## [The Complete Works of Alan of Lille]

[Col. 0009]

# Historical-Literary Notice concerning Alan

(Oudin, *Commentaries on Ecclesiastical Writers and Writings*, vol. II, col. 1387.—Here Oudin sharply rejects the opinion of Charles de Visch, who held that Alan died in 1294, and of others who maintained that the Universal Doctor flourished at the beginning of the fourteenth century. He is mistaken, however, in considering Alan, bishop of Auxerre, who lived around the year 1185, and Alan of Lille, who died in 1203, to have been one and the same person. See *Histoire littéraire de la France* [quarto edition, Paris, Firmin Didot], vol. XIV, p. 358, under **ALAN OF AUXERRE**, and vol. XVI, p. 396, under **ALAN THE GREAT**.)

The common opinion which posits two Alans of Lille—both exceedingly learned men and members of the Cistercian order, but assigning to each wholly different occupations and times—was made the subject of a special Dissertation by Charles de Visch. He prefixed it to his edition of the works of Master Alan, published at Antwerp in folio in 1654 by Guillaume Lestenius and Engelbert Gymnicus. He included a somewhat shorter version in his *Library of Writers of the Cistercian Order*, fols. 12–17 of the final edition of 1656, Cologne, Johann Busaeus. There he endeavours, though with some hesitation, to prove that there were two Alans, separated by entirely different times, one almost a century earlier than the other: namely, a lay brother or convert, and a bishop.

Finally, Caesar Egasse du Boulay composed another highly learned Dissertation on the same subject in the fourth volume of his *History of the University of Paris*, fol. 432 and many following pages, likewise asserting that there were two Alans and assigning them distinct periods. I had held this view after him; but, upon more mature consideration of the matter, and after weighing all the conjectures and arguments of writers on this subject, compelled solely by regard for the truth, I am obliged to adopt the contrary opinion against myself. This point of criticism appeared to me of such importance that it has extracted from me this special Dissertation. I shall therefore say that there was only one Alan, who occupied almost the whole twelfth century and lived from its beginning until A.D. 1203; nor have I been able to derive from all these Dissertations any valid argument compelling me to posit two Alans.

# Dissertation on the One Alan, Abbot of Ripatorii, Bishop of Auxerre, and Finally a Cistercian Monk, Who Died at Cîteaux in the Year 1203

## Chapter I. An examination of the epitaph, the sole basis for distinguishing two Alans

[Col. 0009A]

Charles de Visch, in his historical Dissertation *On the Life and Death of Alan the Great of Lille, Universal Doctor*, §5, states the following verbatim:

“Chrysostom Henriquez writes that he survived seventy-nine years after the aforesaid Lateran Council, reached the age of 116, and at last died with a great reputation for holiness; on this account Henriquez also entered him in his Cistercian Menology on 30 January. John of Cîteaux likewise numbers him among the blessed of our order in the *Catalogue of Saints and Blessed of the Cistercian Order*, appended to the old missals of the same order. The most learned Leo Allatius, in his book *On the Urban Bees*, and our most reverend present General, as well as others commonly, also call him Blessed.

“As for the year of his death, an ancient epitaph engraved upon his tombstone establishes the truth for us; it is still now perfectly legible, in the following form:

> A brief hour buried Alan in a brief tomb—  
> He who knew two, seven, and all knowable things.  
> Despising the affairs of a fleeting age, he became poor.  
> A convert within, entrusted with tending flocks,  
> In twelve hundred and ninety-four,  
> Devoted to Christ, he put off his mortal body.

“Therefore Alan died in the year of the Lord 1294. Hence correct all authors who write that he flourished in 1300. His marble tomb may be seen at Cîteaux, on the left side of the cloister as one enters the church. Beside it, on the wall, hang two other epitaphs, which Gaspar Jongelinus gives us in the *Purple of Saint Bernard*, having himself copied them from the original tablets in 1624, while he was at Cîteaux visiting the blessed man’s tomb.”

### Epitaph I

> This great learned Alan, who was so admirable,  
> Makes this place of Cîteaux everywhere more memorable.  
> For here he was a lay brother, shepherd, and servant;  
> Here still he serves as an example of virtues and honour.  
> Therefore, you religious, lay brothers, and all passers-by,  
> Imitate this Doctor, who lies here below.

### Epitaph II

> Beneath this stone lies Alan, venerable to the whole world,  
> A Doctor whom kindly honour befits.  
> He is deservedly to be ranked with theologians and philosophers;  
> Nor was he himself inferior to the ancient poets.  
> Writing excellently, he lamented, taught, and unfolded  
> Nature, morals, and the mystical words of God.  
> He sang the illustrious deeds of Jesus and His glorious triumphs,  
> Depicting the arts and the warfare of heaven.  
> A painter in speech, censor of morals, lyrist  
> Of the Muses, he was a champion of faith.  
> Here, fleeing the world, he lived beneath religion’s garment;  
> He remains here still: he is present in his tomb.

No one, I think, will deny that the second and last epitaphs are rather recent and smell of the sixteenth century. They therefore do not affect us at all and say nothing concerning Alan’s age, but merely enumerate, however composedly, his works. Thus the question concerns the first epitaph alone, which assigns Alan’s death to 1294 and is the sole basis for distinguishing two Alans.

But I say that it too is recent, renewed and enlarged at the beginning or middle of the sixteenth century. For the ancient epitaph engraved on Alan’s tomb contained only three verses, which in 1501 could scarcely be read because of age and erasure. The fourth volume of the *History of the University of Paris*, fol. 437, reports them in this form:

> A brief hour buried Alan in a brief tomb—  
> He who knew two, seven, subjected the whole world to himself;  
> He could neither impart nor retain his knowledge and morals.

This is reported on the testimony of Matthew Bonhomme, who issued at Lyons in 1501 a printed *Commentary on Alan’s Parables*. He prefixed to it a compendium of Alan’s life and this epitaph of Cîteaux. At that time it consisted of only three verses and had been so worn away by those treading upon it that it could not be read except as Matthew Bonhomme read it, though it ought to have been read thus:

> A brief hour buried Alan in a brief tomb—  
> He who knew two, seven, and all knowable things,  
> Dying, could neither impart nor retain his knowledge.

Since, therefore, by this year 1501 the epitaph had been excessively worn, the brothers renewed it, fashioned it after the pattern of old epitaphs, and enlarged it by four verses, which supplied all the material for the present dispute. For a false chronology was added in the four subsequent, recently added verses—a very easy thing for monks who had not investigated Alan’s dates and eras:

> Despising the affairs of a fleeting age, he became poor.  
> A convert within, entrusted with tending flocks.  
> In twelve hundred and ninety-four,  
> Devoted to Christ, he put off his mortal body.

And the whole matter is confirmed by the passage from Charles de Visch quoted above. What in 1501 could scarcely be read and was then copied conjecturally now in one way, now in another, he affirms is “still perfectly legible, in the following form,” etc.

## Chapter II. Even if admitted as ancient and primary, the epitaph has no force against the testimony of earlier writers

We have said, then, that the epitaph engraved on Master Alan’s tomb at Cîteaux once consisted of only three verses, but after 1501 was read as seven verses; Matthew Bonhomme, before his edition of Alan’s *Parables*, adduced it as ancient along with his account of Alan. Yet the author of the *Belgian Chronicle*, because he is older, is far more authoritative than this epitaph: he ceased writing in 1475. He says that Alan died among the Cistercians in 1201.

[Col. 0012A] “In the year 1202,” he says, “Master Alan of Lille died at Cîteaux, that famous Doctor, author of the *Anticlaudianus*, who in theology composed a certain art of preaching and published a concise booklet against the Albigensians, Waldensians, Jews, and Saracens, addressed to William, lord of Montpellier.”

Nothing could have been said more concisely and expressly by a writer who surpasses the Cistercian epitaph in antiquity both of date and composition.

But let us grant—though wholly gratuitously—the epitaph at Cîteaux over Alan’s ashes whatever antiquity the Cistercian monks desire for it. It will still help their case little, since it cannot have been made before 1300. For it concerns Alan, whom it claims died in 1294; and it is scarcely credible that this epitaph was placed there on the very day he was covered with earth.

But authors a hundred years earlier than this epitaph, contemporaries of Alan, members of the same Cistercian order, all most acceptable in their notes and observations, against whom no objection can be made, and living at least sixty years before the epitaph, assert that Alan died in 1203. Therefore this epitaph is false, belatedly imposed upon Alan, and mendacious. Was it ever read or seen in earlier centuries of the Church, so that historians or chronologists wrote about events a hundred years before they happened through a magical or prophetic spirit? This kind of argument is so demonstrative that it cannot in any way be weakened even by the most acute critics.

The first of these writers is Otto of St. Blasien, abbot in the Hercynian Forest, a contemporary author, who flourished in 1190 and wrote an appendix to the eight books of Otto of Freising’s *Chronicles*, beginning with 1146, when the latter ceased writing, and continuing to 1210. He mentions Alan and the *Anticlaudianus* most expressly, and further places him as contemporary and associate with two most learned twelfth-century theologians:

“During these times, Master Peter the Chanter of Paris, Alan, and the Provost flourished. The first of these compiled with subtlety, by continuous glosses, a book of distinctions, the Book of Psalms, and one Gospel out of the four, besides many other things. The second, writing much, expounded, among other works, the book entitled *Anticlaudianus*, the *Rules of Heavenly Life*, a work against heretics, a book *On Vices and Virtues*, *On the Art of Preaching*, a book of his sermons, and many other sound and Catholic works.”

Thus he flourished a hundred years before the cited epitaph, and is rightly placed between Peter the Chanter and the Provost, chancellor of Paris, both flourishing and alive in 1190. The first died in 1190, the second around 1210, as Caesarius states in his books of *Dialogues*, and as others do. Alan, however, having died in 1203 between the two, is rightly placed between them by Otto of St. Blasien.

The second witness is Alberic, monk of Trois-Fontaines of the Cistercian order, an ancient and weighty author, as Charles de Visch admits in his *Library of Writers of the Cistercian Order*, fol. 15, under Alan. In his *Chronicle* he expressly writes that this Alan died in 1203, in these words:

[Col. 0013A] “At Cîteaux in this year died Master Alan of Lille, the famous Doctor and author of the *Anticlaudianus*, who in theology composed a certain art of preaching, and published a concise booklet against the Albigensians, Waldensians, Jews, and Saracens, addressed to William, lord of Montpellier; and certain other minor works of his are also extant.”

Thus far Alberic, who continued his *Chronicle* to 1241. But how could one writing in 1241, by anticipation, write that Alan died in 1203 if he did not in fact die until 1294? Let those who defend these claims untie these knots.

Charles de Visch therefore speaks correctly regarding this authority in fol. 16 of his *Library of Writers of the Cistercian Order*:

“It follows from this that either Alan’s sepulchral epitaph is erroneous, and Trithemius and all the doctors agreeing with him are seriously mistaken; or Alberic’s *Chronicle* is certainly corrupt, and the aforementioned *Commentaries on Merlin* are by another author. We ourselves followed the latter view as the more probable in the Historical Account prefixed to the recently printed works of Alan, applying all remaining matters accordingly. Yet another view might say that the council at Rome, at which Alan is read to have been present and recognized, was the Third Lateran Council, celebrated in 1180 under Alexander III. I wrote concerning this difficulty to Cîteaux and to various other learned men, but was unable to obtain a resolution; therefore, until I have something more certain, I judged the epitaph should be believed.”

These are Visch’s very words in the final edition of his *Library of Writers of the Cistercian Order*, after the Dissertation on the Alans which he composed for the works of Master Alan published by him. They indicate how much he doubted the Cistercian epitaph and, consequently, Alan’s death being delayed by it to 1294.

Finally, let a third suitable witness of the highest worth be added against this assertion of the epitaph: Caesar Egasse du Boulay reports him in the fourth volume of his *History of the University of Paris*, fol. 434, in the special Dissertation he wrote *On Alan of Lille*, in Egasse’s own words:

“Henry of Ghent is added, a Doctor of Paris and, as they say, alumnus of the Sorbonne house. He studied at Paris before 1270 and died at Tournai in 1293. He places this Alan of ours in the series of illustrious men who flourished in this century, namely from 1110 to 1200, and writes of him thus in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 21: ‘Alan, born at Lille, skilled in the liberal arts, presided over the ecclesiastical school at Paris; and, leaving monuments of his intellect, he wrote a *Summa* useful for the office of preaching. Since he greatly excelled in verse, he wrote a poetic work upon an invented subject concerning a man most good and perfect in every respect, a book which he called the *Anticlaudianus*,’ etc.”

[Col. 0014A] I do not see what can be brought against the authority of these men. For how could both—namely, Otto of St. Blasien, mentioned above, and Henry of Ghent—have remembered Alan and the *Anticlaudianus* if Alan came a hundred years after each of them? Who would believe that Henry of Ghent would have placed Alan among the illustrious men of the twelfth century if he had seen him flourishing in his own time as a member of the Parisian schools? It is thus clear how little firm in their opinion were those who admitted two Alans, one dying in 1182 and the other in 1294, including those who wrote special Dissertations on the matter, such as Caesar Egasse du Boulay and Charles de Visch, mentioned above.

Du Boulay continues:

“Accordingly Gaspar Barth, in the notes on William the Breton, at verse 546, ‘Like Erichtho,’ etc., expressly acknowledges Alan among the authors of this twelfth century. For he says: ‘I have added in brief certain writings of his, suitable to the times of our Breton, from Alan’s sixth book of the *Commentaries on Merlin’s Prophecy*. I have said that that author wrote in this age; those who contradict this are mistaken, since Otto of St. Blasien expressly places him about the year 1194, in the appendix to Freising, chapter 40, also mentioning his *Anticlaudianus*. I wonder why the works of this man worthy of publication have remained hidden until now, while works of far smaller value break through their barriers. Nor are they only those mentioned by writers of catalogues; I myself saw in the Basel library a vast Commentary on the Structure of Metres and Syllables, with testimonies of authors appended, a work which I do not recall any cataloguer mentioning.’

“And at verse 52 of book VII, ‘With level side,’ etc.: ‘In the caesura he neglects a syllable, as often occurs on individual pages, and so do others; and in the work *Anticlaudianus*, written about these same times, Alan of Lille, called the Universal Doctor, whom the author of the chronicle they call the *Great Belgian Chronicle* notes as having died at Cîteaux in 1202.’ These things suffice, since every matter stands by the mouth of two or three witnesses.”

## Chapter III. Many other things fabricated by recent authors in Alan’s favour, which rest upon no foundation of truth or probability

[Col. 0014D]

Charles de Visch, in his *Historical Account of the Life of Alan the Great*, contains three paragraphs in which he recounts many astonishing and prodigious matters intended to commend Alan, matters which I should have wished more firmly proved by him. The second paragraph bears the title: “On what occasion Master Alan, leaving the University of Paris, assumed the habit of the lay brothers at Cîteaux.”

There he recounts a miracle, but adduces no witness other than the Jesuit John Buzelin in his *Gothic Flanders*, vol. II, book VII, under the year 1294. He says that he possessed this same story, though described in a wholly simple style, in the preface to a certain *Commentary on Alan’s Parables*, printed at Lyons one hundred and fifty years ago, at the beginning of a codex—namely, in 1501—without the author’s name, though it is now established that the author was Matthew Bonhomme.

Visch was right and prudent, however, to omit the first, insipid and barbarous printing of this work, so that the exceedingly pure Latinity of John Buzelin might make the tale more credible and less ridiculous. Caesar Egasse du Boulay was not so scrupulous. In the fourth volume of his *History of the University of Paris*, fol. 436, he adduces these stories in the very words of their first inventor. Therefore let Visch, who imagined that these fables would be credible in John Buzelin’s polished Latin, hear them as absurd in faith and wording from the account of Matthew Bonhomme, a Cistercian monk, who issued at Lyons in 1501 the printed *Commentary on Alan’s Parables*. On its title page, under “What were the causes of Alan’s conversion to the Cistercians,” he records the following:

[Col. 0015B] “The author of this book was called Alan. We read of him that, while one day studying at Paris, having mastered the seven liberal arts as well as laws and decrees, he proposed to set forth his learning and turn it to some use, or expound it. And since on the following day he wished to preach about the whole Trinity and to offer true knowledge and understanding of it to his hearers, as he was walking near a certain bank, considering how he might fulfil his intended undertaking, he found a boy who, holding a spoon in his hand, had made a small hole a little distance from the water. Drawing water with his spoon, he carried it to the hole he had made; and as soon as the boy put water into the hole, the water entered the earth because the ground was sandy.

“Seeing this, Alan said to the boy: ‘Boy, what are you doing here?’

“And the boy replied: ‘I have proposed to put this entire bank into my hole, and I shall not stop until I have fulfilled my purpose.’

“Alan said to him: ‘When do you think you will accomplish it? Although your work is childish, it is impossible.’

“The boy said to him: ‘I shall accomplish this sooner than you will fulfil your purpose.’

“And Alan replied: ‘What, then, did I propose to do?’

“The boy said: ‘You proposed tomorrow, through your learning in a sermon, to explain the entire Trinity, which is much more impossible for you.’

“Hearing this, Alan was greatly terrified. He returned home, reflected within himself on the boy’s words, grieved greatly and became sad, and recognized his presumption or arrogance. When the next day and the hour of preaching came, and a great multitude of people had assembled, Alan ascended the pulpit and said in place of his theme: ‘Let it suffice that you have seen Alan.’ Overwhelmed with shame and unwilling to continue at Paris, he went into Burgundy and, in a certain abbey named Cîteaux, became a shepherd of sheep; afterward he became a lay brother of the same abbey, in the manner of a layman. This is the reason and cause of his conversion.”

Immediately thereafter the same Bonushomo, or Bonhomme, the commentator, tells how Alan went to Rome, confounded heretics, and was at last recognized as Alan:

[Col. 0016A] “Moreover, certain heretics had come to Rome who were overthrowing the entire Catholic faith by their arguments and false syllogisms. Therefore the pope commanded all prelates, abbots, doctors, and clergy of all Christendom to come to Rome, in order that they might confound the said heretics. When Alan’s abbot and master heard this, he wished to go to Rome, leaving Alan in the abbey.

“Then Alan, who had now recovered his senses, said to his master: ‘O lord, I am weary of staying here, and it has been a long time since I left the abbey. Therefore I humbly beg that I may go with you to Rome; I shall serve you well and take the best care of the horses.’

“The abbot then went to Rome and took Alan with him. When the day of the disputation arrived, the abbot wished to enter the place of disputation, and Alan wished to enter with him. The abbot said to him: ‘Go to the lodging and care for the horses, for you cannot enter this place because of the guards and attendants here, who permit no one to enter except prelates and important clerics; you might be beaten.’

“Alan said to him: ‘I am willing to be beaten in order to enter.’ Covering himself under the cloak or cape of his master, he entered the said place and, sitting at his master’s feet, heard the disputation.

“The heretics put forward questions and overcame and defeated the Christians. Seeing this, Alan came out of hiding and said to his master: ‘Command, lord, a blessing.’

“The abbot, astonished, said to Alan: ‘Be silent, wretch! What do you wish to do?’

“Then Alan entered, saying as before, ‘Command, lord, a blessing,’ even a third time. Seeing this, the pope permitted him to argue. Alan then recited the questions raised by the heretics, argued against them, and confounded them. Seeing this, a heretic said in confusion: ‘You are the devil or Alan.’

“Alan replied: ‘I am not the devil, but Alan.’

“Then his master the abbot wished to confer his dignity upon him, but Alan refused to accept it. Instead, the pope and abbot granted him that he should have two clerics in the said abbey, and that those clerics should write down under his direction the books which he dictated. There he composed many books, among them this one which begins, ‘From Phoebus, Phoebe,’ etc. When Alan died, he was buried in the said abbey, and these verses are written upon his tomb:

> A brief hour buried Alan in a brief tomb—  
> He who knew two, seven, subjected the whole world to himself;  
> He could neither impart nor retain his knowledge and morals.”

> **[Note: The fourth chapter which follows in Oudin, entitled “The foregoing inventions and new ones are refuted,” and in which he inveighs violently against the patchers-together of this narrative, is omitted. There is no reason for such indignation at a story recounted ingenuously and candidly. Editors.]**

## Chapter IV. Other opinions concerning the life and death of Alan of Lille considered

Since historians do not agree and have differed greatly concerning the time when Alan lived or died, it will not be unwelcome to report two further opinions for a complete discussion of the present matter.

The third opinion was that of John Trithemius, who in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* says that Alan flourished under Emperor Albert in the year 1300. Very many followed Trithemius: Conrad Gesner in the *Universal Library*; Lilius Giraldus, Dialogue V, *On Poets*, where he says of the *Anticlaudianus*:

[Col. 0017A] “The *Anticlaudianus*, a book against Claudian’s *Against Rufinus*, was composed by Alan, who was surnamed the **UNIVERSAL DOCTOR** because of the manifold knowledge of disciplines which the Germans admired in him. He also wrote *On the Lament of Nature*, and everywhere indeed displays learning, but has an uncultivated style and speaks impurely. He was a German from Lille and presided for some time at Paris in the times of Emperors Adolf and then Albert, around the year 1300.”

These are the words of Egasse du Boulay. This author seems never to have read anything about our Alan, whom he says had an uncultivated style and spoke impurely, when it is certain that few men were more distinguished than Alan, not only in the times in which he lived, but also in those that followed.

The Jesuit Antonio Possevino, drawing from the same Trithemian source without further examining or investigating the truth, says that “Alan wrote on the four books of the *Sentences* of Master Peter Lombard, the *Eye of Holy Scripture*, *On Doctrine*, etc.; and finally lived under Emperor Albert, about the year 1300.”

John Gerard Vossius holds the same opinion in his book *On Latin Poets*: “In the year 1300,” he says, “under Emperor Albert, there was Alan of Lille, a German, author of a work against Claudian’s *Against Rufinus*, whence it is called the *Anticlaudianus*. This is he who is called the **UNIVERSAL DOCTOR**.”

Almost the whole multitude of modern authors has written much the same. Yet I can refute this opinion by this single conjecture or argument: namely, that

> **[Note: [Col. 0017D]**
>
> **We do not see what relevance the testimony of William the Breton, who died about the year 1219, has against the opinion of those who maintain that Alan flourished in the year 1300. Moreover, Eberhard, a thirteenth-century writer, in the *Graecismus*, or book written in hexameter verse concerning figures and the eight parts of speech, while listing poets customarily read in schools at that time, mentions Alan’s name in these words:**
>
> > Alan describes the man who cultivates the seven arts;  
> > He teaches the kinds of virtue through their proper attributes.
>
> **See Fabricius, *Library of the Middle and Lower Latin Age*, vol. II, p. 75. Editors.]**

Master William the Breton, who flourished and wrote under Philip Augustus, mentions the distinguished poets Walter and Giles, but nowhere makes any mention of Alan, whom he certainly would not have passed over had Alan then been regarded among the most celebrated and eminent poets.

On the contrary, others maintain that Alan of Lille flourished and lived in the twelfth century [Col. 0017D]; yet they do not agree as to who he was or what manner of life he embraced. Some write that he was a monk of Clairvaux, then abbot of Ripatorium—French *Larivour*—in the territory of Troyes, afterwards bishop of Auxerre, and finally that he returned to Clairvaux, where he spent the last days of his life in 1182. Such is the opinion of Aubertus Miraeus in his scholia on Henry of Ghent’s *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 21:

> “Alan,” he says, “of Lille, a Gallic Fleming [Col. 0018A] called the UNIVERSAL DOCTOR because of his manifold learning, was, from being a Parisian theologian, made a monk of Clairvaux; in 1139 Saint Bernard appointed him first abbot of Ripatorium, in the diocese of Troyes. Thereafter, on account of his piety and learning, he was made bishop of Auxerre in 1151; but, touched by longing for his former solitude, he returned to Clairvaux in 1167, with the permission of Alexander, Roman pontiff, as Robert, the chronicler of Auxerre, relates; and there he died about the year 1182, being buried in the same monastery, according to Geoffrey, bishop of Langres.”

Camuzatus, in his marginal notes on Robert of Auxerre’s *Chronicle*, says that Alan’s will, written in 1182, is still preserved at Ripatorium. The Sammarthan brothers say the same in their *Gallia Christiana*, as does the *Cistercian History*. Camuzatus indeed gives the following in the margin of the *Chronicle of Auxerre*:

> “Ripatorium (Larivour) is a Cistercian monastery, two leagues distant from the city of Troyes, where Alan’s will, written in 1182, is still preserved. His sepulchral monument also may still be seen in the church of Clairvaux monastery, where, wrongly, an inscription attached beside the tomb records that he died in 1181.”

Moreover, as regards writers who would have Alan flourish in 1300 under Emperor Albert, they are all recent; Trithemius is the first among them. They therefore deserve no credit, since they could easily have been deceived, contrary to the authority of the ancients, who place this Alan’s flourishing [Col. 0018C] in the twelfth century, as we said above.

We do, however, agree with the latter writers that Alan, called the Universal Doctor, flourished in the twelfth century; indeed, that he is identical with the bishop of Auxerre who, in 1167, as Robert of Auxerre writes in his *Chronicle*, returned to Clairvaux after resigning his bishopric. But we deny that he died in 1181, as the inscription attached to his fabricated tomb at Clairvaux states, and maintain that he survived until 1203, the year in which ancient writers, authorities of every credibility, report Alan’s death. Indeed, that tablet attached to Alan’s vaunted tomb is modern, as is clear from its composition, which Camuzatus reports in his *Historical Miscellanies*, and after him the fourth century of the *History of the University of Paris*, in its *Catalogue of Illustrious Academics*, fol. 719. Yet there is not one syllable there indicating that Alan died in 1181; it reads only: “He died on the day before the Ides of October.”

As for Alan’s will, written in 1182 and preserved at Ripatorium, I have no doubt that it is a forged document. For what right had a humble monk, who had cast aside a most extensive bishopric in order to live in the utmost poverty, to make a will? Moreover, why should he have made a will at Ripatorium [Col. 0019A], when he was a poor monk either of Cîteaux or of Clairvaux? Finally, the making of a will does not mean that a man dies at once. Alan, having become a poor monk, may in 1182, when afflicted by some illness at Ripatorium, have made a will; afterwards recovering, he may have prolonged his life until 1203, when the ancients say that he died. There is nothing contradictory in all this; indeed, all agrees, if we suppose Alan to have been an old man, as everyone holds.

## CHAPTER V. The more notable epochs of the life of Alan of Lille are set forth

Alan was therefore born at Lille, the principal city of French Flanders, about the fourteenth year of the twelfth century. [Col. 0019B] First, Alan himself expressly declares that he was born in Flanders, at Lille. Thus in Book V of his *Commentaries on the Prophecies of Ambrose Merlin*, fol. 198 of the later Antwerp edition:

> “I too saw in Flanders, while I was still a little boy, at Lille, where I was born, a certain sorceress who had been apprehended in her sorcery, etc. This was at the time when Count Thierry was summoned by the people of Lille, Ghent, and Bruges from his own land into Flanders as the lawful heir of Flanders,” etc.

That Thierry, surnamed of Alsace, son of Thierry the Valiant, duke of Mosellan Lorraine, was summoned and elected count of Flanders in 1128, as is recorded in the *Annals of Flanders*; at which time Alan was still a little boy. Yet this term must not be understood strictly as denoting a child of eight or ten, but comparatively, in relation to the old age in which Alan wrote this commentary. For, writing on the Prophecies of Ambrose Merlin in advanced age, he could call himself a little boy at the time when Thierry of Alsace was summoned to govern the county of Flanders, even if he had reached about fourteen or sixteen years—having been born about 1114.

About the year 1128 he became a monk at Clairvaux under the discipline of Saint Bernard, who drew to himself many young Flemings, especially those distinguished by natural gifts and learning; they gave him exceptional assistance [Col. 0019D] in founding very many abbeys of his order. These *Commentaries on the Prophecies of Merlin the Englishman* are rightly attributed to Alan, and were printed under his name at Frankfurt in 1608 by Johann Spiess, in octavo, under this title: *The Prophecy of Ambrose Merlin*, etc., together with seven books of explanations of the same prophecy, by Alan of Lille, a German, Universal Doctor, most eminent rector of the University of Paris three hundred years ago, the outstanding orator, polymath, and theologian of his age.

For in these commentaries Alan, speaking of himself, admits that he was a member of some order. In Book II, fol. 61, he says: “A certain abbot of the order, a learned man,” etc. Then, at fol. 198, he expressly states that he was native to Lille in Flanders, in these words: “I too saw [Col. 0020A] in Flanders while I was still a little boy,” etc., as we reported above.

In 1139 or 1140, Ripatorium, a Cistercian foundation in the district or diocese of Troyes, was founded on 9 April by Bishop Hatto, in the time of Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux; there Bernard appointed Alan, then about thirty years old, its first abbot. These facts are established by volume IV of the Sammarthan brothers’ *Gallia Christiana*, fol. 790, under “Ripatorium”; by the *Chronology of the Abbeys of the Cistercian Order*, appended by Charles de Visch, prior of Dunes, to his *Library of Writers of the Cistercian Order*; and by the same *Library*, under “Alan, bishop of Auxerre,” fol. 12.

In 1151 Alan was appointed bishop of Auxerre after having been abbot of Ripatorium. Robert, chronicler of Saint Marianus at Auxerre, who may have seen Alan himself, writes:

> “In 1151 Hugh, bishop of Auxerre, a man renowned for character and learning, died. Alan, first abbot of Ripatorium, succeeded him.”

Whoever wishes to know more fully all the remarkable things he accomplished in his bishopric should read the Sammarthan brothers’ *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, p. 276, under “Bishops of Auxerre,” where they are described at considerable length.

In 1167, as the cited chronicler Robert writes under that year: “Bishop Alan resigned his bishopric; William succeeded him, treasurer of the Church of Auxerre and archdeacon of Sens, brother of Hugh, archbishop of that same [Col. 0020C] church.”

In 1180 Alan, having returned to Clairvaux, set out with Peter, abbot of Clairvaux, for Rome and the Third Lateran Council—not in the arrogant and utterly absurd manner stated above, namely, to care for the abbot of Clairvaux’s horses, as Matthew Bonihominis foolishly writes. Rather, he was a theologian of great renown and a monk of extraordinary virtue, who had shown what he could do in the ascetic life by renouncing the distinguished bishopric of Auxerre in order to live as a simple monk. Peter, abbot of Clairvaux, therefore took this most distinguished man with him as his travelling companion; through his company he obtained no small splendour and reputation among the venerable Fathers and theologians of that council [Col. 0020D].

There, as seems quite probable, he received from Alexander III, supreme pontiff of the Church, a commission to write against the Waldensians and the other heretics of those times. At about the same time, Alan seems to have composed in concise form a *Life of Saint Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux*, after the celebrated three or four writers—William, abbot of Saint-Thierry; Arnald, abbot of Bonneval; and Geoffrey, fourth abbot of Clairvaux—all men notable for many writings. The work was composed and dedicated to Peter, abbot of Clairvaux, who is known to have held that abbacy from 1179 to 1186. This little work was therefore composed by Alan within that period.

Having returned from the Lateran Council, where action was taken against the Waldensians [Col. 0021A], Albigensians, and other heretics, he wrote a *Summa* in four books against Waldensians, Albigensians, Jews, and pagans. Thomas Waldensis wrongly calls it a four-part work on the four books of the *Sentences*, in volume II of his *Doctrinal of the Faith*, penultimate chapter. This work long lay hidden in obscurity, but at last appeared for the first time from the library of Papirius Masson at Paris in 1612, and later in the 1654 edition of Alan’s complete works. Since it was published mutilated, Charles de Visch issued, on the authority of a manuscript in the library of Cîteaux, the last two books against Pagans and Mohammedans at the end of the final 1656 Cologne edition of his *Library of Writers of the Cistercian Order*, published by the bookseller Johann Busaeus.

[Col. 0021B] In its prologue Alan writes:

> “To his most beloved lord William, prince of Montpellier by the grace of God—whom not only the title of noble birth distinguishes, but whom the still nobler nobility of mind pre-eminently distinguishes—Master Alan, wholly and in every respect his own, offers his work. Since among all the princes of the world I see you especially clothed in the arms of Christian faith and not abandoning Peter’s little ship amid so many raging storms of this age, I dedicate to your discernment this completed writing on the Catholic faith.”

That William, lord of Montpellier, was surnamed Sibylla after his mother Sibylla. He opposed the count of Toulouse and besieged Toulouse with the English in 1158. He received Alexander III [Col. 0021C] in 1162; and in 1174 he married Matilda, daughter of Manuel, emperor of Constantinople. He was a champion of the Catholic faith against the Albigensian heretics, as is read in the *History of Auch*; he died in 1202, the same year in which Alan is said to have died. Alan therefore dedicated to that William his work against the Waldensians, of whom he speaks in Book II in these terms:

> “How do the Waldensians know letters when they have not learned them? For we see that men holier than they do not preach to them, even though they understand Holy Scripture, as do many Cistercians who have not been sent.”

And elsewhere he mentions the Third Lateran Council in which they were condemned:

> “These Waldensians,” he says, “who preach under pain of excommunication and against the command of the lord pope—indeed, against the whole Church—though the lord pope has commanded them not to preach, lie under sentence of excommunication. For at the Lateran Council a sentence of excommunication was pronounced against them; hence one must not even communicate with them, since by the apostolic sentence they have been cut off from the Church.”

It is clear from this that Alan issued his treatises against the Waldensians after the celebration of the Third Lateran Council, about 1183 or 1184, by command of the Roman pontiff. Nor can anyone object that the Waldensians endured for a long time, and that Alan could thus have written against them even had he not lived in this twelfth century. For in the prologue he says that new heretics had arisen in his own time: “But in our times,” he says, “new heretics [Col. 0022A].” Yet in the time of Emperor Albert—that is, in 1300—the Waldensians, the Paterines, and the other heretics whom Alan refutes in his books had already been buried in oblivion. Everything, therefore, seems to agree fully with Alan’s times and writings. For the Waldensians and Albigensians arose in this century, and the Third Lateran Council was held against them, in which they were condemned, as we said above. Otto of Saint Blasien, a contemporary author, testifies that Alan wrote against them.

From this writing against the Waldensians, which he composed after the Lateran Council and by command of Pope Alexander III, there seems to have arisen among the Cistercians the tale that at this council Alan confounded the heretics. From this work was woven that ample Cistercian—or Clairvaux—abbot’s habit which clothes Alan after his conversion [Col. 0022B] and makes him suddenly appear in public to dispute at that council. At this same time, or somewhat later, Alan is believed to have written his seven books of *Commentaries on the Prophecy of Ambrose Merlin*, which he seems, from the passages cited above, to have composed in extreme old age.

Finally, in 1203, according to the authorities cited above, he died at Cîteaux, in the ninety-third or approximately the ninety-third year of his life, on the calculation given above—namely, if he was born about 1114.

## CHAPTER VI. The works of Alan of Lille, both printed and manuscript, are examined

The works of Alan the Great, so many as could be found, were published in folio at Antwerp in 1654 by Guillaume Lestenius and Engelbert Gimnicus [Col. 0022C], through the labour and care of Lord Charles de Visch, prior of Blessed Mary of Dunes, of the Cistercian Order in Flanders, under this title: *The Moral, Paraenetic, and Polemical Works Which Could Be Found of Alan the Great of Lille, Doctor of Sacred Theology, Surnamed the Universal Doctor, Formerly Distinguished Head of the Ecclesiastical School of Paris and Humble Cistercian Convert*. They are as follows.

*A Commentary on the Song of Songs in Praise of the Most Blessed Virgin Mother of God*, formerly printed at Paris in 1540.

*A Summa on the Art of Preaching*, now first brought to light from two manuscripts of the library of Dunes; it occurs twice and three times in manuscript in the library [Col. 0022D] of the Regular Canons of Saint Victor at Paris, twice also in the library of Cluny, under the letters AA and HH; at Cambridge in the public library, MS 128; and in Pembroke College, MS 81.

Eleven complete *Sermons on Various Subjects*, not previously published.

*A Book of Memorable Sayings or Sentences of Master Alan*, from a manuscript codex of the library of Dunes.

*A Treatise on the Six Wings of the Cherubim*, from a manuscript codex of Saint-Vaast at Arras, wrongly attributed by the Franciscans to Saint Bonaventure and printed among his minor works.

*A Penitential*, or *Book of Penance*, published from manuscripts, p. 181. It was printed from two [Col. 0023A] manuscripts, one in the Cistercian library of Dunes, the other in the library of Saint-Ghislain in Hainaut. The same work is held in manuscript in three codices of the library of Saint Victor, Paris, under Alan’s name, marked MMM. 18, B. 8, and PP. 14, fol. 144; likewise in the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, MS 557, of excellent quality, but under the name of Peter the Chanter, contrary to the authority of the printed editions and the Victorine manuscripts. But there is another *Penitential* of Alan, mentioned by Charles de Visch in his *Library of Writers of the Cistercian Order*, which he says contains four books addressed to Henry, archbishop of Bourges. It survives in manuscript in the library of Marmoutier at Tours, in quarto, under the letter A. 2.

[Col. 0023B] *A Four-Part Work on the Catholic Faith against the Waldensians, Albigensians, and Other Heretics of His Time*. Its first two books were printed here in 1654; its latter two books were published from a manuscript in the library of Cîteaux at the end of the second edition of the *Library of Writers of the Cistercian Order*, fol. 410, issued by Johann Busaeus at Cologne in 1656. This is the very work which Johann Trithemius wrongly calls *On the Four Books of the Sentences*, because this *Summa* is divided into four books; it is in no way a commentary on the four books of the Master of the Sentences. The same manuscript is in the Royal Library of France, MS 5513, fol. 352, entitled: *Alan’s Four-Part Summa against Waldensian Heretics, [Col. 0023C] Jews, and Pagans*. Its prologue to William, prince of Montpellier, begins, “Since among all,” etc. The codex is said to have been written in 1456 by Hervaeus Conseel for Lord Bernard, archbishop of Toulouse. It is also at Cluny under the letter Q. 2, and at Clairvaux in their libraries. The same manuscript exists at Oxford in Merton College Library, MS 230.

*The Book on the Lament of Nature*, mentioned by Henry of Ghent in his *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 21—Henry died in 1293; by Robert Holcot, the celebrated doctor of sacred theology of the Order of Preachers, in his commentary on chapter I of the Book of Wisdom, lecture 118, letter A—he flourished in 1349, according to Bellarmine in his *On Ecclesiastical Writers*; and also in manuscript at Oxford in Balliol College Library, MS 120.

*Anticlaudianus, or On the Office of a Man Perfect in Every Virtue*, in nine books, composed with singular brilliance, charm, and elegance, from two manuscript codices of the Jesuit college at Louvain and a third in the library of Saint-Bertin at Saint-Omer, of the Order of Saint Benedict; from the fourth and fifth editions, at the press of Balthasar Moretus, the celebrated Antwerp printer. It also exists in manuscript in the French royal library, no. 5640, and at Oxford in Balliol College Library, MSS 120 and 122.

Two elegant rhymes: one *On the Incarnation [Col. 0024A] of Christ*, the other *On the Frail and Perishing Nature of Man*.

*The Lesser Doctrinal, or Book of Parables of Master Alan of Lille*, from many earlier editions: Deventer, 1492; Lyons, 1501, with learned Latin commentaries by Matthew Bonihominis; Leipzig, 1516; and elsewhere. All these were printed in 1654 and 1656 by Charles de Visch, prior of Dunes, of the Cistercian Order. Now, omitting the *Penitential*, already discussed above, it remains to deal with manuscripts not yet printed.

Charles de Visch, in his *Library of Writers of the Cistercian Order*, fol. 12, attributes to Alan a four-part work on the four books of the *Sentences* [Col. 0024B], as Thomas Waldensis indicates it in volume II, penultimate chapter, and says that it survives in manuscript among the Dominican friars at Paris. But Trithemius understood Waldensis wrongly, and this work is nothing other than the four-part *Summa against Heretics*, etc.

He also wrote, or reduced to a compendium, the *Life of Saint Bernard the Abbot*.

> [Note: It is by Alan, bishop of Auxerre. See *Patrology*, vol. CCI. EDITOR.]

Lord Jean Mabillon published it from a manuscript codex in the library of Saint Victor at Paris in the preliminary matter to the works of Saint Bernard, Paris edition of 1667, published by Frédéric Leonard, Rue Saint-Jacques, under the sign of the Venetian Shield. It also survives in manuscript in the library of Saint-Vaast at Arras, of the Order of Saint Benedict, and at Vaux-de-Cernay [Col. 0024C], of the Cistercian Order. Discussing this *Life* in volume II of his *Annals of the Cistercian Order*, under the year 1153, Manriquez asserts that it is printed in very ancient copies of the works of Saint Bernard.

He also wrote a *Summa* called *In How Many Ways* (*Quot modis*), for this is how it is called in the manuscript codex and by the author himself. It proceeds in alphabetical order, setting out in that order how many ways each thing is understood in a good or a bad sense in Holy Scripture: a work suitable for preachers. It survives in a small quarto manuscript in the library of Royaumont, of the Cistercian Order, dedicated to Hermengald, abbot of Saint-Gilles by the grace of God. Its opening is:

> “To the most reverend Father and Lord Hermengald, abbot of Saint-Gilles by the grace of God, Alan called Master wishes that he may be so adorned with manifold grace in this present life as to be rewarded with glory in the life to come. Since of old, by diverse …”

Another prologue: “Since, according to the proclamation of apostolic authority, those who are ignorant of the names of virtues,” etc. It begins under the word:

> “Soul, properly speaking, is the rational spirit which, together with the body, enters into the constitution of the human being,” etc.

It also survives in the Royal Library of France, MS 5513, there entitled: *Treatise of Master Alan on the Diverse Meanings of Words according to Alphabetical Order*; and in the Victorine library at Paris, under the letter PP. 12, entitled: “Here begins the book of Master Alan called [Col. 0025A] *IN HOW MANY WAYS*, on the diverse meanings of words according to alphabetical order.” Likewise at Clairvaux and Vaux-de-Luce, Cistercian abbeys, and at Saint-Alyre of Clermont, of the Order of Saint Benedict, in Auvergne. In other manuscripts it is called *The Eye of Holy Scripture*, *The Oracle of Holy Scripture*, or *A Compendium of Both Testaments*.

> [Note: Oudin is mistaken in listing this book of Alan among the unpublished works. It was formerly published under the title: *The Book of the Venerable Alan on the Distinctions of Theological Terms*, at Deventer in the Netherlands, from the press of Richard Paffroet of Cologne, in very large folio, about the year 1477; for the first productions of this printer should be assigned to this period, and his types still display those known to have been used by Gutenberg and Fust. This edition, among the rarest of rare books, was never reprinted. Alan dedicates his *Distinctions* to Ermengald, abbot of Saint-Gilles, who governed that monastery from 1179 [Col. 0026D] until 1195; this contradicts the view of those who make Alan a full century younger. EDITOR.]

It also survives in manuscript in the Cistercian library of Dunes in Flanders.

*A Book on Theological Maxims or Axioms*, Book I, otherwise called *The Higher Doctrinal*, beginning: “Every science employs its own rules,” etc. According to Charles de Visch it survives in manuscript in the libraries of Bruges, Cambron, and Saint-Martin [Col. 0025B] at Tournai, and finally at Cambridge in Pembroke College Library, MS 81.

> [Note: Alan’s *Higher Doctrinal*, or *Book on Theological Maxims or Axioms*, was edited by Giovanni Luigi Mingarelli in his *Collection of Unpublished Texts*, Rome, 1756, quarto, from a codex preserved in the library of San Salvatore at Bologna. EDITOR.]

He also wrote a book *On the Natures of Certain Animals*, as Henry of Ghent testifies in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 21, and after him Johann Trithemius in the same work. This work, nearly always anonymous in libraries, is the second of the four books *On Beasts* found among the works of Hugh of Saint Victor. It begins, “Concerning the lion,” etc., and is entitled *Bestiary*. For Treatise or Book I, on birds alone, belongs to Hugh of Fouilloy; Book II, *On Animals*, to Alan of Lille; Books III and IV to William Peraldus of Lyons, of the Order of Preachers. He wrote two books *On the Properties of Things*, the first of which [Col. 0025C] is chiefly taken from Hugh of Fouilloy’s work *On Birds* and Alan of Lille’s *On Animals*, as is clear from reading it.

*The Prophecy of Ambrose Merlin the Englishman*, etc., together with seven books of explanations of the same prophecy, by Alan of Lille, Universal Doctor, most eminent rector of the University of Paris three hundred years ago, the outstanding orator, polymath, and theologian of his age, printed in octavo at Frankfurt in 1608 by Johann Spiess. The sayings of Alan the philosopher concerning the philosophers’ stone were published by Justus Balbianus at Leiden in 1600, at the press of Raphelengius, together with the secret of Jodocus Grenerus; whether these belong to our Alan, I do not know, since I have not read them.

A work *On Penance* is attributed to him, called in manuscript codices *The Corrector, or Physician of Souls*. Charles de Visch maintains that this is the work [Col. 0026A] he himself edited, but he is mistaken, for that work differs from the published one. It occurs anonymously three times in the library of Saint Victor, Paris: under KK. 17, fol. 106, entitled: *The Penitential Called the Corrector, or Physician of Souls*; under GG. 15, fol. 50; and under Q. 16, fol. 1. It is also in the library of Saint-Germain at Paris, MS 795, of excellent quality, with this title:

> “Here begins the book called the *Corrector* and *Physician*, which fully contains corrections and remedies for souls, and teaches every priest, even a simple one, how and in what manner he may assist every person: ordained or unordained, poor, rich, child, youth, old man, decrepit man, healthy or sick, at every age and in either sex; and when priests of parishes ought, by canonical authority, [Col. 0026B] to compel those at variance to peace and offenders to penance.”

Thus runs the title written in red. The *Penitential* begins: “In the week before the beginning of Lent, parish priests shall summon the people to themselves,” etc.

Johann Trithemius also attributes to him a *Summa of Vices and Virtues*, Book I, and Visch does so after him in the *Library of Writers of the Cistercian Order*. It survives in manuscript under the title *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues* in the celebrated library of Saint Victor, Paris, LL. 14, fol. 166, after his *Summa on the Art of Preaching*, fol. 144. Since it begins: “The apostolic voice proclaims,” etc., it seems to be the same work as the book of the same name read among the spurious works of Saint Augustine, and seems to belong to Ambrosius Autpertus.

Finally, there are letters under Alan’s name in Cambridge, in the library of Saint Benedict’s College, MS 216; but I greatly doubt whether they belong to this Alan of Lille or to another, English Alan. For an Alan, an Englishman by nationality, prior of the church of Saint Augustine at Canterbury and afterwards abbot of Tewkesbury, is recorded to have written many letters.

> [Note: These were recently edited by the distinguished J.-A. Giles, Oxford, 1845, octavo, together with letters and minor works of Saint Thomas of Canterbury and Herbert of Bosham. See *Patrology*, vol. CXC, col. 1475. EDITOR.]

This is what may be said of the writings of Alan of Lille. And let not the Cistercians and other Alanists, I pray, be angry with us for having ridiculed and rejected at once so many tales heaped up in Alan’s favour. Rather, if these men are of serious intelligence and judgment, they should give thanks [Col. 0026D] that we have discussed Alan’s manuscript works so fully, that, if ever anyone of the Cistercian Order should think of gathering them into one collection, he may find everything without difficulty in the indicated places.

## Prolegomena to the Antwerp Edition of the Works of Alan of Lille, Prepared by the Reverend Lord Charles de Visch, Prior of the Monastery of Blessed Mary of Dunes and Professor of Sacred Theology

(*The Moral, Paraenetic, and Polemical Works Which Could Be Found of Alan the Great of Lille, Doctor of Sacred Theology, Surnamed the Universal Doctor, Formerly Distinguished Head of the Ecclesiastical School of Paris and Humble Cistercian Convert; most of them now first brought to light from ancient manuscript codices, while others, formerly printed, are issued after collation with manuscript copies, corrected and variously elucidated; through the labour and care of the Reverend Lord Charles de Visch, prior of the monastery of Blessed Mary of Dunes and professor of sacred theology; with an appended, general, and most copious double index, namely of sermons and of subjects and words. Antwerp: Guillaume Lesteenius and Engelbert Gymnicus, in the street commonly called Hoochtraet, under the sign of the Golden Pelican, 1654.*)

[Col. 0027]

## DEDICATORY EPISTLE

To the most reverend and eminent lord, Lord Bernard Bottyn, abbot of the most illustrious monastery of Blessed Mary of Dunes, and general vicar of the entire Cistercian Order throughout Belgium, etc.

In past years, most reverend lord, I dedicated to your most reverend lordship the first fruits of my studies, adorned by the ornament of the press—I mean the *Library of Cistercian Writers*. You received them with such goodwill that you encouraged my mind and zeal to attempt more elevated matters. And that not without result will be witnessed by that incomparable Alan of Lille, formerly surnamed the Universal Doctor, no less illustrious for holiness of life. Long ago, through the injury of time and the negligence of his own people, he had been consigned to the densest darkness and so worn away and defiled by moths and bookworms that he seemed on the very point of being consumed even by the destruction of oblivion. Yet, through untiring labour and wakeful diligence, I brought him forth, cherished him, and adorned him in various ways, according to my abilities—so that now, restored to his own splendour and strength, he need fear the criticism of none, however exacting and learned.

For as he was in life, so he is in writing: great in the world, humble in the hiddenness of the cloister, but greater and exalted in the public life of the Church; a religious under the bushel, but glorious upon the lampstand; worthy to be heard, more worthy to be read, most worthy to be preached; indeed, worthy to be observed and imitated for the holiness of his life. It is therefore astonishing that a writer so outstanding and singular could have lain hidden for so long. In his writings, when read with attention, there immediately shine forth the brightness of true piety, consistency of exposition, usefulness of moral teaching, aptness of conception and invention, and finally the solidity of proof from Holy Scripture.

Moreover, I shall scarcely persuade those who have never devoted themselves to similar pursuits how much labour I have spent in revising, elucidating, and publishing them. For I frequently found in manuscript copies, here and there, letters and words worn away by age, as well as exceedingly obscure and wholly unfamiliar abbreviations scattered throughout; indeed, entire sentences were often completely corrupted through the scribes’ carelessness or their haste in writing. Thus I necessarily had to obtain several copies of each book, if I wished to establish the genuine reading. Having at last gathered them from every quarter, not without great expense and exertion, I examined and compared them with one another, so as to supply one copy’s mutilated text from another or correct its fault; and I found that in very many places they differed not merely in individual words, sentences, and periods, but in whole pages that had been confused, omitted, or inserted.

Yet when all these difficulties had been overcome through persistent labour—adding or altering nothing of my own, in the utmost good faith—I restored torn-away and transposed portions to their proper place and supplied the text with the reading which I judged truer from the sense of the wording and the agreement of the codices, while recording the alternatives in the margin. Then, besides all citations and certain short annotations added in the margin, and various styles of type by which we took care to distinguish certain matters, we prefixed to every book certain prolegomena or prefaces highly useful to all readers. I have, however, abstained from longer scholia and annotations, by which most modern writers are accustomed rather to disfigure than to elucidate authors otherwise excellent and clear in themselves.

In their place [Col. 0029], I have prefixed encomia and testimonies of distinguished men concerning our Alan and his doctrine, as well as a historical account of his life and death. For it matters greatly to know the author whom one undertakes to read, and the authority of the speaker adds great weight even to his utterances. It is astonishing with what receptive ears and willing minds one absorbs teaching commended by the celebrated reputation of its doctor. All these matters can surely be established nowhere better than from a life and the testimonies of illustrious men.

I therefore present first to your most reverend lordship this author, revised and restored through so many and such great labours, as I am about to bring him before the public in this jubilee—or five-hundredth—year from the most blessed death of our most holy Father Bernard. I present him as a son of that most illustrious house in which that same most holy Father once drew in the spirit of religious life and laid the foundations of his eminent sanctity, which afterwards rose into so magnificent a structure. I present him to you because the most prudent and devout superiors of our order have lately, amid the storms of war and in this most troubled condition of our country, entrusted to you, bearing the distinguished title of general vicar, the government of the numerous congregation of our order dispersed through all the Catholic provinces of Belgium.

I present him, I say, not that you may protect him: through the integrity and excellence of his doctrine, he is sufficient in himself and needs no protecting hand. Rather, I present him that you may receive and embrace him graciously, and finally, fortified by the commission of your authority, may deign to send him forth like a vigorous labourer into the Lord’s field. There—for he is truly mighty in speech as an exhorter, able to stir sinners and spur on the righteous—he will undoubtedly bear abundant fruit, producing many virtues among the people, in religious life, and throughout the universal Church.

With regard to myself and my scholarly labours, since I know well enough, most reverend and most eminent Lord, that the sacred studies of your sons have always been a singular delight to you—and among these, not least should be counted those concerned with rescuing the writings of the ancient Fathers from destruction—I see no great reason to fear that my labours expended on restoring so illustrious an author will displease Your Most Reverend Lordship. Rather, I confidently hope that you will receive them with the same affection with which I have undertaken them: for the splendour of our sacred Cistercian Order, the benefit of the Church, and likewise the everlasting remembrance of your most illustrious name. From the depths of my heart I pray that, as Alan’s name endures, yours too may thereby endure.

Most reverend and most eminent Lord, Your Lordship’s most humble son in Christ,  
F. CAROLUS DE VISCH, Religious and Prior of Dunes.

[Col. 0029]

# TESTIMONIES OF CERTAIN ILLUSTRIOUS MEN CONCERNING OUR ALAN AND HIS LEARNING

[Col. 0029A] The first is that of Henry of Ghent, archdeacon of Tournai, Doctor of Sacred Theology at the Sorbonne, surnamed “the Solemn,” who writes the following about Alan in chapter 21 of his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*:

> “Alan, a native of Lille, skilled in the liberal arts, presided over the ecclesiastical school at Paris; and, leaving monuments of his genius, he wrote a *Summa* useful for the office of preaching. Because he was greatly distinguished in verse, he wrote, in metre, a *Poetics*, on an imagined subject, concerning a man most excellent and perfect in every respect; this book he called the *Anticlaudianus*. He also wrote another work, partly in verse and partly in prose, which he called *The Complaint of Nature*; and another, on the natures of certain animals.”

So far Henry.

Henry of Ghent died in the year of the Lord 1293, [Col. 0029B] one year before Alan. [Note: [Col. 0029] On the opinion of those who maintained that Alan died in 1294, or flourished at the beginning of the fourteenth century, see the *Notice* above. EDITOR.]

The second is Robert Holcot, a most moral and learned professor of Sacred Theology, of the Order of Preachers, in lecture 118, letter A, on chapter 10 of the Book of Wisdom:

> “Against that wicked and most abominable vice of Sodom, Alan the Great of Lille, a renowned doctor of Sacred Theology, composed a book, *On the Complaint of Nature*, in verse and prose, very learnedly and carefully.”

Robert Holcot flourished about the year 1349, according to Bellarmine, in his book *On Writers*.

The third is John Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, of the Order of Saint Benedict, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*:

> “Alan of Lille, a German by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and second to none in secular letters in his own age; a most renowned theologian, philosopher, and poet, [Col. 0030B] who gloriously presided for a long time over the ecclesiastical school at Paris. There, shining forth conspicuously in every kind of knowledge, divine and [Col. 0031A] human, he deserved to be called ‘Universal.’ He wrote almost innumerable little works in verse and prose, by which he made the memory of his name immortal among posterity; but few of these have come to my notice. I found only the following under these titles:

> *On the Sentences*, four books. *Quodlibetal Questions*, one book. *The Eye of Sacred Scripture*, one book. *To the Most Reverend Father*, etc. *On Doctrine*, one book (otherwise, *Theological Maxims*). ‘All knowledge rests upon its own rules,’ etc. *On the Five Books of Moses*, five books. *On the Song of Songs*, one book. ‘Since many, in order to adorn,’ etc. [Col. 0031B] *On Penance, to the People of Bourges*, four books. ‘By God’s grace, to the church of Bourges,’ etc. *On Mystical Equivocations*, one book. *On the Six Wings of the Cherubim*, one book. *On the Complaint of Nature*, one book. *A Summa of Virtues and Vices*, one book. *On Parables*, one book. ‘From Phoebus Phoebe receives light,’ etc. *On the Art of Preaching*, one book. *Anticlaudianus*, one book. *On the Natures of Animals*, one book. Several Sermons, one book. *Letters to Various Persons*, one book.

> “Finally, he is said to have produced notable commentaries and lectures on many books of the Bible, especially [Col. 0031C] on the Prophets, the Gospel, and the Apostle; of these I have been able to find nothing. Certain marvellous things are related about him, to which I neither give credence nor rashly deny it.”

So Trithemius. Yet he is mistaken in writing that Alan flourished in the year 1300, since it is established that he died in the year of the Lord 1294. See the epitaphs appended below.

Trithemius was alive in 1500. He died as abbot of Saint James’s in the suburb of Würzburg.

The fourth is Hartmann Schedel, or the author of the volume entitled *Chronicle of the World*. Under the year 1300 he says the following concerning our Alan:

> “Some assign to these times Alan, the most celebrated doctor, surnamed ‘Universal.’ Since he was admirable in every branch of knowledge [Col. 0031D] but especially eminent in theology and philosophy, he deserved to be marked out by the title ‘Universal.’ His burial is shown at Cîteaux, on the right as one leaves the church oratory, in a marble tomb. Of this Alan the Great, doctor, the following epigram survives:
>
> Here lies Alan [lacuna]
>
> [lacuna] Whom a brief hour buried in a brief tomb,
>
> Who knew the two, the seven, and all that can be known.”

So he writes. It should be noted here that “the two” means the two sacred Testaments, which he understood in their entirety with great ease and upon which he wrote commentaries on almost the whole; “the seven” signifies the seven liberal arts, in which he was exceptionally proficient. Hartmann lived in 1492.

The fifth is James Philip of Bergamo, of the Order [Col. 0032A] of Saint Augustine, in his *Supplement to the Chronicles*, under the year 1300:

> “Some write that Alan the German, surnamed ‘Universal,’ was held in great esteem in these times. Since he was admirable and ready in every branch of knowledge, and especially outstanding in philosophy and theology, he deserved at Paris to be distinguished by the title ‘Universal.’ He accordingly wrote almost innumerable volumes of books in verse and prose,” etc.

There follow word for word the matters reported above from Trithemius. James Philip of Bergamo lived, according to Bellarmine, in 1494.

The sixth is Sixtus of Siena, of the Order of Preachers, in book IV, letter A, of the *Sacred Library*:

> “Alan of Lille, a German, orator, poet, philosopher, and [Col. 0032B] theologian, the most excellent of all men of his age, director of the sacred Parisian academy; because of his all-embracing learning in every subject, he earned the surname ‘Universal Doctor.’ Among the many illustrious monuments of his labours he left five books of commentaries on the whole Pentateuch; likewise one book on the Song of Songs, beginning: ‘Since many, in order to adorn.’ He also surveyed both Testaments in a brief compendium, entitled *The Eye of Sacred Scripture*, beginning: ‘To the most reverend Father and Lord,’” etc.

The seventh is Antonio Possevino, of the Society of Jesus, in his *Sacred Apparatus*, where this is read:

> “Alan of Lille (a city in Belgium), called the Universal Doctor, [Col. 0032C] wrote on the four books of the *Sentences*; *The Eye of Sacred Scripture*; *On Doctrine*; on the five books of Moses; on the Song of Songs; *On Penance to the People of Bourges*; *On Mystical Equivocations*; *On the Complaint of Nature*; *On Parables*; on the art of preaching; on the natures of animals; one book of letters to various persons; *Quodlibetal Questions*; *On the Six Wings of the Cherubim*; *A Summa of Virtues and Vices*; *Anticlaudianus*; several sermons.”

Possevino died in 1611, at the age of seventy-eight.

The eighth is André Saussay, protonotary of the Holy Roman Church, in the *Gallican Martyrology*, published at Paris in 1637, under 30 January:

> “Alan of Lille, called the Universal Doctor, ended his course in a pious death at Cîteaux. There, scorning human glory and loving humility, he took the habit in the lowly and despised rank of the lay brothers; like gold beneath dust, he long remained hidden. Yet after he became known, when the splendours of divine gifts burst forth, he did not allow himself to be called away from this humble and abject class. Nevertheless, persevering in his resolution of voluntary self-abasement until his last breath, he left an altogether astonishing example of self-contempt; and, released from the flesh, fortified by divine aids, and furnished with the most illustrious monuments of wisdom and exceptional piety, he flew away to the enjoyment of eternal glory.”

The ninth is Antoine du Verdier, in the *French Library*:

> “Alain des Isles, a German, wrote in Leonine elegiac verse a book entitled *Alanus on Parables*, or *Doctrinale*. In it are contained many good teachings profitable to everyone, [Col. 0033A] translated from Latin verse into French rhyme, with a prose commentary,” etc.

And below:

> “This is he of whom the proverb is spoken: ‘Let it suffice you to have seen Alan,’ etc. He wrote several other things mentioned in Conrad Gesner’s *Library*.”

The tenth is Jeremias Drexel, of the Society of Jesus, in his *Daniel*, chapter 18, §3. There, discussing the nature and malice of envy, he says that no one has spoken more briefly and significantly concerning it than Alan, whom he calls an outstanding orator and poet; he adduces a passage from Alan’s *Complaint of Nature*.

See volume II of Drexel’s works, folio 582.

The eleventh is John Buzelin, of the Society of Jesus, in his *Gallo-Flanders*, volume I, chapter 7, folio 33:

> “The city of Lille bore Alan, who [Col. 0033B] embraced all studies in his mind and therefore everywhere obtained the name of Universal Doctor, indeed with great glory.”

Likewise, in volume II, book VII, under the year of the Lord 1294:

> “The Cistercian Order mourned that Alan was extinguished from the rolls of the city of Lille, after he had flourished in distinguished renown through many kinds of learning. Some record that he possessed such a genius for every field of study that he was most ready in speech, composed prose discourses and elegant verse, and discussed philosophical and theological matters with the greatest acuteness; no branch of learning escaped his mind, and thence he gained for himself the surname Universal Doctor. For a long time he expounded the sacred writings and questions concerning God at Paris, where he attained the highest laurels of sacred learning. Embracing much both in verse and prose, he published various books,” etc.

Buzelin died in 1626.

The twelfth is Antoine Sander, Licentiate in Sacred Theology, canon and scholasticus of the cathedral church of Ypres, in his book *On the Writers of Flanders*, under the letter A:

> “Alan of Lille, a Fleming, deriving his surname from his birthplace; a man second to none in his time in divine and secular learning. For many years he presided over the Parisian Sorbonne, where, most illustrious for his knowledge of all sciences, he acquired the surname Universal. He wrote almost innumerable little works in prose and verse, by which he transmitted the immortality of his name to posterity,” etc.

[Col. 0033D] The thirteenth is Louis Jacob of Saint Charles, Carmelite of Chalon, royal counsellor and ordinary almoner, in book III of *On the Distinguished Writers of Chalon*:

> “Alan of Lille, monk, a Belgian by nation, Parisian doctor of theology, surnamed Universal, later a lay brother of the monastery of Cîteaux. A man learned to a miraculous degree; a most valiant bulwark of the Catholic Church; a great example of humility; the immortal glory of monks; the most brilliant star of the Muses; hammer of heretics. He was present at the ecumenical Lateran Council, held under Pope Innocent III in 1215, in the company of the abbot of Cîteaux; there he disputed [Col. 0034A] most vigorously and skilfully against a certain heretic, a disciple of Amalric of Chartres, to the great benefit of the Church. Now let us turn to the immense multitude of books which he wrote on almost every subject, than which there can be no richer testimony to his manifold learning.”

He lists the same writings that we have listed above, adding besides *The Mirror of the Church*, which he says survives in manuscript with Matthäus Dresser.

All these authors wrote consistently concerning our Alan: Thomas Dempster, in book I of his *Ecclesiastical History of the Scottish People*, where he testifies that Alan was surnamed the Great and Universal;

[Col. 0034B] Valerius Andreas, Doctor of Leuven, in the *Belgian Library*;

Hippolytus Marracci of Lucca, in the *Marian Library*, published at Rome in 1648 (asserting that he published “many most illustrious monuments of remarkable learning and exceptional piety,” etc.);

Aubertus Miraeus in the *Cistercian Chronicle*, folio 268, and in his scholia on chapter 21 of Henry of Ghent’s *On Ecclesiastical Writers*—except that this last author, by an altogether intolerable error, confuses this Alan with Alan of Auxerre, bishop, who died one hundred and twelve years before Alan the Great, or Universal Doctor, and who was a monk professed in the Cistercian observance at Clairvaux under our most blessed [Col. 0034C] Father Bernard. Having been made first abbot of La Rivour in the diocese of Troyes in 1139, he was subsequently, around 1151, raised to the episcopal see of Auxerre. Resigning it in 1167, he returned to Clairvaux, where he died in 1182 and lies buried beside Godfrey, bishop of Langres. Alan the Great, however, or the Universal Doctor, embraced the state of the lay brothers in the chief monastery of Cîteaux and persevered in it until death—that is, until the year of the Lord 1294—as is most clearly proved by his marble tomb, still visible at Cîteaux and adorned with several ancient epitaphs, which we shall produce below. See our *Library of Cistercian Writers*, [Col. 0034D] published in 1649; Jongelinus, in his notices of Cistercian abbeys and again in *The Purple of Saint Bernard*; Henriquez in the *Menologium*; and others.

Moreover, Miraeus seems to have drawn his error from the fact that Alan of Auxerre too is said to have been Belgian, from the city of Lille, the metropolis of Gallo-Flanders. That Alan the Great also came from this city is the common opinion of all authors, as is evident from the testimonies already cited and as we shall say again below.

Finally, our Alan too is called “the Great” and “Universal Doctor” by the great Angelus Manriquez, recently bishop of Wiener Neustadt, preacher to the Catholic king, and chief professor of Sacred Theology at the University of Salamanca, in volume I of the *Cistercian Annals*, under the year of the Lord 1140, chapter 10, no. 7.

[Col. 0036A] Gaspard Jongelinus, abbot of Eusserthal, in his *Notices*, and again in *The Purple of Saint Bernard*, treatise *On Cardinals*, §30; and many others.

[Col. 0035]

# HISTORICAL ACCOUNT OF THE LIFE AND DEATH OF ALAN THE GREAT OF LILLE, THE UNIVERSAL DOCTOR

## § I. On Alan’s homeland and birthplace

[Col. 0035B]

There is some controversy among authors on these matters. Thomas [Note: [Col. 0035] *Ecclesiastical History of the Scottish People*, 1627; printed at Bologna, book I.] Dempster, excessively eager to magnify the honour of his nation, wrote without any reason whatever that Alan was Scottish by origin and born on the Isle of Man. Jeremias Drexel, in the place cited above, calls him Sicilian, perhaps because he had read that Alan was from “the Island” (*de Insula*) and supposed that “island” was to be understood antonomastically as Sicily.

Gaspard Jongelinus, in his *Purple*, cited above, considers him French. Angelus Manriquez, likewise cited above, writes that he is regarded by some as Spanish and by others as French. But the common opinion of all other authors who mention Alan [Col. 0035C] considers him Belgian, born in the city of Lille, the metropolis of Gallo-Flanders. To this group may be reduced those who wrote that he was German, since the Flemings—indeed all Belgians—are commonly called Lower Germans, and Belgium Lower Germany.

Indeed, all controversy on this matter would cease if it were certain that this Alan was the true author of the *Commentaries on the Prophecy of Merlin the Englishman*, printed in 1608 at Frankfurt under his name by Johann Spiess, in octavo, under the title: *Prophecy, etc., of Merlin Ambrosius—together with seven books of explanations of the same prophecy, by Alan of Lille, German, Universal Doctor, and most eminent rector of the Parisian academy three hundred years ago: an outstanding orator, polymath, and theologian of his age.* In these *Commentaries*, book V, folio 198, the author expressly testifies that he was Belgian by origin, born at Lille in Flanders. His words are:

> “I too saw in Flanders, when I was still a little boy at Lille, where I was born, a certain witch who had been apprehended in the practice of her sorcery, etc.”

But when I recently examined these *Commentaries*, I found several things which made their attribution very suspicious to me and persuaded me that their author was someone other than our Alan. One is that immediately, with very little intervening, after the words just quoted, the following are added:

> “It was the time when Count Theodoric was called back from his own land into Flanders by the men of Lille, and also by those of Ghent and Bruges, as the lawful heir of Flanders,” etc.

So it reads there.

But since Belgian annals commonly report that Theodoric of Alsace was elected count by the Flemings around the year of the Lord 1128 or 1130, if Alan was then a little boy, he cannot have flourished around the year 1300, as many authors write with Trithemius; indeed, he cannot even have survived until 1294, when more exact historians state that he died, and when the ancient [Col. 0036C] epitaph still read at his tomb in Cîteaux proves it, according to Jongelinus and countless other eyewitnesses.

Unless perhaps we say that these latter words drawn from the *Commentaries*—“It was the time when,” etc.—were once added in the margin by someone ignorant of history for the sake of clarification, as he supposed, and were subsequently inserted into the text by the printer.
