Be that as it may, I more willingly subscribe to those who judge Alan to have been Belgian, from Lille by origin, especially guided by the authority of Henry of Ghent, the most celebrated Doctor of Sacred Theology, a Fleming by nation, Alan’s contemporary, and his colleague in the same University of Paris. This opinion is also confirmed by most manuscript copies which I myself have seen, designating him Alan of Lille or Alan of the Isles; the same surname appears in the [Col. 0036D] *Exposition on the Song of Songs*, printed at Paris in 1540 from the library of Saint-Victor.

Nor does it stand against this that Alan of Auxerre, bishop and monk of Clairvaux, is also asserted to have been Belgian and likewise a native of Lille; for it could very easily have happened that, over an interval of one hundred years or more, two men of the same name from Lille entered the Cistercian Order, particularly in different monasteries.

Indeed, within the past few years, several namesakes from the same city of Lille have been received into our Dunes abbey alone and are still alive; and we have seen this happen frequently enough with men from other cities as well. Therefore, following the common and usual opinion, I shall call him Alan of Lille, or Alan of the Isles, since in ancient times, even in Alan’s age—especially in religious orders—everyone commonly took surnames from their birthplace. When I call him also “the Great,” I follow likewise the authority of very many most weighty authors, some of whom the curious reader will find in the encomia above.

## § II. On the occasion upon which Master Alan, leaving the University of Paris, took the habit of the lay brothers at Cîteaux

[Col. 0037B]

Almost all who have written hitherto concerning Alan consistently affirm that, before entering religious life, he was distinguished by a most celebrated reputation for learning and fame and presided over the ecclesiastical or theological school of the University of Paris, as we have seen above from the testimonies of many most learned men. Yet concerning the occasion on which, abandoning the world, he withdrew into a monastery, although most agree sufficiently in recounting it, some nevertheless protest that they merely report it narratively from others and do not wish to affirm or deny anything.

We shall recount it here in the very words of John Buzelin, in volume II, book VII, of his *Gallo-Flanders*, under the year of the Lord 1294:

> “The following reason, I see, is given for Alan’s withdrawal into the Cistercian house. Alan had resolved in a single sermon to set forth the whole teaching of theologians on the mystery of the most holy Trinity, and to explain it in such clear words that anyone could readily understand it. On the day before doing this, he was walking alone beside a river in the evening, considering how he might successfully accomplish what he had in mind. There he found a little boy taking water from the river with a spoon and pouring it into a little ditch which he had made. When Alan smilingly asked him what he intended to do, and learned that he wished to contain the whole river within the narrow limits of the ditch, Alan said that this could not be done. The boy rebuked and instructed him that what Alan intended to do the next day could far less be accomplished. He was immediately struck with great astonishment; sharply reproaching himself and condemning his excessive arrogance, he burst into many tears. Therefore, on the next day, when he ascended the pulpit as though to address the people, who were gathered in the greatest numbers, he said only this: ‘Let it suffice you to have seen Alan.’ Then he rushed away from the midst of the surrounding and astonished crowd and hastened by long journeys to Cîteaux. There, when he requested admission among those called lay brothers, he was entrusted with the care of feeding sheep,” etc.

I possess the same story, written in an altogether simple style, in the preface to a certain commentary on Alan’s *Book of Parables*, printed at Lyons in 1501, one hundred and fifty years ago, without the author’s name.

Chrysostom Henriquez also relates it in his *Menologium*, under 30 January, where he names the author of that commentary Matthias Bonnomius; but he does not state whence he drew this name.

Moreover, that Trithemius, Antoine du Verdier, and many others, both ancient and more recent, read this account may readily be gathered from the testimonies cited above.

Finally, that Alan was a shepherd at Cîteaux and performed other servile tasks of the lay brothers there is proved by his ancient epitaphs, which we shall report below.

## § III. How Master Alan, after living for a long time unknown among the lay brothers of Cîteaux, was finally recognized

[Col. 0038B]

Buzelin says this:

> “After Alan had for some time fulfilled this office, the feeding of sheep, unknown, patiently and humbly, whether later he accompanied the abbot of Cîteaux as far as Rome in order to care for horses, when the supreme pontiff summoned all the prelates there to restrain the arrogance of heretics, and whether, seeing the mouths of Catholic doctors closed by the deceit and empty talk of sectarians, he bore this with great distress and, having first obtained permission, so constrained one of these heretics in disputation that he publicly cried out that either the devil or Alan was contending with him in words—I do not wish to affirm this. At least it is admitted that he afterward became known to the abbot and monks at Cîteaux, and thereafter devoted the remainder of his time diligently either to the writing of books or to piety; and that at his death he was honoured with a distinguished tomb and memorial.”

So he writes. But our ancient commentator, and several others already cited, describe all this much more distinctly and without any doubt, affirmatively. Since their words, in the substance of the story, are the same as those which Buzelin recounts, albeit doubtfully, I judged it superfluous to repeat them here. The curious reader may consult Chrysostom Henriquez, [Col. 0038D] whose *Menologium* is common enough in the more distinguished libraries.

But when this council at Rome was held, at which Alan confuted the heretics, and who was their leader mentioned in the story, I have found no one to declare except Henriquez, in the place cited. He asserts that this disputation occurred at Rome in the twelfth general Lateran Council, held under Innocent III in 1215; and that the heretic there convicted and confounded was a disciple of Amalric, a native of Chartres and Parisian theologian, familiar enough with Alan while he governed that university, who fell into heresy and spread various errors, which Henriquez himself also lists. But neither does he explain whence [Col. 0039A] he derived all this, nor have I found it anywhere.

## § IV. How Alan conducted himself after being recognized at Rome and later at Cîteaux

Buzelin, although doubting the manner in which Alan is said to have become known, nevertheless affirms, as we have just seen, that it is admitted that, once he became known, Alan devoted the rest of his time diligently either to writing books or to piety, and that at death he was honoured with a distinguished tomb and memorial.

The often-cited ancient commentator adds—and so does Matthias Bonhome in Henriquez—that Alan was of such humility that he never wished to accept any dignity, even when it was freely offered to him, but persevered in the humble state of the lay brothers until death. Yet, by order of the supreme pontiff, the abbot of Cîteaux assigned him two clerics in the same abbey to write down all the books which he dictated. Barnabas de Montalbo, in volume I of the *Cistercian Chronicles*, Henriquez in the place cited, and several others also confirm all these things.

Indeed, at Cîteaux itself, as I have learned from the assertion of many persons wholly worthy of belief, so firm and constant a tradition concerning all the foregoing is maintained that all those there most distinguished in religious life and learning would consider it absurd to call any of these things into doubt. Nor could one readily find anyone who has ever categorically denied them or written the contrary, except Thomas Dempster, a Scot, who in his *Ecclesiastical History of the Scottish People*, printed at Bologna in 1627, through an error far too gross, or even deliberate, being in some fashion blind in broad daylight, dared, against the evidence and clear testimonies of all authors who have written hitherto about Alan and of almost innumerable others who have visited his tomb and still visit it daily, to write that Alan the Great of Lille, the Universal Doctor, was Scottish by nation, professed as a monk in the Scottish monastery dedicated to Saint James outside the walls of Würzburg, and died there in 1300 and [Col. 0039D] was buried under this epitaph:

> Scotland bore me; Germany entombs Alan.

All this could be sufficiently refuted from Trithemius alone. After resigning the abbacy of Sponheim, he himself served for several years as abbot of Saint James’s Abbey near Würzburg and wrote an exact chronicle of that abbey, printed at Mainz in 1605 by Johann Albin. In it he recognizes only one Alan, a monk of that monastery and afterwards its twenty-fourth abbot, who died one hundred and sixty-one years after our Alan of Lille, namely in 1455. Indeed, in his book *On Writers*, as we saw above, he expressly testifies that Alan of Lille, the Universal [Col. 0040A] Doctor, was German by nation. Hence the epitaph adduced by Dempster, if any such epitaph exists there, concerns the abbot just mentioned or some private person, monk or layman, but not our Alan. That he was a Cistercian lay brother and was buried there is clearly proved—leaving aside all other authors—by the epitaphs listed in the following section and by the letter immediately appended from our most illustrious and most reverend General, the abbot of Cîteaux.

## § V. On the death and burial of Master Alan

Chrysostom Henriquez, in the place cited, writes that Alan survived seventy-nine years after the aforementioned Lateran Council, reached the age of 116, and finally died with a great reputation for holiness. [Note: [Col. 0039] Louis Jacob of Saint Charles agrees with all this, book III of *On the Writers of Chalon*, folio 145.] For this reason Henriquez included him in his Cistercian *Menologium* under 30 January. John, abbot of Cîteaux, likewise counts him among the blessed of our order in the catalogue of saints and blessed of the Cistercian Order appended to the old missals of that order. The most learned Leo Allatius, in his book *On the Urban Bees*, our present most reverend General in the letter already cited, and others commonly call him Blessed as well.

As to the truth concerning the year of his death, an ancient epitaph carved on his tombstone establishes it for us, and it can still be read perfectly, as follows:

> A brief hour buried Alan in a brief tomb,
>
> He who knew the two, the seven, and all that can be known.
>
> [Col. 0040C] Despising the things of a passing age, he became poor;
>
> inwardly converted, he was entrusted with tending flocks.
>
> In one thousand two hundred and ninety-four,
>
> devoted to Christ, he laid aside his mortal body.

Alan therefore died in the year of the Lord 1294.

Accordingly correct all authors who write that he flourished in 1300. His marble tomb may be seen at Cîteaux, in the left part of the cloister for those entering the church. Beside it, on the wall, hang two other epitaphs, which Gaspard Jongelinus gives us in *The Purple of Saint Bernard*, cited above, as he himself transcribed them in 1624 from the original tablets when he was at Cîteaux and visited the blessed man’s tomb.

## EPITAPH

[Col. 0040D]

### I

> This great learned Alan, so admirable,
>
> Makes this place of Cîteaux more memorable everywhere;
>
> For here he was a lay brother, shepherd, and servant;
>
> Here still he serves as an example of virtue and honour.
>
> Therefore you religious, lay brothers, and all passers-by,
>
> Imitate this doctor who lies here below.

### II

> Beneath this stone lies Alan, doctor,
>
> worthy of reverence throughout the whole world and of noble honour.
>
> He deserves to be numbered among theologians and philosophers;
>
> nor was he inferior to the ancient poets.
>
> Writing nobly, he lamented, taught, and disclosed
>
> nature, morals, and the mystical words of God.
>
> He sang the glorious deeds and shining triumphs of Jesus,
>
> depicting the arts and the warfare of heaven.
>
> [Col. 0041A] A painter of eloquence, censor of morals, minstrel
>
> of the Muses, he was a warrior for the faith.
>
> [Col. 0042A] Fleeing the world, beneath religion’s garment
>
> he lived; he remains here still—behold, he lies buried here.

## TOMB OF ALAN THE GREAT

(*From the Proceedings of the Academy of Inscriptions*, vol. IX, Paris, 1736, p. 229.)

[Col. 0041]

The tomb of Alan the Great was visible at Cîteaux in the cloister, near the entrance to the church. It had been erected in 1482 by Dom John de Cirey, abbot of Cîteaux.

The old epitaph of Alan, engraved in Gothic letters upon a square stone two feet across, set into the pavement of the cloister at the front of the tomb, was read as follows:

> A brief hour buried Alan in a brief tomb:
>
> He who knew the two, the seven, and all that can be known.

[Col. 0043A] Anyone desiring fuller information concerning the learning and writings of Doctor Alan should consult the *Library of Writers of the Cistercian Order*, which we published in the year of the Lord 1649. We are now preparing a second edition, much more corrected and fuller than the first, [Col. 0044A] with shorter works added by various ancient Fathers of the Cistercian Order, distinguished alike by holiness of life and learning. [Note: [Col. 0043A] See above Oudin’s Dissertation, who turned to his own use everything Visch newly wrote concerning the life and writings of Alan in the *Cistercian Library*. EDITOR.]

F. C. D. V. P. D.

[Col. 0043]

# LETTER OF THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS, MOST REVEREND, AND EMINENT LORD CLAUDE VAUSSIN, DOCTOR OF SACRED THEOLOGY, ABBOT OF CÎTEAUX AND SUPREME GENERAL OF THE ENTIRE CISTERCIAN ORDER

In this letter, after approving the *Library of Writers of the Sacred Cistercian Order*, published in 1649, he urges its author to publish his other works, and especially to revise the works of Blessed Alan, Cistercian lay brother.

To the Reverend Lord CAROLUS DE VISCH, our most dear brother in Christ, Prior of our devoted monastery of Dunes.

Reverend Father in Christ,

We ascribe to your labours and learned vigils the fact that the writers of our sacred Cistercian Order, long hidden in darkness, now return from their hiding places into the light and, as though restored from the tomb to life, live again. We therefore regard the publication of your volume as all the more welcome because we trust that it will contribute greatly to the ornament and splendour of our aforesaid Order. Accordingly, in our own name and that of our Order, we congratulate you and render due thanks. With all the paternal affection in our power, we exhort you to strive to complete the works still remaining of those you have begun, for the greater glory of God. We pray that He may deign to crown your labours with His blessings.

If any manuscript works of our Blessed Alan, Cistercian lay brother, besides those presently in your hands, can be found in our Cistercian library, we shall arrange for them to be sent to you for publication. Meanwhile, take courage, Reverend Father, and continue with the zeal you have begun to labour for our Order, which you will have bound to you forever. For our part, awaiting an opportunity to be of service to you, we pray almighty God to grant you an everlasting abundance of His graces as recompense and fitting reward for your labours; and with all the affection of our hearts we commend ourselves to your devout prayers.

At Cîteaux, 12 March 1650.

Your Reverend Paternity’s  
most dear and devoted brother in Christ,  
CLAUDE, Abbot of Cîteaux, General.

[Col. 0043]

# CENSURE
I have read carefully, and with great feeling, these moral, paraenetic, and polemical works of Alan the Great of Lille, as he is now commonly called; and, because they are full of Catholic and learned piety, they may usefully be printed. Such is my judgment. Given at Bruges, 12 April, in the year of the Lord 1652.

John Baptist Vanden ZYPE, Canon of the Cathedral Church of St Donatus, Bruges, Licentiate in Canon Law.

[Col. 0043]

## AUTHORIZATION OF THE ORDER

We, Brother Bernard Bottyn, abbot of the monastery of Blessed Mary of the Dunes, of the Cistercian Order in the Diocese and City of Bruges, Vicar and General Visitor of the same Order throughout Belgium, by the tenor of these presents grant permission that the paraenetic, polemical, and moral works of Alan the Great of Lille—drawn forth, as it were, from Democritus’ well by the untiring study and labour of the Reverend Sir Charles de Visch, theologian and prior of our aforesaid monastery of the Dunes, brought into the light, variously illustrated, examined by different theologians, and warmly commended—may be made available to all and submitted to the press, so that the memory of so great a doctor may flourish anew. Given in our aforesaid monastery of the Dunes on the 24th day of April in the year of the Lord 1652, under our manual signature and the impression of our countersign.

BERNARD, Abbot of the Dunes, Vicar General.

[Col. 0045]

## VERSES

To the Reverend and Most Learned Lord, Sir CHARLES DE VISCH, most deserving Prior of the Abbey of the Dunes, who publishes the works of Alan, the Universal Doctor, applause was offered by the Reverend Sir Peter de WAGHENARE, religious and subprior of St Nicholas at Veurne, of the Premonstratensian Order.

[Col. 0045A]

What does not the desire for wealth compel  
Mortal hearts to do? It drives inhabitants  
Of the solid land onto troubled waves,  
And confidently commits them to the perils  
Of the deep in a vessel far too frail.

They do not fear Africa’s south-west wind, mixing  
Its shrill battles with the north winds; nor the rage  
Of the enraged south wind advancing; nor the savage  
Furies of the Olenian kid; nor the Cyanean mountains  
Accustomed to strike the clouds with waves caught in their narrows;  
Nor Scylla, the maiden with girded womb and dogs,  
Nor infamous Charybdis restrains the sailors’  
Reckless Liburnian vessels.

And you too, Charles, are tormented by no slight desire

[Col. 0045B]

For treasure; and it bids you diligently traverse  
Every retreat—not in a ship, but by frequent letter—  
And fly through east and west.

This treasure, this life-giving treasure, is the glorious  
Doctor Alan’s memorials: Alan, who once  
Leaving the sacred heights of the Parisian chair,  
Did not refuse, while the whole world stood amazed,  
To migrate to the camp of the Cistercians  
And earn the pay of a lay brother.

[Col. 0046A]

O how full these memorials are of piety, holiness,  
Learning, and the charm of eloquence! The more  
They are read by learned persons, the more  
They will be read, not unaware that they stir  
A holy desire.

Are these works not worthier to seek through  
The Symplegades, Charybdis, and Scylla’s  
Barking mouths than any Indian metals  
Or Persian gems?

You, Charles, having sought them with the greatest  
Care and labour, bring them forth from shadowy  
Hiding places; polished by the blessed files  
Of your intellect, you submit them to the press  
And restore them to the world.

Who among the Cistercians, who among others,

[Col. 0046B]

Would not hasten to raise glad applause  
And pay the gifts of thanks?

Certainly now my Muse pays the greatest thanks  
And triumphantly entwines your worthy hair  
With Phoebus’ honours, repeating joyful words  
And praying that the glory which bears Alan  
To the stars may bear you too, and set you  
Among the citizens of the Zodiac, between the Fishes,  
Or in some other exalted place in heaven.

To the Reverend Lord, Sir CHARLES DE VISCH, Bachelor of Sacred Theology in full standing and its professor, most deserving Prior of the Monastery of Blessed Mary of the Dunes, who publishes the little works of ALAN THE GREAT, called the Universal Doctor: with song, applause was offered by Sir Marcus Jacquemont, subprior of the monastery of the Dunes.

While Alan the Great sleeps through very many ages,  
Behold, Charles rouses him from his heavy sleep.

[Col. 0047]

That one potter hates another potter is not well said here:  
Virtue always loves virtue as its companion.

Learning is Charles’s companion in virtue,  
While he restores hidden Alan to the light and celebrates him skilfully.

Recently he brought forth for us all writers universally,  
In order, method, and style.  
[Note: The *Bibliotheca Scriptorum ordinis Cisterciensis* was printed in 1649.]

Now he celebrates before the world, particularly, that Doctor  
Who is universal both in name and in fact.

Since the Universal precedes the particular,  
The learned have here a good ordering of learning.

How well, Charles, by your writings you travel the road of learning:  
In your labour there are fruits, order, and grace.

While pen brings forth pen, your fruitful glory grows,  
And, by lawful interest, becomes doubled:

Your first glory comes to you from your own pen;  
The second, afterwards doubled, comes from another’s.

I should like to make it threefold, if perhaps the Muse favoured me,  
But it cannot be matched to your merits.

Yet I undertake it: I shall try to bring forth such praises  
As I can, if my trembling lyre does not refuse.

Charles is a fish, as he is called by his family name,  
But I do not know what fish he is in species.

What fish shall I sing, Neptune? Shall I place him among great whales?  
Or perhaps call him a sea-horse?  
Shall I sing of a mute dog of the sea that barks?  
It is not permissible to compare Charles with mute creatures.

Shall I mention a Siren? Or call him a remora? He is neither.  
It will be more fitting to call him a dolphin.

Call him a dolphin, who saves men from the waves,  
Keeps them safe, and restores them to dry land.

So, Charles, you do not allow Alan to lie hidden in deep darkness,  
But draw him forth from lofty hiding places.

You restore him to the light, performing a dolphin’s office;  
A fish, you have the name and omen of a dolphin.  
[Note: He alludes to the arms, showing two dolphins on a silver shield sprinkled with several black crosses.]

Continue to give writers their due crown  
And thus to wreath your own head with laurels.

While great constancy overcomes the arduousness of labours,  
It returns more sweetly to the mind again and again.

The more brightly the glory of writers shines through you,  
The more your own glory gleams among them.

**ANAGRAM: CAROLUS DE VISCH — “Decus charo luis” [“You pay honour to the dear one”]. EPIGRAM.**

When virtue brings envy, if without fault  
You pay undeserved penalties, Alan will be your protector.

Be an honour to the dear one whom you love and adorn;  
He will wash away envy’s unjust fires.

You will be dear to the dear one, pleasing to the lover of virtue;  
If you pay the price, he will clear it by just ingenuity.

**ANOTHER: “Charius do, luces” [“More dearly I give; you shine”]. EPIGRAM.**

More dearly you give light to Alan; and, by reflected light,  
you shine, a love made bright by Alan’s radiance.

“I give light to Alan more dearly,” says Charles;  
“You shine with Alan’s light,” says Love.

**CHRONOGRAM.**

“sIs DoCtorIs honor, per teMpora Longa perennIs” (“The honour of this Doctor is everlasting through long ages”).

To ALAN THE GREAT, UNIVERSAL DOCTOR, wise fellow-brother, born from one mother—namely, the Cistercian monastery and Order—heir of the honey-flowing spirit of the most holy Father BERNARD, who celebrates among the heavenly beings the five-hundredth jubilee year of his glory: as this work comes forth from the press into the world in the five-hundredth jubilee year—that is, five hundred years from the death of Blessed Bernard—under the happy auspices, study, industry, and labour of the Reverend and most learned Sir Charles de WISCH, professor of Sacred Theology and most worthy prior of the monastery of the Dunes, Sir Baldwin WINNCEL, religious and priest of the same monastery, offered this song.

[Col. 0049]

“Who will give you to me as a brother sucking the breasts of my mother?” Song of Songs 8.

How many joys does this fiftieth year of triumph give;  
How many jubilations does the spikenard make in heaven!

If you count the years, Bernard, you will mark the number  
In which, weary of earth, your mind was caught up to heaven.

But since we see the stars spreading themselves in applause,  
Why should the Order conceal its own applause?

Let the sacred Order rejoice; let the world rejoice with the Father;  
Let there be equal melody in heaven and on earth.

Let Alan, the lover of piety, come forth from the press,  
So that a brother’s jubilees may flow from a brotherly source.

Do you recognize your brother, Bernard? One parent  
Nursed the two with the rich milk of love.

As each sprang from the foremost ranks of the Cistercians,  
So one house, one mother, belonged to them both.

You would see them flying through the upper air with equal flight  
And say that honey-flowing combs lay beneath each.

For if Bernard the Spikenard hangs sucking at his mother’s breasts,  
Alan possesses those breasts no less happily.

Bernard moves his lips, hanging at the right breast;  
The left gave sweet nectar to Alan.

Each sucked in equal draught; each was filled—  
If one whom love has satisfied can be filled.

Bernard gave honey, but Alan gives honeyed things:  
In this honey-flowing book, Alan, you bring forth honeyed things.

Cease now, Spikenard, to seek your brother  
Who sucks the Mother’s breasts: your brother Alan is here.

Your brother is here because he shares with you the Mother’s breasts,  
Breasts which flow with abundant milk for her children.

While Charles produces this brother for Bernard’s jubilees,  
The book itself celebrates jubilees by this book.

Charles, how great are the proofs of your praise!  
While you live, your work will be full of honour.

You adorn Bernard’s jubilees with the splendour of a volume;  
The earlier brother is honoured by the later one.

Therefore whoever brings Alan forth gives Bernard a brother;  
But this labour was Charles’s.

This book was that labour; this book, the offspring of labour,  
Will not be sparing of your honour.

Charles, in Alan you will live on after death;  
That pen and hand of yours cannot die.

The time will come—I shall meditate silently on the rest—  
When the highest glory will be granted to your writings.

But I am silent: it is burdensome for the modest to hear praise.  
Let others behold this praise; for them, to have deserved it is enough.

**CHRONOGRAMS:**

1. “To blessed BerNarD, these writings of ALan are ConseCrated by CaroL’s Labour and gift.”  
[Note: DDCCCCCLLLIII, 1653.]

[Col. 0051]

2. “To ALan the Great, with a happy song, you sing honours, CharLes.”  
[Note: MCCCCCLLLII, 1652.]

3. “Glory to BernarD and the writer.”  
[Note: MDCLIII, 1653.]

[Col. 0051]

# A SHORT EXPLANATION OF THE SONG OF SONGS IN PRAISE OF THE VIRGIN MARY, MOTHER OF GOD, BY ALAN OF LILLE, MOST CELEBRATED DOCTOR, SURNAMED THE UNIVERSAL DOCTOR

“Those who elucidate me shall have eternal life.” Ecclesiasticus 24.

## PREFACE TO THE READER

1 Here, reader, you have a little book, indeed small in bulk, but remarkable in its efficacy for stirring readers’ affections toward the worship and love of the Virgin Mother of God. From it—as one may know the lion from his claw—you may infer the author’s devout sentiments toward that most holy Virgin, and at the same time the subtlety of his intellect in drawing out mystical meanings from the sacred Scriptures. This is the little book in view of which the most learned Hippolytus Maraccius of Lucca, of the Congregation of the Mother of God, in his *Marian Library*, published at Rome in 1648 from the press of Francis Caballi, included our Alan among the more illustrious writers who have written anything concerning the most blessed Virgin Mother of God, and did so with no undistinguished commendation. This is also the work which Martin Anthony Delrio, the very celebrated writer of the Society of Jesus, writes that, after seeking it in vain for a long time, he finally obtained through the diligence and kindness of Father Andrew Schott, in the introduction to his commentary on the Song of Songs. It had indeed been printed at Paris in 1540 by Jacques Kerver, from the library of St Victor, as these verses inscribed on the title page report:

Now for the first time, reader, the Victorine  
Library brings forth this Alan from its own bosom for you.

But immediately all copies were so dispersed that scarcely anyone could find even one.

Nevertheless, having through the painstaking diligence of the most distinguished Claude Doresmieulx of Arras obtained one copy still remaining of these editions, I offer it for your use, revised by careful comparison with two very ancient manuscript copies—namely, those of St Martin of Tournai, of the Order of St Benedict, and of Villers Abbey, of the Cistercian Order—and illustrated by marginal annotations and by variant readings of a great many words here and there. If you read it attentively, you will also examine the other works of the same author more eagerly, and not without the fruit desired.

Farewell.

Brother Charles DE VISCH, Prior of the Dunes.

# EXPLANATION OF THE SONG OF SONGS

3 ## THE AUTHOR’S PROLOGUE

[Col. 0051A]

Although many offer gold, silver, precious stones, fine linen, scarlet twice dyed, and purple for adorning the tabernacle of God, I, following the custom of others, offer goats’ hair (Exodus 35).  
[Note: The Villers manuscript has *peripsoma* [“a loincloth”] instead of “following custom.”]

[Col. 0052A]

[Col. 0053A]

And although the rich cast treasures from their abundance into the Lord’s treasury, I, with the poor widow, cast in two small coins (Mark 12).  
[Note: The same manuscript has “because, although” instead of “and although.”]

And although many pour out Solomon’s wisdom and Tullian eloquence in praise of the Virgin Mother, who is the tabernacle of God, the palace of the heavenly King, and the treasury of virtues, though they too are endowed with virtues, pure in chastity and inflamed with charity, I—poor in knowledge, abject in life, nothing in grace, bristling with the roughness of sin—offer whatever sort of praise I can in honour of the Virgin. For a spark can be struck from a stone, and honey is often found in a frail reed.  
[Note: The same manuscript reads “in a reed” for “from a reed.”]

As the tongues of human beings and angels proclaim the Virgin’s praise, so from every signifying creature her praise is drawn forth, and in every Scripture the Mother’s dignity is preached.

Therefore, although the song of love, namely Solomon’s wedding-song, is referred specially and spiritually to the Church, yet it is referred most specially and most spiritually to the glorious Virgin, as we shall explain, by divine prompting, to the extent of our ability. Therefore the glorious Virgin, longing for the Bridegroom’s presence, desiring the glorious conception announced by the angel, yearning for the divine Incarnation, speaks thus:

## CHAPTER ONE

“Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

This is what is elsewhere said: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke 1). Therefore she had heard the heavenly best man, the archangel Gabriel, sent to her, who honoured the Virgin with a special and unheard-of greeting; she, filled with a special and spiritual blessing, said: “Hail, Mary, full of grace; the Lord is with you” (ibid.). When she heard that the Son of God would be born from her, she was not puffed up by the announcement, not exalted by the word, not proud because of the Son; but humbling herself to God in all things and through all things, and not distrusting the oracle, she said: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord.”

As though she said, “Let it be done to me according to your word,” that is, at your word I shall conceive the Word of God. And this is what is said here: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

The Son is called the Father’s mouth for many reasons. For just as one person speaks to another with his own mouth, so the Father has spoken to the world through the Son. The mouth is of the same nature as the rest of the body; thus the Son is of the same nature as the Father.  
[Note: The Villers manuscript reads: “For if.”]

And just as a kiss is given by the mouth, so the Father through the Son gives a banquet of grace to the faithful soul.  
[Note: “Thus God the Father.”]

Therefore the Virgin asks for a threefold kiss. One kiss is the Incarnation. For just as two lips are united in one kiss, so through the Incarnation the divine nature is united to the human. Another kiss is the Holy Spirit, by whom the Son kisses the Father, by whom the Father loves the Son, and who unites Father and Son: he is the love, bond, and kiss of both.  
[Note: The same manuscript has “the Holy Spirit” for “of the Holy Spirit.”]

The third kiss

[Col. 0054A]

is the presence of Christ’s teaching: so that Christ himself is not understood by “mouth,” but his teaching is signified by Christ’s mouth, and the presence of teaching by the mouth’s kiss.  
[Note: “Is signified” is read instead of “is figured.”]

Therefore she asks that the Incarnation may be celebrated in her, that the Holy Spirit may come upon her, that the overshadowing of the power of the Most High may occur (ibid.), and that Christ’s teaching may be present.

These are the kisses by which the Father kisses the Son; or the bridegroom, the bride; or the Lord, the handmaid; the son, his mother; the foster-child, his nurse. But Christ, repaying the praise due to her desire, answers the Virgin’s desire:

“For your breasts are better than wine.”

As though he said: You desire my kisses, and I your

[Col. 0054B]

breasts, because your breasts are better than wine. Literally, I can refer this to the Virgin’s natural breasts, of which it is said in the Gospel: “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts which you sucked” (Luke 11). What breasts were more delightful or better than those which gave milk to Christ—not from the foulness of lust, but from the fruitfulness of virginity? Christ desired such breasts, to suck milk from such a breast: milk that did not taste of the slipperiness of flesh, but of virginity’s antidote.

These breasts were sweeter to Christ than all wine, that is, than every delightful drink. Because wine is the privileged drink, every pleasant cup is understood through it.

“Fragrant with the best ointments.”

[Col. 0054C]

That is, comparable to the fragrances of the best ointments. For what ointments accomplish by their scent, those breasts accomplish by virginity’s integrity. For as those draw by their fragrance, so these, by their scent, allure Christ.  
[Note: The Tournai copy reads “by the fragrance of integrity.” The Villers manuscript has the same.]

The foregoing may also be understood mystically: when it is said in the person of the Head, “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth,” the ensuing words may be understood as spoken in the person of the body, that is, the faithful people. For as the Virgin was Christ’s mother through conception, so she was the mother of the faithful through teaching and exemplary instruction. Now there were in the Virgin two examples of good living, chastity and humility, which she set before us as an example. With these, as with breasts, she nursed the faithful people

[Col. 0054D]

as a mother nurses her son. These are sweeter to the faithful than wine, that is, than carnal pleasures; for examples of humility and chastity taste sweeter to the palate of the mind than any delights taste to the palate of the belly.

Or what is said, “Your breasts are better than wine,” may be understood thus. The breasts of married women are the falls of the flesh, the movements of concupiscence, by which the milk of weakness is given and by which children are nursed or the sick restored. The breasts of widows are the austerity of continence and the restraint of experienced lust.

[Col. 0055A]

These breasts do not give honey  
[Note: The Tournai manuscript has “milk” for “honey.”]

of sweetness, but the wine of austerity. The breasts of the Virgin are virginity of mind and integrity of body. These give the wine  
[Note: Both manuscripts have “honeycomb” for “wine.”]

of eternal delight and the honey of pleasant rest. These breasts surpass all wine, that is, the state of widows and married women.

“Fragrant with the best ointments.” Because  
[Note: In the Villers manuscript all the following is added here: “because in many humility is feigned and chastity false, and in them the spiritual ointments—that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit—do not give forth fragrance; therefore there is added, ‘fragrant with the best ointments,’ because…”]

the ineffable humility of the Virgin and her refined virginity shine forth accompanied by other spiritual gifts.  
[Note: The Villers manuscript reads “communicating” for “accompanied.”]

Therefore it follows:

“Your name is oil poured out.”

For because of the distinguished gifts of the Holy Spirit which shine forth in the glorious Virgin, the renown and glory of her name have been spread throughout the whole world. Whose name does the world proclaim if not this Virgin’s? Whose praise is celebrated in the mouths of the

[Col. 0055B]

faithful people if not the Virgin Mother’s? Whose humility is set before us as an example if not the virgin Mary’s? Whose virginity is given us as a mirror if not that of the incorrupt Mother of God?

And elegantly the renown and glory of her name are compared to poured-out oil. Oil refreshes the hungry, heals the sick, soothes weary limbs, produces fragrance, and nourishes flame. So too, in the Virgin’s praise we are refreshed; by her example we are invited to the remedies of virtue; weary in adversities, we are restored by her patience; we are enlightened by the pattern of her life. The renown of her name is diffused; and her name is compared not merely to oil, but to poured-out oil. For as oil poured out gives a stronger fragrance, so the more widely the Virgin’s name is spread, the more her glory increases.

[Col. 0055C]

Therefore it follows:

“Therefore the young maidens loved you.”

For the more her beauty is made known, the more other virgins are invited to imitate and love her. And, in relation to the Virgin Mother, certain virgins are elegantly called young maidens, because she is mother and they daughters; she queen and they handmaids; she matron and they young maidens; she teacher and they pupils.  
[Note: Both manuscripts read “other virgins.”]

“Draw me after you.”

These are the words of one seeking the companionship of the heavenly Bridegroom, the words of a mother sighing for the presence of her Son. As though she said: I asked for your presence and obtained that presence; I asked for your teaching and was consoled by that teaching; but you ascended into heaven

[Col. 0055D]

by miraculous ascension. Therefore, grieving at your absence and filled with the presence of worldly misery, I cry to you: “Draw me after you.”

She elegantly says “draw.” For it does not belong to human nature to ascend of itself into heaven unless divine grace grants this by miracle. And note that as the glorious Virgin desired Christ’s coming in the flesh, so after his Ascension she desired with every prayer to come to him: that, as she had journeyed on earth with her Son, so she might reign with him in heaven. For as sorrow passed through Mary’s soul in the Passion (Luke 2), when the Son died, so it did in the Ascension, when she was separated from her Son.

[Col. 0056A]

And therefore, desiring her Son’s presence, she says: “Draw me after you.” And she rightly says “after you,” because the Virgin ascended after the Son and by the Son’s aid. Meanwhile, before I am drawn, so that I may deserve to be drawn:

“We shall run after the fragrance of your ointments.”

That is, I and the young maidens, drawn by the fragrance of your ointments—that is, imbued with the fragrance of the spiritual gifts with which you spiritually anoint us, which are called yours because they are specially given by you—we shall run. We shall not stand still in delight upon the road of the world, under the shadow of the age or the illusion of earthly pleasure; rather, we shall run by doing good works, ascending from virtue

[Col. 0056B]

to virtue. We shall run through the course in order to attain the prize (1 Corinthians 9).

“The king brought me into his cellars.”

After the King of kings and Lord of lords brought himself into the chamber of the virginal womb, he subsequently, after his Ascension, brought the Virgin into the chamber of Paradise. The property of heaven is elegantly signified by the name “cell” or “cellar”: for, to offer an allusion from the word, as wines are stored in a cellar which satisfy a person, intoxicate him, and remove him from worldly cares, so heavenly blessedness intoxicates the blessed so that it makes them solitary  
[Note: Both manuscripts read “sober” for “solitary.”]

and wholly separates them from love of earthly things.  
[Note: “Leads them astray.”]

Hence it is read in the Psalm: “They shall be intoxicated with the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Psalm 35).

[Col. 0056C]

And as one who is in a cell, like a solitary hermit, is separated from the clamour of the age, so one who is in heaven is separated from the tumult of the world. Or by “cellars” is understood the storehouse of the treasures of God’s wisdom and knowledge. As things to be kept are stored in a cellar, so in the glorious Virgin, as in a spiritual cellar, are the secrets of God’s wisdom and knowledge.

But the young maidens—that is, the other virgins—hearing the commendation of the glorious Virgin taken from the Virgin’s breasts, congratulate the Virgin and say:

“We shall exult and rejoice in you, remembering your breasts more than wine.”

We shall exult in devotion of mind and rejoice in bodily

[Col. 0056D]

applause.  
[Note: The Tournai manuscript has “spiritual” for “bodily.”]

“In you,” that is, in your praise and imitation; “remembering your breasts,” that is, calling to mind your breasts, namely humility and virginity, by which you make young maidens eager to imitate you, above wine—that is, above earthly delight—thus inviting the righteous who imitate and love you.  
[Note: The Villers manuscript reads “imitating” for “inviting.”]

And this is what follows:

“The upright love you.”

Those are called upright who go straight along the royal road,

[Col. 0057A]

not turning aside to the right, enticed by prosperity, nor to the left, broken by adversity; who are not bent down to worldly things by love of the earthly, but are directed to heavenly things by love of the heavenly; who do not love God for the sake of the world, but for God himself.

Or those are called upright who do not limp on one foot. A person limps on one foot who does not preserve both virginities, namely that of body and mind. Such a person does not follow the Lamb wherever he goes (Revelation 14), nor the Lamb’s mother. But those who walk uprightly on both feet truly remember the Virgin’s breasts and rightly love her. Especially upright, too, are those who, by loving and imitating, suck the Virgin’s two breasts, namely humility and virginity, and thus particularly remember those breasts.

Thus Christ was brought into the chamber of the maternal womb by conception, but, so far as human opinion was concerned, that chamber seemed blackened and darkened by concupiscence. This is what she says:

“I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the skins of Solomon.”

I am black, that is, pregnant, and so I seem not to possess intact virginity; yet I am beautiful, because I am a virgin in integrity of mind and body. Therefore, directing her words to the other virgins of Judaea, she says: Daughters of Jerusalem, I seem black according to human opinion, but I am beautiful, that is, a Virgin in the truth of the matter.

I am black, I say, like the tents of Kedar. By the tents of Kedar is signified the onslaught of tribulations

[Col. 0057C]

to which the glorious Virgin was exposed, not only in herself but also in her Son’s distress. For she called her Son’s tribulations her own and did not regard his adversities as foreign to herself. Hence it was said to her: “A sword shall pierce your own soul also” (Luke 2).

And tribulations are elegantly represented by Kedar’s tents. For it is read of Kedar that he always dwelt in tents; hence his tents were exposed to diverse whirlwinds and storms of wind and rain. Therefore the Virgin is elegantly represented by the tents of Kedar, she who is read to have been exposed to tribulations in herself and in her Son.  
[Note: The Villers manuscript reads: “the Virgin Mother is signified.”]

But she is beautiful like the skins of Solomon. Solomon’s skins were made from the hides of dead animals, painted with a variety of colours. The Virgin is therefore elegantly compared with Solomon’s skins because of the variety of virtue; the true peaceful one, Jesus Christ, was clothed in her flesh.

[Col. 0057D]

And because Joseph, the Virgin’s husband (Matthew 1), seeing the Virgin pregnant, was astonished  
[Note: The Villers manuscript omits the word “was astonished.”]

and did not know how that pregnancy had occurred, she may be introduced as speaking to her bridegroom in this manner:

“Do not look upon me because I am dark, because the sun has discoloured me.”

Do not look upon me because I am dark, that is, because I seem dark on account of pregnancy. For it was not a man,

[Col. 0058A]

but the Sun of righteousness, that discoloured me, that is, coloured me greatly: not with a colour of evil,  
[Note: The same manuscript has “material” for “evil.”]

but with a colour of the mind. For the grace of the Holy Spirit made me pregnant in such a way that it did not take virginity away; or it made me pregnant so that it discoloured me, that is, set me beyond the proper condition  
[Note: “The proper condition of colour.”]

of colours—namely, beyond the nature of other pregnant women. And I am truly black through tribulations, because:

“My mother’s sons fought against me; they made me keeper in the vineyards.”

“My mother’s sons,” that is, the Jews, sons of the Synagogue, fought against me in my Son, as against another self, when they persecuted my Son even to death. And thus they made me keeper in the vineyards.

“I did not keep my own vineyard.”

For the Virgin, who had previously been the Synagogue’s pattern for right belief

[Col. 0058B]

and conduct, ceased, after the Synagogue became unbelieving, to be its keeper. Passing to the Gentiles, she instructed them by her example and fortified them by her protection. Thus she became keeper of different vineyards, that is, churches from among the Gentiles, having left her own vineyard, that is, the Synagogue.

For it must be known that whatever is said in this song concerning blessed Mary is referred to her bodily or spiritual acts. Therefore it follows:

“Tell me whom my soul loves.”

This refers to the time of the Passion, and these are the Virgin’s words to Christ. At the time of the Passion, the disciples fell away from faith, but the Virgin did not fall from the state of faith. She wondered in whom he then rested by faith,

[Col. 0058C]

whom he joined to himself spiritually. For it is read that only the thief then ate, that is, was incorporated.  
[Note: The Villers manuscript reads: “was spiritually incorporated.”]

Therefore she is introduced as asking in this manner: “Tell me whom my soul loves,” for I see your fellow-countrymen raging against you; I see the apostles fleeing; and therefore I do not know in whom you dwell by faith. Therefore tell me whom my soul loves: show me in whom I may know that you dwell by faith.

She says “whom my soul loves” more expressly than if she had said “you,” in order that the mother’s ineffable love for her Son may be expressed: she did not abandon him at the crisis of the Passion, when the ardour of charity had failed among the apostles.  
[Note: There: “had failed.”]

For she loved Christ with her whole heart, she who so nourished and cherished Christ’s flesh that, suspended from love of her own flesh by love of his flesh,

[Col. 0058D]

she poured out every affection of her heart upon the needs of the newborn, nursing, crying, and growing child.

She also loved Christ with her whole soul, because such strength of the Holy Spirit aided her that, strengthening her toward every wholesome and most holy thing, it kindled her in Christ’s love. Finally, she loved Christ with such great strength that it is sufficient for the title of her praise that such force of love occupied her mind that, when the disciples fled, forgetting her frail sex, she herself stood weeping at the cross

[Col. 0059A]

and grieving with the dying one; though she did not lay down her soul for her Son by suffering, she nevertheless exposed it through compassion.

“Where you pasture, where you lie down at noon.”

Tell me, therefore, where—that is, in whose mind—you pasture by faith; where you lie down, in whose soul you rest by charity, while outwardly you labour in the Passion. And this at noon, that is, at the time of the Passion. The time of the Passion is elegantly designated by noon, because, according to John, Christ was crucified at the sixth hour (John 19). And as the sun’s heat rises at noon, so at the time of Christ’s Passion the heat of tribulation burned Christ. This, I say, I ask:

“Lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions.”

[Col. 0059B]

By Christ’s companions are represented the disciples, who, when the shepherd was struck, wandered as sheep of the flock (Matthew 24). Then the Virgin would have wavered with the disciples if she had remained in uncertainty and believed faith to have failed altogether. Christ is introduced as answering this as follows:

“If you do not know yourself, O beautiful [most beautiful] among women, go forth and follow the tracks of your flocks.”

Who is beautiful among women except the Virgin Mother, who above all others is privileged with spiritual gifts, the Mother of God, the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, the seal of virginity, and the mirror of humility? Therefore Christ says to her: “If you do not know yourself,” as though he said: So long as you love me, you will know yourself and know that I rest in you through love. But if you were ignorant that you are the Mother of God and did not love me as a mother loves her son, you would depart from me through ignorance and unbelief, and go after the tracks of your flocks—that is, you would become like the unbelieving apostles through ignorance and unbelief. And you who are now an example to others through faith would, by the example of unbelief, disfigure the apostles, comparable to goats by reason of unbelief. This is what he says: “Go forth and follow the tracks of your flocks.”

“And pasture your kids beside the tents of the shepherds.”

The churches of God are called kids,  
[Note: The Villers manuscript reads: “The tents of the shepherds are called the churches of God, which shepherds govern.”]

and ecclesiastical shepherds govern them. But the apostles, who had failed in faith, were no longer in the Church or of the Church; rather, they wandered, as it were, beside the Church through unbelief.  
[Note: Both manuscripts here insert the following: “and rightly so, because even though they wandered for a time…”]

Yet they were predestined. If, I say, you did not know yourself,

[Col. 0059D]

these things would happen; but you do know yourself. Indeed, I sit in you by faith and rest in you by charity. Therefore:

“I have compared you, my beloved, to my cavalry among Pharaoh’s chariots.”

Who is God’s cavalry, if not the Church, which accepts the bridle of his discipline, bears the yoke of his gentleness, and is recognized by the Spirit of God—and in this lies its salvation? Hence we read: “Your cavalry is salvation” (Hab. 3). This, then, is the meaning of: “I have likened you to my cavalry among Pharaoh’s chariots.” By contrast, Pharaoh’s chariots are those who are subject to the spiritual Pharaoh, that is, to the [Col. 0060A] devil; and they are his four-horse teams, which he himself drives and leads in pursuit of God’s people and to oppress Israel. Those who turn to faith become God’s cavalry, bending their backs—that is, the freedom of their will—in order to receive Christ as rider upon themselves, and enduring his reins so that he may turn them wherever he wills.

The sense is: My beloved, that is, Virgin Mary, my beloved bride, singular and unique, I have likened you—that is, made you like—to my cavalry, that is, to my Church, which was formerly among Pharaoh’s chariots while it was subject to spiritual vices or wickednesses. [Note: [Col. 0059] MS Villar: “vices or wickednesses.”] For the Virgin Mary resembles the Church of God in many respects. As the Church of God is Christ’s mother in his members through grace, so the Virgin is mother of Christ the head according to his human nature. And as [Col. 0060B] the Church is without spot or wrinkle, so too is the glorious Virgin. And as the Church possesses, in diverse persons, the universality of gifts, so the Virgin Mary possesses in herself the universality of charisms.

Because Christ seemed to declare to the Virgin that, unless she knew herself, she would go out after the tracks of the flocks in order to feed not sheep but kids, the Virgin seems, as it were, to have blushed at the severity of the warning and, with the purple of modesty spread over her face, to have made her cheeks beautiful. The Bridegroom says:

> Your cheeks are beautiful like those of the turtledove.

The nature of turtledoves is said to be such that neither does the male mate with any female except his own, nor does the female endure more than one male; so that, if one of the pair is killed or taken away and the other survives, the surviving bird’s desire for union perishes together with its mate. The comparison with the turtledove is therefore fittingly applied to the Virgin Mary: she knows no union with any man other than Christ; and in her there flutters, as it were, a multitude of turtledoves—continence and chastity. Cheeks are the sides of the face, in which honour and modesty are recognized. Her cheeks are elegantly compared to turtledoves, because in such birds both modesty of appearance and simplicity are denoted.

In accordance with this interpretation, the Virgin’s neck, or throat, is understood when it follows:

> Your neck is like necklaces.

Observe that he compared her neck to the very ornament customarily placed upon necks and throats. This should be understood thus: by the neck, which [Col. 0060D] we are accustomed to bend as a sign of obedience, are signified the obedience and submission she offered to Christ, because she accepted, as it were, Christ’s yoke and rendered obedience to his faith. Therefore Christ is the ornament of the neck—that is, obedience. For he himself first “became obedient unto death” (Phil. 2). Thus the adornment and necklace of her neck—that is, of the Virgin’s obedience—is Christ’s obedience. Her neck, moreover—that is, her obedience—was made like Christ’s obedience, which is Christ’s necklace. Great, then, is Mary’s praise in this; great is her [Col. 0061A] glory, that the imitation of her glory is made equal to the obedience of Christ which she imitates.

Hearing, the heavenly friends of the Bridegroom—the bridal attendants—that such great grace had been granted the Virgin by God, wish also to offer her their gifts. Hence follows the voice of the friends:

> We shall make for you little golden chains, patterned with silver.

A *murenula* is a fish hidden in water, very slippery and elusive. By these little *murenulae*, therefore, are understood the teachings of divine wisdom, hidden in the depth of Holy Scripture, elusive and slippery because they easily slip from human memory and understanding. They are golden because of the dignity of their knowledge; “patterned with silver,” that is, distinguished by a variety of expression in accordance with the beauty of eloquence. A little worm ordinarily marks the earth with various furrows; therefore the author used *vermiculatae* (“worm-patterned”) for “distinguished.” Or, since *vermiculus* denotes a certain colour applied to a thing for adornment, he understood “patterned” to mean “adorned.”

The holy Fathers set forth these little *murenulae*—that is, divine sayings—in praise and honour of the Virgin. Isaiah says: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isa. 31). Jeremiah likewise says: “The Lord shall create a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. 31). David says: “He has placed his tent in the sun” (Ps. 18). And in Daniel we read that a stone was cut from a mountain without hands (Dan. 2). And, as though the Bridegroom had entered the bride’s chamber, the bride speaks in this manner concerning the Bridegroom. [Note: [Col. 0061] MS Villar adds: “concerning the Bridegroom.”]

[Col. 0061C] **10. While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance.**

After the glorious Virgin conceived not only in mind but also in womb, Christ’s spiritual reclining took place within her. For where did he especially dine with the Father and the Holy Spirit? Where did he make his particular dwelling? Where did he recline spiritually and fully, if not in the Virgin’s mind? [Note: [Col. 0061] MS Villar reads “spiritually” for “especially,” and likewise later “spiritual.”] In her womb he reclined perfectly according to his human nature. O happy mind in which the heavenly guests—that is, the three Persons—are specially and spiritually refreshed! Peace is there the first food. Humility is served together with patience, likewise gentleness and mildness; and, above all, sweetness and purity of heart. But charity holds the principal [Col. 0061D] place in such a banquet.

Therefore, while Christ the King—who rules me and others—was at his table, that is, in me, in whom he was not only in mind through grace but also in womb through human nature, my nard gave forth its fragrance. That is, my frail flesh, signified by the humble nard-tree, cleansed by the coming of the Holy Spirit and with the tinder of sin extinguished, gave forth its fragrance and was proposed to others as an example, that through mortification of the flesh they might cleanse their own flesh. Or: while the King was at his table—that is, while the Lord Jesus was received into repose—my nard gave forth its fragrance, [Col. 0062A] that is, my fame, formerly humble and lowly, was spread throughout the whole world. [Note: [Col. 0061] The same exemplar here adds: “most sweet.”]

> My beloved shall dwell for me as a bundle of myrrh between my breasts.

But before my beloved, whom I love above all things, was taken up into heaven, he was for me, in the time of his Passion, a bundle of myrrh—that is, a great and manifold bitterness—because I shared his Passion with inward grief. The bitterness of sorrow is elegantly signified by myrrh, because *myrrh* is interpreted “bitterness.”

And because he suffered for our redemption, he shall dwell between my breasts—that is, he shall be held in the love of my inmost heart. The Virgin’s two breasts are the two arms of charity: one by which she loved Christ as God; the other by which she loved him as her son. With these two arms of charity she embraces him. The two streams of charity are elegantly called breasts, because women are accustomed to offer their breasts for suckling to the little ones whom they love. She proposed these two streams of charity to others as an example and for their instruction, like a mother offering breasts for suckling.

Or Christ is called a bundle of myrrh to the Virgin Mother because, coming in the flesh, he excluded from the Virgin every corruption of concupiscence, just as myrrh preserves flesh free from decay. Hence what follows may also be understood literally: “He shall dwell between my breasts,” because, born from the Virgin, he was suckled by the Virgin alone; he did not suck the breasts of any other [Col. 0062C] woman but of his Virgin Mother. O blessed mother, who nurses at her breast him who offers the breasts of mercy to all! O wondrous thing: the daughter nurses the Father, the creature the Creator, the handmaid her Lord!

And because the breasts signify the Virgin’s twofold love, it follows:

> My beloved is for me a cluster of cyprus in the vineyards of Engaddi.

A cluster on the vine possesses fragrance in its blossom and, in its fruit, is said to have the power of warming and nourishing. Christ, therefore, was a cluster to the glorious Virgin: first, before Christ’s own advent, he sprinkled the Virgin with the fragrance of his fame when he made himself known to her through the Law and the prophets; he made her grow warm toward faith in him and [Col. 0062D] charity; and, coming in the flesh, he refreshed her like spiritual wine. Thus she grew warm with such fervour of charity that she was ready to endure every tribulation, grief, and temptation.

Accordingly, *cyprus* fittingly follows, for *cyprus* is interpreted “sorrow and sadness.” **11.** For the Virgin, in those tribulations and temptations, [Note: [Col. 0061] Both manuscripts insert: “and fittingly: always the character of her temptation.”] knew the character of her temptation, so that in all these things she could say of herself: “I have not sinned with my lips before God” (Job 1); and she understood how a person is delivered by God from temptation, and how human life upon earth is [Col. 0063A] temptation (Job 7). Thus “in the vineyards of Engaddi” is appropriately added. *Engaddi* is interpreted “eye of temptation.” The vineyards, moreover, are understood as assemblies of the faithful established in Engaddi, because, illuminated by the eye of temptation, they understand the character of their temptation and are delivered from temptation through God’s mercy.

Christ, seeing that the Virgin attributed the good things she had not to herself but to Christ, is introduced as responding to the Virgin and, in turn, praising her in this manner:

> Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved; behold, you are beautiful: your eyes are those of doves.

Christ exalts and confirms this title of praise because she is his bride not only when she is near him in body, but even, should it happen that she is absent from him, she remains his bride. This is indicated by the fact that, after saying, “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved,” he added thereafter, absolutely and without qualification: “Behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are those of doves.” That her eyes are compared to doves’ eyes is certainly because she understands the divine Scriptures no longer according to the letter but according to the Spirit, and beholds spiritual mysteries in them. For the dove is a sign of the Holy Spirit. To understand the Law and the prophets with spiritual meaning, therefore, is to have the eyes of a dove.

Perhaps, by a deeper mystery, “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved” may be understood as spoken of the present age, because here too the Virgin Mary was the Bride when she was near Christ. But because [Col. 0063C] he repeated himself and said, “Behold, you are beautiful,” it belongs to the future age, where she is beautiful and Bride not merely by imitation but by her own perfection itself. The dove’s two eyes signify the Virgin’s two understandings: by one she understood Christ while remaining on the way; by the other she now beholds him while remaining in the homeland. Both are dove-like—that is, simple—because free from error.

Hearing herself praised by Christ, the Virgin returns praise to him, saying:

> Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, and fair.

My beloved, whom I love more particularly than all others and more particularly than all else: behold, you are beautiful according to humanity and fair according to divinity. Nor are you alone beautiful, but I too am beautiful.

> Our little bed is flowering.

[Col. 0063D] Christ’s bed is called the flesh which he assumed, because a bed has two uses: on a bed a person suffers in sickness and rests in health. Similarly, Christ suffered in human weaknesses in human flesh before the Passion, and rested in the same flesh after the Resurrection. And she elegantly says, “Our little bed is flowering,” because Christ’s flesh—which was formerly in bloom in life—bloomed forth through death and bloomed anew through the Resurrection. [Note: [Col. 0063] MS Villar inserts here: “because Christ’s flesh was in some manner the Virgin’s flesh, since he assumed it from virginal flesh.”] Hence in the Psalm: “My flesh also bloomed anew” (Ps. 27).

[Col. 0064A]

> The beams of our houses are cedar; our ceilings are cypress.

These houses are understood as Christ’s body and the Virgin’s body. The beams of the houses are the substances of their bodies, called cedar because they are incorruptible—for cedar is incorruptible. As we believe that Christ’s body was not dissolved in decay—hence we read: “You will not give your Holy One to see corruption” (Ps. 19)—so it is probable that Mary’s body too was free from the corruption of decay. Thus Augustine says in his sermon *On the Assumption of the Virgin*: “We believe that not only the flesh which Christ assumed, but also the flesh from which he assumed it, was taken up into heaven.” Hence in a published prayer we read: “Yet she could not be crushed by the bonds of death,” [Col. 0064B] etc. And if she did not rise again, why is it said of her: “Mary was taken up into heaven”?

“Our ceilings are cypress.” The ceilings attached to the beams signify the bodily weaknesses attached to the bodies of Christ and the Virgin. They are elegantly called cypress, because cypress is customarily used for bodies that are burned and gives forth from them a marvellous fragrance. So too the weaknesses belonging to death, in both the Virgin and Christ, give forth a more wonderful fragrance through the sufferings which they endured in weakness.

Or the houses are understood as churches. They are called Christ’s houses by reason of his governance and spiritual indwelling; they are called Mary’s by reason of formation, because the Virgin formed them by her example. [Col. 0064C] The beams or timbers are called the doctors of the Church, cedar because of their unfailing strength and the fragrance of their virtues. For cedar is incorruptible wood and sweet-smelling. Hence the Apostle says: “We are Christ’s good fragrance to God” (2 Cor. 2). The ceilings which adhere to the beams or timbers are the hearers who, through the teaching of their superiors, adhere to God and to God’s Church and complete the beauty of God’s house. Therefore these ceilings too are called cypress, a wood that is incorruptible and sweet-smelling, because these hearers become both hearers and doers of God’s word, and are of good fragrance.

Because the Virgin had called the bed flowering, Christ next declares by what flower it is flowering, saying:

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 0064D]

> I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.

The field is called Christ’s human nature. As a variety of flowers springs up in a field, so in Christ’s human nature there is a multitude of virtues: there was the violet of humility, the rose of patience, and the lily of chastity. Christ was the flower of this field—that is, its beauty—according to divinity, because through the power of divinity he possessed in human nature the fullness of gifts. [Note: [Col. 0063] MS Villar: “The flower—that is, the beauty—of this field was Christ.”] Christ’s human nature is elegantly signified by a field on account of its breadth and levelness, because [Col. 0065A] Christ’s human nature possessed breadth of virtue and the levelness of truth [Note: [Col. 0065] “Purity.”]; for in him there was no trace of error.

Thus the same one is also called “the lily of the valleys,” because perfect humility existed in Mary and in Christ’s human nature. Therefore the person of the Virgin and the human nature of the Word are called valleys because of the eminence of their humility; not merely valleys but adjoining valleys, by reason of resemblance, because the Virgin was especially like Christ. Christ was the lily of these valleys because, corresponding to the perfection of her humility, he gave perfection of chastity. Hence the Virgin herself is elegantly called “a lily among thorns.” Thus it follows:

> As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among daughters.

[Col. 0065B] These are Christ’s words concerning the Virgin. The sense, therefore, is: As she is most chaste among the lustful, [Note: [Col. 0065] “Among the lustful women.”] so is my beloved—that is, the Virgin Mary—among daughters. We may observe that these daughters, among whom the Virgin stands as a lily among thorns, are called not daughters of God but daughters of the devil, whom they have as father by imitation.

As Christ compared his mother to a lily, so she fittingly compares her Son to a tree. Hence it follows:

> As an apple tree among the trees of the woods, so is my beloved among sons.

[Note: [Col. 0065] MS Villar reads: “he compares [him] to an apple tree.”] Since all heretics are fruitless among the trees of the woods, [Note: [Col. 0065] For “among,” it reads “as.”] he alone, with his members and the fruit of the Church, feeds and delights by the fragrance of good repute. [Col. 0065C] The trees of the woods feed swine [Note: [Col. 0065] In place of *priusquam* (“before”), another manuscript has *plusquam* (“more than”), rather than [uncertain reading/context].] before they feed people, because the devil with his members, namely heretics, feeds unclean souls through unclean desires. The shadow of this apple tree is the protection of the Holy Spirit. Hence it follows:

> Under the shadow of him whom I had desired I sat.

These are the words of the Blessed Virgin, as though she said: I, humbled by Gabriel’s words, sat—that is, rested—under his shadow, that is, under the protection of the Son of God, effected through the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit, of which it is said: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1). At the time of the Incarnation, the grace of the Holy Spirit was in her as a tent or shelter against the incitement of concupiscence.

“Under the shadow of him whom I had desired I sat”: I did not stand in the rigidity of pride, did not walk in restless curiosity, did not lie down in abandoned pleasure. Therefore she was full of grace: before God through humility, before angels through virginity, and before human beings through fruitfulness. She is the one of whom it is said in Proverbs: “A gracious woman shall find glory” (Prov. 11); and “a wise son is the glory [Col. 0065D] of his father” (Prov. 15). Thus she found glory, namely the Son of God the Father.

> And his fruit is sweet to my throat.

The fruit of this tree is divine wisdom, remembered as sweet because all things that are desired [Col. 0066A] cannot compare with it. To whom was Christ’s wisdom sweeter than to the glorious Virgin, who drank more fully from the fountain of God’s wisdom, from which Wisdom itself was also incarnate? She especially tasted and saw that the Lord is sweet: that is, the tree planted beside the courses of waters (Ps. 1); that is, the tree planted in the paradise of delights (Gen. 2). Nor is it surprising that his fruit was sweet to my throat, because:

> The king brought me into the wine cellar.

The Old Testament is signified by the wine cellar. For as provisions are stored in a cellar, so heavenly secrets lay hidden beneath the figures of the Old Testament, by which the soul is spiritually nourished. The Mosaic Law is rightly signified by a wine cellar because of the Law’s severity and rigour, and because, as has been said, those who understand the Law spiritually are made drunk by spiritual wine. Christ brought the Virgin into this cellar when he revealed to her the spiritual understanding of the Law. Hence it is written of her: “But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart” (Luke 2), because she compared the events concerning Christ with what the Old Testament promised.

> He set charity in order within me.

In whom was charity ordered, if not in the Virgin Mary, who loved Christ with her whole heart, without error of understanding; with all her mind, that is, with memory without forgetfulness; and with all her soul, that is, with will without sluggishness? And after God, she loved herself. Because the Virgin, in the time [Col. 0066C] of the Old Testament, especially bound herself by a vow of virginity and was strong against every enticement, she invited other women to the flower of virginity and the strength of fortitude. Wishing to have companions in virginity and comrades in steadfastness, she says:

> **14.** Sustain me with flowers; surround me with apples, for I languish with love.

May I have in your virginities the consolation of my own virginity, and in your patience the example of my own strength, because I languish with this love.

Or the wine cellar signifies a rapture of mind, also called ecstasy, by which the Virgin was carried away to contemplation of heavenly things; this is also called *apotheosis*, that is, deification, or *theophany*, divine manifestation. Into this she was carried, lifted above love of earthly things. [Col. 0066D] This contemplation is rightly called a wine cellar because spiritual wines—that is, heavenly secrets—were served from it; they make the soul drunk in order to make it sober. In this contemplation true charity is ordered. For the more the human mind is lifted above love of earthly things, the more charity is directed along the straight path toward love of God. Love of earthly things in some manner hinders the order and course of charity.

This contemplation is elegantly called a flower, [Col. 0067A] because, as a flower contains hope of fruit and from the flower one comes to fruit, so through this enigmatic contemplation we yearn for the eternal one. By the apple, however, which is stronger, is signified the fortitude found in contemplation, which no earthly desire and no onset of tribulations can weaken. Therefore the Virgin, strengthened in contemplation and inviting her companions to the strength of contemplation, says: “Sustain me with flowers; surround me with apples, for I languish with love”—that is, with desire for eternal life.

> His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me.

Because I desire that his right hand—that is, his divinity—may embrace me, making me a participant in divinity. Christ’s left hand is called his human nature; his right, his divine nature. Inflamed, therefore, with love of divinity, she desires not merely to enjoy the presence of his human nature, but also his divine nature, because the divine is preferred to the human: human nature is from Christ and beneath Christ, to whom it owes everything.

Or by the head may be understood the Virgin’s natural understanding, which Christ formed in his human nature. Thus Christ’s left hand was beneath the Virgin’s head because, by supporting her natural understanding in some manner, he formed it. And because the Virgin was not awakened from the sleep of contemplation until she came down to the wakefulness of activity, to the time of her conception and childbirth—also because after conceiving she attended Elizabeth in her childbirth, and after giving birth [Col. 0067C] she cared for the nourishment and upbringing of her Son—it fittingly follows:

> I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles and stags of the fields, that you do not rouse or awaken my beloved until she herself wishes.

The daughters of Jerusalem are called the virgins of Judaea who aspired to marriage and wished to be granted the fruitfulness of conception and the honour of offspring, lest they incur the curse of the Law if they were barren. Therefore the Virgin’s kinswomen invited her to do likewise: to marry, conceive, and bear children, lest she incur the Law’s curse. But the Virgin had resolved by a contrary divine disposition to keep her vow of virginity unless God ordered otherwise, and thus not to descend from the sleep of contemplation to the tumult of activity. Virgins are freer for contemplation than married women, for many temporal cares adhere to the married state, as the Apostle says—for example, the rearing of children (Eph. 6).

Before she conceived, the Virgin was unwilling either to conceive or to rejoice in offspring until she received from the angel the fruitfulness of her conception and the honour of offspring. Then for the first time she desired conception and childbirth, when she said: “Let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke 1). The Son of God therefore so ordained that no exhortation and no example of other virgins should invite her to desire conception or childbirth before she had heard the divine oracle from the angel. Thus the Son of God is introduced [Col. 0068A] as speaking to the kinswomen of the glorious Virgin in this manner: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem,” that is, virgins of Judaea: I have established this concerning you, that by no example and no exhortation of yours—you who have right faith and right conduct in this matter—may you awaken the Virgin Mary from the sleep of contemplative life to the wakefulness of active life, except when she wishes, by divine inspiration, both to conceive and to bear.

By gazelles is understood faith, because, as gazelles possess keen sight, so faith possesses the first apprehension by which God is understood. By the stag, a larger and stronger animal, perfect action is signified. Or thus: “I adjure you, I forbid you by the gazelles and stags of the fields”—that is, if you wish to imitate the patriarchs and prophets, who foretold and understood this beforehand—“do not rouse or awaken my beloved until she herself wishes.”

Understanding this divine ordering, the Virgin rejoices with her beloved and says:

> The voice of my beloved.

As though she said: This ordering was made by my beloved—that is, by the Son of God—so that he might choose me beforehand and love me especially, so that I might conceive without concupiscence and give birth without pain. This is what follows:

> Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains, springing over the hills.

The mountains are the patriarchs; the hills, the prophets. Christ leaps upon them because they announced his coming, Passion, descent into hell, Resurrection, [Col. 0068C] and Ascension into heaven. All these were, as it were, certain leaps, which he nevertheless surpassed altogether, because, coming into the world, he did and taught more than all the patriarchs and prophets before him. Hence David says: “His word runs swiftly” (Ps. 147).

> My beloved is like a gazelle, or a young stag.

He is said to be like a gazelle according to divinity.
