Those skilled in medicine assert that this animal possesses within its entrails a certain moisture which dispels dimness from the eyes and sharpens dullness of vision. He is therefore rightly compared to a gazelle, because he not only sees the Father himself but causes himself to be seen by those whose sight he himself created. He is compared to a young stag because, according to the flesh, he is the son of the ancient fathers, who are denoted by the name of stags. And he is truly like a young stag because he assumed human flesh. Hence it follows:

> Behold, he stands behind our wall, looking through the windows, gazing through the lattices.

Our wall is called our flesh, set between us and God, preventing us from comprehending God with clear sight; rather, we see as in a shadow [Note: [Col. 0067] MS Villar: “shadowily.”] and through a mirror and in an enigma (1 Cor. 13). For as long as we are placed in the prison-house of flesh, our flesh prevents the gaze of our mind from being directed to comprehend the sun of divinity. The Son of God stands beside this wall, not within the wall, because though he assumed the reality of flesh, he did not assume fleshly concupiscence; though he assumed nature, he did not assume guilt. Hence he is said to have been made not in sinful flesh but in the likeness of sinful flesh (Rom. 8).

Thus David, speaking of Christ as of a tree, says: “He shall be like a tree planted,” not *in* the watercourses but “beside the watercourses” (Ps. 1). For whereas waters signify human nature, Christ was not incarnate in the flow of human nature so as to incur guilt; but he was incarnate beside the course of human nature, because he assumed both the defect of punishment and the reality of nature: he had the sack, but not the sack’s defect. It is elegantly said that he stands, not lies down, [Col. 0069B] because we wretched people do not stand beside the wall but are within the wall and are crushed by it, since, remaining in flesh, we are overwhelmed by both punishment and guilt. But Christ, existing in flesh, truly stood within it, because no enticement of the flesh moved him from rectitude.

After the Passion, moreover, he looked through the windows and lattices. The windows are broader; the lattices narrower. By the windows is understood the manifest teaching which Christ offered to lesser disciples; by the lattices, the loftier and more obscure teaching offered to the greater. Hence Christ says to the apostles: “To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God” (Matt. 13). Thus Christ, through the Incarnation, stood behind our wall, looking through windows and lattices—that is, revealing greater and lesser things to the disciples and especially to the glorious Virgin.

Afterward he endured the Passion for humankind, a Passion with which the Virgin Mary especially shared in suffering. Then he consoled his mother through the Resurrection. Therefore the Virgin Mother is introduced as speaking of her Son in this manner:

> Behold, my beloved speaks to me.

Observe that Christ’s mother loved her Son above all things; she therefore calls him emphatically “my beloved,” saying: “My beloved speaks to me,” giving me consolation after the Resurrection in this manner:

> Arise, make haste, my beloved, my dove, my beautiful one, and come.

O my beloved through faith, my dove through simplicity, [Col. 0069D] my beautiful one through the beauty of virtues: arise from grief and come to me, where you will have consolation.

> For now winter has passed; the rain has gone away and withdrawn.

Winter has passed—that is, the freezing cold of unbelievers [Note: [Col. 0069] Both manuscripts read “of unbelief.”] has departed; the rain has gone away and withdrawn—that is, the flood of temptation has departed from the minds of the apostles.

> Flowers have appeared in our land.

That is, our flesh has flowered anew through the Resurrection and immortality.

> The time of pruning has come.

That is, the time of cutting away, because every superfluity of weaknesses [Col. 0070A] has been cut away from me, and all unbelief from the hearts of the apostles.

> The voice of the turtledove has been heard.

By the turtledove, which, as was said, grieves inconsolably when it has lost its mate, Mary Magdalene is signified. She grieved most deeply because she was bereaved of her spiritual husband, Christ. Her voice was heard in our land—that is, Judaea—when she announced the Resurrection:

> The fig tree has put forth its green figs; the flowering vines have given their fragrance.

The synagogue, called the fig tree, brought forth the apostles through faith, because, born from it, they became the sweetest food of teaching and by their example summoned the nations of other peoples to the flower of belief. “The flowering vines have given their fragrance”: that is, the faithful in [Col. 0070B] the primitive Church, flourishing in virtues after the Resurrection, gave forth the fragrance of good repute. Therefore:

> Arise, my beloved, my sister, and come, my dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the wall.

O my beloved through faith, my bride through love of God, and my dove through love of Christ. [Note: [Col. 0069] Both manuscripts have “of neighbour” in place of “of Christ.”] For this kind of bird is accustomed to fly in flocks, signifying love directed above. Arise from grief to joys, and come to me, now glorified. I mean you rejoicing and exulting in the clefts of the rock—that is, now joyful at Christ’s wounds, by which the rock, Christ, [Note: [Col. 0069] MS Villar: “Christ.”] was pierced. As though he said: You who formerly grieved at the bitterness of the Passion now joyfully [Col. 0070C] see that from it have proceeded the redemption of humankind and my glorification.

Thus “in the hollow of the wall” follows, with reference to the piercing of his side. A hollow is usually larger than a cleft; hence by the clefts are signified the piercings of Christ’s hands and feet, while by the hollow is signified the opening of his side. Christ is called a rock because of firmness; but a wall, because in respect of his spiritual body—that is, the Church—it is made up of many stones, namely believers.

> Show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears.

“Show me your face”: as the mother desired to see her Son, so the Son desired to look upon his mother, and not merely to gaze upon her but also to speak with her. Hence follows: “Let your voice sound in my ears.” Therefore I desire your voice:

> For your voice is sweet, and your face beautiful.

The voice of the humble, and especially of virgins, is usually kindly and sweet. Whose voice has greater sweetness, both in outward sound and inward meaning, than that of her who was humblest among all and especially marked with the seal of virginity? As though he said: I heard, at the time of my Passion, the voice of your lamentation; at the Resurrection I wish to hear the voice of your rejoicing. [Col. 0071A] Nor do I rejoice merely in hearing but also in seeing, because your face too is beautiful. We believe that the holy and glorious Virgin was beautiful in outward appearance, but especially adorned with the beauty of virtues.

Because many heresies arose against Christ and against his mother, which were destroyed through the Virgin herself, it is added:

> Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards.

By foxes, deceitful animals dwelling in holes in the ground, are understood heretics; by vineyards, churches. Heretics destroy these vineyards as far as they can. In disparaging Christ and his mother, they strive to destroy [Col. 0071B] the Church’s faith. These may therefore be the words of the faithful to Christ and the Virgin: “Catch for us”—that is, destroy for our benefit—the little foxes, that is, the heretics, “little” because of their weakness; for although they strive against the Church, they are nevertheless weakened. They destroy the vineyards—that is, they disparage ecclesiastical faith—

> For our vineyard has blossomed.

While it was still tender—that is, while the Church was new and, as it were, set in flower—they raged most fiercely against it, both through open persecution and through the cunning of perverse teaching. [Note: [Col. 0071] MS Villar: “through the cunning of perverse teaching.”] It should be noted that, whether “vineyards” is said in the plural or “vineyard” in the singular, the Church is one.

And, as though the Virgin had heard her Son’s voice, she says, as though speaking of him to others:

> My beloved is mine, and I am his.

[Col. 0071C] My beloved speaks to me, calling me to himself; and I am obedient to him.

> Who feeds among the lilies.

That is, he who delights in my virginity and humility. The lily, because of its whiteness, signifies virginity; and because it grows in valleys, humility.

**18. Until the day breathes forth.**

That is, until, when I have been assumed into heaven, the day of eternal blessedness dawns for me.

**And the shadows decline.**

That is, the weakness both of body and of soul perishes in me. And because the Virgin Mother, moved by excessive longing, yearned for her Son’s resurrection, she says:

**Return; be like, my beloved, a gazelle and a fawn of stags.**

O my beloved, who came to us through the flesh, return through the resurrection. And thus be like a gazelle in respect of the agility and subtlety which Christ’s human nature assumed in the resurrection; and like a fawn of stags in respect of the renewal of human nature. As though she said: Put off the oldness of punishment, and assume the newness of immortality and glory. Thus, by what is said, “Be like a fawn of stags,” the resurrection is signified. Hence also the Psalm which treats of the resurrection is entitled *For the morning dawn* [Note: [Col. 0071] Ms. Villar.: instead of “for the morning dawn,” it has “a hind.”] (Ps. XXI).

[Col. 0072A]

**Upon the mountains of Bethel.**

Be like this, I say, being upon the mountains of Bethel—that is, surpassing the other mountains in this, that you rose first and by your own authority. For you are “the firstborn from the dead, the firstfruits of those who sleep” (Col. I), or of those who rise again. The mountains are called holy because of their eminence in virtues; and Bethel is interpreted “house of God,” because God dwells in the saints through grace (I Cor. XV). Hence one reads that the throne of God is the soul of the righteous. But I say “Return” because I long for your return through the resurrection; therefore, from excessive affection, I sought you:

## CHAPTER III

**Upon my little bed through the nights I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him and did not find him.**

[Col. 0072B] This is manifest in Mary Magdalene, who frequently, “while it was still dark, went to the tomb” (John XX); and when she did not find Jesus’ body, she began to seek him in different places, and at last found him when she supposed Christ, appearing to her, to be the gardener, saying: “If you have taken him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away” (ibid.). And afterwards, recognizing that he was Christ, she said, “Rabboni,” as the Gospel narrative attests.

By analogy this might be understood of the glorious Virgin: that she frequently went to the tomb [Note: [Col. 0071] Ms. Villar.: instead of *fuerit* (“went/was”), it has *ierit* (“will have gone”)], that she sought him with great diligence, and that Christ appeared to her. But we do not have this as certain from the Gospel reading. Yet even if it was not so, perhaps she may nevertheless be introduced as speaking, to express [Col. 0072C] the excessive affection of the virginal mind.

The bed, moreover, is understood as the tomb in which the Lord’s body rested, which is said, by reason of its origin, to belong to the Virgin; for the body which rested in the tomb was that which Christ assumed from virginal flesh. Therefore by nights—that is, through the many tribulations which she had endured from the most bitter passion of her beloved Son, and especially during the three days of Christ’s death—she sought in desire him whom her soul loved, lest he should leave his mother, utterly bereft by his death, without any Paraclete at all—that is, Comforter. As though she said with the Prophet: “I looked for one to grieve with me, and there was none; and for one to comfort me, and I did not find one” (Ps. LXVIII).

Here, therefore, she first sought upon the little bed [Col. 0072D] and did not find him. A bed is that upon which bodies wearied by the day’s exertions customarily rest; by it is elegantly signified the repose of the mind, in which God must be sought. But because, in the condition of this life, such repose is slight and narrow, she is said to have sought her beloved not on a bed but on a little bed.

By the bed may also, not unreasonably, be signified that house situated on the height of Zion, in which Christ celebrated the Last Supper with his disciples, and to which, after Christ’s passion, the glorious Virgin is said to have withdrawn. There she sought, through frequent sighs and holy desires, him whom her soul loved; and there [Col. 0073A] she venerated those places, and with the reverent mouth of her heart kissed those places in which she could imagine that her beloved Son had reclined with the disciples, or had lain prostrate in washing their feet, or had sat somewhere. But what did she seek by such devout offices except her beloved? Yet she did not find him at all, because she received no consolation from them. Therefore she says:

**I will arise and go about the city through the lanes and streets; I will seek him whom my soul loves.**

It did not satisfy the burning desire of that glorious Virgin to seek her beloved on the little bed—that is, in that house in which she knew her Son had stayed and which he had consecrated by holy mysteries. Rather, rising, she also went out, in order to seek him through the lanes and streets of the city, [Col. 0073B] while she traversed in devout veneration even the holy places in which he had suffered.

For they say that the glorious Virgin herself, after her Son’s passion, diligently visited the places of his passion in devotion, so that until she was assumed to rest she might receive from them whatever consolation she could. But because they could not perfectly console her, it rightly adds:

**I sought him, and did not find him.**

For it is devoutly to be presumed that, just as the glorious Virgin enjoyed frequent visits from angels even before Christ’s conception, so after Christ’s passion these were granted her, by whom indeed she was consoled. Of them she seems to have said:

**The watchmen who guard the city found me.**

[Col. 0073C] By the watchmen guarding the city are elegantly signified the holy angels, who guard the Church and each one of the faithful.

For they keep watch and are solicitous concerning the elect: that they may draw them back from evil, stir them up toward good, and make each one concerned for his own salvation. As the Apostle says: “They are ministering spirits, sent for service on behalf of those who are to receive the inheritance of salvation” (Heb. I). And it is as though they came to console the Virgin, who was oppressed by sad grief and anguish at the absence of her beloved Son, and in that state was found by them. But she received no discourse concerning other matters; she wished for no consolation other than the presence of her Son, saying to them:

[Col. 0073D]

**Have you seen him whom my soul loves?**

As though she said: I do not seek you, but my Son; not creatures, but the Creator; not angels, but the Lord of angels. Have you seen him? Without doubt she knew that the holy angels enjoy the blessed vision of God and are not unaware of him through love and longing for him. Hence she judged it unfitting that they should see God, while leaving her deprived of the vision of him whom she so greatly desired.

**A little while after I passed them, I found him whom my soul loves.**

For the glorious Virgin was not assumed [Col. 0074A] immediately after Christ’s ascension; but for a little while—considering the brevity of the present life—she was left upon earth. Yet there she chose not to fix the steps of her desires upon the angelic vision, but always to tend toward him in whom alone her soul could rest. Thus it came about that at last she attained what she desired, and was assumed to the wished-for vision of her beloved. And this is what is said: “A little while after I passed them, I found him whom my soul loves.” It fittingly follows:

**20. I held him, and I will not let him go, until I bring him into my mother’s house, and into the chamber of her who bore me.**

I held him through his presence, and I shall not let him go without dwelling with him in his presence, until I bring him in—that is, until I see him brought into my mother’s house, that is, into the empyrean heaven, where the Church triumphant dwells, which is the mother of the Church militant. Hence, as though explaining, it is added: “and into the chamber of her who bore me,” that is, the empyrean heaven. It is called the chamber of the Church triumphant because there is the repose of our mind [Note: [Col. 0073] Ms. Villar. reads “mother’s.”].

Or, by “mother” and “she who bore me” is understood the Church drawn from Gentiles and Jews, from which the Virgin descended in the line of the flesh. Its house was already the empyrean heaven by hope, and will be so in the future by sight. Therefore Christ rose again, and after his resurrection ascended into heaven. But whether the Virgin Mother rose again and ascended bodily into heaven, or when she rose or ascended, is uncertain. Therefore Christ warns the daughters of Jerusalem, [Col. 0074C] that is, the Churches, never to make a definition concerning the resurrection of the glorious Virgin, nor concerning the time of that resurrection, which has not been distinguished [Note: [Col. 0073] Ms. has “defined.”] by patriarchs, prophets, and apostles. This is what follows.

**I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles and stags of the fields, do not arouse or awaken my beloved until she herself wishes.**

O daughters of Jerusalem, that is, Churches, I adjure you by the gazelles and stags of the fields—that is, in this imitating ancient and modern teachers—not to arouse or awaken my beloved; that is, do not firmly assert, as certain from authorities, that the Virgin has been raised or awakened from the sleep of death, until [Col. 0074D] she herself wishes. As though he said: This has been reserved to the will of the Virgin, which accords with the divine will: that she should wish it to be known that she has been raised. Hence, concerning when she wishes this to be revealed or not revealed, in her assumption the Holy Spirit, wondering in the person of the citizens above, says:

**Who is this who comes up through the wilderness like a slender column of smoke, from spices of myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer?**

She is aptly like a slender column of smoke, because she is slight and delicate; because she has been refined by divine disciplines and consumed inwardly as a holocaust by the fire of devout love and the longing of charity. “Like a slender column,” he says, “of smoke from spices,” [Col. 0075A] surely because she was filled with many fragrances of virtues: the sweetest fragrance flowing from her diffused its scent even among angelic spirits. But the rod, once sprung from the root of Jesse, ascended from the wilderness of the present age. Yet the souls of the elect lingered in joy, asking who she was who surpassed even the dignity of angels by the powers of her merits.

As the citizens above marvel at the Virgin assumed into heaven, so the faithful in the Church of God praise her together upon earth, saying:

**Behold, sixty mighty men surround Solomon’s little bed, from among the mightiest of Israel.**

Solomon is interpreted “peaceful,” and therefore signifies Christ, the true Peaceful One, who restored peace between Gentile and Jew, between man and God, and between man and angel. His little bed is the glorious Virgin, because Christ reclined in her when he assumed humanity. Sixty mighty men surrounded this little bed. By these mighty men is understood the totality of good works [Note: [Col. 0075] “Totality,” thus found in both manuscripts], which are strong against demons or vices.

For the number sixty contains six and ten. For six times ten, or ten times six, makes sixty. By six are understood the works of mercy found in the Gospel; by ten, the ten commandments of the Law. Therefore, by sixty [Note: [Col. 0075] Ms. Villar. has “the sixtieth number.”] are expressed the most perfect works, which by their exercise and intention protected on every side the little bed of Solomon—that is, the blessed Virgin. [Col. 0075C] These are represented by the mighty and chosen ones among the mightiest of Israel, because the Virgin Mary always possessed better and stronger works, which she appointed for her own protection. They are said to hold swords because of the defense and fortification by which they defend and protect the Virgin. Therefore it is said:

**All holding swords and most skilled in war, each man’s sword upon his thigh because of fears in the night.**

Each man’s sword was upon his thigh—that is, the defense of each good work was over bodily works or against pleasures—because the Virgin herself had so strengthened her heart with good works and thoughts that she utterly extinguished the flow of carnal pleasure, which is understood by the thigh. “Because of fears [Col. 0075D] in the night,” that is, in order to drive away temptations which ought to be feared and which customarily arise in the night of the present life.

And after the little bed of Solomon, which was so fortified:

**King Solomon made himself a litter of the wood of Lebanon.**

Literally, a *ferculum* is called a seat from sitting, because it bears one who sits. Hence even a judge’s throne may be called a *ferculum*. By this litter which Solomon made for himself is represented the human nature of the true Solomon—that is, of Christ the true Peaceful One. Christ fashioned this [Col. 0076A] in the virginal womb by taking flesh from the Virgin, forming it into a human body, and infusing into the body a created soul.

He made this human nature from the wood of Lebanon—that is, from the most pure substances, namely soul and body. For Christ’s soul was immune from every sin, and so was his flesh. Lebanon is a mountain of Phoenicia, whose trees excel in height, endurance, and beauty. Hence by the wood of Lebanon are understood the parts of Christ’s human nature, because [Note: [Col. 0075] Ms. Villar.: “which.”] they were taken from a more excellent kind [Note: [Col. 0075] Ms. inserts “of human nature.”], beautiful in purity and everlasting in endurance.

This human nature of Christ is elegantly called a litter, because through its mediation the Son of God was borne into the world; and, seated in it as upon his throne, [Note: [Col. 0075] Ms. Villar.: instead of “seated,” it has “appearing.”] he will judge the world. And of this litter:

[Col. 0076B]

**Its pillars he made of silver, its backrest of gold, its ascent of purple.**

These pillars signify the gifts of the Holy Spirit, upon which Christ’s soul rested as though upon certain pillars. Of these pillars one reads in the book of Wisdom: “Wisdom has built herself a house and hewn out in it seven pillars” (Prov. IX). These pillars were silver—that is, resplendent in God’s preaching and working. And he made its backrest golden—that is, the soul in which he reclined, full of graces and endowed with every wisdom. Its ascent was purple—that is, the passion which he endured in mounting the cross, and by whose merit one ascends into heaven, [Col. 0076C] which is signified by the ascent. It is called purple because Christ’s flesh was thereby made purple [Note: [Col. 0075] Ms. Villar. adds “with blood.”], for purple represents the color of blood. All these things

**22. He paved in the midst with charity, because of the daughters of Jerusalem.**

That is, he established them with charity placed in the midst, because charity is, as it were, the mediator and form of the other virtues. For, placed as it were in the midst of the virtues, it enlightens and forms the rest and relates equally to all. And this is because of the daughters of Jerusalem. Jerusalem is called the mind of Christ’s soul; for Jerusalem is interpreted “vision of peace,” and therefore that mind is elegantly called a vision of peace, because it experienced “the peace which surpasses all understanding” (Phil. IV). The virtues of this [Col. 0076D] Jerusalem are daughters, because they proceed from the mind.

The meaning, then, is: Charity is placed in the midst to enlighten and form the surrounding virtues of the soul, which proceed from the mind. Nor is Christ’s human nature called only a litter, but also a diadem, because, having won triumph over death in his human nature, Christ deserved to be crowned and to sit at the right hand of God the Father [Note: [Col. 0075] Ms. Villar. here inserts the following: “In this crowning, two things are removed: the infirmity of the mind and the punishment of the soul.”]. Thus it is as though the Virgin’s voice says to the young women:

**Go forth, daughters of Zion, and see King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him, on the day of his espousal and on the day of the gladness of his heart.**

[Col. 0077A] O daughters of Zion, who desire to behold God—for Zion is interpreted “contemplation”—go forth from carnal understanding into spiritual understanding, and see King Solomon—that is, understand Christ, the true Peaceful One—in the diadem, that is, in the human nature with which his mother, the Virgin Mary, crowned him. She crowned him, I say, because she did not give him back disfigured by the stain of original sin, as mothers give back their sons.

Rather, she crowned him—that is, she gloriously conceived without a man’s seed, and bore him clothed in noble flesh. See him, I say, on the day of his espousal—that is, in clear consideration of his incarnation, when he espoused the Virgin not only through the union of spirits, [Col. 0077B] but also of natures [Note: [Col. 0077] Ms. Villar.: “natural [things].”]. Therefore here the incarnation is called an espousal, because it was like a certain marriage and an inexpressible joy. Hence it follows: “and on the day of the gladness of his heart,” because this incarnation was the supreme exultation of the Virgin’s heart.

## CHAPTER IV

**How beautiful you are, my friend; how beautiful you are [and lovely]!**

The bridegroom answers the voice of the bride praising him, himself praising and saying: “How beautiful you are, my friend,” outwardly through the practice of action; “how beautiful and lovely you are,” inwardly through the subtlety of contemplation. This is what he means in commending her beauty by repetition:

[Col. 0077C]

**Your eyes are those of doves, apart from that which lies hidden within.**

The Virgin Mary has the eyes of doves because, raised by hope of heavenly things, she desires neither earthly nor perishable things. She sees all things simply and takes nothing belonging to anyone [Note: [Col. 0077] Ms. *trumuque*: “She sees all things simply, takes nothing belonging to anyone.”]. Though she is beautiful outwardly through simplicity and purity of deed, inwardly, where no one sees except God alone—for man sees the face, but God the heart (I Sam. XVI)—there she is far more beautiful. This is what he says: “apart from that which lies hidden within”: it is hidden indeed from human beings, but open to God. Hence it is said: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard,” etc. (I Cor. II). Christ continues his praise of the glorious Virgin as follows:

[Col. 0077D]

**23. Your hair is like a flock of goats that have come up from Mount Gilead [appeared from Gilead].**

Hair is fine, elevated, and adorns the head. Such are the Virgin’s thoughts: fine through contemplation, elevated through divine love, adorning the head—that is, the mind—and taking their origin from the mind as hair does from the head. The head elegantly signifies the mind, because just as the head excels and presides over all the members, so the mind presides over all thoughts.

The meaning, then, is: Your hair—that is, your thoughts—is like a flock [Col. 0078A] of goats that have come up from Mount Gilead. They are comparable to movements of contemplation, because such thoughts belong to contemplation. The modes of contemplation are elegantly signified by gazelles. For just as gazelles, which feed in the mountains, gaze keenly, so such movements delight in heavenly things and contemplate the heavens.

Nor is the following without reason: “which have come up from Mount Gilead.” For they do not descend to lower things but ascend to higher ones; and they do this from the lofty abundance of the testimony of sacred Scripture’s authority. For Gilead is interpreted “heap of testimony.” Many authorities bear witness to such movements of contemplation [Note: [Col. 0077] Ms. Villar.: instead of “movements of contemplation,” it has “such understandings.”].

**Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep that have come up [Col. 0078B] from the washing.**

By teeth are signified the exercises which the Virgin had in sacred Scripture. By them sacred Scripture itself is in some fashion ground up and thereby made edible—that is, intelligible—and thus passed into the stomach of the mind. These teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep. By shorn sheep are understood interpretations of sacred Scripture, removed from carnal interpretation. For just as shorn sheep lay aside the excess of their fleece, so spiritual interpretations put off the excess of carnal understanding.

Thus the teeth are comparable to flocks of shorn sheep because exercises in sacred Scripture belong to those understandings which are simple rather than perverse, and stripped of the excess of carnal understanding. [Col. 0078C] Fittingly, moreover, it adds: “which have come up from the washing.” By the washing is understood the cleansing of the mind from love and thought of earthly things, from which proceed pure and wholly spiritual interpretations of the Scriptures. Or baptism is understood by the washing, in which those who are baptized are granted the power to understand spiritual things.

**All bearing twin offspring, and none among them is barren.**

For from such interpretations proceed two modes of understanding, which are like two offspring of spiritual intelligence—namely, the allegorical and the moral. And none among them is barren, because no such understanding is fruitless.

**Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon.**

By the lips, which are instruments of speech, is signified [Col. 0078D] the Virgin’s outward speech or instruction, which was like a scarlet ribbon. For just as a scarlet ribbon outwardly displays a red color and binds the hair round about, so the Virgin’s words recalled and proclaimed Christ’s passion, in order that her hearers might bind and restrain their thoughts by the discipline of the fear of the Lord. Hence follows:

**Your speech is sweet.**

Because even in words she showed how greatly God loved human beings, and what heavenly rewards God promised to his own.

[Col. 0079A]

**24. Your cheeks are like a fragment of pomegranate.**

The pomegranate has a reddish skin and within is full of a multitude of seeds; it is rightly called both a seeded apple and a Punic apple. By the cheeks, which appear more than the other members, is signified the representation of the Lord’s passion, which she bore in her body through mortification of the flesh. Hence she is compared to the pomegranate. In the mortification of the flesh, therefore, a redness appears outwardly, in respect of remembrance of the passion.

But when she considered how great a benefit for our redemption proceeded from it, and how through Christ’s passion man is not only justified from sins [Note: [Col. 0079] Ms. Villar.: “is justified”], but also has merited fellowship with the divine, then that which lay hidden within was, as it were, white. This is what follows:

[Col. 0079B]

**Apart from that which lies hidden within.**

Because many spiritual things were in the Virgin which lay hidden from people but were open to God. It follows:

**Your neck is like the tower of David, built with battlements.**

By the neck, which we customarily bow down when something is borne by us, and through which the head is joined to the members, is signified the Virgin’s humility, which is transmitted to others by example [Note: [Col. 0079] Ms.: “is transmitted”]; for she was especially united to Christ. This was like the tower of David—that is, like Christ’s humility, which is signified by David [Note: [Col. 0079] “Figured.”]. For the humility which Christ bore in the flesh was strength, fortification, and refuge for others. It was built with battlements. The battlements of this tower [Col. 0079C] are obedience, patience, and abstinence, which fortify humility itself [Note: [Col. 0079] Ibid.: “which are fortified through that humility itself.”].

**A thousand shields hang from it, all the armor of the mighty.**

They are innumerable defenses by which the Virgin’s humility is encircled and defended: that is, all the armor of the mighty—namely, of the patient, who are strong against the assaults of tribulations.

**Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a gazelle, feeding among lilies, until the day breathes forth and the shadows decline.**

As was said above, the two breasts of Mary the Virgin are understood as the two streams of charity by which she loved Christ [Note: [Col. 0079] Ms. adds: “and as streams in comparison with Christ’s charity”]: one by which she loved him as [Col. 0079D] God, the other by which she loved him as man. They are called fawns of a gazelle—that is, offspring of Christ, signified by the gazelle—which were both implanted in Christ and proceeded from Christ.

Christ is understood by the gazelle because of the swiftness of his ascension and the course of mortal life which he overcame by swift running. These are called twins because these two movements arise together from the one fountain of charity. They feed among lilies—that is, they are formed by chastity of mind and body—until the day breathes forth, that [Col. 0080A] is, until Christ comes or rises, who is the true Day and Sun of righteousness; and until the shadows decline, that is, until the clouds of sorrow pass away [Note: [Col. 0079] Ms. adds: “or the shadows of this age.”].

The adverb “until” is not used here exclusively, as though these movements of charity were to endure in the Virgin only until the day of judgment and no longer; rather, it is used inclusively, so that the sense is: “until the day breathes forth,” etc.—that is, forever—according to the saying: “Until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet” (Ps. CIX). And because the Virgin Mary is such and so great, Christ says:

**25. I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense.**

I will go, through assumption of flesh and inward inspiration, to the mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense—that is, to the glorious Virgin, who is a mountain because of the height of her virtues, and of myrrh because of [Col. 0080B] mortification of the flesh. She is also compared to a hill of frankincense because she offered to God the sweet fragrance of prayers, and through the pursuit of holy meditations rendered herself an offering pleasing to God. And as though Christ, coming to the Virgin, were speaking, it follows:

**You are wholly beautiful, my friend, and there is no stain in you.**

You are wholly beautiful—that is, in body and soul—my friend through grace and works; and there is no venial [Note: [Col. 0079] Ms.: “or.”] or mortal stain in you. For we believe that in the Virgin there was no sin before or after the conception. And because you are wholly beautiful and no stain is in you, you are now worthy of royal embraces.

**Come from Lebanon, my bride; come from Lebanon, come.**

[Col. 0080C] Come from Lebanon, my bride; come from Lebanon—that is, from the whitening and purification of virtues. Notice that Christ calls her three times, signifying that God called the Virgin through faith, hope, and charity, and calls her in the faith of the Trinity. And, rejoicing with me [Note: [Col. 0079] Ms. Villar.: “rejoicing with himself.”] in the homeland, many established in the Church will crown and praise you in blessedness. Concerning their remarkable grace and glory it follows:

**You shall be crowned from the summit of Amana, from the peak of Sanir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards.**

Amana is a mountain of Cilicia, also called Taurus, and is interpreted “God of watchmen.” But “God of watchmen” expresses the devil, who “goes about seeking whom he may devour” (I Pet. V). Sanir and Hermon are mountains [Col. 0080D] of Judea, in which lions and leopards are said to dwell. Sanir is interpreted “night bird.” By Sanir are denoted the nocturnal snares of demons. [Note: [Col. 0079] The same manuscript here inserts: “Hermon is interpreted ‘anathema.’”]

By these mountains, however, are understood the powerful of this world, namely kings and princes, because they are raised up in pride like a mountain. They provide dens within themselves to evil spirits, as to lions and leopards. Evil spirits are called lions because of pride, leopards because of ferocity, or also because of their thousand arts of harming, since the leopard is a variegated animal.

Therefore from these [Col. 0081A] mountains the glorious Virgin is crowned when the princes of the world are converted to faith, received into eternal blessedness, and added to the Virgin’s fellowship and praise. She is crowned from the summit of these mountains when, their rulers having been subjected to the Catholic faith, she is honored and glorified by them in Christ. And because she is distinguished by the gifts mentioned above, it adds:

**You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride.**

He speaks in the manner of lovers: my sister through grace, my bride through love.

**You have wounded my heart with one of your eyes.**

Repetition is confirmation. “With one of your eyes,” as though he said: Although you are wholly beautiful, O Virgin, and although I love you for many things, yet especially [Col. 0081B] the brightness and purity of the contemplative life which is in you delights me. By the two eyes of the Virgin Mary are signified the two lives, contemplative and active. The former is happier, the latter more fruitful; the former freer, the latter involved; the former simple, the latter manifold; the former one, the latter many-formed.

Confirming this [Note: [Col. 0081] Ms. Villar.: “indicating this.”], Christ says in the Gospel: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things; but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke X).

**And with one lock of your neck.**

As was said above, by the neck is understood humility or obedience, and by the lock a thought. Thus this signifies that thoughts which proceed from humility [Col. 0081C] toward obedience are pleasing to God. Nor is it surprising that you have wounded my heart, because:

**How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my bride!**

They judge that *mammae* (“breasts”) concern the blessing of fruitfulness, but *ubera* (“breasts”) the glory of virginity. For in mothers they are called *mammae*, in virgins *ubera*. Therefore *mammae* in the Virgin denote fruitfulness; *ubera*, the blessedness of both forms of virginity, namely of body and mind. Hence it is said:

**Your breasts are more beautiful than wine,**

That is, than every carnal pleasure.

**And the fragrance of your ointments above all spices.**

That is, the good reputation of your virtues above all vain [Col. 0081D] glory.

**Your lips, O bride, are a dripping honeycomb.** [Note: [Col. 0081] The same manuscript immediately adds here: “A honeycomb is honey in wax; therefore by the honeycomb is represented divinity hidden in human nature. Thus the Virgin’s lips were a dripping honeycomb, because in her mouth, etc.”]

Because in her mouth, heart, and flesh she had Christ hidden in his humanity: in her mouth, because she preached nothing else; in her heart, because she loved nothing else; in her flesh, because she conceived nothing else.

**Honey and milk are under your tongue.**

Christ still speaks to the Virgin. Honey and milk are God and man: honey, divinity; milk, humanity. Honey comes from the dew of heaven, because the divine nature is above all things; milk [Col. 0082A] is pressed out below, because human nature was assumed below.

What are honey and milk under your tongue? They are the Word of the Father and man [Note: [Col. 0081] Ms.: “God and man.”] beneath your flesh. “Under the tongue,” because the Word is hidden under the tongue and not upon the tongue. Therefore it is milk, not flesh, beneath your tongue—and yet flesh from flesh: from native flesh [Note: [Col. 0081] Instead of *patria* (“native/fatherland”), the reading is *pura* (“pure”).], a second flesh; from old flesh, new flesh; from flesh needing purification, sacrificial flesh. Therefore honey and milk are under your tongue, because in your flesh are God and man, and beneath your flesh are God and man.

**And the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of frankincense.**

That is, the reputation of the spiritual goods with which you are clothed [Col. 0082B] and adorned, as a body with garments, is as sweet and pleasant as the scent of frankincense is to the body.

**A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain.**

A garden of delights in which neither the roses of patience nor the lilies of virginity are lacking; in which is the rose of the Lord’s body and blood, in which the lily of chastity. “Enclosed,” because shut on both sides by the pursuit of good intention and the consideration of reason. My sister, my bride, is a garden enclosed because she is sealed by the valley of charity, lest the evil one break in. Enclosed, because surrounded by the guardianship of angels. My sister through love, my bride through the union of natures.

“A garden enclosed” is repeated here in order that the Virgin’s perfection [Col. 0082C] in action and contemplation may be noted. Or it is appropriate to the garden in the twofold kind of virginity that it should be level, enclosed, planted, arranged, straight [Note: [Col. 0081] Ms.: “restored/refreshed.”], and fertile: level, that it may be watered; enclosed, that it may be preserved; planted, that it may bear fruit; arranged, that it may delight; straight, that it may receive air; fertile, that it may provide abundance.

And you, O Virgin Mother of God, were a fertile garden through the abundance of fullness [Note: [Col. 0081] Here the following is missing: “a level garden through the affection of mercy, enclosed by heavenly thought, planted by the exercise of good works, arranged by the variety of virtues, refreshed by confession of divine praise.”], a fountain in which is the stream of ineffable mercy, in which is the irrigation of every grace; a fountain which receives within the bosom of its compassion the outpouring of our tears. Sealed by the seal of faith, the seal of Gospel truth, and the bolt of virginity, so that neither heretics nor demons can weaken in you faith or the truth of the Gospel.

**Your offshoots are a paradise of pomegranates with the fruits [Col. 0082D] of orchard trees.**

Your offshoots—that is, the works proceeding from you—are a paradise, that is, delightful, because they produce delights in the minds of the faithful. For “paradise” in Greek is called *eden* in Hebrew, which in Latin is interpreted “garden of delights.” And not merely a paradise, but one of pomegranates. The pomegranate is red outwardly and contains a multitude of seeds within one rind; so in the Virgin a multitude of good works is held enclosed [Col. 0083A] within faith in the Lord’s passion.

“With the fruits of orchard trees.” By the fruits of orchard trees are signified the honorable and chaste utterances of the Virgin, from which there proceeded into the minds of the faithful the fruit of instruction. Hence follows:

**Henna with nard; nard and crocus; cassia and cinnamon, with every tree of Lebanon; myrrh and aloe, with all the finest ointments.**
That is, diverse kinds of virtues are fragrant in you, as these aromatic kinds signify. Cyprus is an aromatic tree, having seed like coriander, as is said of manna; and it signifies the heavenly life, that is, virginity. Nard is a precious ointment, and signifies true charity, which surpasses the other virtues. Saffron is golden in colour [Col. 0083B] and signifies divine wisdom. The fistula is a small shrub, called cassia, and signifies humility and patience. Cinnamon is a very sweet bark and signifies the sweetness of inward contemplation. “With all the trees of Lebanon,” that is, with all the other virtues that possess some strength and spiritually make the mind white. Myrrh signifies the mortification of the flesh because of its bitterness. Aloe, which has a wonderful fragrance, signifies good repute. “With all the chief ointments,” as though he said: These virtues are in the Virgin together with the other gifts of the Holy Spirit. Having enumerated the trees and aromatics that are in the paradise of the virginal mind, he shows by what fountain such cultivation is watered, so that it may grow with everlasting greenness and not wither.

[Col. 0083C] “A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, which flow with force from Lebanon.”

As though he said: Rightly, O Virgin, are you adorned with such beauty of trees and aromatics, because in you is a fountain springing up into eternal life. That fountain is a well, that is, inexhaustible and deep because of the depth of knowledge. Yet living waters do not flow from you, but from Lebanon, that is, Christ, who is made bright by the beauty of every virtue and says: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink; and living waters shall flow from his belly.” Hence the Apostle: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase” (1 Cor. 3).

28. “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden, and its aromatics shall flow.”

[Col. 0083D] The north wind is the coldest wind, and the south wind warm; therefore, by the north wind terrors and threats are denoted, or the devil himself. By the south wind the Holy Spirit is signified. This is what the bridegroom says: Because I have planted my garden on earth [Note: [Col. 0083] The Villar manuscript has “now” in place of “on earth.”] and sown it with many trees [Note: [Col. 0083] Manuscript: “with trees and aromatics.”], O north wind—that is, O demon, who makes cold everything you can blow upon—arise, that is, depart far from my garden. Or: “Arise,” that is, rise up and attack Mary as much as you can; for the more she is attacked, the more she increases and grows. And you, south wind—that is, Holy Spirit, who blow warmly and make things germinate—come and overshadow the Virgin with the protection of virtues. “Blow through my garden,” [Col. 0084A] that is, the same Virgin, who is called a garden for the reasons already given. And it is “my” garden because by your breath—which is both mine, and not by her own power—she will bring forth good works. Hence follows: “and its aromatics shall flow,” that is, good works which give forth a sweet fragrance. Hearing the bridegroom say that the south wind should come and blow through his garden, the bride, as though saying, “The south wind has already come and blown through the garden; its aromatics flow; therefore I desire that,” says:

## CHAPTER V

“Let my beloved come into his garden and eat the fruit of his apple trees.”

Let him come, that is, visit; and eat, that is, gladly receive the fruit of his trees, that is, my fruitful works. The bridegroom, knowing that the bride [Col. 0084B] longs for his coming, says to console her:

“Come into my garden, my sister, my bride.”

O my sister, my bride: formerly I came into you, who are my garden; now come to me, who am your garden. Come to me by ascension, as I came to you by assumption of flesh. Come, I say, into the garden, that is, into the heavenly paradise, which is the garden of delights, which is eternal life.

“I have gathered my myrrh with my aromatics.”

That is, I have cut away every bitterness of suffering together with the works of the active life.

For Christ, having become immortal, cut off from himself the works of the active life, being intent upon the contemplative life.

“I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey.”

[Col. 0084C] That is, by the resurrection I reunited to the body the soul that had been separated from the flesh through death. This is elegantly represented by the honeycomb: for as the honeycomb is honey hidden in wax, so Christ’s soul lay hidden in the cell of flesh. And this was with honey, because I also gave life to the body; and the enlivening of that body, the reunion of the soul with it, and the glorification of both, were for you the highest sweetness.

“I have drunk my wine with my milk.”

That is, I overcame the hardships of the passions together with the need for bodily food. By milk, which is the food of children and which little ones need, is signified the need for bodily food, which in Christ was swallowed up through the resurrection, like every other weakness. All this was figured by the fact that Christ, risen [Col. 0084D] from the dead, ate broiled fish and a honeycomb, and drank wine (Luke 24).

29. “Eat, friends, and drink; be intoxicated, beloved ones.”

By comparison: you, my friends, delighting in the garden of eternal blessedness, eat the bread that came down from heaven (John 6), not in the sacrament but in reality. And drink the living water that waters the heavenly paradise. And be intoxicated with heavenly joy, beloved ones, through true love; so that, intoxicated with the abundance of God’s house and given drink from the torrent of delight, you may say: “How glorious is your intoxicating cup” (Ps. 22). Since above mention was made of Christ’s ascension, the author consequently returns, in prophetic fashion, to the assumption of flesh. For it is the custom of prophets, when they speak at one moment of present and future things, immediately to return to the past, as the Holy Spirit touched their hearts. Therefore the Virgin is introduced speaking according to her state before the Incarnation, in which, occupied with contemplation, she had put off every worldly care. Thus she says:

“I sleep, and my heart keeps watch.”

I sleep as regards worldly care, and my heart keeps watch in contemplation. But while I was occupied with contemplation:

“The voice of my beloved knocking”—

that is, heard by me through an angel announcing to me his coming by the Incarnation—in this [Col. 0085B] manner:

“Open to me, my sister, my friend, my dove, my undefiled one.”

Open to me through humility and obedience, so that I may come into you by the Incarnation. For through humility and obedience the Virgin made herself fit for God’s wisdom to be incarnated in her. Open, I say, my bride and future friend, through companionship in the flesh; my friend, through present love; my dove, through simplicity; my undefiled one, through virginity. Isaiah says of this opening: “Let the earth be opened and bring forth the Saviour” (Isa. 45). What, then, is the meaning of the Lord’s testimony to Ezekiel: “This gate shall be shut and shall not be opened” (Ezek. 44)? It was indeed opened to the Lord, but not to a man, as it is there said to Ezekiel himself: “No man shall pass through it, because the Lord God of Israel has entered through it” (ibid.). Yet it shall be opened to the Lord—not the virginal integrity of the body, since, as Ezekiel added after the foregoing: “It shall be shut even to the prince himself” (ibid.)—but the gate of the ear and the gate of the heart shall be opened. For the Word, about to be incarnate, entered through the Virgin’s ear, and, incarnate, came forth through the closed gate of the body. I desire to come to you by the Incarnation in order that, according to my humanity, I may receive from the Father the fullness of graces, and that from my fullness an abundance of grace may distil. Hence follows:

“For my head is full of dew, and my locks with drops of the night.”

[Col. 0085D] Christ’s head is God, who is said to be full of dew because every heavenly grace flows from him into Christ and from Christ into the Virgin. Hence follows: “and my locks,” that is, your thoughts, which I call mine because they are from me and tend toward me, “are full of drops of the night,” that is, they are filled with obscure and profound wisdom. They are called locks because they do not flow down loose and unbound, but are gathered by the bond of fear and love of God. In reply to this, the Virgin says:

“I have put off my tunic; how shall I put it on?”

This is what is read in the Gospel: “How shall this be, since I do not know a man?” (Luke 1), [Col. 0086A] that is, since I have a purpose of not knowing one? As though she said: I have cast away every concern for conception and childbirth, having surrendered myself to the divine will; how shall I take up concern for conception and childbirth? I have put off worldly care; 30. how shall I resume it?

“I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?”

I have washed my feet, that is, I have purified my affections from every worldly care and desire. How shall I defile them, so far as concerns the opinion of those who thought that I had conceived from desire? But now I understand the manner of conceiving.

“My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my belly trembled at his touch.”

My beloved put his hand—that is, he showed me the work of his mercy—through the opening, that is, [Col. 0086B] through a hidden inspiration: how I should conceive by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit alone. “And my belly trembled at his touch,” that is, my memory rejoiced at such a revelation.

“I rose to open to my beloved.”

That is, I immediately obeyed, saying: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke 1), so that I might open to my beloved by humility and obedience. And then the Holy Spirit came upon me, and the power of the Most High overshadowed me (ibid.). Through this:

“My hands dripped with myrrh”—

that is, my works accomplished the mortification of vices. And this is what follows:

[Col. 0086C] “My fingers are full of the finest myrrh.”

That is, my particular works were performed together with a mortification of the flesh approved by God. And thus:

“I opened the bolt of my door to my beloved.”

The door is called faith or obedience, through which Christ enters a human being by means of grace. Therefore I opened the bolt of my door to Christ when I both obeyed and believed [Note: [Col. 0085] Here the Villar manuscript adds: “and thus I removed from my mind every doubt, which is understood by the bolt.”].

“But he had turned aside and passed on.”

But he delayed entering, though he had already inclined himself. Christ inclined himself when, by the Incarnation, he “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2). And he passed on, coming from the Father’s bosom into the Virgin’s womb. In this passage he so assumed what he was not that he did not abandon what he was. [Col. 0086D] And thus:

“My soul melted when [my beloved] spoke.”

That is, the Son of God, spiritually giving me life and quickening me, melted, that is, was emptied through the weakness of the flesh. Because of the union of will and spirit, he is also called the Virgin’s soul, according to which the following might also be read: “A sword shall pass through your own soul” (Luke 2), that is, he who is your soul by love shall be passed through by a sword. Or, “My soul melted,” that is, it was warmed by divine fire; and what had previously been less able [Col. 0087A] and somewhat hard to grasp the manner of the Incarnation was melted, that is, softened and made capable of understanding, when the beloved spoke to me through the angel; or after Christ the Word united himself to my flesh, that is, to that flesh which he assumed from me.

31. “I sought him and did not find him; I called him and he did not answer me.”

And although my soul has melted so as to understand, nevertheless I sought in the Scriptures, that is, I inquired more fully into the manner of the Incarnation. And I did not find him completely. I called upon him by inward devotion that he might reveal it, and he did not answer me fully.

“The watchmen who guard the city found me.”

[Col. 0087B] That is, the prophets and other ancient Fathers, who diligently guarded the Church through sacred teaching and diligently provided for it.

“They struck me and wounded me.”

They struck me with divine love and wounded me with the sword of God’s word in their Scriptures.

“The watchmen of the walls took my cloak away from me.”

That is, the patriarchs and prophets took from me the veil of ignorance. And because the Virgin studied the sacred Scriptures with the utmost attention, that she might have knowledge of Christ, it follows:

“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem: if you find my beloved, tell him that I am sick with love.”

As though she said: O holy Fathers, I earnestly require [Col. 0087C] this of you—that is, of your Scriptures—that I may understand those things you have said about Christ, because I am sick with love for him. Thus the Virgin sought knowledge of Christ from the holy Fathers, that is, from their Scriptures; but because more things about Christ were revealed to her than to the Fathers, it is therefore said that the Virgin taught certain evangelists more about Christ. It follows:

“What is your beloved, more than a beloved, O fairest of women?”

As though the holy Fathers said: You seek from us knowledge of Christ; but rather we ought to inquire of you, who are his special keeper of secrets, mother, and daughter. This is the meaning of “O fairest of women.” Who is fairest except she who is “blessed among women”? (Luke 1).

[Col. 0087D] Indeed, above all women she is full of grace: an untouched Mother, full of God; Mother and Virgin. “What is your beloved”—that is, your Son, whom you love with a special love, born from you according to the flesh—“more than a beloved,” that is, God the Father according to divinity? And to indicate more strongly that the Virgin possesses fuller knowledge or understanding of Christ than they do, the question is repeated with the addition:

“What is your beloved, more than a beloved, that you have thus adjured us?”

And note that above the Virgin is called the fairest [Col. 0088A] of women, but here she is simply called [Note: [Col. 0087] The manuscript adds: “fairest.”] this, in order to signify that she was not only beautiful above women, but also above the choirs of angels. And because the Virgin is believed to have taught many concerning her Son’s Incarnation, the Virgin’s reply follows:

“My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen from among thousands.”

White, that is, virginal and without sin: “he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2). And ruddy, that is, sprinkled with blood, because “he washed us from our sins in his blood” (Rev. 1). “Chosen from among thousands,” because he alone from the multitude of believers was worthy to hear: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. 3). 32. For the man Christ shone with singular grace in the mass of the human race, [Col. 0088B] because God proposed [Note: [Col. 0087] The manuscript adds: “through him.”] to save the human race; and he is “the mediator of God and human beings” (1 Tim. 2), of whom David says: “There is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. 13).

“His head is the finest gold.”

The bridegroom’s head is God, who is compared to the finest gold because, just as gold is more precious than all metals, so God surpasses all goods made by him. Hence the Lord says: “No one is good except God alone” (Luke 18). Therefore the bridegroom’s head is the finest gold, because God’s goodness is ineffable, surpassing the goodness of all things, since nothing is good except by participation in this good.

[Col. 0088C] “His hair is like the lofty branches of palm trees, black as a raven.”

The lofty branches of palms are the longer branches, sometimes curling with a rosy colour; they always tend upward and never lose their greenness. Thus the Virgin Mary says that her bridegroom’s hair is such: curling and ruddy. His hair, then—that is, those who cling to him—is compared to the lofty branches of palm trees, because the multitudes of believers rejoice in the greenness of faith, are raised toward the desire for eternal joys, and taste the sweetness of heavenly delight. They are also signified as ever victorious by the palm, because they are strong in adversity. The more righteous they are, the more they see themselves as sinners and contemptible in their own eyes. Hence follows: “black [Col. 0088D] as a raven,” because the multitudes of believers remember their own frailty [Note: [Col. 0087] In the Tournai manuscript the following is inserted: “Because the saints, who through penitence and remembrance of death foretell dangers, hasten as though toward corpses, awaiting their reward at hand. Hence: ‘Tomorrow my righteousness shall answer for me,’ because, etc.”]; and know that they possess no good from themselves.

“His eyes are like doves beside streams of water, washed with milk, and sitting beside very full channels.”

The doctors of the Church are the eyes of the Holy Spirit, who, set in a higher rank, watch over the Church lest anything of heretical perversity insinuate itself, and enlighten it. They are compared to doves because of simplicity and innocence. These doves sit beside streams of water [Col. 0089A] in order [Note: [Col. 0089] The Villar manuscript inserts: “Because holy teachers linger over the streams of the divine Scriptures. Doves sit beside streams of water in order”] to guard themselves against the hawk, because holy teachers, drenched with the water of doctrine, are secure from the evil one. They sit beside the streams of the Old Testament, from which flow rivulets—that is, expositions and interpretations—and also beside the very full channels, that is, beside the abundant teaching of the holy Gospel, in which hearers are more fully instructed than in the Old Testament.

“His cheeks are like beds of aromatics, planted by perfumers.”

The bridegroom’s cheeks are those who are ashamed of their own sins and those of others. And because through them food is ground for others, and they pass on to their hearers what they could chew and ruminate from the holy Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0089] Manuscript: “could.”]. These cheeks are compared to beds, because just as beds of aromatics, most [Col. 0089B] well arranged and ordered, delight those who look upon them and offer them their fragrance through the abundance of aromatic herbs, so those who are the bridegroom’s cheeks give fragrance to God through a multitude of good works, whether they are preachers or hearers. He used the diminutive “little beds” because of humility. “Planted,” that is, well established and set in place by perfumers, that is, by their planters. These perfumers—that is, planters—are the apostles and prophets, of whom the latter described all these things as future, the former as already accomplished.

33. “His lips are lilies, dripping the finest myrrh.”

That is, those who disclose his secrets are lilies, that is, sweetly fragrant. Lilies, I say, dripping [Col. 0089C] the finest myrrh—that is, their own mortification, not for appearance’s sake and not feigned. In this passage virgins in the Church are denoted, for to none were heavenly secrets disclosed more than to the holy Virgin.

“His hands are rounded gold, full of hyacinths.”

He has the foregoing members of such a kind. But his hands are those who have little strength in preaching but are strong in action and in the generous distribution of alms. Such persons are “rounded,” that is, turned and cleansed of vices, so that nothing superfluous remains in them.

His hands, I say, are golden, that is, filled with divine wisdom. A person is wise, even if lacking knowledge of letters, who labours and works so as to give to one suffering need (Eph. 4). Therefore the bridegroom’s hands in [Col. 0089D] the holy Church are good workers. “Full of hyacinths”: hyacinth is a stone of sky-blue colour. What, then, is understood by hyacinths except heavenly hope and desire? Therefore the bridegroom’s hands are full of hyacinths, because good workers direct their works toward heaven, hoping from them for nothing except heavenly things.

“His belly is ivory, set with sapphires.”

Among the members of the human body nothing is more fragile, nothing more tender, than the belly; therefore by the belly are understood the more fragile and less powerful persons in the holy Church, such as peasants and unlearned people. Yet they are [Col. 0090A] ivory, that is, cool and chaste. Ivory is the bone of the elephant, an animal said to be most chaste and of a cold nature. Thus, in the holy Church, the simpler and less learned are usually more chaste and continent. His belly, I say, is set with sapphires. Sapphire is a stone [Note: [Col. 0089] Manuscript: “of an ethereal colour.”] of saffron colour and signifies blessed hope, because those who are the bridegroom’s belly perform the good things they do for ethereal hope.

Nor is that belly said to be full, but “set with sapphires,” so that the whiteness of ivory appears between the sapphires; because they seek heavenly things in such a way that they do not abandon earthly things, since through these earthly things they come to those heavenly things.

“His legs are marble columns, founded upon bases of gold.”

[Col. 0090B] The bridegroom’s legs are the bearers of his name, such as holy preachers, who bear Christ through the world and proclaim him before kings, princes, and others who are strong and upright, because they resist the vices and desires of this life. They are founded upon golden bases, that is, the sayings of prophets and apostles, which are called firm bases because they cannot be overthrown by any art, any disputation of human wisdom, or any height [Note: [Col. 0089] Manuscript: “can be overthrown.”]. And they are golden because they shine with divine wisdom and doctrine. Nothing in worldly things is more precious than gold; nothing is better and dearer than divine wisdom, which is fitting and harmonious in every respect.

“His appearance is like Lebanon, chosen as the cedars.”

[Col. 0090C] Lebanon is a mountain of wonderful beauty in the adornment and loveliness of its trees and groves. So too my beloved, with all his members, is beautiful and radiant in every adornment and harmony [Note: [Col. 0089] Villar manuscript: “harmony of body.”].

34. “His throat is most sweet, and he is altogether desirable.”

Thus far the bride has discoursed on the beauty and harmony of the bridegroom’s body; now she has added a few words about his divinity. For through the throat we taste every food, whether sweet or bitter; so the subtlety of divine understanding searches and examines all the inward things of the heart. Therefore the bridegroom’s divinity is rightly understood through his throat, which is called most sweet because divine sweetness surpasses every sweetness. [Col. 0090D] Hence follows: “and he is altogether desirable,” because he exceeds every desire; the angels long to look into him (1 Pet. 1).

“Such is my beloved, and he is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem.”

Behold, I have described for you the one of whom you asked what he was like; and therefore, because he is such, he is my friend in true love. And because the holy Fathers have been instructed about Christ by the Virgin, they still speak to her in the following manner in their search for Christ himself:

[Col. 0091A] “Where has your beloved gone, O fairest of women? Where has your beloved turned aside, that we may seek him with you?”

Why Christ is called the Virgin’s beloved in a special sense, and why she herself is the fairest of women, has been explained above. But note that it is said, “has gone.” To go away is to go farther off. Therefore he goes away when he seems to come very slowly to those who seek him. He turns aside when he returns more quickly to those who seek him. But he goes away and turns aside for a time, in order to kindle a greater desire to seek him. It is well said, “We shall seek him with you,” because anyone who seeks Christ without faith in the glorious Virgin can err and cannot make progress. The Virgin answers this, saying:

## CHAPTER VI

[Col. 0091B]

“My beloved has gone down into his garden, to the bed of aromatics, to feed in the gardens and gather lilies.”

Christ’s garden is called human nature, into which Christ especially went when he united it to himself; and he turned aside into it when, humbling himself, he emptied himself (Phil. 2). For Christ’s human nature possessed full and perfect knowledge of God. Christ prepared and cultivated it as his garden, sowed it with the shoots of virtues, and, by the merit [Note: [Col. 0091] Manuscript: “of the wall.”] of his protection, defended it from the attacks of evil spirits. And he is fittingly said to have gone down into his garden, for he wished to be buried in a garden, and [Col. 0091C] first appeared to Mary Magdalene in a garden (John 19 and 20). He is said to have gone down because he came from the heights into the garden which he had planted in a low place. “To the bed of aromatics”: Christ’s soul is understood as the bed, cultivated by heavenly discipline and carefully ordered, “to feed in the gardens,” that is, to delight in the pursuits of the saints, “and gather lilies,” that is, to receive chastity and holiness from the saints. And because my beloved feeds in the gardens:

“I am for my beloved, and my beloved is for me.”

I prepare a pleasing dwelling for my beloved; and my beloved prepares for me a heavenly reward, or the grace of the perfect. And because he dwells in me and makes me dwell in him, as he himself says: “I in you, and you in me” (John 14).

[Col. 0091D] “He feeds among the lilies.”

That is, he cares only for those holy persons who are white in innocence, bright in chastity, and fragrant in good repute. Christ, 35. returning the bride’s commendation, says:

“You are beautiful, my friend, sweet and lovely, like Jerusalem.”

You are beautiful in faith, sweet in hope, lovely in charity, like Jerusalem. Jerusalem is interpreted “vision of peace.” What, then, is more truly Jerusalem than the glorious Virgin, in whom are peace of heart and peace of eternity? This is Noah’s ark, [Col. 0092A] in which the beasts were at peace, because in her there were no disordered thoughts.

“Terrible as an army drawn up in battle array.”

Because in life she was supported by many virtues, and in death surrounded by troops of angels. And as she became terrible through her virtues, destroying the errors of heretics and repelling the suggestions of demons, so also [Note: [Col. 0091] Villar manuscript: “and” in place of “so also.”] in her Assumption she was supported by the guards of those same angels and crowned by the choirs of saints. And lest the Virgin should believe that in the present life, by searching the Scriptures and evangelical contemplation, she could fully comprehend God, Christ says:

“Turn your eyes away from me, for they have made me flee away.”

Although you are beautiful, although you are my friend, turn [Col. 0092B] your eyes away from me. As though he said: I have given you dove-like eyes, by which you can behold me and penetrate the mysteries of Scripture; but beware lest you desire in this present life to fix them upon me so as to see me fully, because you cannot do so in the present. Hence he says to Moses: “No human being shall see me and live” (Exod. 33). But when, assumed into my presence, you arrive, then you will see me in open vision. When it is said, “they have made me flee away,” it should not be thought that God abandons those who seek him and withdraws from them, since he himself commands: “Seek, and you shall find” (Matt. 7). Rather it is to be understood thus: the more anyone seeks to investigate God’s divinity, the more fully that person understands it to be unsearchable and incomprehensible. This is what [Col. 0092C] the Psalmist says: “Man shall approach the deep heart, and God shall be exalted” (Ps. 63) [Note: [Col. 0091] The Villar manuscript inserts here: “as though he said: although he raises himself up to behold God, God shall be exalted, because, etc.”], because how great he is cannot be comprehended. And though you cannot see me fully, nevertheless:

“Your hair is like a flock of goats which appeared from Gilead.”

Your hair, that is, your thoughts proceeding from the spiritual head, that is, the mind, are like a flock of goats, that is, like the motions of contemplation, which are represented by goats, as was said above. They appeared from Mount Gilead because such motions proceed from the eminence of the human condition and furnish manifold testimony to the truth [Note: [Col. 0091] Manuscript: “bring.”].

“Your teeth are like flocks of sheep, which have come up from [Col. 0092D] the washing.”

That is, your exercises in the sacred Scriptures are like flocks of sheep, that is, they pertain to spiritual understandings, represented by sheep because of simplicity and purity. They have come up from the washing, because such understandings, cleansed from carnal interpretation and purified from images, have ascended to the contemplation of God.

“All bearing twins, and none among them is barren.”

For such understandings also conceive a good intention and bring forth an honourable action. Hence [Col. 0093A] it follows: “and none among them is barren,” namely in good works.

36. “As the rind of a pomegranate, so are your cheeks, apart from what lies hidden within [your hidden things].”

Above, we said that in the cheeks is signified the Virgin’s chaste modesty; in the rind of the pomegranate we understand remembrance of Christ’s Passion. Therefore the Virgin’s cheeks were like the rind of a pomegranate because she was not ashamed of Christ’s cross. Hence the Apostle: “Do not be ashamed of the cross of Christ, nor of me, his prisoner” (2 Tim. 1). And these things that are outwardly visible are indeed great; but greatest are those things within, that is, those reserved for the Virgin in the future. And though there are many holy souls spiritually joined to me, yet there is one whom I love more specially because of her simplicity [Col. 0093B] and perfection of virtues. By this I mean the glorious Virgin, and this is what he says:

“There are sixty queens, and eighty concubines, and maidens without number.”

The queens are doctors of the Church who, by the merit of faith and knowledge, are worthy of the embraces of the eternal King; they bring forth spiritual children for God and govern themselves well. Hear a queen governing herself well and bringing forth children for God: “My little children,” she says, “whom I am again bringing to birth until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. 4). These queens are fittingly signified by the number sixty, which is completed by multiplying ten and six. By ten are signified the Ten Commandments of the Law; by six, perfection in work, because in six days God completed his works (Gen. 1). “And eighty [Col. 0093C] concubines.” The concubines are those who are not chaste, that is, who proclaim the Gospel not with true and sole love of God, but for earthly gain or human praise. Yet it is remarkable why such persons are signified by the number eighty, when this number is found to be most perfect in every place of the divine Scripture, whereas these persons are shown to be imperfect and perverse. Therefore I think that, although they are imperfect, they nevertheless display perfection in their outward appearance and speech through hypocrisy; though they are most wicked, they still beget others to perfection through the Gospel. Of them the Saviour says: “Beware of false prophets, etc.” (Matt. 7). “Satan himself also transforms himself into an angel of light” (2 Cor. 11). “And [Col. 0093D] maidens without number.” Maidens are those already reborn in Christ, who, having put off the oldness of the first human being, have been renewed in Christ, but are not yet marriageable or fit for the King’s bed, because they have not yet reached preaching about Christ. They are without number because the number of souls believing in Christ is known to God alone. And though there are so many queens, so many concubines, so many maidens, nevertheless:

“My dove is one, my perfect one is one; she is the only one of her mother, chosen for her that bore her.”

She is one, my dove, by special simplicity; one, my perfect one, by fullness of virtues; she is the only daughter [Col. 0094A] of her mother, chosen for her who bore her—namely, the Synagogue, from which Christ descended according to the flesh, and which is therefore called his mother. This special one was the Virgin Mary, most worthy among all, unique among all, blessed among all.

“The daughters of Zion saw her and proclaimed her most blessed; queens and concubines praised her.”

The daughters of Zion, that is, holy souls which now by faith and hope are in contemplation, saw her and proclaimed her most blessed. They did not call her blessed, but proclaimed her most blessed: she who bore God’s Son; who remained a virgin; endowed with humility, blessed in virginity, praiseworthy in reverence, distinguished in obedience. Note that above he called those whom he now calls daughters the maidens of Zion. The queens, [Col. 0094B] as was said above, are called doctors of the Church, who by the proclamation of their preaching praise the Virgin, declare her most blessed, and invite the daughters of Zion to imitate her. “And the concubines praised her.” As was said, concubines are those who proclaim God’s glory for the sake 37. of human favour or earthly gain, and do not fail to praise the Virgin Mother [Note: [Col. 0093] The Villar manuscript has “deny” in place of “fail to.”], praising her in this way:

“Who is this that comes forth like the rising dawn?”

How great is the dignity of her who comes forth with such honour and glory that, by the merit of her beauty, she is compared to the dawn? She comes forth, I say, from virtue to virtue (Ps. 83), like the dawn; for as the dawn brings into the world the sun shining over the earth, so the Virgin Mary, like a heavenly dawn, bears into the world the Sun of righteousness. The dawn precedes the sun, yet proceeds from the sun’s power; so the Virgin is the forerunner of the true light, that is, the herald of the Sun of righteousness, yet she herself is enlightened by spiritual grace from him. And she is truly like the dawn rising, that is, rising wholly together, because she was wholly holy, shining both in body and spirit.

“Beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun.”

For just as the moon illumines the night, so she enlightens us by her example; by bearing the Sun of righteousness, she removes the darkness of our ignorance. And as the moon is illuminated by the sun, so the Virgin is illumined by the brightness of the true sun.
