And as she is beautiful as the moon—indeed, more than the moon, [Col. 0094D] because the moon sometimes wanes, while she always advances; the moon decreases, while she always increases; the moon has some stain in itself, while she has none—therefore she is chosen as the sun, which has in itself no defect of light. As the sun is preferred to all worldly things, so she is preferred to all creatures and strives to imitate the true sun himself by living in all humility, gentleness, righteousness, and holiness. And as the sun does not change the accustomed reins of its course, so the blessed Virgin did not change the resolve she had once undertaken.

“Terrible as an army drawn up in battle array.”

Terrible to whom? To the princes of darkness—to the devil and his angels. She terrifies and pierces them; and, for the strengthening of her servants, she often restrains the wicked and beats back the assaults of the malicious. Terrible, I say, to heretics, whom you confound by your power, and to the faithless, whom you turn away from your lovers. [Note: [Col. 0095] The manuscript has *dilectoribus* (“lovers”) in place of *delectationibus* (“delights”); and thus it should also be read.] Like an ordered battle-line of camps: that is, so fortified by faith, hope, and love that she cannot be penetrated by any temptations of the enemy. Note that the queens called her dawn, moon, and sun, and ordered like a battle-line of camps; but Christ calls her his garden, saying:

> I went down into my garden, to see the fruits of the valley.

As though he said: Because the Virgin is such, I have now become man in the bridal chamber of the virginal womb. [Note: [Col. 0095] The Tournai manuscript: “therefore I was born man”; the Villers manuscript: “I was humbled in the bridal chamber of the virginal womb.”] This is the garden in which the fragrances of virtues breathe, in which the rosebeds of patience give forth their scent. This is a garden overflowing with fruits, abounding in riches, blooming with the flower of virginity; no harsh south wind touches it, where the grace of a gentler breeze continually breathes and springtime loveliness attracts those who behold it. Note also that where our text has *my*, some codices have *of nuts*, which aptly suits the glorious Virgin. For the nut has a bitter husk, a hard shell, and a very sweet kernel. So the Virgin Mother outwardly had the weakness of flesh and a hard shell—that is, firm constancy of faith and perseverance in virginity—and the most sweet kernel, Christ; for she bears Christ for the world, from whom the sweetness of eternal blessedness has been given to us. Thus Christ descended into the Virgin through the humility of his Incarnation, in order that he might see—that is, cause to be seen—the fruits of the valley: that is, the fruits which are preserved in humility. God is said to “see” something, that is, to make something seen, as it was said to Abraham: “I have known,” that is, “I have caused others to know,” “that you fear God” (Gen. 22).

> And that I might look to see whether the vine had flowered and the pomegranates had budded.

That is: I might consider how the Church, spread throughout the world, flourishes in virtues; and I might carefully inspect those who are already ripe to endure martyrdoms. For all these things commend the great watchfulness, concern, and love which he has for the Church.

> [Col. 0095D] I did not know; my soul troubled me because of the chariots of Amminadab.

Thus Christ came in the flesh and took flesh from me, says the Virgin; but before he came into me, I did not know that he would come into me. I knew that he would be born of a virgin, but I did not know which virgin. This is what she says: “I did not know the Son of God”—namely, that he would be born from me before the angel’s coming. Hence at the angel’s address she says: “My soul troubled me,” because I wondered what sort of greeting this might be. This is what is read in the Gospel: “When she heard it, she was troubled at his saying, and considered what sort of greeting this might be” (Luke 1). And this was because of the chariots of Amminadab.

Note that there were four means by which Christ came into the Virgin Mary: humility, love, mercy, and wisdom. For the Son of God came to the Virgin in supreme humility, so that the humility in the Redeemer might be as great as the pride in the first sinner had been. So great was the pride in the first parent that he raised himself up against his Creator; so great was the humility in the Son of God that he stooped [Note: [Col. 0095] Villers manuscript: “emptied himself.”] even to the assumption of our flesh of misery (Phil. 2). The first woman wished to make herself equal to God; the glorious Virgin declared herself the humble handmaid of God.

Likewise, out of supreme love the Son of God stooped down. [Note: [Col. 0095] “He was incarnated.”] For what love is greater than that the Son of God should come into the world to redeem the slave, [Note: [Col. 0095] The same manuscript here inserts: “and wound the physician, in order that,” etc.] to heal the sick? Likewise, supreme piety and mercy caused the Son of God to be incarnate. What piety and mercy are greater than that God should empty himself and take the form of a servant (ibid.), than that the Maker should rescue his work from the pit of filth and misery (Ps. 39)? And it was also supreme wisdom that the Wisdom of God was incarnate, so that man might redeem man. These four—humility, love, mercy, and wisdom—were like the chariots by which the incarnate Son of God came to us. The Virgin marvelled at these four things in the angelic address: the humility, love, mercy, and wisdom which Christ displayed to us when he assumed flesh in the virginal womb. These are called the chariots of Amminadab, that is, of Christ. Amminadab was the great-grandson of the patriarch Judah, through whom Christ’s genealogy is woven; his name means “the willing one of my people.” He signifies Christ, who was willing for his people, because, though he was God, he gave himself up for them.

But as though the angel answered the Virgin, troubled at his words, it follows:

> Return, return, Shulamite [Sunamite], return, return, that we may behold you.

Return to yourself: “Do not fear, for you have found favour with the Lord” (Luke 1). Return to the Scriptures, so that from the Scriptures you may understand what I say. “For behold, you shall conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel” (ibid.). And you who formerly were a Shulamite—that is, captive under the burden of the Law, for *Sunamite* is interpreted “captive”—return to the freedom of evangelical dignity. And you who do not know the manner of this conception, return from this ignorance to knowledge of the mode of conceiving. For “the Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (ibid.). “That we may behold you,” not only through knowledge or grace, but also through the presence of the Incarnation.

Or these may be the words of the holy spirits, who desire the Virgin’s assumption. When they say, “Return, return,” it is as though they say: First, return from the captivity of the world, because you ought not be subject to worldly captivity—you through whom captives have been freed from their captivity. Second, return from the burden or corruption of flesh, because just as you are free from the corruption of sin, so you ought to pass into immortality, mortality being swallowed up by God’s grace. Third, return to the freedom of the children of God (Rom. 6), because, just as sin never reigned in your mortal body, so you are worthy to enjoy in your virginal flesh that same freedom of spirit which the angels have enjoyed in spiritual knowledge [Note: [Col. 0097] The same Villers manuscript has *substantia*, “substance,” in place of *scientia*, “knowledge.”] from their creation itself, or rather from their confirmation. Fourth, return, “that we may behold you”: from the dignity of angels to the surpassing excellence of spirits now made blessed. For just as we desire to look upon the face of your Son, so we wish to fix our gaze upon your countenance in your form and beauty, and strive in every way to be illumined by the light of your face.

And as though Christ, speaking these things, directed his speech to the Holy Spirit, there follows:

## CHAPTER VII

> What will you see in the Shulamite, but the choirs of camps?

The choirs of camps are gatherings of virtues, ordered in the Virgin, by which she is fortified against vices, demons, and heretics. Note that choirs belong to singers, but camps to fighters. Therefore in the Virgin there were choirs of singers in respect of the harmony of virtues, and camps of fighters in that, protected on every side and instructed in holy disciplines, she repelled the assaults of vices and demons. And Christ, still directing his speech to the Virgin, says:

> How beautiful are your steps in sandals, daughter of a prince!

Your steps, glorious Virgin, are nobility, virginity, and fruitfulness: nobility of lineage, integrity of flesh and mind, and fruitfulness of offspring. The sandals are affections, actions, advances, and ecstasies: affections in meditations, actions in works, advances in desires, ecstasies in joys. But you are the princely daughter of the Prince, namely God, who is Prince of princes and Lord of lords, because he begot you specially by grace and specially formed you—yet you are so God’s daughter that you are also his inviolate Mother. Or by feet and steps are understood the dispositions of the mind, which were altogether purified and adorned in Christ’s Incarnation. The sandals signify the divine Incarnation.

For a sandal is customarily made from the skin of a dead animal; yet not the whole skin is made into a man’s sandal, but rather part of it. Human nature had been put to death by punishments and guilt. Christ assumed this skin of human punishment in respect of the substance of nature, but not wholly in respect of the circumstances of nature: for he assumed punishment, but not guilt. Thus he applied it as a sandal when he assumed human nature. Continuing the Virgin’s beauty, he says:

> The joints of your thighs [feminum] are like necklaces.

The thighs are ordinarily signs of generation. The joining of the thighs signifies nothing other than the harmony of the two fruitfulnesses which were in the Virgin: one of the mind, the other of the womb. This joining was like a necklace; that is, it had as its twofold companion virginity of flesh and virginity of mind. Chastity is commonly signified by a necklace, for a necklace is placed upon the breast for adornment and as a sign of chastity; whence it is called *monile*, that is, something “admonishing chastity.” The sense, then, is: “The joints of your thighs are like necklaces”: as you are endowed with twofold fruitfulness, so you are endowed with twofold virginity.

> Which were fashioned by the hand of the craftsman.

That is, by the hand of almighty God, through whose generosity every virtue was bestowed upon the Virgin; or by the hand of the craftsman, that is, the Son of God. For he is the hand of God the Father, through whom he also made the ages (Heb. 1).

> Your navel is a rounded bowl, never lacking cups.

Just as in a man the power of desire has its seat in the loins, so in a woman the power of desire is in the navel. The navel is also in the middle of the belly. Therefore by the Virgin’s navel is understood the power of understanding [Note: [Col. 0097] The Villers manuscript has *diligendi*, “loving,” in place of *intelligendi*, “understanding.”] by which she loved God, namely love. In the Virgin this was like a bowl, because through it the Virgin offered the world the wine of joy, of which it is said: “My inebriating cup, how excellent it is!” (Ps. 22). And elsewhere: “Wine gladdens the heart of man” (Ps. 103). It is rightly called a rounded bowl, because we work more easily with a lathe. And the Virgin herself, without any difficulty, any allurement, or any distress of the flesh, conceived and gave birth.

“Never lacking cups”: it says less and means more—that is, full of cups—because they offer to the world the wine of love, the wine of salvation, the wine of joy, the cup of life. Nor is it surprising if your navel is such, because:

> Your belly is like a heap of wheat, surrounded by lilies.

The Virgin’s belly is elegantly compared to a heap of wheat because from it came forth the grain of wheat which, falling into the earth and dying, brought forth abundant fruit (John 12). From it proceeded in God’s Church the multiplied harvest of the faithful and believing. Your belly, I say, is surrounded by lilies because, though full of fruitfulness, it is nevertheless adorned with virginity.

> Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a gazelle.

The Virgin’s two breasts may be understood as her flesh and soul: her flesh, cleansed of every desire and adorned with virginity; and her soul, filled with the delights of virtues, in which, because Christ delighted, they were to him like breasts from which he especially drew nourishment of joy and love. These were like fawns of a gazelle. The gazelle is Christ, because, as that animal is distinguished by keenness of vision and dwells in high places, so the Son of God dwells in heaven and penetrates all things by his wisdom. Its two fawns are Christ’s body and soul; for just as fawns proceed from the gazelle and do not depart from it, but rather accompany it and are nourished from its breasts, so Christ’s flesh, formed by Christ himself, and his created soul follow him as he goes into heaven and are delightfully nourished from the breasts of his divinity. [Note: [Col. 0099] Here the Villers manuscript adds: “which he never dismissed from the time he assumed them; for whatever good the soul or flesh has, it has from the Word of God. Thus the Virgin’s two breasts are like two fawns of a gazelle, because the Virgin is conformed in body and soul to the body and soul of Christ.”] Besides all this:

> Your neck is like an ivory tower.

That is, your teaching, by which you instructed the evangelists, was firm, wavering in nothing and doubting in nothing; it taught simply, mingling in no falsehood, and taught in all holiness and sanctity. For ivory signifies chastity and purity in Scripture. Likewise:

> Your eyes are like pools in Heshbon, which are at the gate of the daughter of the multitude.

The Virgin’s eyes are called the contemplative life and the active life: in the one, the active, she sees what ought to be done; in the other, the contemplative, what ought to be loved. They are compared to pools because they both satisfy the Virgin with spiritual refreshment and free her from the stain of sin. These are in Heshbon, that is, “in the girdle of sorrow”; for this is the interpretation of that name. In respect of the active life, the Virgin is encircled by a girdle of sorrow because of the length of labour and misery; and in respect of the contemplative life, because of the delay of the homeland. These pools are at the gate of the daughter of the multitude. The holy Church is rightly called the daughter of the multitude because she daily gathers a great number of nations. This gate is faith or the washing of baptism, through which entrance into God’s Church lies open. Therefore these pools are at the gate of the daughter of the multitude, because through the Church’s faith the lives aforesaid are acquired. By a similar comparison:

> Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, which looks toward Damascus.

The Virgin’s discernment is figured by the nose, through which she distinguished the stench of vices from the fragrance of virtues. Hence [Note: [Col. 0099] Manuscript: “this.”] it is compared to the tower of Lebanon, because, like a tower, it defended [Note: [Col. 0099] The same manuscript: “it defended her.”] against the incursions of the malicious. It is rightly said to be like the tower of Lebanon. For *Lebanon* is interpreted “whitening,” because it adorned her with the brightness of virginity and defended her against vices. This is said to look toward Damascus. *Damascus* is interpreted “drinking of blood” or “eye of blood”; it therefore signifies the pleasures and allurements of the flesh, whereby it is shown that the Virgin’s discernment was contrary to pleasures and allurements.

> Your head is like Carmel, and the hair of your head like royal purple, joined to channels.

Carmel, also called Chermel, is a mountain; its name means “knowledge of circumcision,” and it signifies Christ, who knows how by true circumcision to cut away all vices from his faithful. He is the Virgin’s head, and her hair is all the faithful. This hair is dyed like royal purple because it is adorned by the blood of the true King.

“Joined to channels.” Christ’s Passion is signified by the purple, and our hearts by the channels. For just as water usually runs through channels, so contrition runs through our hearts from remembrance of Christ’s Passion. Therefore the King’s purple, that is, Christ’s Passion, is joined to channels, that is, to our humble hearts, when with true love in the very depths of our hearts we suffer with Christ in his Passion; for “if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (2 Tim. 2). Therefore:

> How beautiful you are, and how lovely, dearest one, in delights!

How beautiful you are outwardly through the active life, and how lovely inwardly through the contemplative life! “Dearest in delights,” that is, in love of God and neighbour, because:

> Your stature is like a palm tree, and your breasts like clusters.

The palm has a somewhat rough root, a harsh bark, strength of wood, loftiness of trunk; it is beautiful at its crown, delightful in flower, and sweet in fruit. It is also customarily carried as a sign of victory. Therefore the stature of the glorious Virgin, that is, the course of her life, is compared to a palm. For she came forth from a rough root—that is, from the sinful Synagogue—as a rose from a thorn. She had harsh bark, because in regard to worldly honour she was steadfast, and in regard to temporal riches she was poor; but she had strength of wood through constancy of mind. She stood upright in her trunk because her intention of mind was raised toward heaven.

She was beautiful at the crown in the loftiness of virginity and humility; delightful in flower because without desire she conceived the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys. She was sweet in fruitfulness because without pain [Note: [Col. 0099] Manuscript: “sorrow” in place of “pain.”] she bore the Redeemer of the world. She is set before us as a sign and example of victory, so that, as she conquered the world, sin, and the devil, we also may conquer according to our ability.

“And your breasts like clusters,” because, as we said above, Mary’s breasts are called virginity and humility, in which Christ delighted. They are set before us to form and instruct us, that we may follow her footsteps. They are compared to clusters because a cluster gives fragrance in flower and sweetness in fruit; it also warms and refreshes. So the Virgin’s virginity and humility are fragrant with the odour of good repute, offer the fruit of sweetness [Note: [Col. 0101] The manuscript adds: “to imitators of the Virgin.”], warm us to love, and refresh us unto spiritual satisfaction.

And just as I descended into you, the palm, so I shall ascend the palm, that is, the cross. Thus he speaks to the bride about his Passion and reveals to her his counsel, which from eternal times had been ordained with the Father and which he did not wish to conceal from the Virgin. This is what he says: “I said,” that is, I established eternally and unchangeably, “I shall ascend the palm,” that is, the cross. He calls it a palm because it is a triumphal sign against every power of the enemy. “And I shall seize its fruit.” The whole world is known to be the fruit of that palm, redeemed through the cross; hence the same Saviour says: “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, shall draw all things to myself” (John 12). This is what is said:

> I said: I shall ascend the palm and seize its fruits.

Hence it follows:

> And your breasts shall be like clusters of the vine.

After Christ suffered, and the fame of Christ’s name was spread abroad through the Resurrection, Ascension, and sending of the Holy Spirit, the Virgin’s breasts—that is, humility and virginity—gave forth the fragrance of good repute, refreshing the Virgin’s imitators by their example and inflaming them with love of him. Or the two breasts are called the two arms of love with which the Virgin loved Christ; in the Passion they were like clusters, because the Virgin’s love blazed more intensely in her Son’s Passion through its manifestation, and soberly intoxicated her through grief. And then:

> And the fragrance of your mouth like the fragrance of apples.

That is, the fame and repute of your works shall be like the fragrance of apples, because they shall come to maturity and offer others a most sweet fragrance.

> Your throat like the finest wine.

That is, your meditation upon the Scriptures, through which the word of holy instruction is formed and the spiritual food of Sacred Scripture passes into the stomach of the mind, is like the finest wine—that is, it is compared to excellent wine—because it both intoxicates soberly and frees one from the cares of temporal things. As Christ said these things, the Virgin, as though interrupting his words, [Note: [Col. 0101] The Villers manuscript adds “the Virgin.”] replies:

> Worthy for my beloved to drink, and for his lips and teeth to chew over.

For my meditation upon the Scriptures pleases God, my beloved, as a cup pleases someone by its fragrance and taste, and as something to be chewed over pleases his lips and teeth. Teachers are understood by the lips, and preachers by the teeth: they have their meditation in Sacred Scripture. Nor is it inappropriate that wine is drunk and not chewed, since chewing pertains more to food than to drink. For holy teachers chew spiritual wine when they diligently investigate spiritual precepts, search them by repeated meditation, and compare them with one another. Thus I offer the finest wine to my beloved. This is what follows:

> I am for my beloved, and his turning is toward me.

I offer my beloved the cup of holy meditation, and his turning is toward me in help, because without him I can do nothing. And because my meditation upon Sacred Scripture has no strength without your inspiration, therefore:

> Come, my beloved; let us go out into the field.

Come to me through the revelation of Sacred Scripture, and thus let us go out into the field, that is, into the searching of Sacred Scripture. Note that Sacred Scripture is elegantly called a field, because just as in a field there spring up a diversity of flowers and a variety of herbs, so in Sacred Scripture there is a multiplicity of meanings. The meaning which urges chastity bears the image of the lily; that which urges patience in martyrdom bears the likeness of the rose; that which urges repentance presents the form of the violet.

> Let us remain in the villages.

Let us remain in the villages, that is, applying diligent study to the obscure books, so that we may draw light from smoke, sun from night, brightness from obscurity. Villages elegantly signify the obscure books of Sacred Scripture, because, just as in villages there is not the frequent noise of people nor such a tumult of citizens as in towns and cities, so in obscure places of Sacred Scripture there is not such chattering of people as in open places. For obscure passages of Sacred Scripture are far removed from popular understanding [Note: [Col. 0101] Manuscript: “intelligence.”]; and thus:

> Let us rise early to the vineyards; let us see whether the vine has flowered, whether the flowers bear fruit, whether the pomegranates have blossomed.

Let us rise early to the vineyards: that is, rising from the letter to the spirit, from history to the mystical sense, let us approach the Sacred Scriptures. In them the foliage of history is green, the flower of allegory is fragrant, and the fruit of tropology satisfies. And this is “early,” that is, through the dawn of spiritual understanding. Thus let us see—that is, let us experience; that is, cause me to experience—whether the vine has flowered, that is, whether Sacred Scripture has flowered in me through the allegorical sense; whether the flowers bear fruit through the moral understanding. For as fruit follows the flower, so moral understanding follows allegorical interpretation for our instruction. “Whether the pomegranates have blossomed.” The pomegranate has a rind outwardly and contains an abundance of seeds within. Such is Sacred Scripture: outwardly it presents the rind of the letter, inwardly it contains the fruitfulness of spiritual understanding. Therefore the pomegranate blossoms in the mind when Sacred Scripture exhorts a person, by hope of eternal blessedness, to patience [Note: [Col. 0101] Villers manuscript: “endurance of sufferings.”] in suffering. For the firmness and redness which the pomegranate outwardly displays signify endurance of sufferings.

> There I shall give you my breasts.

That is, in this meditation upon Scripture I shall reveal the twofold love with which I love you, both inasmuch as you are God and inasmuch as you are man. For love is inflamed through frequent meditation on Sacred Scripture; there one finds what Christ bestowed upon us both inasmuch as he is God and inasmuch as he is man.

> The mandrakes gave forth their fragrance at our gates.

What is understood by mandrakes, a medicinal and fragrant herb, except the perfection of the glorious Virgin’s virtues? While she distributes examples of good works everywhere through good repute, she sprinkles, as it were, a fragrance by which the sick are healed. And this is at the gates, that is, in virtues, which are gates to life. Nor have the mandrakes alone given forth their fragrance, but also:

> All fruits, new and old, my beloved, I have kept for you.

That is: I have kept for you the precepts, sayings, or promises of the New and Old Testaments—that is, I have understood them to be fulfilled in your name, in you, and through you. For I know that all things announced in the Old Testament can be fulfilled only by your authority. By fruits are understood the senses of the Sacred Scriptures; when they reach us from the holy Fathers and are believed, they produce, as it were, a certain fragrance through understanding and spiritually refresh the mind. [Note: [Col. 0103] Manuscript: “spiritually filling [it].”] Therefore, O Christ, you who are now in the Father’s bosom, assume the form of man.

## CHAPTER VIII

> Who will grant me you as my brother, sucking the breasts of my mother, that I may find you outside?

But who will grant me you as my brother—that is, who can bring it about that, sharing in my nature, you may be called brother? You, I say, “sucking the breasts of my mother”: that is, assuming everything that belongs to human nature, apart from sin—who but God the Father? The Virgin’s mother is called the Synagogue, from which Christ also descended. Therefore to suck the breasts of the Virgin’s mother is to suck the breasts of the Synagogue.

Here the Virgin Mary is introduced speaking according to the state in which she was when, answering the angel, she said: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke 1). And who will also grant that I may find you alone outside—that is, that I may recognize you as incarnate in human nature, from my own substance? For God was, as it were, within when he lay hidden in the Father’s bosom; but he was found outside when he made himself visible to the world.

> And I shall kiss you, and now no one shall despise me.

“I shall kiss you,” that is, I shall take great delight in you, and you shall delight in me; and no one shall now despise me as before you came into me. For before the Incarnation of the Son she seemed of no consequence; but after conception and birth she was held in great honour, not only by human beings but also by angels, because she was blessed among women—indeed, exalted above the choirs of angels. And when you have come in the flesh:

> I shall take hold of you and lead you into the house of my mother.

“I shall take hold of you,” that is, I shall embrace you with supreme love, and lead you into the house of my mother. The Virgin’s mother is the Synagogue, and the house and chamber of that Synagogue is the old Law in which she dwells. The Virgin Mary therefore leads him into this house or chamber when she carefully considers all that was written concerning him in the Old Testament and understands that it was truly fulfilled in Christ. This is what follows:

> There you will teach me, and I shall give you a cup of spiced wine and new wine of my pomegranates.

There—that is, in the Old Testament—you will teach me: you will open its meaning to me, so that I may understand all that is written concerning you in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms. And I shall give you a cup of spiced wine. The Virgin Mary gave Christ a cup of spiced wine when she understood that the New Testament accords in him with the Old. She spiced the cup, as it were, with wine, because she knew that the sweetness of the Gospel ought to be steeped with the testimonies of the Law, which is harsh, so that it may be held more firmly. Moreover, I shall give you the new wine of my pomegranates: that is, in the manner aforesaid I shall refer to you spiritual understanding, fervent within me through frequent meditation. She fittingly calls the mystical sense “new wine,” since it is so intensely fervent that it burns out from itself every impurity by its excessive heat. For the spiritual understanding of the Mosaic Law removes from itself the literal sense as though it were dregs.

And therefore, because I perceive its grace and ineffable sweetness, I now set aside all earthly things, despise even the life of the flesh for love of it, and with all desire pant to behold its blessedness. For the Virgin subjected to her mind the things which she saw, and with every effort and all her thoughts sought the things which she did not see. She pursued heavenly things with such desire that she reckoned all visible things as nothing, occupying her mind with heavenly desires. [Note: [Col. 0103] Villers manuscript: “occupies [it] without interruption.”]

> His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me.

She therefore had his left hand under her head, because, with her mind raised toward blessedness, she bore the present life beneath herself. [Note: [Col. 0103] The same manuscript: “sees.”] And Christ’s right hand embraced her, because heavenly love protected her on every side. Since the Virgin was in contemplation when he came, Christ instructs the evangelists not to rouse the Virgin from the sleep of contemplation by asking her what Christ did in the flesh, except when she herself should wish to reveal it to them. For there was a time when the Virgin gave herself to contemplation, and a time when she revealed many of Christ’s deeds to the apostles. This is what is said:

> I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, do not rouse or awaken my beloved until she herself wills it.

Because the Virgin was of such great merit, the hosts of heavenly spirits praise her, assumed into heaven, with wonder in this manner:

> Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, abounding in delights, leaning upon her beloved?

The Virgin descended into the wilderness; she ascended through the wilderness; she ascended above the wilderness; she ascended from the wilderness. She descended into the wilderness through birth; she ascended through the wilderness by advancing from virtue to virtue (Ps. 83); she ascended above the wilderness by despising every worldly height; she ascended from the wilderness into eternal blessedness. This is what is said here: “Who is this?”—that is, of how great merit and dignity is she who ascends from the wilderness, that is, from the world to heaven, abounding in delights, that is, distinguished by many virtues; leaning upon her beloved, because she clings to Christ through love and trusts in the help of Christ alone? By generosity [Note: [Col. 0105] Tournai manuscript: “God bestowing”; Villers manuscript: “he bestowing.”] she is transferred from exile to her homeland.

The Beloved explains whence she receives the power to ascend from the lowly to the heights, from wilderness to kingdom, when he adds:

> Under the apple tree I raised you up.

Christ calls his cross not an evil tree but an apple tree, because of the fruit of eternal blessedness which the Virgin Mother received through the cross, along with the other faithful souls, though she more fully. Yet [Note: [Col. 0105] The same Villers manuscript reads “and” instead of “yet.”] because of the good fragrance of Christ’s cross among all nations, and because she, glorious as she was, endured evil, of whom it was said above: “As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons”:

> There your mother was corrupted.

Namely, beneath that cross the Synagogue, from which the Virgin Mary descended according to the flesh, was corrupted through unbelief. Hence it follows:

> There she who bore you was violated.

“She who bore you,” that is, that same Synagogue, was there violated by the devil. Or thus: “Under the apple tree I raised you up”: that is, under me, who am called an apple tree for the reasons stated, I raised you up—that is, I exalted you to the fullness of virtues. Because I was incarnate in you and from you, you have been exalted above the choirs of angels. “There your mother was corrupted,” that is, in me the Synagogue sinned. This is what follows: “There she was violated.” And because I exalted you, therefore:

> Set me [Note: [Col. 0105] The same manuscript immediately adds: “‘Set me,’ that is, ‘you will set me’: the present imperative is used for the future indicative, as is frequently read in Sacred Scripture.”] as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm.

A seal is called that whose signet, form, or image is customarily impressed upon wax, so that the wax receives the form of the signet, secrets may be concealed from strangers, and disclosed to those known. Thus the Virgin Mary placed Christ upon [Note: [Col. 0105] “Upon [her] heart.”] her heart as a seal, because by imitation she was conformed to him and marked with his grace. Hence it is read: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us; you have given joy in my heart” (Ps. 4). This was unknown to the devil but known to the angel.

“And set me as a seal upon your arm”: that is, in all your works you shall remember me. The Beloved is set as a seal upon the Virgin’s heart and arm because in her thoughts and actions the Virgin Mary imitated her Son. Thought is signified by the heart, and action by the arm. You do this because:

> For love is strong as death.

For just as death separates the soul from the body, and a person thereafter may desire nothing in the present life, so the love by which the Virgin loved Christ utterly mortified her to this world and rendered her insensible to it, living for Christ alone and dead to the world. And that love is truly strong in the Virgin, because:

> Jealous devotion is harsh as hell.

That is, the execution and effect of love is harsh as hell. For just as hell never releases those whom it has once received, so love, once it came into the Virgin, never left her. Nor, he says, is it surprising that your love should possess such strength, because:

> Its lamps are lamps of fire and flames.

The lamps—that is, the ardours and compunctions—of that love are lamps of fire and flames because they pour out to others the light of good example. Therefore the lamps of love are the Virgin’s inner parts, in which love dwelt as in vessels. Thus they were lamps of fire because inwardly they burned with love, and lamps of flames because outwardly they shone in action. These lamps, I say, are like flaming fire, as may be proved by this, since:

> Many waters could not [will not] extinguish love, nor shall rivers overwhelm it.

Many waters—that is, the threats of persecutors, the blandishments of the world, or tribulations, which are signified by waters—could not extinguish the love that is between me and you. Nor will rivers—that is, violent persecutions—overwhelm that love. For although persecutors kill the body, they cannot kill the soul [Col. 0106D] (Matt. 10). Therefore your love is of such dignity as has been said, although not everyone ought to possess so great a love, that

> If a man should give all the substance of his house for love, he would regard it [him] as almost nothing.

For all the substance of this world is worthless, and like a little grain of sand in comparison with love. Hence the elect have surrendered not only their possessions, but even themselves to death for Christ’s love. Thus far Christ has spoken [Col. 0107A] of the Virgin according to her state after the Incarnation; now he speaks of her according to the state she had before the time of the Incarnation. He is introduced as speaking to the angels concerning the sending of a messenger to the Virgin and the Incarnation to be accomplished in the Virgin. Thus he says:

**48. Our little [small] sister has no breasts.**

The Virgin Mary is little in humility; little in age, according to some who say that she was thirteen [Note: [Col. 0107] In the Villar. manuscript it reads fourteen.] years old when the Son of God sent an angel to her; little also in the scantiness of her earthly possessions; little in public estimation. And she has no breasts, that is, she is not fruitful by conception. Or, she does not yet have breasts as great as she is to have—namely, [Col. 0107B] breasts of love: that is, she does not yet have such fullness of love as she will have after the Incarnation, for loving me as God and man.

> What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be addressed?

This question is not that of one who does not know, but is administrative. For God knows what he will do. “What,” says the angel, “shall we do for our sister?”—that is, for the Virgin Mary, who is called Christ’s sister by reason of human nature, according to which the Virgin was in some manner to become Christ’s sister, because she was akin to him in human nature. She was also the sister of the angels, insofar as she shared in spiritual grace, in which Christ was to be [Col. 0107C] like Mary and like the angelic nature. “On the day when she is to be addressed,” that is, at the time when the archangel Gabriel is to address her.

> If she is a wall, let us build upon her battlements of silver.

That is: if she has the firm purpose of preserving the virginity she has vowed to God—and indeed she does—let us build upon her battlements of silver; that is, let us instruct her in the knowledge of the divine word, so that she may believe that the Son of God can be born [Note: [Col. 0107] The same manuscript: “can be born.”] from her, according to the authorities of the divine word, if she preserves the virginity of body and soul.

> If she is a door, let us fasten it with cedar boards.

If she is a door—that is, if through faith, obedience, and humility she provides me access to herself, so that I may [Col. 0107D] be incarnate from her—let us fasten it with cedar boards; that is, let us instruct her in the sacred Scriptures, so that she may understand that the things foretold by the prophets concerning the Virgin were spoken of her. And as though she answers this [Note: [Col. 0107] The same manuscript inserts the word “Virgin.”], there follows:

> I am a wall, and my breasts are like a tower; from the time when I became before him as one finding peace.

“I am a wall,” that is, I have the firm resolve of virginity; this is what is read in the Gospel: “How shall this be, since I do not know a man?” (Luke 1)—that is, I have the intention not to know one. [Col. 0108A] “And my breasts are like a tower,” that is, my humility and virginity keep me immovably guarded, and are themselves immovable in me. “From the time when I became before him as one finding peace,” that is, from the time when I possessed humility and virginity, in which I especially pleased Christ and the angels, because like things delight in like things.

Note that he elegantly says “as one finding peace,” to indicate that in the world there is no true peace, but only a seeming peace and a shadow of peace. Hence Christ says to the disciples: “I give you my peace” (John 14), that is, for the future; but for now I leave you peace, that is, the remnants of peace. Nor is it surprising if Christ thus fortifies me, for Christ fortified his Church from the beginning, and first in righteous Abel. This is what follows:

**[Col. 0108B] 49. There was a vineyard for the Peaceful One, in that which has peoples; he entrusted it to keepers.**

“There was a vineyard for the Peaceful One,” that is, the Church was joined to Christ, which Christ, as the peaceful vinedresser, cultivated by redeeming it from sins, forming it in virtues, and delighting in its fruits—that is, its good works. That he was peaceful appears in the peace that holds peoples together; for unless he were peaceful, there would not yet be peace on earth between man and angel. For through him those things which are in heaven and those which are on earth have been reconciled (Col. 1).

Or the phrase “which has peoples” may be referred to the vineyard, that is, the Church, because the peoples converted to faith belong to the Church. Christ did not leave it carelessly, but entrusted [Col. 0108C] it to keepers—that is, to the preaching apostles and their successors, and also to the angels, who always guard it.

> A man brings a thousand silver pieces for its fruit.

Insofar as [Note: [Col. 0107] Manuscript: “to such an extent.”] that peaceful vinedresser cultivated it and gave it both the capacity to work and the reward of possessing peace, the man—that is, one not soft but strong—brings for its fruit the remuneration promised to the Church: a thousand silver pieces, that is, all his substance. For a thousand silver pieces signify everything that can be possessed in this world. The number one thousand is used for the fullness of perfection. Therefore the man brings a thousand silver pieces for fruit, because holy men leave everything and distribute it to the poor, that they may obtain the eternal reward. And what you say is true, [Col. 0108D] O Virgin, because:

> My vineyard is before me.

That is, I am with it until the consummation of the age.

> A thousand are yours, O Peaceful One [peacefully], and two hundred for those who guard its fruit.

As though he said: O Virgin Mary, you are certain of eternal reward, because a thousand belong to you, O Peaceful One. Perfection is signified by the number one thousand; by the term “peaceful,” eternal recompense is signified, in which true peace exists. Thus, by the thousand peaceful ones, the Virgin’s perfect recompense [Col. 0109A] is indicated. A double crown, in body and soul, together with the fruit of eternal life in heaven, is reserved for her; this is signified by the two hundred. Christ, still speaking to the Virgin, says:

> You who dwell in the gardens, your friends are listening.

As if he said: I have praised your beauty in many ways. But in this final address I admonish you of this:

> Make me hear your voice.

That is, your prayer; for whatever tribulation you cry to me from, I shall hear you. This, O Virgin Mary, is the meaning of “you who dwell in the gardens”: bodily, in the garden of the Church; spiritually, in the garden of virtues that spring up unto eternal life; [Col. 0109B] in the garden which is Christ through love, and in the garden of eternal life through hope, where you will subsequently dwell through sight. “Make me hear your voice,” that is, direct your voice to me, that I may fulfill it, because you cannot pray in a disordered way. This is so because your friends listen—that is, the angels who love and guard you, ever ready to report to me your words, thoughts, and works.

Since Christ had admonished the Virgin that after his Ascension she should direct her prayer to him, conversing with him in heart and voice, the Virgin afterward, consenting to Christ’s Ascension, says:

**50. Flee, my beloved, and make yourself like a gazelle and a young stag upon the mountains of spices.**

[Col. 0110A] By a remarkable exhortation Christ urges the Virgin to persist in prayer so that he may hear her voice; and she urges him to flee. Yet the sequence of the mystery is profound. For since Christ’s birth has been foretold above, when he said, “Who will give you to me as my brother,” etc.; and his Passion where it was said, “Under the apple tree I raised you up”; now, accordingly, the Mother urges the Son to flee—that is, to return with the greatest speed to the Father through the Ascension.

The sense is: You command me to persist in prayer, as you have ordained; I do not wish to oppose that ordinance. Flee—that is, when the mystery of the Incarnation and Passion has been completed, return to heaven, so that I may begin henceforth to think of and pray to you not as man, but always as God; then you will hear my voice. Yet do not let your visitation abandon me in [Col. 0110B] the present life. Deign frequently to visit me anew by an infusion of greater grace, and more often grant yourself to be seen by me. This is what she says: “Be like a gazelle and a young stag upon the mountains of spices.” Just as gazelles and young stags, untamed animals, flee human company, yet are more often seen in the mountains, so you too, after your Ascension, although invisible, deign to appear to me through greater gifts of your grace. And this is “upon the mountains of spices,” that is, upon the heights of virtues. The mountains of spices are called the excellences of virtues nearest to heavenly conduct, whose fragrance and renown of upright action spread far and wide.

**End of Alan of Lille’s exposition of the Song of Songs, composed in praise of the God-bearing Virgin Mary at the request of the prior of Cluny.** [Note: [Col. 0109] This final clause is added in the very ancient manuscript of St Martin at Tournai.]

[Col. 0109]

# SUMMARY OF MASTER ALAN, THE UNIVERSAL DOCTOR, ON THE ART OF PREACHING

*In which excellent concepts are suggested for framing sermons on almost every moral subject; now published for the first time.*

**51. TO THE READER.**

I had two manuscript copies of this *Summa*, on parchment, from our library at Dune: one written in very ancient characters and filled with the most obscure abbreviations of words; the other copied in a somewhat more recent hand, as it appears, and much fuller than the former. I have therefore followed the latter here, while noting in the margin the differences in words and meanings by which it differs here and there from the other copy. For readers’ benefit I have added the places of sacred Scripture corresponding to each proposition drawn from it and here set forth in the text.

# SUMMARY ON THE ART OF PREACHING

[Col. 0111]

**52. PREFACE OF THE AUTHOR**

[Col. 0111A]

He saw Jacob’s ladder reaching from earth to heaven, by which angels ascended and descended (Gen. 28). The ladder is the progress of the Catholic man, which is built up [Note: [Col. 0111] The other copy has, “is woven together.”] from the beginning of faith to the perfection of the complete man. On this ladder the first step is confession; the second, prayer; the third, thanksgiving; the fourth, searching the Scriptures; the fifth, when something doubtful occurs in Scripture, inquiry from one more learned; the sixth, exposition of Scripture; the seventh, preaching.

Therefore, a person repenting of sin must first set his foot on the first step of this ladder by confessing sin; second, he must ascend the second step by praying to the Lord that grace may be bestowed on him. The third step is ascended [Col. 0111B] through thanksgiving for the bestowal of grace. The ascent to the fourth step comes through scrutiny of Scripture, in order to preserve grace that has been bestowed; for sacred Scripture teaches how bestowed grace may be preserved. Then comes the fifth step, when a doubt arises and the reader seeks understanding from one more learned. The sixth step is ascended when the reader expounds sacred Scripture to others. He ascends the seventh step when he publicly preaches what he has learned from Scripture.

But because various writers have set forth diverse treatments of the other steps—how and when one ought to ascend through them [Note: [Col. 0111] Another copy reads: “But because concerning the other steps it is sufficiently clear how and when one ought to ascend through them, concerning which various writers, etc.”]—whereas concerning preaching, what it ought to be like, whose task it is, to whom it should be offered, and concerning what, how, [Col. 0111C] when, and where, few things have been said [Note: [Col. 0111] “Because few things have been said.”], we have judged it fitting at present to compose some treatise on these matters for the benefit of our neighbors.

First, therefore [Note: [Col. 0111] Another copy begins the chapter here, placing all that follows at its head: “First, therefore,” etc. Its title is: “What is preaching, and what ought it to be like?” etc.], one must consider what preaching is; what it ought to be like with respect to the surface of its words and the weight of its meanings; and how many kinds of it there are. Second, whose preaching should be; third, to whom it should be addressed; fourth, why; fifth, where.

## 53. CHAPTER ONE. On preaching: what it is and what it ought to be like, etc.

Preaching is a clear and public instruction in morals and faith, serving the formation of people, proceeding from the path of arguments and the wellspring of authorities. Preaching ought to be clear because it must be offered openly. Thus Christ says: “What I say to you in the ear, preach upon the rooftops” [Col. 0111D] (Matt. 10). For if preaching were secret, it would be suspect and would seem to have the odor of heretical doctrines. For heretics preach secretly in their conventicles [Col. 0112A] [Note: [Col. 0111] Another copy: “councils/conventicles.”], so that they may more easily deceive others.

It must be public because it is to be offered not to one person but to many. For if it were offered to only one, it would not be preaching but teaching. There is this difference between preaching, teaching, prophecy, and public address: preaching is the instruction given openly to many people, for moral formation; teaching is that given to one or to many for the education of knowledge; prophecy is admonition given through the revelation of future things; a public address is civic admonition delivered for the strengthening [Note: [Col. 0111] “Preservation.”] of the commonwealth.

By calling preaching an instruction in morals and faith, two parts of theology are indicated: the rational, which pursues knowledge concerning divine things; [Col. 0112B] and the moral, which promises instruction [Note: [Col. 0111] “Weakening.”] in morals. For preaching sometimes instructs in divine things and sometimes in morals; this is signified by the ascending and descending angels. These angels are preachers: they ascend when they preach heavenly things; they descend when, through moral matters, they adapt themselves to those below.

By the phrase “serving the formation of people,” the final cause, or usefulness, of preaching is indicated. And because preaching ought to be supported by arguments and strengthened by authorities, there follows: “proceeding from the path of arguments and the wellspring of authorities.” [Note: [Col. 0111] In another copy a new chapter begins here, entitled: “On spiritual preaching.”] Preaching itself ought not to contain buffoonish or childish words, or the melodies of rhythms and metrical harmonies, which are made more to soothe the ears than to instruct [Col. 0112C] the mind [Note: [Col. 0111] “Form.”]. Such preaching is theatrical and mimetic and therefore to be rejected in every way. Of such preaching the prophet says: “Your innkeepers mix water with wine” (Isa. 1).

In that preaching water is mixed with wine in which childish and buffoonish words, which in some way effeminate minds, are introduced. Preaching should not glitter with verbal trappings or the purple dyes of rhetorical ornaments, nor should it be debased by words too bloodless, but:

> The blessed have held the middle course.

For if it were too elaborately embellished, it would seem to have been devised with excessive care, and crafted more for human favor [Col. 0112D] [Note: [Col. 0111] “Human.”] than for the benefit of one’s neighbors; and so it would move the minds of listeners less. Those who preach in this way are comparable to the Pharisees, who enlarged their fringes [Col. 0113A] and broadened their phylacteries (Matt. 23).

Such preaching may be called suspect; yet it is not to be rejected, but tolerated. Thus the Apostle says: “By whatever occasion Christ is preached, in this I rejoice, and shall rejoice” (Phil. 1). Nor should [things] be inserted for Christ’s greater praise [Note: [Col. 0113] Another copy: “for the greater praise of the Christian religion.”], because Christ is no less angered by false praise than by truth denied. Such preaching is customary among heretics, who put forward true things and then insert false ones [Note: [Col. 0113] “Conclude false things.”], 54 concerning whom it is said: “The lamiae bared their breasts and suckled their sons” (Lam. 4) [Note: [Col. 0113] The text of Lam. 4 has “their cubs.”].

The *lamiae* have virginal faces but equine feet. Equine feet do not divide the hoof, but fix it firmly upon the earth [Note: [Col. 0113] “Drive it in.”]. Therefore heretics are understood by the *lamiae*: they display a virgin’s face [Col. 0113B] but end with the sting of a scorpion. For first they present true things and then conclude false ones. Their feet are equine because their affections are not divided in the love of God and neighbor [Note: [Col. 0113] “Because they do not divide their affections, etc.”], but fix all their affections upon earthly pleasures [Note: [Col. 0113] “Drive [them] in.”]. Such preaching is to be wholly rejected, because it is vicious and destructive.

In its propositions, however, preaching ought to possess weight, so that by the force of its propositions it may soften [Note: [Col. 0113] Another copy adds here: “Move [them] to tears.”] the minds of hearers, arouse the mind, bring forth contrition, shower with teachings, thunder with threats, soothe with promises, and thus be directed wholly to the benefit of one’s neighbors. For some people make earthly payment the end of their preaching; their preaching is therefore mercenary. Such persons [Col. 0113C] are hirelings rather than preachers; nevertheless their preaching should be heard and tolerated.

Thus the Lord says: “Do what they say; but do not do what they do” (Matt. 23). There are three kinds of preaching. One is in word, concerning which it is said: “Go, preach the Gospel to every creature,” etc. (Mark 16). Another is in writing; hence the Apostle says that he preached to the Corinthians (1 Cor. 5), because he wrote letters to them. Another is in deed; hence it is said: “Every action of Christ is our instruction.”

This should be the form of preaching: its beginning should be drawn from theological authority as from its proper foundation, especially from the Gospels, Psalms, Epistles of Paul, and books of Solomon, because moral instruction resounds especially in these. Authorities should therefore be taken from other [Col. 0113D] [Note: [Col. 0113] “Also.”] books of sacred Scripture if they are necessary and useful to the subject.

Next, the preacher must win the goodwill of the hearers by humility in his own person, and by the usefulness of the matter he proposes. He should say that he offers them the word of God so that it may bear fruit in their minds, not for earthly gain but for their advancement and progress; not because he is stirred by the empty shouts of the crowd, not because he is caressed by a favorable [Col. 0114A] breeze, not because he is delighted by theatrical applause, but so that their minds may be formed. They ought not to consider who speaks, but what [Note: [Col. 0113] Another copy: “Who is it that speaks?”]. For in a thorn bush one should not consider the thorn’s harshness, but the rose’s loveliness; indeed, honey is found [Note: [Col. 0113] “Received.”] even in a fragile reed, and flame is struck from stone. Next, he ought to show how useful it is to hear God’s word, if it is put into effect.

He should also promise to say a few useful things; that he is drawn to this only by love of his hearers; and that he does not speak because he possesses greater learning or prudence, or a better life. For things are sometimes revealed to one less great that are not revealed to one greater; then the greater ought to be silent. And because those greater than oneself sometimes refuse to preach, it is no wonder if lesser persons occasionally [Col. 0114B] stammer: if the learned are silent, the stones will speak or cry out.

Next, he should proceed to explain the authority he has proposed and turn the whole exposition to the instruction of the hearers. He should not propose an authority that is too obscure or difficult, lest the hearers become weary of it and thus listen less attentively. Nor, in expounding an authority, should he depart too quickly from his subject, lest the beginning disagree with the middle, or the middle with the end. He should also introduce other authorities to establish the point, especially those relevant to the subject.

He may also, when occasion arises [Note: [Col. 0113] “From knowledge of the cause.”], insert sayings of the Gentiles, just as the Apostle Paul sometimes inserts authorities from philosophers in his Epistles, [Col. 0114C] because he will have an elegant expression, 55 if, by a skillful joining, he renders a word new.

He should also insert stirring words that soften minds and bring forth tears. But the discourse should be concise, lest length produce weariness. When the preacher has discerned that minds have been softened, tears are flowing, and faces lowered, he should linger a little, but not too long; for, as Lucretius says, “Nothing dries more quickly than a tear.”

At the end, he should employ examples to prove what he intends, because exemplary teaching is familiar teaching. For example:

## CHAPTER II. On contempt for the world

[Col. 0114D] If a preacher wishes to invite hearers to contempt for the world, let him bring forward this authority: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity,” etc. (Eccles. 1). What authority so conveys the vanity of worldly things and the worthlessness of human beings, that all things are slippery and none stable, as this authority does? In accordance with this authority, he should distinguish a threefold vanity of the world. There is the vanity of mutability, the vanity of curiosity, and the vanity of falsity.

The vanity of mutability is that according to which [Col. 0115A] all things are naturally subject to change. Of it the Apostle says: “Every creature is subject to vanity” (Rom. 8). The vanity of curiosity is that according to which a person spends all care upon worldly matters. Hence: “The Lord scatters the thoughts of men, because they are vain” (Ps. 93; 1 Cor. 3). Of this the comic poet Persius says:

> O the cares of men! O how much emptiness there is in things!

The vanity of falsity is the eagerness for lying, of which it is said: “Each one has spoken vain things to his neighbor” (Ps. 11). Thus the preacher ought to strengthen every division he proposes with authorities; otherwise the whole division is unstable and slippery [Note: [Col. 0115] Another copy here inserts: “He should compare the members of the divisions with one another by certain compositions, for example: through the vanity of mutability man passes away; through the vanity of curiosity man kills himself; through the vanity of falsity he perishes spiritually. The vanity of mutability changes man; the vanity of curiosity exchanges man; the vanity of falsity changes man for the worse. Through the vanity of mutability man flows away; through the vanity of curiosity he flows out; through the vanity of falsity, he flows utterly away.”].

Next he should show where there is vanity, where vanity of vanities, and where all is vanity [Note: [Col. 0115] Another copy inserts: “How, in a person’s birth, there is vanity; in life, vanity of vanities; in death, all is vanity.”]. This is clear in all [Col. 0115B] worldly things: if riches come to a person, there is vanity, because they soon pass away; if they remain, they take the person away from himself—behold vanity of vanities; if they depart, all is vanity.

In riches there is the vanity of mutability, because they pass away; the vanity of curiosity, because people spend all their care upon them; and the vanity of falsity, because in acquiring or retaining riches people spew forth lies. Where is there greater vanity than in riches, which promise happiness but take it away, promise security but bring fear? Where is there greater fear than among the rich, who fear everything lest they lose their wealth? They do not trust their children; a wife’s love is suspect; they fear their superiors; they dread [Col. 0115C] thieves; they dream false things and disbelieve true ones. Where is greater vanity than in riches, which promise satiety and produce hunger, bring drunkenness from thirst, do not diminish desires but rather add to them, do not fill the mind but exhaust it, and are full with some unknown emptiness and empty with a kind of fullness?

Where is there vanity but in honors [Note: [Col. 0115] Another copy: “earthly honors.”], which favor a person in order to cast him down, raise him up in order to destroy him, suspend him in order to hurl him down more heavily? In them there is vanity of vanities, because honor is an unbearable burden, and a phantom honor lies in a burden; and in them all is vanity when they utterly 56 depart from a person [Note: [Col. 0115] Added: “Because the highest things are not permitted to stand long, and falls are grievous in excessive height.”].

There is vanity in worldly allurements when at first they flatter; vanity of vanities when they become wearisome; [Col. 0115D] and all is vanity when through them we are brought to death. First they make sweet as honey; second, they sting; third, they kill. Likewise, there is falsity in venial sin, falsity of falsities in mortal transgression, and all falsity in obstinacy. There is falsity in punishment, falsity of falsities in guilt, and all falsity in hell.

Therefore, abhorring vanity and fearing falsity, let us run [Col. 0116A] to the highest truth, that is, to God, in whom is truth of truths through the fulfillment of promises; in whom all is truth, because he is all in all (1 Cor. 12) among the saints.

Having thus established contempt for the world by the condition of temporal things, he should establish it also from its final cause, which consists of two things: the attainment of advantage and the avoidance of disadvantage. Contempt for the world is established through attaining an advantage thus: O man, if you despise the world, you shall have as your reward God, who is the world’s creator and lord. Through avoidance of disadvantage, contempt for the world can be established thus: O man, if you despise worldly and vain things, fear will not shake you, hope will not make you slack [Note: [Col. 0115] “You will not be relaxed by hope.”], sorrow will not constrain you, joy will not dissolve you. You will serve no one; [Col. 0116B] you will be free; you will not fear the assault of adversity; your conscience will be serene; you will peacefully await the coming of death; death will be welcome, and after death expectation blessed.

But if you cling to worldly pleasures, entangled in earthly allurements, your conscience will be seared, death hateful, and after death you will be shut up in eternal punishment. What courage will you then have, O man, when at death itself demons—horrible enemies—will appear to you, awaiting your soul in order to carry it to hell? Those whom you found flattering in life, you will find raging at death. Where then will be your delights? Where your earthly friendships? Where worldly pleasures? From riches will follow eternal poverty; from honors, abasement; from pleasures, perpetual [Col. 0116C] bitterness.

After this, the preacher should conclude his admonition with exemplary teaching, showing how the ancient Fathers despised the world. Yet the world then flourished when it withered in their hearts; now, when the world itself is withering, it ought not to flourish in our hearts. Rather, we ought to flee what flees, and abandon what slips away, lest we slip with what is slippery and fall with what is unstable [Note: [Col. 0115] “Falling.”].

## CHAPTER III. On contempt for oneself

If the preacher intends to invite hearers to contempt for themselves, let him bring forward this authority: “Remember, son, your last things, and you shall never sin” (Ecclus. 7). Or this: “I am a worm, and not a man” [Col. 0116D] (Ps. 21). Or again: “Man, born of woman, is filled with many miseries” (Job 14), etc.; or a similar passage in which human misery is expressed.

He should proceed thus: remember your last things; remember the last things of the world; remember the last things of the day. Remember your own last things by considering that your conception is guilt, your birth a kind of punishment, [Col. 0117A] your life a state of punishment, and your dying a necessity: that life either eludes you or promises its own absence, while death either presses near or threatens its imminence. Therefore, what ground has man for pride, whose conception is guilt, birth punishment, life labor, and death necessity?

O man, remember that you were fluid semen; how you are a vessel of excrement; how you will be food for worms. After death, a worm will arise from the tongue, to mark the sin of the tongue; intestinal worms from the stomach, to signify the sin of gluttony; a scorpion from the spine, to signify the sin of lust; a toad from the brain, to signify 57 the sin of pride. Therefore, man, you are a worm born from earth; a worm while you live, because intent on earthly things; a worm when you die, because given to worms as food.

Remember, O man, that you are earth and [Col. 0117B] shall go into earth; that you are ash and shall return to ash; that you are dust and shall be reduced to dust. Job said in your person: “I have said to corruption, ‘You are my father’; to the worms, ‘My mother and my sister’” (Job 17). O man, remember the last things of your beauty: how all flesh is grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass (Isa. 40); for:

> Beauty is a fragile good; and, as it advances in years,  
> It becomes smaller and is consumed by its own passage of time.

Remember how death destroys it, the scratch of a single needle kills it, sickness demolishes it, and old age plunders it. If you boast of strength, remember the last things of your strength: how old age weakens it, sickness enervates it, and death utterly uproots it. If you boast of wisdom, hear what the Lord says through Isaiah: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and reject the prudence of the prudent” [Col. 0117C] (Isa. 29; 1 Cor. 1). And elsewhere: “The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Cor. 3).

Consider how knowledge puffs up, but love builds up (1 Cor. 8). Consider how philosophers comprehended God’s invisible things through the things made, but, because they became vain in their thoughts, were handed over to a reprobate mind (Rom. 1). If you boast of lineage, remember the last things of every lineage:

> Every race of humankind rises from a similar origin.

For all share one condition of birth and one ending in death. Nobility that is achieved is better [Col. 0117D] than nobility that is born: the former is more universal, the latter more highborn.

Royal purple is not exempt from the rule of death, because death strikes equally at the palaces of kings and the huts of the poor. If you boast of riches and earthly pleasures, consider that they are rather snares than friendships, and that toward them you should be watchful and afraid rather than secure. Consider that naked you came forth from your mother’s womb, and naked you shall return there (Job 1). Learn to open your mother’s house to poverty and to keep pleasures under the yoke of reason [Note: [Col. 0117] Another copy here inserts: “I desire you to possess this thing, so that you may rejoice spiritually; let this joy never fail.”].

The fruit of earthly goods is superficial, and the brightness [Note: [Col. 0117] “Usefulness.”] of light metals shines upon the surface; those things are most rich whose vein lies hidden in the depths [Col. 0118A] and will continually yield more fully to the miner. Direct your mind toward these heavenly treasures, so that where your treasure is, there your heart may be. Therefore do not lay up treasure on earth, where thieves dig through and steal, but lay up treasures in heaven, which neither rust nor moth destroys (Matt. 6). For, as Seneca says: “Those things in which the crowd delights have a thin and superficial pleasure; and every joy of living things lacks a foundation.”

Learn, therefore, to trample underfoot those things that shine outwardly, which are granted to you by another or from another. Strive toward the true good, and rejoice in what is your own.

Do not boast of distinguished clothing. For what glory is there in sheep’s fleeces and the excrement of worms? What benefit is there in preparing the mud of the body, in gilding the dung-heap of the flesh? [Col. 0118B] Therefore remember your last things in the book of knowledge, so that you may read yourself in the book of experience and find yourself in the book of conscience: so that the book of knowledge written in a codex, and the book of experience written in the heart, may rebuke you.

In the book of knowledge you read: “Know yourself.” In the book of experience you read: “The flesh fights against the spirit” (Gal. 5). In the book of conscience you read:

> The cruel day circles about the mind  
> With unceasing wings.

O man, look at yourself in a threefold mirror, and you will displease yourself. There is a threefold mirror in which you ought to see yourself: the mirror of Scripture, the mirror of nature, [Col. 0118C] and the mirror of creation. In the mirror of Scripture you read your condition; in the mirror of creation you will see yourself wretched; in the mirror of your own nature you will consider yourself guilty.

Within your nature, however, a threefold mirror is reflected: the mirror of reason, sensuality, and flesh. As the philosopher says, there is one kind of mirror in which the left appears left and the right appears right. The right in this mirror is reason [Note: [Col. 0117] Another copy reads: “This mirror is reason, which declares, etc.”], which declares that the right-hand things—that is, heavenly things—are to be sought, and the left-hand things—that is, earthly things—are to be fled. But there is another mirror in which the right-hand parts appear left and the left-hand parts appear right: this is sensuality, which declares that earthly things are to be sought and heavenly things postponed.

Another mirror is one in which the face appears reversed [Col. 0118D]: this is the flesh, which turns the whole of human nature upside down. Therefore look at yourself in the mirror of reason, so that you may obey it; look at yourself in the mirror of sensuality, so that you may subject it to reason; look at yourself in the mirror of the flesh, so that by chastising it you may cast it down. And, that you may be able to overcome carnal things, place yourself in a threefold watchtower: first, in the watchtower of foresight, that you may guard against impending dangers; second, in the watchtower of circumspection, that you may avoid opposite vices, keep the mean, and go most safely by the middle way—for nature too is a friend of moderation; third, in the watchtower of caution, lest vice conceal itself beneath the cloak of virtue. For cruelty often pretends to be justice, and laxity mercy; and thus through the threefold watchtower you will attain the threefold mirror [Col. 0119A]: of a pure conscience, of divine contemplation, and of eternal life.

## Chapter IV. Against Gluttony

If a preacher wishes to invite his hearers to flee gluttony, he may use this authority: “I chastise my body and reduce it to servitude” (1 Cor. 9). Likewise: “Let us live soberly, justly, and piously in this world” (Titus 2). The body, I say, must be chastised so that it may serve us; it must be indulged, not served. For he who serves the body must serve many masters: he fears excessively on its behalf who refers everything to it. What is honourable is cheap to the person to whom the body is excessively dear. The Lord says in the Gospel: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with carousing and drunkenness and the cares of this life” (Luke 21). [Col. 0119B] Paul also says: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which is debauchery” (Eph. 5). Solomon likewise says: “Wine is a luxurious thing and drunkenness tumultuous; whoever delights in them is not wise” (Prov. 20). Jesus son of Sirach: “A drunken workman shall not grow rich. Wine and women cause even wise men to fall away and expose the prudent to rebuke” (Ecclus. 19). For a wise and learned man a little wine is sufficient: when sleeping, you will not be troubled by it, nor feel discomfort. Wine drunk in moderation is health for body and soul (Ecclus. 31).

> [Note: Col. 0119] Another copy inserts the following: Isaiah (ch. 5): “Woe to you who are mighty at drinking wine, men strong at mixing drunkenness.”

Isidore says: “Wherever satiety and drunkenness are found, there lust rules.”

> [Note: Col. 0119] “Show yourself sober in all things, that sobriety may show you pure.”

Therefore, O man, you ought so to conduct yourself that you may seem not to live for the body, but may be able, as though without a body, to use yourself and the best part of yourself. Regard the flesh more as a necessary thing than as a great one. From it pleasures arise only incidentally—brief, regrettable, and, unless restrained, immoderate and destined to turn into their opposite. [Col. 0119C]

> [Note: Col. 0119] There follows: “They rush headlong toward pain unless they keep measure; but it is difficult to keep them within measure in any other way.”

Therefore chastise the flesh, which is like a dog, a slave, or a beast of burden.

The more a slave is indulged, the more he is corrupted by idleness; the more a dog is beaten, the more he indulges in barking; the more a beast of burden is fed, the more it kicks against its master. How earnestly, then, must gluttony be avoided! It turns the body’s dwelling, the spirit’s and soul’s receptacle, into a dung-heap, and reduces the mass of our flesh to mud. It bends the soul—the true school of virtues, rule of reason, temple of the Godhead, [Col. 0119D] foundation of immortality—toward the pageant of vices, the feast of crimes, the mud of sin, the theatre of uncleanness.

This is gluttony, for which you engage in lawsuits, labour in military camps, serve the rich, endure their [59] arrogance, cloak flattery, and soften your speech. Therefore, in avoiding gluttony, do not serve the flesh; rather indulge it. Sustain it; do not fatten it. Govern it; do not exalt it. O man, do you know what gluttony is? Surely gluttony is the mind’s [Col. 0120A] tomb, a heap of dung, the origin of lust, the mother of nausea. O man, if it could speak, the stomach would complain of gluttony, saying: “O man, I demand what necessity requires; I reject what is superfluous. Do not give me things that burden me, but things that nourish me when I ask for them. I seek what nature asks and necessity demands; what is beyond this comes from evil.” For:

> A river and grain are enough for the people.

O man, why trouble yourself over the means by which excrement is produced and dung-heaps enlarged? Consider your nature; observe the stomach’s capacity. Do you know whence bodily infirmities and derangements of mind arise? Certainly from excessive food, from a flood or overflow of drink. Whence comes fever, if not from gluttony? Whence [Col. 0120B] epilepsy, if not from carousing? Does not paralysis arise from drunkenness, and dropsy from wine-bibbing? What is drunkenness but alienation of the mind, plundering of virtues, an image of death, a likeness of madness?

Through drunkenness grow insolent pride, cruelty toward a servant, and malice toward an envier. Drunkenness entangles speech, distorts sight, makes a man stumble in his wandering, brings torments to the stomach, distends the very entrails, and causes dizziness in the head. It drives out the mind’s very sense of shame and the guard upon the mouth; it expels the mark of modesty and breaks the seal of chastity. This is drunkenness, through which whatever evil lay hidden comes forth once excessive wine has taken possession of the mind. And just as a cask bursts with fermenting must and what is in the wine [Col. 0120C] rises to the top, so, when drunkenness floods in, the secret that lay hidden in the mind rises from the depths of the heart to the height of the mouth. For as wine travels from the stomach of the body to the mouth, so the secret comes forth from the stomach of the mind into words: as the drunkard cannot hold wine, so he vomits out his secret externally.

This is a daughter of idolatry, whose god is the belly (Phil. 3), which offers *latria*—divine worship—to Bacchus; hence it may, by a coined word, be called *bacchilatria*.

For he is quite an idolater who puts his belly before God, who worships Bacchus more than God, who rots in his carousing and, like a beast of burden, becomes foul in his own dung.

O man, consider the rich man (Luke 16), who feasted splendidly every day; consider, by contrast, [Col. 0120D] Lazarus, lying at his gate, covered with sores. The rich man rejoiced at the feast and was thereafter buried in hell; he feasted splendidly in life and after life thirsted for a drop of water. First he was clothed in purple; thereafter he was surrounded by the fire of Gehenna. Lazarus, however, was a beggar in life and after life was placed in Abraham’s bosom: poor here, rich there; covered with sores here, comforted there by blessed hope.

> [Note: Col. 0119] In another copy the following is added: “Surely, through the utmost misery we ought to aspire to that heavenly draught of wisdom which, when drunk, gives sobriety of mind, not to that which gives drunkenness to the mind. The drink that takes wisdom away must be avoided.”

[Col. 0121A] Consider, O man, how Adam through gluttony lost paradise; Elijah through abstinence ascended to heaven; Noah through gluttony exposed his thighs; Moses through abstinence deserved converse with God; Lot through drunkenness fell into incest; David through penitential abstinence obtained a remedy. O man, consult nature: it will tell you what ought to be the law of life. It is nature’s law that you should drive away hunger and thirst.
