For this there is no need to cross seas or follow armies: what nature desires is readily obtainable and at hand. Therefore take up arms against gluttony; fortify yourself against carousing. Take up the medicines of fasting against the attacks of so great a disease: fast from food, lest the flesh become wanton; fast from temporal pleasure, lest the mind grow weak; fast from sin, lest the spirit [Col. 0121B] grow torpid.

By this threefold fast we must chastise our beast of burden—that is, our flesh—lest it raise its heel against us. Our beast of burden must be corrected with a staff, spurs, bridle, and goad.

[60] For if our flesh wishes to stray into forbidden things, it must be checked with the bridle of discernment; corrected by fasts as by certain spurs; chastised by vigils as by certain staffs; and stirred up by the goad of fear.

## Chapter V. Against Lust

If a preacher wishes to instruct his hearers to flee lust, he may begin with this authority: “Flee fornication.” The Lord says in the Gospel: [Col. 0121C] “Let your loins be girded and lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 12). Paul says: “God will judge fornicators and adulterers” (Heb. 13). Solomon: “A harlot is a deep pit; she lies in wait on the road like a robber; those whom she sees off guard she kills” (Prov. 23). Jesus son of Sirach: “Do not give a woman power over your soul, lest she enter through your strength and you be put to shame” (Ecclus. 9). Jerome: “Woe to him whose limit to lust came only with the end of life. For chastity is difficult to preserve amid riches: shining skin displays a filthy mind; and lust rules alike in silks and rags. He who lives in luxury is dead while living; and he who becomes drunk is dead and buried.” Gregory: “While the belly is stretched by fullness, the sting of lust is roused.”

He who restrains the pleasure of a lustful suggestion does not proceed to lustful consent. If the pleasure of fornication delights the mind more than love of chastity, sin still reigns in that person. Every unclean defilement is called fornication. Better to die than to commit fornication; better to die than to be stained by lust. Lust plunges a human being into hell. Lust burns more fiercely the one whom it finds idle. Draw nearer to blazing fire than to a young woman when you yourself are young. Though material monsters [Col. 0122A] are to be fled and dreaded, spiritual monsters must far more be fled and driven away. What monster is more monstrous than lust, which bears on its head the face of a virgin and the image of pleasure; in its middle, the goat of fetid lust; and at its end, a she-wolf, through the plundering of virtue?

> [Note: Col. 0121] Another copy reads thus: “The image of pleasure; in the middle, a goat with the stench of lust.”

This is that pestilence which has a resemblance especially close to Gehenna. In Gehenna there are three things: a foul smell, the burning worm of conscience, and consuming flame. So lust stinks through disgrace, burns through conscience, and consumes through concupiscence.

> [Note: Col. 0121] Added: “O miserable fire of lust! In it gluttony is the fuel, concupiscence the flame, disgrace the smoke, uncleanness the ash. O dreadful pestilence of lust, which, sleeping in a person’s bosom, deceives him through flattery and turns him to stone.”

This is a pestilence more harmful than every monster: it empties the purse, enfeebles the body, intoxicates the mind, makes the mind’s disposition effeminate, defiles the soul, ruins reputation, injures one’s neighbour, and loses God. This is that pestilence in which what delights quickly passes [Col. 0122B], while what torments endures without end; whose desire brings anxiety and madness, whose act brings abomination and dishonour, and whose outcome brings repentance and shame. In this plague three things are detestable: burning in its onset, toil in its execution, and stench in its completion. See how base are lust’s chambers, full of dung: a hungry satiety, pleasure full of repentance, momentary delight, eternal bitterness. This is the pestilence that hates light, seeks darkness, looks for a covering, and sets a doorkeeper at the gate. This is the fly that ruins the sweetness of ointment: a fly is born from a dung-heap and dwells in filth; the place on which it settles is infected. This is lust, the daughter of gluttony—

> [Note: Col. 0121] Added in another copy: “The offspring of feasting”—

the stench born from the dung-heap of the flesh, the odour produced by the body’s mud. [Col. 0122C] It feeds on unclean things and delights in carnality.

Ointment, however, is chastity, in which the fragrant spices are purity of mind, cleanliness of body, modesty in [61] bearing, chastity in dress, abstinence in food, and restraint in speech. Lust corrupts this ointment, because it pollutes the mind, defiles the body, relaxes bearing, effeminates dress, enlarges one’s diet, and loosens speech. Thus lust assaults chastity with its own weapons, which are:

> Sight and conversation, touch and kisses, the deed.

First, lust entices a person through sight to desire and attacks chastity; second, through conversation it heaps insults upon chastity; third, through a kiss it spits in the face of modesty; fourth, [Col. 0122D] through touch it strikes chastity; fifth, through the deed it kills it. Battle against lust must be undertaken in the manner of the Parthians: just as the Parthians put their enemies to flight by fleeing and conquer by turning their backs, so lust must be driven away by flight and struck down by retreat.

This is the pestilence that comprises the three things by which a man is driven from his house: smoke, dripping, and a wife. The wife is carnality; dripping is the flowing instability of lust; smoke is the enormity of disgrace. These three drive the soul from the peace of the breast, the serenity of the mind, [Col. 0123A] and the tranquillity of the heart. O man, read in examples what the vice of lust brings about, so that another’s deed may be your lesson. David through lust fell into homicide; Amnon through incest experienced Absalom’s sword; Daniel through chastity merited understanding of dreams; Joseph through chastity the supremacy of Egypt; Jezebel through prostitution experienced the downfall of death; the blessed Virgin through virginity merited to give birth to God. Do you wish to avoid lust? Beware of gluttony, which is fuel for lust, a prologue to incest, a bridge to shamelessness, a preface to incontinence.

O man, this is lust through which imagination grows torpid, sensation dull, understanding darkened; indeed, to say more, it turns a human being into a beast. [Col. 0123B] Indeed, by it a person degenerates beneath a beast: for a beast observes the seasons of desire, whereas you desire at every hour; a beast observes nature, whereas you rage against it; a beast observes the unity of a mate, whereas you run after many.

## Chapter VI. Against Avarice

If a preacher wishes to incline his hearers’ minds to flee avarice and covetousness, let him begin his sermon with the authority that says “avarice is the service of idols” (Gal. 5), or with that which says “there are three insatiable things, and a fourth that never says, ‘Enough’” (Prov. 30), because:

> The more waters are drunk, the more they are thirsted for.

[Col. 0123C] O plague, than which nothing is better equipped for crime when the thirst to possess is inflamed! For:

> To what do you not compel mortal hearts,  
> accursed hunger for gold?  
> —Virgil, *Aeneid* III.56

Though all other things are bounded by fixed limits, avarice is enclosed by no limit. The earth is bounded by its borders, water by its confines, air by its limit; heaven is restricted by its bounds; avarice alone is not held within measure.

> [Note: Col. 0123] Another copy continues: “O plague crueller than a demon! The demon wished to be like God; it wishes to be more than God. This is avarice, for which, O man, you ruin yourself, run to lying, break treaties, deceive a friend, overturn kingdoms, and suffer shipwrecks!”

O man! For avarice many things arm themselves against you and complain of you: fortune, nature, your own flesh, charity, your neighbour, the world, and God. Hear what fortune says against you: “O man, why do you seek my intimacy? Why desire my favour? If [Col. 0123D] I give you riches, I give them in order to take them away; I bestow them in order to snatch them away; I flatter you in order to torment you more severely; I become serene in order to strike with lightning more terribly.”

> [Note: Col. 0123] Added: “I give light in order to darken more deeply.”

“You who are safe, why seek turbulence with me? You who stand on level ground, why aspire to my precipice? You who are in harbour, why long for my shipwreck?”

Hear what nature says against you: “O man, I gave you birth without honours; return without honours. I bore you [62] without riches; come back to me without riches. You entered without worldly glory; depart without it. O man, do you seek to make your own what belongs to another? Certainly those things are alien to you which were not born with you; they cannot be yours, since they cannot remain with you long or always.”

> [Note: Col. 0123] Omitted in our copy: “For what does it matter to him how much lies in his chest, [Col. 0125] how much in his granaries, how much he feeds or lends at interest, if he longs for what belongs to another, if he reckons not what he has acquired but what remains to be sought? Do you ask what measure of riches there is? The first measure is to have what is necessary; the second, what is enough. Consider that these goods of fortune are trifles and snares. Whoever wishes to live securely should avoid those baited benefits. He alone is happy who enjoys himself and does not depend upon another.”

Consider the philosopher’s saying: “Cheerful poverty is an honourable thing.” Yet it is not poverty if it is cheerful. The person to whom poverty agrees well is rich; not the one who has little, but the one who desires more, is poor. If you live according to nature, you will never be poor; if according to opinion, never rich. Nature desires little; opinion, the boundless. Natural desires are finite; those arising from false opinion have no point at which they cease.

For there is no limit to false opinion. Withdraw, therefore, from vain things; and when you wish to know whether [Col. 0124B] they have a natural desire or a blind one, consider whether they can stop anywhere. If, when you have advanced far, something farther always remains, it is unnatural. O how desirable is honourable poverty! Riches have hindered many from acting well. Poverty is unencumbered and secure. If you wish to serve God, you must either be poor or like a poor person.

Hear, O man, what your own flesh says against you: “O man, why do you complain against me? Why bring a complaint against me? Do you call me the tinder of sin, a tyrant raging in the members, the weakness of nature, the thorn of Satan? Why do you charge me with being afflicted by avarice and loosened by covetousness? I could bring more complaints against you, advance more arguments: while I lie without tinder and languish without incentive, you provoke me to covetousness, you stir me to avarice; you give me arms with which to fight against you, you give me instruments with which to contend; you incite me to strike, you invite me to rage.” [Col. 0124C]

Hear what charity says against you: “O man, why do you enrich yourself with things your neighbour needs? Why appropriate to yourself things that ought to be shared with the poor? Why do you feed moths and worms with what ought to feed the poor? Do you wish to be the finest merchant, an excellent moneylender, and a prudent trader? Give what you cannot retain, that you may obtain what you cannot lose. Give a little, that you may obtain a hundredfold. Give away an alien possession, that you may obtain an eternal inheritance.”

[Col. 0124D] Hear what your neighbour says against you: “O man, why do you wrong me? Why do you plot death against me for the sake of what is mine? Why do you bring false charges and fabricate crimes, in order to empty my purse and squeeze out my money? If you wrong me, vengeance will be taken upon you at once; if you plunder me of money, you will first plunder yourself in soul; if you wound me in body, you will first be wounded in mind.”

Hear what the elements say against you, and especially [Col. 0125A] the earth, your mother: “Why do you wrong your mother? Why do you inflict violence upon me, who brought you forth from my entrails? Why do you harass me with the plough, that I may render a hundredfold interest? Why harass your mother so that I may vomit forth gold? Are the things I freely bestow upon you not sufficient unless you extort them by violence? A time will come when you will return to your own origin, when I shall receive you and enclose you in my entrails, when I shall expose you to worms—you who exposed me to blows.”

Hear what the sea says against you: “O man, why do you furrow me with ships, beat me with oars, search my entrails with nets? It is no wonder if I drown you, bring shipwreck upon you, and assail you with storms and diverse blows.”

Hear what God says against you: “What is this, O [Col. 0125B] man, that you place your Creator [63] after the creature? Do you prefer a coin to him, the creature to God, earth to heaven, the perishable to the heavenly, the transitory to the eternal? Consider that I made you from mud and formed you in my image; consider that my hands made you and fashioned you wholly round about.”

> [Note: Col. 0125] There follows: “Consider that I clothed you with skin and flesh and bound you together with bones and sinews. Why do you despise me and stand convicted of such great ingratitude?”

“Would you be grateful to a man for money, yet ungrateful to me for life? If you are not grateful for gifts already given, at least be grateful for those yet to be given; so that, if what I have given does not move you, at least what I promise may move you; and if hope of eternal life does not move you, may fear of Gehenna move you.”

Thus warned, let man avoid avarice and not set his heart upon riches—

> [Note: Col. 0125] “Let him flee covetousness and lay aside ambition”—

because Scripture says: “As difficult as it is for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle, so difficult is it for those who trust in money to enter [Col. 0125C] the kingdom of God” (Matt. 19). Paul likewise says: “Covetousness is the root of all evils. In seeking it, some have gone astray and entangled themselves in many sorrows” (1 Tim. 6). Covetousness profits no one in whom covetousness dwells. Avarice and love of money are worse than every sin. Hence the Lord in the Gospel says: “Beware of all avarice” (Luke 12). And Paul: “No fornicator, unclean person, or covetous person has an inheritance in the kingdom of God” (Eph. 5). Likewise Solomon: “The greedy person is not satisfied with money” (Eccles. 5). And: “He who loves riches will not receive fruit from them” (ibid.). Cyprian likewise says: “An avaricious man is like hell.” Another has said: “The avaricious man lacks what he has as much as what he does not have.” Brothers, you leave many things behind [Col. 0125D] if you renounce desires; for God asks for the heart and does not count napkins.

## Chapter VII. Against Sloth

If a preacher wishes to arm a person against sloth, let him use these authorities: “The sluggard shall be stoned with the dung of oxen” (Ecclus. 22). Likewise: “Rise, you who sleep, and Christ will enlighten you” (Eph. 5). Likewise: [Col. 0126A] “You who lie in tombs, rise and hasten to meet the judgement of the Saviour.” Seneca also says: “The greatest loss is that which occurs through negligence.”

From these the preacher should proceed as follows: Dearest brothers, see how Scripture arms us against sloth or laziness. This is the sloth that draws the Christian’s hand back from the plough; that looks back into Sodom with Lot’s wife; that fears to climb the mountain with Lot; that refuses to return with Ruth to the land of Bethlehem. This is the sloth that makes a monk’s vow grow lukewarm, through which he loathes the rigor of the cloistered order; that wishes to use more delicate foods, recline upon softer bedding, attend fewer vigils, and practise less silence—or none at all. This is the sloth that fears to undertake great things, loathes what it has begun, finds everything burdensome, everything difficult, and nothing light. [Col. 0126B] It keeps the cleric from study, excludes the cloistered person from the cloister, nourishes vices, and shuts out virtues. For it produces lust, nourishes gluttony, sows detractions, and begets quarrels. Hence the poet:

> Why is Aegisthus said to have become an adulterer?  
> The reason is ready: he was idle.  
> —Ovid, *Remedies for Love* I

To such a sluggard it is said: “Rise, you who sleep.” The sluggard, I say, sleeps with the eyes of his mind closed: he neither directs his gaze toward good things nor opens the mind’s eye to see what is necessary. But while he bends himself toward earthly things in desire, he is placed in the sleep of the mind and, as it were, dreams phantasms. There are three kinds of sleep. The first and highest is that of contemplation, by which a person is caught up to see heavenly things. The second is that of imagination, by which visible things are imagined. The third is that of laziness, by which foolish things are dreamed. Of the first it is said: “The Lord sent sleep upon Adam” (Gen. 2). Of the second it is said [Col. 0126C] that God gave Solomon wisdom in dreams (3 Kings 3). Of the third it is said against the sluggard: “Rise, you who sleep,” etc. (Eph. 5). By the first sleep a human being becomes [64] God; by the second a human being becomes spirit; by the third, a beast. In the first God appears, in the second a spirit, in the third the devil.

Ish-bosheth was torpid in this sleep at midday (2 Kings 4), when, while the female doorkeeper slept, the chiefs of robbers entered and cut off the head of the sleeping man. The sleeping Ish-bosheth is the soul lulled by the sleep of idleness. The chiefs of robbers—that is, demons—enter it to kill it, because, while reason’s circumspection guards the gate of the mind less vigilantly, the devil cunningly enters through this gate to kill the soul. This sleep of torpor is induced by whispering, a gentle breeze, shade, or excessive weariness. [Col. 0127A] For just as bodily sleep is induced by a soft murmur of a fountain, a gentle breeze, or the sweetness of song, so the mind is led into the sleep of torpor by the prompting of prosperity, as by the breath of a gentle breeze, or by the whisper of carnal pleasure. The shade of ignorance also produces this sleep; the fatigue of honourable labour likewise gives rise to it.

To the sleeper Scripture cries: “Rise, you who sleep” (Eph. 5). Rise, I say, through reason’s circumspection; rise through rejection of evil; rise through doing good; “and Christ will enlighten you” (ibid.), because night has passed and day has drawn near.

> [Note: Col. 0127] Another copy reads: “Let him who sleeps the sleep of sloth therefore cry to the Lord: ‘Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?’ O God, who are the true Samaritan, the true guardian of soul and body, why do you not deliver me from the death of idleness, from the darkness of sloth? If a person cries this with the whole intention of his mind, he will hear the Lord saying: ‘Morning comes and night withdraws,’ as if to say: when you strive to keep watch for me and shake off torpor, behold, I offer you the morning of eternal illumination, the dawn of heavenly grace; and thus the night of negligence will withdraw, provided that you strive to persevere in vigils.”

Therefore you who lie in the tombs of negligence, whitewashed outwardly with respect to the outward surface of righteousness, but inwardly foul through the mind’s torpor and dissolved into worms [Col. 0127B] by the multitude of wicked thoughts: rise from earth to heaven, from idleness to exertion, from ruinous torpor to the work of virtue, and hasten to meet the judgement of the Saviour.

> [Note: Col. 0127] In another copy: “So that he who judges you with the judgment of discernment may find you at work, and thus in the future may exclude from you the judgment of condemnation.”

Hear what Scripture says: “The sluggard shall be stoned with the dung of oxen” (Ecclus. 22). The ox is one who labours on the Lord’s threshing-floor, who chews Holy Scripture with spiritual understanding as it were with his teeth, draws spiritual understanding from Holy Scripture, and conveys it into the mind’s delight as into a stomach. From this spiritual food, the literal surface is cast out as dung: it sometimes savours of heresy and kills by torpor the person who is sluggish in understanding the Scriptures.

O man, why is it that other creatures devote themselves to their appointed duties? The sun completes its yearly course; the moon runs through its monthly changes; the other stars perform their assigned offices; brute animals do not grow torpid in their natural activities—yet you alone, lulled by idleness, depart from your office, disfigure God’s image in yourself, die while living, and live while dying? Let at least the diligence of the least and lowliest creature, namely the ant’s foresight, move you to shame: in summer it gathers grains with great diligence, by which it may live when winter’s severity comes on. Thus in the present life you ought to acquire the fruits of good works, so that when the wintry day comes—that is, on the day of judgement—you may have fruits of good works to refresh you for eternity. [Col. 0127C]

See, then, how ruinous sluggishness is. So long as David exercised himself in war, lust did not assail him; but after he sat down in the palace, he fell into adultery. So long as Samson had battle with the Philistines, he was not captured by enemies; but sleeping in Delilah’s lap, he was blinded by the enemy. Solomon, [Col. 0128A] while labouring at the building of the Temple, did not experience the ruin of lust; but, released from labour, he experienced the assaults of wantonness. This is idleness, which offers a person unarmed to the devil, exposes him naked to suggestion, and weak to temptation. It deprives a person of the spiritual goods—

> [Note: Col. 0127] “For goods” another reading has “weapons”—

of the garments of virtues. It summons the devil to battle, the flesh to wantonness, the mouth to gluttony, and the mind to negligence. Therefore be occupied in honourable [65] work, so that by what is to come you may redeem what you lost in the past. Embrace every hour; make every moment serve your benefit, so that at least you may offer God the dregs of old age—you who offered the devil the flower of youth; so that at least in old age you may become a soldier of Christ—you who in youth were the devil’s servant.

## Chapter VIII. Against Envy

[Col. 0128B]

Against envy a preacher may arm his hearers with these authorities. The Lord says in the Gospel: “Do not envy one another.” Likewise Peter says: “Putting away all malice, all guile, hypocrisies, detractions, and every envy” (1 Pet. 2).

> [Note: Col. 0127] Chapter 8. In another copy the following is inserted here: Paul also says: “Charity is not envious” (1 Cor. 13).

Solomon says: “The life of the flesh is health of heart; envy is rottenness of the bones” (Prov. 14). Augustine likewise says:

> [Note: Col. 0127] St Prosper, book III, *On the Contemplative Life*, ch. 5.

“Envy burns up all virtues. The envious person is surely one who, through envy, makes another’s good his own punishment.” Isidore says of the same: “From that by which the good person prospers, the evil or envious person wastes away.” Another authority says: “Through the envy [Col. 0128C] of the devil death entered into the world” (Wis. 2). Likewise the poet:

> There is no laughter except that produced by the sight of pain.

Likewise:

> The Sicilian tyrants found  
> no greater torment than envy.  
> —Horace, *Epistles* I.2.5–8

In accordance with these authorities, the preacher should proceed thus: You have heard, dearest brothers, how Holy Scripture pursues the pestilence of envy and execrates the evil of spite. Therefore the pestilence of envy must especially be avoided, since it first torments itself and afflicts its own possessor; it harms itself before it wounds another, and its own wounds return upon itself. It grieves at another’s prosperity, mourns another’s joys, and rejoices in [Col. 0128D] another’s adversity. O vice, more contemptible than every vice and more debased than every plague! Virtue troubles it, happiness afflicts it, blessedness torments it, joy crucifies it! Though the other vices have some fleeting pleasure, a shadow of joy, an image of happiness, this pestilence is torment without relief, disease without remedy, labour without respite, punishment without interruption. This is the sin that punishes itself and does not leave itself unpunished; at once it defiles and tortures, at once it punishes and corrupts. This is the worm born from manna; this is the worm by which Jonah’s ivy is dried up (ch. 4); this is the fiery serpent by which the children of Israel are stung; this is the locust by which the fruits of the earth are devoured. [Col. 0129A]

We read that manna was given from heaven to the children of Israel (Exod. 16), and that, when it was stored up, a multitude of worms issued from it. Thus, from heavenly grace bestowed upon a faithful person, envy arises incidentally in the mind of the proud; and the more the faithful person is strengthened in the manna of heavenly grace, the more the proud person’s mind dissolves into the worm of envy. We read that a worm born from the ivy, by whose shade Jonah (ch. 4) was shielded from the attack of heat, gnawed the ivy away to its roots. Thus envy, like a worm born from the brightness of virtue, wholly gnaws away the purity of conscience by which a person ought to defend himself against the heats of vices, and exposes Jonah’s head—that is, the human mind—to the heats of vices. We read that fiery serpents stung the children of Israel wandering in the desert (Num. 21). Thus cloistered persons exiled in this wilderness of the world, who ought to be true children of Israel, frequently suffer from envy; for this worm dwells in ashes and haircloth and, lurking in the dust, stings unto death. This is the moth that destroys the purple garments of virtues. This is [Col. 0129C] the rust that plunders the treasure of wisdom. This locust consumes the earth’s green growth: whatever good work flourishes in a person, it destroys.

This is the pestilence that cast an angel out of heaven and banished humankind from paradise. [66] It struck the children of Israel in the wilderness; it armed Joseph’s brothers against him; it cast Daniel into the lions’ den; it finally fastened our Head to the gibbet of the cross. O man, what benefit is there to you if you envy, what gain if you are envious? You open a snare and dig it out, and do you yourself fall into the pit you make? While you labour to bind others, you yourself are bound; while you seek to defraud others, you are deceived. O man, you attack nature, wage war against charity, trouble yourself, go astray against your neighbour, and offend God. Whereas you ought to make another’s [Col. 0129D] joys your own by rejoicing with them, and another’s sorrow your own by suffering with them; whereas in another’s misery you ought to read your own misery and recognize in yourself your neighbour’s condition. Where does spite tend? Where does jealousy leap? Where is envy carried? It breaks the bond of friendship, the glue of charity, the covenant of love, and the law of natural justice.

## Chapter IX. Against Anger

If a preacher wishes to arm a person against anger, let him use these authorities: “Everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgement” (Matt. 5). And Paul says: “Let not the sun set upon your anger” (Eph. [Col. 0130A] 4). And James: “The anger of man does not work the righteousness of God” (Jas. 1). And Solomon: “Fools immediately reveal their anger; but he who conceals his anger is prudent” (Prov. 12). “An angry man provokes quarrels; one who is patient calms those that have been stirred up” (Prov. 15). “Anger rests in the bosom of a fool” (Eccles. 7). Gregory: “Who can endure a spirit easily inclined to anger?” And in the Psalm: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. 4); the poet also says:

Anger is a brief madness: rule your mind; unless it obeys,

it commands. Restrain it with reins; curb it with chains. And Claudian says:

If you are moved by fear, if you desire what is wrong, if you are led by anger,

you will endure the yoke of slavery.

Behold the authorities with which a Catholic ought to arm himself against anger as with spiritual weapons. See, O man, how fruitful anger is in evil offspring. From anger proceeds the rancour of hatred. For what is hatred but anger grown old? From it are born murder, insult, detraction, and injury. O man, if you are angry, if you hate your neighbour, you contradict yourself when in prayer you cry to the Lord: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6). With what face do you ask that debts be forgiven you, when you do not release your neighbour from the rancour of your heart?

There are three kinds of anger. One arises in the mind but is not carried as far as outward anger. This is the anger of which it is said: “Whoever is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment” (Matt. 5). For one who conceives and retains anger inwardly [Col. 0130C] will not escape the judgment of eternal condemnation. This anger is signified by the dead daughter of the ruler of the synagogue in her chamber.

There is another anger which proceeds as far as general insults. It is more serious and nearer to Gehenna; of it it is said: “Whoever says to his brother, Raca”—that is, who heaps general insults upon him—“shall be liable to the council” (ibid.), that is, liable to a more serious judgment. This is signified by the widow’s son (Luke 7). For when someone is stirred from the mind outward into the act of anger, the soul is borne dead beyond the enclosure of the mind into the practice of wicked action. But when an insult bursts forth into specific acts of malice, it rages more gravely. Of this it is said: “Whoever says to his brother, ‘Fool,’ shall be liable to the fire of Gehenna” (Matt. 5).

[Col. 0130D] For the graver the insults, the more the person who inflicts them corrupts another with the stench of disgrace. If anger arises in the mind, let it be restrained at once: for little ones must be dashed against the rock before they grow; little foxes must be caught before they gnaw away the vineyard; the firstborn must be slain in the morning; and the Canaanite must be driven out of the land of promise. Thus “let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Eph. 4).

For we must be angry at the first stirrings in such a way that we do not sin by consent. It is human to rise in anger, but devilish to persist in it. It is not shameful to be angry, but it is shameful to fall into fault.  
[Note: [Col. 0129] In another copy the following occurs: “For if anger persists, the Sun of Justice will set upon it”—[Col. 0131] Christ, who works in us in the morning, when grace is poured into us. Then indeed the dawn of grace rises within us, while day breaks in us through the light of justification. Then the sun tends toward noon, when greater charity burns in the mind. But it tends toward evening when charity feels the little cloud of the body. Yet when the clouds of anger arise, the rays of the heavenly sun withdraw themselves from the human mind. O man, flee anger, which is the enemy of wisdom: it degenerates from reason, exceeds the measure of justice, breaks friendship and concord, and takes away the peace of the heart, the Sabbath of eternity.]

O [Col. 0131A] man, hear what the teaching of the heavenly Master says: “If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there,” etc. (Matt. 5). There you have it: if you wish to offer your material gift at the altar, you ought first to be reconciled with your brother if you retain rancour in your mind; for the offering of an outward gift profits nothing unless inward tranquillity of mind is offered to God. Likewise, if at the altar of faith you wish to offer the sacrifice of good action, first drive the clouds of rancour from your mind. For if your brother sins against you, you must forgive him not merely seven times, but seventy times seven (Matt. 18). Our head, Jesus Christ, at the moment of his Passion prayed for his persecutors, and Stephen, the chief among the martyrs, [Col. 0131B] interceded for those who stoned him (Acts 7). Even if we are not of such perfection as to return good for evil, at least let us by no means repay evil for evil.

We ought often to recall what the teaching of the Gospel parable impresses upon us: we read there of the man whose master forgave his debt, but who would not forgive his own debtor; therefore he was cast into prison and compelled to pay to the last farthing (Matt. 18). Likewise, if someone does not forgive injuries to his neighbour, the supreme Exactor will exact penalties from him for every fault.  
[Note: [Col. 0131] Yet injuries are not to be forgiven through negligence, as the philosopher says, but rather through wisdom. O how great is the stain of fraternal hatred, through which sins return, vice sprouts anew, and a person suffers a relapse of illness! O man, consider that you should not do to another what you would not wish done to yourself (Tob. 4).]

When you retain rancour in your mind, you do not harm your enemy, but destroy yourself in soul; you punish yourself inwardly through rancour while wishing to oppose another. [Col. 0131C] What is this malice? What vengeance is this, in which, while you wish to hold your enemy, you are held; while you wish to strike your foe, you destroy yourself? Attend carefully and understand more cautiously that commandment: “Love your enemies, and do good to those who hate you” (Matt. 5).

## CHAPTER X. Against Pride

If a preacher intends to stir his hearers to flee pride, let him employ these authorities: “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled” (Luke 14). Again: “What is exalted among men is an abomination before God” (Luke 16). Again Paul: “Do not think high things, but fear” (Rom. 11). Again Jesus son of Sirach: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. 10). Again: “He has cast down the mighty from their seat and exalted the humble” (Luke 1). Again Peter: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (1 Pet. 5; Jas. 4).

O man, consider what pride takes away, and what humility, the foster-child of virtues, bestows. Pride made demons out of angels; [Col. 0132A] humility, however, makes human beings like the holy angels. Pride is heavenly by birth, yet hides in ashes and sackcloth. Let the cloistered religious take care not to say with the Pharisee: “I am not like other men” (Luke 18). Rather, let him cry: “I am a worm and no man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people” (Ps. 21). If he is learned, let him not thunder with the Pharisee: “Our lips are our own; who is lord over us?” (Ps. 11). Rather, let him cry with the tax collector: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18).

O man, it is yours to take the lowest place; it is dangerous to stand on a precipice. To the humble the Lord says: “I am the dew, and Israel shall blossom like the lily” (Hos. 14). The lily grows better in the valley than upon the mountain, because there [Col. 0132B] it is more abundantly nourished by water, retains its greenness longer, and preserves its whiteness more enduringly. Hence it is called “the lily of the valleys” (Song 2). Thus the one who is true Israel, truly seeing the Lord, planted in the valley of humility, is more abundantly nourished by the water of heavenly grace and blossoms more richly in spiritual things.

He retains more fully the brightness of charity and the whiteness of innocence.  
[Note: [Col. 0131] St Gregory, *Homilies on Matthew*, 25.] “Therefore, the greater the gift that anyone has received, the humbler he ought to be, because he sees himself more obligated to render an account.” Indeed, whatever works there may be are deprived of their merit unless they are seasoned with the sweetness of humility. For [Note: [Col. 0131] St Gregory, *On Psalm 3, Penitential*.] “he who gathers virtues without humility is like one who carries dust into the wind.”

This is the humility that cries: “Let him who is greater become as one who serves” (Luke 22). And elsewhere: “The greater you are, humble [Col. 0132C] yourself in all things” (Ecclus. 3). This is what caused the Son of God to descend from the bosom of the Father into the womb of the Virgin; what wrapped him in lowly swaddling-clothes so that he might clothe us in the adornments of virtue; what had him circumcised in the flesh so that he might circumcise us in mind; what allowed him to be scourged bodily so that he might free us from the scourge of sin; what crowned our King with thorns so that he might crown us, his servants, with the roses of eternal blessedness.

O how unlike humility is pride! Pride cast Lucifer out of heaven, deprived Adam of paradise, and transformed Nebuchadnezzar into a beast. This is pride: while it insolently raises itself above itself, it falls ruinously beneath itself. While it seeks itself outside itself, it does not find itself within itself. It makes a human being special within the generality, singular within the universality, solitary in public, and private in an assembly. It was the first thing to cast humanity down, and it is the last thing to oppose a person returning to the Lord.

[Col. 0133A]

When you fight well, when you suppose that all things have been subdued,

then pride remains as the evil still to be conquered.

This is what feminizes one’s bearing, puts one’s manner outside the rule; through it words overflow, threats thunder, what is lacking is claimed, and what is present is disregarded. It delivered philosophers over to a reprobate mind, blinded the Jew, destroys the obstinate, and casts down the exalted.

[Note: [Col. 0133] In another copy the following was inserted here: Pride strikes prelates, raises the rich into arrogance, and deceives religious persons. It blinds a person so that he cannot know himself, and by a kind of illusion deceives him, so that he neither believes of himself what he is nor thinks of himself what he is not.]

It is signified by the north wind when it is said: “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind” (Song 4). The north wind is hostile to flowers, ravages the grasses, and binds waters with frost. So pride acts as a stepmother toward good things, destroys the fruit of work, and binds the mind with the frost of perversity. Of it it is said: “Every evil is opened from the north” (Jer. 1), because pride is the mother of every wickedness. [Col. 0133B] It is also said of this: “What do you see, Jeremiah? I see a boiling pot from the north” (ibid.). This pot belongs to the servants of pride: in it are boiled the children of darkness, followers of honours, hunters after riches, those who seek the chief seats, who wish to be greeted in the marketplace and called rabbi by men. Nebuchadnezzar—that is, the devil—kindles this pot; the arrogance of pride supplies its flame; the proud person is boiled in it; Egypt consumes what has been boiled—that is, the unclean spirit draws him into its own body and subsequently carries him off into hell.

Pride is a wind that casts dust from the face of the earth, because it expels the proud from the stability of eternal life. It is a swelling that repels medicines poured into it, because pride does not receive offered grace. [Col. 0133C] There are four kinds of pride, which, like four winds, blow through the whole world because they inflate worldly people with swellings: arrogance, which ascribes to itself what it does not possess; insolence, which appropriates to itself what it owes to others; haughtiness, which believes many things of itself beyond the truth; and obstinacy, which exalts itself above a prelate. These are the four smiths who shake the whole world and present various phantasms to human beings.

## CHAPTER XI. On Contempt for Worldly Fear

If the preacher wishes to invite his hearers to contempt for worldly fear and to desire for heavenly fear, let him use these authorities: “Do not fear [Col. 0133D] those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matt. 10). In the book of Wisdom it is read: “Fear God and keep his commandments” (Eccl. 12). Again elsewhere: “Blessed is he who is always fearful” (Prov. 28). And again: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. It shall go well in the end for those who fear God, and they shall be blessed in the day of his protection” (Ecclus. 1).

[Col. 0134A] “Those who fear the Lord keep his commandments and shall have patience until his visitation” (Ecclus. 2). Jerome says: “Nothing keeps us so free from sin as fear of punishment and love of God.” Gregory says: “To fear God is to omit none of the good things that ought to be done.” From these authorities one should proceed thus:

O man, every worldly fear must especially be avoided: it flees tribulations before they come; it magnifies pain amid torments; in prosperity it gives birth to adversity, and in joy to sadness and death. It is the worst augur in uncertainties, a liar in truths, abundant in falsehoods. It helps its possessor toward no good unless the mind is prepared for its loss.

Therefore, against everything that may happen, [Col. 0134B] exhort yourself even most forcefully.  
[Note: [Col. 0133] Added in another copy: “And harden yourself.”]

Even the end of desires contributes to remedies against fear, and, as Seneca says: “Fear follows hope.” Foresight, the greatest good of the human condition, has been turned into an evil. Beasts flee dangers that they see when they can safely escape them; we are tormented both by what is to come and by what has passed. Many of our goods harm us. Memory recalls the torment of fear; foresight anticipates it. No one is miserable only in present things.

O man, conquer fear, the conqueror of all; if you conquer it, adversity will be prosperous, tribulation sweet, and pain delightful. O man, do you wish to escape fear and set earthly things aside? Do not cling to earthly things; do not indulge transient things. If you love earthly things, you fear giving offence and fear loss. If you wish to conquer fear, fear God. [Col. 0134C] Thus art is deceived by art; thus one nail is blunted by another. Fear God so that you may not fear; serve God so that you may not be enslaved; and keep his commandments in mind.  
[Note: [Col. 0133] Added: “So that you may be able to say, ‘Your commandments are my meditation.’ Keep them with your mouth, so that you may cry to the Lord, ‘I shall teach the wicked your ways’; keep them in deed, so that you may say, ‘I have sought your commandments exceedingly.’”]

This is the whole human being—that is, every human being has been made for this purpose: to read within himself the whole power of God. Set yourself, O man, between two millstones: the millstone of fear and that of hope. Hope in such a way that the mind does not grow slack; fear in such a way that thought does not become overextended.

O man, do not fear the imminence of death, nor refuse the military service of life. The latter gives the just person greater merit; the former bestows his pay. Consider not how long you live but how. One must not take care to live long, but to live well enough. To live long belongs to circumstance; to live well enough belongs to the mind. Life is long if it is full; and the mind is made full when it renders itself full of virtues [Col. 0134D] and does not recoil from its own mastery over itself. What does it profit a man if he has spent eighty years in the torpor of idleness? He has not lived, but lingered in life; he did not die late, but merely died after a long time. But that person dies full of days who makes old age weighty through virtue, who extends a constrained lifetime by merits. For though his age be incomplete, his life is nevertheless complete.  
[Note: [Col. 0133] Do you ask, O man, what span of life is the highest? To fear until wisdom: whoever reaches that end has attained an end not the longest, but the greatest.]

I beseech you, O man, [Col. 0135A] live in such a way that, just as you consider precious things to depend upon chance, you do not doubt that the span of life hangs in the balance. Let us measure it by action, not by time. Let a person recover by good action what he has lost in passing time. We do not suddenly fall into death, but proceed toward it little by little: every day we die; every day we take away something from life. Let us ensure that, as much as temporal life decreases, eternal life increases. Let the loss of temporal life become an increase of eternal life.

Let us arm ourselves with patience for life’s course and for death’s assault. For we must be admonished and strengthened for both, so that we neither love life too much nor fear death’s attack too greatly, but weigh both in the balance of reason. Otherwise there is an unconsidered inclination of mind toward dying, since some, weighed down by idleness, wish to end their weariness by death. [Col. 0135B] The adversity of worldly trouble ought not to drive a person to death; rather, the ardour of divine charity ought to do so, so that a person does not place the end of desire at the point of death, but rather in desire for eternal blessedness.

## CHAPTER XII. On Hope for Heavenly Things and Contempt for Earthly Things

If a preacher wishes to invite his hearers to hope for heavenly things and restrain them from hope in earthly things, he ought to use authorities which foster the former hope and draw the mind away from the latter. For example: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh [Col. 0135C] his arm” (Jer. 17). Again: “How difficult it is for those who trust in riches to enter the kingdom of heaven!” (Mark 10). And elsewhere: “It is good to hope in the Lord rather than to hope in princes”  
[Note: [Col. 0135] In another copy the following is added here: “And the poet: ‘The greatest care added to mortals comes when hope is prolonged.’ The same says: ‘It consumes joys by long desire.’ Conversely, concerning heavenly hope it is said: ‘Cast,’ etc.”]  
(Ps. 117). Again: “Cast your thought upon the Lord, and he shall sustain you” (Ps. 54). Again: “Hope in the Lord, and do good” (Ps. 36).

From these authorities one should proceed thus: hope in earthly things stretches toward future wishes and consumes joys before they arrive. Through excessive anxiety it corrodes the mind, because fear assails hope, sells future joys, and extends desire to infinity. O man, you who lean upon earthly things, trusting in uncertainties, lean upon a reed-staff that breaks easily. Therefore do not trust one who is frail and slippery, who quickly falls and [Col. 0135D] destroys you. Rather establish your mind in the cloudiness of adversity than in the clear weather of prosperity.

If you place hope in earthly prosperity, it is deceptive and misleading. When you grasp it, you will not find what you had hoped for. From the forewarning you will learn that hope ought not to be placed in slippery things. Why do you hope for what you cannot retain for long, where you will not find what you believe, where the pleasure in experience is less? Nor will you find in them merely what you hoped for; rather, you will find fuel for fault, fuel for ruin, a snare for the soul, and leaven of justice.

Rather direct hope amid tribulations, which, [Col. 0136A] although outwardly they display bitterness, nevertheless produce in the steadfast mind the sweetness of heavenly hope. No one will enjoy the sweet fruit of patience who has not been pierced by the bitterness of tribulation. For tribulation is a furnace that refines gold, a file that polishes iron, a scourge by which grain is separated from chaff. In this warfare of tribulation, patience is exercised, courage serves, steadfastness is strengthened, and hope is invited toward heavenly things.

Therefore let the anchor of hope be fixed in the harbour of salvation, in the mercy of the Saviour. This hope does not confound but restores; it enlightens rather than blinds. There more is found than is sought, or than hope can contain; there more is done than hope can understand; there hope does not consume joy, and desire does not diminish joy. For this reason desire awaits nothing where hope fixes its step.

[Col. 0136B] O how blessed is that heavenly hope which fear does not storm, in which fear foretells no false things, where desire dreams no unheard-of things, but charity “bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things” (1 Cor. 13)—things to be believed or hoped for to which the boundary of reason invites us. What fear can weaken the human mind if heavenly hope pleads for it before God? How can the thunderbolts of tyrants, the precipices of fortune, bodily infirmities, or the clamour of poverty harm it, if the mind is defended by heavenly hope? This is the hope that governs communities and directs actions. This is what gives charity height, so that we direct our actions toward God; this is what measures charity’s breadth [Col. 0136C] so that we extend it even to an enemy; this is what stretches charity’s length, so that we persevere in it to life’s end.

Between this hope and fear, as between two millstones, the Christian, gentle and delicate, ought to be ground. Hence it is said in Deuteronomy (ch. 24): “You shall not take the upper or lower millstone as a pledge.” The upper millstone is hope; the lower is fear. The former must not be taken without the latter. For one who hopes and does not fear is negligent; but one who fears and does not hope is dejected.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Spiritual Mourning

By these authorities and reasons one may be invited to spiritual mourning: “Blessed are those who mourn, [Col. 0136D] for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5). Elsewhere: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep” (Luke 6). James says: “Be wretched, mourn, and weep. Let your laughter be turned into mourning and your joy into sorrow” (Jas. 4). Solomon says: “It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting” (Eccl. 7). Gregory says: “Present joys are followed by everlasting lamentations. No one can rejoice here with the world and reign there with God.”

There are three mournings with which a person is bound to water his mind: mourning for one’s own sin, mourning for another’s sin, and mourning over [Col. 0137A] the delay of eternal blessedness. The first mourning is directed toward oneself, the second toward one’s neighbour, and the third toward God. Of the first it is said: “My tears were my bread by day and by night” (Ps. 41). Of the second: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11). Jesus too wept with this weeping over Jerusalem, saying: “If only you also had known!” (Luke 19). Of the third weeping we read in the Psalm: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down and wept,” etc. (Ps. 136).

These are the Lamentations of Jeremiah, by which one laments the soul’s sin, mourns the assault of misery, and laments the delay of the homeland. A person ought to water the soil of his mind with the rains of these tears, so that it may bear the fruit of good works and the diverse flowers of virtues. These are the early and latter rain: [Col. 0137B] the early rain is weeping for one’s own sins, through whose watering the germ of good work rises in the mind. But after the shoot of penitence has reached the ripeness of perfect justice, the latter rain must be present—that is, weeping over the delay of the homeland—so that by such a seasoning of lamentation we may harvest the fruit of good works more fittingly.

These are the waves of grace through which the children of Israel passed as they went up to the land of promise. For sinners leaving the Egypt of vices first pass through the Red Sea, in which their enemies are submerged—that is, they first undergo the waves of penitence, where the errors of vices are erased. Therefore through weeping we ought here to sing the song of Moses, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified; horse and rider he has cast into the sea” (Exod. 15).

[Col. 0137C] Subsequently the children of Israel come to the torrent of Hermon, and the rocks are bowed down, when the faithful, placed in the desert of the mind, freed from worldly cares, and established upon the throne of virtues, weep for others’ sins, suffer with their neighbours, judge another’s error as their own; and thus the rocks are bowed down. At last the children of Israel come to the Jordan and cross it dry-shod, when the faithful, established in the summit of perfection and their affections cleansed from the streams of carnal thoughts, enter into lamentation because of the loss entailed by present misery.

The first weeping is that of penitence; the second comes from compassion for one’s neighbour; the third from compassion for oneself. O man, make [Col. 0137D] your mind that book which Ezekiel saw (ch. 2), in which was written: “Woe, lamentations, and songs,” so that, if you are entangled in sin, you may turn to penitence; so that, if the woe of mortal sin has preceded, the lamentation of penitence may follow—or rather, three lamentations: the lamentation of penitence, the lamentation of compassion for another, and lamentation over the delay of the homeland.

O man, turn yourself to these groanings. Embrace these sorrows; turn yourself away from other earthly sorrows. If Fortune acts as your enemy, do not increase your grief on account of her enmity. She has nothing with which to harm you unless you provide her strength. Certainly she does not harm you unless [Col. 0138A] you harm yourself; if you grieve, you have supplied her weapons.

Why are you sad over the loss of things that contain a cause of pain in the midst of pleasures, a cause of dissension in the midst of peace, and which, though they ought to be nourishment for security, are turned into fear? If you grieve over the death of a friend, grieve more over the danger to his soul than over the cutting-off of this temporal life. If you weep for him, rather pour out the tears of your mind for him before God than an outward wailing to the world.

If natural weakness invites you to mourning, do not surrender your mind to grief. I do not forbid tears which necessity naturally presses forth and human weakness expels, for such tears fall by an involuntary outburst. Often, without impairing the authority of the wise person, tears have flowed for a friend for such a time [Col. 0138B] that neither humanity nor dignity was lacking to them. It is permissible, provided gravity is preserved, to yield to nature. Yet although nature invites you to mourning of mind, do not let tears suffocate your mind. In the midst of tears let the mind remain steadfast and unmoved; let it read its own misery. Let mourning be conquered by the mind; let the mind absorb weakness; let the spirit diminish the flesh; reason, sensuality.

If death threatens, do not grieve, but prepare yourself for its imminence through steadfastness of mind. Prepare yourself so that you cannot fear death; so that you may begin to live after death, having lived by dying before death. Yet I do not say that, overcome by idleness, you should flee to death, because it is sometimes as shameful to seek refuge in death [Col. 0138C] as to flee death. Let desire for eternal life invite you to death; let desire for greater merit keep you in life.  
[Note: [Col. 0137] In another copy the following occurs: Do not desire death from weariness of pain; do not desire life from love of earthly flattery. Bear the latter patiently; await the former steadfastly.]

Do not be dissolved by prosperity; do not be suffocated by adversity. Do not be among those women whom Ezekiel saw (ch. 8) mourning Adonis. By Adonis—who is said to have died and afterward returned to life, and for whom the women appeared to mourn when dead and rejoice when alive—is understood temporal prosperity, which ends in a moment and rises again for a moment, because it is always in flux and never remains in the same state. Effeminate people mourn him dead and rejoice in him revived: people who are always changed according to Fortune’s game, who mourn with mourning Fortune and rejoice with rejoicing Fortune; who have as many changes of mind [Col. 0138D] as Fortune has varieties.

This temporal mourning is not to be embraced; rather, eternal mourning must be guarded against from the heart, where there will be weeping without remission, pain without interruption, labour without rest; where the whole soul will be in the weeping of conscience and the whole body in the mourning of misery, because from the first gate there will be a cry, from the second misery.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Spiritual Joy

The following authorities and reasons can invite a person to spiritual joy: “Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous” (Ps. 31). Again: “Rejoice [Col. 0139A] because your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10). Again: “We shall exult and rejoice in you” (Isa. 25). Again: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice” (Phil. 4). Again: “Make joyful noise to God, all the earth; serve the Lord with gladness” (Ps. 65).

By these authorities we are admonished toward spiritual gladness of mind, which is produced not by abundance of riches, nor by the deceptive glory of the world, nor by secular power, nor by fruitfulness of offspring, nor by bodily health, but by purity of conscience and cleanness of life. No misery interrupts this joy; no adversity demolishes this prosperity; no bitterness mingles with this sweetness. O blessed delight of a pure conscience, which excludes the inward worm, frees reason from the prison of pain, and cleanses the mind from impurity!

[Col. 0139B] This is the paradise of delights, planted with diverse trees of good works, adorned with diverse flowers of virtues, and watered by the fountain of heavenly grace.  
[Note: [Col. 0139] In another copy follows: This is the paradise in which the tree of life is planted, that is, the flourishing of heavenly wisdom; where the tree of the knowledge of good and evil flourishes, that is, freedom of choice. In this a person is placed so that he may rejoice in everlasting happiness.]

This purity of conscience is an image of eternal life and a preface to the heavenly kingdom. Against this serenity of mind no storm of Fortune can prevail; against these fortifications of the mind the engines of the world avail nothing. Whoever has purity of conscience rejoices amid pains, laughs amid lamentations, and is happy amid adversity.

This is Solomon’s house, filled with various perfumes, because in purity of heart the sweet gifts of charisms give forth their fragrance. This is God’s bridal chamber, Christ’s palace, the bed of the heavenly bridegroom. There the bride—that is, the soul—rests with Christ her bridegroom. There Rebecca meets [Col. 0139C] Isaac coming from the field. There Jacob delights in Rachel’s delightful embraces. There Mary Magdalene offers Christ most precious ointments.

O, if such is the happiness of a pure conscience, how great is the misery of a seared mind, before whose judge no guilty person is acquitted, where the worm of conscience constantly demolishes the mind; where the savage day of the soul flies about with unceasing wings; where the monsters, the beasts of sins, confront it. This is the handwritten book of the devil, disfigured by most foul marks. There the page is the mind conscious of evil; the pen is freedom of choice; the ink [Note: [Col. 0139] Another copy has *incastum* (“unchaste”) instead of *incaustum* (“ink”).] is the enormity of sin. There, O most wretched man, you recall whatever you wrote from earliest age onward, by which you offended God, opposed your neighbour, and [Col. 0139D] harmed yourself.

O condemnable book, in which not songs but lamentations and woes are written! But now, O man, erase by confession what you wrote by false speech; erase by contrition what you wrote by evil thought; erase by satisfaction what you wrote by wicked action. Erase the book of perverse conscience, lest reason read there what will condemn you, lest the devil find there what will accuse you, lest God see there what will judge you; so that you may return to spiritual joy of mind, return to yourself, and return to God.

## CHAPTER XV. On Patience

[Col. 0140A]

If you wish to instruct your hearers in patience, use these authorities: “Patience has a perfect work” (Jas. 4). Again: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. 5). Again: “A man’s teaching is known by patience” (Prov. 19). And the philosopher says: “Patience is the highest of dispositions.” It is that through which the martyr, by dying, overcomes one who lives; triumphs by suffering; finds sweetness in tribulation and rest in labour. From gall it draws honeycomb, from vinegar something honeyed. The shield of patience shatters the arrows of insults; the strength of endurance drives away the darts of injuries.

There are four kinds of injuries which victorious patience repels and overcomes by resisting them. [Col. 0140B] The first is injury of words, which patience either absorbs through the tranquillity of silence or soothes through gentleness of speech. The second is injury of hatred, which patience forgives and repays hatred with charity. The third is injury to possessions, which patience overcomes, content with a small provision for the journey. The fourth is injury to one’s own body, which bodily discipline repels.

Many are read to have possessed the shadow of patience; many, we read, falsely claimed constancy in order to obtain worldly prosperity. We marvel at certain animals which pass through the midst of fires without bodily injury; but we ought to marvel much more at those who pass through sword, ruin, and fire unhurt and unharmed in mind. It is shameful to yield to suffering, more shameful to succumb. Wrestle against it: once it has been conquered, it will not renew the contest. Increase your spirit, enlarge your virtue. A strong or vigorous man is not one who flees labour. Patience, I say, ought to have a place in those labours where the cause of heavenly work presents itself; otherwise you will continually weary yourself in sordid labour.

Therefore, if you see grave things pressing upon you, do not turn your back, but retreat step by step to safety. It is easy through patience to escape the stings of tribulations; it is easy through patience to despise temporal goods. What is more shameful than to be anxious at the very threshold of security? This is the reason that makes us impatient: we are empty of heavenly good.

There are seven kinds of patience, which are contained in the seven petitions of the Lord’s Prayer.

[Col. 0140D] The first is against the assault of the world, against the desire for vain glory, against desire for earthly labour, against the tether of cupidity. It is sought when one says: “Deliver us from evil” (Matt. 6), as though the faithful person said: Grant patience against the evil of the age, against the world’s assault. The same patience is spoken of when it is said in the catalogue of beatitudes: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. 5). For the first kind of patience consists in spiritual poverty: in renunciation of outward possessions; in [Col. 0141A] renunciation of natural gifts, when a person does not become inflated because of the natural endowments of the soul; and in renunciation of things belonging to bodily endowments, such as strength, beauty, and so forth.

The second patience is against the assaults of the devil. This kind of patience is sought when one says: “And lead us not into temptation” (Matt. 6). A person does not ask not to be tempted, but not to be led into temptation. For one may be tempted and not led into temptation, as is the just person who resists the devil; another is tempted and led into temptation when, by sinning, he submits to the evil one. Of this patience it is said: “Blessed are the meek,” etc. (Matt. 5). For in this patience the highest meekness appears: a person gives no assent to the evil demon.

[Col. 0141B] The third kind of patience is against injuries from one’s neighbour, when a person patiently endures insults. This is sought when it is said: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI). Of the same it is said: “Blessed are the merciful,” etc. (Matt. V). For the effect of spiritual mercy is the forgiveness of injuries.

The fourth kind of patience is against the pressure of natural poverty, when someone steadfastly endures the onset of want. This is sought when it is said: “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matt. VI). What is this daily bread, if not patience against poverty amid the losses of this life? For this is the patience which counts a little provision for the journey [Col. 0141C] as immense, which richly feeds the mind although it does not fill the stomach. This patience makes fasts fruitful; it finds fine wheat flour in millet, salmon in a goby, seasoning in water. Of this it is said: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matt. V). For patience which finds satisfaction in material fasting thirsts and hungers for righteousness; and the more it despises material food, the more it desires spiritual food.

The fifth patience is against the assault of the flesh, when a person manfully restrains the assault of the flesh and chastises the beast, so that sensuality serves reason and the flesh the spirit; when the spirit holds dominion over the flesh, and reason obtains rule against the flesh. This kingdom is sought in the Lord’s Prayer, [Col. 0141D] when it says: “Thy kingdom come” (Matt. VI); that is, make it so that, just as all things obey thee, so sensuality in us may obey reason. And just as all things in thy kingdom are peaceful, so may all things in the kingdom of our mind be tranquil.

Oh, how greatly this duel between flesh and spirit must be feared, where the flesh is armed against the spirit with the enticements of the senses and the pleasures of bodily delights. Consider the army of the flesh, which serves in its camp and comes with the flesh to battle: the beauty of an object that deceives sight; the blandishment of sound that seduces hearing; the fragrances of things that suspend the sense of smell; the flavour of food that [Col. 0142A] attracts taste; the softness of a thing that provokes touch. Against this army patience arms the mind: it alone can overcome these enemies, it alone can end the conflict, it alone can restore exiled reason to its own kingdom.

This war is more than civil, and therefore must be guarded against more carefully. There is an external war between man and the devil, of which it is said: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the principalities and powers of this air” (Eph. VI). There is a civil war between a person and his neighbour, of which it is said: “The children of my mother fought against me” (Song I). There is a war more than civil, between flesh and spirit, of which it is said: “The flesh fights against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. V). This war can be quieted by spiritual mourning: if one mourns the absence of the bridegroom; if one weeps over the onset of sin; if one grieves by abstaining from fleshly desire; if one weeps by ceasing from love of the world. Of this mourning it is said: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. V).

The sixth patience is against the miseries of the body, which are found in toil, sickness, cold, heat, hunger, and thirst. These are the wounds inflicted by the robbers upon the man going down from Jerusalem to Jericho (Luke X): that is, the demons upon Adam when he sinned, he who went down from Jerusalem—the vision of heaven—to Jericho, that is, into the failing condition of our mortality. Against these there is patience when the mind, in sickness, overcomes the severity of disease while giving thanks to God, and thus finds health of mind in the weakness of the flesh; and when, even in labour, the mind finds [Col. 0142C] rest, referring punishment to its due end, so that the bodily ailments may become remedies for minds. Against these bodily miseries patience is sought when it is said: “Thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth” (Matt. VI); that is, make it so that, just as in heaven—that is, in Christ’s human nature—thy patience was steadfast, at the prompting of thy will, against these miseries of the flesh, so also on earth—that is, in us earthly people—there may be patience against bodily infirmities. Of this it is said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V). Through this patience the eye of reason is cleansed, lest through sickness it fall into despair, or through labour collapse into lethargy.

The seventh patience is against the chastisements [Col. 0142D] of God, which test the righteous, prove the servant, and show forth the son. This is sought when it is said: “Hallowed be thy name” (Matt. VI). For when someone is patient under God’s chastisements, the name of sonship is sanctified in him; and the more patiently he bears God’s chastisements, the more the paternal name is sanctified in him, because “the Father chastises by punishment every son whom he receives through patience” (Heb. XII). Of this patience it is said: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the children of God” (Matt. V). For those who retain peace of heart through patience while they are chastised by the Father are rightly proved to be children of God.

> [Note: [Col. 0141] In another copy, this is added here: This sevenfold patience appears in Job: loss of earthly honour did not break him; Satan tempted him but did not conquer him; he manfully resisted his wife when she insulted him; deprived of all temporal goods, he did not succumb to want; the fleshly love of his children did not cast him down; in strength of mind he absorbed the sores of the flesh; he patiently endured God’s chastisements.]

Therefore, if anyone desires to be patient, let him diligently consider Job’s patience, Christ’s end, and the steadfastness of the martyrs; and thus, by the power of patience, let him mock all worldly assaults. As is read in the book of Macrobius: “The impulses of the mind must be bound by the bond of patience; great is the glory of the person who is not raised by anyone’s praises nor diminished by anyone’s reproaches.” Plato says of patience:

> [Note: [Col. 0143] Added: No one ever seemed to him sufficiently self-controlled or temperate whose life had not been tested amid the very dangers of errors, among the enticements of pleasures. And afterwards: Therefore we must contend, etc.]

“We must contend with pleasurable things, so that we may be secure against them not by flight or absence, but by vigour of mind, constant presence, and moderate use; and so that, while the mind is at once warmed and refreshed, we may dissipate whatever cold sadness or sluggish dullness there may be in it.”

Aristotle also says: “Who possessing any human sense of shame congratulates himself on having pleasures in common with a sow and [Col. 0143B] an ass?” Likewise Socrates said that many people wish to live in order that they may eat and drink, not eat and drink in order that they may live. Gregory also says: “Do not impose upon another what you yourself cannot endure.” And again Socrates: “It belongs to the wise person to guard against falling into a snare, and, should someone perhaps fall, to endure it courageously. For a person cannot be judged brave unless he is also wise; for virtue without wisdom must be regarded as dangerous rashness.” Again Socrates: “It belongs to a good man to know how to suffer and not to commit injury.” Again, the same: “Patience is a harbour amid miseries.”

## CHAPTER XVI. On Obedience

By these authorities hearers may be instructed in patience: “Christ became obedient for us unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. II). Samuel also says: “Obedience is better than sacrifices” (I Sam. XV). Likewise the Apostle: “Servants, obey your superiors and masters, not only the good and gentle, but also the harsh” (I Pet. II). And: “Whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance” (Rom. XIII).

From these authorities one must proceed thus: O man, the Son of God became obedient for us even to the disgrace of the gibbet; and do you refuse to obey the commands of the Gospel? When an angel obeys God in all things, do you, who are mud and ashes, contradict God’s command? Insensible things obey God; do you, alone endowed with reason, oppose God’s will? The sun does not depart from its path, the moon does not stray from its course, the stars perform their offices; at God’s command the field is made pleasant with flowers, the earth is watered by rains, the forest is clothed in rippling foliage, and the little bird makes music in the grove. Thus all things obey God; you alone oppose his commands!

Consider, O man, that “obedience is better than sacrifices” (I Sam. XV), [Col. 0144A] because in sacrifices another’s flesh is immolated, but through obedience one’s own will is slain. Therefore each person pleases God the more swiftly, the more he represses the pride of his own choice and immolates himself with the sword of command. Indeed, disobedience is called “the sin of divination” (ibid.), so that the greatness of obedience’s power may be shown by its opposite.

Solomon says of this obedience: “An obedient man speaks of victories” (Prov. XXII). For while we humbly submit to another’s voice, we overcome ourselves in our hearts.

It should also be known that obedience sometimes ought to have nothing of its own. For when a higher position is commanded, a person who yearns for it through personal desire empties obedience of its strength. At other times, however, obedience ought to have something of its own: when insults and reproaches are commanded, if the mind does not seek these of itself, a person who descends to them unwillingly diminishes the good of obedience for himself. Obedience, therefore, ought to have something of its own in adversities, and again to have nothing of its own in prosperities. Thus Moses humbly refuses the leadership of the people (Exod. III). Paul boldly says: “I am ready not only to be bound at Jerusalem, but also to die” (Acts XXI). But beware lest you err in obedience.

> [Note: [Col. 0143] The following is inserted here: For here gall may be concealed beneath the appearance of honey, a wolf beneath a sheep’s fleece, poison in drink, and death-dealing matter in food.]

Know, therefore, that true obedience is the honourable effect, with discernment, of a just command upon a deliberating mind. See what companions obedience ought to have: namely, justice, so that what is commanded may be just—hence it says, “the effect of a just command”; secondly, that what is deliberated may be honourable—hence, “of a deliberating mind, honourable”; thirdly, that it may proceed from discernment—hence the addition, “with discernment.”

Therefore obedience without discernment is empty; obedience without honour is abject, because one who obeys in dishonourable things through excessive enlargement of obedience indicates pride of mind. But if it is not joined with justice, it is irregular and anomalous. It should be known, moreover, that evil must never be done through obedience, although sometimes a good action may have to be omitted. The tree in paradise which God forbade to be touched was not evil; yet it was fitting that he should forbid this good thing, so that man might grow blessed through the merit of obedience. Note, moreover, that it says there: “Eat of every tree of paradise” (Gen. II), etc. For whoever forbids his subjects one good thing must grant many things, lest a mind repelled from all things perish as though fasting.

Four things, therefore, accompany rational obedience: discernment, honour, justice, and humility.

> [Note: [Col. 0143] In another copy this is again added here: These so surround obedience itself that it cannot collapse altogether or falter even in a small matter.]

There are three kinds of regular obedience: sufficient obedience, by which one obeys a superior; perfect obedience, by which one obeys an equal; and abundant obedience, by which one serves an inferior. The first is, as it were, positive; [Col. 0145A] the second comparative; the third superlative. The first belongs to command, the second to supererogation, the third to counsel.

> [Note: [Col. 0145] Added: The first is a good measure, the second heaped up, the third overflowing.]

Christ fulfilled these in himself: obedient to a superior when he obeyed the Father, who was greater than him according to his humanity; obedient to an equal when he obeyed the Father, to whom he was equal according to divinity; and obedient to an inferior when he obeyed his mother.

Furthermore, there is a certain obedience which is direct: it is performed with a due end and a suitable office, as when we obey God with a good intention. Another is right but not direct: as when we obey God but with an unsuitable office—such obedience as the Jew renders to God his creator, but which lacks the form of office, that is, the rule of charity and faith. Indirect obedience is when we obey the Creator for the sake of human favour. Retrograde obedience is when demons obey God, because they thus obey by doing [Col. 0145B] what they do not wish.

The first is meritorious; the second introductory; the third gainful; the fourth destructive. The first is effective; the second, doing; the third, failing; the fourth, infecting.

Oh, how effective is the rule of obedience, which preserves concord among the angels, nourishes peace in cloisters, and without which neither a commonwealth can stand nor even the smallest household be governed. It suggests natural law even to brute animals; inanimate things keep it as law. By it earthly things are bound to heavenly, and divine things to human; it is the ladder by which ascent to heaven is made. This obedience also nourishes humility, tests patience, and examines gentleness. Let the cloistered person [Col. 0145C] strive to embrace it with the arms of charity, so that he may render to God what is God’s and to his neighbour what is his neighbour’s. This is obedience which, according to the rule of justice, renders to each person what is his own. And as every good proceeds from obedience, so every evil arises from disobedience, when through sin man scorns to obey his Creator.

## CHAPTER XVII. On Perseverance

By these authorities one is admonished toward perseverance: “Whoever perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. X). Elsewhere likewise: “If he perseveres in knocking, I tell you, even if he does not give to him because he is his friend, yet because of his importunity he will rise and give him as many things as he needs” (Luke XI). And the Apostle says: “All run in the stadium, but one receives the prize” (I Cor. IX). And: “He who has contended lawfully shall be crowned” (II Tim. II).
