Elsewhere it is said that “the Lord will judge the ends of the earth” (Ps. IX). And: “Wherever the tree falls, whether to the south or to the north, there it shall remain” (Eccl. XI). And elsewhere: “It is the finish, not the contest, that crowns.”

Many undertake great things but fail on the way. Many leave Sodom but quickly look back. [Col. 0146A] Many go out from Babylon but die on the way and do not reach the city of eternal peace, the heavenly Jerusalem. Perseverance gives form to merit, colours a good purpose, rewards the runner, crowns the combatant. It leads to the prize, leads to the harbour, gives form to the work and rule to the action. It is Joseph’s long robe, reaching to the end of life; it is the priestly robe reaching to the feet; it is the tail of the sacrifice which we are bound to offer God.

This is the heel of good action, which we must guard against the serpent’s bites. This is the virtue which gives form to every good vow, by which martyrs gain their laurels and virgins receive their crowns. This is what reduces difficult things to what is attainable and overcomes every difficulty. It is a garment without wrinkle, a robe [Col. 0146B] without stain. It makes good action of one colour and virtue uniform.

And it should be noted that there is a kind of perseverance which is, as it were, hay-like (*fenalis*): like hay it flourishes for a time and withers in a time of adversity. It comes forth like a flower and is crushed; it flees like a shadow and never remains in the same condition. Final perseverance, however, is that which endures to the end. It is a living fountain, a sealed garden, in which no stranger shares, which always flows and always springs up. Let the faithful labour to possess it, the cloistered to retain it, virgins to be formed by it, and widows to persevere in it.

At times the devil incites a person to good in order to draw a more grievous evil from that good. Against this assault of the devil perseverance avails, so that good beginnings may be concluded [Col. 0146C] by a good end:

> Let the middle not differ from the beginning, nor the end from the middle.

For to begin well and conclude with an evil end is to produce something monstrous.

For that action is like a chimera which has its beginning in reason and its end in sensuality. Thus it is done:

> The painter joins a horse’s neck to a human head,  
> and then adds diverse feathers of fruitlessness.

There are some whose life produces a marvellous monster: its good beginning displays, as it were, a human head; its middle, descending into lust, displays the belly of a goat; at last, swerving into rapacity, it has the feet of a she-wolf. O man, what good does it do you [Col. 0146D] to begin well and not to conclude with a right end? “It is better not to know the way of truth than, after knowing it, to go back” (II Pet. II). Through this fickle instability you are accused, you incur apostasy, and you set aside steadfastness of mind.

> [Note: [Col. 0145] In another copy: O man, through perseverance you redeem the brevity of life; you allow no work to pass in vain; you embrace every hour, so that you may depend less upon tomorrow.]

Seneca says: “It belongs to an ordered mind to be able to stand firm and remain in the good.” Nothing is so useful that it can profit while merely passing by. Perseverance brings good [Col. 0147A] up and leads what is tender to maturity. It does not seek a childish mind but an adult one: it seeks mature character, not tender or misshapen character.

> [Note: [Col. 0147] Here the following occurred: If you wish to attain perseverance, strive to rest in good things, so that habit, which is a second nature, may produce perseverance in you, and the companionship of good people may bring forth endurance in life.]

If perseverance does not illumine the whole life, let final perseverance at least complete the end. If you have offered the flower of youth to the devil, offer Christ at least the dregs of old age. At evening the serenity of the day is praised; at the end, the condition of a good work. Consider from how great a good Judas fell, because he did not persevere in good.

Consider what Solomon lost through instability of mind, and into what calamity Saul fell. We may infer how great the merit of perseverance is from the grievousness of the opposing vice, namely impenitence. For it is said of impenitence that the stain of this sin is so great that it cannot submit to the humility of asking pardon. This is sin against the Holy [Col. 0147B] Spirit; this is sin unto death, concerning which John says: “There is sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it” (I John V). Impenitence, moreover, is born of despair or arises from presumption; and, so far as it lies in it, it either detracts from God’s justice or diminishes his mercy. Blessed therefore is perseverance, which excludes impenitence, drives out obstinacy, eliminates contempt, and conquers hardness of heart.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Mercy

These authorities may invite a person to mercy: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. V). “I desire mercy and not sacrifice” (Matt. IX, XII). Likewise: “Blessed is the man who shows mercy and lends” (Ps. XXXVI). And James in the Catholic Epistle: “Mercy exalts itself over judgment” (Jas. II). Likewise Solomon: “Mercy and truth preserve a king, and his throne is strengthened by clemency” (Prov. XX). And in the Gospel: “Whatever things you wish people to do to you, do also to them; this is the law and the prophets” (Matt. VII).

O man, if you considered God’s mercy carefully, you could possess in yourself the pattern for showing mercy. What made Christ incarnate except mercy? What subjected him to our misery except his clemency? This is the one way of man to God and of God to man. O blessed way, which alone knows the exchange that brings our salvation, which alone directs man to God and [Col. 0147D] brings God down to man! It alone is the mediatrix: reconciling those estranged, joining those divided, in some way making equals of unequals; humbling God, exalting us, drawing him to the lowest things and raising us to the highest—yet so that his descent is not abased, nor our exaltation proud but glorious. For mercy possessed great power: it alone could draw God from heaven to earth and lead man back from exile to his homeland. O great bond of mercy, by which God could be bound and bound man burst the bonds of iniquity!

O man, if you considered your misery, in God’s action toward [Col. 0148A] you you would find nothing but mercy. It is mercy if he bears with the sinner; if he chastises in order to correct; if he frees from sin; if he preserves in righteousness. It is mercy also if he punishes eternally, because he punishes less than is deserved; it is mercy if he rewards eternally, because he rewards beyond merits. Nor is his justice thereby diminished, since his justice requires the exercise of mercy. Justice must always have mercy as its companion, because the truth of justice turns into severity unless it is seasoned with the sweetness of mercy. Hence it is said: “Mercy and truth have met together; justice and peace have kissed” (Ps. LXXXIV). Justice must, as it were, kiss mercy, so that it may not depart from the path of mercy; and mercy must not escape the line of justice.

[Col. 0148B] Thus judgment is said to be above mercy’s altar, because justice is sunk into an abyss of cruelty unless it is relaxed by the grace of mercy. Mercy is the seasoning of justice and the remedy of judgment. Yet mercy ought not, on account of misery, to be either indiscriminate or cut short; for, as Seneca says: “To forgive everyone is as much cruelty as to forgive no one.” For discipline is greatly destroyed by mercy, or mercy by discipline, if either is held without the other. Rulers ought to possess both toward their subjects: mercy that consoles justly, and discipline that rages piously.

Let us consider how much Moses loved the people, for whose life he asked to be blotted out; and with what zeal for righteousness, after he had obtained pardon, he said to the people: “Let every man put his sword upon his thigh,” etc. (Exod. XXXII). Behold, he who sought the life of human beings at the cost of his own death extinguished the lives of a few by the sword. Inwardly he burned with the fire of love; outwardly, before God, he was kindled with zeal of severity. A strong ambassador in both respects, he pleaded the people’s cause before God by prayers, and God’s cause before the people by swords.

O man, pursue mercy toward your neighbour not with regard to fortune but to the cause. Let not weakness of mind but the charity of God stir up clemency. For many are moved by the tears of the most guilty, who, if permitted, would break open a prison; these are moved not by charity but by weakness of mind. Therefore let charity render compassion to a person, and equity punish the enormity of vice. Most of all one must strive [Col. 0148D] in works of mercy: that the hungry be fed, the thirsty refreshed, the naked clothed, the stranger received, the orphan comforted, and the sick visited. These are works of mercy, which the righteous man will order in judgment (Ps. XXXVI), and which will plead for him on the day of judgment. For works of mercy alone will speak for a person in the final cause, because “judgment shall be without mercy for him who has not shown mercy” (Jas. II).

O man, recognize yourself in another’s misery; in another’s affliction read your own. If you are righteous, you can fall; if you are rich, this is a gift of fortune, not of nature. If you are healthy, infirmity either presses upon you or threatens to do so. [Col. 0149A] If you are wise, human wisdom has no constancy. O man, if you depart from the path of clemency, as far as you are concerned you muddy the fountain of mercy. You who have experienced in God the fountain of mercy and loving-kindness, at least allow a stream of mercy to flow forth toward your neighbour. What will happen if your Saviour is clement and loving, while you are merciless and harsh toward your neighbour? You have received mercy from the Lord and commit malice against your neighbour. In God’s mercy you can read what you ought to do and what rule of clemency you can observe.

And certainly you ought to embrace mercy more readily than justice. Every person ought by nature to be more inclined toward mercy than toward justice, because mercy produces love and justice fear; because charity drives out [Col. 0149B] fear, and love is more worthy than fear. There are also many things that admonish us to relax something of justice: the weakness of human nature, the usefulness of the matter, and the dignity of mercy itself, which exalts itself over judgment. Therefore let mercy arise not from negligence, not from faint-heartedness, not from lack of discernment, not from weakness of mind; but let it in every respect be bounded, so that it may retain its own proper character and not take away what is due to justice.

See, O man, in Joseph the mercy that forgot the injury of his brothers (Gen. XLIII). Read in David the grace of clemency, he who mourned the madness of his persecuting son (II Sam. XVIII). Set before yourself these and similar examples if you wish to follow the straight path of mercy. If you close the bowels of mercy against the needy, you close to yourself the door of Christ’s mercy. For mercy is the key by which heaven is opened and guilt released. This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it. This is the mercy that illumines the New Testament and tempers the strictness of the old law. This is the wood which sweetens the waters of Marah (Exod. XV). By this salt Elisha removed the bitterness of the waters (IV Kings II). By this flour Elisha removed death from the pot (IV Kings IV). This is the oil which the Samaritan poured into the wounds of the wounded man [Col. 0149C] (Luke X).

Clemency makes a person not only honourable but safe. Clemency is the ornament and surest light of rulers. It alone distinguishes the cruel from the pious, the king from the tyrant. A king is armed with clemency; a tyrant provokes hatred by arms. O man, where would you submit, unless clemency came to your aid? If God dealt with you in strict justice, no punishment could be imagined to answer your merits, no torments to equal your offences. Therefore attribute all things to God’s mercy, and by analogy exercise mercy toward your neighbour. Do not be miserly in showing mercy, since you have experienced the abundance of mercy in God.

## CHAPTER XIX. On Justice

These authorities exhort us to justice: “Love justice, you who judge the earth” (Wis. I). Likewise: “I have done [Col. 0150A] judgment and justice; do not hand me over to those who slander me” (Ps. CXVIII). Likewise: “Blessed is the man who will remain in wisdom and meditate upon justice” (Ecclus. XIV). Likewise: “Judge for the orphan and the humble, that man may no longer presume to magnify himself upon earth” (Ps. IX).

You must beware, O man, in what manner you consider judgment: do not sharpen judgment with hatred, inflame it with cruelty, soften it through love of money, or curtail it through fear. Let neither the purple of the rich nor the sackcloth of the poor move you. Walk the royal road: do not turn to the right by softening judgment, nor to the left by aggravating punishment. To punish guilt is not cruelty but justice; it is not tyranny but a judgment of divine rectitude. But beware lest you cast the mote from another’s eye while failing to see the beam in your own eye. Do not wish to uncover another’s fall while neglecting your own downfall; do not cure another’s illness while leaving yourself sick behind. And let it be said to you: “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke IV).

Hear what the Lord says to the Pharisees accusing the adulteress: “Let him who is without sin be the first to cast a stone at her” (John VIII). If you, a sinner, judge another sinner, you condemn yourself. O man, with what brow do you rebuke in another what you find more gravely in yourself? With what face do you judge your neighbour, when you know that you yourself must be judged more severely?

Justice befits a ruler when it is cut off from every vice, bounded by due limits, and fortified with companions: rectitude should accompany it, lest in judging it stray from what is right; discernment, lest it depart from the path through error; charity, [Col. 0150C] so that it may exercise the sword of vengeance not through the rancour of hatred but through zeal for justice; mercy, lest justice become cruelty; deliberation, so that the ruler may long consider or deliberate within himself concerning the punishment. Hence Seneca says: “He who condemns quickly is close to condemning gladly; he who punishes subjects excessively is close to punishing unjustly. To rule moderately is praiseworthy.”

Nature proves what a king ought to be, as can be known from other animals over which nature appoints a king, such as bees. Yet nature willed that their king should neither be savage nor seek vengeance with excessive constancy. It also curbs his zeal and leaves him unarmed, because, as Seneca says, bees are most irascible and, relative to their bodily capacity, most combative; they leave their stings in the wound, but the king himself is without a sting, set forth as an example for great matters. [Col. 0150D] One should be ashamed not to derive morals from these animals, since the human mind ought to be so much more moderate as it can do greater harm.

Whoever is endowed with justice will, with Moses, pass dry-shod through the sea of worldly vices reddened with blood. This is the rod by which the rock is struck and flows forth in streams, making the stony hearts of subjects overflow in rivers of virtues.

> [Note: [Col. 0149] In another copy it is inserted: This is Aaron’s rod, which flowered, put forth leaves, and bore fruit. For justice in some way puts forth leaves when it is conceived in the mind, flowers when it is exercised materially, and bears fruit when the subject is corrected.]

This is the winnowing fan by which grain is divided from chaff; the furnace in which silver is separated from dross; the sword by which the living are separated from the dead; the iron by which the healthy are divided from the sick. For against the disease of sin a biting plaster must be applied, lest an excessive corruption of vices [Col. 0151A] grow unchecked, and unpunished iniquity return to life for an increase of crimes.

> [Note: [Col. 0151] In another copy, *recidivit* (“has relapsed”) is read instead of *redivivat* (“may revive”).]

This is the measure by which we ought to measure punishments and weigh merits. It is what gives each person his due, while preserving the common good. Sometimes punishment must be relaxed because of scandal to others; sometimes punishment must be increased so that others may be warned. This is the medicine of vices and antidote of sins. This is the sword that defends both parts of a person: the body from outward injuries and the soul from inward afflictions. This is the stone by which David struck Goliath and delivered Israel from slavery. Justice without discernment is a sword in the hand of a madman; without power, a sword in the hand of one crippled; without mercy, a sword in the hand of a tyrant.

The exercise of justice must be undertaken with the greatest [Col. 0151B] discernment, so that we may judge not from suspicion but rather from rectitude.

> [Note: [Col. 0151] Hence the authority: “Do not judge, and you shall not be judged”; and, “Do not judge according to appearance, but judge righteous judgment.”]

Condemn no one before trial; first prove the case and then judge. For the guilty person is not the one accused, but the one convicted.

## CHAPTER XX. On the Love of God

These authorities set forth the pattern of charity: “You shall love the Lord God with all your heart and with all your soul” (Matt. XXII). John says: “God is charity, and whoever remains in charity remains in God, and God in him” (I John IV). Likewise Peter: “Above all, having mutual charity among yourselves, because charity covers a multitude of sins” (I Pet. IV).

[Col. 0151C] Likewise Paul: “Charity is patient, is kind,” etc. (I Cor. XIII). Likewise Augustine: “Whatever we do without charity profits us nothing to do, and we spend a futile effort if we do not possess charity, which is God.” Likewise Gregory: “The more the heart of a sinner is burned with the fire of charity, the more abundantly the rust of sins is consumed.”

From these one must proceed thus: Who, endowed with Tullian eloquence, who formed by every wisdom, is sufficient to express the praises of charity and expound its virtues? This is the charity which teaches us to flee enticements, trample pleasures, restrain the lust of the flesh, despise honours, and break unlawful desires; finally, to reject all the blandishments of this present life. Of this the Bridegroom admonishes in the Song of Songs, saying: “Set me [Col. 0151D] as a seal upon your heart, set me as a seal upon your arm; for love is strong as death, jealousy hard as hell” (Song VIII). For death extinguishes the living, while hell spares not even the dead. Love, therefore, is like death, because, as the one destroys bodily perception, so the other punishes the inclination of fleshly desire. Jealousy is hard as hell, because those whom desire for eternal things draws inwardly, it compels not only to reject outwardly pleasing things, but also to endure adversities [Col. 0152A] and hardships in order to attain what they love.

> [Note: [Col. 0151] In another copy the following is added: This is the Charity which made Abel a martyr; this is what led Abraham out of his land. This preserved Joseph in Egypt. This extinguished the flames for the three boys in the furnace. This is the greatest of all goods; apart from it nothing has savour, and in it nothing is harsh or hard.]

Charity strengthens the other virtues by the protection of its perfection. Whoever is grafted into its root neither fails in greenness nor is deprived of fruit.

> [Note: [Col. 0151] For *evanescit* (“fades away”), the reading is *defraudatur fructibus* (“is deprived of fruits”).]

Isidore also says of this: No reward is obtained without the love of charity; however rightly one may believe, without charity one cannot attain blessedness. For charity’s power is so great that even prophecy and martyrdom profit nothing without it. Charity holds primacy among all virtues. Hence it is also called by the Apostle “the bond of perfection” (Col. III), because all virtues are bound together by its bond. Therefore love God so that you may be loved by him; and you will reach him more quickly in order to be with him, for through love you will lay hold of him, [Col. 0152B] possess him, and enjoy him. This is the surpassing way, the pre-eminent way, directing crooked paths and showing straight paths.

This is the charity that prevailed so greatly with God that it brought him down from the seat of supreme majesty to the lowliness of our mortality; it wounded the impassible, drew the immutable, bound the unconquerable, and made the eternal mortal.

If charity could do so much in God, how much, O human being, ought it to be able to do in you yourself? If God endured such things for humankind, what will a human being refuse to endure for God? Let a human being be ashamed not to submit to charity, which subjected to itself the Creator of the world! It is not jealous, does not behave improperly; rather, in the person [Col. 0152C] in whom it dwells, it uproots the root of vices. Charity is the origin of all virtues: it enlightens the mind, cleanses the conscience, gladdens the soul, and shows God. The soul in which charity dwells is not puffed up by pride, ravaged by envy, scattered by anger, troubled by evil sadness, blinded by avarice, inflamed by gluttony, or defiled by lust.

It is always chaste, always pure, always tranquil, always kind. Secure in adversity, restrained in prosperity. This is the spiritual cross which everyone is bound to carry, so that, by taking up this cross, he may follow Christ’s footsteps. Its height rises toward God, its breadth extends toward the enemy, its length reaches to life’s end, and its depth tastes the immensity of divine grace. This is the charity which is a shield to one fighting, [Col. 0152D] a reward to one triumphing; which is begun on the way in such a manner as to be perfected in the homeland. “For there is a fire in Zion, and a furnace in Jerusalem” (Isa. 31). Charity brings forth, as it were, a created Trinity: in this Trinity, as it were, the Father is love of God, from which proceeds the love by which a human being himself is loved, as offspring by a father. [Note: [Col. 0151] In another copy: “By which a human being loves himself.”] From both, however, proceeds love of neighbor, as the Holy Spirit from both. Likewise, there are three distinctions in the one substance of charity, though they are distinct in their proper character. [Col. 0153A] Therefore beware, O human being, if you wish to pursue love, lest you be deceived by love’s shadow. For there is a love of fortune, which comes with prosperity. [Note: [Col. 0153] Added: “But in adversity it departs.”] By this the carnal person loves God when God has done well by him. There is a love of nature, by which every rational being loves God. For, as blessed Augustine says: “No mind has ever been able to hate God.” There is a love of grace, which alone possesses merit, by which God is loved so as to be possessed as a reward.

The first is failing, the second effecting, the third perfecting. The first belongs to the flesh, the second to sensuality, the third to reason. The first belongs to the false brother, the second to the humble sinner, the third to the justified person. O human being, consider how sweet is the love of God, how impure is the love of this world! The love of God is the mother of all virtues; [Col. 0153B] the love of the world is the mother of all vices. In the latter love all things are imperfect; in the former all things are brought to perfection. Through charity God is sought with the whole heart, sought above all things, found outside all things, loved more than all things. This is the fire which God came to cast upon the earth (Luke 12), that it might burn away the rust of sins and consume the chaff of vices. Charity has established its tribunal on high; worldly fear, earthly love, hope in carnal things, or sorrow over adversities cannot storm it. For who can investigate its breadth, which extends even to the enemy? Who can comprehend its height, which rises even to God? Who could search out its depth, which [Col. 0153C] is lowered to the abyss of divine wisdom? “Charity is God; and whoever remains in charity remains in God, and God in him” (1 John 4). Hear, O human being, and no longer think it a small thing if you have charity: hear that charity is God. Is it a small thing to have God himself dwelling within? Certainly it is a great thing to have charity within oneself, because God is charity. Charity alone has this privilege: that it is called God and indeed is God, such that this can belong to no other thing. For although every virtue is a gift of God, none but charity alone has this: that it may be called not only a gift of God, but God himself.

## CHAPTER XXI. On love of neighbor

By these authorities a human being is instructed concerning love of [Col. 0153D] neighbor: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 22). “Whatever you want people to do to you, do likewise to them” (Mark 12). “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Matt. 7; Luke 6). Sixtus also says: “The foundation and beginning of the worship of God is to love human beings.” St Gregory: “Charity is true if a friend is loved in God and an enemy is loved for God’s sake.” God himself is not loved without one’s neighbor, nor is one’s neighbor loved without God. Again Bede: “It is called *dilectio* [love] because it binds two—God and a human being—or joins each neighbor to another.” Although love of God is greater in the dignity of charity, nevertheless love of neighbor is greater in operation, because through love of neighbor one arrives at love of God. O human being, love your neighbor as yourself. Do not begrudge another the good things that you desire for yourself. If you desire something greater for yourself than for another, you are envious; if something greater for another than for yourself, you are foolish. Consult nature: it will teach you to love your neighbor as yourself. For nature made all things common and made one origin for all, because:

> The whole race of humankind descends from a like beginning.

If you deny another what you wish done to yourself, you oppose nature and weaken the common law.

Do not impose upon anyone what you yourself could not endure; offer others what you desire to be offered to yourself. How can you [Col. 0154B] despise your own nature in another when you embrace that same nature in yourself? Every animal loves what is like itself; thus every human being ought to love his neighbor. All flesh is joined in fellowship with its like. The Samaritan of the Gospel, though he was a stranger to the wounded man, nevertheless cared for the sick man; and how then can you fail to love your neighbor? Therefore be a friend to every neighbor in time of persecution, and not only in prosperity. Do not be a friend of table or fortune, but of tribulation, so that through compassion you make his adversities your own; through shared sorrow, make his pain your own; through compassion, make his suffering your own. This is a greater charity than to lay down one’s life for one’s friends and to extend charity even to [Col. 0154C] enemies. These are wonders in the law of the Lord. As God has mercy on his creature, so have mercy, in your neighbor, on your own nature. How praiseworthy is the charity which binds neighbors, joins those who differ, reduces plurality to unity, and transforms diversity into identity! This is harmonious discord, united plurality, consenting disagreement, uniting variety. This is Christ’s seamless garment, woven from above throughout (John 19).

This is Joseph’s garment, distinguished by embroidered work (Gen. 37). This is the variety in which the queen is read to be clothed, of whom it is said: “The queen stood at your right hand in gilded clothing, surrounded with variety” (Ps. 44). Of this unity of charity it is said: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell [Col. 0154D] together as one!” (ibid.). “As one”: not so much with regard to place as with regard to mind. For to dwell in one place and not to be of one mind is punishment, not delight. This unity leads to the heavenly unity, of which it is said: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this will I seek” (Ps. 26), etc. This unity enriches a person in his neighbor and makes him rejoice in another’s happiness. It brings a private good into common possession; it enlarges another’s good and does not extinguish it. Let Christians be ashamed not to be bound to one another by the bond of charity, when we read that Gentile equals were bound in friendship by the very tie of natural love! Since temporal [Col. 0155A] love has made many into one in friendship, will heavenly love fail to bind the faithful with the bond of charity? If trivial causes produce friendship among many, will eternal rewards not be able to do the same? O how great is the sweetness in true love of neighbor—a love produced not by human favor, earthly advantage, or human carnality, but by charity alone! This is what prays in Samuel for Saul (1 Sam. 15); what pleads with God for the people in Moses (Gen. 32); what weeps in David (2 Sam. 1) for Jonathan, and in Jeremiah for Jerusalem. Certainly he departs from the love of God who separates himself from love of neighbor, because: “He who does not love the neighbor whom he sees, how can he love God whom he has not seen?” (1 John 4). O human being, do you not wish your neighbor to love you for God’s sake? Love him for [Col. 0155B] your own sake. As the moral philosopher Seneca says: “If you wish to be loved, love.” O happy love, driven not by external causes but by the innate form of the highest good; free from envy, it is content with itself. Such love has its own affection within itself and is not anxious; it is set in tranquility and does not dissolve into mockeries. O how pleasant it is to find yourself in another! It is sluggishness and negligence to leave the practice of charity obsolete and not to exercise the noblest virtue.

It is glorious to be a maker of true friendship, which cleanses away the dregs of superficial love. Have a friend, not so that he may visit you when you are sick, feed you when hungry, or comfort you when imprisoned, but so that you may [Col. 0155C] visit him in prison, feed him when hungry, give drink to him when thirsty, and receive him when wandering. If you love your poor neighbor, you give alms from love alone; for the almsgiving of the heart is much greater than that of the body. Charity is sufficient in almsgiving even without earthly substance. Nor is that which is given bodily sufficient unless it is bestowed with a kindly disposition. Keep, therefore, the order of charity. Love God above all things; yourself below him; your neighbor alongside yourself; the flesh beneath. Love your flesh not in order to serve it, but in order to correct it by discipline; love it for good, not for the world’s luxury. Do not follow its will, but compel it to follow your will. Like a good physician, treat in it what is weak, what is diseased, what is sick; so that it may suffer for a time [Col. 0155D] and rejoice together for eternity, feel for a time the sharpness of medicine, and attain the benefit of eternal health.

## CHAPTER XXII. On peace

The following authorities instruct us concerning peace: “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give you” (John 14). Likewise: “Have peace among yourselves” (Mark 9). Likewise: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God” (Matt. 5).

Concerning peace it is also said: “Peace which surpasses all [Col. 0156A] understanding” (Phil. 4). And: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2). And Gregory says: “If we have shown how great is the power of peace, we recognize with what zeal it ought to be cultivated by us,” etc. We sufficiently recognize the dignity of this virtue from the fact that our Lord and Redeemer deigned to leave it to his disciples as a great gift, so that through it they might make their companions at peace with him. The law of nature teaches this; the elements, planets, and other insensible things embrace one another peacefully in their arms. [Note: [Col. 0155] In another copy the following is added: “This is what orders the hierarchies of angels in heaven. In human beings it stills the waves of thought, makes the wavering mind serene, cleanses the conscience, and banishes tumult from the soul.”]

There are three kinds of peace: the peace of time, the peace of the breast, and the peace of eternity. The first is peace’s shadow; the second, peace’s attendant condition; the third, peace’s substance. In the first are peace’s torches; in the second, peace’s remnants; [Col. 0156B] in the third, delightful banquets. The first is imaginary, the second invitatory, the third substantial. The first peace consists in temporal prosperity; the second arises from tranquility of mind; the third exists in the joy of heavenly life. The first peace [Note: [Col. 0155] Added: “The first gives fortune, the second conscience, the third eternal life.”] is not to be desired, because it is deceptive, slippery, and transitory; when it is thought to be held, it flees. It is a womanly storm, prosperous adversity, delightful bitterness, bitter sweetness. In serenity this peace produces cloud; in tranquility, tumult. Like a worldly breeze it flatters, then rages like the sea; now it is calm, then immediately it overturns and, as Seneca says, on the very day on which ships have sailed, they are swallowed up. Princes have experienced these pleasures of peace; [Col. 0156C] persons of middling rank have experienced them; the poor also have experienced them. Whoever hopes in this peace sets his foot on slippery ground, places his ship in shipwreck, stands on a precipice, and sows in sand.

The second peace is far more excellent than this: it does not fear the slipperiness of outward peace, shudder at fortune’s cloud, and cleanses the mind of vices; it is not demolished by the worm of conscience. The thunderbolts of rulers cannot destroy it, nor can the assaults of enemies shut it out. With this alone as companion, a person is rich; with this alone, the wise person is content; with it as companion, he is safe in adversities and secure amid dangers. This makes a person a child of God. It is produced by the gathering of virtues and the departure of vices. Of it it is said: “In peace, in the selfsame, I shall sleep and rest” (Ps. 4).

[Col. 0156D] In this peace of mind there are tranquil sleep, peaceful rest, and true vision. Whoever’s mind depends upon external goods does not possess this peace.

Whoever is not content with himself lacks such peace. Whoever keeps peace within himself retains that same peace with his neighbor.

A person cannot shut it up within if he does not exercise it outwardly. But the peace of eternity is that which surpasses every peace, where God is all in all; where all will one thing and reject one thing, [Col. 0157A] There the flesh does not clamour against reason; every will submits itself to the will of God; and a person has peace with God and peace with himself. There Simon Magus does not deceive; the Pharisee does not enlarge his phylacteries; the Jew does not murmur; Linus rejoices as much in Peter’s good as in his own; there is reciprocal love and vicarious affection. There discord does not shatter peace; fraud does not make divorces in peace; all things turn out according to desire; nothing opposes affection; effect accompanies the will; affection does not precede effect. [Note: [Col. 0157] “What tumult can exist where Wisdom itself reigns? Where one mercy orders all things? Where justice holds dominion?”] No one will come to this peace unless he has first ordered peace in his mind, first stilled tumult within himself, first excluded from himself the strife of carnal thoughts, and first [Col. 0157B] become ruler of himself. The aforesaid threefold peace was once signified by various figures. By the rest which the children of Israel had in the promised land was signified the peace of time, because, just as that rest was strewn with various adversities, so the peace of time is troubled by many adversities. But by the solemn Sabbath in the old law is signified the peace of our conscience, because, just as on the Sabbath people rested from servile work, so in peace of heart one rests from the slavery of sin. By that rest in which God rested on the seventh day from his work (Gen. 2) is signified eternal peace, in which one must rest from every labor. The first peace is to be trodden underfoot, the second held fast, the third desired. If Cain had possessed peace in [Col. 0157C] his breast, he would not have attacked his brother (Gen. 4). If Absalom had held the peace of mind, he would not have attacked his father (2 Sam. 15). If the tranquility of conscience had made Judas’s soul serene, he would not have resorted to the noose (Matt. 27). O how safely is he placed upon a throne whom tranquility of mind delights; how elegantly has he spread his bed who orders his soul in peace of heart; how securely does he lie in bed who disposes peace in his mind! In this especially a person ought to remain until he passes over. Striving toward it, let him sleep and rest.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On prudence

If anyone wishes to have instruction concerning prudence, let him proceed by this path: “Be prudent as serpents and [Col. 0157D] simple as doves” (Matt. 10). Likewise: “Wisdom conquers malice” (Wis. 7). And elsewhere: “Blessed is the person who dwells in wisdom” (Ecclus. 14). Likewise: “A fool stirs up quarrels, but a wise person calms those that have been stirred up” (Prov. 15). Seneca says: “Whoever desires to follow prudence should begin to live well under reason’s guidance, and should establish the worth of things not from opinion but from their nature.” Prudence is the discernment of good and evil things, and of each kind among themselves, together with the avoidance of evil and the choice of good. It is said “of each kind,” because it is not enough [Col. 0158A] to separate good and evil things from one another, but also good things from one another and likewise evil things: good from better and less good; evil from worse and less evil. It is not enough to discern them unless the choice of good and contempt for evil follow. Prudence teaches what seem to be goods but are not, and what do not seem to be goods but are. O human being, prudence teaches you not to marvel at the transitory things you possess or to think highly of what is perishable. Prudence will teach you to administer wisely what you possess as though it belonged to another, and fruitfully to let go what you cannot keep forever. If you embrace prudence, you remain the same everywhere, suffer loss in nothing, and, as the variety of things or times requires, adapt yourself to time, [Col. 0158B] place, person, and circumstance; you will not change yourself in any of them but rather adapt yourself to all of them, like a hand, which is the same whether extended into a palm or clenched into a fist. Prudence neither wishes to deceive nor can be deceived. Prudence praises sparingly and criticizes more sparingly; for excessive praise is as blameworthy as immoderate criticism: the former is suspect of flattery, the latter of malice. Prudence bears witness to truth, not friendship. It promises with discernment, hastens to fulfil its promise, and gives more fully than it promised. Prudence is administered through three times: it orders the present, foresees the future, and remembers the past. For one who thinks nothing of the past loses life; one who makes no preparation for the future proceeds incautiously into everything. The prudent person sets before his mind both future evils and goods, that he may endure the former and restrain the latter. He is not always active, but sometimes refreshes his mind by the pause of rest. That rest itself is full of studies of wisdom and good thoughts. For the prudent person never grows dull in idleness, never becomes torpid in sloth; at times he has a relaxed mind, but never a lax one; he hastens what is slow, untangles what is perplexed, softens what is hard, and undertakes what is difficult. [Note: [Col. 0157] In another copy: “For he knows by what way he ought to proceed; he orders each thing safely; from things open he judges obscure things, from obscure things he declares open things, from small things great things, from near things distant things, from parts the whole, from evils goods, and from idle things serious matters.”] The wise person is not moved by the authority of the speaker, the eminence of lineage, nor by what someone says or does, nor by how much he says or does, but considers what sort of things win approval. He desires 88 and seeks what can be desired before all people. Nor does he impose upon himself something higher, in which he must fear either while standing or falling as he descends.

[Col. 0158D] He calls salutary counsels to himself when prosperity of life or worldly rank flatters him; then, as on slippery ground, he checks and plants his foot, and allows his step to go forward not rashly but cautiously. Circumspection and caution belong to prudence. Prudence measures the future by the past: if a prudent person sees someone have fallen into a particular vice on a particular occasion, he measures the future accordingly, lest he fall from a like occasion into a like sin. O what great prudence it is to measure the future by the past—[Col. 0159A] the present by prior deeds, like things by like things, consequences by signs! Circumspection also belongs to prudence; it is nothing other than caution regarding opposite vices, by which we avoid one vice in such a way that we do not incur its opposite. For example: we guard against avarice in such a way that we do not incur prodigality. Solomon recommended this virtue when he said: “Guard your heart with every guard” (Prov. 4). Intending to say “guard,” he first said “with every,” lest, when you close bolts at this door, you open an entrance from another side. For there are many who so escape the assault of one vice that they fall into the snare of another. Thus vices supply one another: while someone secretly escapes one, another by reciprocal succession holds the fugitive. Caution also belongs to prudence, by which prudence discerns vices that bear the appearance of virtues. Hence Isidore says: “Vices bear the appearance of virtues and thereby deceive their followers more ruinously, because they cover themselves under the veil of virtue. For under the pretext of justice cruelty is practiced, and lax sloth is thought gentleness. Often the negligence of sluggishness does what indulgence is believed to do.” From this it is clear that the prudent person is self-sufficient for living happily. Hence Crispus says, “The wise person lacks nothing,” for he possesses the highest good within himself, and therefore the instruments of goodness need not be sought externally. The highest good is cultivated within the mind; inwardly, the wise person embraces it wholly, because outwardly he does not embrace *form*. [Note: [Col. 0159] In another copy, *fortune* is read instead of *form*.] He begins [Col. 0159C] to be subject to fortune who seeks any part of goodness externally. But the prudent person confines every good within himself; even if he loses every good of fortune, he will cry: “All my things are with me,” namely prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance. He does not consider goods that can be taken away to be goods. Nothing is enough for the imprudent person, but he is not content and should not be left to himself. If he has need of no thing, he knows how to use no thing, but lacks everything.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On fortitude

These authorities invite us to fortitude: “Be strong in battle, and fight against the ancient serpent.” [Note: [Col. 0159] Another copy has: “Fight against ancient vices.” And Claudius says: “For what could make noble human nature reluctant to undertake, or weary of its undertaking?”] Seneca says: “If you are magnanimous, you will never judge that an insult has been done to you. Of your enemy you will say: ‘He did not harm me, but he had the intention of harming me.’” O [Col. 0159D] how noble is the magnanimity which, when it has its enemy in its power, judges that it has avenged itself by having been able to take revenge. It judges forgiveness to be the honorable and highest kind of vengeance. It attacks no one unexpectedly but openly; it does not engage in conflict unless it has declared it; adversities do not cast it down, prosperity does not exalt it. The courageous person does not seek dangers like a rash person, nor fear them like a coward. [Note: [Col. 0159] “We marvel at certain animals which pass through the midst of fires without bodily harm; how much more wonderful is the courageous man who passes unharmed and uninjured in spirit through iron, coals, and fires!”] This is what made Vincent [Col. 0160A] more powerful while he was being tortured than the one who tortured him.

O human being, if you have embraced this virtue, you will not fear fortune’s dart; you will laugh at it when flattering and despise it when angry. Whoever is courageous is free: he does not serve fortune or the world’s changes. See how great was the fortitude of the martyrs, who conquered torments, mocked the tyrants themselves by their magnanimity, were cast down in body but not in mind, did not turn their backs upon adversity but resisted magnanimously. There are three kinds of fortitude: the fortitude of the whitewashed hypocrite, the fortitude of the philosopher, and the fortitude of the just person. The first hunts empty glory, but by hunting earns the disgrace of eternal condemnation. It draws glory to itself in such a way that it is not in glory. This is [Col. 0160B] weakness rather than magnanimity, infirmity rather than strength. Heretics put it on display; false brethren presume upon it. The second is that by which philosophers despised worldly fortune, scorned glory, rejected riches, and renounced human powers. But this fortitude was insufficient for merit and incapable of earning life’s reward because it lacked form—that is, charity, which is the form of every good affection. According to this fortitude, Cato is said to have had sternness, Socrates magnanimity, and Diogenes contempt of the world.

But because this lacked the foundation of faith, was not raised by hope, and was not perfected by charity, it lost virtue’s merit. The fortitude of the just person, however, is that which establishes God as its end and does not omit its due [Col. 0160C] duty. This fortitude despises death, opens the house to spiritual poverty, and compels pleasures to lie beneath the bridle of reason. There are three kinds of accidental misfortunes: poverty, sickness, and a tyrant’s violence. Fortitude is effective against poverty so that the spirit is not broken but is greater inwardly, and grows richer in mind in proportion as it has less abundance in the goods of fortune. Fortitude is effective against the assault of sickness; in pain it gives thanks to God and finds spiritual delights in tribulation, [Note: [Col. 0159] Another copy reads: “In tribulation it finds spiritual delights.”] so that illnesses may yield rather to the mind’s benefit than to bodily damage. Thus sickness brings medicine, infirmity health, and sorrow joy. Fortitude conquers a tyrant’s violence, weakens his cruelty, [Col. 0160D] rejects prison, and does not fear death. [Note: [Col. 0159] Added: “It embraces the rack, desires chains, and willingly runs to death.”] Human being, your work is of no value unless it is strengthened by the pillar of fortitude. The building of good works totters unless it rests on the pillar of fortitude; once this is broken, the whole building collapses, and Samson—that is, the strong man—kills himself. [Note: [Col. 0159] Added: “If Peter had possessed this, he would not have departed from faith at a servant-girl’s voice; if the children of Israel had been endowed with it, they would not have murmured at the waters of contradiction.”] This makes adversities equal to prosperities and prosperities to adversities, so that one is not more exalted by prosperities than cast down by [Col. 0161A] adversities. It judges prosperities to be smoke and like passing foam, adversities like fleeing mist. Magnanimity itself shows that weakness makes a person powerful in tribulation, though it has no power of itself. Prudence is the queen of the other cardinal virtues. In it they find their form; from it they seek their measure. Without it, what seems to be virtue falls into foolishness, and what appears good lapses into rashness. Prudence teaches what is to be thought, what is to be done with what intention, and how it is to be brought to its end. It measures human strength, sets bounds to thoughts, directs the movements of the mind and the insights of reason, weighs goods, and examines evils. What good is religion unless it receives prudence’s seasoning? What good is fasting [Col. 0161B] unless it is seasoned with the salt of wisdom? Therefore, O human being, before undertaking anything, consider in the mirror of prudence the measure of your action; read in the book of prudence what is to be done and what avoided. That book does not err and deceives no one: all its judgments are true and honorable assertions.

## CHAPTER XXV. On temperance or moderation

Let the preacher proceed in this manner in a discourse on temperance or moderation:

“Let your moderation be known to all people: the Lord is near” (Phil. 4). Likewise the Apostle: “Let us live soberly, justly, and devoutly in this world” (Titus 2). Likewise: “Pursuing sobriety” (ibid.). And Jerome: “Moderate [Col. 0161C] and temperate food is beneficial to soul and body.” Again he says: “All things are prepared for the virtue of continence.” St Gregory: “The elevation of minds is the purity of the continent.” And elsewhere the poet says:

> The blessed have held the mean.

And:

> You will go most safely in the middle.

Consider how much nature requires, not how much the appetite desires. If you are self-controlled, you will attain the point of being content with yourself. For whoever is sufficient to himself is born amid delights. Put a bridle upon desire. Reject everything that draws the mind by blandishment or pleasure. Eat short of fullness; drink short of drunkenness; satisfy your desires with little, because you should care only that they cease. Approach food [Col. 0161D] not for pleasure; let hunger awaken your palate, not flavors. Let poverty never seem filthy to you, thriftiness never sordid, simplicity never neglected, nor lightness feeble; do not lament your own possessions or marvel at those of another. If you love continence, flee shameful things before they occur. [Note: [Col. 0161] In another copy: “Allow everything tolerable except shamefulness.”] Maintain not bitter but gentle words. Be yourself a fugitive from vices, but do not be a curious investigator of others or a harsh reprover; rather, correct without condemnation, so that by admonition you anticipate cheerfulness and readily grant pardon for error. Do not exalt anyone beyond measure, nor cast anyone down. Be a silent listener to those who speak, [Col. 0162A] [Note: [Col. 0161] Added: “A ready receiver of those who listen.”] Answer readily the one who asks; yield readily to the contentious; do not descend to insult and curses. If you wish to be continent, observe the movements both of mind and body, lest they be unbecoming. Do not despise them because they are hidden: it matters nothing that no one sees them, when you yourself see them. Be familiar with few, fair to all; more severe in life than in expression; a merciful avenger, a detester of cruelty, desirous of a good reputation but not a sower of empty glory—indeed, outside empty glory, a hider of virtues, as others hide vices; a despiser of vain glory and honors. Endowed with these qualities, you will not be a harsh exactor. O how

> Rare a bird upon the earth, and most like a white crow,

is one who maintains the measure of this moderation! O how glorious is the virtue of temperance, which makes virtue [Col. 0162B] hold the mean, lest there be a lapse into deficiency or an excess into superfluity. This is spiritual circumcision, which cuts away with reason’s file the excess of each of the senses. This is what Seneca, inviting us to it, says: “Let life be regulated between good morals and public custom. Great is the person who uses earthenware in the same way as silver; nor is he less great who uses silver in the same way as earthenware.” He also says: “Let clothing be neither shabby nor excessively splendid. Virtue lies in moderation, not in abjection.” O human being, bind yourself within the bounds of temperance. Beware of being avaricious, yet do not disgracefully incur the mark of prodigality. Measure the other virtues also by the rule of temperance. Temperance must be maintained in justice, so that reverence for its discipline [Col. 0162C] does not become cheap through neglect arising from excessive familiarity, nor lose the grace of human lovableness through harsher severity. It sets a measure upon fortitude, so that it knows how to accept [Note: [Col. 0161] Another copy reads *endure* instead of *accept*.] prosperity and does not rashly seek adversity. It orders prudence, so that it does not be wise beyond what is due, but is wise unto sobriety and does not shamefully grow obsolete beyond [Note: [Col. 0161] *Within bounds* is read instead of *beyond*.] the measure of inquiry. Temperance adorns every substance in every respect with good works and gives form to circumstance. By it one so measures times, places, persons, and causes that, walking according to its limit, one cannot suffer ruin amid this world’s abrupt places and the precipices of temporal life. If anyone is armed with this, the sting of envy and the heap of detraction can do nothing against him; the devil finds [Col. 0162D] nothing in him to accuse, conscience nothing to uproot, the world nothing to mock, and purgatorial fire nothing to cleanse.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Against wordiness and the wandering of the tongue.

If anyone is anxious to guard against wordiness and the unbridled wandering of the tongue, let him diligently attend to the following. The Apostle says: “Avoid foolish and worthless tales” (1 Tim. 4). Jerome says: “Let buffoonery and wantonness have no place in your presence.” Everything that does not edify its hearers turns to their danger; for “evil conversations corrupt good morals” [Col. 0163A] (1 Cor. 15). Sixtus also says: “A malicious tongue is evidence of a malicious mind.” Your tongue follows your understanding; a word without understanding is a reproach. Augustine likewise says to Nepotianus: “Let it be your duty, dearest one, not only to keep your eyes chaste, but also your tongue: let neither the body be moved toward lust nor the tongue toward jokes or empty words.” Sixtus also says: “An empty utterance is an indication of an empty conscience: as speech is shown to be, so the mind too is proved to be. O human being, what will you be in deeds if you are found dissolute in words? It is no greater glory to say what is known than to keep silent about idle matters. He is foolish who does not first bring a word to the file of reason before sending it forth upon the tongue of his mouth. A person ought first [Col. 0163B] to scrutinize a word before assuming the office of speaking. Beware, when you are about to speak in public, lest your wordiness produce shame in the unlearned and indignation in the learned. A flood of words signifies a fickle mind; wordiness on the lips portrays what a person is in mind. Wordiness makes a person into a buffoon, transforms him into an actor, degrades him into a jester, and lays aside the dignity of human nature. The tongue must be restrained, as James says (ch. 3), for it sets ablaze the wheel of our birth.

“The wheel of our birth” is this present life, which from the beginning of life revolves in manifold changeability. The mobility of the tongue sets it ablaze: in youth toward jesting, in mature age toward deceit, in old age toward slander. This spark [Col. 0163C] must be quenched lest it become a flame; this shoot, lest it grow into a forest; this drop, lest it swell into the abundance of a torrent. It is a greater thing to restrain the tongue than to capture a city, because the former assaults inwardly, the latter outwardly. Here weapons are taken against you from yourself; there, battle is waged over what belongs to another. Yet it is the height of shame and abject humiliation to be unable to restrain one member, unable to subdue a worthless servant to oneself. If the tongue is placed in a moist place, let it be held fast by steadfastness; if it wishes to go out, let it be restrained by temperance; let the bolt of reason be applied, and let it be trimmed by the file of discernment. If a bridle is put upon a horse lest it wander contrary to its rider [Note: [Col. 0163] Another copy continues: “Lest it be carried over precipices, lest it fall into steep places.”], where no danger threatens except that of the body, much more should a bridle be applied to the tongue, through [Col. 0163D] which danger threatens the soul [Note: [Col. 0163] The following is added: “Lest it carry us into the grove of buffoonery, into the precipice of perdition, into the poison of slander, and finally into the abyss of Gehenna’s punishment.”].

True simplicity is better than abundant talkativeness; holy rusticity is better than sinful eloquence. One who frequently breaks into chatter uninvited is easily despised. Accustom your tongue, therefore, to speak well. Precious is the tongue that knows how to frame words only about divine things; and holy is the mouth from which heavenly sayings always proceed. Consider that you will render an account of every idle word. An idle word, as Gregory says on Matthew 12, is “one which lacks either the usefulness of uprightness [Col. 0164A] or the reason of just necessity.” Wordiness is seed that bears no fruit; foolish salt, good for seasoning nothing, but rather making the earth barren, because it turns its hearers to laughter.

Do not, O human being, strive for a multitude of words, but for fruitful brevity of meaning; for, as Jerome says, when striving for brevity, you ought not to say more. And if you have chastity in your mind, do not defile it by disgraceful speech: “Show yourself wise, not by talking and running about, but by keeping silent and sitting still.” A chatterer is never ashamed to speak; he considers not what he says, but how much; he measures not an abundance of meanings but of words. Moderate speech is holy reverence; immoderate speech is the mark of shamelessness. Some, in order to indulge wordiness, rashly expound Scriptures which they nevertheless do not understand; and, once they have persuaded others, they assume the haughty bearing of learned persons. Truly, chatterers [Note: [Col. 0163] Another reading: “Gossipmongers are to be avoided.”] are to be avoided like venomous animals: by their wordiness they make others foolish, and imprudently belch forth things useful neither to themselves nor to others. And, as Jerome says: “Some spread most disgraceful rumours, and say that they have heard what came forth from their own lips.” Some are talkative and garrulous against others, but tongue-tied and mute on their own behalf. Wordiness is the mirror of the mind, and a garrulous tongue the writing of the heart.

Hear what the Gospel says: “A good man brings forth good things from the good treasure of his heart” (Matt. 12). [Col. 0164C] Solomon likewise says: “In much speaking sin will not be absent, but he who moderates his lips is most prudent” (Prov. 10). “He who guards his mouth guards his soul; but he who is inconsiderate will suffer evils” (Prov. 13). A wise person will keep silent until the proper time; but the wanton, the imprudent, or the shameless will not observe the time. David likewise says: “A man of tongue shall not be directed upon the earth” (Ps. 138). And Gregory: “A man of many words is unskilled; the prudent person uses few words. Brief speech produces knowledge; much speaking is folly. Listen first; speak last: the end has greater honour; the last speech is better than the first.”

## CHAPTER XXVII. Against lying.

[Col. 0164D] Whoever wishes to avoid the ruin of lying should form himself by these maxims. We read in the Gospel: “You shall not bear false witness” (Matt. 19). And Paul says: “Putting away lying, speak the truth, each one with his neighbour” (Eph. 4).

Solomon also says: “He who lies is a deceitful witness. Lying lips are an abomination to the Lord, but those who act faithfully please him” (Prov. 12). “The mouth which lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1). And David says: “You will destroy all who speak falsehood” (Ps. 5). Isidore likewise says: “Everything that disagrees with truth [Col. 0165A] is iniquity.” O human being, how far you depart from the supreme Truth while you devote yourself to fabrications of lies! How do you suppose that you will come to the True One, if in your words you disagree with truth? With what conscience, I do not know, does one ask God with the tongue that has belched forth a lie? There is no sin by whose mark the conscience is so branded as by that of lying. Although every mortal sin alienates a person from the true, no evil does so more than lying, which detracts from the nature of truth.

This is the vice that devises false testimonies, fashions flatteries, invents frauds, and completes acts of detraction. By this vice one speaks with heart and mouth, and is made divided within oneself. One denies with the mouth what one holds in the heart. By this vice heart contradicts heart, mouth opposes heart. [Col. 0165B] This vice gives birth to heresy, makes schisms, generates suspicions, fabricates unheard-of rumours, colours disgraces, conceals things that should be exposed, and exposes things that should be concealed. It stands by perjuries, sits beside dishonourable actions, and, contrary to all things that by natural law tend toward the neighbour’s benefit, attacks even truth itself. It contains such a rust of malice that it can by no reasoning be excused. Natural affection did not free the midwives from guilt (Exod. 1); reasonable fear did not free the Gibeonites (Josh. 9); error of mind did not free Peter (Matt. 26); necessity’s provision did not free Ananias (Acts 5).

No sin so breathes toward guile, tends toward fraud, looks toward deception, or pants [Col. 0165C] after betrayal as the vice of lying, the crime of falsehood. “O children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek lying?” (Ps. 4). You excessively desire to pursue the vanity of our nature, you who even in speech exchange truth for falsehood. But if fault now lies in falsehood, punishment in the future will not be absent from truth; and whoever is now false through lying will in the future be true in Gehenna. You know that through lying you imitate the devil, the father of lies, who did not stand in truth but fell through the vanity of pride. Those who depart from truth are his children; those who indulge falsehoods are his accomplices. O human being, if in your lie there is falsehood, in your guilt there will be truth. O wretched effect of lying: by a false proposition it consequently [Col. 0165D] brings in a true punishment! O how great the imprudence, how great the folly, to endure the blows of eternal punishment for a lying word! How far from the office of the tongue does one depart who is defiled by the filth of lying! A person adequately displays the wheel of his birth when he slips through the offense of falsehood. O human being, if you wish to avoid lying words, train your tongue for truth and turn it away from the buffoonery of words.

Lying is a servitude that turns the whole substance of speech into its own bitterness. There are three kinds of lie: the lie of vanity, the lie of falsehood, and the lie of intention. Of the first it is said: “They have spoken vain things, each one to his neighbour,” etc. (Ps. 11). [Col. 0166A] Of the second it is said: “Every human being is a liar” (Ps. 125). Of the third: “You will destroy all who speak falsehood” (Ps. 5). The first is miserable, the second culpable, the third abominable. The first belongs to punishment, the second to guilt, the third to malice. The first is inborn, the second devised, the third deliberately wrought.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Against detraction.

These authorities furnish a remedy against acts of detraction. Jerome says: “When some deed is invented by a slanderer, another person’s reputation is harassed.” He also says: “You cannot rightly rebuke in others what you yourself do, nor can you accuse hypocrisy when you yourself are held guilty.” Likewise: “Beware lest you have either an itching tongue or itching ears: that is, lest you either slander others or listen to others slandering.” “Slander no one, nor consider yourself holy in this, if you tear others to pieces and wound them by your detractions. This is not correction, but satisfying your own vice.” Likewise: “It is incongruous for the body to lie concealed while the tongue wanders throughout the whole world. See that, while you rebuke vices, you do not incur the vice of detraction.” Likewise: “Servants are a complaining sort; however much they receive, it is too little for them. For they consider not what is given but how much, and console their pain only through detractions.” He also says: “One who frequently detracts from others offends very many. It is disgraceful to tear apart the absent and describe another’s life; he is less eloquent who excuses himself by another’s error.”

The detractor [Col. 0166C] bears the image of a scorpion, because, just as a scorpion displays a maiden’s face and then emits its sting, inflicting from above a sharp wound [Note: [Col. 0165] Another copy reads: “curved” (*arcuatum*).], so the detractor puts forward favourable words in people’s presence, conceals the sting of detraction in secret, and, as though wounding from above, detracts from those who are better. O human being, what do you think of yourself when you hurl the javelin of detraction? The first arrow returns upon you, and the wound is inflicted on you before it is inflicted on others. You conceal badly the enormity of your own deed when you desire to cover it over by another’s detraction. While you detract from people, you make yourself suspect, make yourself hateful to all, and strive to make enemies, by the poison of detraction, of those whom you ought to make friends by honourable speech. While you endeavour to disgrace others, you infect yourself more deeply; and what falsehood you devise against others [Col. 0166D] you find true in yourself.

Of detractors it is said: “Their throat is an open sepulchre,” etc. (Ps. 5, 13). A whitewashed sepulchre is outwardly fair but holds the stench of a corpse within; so the detractor, wishing to colour his inward malice, breaks out into the bites of detraction. Yet by this very act the sepulchre is opened and the stench of inward malice goes forth. Detractors bear the image of dogs, which apply themselves indiscriminately to barking and inflict bites upon all. These are those who find a knot in a reed, a stain in what is spotless, a corner in what is round, darkness in what is bright. This is the plague of hypocrites, the bite of the envious; that plague spares no one, increases guilt, diminishes grace, errs against the neighbour, and sins against the Holy Spirit. Sounding forth with this malignant plague, the scribes and Pharisees said: “By Beelzebub, prince of demons, he casts out demons” (Luke 12; Mark 3). And others cried: “You are a Samaritan and have a demon” (John 8).

O human being, what advantage is there in detraction? What benefit in a malicious tooth? While you believe that you harm your neighbour, you rather advance his honour; for good persons are customarily slandered, and the wasting sickness of envy rages into virtue. For the malicious tongue disdains to exercise its malice upon vices, arms itself wholly to lessen a neighbour’s righteousness, and so polishes another’s reputation with the rust of its own detraction and, by its own biting, purifies and exalts another’s glory. Detraction proclaims envy and lays bare the mind’s malice; and what is inwardly unknown, [Col. 0167B] it vomits outwardly through the poison of detraction [Note: [Col. 0167] Everything following was absent from our copy, but has been taken from another, older copy.].

O human being, if you accuse, accuse with measure; if you rebuke, rebuke cautiously: not that your neighbour may be scandalized, but that he may be corrected. Accuse, not in order to cover up your own crime, but in order to heal another’s wound. Detraction belongs to buffoons, who flatter in order to squeeze out money; who slander in order to incite the rich to make gifts; who play the cithara in the ears of the powerful through flatteries; who weigh praises according to the measure of table-gifts; who gain through detractions what they cannot gain through virtues. Their tongue, which hunts food, will be food for eternal fire; and the tongue which draws gifts through detraction will be torn apart by Gehenna’s punishment.

[Col. 0167C] Detraction is the enemy of the mother of virtues, namely charity. Whoever wounds his neighbour with detraction drives charity away from himself, because the Holy Spirit will flee the contrivance of detraction and abhors the falsehood of reproach, the sin of detraction. Neither here nor in the future scarcely finds a place of forgiveness one who offends the Holy Spirit. O human being, who are ash and dust, with what face, with what brow marked by shame, do you dare to vomit the poison of detraction against one better than yourself, or to pronounce a judge’s sentence against one who is less evil, or only slightly so? If you judge your neighbour unjustly, you will be judged justly by one greater; for a judgment of detraction, you will feel the eternal judgment of condemnation.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Exhortation to prayer.

[Col. 0167D] This is teaching concerning prayer: “All things whatsoever you ask in prayer, believing, you shall receive” (Matt. 21). “Pray for one another, that you may be saved; for the constant prayer of the righteous avails much” (Jas. 5). “The Lord is far from the wicked, and he will hear the prayers of the righteous” (Prov. 15). “Before prayer prepare your soul, and do not be like one who tests God” (Ecclus. 18). “God will hear the prayer of the injured” (Ecclus. 35). Son, in your infirmity do not despise yourself, but pray to God, and he will heal you. Rise from your bed, turn away from [Col. 0168A] sin, direct your hands, devote yourself to prayers and readings night and day; and when sleep has fallen from your eyes, then let the mind awaken in prayer. As it is unfitting for a soldier to go out to battle without arms, so it is not expedient for any Christian to proceed without prayer. Hence Jerome: “Let prayer arm one going out from his lodging.” The more heavily we are pressed by the tumult of carnal thoughts, the more ardently we ought to persist in prayer [Note: [Col. 0167] An old copy adds: “Hence Isidore: The judge is more quickly bent to prayer if the sinner is corrected from his perversity.”].

It is better to pray with the silence of the heart than with words alone, without the mind’s attention; for the benefit of psalmody consoles the heart’s sadness.

One’s affection in praying toward God ought to be so great that one does not despair of obtaining the effect sought by prayers. We pray in vain if we lack the confidence of hope. Whoever turns away from God’s commandments will not deserve what he asks in prayer. Caesarius said: “We ought to apply ourselves to prayer and reading in such a way that at times we may also perform some work with our hands.” Just as stronger herbs or medicinal compounds drive away venomous animals, so pure prayer drives away filthy thoughts. Do not, O human being, disfigure prayer by any circumstance. Ask for eternal things, not temporal ones. If you ask for earthly things, your prayer lacks matter; if it is not from charity, it lacks form. Therefore ask devoutly, that prayer may be formed; perseveringly, that your intention may be rooted; and for those things which pertain to eternal salvation, that they may cleave to a stable foundation. Do not ask for monstrous things, lest your prayer be turned into sin for you, as was Judas’s prayer. Do not ask from [Col. 0168C] bitterness of mind, like the sons of Zebedee, who asked Christ that fire might come down from heaven and destroy the Samaritans (Luke 9). For they did not ask with an eye to justice, but from a love of vengeance.

If you pray, exclude from your mind the tumult of thoughts; close the door of your mind; enter the chamber of your heart. When you pray to God, preserve the sweetness of your ointment, lest dead flies spoil the sweetness of the holy incense (Eccl. 10); that is, beware lest evil thoughts mingle with your prayer and destroy its merit. If you offer God the sacrifice of prayer, drive away with Abraham the birds from the sacrifice (Gen. 15), lest they lie in wait for the offerings and defile them; for one must fear lest impure thoughts corrupt the sweetness of the prayer offered. For many have [Col. 0168D] God on their lips but the devil in their minds; with their voice they praise God, but in mind they blaspheme; while their tongue is in hymns, their spirit is among the dishes; and what they confess with their mouth, they deny in spirit. Such people, so far as lies in them, mock God and blaspheme the divine majesty; and, while they pray that the sins of the tongue may be forgiven, they do not hesitate to retain those sins in their minds. Indeed, some pollute their mouths in prayer and infect their souls. Seneca says of them: “How great now is human madness! They whisper most shameful vows to God; if anyone should remove his ear, they would fall silent. What they do not wish human beings to know, they tell God.” “Live with people as though God sees; speak with God as though people hear.”

O human being, if you wish to be heard, ask worthily for worthy things; thus you will ask God for what pertains to God to give. There is, however, a dangerous kind of prayer, by which we ask for evil things, such as the prayer of Judas the traitor, because he sought the betrayal of the Saviour. Another is profit-seeking, by which temporal things are sought, such as the request of the sons of Zebedee, by which they asked that one might sit at God’s right hand and the other at his left in his kingdom, which they believed he would rule temporally (Matt. 20). Another is fruitless, by which an obstinate person asks for eternal salvation; concerning this it is said: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ shall enter [Col. 0169B] the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 7). Another is fruitful, in which nothing fitting is omitted; of this it is said: “Whatever you ask the Father in my name shall be done for you” (Mark 11; John 16). Here the power of the name is understood rather than the name of the divine power. The person truly asks in the name of Jesus who asks with a saving intention and for eternal salvation. This prayer alone pleads before the Judge and makes its case before the heavenly Prince. Of it the Song of Songs says in the language of love: “Who is this who comes up through the wilderness like a little column of smoke, from the spices of myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer?” (Song 3). For this prayer truly ascends: it penetrates paradise and rises even to God’s throne.

This is aptly called a little column, and straight, because, as a rod is directed straight upward, so [Col. 0169C] fruitful prayer is not bent toward earthly things but is directed inflexibly toward heavenly ones. It is aptly compared with smoke because, as smoke born from fire tends upward, so fruitful prayer, arising from the furnace of charity, ascends on high. It is also aptly said to ascend through the wilderness because the mind through which such prayer is poured out is separated from every tumult of evil thoughts. It is from the spices of myrrh and frankincense. Frankincense brings fragrance; myrrh, bitterness. Frankincense therefore signifies the devotion of the mind; myrrh, the bitterness of penitence. Thus the ointment of prayer ought to consist of the bitterness of repentance for sins and the fragrance of inward devotion. For whoever desires to pray fruitfully [Col. 0169D] must necessarily, repenting of sins, give forth in prayer the fragrance of the mind’s devotion. “And every powder of the perfumer.” Christ is the perfumer, who adorns his own with the diverse spices of virtues and intoxicates them, as it were, with perfumer’s nectar. The whole powder of this perfumer is manifold virtue, from which we ought to prepare the ointment of prayer.

## CHAPTER XXX. On compunction, or contrition.

By these authorities someone may be instructed unto compunction [Col. 0170A] and contrition of heart. The prophet says: “Rend your hearts and not your garments” (Joel 2). And John: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” (Matt. 3). And the Psalmist: “A troubled spirit is a sacrifice to God” (Ps. 50). Saint Augustine likewise says: “He who does not have compunction does not have pure prayer.” And Saint Isidore: “The vices we have committed must first be cleansed by tears; then, with the mind’s vision purified, let us contemplate what we seek.”

Compunction of heart is humility of mind with tears, arising from remembrance of sin, love of the Judge, and fear of judgment. The more perfect effect of compunction is that which repels from itself every affection of carnal desires and fixes its intention, with the whole effort of the mind, upon contemplation of God. The soul of the elect is likewise affected by a twofold compunction: when it considers the evils of its deeds, and when it sighs with desire for eternal life. There are four dispositions by which the mind of the righteous is beneficially pierced: first, remembrance of past deeds; second, consideration of its pilgrimage in this life; third, remembrance of its punishments; fourth, desire for the heavenly homeland, so that it may be able to arrive there more quickly.

For tears of repentance are reckoned before God in place of baptism. Love tears, and be so much the more inclined to lamentation as you were inclined to guilt. Great sins require great lamentations; blessed, moreover, is the person who has compunction according to God. Compunction is health for the soul; compunction is remission of [Col. 0170C] sins; compunction is the second plank after shipwreck, the second remedy after sin’s remedy.
