Compunction is a spiritual washing of inward regeneration, without which baptism does not avail adults; without which Christ’s body is received unto judgment; without which confession is fruitless; without which satisfaction is vain. This is the water that cleanses the mind, makes intention fruitful, waters confession, and satisfies the soul. This is the water that drowns the Egyptians—that is, extinguishes the first motions. This is the spiritual flood that kills all flesh—that is, extinguishes every carnal thought [Note: [Col. 0169] Another copy here added the following: “O happy remedy, by which the disease of sins is expelled, by which the poison of guilt is vomited forth! O happy plank, by which the shipwrecked person returns to the harbor of salvation! Saving water by which sin is washed away; the way by which one returns to the homeland; the spiritual remedy by which one returns from the trackless place to the way!”].

There is a threefold washing: of baptism, of penitence, and of martyrdom. The first is for those entering, [Col. 0170D] the second for those returning, the third for those arriving.

Of the first it is said: “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isa. 1). Of the second: “Wash me yet more from my iniquity” (Ps. 50). Of the third: “They washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb” (Rev. 7). The first washing is prefigured by the sprinkling performed in the Old Testament with living waters; the second by sprinkling with ashes; the third by the blood of the red heifer (Num. 19). For what is living water but baptism? What is the sprinkling of ashes but the humility of compunction, [Col. 0171A] through which a person shows himself to be ash and sits in ashes and sackcloth? And what is the blood of the red heifer but martyrdom, reddened with blood, which had efficacy from Christ’s Passion? Thus there is a threefold baptism: baptism of the stream, performed in water; baptism of the breath, performed in penitence through the grace of the Holy Spirit; and baptism of blood, performed in the struggle of martyrdom. By the first a person is clothed with the first robe; by the second one who has become misshapen is renewed; by the third the second is prepared. In the first, the old person is blotted out; in the second, the inward person is renewed; in the third, the flesh dies. The first belongs to all, the second to many, the third to few.

O happy washing of penitence, which has power to cleanse as often as the human heart needs cleansing. This is the heavenly fuller’s herb, by which he cleanses his garments, disfigured by stains. This is the heavenly nitre which, descending from the dew of divine grace and refined by the sun of righteousness, wipes away the stains of sins. This is the lye with which the head of the inward person—that is, the mind—teeming with the worms of vices is washed; it is prepared from the ash of humility and the water of compunction. This is the sole consolation against human falls: standing in place of Christ’s Passion, it provides a remedy against sins, lest Christ be compelled to die as often as a person falls into the abyss of sin. This is spiritual circumcision, performed through the rock, Christ; through it the foreskin of the flesh—that is, the desire of carnal uncleanness—is cut away.

If, therefore, you suffer shipwreck in the abyss [Col. 0171C] of sin, cling to the plank of contrition. It excludes shipwreck; it brings you to the harbor. Enter into your conscience and examine it. First consider the state of your prudence: whether sight has bent you down through desire, the throat through gluttony, hearing through enervating melody or willing listening to detraction; whether the tongue has stumbled in speech, smell has gone astray through scent, touch has gone astray through theft, or your steps have strayed upon level ground. If in these things, or in any one of them, you find guilt, wash it away by the mark of compunction. Measure the extent of washing by the quantity of filth; apply the measure of remedies according to the magnitude of diseases; weigh the degree of punishment according to the excess of guilt.

Penitence is so called from punishing, because the guilt that is punished by contrition is erased. Fear is the mother and origin of penitence: it conceives penitence and gives birth to contrition. Hence Isaiah: “From your fear, O Lord, we have conceived and brought forth a spirit of salvation” (Isa. 26). Penitence, then, is to weep over sins already committed and not commit those which must be wept over. For one who weeps over some sins in such a way as to commit others again either does not know how to do penitence or pretends to do so. What good is it to someone, for example, to weep over sins of lust while still panting with the heats of avarice? Isidore says: “He is a mocker and not penitent who still does what he repents of; nor does he seem to ask God as one subject to him, but to mock him as one proud.” “A dog returned to its vomit” (Prov. 26) [Col. 0172A] is the penitent person returning to sin. Many weep without ceasing and do not cease to sin. I see some receive tears for penitence, yet I observe that they lack penitential feeling: for they shed tears through the mind’s sense of justice, not from remembrance of sin; and, when the habit immediately comes back to life, they commit again the things over which they had wept.

Here our most ancient copy ended, with the word: “It is finished.” Yet in another copy everything following was appended.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On confession of sins.

Authorities: “Confess your sins to one another” (Jas. 5). And elsewhere: “I said: I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord” (Ps. 31). Job likewise [Col. 0172B] says: “I will speak in the bitterness of my soul” (Job 10). For one speaks in the bitterness of one’s soul who, in accordance with contrition of heart, confesses sin with the mouth. The Apostle likewise says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10). In the Old Testament it was commanded that a person cured of leprosy should show himself to the priest (Lev. 14). By this it is shown that the penitent person, cured by contrition of spiritual leprosy, is bound to show himself to the priest through confession.

Therefore confess your sins that you may be absolved; accuse yourself that you may be excused. If in the present you are not your own accuser, you will have three accusers on the day of judgment: God as accuser and judge; conscience accusing and punishing; and the devil accusing and punisher. This is the difference [Col. 0172C] between the judge of the earth and the judge of heaven: one who accuses himself before the judge of the earth is regarded as guilty, but before the judge of heaven one who confesses his sin is absolved. Before the judge of the earth, reporting a crime or shifting it elsewhere has force. A defendant who removes the crime from himself or attributes it to someone else is in some fashion excused; but one who, before the judge of heaven, ascribes the crime to himself, neither attributes it to another nor assigns the cause of sin to fortune or fate, is excused.

Confession may be fourfold: confession under compulsion, confession of despair, confession of penitence, and confession of praise. Confession under compulsion is that which arises in some sense from being compelled, such as that by which the demons confessed the Son of God, saying: “Jesus, Son of the living God, why have you come before the time to destroy us?” (Matt. 8). [Col. 0172D] Confession of despair is that by which Judas confessed, saying: “I have sinned in betraying innocent blood” (Matt. 27), and Cain: “My iniquity is greater than that I may deserve pardon” (Gen. 4). Confession of penitence is that which arises from penitence, concerning which James says: “Confess your sins to one another” (Jas. 5). Confession of praise is that by which we confess God’s goodness, saying: “Confess to the Lord, for he is good” (Ps. 135), and by which Christ too confessed, saying: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth” (Matt. 11).

There is a twofold confession of sin: one general, the other special. General confession is made daily at the morning and evening sacrifice—that is, at Compline—for venial and hidden sins. [Col. 0173A] Special confession is made for mortal and manifest sins [Note: [Col. 0173] “Manifest sins” here means sins known to the person confessing them.]. Clerics are bound to make it every Saturday; laypeople are bound to make special confession three times yearly: namely, at the Nativity of the Lord, at Easter, and at Pentecost. This was prefigured in the old law by the command that the children of Israel should present themselves to the Lord in Jerusalem three times each year, and not empty-handed. Thus we too are commanded to offer ourselves to God three times yearly through confession in the spiritual Jerusalem—that is, in the Church—and not empty of good works. But today the practice has become prevalent that scarcely a layperson or cleric confesses even once a year; and when one does confess, one must fear that the confession is made rather to satisfy custom than from contrition of mind. Some are kept from confession by negligence; some by shame; some [Col. 0173B] by evil habit; some by fear of the satisfaction to be imposed; some by a resolve to live in sin.

These are the little frogs which, cast into a dog’s mouth, make the dog mute. Some maintain that a *calamites* is a frog living among reeds, which, if cast into a dog’s mouth, makes the dog mute. The dog is the unclean sinner, from whom the aforesaid plagues take away barking, or the sound of confession, like little frogs cast into a dog’s mouth. These are the foreigners who stopped up Abraham’s well (Gen. 26). Abraham’s well signifies confession, from which the faithful draw water springing up to eternal life. The aforesaid plagues stop it up, so that a person may not draw the water of salvation from the well of confession. This is the cistern [Col. 0173C] of Bethlehem, which the Philistines besiege and from which David desires to drink (2 Kings 23); for the faithful person, figured by David, desires the water of confession and salvation, but the wedge of the Philistines—that is, the multitude of the aforesaid plagues—besieges it and prevents the faithful from drawing it.

Confession, however, ought to be universal, not particular: confession should be made specifically of known sins and generally of unknown ones. For it belongs to devout minds to reckon guilt where guilt is not present, and by confession to acknowledge it where it is not manifest to recognition. For as remission is universal, so confession too ought to be universal; for the grace of the Holy Spirit does not know slow processes: whom it heals, it heals wholly.

Three things must be present for confession to be true: [Col. 0173D] contrition of heart, profession of the mouth, and satisfaction in deed. Therefore, if any of these is lacking, there is no confession, but only a gaping of the mouth; for confession is a complex expression and denotes three things. This is the three-days’ journey by which we must go into the wilderness—that is, strive toward the heavenly homeland—in order that we may sacrifice to our God.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On penitence, or satisfaction.

“Bring forth fruits worthy of repentance” (Matt. 3). And elsewhere it is said: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (ibid.). And Job says: “I repent in ashes and dust” (Job 47). Outward repentance, therefore, [Col. 0174A] had its beginning from Christ through preaching, its example from Job through satisfaction, and from David through teaching and instruction, who says: “Against thee only have I sinned,” etc. (Ps. 90). The fruits of repentance are remedies: prayers, fasts, psalmody, vigils, offerings, readings, almsgiving, and austerity of dress. Against the disease of lust, prayers and fasts are medicines: prayers, that God may temper the fire of concupiscence with the dew of heavenly grace; fasts, that they may chastise the beast of our flesh. “This kind of demon is not cast out except by prayer and fasting.” Psalmody and reading avail against the sin of sloth, so that the mind may be roused from torpor and learn to reject idleness and pursue serious matters. Almsgiving likewise becomes a remedy against avarice; scantiness of food [Col. 0174B] against gluttony; for, as Gregory testifies, “Contraries are cured by contraries.” Thus the seven principal virtues must be opposed to the seven principal vices: humility against pride; charity against envy; the long-suffering of patience against anger; cheerfulness of mind against sloth; generosity against avarice; sobriety against gluttony; chastity against lust.

As we sin in three ways, so we must repent in three ways. Because we sin in thought, let us apply to this disease the remedy of contrition; because we sin in speech, let us apply the antidote of confession; because we sin in deed, let us set against it the medicine of satisfaction. Repentance is twofold: one kind is momentary and passing; the other [Col. 0174C] persevering and lasting. The former is insufficient for the blotting out of sin; the latter is sufficient for forgiveness. The former is imperfect; the latter perfect. Of the former Isidore says: “He is a mocker, and not penitent, who does what he repents of.” Of persevering repentance it is said that it ought not to end until death. For through repentance the sinner ought to offer from himself as many holocausts of satisfaction as he had offered vices from himself to the devil; so that our flesh, which previously produced the thorns and briars of vices, may through repentance be ploughed for the increase of virtues. And as our sins must always be kept in memory in order to erase them, so repentance must be remembered, that repentance may produce memory and memory draw forth sorrow. In the present life one ought to be set in this purgatorial fire, lest one be tormented [Col. 0174D] definitively in the flame of Gehenna.

There are three fires: purgatorial, testing, and definitive. The purgatorial is satisfaction; the testing is temptation; the definitive, eternal condemnation. Of the first it is said: “He shall cleanse us in spirit and fire” (Matt. 3). Of the second we read: “Thou hast tested us with fire” (Ps. 16). Of the third: “Go into eternal fire” (Matt. 25). Purgatorial fire is twofold: one is on the way, namely repentance; the other after life, namely purgatorial punishment.

If we are cleansed in the first, we are delivered from the second and third; if we do not undergo the first, we shall experience the second—indeed, what is more grievous, the definitive fire. The first [Col. 0175A] purgatorial fire excludes two fires, namely the second purgatorial fire and the eternal definitive fire. For the first purgatorial fire is, as it were, a shadow and picture of the second. Just as the shadow and picture of a material fire inflict no pain, while the material fire itself brings torment or burning, so the fire of repentance has no bitterness in comparison with the second purgatorial fire. For, as Augustine says, the punishment of purgatory is much more severe than any temporal punishment. O man, God’s patience invites you to repentance, his power to fear, his kindness to love. Consider how great is his power to punish, how great his patience for repentance. See how merciful he is, who gives you time to repent. He no longer wills the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live (Ezek. 33). [Col. 0175B] And all this proceeds from his sweetness and love. For “the Father chastises every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12), or loves.

## Chapter XXXIII. On Almsgiving

“Break thy bread for the hungry, and bring the needy and wandering into thy house” (Isa. 58). And elsewhere: “Give alms, and all things are clean for you” (Luke 11). Likewise: “Give to everyone who asks of thee” (Luke 6). Likewise: “Blessed is he who anticipates the hand of one perishing.” Likewise: “If you see someone perishing from hunger and do not help, you have killed him.”

O man, almsgiving is the seasoning of fasting, the ornament of prayer, the glory of vigils, the badge of generosity, a special remedy for sin. Christ invites you to it, giving away all things by the example of poverty and [Col. 0175C] preaching works of mercy in word. Let no poverty excuse you from it. If you cannot give money, give a piece of bread; if you cannot do this, at least give a drink of cold water. If you cannot aid your neighbor by deed, aid him by word, either interceding for him or instructing him. For almsgiving is manifold: of the hand, by giving to the poor; of service, by ministering to one who gives; of the tongue, by instructing one’s neighbor or interceding for him; of the mind, by compassionating the sinner or forgiving injuries.

Some alms are ordered, others disordered. Ordered alms are those shaped by their proper circumstances; disordered alms are those deprived of them. The circumstances of almsgiving are these: who, what, how much, to whom, where, when, [Col. 0175D] and why. “Who”: whether the giver is rich or poor; for the alms of a poor person are more pleasing than those of a rich person. Thus the Lord says in the Gospel (Mark 12) that the poor woman who put two small coins into the treasury gave more than the rich who put in large sums. By “who” is also understood whether the giver is just or unjust. For if a just person gives alms, they avail for both ends; but if an unjust person gives alms, they avail him for escape from punishment, not for the merit of glory. By “what” it is indicated that almsgiving ought to be made from one’s own possessions, not another’s. For almsgiving is not rightly made from theft or robbery; since, as the authoritative text says: “To make alms from the substance of the poor is to slaughter a son in the sight of his father” (Ecclus. 34). By “how much” it is shown that one should not give everything [Col. 0176A] to one person, but distribute portions among many. By “to whom” it is indicated that alms should be given rather to the poor than to the rich; rather to a relative or connection than to a stranger; rather to members of the household of faith than to ill-disposed persons. Thus, to indicate how much and to whom, it is said: “He dispersed, he gave to the poor” (Ps. 111): openly, indeed, for the instruction of others, but with every desire for human praise removed. Hence the Lord says: “So let your works shine before men that they may glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5). 101 “When”: in a time of need. “Why”: for the sake of God, not earthly gain or human favor.

Almsgiving is heavenly dew, extinguishing the furnace of sin; it alone pleads with God; it alone will plead for you before the strict [Col. 0176B] Judge. For what will cause the blessed to be praised by Christ in judgment? Because they kept silence? No. Because they were continent? Not at all. Because they devoted themselves to vigils? Certainly not; but because they applied themselves to almsgiving.

Almsgiving bears the likeness of oil, fasting that of light. For as light is extinguished when oil is removed, so fasting without almsgiving is deprived of the power of merit. He opposes that special and natural command in which it is said, “What you wish men to do to you, do also to them” (Matt. 7), who refuses alms to one in need.

Almsgiving is threefold: cold, lukewarm, and hot. Cold almsgiving is that which is done not from the prompting of natural compassion or the fervor of charity, but solely for [Col. 0176C] human favor. Lukewarm almsgiving is done from the prompting of natural compassion, as that done for unbelievers from natural affection. Hot almsgiving is done in the heat of charity. The first merits punishment, the second avoids it, the third obtains glory.

Almsgiving should be made not only from superfluities but even from necessities. Hence it was said: “He who has two tunics, let him give to one who has none” (Luke 3). He names the tunic, not the cloak, because the tunic is more necessary; indicating that we are bound to give not only superfluities but also necessities. This was made clear in the blessed confessor Martin, who, in the harshness of the weather, gave to a poor man part of the cloak with which alone he was clothed. There are some who give to the poor things scarcely fit [Col. 0176D] to be set before pigs, supposing that their sins are redeemed by them. This is almost blasphemy against God: honoring the divine with unworthy things and offering heavenly pearls what ought to be trampled by pigs.

## Chapter XXXIV. On Fasting

The prophet (Joel 2) exhorts penitents to be in fasting, weeping, and lamentation. And the Lord says: “When you fast, do not become sad like the hypocrites” (Matt. 6). Gregory likewise says that the sinner ought even to give himself to fasts, so that God may at some time turn his heart to repentance. Fasting weakens the flesh, lifts up the soul, restrains the fuel of concupiscence, and awakens reason. By fasting Moses deserved converse with God, Daniel the interpretation of dreams, [Col. 0177A] Elijah aid, and the Ninevites forgiveness of sins. Christ gave us the example of fasting: in the wilderness he fasted for forty days and forty nights (Matt. 4).

Yet bodily fasting is of no benefit without the fasting of the mind; otherwise it is deceitful and deceptive. What good is it if the mouth fasts from food while the tongue is loosened for lying, the eye feasts on vanities, the ear delights in tales, the nostrils idle amid perfumes, touch roams over smooth things, the hand engages in robbery, and the foot strays outside the ordinary path? Let the other senses fast with taste, so that those who were companions in pleasures may be partners in sufferings.

There are many kinds of fasting. There is the fasting of custom, not done from charity but merely from [Col. 0177B] custom, lest a person seem to sail against the public course. This profits only in avoiding a bad example and giving no offense. There is the fasting of avarice and greed, in which the stomach is emptied so that the purse may be filled; this is destructive. There is the fasting of illness, so that health may be obtained; and this is indifferent, since it is neither good nor bad. There is also the fasting of gluttony and voracity, so that food may be consumed more eagerly; and this is the worst. There is the fasting of praise and appearance, used by hypocrites in order to gain human praise; and this is evil.

102 There is the fasting of want and necessity, by which the poor fast; and this is indifferent. There is the fasting of compulsion, practiced by many religious in cloisters; [Col. 0177C] and this is insufficient. Therefore, leaving aside the other fasts, one should aspire to the fasting that belongs to charity: by it the body is chastised, the spirit rules, and man thus lives like an angel. For by fasting a man becomes spirit; by moderate food, a human being; by superfluous food, a beast.

There are many circumstances that shape fasting: namely, from what, where, when, and why. “From what”: that one abstain from delicious foods; for what profit is there in fasting from food if one recovers in pleasure or quantity what was lost in time? At the time of a meal, the faster ought to use moderate food, so that he may partly help his neighbor and thus afflict himself in order to refresh his neighbor. One must also consider [Col. 0177D] “where”: the custom of one’s country must be kept, as the saying goes:

> When you are in Rome, live by Roman custom.

Hence Augustine says: “When I am in Rome, I do not fast on Saturday; when I am in Milan, I fast.” “When”: fasting should take place on the appointed days. For there are certain days on which one should not fast, such as Sundays and some great feasts, because of offense. “Why”: that it be done in charity for God’s sake. As many as are the kinds of abstinence from carnal things, so many are the different forms of fasting. There is fasting in continence, abstinence, humility, meekness, and rejoicing. Augustine says of fasting: “Let fasts praise thee, not belching entrails.”

[Col. 0178A] Fasting avails as medicine for body and soul. It preserves the body from illness and the soul from sin. In this medicine heavenly philosophy agrees with natural philosophy. For this medicine both purges the stomach of the vice of gluttony and the soul of indignation. If Adam had fasted in Paradise from the forbidden food, he would not have been condemned to exile (Gen. 3). If Esau had fasted from the lentil, he would not have lost his birthright (Gen. 25). If Noah had fasted from wine, he would not have uncovered his thighs or private parts (Gen. 2). Therefore, by fasting the body is purified in order to receive the Eucharist sacramentally, and the spirit in order to receive it spiritually. This ought to be the preliminary to receiving the Eucharist. Let a person therefore despise material food in the present, lest in the future he feel the fire [Col. 0178B] of Gehenna.

Let these three things be present to shape fasting: good intention, generosity in almsgiving, and the kindling of charity. If the flesh desires the pleasures of food, let a person consider that it makes no difference from what material excrement comes. If the flesh wishes to anticipate the hour of the meal, let it flee to the refuge of work, lest idleness awaken gluttony and increase appetite. O man, if you consider the ancient Fathers, who used scant food only twice or once a week, none of your fasts, or only few, would seem great to you. But if the examples of the ancients do not move you, at least let the infancy of blessed Nicholas move you: on Wednesday or Friday he suckled at the breast only once.

Let an adult be ashamed not to have fasted when he sees [Col. 0178C] a little child fasting. The example of a small child turns to our shame, when infants and children correct us.

## Chapter XXXV. Instruction Concerning Vigil

“Blessed is that servant whom, when the Lord comes, he shall find watching” (Luke 22; Matt. 24). Likewise: “If the master of the house knew at what hour the thief would come, he would certainly keep watch,” etc. (ibid.). Likewise: “Watch therefore, because you do not know at what hour your Lord will come” (Matt. 24). Likewise: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matt. 26). And Solomon: “Those who watch early shall find me” (Prov. 8). Christ invites us by his own example to vigils, spending the night in prayer and watching for our instruction. Material [Col. 0178D] vigils are to be observed for bodily exercise, to exclude torpor, avoid nocturnal illusions, and guard against the slippery passions of the flesh, so that room may be given to prayer and denied to the enemy.

Every faithful person ought, like a most valiant man, to surround Solomon’s bed (Song 3) and hold a sword upon his thigh because of the terrors of the night. Every faithful person ought to provide this not only by material but also by spiritual vigils for God’s Church, which is Solomon’s bed—that is, Christ’s—in which he himself rests, because “his delights are to be with the children of men” (Prov. 8). He ought also to hold a sword upon his thigh—that is, use the sword of discernment—to restrain the movements of the flesh and the assaults [Col. 0179A] of the devil, which must especially be guarded against and feared in the darkness of this world. But one should devote oneself more to spiritual than to material vigils, so that each person’s mind may watch over its flock, that is, the movements of the soul, lest the lurking wolf—that is, the devil—force any movement to depart from what is right.

We must watch lest the thief, that is, the devil, enter the enclosure of our breast through lust, the chamber of the mind through sloth, and steal the soul’s garment, that is, the ornaments of virtues. This invisible thief is sometimes a robber, when he rages through the tyranny of rulers; sometimes he attacks us as a thief through a heretic; now as a bird, when he bears himself aloft through pride; now as an asp, when he deceives through lust; now as a lion, when he rages through open cruelty; now as a dragon, when he acts through hidden [Col. 0179B] temptation.

There are four parts of the night of sin. The first is called *intempestum*, the dead of night, when someone delights in a wicked thought. The second, *conticinium*, is when people—that is, rational movements—lie beneath a seduced will. The third is cockcrow, when the will sounds forth in action. The fourth is before dawn, when the deed comes into public manifestation. Not without reason have nocturnal vigils been instituted, signifying that one must rise at midnight for nocturnal hymns, so that not even that hour may lack divine praise and the material vigil may awaken the spiritual one. Let a person be ashamed that the sunrise should outrun his vigils and that the cock should give himself to its songs at night while he himself is idle from divine praises. O man, beware of the watching rod, lest it find you asleep; beware of the thief, lest he suffocate you while you are torpid.

[Col. 0179C] The watching rod, or rod of vigils, is the rod which, when inserted into a house, a thief uses to test whether the master of the house is sleeping or the household is sluggish. If the master sleeps, the thief plunders everything he finds; if he is awake, the thief flees. Spiritually, the rod of vigils is Christ, of whom Jeremiah says: “I see a rod of watching” (Jer. 2). This is the rod which by its discernment tests whether the master of the house sleeps in his house—that is, whether a person is sluggish in his own self-restraint. If it finds him sleeping, it condemns him; if it finds him watching, it finds in him nothing by which it can harm him. Likewise, the devil, who is a spiritual thief, flees if he finds a person watching; if he finds him sleeping, he carries off everything. Because Ish-bosheth slept at midday, he was killed by robbers [Col. 0179D] (2 Sam. 4); Samson, when put to sleep, was captured by enemies (Judg. 16); Sisera, sleeping, was killed by a woman (Judg. 4); Gideon killed his drowsy enemies (Judg. 7). When his Passion was imminent, Christ rebuked the disciples for sleeping.

## Chapter XXXVI. Exhortation to Learning

Learn as though you were always to live; live as though you were to die tomorrow. Likewise the Apostle: “Read books.” And: “Bring the books with thee” (2 Tim. 4). Likewise Seneca: “Life without letters is death, and the burial of a living man.” Likewise Jerome: “My head was already sprinkled with gray hairs, yet my zeal for learning saw no end.” And elsewhere: “I prefer to learn from others with modesty than [Col. 0180A] shamelessly to thrust forward my own views. Reading sharpens understanding, multiplies intelligence, prepares eagerness for learning, supplies eloquence, warms the coldness of the mind, drives out torpor, extinguishes the darts of lust, awakens the groaning of the heart, draws forth tears, and brings us near to God.” The writer on love says:

> If you take away idleness, Cupid’s bows are lost.  
> —Ovid

If you read, idleness flees; the devil finds you occupied. Enter the wine-cellar (Song 2), in which charity is ordered: that is, read the Scriptures and examine their meanings. In this cellar a person is so intoxicated that he is made sober. And when you have read much, assign one thing especially to yourself; chew over one thing to the marrow, what sits most fittingly in your mind and [Col. 0180B] best pleases the palate of the mind.

If you approach some reading, do not abandon it at once, but adhere to it faithfully, nor, as though disgusted, pass to another. For, as Seneca says: “A plant that is often transplanted does not thrive, and a medicine frequently changed does not bring about the scarring of a wound.” And if it happens that you pass from books of theology to books of earthly philosophy, as you pass examine whether perhaps you find in them something that instructs morals or accords with the Catholic faith, so that the Hebrews may be enriched by those things of which the Egyptians are despoiled; that gold may be borrowed from the Egyptians for building the tabernacle, and timber for building the temple. Let Hiram, king of Tyre, bestow his riches; [Col. 0180C] let the children of Israel drink from the wells of the Amorites. And let the hostility of Goliath be beaten back by his own sword. Yet we must pass into foreign camps in such a way that we are scouts and pilgrims, not inhabitants.

O man, read in order to understand; apply yourself in order to read. For, as the moral philosopher says: “To read and not understand is to neglect.” Consider the words of the philosopher Papinian, who said: “If I now had one foot in the grave, I would still wish to learn something.” Nor should a greater person disdain to learn from a lesser, because what is not revealed to the greater is sometimes revealed to the lesser. The Apostle says: “If it has been revealed to the lesser, let the greater be silent” (1 Cor. 14). Moses, skilled in all the learning of the Egyptians, did not disdain to receive counsel from the Gentile Jethro. And Solomon, [Col. 0180D] to whom the treasure of knowledge was given, did not disdain to hear wisdom from the Queen of the South. Water descends through channels of stone into beds of spices. Plato, a Gentile, endured many storms and went down into Egypt to read Genesis; yet the Christian disdains what is present, offered, and obtainable—what would instruct him.

For the clerics of our time follow the schools of Antichrist rather than those of Christ; they are more devoted to the gullet than to the gloss; they prefer gathering pounds to reading books; they more willingly look upon Martha than Mark; they prefer to read in Solomon rather than in Solomon (*sic*). Now every branch of learning is cheapened, every reading grows languid, and there is no one to read books. “There is none, not even one; all have turned aside, together they have become useless” (Ps. 13). Now [Col. 0181A] Christ’s school is deserted, which consists in two things, life and teaching; but true life is despised and teaching buried. Formerly, even if a good life was not loved, learning was nevertheless embraced; but now the utmost deviation, the utmost obstinacy, the utmost estrangement prevail, when not only good morals are set aside, but even their adornment—that is, learning—is despised.

And if perhaps anyone learns, he does not direct the end to God, but to earthly gain or human favor: in reading he seeks not Christ but money, earth rather than heaven. Such men deflower virgins—that is, corrupt virginal branches of knowledge—because they prostitute them for profit and, insofar as lies in them, infect them. And what is worse, more monstrous than every monster! [Col. 0181B] hearers of theology sell their ears in order to hear, while teachers buy them in order to expound their learning boastfully. Theology is now prostituted for sale, and sits in the marketplace as a harlot. Formerly teachers were held in the highest honor; but now they are deservedly considered foolish and stupid. Now the question is not what is in the storehouse of the mind, but what is in the treasury. Who are honored? The rich. Who are despised? Teachers. Who stand in royal palaces? Those with money. Who are excluded from court? The learned. Now the household of Croesus is honored, while the household of Christ is despised.

How glorious it is to read, how fruitful to labor over the Scriptures, to search out the mind of God, to investigate instruction concerning oneself! Everyone ought to read in a threefold [Col. 0181C] book: in the book of creatures, in order to find God; in the book of conscience, in order to know oneself; in the book of Scripture, in order to love one’s neighbor.

## Chapter XXXVII. On Hospitality

Paul says: “Do not neglect hospitality” (Heb. 12). Likewise Peter: “Be hospitable to one another without grumbling” (1 Pet. 4). And Isaiah: “Bring the needy and wandering into thy house” (Isa. 58). Hence Truth says: “I was a stranger, and you received me” (Matt. 25). O man, Christ cries at the door in his members and asks for lodging. Receive the pilgrim on earth, that he may receive you rejoicing in the homeland. Abraham [Col. 0181D] received angels in the appearance of guests and deserved to be given a son (Gen. 18). Lot received angels as guests and deserved to be delivered from the burning of Sodom (ibid., Gen. 19). The widow who honored Elijah by the benefit of hospitality deserved the restoration of her son to life (3 Kings 17). The disciples going to Emmaus were enlightened through Christ’s teaching, but by performing the service of hospitality they deserved to be enlightened more fully and perfectly by him (Luke 24).

O man, if you know yourself to be a sojourner and pilgrim in this age, if you recognize the condition of your pilgrimage, you will not deny lodging to a pilgrim. For if you exclude Christ’s poor person from your roof, you exclude Christ himself from the lodging of your heart. Hear what he himself says: “What you did to one of my least ones, you did to me” (Matt. 25). [Col. 0182A] Hospitality itself ought to be cheerful and generous, displaying humility and embracing liberality. For an important part of honorable hospitality is serenity of countenance. Hence it is said:

> Above all, good faces  
> have drawn near.

Generosity is also a part of hospitality: we should not receive a person asking only when overcome by annoyance, but should even anticipate him with outstanding service. By the example of those going to Emmaus, guests are not merely to be invited but drawn in. Humility must also be shown to guests, so that through the grace of humility—which brings hospitality itself to completion—the service rendered may be more welcome.

Let us therefore receive in the pilgrim him who for our sake journeyed on earth [Col. 0182B] from heaven; who, leaving his homeland for our sake, became a beggar on the road. O happy hospitality shown to Christ in the poor! O happy bed upon which Christ rests in the body! Blessed table at which man sits—God in man! O man, among Gentiles the laws of hospitality are observed; among believers they are broken. Brute animals rejoice at the arrival of creatures like themselves and in some manner show them the right of kinship; but human beings refuse the duty of humanity. “Be ashamed, Sidon,” says the sea (Isa. 23); let the sea be ashamed to be aided by rivers. Let the rational be ashamed to be instructed by the irrational. Let the sun be ashamed to be warmed by a furnace and torches.

But just as the faithful person is bound to render the work of charity to Christ in his members, so he is bound to render [Col. 0182C] spiritual service in his own mind to Christ himself, the head. Each person must invite Christ into the house of his mind by the inward cries of the heart, prepare for him a table in the house of the mind with honorable and pure thoughts, and offer the wine of charity. Every faithful person must also prepare a third lodging for Christ: namely, to receive the heavenly viaticum, the spiritual Eucharist, the Lord’s body. At the coming of so great a guest, let him cleanse the house of his own body; let him clean it from the dung of lust, the dust of vain glory, and the mud of gluttony, so that when Christ comes he may deign peacefully to rest there, as he himself says: “I and the Father will come, and we shall make our dwelling with him” (John 14); lest the uncleanness [Col. 0182D] of the lodging offend the eyes of so great a guest.

## Chapter XXXVIII. That Preaching Ought to Belong Only to Prelates

It has been said what preaching is, what it ought to be like, and what it ought to concern. It remains now to show whose task preaching ought to be. Preaching ought to belong to prelates and be undertaken by them. For two things belong to them: teaching, that they may instruct others; and life, that they may offer others an example of right living. To signify this, it was commanded that in sacrifice the mouth of a turtledove be bent back toward its wings (Lev. 1). By the turtledove the simplicity of the preacher is figured; by its being bent back toward the wings is understood that the preacher ought to have in deed what he sets forth in speech.

[Col. 0183A] The same is also signified by the crook of the pastoral staff: what he preaches to others he should turn back upon himself through good works. To indicate these two things, namely prudence and a good life, it is said of the steward: “Who, thinkest thou, is the faithful and prudent servant?” etc. (Matt. 24). A preacher ought to be faithful in word and deed: faithful in word, lest he mix falsehood with truth; faithful in word, lest he proclaim the word for human favor; faithful in word, lest he sell preaching for earthly gain; faithful in word, lest his deeds contradict his words. Hence it is said of false preachers: “Our tavern-keepers mix water with wine.” They mix water with wine who preach falsehood together with truth, as heretics do; likewise those who sell the word for human favor, as hypocrites do; those who drain earthly goods through preaching, as hirelings do; and those who contradict their word by deed, as false Christians do.

[Col. 0183B] He must also be faithful in deed, so that he does what he does with a right intention and sets God as the end of the deed itself. Thus he must be prudent in word and deed: in word, so that he knows what should and should not be preached; in deed, so that he knows to whom and when matters ought to be preached—namely, greater things to the greater, lesser things to the lesser. “To whom”: lest the holy thing of God be set before the unworthy as before dogs, and lest pearls be handed over to be trampled under the feet of swine (Matt. 7). “When”: that he may propose the word when the time requires it, and remain silent when occasion is lacking; for Solomon says: “There is a time to speak and a time to be silent” (Eccl. 3).

Knowledge belongs to preachers, so that they may be practiced in both Testaments, discerning in the examination of propositions, eloquent in sermons, circumspect in all their actions, despisers of the world, and diligent in their office. For Malachi says of a prelate: [Col. 0183C] “The lips of priests preserve knowledge, and the law is sought from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 1). And Jesus son of Sirach says: “If thou hast knowledge, answer thy neighbor; if not, let thy hand be upon thy mouth, lest thou be caught by an undisciplined word” (Ecclus. 5). For one must greatly fear that Gospel saying: “If the blind lead the blind, both fall into the pit” (Matt. 15; Luke 6). And that saying of the Apostle: “He who is ignorant shall be ignored” (1 Cor. 14). And what will the Lord say to the foolish virgins? “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. 25). And the saying: “Cursed is the old beginner.” Likewise: “The sinner being a hundred years old shall be accursed” (Isa. 65).

There is a kind of affected ignorance, when someone can know but does not wish to know. This is gross, utter, and conquerable ignorance, and therefore inexcusable. Of it it is said: “He did not wish to understand so as to do good” (Ps. 34). Likewise: “Man, though he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48). This ignorance pertains to prelates who through contempt fall into ignorance and through pride remain in folly: priests and prophets without reason; teachers of impossibilities; judges of hidden matters.

[Col. 0184A] O vile ignorance, abominable folly, which imposes silence upon the prelate and makes our dog—that is, our shepherd—mute! This is the reed which, cast into a dog’s mouth, takes away its bark. The prelates of our time first sit 107 in the chair before they have been taught under the rod; they first receive the honor of mastership before they have borne the burden of discipleship. They wish to preside, not to benefit; they seek the price of honor, not the weight of the burden. To such a prelate it may be said: “Physician, heal thyself” (Luke 4); advocate, plead for yourself; you who are Christ’s vicar, imitate his work, he who “began to do and to teach” (Acts 1). For he who teaches but does not do contradicts Christ; he imposes unbearable burdens on his subjects, yet will not move them with a finger.

Some hide in a napkin the talent of divine wisdom entrusted to them: namely, those who through negligence refuse to preach. Some hide it in dung: namely, those whose deeds contradict their words. Others hide it in mud: those who conceal the word through envy.

## Chapter XXXIX. To Whom Preaching Should Be Addressed
Having stated whose office preaching ought to be, and what sort of men preachers ought to be, it remains to show to whom preaching should be offered. Namely, to the faithful, who with a certain desire of mind wish to hear the word of God; concerning whom the Lord says: “Lift up your eyes and see that the fields are already white for harvest” (John 4). The fields white for harvest are called the minds of human beings, ready to receive the word of God. This is the good soil that receives seed and bears fruit.

But preaching is to be withheld from the unworthy and obstinate, because those who reject God’s word make themselves unworthy. Hence the Apostles said to the Jews who rejected their preaching: “Since you have rejected the word of God and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13). He diminishes the majesty of secrets who divulges secrets to the unworthy; and the vessels of the Lord are not to be displayed in Babylon. To lesser persons it is fitting to speak in parables; to greater persons, to reveal the mysteries of God’s kingdom. Little children are to be nourished with liquid food, adults strengthened with solid food, lest the child be choked by solid food and the adult loathe liquid food; so that each thing may fittingly occupy the place allotted to it.

It belongs to the preacher to assume the role of a bodily physician or doctor. For just as a bodily physician varies kinds of remedies according to the variety of diseases, so the preacher ought to apply the remedies of admonition. Thus, if he preaches to the lustful, he should bring forward authorities against lust and introduce arguments; he should show it to be abominable before God and before men—how it stinks in infamy, stinks in one’s own flesh, stinks before one’s neighbour, stinks before God. Now let him cut with iron through threats; now soothe through consolation. In like manner let him argue against other vices, according as he sees his hearers entangled in various vices.

If he preaches to the poor, let him speak of poverty, commending poverty and taking as his example our head, Jesus Christ, who, though rich in heaven, became poor for us on earth, that by his poverty he might make us rich. Let the ancient Fathers also be brought forward as an example, who, naked, followed naked Christ. Let him show how blessed are the poor in spirit (Matt. 5), not those rich in possessions. If he preaches to the rich, let him invite them to almsgiving, contempt for riches, and love of heavenly treasures: so that, if riches abound, they may not set their heart upon them; if they possess them, they may nevertheless not covet them. For possessing belongs to one’s substance; coveting, to one’s fault.

If he preaches to soldiers, let him move them to be content with their own pay, not laying hands upon what belongs to others; let them exact nothing by violence, extort from no one, be defenders of their country and guardians of orphans and widows; [Col. 0185B] thus may they bear the arms of the world outwardly, while inwardly they are armed with the breastplate of faith.

If to advocates, let him warn them not to support an unjust cause for a fee, or weaken a just cause from the rancour of hatred; not to sell their tongue or prostitute wisdom, nor pursue falsehoods or revere lies.

If he preaches to teachers, let him warn them to teach with God in view, making God alone the end of their labour; let them not hunt after favourable applause or an earthly reward; let them demonstrate in deed what they set forth in speech.

If he directs his discourse to prelates, let him exhort them concerning the governance of their subjects: that they may raise them by hope of heavenly things, correct them by threats, and guide them by gentleness.

If he preaches to rulers of the earth, let him warn them to pursue prudence, abhor avarice, not depart from the path of justice, and temper severity with gentleness.

If he speaks to cloistered and religious men, let him offer for their instruction examples of the ancient Fathers, who spent their present life in excessive mortification of the body. Let him show that it is little merely to begin, unless what has been begun is concluded with a good end, because “no one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9). And Lot’s wife, looking back, was changed into a pillar of salt (Gen. 19).

If he addresses married persons, let the state of marriage be commended: fidelity to the marriage-bed and the power of the sacrament. Let him show how marriage had its beginning in paradise, and how the ancient Fathers in the married state deserved to attain eternal life.

If widows, let the burdens of marriage be set forth: the care of children, the acquisition of necessities, and the management of household affairs; and how glorious it is, after the pleasures of the flesh have been tested, to avoid them and serve God freely.

If virgins, let purity of body and purity of mind be commended, by which a human being is above the human, overcoming the flesh and bearing the likeness of angels.

## CHAPTER XL. To Soldiers

John the Baptist says to soldiers: “Extort from no one, do no one injury; be content with your pay” (Luke 3). Let soldiers have as an example for their life the blessed martyr Sebastian, a soldier, who under the emperor Diocletian so performed temporal military service that he did not abandon the spiritual contest: rendering to Caesar what was Caesar’s, and to God what was God’s. Likewise blessed Victor, blessed Hippolytus, and many others, who by vigorously carrying out material military service deserved happily to be raised to the eternal military service of the highest King. The Theban legion also so wore the belt of military service outwardly that inwardly it devoutly served God.

For outward military service is a figure of inward warfare; and without the inward, the outward is empty and void. And just as a human being has two parts, bodily and spiritual, so there are two swords for repelling the various assaults upon human beings: the material sword, by which injuries are repelled; and the spiritual sword, by which afflictions of the mind are repelled. Hence it was said: “Behold, here are two swords” (Luke 22). Therefore let the soldier gird himself outwardly to restore the violently disturbed peace of the time; inwardly also, with the sword of God’s word, to restore the peace of his own breast.

Soldiers were instituted especially for this: to defend their country and repel from the Church the injuries of violent men. But soldiers have now become predatory leaders of others; they have become cattle-thieves. They no longer practise military service but robbery; and under the appearance of a soldier they assume the cruelty of a robber. They do not so much fight enemies as prey upon the poor; and those whom they ought to protect with the shield of military defence, they persecute with the sword of savagery. They now prostitute their military service: they serve in arms in order to make gain; they take up arms in order to plunder. They are no longer soldiers but thieves and robbers; not defenders but invaders.

They whet swords against the entrails of mother Church, and expend upon their own people the force that they ought to expend upon enemies. But their enemies—either cast down through sluggishness or terrified by fear—they cease to attack; and against Christ’s defenceless servants they compel their swords to rage. To honourable military service both temporal gifts are due and the rewards of eternal recompense are not denied. And while some are bound by their office to undertake bodily military service, all are bound by precept to undertake spiritual warfare.

The material soldier dwells in camp, abstains from a wife’s embraces, is content with simple food, intent upon watchfulness, clothed in arms, resisting enemies, and caring for his fellow-soldiers. Such in spirit ought every person to be as the material soldier is in act. Of Christ’s soldier it is said: “The life of man upon earth is warfare” (Job 7). And elsewhere: “Here we have no lasting city” (Heb. 13). Likewise the Apostle says that here we are strangers and sojourners, but in the future citizens of the saints and members of God’s household (Eph. 2).

Therefore, in the pilgrimage of this life the Christian ought to live as though in camp: not thinking that he has here a lasting dwelling, but awaiting in heaven an eternal habitation. Of these dwellings it was said: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 14). Let him live as one about to die in a moment; dwell in the tent of flesh as one about to depart in a moment; abstain from the embraces of earthly pleasure; flee the flood of gluttony; watch against the snares of the spiritual thief; be clothed in spiritual weapons; put on the breastplate of faith; gird himself with the sword of God’s word; arm himself with the spear of charity; take up the helmet of salvation.

Armed with these, let him fight against the threefold enemy: against the devil, lest he seize him; against the world, lest it entice him; against the flesh, lest it seek unlawful things. Let him provide for his fellow-soldiers, that is, the faithful: giving generously if they are needy, admonishing if they need it, suffering with the sick, and rejoicing with the healthy.

## CHAPTER XLI. To Orators, or Advocates

Scripture says to advocates: “Judge for the orphan and the humble” (Ps. 10). And Isaiah says: “Help the oppressed; defend the widow” (Isa. 1). For an advocate ought to be fortified by truth, ready in discernment, fervent in charity, a despiser of avarice, and a pursuer of justice: lest falsehood cloud his reason, indiscretion weaken the truth of his speech, or hatred introduce suspicion. Let not avarice bend his mind; let not injustice lead him into a pathless place; let not his tongue hunt money; let him not seek popular applause through elegance of words. Rather, let him make the end of his pleading righteous and the conclusion of his speech honourable.

Let him not prostitute his tongue, offer his speech for sale, sell God’s gift, or lease out God’s freely given benefit. What he received solely as the gift of grace, let him not debase by selling it. O how execrable is the simony of selling the poor person’s patrimony and hiring out assistance to the needy!

Among almsgivings, he occupies no small place who provides help to a widow in a lawsuit; for he who by the power of argument preserves for her what is her own not only defends but also gives. Yet neither anyone’s poverty nor misery ought to bend advocates toward falsehood, nor anyone’s prosperity draw them toward injustice.

Let truth always give strength to argument, and let one bring aid to the needy through speech. He who does not uphold what is right when he can uphold it is the same as one who gives assent to injustice. For this is to visit the wretched person in prison: to bring advocacy to the oppressed in a lawsuit. This is to clothe the naked: to bring the assistance of advocacy in a case to one stripped of advocacy. This is to feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, provide medicine to the sick, receive the stranger, and take up the person deprived of every aid in order to advocate for him in court. Therefore, whoever provides advocacy to one in need in a just cause fulfils every work of mercy.

Advocate, why do you omit to defend widows in their necessities? You lose nothing in expounding your knowledge; you forfeit nothing in distributing this treasure. This is a noble possession, which disdains an avaricious possessor and slips away when it is not made public.

The spiritual advocate also—that is, the just man whose prayer pleads before God—should plead before God with devout prayers on behalf of the accused, so that although condemnation is due to the accused according to the strictness of his deserts, God’s merciful compassion may grant him time for true repentance and amendment of life. For the persistent prayer of a righteous person is very powerful (James 5). Let the righteous person plead for the accused before divine mercy, so that, because human weakness can do nothing without divine compassion, by God’s grace the accused may be delivered from sins and directed to salvation.

And although the prayer of the righteous does not always obtain the desired end in another person, the one praying always obtains the end in himself. For even if the sin of the one for whom he prays is not forgiven, the prayer returns into the bosom of the one praying. A doctor does not always heal, nor does an advocate always persuade; but if he has omitted nothing among things contingent, he has attained his end.

## CHAPTER XLII. To Princes and Judges

To the rulers of the earth it is said: “Love justice, you who judge the earth” (Wisdom 1). And elsewhere: “And now, kings, understand; be instructed, you who judge the earth” (Ps. 2). O rulers of the world, whom the Lord has set over the heads of men, do not be lifted up by pride, blinded by avarice, or rage with cruelty. Consider the greater power above you, which will judge you at the judgment.

Even if a ruler is surrounded by the splendour of a household, even if placed upon a royal throne, he will nevertheless not be able to resist the divine will; for who can resist God’s power? Therefore let every ruler humble himself under God’s mighty hand. Nebuchadnezzar, because he did not acknowledge divine power above himself, put on a bestial form. Because Manasseh, king of Israel, did not acknowledge divine power above himself, divine power subjected him to extreme captivity.

O ruler, if you wish to judge rightly the earth of the world, judge rightly the earth of your body. For there is a threefold earth: the earth we tread, the earth we bear, and the earth we seek. The earth we tread is material earth, which ought to be trampled. The earth we bear is the earth of our body, which ought to be cultivated. The earth we seek is eternal life, which ought to be inhabited. Therefore, just as a king guards material land lest an enemy invade it, so he ought to guard the land of his body lest the devil steal away the land’s goods—that is, the endowments of body and soul.

And just as in material land there is diversity among inhabitants, some ruling, as princes; some working, as soldiers; and others obeying, as common people: so in the land of his body a king ought to order the diversity of three movements. The movements of reason should rule; the movements of sensuality should work; the movements of the flesh should obey. And just as it befits a ruler to labour for the peace of material land—that is, for the preservation of peaceful tranquillity—so it is said to the rulers of this land: “Be instructed,” that is, instruct the roughness of carnality, “you who judge the earth,” that is, who condemn earthliness in your bodies.

What then will your mind say to you, O ruler of the earth, when the poor person judges you on the day of judgment, if you have governed the world badly and judged the poor unjustly? O king, do not regard your rule as an honour; consider rather that earthly honour belongs not to nature but to fortune. That honours are not true honours is proved by their slippery reversals, and their mutability demonstrates their vanity. Many kings are led with the honour of a funeral to the tomb, and their bodies, with a kind of superficial happiness, are carried to the grave; but their wretched souls, surrounded by a horrible host of demons, are miserably tortured in hell. Where then is worldly honour? Where popular applause? Where the household crowd? Where worldly riches? Where nobility of lineage? Where the fruitfulness of offspring? Where the beauty of a wife? These things will not benefit wretched souls after death; indeed, they will contribute to the increase of their pain.

## CHAPTER XLIII. To the Cloistered

Scripture, speaking to cloistered persons, says: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132). And elsewhere, the Psalmist, in the person of a cloistered person: “One thing have I asked of the Lord; this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord,” etc. (Ps. 26).

Although unity is marked with the most celebrated praises among moral philosophers, among theologians it is grounded in no small mysteries. For without spiritual unity, grace is possessed neither in the present nor glory conferred in the future. Without unity all religious life is puffed away, heavenly love languishes, faith itself perishes, and obedience fails.

Unity produces harmony in divine things, concord among angels, and obedience in churches. For there is a supercelestial unity, a celestial unity, and a subcelestial unity. Supercelestial unity is in the concord of the Trinity, where there is a unity that unites and is united.

The unity which unites and is united is the Holy Spirit, who unites the Father with the Son; hence it is said: “One with the Father and the Son.” Elsewhere he is called the kiss and love of the Father and Son. And he is a unity united, because he is united to the Father and Son through the divine nature. The unity which unites but is not united is the divine nature, which unites the three persons with one another, but is not itself united to them, because it is not a person. The unity which is united but does not unite is the Father, because he is united to the Son and Holy Spirit, but neither of them is united to him, or through him.

Of unity uniting and united it is also said: “Now, Holy Spirit, one with the Father and the Son.” Of unity not united it is also said: “Unity in majesty.” But Hilary says of unity united but not uniting: “Unity is in the Father,” etc.

Celestial unity is in the concord of angels, and there is there a threefold unity: unity of nature, unity of grace, and unity of glory. Unity of nature, because all are ministering spirits; unity of grace, because they are confirmed in grace; unity of glory, because all are glorified in eternal blessedness. In this threefold unity there is diversity in the offices of dignities and in knowing the mysteries of hidden things. There is also harmonious dissonance, consonant discord, diverse unity, united diversity, consenting disagreement, and uniting diversity.

But subcelestial unity ought to exist in the Church, and it is threefold: unity of faith, unity of charity, and unity of obedience. Let inferiors obey superiors, and let superiors condescend to inferiors according to a moderated custom. To indicate the merit of this unity, one man descending into the pool is healed (John 5); one widow’s son is raised up (3 Kings 17); the ark is completed in one cubit (Gen. 6); one person is sent to announce victory to David; one announces to Job the death of his children, he alone being delivered from danger (Job 1).

Unity embraces all things belonging to the ecclesiastical state; singularity gives form to all things. For there is one God, one faith, one baptism (Eph. 4), one law, one king, one Church, one grace, one glory. Therefore among religious persons likewise there ought to be a threefold unity: unity of religious observance, unity of possession, and unity of charity.

Unity of religious observance requires that they be uniform in clothing, food, vigils, and fasts. But certain irregular persons exempt themselves from the rule of this unity, desiring to recline on softer beds, attend fewer vigils, use more delicate foods, and observe little or no silence. For certain monks embellish a lowly habit in one way or another—by shaking off dust, or by a certain elegant arrangement of its parts: they fit their feet more tightly into shoes, tighten their sleeves, or turn their hoods back over their ears. They also desire, as far as they can, more delicate foods; and as far as possible, if they cannot change the material, they at least change its form. Thus, if one wishes beans or other plain foods prepared in one fashion, another wishes them prepared in another.

Some break silence; if not with words, then at least with signs, and so redeem the sparks of words by a multitude of signs. Some either omit or cut short vigils. There ought also to be unity in possession, so that all things are held in common by them. A monk ought to have nothing of his own, because he ought to have nothing private either in possessing or in willing. That they ought to possess nothing as private property they may understand from the example of Ananias, who expired at Peter’s feet (Acts 5), because he had retained something as his own. And for the instruction of cloistered persons the Lord says: “Unless anyone renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14).

Yet it is not enough to renounce one’s possessions in fact unless they are renounced in will; hence Peter also says of this renunciation of will: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you” (Matt. 19). Therefore the cloistered person who desires to have private property looks back with Lot’s wife, withdraws his hand from the plough, and, like Dinah the daughter of Jacob, desires the adornment of foreigners. Those, therefore, who make any private exception from the community of possessions purchase the place of Judas, traitor and thief.

O cloistered person, you who left many things in the world, do not return to the world by desiring a single coin. Let not the desire for one coin ensnare you whom the treasury of riches did not deceive. Fear lest the devil’s snare take you in the least thing when it did not deceive you in the greatest. The cloistered person ought also to reject his own will, so that, just as there is community in religious observance, so there may be community in will: so that all things may be common to them not only with respect to property, but also with respect to agreement; so that all may meet in one will and agree in one charity, so that it may truly be said of them: “They had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4).

Cloistered persons are also bound to possess unity of charity, so that in their neighbour’s advancement they may find their own advancement, and in another’s failing may grieve for their own failing. Let the wiser instruct the less skilled; let the healthy suffer with the sick; let the sound rejoice with the healthy. Thus may cloistered life be an image of heavenly life: so that, just as in eternal life joy is equal amid unequal brightness, so in the cloister, amid unequal charity, may the bond of love be uniform.

From this threefold unity the cloistered person is called a monk, as though a guardian of unity. For if he does not preserve the first unity, he becomes irregular; if the second, an apostate; if the third, a schismatic. Let there be in the cloistered community a unity that unites and is united—that is, the prelate uniting subjects by authority and united to subjects by charity. Let there be unity united but not uniting—that is, the subject who, although he does not unite others, nevertheless joins himself to others through charity. Let there be unity uniting but not united—that is, charity, which, though it unites cloistered persons, is nevertheless not firmly joined in the present to any one person.

Let there be in them unity of nature, that they may love it in themselves; unity of grace, that they may share with one another the grace bestowed upon them; unity of glory, that with one hope they may tend toward the glory of eternal life; unity of faith, lest they be heretics; unity of charity, lest they be schismatics; unity of hope, lest they be obstinate. Thus it may especially be said of them: “Behold, how good”—in respect to human opinion—“and how pleasant”—in respect to the devotion of the mind—“for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132): in unity of religious observance, unity of possession, and unity of charity, so that they may attain that unity of which the Prophet said: “One thing have I asked of the Lord,” etc. (Ps. 26).

## CHAPTER XLIV. To Priests

The Lord says to priests: “You are the salt of the earth; but if salt has become foolish, with what shall it be salted?” (Matt. 5). Salt does four things: it makes ground barren, seasons food, preserves flesh from decay, and keeps worms from the flesh itself. These four things befit spiritual salt, that is, the priest. He ought to plough with the ploughshare of preaching the land of his subjects—that is, their earthly thoughts—lest they sprout into thorns and thistles of vices; and thus he ought to render it barren of evil works. From his own land also—that is, his flesh—he is bound to exclude the fertility of vices and keep that flesh free from decay, that is, from lust and gluttony.

Lust is aptly compared to decay. For just as decay corrupts flesh and makes it stink, so lust makes a person stink through infamy, the flesh through uncleanness, and the human being through an evil conscience. Gluttony also is compared to decay because through gluttony a person is corrupted in body, infected by stench, and hastens more quickly toward non-being.

He ought to guard his flesh from worms, lest the flesh generate evil thoughts or fall into disordered appetites. He ought also to season the food of sacred Scripture by diligent inquiry, because sacred Scripture in some places seems tasteless unless it is searched out through diligent investigation. He ought to season the food of the Eucharist by good works, because unless the food which is sweet in itself is received worthily, it becomes bitter; and what is an electuary for the righteous is wormwood for the unrighteous. He ought to season the food of doctrine by the example of a good life, lest, if his life is despised, his preaching rightly be held in contempt.

But if that salt has become foolish, with what shall it be salted? This salt becomes foolish in three ways: through ignorance, negligence, and avarice. For the priests of our time are aged schoolboys, children of a hundred years, of whom the Lord says through the prophet: “Those who hold the law did not know me” (Jer. 2). How will such men be able to season others, when they know neither how to instruct themselves nor others? It often happens that, when priests through their own fault lack the light of knowledge, those who follow them too stumble through their ignorance.

Hence the Lord says: “If the blind lead the blind, both fall into the pit” (Matt. 13). If such men have become foolish through the error of ignorance, who will season them with the salt of wisdom, when they ought to teach rather than be taught, instruct rather than be instructed? They have no greater persons over them to correct them, nor ought they to have wiser persons to instruct them.

They become foolish through negligence, because in all their works negligence induces torpor and destroys the fruit of their works. In the Psalms there is no devotion; in reading, no attentiveness; in imposing penance, no diligence; in celebrating Mass, no caution; in governing subjects, no discernment; in good works, no practice.

But if they have become foolish, by whom shall they themselves be salted? Who can free them from so great a precipice of negligences? Who can season them with the savour of diligence? They are also made foolish through avarice, because they sell Christ himself for money, and thus occupy the place of Judas the traitor. They put baptism up for sale, prostitute burials for selling; they flatter the vices of subjects in order to squeeze out money; they flatter vices in order to fill their purse.

Such salt is not offered in sacrifice to the Lord, but is cast out, trampled under foot, and reduced to a dungheap. For such priests do not worthily offer themselves to God in sacrifice, nor season their sacrifices with the salt of wisdom; they handle the sacraments unworthily and consecrate unworthily. Thus the salt of the offering is withdrawn, although the Lord forbids an offering without salt to be offered. Thus salt is cast outside, because although such priests belong to the Church in name and number, they do not belong to it in spiritual power and merit, but are worthy to be trampled under foot.

The feet are the subjects for whom ecclesiastical priests are bound to provide, lest they stumble on the way of this life into the scandal of sin. Evil priests are trampled by these feet because, when subjects see them darkened by ignorance and cast down by sloth, those whom they ought to have as a model of good they have as an example of evil; and those who ought to be a model for the flock are the people’s mockery. Thus salt is turned into a dungheap: such priests stink with the odour of infamy, rot through the corruption of guilt, and putrefy in the filth of evil habit. Therefore let there be salt in priests, and let them have peace among themselves.

## CHAPTER XLV. To Married Persons

The Apostle Paul says: “Let each man have his own wife, because of fornication” (1 Cor. 7). Likewise: “It is better to marry than to burn” (ibid.).

The Lord also, establishing marriage in paradise, said: “Increase and multiply” (Gen. 2). In the Gospel Christ likewise says: “What God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19; Mark 10). O how great is the dignity of marriage: it had its beginning in paradise; it removes the vice of incontinence; it contains within itself a heavenly sacrament; it keeps faith with the marriage-bed; it preserves between spouses an indivisible fellowship of life; it frees offspring from disgrace; and it excuses bodily intercourse from sin. In this state the patriarchs were saved, and in it some of the Apostles were chosen.

O how great is the power of this sacrament, through which, lest anyone fall into the precipice of lust or incontinence, he is received into the honourableness of marriage! O how greatly does one assail honourableness who breaks faith with the marriage-bed! When, abandoning the marriage-bed, he commits adultery with another, he defiles the sacrament, so far as lies in him; he sins against his own body, divides the unity of marriage, and breaks the laws of matrimony.

O how great is the danger in adultery, where sin is committed against God, one’s neighbour is wronged, murder is often perpetrated, a legitimate son is frequently disinherited, and a daughter often marries her father, a sister her brother! Adultery is commonly the cause of manifold wickedness. Through adultery David falls into homicide; Reuben is subjected to his father’s curse. But in commendation of marriage, Christ is born of a betrothed woman, and at Cana of Galilee the wedding is consecrated by his presence.

Yet although bodily intercourse is excused from sin, it is performed for the receiving of offspring, not for the pleasure of the flesh. Therefore let the joined fellowship of bodily intercourse be restrained by regard for place, time, and religious duty. Let a person also observe the spiritual marriage between flesh and spirit: that the flesh, like a wife, may obey the spirit, and the spirit, like a husband, may rule the flesh as a wife.

Let there be fidelity to the marriage-bed, lest either the flesh, having abandoned the rule of the spirit, commit adultery with the world, or reason, seduced by the enticement of the flesh itself, commit fornication with it; according to the saying that “a vehement lover of his wife is an adulterer.” Let there also be hope of offspring, namely the intention of good work; let there be the sacrament of spiritual union; let good works be brought forth as children; and let there be the rational bond of flesh and spirit.

## CHAPTER XLVI. On Widows

The Apostle says of widows: “To the unmarried and widows, it is good for them if they remain as I do,” that is, chastely (1 Cor. 7). And elsewhere: “I wish all people to be as I myself am” (ibid.), that is, continent. Though the married state is good, the widowed state is more advantageous.

For in marriage there is danger in keeping faith with the marriage-bed; danger in moderating the claims of bodily intercourse; labour in anxiety over household affairs; the burden of rearing offspring; a wife’s pain in giving birth and pain while carrying the womb; the wife’s subjection, even by force, to the authority of her husband; the husband’s fear lest his wife become an adulteress; the husband’s authority is not absolute; and there is an inordinate movement, though venial.

Therefore let the widow not proceed to a second marriage. Second marriages raise the suspicion of lust and are an indication of incontinence. Bereft of an earthly husband, let her be joined to a heavenly bridegroom, where conception is without labour and birth without pain; where justice is strict and God is eternal life; where conception is ordered will and birth is good work; where desire is charity, fidelity to the marriage-bed is long-suffering, the sacrament is the truth of the sacrament, the marriage-bed is chastity, sight is contemplation, speech is prayer, touch is eternal love, the kiss is tranquillity of mind, and bodily intercourse is eternal joy.

O widow, if you seek an example of the widowed state, you find a model of widowhood in Anna the prophetess (Luke 2). By the merit of her continence she deserved prophecy; by the merit of chastity she deserved to see the Messiah. Therefore let the widowhood of the turtledove, faithful to its mate, invite you to chastity, because, bereft of its mate, it seeks neither to love nor to be loved.

And if it lacks its mate, it settles neither upon a green branch nor upon flourishing grass. This admonishes you, O widow, that in the time of widowhood you should despise the flower of the aging world and scorn the freshness of worldly delight. O widow, if you are joined to a temporal husband, you serve the heavenly bridegroom less freely. For no one can serve two masters (Matt. 6); and while you attend to the flesh, you attend less to the spirit.

## CHAPTER XLVII. To Virgins

It is said to virgins: “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11). And the prophet says: “Hear, daughter, and see,” etc. (Ps. 44).

O virgin, marked by the seal of virginity and the title of chastity, do not betray that which nature entrusted to you in a special manner and by which it marked you out more graciously. Do not lose for a slight pleasure what can in no way be restored. This is nature’s treasure, which, once lost, does not return; this is the flower which, having bloomed, does not bloom again. This is the star which, when it sets, does not return to its rising; this is the gift which, once lost, is not compensated. And because it alone is what you cannot restore, you ought to preserve it more diligently.
