By this alone a human being living in the flesh imitates an angel; by this alone a human being conquers himself; it preserves the integrity of reputation and guards the flesh from uncleanness. Therefore hear, daughter, not only with the ear of the body but also with the ear of the mind; see with the eye of the heart, that you may understand; incline your bodily ear, that you may obey; and so forget your people (ibid.).

The people are the assembly of carnal thoughts, which suggests to the virgin that she should obtain marriage, rejoice in a spouse’s embraces, be made fruitful by offspring, and enjoy carnal pleasure. But forget such a people, because it is the people of Babylon, the nation of confusion, which attempts to lead the daughter of Zion captive. Forget also your father’s house (ibid.).

Your father is the tinder of sin that begot you and brought you forth from your mother; its house and dwelling is concupiscence, in which that tinder rules, reigns, exercises lordship, and commands. And thus “the king shall desire your beauty” (ibid.): namely, that king who is King of kings and Lord of lords, of whom it is said: “The sides of the north, the city of the great King” (Ps. 47). And elsewhere: “The earth and its fullness are the Lord’s” (Ps. 23).

O virgin, if you wish to marry an earthly man because of the flower of youth, consider that death plucks that flower, or at least it withers in the winter of old age.

Marry, then, that man who alone possesses immortality, with whom there is no change nor shadow of alteration (James 1). If you wish to marry an earthly [Col. 0195C] husband because of riches, consider that earthly riches are deceptive and transitory: they either pass away in this present life, or at least depart at death. Marry, then, him with whom are incomparable treasures and unchangeable riches, which neither thief steals nor moth destroys (Matt. 6). But if you wish to marry an earthly man because he is distinguished by beauty, consider that sickness diminishes beauty, old age uproots it, or at least the moment of death utterly removes it. Marry, then, him “whose beauty the sun and moon admire.” If you wish to marry an earthly man because of nobility of lineage, marry him of whom it is said: “Who shall recount his generation?” (Isa. 53). If you wish to marry an earthly husband because of worldly honour or earthly rank, [Col. 0195D] consider that it is denied even to the highest to stand long, and that falls are grievous beneath an excessive weight. Marry, then, him of whom it is said: “Who can resist his power?” (Job 9). And elsewhere: “Of his kingdom there shall be no end” (Luke 1).

## CHAPTER XLVIII. To the Drowsy

“Knowing that it is now the hour for us to rise from sleep” (Rom. 13): it should be noted, dearest brethren, that sleep is threefold. There is a sleep when someone is carried away to contemplation of heavenly things, and then the natural powers rest; of this it is said: “The Lord cast a deep sleep upon Adam” (Gen. 2). There is another sleep, when the animal faculties rest and the natural powers operate; of this it is said that an angel appeared in dreams to Joseph (Matt. 1–2). The third sleep is [Col. 0196A] when reason sleeps and sensuality goes beyond bounds. The first sleep occurs above man; the second, according to man; the third, below man. The first is miraculous, the second imaginary, the third monstrous. By the first, a man becomes God; by the second, spirit; by the third, a beast. In the first he dreams true things; in the second, monstrous things. But the third occurs in the night of sin, in the darkness of vice, in the shadow of transgression.

Therefore now, in the time of grace, it is the hour for us to rise from the sleep of error, to arise from the sleep of sin. For four things ought to awaken us from sleep: the rising sun, the cock’s crow, fear of a thief, and care for one’s household. The Sun of righteousness awakens us from the sleep of sin; it has already risen for us through grace in baptism, when we renounced sin. Therefore, through the grace which we have already received, we are invited [Col. 0196B] to watchfulness of mind and to its safeguarding.

The cock’s crow awakens us from sleep—that is, the admonition of the preacher. So too does fear of the thief, that is, the devil, who, if he finds us sleeping, will enter the body through lust and the soul through pride, carrying off the purple garments of virtues and the riches of good works. Care also for one’s household ought to awaken us from the sleep of sin. Let us therefore awake, because so many things awaken us; let us keep watch, because so many things invite us to watchfulness, and because our salvation is nearer than when we believed. Let us persevere in grace, because glory is at hand. Let us run through the racecourse, because the prize is at hand.

The righteous person approaches eternal salvation in a double way: through the course of natural life and through the course of spiritual life, [Col. 0196C] because the more of the course of temporal life the righteous person completes, the more he approaches the life of glory.

The more fully he completes the course of spiritual life, the more he draws near to the salvation of eternal life. Therefore, the holier the righteous person, the nearer he is to salvation; and the older he is, the nearer to that same salvation. “Our salvation is nearer than when we believed” (Rom. 13), because, when faith was first bestowed upon us, the greater part of life’s course remained, and therefore the greater part of righteousness still had to be completed. “The night has passed, and the day has drawn near” (ibid.). Night is threefold: the night of ignorance, the night of guilt, and the night of worldly tribulation. Of the night of ignorance it is said: “The night has passed, but the day has drawn near.” Of the night of guilt it is said: “Every night I shall wash my bed” (Ps. 6). Of the night [Col. 0196D] of worldly tribulation it is said: “By day the Lord commanded his mercy, and by night his song” (Ps. 41). In the first walk fools, in the second the ungodly, in the third the miserable.

But the night of ignorance has receded, because we have now been instructed by the Law, formed by reason, and taught by every creature. For the Law teaches what must be done; reason, how it must be done; and creation, for whose sake it must be done. For every creature, while serving its Creator, instructs us to serve God. The night of guilt too has receded, because, from the time grace was bestowed upon us in baptism, guilt has been banished from us. The night of worldly tribulation has receded, because, although the primitive Church endured various tribulations—from the assaults of tyrants, the violence of false brethren, and the attacks of heretics—the storm has now in part [Col. 0197A] been calmed, so that the Church may serve God in peace.

Therefore the day has drawn near: namely, the day of knowledge, to enlighten the ignorant; the day of grace, to direct those who stray; the day of worldly prosperity, to soothe those who labour. “Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness” (Rom. 13). As the kinds of night are diverse, so too are the kinds of darkness. There is the darkness of ignorance, of which it is said: “The people of the nations who walked in darkness saw a great light” (Isa. 9). There is the darkness of sins, of which it is said: “He who walks in darkness does not know where he is going” (John 12). There is the darkness of punishments, of which it is said: “Cast him into the outer darkness” (Matt. 22, 25). The darkness of ignorance is inward; the darkness of sins is most inward; the darkness of punishments is outward.

“Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness” [Col. 0198A] (Rom. 13), so that we may act well; let us flee the works that bring punishments, lest we live miserably. Let us cast off the works of ignorance, that we may be prudent; the works of sins, that we may be guileless; the works that bring punishments, that we may be happy. And so let us “put on the armour of light” (ibid.), armed with the light of wisdom against heretics, the light of grace against the devil, and the light of glory against hell. “Let us walk honourably as in the day” (ibid.). One who walks by night often walks dishonourably: he either stumbles over an obstacle, falls into mud, slips into a precipice, or plunges into a pit. So too one who walks in the night of sins sometimes stumbles upon the mountain of pride, falls into the precipice of gluttony, or plunges into the pit of avarice. Let us therefore walk honourably in the day of good works, that we may reach the day of eternity.

[Col. 0197]

[SERMONS.]

## EIGHT SERMONS OF MASTER ALAN OF LILLE

Now brought to light for the first time from a most ancient codex of the library of Blessed Mary of Alne, of the Cistercian Order, in the diocese of Liège.

### 118 SERMON I. ON THE SPIRITUAL UNITY OF ABBOT AND MONKS

“Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth,” etc. (Song 1).

[Col. 0197B]

It should be noted, dearest brethren, who asks, what she asks, and from whom she asks it. The Virgin of virgins asks; she asks for a kiss; she asks it from the true bridegroom—that is, from Christ. What kiss? Not that from which the ferment of lust flows, but that from which the honeycomb of heavenly grace distils. The virgin asked for a threefold kiss, and obtained what she requested.

The first kind of kiss takes place through the spiritual union of soul and God. The second kiss is that by which the Father kisses the Son; for the Holy Spirit is the love and bond of Father and Son. The third kiss is that of the Incarnation, by which Christ, through the humanity he assumed, kissed the Virgin Mary. The first kiss is of inspiration; the second, of breathing forth; the third, of incarnation. The first kiss is of the heart; the second, of the mouth; the third, of the body. The first yields honeycomb, the second balsam, the third oil. Therefore, before the Incarnation, the Virgin sought the kiss of inward visitation, that through it she might keep intact the seal of virginity; nor was she cheated of her request, but was visited by inward inspiration.

Therefore she experienced the first kiss when she did not lose the seal of virginity; and so, through inward visitation, [Col. 0198B] she in some sense made herself worthy of the incarnation of the Word. But by what worthiness? A threefold worthiness: the worthiness of pre-election, of election, and of sub-election. The worthiness of pre-election was hers when, by the eternal decree of predestination, she was pre-elected to be the untouched Mother of God. But after the Holy Spirit overshadowed her, he chose her to conceive the Son of God and bring forth the one conceived into the light through an ineffable birth. She was also sub-elected in relation to that human nature which was beloved by the Word of God with ineffable love.

That human nature was principally elected, to which the Blessed Virgin, sub-elected, was to be united, so that from her the Son of God might be born. But she sought the second and third kisses when, hearing from the angel, “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1), [Col. 0198C] she said: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (ibid.). And when she said this, she received both kisses: the Spirit for her own strengthening, and the Son of God in conception.

But just as this name “kiss” is written in Sacred Scripture now in golden, now in black letters, so kisses too are diverse. For, just as Christ has his kisses, so Antichrist—that is, the devil—has his kisses, that is, his sweetnesses. For he sometimes [Col. 0199A] kisses a person by flattering him through worldly things, sometimes by deceiving him through lust, sometimes by tempting him through inward suggestion. The first kiss is poisonous, the second foul-smelling, the third muddy; the first belongs to the deceiver, the second to the adulterer, the third to the robber and thief.

But when these kisses have been banished, three kisses ought to be observed in the Church of God: one of charity toward one’s neighbour; a second of obedience toward one’s superior; a third of compassion toward one’s subject.

This is the threefold cord that is not easily broken, by which cloistral unity is preserved. It consists in three things: unity of distinctness, unity of union, and unity of integrity. From this threefold unity the cloistered monk is called, as it were, a guardian of unity.

A monk ought to possess unity of distinctness, [Col. 0199B] so that he does not consent to the sins of his neighbours, but at least in mind keeps himself apart from their enormities. The unity of union must likewise be preserved in him, so that he compassionately shares the sufferings of his neighbours, is bound by the bond of religious life, and is united by the tie of compassion. Nor should the cloistered man depart from the unity of integrity; indeed, he ought to preserve integrity of mind and body, so that the enemy may find nothing broken within him by which, when attacking, an entrance into his inward parts may lie open.

Nor is the Bridegroom praiseworthy only in the kisses mentioned above, but also in his breasts; hence it follows: “Your breasts are more beautiful than wine” (Song 1). The Bridegroom has two breasts; from one milk flows, from the other wine. By milk mercy is denoted; by wine, justice. For just as milk is sweet and the food of little ones, so mercy is kindly exercised toward little ones; and by wine, justice, because, just as wine is harsher and the drink of those more mature, so justice is harsher and is exercised upon those more mature. But these two breasts are sweeter than wine—that is, than the harshness of the Old Law, where justice existed without mercy, misery without compassion. Yet in the time of the New Testament the severity of justice is tempered by the sweetness of mercy, and the sweetness of mercy is sharpened by the severity of justice. Every prelate ought to possess these two breasts, by which bishop may nourish subject, teacher disciple, and abbot monk: offering him a mother’s breasts, and also a father’s blows; now flashing forth corrections and threats, now raining down admonitions and [Col. 0199D] benefits. These breasts, moreover, ought to be fragrant with the finest ointments.

There are three kinds of ointment: cleansing ointment, soothing ointment, and healing ointment. Christ applies cleansing ointment when, through scourges, he cleanses sin in a person; soothing ointment when, through mercy, he raises up one who has gone astray; healing ointment when he strengthens through admonitions and teachings. An abbot ought to offer this threefold ointment to his subjects: to cleanse the disobedient from sin through corrections and discipline, or, should they be obstinate, to remove them from the fellowship of the others; to support the weak through the remedy of allowances and dispensations; and to enlighten the unlearned through teaching. For a prelate ought to be a pattern for the flock, so that he may conform himself to others and form others in himself.

[Col. 0200A] But care must be taken lest such a pattern be deformed, such a face defiled, such a mirror darkened. For a prelate ought to be a mirror—but not just any mirror. There are three kinds of mirrors. There is a mirror in which the left parts appear left and the right parts right; by this mirror is signified the prelate who in works and teachings makes clear what things are left—that is, earthly—and what are right—that is, eternal. There is another mirror in which left parts appear right and right parts left; by this is signified the prelate who puts earthly things before divine things as better and puts divine things after them as worse.

The third mirror is one in which the upper parts of a person appear lower and the lower parts upper; [Col. 0200B] by this is denoted the prelate who, according to sensuality, is always so intent upon earthly things that he does not look with reason toward higher things. Therefore let every prelate conform himself to the first mirror, so that from hope he may come to sight, from the way to the homeland, from mercy to glory. May Jesus Christ deign to grant this to us. Amen.

### SERMON II. ON THE ANNUNCIATION OF BLESSED MARY, WHEN IT FALLS ON PALM SUNDAY

“Glorious things have been said of you, city of God” (Ps. 86).

Dearest brethren, the King of kings, who commands winds and sea, whose city is “the sides of the north,” in order that in all things he might represent the image of his Trinity, has built for himself a threefold city: the first is the world, [Col. 0200C] the second the Church, the third the Virgin of virgins. For the world is aptly designated by the name of a city, because, just as the majesty of a commonwealth is preserved in a city, so the world is not without its own commonwealth. For just as a commonwealth is an ordered assembly of things, among which some rule, others act, and others obey, so in the world, as in a great city, God rules, the angel acts, and man obeys.

Likewise the Church is aptly designated by the title of a city, in which the greater prelates govern by authority, those of middle rank order each thing by action, and the lower submit themselves to the authority of their superiors. In this city the wall is the foundation of Christian faith; the cement is [Col. 0200D] the blood of martyrs; the battlements are the authorities of the saints; the streets are the breadth of charity; the rampart is the height of humility; the bridge is obedience; the gate is almsgiving.

Nor without reason does the Virgin of virgins receive the name of city. In her the authority of reason ruled, sensuality acted, and carnality served; in her the citizens were rational motions. By these, armed with discernment, the city was guarded lest the hostility of the devil rage within it. In this city constancy was the wall, temperance the cement, fortitude the battlement, prudence the rampart. The eastern gate was faith, through which the Sun of righteousness shone upon her; the southern gate, charity, through which the warmth of the Holy Spirit burned in her; the northern gate, virginity, through which carnal concupiscence [Col. 0201A] was extinguished in her; the western gate, humility, through which worldly temptations were repelled in her. The river of heavenly grace so flows beside her that it continually flows back into her, thus fortifying the city so that it need not fear a hostile attack. Of this river it is said: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. 45).

In this city is a garden enclosed, a garden sealed (Song 4), a watered garden, a garden planted with trees, adorned with herbs, decorated with flowers: that is, the mind of the Virgin. In it, as in a heavenly garden, upright habits, in the likeness of trees, bear the fruits of good works; good thoughts, after the pattern of herbs, send forth the greenness of inward devotion; virtues, after the example of flowers, produce the fragrance of good repute. In this garden flourish [Col. 0201B] the myrtle of temperance, the rose of patience, the lily of chastity, and the violet of eternal contemplation. Thus the King of kings built these three cities, that he might dwell with the children of men.

In the first city he was Creator; in the second, Saviour; in the third, Merciful One. In the first his power resounded; in the second, his wisdom; in the third, his grace. Of the first it was said: “The sides of the north are the city of the great king” (Ps. 47). Of the second: “How beloved are your tabernacles, O Lord of hosts!” (Ps. 82). Of the third: “Glorious things have been said of you, city of God” (Ps. 86). But let us see what glorious things have been said of the Virgin Mary.

Balaam says: “A star shall arise from Jacob” (Num. 24). She is the one who, in the heavenly Arcturus, [Col. 0201C] bears the image of the immovable pole. According to the philosophers, Arcturus is that group of seven stars which is now called *arctos*, now the Bear, now the North, and in which the star called the pole, occupying the last position, remains immovable and provides a route for sailors. Thus by Arcturus the Church is signified; for just as Arcturus is always pressed upon and never submerged, so the Church is always scourged and never bent. In this heavenly Arcturus Mary is the immovable pole: moved by no temptation and shaken by no tribulation, she offers a harbour of salvation to those who fear shipwreck on the sea of this world.

Isaiah says of the same: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse,” etc. (Isa. 11). Accordingly, the Virgin is compared to a rod on account of straightness, correction, and fruit-bearing. [Col. 0201D] For as a rod is directed upward, so the Virgin is raised to eternal things; as excesses are corrected by a rod, so sins are remitted through the Virgin; as a rod bears fruit, so the Virgin bears the bread of angels. Nor is the Virgin compared to a rod merely on account of the office, but also on account of the name: by changing one letter in the word, *virga* (“rod”) becomes *Virgo* (“Virgin”). And while the Virgin Mary proceeded from the flowers of mother Eve like a golden rose, the rod became Virgin; and alpha was changed into omega, because the beginning became the end—that is, the Eternal became temporal.

She is the fortress, or little castle, of which it was said: “Go into the village that is opposite you, and you will find an ass tied, and a colt with her,” etc. (Matt. 21). When the Son of God wished to assume the garment of humanity in the tabernacle [Col. 0202A] of the Virgin, he commanded the angels to guard her against every enticement of the flesh, saying to them: “Go to the little castle; go to the Virgin by guarding her; go to the Virgin by counselling her; go to the Virgin by accompanying her.” Accordingly, this Virgin is also called a little castle.

But Eve, the first woman, was formerly also a fortress, because she was fortified with natural and gratuitous gifts. Afterwards she was reduced to the likeness of a most worthless town—indeed, she became a decayed village—open to every enemy: flesh, world, and devil. Thus the human race plainly remained desolate, until the King of kings “set his tabernacle in the sun” (Ps. 18), that is, established a fortress in the Virgin, when through the coming of the Holy Spirit the Virgin was so strengthened that the enemy had no entrance open to her.

Nor is it without reason that it is said: “which is opposite [Col. 0202B] you.” Before the Incarnation, human nature was opposed to angelic nature. In this little castle the ass and colt were tied: that is, sensuality and the first movements of sensuality. Of themselves they were not bound to good, but through the ministry of angels they were released for good. And after Christ came through the Incarnation, he sat upon the ass and colt, because both sensuality and its first movement obeyed him. Christ entered this little castle to fight against the devil; but he entered through the golden gate while its doors remained closed, because neither at his entrance nor at his departure was the seal of virginity broken in her.

This is that famous Jerusalem in which the true Solomon built the solemn temple. For what could more fittingly be called Jerusalem—that is, “vision of peace”—than she in whom the peace of eternity rested, in whom the true Solomon, that is, Christ, built the temple of his body, of which it was said: “Destroy this temple,” etc. (John 2)?

But in building this temple neither hammer nor axe was heard, because Mary experienced no commotion of flesh or pains either in conception or in childbirth. But because three altars belonged to Solomon’s temple—the first, of burnt offerings, in which animals were sacrificed; the second, of incense, in which aromatic substances were offered; the third, the propitiatory, in which the divine glory appeared—so in the temple of Christ, that is, in his human nature, three altars are present. The first altar is that of burnt offerings, [Col. 0202D] namely, his glorious flesh, in which our sins were consumed. The second is his soul, because, just as aromatic spices were offered on the altar of incense, so Christ’s soul is filled with various virtues. The third is his divinity, in which the majesty of divine authority shines forth.

Therefore, dearest brethren, after the likeness of the Virgin, if we cannot prepare a city, at least a village; if not a fortress for the King of kings, at least let us prepare lodging in our souls—indeed, even a little lodging in our minds—so that he may deign to set his tabernacles therein. But first let us cleanse our minds, so that we may invite one who is willing. A lodging is commonly defiled by three things, 122 from which we must cleanse the tabernacle of the mind: dung, dust, and mud.

Dung [Col. 0203A] is lust, which stinks in the flesh and stinks in one’s reputation. For just as dung smells the more foul the more it is stirred, so lust smells the more foul the more it is practised. Yet in this respect dung is better than lust: added to our soil, it makes it fruitful; lust clinging to the soil of our flesh makes it weak. Dust is vainglory, which the wind casts from the face of the earth because it is reduced to nothing by the breath of pride. Gnats, which sting with stings, are born of dust; from vainglory arise perverse thoughts, which penetrate the storehouse of the heart. Dust darkens the eye; vainglory blinds the mind.

But mud, which is unclean and sticky, signifies avarice, which both entices a person with the glue of tenacity and defiles him with the filth of cupidity. This avarice [Col. 0203B] compels the people of our age to return to idolatry. Of it the Apostle says: “Avarice, which is the service of idols” (Eph. 5). It compels a person to put God behind and worship money. The idolatry of our age has three daughters: the first causes the belly to be worshipped through drunken excess; the second, the world to be loved through covetous desire; the third, the flesh to be worshipped through lust. To permit ourselves coined names, the first may be called *bacchilatria* (“worship of Bacchus”); the second *nummilatria* (“worship of money”); the third *carnilatria* (“worship of the flesh”).

Let us therefore cleanse the lodging of the mind from dung by continence; from dust by patience; and from mud by almsgiving, so that in this way we may prepare within ourselves a dwelling worthy of God. May Jesus Christ our Lord [Col. 0203C] deign to grant this to us. Amen.

### SERMON III. ON FEAR OF JUDGMENT, IN LENT

“You have given a sign to those who fear you, that they may flee from before the bow” (Ps. 59).

Brethren, the Apostle, conscious of nothing against himself yet not presuming upon the prerogative of merits, when speaking of himself said: “My glory is the testimony of my conscience” (2 Cor. 1). But I, whom the worm of an evil conscience gnaws, whom the spark of reason—unextinguished even in Cain the fratricide (Gen. 4)—accuses and rebukes, can say: “My shame is the testimony of my conscience” (Heb. 11); for “all day long my shame is before me, and my sin is always before me” (Ps. 43).

Therefore I have set before you not my own words but those of the prophet, who, by the privilege of prophecy, deserved to be called the trumpet or organ of the Holy Spirit. Stirred by no outward assistance—not through deeds, dreams, sayings, or visions, but by the revelation of the Holy Spirit alone—he foresees future things and foretold what he foresaw. These are indeed the words of one of the modern Fathers speaking in his person to him who “gives a word to those who proclaim the Gospel with great power” (Ps. 67). Likewise: “Who gives snow like wool, who scatters mist like ashes” (Ps. 147). He declares that he gave, and specifies to whom he gave, what he gave, and why. To whom? “To those who fear you.” What? “A sign.” Why? “That they may flee from before the bow.”

Here [Col. 0204A] it must be carefully observed that he did not say simply “those who fear,” but “those who fear you,” thereby indicating what fear he means. For fear is threefold: the fear of horror, the fear of caution, and the fear of reverence. The fear of horror is that by which we fear or dread punishment; the fear of caution, that by which we avoid guilt and also punishment; the fear of reverence, that by which we revere the divine majesty. The first instructs, the second advances, the third completes and perfects.

Of the first it is said in the person of Christ the head: “Fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness covered me. And I said: Who will give me wings like a dove?” etc. (Ps. 54). And of the same in the Gospel: “Jesus began to be dismayed and afraid” (Mark 14). For our Redeemer assumed real fear and real sorrow, just as he assumed real flesh—not from the necessity of one who suffers with another, but by the willing purpose of mercy. Of the second, Solomon says: “Blessed is he who is always afraid” (Prov. 28). And on the same passage: “The less the punishment of judgment is feared, the more strictly will it be borne.” And elsewhere: “Whatever can happen is prudently feared.” Of the third Isaiah says: “From fear of you, O Lord, we have conceived and brought forth a spirit of salvation” (Isa. 26).

The Psalmist commends the same fear, saying: “The holy fear of the Lord endures for age upon age” (Ps. 18). And elsewhere: “The angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear him, and will deliver them” (Ps. 33).

To these, indeed, a sign has been given in three things: namely, in the Scriptures, in the sacraments, and in examples of works. [Col. 0204C] In the Scriptures: for the volumes of Sacred Scripture contain commands and prohibitions, which are signs of the divine will, since they commonly command those things which he wishes you to fulfil and prohibit those which he wishes you to avoid. This decree, whether command or prohibition, is sometimes customarily called “will.”

He gave a sign in the sacraments, because a sacrament is nothing other than a sign of invisible grace; this can be shown in baptism and in the others. For the outward washing of the body performed in baptism signifies the inward washing away of the stain of original sin; the anointing performed both in baptism and confirmation represents the inward anointing of the soul; likewise, the visible form of bread on the altar signifies the invisible body of the Lord. These are the darknesses of which the Psalms say: “He made darkness his hiding-place” (Ps. 17). For divine grace lies hidden, or is contained, beneath the sacraments. Hence the sacraments themselves are called vessels in the Gospel (Matt. 25), where it says: “Store oil in your vessels.” And in Isaiah: “Be cleansed, you who carry the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. 51).

These vessels are empty in some, half-full in others, and full in still others. They are empty in apostates, who, having fallen away from faith, are Christians neither in name nor in divine reality; they are half-full in false brethren, who are Christians only in name; they are full in those in whom both the name and devotion are found. These are the bandages which our Samaritan, who was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho (Luke 10), applied. They are likewise the dark mountain of which Isaiah says: “Raise a sign upon [Col. 0205A] a dark mountain” (Isa. 13). This is fulfilled by priests raising the sign of the holy cross over the sacraments, as in the consecration of baptism and the celebration of the Eucharist.

The Lord gave a sign in examples of works, of which we may select two: prayer and fasting. For the Lord prayed when he ascended the mountain, spending the night in prayer (Matt. 14); he also prayed in the garden beyond the torrent of Cedron, once, twice, and a third time; and he invited his disciples to do the same, saying: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matt. 26). The evangelical priest represents these things in that threefold silence which occurs in the canon of the Mass.

The Lord also fasted forty days and [Col. 0205B] forty nights (Matt. 4), not only in his own person but also in his heralds Moses (Exod. 24) and Elijah (3 Kings 19), so that he who had said through Moses, “Every word shall stand in the mouth of two or three,” might commend fasting to us in the deed of two or three. We believe that Christ assigned the forty-day number to Christian warfare, or fasting, not rashly or by chance, but by deep counsel; in it he indicates the weapons with which we ought to fight. For since forty arises from ten multiplied by four, ten belongs to the Old Testament because of the Decalogue, and four to the New because of the grace of the Gospel. The faithful ought to fight against [Col. 0205C] the flesh, the world, and the devil by observing the commandments of the Old and New Law.

Behold: “The Lord gave a sign to those who fear him” (Ps. 59). Why? “That they may flee from before the bow” (ibid.), that is, from the terrible sentence of the future judgment, which is figured by the bow: for the more vigorously the wood is bent backwards, the more forcefully the arrow is driven forward. So too, the longer judgment is deferred, the heavier and harsher will be the sentence that says: “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25).

Yet it may be said, without prejudice to the preferable interpretation, that divine judgment is prefigured in the bow. For although the bowstring is flexible, it bends and curves the stiffness of the wood; so, in the divine assize, the gentleness of mercy tempers the rigour of justice. “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24). And in judgment, [Col. 0205D] “mercy and truth shall meet; justice and peace shall kiss” (Ps. 84). Hence it is compared to a cup full of mixed wine, when it says: “A cup of unmixed wine, full of mixture, is in the hand of the Lord” (Ps. 74). There justice punishes and mercy has compassion.

Therefore, brethren, that we may flee from before the bow, let us fulfil what he commands, avoid what he prohibits, receive the sacraments he instituted, and imitate the examples of works which he set forth. Let us go and show ourselves to the priest; let us pour out our consciences before Christ’s vicar, asking from him medicine for our wounds. For he is the physician of whom Jeremiah says: “Is there no balm in Gilead, or is there no physician there?” (Jer. 8).

He is the wise man of whom it is said: “Their fury is according to the likeness [Col. 0206A] of a serpent, like that of a deaf asp stopping its ears, which will not hear the voice of charmers or the medicine compounded by the wise man” (Ps. 57). If he should wish to contend with us in private judgment and take our tunic, let us leave him also our cloak: that is, let us carefully disclose not only inward sins but also outward sins performed through the service of the body. If, namely, we have sinned by looking at vain things or listening to frivolous entertainments, in the smell of perfumes, in the taste of flavours, or in touching another’s skin, let us confess the kinds of sin and offer the gift which Moses commanded to be offered.

Moses indeed commanded that no one be excluded from the camp on suspicion of leprosy without examination by a priest; he also forbade anyone, even one who was clean, to be received within the camp unless he presented himself to the priest [Col. 0206B] (Lev. 13). He likewise ordained that the person whom the priest cleansed and judged clean should offer a yearling ewe, two unblemished lambs, three tenths of fine flour, and a sextary of oil (Lev. 14).

Let us therefore offer perfect obedience to the priest—that is, let us obey one who imposes upon us fitting satisfaction—lest we be like a heifer that grows wanton and throws off the yoke, but rather like a trained heifer that loves threshing. Let us also offer two unblemished lambs: fasting and almsgiving, so that vainglory may not defile our almsgiving, nor the wish to amass money corrupt our fasting. For it is taught that one who distributes alms ought to take care not to sell the treasure of a good conscience for the cheap price of a slight reputation. It is also fitting that one who fasts should consider that our hardships bear no fruit unless we grant relief to another.

Let us also offer three tenths of fine flour: that is, faith in the Trinity, whose subtlety is incomprehensible. Finally, let us offer a sextary of oil: that is, let us bestow upon our neighbours the six works of mercy which the Lord indicates in the Gospel of Matthew (chapter 6), and Isaiah in part, saying: [Col. 0206C] “This is the fast which I have chosen, says the Lord: loosen the bonds of impiety, untie the bundles that weigh down, let those who are broken go free, and break their burden. Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the needy and wandering into your house; when you see one naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh. Then your light shall break forth like the morning, and your health shall arise more swiftly.”

Behold, wholesome counsel! For whoever does these things, placed at the right hand on the day of the last sifting, will hear: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom,” etc. (Matt. 25).

May Jesus Christ our Lord deign to grant this to us: he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for all ages of ages. Amen.

## 125. SERMON IV. ON EASTER, TO THE MASTERS OF CLERICS

“Hurry; mix three measures of fine flour, and make bread baked under the ashes” (Gen. 18).

These are Abraham’s words to Sarah. While Abraham was dwelling as a guest in the valley of Mamre, he saw three men and worshipped one; and, entreating them, obtained that they should turn aside to him at night and take food. Therefore, entering the tent, he commanded Sarah: “Hurry,” etc. [Col. 0207A]

My brothers, we believe that a profound mystery lies veiled beneath these words. This will be clearly evident if we draw honey from the rock and oil from the hardest stone (Deut. 32), that is, spiritual understanding from the historical sense. Let us therefore seek the sun beneath the cloud, the marrow beneath the bark, the life-giving spirit beneath the killing letter. Let these words then be those of the Father to the Son; for both the change of names and the designation of ages agree well with this. Abraham was first called Abram, that is, “exalted father,” before the creation of the world; whence the Father says to the Son: “With thee is the beginning in the day of thy power” (Ps. 109), etc. And the Son says of him: “The Lord said unto me, Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee” (Ps. 2). That is, “I begot thee from eternity”; but around the beginning of the world’s course he became the father of many nations. [Col. 0207B]

Hence the Church cries: “Abba, Father” (Rom. 8). Jew and Gentile have come together into the one Church of Christ. Thus the Jew cries “Abba,” the Gentile “Father.”

Sarah, however, was first called Sarai, as though “my princess,” and afterward Sarah, as though princess absolutely and universally. She was therefore first Sarai, for the Jewish people could say to Christ: “Thou art my prince”; whence the Psalmist says: “God is known in Judaea, and his name is great in Israel” (Ps. 75). Now she is Sarah, because he is prince of many. For all kings worship him; all nations serve him. And it is said of the same one: “The Lord is exalted above all nations, and his glory above the heavens” (Ps. 112). [Col. 0207C] Yet he is not only prince, but beginning; whence in the Gospel: “I am the beginning, who also speak unto you” (John 8). He is beginning from beginning; he is Alpha and Omega, that is, beginning and end.

Likewise, at Isaac’s birth Abraham was a hundred years old and Sarah ninety, according to the words: “Shall a son be born to one a hundred years old? And shall a woman of ninety bear?” (Gen. 17). The number one hundred is square; it passes from the left to the right and is produced by multiplying ten by three. But ninety does not attain so great a perfection. In these things is indicated that the Father possesses authority as the source of the Son. Let these words therefore be those of the Father to the Son: “Hurry; mix three measures,” etc. [Col. 0207D] The Son, obedient in reverence to the Father, hastened. He is the one of whom it is said: “He rejoiced as a giant to run his way” (Ps. 18). And elsewhere: “He sends forth his word to the earth; his word runs swiftly” (Ps. 147). Truly swiftly: in a brief span of time, almost three years, his most saving preaching became known to all.

He mixed three measures—that is, by preaching he implanted in the minds of believers the ineffable Trinity of Persons, aptly figured by measures of fine flour, that is, most delicate flour. This is the Trinity to which, if a human being draws near, he is exalted more and more. This is the Trinity which ascended above the Cherubim; this is the Trinity which flew upon the wings of the winds. [Col. 0208A] It transcends the keenest powers of subtle minds. It is that in which there is unity without singleness, distinction without diversity.

From this came bread baked under ashes, that is, teaching veiled by words transferred from elsewhere. For ashes are in a certain manner transferred from wood; so we transfer words from created things to the creating and ineffable Trinity, calling the Father “paradise,” the Son “the fountain from paradise,” and the Holy Spirit “delight,” according to the words: “A fountain went out from the paradise of delight” (Gen. 2). Scripture also sometimes calls the Son the right hand, [p. 126] sometimes the arm, sometimes the hand, according to: “The right hand of the Lord has wrought strength” (Ps. 117), etc.; and elsewhere: “Send forth thy hand from on high” (Ps. 144), etc.; and: “With a mighty hand and an uplifted arm” (Ps. 136). But when it is said, “If I cast out demons by the finger of God, by whom do your sons cast them out?” (Luke 11), by “finger” we understand the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0208B] With this bread are refreshed the three men—that is, believers summoned to faith from all parts of the world, or the human beings scattered throughout the earth from Noah’s three sons.

The same words may be words of the Father to a Christian—not to just anyone, but to a minister of the altar entrusted with pastoral care. For he was first Sarai, that is, prince of one, while he was governed by another; he became Sarah, or prince of many, when Christ set him as shepherd over a frail flock. Therefore he is told: “Hurry”—as though to say, remember [Col. 0208C] that you must render an account of your stewardship; beware lest you be found an unprofitable servant (Matt. 25); beware lest you be a dumb dog unable to bark (Isa. 56). “Mix three measures of fine flour,” that is, impose the threefold work of satisfaction and punishment: namely, prayer, fasting, and almsgiving.

Prayer: for this is the evening sacrifice; this is the incense of sweet savour which must be kindled upon the altar of the heart (Exod. 25). This is the column of smoke which rises from the spices of myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer (Song 3). The prelate must impose fasting, for it is able to restrain the wantonness of our flesh. Flesh is an untamed beast: unless its insolence is checked, it draws us into destruction and death. Therefore spiritual fasts must be imposed; let some be general, binding all alike. [Col. 0208D] For just as the fathers of the Old Testament were bound to offer tithes and firstfruits of their produce to the Lord, so people of the present day are bound to pay not only tithes of their days but also firstfruits.

This is done in the fasts of the Four Seasons and in the Lenten season. In the fasts of the Four Seasons we pay the firstfruits; in Lent, however, both tithes and firstfruits. For the solar year has 365 days; therefore, when we fast for thirty-six days, we pay tithes. Five days remain; and because it is better to give beyond what is required than to fall short, we pay one day as though it were an alms. Let the three days belonging to the fast of the Four Seasons intervene, and thus the forty-day number is completed. But since fasting is useless unless almsgiving commends it, almsgiving must be imposed. [Col. 0209A]

For there is a fast of ambition, a fast of superstition, and a fast of religion. The fast of ambition is also one of avarice, when someone mortifies the flesh in order to fill his moneybags; but, says the Lord, “my soul does not know such a fast.” The fast of superstition is the fast of hypocrisy, which disfigures and emaciates the face in order to be seen by people as fasting. The fast of religion is that accompanied by almsgiving, which you are bound to distribute, first to yourself and then to your neighbour.

From these is made bread baked under ashes, that is, penitence; for ashes and haircloth are the arms of penitents. With this bread are refreshed the three men whom Ezekiel saw saved (Ezek. 14): Job, Daniel, and Noah. In Job [Col. 0209B] we understand married persons; in Daniel, continent persons; in Noah, who took charge of the ark in the time of the flood, rulers. Or they are the three dead persons mentioned in the Gospel: the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, who died in the house (Mark 7); the widow’s son, who was being carried outside the gate (Luke 7); and Lazarus, four days dead and stinking (John 11). For penitence is needed both by the person who has thought wickedly, by the one who has fallen through evil action, and by the one caught in the habit of sinning, who, like a beast, has rotted in his own dung (Joel 1).

Let the Master understand these words as addressed to himself—not any person whatever, but one to whom heavenly secrets have been revealed and to whom it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 13). He was Sarai, as though prince of one, while he studied under another; [Col. 0209C] he became Sarah, that is, prince of many, when he undertook the honour of the chair. To him the Church says, “Hurry”: that is, turn over often the volumes of Sacred Scripture. Watch diligently for the benefit of your hearers; do not be a gambler; go about your flock and rouse the sluggish.

“Mix three measures of fine flour,” that is, employ a threefold exposition in reading: the first historical, the second tropological, the third allegorical. The first is the foundation; the second, the wall; the third, the roof laid upon the other two. [p. 127] The first is plainer, the second more pleasing, the third more penetrating. The first begins, the second advances, the third completes and perfects. From these is made bread baked under ashes, that is, theological reading, which seeks not verbal ornaments or the trappings of diction but humble meanings. With this bread [Col. 0209D] are refreshed three men: the greater, the intermediate, and the lesser. To the lesser is offered the milk of history; to the intermediate, the honey of tropology; to the greater, the solid bread of allegory. These are the three loaves which a friend ought to lend to a friend. This is the journey of three days which we must undertake, that we may at length sacrifice to the Lord in the wilderness.

But someone will say: “You impose upon us burdensome forced labours; but what will be the fruit of this work?” Hear: in the present life its benefit will be that one may say: “How sweet are thy words to my palate, more than honey to my mouth. From thy commandments I have gained understanding; therefore I have hated every way of iniquity” (Ps. 119). And thus you will celebrate the Passover to the Lord—that is, the passage from death to life, from darkness to light, from labour to rest, from vices to virtues; for *pascha* is called, as it were, *phasea*, that is, *phase*, “passage.” [Col. 0210A]

But someone will again object: “By whom, how, and when is Passover to be celebrated?” By those existing in Egypt—that is, in the Church militant, of which Egypt bore the type. When the people of the Lord were mingled with Egyptians, so in the Church nettles are mingled with roses, and leaves with lilies: that is, evil persons are mingled with good. Do you wish to know how and when? This is explained to you where it says: “On the fourteenth day, at evening” (Lev. 23). In the phrase “the fourteenth,” the manner or pattern of passing over is prefigured for you: namely, in the observance of the Old and New Law. Ten refers to the Old Testament because of the Decalogue, but four to the New because of the Gospel. In the phrase “at evening,” however, the time is fixed: namely, the sixth age, in which the true sun knew his setting and, after three days, rose again without delaying his rising. Hence: “He who ascends above the setting: the Lord is his name” (Ps. 68). [Col. 0210B]

In the life to come the benefit will be so great that you may deserve to hear: “Well done, good servant,” etc. (Matt. 25). It will not be said, “Enter unto joy,” but “Enter into joy” (ibid.). “His truth shall surround us as a shield,” etc. (Ps. 91). “His left hand shall be under our head, and his right hand shall embrace us” (Song 2). Then we shall sing a hymn to the Lord; then we shall render our vow in Jerusalem; then we shall celebrate the feast on the fifteenth day, namely at the full moon. Then the number of the elect will be full and complete; then the moon—that is, the triumphant Church—will be fully illuminated by the sun. [Col. 0210C] Then she will possess both sabbath rests; she who is now content with one single robe will then receive the second also.

For Septuagesima, which ends on Saturday in white garments, bears the type and figure of the present life. The present life, extending from the creation of the world to the day of the final judgment, proceeds through the recurrence of seven days and is distinguished into seven ages. Hence the Church sings a single *alleluia* near the end of Septuagesima, that is, on the Vigil of Easter and during the Easter days; but at the end, that is, on Saturday in white garments, she doubles it, to signify that those who now rejoice in one robe will triumph when they have received both. Truly they will triumph: for they will receive the diadem [Col. 0210D] of the heavenly kingdom; and those set over others will receive not only a golden crown but also an aureole. May the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit deign to grant this to us: God who lives and reigns for all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON V. ON THE GUARDIANSHIP OF THE CHURCH, TO PRIESTS IN SYNOD

“My peaceable one had a vineyard, which has peoples, and he entrusted it to guardians” (Song 8).

My brothers, whenever I recall that great men have said great things about the Peaceable One, I open my lips to speak of him, not presumptuously, indeed, but fearfully. Yet I beg from this source some strength and consolation, because you gladly endure foolish people, being yourselves wise (2 Cor. 11). I also remember what is written—and it is a pleasure to remember it: [p. 128] “Mountains and hills shall sing praises before God, and all the trees of the forest shall clap their hands” (Isa. 55). [Col. 0211A] Behold: from this universal joy neither the cedars of Lebanon nor the shrubs of the wilderness are excluded. I therefore, a humble shrub, a worthless little willow, propose to set before you a few matters drawn from the slenderness of my substance: briefly explaining what this Peaceable One is, what is called his vineyard and why; to which guardians he entrusted it, and what kind they ought to be.

This Peaceable One is the Word of the Father, eternally uttered from the Father’s heart, and he is truly peaceable. For he himself says of himself in the Gospel: “My peace I give unto you; my peace I leave unto you” (John 14). He is the one who reconciles the highest with the lowest. He is the one who joins together in himself, as the corner-stone, two walls coming from opposite directions. [Col. 0211B] He is the peace which surpasses all understanding (Phil. 4).

This vineyard is the Church, planted by him in a horn, in a fruitful place; he dug it with his own flesh, watered it with his own blood, and dug around it with the spiritual ploughshare. This is the vineyard whose fruit is gathered every day and yet is never exhausted. What more need be said? This is the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth—that is, of hosts—not of human beings only, but also of angels. But someone will say: “This figurative application is far-fetched.”

Nevertheless, the comparison of the Church with a vineyard is explicit. For it has its root in the angels, its trunk in the patriarchs, its vine in the prophets, its branches in the apostles, and its fruit in the *excussorum* [reading uncertain], that is, in the apostles’ children. [Col. 0211C] This same Church has its root in charity, its trunk in devotion, its vine in the love of neighbour, its branches in reverence for the clergy, and its fruit in blessedness.

Behold the root of the Church: charity, of which it is said, “A rod shall go forth from the root of Jesse” (Isa. 11)—that is, devotion from charity, which is aptly called the root of Jesse. For Jesse is interpreted “fire,” and charity is the fire of which Truth says in the Gospel: “I came to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I desire but that it should burn?” (Luke 12). And elsewhere: “The Lord lives, whose fire is in Zion and whose furnace is in Jerusalem” (Isa. 31). It should be noted that this root does not penetrate the inward parts of the earth, but rises toward heavenly things; just as the foundation of the Church is not laid beneath the other, lower parts, [Col. 0211D] but is raised aloft above all things.

We believe, moreover, that this happens sufficiently properly and carefully in the Church which has *populi* (“peoples”), not in that which has *gentes* (“nations”). For *gentes* are properly those who show themselves such as they were born, not distinguished from others by the mark of circumcision or baptism. A *populus*, on the other hand, is an aggregation of human beings who have come together into one place in order to live under law.

Behold, as we have said, how our Peaceable One has laboured in cultivating this vineyard: he transplanted its shoots from Egypt into the land of promise; then, with the greatest labour, he grafted the shoot of the wild olive upon the trunk of the olive tree. Thereupon he judged that it should be entrusted to faithful guardians. For the boar from the forest goes about it, to destroy it; [Col. 0212A] the solitary wild beast goes about it, to feed upon it (Ps. 80); and the lion also prowls about, seeking someone to devour (1 Pet. 5). Hence, even if it does not incorporate fruitful vines, it incorporates wild outer vines.

Foxes also destroy this vineyard, namely heretics, prefigured by Samson’s foxes. For the history of Judges relates that Samson, pursuing the Philistines (Judg. 15), sent foxes into their fields. Their heads were turned apart, but their tails were bound and joined together with burning torches, so that the fields might be burned. I judge it useful briefly to explain the figure of this event. Because of the people’s sins, the Lord often allows heretics to reign and to burn the harvest of the Church with the torches of false doctrines. These heretics are aptly represented by foxes: their heads are different, [Col. 0212B] but their tails joined together; for though they teach different things, they agree in error.

Guardians are therefore necessary. But who are they, and what ought they to be? They are the ministers of the altar, of whom the Bride says in the Song of Songs: “The guardians of the city found me” (Song 5); and elsewhere the Bridegroom says of the same: “Upon thy walls, O Jerusalem, I have set guardians” (Isa. 62). They are those of whom it is said: “Blow the trumpet in Zion; call the nations; announce to the peoples that our Lord will come,” etc. (Joel 2). Their character is made known to us in the Gospel when it says: “Who, thinkest thou, is the faithful and prudent servant whom the Lord set over his household, to give them food in due season?” (Luke 12). Behold, it is briefly shown that a minister of the altar ought to be faithful [p. 129] and prudent, a dispenser of heavenly nourishment [Col. 0212C] at the appropriate time.

But the minister of the altar may say: “I am faithful, for I know the articles of faith by heart and, by the seal of faith in the Lord’s cross, arm and mark myself against the various assaults of the devil.” But this is not enough. For if the minister of the altar defiles himself by lust, stuffs himself with food, becomes drunk with wine, whispers among the people, is a gambler, or becomes a usurer, I declare that such a person is not faithful. I fear that, when he approaches the altar, he may deserve to hear: “You grown old in evil days, what advantage is a whitened garment to you when the mind within is blackened with soot? What advantage is a broad tonsure to you, when your hand is clenched against your neighbour? Go backward. My soul does not care for new moons and Sabbaths. I will not take calves from thy house nor goats from thy flocks” (Ps. 50). [Col. 0212D]

Behold, this is the true Leviathan, entangled in knots. Therefore such a person should withhold his hand from the ministry or amend himself, unless he wishes to incur severe judgment. He must not only be faithful but also a prudent steward—truly prudent, so that he does not set every matter indiscriminately before his hearers, but preaches spiritual things to the spiritual, lesser things to the lesser and newly instructed. Thus the sun is for the day, the moon for the night; day pours forth speech to day, and night declares knowledge to night (Ps. 19). Let him follow the rule laid down by the Apostle for preaching and say: “We speak wisdom among the perfect; but I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Cor. 2).

Let him remember that in the tabernacle of the Lord there were bowls and cups upon the table of the offering: that preaching concerning divine matters might be figured in the cups, but preaching concerning things pertaining to Christ’s humanity in the bowls. [Col. 0213A] Therefore, whoever wishes to be a prudent steward should call to mind that Jacob saw a ladder, and angels ascending and descending upon it (Gen. 28), and should also consider the opportunity of the time. If he has hearers eager to bark back, slow and sluggish in yielding assent, let him judge within himself that the pearls of the divine word must not be laid before dogs. If he perceives that the minds of his hearers are not barren but suited to receive seed, let him preach and not delay to water the fertile plots with heavenly dew.

We believe this also pertains to the character of a guardian: that he should not be driven to preach by avarice, vain glory, or reckless talkativeness; that he should not thirst for shameful gain; that he should not think his knowledge to be nothing unless another knows that he knows it; that he should not consider it beautiful to be pointed out with the finger and called, “There he is!” Let him not produce disgust in his hearers by a torrent of verbosity. Let him remember that:

> “A word once sent forth flies onward, irrevocable.”

Let him watch attentively over the flock entrusted to him, so that, when another receives a hundred, he may receive two hundred talents; so that he may come bearing his sheaves with exultation; so that, crowned not only with a golden crown but also with an aureole, he may be able to triumph. May he who lives and reigns for all ages of ages deign to grant this to him. [Col. 0213C] Amen.

## SERMON VI. ON THE LOOSENING OF SINS AFTER CONFESSION

“Loose him, and let him go” (John 11).

“The Lord has spoken once, and two things have been heard.” These are the words of Truth to the apostles concerning the loosening of Lazarus, whom the Lord had raised, though four days dead and stinking, at the prayers of his sisters Martha and Mary; but because he was bound with bands, he could not go away. These same words may be those of the Mediator to the ministers of the Church. In his words there is nothing discordant, nothing idle; all are full of mysteries and fruitful. He speaks to ministers, not to just anyone, but to those established in the highest rank, namely that of the apostles. [Col. 0213D] For although someone raised to the priesthood stands there, he should not determine to remain there; rather, he should advance from virtue to virtue until he sees the God of gods in Zion (Ps. 84). For the kingdom is promised to those who watch, not to those who sleep, etc.

These may be called ministers for two reasons: first, because they minister to the supreme priest, [p. 130] of whom it is said: “Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 110). And elsewhere: “Behold the great priest” [Note: [Col. 0213D] Office of the Church], etc. And again: “Christ, standing forth as high priest of the good things to come,” etc. (Heb. 9). Second, because those of lower rank minister to them, namely deacons, subdeacons, and others.

This four-day-dead man [Col. 0214A] signifies a person entangled in grave sins and slain by a fourfold death. The first day of burial means the sin of thought; the second, the sin of perverse speech; the third, evil action; the fourth, the habit of sinning. The Lord raises such persons when, granting remission of sins, he pours in the dew of spiritual grace. He does this through the intervention of active and contemplative persons; and because it is difficult to leave habitual sins behind, we read that the Lord wept, groaned deeply, and cried aloud: “Lazarus, come forth” (John 11). For one firmly bound by the chains of sins is not easily loosed; and the person who sins through obstinacy and evil habit is bound more firmly than the person who sins through ignorance or some sudden temptation. [Col. 0214B]

But because inward resurrection is insufficient if confession is despised and outward loosening does not follow, the ministers are told: “Loose him.” For although the sinner has been raised inwardly by God through the resolve to turn back from sin, he still needs priestly absolution, so that he may be absolved not only from punishment but also, ordinarily, from guilt, and likewise from the sentence, when through anathema he has been banished outside the Church; thus he may be received into the bosom of the Church and be able to communicate with the faithful. But because the end, not the struggle, crowns, it adds: “Let him go”—that is, intercede for the perseverance of such persons. May he who lives and reigns for all ages of ages deign to grant this to us. [Col. 0214C] Amen.

## SERMON VII. ON THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

“Drop down dew, ye heavens, from above,” etc. (Isa. 45).

As the holy Fathers testify, Sacred Scripture tells us of a threefold advent of the heavenly King. The first advent is in charity, when Christ visits us by grace. The second was in the flesh, when he visited us in mercy. The third will be in charity, when he judges the world in glory. The first is one of loving-kindness; the second was one of humility; the third will be one of majesty. The first is so that a human being may judge himself; the second was so that God might be judged by a human being; the third will be so that God may judge the human being. Of the first it is said: “We will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14). Of the second it is said: “Drop down dew, ye heavens, from above,” etc. Of the third it follows: “The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of the earth” (Prov. 31). [Col. 0214D]

Since the name “heaven” is used in Sacred Scripture with various meanings, in this place it is understood as a sign of the three Persons. For the three Persons may be compared to the empyrean heaven. Just as the empyrean heaven has one property of fire—not destructive but soothing, illuminating but not consuming—so the three divine Persons, shining upon the faithful by grace, soothe them by the consolation of inward inspiration, not by punishment. They may also be compared to the starry heaven: just as various stars shine in the starry heaven, so in the three Persons, as in a starry heaven, manifold stars of wisdom and knowledge shine. They may likewise be compared to the aerial heaven: just as from the aerial heaven come frost and snow, rain and hail, refreshing dew and breezes, lightning and flashes, and an abundance of various things, so from the three Persons, as from aerial heavens, come snow and frost by God’s permission alone; hail and rain, flashing and lightning by God’s authority alone; dew and refreshing breeze by God’s mercy alone; and sufficiency of all things by God’s goodness alone. [Col. 0215A]

Moreover, the eternity of time which began with the world and will endure for ever bears a likeness to one great year. Then it was winter, from the beginning of the world to the time when the Law was given; in that time human [p. 131] hearts were constrained by various vices and frozen, as it were, with frost and snow. In it the north wind blew, because the devil bound the waters—or peoples, understood by “waters”—with the freezing cold of unbelief. But in the time of the Law, as in spring, hail came down through the threatening of punishments, and rain flowed forth with the promise of rewards. In spring the south wind blew, a warm and moist wind, because in the time of the Law there was warmth with moisture, when love adhered to the hearts of human beings together with the fluid love of earthly things. [Col. 0215B]

But in the time of grace, as in summer, the dew of heavenly grace distilled upon us, and the refreshing breeze of apostolic preaching sounded forth; indeed, flashes of lightning and threats still shine out and flash. In this season the west wind blows, when the grace of the Holy Spirit fills the Church—like a garden planted with various flowers—with various virtues. But in eternal life, as in autumn, there will be sufficiency of all things, when blessedness is perfect and Christ will be all things in all (1 Cor. 15).

In the aforesaid summer a threefold dew is poured into us, of which Sacred Scripture speaks. There is common dew, which descends upon the earth in the morning; there is dew appearing upon the surface of a field, which has the sweetness of honey; and there is heavenly dew, namely manna, which fed the Jews in the wilderness. By the first dew, which descends upon the earth in the morning, is understood the first grace, which came to us after the darkness of vices in the morning of faith; concerning it Scripture says: [Col. 0215C] “Like the dew of Hermon, which descends upon Mount Zion” (Ps. 133). For the dew of grace first descended upon Mount Zion—that is, upon the Jews—and afterward came to the Gentiles.

By the second dew, which bears the likeness of honey, is understood contemplation of divine things, in which the sweetness of love is given to a human being when that person is carried up to heavenly things. Of this dew it is written: “Mountains of Gilboa, let there be neither dew nor rain,” etc. (2 Sam. 1). For obstinate sinners, comparable to mountains on account of their pride, receive neither the rain of inward inspiration nor the dew of divine contemplation.

By the heavenly dew which fed the Jews on their wilderness journey is signified the Eucharist, by which the soul journeying in the wilderness of this life is fed. The first dew waters; the second delights; the third satisfies. The first purges sickness; [Col. 0216A] the second gives health; the third preserves the health given. The first prepares for health, the second effects it, the third perfects it.

Therefore the Fathers of the Old Testament, awaiting the second advent of Christ, asked for this heavenly dew and said: “Drop down dew, ye heavens, from above,” etc. As though they said: “Until now you have dropped dew downward, giving us earthly dew; until now you have given us temporal things, promised earthly things, and held back eternal things. But now, drop down dew, ye heavens, from above, giving us that food which is the bread of angels in heaven, manna for travellers in the wilderness of this life, liquid food for the sick but solid food for the healthy.” And thus let the clouds rain down the Just One.

There is a threefold cloud: the cloud of God’s mercy, the cloud of the Holy Spirit, and the cloud of Christ’s body. A cloud is usually formed when the sun draws waters upward, to temper them by its heat. [Col. 0216B] The Fathers of the Old Testament poured forth many waters of tears and prayers that the Son of God might come into the world. From these waters the Sun of Justice draws certain drops to himself, when, moved by their manifold prayer, he gave us the refreshing mercy that tempers the heat of his justice. For if he dealt with us according to justice, he would not send his Son to us, but would justly condemn us. He therefore placed between us the cloud of his mercy, to temper the heat of his justice.

The cloud is the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit, by which he gave the blessed Virgin refreshment against the incitement of vice; he gave her the overshadowing to endure the heat of divine majesty. The cloud is also the body of Christ, by which he gives us refreshment against the fires of vices and rains upon the hearts of the faithful. Of the first cloud it is said: “I saw in the vision of God, and behold, a great cloud and enfolding fire” (Ezek. 1). Of the second it is said: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon thee, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow thee” (Luke 1). [Col. 0216C] Of the third it is said: “The Lord shall ascend upon a light cloud and shall enter Egypt” (Isa. 19). The first tempers; the second flashes with miracles; the third shines with holiness. The first is placed between us and the heat of divine justice; the second between us and the heat of temptation; the third between us and the heat of vices. When we are rained upon inwardly by these three clouds, the earth is opened and the Saviour springs forth (Isa. 45).

There is likewise a threefold earth. The first is the land of the living, namely eternal life, of which it is written: “Not so [p. 132] the wicked, not so; but like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth” (Ps. 1). The second earth is Sacred Scripture, of which it is written that it was said to the first parent: “The earth shall bring forth thorns and thistles to thee” (Gen. 3). For Sacred Scripture does not bring forth for the unworthy the fruit of delight, but the thorns and thistles of error. The third earth is the Virgin Mary, of whom it is written: “Truth has sprung from the earth,” etc. (Ps. 85). [Col. 0216D] The first earth is that toward which we must journey; the second, that through which we must journey; the third, that beside which we must journey. The first is supercelestial; the second celestial; the third subcelestial.

The first earth was opened threefoldly at Christ’s birth: through the emptying of the Son of God, through the knowledge of Christ, and through his preaching. The second was likewise opened threefoldly: through the fulfilment of the promise, through the exposition of obscure things, and through the revelation of figures. But how was the third earth, that is, the Virgin Mary, opened? Certainly, she was closed in three ways and opened in three ways: closed by the seal of chastity, circumspection of mind, and mortification of the flesh; [Col. 0217A] but opened threefoldly by the love of charity, by the separation of flesh—which occurred solely through the operation of the Holy Spirit—and, as it were, by faith, when she believed those things which the angel foretold to her. Thus she was opened by the separation of flesh without losing the seal of virginity; opened by the enlargement of charity without losing circumspection of mind; opened by faith without losing mortification of flesh. And thus she brought forth the Saviour.

We must now see what the earth is, who the sower is, what the seed is, and what the shoot is. The earth is the Virgin Mary: unploughed earth, land of promise, land flowing with milk and honey. This is the earth which, unlike our weakness, did not produce fruit after being troubled by the rakes and hoes of desires, nor bring forth after being flooded by the waves of lust, but bore the Son through the dew of the Holy Spirit alone. [Col. 0217B] The seed was the Virgin’s flesh, separated from the rest of her flesh through the work of the Holy Spirit and formed into Christ’s body—if, indeed, that should be reckoned seed which was separated not by the itching of lust but by the refreshment of the Holy Spirit. The shoot was Christ’s body, which proceeded from the aforesaid flesh; and thus the Saviour sprang forth—that is, Christ, in whom is a threefold salvation, just as in bodily matters there is a threefold salvation: in the removal of sickness, the bestowal of health, and the preservation of health.

The first salvation for a human being is iron. Christ’s first advent took place for the remission of sin; the second occurs for the bestowal of righteousness; the third for its preservation. We, dearest brothers, having Christ’s advent in the flesh, should ask for his advent through charity, saying: “Drop down dew, ye heavens, from above,” etc., so that the heavens may rain upon the earth of our mind with divine dew.

The earth is customarily barren and unfruitful in three ways: when it is not cultivated with rakes and hoes, when it is ruined by excessive dryness, or when it is submerged by excessive flooding. So too the earth of our mind becomes barren [Col. 0217D] and unfruitful when we do not correct the dryness of desire by fasts, prayers, and vigils; when we do not temper it with the streams of charity; or when we do not restrain the streams of concupiscence through continence. Thus may the heavens deign to rain dew from above—that is, to pour the dew of heavenly grace into the earth of our mind—and thus may the clouds rain down the Just One, by suspending clouds above, that is, by directing our tears to heaven, so that our tears may be clouds against the burning heat of divine justice: that the heavens may not strike us with lightning in justice, but may water us in mercy; so that, through our tears as though through clouds, Christ may rain down within us, the earth may be opened, and the Saviour may spring forth.

Let the earth of our mind therefore be opened by confession of the mouth, [Col. 0218A] contrition of heart, and outward satisfaction; and thus let our earth bring forth the Saviour. As the blessed Virgin Mary conceived Christ materially, so may our mind conceive him spiritually; as she conceived through the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit, so may our mind conceive through inward inspiration; and as she conceived while remaining inviolate, so may our mind conceive while remaining unviolated. O happy mind of that soul which deserves, together with the Blessed Virgin Mary, to be the mother of Christ, in some measure following her footsteps from afar: so that, just as the Virgin conceived Christ through faith, the mind may conceive through faithfulness; just as she did in the flesh, so this mind may do in charity. May Jesus Christ himself, who lives, etc., deign to grant this to us. Amen.

### 133. SERMON VIII. ON THE HOLY DAY OF PENTECOST

*When the days of Pentecost were fulfilled*, etc. (Acts II.)

[Col. 0218B]

Just as the three Persons are distinct from one another, though they have one common essence, so three solemnities are celebrated in the year as pertaining to the three Persons: namely Christmas, Easter, and Pentecost. Yet there is one solemnity common to the three, called the feast of the Trinity, which is celebrated, that is, in the octave of Pentecost. For although the feast of Christmas is called the feast of the Son, it may nevertheless properly be called the feast of the Father also, because in that solemnity the eternal generation of the Father is treated. Hence it is said: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today [Col. 0218C] I have begotten you” (Ps. II). The Easter solemnity properly belongs to the Son, in which the resurrection of the Son is considered. Pentecost properly belongs to the Holy Spirit; but the solemnity held in the octave belongs to the whole Trinity.

Nor is it without a mystical reason that, when the days of Pentecost were fulfilled, the Holy Spirit descended upon the disciples. For the fact that the Holy Spirit was given to the Apostles after seven weeks signifies that, after the cycle of seven spiritual weeks, the Holy Spirit fully enters into the minds of the faithful. The first week is the absence of the seven deadly vices, which is the first stage in every justification. The second is the seven ways of remitting sin: through baptism, penance, martyrdom, charity, almsgiving, [Col. 0218D] forgiving resentment against one’s neighbour, and converting a brother to the faith. The third week consists of the seven petitions set forth in the Lord’s Prayer. The fourth is the bestowal of the seven gifts explained in Isaiah, where it is said: “The Spirit of wisdom,” etc. (Isa. XI). The fifth is the bestowal of the seven virtues: faith, hope, and charity, and the four cardinal virtues. The sixth is the bestowal of the seven beatitudes, set forth in Matthew, where it is said: “Blessed are the poor,” etc. (Matt. V). The seventh is the seven stages of ascent from virtue to virtue (Ps. LXXXIII), explained in that Psalm: “Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle?” etc. (Ps. XIV). After all these have been confirmed in a person, the Holy Spirit fully takes possession of that person.

Nor is it without mystical reason [Col. 0219A] that the solemnity continues for seven days; for the seven days signify the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which were then fully bestowed upon the Apostles. Therefore it is said: “When the days of Pentecost were fulfilled, they were all together.” Unity of place signifies the threefold unity of the mind: unity of faith, unity of hope, and unity of charity. These three make that threefold cord of which it is said: “A threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Eccl. IV). This is the cement with which Noah’s ark was coated, inside and out. These are the three unities which make, as it were, a created trinity in the Church: faith is as the Father, from whom hope is born as the Son; and from hope and faith comes charity, as the Holy Spirit. Whoever therefore sins against faith sins against the Father; whoever sins against hope sins against [Col. 0219B] the Son; whoever sins against charity sins against the Holy Spirit. Whoever sins against the Father is forgiven, because one who sins through unbelief often sins through ignorance. But whoever sins against the Son—that is, against hope—is forgiven, though not easily; but whoever sins against the Holy Spirit—that is, against charity—is not forgiven, because it is erased with still greater difficulty.

“And suddenly there came from heaven a sound” (Acts II), when they were all in one place. By the sudden sound heard when the Holy Spirit descended upon the Apostles, it was signified that there would be a twofold sound among the Apostles: the sound of preaching, whence: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth,” etc. (Rom. X); and the sound of penance and confession, whence: “I cried with my whole heart” (Ps. CXVIII). And there is the sound of jubilation, [Col. 0219C] whence: “Praise him with tuneful cymbals,” etc. (Ps. CL).
