Thus the Apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, preached, invited others to penance and confession, praised the Lord, and even contradicted evil people.

“Suddenly there came a sound.” The fact that the sound came suddenly signifies the sudden coming of the Holy Spirit; for he visits the mind in such a way that it is not known whence he comes or whither he goes: how he enlightens the sinner’s mind, justifies the penitent, and heaps grace upon one already justified. This sound came from heaven, not from earth. For there is a sound arising from earth, produced by the collision of solid bodies. There is a sound arising from water, produced by the clash of waves. There is a sound descending [Col. 0219D] from heaven, produced by the collision of clouds. By the first sound is understood the contradiction of people arising from love of earthly things; by the second, contradiction arising from carnal pleasures; by the third, preaching proceeding from clouds—that is, from preachers, who are compared to clouds because they rain down teachings, flash with miracles, and thunder with threats.

This sound came “as of a mighty rushing spirit” (Acts II). There is a twofold spirit: a spirit of fear and a spirit of swelling pride; a spirit of the sun and a spirit of the pole. The spirit of swelling pride is the devil, who breathes the swelling of pride; the spirit of fear is the Holy Spirit, who inspires fear and charity. The spirit of the sun is the devil, who invites us to the love of earthly things; [Col. 0220A] the spirit of the pole is the Holy Spirit, through whom we desire heavenly things and avoid earthly ones.

The Holy Spirit sometimes goes before us, sometimes comes to us, sometimes comes to our aid. He goes before us through the infusion of grace; he comes to us through the multiplication of virtues; he comes to our aid by strengthening us against tribulation. In going before, he is a physician, healing from sin; in coming, he is a Lord, enriching his servant; in coming to aid, he is a protector, fortifying one who is fighting. Hence he is aptly called *vehemens* (“mighty”), as though *vae demens* (“removing woe”); for he takes away the fourfold woe, that is, the fourfold punishment. For punishment may test, as in Job; purify, as in Paul; defile, as in the sinner entangled in offenses; or afflict, as in hell. Or he is called *vehemens*, as though “carrying one outside the mind,” [Col. 0220B] because he carries a person beyond the carnal mind to spiritual things.

“And it filled the whole house where they were sitting” (ibid.). The fact that the outward sound filled the house signified that the Holy Spirit was breathing within through the temple of the mind. Outwardly, the sound touched the ear; inwardly, the Holy Spirit soothed the mind. Nor is it without a mystery that the Apostles were sitting. Some lie prostrate; others sit; others stand erect. Those lie prostrate who indulge only in earthly things. Those sit who, although they direct their minds to heavenly things, nevertheless at times lower their minds to earthly things. Such were the Apostles while they had not yet been strengthened by the Holy Spirit. Those stand erect who contemplate only heavenly things; such the Apostles became after they had been strengthened by the Holy Spirit.

“And there appeared to them divided tongues, as of fire” (ibid.). One must not believe that actual tongues appeared above the Apostles’ heads; rather, [Col. 0220C] rays of fire in the likeness of tongues appeared. Nor is it irrational that the Holy Spirit is said to have appeared in the form of fiery tongues, since fire has two properties: a soothing one, in that through grace it makes the mind serene; and a burning one, in that it purges sins; a soothing one, in that it infuses the light of grace; and a destructive one, in that it consumes sins. Moreover, the fire bore the form of a tongue. The tongue is the instrument of speech; the tongue is the instrument by which flavours are distinguished; the tongue speaks on behalf of the other members when it sympathizes with them. For when the members are injured, [Col. 0220D] the tongue says: “You are injuring me.” Appropriately, then, the Holy Spirit appeared in fiery tongues: he gave the Apostles power to speak in diverse languages; he also bestowed on them the power of discerning good from evil; and he unites the members of the Church into one body, so that, suffering with another, one may say: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (II Cor. XI).

Let us therefore come together, dearest brethren, in the threefold unity of faith, hope, and charity, that we may thus deserve to receive the coming of the Holy Spirit; that the Holy Spirit may deign to visit the house of our mind, in which there ought to be three things: a bridal chamber, a council chamber, and an upper room. The upper room of God is love, in which the soul feasts; the bridal chamber is divine contemplation, in which [Col. 0221A] the soul delights with the bridegroom; the council chamber is discernment, in which good is separated from evil by the judgment of reason.

Let us therefore pray to the Holy Spirit that he may purify our senses, the upper room of charity, adorn the bridal chamber of divine contemplation with virtues, and clothe the throne of discernment with the gold of prudence. May Jesus Christ, our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, deign to grant this to us. Amen.

### 135. SERMON IX (Fragment). ON THE FEAST OF SAINT AUGUSTINE

“Blessed is the man who endures temptation, because, when he has been proved, he shall receive the crown of life,” etc. (James IV).

How glorious, dearest brethren, it is to overcome temptations, to endure the assaults of temptations, to confront temptations, since through the contest of temptations one comes to the prize of eternal life; since through the merit of earthly tribulation one comes to the reward of eternal [Col. 0222A] blessedness; since through enduring tribulation one comes to the crown of eternity. Temptation is threefold: human temptation, produced by the weakness of the flesh; diabolical temptation, arising from the devil’s suggestion; and divine temptation, proceeding from God’s authority. Of the first it is said: “Let no temptation overtake you except a human one” (I Cor. X). Of the second it is said: “And lead us not into temptation” (Matt. VI). Of the third is added: “God tested Abraham” (Gen. XXII). The first belongs to human frailty; the second to diabolical perversity; the third to divine authority. The first occurs to restrain pride; the second to destroy righteousness; the third to test patience. By the first Paul was buffeted (II Cor. XII); by the second Vincent was attacked; by the third Job was tested. [Col. 0222B] Human temptation is threefold: for at one time the flesh tempts through lust, at another time . . . [lacuna]

The remainder was absent from the Alne exemplar.

The following sermons are issued from a very ancient manuscript codex of the monastery of Blessed Mary of Dunes.

[Col. 0221]

### SERMON I. ON THE HOLY SPIRIT

“The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world, and that which contains all things has knowledge of speech” (Wis. I).

[Col. 0221C]

Although the world is filled by the whole Trinity, the Holy Spirit is nevertheless said to fill it in a special sense, because the name of goodness is appropriated to him, and a thing is preserved in its being through goodness. For although the whole Trinity creates, orders, and preserves, the Father is specially said to create; the Son to order or dispose; and the Holy Spirit to preserve things in their being. Therefore he is specially said to fill the world. The Holy Spirit, I say, fills all creatures with his essence; he fills them with sufficiency; he fills them with efficacy.

This is the Spirit of the Lord who, at the beginning of the world, moved [Col. 0221D] over the waters (Gen. I). This is the Spirit of the Lord who descended upon the Apostles as fire. He is aptly called, as it were, a mighty fire, *quasi aeternum vae demens*—“as though removing eternal woe” (Acts II). For he takes away three woes: the woe of guilt, the woe of punishment, and the woe of Gehenna. He also carries the mind to contemplation of heavenly things. Hence he is called *vehemens*, as though *mentem vehens*, “carrying the mind.” He is called the Spirit of the Lord both because he is Lord and because he proceeds from the Lord Father.

This Spirit, I say, fills the world. He fills inanimate things by preserving them in being; he fills animate but insensible things, such as plants, trees, and so forth, by supplying vegetative life; he fills irrational sentient things [136] by bestowing sensory power; he fills rational beings by conferring diverse gifts. Nature indeed—to speak so—produces everything, but perfects nothing; it brings forth but does not create, nor does it fill. To the Holy Spirit alone belongs the work of perfecting, creating, and filling.

The Holy Spirit filled the world—that is, the Church gathered in the upper room on [Col. 0222C] Mount Zion, awaiting his coming. He filled it with the fullness of virtues; he filled it with a diversity of languages, for the Apostles spoke in various tongues. He filled it with the fire of charity; he completed in them what had been begun and fulfilled what had been undertaken; he banished fear and increased charity. The Church is aptly called the world because it is both scattered throughout the whole world and gathered from different regions of the world. Hence it is said: “And that which contains all things has knowledge of speech” (Wis. I). That is, the Church, which contains some persons from every nation, contains all the gifts of the Holy Spirit. It has knowledge of speech, that is, it knows how to speak various languages.

Or, “that which contains all things” means the Holy Spirit, who contains all things by preserving them in being, who contains [Col. 0222D] all things by governing them, and who has knowledge of speech—that is, possesses every kind of knowledge expressed by speech. Or “the world” means the human being, who has some likeness with every creature: being with stones, life with trees and plants, sensation with beasts, and reason with spirits. On the day of Pentecost the Holy Spirit filled this human being when he gave him manifold knowledge, when he instructed him in every kind of language, when he strengthened him in faith, raised him in hope, and inflamed him with charity. Hence follows: “And that which contains all things,” that is, the human being, who has something in common with every creature—thus elsewhere “every creature” is said to mean a human being, where it says: “Preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark XVI), that is, to humankind—“has knowledge of speech,” as has been explained: that is, knowledge of speaking in various languages.

This filling was specially bestowed upon the Apostles on Pentecost, in fiery tongues (Acts II). The form of fire signified the ardour of charity, the brightness of knowledge, [Col. 0223A] and the consuming of ignorance. The form of the tongue signified diversity of speech. The tongue sympathizes with the other members, speaks for them all, distinguishes flavours, enables speech, and speaks on behalf of all the members. For if a foot is injured, the tongue says, “You are injuring me”; if a hand is injured, it cries in the same way; and so with the other members. Thus the form of the tongue that appeared over the Apostles represented in them the compassion of charity, so that they might know how to sympathize with the other members, saying: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (II Cor. XI). It represented in the Apostles the power of discernment, by which they might know how to distinguish wise people from foolish, cold from hot and lukewarm. It represented in them knowledge of speaking in diverse languages.

O human being, labour that [Col. 0223B] the Spirit of the Lord may fill you, so that he who made you by creating may restore you by re-creating; that he who, so to speak, made you through natural subsistence may fill you through the efficacy of grace; that he who finds you empty of good may fill you with a heavenly gift, so that you may not be an empty vessel but one full of heavenly liquid, and so that it may be said of you as of the city of God: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. XLV). May he contain in you all things sufficient for the merit of life, and thus may you have knowledge of speech—not that you may speak diverse languages, but that, according to your ability, you may give attention to Holy Scripture, which is customarily expressed by speech.

Knowledge of speech includes reading, prayer, preaching, and psalmody: so that, when the occasion demands it, you may devote yourself to reading, apply yourself to psalmody, give yourself to preaching, and not neglect reason.

### SERMON II. ON THE HOLY CROSS

“I will climb the palm tree and grasp its fruits” (Song VII).

The words of the Bridegroom in the Song of Songs, dearest brethren, lead us to understand the palm tree as the Lord’s cross for three reasons: its substance, its circumstances, and its efficacy. By reason of its substance, [Col. 0223C] because the gloss on the Song of Love states that palm wood was the material of the Lord’s cross. By reason of its circumstances, because the qualities found in the palm tree are mystically reflected in the Lord’s cross. The palm tree is formidable at its root, rough in its bark, upright in height, beautiful at its summit, and sweet in the savour of its fruit. So the Lord’s cross was formidable at its root, because it was initially detestable because of the ignominy of its punishment; rough in its bark, because of the pain; firm in its strength, because of patience; upright in its height, by reason of its end; beautiful at its summit, in view of the resurrection; and sweet in its fruit, in view of our redemption.

The Lord’s cross is also figured by the palm tree by reason of its efficacy, because just as the palm is the prize of victors, so Christ obtained triumph through the cross. This is Jacob’s ladder, reaching [Col. 0223D] to heaven (Gen. XXVIII); Moses’ serpent, devouring the serpents of the magicians (Exod. VII); the *tau*, defending the Hebrews from the destroying angel (Exod. XII); Moses’ rod, dividing the Red Sea (Exod. XIV) and governing [Col. 0224A] the Israelite people in the wilderness; the wood that turned bitter waters sweet (Exod. XV); the wood that drew abundant water from the rock (Num. XX). This is the wood upon which the bronze serpent was hung (Num. XXI); the pole upon which the heavenly cluster of grapes was carried. He saw, I say, Jacob’s ladder reaching from earth to heaven, upon which angels ascended and descended, and the Lord leaning upon the ladder (Gen. XXVIII). And of that ladder he prophetically declared: “How terrible is this place! Truly this is the house of God and the gate of heaven” (ibid.).

Truly, Christ’s cross is a ladder reaching from earth to heaven, because through faith in the cross and imitation of the Passion, a human being returns from exile to his homeland, from death to life, from earth to heaven, and from the wilderness of this world to paradise. Upon this ladder [Col. 0224B] angels—that is, Christ’s preachers—ascend and descend. They descend when they preach the weakness of the cross; they ascend when they preach God’s wisdom and power. For “what is foolish in Christ is wiser than human beings, and what is weak is stronger than powers” (I Cor. I). Christ leaned upon this ladder when he was fastened to the cross. This place is terrible because it presents a stumbling block to the Jew, horror to the devil, and fear to the Christian. This is Christ’s gate and the door of paradise.

This ladder had six steps by which Christ ascended: the first, mercy; the second, humility; the third, obedience; the fourth, punishment; the fifth, patience; the sixth, a most bitter death. In the Passion, I say, there was mercy, which drew the Son [Col. 0224C] of God down from heaven, enclosed him in the narrow womb of a woman, wrapped Christ in swaddling clothes, marked him with the sign of circumcision, subjected him to hunger, delivered him over to thirst and death, exposed him to suffering, punished him with the scourge, and fastened him to the gallows. This is the mercy that crowned the king with thorns so that it might crown the servant with glory. This is what bound the Lord in order to free the servant; what wounded the physician in order to heal the sick person; that through which the physician is made ill so that the sick person may be cured.

The second step was humility. For what humility is greater than for God to suffer, Life to die, a king to be exiled, one who is rich to beg, the maker to obey his work, and the Creator to be subjected to his creature? The third step was obedience. In Christ there was not only the first degree of obedience but also the last: not only its first line [Col. 0224D] but its farthest limit. For there are three degrees of obedience: the first is positive, to obey a superior; the second comparative, to obey an equal; the third superlative, to obey an inferior. Christ was obedient to the Father unto death (Phil. II); to his mother according to the lot of his human nature; to the flesh even unto fear; to sensuality even unto a will of compassion; to reason even unto the Passion; to death even unto the dissolution of soul and body; and to the law even unto fulfilling its precepts.

The fourth step was punishment. What punishment? An ignominious one. What punishment? A cursed one: the punishment of thieves, robbers, guilt, and disgrace. The fifth step was patience, surpassing every patience.

For just as manifold injury was inflicted upon Christ, so manifold was his patience against injury. He endured [Col. 0225A] injuries of intention, injuries of words, and injuries of deeds. The injuries of intention were manifold: some crucified Christ from ignorance, some from envy, some from pride, some from avarice. Yet against these injuries he gave no answer, but prayed for the sinners themselves, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke XXIV). He was likewise patient against the manifold injury of words: when they accused him, saying, “He is deserving of death” (Matt. XXVI); when they condemned him, saying, “Crucify him” (Luke XXIII); and when they mocked him, saying, “Ha! You who destroy the temple of God!” (Matt. XXVII). Against these injuries he was most patient, because he did not answer even a word; hence: “Like a sheep he was led to slaughter” [Col. 0225B] (Acts VIII).

He was patient against injuries of deeds, because, although he could have resisted through his divinity, he was patient through his humanity. For when they came to seize him, he went out to meet them; when they bound him, he did not resist; when they scourged him, he offered his back; when they struck him with their palms, he did not turn away his face; when they led him to crucifixion, he carried the cross; when they crucified him, he endured it patiently. O wondrous injuries! The disciple wrongs him in order to betray him; Pilate, in order to sentence him to death; the Jew, in order to condemn him; Peter, in order to deny him; his kinsman, in order to flee; the Gentile, in order to crucify him. On the other hand, Christ gave a kiss to the disciple, spoke humbly to Pilate, answered the Jews patiently, looked upon Peter, consoled the fleeing disciple, and endured the insults of those who crucified him.

The final step [Col. 0225C] in the Passion was death: an admirable death, a death that slays death itself, gives life, weakens death’s sting, overcomes the devil, and uproots sin. By these steps of the ladder Christ ascended to heaven. Christ’s ascent was threefold. First, he ascended in order to suffer; second, he ascended in order to rise again; third, he ascended in order to be glorified at the Father’s right hand. In the first ascent he ascended to death; in the second, to immortality; in the third, to majesty.

He therefore climbed this palm tree and grasped its fruits. Its leaves were the words Christ spoke in his Passion; its flowers, the example of patience; its fruit, the glory of eternal blessedness. The tree of this palm was planted from the origin of the world, [Col. 0225D] when he marked the wood in order to undo the harms caused by wood; it was rooted at the time of the Incarnation; green in Christ’s insults; leafy in his words; flowering in the example of patience; blossoming among the obstinate Jews; blooming again among the converted Gentiles; and bearing fruit among the redeemed.

Let us therefore, dearest brethren, climb this palm tree, that we may grasp its fruits. The palm is indeed bitter at its root but sweet in the savour of its fruit. Let us therefore suffer with Christ, that we may be glorified. For one who abhors the bitterness of the root will not taste the sweetness of its fruit. Let us therefore ascend the threefold cross: the cross of penance, that we may be freed from sin; the cross of compassion, that we may reign with our neighbour; and the cross of suffering, that we may be glorified with Christ.

The cross of penance has four [Col. 0226A] dimensions: height, breadth, length, and depth. The dimension of height is that by which one is raised to God; the dimension of breadth is that by which punishment is extended to one’s neighbour; the dimension of length is perseverance, by which it is extended unto death; the dimension of depth is satisfaction with regard to oneself. The cross of compassion has the dimension of height, love of God; the dimension of breadth, love of neighbour; the dimension of length, the continuance of charity; and the dimension of depth, by which a person loves himself. The cross of patience has the dimension of height, the loftiness of hope; the dimension of breadth, greatness of fortitude; the dimension of length, long-suffering; and the dimension of depth, purity of conscience.

On this manifold cross the faithful person stretches out his hands and treads with his feet, by making satisfaction, by compassionating, and by suffering. On the cross of penance was crucified the thief who repented on the cross; on the cross of compassion, the Blessed Virgin who shared Christ’s Passion. Hence it is said of her: “And a sword shall pierce your own soul also” (Luke II). On the cross of patience was Christ, who was patient [Col. 0226B] even unto death. In imitation of Christ, let us ascend to heaven through the aforesaid steps of the cross.

Let mercy be in us, as we show compassion to the wretched, support the weak, give alms, instruct the less learned, visit prisoners, and clothe the naked. Let humility be in us in dress, gesture, food, speech, and mind. Let obedience be in us, so that we obey our prelates in counsel, command, acceptance of penance, and its execution. Let punishment be in us through satisfaction; let patience be in us through steadfastness of mind. Let death be in us through chastisement of the flesh and the diminution of concupiscence, so that we may rise from vices to virtues, from guilt to glory, and from death to life, through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

### SERMON III. ON SAINT NICHOLAS, BISHOP AND CONFESSOR

“For you are he who drew me out of the womb; my hope from my mother’s breasts; on you I was cast from the womb” (Ps. XXI).

[Col. 0226D]

The faithful have a threefold mother: a natural mother, a carnal mother, and a spiritual mother. The natural mother is the woman who gives birth; the carnal mother is concupiscence, through which a person degenerates; the spiritual mother is that which regenerates the one born. From the natural mother one draws flesh; from the carnal mother, carnality; from the spiritual mother, the life-giving spirit.

Among the faithful, one was conceived without concupiscence, born without concupiscence, lived without concupiscence, and completed the course of life without concupiscence: Christ. Another was conceived in concupiscence yet born without concupiscence, as the prophet Jeremiah, John the Baptist, and perhaps anyone else sanctified in the womb.

[Col. 0227A]

But although the glorious Nicholas was conceived in concupiscence and born in concupiscence, nevertheless from his birth Mother Grace received him and, until the end of his life, shut up within him the streams of concupiscence. But we wretches are conceived in concupiscence, born in concupiscence, live in concupiscence, and die in concupiscence. O how unlike our birth is to the birth of the glorious confessor! O how unlike our origin to his beginning! From birth Mother Grace received Nicholas to give life; from birth Mother Concupiscence led our beginning toward death. Experiencing this grace in himself and reading this mercy in the book of experience, the glorious confessor could cry: “O fountain of mercies! O fullness of compassion! O height [Col. 0227B] of grace! O greatness of the treasury of wisdom! In myself I have experienced the greatness of your mercy, the depth of your grace, the treasury of your wisdom. For you drew me out of my mother’s womb.”

Just as there is a threefold mother, so there is a threefold womb. The womb of the first mother is the seal of conception; the womb of the second mother is the abundance of concupiscibility; the womb of the third mother is the depth of divine compassion. From the womb of the first mother you drew me, that I might live; from the womb of the second mother, that I might not live wickedly; from the womb of the third mother, that I might live well. From the womb of the first mother you brought me to the birth of nature; from the womb of the second, to the birth of grace; from the womb of the third, to the birth of glory. Therefore you are my hope from my mother’s breasts.

[Col. 0227C]

Just as mothers differ, so breasts differ. The breasts of the first mother are breasts of milk; the breasts of the second mother are breasts of gall; the breasts of the third mother are breasts of honey. The breasts of the first mother nourish children; the breasts of the second mother kill little ones; the breasts of the third mother strengthen adults. Of the breasts of concupiscence it is said: “The sea-monsters have laid bare their breasts; they have nursed their young” (Lam. IV). Concupiscence has two breasts, gluttony and lust; by these children in sense-perception and little ones in understanding are nursed—or rather made drunk. For who, if not fools, are made drunk by lust and nursed on incontinence? Who, if not fools, are submerged in the flood of gluttony and killed by the poison of drunken feasting? The breasts of the third mother are the grace of justification and glory, or the grace [Col. 0227D] of glorification. Of these John said: “Receiving grace for grace” (John XVI). Of these breasts also it is said in the Song of Love: “Your breasts are sweeter than wine” (Song I). Wine signifies earthly delight, which, although it presents sweetness on the surface, nevertheless brings drunkenness to the mind. But divine grace is sweeter than every earthly delight, and so intoxicates the righteous that it makes them sober.

[Col. 0228A]

The glorious confessor Nicholas therefore placed his hope in Christ from his mother’s breast. While as a little child he drew milk, he abstained as an adult. While he hung from his mother’s breast, he aspired to the Father’s table. In the cradle he prophesied what he would be in heaven; in liquid food he prophesied what he would do with solid food. Abstaining from the infant’s breast, he passed beyond the bounds of infancy: a child in age, an old man in deed. He lived well before he knew how to live, for he fasted before he knew how to eat. Not yet speaking, he prophesied by deed; untaught by another, he taught others. Let the old man therefore be ashamed to break the fasts which Nicholas observed in the tenderness of his age; let the grown man be ashamed to dissolve into lasciviousness, which this infant restrained.

By abstaining from [Col. 0228B] the breast of flesh, he represented that he would abstain from the breast of carnality. By scorning the breasts of nature, he represented that he would aspire to the breasts of grace. Abstaining, therefore, from the breasts of concupiscence, he placed his hope in Christ because, from his earliest age, by rejecting lust and avoiding gluttony, he fixed the anchor of hope in God. From the breasts of Mother Grace he directed his whole mind toward Christ, because, from the time Mother Grace received him, he established in God the purpose of his intention. Thus he was cast upon him from the womb, because from his earliest age, lest he perish in the shipwreck of concupiscence, he was made firm in Christ as in a harbour of salvation.

This is Nicholas who relieved the poverty of an indigent father from his own abundance; who through his mercy rescued girls from the misery of public prostitution; who was [Col. 0228C] chosen by the proclamation of a divine voice; who raised a dead person at a crossroads; who was proved by the increase of grain; who saved sailors from shipwreck; who restored a son to his father; who freed three youths from the danger of death; and from whose tomb an anointing of oil flows. Let us therefore, in imitation of him, enrich with the treasure of good works the three daughters of our spirit—that is, the three powers given from the origin of the soul—lest they commit fornication with the seductions of the world. Let us be raised through the admonition of Holy Scripture to mastery over our thoughts. Let us raise our spirit from the death of sin. Let the bread that came down from heaven increase within us through faith—the bread which, being the grain of angels, became the grass of human beings. Let us rescue spiritual sailors—that is, the virtues which ought to be [Col. 0228D] the rulers of the soul—lest they suffer shipwreck in the whirlpool of vices. Let us restore the son—that is, the spirit—to the Father, the Creator. Let us preserve the youths—that is, wanton thoughts—lest they proceed unto the death of sin. Let us draw forth from our mind the anointing of holy charity; through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0229]

## BOOK OF SENTENCES AND MEMORABLE SAYINGS OF MASTER ALAN OF LILLE

Most useful for preachers and, in general, for all devoted students of divine love;

now for the first time brought to light from an ancient manuscript codex of the library of Dunes.

[Col. 0229A] 141

1. At Christ’s Nativity, two suns appeared at Rome; from those two there came to be one sun: signifying that the sun of human nature and the sun of divine nature were united in the unity of one person.

2. Jerome, in the *Annals of the Hebrews*, says that he found signs for the fifteen days before judgment. But he did not state whether they are to occur continuously or at intervals. On the first day the sea will rise forty cubits above the height of the mountains, standing in its place like a wall. On the second it will sink so low that it can scarcely be seen. On the third sea-monsters will appear above the sea and give roars reaching to heaven. On the fourth the sea will burn. On the fifth plants and trees will yield a bloody dew. On the sixth buildings will collapse. On the seventh rocks will strike against one another. [Col. 0229B] On the eighth there will be a general earthquake. On the ninth the earth will be levelled. On the tenth people will come out of the caverns of the earth and walk like madmen, unable to speak with one another. On the eleventh the bones of the dead will rise and stand above their graves. On the twelfth the stars will fall. On the thirteenth the living will die, so that they may rise with the dead. On the fourteenth heaven and earth will burn. On the fifteenth there will be a new heaven and a new earth, and all will rise again.

3. O man, what courage will you have when the angels tremble? What will the little rod of the wilderness do when the cedar of paradise is shaken? All things will rise against you. God the Trinity will judge you by authority; Christ the man will judge you by carrying out judgment; the angels will judge you by approving the sentence; the saints will judge you [Col. 0229C] by their deeds; conscience will judge you by revealing your sins; the devil will judge you by accusation. Gehenna will judge you by condemnation—unless you judge yourself in the present.

4. “You who sit upon the cherubim,” etc. (4 Kings 19). “Cherubim” means a heavenly order; it also means fullness of knowledge and perfection of charity. God sits above the first cherub, that is, above the angelic order, by its subjection, because that order is subject to him, to serve and obey him and to carry out his ministries. [Col. 0230A] He sits above the second cherub, that is, above the fullness of knowledge, by incomprehensibility, because every fullness of knowledge fails to comprehend him. He sits above the third cherub by surpassing charity, because God’s charity exceeds every charity.

The first cherub has two wings: subtlety of nature and keenness of intellect; by these two wings, as it were, it flies to comprehend mysteries. The second cherub has two wings, namely the two Testaments, by which it veils divine mysteries. To signify this, the cherub in the tabernacle covered the mercy-seat with two wings; for beneath the two Testaments, as beneath the cherub’s wings, the secret of the divine majesty lies hidden.

[Col. 0230B] The third cherub, that is, charity, is distinguished by two wings: love of God and love of neighbour. One rises to love God; the other descends to love one’s neighbour. With these two wings the cherub covers the mercy-seat, because the whole propitiation of divine mercy is fulfilled in the commandment of charity. These two cherubim, with faces turned toward the mercy-seat, look upon one another, because fullness of knowledge and perfection of charity tend toward the propitiation of the divine majesty; and they turn their own faces back upon themselves, because neither is knowledge perfected without charity nor charity brought to completion without knowledge. Hence it is said: “As much as you love, so much you know.”

5. “Stir up your power and come” (Psalm 79). That is, send your Son into flesh—that is, come into [Col. 0230C] the world through the incarnation of the Son. The Son is said to sleep in three ways and to be awakened in three ways. Before the incarnation, the Son slept in the bosom of the Father, where sleep was eternal rest. The Father awakened the Son from this sleep of rest when he sent him into flesh, so that he might watch over the advancement of humankind. Before the incarnation he also seemed to sleep in human hearts because of the lukewarmness of faith.

The Son of God is also said to have slept in death. There death was sleep, and resurrection awakening. Likewise, in the condition [Col. 0231A] of the present life, when God allows the wicked to flourish in temporal things and the good to flourish, the faithful people cry to the Father: “O Father, stir up your power and come.” As though saying: “Your Son now seems to sleep, since he does not render rewards to the righteous and punishments to the unrighteous; awaken your Son to judge, and come in Christ to judgment.”

6. “Give ear, O ruler of Israel” (Psalm 79). That is, you who rule the faithful people, who spiritually see God: preserving them in being, justifying them in grace, and glorifying them in glory. “Give ear” means: send the Son.

“You who lead Joseph like a sheep” (ibid.). Joseph, whose name is interpreted “increased,” prefigured Christ. Joseph increased joy for his mother by being born; for Egypt by his counsel; [Col. 0231B] for his brothers by freeing them from famine; and for his father by presenting himself bodily before him. So Christ increased joy for the Virgin Mother by his generation; for the Church by regeneration; for sinners by giving counsels of life; and for the Father by presenting the signs of victory. Hence he himself was like a heavenly Augustus. For just as the earthly Augustus enlarged the commonwealth of the world, so Christ enlarged the commonwealth of heaven.

Therefore the Lord Father led this Joseph, that is, Christ, like a sheep, because like a sheep he was offered to the Father for slaughter, led without complaint. A little sheep recognizes its mother’s bleating in the flock; Christ recognized his Father by obedience, his mother by care—because he entrusted her to John—and his disciples by love—because he prayed for them. Thus Christ is also called the Lamb (*Agnus*) from *agnosco, agnoscis*, “I recognize, you recognize.” Accordingly, in the Mass the address is made to him under the name of the heavenly Lamb, with this meaning: “Lamb of God, you who recognized the Father by obedience, have mercy on us; Lamb of God, you who recognized your own by love, grant us peace.”

7. “The Lord is near” (Philippians 4): he is near to everyone, to free them from evil and preserve them in good. Death threatens sufficiently near at hand; the Lord is near to humankind because the day of judgment approaches, and therefore “be anxious about nothing” (ibid.).

There is anxiety arising from necessity, and there is anxiety arising from curiosity. The Lord does not forbid the anxiety necessary for need, but that which concerns superfluity, lest anxiety about earthly things be preferred [Col. 0231D] to anxiety about eternal things. Concern for nature is allowed, but concern for luxury and avarice is forbidden. Hence the Gospel says: “Do not be anxious about tomorrow” (Matthew 6), that is, about the future. This prohibition of anxiety applies especially to those who have recurring income, because an income ought to exclude excessive anxiety. Concern for obtaining provisions up to a year is allowed, but it is not permissible to extend it to the end of the year, because in the following year provisions return through nature’s providence.

It follows: “But in every prayer and expectation” (Philippians 4). Here it is suggested that, if eternal things are sought, earthly things will be added. Hence it was said: “Seek first the kingdom of God,” etc. (Matthew 6). It is suggested that excessive anxiety concerning temporal things should therefore cease, [Col. 0232A] because the petition for eternal things includes temporal things. Yet a faithful person may lawfully ask for earthly things, not so that the end may be established in them, but so that the petition may be directed toward the highest end, namely God. Earthly things should be sought so that the human mind may not be distracted by anxious care for them, but may serve the Lord freely.

How our petitions become known to God—that is, become pleasing to divine mercy—he shows when he says: “In prayer and expectation” (Philippians 4). Two things ought to shape a petition: prayer and expectation, because prayer without perseverance does not attain its effect. God’s “knowing” a prayer is nothing other than his approval of it. Thus the Lord, speaking to the wicked, says: “I do not know you” (Matthew 25), that is, “I do not approve you.”

[Col. 0232B] 8. Sometimes we pray verbally for something good, but we do not direct our mind to it, but to some other good. For example, someone may ask God to preserve him in good things, while meanwhile thinking of giving alms generously to a poor person. This prayer is good but in a sense disordered, because the voice sometimes disagrees with the mind; and here venial sin intrudes when this happens through negligence. Against this the Lord says: “When you pray, enter into your chamber, and, having shut the door, pray to your Father in secret,” etc. (Matthew 6). As though saying: “When you pray with your voice, direct your mind to that for which you pray.”

Sometimes we pray verbally for something good, yet direct our mind to another evil; and to pray thus is a mortal sin. Hence it is said: “This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matthew 15; [Col. 0232C] Mark 7). Sometimes someone prays for evil with an evil mind, and that is worst of all. Sometimes one prays for good, and rightly, and holds in one’s heart what one says; this is best of all.

## ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

9. “For Zion’s sake I shall not be silent, and for Jerusalem’s sake I shall not rest, until her righteous one goes forth as brightness and her Saviour is kindled as a lamp” (Isaiah 62).

Isaiah speaks as though saying: “For Zion’s sake”—that is, so that the Church from the Jews may understand the coming of the Saviour—“and for Jerusalem’s sake I shall not rest”—that is, so that the Church from the Gentiles may acknowledge the coming of its Redeemer—I shall not be silent from preaching the Word of God; I shall not rest [Col. 0232D] from the office of preaching, until her righteous one goes forth as brightness, that is, until through my prophecy Christ’s coming becomes known to humankind.

Christ is called, by antonomasia, the Righteous One of the Church, because according to his divine nature he is justice itself; according to his human nature he is filled with the consummate fullness of justice; and from him proceeds the justice of the whole Church. He is said to go forth as brightness according to both natures. In his divine nature he goes forth from the Father as brightness from fire: for just as brightness is coeval with fire, so the Son is coeternal with the Father; and as knowledge of fire is gained through brightness, so knowledge of the Father is effected through the Son. As brightness proceeds from fire without any alteration of the fire, so the Son proceeds from the Father without any alteration of the Father.

[Col. 0233A] He also went forth according to his human nature, as brightness into the Virgin’s womb; for as brightness proceeding from the sun enters a glass window, illuminates it, and in no way breaks or violates it, so the brightness of the heavenly sun entered the Virgin’s womb, illumined her by the grace of the Holy Spirit, and in no way broke or violated the seal of virginity. He also goes forth from the Father as brightness into the mind of the human soul when he removes from it the darkness of vices and illumines it with the brightness of heavenly grace.

It follows: “And her Saviour shall be kindled as a lamp.” The lamp figures human nature. A lamp does not emit light from itself; likewise human nature has no brightness of grace from itself. Yet from the meeting of oil and flame the lamp is flooded with light. [Col. 0233B] Before Christ’s coming human nature was a lamp without light. But this lamp was kindled when Christ assumed humanity, and then the oil of divine grace was poured into the lamp, that is, into human nature, and the flame of divine nature shone within it. Therefore the Saviour was kindled as a lamp when he flooded human nature in himself with the oil of divine nature and the flame of divinity was kindled; thus, in the night of this world, he gave light to minds.

“And the nations shall see your righteous one,” etc. (Isaiah 62): some with material sight in the flesh, others with mental sight in the Godhead. “And all kings your glory”: those kings, I mean, who judge the earth, that is, who condemn earthliness in themselves. “Your glory”: Christ is called glorious, that is, exceedingly glorious. “And you shall be called [Col. 0233C] by a new name, which the mouth of the Lord has named” (ibid.). By Christ’s coming the Church’s name was changed, because she who was formerly called barren and was not named mother of many, and who was formerly said not to have received mercy, is now said to have received mercy. This was signified by the change of Sarah’s name: she was formerly called Sarai, but afterwards Sarah (Genesis 17).

“And you shall be a crown of glory in the hand of the Lord, and a royal diadem in the hand of your God” (Isaiah 62). We read of a manifold diadem. Christ’s human nature is called his diadem. A diadem lacks beginning and end because it is circular in shape. Hence *diadema* is said as though “two lacking,” namely beginning and end. A diadem shades the head and signifies kingship. Gold provides the material of the diadem. Now concupiscence is the beginning of our human nature, and death without return its end; but Christ’s human nature lacked this beginning and this end, because concupiscence did not conceive him, but charity begot him; and although life departed for a time from Christ’s human nature, it returned to it more quickly.

[Col. 0233D] This crown crowned Christ’s head, because the sun of deity lay hidden beneath the shadow of humanity. It was a sign of kingship because, in assuming humanity in its more excellent kind, in which was fullness of graces, he signified that he would be king of humankind. This crown was made of gold because it proceeded from a purer condition of human nature.

Of this diadem it is said to the daughters of Zion, that is, to faithful souls: “Go forth, daughters of Zion, in mind, and see, by faith and devotion, King Solomon,” that is, the peaceful Ecclesiastes, namely Christ, “in the diadem,” that is, in human nature, “with which his mother,” that is, the Virgin Mary, “crowned him, on the day of his espousal and on the day of the joy of his heart” (Song of Songs 3). For on the day when he entered the bridal chamber of the virginal womb, he espoused a virgin to himself and endowed her with spiritual joy of mind.

The second diadem of Christ is the ordered succession of the faithful, of which it is said: “Like an army arrayed in order” (Song of Songs 6). In a crown, certain things are arranged in proper order; a crown is adorned with stones; a crown contributes to a people’s honour. So, in the assembly of the faithful, the saints are arranged in proper order; [Col. 0234B] the assembly of the faithful is adorned with saints as with precious stones; and it contributes to Christ’s honour, because in a sense the life of the faithful adorns Christ. This diadem lacks beginning and end because it excludes from itself the beginning of misery, namely sin, and the end, namely Gehenna. Of this crown it is said: “You have set, O Lord, upon his head a crown of precious stone” (Psalm 20). This is said of the Church: “And you shall be a crown of glory in the hand of your God.” His mother, that is, the Church, crowned him with this diadem.

The third crown was of thorns, with which his mother, that is, Judaea, crowned him. Of it it is said: “And plaiting, they put upon him a crown of thorns” (John 19). The fourth crown is of glory and immortality, of which it has been said: “You crowned him, O Lord, with glory and honour” (Psalm 8).

## ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD AGAIN

[Col. 0234C]

10. “The people of the Gentiles who walked in darkness saw a great light” (Isaiah 9). Before Christ’s coming the Jew walked in the darkness of ignorance, the Gentile in that of sin, and the faithful after death in the darkness of punishment. The Jew walked amid uncertainty, the Gentile on slippery ground, and the faithful after death sat in obscurity. But the people who walked in darkness saw a great light: Christ, who is “the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1). The Jew saw this light in the flesh, the Gentile in faith, and the faithful after death in blessed expectation. This light came into the world so that the Gentile might believe and so that it might free the faithful from death.

Accordingly, the Jew saw a small light of this light in the understanding of the Law; the Gentile saw a small light in rational inquiry; the faithful after death saw a small light in the bosom of rest. The Jew saw a small light in the seal of the Law; the Gentile in the mirror of creation; the faithful after death in refreshment.

[Col. 0234D] “But to those sitting in the region of the shadow of death, a light has risen” (Isaiah 9). There is a threefold death, a threefold shadow, and a threefold region. Bodily or natural death is the separation of body and soul. The second death is death of the soul, namely its separation from God. The third is Gehenna. The shadow of the first death is infirmity, because as the image of a thing appears in a shadow, so natural infirmity is the likeness of death. The shadow of the second death is sin, because in mortal sin the soul is separated from God; and just as one comes from image to thing, from shadow to truth, so through sin one comes to death. But the darkness in which the faithful, existing in Abraham’s bosom, were after death was like the shadow of eternal death, because the darkness in which they were there signifies that into which the damned will be plunged.

[Col. 0235A] The region of the shadow of the first death is the world; the region of the shadow of the second death is the assembly of the wicked; the region of the shadow of the third death is Abraham’s bosom. Therefore, both for Jews and Gentiles lying numbed by the torpor of vices in the region of the shadow of the first death—that is, living in the world—and in the region of the shadow of the second death—that is, languishing in the assembly of the wicked—a light rose, namely Christ through the incarnation, that he might illuminate both to understand and shine upon both to believe. For those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death, that is, for the saints resting in Abraham’s bosom, the Sun of Justice rose, both to free them from the darkness of hell and to flood them with eternal light.

Nor is this surprising: “For a little child has been born to us, and a Son has been given to us” (Isaiah 9): little in age, greatest in majesty. He appears to us in the world so that we may appear before him in heaven.

“And therefore dominion is upon his shoulder” (ibid.). The cross which Christ bore on his shoulders is fittingly called dominion, because through it he triumphed over the devil, lest he stretch out the hand of his power against us; over the world, lest it approach us by love; over sin, lest it reign in us; over death, lest it remain; and over the old man, lest he rise up.

[Col. 0235C] “And his name shall be called Wonderful” (ibid.). O how fitting is this naming! Christ is wonderful in the nature which lacks a beginning in begetting, because he was begotten from eternity; wonderful in his mother’s conception, in his birth, in death, and in resurrection. He is also found wonderful in counsel, whence he is called “Counsellor” (ibid.). For by the deep counsel of God it was ordained that, as sin entered through a human being, so grace should return through a human being; that, as transgression came first through wood, so redemption should likewise be celebrated through wood; and that, as Christ’s passion was for the Jews “an odour of death unto death,” so it should be for the Gentiles “an odour of life unto life” (2 Corinthians 2).

He also brought a manifold counsel of salvation: he wrote for human beings the natural law in the heart, the Mosaic law in a book, and the law of the Gospel—that is, the law of patience—in flesh. [Col. 0235D] And because he is so wonderful and so great a counsellor, therefore he is God. Here Christ’s two natures are expressed: the human, when it is said, “A little child has been born to us”; the divine, when “God” is added. And what God? “Father of the age to come.”

11. By Christ’s circumcision in the flesh on the eighth day, it was figured that on the eighth day of resurrection he was to be circumcised from the passibility of flesh; and that his body, namely the faithful people, in the eighth age was to be circumcised from the penal condition of body and soul. Nor was there in Christ only perfect and complete circumcision—that is, circumcision circumcised—but also circumcision that circumcises. For he circumcised his mother’s conception from sin; birth from punishment; water, through baptism, [Col. 0236A] from inability to sanctify; the cross from ignominy; the tomb from corruption of the corpse; and flesh from the bond of death—not because he needed it, but to remove our need.

12. It is not without mystery that Christ was circumcised as a child. For this signifies that we, children not in age but in purity, ought to circumcise ourselves from childishness; or that from our earliest age we ought to circumcise ourselves from vices.

13. Some prophets were prophets in word, others in deed. An angel was such in word when he said: “You shall call his name Jesus” (Luke 1). Joseph was such in deed, because by becoming the saviour of Egypt through saving it from famine, he signified that Christ would be the Saviour of the world by freeing it from spiritual hunger.

[Col. 0236B] 14. The three kings offering gifts signify the three potential powers of the soul. They are fittingly called kings because they rule the soul; they are reason, intellect, and intelligence. They journey from the east because they pass into the soul’s endowments from the heavenly east, that is, from God.

By myrrh, which is applied to dead corpses, history is signified, because it is concerned with perishable and transitory things. Reason offers this, because its consideration is concerned with historical matters. By incense, tropology or morality is signified; it gives forth the fragrance of sweetness. Intellect offers this, because its contemplation is concerned with its forms.

By gold anagogy is signified, that is, consideration of heavenly things, because as gold retains precedence among metals, so anagogy retains primacy among modes of understanding. Hence *anagoge* means, as it were, “leading upward.” The higher power of the soul, namely intelligence, offers this, for it alone contemplates divine things.

[Col. 0236C] 15. “Behold, I send my angel, who will prepare the way before your face” (Malachi 3; Matthew 11). The Son of God is called the brightness and form of the Father’s substance (Hebrews 1), and therefore is called the face, because as a person’s will is perceived in the face, so the Father’s will is known through the Son. The Father’s face is manifold. His only offspring is called his face; hence it is said: “Behold, I send my angel before your face.” Mercy is called a face; hence: “Do not turn away your face from me” (Psalm 68). Presence is called a face; hence: “They shall be weakened and perish before your face” (Psalm 9). Manifest knowledge is called a face; hence: “We shall see God face to face, as he is” (1 Corinthians 13).

[Col. 0236D] 16. God’s temple is fourfold. In each, the Son was offered to God the Father. Human nature is God’s temple, of which it is said: “Destroy this temple, and after three days,” etc. (John 2). The material temple is also called God’s temple, of which it is said: “And he came in the Spirit into the temple” (Luke 2). The present Church is also called a temple: “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Corinthians 3). Eternal life is called a temple; hence: “I shall worship toward your holy temple in your fear” (Psalm 5). Christ came to the first temple through the incarnation; to the second according to the custom of the Law; to the third through the visitation of the human [Col. 0237A] race; and to the fourth through the ascension.

17. A threefold coming of Christ is read of: first, into flesh through mercy; second, into the human mind through grace; third, to judgment through glory. “Who can conceive the day of his first coming?” (Malachi 3). Who can comprehend the day or hour, the manner or form of his coming? How could the heavenly be united to the earthly, the invisible to the visible, the non-local to the local, by an ineffable union? Who also can conceive the day of the other coming, when the Holy Spirit enters the soul through grace?

For what is more incomprehensible than a coming without motion, an entering without passage, movement in stillness, a descent in rest? Who can also conceive the third coming, [Col. 0237B] when he will come to judge the living and the dead, when he will judge in majesty, though he was judged in humility, when the angels will fear? “Who shall stand to see him?” (ibid.). As though saying: Few who are raised toward heavenly things will see Christ’s first coming; few will stand firm in virtues so as to understand Christ’s spiritual coming to themselves. Who will stand in virtue on the day of judgment, daring to behold him in majesty?

“The groanings of death surrounded me, and the pains of hell surrounded me” (Psalm 17): that is, sins for which one should grieve, and which lead to hellish torment, surrounded me. There are three kinds of the pains of hell: demons, mortal sins, and infernal punishments. The kinds of infernal punishment are four: the worm of conscience, the flame of Gehenna, the disclosure of sin, and deprivation of the divine vision. The first punishment is more hidden, the second more grievous, the third more shameful, the fourth more damaging. [Col. 0237C] Therefore those who are in the punishments of hell may cry: “The groanings of eternal death surrounded me.” By a contrary analogy, any faithful person established in rest may say: “The joys of life surrounded me, and the delights of paradise surrounded me.” Consider, O man, by how many and how great miseries you are hemmed in, and you will find nothing in the human condition that is not full of pain and groaning.

18. “Tear your hearts” (Joel 2). The human heart is torn in many ways. It is torn when it is drawn in different directions, as is the heart of the avaricious person; it is torn when partly divided toward God and partly toward the world, as is the heart of the lukewarm person.

The heart is torn through contrition, though it was formerly closed through obstinacy. The first is the heart of a cold person, the second of a lukewarm person, the third of a fervent person. Greed tears the first heart, duplicity the second, charity the third. Of the first it is said: “They have spoken with heart and heart” (Psalm 11). Of the second: “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew 6). Of the third: “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Psalm 50). Our heart must be torn open in order to love God, to understand, and to repent.

19. “We ask and beseech you,” etc. (1 Thessalonians [Col. 0238A] 4). We ask when we simply request something; we beseech when we pray with earnestness.

It is fittingly said: “that you walk” (ibid.). For walking denotes progress from one stage to another. Nor is it simply said, “that you walk,” but “as you received from us.” A person walks in the manner received from the preacher when he fulfils what he hears for the end for which it was spoken by the teacher—when he fulfils not only the substance of the matter but also its circumstances. It follows: “that you so walk as to abound more” (ibid.). Walking denotes not only progress in virtues but perseverance in good work: “that you may abound more,” not only by persevering but also by advancing from virtue to virtue [Col. 0238B] (Psalm 83). For as it is just that one who is in filth should “be filthy still” (Revelation 22), so it is just that one who is in virtues should abound still; for charity given deserves to be increased, and increased charity deserves to be perfected.

“For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from fornication” (1 Thessalonians 4). Fornication is twofold: carnal and spiritual. Carnal fornication is committed in the body; spiritual fornication is committed in the mind through mortal sin. Wherever carnal fornication is, spiritual fornication is also present, but not conversely. The whole of Scripture, New and Old Testament alike, forbids fornication because it sees human beings as more prone to this sin.

For a human being is more inclined toward the slipperiness of the flesh, [Col. 0238C] because, conceived in lust, the flesh seems by a kind of hereditary right to desire lust. Therefore a person should not believe that he can lawfully give himself to libido because he is bound to its origin. Fornication is more frequently and more openly prohibited than other human deviation; and under the designation of carnal fornication, spiritual fornication is forbidden. For the soul commits spiritual fornication when it falls into mortal sin, because then it withdraws from God and fornicates with the devil. Therefore one must abstain from fornication: “That each one of you may know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honour” (ibid.).

A human being has a threefold vessel: Sacred Scripture, human flesh, and one’s own wife. Sacred Scripture is called a vessel because it contains the wine of spiritual understanding; human flesh is a vessel because the soul is received in it; one’s own wife is a vessel because offspring is conceived in her. The first vessel is golden because of wisdom, silver because of eloquence. The second is earthen because of the corruption of flesh. The third can be called fleshly because carnal intercourse is performed in it. We ought to possess the first in sanctification and honour, so that we may not corrupt it by heretical exposition, but sanctify it through lawful inquiry into spiritual understanding.

[Col. 0238D] We must also possess the second vessel, that is, our body, cleaving to sanctification in virtues and honour, lest it be dishonoured by any shamefulness. For just as a person strives to keep the vessels used in his service clean, so he ought through continence to keep honourable the workshops of his members. Every married person is likewise bound to possess his vessel, that is, his wife, in sanctification: not abusing her shamefully, not in passion of desire, so that there may not even be desire there, which is an injury and a passion of the soul. O miserable man! You think lust is pleasure, while the Apostle calls it passion. If there is pleasure there, it is false, momentary, unclean, and destructive.

20. “My eyes are ever toward the Lord” (Psalm 24). Some direct their physical eyes toward creatures in order to take delight in them through concupiscence. Against such delight it is said: “Turn away my eyes, lest they see vanity” (Psalm 118): vain things, [Col. 0239B] and vainly. For someone can see vain things without seeing vainly, when one sees visible things so that God may be praised in them. But one sees vain things vainly who beholds them in order that the senses may take delight.

Not only the physical eye must be turned from vanity, but also the spiritual eye, namely the mind, lest it behold vain things vainly—that is, conceive carnal delights with the intention of delighting in them. Rather, it should behold vain things not vainly—that is, consider them in order to flee from them.

Let the inward eyes, however, be turned toward truth, so that they may behold true things, and truly—that is, eternal things, and from charity. This is what he says: “My eyes are ever toward the Lord.” Yet there are some who, putting on beastly manners, lower their eyes to the earth and think only of earthly things. [Col. 0239C] They are like “a sow in the mire of mud” (2 Peter 2), sunk in deep slime. They keep their wisdom in worldly phantasms. Of them Solomon says: “A beautiful and foolish woman is a golden ring in her nostrils” (Proverbs 2). For a sow soils the ring in mud, and the woman soils beauty in the stench of lust. Such wisdom is like a golden ring in her nostrils.

The sow is a gluttonous and unclean animal, given over to mud. Such is the person devoted to worldly things, whose greed devours all things, whom sin stains, and who longs for the dregs of earthly things. In that person’s nostrils is a golden ring. His nostrils are fear and love of the world, by which he draws the delights of the world to himself as a kind of scent. Fear takes care lest he lose them; love draws him to acquire them. In these nostrils, as it were, a golden ring is a person’s wisdom, expended in fear and love of the world; and while these nostrils are applied to the mud of earthly things, the golden ring is defiled.

[Col. 0239D] But the wisdom of the righteous is a golden ring on the finger of a discerning person. By the finger good action is understood, for we work with our fingers. Thus the rich man, buried in hell, speaking to the soul of the poor man resting in Abraham’s bosom, says: “Let him dip the tip of his finger in water, that he may cool my tongue” (Luke 16). That is: if I had the least of his good works, I would endure a lesser punishment.

21. “Let us exult from the breasts of our consolation” (Isaiah 66). Some breasts are of desolation, others of consolation, and others of absolution. The breasts of desolation are the delight of sin and its continuance; Mother Habit offers these breasts to drink. Thus Job, in the person of the human race, laments that he was nursed at the breasts of evil habit. The person who, wishing to approach the Lord’s table, grieves over sin, withdraws from sin, and repents, is weaned from these breasts. This usually happens when something bitter is applied to the breasts of evil habit; and this happens when a child is chastised by the Father through temporal tribulation.

The breasts of consolation are the breasts of Mother Church, namely doctrine and life. Milk flows from one breast, namely doctrine; honey drips from the other, namely life, because doctrine nourishes and life delights. Of these breasts the Bride says: “He shall dwell between my breasts” (Song of Songs 1). The breasts of absolution are the breasts of our mother, the heavenly Jerusalem, which triumphs in heaven. These are freedom from sin and freedom from punishment. Those who triumph in heaven exult from these breasts. Of them it is said: “Your breasts are sweeter than wine” (ibid.).

[Col. 0240B] Therefore let us exult from the breasts of consolation; let us drink the milk that doctrine offers, and be satisfied with the honey that the life of the faithful offers. Hence it is said of the Church: “Honey and milk are under your tongue” (Song of Songs 4).

Sacred doctrine, or Sacred Scripture, is aptly figured by milk, because as milk has a threefold substance—whey, cheese, and butter—so Sacred Scripture has a threefold sense: historical, allegorical, and tropological. By whey history is figured, because, as whey is of inferior substance and lesser flavour, so history is of inferior substance and lesser delight. By cheese, which is of more solid and nourishing substance and is separated from whey, allegory is figured, for it nourishes the soul’s understanding and feeds the soul more solidly. By butter, which is richer and has a soothing substance, tropology is figured, for it tastes more sweetly to the palate of the mind. By honey, which lies hidden in cells, the life of the faithful is figured, hidden in the shell of the human body as a honeycomb in its cell.

Therefore let us exult from the breasts of our consolation, so that we may attain the breasts of absolution.

22. Christ’s tabernacle is threefold: the tabernacle of human nature, the tabernacle of the Church, and the tabernacle of eternal life. Of the first it is said: “He set his tabernacle in the sun” (Ps. 18). Of the second: “How beloved are thy tabernacles, O Lord!” (Ps. 83). Of the third we read: “Lord, who shall dwell in thy tabernacle?” (Ps. 14). In the first he was fighting; in the second, reigning; in the third, triumphant. The first tabernacle was made of curtains of haircloth; the second, of dyed-red skins; the third, of hyacinth-blue skins. For Christ’s human nature was, in a manner, haircloth, since it was rough because of human infirmities. Christ assumed the sackcloth of merit, not the merit of sackcloth—that is, penalty, not guilt. Hence Christ in the Psalm says that he is clothed in sackcloth (Ps. 34). The second tabernacle, that is, the Church, is made of dyed-red skins (Exod. 36), that is, of saints reddened by the blood of various tribulations. The third tabernacle, that is, [Col. 0241A] eternal life, is made of hyacinth-blue skins (ibid.). Hyacinth displays a heavenly colour; therefore the hyacinth-blue skins signify the diverse heavenly rewards in which and from which eternal life consists. O man, who are established in the tabernacle of the body and set in the tabernacle of the Church, aspire with your whole heart to the heavenly tabernacle, so that you may deserve to enter the Holy of Holies—that is, eternal life. There are the cherubim, that is, the angelic nature; there is the ark of the covenant, that is, Christ’s human nature; there is the urn full of manna, that is, Christ’s soul, full of heavenly grace; there is the golden crown, that is, heavenly blessedness; there is the aureole, that is, a certain addition to blessedness; there is the mercy-seat, that is, the divine majesty.

[Col. 0241B] 23. “Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as thou wilt” (Matt. 26). See how two speak in Christ, and speak of different things: sensuality speaks; reason speaks. Sensuality speaks from our weakness; reason speaks from divine steadfastness. Sensuality speaks from human feeling; reason speaks from divine effectual power. Sensuality says: “Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me.” Reason says: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as thou wilt.” These wills are different, not opposed: they will different things, but do not tend toward contrary ends. Sensuality proposes; reason disposes. In us sensuality and reason are often not merely different but opposed, when sensuality wills evil and reason good.

[Col. 0241C] Hence the Apostle says in the person of the human race: “I perceive another law in my members, resisting the law of my mind” (Rom. 7). The one compels a human being to rage with the beasts; the other makes a human being reason with the angels. This is the perpetual duel in the human mind: although reason sometimes restrains sensuality, sensuality nevertheless always murmurs back. For it is like the wheel of a cart that carries hay and yet creaks. But in Noah’s ark all the beasts were peaceful, because all sensual motions in Christ’s human nature were peaceful—that is, obedient to reason. Christ therefore, speaking according to sensuality, says: “Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me.”

The cup has many meanings. The cup is passion; the cup is the receiving of the Lord’s body [Col. 0241D] and blood; the cup is earthly pleasure. Of the first it is said: “Let this cup pass from me.” Of the second: “How excellent is the intoxicating cup!” (Ps. 22). Of the third it is said that all nations were made drunk by the golden cup of Babylon (Jer. 51). The first cup intoxicates unto the sleep of death; the second unto sobriety; the third unto eternal damnation. The first cup is mingled with myrrh; the second with honey; the third is honey-sweet. Hence it is said of that very cup: “The lips of the harlot drip honey” (Prov. 5). O man, if a passion leading to death hangs over you, if the flesh entices you, let reason stand firm; cry out: “Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as thou wilt.” If fear precedes the passion, let not the passion press on and disturb reason. Be ready [Col. 0242A] to receive the second cup—that is, the Lord’s body and blood—and cry: “Father, if it be possible, let this cup remain in me.” If the third cup threatens, that is, earthly pleasure, cry: “Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me.”

24. “Purge out the old leaven” (1 Cor. 5). Leaven is wickedness, which corrupts the whole mass of works. There is a twofold leaven: that of charity and that of iniquity. Of the leaven of charity it is said that a woman mixed a little leaven into three measures of meal (Matt. 13). To mix leaven into three measures of meal is nothing other than to join charity to faith in the Trinity. As leaven converts into its own nature the whole mass of the thing to which it is added, so charity makes all things to which it is joined like itself.

[Col. 0242B] Let leaven be purged out from us, so that we may be a new dough, as we were unleavened.

We were unleavened through baptism: that is, purified from the leaven of original sin. Remaining therefore in innocence, let us be new dough, moistened with heavenly grace. Dough is nothing other than flour sprinkled with water. Thus the faithful person sprinkled with the dew of heavenly grace is new dough. Observe that, in order that the faithful person may become Christ’s food, and Christ the food of the righteous, he must first be ground and crushed between two millstones—namely, fear and hope—and thus reduced to spiritual flour; then sprinkled with the more abundant water of charity and so made into bread; afterward baked by the fire of tribulation and thus converted into Christ’s food. [Col. 0242C] “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5).

“Passover” also means the evening hour at which the lamb was eaten. Hence it was said: “Before the feast-day of the Passover” (Matt. 26); and it means the paschal lamb that was eaten, whence it was said: “Where wilt thou that we prepare for thee to eat the Passover?” (ibid.); and it means the paschal solemnity, whence it was said that they might not defile the Passover (John 18), that is, the paschal solemnity. Christ, then, is called Passover, as it were the paschal lamb sacrificed for us. Passover may also be called a “passing-over,” because he passed from death to life, from the world to the Father.

25. “Christ, ascending on high, led captivity captive” (Eph. 4). Christ’s [Col. 0242D] descent is read as manifold. His first descent was from the Father’s bosom into the Virgin’s womb; his second, into the manger; his third, into hell. The first was to visit, the second to signify, the third to liberate. Likewise, his ascent was manifold: he ascended onto the gibbet of the cross; he ascended to the triumph of the resurrection; he ascended into heaven. By the first ascent he ascended in order to capture death; by the second, to destroy it; by the third, to lead captivity captive.

The human race had been made captive in many ways and by many powers: by the devil’s power, by guilt, and by punishment. But what the devil had made captive by the captivity of error, the Lord captured by the captivity of salvation, so that it would no longer be subject to tribute to the devil but bound to God. What guilt had captured through the devil, grace captured through [Col. 0243A] Christ; and what punishment had captured, glory captured. But that captivity was one of servitude; this one, of freedom.

Nor did Christ alone capture the human race with a good captivity: he also captured hell, the devil, sin, and punishment. He captured the human race, that it might be free; hell, lest it destroy his own; the devil, lest he rage cruelly against his own; sin, lest it abound excessively; punishment, that man might fear it less. But he, ascending as victor, “gave gifts to men” (ibid.), because he distributed rewards to his soldiers.

Behold the worm which is born without mating, feeds upon green leaves, emits silk from its mouth, and then is enclosed in death; it is raised again, and afterward receives wings for flight. This is he who was born without male seed, delighted in green leaves—that is, in the prayers [Col. 0243B] of the saints—emitting silk from his mouth, that is, supplying us through his preaching with garments of virtues; afterward dead, again raised from the dead, and at last, having received the wings of immortality and agility, impassibility and subtlety, seated at the right hand of the Father.

## ON SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST

26. “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord,” etc. (Matt. 3).

A word is one thing, the voice of a word another. A word properly means an inward conception of the mind expressed by an outward voice. Hence *verbum* (“word”) is said to derive from the striking of the mind (*verbere mentis*), that is, from passion, because in a certain sense the soul undergoes something when it receives an understanding of a thing. Hence Aristotle says in the book *On Interpretation*: “Things in the voice are signs of things in the soul.”

The Son of God is therefore elegantly called the Word, because, as the conception of the mind proceeds from the mind, so the Father begot the Son. As the mind begets understanding without any diminution of itself, so the Father begets the Son without any diminution of himself. As a word is expressed by outward speech, so the Son, as it were the tongue of God, announced the Word to diverse prophets. And as the word is called the inward conception of the mind, so the voice of the word is called the outward sound. Hence, as Christ is called the Word, so anyone preaching the Word is called the voice of the Word. Although any prophet might be called the voice of the Word, as one preaching the Word, John the Baptist is called the voice of the Word by antonomasia, because he not only foretold him to come, but also pointed him out as present. It was therefore elegantly said of him that he is the voice of the Word crying in the wilderness.

Observe that, as logicians distinguish, one sound is not a voice and another sound is a voice; one voice is significant and another not significant; one is significant naturally and another by convention. Certain inanimate things were signs of the Word, but proclaimed the Word itself by no voice. Such a sign may be called the sound of the Word, but not the voice of the Word. Thus manna which descended from heaven was a sign of Christ. Some voice of the Word was significant, some was not.

A significant or articulated voice is one uttered [Col. 0244A] with the speaker’s understanding, when he understands what he says aloud. Isaiah and Jeremiah, then, were significant voices of the Word, because each understood what he said. But Balaam, Caiaphas, and others were non-significant voices of the Word: although they prefigured something concerning Christ, they nevertheless did not understand what they were saying. Again, one voice of the Word was naturally significant, another significant by convention. Some philosophers naturally, led by reason, apprehended the Father’s wisdom, and thus foretold the Word and many things about him. For example, one of them—

> [Note: [Col. 0243D] Mercurius Trismegistus.]

—said of the Son of God: “The highest God made a second God, loved him as his only-begotten Son, and called him the Son of eternal blessing.” Such a significant voice of the Word was natural, because it proceeded under the guidance of natural reason. That significant voice was by the appointment of the one imposing it—that is, by the good pleasure of God inspiring it—as in the holy prophets.

[Col. 0244B] Such a voice was John the Baptist; hence it is said of him: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness.” The Word, that is Christ, cried out in him in a manifold wilderness: in the wilderness of the world, through creatures proclaiming God, and thus he cried in the wilderness of the world by deed; in the wilderness of Judaea, by word; in the wilderness of the righteous soul, by a divine prompting. What does he cry? “Prepare the way of the Lord.”

The Lord’s way has many meanings. It is the way from which one must travel, as repentance; the way beside which one must travel, as a good prelate whose example we ought to follow; the way in which one must travel, as the divine commandment; and the way toward which one must travel, as Christ.
