Of the first it is said: “Prepare the way of the Lord”; of the second: “The ways of Zion mourn” (Lam. 1); of the third: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way” (Ps. 118); of the fourth: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14). Therefore the way must be prepared by repentance, contrition, confession, and satisfaction. The way must be prepared so that the mud of lust, the dust of vain glory, and the stone of the hardened mind may be cast out. “Make straight the paths of our God” (Matt. 3).

A way is one thing, a path another. A way is a public road on which all proceed together; a path is a narrow and hidden road on which few travel, and more straitly. Hence *semita* (“path”), as it were *semis iter* (“a half-journey”). Thus the way is a commandment; the path is counsel. [Col. 0244D] The commandment must be fulfilled by all; the counsel is fulfilled by few, because it is narrower.

A path is sometimes straight, sometimes crooked. It is crooked when someone fulfills counsels outwardly, from a certain natural impulse and not from love of God—as philosophers did, who abandoned everything but did not follow Christ. A path is straight when counsels are fulfilled solely with a view to God. John the Baptist was the voice of this Word crying thus.

## ON SAINT PETER THE APOSTLE

27. “Thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16).

Peter figures the Church. As Peter is named from Christ the Rock, so the Church inwardly derives its name from Christ, the cornerstone. As he himself received his name from Christ the Rock, so the Church received its name from Christ the Rock. As Peter is endangered amid waves, so the Church is endangered amid the storms of the world. Like the northern star, it is tossed but not submerged; endangered but not shipwrecked. As Peter was called Barjona, as it were “son of the dove,” so the Church is daughter of the heavenly dove, that is, the Holy Spirit.

Therefore the Lord, speaking to Peter, says: “Thou art Peter”—understand, “thus named by me, the Rock”—“and upon this rock,” that is, upon me—

> [Note: [Col. 0245D] Our Alan, in his exposition of this passage, followed the opinion of Saint Augustine, who in *Retractations*, book 1, chapter 21 (and often elsewhere), judges that this passage should be expounded in this way—though he does not reject the other exposition either, according to which “the Rock” is understood as Peter, the common view of all the other holy Fathers and Catholic expositors. Augustine’s words in the passage cited are these: “In a certain place I said concerning the apostle Peter that the Church was founded upon him as upon a rock. This sense is also sung by many in the verses of the most blessed Ambrose, where, speaking of the cock, he says: ‘At his crowing, the very rock of the Church washes away its guilt.’ But I know that I afterwards explained it very often in such a way that by ‘this rock’ should be understood him whom Peter confessed. For it was not said to him, ‘Thou art the rock,’ but ‘Thou art Peter’; but the Rock was Christ (1 Cor. 10). Which of these two opinions is the more probable, let the reader choose.” Thus Augustine. See Bellarmine, *On the Roman Pontiff*, book 1, chapter 10, and others.]

—“I will build [Col. 0245A] my Church. And I will give thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (ibid.). What is this kingdom, whose keys were bestowed upon Peter and upon every successor of his? One key is the power of binding [Col. 0245B] and loosing; the other is discernment for distinguishing leprosy from leprosy, that is, sin from sin. The power of binding and loosing is aptly called a key, because, as a key locks and unlocks, so that power has two uses: one in binding, the other in loosing.

A priest is said to bind for three reasons: either because he leaves someone bound, imposes satisfaction, or pronounces a curse upon one excommunicated. Likewise, he is said to loose in three ways: because he sacramentally absolves, remits punishment, and prays for salvation. The office of discerning between sin and sin is also called a key, because by such an office he must assign the difference between one sin and another. These are the keys of the kingdom of heaven.

The kingdom of heaven is fourfold: Christ, sacred Scripture, the Church, and eternal life are each called a kingdom. Of the first it is said: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17). Of the second: “The kingdom of heaven is like a man who went out early in the morning to sow his seed” (Matt. 13). Of the third: “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18). Of the fourth: “For the kingdom of heaven draws near” (Matt. 3). The key mentioned above is said to belong to the first kingdom because, through the priest’s office and the power given by Christ, the first kingdom is opened to the faithful and the way to Christ is prepared. For when the priest distinguishes one sin from another and absolves the penitent, he prepares the faithful person’s way to Christ.

Likewise, by these keys the entrance to the second kingdom, sacred Scripture, is unlocked. For when the priest looses the penitent, remits punishment, reveals the gravity of sin and also the suitability and difference between sins, he directs the person toward understanding sacred Scripture. By these keys the entrance to the third kingdom, that is, the Church, is likewise unlocked; [Col. 0246A] and in the same manner to the fourth kingdom, eternal life. Thus, in respect of the fourfold kingdom, they are called the keys of the kingdom of heaven.

These keys belong to priests, who ought to be gatekeepers of heaven and key-bearers of paradise. But now these lawful keys have been changed into adulterous ones, because they bind and loose no longer with God in view and under reason’s guidance, but, out of love of money, bind those who ought not to be bound. Thus it may truly be said of them: “Whatever thou shalt bind on earth shall be loosed in heaven; and whatever thou shalt loose on earth shall be bound in heaven” (Matt. 16). Behold: these key-bearers derive their name not from the key (*clavis*) but from the club (*clava*). They change keys into clubs, because they do not open the way for people but instead, by deceiving them, strike them toward eternal death.

[Col. 0246B] These men seem rather to possess the keys of hell than those of the kingdom of heaven. These wretches are not vicars of Simon Peter, but of Simon Magus.

## ON SAINT MARY

28. “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse” (Isa. 11).

The Lord God planted man, as it were a tree of life, in the midst of the world, as it were in the midst of paradise.

Man, I say, was a tree before sin, on account of the solidity of his nature and life, because he possessed spiritual life. But through sin this tree was turned into “a leaf carried away by the wind” (Job 13), and it flees like a shadow and never remains in the same state (Job 14). Many branches proceeded from this tree: some green, some dry—that is, Adam’s posterity. Of these, some bore the fruit of good works, like green branches; others lacked the dew of heavenly grace and therefore withered away from good works.

From the root of this tree, from which Jesse proceeded—that is, from the stock of the ancient fathers—there came forth a rod, the Virgin Mary. By the sweetness of her fruit this rod redeemed the bitterness of the ancient root. She redeemed in the shoot the defect that was in the trunk. She is aptly called a rod by reason of her name, signification, and property. [Col. 0246C] By reason of the name, because, by changing *a* into *o*, *virga* (“rod”) becomes *virgo* (“virgin”). By reason of signification, because the Virgin Mary was figured by Aaron’s rod. As that rod, without any external assistance, put forth leaves, flowered, and bore fruit, so the Virgin [Col. 0246D] Mary, without male aid, flowered in conceiving Christ and bore fruit in giving birth. By reason of property, because, as a rod is the instrument of a king, of one who corrects, and of one who measures, so the glorious Rod Mary was the instrument of the heavenly King, which he used to rule his people; the instrument of one correcting, which he used to correct the human race; and the instrument of one measuring, which he used to enclose himself within the measure of humanity.

And as a rod, when raised on high, is directed in a straight line, so the Virgin Mary was raised to the height of blessedness and directed along the path of virtues. Hence it is said of her: “Who is this that ascends through the wilderness?” etc. (Song 3). From this rod came forth the flower, that is, Christ was born. A flower produces fruit, gives fragrance, and grants beauty to the field. Thus Christ produced the fruit of our redemption, spread the fragrance of his name everywhere, and gave spiritual beauty to the world.

29. The seal-mark of God is one thing, the seal another; an image is one thing, a sign another. The seal of God the Father is [Col. 0247B] the Son, as it were marking him in every respect, because he is equal, coeternal, and consubstantial with the Father. An angel is God’s seal-mark, as it were marking him in some respects, because it is like God in many things, though not in all. Hence Lucifer is said, according to the state which he possessed before his fall: “Thou, the seal-mark of God’s likeness” (Ecclus. 28). But the Son is the Father’s seal according to unity of essence, whereas an angel is the seal-mark of imitation by reason. Man is called the image of God, as it were an *imitago* (“imitation-image”), because he is not so expressly like God as an angel is. Every creature, however, is called a sign of God, because by its essence, its ordering, and its beauty it proclaims God.

30. Eternal life is called not only a promise but also a re-promise, because it has been promised not only in words but also in deeds: promised through the patriarchs, through the prophets, through Christ, and through the senate of the apostles. What saint doubts the attainment of eternal life, which has been confirmed by the proclamations of so many saints and the examples of so many saints?

[Col. 0247C] Vincent would not laugh upon the rack unless he were certain of the reward. Lawrence would not rejoice upon the gridiron if he doubted the glory. Faith accomplishes all this: it conquers kingdoms, performs righteousness, and obtains the re-promise.

31. The Blessed Virgin Mary is like a lily among thorns (Song 2), like a beautiful olive tree in the fields, like a planting of roses in Jericho (Ecclus. 24). The more a lily rising among thorns is pricked by the thorns, the greater fragrance it sends forth. The lily surpasses the thorns in scent and excels them in colour. Likewise, the more severe the persecution which the Blessed Virgin endured from the Jews, the more her patience gave forth the fragrance of good repute. She is like an olive tree in the breadth of this world, as though in the middle of a field: retaining the beauty of virtues, green with holy thoughts, flowering with good works, bearing for us the fruit of eternal blessedness, fruitful with heavenly oil—that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit. She is like a planting of roses in Jericho. A rose planted in Jericho rises more beautiful, breathes a more fragrant scent, is clothed in a deeper red, and retains the colour of its beauty longer. Since Jericho is interpreted as “defect,” the Blessed Virgin, like a rose planted amid the defects of human nature, was [Col. 0248A] fairer than other women in virtue, more lovely through the redness of earthly tribulations patiently endured, and more fragrant in the scent of good works.

32. These are the three steps by which a person ascends to heaven: poverty, humility, and charity. For a person to be justified, he must first be poor in spirit—that is, humble—and not set his heart upon riches, so as not to depart after them in mind, even though he possesses them materially. One must possess a fourfold poverty against the fourfold kind of riches. There are riches of fortune, [Col. 0248B] consisting in gold, silver, precious stones, and earthly honours; these depart with the same fickleness with which they arrive, and therefore are called fortunes. If they abound, a person ought not set his heart upon them.

There are also riches of nature, consisting in gifts of the body—such as beauty, strength, and health—and gifts of the soul, such as memory, understanding, and reason. A person ought not be proud of these, but should always maintain poverty in opposition to them. There are riches consisting in virtues and gifts of the Holy Spirit. A person ought not be proud even of these riches, lest through human pride they depart as they came through divine grace. The riches of glory consist in eternal blessedness. Nor ought one be proud of that in the present life because of the distinction of one’s merits, since pride takes away not only the distinction of merit but even the distinction of reward.

The second step by which [Col. 0248C] a person ascends to heaven is humility. It has three kinds. The first is sufficient humility, shown to a superior; the second is abundant humility, rendered to an equal; the third is perfecting humility, paid to an inferior. This is the fulfillment of all righteousness, of which the Lord says to John: “It is fitting for me to fulfill all righteousness” (Matt. 3), that is, the highest degree of humility. The highest degree, however, is charity, according to which a person is bound to love God above himself, himself beneath God, and his neighbour within himself.

33. The three boys, Ananias, Azarias, and Misael, are taken captive so that they may not fulfill God’s law (Dan. 1), because in this world the three powers of the soul are taken captive so that they may not exercise themselves fully: namely, the irascible power, the concupiscible power, and the rational power. The irascible is taken captive lest it restrain vices; the concupiscible, lest it appear upright; the rational, lest it examine each thing. But the fourth, contemplative Daniel, rejoices and sees visions, because the higher part of reason, which cannot be extinguished, sees truth in a mirror.

Therefore, lest the captivity of the northern land invite us through anger to quarrels, inflame us to insults, move us to detractions, and kindle us to hatreds; lest concupiscence stir up gluttony, summon lust, feed covetousness, and nourish avarice; lest reason be deceived or seduced by imaginings—the Lord cries to us: “Ho, ho, ho, flee from the land of the north” (Zech. 2). The land of the north is the city of Babylon. What is Babylon but this world, in which the spiritual Nebuchadnezzar—that is, pride—reigns? Flee from this land, lest the irascible power go astray; flee, lest [Col. 0249A] concupiscence deviate; flee, lest rationality stray beyond bounds. Upon us in the land of northern captivity hangs a threefold woe: woe, because anger is inflamed; woe, because concupiscence burns; woe, because reason is darkened.

Jeremiah, indicating this, says: “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God, for I am a child and do not know how to speak” (Jer. 1). “Ah,” because anger boils; “ah,” because concupiscence burns; “ah,” because reason sleeps; and therefore I am a child and do not know how to speak. From this land of the north every evil is opened: evil against God through blasphemy; evil against one’s neighbour through pride; evil against oneself through lust.

34. Three things provide fuel for the fire of lust: namely, the vine-branch, sulphur, and dung.

[Col. 0249B] Outward bodily beauty is aptly compared to a vine-branch. As a vine-branch is green for a little while in spring, withers in winter, dries up in hail, and is kept for the flame, so outward bodily beauty now blooms in the face, now is banished by the winter of old age, now is uprooted by death, and now supplies fuel to the flame of lust. What is outward beauty but nourishment for pride, gilded mud, whitewashed dung, a vine-branch reserved for the fire of lust?

Sulphur, moreover, is gluttony: as sulphur stinks and burns, so gluttony stinks through disgrace and burns through concupiscence. What is gluttony but the seedbed of lust, the tomb of reason, a heap of filth, the robber of modesty, the enemy of chastity, the origin of uncleanness, the mother of nausea? Dung, [Col. 0249C] which fattens the ground and emits from itself a most foul odour, is sloth. It fattens the flesh for lust and bears in itself only disgrace. Hence David, idle in the palace, fell into adultery. And:

> “Why, it is asked, did Aegisthus become an adulterer?  
> The cause is ready at hand: he was idle.”
>
> (Ovid, *Remedies for Love*, book 1.)

O wretched fire of lust, whose fuel is sulphur, whose spark is sloth, whose smoke is disgrace, and whose ashes are uncleanness!

35. Riches provide the material for avarice, because many who are cast down by poverty do not burn with avarice, but after becoming rich suffer from it.

[Col. 0249D] 36. Earthly honours and worldly powers are aptly comparable to hay and straw. As hay or straw is now green and now cast into the oven, now flowers and now is crushed, so worldly glory now flourishes and now dies, now shines and now is worn away. What, then, are earthly honours but images of goods?

What are worldly powers but actors playing powers? What are secular dignities but masks and apes of dignities? What are earthly goods but phantasms of goods? Certainly earthly goods are not goods. If they were goods, they would never fail; they would not be absent from the righteous or present with the unjust.

If they were goods, they would fill the soul rather than drain the mind; they would not be things through which the mind becomes full by a certain emptiness and empty by a certain fullness. If they were goods, the earth would not rejoice in them and paradise would not lack them. These earthly goods are the material of avarice.

37. If you wish to avoid lust, restrain gluttony, persist in vigils, and devote yourself to prayer. If you wish to avoid avarice, consider that avarice is the service of idols (Eph. 5). If you wish to avoid vain glory, consider that “vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccles. 1). Consider that vain glory retains for itself only this glorious trait: it despises its seekers, seeks those who despise it, scorns those who desire it, and pursues those who flee it.

38. The punishments of hell which the damned will suffer in hell [Col. 0250B] are nine. The first is unquenchable fire, a fire exceeding our fire as much as our fire exceeds an imaginary fire. Of it it was said: “Go, ye cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25); and elsewhere: “Their fire shall not be quenched” (Mark 9; Isa. 66). Note the double effect of this fire: it will neither consume nor be consumed. The second punishment of the damned will be incomparable cold. Hence Job: “They shall pass from snow-waters to excessive heat” (Job 24). The third is the immortal worm: “Their worm shall not die” (Isa. 66). The fourth is intolerable stench; indeed, the damned will scarcely endure that stench. The fifth is palpable darkness, so dense that it could almost be cut. Hence the Lord says: “Cast him into the outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 22). And Job: “If I wait, hell is my house, and in darkness I have spread my bed” (Job 17). And the prophet: “The wicked shall be silent in darkness” (1 Sam. 2). The sixth is the lashes of those who beat them, for the wicked will be afflicted by most grievous lashes. The seventh is the sight of demons, serpents, and four-footed beasts. The eighth is the confusion of sinners, because the wicked will see before their eyes all their sins, and the evil deeds of each will be manifest not only to himself but also to all others. The ninth and final punishment will be despair, for none of them will henceforth hope ever to obtain rest.

39. A person will flee the nine punishments mentioned above in four ways: by flight, shame, sorrow, and fear. By flight: while he lives, he should flee sins as far as he can. Some sins are conquered more by fleeing than by resisting, as lust is. Hence Paul says: “Flee fornication” (1 Cor. 6), because one should not fight with it except by turning one’s back. By shame: one should now be ashamed of one’s most evil life and, being ashamed, do penance. By sorrow: one should grieve for past sins and because one has offended God. By fear: one should fear one’s Creator and also punishment, and thus undertake worthy penance now, lest in the future one suffer without end the nine punishments mentioned above.

40. “Rejoice in God our helper” (Ps. 80). We must rejoice in spiritual, not earthly, joys, which promise delight and [Col. 0251A] take it away. If you wish to flee these earthly joys, consult reason. If you are willing to hear it, it will say to you: “Leave these things, toward which people rush without discernment. Leave riches, because of the dangers and burden of possessing them. Leave bodily pleasures, because they soften and enfeeble. Leave ambition: it is a swollen thing, vain and windy, having no end.” You see how wretched it is to desire earthly pleasures, how wretched to sit at the thresholds of the powerful. You suffer many insults in order to enter, and more after you have entered. Pass beyond these steps of the rich and honours suspended in great arrogance.

Though these earthly things are utterly low and abject, they are nevertheless approached by difficult and steep steps. The road to the summit of dignity is dangerous. Direct, therefore, [Col. 0251B] the path of your intention toward the spiritual riches of the mind, things most ample and tranquil. If you ascend to that summit of reason, Fortune will bow her head beneath you.

You will behold beneath yourself all things thought most excellent. The better part of you—reason—is secure; Fortune cannot harm it. This is the path that must be taken, and in this manner of life a person must be ordered: calmly indeed, but not softly. The long and everlasting joy of reason awaits. Receive that joy which is immortal and delights continually. For one who gives oneself to reason relies upon oneself, not upon another; but one supported by another’s help can fall.

Who prudent, moreover, trusts in Fortune? Or who prudent marvels at himself because of things belonging to another?

What is the blessed life but security of mind and perpetual tranquillity? Greatness of spirit will give this; steadfast constancy in right living will give it. One reaches these things if purity of mind is wholly perfected; if, in matters to be done, order, measure, beauty, and a harmless and benevolent will are kept—intent upon reason and never departing from it.

### 41. “You will destroy all who speak falsehood” (Psalm V).

O man, how far you depart from the highest truth when you devote yourself to the fabrications of lies! How do you think to come to the true, if even in your words you dissent from truth? I do not know with what conscience anyone asks God with the tongue with which he has belched forth a lie. [Col. 0251D] He cuts off the tongue’s proper function who employs it for lying; and in this way the conscience is branded [Col. 0252A] with the mark of falsehood.

Although every mortal sin estranges a person from true being, none detracts from the nature of truth more than lying. This is the vice that devises false testimony, manufactures flattery, invents frauds, and completes acts of slander. By this vice a person speaks with heart and mouth and becomes divided within himself: with his mouth he denies what he holds in his heart. By this vice the heart contradicts the mouth, and the mouth opposes the heart. This vice gives birth to heresy, creates schisms, generates suspicions, composes unheard-of rumours; it colours shameful disgraces, flatters what should be exposed, exposes what should be covered, lends support to perjuries, and attends dishonourable proceedings.

Although every thing by the law of nature tends toward the benefit of one’s neighbour, lying alone assaults truth; it contains in itself so great [Col. 0252B] a corrosion of malice that no reasoning can excuse it. Natural affection does not release it from guilt in the midwives (Exodus I); rational fear does not do so in the Gibeonites (Joshua IX); terror of mind does not do so in Peter (Matthew VI); nor does necessity’s foresight do so in Ananias (Acts V). O man, if falsity is committed in your lie, will truth be in fault? O wretched effect of lying: it proposes falsehood in intention and consequently takes upon itself a true punishment! How far from the tongue’s office is one who defiles his mouth with the filth of lying! A lie is leaven which corrupts the entire mass of speech and turns whatever good there is in speech into its own bitterness.

[Col. 0252C] There are three kinds of lie: that of vanity, that of falsehood, and that of intention. The first is pitiable, the second culpable, the third abominable. The first belongs to punishment, the second to fault, the third to malice.

158 The first is inborn; the second devised; the third elaborated.

### 42.

By Christ’s changing water into wine at the wedding (John II) is signified that, in those nuptials which he celebrated in the chamber of the virginal womb, by joining human nature to divine nature, he changed the tastelessness of the old Law into the flavour of the new Law. In this house of the virginal womb, the order of the three virtues—humility, virginity, and charity—was as it were a dining-hall; Christ was the steward of the feast, as it were the prince of the banquet. There a threefold water was changed into a threefold wine: [Col. 0252D] punishment into penitence, austerity into grace, misery into mercy.

[Col. 0253]

## Other Sayings of Master Alan of Lille

Commonly called *Mirabilia* (“Wonders”), but perhaps better *Memorabilia* (“Things Worth Remembering”).

Extracted from the same manuscript codex of the monastery of Dunes.

[Col. 0253A] 159 God, the creator of the universe, created all movements of the soul for good; yet through our use it often happens that things good by nature lead us into sins when we use them badly. Love is one of the soul’s movements. We use it well if we love wisdom and truth, but badly if we love flesh or blood. Therefore, being spiritual, hear love-songs sung spiritually, and learn to transfer the movement of your soul and the fire of carnal love to better things.

A friend is love’s companion: attach your mind to him so that one thing may arise from two; entrust yourself to him as to yourself; fear nothing from him, and ask nothing dishonourable of him. For friendship is not mercenary, but is wholly honourable. Hence the Lord says: “You are my friends [Col. 0253B] if you do what I command you” (John XV). The Lord gave us a model of friendship to follow: that we should do a friend’s will, reveal secrets to him, and he to us. Thus Ecclesiasticus also says: “A faithful friend is a strong protection; whoever finds him finds a treasure” (chapter VI). A faithful friend, that is, one according to God, discusses with his friend those things necessary for the medicine of eternal life and immortality; for, as Cicero rightly says, friendship can exist only among good persons. Friendship ought also to be free and inclined toward every happiness. “He who fears God will likewise have good friendship.”

The full and perfect grace of friendship can endure among perfect men possessing the same virtue. It is attained by certain steps. The first [Col. 0253C] step is contempt for worldly things; the second, that no one, judging himself wise and prudent, should prefer to trust himself rather than his friend. The third is that a person should place every thing he judges useful and necessary after the good of charity. The fourth, that he should wholly cease from anger. The fifth, that he should desire to cure even his brother’s irrational anger, because another’s grief is as destructive as one’s own unless, so far as lies in you, you drive it even from your brother’s mind. The last step, destructive of all vices, is to believe that you are to depart from this world daily.

“Do not seek to become a judge,” etc. (Ecclesiasticus VII). Each person ought to weigh his own virtues and, in proportion to his strength, undertake the care of others, lest, while he delights in a place of glory, he become the cause of ruin to those subject to him; and lest one weighed down by the burden of his own faults should wish to become a judge of others’ faults. The one who fears no adversity ought to be brought forward as an example of life.

[Col. 0254A] “God created man from the earth and made him according to his own image” (Genesis I): namely, so that he may live, know, and possess memory, understanding, and will. Hence: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart,” etc. (Matthew XXII; Mark XII), that is, with all your understanding, will, and memory. But as the Son proceeds from the Father, 160 and the Spirit from both, so will proceeds from understanding, and memory from both. Nor can the soul be perfect without these three; nor, as regards blessedness, can any one of them be whole without the others. And just as God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit are not three gods but one God having three persons, so the soul’s understanding, the soul’s will, and the soul’s memory are not three souls but one soul, having three powers, in which it marvellously bears [Col. 0254B] God’s image. With these, as with its highest powers, we are commanded to love the Creator, so that whatever is understood and loved may always be held in memory.

Understanding does not suffice for God unless the will is in love of him; nor do these two suffice unless memory is added, by which God continually remains in the mind of the one who loves and understands.

For just as there is no moment in which a human being does not use or enjoy God’s goodness, so God ought always to be present in memory.

Man was also made in God’s likeness, so that, as God is charity, good, just, gentle, and merciful, so man may possess charity and be good, [Col. 0254C] just, and so forth.

“He who lives for ever created all things together” (Ecclesiasticus XVIII). The substance of things was created together, but they were not all formed simultaneously according to their species. They existed together in the substance of matter, but did not all appear together in the appearance of form. For when heaven and earth are described as made, spiritual and bodily things alike, and whatever is produced from heaven or earth, are indicated as having been made.

“Do not be humble in your wisdom” (Ecclesiasticus XIII). It does not reject the virtue of humility, but teaches that one should maintain firm authority against assailants of truth, whom one must resist courageously.

“The fornication of a woman will be recognized in the lifting up of her eyes and in her eyelids” (Ecclesiasticus XXVI). By these three things it shows the curiosity of the human mind, which is always prone to evil. Hence: “All that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, and the desire [Col. 0255A] of the eyes, and the pride of life” (I John II). All vices are contained in these three.

The desire of the flesh is whatever pertains to bodily pleasure: food, drink, sexual intercourse. The desire of the eyes is all curiosity, as in a shameful spectacle, in acquiring superfluities, in learning and censuring one’s neighbours’ faults. Pride of life is when someone boasts of honours and serves through the exaltation of empty glory and through arrogance. Adam was tempted through the desire of the flesh when the enemy urged him to eat from the forbidden tree; through the desire of the eyes when he said, “You shall know good and evil”; through pride when he added, “You shall be like gods” (Genesis III).

“The beginning of a man’s life is water, bread, clothing, [Col. 0255B] and a house” (Ecclesiasticus XXIX). It teaches frugality and hospitality: that we should be temperate in food and clothing, while giving generously to worthier brethren who are to be received. In the beginning there was not such luxury of food and drink, nor such ambition for garments, towers, and palaces; rather, the ancients lived on the fruits of trees and the vegetables of herbs, and after sin the Lord made garments of skins for the first parents.

“Let a little please you in place of much” (ibid.). Let what you have suffice for you, lest you seek superfluously what you cannot attain. Hence someone says: “It is better for you not to have something to give than shamelessly to ask for what you do not have.”

“Jealousy and anger shorten one’s days” (Ecclesiasticus XXX). A disordered affection of the mind weakens the body. Hence: “A sorrowful spirit dries up the bones” (Proverbs XVII). “Men of blood shall not halve their days” (Psalm LIV), that is, they cannot possess for ever the prosperity 161 which they promise themselves.

“Have you sat at a great table? Do not open your mouth first over it” (Ecclesiasticus XXXI). Literally, it teaches continence and temperance. Mystically, it teaches that we should be cautious and provident in God’s Law; for the great table is the abundance of the Scriptures, at which we ought not to be presumptuous and snatch something from it without a teacher, but should follow the path of holy teachers.

“Do not provoke lovers of wine; flee the drunk, for they are easily angered; for wine has destroyed many” [Col. 0255D] (ibid.), that is, drunkenness has overthrown many. It diminishes understanding, stirs up anger, inflames lust, and reveals the mind’s secrets. “Fire tests hard iron; so wine, drunk in drunkenness, will expose the hearts of the proud” (ibid.), that is, as fire softens iron’s hardness, so wine, inflaming proud hearts, drives them to wickedness.

“Wine soberly drunk is life equally shared among men” (ibid.). Wine drunk soberly does not take away a life of equity, but brings sobriety and the other adornments of virtues.

“A stallion, so too a mocking friend: under every rider he neighs” (Ecclesiasticus XXXIII). As there is no reason in a beast of burden, so there is no order of fairness in a false friend. For just as a lascivious horse does not distinguish by its neighing [Col. 0256A] between its own master and a stranger, so a fool and scoffer does not distinguish a hypocrite from a faithful friend, but reveals secrets equally to both through the offices of his mouth.

“To son and wife, brother and friend, do not give power over yourself during your life” (ibid.). Literally, it teaches fathers to govern their sons and raise them with discipline until they attain mature age and can be worthy heirs of their fathers. Spiritually, however, it instructs rulers of churches to maintain their dignity to the end and leave their disciples, well brought up, as heirs of their labour. For rulers of the Church ought outwardly to retain what they undertake for the benefit of others.

“Food, a rod, and a burden for an ass; bread, discipline, [Col. 0256B] and work for a servant” (ibid.). It is necessary that wicked servants be restrained by their masters’ severity, lest they enjoy unlawful freedom. Yet in them nature is not to be despised, but wickedness restrained, so that they may know themselves to be subject. Those are rightly servants who serve vices; but those who obey righteousness are truly free. Hence: “If the Son sets you free, you shall truly be free” (John VII); for no power is better or greater than serving God, whom love serves well. Thus it is described what provision and discipline ought to be given to servants: namely, that they should have food and clothing, not leisure for wandering. If servants are kindly disposed and obedient, they are to be regarded as brothers; but if harsh and proud, they are to be restrained under discipline.

[Col. 0256C] “If you have a faithful servant, let him be to you as your own soul” (Ecclesiasticus XXXIII). For in him we ought to love our common nature and, if necessary, lay down our life for him; for it is not the human being who should be persecuted, but vices.

“He who grasps a shadow and pursues the wind is like one who attends to lying visions” (Ecclesiasticus XXXIV). This signifies that deceptive dreams often mock people and lead them into errors unless they are cautiously discerned. Hence the Law commands: “You shall not observe dreams or divinations” (Leviticus XIX; Numbers XXIII). Yet revelations sometimes occur through dreams. Thus Gregory says in the *Dialogues*: “You should know, Peter, that dream-images touch the mind in six ways: sometimes through the fullness or emptiness [Col. 0256D] of the stomach; sometimes through illusion; sometimes through thought together with illusion; sometimes through revelation; sometimes through thought together with revelation.”

“He who has not been tested, what does he know?” (Ecclesiasticus XXXIV)—that is, tested by tribulation. Hence: “The furnace tests the vessels of the potter, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous people” (Ecclesiasticus XXXVII). For one who preserves patience amid tribulations is made stronger.

“He who offers sacrifice from the substance of the poor is like one who sacrifices a son before his father” (Ecclesiasticus XXXIV). A sacrifice is utterly detestable when it is compared to the sorrow of a bereaved father. 162 Some weigh how much they give, not how much they seize; they gather wages and put them into a bag [Col. 0257A] with holes (Haggai I). Money appears to be put into a pierced bag when it is deposited, but not when it is lost. Therefore those who look at how much they give but not how much they seize put wages into a pierced bag, because they gather them while contemplating them in the hope of confidence, yet lose them by not contemplating themselves.

“He who is cleansed from a dead person and touches him again, what does his washing profit?” (Ecclesiasticus XXXIV). He neglects to remain clean after washing who does not preserve innocence of life after tears. Some are washed and yet are not clean, because they do not cease to weep for sins committed and then commit anew deeds that must be wept for.

“The Lord who repays will render to you sevenfold” (Ecclesiasticus XXXV): namely, a perfect recompense. For the number seven, because it signifies the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0257B] is perfect; and because it embraces the inner and outer substance of man, it signifies the soul in the number three—hence, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart,” etc. (Matthew XXII; Mark XII)—and the body in the number four, because the body consists of four elements.

“Do not offer wicked gifts, for he will not receive them” (Ecclesiasticus XXXV). With God there is no concern for the quantity of a gift or desire for a powerful person; rather, there is love and humility of heart. Therefore no one ought to offer sacrifice from iniquity, but from just labour.

“Do not be greedy at every feast, and do not pour yourself out over every food” (Ecclesiasticus XXXVII). In its historical sense, it praises thrift and censures gluttony, which brings its devourer to sickness. [Col. 0257C] Mystically, it warns us to be temperate in temporal things. Hence: “Have you found honey? Eat what is enough for you” (Proverbs XXV). And elsewhere: “Do not be wise beyond what it is fitting to be wise” (Romans XII).

“Honour the physician because of necessity, for the Most High created him” (Ecclesiasticus XXXVIII). It wishes us to be discerning in all things, because all God’s works are very good (Genesis I). Therefore we ought not despise those whom the Creator plainly made for our benefit. There are bodily physicians and spiritual physicians: bodily physicians cure bodies; spiritual physicians cure souls. Both, therefore, are to be honoured, but spiritual physicians are to be preferred.

“It is not for one to say, ‘What is this?’ or ‘What is that?’” [Col. 0257D] (Ecclesiasticus XXXIX). It forbids us to be curious and investigate what it is not fitting to know. For all things will be revealed in their time, when the Lord “will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts” (I Corinthians IV).

“Fire, hail, famine, and death: all these were created for vengeance” (Ecclesiasticus XXXIX). Before sin, all things obeyed man; after sin, the world’s order fights against him—famine, death, and a thousand perils of death. Beasts also rage against him, as does the sword of heavenly vengeance.

Therefore the wicked will be tortured in punishment because, in the time given them for repentance, they do not cease to sin. For, deceived by prosperity as though by sleep, they suppose it to be a time of peace, not of war, although the present [Col. 0258A] life is granted to man so that through a good contest he may attain blessedness.

Therefore, in the time of his salvation, while it was an acceptable time for him, he rose up in pride and burned with desire for earthly things, without any fear of God.

“Besides these: death, blood, contention, and the sword, oppressions, famine,” etc. (Ecclesiasticus XL). Multiple punishments were appointed for sinful man, so that, corrected, he might repent and thereafter take heed. But because he neglects this and falls into worse things, the Lord brought the flood upon the world so that he might destroy the man whom he had created. Yet in comparison with future punishment, what man suffers in the present is nothing. For then full and profound vengeance will come, so that those who do not cease to sin in the present life may be tortured without end.

[Col. 0258B] “The life of a man who looks to another’s table is not to be reckoned life” (ibid.). It is foolish to be idle and seek a reward from another’s labour. “Each one will receive according to his works” (Romans II). Whoever delights in languishing idly and in not benefiting neighbours through teaching will at last burn with the pains of hell and late repentance.

“O death, how bitter is your remembrance to a man at peace amid his possessions, to a quiet man whose ways are straight in all things and who is still able to take food!” (Ecclesiasticus XLI). Death of the body is bitter to one who loves the world’s prosperity and riches, because he neglects the joys of the life to come.

“O death, your judgment is good for the needy man, and for one whose strength is failing, worn out by age,” etc. (ibid.). [Col. 0258C] The judgment of death is good for Christians, because through it they pass to eternal life. Do not fear the judgment of temporal death, but rather: “Fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matthew X).

With respect to the equality of scales and weights, fairness must everywhere be preserved and the rule of scales and weights observed, lest we defraud our brother in buying. How greatly hypocrisy and deceit displease the Lord he shows in these words: “A deceitful balance is an abomination to God, but a just weight is his will” (Proverbs XI). Whoever weighs the cause of the poor and the powerful differently, considers his own errors lighter than those of others, places unbearable burdens upon people’s shoulders, [Col. 0258D] or is good in public and evil in secret, is abominable to the Lord.

“Do not fix your gaze upon every person’s appearance, and do not linger among women” (Ecclesiasticus XLII). It teaches us to preserve purity of heart and body. Hence: “The person whose face you frequently look upon serves you dangerously”; for shameless eyes do not know how to contemplate the beauty of souls, but only that of bodies.

“From garments comes the moth, and from a woman a man’s wickedness; for better is a man’s wickedness than a woman doing good, and a woman bringing shame into reproach” (ibid.). “Woman” may signify sex, as there: “God sent his Son, born of a woman” (Galatians IV); or weakness, as here: “Man, born of woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries” (Job XIV). [Col. 0259A] “Man,” therefore, in this place means the strong and discerning person; “woman,” a weak and undiscerning mind. It often happens that the discerning person slips into fault while the weak person performs a good work; but the undiscerning person, becoming proud of his good deeds, falls more grievously, while the discerning person, repenting, returns to the rule of discernment and thereafter acts more strongly and cautiously. For the fault of the strong often becomes an occasion of virtue, and the virtue of the weak an occasion of sin. This woman brings shame into reproach because she does things deserving shame.

“How desirable are all his works; and we can consider them only as a spark!” (Ecclesiasticus XLI). We consider God’s works as a spark because we scarcely receive a small knowledge of them.

God so ordered all things that things which seem [Col. 0259B] contrary to one another may agree, such as the elements or the four seasons.

“The height of the firmament is its beauty, the appearance of heaven in a vision of glory” (Ecclesiasticus XLIII). The beauty of the firmament displays the Creator’s power through the brightness of the stars; yet more fully the beauty of the Church, in the virtues and miracles of the saints, makes known the excellence of the Redeemer, who illumines believers by his radiance and will punish sinners by the heat of judgment. Hence he adds:

“The sun, announcing in its rising, is a wondrous vessel,” etc.; “guarding a furnace in the works of burning heat” (ibid.), because it prepares the punishments of Gehenna for sinners.

“The sun, burning the mountains in three ways” (ibid.), because the eternal flame tortures the proud [Col. 0259C] for evil thought, speech, and action.

“And shining with its rays, it blinds the eyes” (ibid.), because by mystical words it confounds the understanding of the proud. Hence: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God” (Mark IV; Luke VIII).

“Great is the Lord who made him” (Ecclesiasticus XLIII): namely, the dispensation of the Incarnation, so that the proud might be confounded and the humble exalted by the knowledge of God.

“And the moon in all things in its season: an indication of time and a sign of the age” (ibid.). After discussing the sun, he discusses the moon, because the Church follows Christ and is illumined by him as the moon is by the sun. For the moon has no native brightness but receives it from the sun; so too does the Church from Christ. In persecution she seems [Col. 0259D] to diminish, but in peace she shines brightly, and at the consummation she will grow marvellously.

“A vessel of the camps on high, shining gloriously in the firmament of heaven” (ibid.), because in her consists the multitude of the faithful, who shine gloriously throughout the whole world in the firmament of truth and divine preaching.

“The beauty of heaven is the glory of the stars, illuminating the world on high: the Lord” (ibid.). The adornment of the Church is the multitude of saints, whom God Most High ordained to be illuminated through the preaching of the Gospel. These saints, abiding in the words—that is, in the teaching of the true faith—await God’s judgment.

“Look upon the rainbow and bless him who made it” (ibid.): namely, the writing of the New and Old Testaments. Hence: [Col. 0260A] “He bent his bow and made it ready” (Psalm VII). Here a sweet yoke is shown to the faithful, terrible weapons to the rebellious.

“It is exceedingly beautiful in its brightness” (Ecclesiasticus XLIII), because Scripture is exceedingly illustrious in its meaning.

“It has encircled heaven in the circuit of its glory” (ibid.), because it tells of things above and things below.

“The hands of the Most High opened it” (ibid.), when, through the power and wisdom of God in Christ, the Old and New Testaments were established. “By his command he hastened the snow” (ibid.), that is, he brought the cold to the brightness of righteousness.

“And he hastens to send out the lightnings of his judgment” (ibid.), that is, the terrors of judgment and the miracles of virtues.

[Col. 0260B] “And the stones of hail were broken” (ibid.). Teachers who water the earth of the human heart bear within themselves the storm of rebuke; they pour it out in due time and break the stones of hail, rebuking, that is, the hardness of a perverse heart lest they stone the life-giving seed.

“Let us praise glorious men and our fathers in their generation” (Ecclesiasticus XLIV). Because he has added many mysteries of the divine sacrament by discussing moral matters and touching in many places upon allegory and anagogy, he now begins to speak of the holy Fathers.

“Men great in virtue and endowed with prudence” (ibid.), because many of them were kings, abounding in knowledge and riches, yet for the greater part ruling themselves.

“All these attained glory [Col. 0260C] in the generations of their nation,” etc. (ibid.). In the historical sense, these words are understood of the patriarchs and prophets, whose seed—that is, the Israelites—was often delivered from straits because of their merits and promises. Thus Moses, praying for the people’s sins, recalls Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, so that God, appeased by their merits, might grant pardon to their sinning children. David’s merit preserved the kingdom for his children for a long time. But in a more sacred sense, the men of mercy are the apostles and preachers of the New Testament, who daily beget children of God through the word of the Gospel and the ministry of baptism. These children imitate their parents and follow their examples; their bodies rest in hope of resurrection, when the seed of good works will be repaid with a heavenly reward.

[Col. 0260D] “Enoch pleased God and was translated into Paradise, that he might give repentance to the nations” (ibid.). He did not begin to enumerate the fathers from Adam, who transgressed and was expelled from Paradise, but from 165 Enoch, who was translated into Paradise; for in this is displayed the election of the saints, who have passed from the misery of the age to the rest of the kingdom. He is believed to be coming at the end of the world in order to give all people counsel to repent.

“Noah was found perfect and righteous,” etc. (ibid.). When the world was perishing, he was preserved so that he might preach repentance to the nations and demonstrate by example that those who serve God devoutly are delivered from eternal destruction. God established a covenant with him that he would no longer destroy all flesh by the waters of the flood. He signifies rulers who, amid the waves of the age, [Col. 0261A] govern the ark—that is, God’s Church—and preach the baptism of repentance, appeasing God for humankind through prayers and sacrifices.

“Abraham, the great father of many nations,” etc. (ibid.): of many nations, namely, those believing in Christ, because children of the flesh are not reckoned in the seed. Abraham’s promise is twofold: in the sand of the sea are represented the barren people of the world; in the likeness of the stars, faithful Christians, who will shine with the light of resurrection like the stars of heaven.

“Phinehas, son of Eleazar, is third in glory” (Ecclesiasticus XLV). Phinehas son of Eleazar, as is written in the book of Numbers (chapter XXV), received from the Lord the covenant of peace because, in zeal for God, he killed an Israelite man and a Midianite woman engaged in fornication.

[Col. 0261B] This mystically signifies that one who, in zeal for God, kills the lust of his own flesh and that of those subject to him deserves from the Lord even the dignity of priesthood, and belongs to that priest of whom it is written: “You are a priest for ever,” etc. (Psalm CIX).

“Therefore he established for him a covenant of peace,” etc. (Ecclesiasticus XLV). This signifies that David, in his distribution of God’s ministers (I Chronicles XXIV), whom he divided into twenty-four lots so that they might minister to the Lord in turns, did not diminish Phinehas’s glory but increased it.

Hence in Chronicles: “Phinehas son of Eleazar was their leader before the Lord.”

Hence the Hebrews hand down that he was still living bodily and arranged the turns of the ministers of the tabernacle.

“Wisdom has built herself a house; she has cut out [Col. 0261C] seven pillars” (Proverbs IX). Hence: “Where is wisdom found, and what is the place of understanding? Man does not know its price, nor is it found in the land of those who live pleasantly” (Job XXVIII). “Behold, the fear of God is wisdom itself, and to depart from evil is prudence.” That it may appear clearly what wisdom built the house, one must distinguish among wisdoms. There is the wisdom of the world, the wisdom of the flesh, wisdom from above, and wisdom on high. Of the wisdom of the world the Apostle says: “The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (I Corinthians V).

Of the wisdom of the flesh he says likewise: “For the prudence of the flesh is death” (Romans VIII). Of wisdom from above it is said that it is “chaste and peaceable,” etc. (James III). Of wisdom on high it has been said that [Col. 0261D] “it reaches mightily from end to end and disposes all things sweetly” (Wisdom VIII).

The wisdom of the world lies in vanity; the wisdom of the flesh in pleasure; wisdom from above in truth; wisdom on high is truth, is eternity.

Therefore wisdom on high, which is God, built itself a house: namely, the Lord’s body, in which it dwelt bodily. There it cut out seven pillars, that is, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. For Christ, inasmuch as he is man, received the sevenfold Spirit not by measure but in fullness. Hence Isaiah: “The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding,” etc. (Isaiah XI). Again, “Wisdom has built herself a house,” [Col. 0262A] etc. (Proverbs IX): namely, the holy Church, in which she likewise cut out seven pillars, because the Church herself receives the sevenfold Spirit. Hence John: “And from his fullness we have all received” (John I). We may also say that wisdom built herself a house, namely, the Blessed Virgin, in whom she cut out seven pillars: the four cardinal virtues—prudence, temperance, fortitude, justice—and the three divine virtues, that is, faith, hope, and charity. But since we read, “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom,” in this house, that is, in the soul of the righteous, we can also find seven pillars: seven moral virtues, cut and marvellously polished there with much labour. The seven pillars, that is, the seven virtues, are charity, [Col. 0262B] humility, sobriety, chastity, obedience, discipline, and patience. And because all—that is, perfect—praise is sung at the end, let us join perseverance to these. These eight virtues, although each belongs to diverse persons, all together are proper to monks. Charity is the form of virtues; humility their seat or chair; sobriety their measure; chastity their adornment; obedience their charioteer; discipline their school; patience their shield; perseverance their crown.

Charity is the queen of virtues; humility their guardian; sobriety their handmaid; chastity their beauty; obedience their direction; discipline their correction; patience their testing; perseverance their completion. The Lord commends charity to us, saying: “No one has greater charity than this, that one lay down his life for his friends” [Col. 0262C] (John XV). He teaches humility, saying: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matthew XI). Of sobriety: “Be sober and watch,” etc. (I Peter V). Of chastity: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke XII). Of obedience: “Obedience is better than sacrifices” (I Kings XI). Of discipline: “Lay hold of discipline” (Psalm II), and: “He who rejects discipline is unhappy” (Proverbs XV). Of patience: “In your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke XXI). Of perseverance: “He who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matthew X and XXIV). Our place and food commend charity to us; the lowliness of our clothing, humility; the measure of food and drink, sobriety; sameness of sex enjoins chastity upon us; our mutual bowing suggests [Col. 0262D] obedience; our having teachers, discipline; our being as though mute through silence, patience; and our being enclosed by cloisters, perseverance. These things have been said briefly concerning virtues, because “the kingdom of God is not in word but in power” (I Corinthians IV); indeed, virtue and the kingdom of God are so joined that virtue itself is called the kingdom of God. Hence the Apostle says: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Romans XIV). And the Lord says: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke XVII). Virtue is the road; the kingdom of God is our homeland. Let us hold to the road so that we may arrive at our homeland. Let us eagerly undertake the citadel of virtues; let us swiftly run the way of the commandments, so that we may arrive happily [Col. 0263A] at our Creator, to whom be honour for ages of ages. Amen.

“How beautiful you are, and how lovely, dearest one, in delights!” (Song of Songs VII). This is the voice of Christ praising and admiring the beauty of the faithful soul. Therefore he does not say merely, “You are beautiful,” but says in admiration: “How beautiful you are!” There is a twofold beauty, natural and artificial: natural beauty comes from creation; artificial beauty from adornment. The soul was indeed created beautiful by God, but she herself has willingly defiled herself by heaping upon herself the dung of vices. Therefore, in order to recover her natural beauty, she must wash away the accumulated filth with worthy tears and fruits of repentance: first, that of deed; second, that of speech; third, that of heart. Purity of action consists in three things: that it may be [Col. 0263B] without iniquity, without softness, and without frivolity—innocent, clean, and serious.

Purity of speech is likewise threefold: that it may be without lying, without boasting, and without much speaking—truthful, humble, and restrained.

167 And purity of heart likewise consists in three things: in a right intention, which devises nothing wicked; in a steadfast affection, which admits nothing idle; and in a clean thought, which admits nothing foul. From the twofold purity, namely of deed and speech, the soul may be called beautiful by human beings—for it has glory among human beings, but not before God. But when purity of heart is present, how beautiful it will be called, not by human beings alone, but by Him who searches hearts. Yet, once the beauty of its native purity has been restored, it must display another adornment through every art and effort: that is, having acquired the colours of the virtues, it must adorn the soul and make for it a wedding-garment, so that, pleasing the Bridegroom by its form and beauty, it may deserve to hear, in the doubled proclamation of its praise: “How beautiful you are, and how lovely!” This beauty is brought about chiefly by charity, which is love for God and neighbour.

Love for God is threefold, because God is Trinity: with the whole heart, so that He alone may please the reason; with the whole soul, so that He alone may be sweet to the will; with the whole strength, so that He alone may draw it into desire for Himself. Love for one’s neighbour is twofold, because pride is twofold: first according to the soul, then according to the flesh; for those who love the flesh alone or the soul alone love neither.

[Col. 0263D] For both, those two precepts suffice: “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another”; and: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do likewise to them” (Matt. VII; Luke VI). In the one is innocence; in the other, beneficence. [Col. 0264A] Innocence means neither harming nor wishing to harm; beneficence means doing good if you can, and grieving if you cannot.

Thus you will deserve to hear: “How beautiful you are, and lovely!” But if you are also to be called most beloved, add something greater even than the virtues themselves: “Do not think highly of yourself, but fear” (Rom. XI). This is humility: the nurse of virtues, the glory of virtues, the life, name, and merit of virtues.

Without it, virtues are not worthy either to be called virtues or to be counted as virtues. Therefore, whoever you are, devout soul, attach it to yourself; attach yourself to it; have it as your companion, have it as your most beloved. And if by purity you are beloved, by charity more beloved, by humility you shall be most beloved. Or indeed, because there are three kinds of humility—submission to a superior, to an equal, and to an inferior—rightly is it called beloved in the first, more beloved in the second, and most beloved in the third, since it omits no rank.

Let us now come to delights: “Most beloved,” he says, “amid delights.” If blessed is the soul that shall eat the labour of its hands (Ps. CVII); that suffers poverty, mourning, and persecution for righteousness’ sake (Matt. V), what then of that soul which dwells amid delights, which abounds in delights, leaning upon its beloved?

Here too several degrees are to be observed. There is a soul that eats its bread in the sweat of its face, and that, though it has worked its land, does not receive its fruits, but has thorns and thistles spring up for it (Gen. III). There is also one that rejoices when it has done well and exults in the best things, saying: “It is good for me, Lord, that you humbled me, that I may learn your ordinances” (Ps. CXVIII). There is also to be found—rarely indeed, I confess—a soul for which to live is Christ and to die is gain (Phil. I), which glories in tribulations and rejoices that it is worthy to suffer insult for the name of Jesus. Why should I not say that such a soul is amid delights—indeed, that it abounds in them?

For the first is among thorns: it labours in its groaning, lamenting and saying, “I have become wretched and bowed down utterly; all day long I walked in sorrow” (Ps. XXXVII). The second [168] is among foods: it eats not without delight of that bread concerning which He Himself bears witness when He says, “My food is to do the will of my Father” (John IV). Great is the one that endures thorns; greater, the one that feeds upon the foods of its Father; but greatest of all [Col. 0264D] is the one that abounds in delights and is carried from delights to delights, through the co-operating grace of the Bridegroom, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0265]

## A Short Work of Master Alan of Lille, the Universal Doctor, on the Six Wings of the Cherubim

In it is contained a concise and sound doctrine concerning compunction, confession, satisfaction, love of God and neighbour, and so forth.

Now for the first time published complete from an ancient manuscript codex of the library of Saint Vedast at Arras.

## To the Reader

169 Do not be surprised, reader, if perhaps you have seen this short work—largely in part—printed on several occasions among the works of Saint Bonaventure, and now see it attributed to Alan. For that Alan is its true author is affirmed, besides by the most distinguished men Antonio Possevino in his *Sacred Apparatus*; Valerius Andreas in his *Belgian Library*; Antonius Sanderus in *Writers of Flanders*; and many other more recent writers, also by John Trithemius, an author most expert in knowledge of ancient writers. Indeed, its style strongly suggests it, and several very ancient manuscript copies clearly prove it, since they expressly bear Alan’s name [Note: [Col. 0265] Thomas Dempster, in his *History of Scotland*. Claude Doresmieulx, in a letter to me written on this matter.]. One of these, from the distinguished library of the nobleman P. M. Toussani Desbarbieuz of Lille, lord of Despretz, etc., was procured for me by Claude Doresmieulx of Arras, a most learned man, especially through his reading of ancient authors. On the other hand, no ancient copy has hitherto appeared bearing the name of Saint Bonaventure.

Thus, whoever has hitherto arranged for this short work to be printed together with the works of the same Saint Bonaventure has always noted that it was uncertain whether it was truly an authentic offspring of the Seraphic Doctor or of Alan. Witnesses to this are the two most exact editions of the works of that Seraphic Doctor: namely, the Roman Vatican edition prepared in 1587 by command of Sixtus V, and the Mainz edition of 1619. At the end of volume VII you will find this short work—although mutilated by almost a third—relegated to the series of uncertain works, under the following title: *Treatise on the Six Wings of the Cherubim. Yet it has been ascribed by some to Alan.* This is how the work is prefaced in all printed editions.

John Trithemius, however, in his catalogue *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, recognizes Alan of Lille as its author and entitles it *On the Six Wings of the Cherubim*. But whoever its author may be, it contains a brief and sound teaching on compunction, confession, satisfaction, purity of the flesh, purity of mind, and love of God and neighbour. So much there.

Moreover, I would have you know that this work has never before been printed complete, but always mutilated. For at the beginning of the work the author, having set forth an explicit image of a seraph, explains it clearly according to the vision of Isaiah VI, “I saw the Lord sitting,” etc., which he expounds learnedly and elegantly. Having supplied this exposition, he fittingly applies the whole subsequent work to the said image. This exposition—which comprises easily a third of the work—is missing from all printed copies; we restore it here from a very ancient manuscript codex, as mentioned above, from the library of Saint Vedast.

Furthermore, although, in view of the image of the seraph and its explanation according to Isaiah’s vision—in which only seraphim, and not cherubim, are mentioned—this little book might perhaps more suitably be entitled *On the Six Wings of the Seraphim*, nevertheless, because not only all printed copies, but also Trithemius and the ancient manuscript communicated to us, entitle it *On the Six Wings of the Cherubim*, we have retained the same title here. This is especially so because, at the end of the exposition so often mentioned, the author asserts that in composing the work he also had regard to the vision of the prophet Ezekiel, who speaks only of cherubim, with no mention of seraphim. Meanwhile, the book is good and useful, and therefore worthy of being printed again.

D. Charles de Visch, prior of the Dunes.

[Col. 0267]

## On the Six Wings of the Cherubim

[Col. 0269]

[Col. 0269A] 172–173 For the explanation of this figure, an examination of this authority seems necessary: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up” (Isa. VI). “High” is that which is situated on high; “lifted up,” that which has been transferred from lower things to higher. The high throne, therefore, is the angelic spirits; the lifted-up throne is the souls of the saints, transferred from the abyss of this world to the joys of heavenly peace. And because God presides over both, He is therefore said to sit upon a throne high and lifted up.

What is said in the following words, “The whole earth is full of His majesty” (ibid.), signifies by “earth” every bodily creature, which is full of God’s majesty, because the divine essence, just as it presides over spiritual creatures through thought, so fills bodily creatures by governing and ordering them. Thus what is elsewhere said, “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. XXIII), and again, “Heaven is my throne and earth the footstool of my feet” (Isa. LXVI), is here said: “I saw the Lord sitting,” etc.

“Those things which were beneath Him filled the temple” (Isa. VI). The temple is the receptive capacity of the intellect of angelic spirits and human beings; and this temple is filled by those things which are beneath God Himself, because the immensity of divine works is so great that no intelligence suffices perfectly to comprehend them. Consideration of them fills my heart; their immensity is not comprehended by my heart. How, then, shall we be able [Col. 0269C] to comprehend the maker of the work when we cannot fully grasp the work of the maker itself?

We may also say that this high and lifted-up throne upon which the Lord sits is the eternity of the Godhead, of which alone it is said: “Who inhabits eternity” (Isa. LVII). Not that God is one thing and His eternity another, but because the throne belongs to those who reign; and therefore He is rightly said to sit upon the throne of eternity, since, just as no beginning or end is found for His essence, so none is found for His omnipotence. He always was and was always almighty; He was always full and perfect in Himself and of Himself, and did not overflow beyond Himself.

He says, therefore: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up.” By the power of His divinity He precedes every creature and surpasses it in eternity and dignity; by His power He disposes all things. It follows: [Col. 0269D] “Those things which were beneath Him filled the temple.” Here may be understood the circuit of times and the course of ages: for times, as they return into themselves in their course, circumscribe a kind of enclosure of the temple by producing it. Thus the words, “Those things which were beneath Him,” are rightly understood to mean that all the times of the ages are full of God’s works, and every generation stands in awe of God’s wonders.

Or you may read it thus: “Those things which were beneath Him filled the temple”; that is, those things which filled the temple were beneath Him, because whatever turns in temporal course is found beneath eternity. For the immensity of eternity encloses temporal narrowness beneath itself: He is before time, who never began; He is after time, who knows no end; and He is above time, who admits no change.

“Seraphim stood above it” (Isa. VI). The two seraphim are the two Testaments. And fittingly the seraphim—which is interpreted “burning”—signify divine Scripture, which first illumines through knowledge those whom it afterwards causes to burn strongly through love; for one who does not burn does not set others aflame. For when it shows our mind what it ought to desire, it first illumines it and then [Col. 0270B] makes it burning.

It burns, therefore, because it makes others burn, just as elsewhere one is said to shine who illumines. Of this Scripture the apostle Peter says: “We have the more certain prophetic word, to which you do well to attend, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawn and the morning-star, the light, arise in your hearts” (II Pet. I). And perhaps, according to the likeness attributed there to Scripture in order to signify the effect which it produces in the hearts of its hearers, it is said: “Seraphim stood above it.” For it rises when it raises us; it walks when it makes us progress; it stands when it fixes us in blessed purpose.

But we must inquire why God is said to sit upon the throne, while the seraphim are reported not to sit but to stand above the throne. Since above we have interpreted this throne in three ways, we must adapt the exposition to each sense. If, then, we take God’s throne to be spiritual creatures, God is rightly described as sitting upon the throne, because the divinity of the Godhead is above all things and neither advances in power nor increases in wisdom, since neither fullness can be enlarged nor eternity changed.

But whenever the human mind has been illumined through knowledge of Scripture, it is raised up to contemplate heavenly things. If, transcending even the choirs of angels, it has progressed as far as the presence of its Creator, it ascends above the throne indeed, but stands and does not sit, because by laborious progress it comes to that place where it did not possess by nature the ability to remain. For standing belongs to one who labours, but sitting to a mind at rest.

But upon the throne of eternity none but God sits; we stand, because through grace we begin to be where He is by nature, nor can we reach that throne except through the labour of death. Yet although by our condition we are servants under obligation, by adoption we are made heirs of eternity.

[Col. 0271A] “Six wings to the one, and six wings to the other” (Isa. VI): that is, each had six wings. Each covered its own body with two wings, not the Lord’s: this is the first pair. Each extended two wings: one to cover the head—not its own but the Lord’s—and the other to cover the feet—not its own but the Lord’s: this is the second pair. Each flew with two wings, one toward the other: this is the third pair.

If, then, the seraphim signify sacred Scripture, the three pairs of wings are the three senses of that Scripture: history, allegory, and tropology. Each is twofold because each kindles readers’ souls toward love of God and neighbour. The two wings that cover the body of the seraphim are history, which conceals mystical meanings beneath the veil of the letter. The two wings that extend from the Lord’s head [Col. 0271B] down to His feet are allegory, because when we learn the mysteries of divine Scripture, we penetrate, through illumination of the mind, to knowledge of the Godhead itself, which is before all things.

But it should be known that the wings extended as far as the head also touch the feet, and, touching both, cover them; because whenever we are carried away in an ecstasy of mind to think upon His eternity, we find in Him neither beginning nor end. We extend wings to His body when we think that He was before all things; but with those same wings we veil His head from ourselves insofar as we find in Him no end. We also touch His head when we consider that He is after all things—not in time but in eternity; yet we touch His feet because, the more the human mind strives to investigate eternity, the more we marvel that He is incomprehensible.

The censers hanging on either side signify the prayers of contemplatives and of others engaged in active life, offered to the divine presence through the ministry of the holy angels. But what is written in Isaiah, “They veiled His face” (ibid.), and not His head, is to be understood in the same way as the words said to Moses: “You cannot see my face, for no human being shall see me and live” (Exod. XXXI). For this is the full knowledge of the Godhead, promised to the saints in eternal life, concerning which the Apostle says: “We shall see Him face to face” (I Cor. XIII); and again, “Then I shall know as I am known” (ibid.).

While we still live in this mortality, this knowledge is veiled and hidden; but in that eternity it is not veiled but revealed and manifest, as the Lord says in the Gospel concerning the good angels: “Their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVIII). Therefore, since it pertains to the present treatise that the face remain uncovered, we do not alter the words of prophecy but pass over them, so that, since it is true that no beginning is comprehended in God, the saying may stand: “Their angels always see the face of my Father.” We leave the face uncovered. All the other features said to be otherwise represented must likewise be referred not to the prophecy but to the picture.

“They flew with two wings” (Isa. VI). These two wings with which the seraphim flew signify tropology, because when through reading divine Scripture [Col. 0272A] we are instructed in good works, we are raised as it were on certain wings to the heights. With these we also fly “one toward the other” (ibid.), when we exhort one another to zeal in good works. And while flying we cry, “Holy, [175] holy,” if through our good works we strive to magnify not our own glory but that of our Father who is in heaven. For what is it to cry “Holy, holy,” except publicly to proclaim the glory of our creation that we have recognized inwardly?

It remains, now that we have shown what is meant by the Lord’s head and feet being read as hidden, to demonstrate what should be thought about the rest of the body. If, then, we say that God’s head is what was before the foundation of the world, and His feet what will be after the establishment of this age, then by the length of His body we rightly understand the intervening space of time between beginning and end. The head and feet, therefore, are covered because we cannot investigate first and last things; the body appears because we see what is done in the middle, in this present age.

This body is the Church, which began from the beginning of the world and will endure until the end of the age. This is the ark that extends from head to feet, because from beginning to end the holy Church extends itself through the succession of generations, so that it may bring forth the complete—not diminished—body of the Lord. For if it were already complete, as the Apostle says, the end of the world would already be at hand.

But it should be known that, just as in the person of a human being some things are around the feet and are neither in the body nor of the body, while other things are in the body yet are not of the body, so it is also in the body of Christ—that is, the Church—which dwells in the midst of a perverse nation. While it receives the assaults of unbelievers, the ark is battered from without, as it were by stormy waves; while it suffers tribulation from false brethren, the body is tormented within, as it were by harmful humours. Whatever is hostile to the body, therefore, whether within or without, is not of the body.

But the Lord’s arms embrace all things on either side, signifying that all things are under His power, and that no one can escape His hand—His right hand for reward or His left for condemnation. Why, then, should the members be further anxious about the safety [Col. 0272D] of the body, when they have known such power in the head? He knows what benefits His body: through compassion He feels its danger, and through power He prepares its remedy. He who makes a way in the sea also knows how in many ways to guide His body—that is, the Church—like an ark in the flood. This is Christ: both helmsman and harbour. Amid the storms of this life, He guides the ark, or Church, which is His body, through the middle, by Himself, unto Himself.

But that this model may be clearer to you, I have depicted the whole person of Christ—that is, the head together with the members—in visible form, so that when you see the whole, you may more easily understand what is said about the invisible part. I wish to represent to you here such a person as Isaiah testified that he saw (ibid.), so that the person placed before your eyes may correspond with the exposition of the authority. And lest we exceed the bounds of so great a subject, let it suffice for the writer, if not for the hearer, to have recalled these things concerning the feet of Him who sits upon the high throne, which the seraphim covered with two wings. Beginning from the face of the One sitting, he proceeded by the middle, with the way as guide, as far as the feet, according to the visions of Isaiah and Ezekiel.

### The First Feather of the First Wing

The first wing is confession—not confession of praise, whence: “Confess to the Lord, for He is good, for His mercy endures for ever” (Ps. CXVII), but confession of sin, whence: “Confess your sins to one another” (Jas. V). This confession is an accusatory disclosure of sin. It is a sorrowful recounting, under the pricking of conscience, of one’s own weakness, ignorance, and wickedness.
