[Col. 0273B] The first feather of this wing is truth, which excludes every pretence; for confession ought to be true, not feigned or simulated.

### The Second Feather of the First Wing

The second feather is completeness, which excludes curtailment and division. Confession ought to be complete, not curtailed or divided. Curtailment conceals something: it keeps back something which one regrets having committed, yet not altogether; it retains something in which one takes pleasure. But it is the impiety of unbelief to hope for a diminished pardon from Him who is just and is justice. And one wound is enough for death.

Division, however, reveals everything, but not to one person. For there are some, as blessed Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0273] Book *On True and False Penance*, chapter 15, vol. IV.], who altogether repent of having sinned but, led by shame, divide their confession among themselves: they wish to confess different matters to different priests, and keep what they conceal from one in reserve to disclose to another. This is in a certain way to praise oneself, to tend toward hypocrisy, and always to lack the pardon which they think they find in fragments.

Therefore everything, and especially grave sins, must be disclosed in confession to one person; nor are evil actions alone to be disclosed, but also their circumstances—that is, place, time, manner, number, person, and anything similar. These are not to be carelessly suppressed but diligently explained in confession. For there is great difference between one place and another, one time and another, one manner and another, one person and another.

[Col. 0273D] Persistence in a habit, which pertains to time, and multiplication in number exasperate God’s patience—which calls to repentance—and provoke divine vengeance against themselves. With respect to the person, sex, age, knowledge, condition, relationship, and rank must be carefully weighed and expressly disclosed. Therefore one who confesses should dwell upon each of these matters.

### The Third Feather of the First Wing

The third feather is firmness, because confession ought to be strong and firm. This firmness drives out ten things that impede confession. What are they? Shame, fear, contempt for the priest, despair, presumption, perversity, ignorance, forgetfulness, negligence, and necessity—the last alone excusable.

Against shame, the virtue of courage should resist manfully, considering the necessity arising from the danger that threatens unless sins are disclosed. The fruit of patience should drive out the fear inspired by the penance to be imposed. Reverence, veneration, and the love owed to Christ’s representative should utterly remove contempt for the priest. The kindness of divine mercy should exclude despair; the strict severity of divine justice should uproot presumption.

Reason should extirpate perversity of faith. Prudence should avoid ignorance. Diligent examination and recollection of one’s conduct and actions should illuminate the darkness of forgetfulness. Fervour of spirit should tear out and destroy torpor and the lukewarmness of negligence. And no negligence whatsoever should anticipate necessity.

### The Fourth Feather of the First Wing

The fourth feather is humility, which excludes the pattern of pride (Prov. III). The mind, tongue, and countenance of one confessing ought to be humble. “For the Lord resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. IV).

### The Fifth Feather of the First Wing

The fifth feather is simplicity. It accuses one’s own weakness, one’s own ignorance, and one’s own wickedness, defending nothing, excusing nothing, diminishing nothing. Therefore confession ought to be true, complete, firm, humble, and [Col. 0274C] simple: true, without pretence; complete, without diminution; firm, without wavering, hesitation, or despair; humble, without boasting or presumption; simple, without comparison with another, excuse, or defence. This is the first wing with its feathers.

## The Second Wing

Satisfaction follows confession. Compunction creates and forms these first two wings. For in every act of penance these three are proved necessary: compunction, [177] confession, and satisfaction. Compunction disturbs; confession accuses; satisfaction strengthens. Compunction investigates the cause of illness; confession makes it manifest; satisfaction heals. Compunction enumerates evils; confession condemns them; satisfaction amends them. Compunction pricks the abscess; confession presses out the pus; satisfaction applies the poultice. Compunction finds the wound; confession opens it; satisfaction restores health.

Compunction is contrition of heart, or a pain of the spirit that binds up what has been broken; it is a bitterness of soul that gathers together what has been divided; and it generates the sweetness of wondrous sweetness. It is written: “Rend your hearts and not your garments” (Joel II); and elsewhere: “Be pierced with compunction in your beds” (Ps. IV).

A twofold cause produces compunction: fear and hope. Fear is the initiating cause; hope the completing cause. Fear carefully reckons how wonderfully a human being has been created by the Creator, how freely sustained, how upright in substance and enriched with reason in the very act of creation; it reckons also all the other goods the Creator has bestowed upon him, and what evils he has himself returned for those goods. It also sets forth the strict Judge and the threats of punishments; it strikes the mind with horror at penalties, confounds it with shame, rebukes unlawful impulses, and disturbs the repose of harmful security.

Thus fear, examining the degree and number of faults and considering the severity of divine justice and the strictness of the future judgment, pricks the mind and, by pricking it, expels sin. Whence does fear have this expulsive power? Hope, which strengthens, grants and reinforces it.

For vain is the fear that confidence does not make firm. Those who fear God lack nothing; if hope is absent, no good is present. It is written: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you!” (Ps. XXX). Yet it will not be bestowed unless hope presents it. Contrition of heart, therefore, comes from fear; but the fruit of labour comes from hope.

But whence comes hope’s strengthening power? From the divine promise. Hear Scripture: “Hope in the Lord, and you shall be fed in His riches” (Ps. XXXVI). Again: “Hope in Him, and He Himself will act” (ibid.). Again: “The Lord does not abandon those who hope in Him” (Judith XIII). Again: “Blessed are all who trust in Him” (Ps. II).

Therefore, if you fear in order to be moved to compunction, hope in the Lord in order to be reconciled to Him. If you fear God because He can destroy in Gehenna, hope in Him because [Col. 0275C] He does not will the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live (Ezek. XXVIII). If you fear because, being wise, He knows the hidden things of the heart (Ps. XLIII), hope because He will bring to light the hidden things of darkness (I Cor. IV). If you fear because He leaves nothing unpunished, hope because He will redeem Israel from all its iniquities (Ps. CXXIX).

Therefore, just as fear precedes and accompanies the power of compunction, so hope advances it and brings it to the fruit of reconciliation. Through fear, then, compunction is aroused; through hope, the grace of desired reconciliation is merited. “In whatever hour he groans, he shall be saved” (Ezek. XXXIII). Yet fear produces the groaning; hope merits salvation. What compunction of heart is, whence it comes, and for what end it exists has now been briefly explained. Let us now briefly discuss satisfaction, which is the second wing.

## On Satisfaction: The Second Wing

Satisfaction is the complete performance of the penance imposed, or the fitting chastisement and correction of sins.

For the measure of chastisement or correction must be weighed according to the quality or quantity of the offence. “Produce,” he says, “fruits worthy of repentance” (Matt. III; Luke III). For repentance is one thing and the fruit of repentance another, just as a tree is one thing and its fruit another. Repentance is sorrow for the past, when you grieve that you have done what is evil.

When, therefore, you disapprove and condemn your evils, you have repentance. But when, by the satisfaction that follows, [Col. 0276A] you punish and correct your evils, you have the fruit of repentance. If what you have done displeases you, you repent; but if you pursue and punish what you have done, you produce the fruit of repentance. Repentance is disapproval of the deed; the fruit of repentance is correction of the offence.

But because the measure of correction must be weighed by the measure of the offence, fruits worthy of repentance must be produced. If the affliction in correction is less than the pleasure was in sin, the fruit of your repentance is not worthy. But you say to me: “How can I know when my penance is proportionate?” Because you cannot know this, you must always repent. You can make satisfaction; you cannot do too much. It is better to do more than less. Therefore be diligent, labour, make every effort, devote yourself, apply zeal, [Col. 0276B] so that guilt may have an end but devotion no end.

Nevertheless, so that a sinful conscience may at some point be consoled, a limit and measure have been established for outward penance: when this has been completed or fulfilled, you may begin to have confidence and, with a sound kind of assurance, hope in divine mercy and trust in the pardon and remission of sins. And this is truer in proportion as you have more sincerely completed the penance imposed.

### The First Feather of the Second Wing

The first feather of this wing is renunciation of sin, which closes the door against the devil. To renounce sins is to turn away from evil. “Turn away,” he says, “from evil” (Ps. XXXVI). From what evil? From the evil of vanity, the evil of iniquity, the evil of malice, and the evil of impiety.

“I have not sat,” says the Psalmist, “with the council of vanity, and I shall not enter in with those who work iniquity; I have hated the assembly of the malicious, and I shall not sit with the impious” (Ps. XXV). These four vices generate four affections: self-love, love of the world, hatred of one’s brother, and slackened love of God. The first affection generates vanity; the second, iniquity; the third, malice; the fourth, impiety. Vanity turns back upon oneself; iniquity is directed against one’s neighbour; malice is bent against one’s brother; impiety extends toward God.

Vain and foolish is the person who seeks what is his own; unjust is the one who, so as to glory in the abundance of his riches and fill the sack of avarice, deceitfully acquires what belongs to neighbours; malicious is the one who desires to do harm even when he cannot; impious is the one who either does not believe in God or, if he believes, despises Him.

[Col. 0276D] The second feather is the outpouring of tears. This washes and cleanses the wounds of sins.

The third feather is mortification of the flesh. This wipes and dries the wounds once washed.

The fourth feather is generous almsgiving. This binds up what is broken, strengthens what is fractured, and heals all things.

The fifth feather is devotion in prayer. This preserves what has been healed.

## The Third Wing

The third wing is purity of the flesh. Flesh is pure when no lust defiles it; lust uproots the shoots of every virtue.

The first feather of this wing is modesty of sight. This excludes wantonness. It circumcises the eye, lest it covet what belongs to another, lest it look upon a woman in order to desire her. For the one whose gaze wanders lasciviously and inquisitively over women’s forms is unchaste in mind as well.

The second feather is chastity of hearing. Chaste ears are those that do not admit the voice of a detractor, do not listen to the words of the slanderer and blasphemer, give no aid to false accusations, lying, provocation, indecent songs, and theatrical entertainments; they are closed lest they hear a judgment of blood, receive nothing obscene, and turn away from every mire of corruption.

The third feather is moderation of smell. If anyone takes in a good fragrance and seeks the fragrance of sweetness through works of mercy, that person’s sense of smell is moderate. But the one who walks about anointed with the finest perfumes has a sense of smell that breathes not the fragrance of virtue but of stench; for the fragrance of such sweetness is the stench of a most monstrous vice.

The fourth feather is temperance of taste. This overthrows the excess of gluttony and drunkenness. “Woe to those whose god is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who savour earthly things” (Phil. III). Hence Gregory says: “When the belly is not restrained from fullness, through the lust of the flesh all virtues together are overwhelmed.” Hence it is read (IV Kings XXV) that the chief of the cooks destroyed the walls of Jerusalem: the chief of the cooks destroyed Jerusalem’s walls because, when indulgence is granted to the belly, the virtues [179] of the soul are endangered.

Concerning surfeit and drunkenness the Lord says: “Take heed lest perhaps your hearts be weighed down with surfeit and drunkenness, and that sudden day come upon you” (Luke XXI). Drunkenness is the parent of quarrels, the mother of fury, and the shameful teacher of wantonness. Whoever has it does not possess himself; whoever has it is not a human being; whoever has it does not commit sin, but is himself sin. Drunkenness is a pleasing demon, sweet poison, voluntary madness, a seductive injury to honour and modesty. No Christian should know it.

The fifth feather is holiness of touch. Let not the Christian’s hand handle the filth of sin; let his flesh touch nothing unclean—if it touches it, it will be unclean. If the individual members serve in the offices of God’s commandments [Col. 0277D], they are to be called clean; but if they luxuriate beyond the laws prescribed or divinely given, they are to be called, or accounted, unclean; and these things are shameful. And this, I think, is what the Apostle says: “For just as you presented your members to serve iniquity unto iniquity, so now present your members to serve righteousness unto sanctification” (Rom. VI). Therefore let the eye be modest, the ear chaste, the sense of smell restrained, the taste sober, and the touch holy.

Fourth wing.

The fourth wing is purity of mind. The first feather of this wing is the rightness of sincere affection. Let the affection of your desire be upright and sincere. It will be upright if you seek what you ought to seek; sincere, moreover, if you seek it in the manner urged by the virtue of honourableness. Amnon loved his sister [Col. 0278A] (II Kings XIII); the affection of his love was upright, but because he did not love his sister as he ought, that affection was not sincere.

The second feather is the mind’s delight in the Lord. It is written: “Delight yourself in the Lord, and he will give you the desires of your heart” (Ps. XXXVI). The virtue of contemplation creates and shapes this feather. Of it the Lord says: “Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke X).

The third feather is clean and ordered thought. Let the mind conceive nothing unclean; but let discretion also adapt a clean conception to place and time.

The fourth feather is holiness of will. The angels [Col. 0278B] brought down from heaven peace to people of good will. “There is no peace for the wicked,” says the Lord (Isa. XLVIII). “Great peace have those who love your law, and for them there is no stumbling-block” (Ps. XI). O how desirable is the name of peace! How it establishes the firm foundation of the Christian religion. Thus, when it was said, “Glory to God in the highest,” there was rightly added, “and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II). For the angels hasten to have fellowship with those in whose minds they perceive the purity of good will to reside. After their release from the flesh, they rejoice to bear with themselves to the contemplation of true peace those whom, while dwelling in the flesh, they see bringing forth from the root of good will all that they do or say. For such persons, even if weakness perhaps sometimes [Col. 0278C] or ignorance delays them from accomplishing the good work they desire, are nevertheless excused before the eyes of the supreme Judge by the integrity of good will which they hold in their hearts.

The fifth feather is a simple and pure intention. Of this the Lord says: “If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light” (Matt. VI). By “eye” he signifies intention, by “body,” action. For this passage of the Gospel must be understood thus: all our works are then clean and pleasing in God’s sight if they are done with a single heart—that is, with a heavenly intention, or the eye of charity—because “charity is the fulfilment of the law” (Rom. XIII). Therefore we must here understand the eye to be intention itself, [Col. 0278D] by which we do whatever we do. If it is simple and pure, and looks upon what ought to be looked upon, all the works which we perform according to it must be good. He called all these works “the whole body,” just as the Apostle calls certain works which he disapproves “members,” and commands them to be put to death: “Put to death therefore your members which are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, avarice” (Col. III), and other evils of this kind. Therefore one must consider not what a person does, but with what intention he does it; for the entire fruit of a work consists in the simplicity of intention. Whatever, then, our thought suggests ought to be done, let us reconsider it without any scruple and place it in the balance of our breast; let us weigh it with an even and most just [Col. 0279A] weighing: whether it is full of common honourableness; whether it has weight through the fear of God; whether it is sound in meaning; whether it is light through human display or some presumption of the will; whether empty vainglory has diminished its weight of merit, or glory has smiled upon it. And thus, having weighed it for public examination—that is, having compared it with the deeds and testimonies of the prophets and apostles—let us either retain it as whole and perfect, worthy of recompense, or reject it, with every caution and diligence, as imperfect and harmful, not corresponding to their weight.

Fifth wing.

The fifth wing is love of neighbour. Its first feather is to harm no one by word or deed. Of this it is written: “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another” [Col. 0279B] (Matt. VII). The virtue of innocence forms this feather. Innocent is one who, even when able, wishes to harm no one. “Who,” he says, “shall ascend the mountain of the Lord? He who is innocent in hands,” etc. (Ps. XXIII). Who is innocent in hands? One who has done no evil to his neighbour. “The malignant one has been brought to nothing in his sight” (ibid.). Who is this malignant one but the devil? Whoever wishes to harm no one has already felt the first stirring of love, time being set aside.

The second feather is to benefit everyone, by word and deed. “A brother helping a brother is a fortified and strong city” (Prov. XVIII). The virtue of mercy raises this feather and advances it to the summit of perfection. “Blessed,” he says, “are the merciful” (Matt. V). Whoever strives to benefit all breathes the living warmth [Col. 0279C] of true love.

The third feather is not merely not to grieve over losses incurred through things spent for a friend, but, with the strength of true liberality, not even to feel them; and always to rejoice in one’s heart at the magnitude of benefits bestowed for the use of one’s brethren. Whoever feels it is an accountant, not a giver; whoever does not rejoice grieves. Of this feather it is written: “He who disregards loss for a friend is righteous; but the way of the greedy will deceive him” (Prov. XII).

[Col. 0280A] In this, understand “friend” as the friend of love.

The fourth feather is to lay down one’s life for a brother. What is it to lay down one’s life for a brother? Even for a neighbour’s temporal safety, to abandon one’s own will; and, in a moment of necessity, willingly to undergo the hazards of death for a brother’s eternal salvation. Of this it is written: “No one has greater love than this: that he lay down his life for his friends” (John XV). No greater ardour of love can boil forth.

The fifth feather is to persevere in these things. The virtue of perseverance brings it to completion. The end, not the struggle, crowns. Whoever perseveres does not know how to cease.

Sixth wing.

The sixth wing is love of God. This, like the others, has five feathers.

[Col. 0280B] He has its first feather who desires nothing other than God. This is the motive force of this love.

He has the second feather who distributes his possessions for God’s sake, retaining one part but giving another. This is the warmth of this love.

He has the third feather who reserves nothing for himself for God’s sake, but leaves everything behind. This is the keenness of this love.

He has the fourth feather who denies himself for God’s sake. He denies himself who abandons his own will, so as to do the Lord’s will alone. This is the fervour of this love.

He has the fifth feather who perseveres in these things. For “he who perseveres unto the end shall be saved” (Matt. X). This is the unceasing quality of this love.

[Col. 0280C] These are the wings of which the Psalmist says: “Protect me under the shadow of your wings, from the face of the wicked who have afflicted me” (Ps. XVI). Likewise: “I shall hope in the shadow of your wings until iniquity passes away” (Ps. LVI). These are the feathers of which the same Psalmist says: “Who will give me feathers like a dove’s, that I may fly and be at rest?” (Ps. LIV). “I shall fly,” he says, abandoning earthly things and seeking heavenly things; “and I shall rest” in true freedom, enjoying eternal blessedness. Amen.

[Col. 0279]

THE PENITENTIAL BOOK OF MASTER ALAN OF LILLE, OR A METHOD FOR WORTHILY ADMINISTERING AND RECEIVING THE SACRAMENT OF PENANCE.

PREFACE TO THE READER.

181 John Trithemius, in his Book on Writers, Antonio Possevino in the *Apparatus Sacer*, and many others, when cataloguing the works of Master Alan of Lille, list among them Four Books on Penance, addressed to the people of Bourges [Col. 0281], whose opening is: “By the grace of God, to the church of Bourges,” etc. They make no mention, however, of this book. Yet I was unable to discover that former work, though I diligently sought it through the more celebrated libraries of all Belgium, and also some of foreign provinces. This present work, on the other hand—also distinguished by the author’s name—I found in several places. First, the catalogue of the library of the distinguished George Colvenerius, recently chief professor of sacred theology at the renowned University of Douai, testifies that it contains this work; this catalogue, recently sent to me, will shortly be printed in the third part of the manuscript Belgian library of Antony Sander, canon of Ypres. [Note: [Col. 0281] John Bunderius, in his indexes of Belgian manuscripts, etc., testifies that he found this little book in many libraries, in different copies, entitled *The Corrector and the Physician*.]

I found another copy in our own library at Dunes, a very ancient manuscript written on parchment. A third, from the library of Saint-Ghislain, of the Order of Saint Benedict in Hainaut, was most graciously sent to me, with the permission of its abbot, by the Reverend Simon Guillemot, librarian of that monastery. It is plainly extremely old and nevertheless agrees in every respect with our Dunes copy, except for a few words here and there which I noted in the margins.

182 Moreover, whether Alan first wrote this little work and later enlarged it, or composed another work wholly different from this one which he dedicated to the Archbishop of Bourges, I do not know. Meanwhile, for the instruction of confessors and penitents, I considered it worthwhile to publish this little work, adding in the margins the places in Holy Scripture whose statements it cites. For it contains a good and concise method for worthily administering and receiving the sacrament of penance, and is therefore, in the judgment of very learned men, worthy of publication. Yet I wished to warn the reader concerning this: when Master Alan treats of the circumstances of sins that must be explained in confession, he follows the opinion which maintains that aggravating circumstances within the same species must be confessed, even when they do not greatly aggravate it. Although modern practice now almost universally follows the contrary view, very many ancient authors formerly taught Alan’s opinion; and not a few more recent writers, men of most distinguished learning, still defend it. Diana cites them in considerable number, Part I, Treatise VI, Resolution I. Indeed, the very learned Franciscus Sylvius, in his commentary on Question 9 of the Supplement to Saint Thomas, article 2, question 1, while treating this subject, demonstrates well that it is sometimes useful in confession to state not only aggravating circumstances but also mitigating ones. Read him, and you will not be surprised if you find similar things in our Alan.

Brother Carolus de Visch, of Dunes.

ANAGRAM.

ALANUS:—“Washing.”

He who teaches that sins are to be WASHED  
by tears poured forth  
rightly deserves the name of a WASHER.

THE PENITENTIAL BOOK BEGINS.

[Col. 0281A] 183 “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God, for I am a child and do not know how to speak” (Jer. I). If Jeremiah, sanctified from the womb, chosen by the Lord as a prophet, free from the stain of grave sin, instructed by divine inspiration, fearing to undertake the office of preaching and to sound forth God’s words, confessed [Note: [Col. 0281] “Professed.”] himself to be a child, confessed himself to be tongue-tied: how do people of our own time, unclean from the womb, rejected by the Lord, entangled in knots of grave sins, deserted by divine visitation, dare to ascend the height of the priesthood and stammer out heavenly mysteries, when they are not merely infants in wisdom and childish in understanding, but old men in folly? When they are not merely tongue-tied in preaching, but mute in speaking? [Note: [Col. 0281] Another copy here inserts the following: “If Jeremiah, a child in malice, shrank from the burden of preaching, how does a priest, a child in knowledge, seize upon the honour of the priesthood?”] If Jeremiah, who was eloquent, confesses himself mute for preaching God, how does a mute priest [Col. 0281B] profess [Note: [Col. 0281] “Confesses.”] himself eloquent for speaking about God?

The priests of our day are old men and children, [Col. 0282A] of whom it is said: “Cursed is the old man still learning his letters.” [Note: [Col. 0281] Seneca, Book V, Epistle.] And elsewhere: “Cursed is the child a hundred years old” [Note: [Col. 0281] The scriptural text has: “He shall die as cursed.”] (Isa. LXV). They are old in the foolishness of their conduct, children in wantonness; old in weakness of spirit, children in instability of spirit; old through lack of divine heat, children through the effect of adulterous heat. If poverty drives such men to orders, the Church’s need constrains them, or the authority of superiors compels them, let them cry “Ah,” because poverty drives them; let them cry “Ah,” because the Church’s need constrains them; let them cry “Ah,” because the authority of superiors compels them. Let them first endure poverty’s assault rather than rashly undertake the burden of the priesthood. Yet if necessity presses and a superior’s authority reasonably enjoins it, let them prepare themselves as persons worthy of orders and suitably adorn themselves [Col. 0282B] with worthy morals [Note: [Col. 0281] “Adorn.”], so that they may receive the burden of priesthood while rendering honour to its honour. Reckoning themselves unworthy, let them cry with Jeremiah: [Col. 0283A] “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God, for we are children and do not know how to speak”—children in understanding, tongue-tied in speaking, lame in acting.

Some priests are tongue-tied, others silent, others mute.—And indeed, some of our priests are tongue-tied, some silent, some mute. Those are tongue-tied who form words badly: they are priests who preach divine matters but turn the force of their preaching toward the gain of earthly things. Those are silent who speak rarely: they are priests from whom heavenly mysteries are preached too seldom, held back either by negligence, diverted by love, or repelled by fear. Negligence makes them sluggish, love foolish, fear faint-hearted. Those are mute who either do not know how to preach or disdain to know. Of them [Col. 0283B] it is said: “Woe to you, mute dogs unable to bark” (Isa. LVI). Unable because you do not know; unwilling because you disdain. Let all these cry: “Ah, ah, ah,” because they are weak for acting, frail for knowing, lukewarm for loving. For these three miseries belong to priests; these three weaknesses assail such priests: inability to act well, ignorance in knowing, and negligence in loving God.

Walls between God and priests are inability, ignorance, and negligence.—The wall of inability is pierced in four ways.—The same concerning the wall of ignorance.—The wall of negligence too is pierced in four ways.—The aforesaid walls are sometimes wholly destroyed.—These [Col. 0283C] three walls are set between priests and God, so that they cannot see God through knowledge, cannot advance to God through good action, and cannot reach God through charity. Some are shut up enclosed by these three walls, and pierce the same walls; some destroy the walls completely; some rise above them by a heavenly ladder. Those are hindered by these walls who are delayed from good action by inability, impeded from knowing God by ignorance, and checked from loving God by negligence. These, bound hand and foot, will be cast into outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matt. XXII). Some pierce the walls because they strive to weaken weakness, drive out ignorance’s darkness, and shake off negligence’s torpor. [Col. 0283D] These pierce the wall of inability with a fourfold engine and make four windows in it: through giving alms, the austerity of fasts, the continuance of vigils, and devotion in prayer. As if through four windows, they thus look toward God so that he may look upon them; thus pray to God so that God may hear them; thus come to him so that he may come to them. Of these windows one reads in the Song of Love: “Behold, the bridegroom stands behind the wall, looking through the windows, gazing through the lattice” (Song II). Yet these windows are sometimes blocked by the *allophyli*, that is, foreigners: the aforesaid works through which we look toward [Col. 0284A] God are hindered by vices—avarice uproots almsgiving, gluttony fasting, drowsiness vigils, and sloth prayer. In the second wall, namely that of ignorance, there are four windows: God is known through creatures, for “through the things that have been made, the invisible things of God are understood” (Rom. I); reason is moved to understand God [Note: [Col. 0283] The Dunes copy has: “to understand divine things.”]; a person is inspired [Note: [Col. 0283] “enlightened.”] by divine inspiration; and Holy Scripture is investigated. When people seek God by this fourfold inquiry, they look upon him as if through four windows. But these windows are frequently blocked: when the Creator is not read in creatures; when a person is deserted by divine enlightenment [Note: [Col. 0283] “visitation.”]; when reason is enslaved to sensuality; and when Holy Scripture is despised. The third wall, namely [Col. 0284B] that of negligence, is furnished with a fourfold opening: when we love God above ourselves, our neighbour beside ourselves, our body below ourselves, and our soul within ourselves. But we block these windows when we put God second, neglect ourselves, despise our neighbours, and nourish our bodies too delicately. Those who have already been received into eternal dwellings and live eternally wholly destroy the aforesaid walls: they are neither bowed down by inability, darkened by ignorance [Note: [Col. 0283] “obscured.”], nor slackened by negligence in charity.

Some rise above these walls.—But those rise above these walls by a heavenly ladder who, although placed in the flesh, are endowed with sevenfold grace and attain divine contemplation, where there is power in inner action, knowledge in contemplation, and charity in devotion. These walls hinder our priests, block their way, impede their sight, and frustrate their intention.

Priests are compared with children.—Therefore let our priests cry: “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God, we do not know how to speak, because we are children and do not know how to use more solid food.” For these three human weaknesses attend childhood: children cannot walk, stammer in speaking, and cannot use solid food. Thus our priests are children in this: in walking—that is, in acting well—they either move backwards when they look behind, that is, to earthly things; or stumble at the scandal of grave sins; or rush into the abyss of obstinacy. They do not know how to speak [Col. 0284D], because they either utter foolish things, commend earthly matters more than heavenly ones, keep true things silent [Note: [Col. 0283] “Dissemble.”], or remain wholly silent.

The Lord’s Body is wholesome food for some, unwholesome for others.—They cannot use more solid food because they are weak in swallowing or chewing. The solid food of the mature is the Lord’s Body; it kills children in understanding but gives life to those who have advanced; for the gravely ill it brings ruin, for the healthy it safeguards health. Yet this food is medicine for the ill if received with the caution of due reflection, so that one sick through guilt may be led [Note: [Col. 0283] “may be troubled.”] to repentance [Col. 0285A] and promise obedience to the heavenly physician, in order to avoid the disease. The same food is refreshment for the healthy—that is, advancement for the righteous. Thus our priests are comparable to children because, just as children cannot use solid food because their hands are too weak to hold, their mouths to eat, and their stomachs to receive, so priests have hands too weak to handle heavenly food: hands 185 which they unjustly stretch out toward money they then extend toward the Eucharist; hands with which they touch unlawful things they employ in handling the divine mysteries.

They also have mouths weak and unclean for receiving heavenly food. For it is unworthy that the mouth which is choked by the gluttony of many foods should be filled with heavenly bread. It is surely unworthy that truth should enter [Col. 0285B] a mouth through which falsehood is belched forth. The stomach of the mind, filled by appetite for earthly things, rejects heavenly provisions; and the mind that embraces earthly food rejects [Note: [Col. 0285] “disdains.”] the heavenly viaticum. Therefore the aforesaid cry of lamentation comes upon the evil priest: “Ah, ah, ah,” etc.; but the cry of exultation rejoices with the good priest: “Well done, good and faithful servant: because you have been faithful over a few things, dispensing wisdom, I shall set you over many things,” loving God (Matt. XXV). But on the day of judgment that fearful and dreadful cry will come upon evil priests: “Woe, woe, woe, because we were children and did not know how to speak.” And indeed, they did not know how to speak in preaching, twisting preaching toward earthly things. They did not know how to speak in prayer, praying for improper things; they did not know how to speak in counselling their subjects, saying unsuitable things [Note: [Col. 0285] “improper things.”]. For those whom they ought to cleanse from vices they defile further through bad counsel; those whom they ought to raise to heavenly things they bend further toward earthly things; those whom they ought to heal they wound more deeply.

Priests are spiritual physicians.—A sinner is a spiritual patient.—How he is to be led to confession.—For a priest ought to perform the role of a spiritual physician, and a subject the role of a spiritual patient. Just as a bodily physician who approaches a sick person first soothes the patient with words, sympathizes with the sick person, adapts himself to the infirm person, speaks kindly, and promises health, so that the patient may confidently disclose the extent of the illness and the sharpness of the pain; and, having learned [Col. 0285D] the extent of the illness and sharpness of pain, then inquires when the disease began, the place where it seized the patient, and the patient’s age. He also investigates the cause and origin of the illness, the duration of the illness, the habit of life tending to reduce it [Note: [Col. 0285] “habit of life.”], the person’s condition, the force of the pulse, the bearing of the body, and the appearance of the face. When the circumstances of the illness and the accidents of infirmity are well known, the physician, according to the extent of the disease, makes the diet more or less strict, forbids some foods, and prescribes others; [Col. 0286A] he threatens the patient with worse things unless he observes what is imposed, and then cures opposites by opposites. So a priest, as a spiritual physician, when a sinner who is a spiritual patient comes to him, ought first to draw the sinner with words and soothe him with gentle encouragement, so that he may more readily disclose the illness, disclose the sin; and then, after the sin has been revealed, having first set forth words of encouragement, may more effectively add words concerning satisfaction. He should warn the sinner not, led by shame, to deny his guilt; not to fear to confess crimes before a human being, because the person confessing speaks not to a human being but to God. Nor, having confessed before the Judge of heaven, will he be regarded as condemned, but as absolved. This should be shown by many authorities: guilt is erased through confession of sin. For Authority says: [Col. 0286B] “Confess your sins to one another” (Jas. V). And elsewhere: “I said, I will confess,” etc., “and you forgave the impiety of my sin” (Ps. XXXI). Likewise, Christ commanded the ten lepers whom he had healed to show themselves to the priests (Luke XVII). This signifies that one who suffers from spiritual leprosy ought to show himself to a priest through confession of sin. Further, he should teach that the sin disclosed in the present will be covered on the day of judgment, whereas what is concealed in the present will be revealed in the future. Then, so that the guilty person may be less afraid to confess sins, if the priest sees him led by shame, he should ask him generally whether he has suffered from this or that fault, so that, when questioned, the guilty person may confess what at first he was ashamed [Col. 0286C] to say. For example, he asks whether the person has been involved in unlawful intercourse, theft, or robbery, and likewise concerning other matters.

In sins of the flesh excessively minute details should not be investigated.—But if the person has confessed that he has been involved in unlawful intercourse, the priest should ask concerning its kind: whether he committed fornication, adultery, incest, or deviated into a sin against nature. But he ought not descend to minute details, because Christ commands one who descends to the individual particulars of sins to stop, lest investigation of an unknown sin provide an occasion for sinning; for “he who squeezes too hard draws blood” (Prov. XXXIX). And since the sound of preachers has already gone out into all the earth, we say that investigating such minute details is idle, since such inquiry is accustomed to be an occasion of error. For:

> We always strive toward what is forbidden, and desire what is denied.

Therefore it is also said of the old law: “The law entered in so that the offence might abound” (Rom. V). Through the giving of the law certain things became known to be sinful, and then people burned all the more in them. Therefore let excessively subtle inquiry cease. By way of example: if someone confesses that he has known a woman, I shall not ask whether he knew her from the front or the rear, or anything of that kind. The same inquiry is to be made concerning other matters.

[Note: [Col. 0285] On this and the several following circumstances, see what we noted above at the end of the preface.] Once the illness has been well understood and the sin disclosed, the priest ought to investigate [Col. 0287A] the time: namely, whether the sin was committed on a feast day, when one must especially rest from servile work—that is, sin. For what is done on feast days is more serious.

Furthermore, whether the person sinned at the hour appointed for prayer or at another time; for one who gives himself to embraces at a time appointed for prayer sins more seriously than at another time.

Likewise, the circumstances of time must be considered in other sins, by which faults are aggravated or diminished. [Note: [Col. 0287] One may also read usefully Cominck, *On Penance*, question 7, doubt 3; and Sayrus, Book XXI, chapter 3.]

The status of the place must also be considered: whether the subject sinned in a sacred or a profane place, in a public or a private place. For one who sins in an oratory sins more seriously than in a profane place; likewise, one who sins in public more seriously than in private.

[Col. 0287B] Age must also be investigated: whether the guilty person is old or young. An old person, who has experience of things, sins more seriously than a child who has none. Sex too must be considered, whether the person is male or female; for according as the sex is stronger or weaker, the fault is lesser or more serious.

Furthermore, the origin and cause of sin must be confessed. Thus, if the guilty person has perhaps committed fornication, it should be asked whether he was deceived by money, by the sweetness of sin, or by drunkenness. For he sins more seriously when deceived by the scent of gain or the sweetness of allurement than when deceived by drunkenness. In like manner, the cause and origin of another sin must be investigated.

[Col. 0287C] The duration of sin must also be considered, since according as the sin lasted longer or less long it is less serious or more serious.

The habitual manner of living must also be considered: whether the guilty person is held by the vice of an evil habit.

The person’s state must sometimes also be considered: whether the sinner was rich or not. For a rich person sins more seriously if he steals than a poor one, because the poor have a greater impelling cause for theft than the rich.

Condition must also be considered: whether he is a layperson or a cleric, of higher or lower order; for the higher the rank, the more serious the fall.

[Col. 0287D] Temperament also must be considered, insofar as it can be weighed from outward signs. For according to differing temperaments one person is more impelled toward a particular sin than another: if he is choleric, he is more impelled toward anger; if melancholic, more toward hatred; if sanguine or phlegmatic, toward lust.

It must also be considered whether the guilty person has suffered a relapse into some sin; for if someone has been contrite for a sin and falls into it again, he is held more seriously accountable than before.

The face is an image of the mind.—The bearing of the body or the expression of the face must also be considered, so that inward things may be understood from outward ones: namely, whether the mind’s movement toward continence is intense or slack. For, since the face is as it were the seal and image of the mind, one may in some degree perceive through the face what the inner will is. If the face is cast down toward the earth and moistened with tears, it signifies the inward torments of contrition; but if the face is raised and bears no marks of sorrow, repentance appears to be less.

Sins of body and spirit.—Spiritual sins are graver than bodily ones.—Not only the sinner’s condition but also that of the sin must be considered. One must consider whether the sin is bodily or spiritual—namely, whether it arises from weakness of the flesh or a vice of the soul. 187 Bodily [Col. 0288B] sins are those arising from weakness of the flesh, such as lust, gluttony, and so forth. Spiritual sins are those arising from a vice of the soul, such as envy, avarice, and pride. With all other circumstances set aside, a spiritual sin is more serious than a bodily one. For as Gregory testifies: “A carnal sin carries greater disgrace and lesser guilt; a spiritual sin greater guilt and lesser disgrace.”

One must also consider whether the sin belongs to the class of venial or mortal sins, for accordingly greater or lesser satisfaction must be imposed.

Furthermore, one must inquire whether it was done knowingly [Col. 0288C] or ignorantly, for knowledge aggravates fault and ignorance lightens it; and one to whom the gift of greater knowledge has been given will be subject to greater guilt as a transgressor.

It must also be investigated whether the sin is only of the will, or of will and deed; for a sin of will and deed is more serious than a sin of will alone. Likewise, whether the sin consists only in delighting, or also in willing.

Furthermore, the differing condition of the person against whom the guilty party sinned must be considered. For example, if he has known a woman, whether she was unmarried or not, and whether he who knew her was married or not. If he is not married, the sin is less; if married, greater. But if a married man knows a woman joined to another man, [Col. 0288D] he sins most grievously. If, however, an unmarried man has known an unmarried woman, it should be investigated whether he deflowered her or not; for he sinned more seriously if he deflowered her than if he knew her already corrupted. It should also be investigated how often he knew her. Furthermore, whether he violated her by force or not, for one who violates by force sins more than one who knows a willing woman.

It is also necessary to investigate whether she is his blood-relative or relative by marriage. Likewise, whether she is simple or shrewd; for one who deceives a simple woman sins more seriously than one who deceives a shrewd one.

Likewise it must be observed whether he has sinned with a sin against nature or not; for adultery is a more serious sin than simple [Col. 0289A] fornication, incest than adultery, and a sin against nature than incest.

Sins against temperance.—In the same way, if he has sinned in food or drink, one must inquire whether, led by abstinence, he anticipated the time of eating; whether, deceived by immoderation, he exceeded the measure in desiring food or drink; or whether, deceived by unseemliness, he sought out overly delicate dishes and devoted himself to them.

On lying.—Whether, too, overcome by shamelessness, he burst out into shameful words; whether he lied; and, if he uttered a lie, whether he lied in jest, or led by natural compassion—as the midwives who lied to Pharaoh (Exod. I) in order to preserve [Col. 0289B] the lives of the children of Israel—or whether he lied so as to benefit no one and harm someone, through a desire to deceive or a craving to please. For according to these circumstances lies are greater or lesser.

On homicide.—Likewise, if he killed someone, whether it was from a sudden movement of anger, long-established rancour of mind, vengeance, hope of money, repelling force by force, avenging or repelling injuries inflicted upon himself, fear, another’s request, or love. These and other circumstances concerning the matters in which, or against which, we have sinned must be considered.

And let what has been said concerning circumstances suffice. For it will be the prudent reader’s task to infer others from these.

[Col. 0289C] The confessor’s prudence in imposing satisfactions.—When the illnesses have in this manner been disclosed by the sinner, the spiritual physician ought to impose different satisfactions for different sins, as it were different medicines and different diets. First he should show, through threats and fear, in how great sins the guilty person lay; how great the penalties due to them would be if he departed with them; and from how great penalties he will be freed if he grieves through repentance. He should adduce as examples David, who through contrition of heart was freed from the sin of homicide and adultery (II Kings II); Mary Magdalene, freed from seven demons through the lamentations of repentance (Luke VII–VIII); and the thief to whom, as he hung on the cross, it was said: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII). For God does not wish the sinner’s death, but that he [Col. 0289D] should be converted and live (Ezek. XVIII). And elsewhere: “At whatever hour the sinner groans, I shall remember his iniquities no more” (Ezek. XXXIII).

### Stirring Contrition

**The practice of stirring contrition.**—He should also admonish the penitent that contrition be genuine and not sophistical, and that the tears likewise be not artificial but flow from the fountain of the heart; teaching that three things ought to be present in contrition of heart: contrition of heart, confession of the mouth, and satisfaction in deed. He should also admonish the sinner to search the corners of conscience, lest any sin which he remembers and does not confess be omitted; for a partial confession is of no avail, just as neither is a partial contrition. But if the guilty person confesses sins and yet says that he does not wish to repent, or cannot refrain from sin, he should admonish him in many ways, [Col. 0290A] and deter him in many ways, showing how God punishes sinners not only in the future but also in the present; showing that it is human to sin, but devilish to persevere. He should set before his eyes the bitterness of the punishment that awaits the unrepentant, so that, at least thus pierced by servile fear, he may be led to repentance; and then this servile fear may introduce charity, as a bristle draws a thread.

### Sin Is Punished by Sin

He should also teach how the inward disposition of a depraved habit draws a person toward worse things, because crimes are avenged by crimes. For it is just that one who is filthy should become filthier still (Rev. 22); and sin that is not washed away through repentance draws, by its own weight, toward another sin. By way of [Col. 0290B] example, let him set before him Saul, who through the sin of disobedience, for which he did not repent, fell into idolatry and avarice (1 Sam. 15, 28); and Judas, who, because he did not repent of his betrayal, hanged himself with a noose (Matt. 27). The priest should also show the guilty person the face of one who sympathizes, so that the guilty person, at least led by shame, may be invited to repentance. Let the tears of the admonisher call forth the tears of the penitent.

### How an Unrepentant Guilty Person Is to Be Treated

He must also instruct the guilty person who is excessively confident in God’s mercy not to sin in hope; for this is to sin against the Holy Spirit, and cursed is the person who sins in hope. But if the guilty person is unwilling by any means to be led to repentance, the priest ought not wholly to deprive him of his counsel [Col. 0290C]; indeed, he should admonish him not to desist from devout prayers, almsgiving, and fasts, so that God may thus turn his heart to repentance. Yet in this matter he should in some sense leave him without counsel: he should neither urge him, while he persists in such a purpose, to receive Christ’s body, nor command him to abstain. But he should instruct him that, if he receives it while remaining in this state, he will eat judgment upon himself (1 Cor. 11). But if a guilty person remaining in such a state approaches the priest in order to receive the Eucharist, he must warn the claimant, but cannot forbid him.

### Satisfaction Is Ordinarily Always to Be Imposed

But if the guilty person, as seems sufficient to the priest, repents, let him impose satisfaction according to the condition of the sin. Yet contrition might be judged so great that no [Col. 0290D] satisfaction ought to follow; as Christ, seeing in Mary Magdalene the greatness of contrition, and in the thief the power of repentance, said to the former: “Go, and sin no more” (Luke 12); but to the latter: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23).

Contrition is sometimes sufficient when it suffices for the removal of guilt, but not of punishment.

### Contrition Is Sometimes of Itself Sufficient for Removing Guilt, and Even Punishment

**Satisfaction must be proportioned to guilt.**—It is sometimes complete, when it removes both punishment and guilt; sometimes abundant, when not only punishment and guilt are removed, but the crown also is increased. Yet punishment ought rarely to be relaxed unless manifest external signs of immense contrition are present, lest the sinner more readily fall back into guilt when he feels no punitive effect of satisfaction [Col. 0291A]; for unpunished iniquity is accustomed to overflow into an increase of crimes. Therefore satisfaction should be imposed even upon one who is most contrite, for caution and for preserving humility. For just as a regimen should be prescribed according to the extent of illness, and medicine applied according to the patient’s strength, so satisfaction must be measured according to the extent of sin; punishment must be diminished or increased according to the weakness and means of the guilty person, and proportioned to the degree of contrition. For the graver the sin, the greater ought to be the increase of satisfaction.

> [Note: Col. 0291: The Dunensis exemplar has: “grow greater” (*excrescere*).]

The lighter the guilt, the lesser the satisfaction. When it is necessary to impose a heavier satisfaction, he should admonish the guilty person not to recoil from the severity of repentance, [Col. 0291B] showing that the gravity of sin demands a greater repentance, but that he wishes to proportion it to the incapacity arising from human frailty. For example: if he wishes to impose satisfaction for the sin of lust, even though he imposes a great satisfaction, lest the sinner be scandalized he should make clear that a greater satisfaction is due for such guilt, but that something must be remitted from the punishment in view of the incapacity of human frailty. Hence he should further indicate that lust is a very great sin and must be avoided as much as possible, because it weakens, corrupts, and exhausts the body,

> [Note: Col. 0291: “Defiles” (*contaminat*).]

brings disgrace upon a person, corrupts the soul, and eternally condemns. Likewise, when imposing penances for other sins, he should indicate [Col. 0291C] what punishments are due to such sins, lest the sinner be scandalized by the amount of satisfaction.

### The Person’s Condition Must Also Be Considered in Imposing Satisfactions

The punishment must likewise be adjusted to the strength of the guilty person.

> [Note: Col. 0291: “Penance” (*poenitentia*).]

Thus, if the guilty person is able to bear the austerities of fasts and the labours of vigils; but if he is too weak to sustain these labours, let him compensate by the remedy of prayers. Thus, if he cannot fast, let him at least pray, and season his prayers with almsgiving. But if he is poor, let him have recourse to prayers; let him visit, if able, the thresholds of the saints on pilgrimage; and thus let good works be substituted for him by a reciprocal necessity. If almsgiving is lacking, let fasts take its place; if fasting is lacking, let prayer supply the deficiency. Nevertheless, lest anyone excuse himself from almsgiving on account of poverty, God attends not to how much, but to how much one has. The widow who put two mites into the treasury contributed as much

> [Note: Col. 0291: “Deserved” (*meruit*).]

[Col. 0291D] as the rich, who offered much from their abundance (Mark 12). Hence the Lord says: “Whoever gives you a cup of water to drink in my name—because you belong to Christ—amen, amen, I say to you, he shall not lose his reward” (Matt. 9). Hence the Apostle says, lest anyone excuse himself on account of poverty: “Do not be deceived: God is not mocked; for whatever a man sows, that shall he also reap” (Gal. 6). Nor should punishment be conformed only to the quantity of the illness, but also to its kind, [Col. 0292A] so that, as medicine or a bodily physician heals opposites by opposites, so the spiritual physician may expel opposites by opposites. Thus, if the guilty person has been ensnared by the sin of gluttony, let fasts be imposed upon him, so that by fasting the liability of sin may be removed.

> [Note: Col. 0291: “The punishment of fasting” (*poenam jejunii*).]

If he has been led astray into drunkenness through wine, let him be urged to drink water.

But since gluttony and lust are related—for a belly heated with unmixed wine easily boils over into desire—as fasting acts against gluttony, so it serves against lust. Therefore, for the sin of lust, the guilty person is to be afflicted with fasting, because fasting chastens the body and reduces it to servitude (1 Cor. 9).

Therefore let the penalty of satisfaction be imposed in proportion to the degree of contrition: so that where there is less in contrition, there may be more in [Col. 0292B] satisfaction; or where there is more in contrition, there may be less in satisfaction.

### How the Guilty Person Is to Be Moved to Accept Penance

But let the priest beware lest, moved by hatred, he increase the satisfaction; or, drawn by affection, diminish what is due; or, enticed by money, remit the penance. He should also admonish the sinner that if he has at some time worthily repented of sins and made satisfaction, and afterwards falls into any of them, he should confess not only that sin but also the past sins for which he was contrite, because Sacred Scripture seems to proclaim (Matt. 5) that sins return by reason of contempt. It is therefore safer to confess than not to confess. If he confesses those sins, the priest ought not to impose upon him as great a penance as he would impose if he were actually [Col. 0292C] engaged in them.

### What Is to Be Imposed on Usurers and Thieves

But if the guilty person has confessed the sin of usury, the priest should advise him to restore what he seized through usury, if he has the means of restoration; otherwise there would be no salvation for him. The authority is: “Forgiveness is not granted unless what was taken is restored.” But if he does not have the means to make restoration, let him offer the will to do so, because intention suffices where the deed is lacking; and let him restore spiritually to those whom he robbed; if they are absent, to their relatives; if relatives likewise cannot be found, let it be distributed to the poor. Yet almsgiving made from robbery is of no avail if those from whom he robbed still survive and he refuses to restore it. For one who offers God a sacrifice from the robbery of a poor person (Ecclus. 34), as the authority says, does the same as if he [Col. 0292D] were sacrificing a son in the presence of his father. For the offering of the wicked is abominable to God (Prov. 21).

Likewise, if through false advocacy in a legal case, false judgment, violence, any violent exaction whatsoever, or any fraudulent commercial transaction, he has extorted anything, let him restore it; for without repayment there is no salvation.

### What Simoniacs Must Be Admonished About

Likewise, if he has acquired anything simoniacally, whether as ordainer or ordained, he is bound to restore it. But if a prelate has extorted anything simoniacally from his subjects, he is bound to repay it; yet not [Col. 0293A] to those from whom he received it: rather, let it be left to the Church or distributed to the poor. But a subordinate who acquired a canonical prebend simoniacally should relinquish it, do penance for simony, and, if he can, restore its usufruct to the Church. But if he was simoniacally invested with a canonry before reaching the years of discretion, through the intervention of his friends’ money, then when he reaches the years of discretion and understands this simony, let him renounce the canonry and, if he can, restore its usufruct to the Church.

But since we have mentioned punishment,

> [Note: Col. 0293: “Penance” (*poenitentia*).]

let us see why the ancient Fathers imposed such burdensome satisfactions for sins, and whether in our times something of that ancient rigor ought to be remitted according to the condition of sinners and the differing kinds of those who sin; [Col. 0293B] or whether the same rigor ordained by the ancient Fathers ought to be retained.

### Penances Were Formerly Imposed Far More Strictly than Now

**The reason for strictness.**—In the primitive Church, when the faithful were in some manner bound together by greater charity, if anyone fell into mortal sin, stricter rigor was observed in the imposition of penance, for greater caution: so that sinners, constrained by the strictness of punishment, might provide more carefully for themselves in avoiding sin. Just as an emperor, when he first promulgates a law, imposes a stricter penalty upon transgressors of the law so that the people may be more careful in observing it, so the Emperor of heaven and earth, in the first promulgation of his law, wished transgressors of that law to be punished more severely [Col. 0293C] so that they might be more diligent

> [Note: Col. 0293: “More prudent” (*solertiores*).]

in avoiding violations of the command.

Thus Ananias, together with Sapphira, was struck dead in Peter’s presence (Acts 5), because he retained part of his property, so that others might fear more and avoid a similar sin. But as God’s Church increased, the diseases of sins grew strong; and because numbers protect them, it was necessary to relax the strictness of punishment, lest that strictness be an offense rather than a medicine.

### Penances Must Now Be Moderated

Therefore punishment had to be remitted, so that those who could not be recalled through rigor might be called through the mercy of indulgence. Accordingly, since some people of modern times could not bear fasts and vigils, offerings, prayers, [Col. 0293D] and pilgrimages were imposed. The rigor of penances imposed in ancient times must also be relaxed because human nature was formerly stronger in bearing the burdens of penance than it is now; therefore penance must be moderated. Just as the bodily physician moderates for present-day constitutions potions devised long ago, when people were stronger, on account of the weakness of human frailty.

### The Penitent Must Be Accommodated in Imposing Penance

Penances must therefore be moderated. If a penitent cannot bear greater burdens, or is unwilling or unable to bear or fulfil any of those imposed, he should be asked [Col. 0294A] what he will be able to bear; and according to his answer the priest should impose a penance. Nor should he leave him wholly without counsel concerning penance, because through such great charity he will be able to fulfil lesser things; and he who would be crushed by a greater burden will not succumb to a lesser load. Therefore the priest, like a good steward, should distribute provisions discreetly, so that, according to the Apostle’s saying, “he who is weak may eat vegetables” (Rom. 14).

We must therefore see what the ancient satisfactions were, and how, according to the circumstances of modern people and the conditions of sinners, something appears to require relaxation from their rigor.

### “Penitential Canon concerning Voluntary Homicide

It is read in the penitentials that if anyone has committed homicide [Col. 0294B] voluntarily and not from necessity—not against an enemy but through his own greed—he shall do penance continuously for forty days, which the common people call a *carena*, fasting, as is customary, on bread and water; and he shall observe the following seven years in this manner. In the first year after those forty days, he shall spend the whole year without a drink capable of causing intoxication, abstaining from meat, blood, cheese, and every fatty fish, except on those feast days which are celebrated by all the people in that bishopric;

> [Note: Col. 0293: The Dunensis exemplar reads *episcopio* (“bishop’s see”).]

and except when he is on a long journey, or in such company that he cannot abstain, or is held by some illness. Then he may redeem Tuesday,

> [Note: Col. 0293: There, “Tuesday” (*feriam tertiam*) is absent; only Thursday and Saturday are found.]

Thursday, and Saturday by one denarius, or by the value of one denarius, or by feeding three poor persons, [Col. 0294C] so as to use wine, mead, or beer; provided nevertheless that, after returning home and being restored to health, he has no permission to redeem them.

“When the course of the year has been completed, let him be admitted to church and granted the kiss of peace. In the second and third years likewise let him fast, except that on Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday he may have the power, wherever he is, to redeem them at the aforesaid price. Let him diligently observe everything else as in the first year.

“Another, stricter canon.—During each of the remaining four years, he must fast three Lents on the prescribed fast days: the first before Easter, with the other Christians; another before the feast of Saint John [Col. 0294D] the Baptist, and, if anything remains, let it be completed after the feast; the third before the Nativity of the Lord. At those times let him abstain from wine, every other drink capable of causing intoxication, meat, cheese, and fatty fish. And, lest he be without penance for as long as he lives, throughout his whole life let him do penance every Friday on bread and water; and if he wishes to redeem it, he may redeem it by one denarius or feed three poor persons. This appears to be granted according to mercy, not according to canonical censure; for the canons prescribe thus: If anyone through deliberate contrivance and greed [Col. 0295A] has committed homicide, let him leave the world and enter a monastery, and there serve God continually.”

Behold: one of these penances appears to be imposed from rigor, the other from gentleness. Yet each seems to bring excessive rigor in our times.

Therefore, in order that it may become clearer how penances ought either to be remitted or increased,

> [Note: Col. 0295: Another exemplar reads “made more severe” (*exaggerandae*).]

we must consider: first, in how many senses “penance” is said; second, in which sense it is understood here; third, how many kinds of penances there are;

> [Note: Col. 0295: “Kinds of penances.”]

fourth, why penances are more frequently imposed under the number seven; fifth, how penances should be made more severe or remitted according to differing conditions.

[Col. 0295B]

### Various Senses of “Penance”

**Interior penance. Exterior penance.**—Penance is sometimes called contrition of heart, by which someone bewails offences and is unwilling to repeat what has been committed. In this sense, the authority says that to repent is to bewail sins and to be unwilling thereafter to commit things that must be bewailed. Penance is also called satisfaction accompanying repentance; it is called *poenitentia*, as though “holding a person in punishment” (*poenam tenens hominem*). This is called exterior penance, while the preceding is interior. Of interior penance Peter says in the Acts of the Apostles (ch. 2): “Repent, and let every one of you be baptized.” But of exterior penance Ambrose says, in his commentary on the Epistle to the Romans: “The grace of God in baptism does not require groaning or lamentation.”

### Civil, Solemn, Private, and Ecclesiastical Penances

**Concerning the carena. He approves reservation of cases. A carena is not to be imposed on clerics.**—Some penances are civil, others ecclesiastical. Civil penances are those imposed upon people according to the decrees of civil laws; some of these are solemn and others private. Solemn penances are those publicly imposed for graver offences; private penances are imposed secretly. These civil penances are softened or made harsher for various reasons, and they ought rather to be called punishments than penances. Ecclesiastical satisfactions are properly called penances because they commonly proceed from interior repentance. Of ecclesiastical penances, one kind is solemn and another private. Solemn penance is that imposed for graver or [Col. 0295D] notorious crimes, or for crimes that a person has confessed or of which he has been convicted; it is commonly called a *carena*. And as it concerns graver crimes, so its imposition belongs to the higher prelates of the Church. For although lesser priests have the power of binding and loosing, it belongs especially to them to bind or loose in lesser matters; but greater matters are reserved to higher prelates as more learned and more worthy persons.

And note that the solemn penance called a *carena*, which is imposed on laypeople, is not to be imposed on clerics, [Col. 0296A] on account of the dignity of the clerical state and because clerics’ sins ought especially to be concealed, lest, when made known, they become an example and scandal to laypeople and, because of them, the name of God be blasphemed among the nations.

> [Note: Col. 0295: “The word of God.”]

Nevertheless, some public penance must be imposed upon clerics for grave and public sins, though not such as is imposed on laypeople: they are not to be in choir with the others who chant, nor at table with those who eat. But the solemn penance imposed on laypeople should not be repeated, because of that penance’s solemnity, lest repetition make it contemptible. Hence Augustine says to Macedonius: “The place of that most humble penance has been provided carefully and subtly

> [Note: Col. 0295: “Wholesomely” (*salubriter*).]  
> [Note: Another exemplar reads: “Provision has been made that the place of that most humble penance be granted only once in the Church.”]

so that it may be granted only once in the Church, lest a cheap remedy be less useful to the sick, because [Col. 0296B] it is so much the more salutary as it is the less contemptible,” etc.

### A Person Who Has Sought Absolution by Gestures Alone Must Be Absolved

**Even if, at the time of absolution, he lacks the use of his senses.**—Those who do penance solemnly are customarily excluded from the sacrament of the altar during the time of penance, and from certain other things. Yet if the hour of death approaches, nothing should be denied them; indeed, everything should be solemnly celebrated for them. Moreover, if anyone existing in mortal sin, when necessity presses, requests the aid of penance, he must obtain what he asks; neither penance nor the grace of communion is to be denied him, even if, having lost the function of speech, he is shown to request it by definite gestures.

> [Note: Col. 0295: The Dunensis exemplar: “is seen” (*videatur*).]

Hence Bishop Leo says: “To those who, at a time of necessity and under the pressure of impending danger, ask for the aid of penance and immediate reconciliation, neither satisfaction is to be forbidden nor reconciliation denied; for we cannot set a measure to God’s mercy or determine times for him with whom the granting of pardon suffers no delay.” Necessity must therefore be aided in such a way that neither the performance of penance nor the grace of communion is denied to one shown to seek it, having lost speech, by evidence of an unimpaired mind. But if he is so burdened by illness that he cannot at the present moment signify what he had asked a little earlier, the testimony of the faithful standing around him should avail him; and in like manner he shall obtain the benefit of penance and reconciliation.

[Col. 0296D]

### What Penances Are to Be Imposed on the Sick

Behold, we have that penance must not be denied to someone in danger. Yet penance should not be imposed on him simply and unconditionally, but should be prescribed in such a way that he fulfils it if God grants him a span of life. The sick person himself should also be enjoined, as a kind of penance, to endure with patience and devotion of mind the scourge of God the Father. Thus also those who are led away to punishment for offences should be enjoined, as penance, to bear their penalty devoutly. Yet the grace of communion, [Col. 0297A] or the Eucharist, is customarily denied them—not because of the guilt of sin, but because of the dignity of the sacrament.

That the Eucharist cannot be denied to one undergoing solemn penance if necessity approaches is shown by Pope Nicholas, speaking of a matricide: “We have learned that the bearer of this letter is a matricide. We command him to remain under the yoke of penance: for a whole year he is not to enter church, but is to stand before the doors of the basilica, praying and beseeching God, and persevere in this. But after three full years have been completed, let the grace of holy communion be granted him. If, however, the end of his life approaches before the third year, let him partake of the body and blood of the Lord.”

From what has been said it is also clear for what causes solemn penance is given, and to whom; what solemn penance is, and what public penance is—yet solemn penance is not that which may be imposed on both clerics and laypeople.

### Diversity of Penances for the Same Sin

From these things it is also clear what private penance is: that which is imposed for lesser and hidden sins. Therefore, since a diversity of penalties for a similar sin is found in the penitentials, we understand that diversity according as solemn penance is imposed on one, private on another, public on another; or we may understand one as given out of rigor and another out of gentleness; or according to the differing condition of the Church, the sin, or the person.

But it is asked how one should understand [Col. 0297C] what is said concerning the imposition of solemn penance:

> [Note: Col. 0297: The Dunensis exemplar: “seven-year.”]

“Perform three years on bread and water, and

> [Note: Col. 0297: In place of *and*, it has “or.”]

perform three Lents in each year.” Is this to be understood as requiring fasting every day, or every other day?

To this we answer—without prejudicing a higher interpretation—that the rigor of canonical censure is indicated when fasting on bread and water for three years is commanded. Some understand this to mean

> [Note: Col. 0297: Here the following is inserted, and rightly: “that for three years he abstain three times in each week.” Others, however, understand it thus: “that for,” etc.]

not that bread and water are to be eaten for the whole week throughout three years, but only during the three fasts mentioned above. The statement, “perform three Lents in each year,” means during those three fasts. It is not said that he must abstain continuously throughout those three fasts—unless perhaps he is doing solemn penance—[Col. 0297D] but that during those three fasts he must confess his crimes to the priest and receive, according to the priest’s judgment and the magnitude of his guilt, a corresponding measure of satisfaction.

### Penances Are Left to the Judgment of the Priest Hearing Confessions

As we have said, a reasonable mode of penance must always be fixed at the priest’s discretion. Hence Jerome says: “The canons do not sufficiently explicitly prescribe a measure of time for performing penance for each crime, so as to state for individual offences how they are to be corrected; rather, they determine that this should be left to the judgment of an understanding priest, because before God the measure of time is not worth as much as the measure of sorrow, nor abstinence from food as much as mortification of vices.” Some direct that the periods of penance should be shortened according to the penitents’ faith and manner of life, and prolonged because of negligence. Yet prescribed modes of penance have been established for certain offences.

Behold, you have that penances are discretionary. But note that he says, “of an understanding priest.” If a priest is insufficiently discerning, so that he does not know how to distinguish between leprosy and leprosy—that is, between sin and sin—nor between medicine and medicine—that is, between penance and penance—the priest [Col. 0298B] ought to have recourse to a more experienced person and consult him, or send the penitent to someone more experienced.

### Why Was a Seven-Year Penance Formerly Common?

It should be noted that a seven-year penance is frequently imposed. The holy Fathers did not establish this by the choice of their own judgment, but rather by the sentence of divine judgment.

> [Note: Col. 0297: Another exemplar: “of the Lord” (*Dominici*).]

For it is read that Miriam, Aaron’s sister, a prophetess, when she incurred the offence of dissension

> [Note: Col. 0297: “Detraction,” i.e. slander.]

against Moses, was immediately struck with leprosy (Num. 12); and when Moses asked that she be cleansed, God commanded her to go outside the camp for seven days and, after her cleansing, to be admitted again into the camp.

In imitation also of that divine judgment, David, reproved for homicide and adultery [Col. 0298C] (2 Sam. 12), is read to have offered God a fast of one week in satisfaction for what he had done. Hence the laws of ecclesiastical custom also establish that penance for grave crimes should be limited to a period of seven years—unless either the eminence of one’s office or the magnitude of the crimes exceeds ordinary custom

> [Note: Col. 0297: “Exceeds” (*excedens*).]

and compels the stated period to be exceeded; as, for example, when we attach ourselves indecently to parents, children, or other such persons, contrary to the nature of human society; or, abandoning natural intercourse, commit fornication against nature.

### Forgiveness of Sins Takes Place in Seven Ways

A seven-year penance is also imposed because forgiveness of sins occurs in seven ways: namely, through baptism, almsgiving, martyrdom, conversion of a brother, forgiving the injury of one who sins [Col. 0298D] against us, weeping, satisfaction for sin, and communion of the body and blood of the Lord. Or because whatever is committed in the sevenfold span of this life is wiped away through sevenfold grace.

### A Confessor Must Not Hear a Woman with Whom He Has Had Sexual Relations

**Shame Is a Part of Penance.**—Although this is so, penance nevertheless ought to be increased or diminished according to the aforementioned circumstances, lest a heavier burden crush the weak or an overly lax one lead the obstinate to contempt. But the priest must take the utmost care [Col. 0299A] that, if he himself has had sexual relations with his own female parishioner or another woman and she wishes to confess to him, he does not hear her, but admonishes her to approach another priest, so that in confessing to him she may be more ashamed of her sin.
