For shame at confession is a part of penance. For although confession of sin has been instituted for other reasons, it has also been instituted for this reason: that shame for sin may serve as punishment.

### Religious Cannot Hear the Confessions of Secular Parishioners

But if a parishioner of another priest approaches a different priest, the priest whom he approaches should send him back to his own priest if he knows this. But if he learns that the person has confessed to his own priest, he should not reject his confession. Those living in cloisters, however, may not hear the confessions of parishioners [Col. 0299B] or impose penances, unless this has been specially assigned to someone by the minister of the parish or by a higher prelate.

### After Imposing Penance, the Priest Is Bound to Pray for the Penitent

In these three things consists the spiritual power of loosing possessed by the priest: that he grants absolution from sin; that he is bound to pray for the penitent; and that he may remit part of the punishment.

### How Conscience Is to Be Examined

Thus far we have spoken of the priest’s office—how he should conduct himself in advising a sinner. It remains to discuss the penitent’s condition: namely, how he ought to confess his sins. Just as a bodily sick person ought, as far as he can, to investigate the causes and location of his pain, so that he may know how to answer the physician who comes to him about his condition; so a sinner, as a spiritual sick person, before approaching his physician—that is, his own priest—ought to search the corners of his conscience, asking what sins may lie hidden in those corners; examining how he has conducted himself at each stage of life, in childhood, adolescence, and his other ages; in one place and another; in this company and another; what he has contracted from association with those people or others; and thus he must inquire how, in his different conditions, he has offended God.

But if he is conscious of nothing in himself, so that with the Apostle he can say, “I am conscious of nothing against myself” (1 Cor. 4), let him pray to God, saying: “Lord God, [Col. 0299D] I am conscious of nothing against myself; yet who understands transgressions? Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults” (Ps. 18).

### One Conscious of No Sin Must Approach the Confessor at Easter

Although hidden sins are forgiven in general confession, it is nevertheless advisable that he approach the priest, lest he seem to neglect the rule of ecclesiastical institution. Let him tell the priest that he is conscious of no sin in himself; but because “we all offend in many things” (Jas. 3), and “the righteous falls seven times a day” (Prov. 24), let him call himself wretched and a sinner, asking the priest to impose some satisfaction by which sins may be cleansed—if not manifest sins, yet hidden ones, if [Col. 0300A] there are any. But if no sins are cleansed by it, because there are none, the satisfaction will nevertheless avail toward the merit of a greater crown.

### No One Must Confess What He Has Not Done

But let him beware lest, from false humility, he say that he is guilty of a sin of which he is not guilty; for by that very act he makes himself guilty of the same sin which he says has ensnared him.

### Venial Sins Dispose One toward Mortal Sin

**Three Things Are Required for Confession.**—If someone knows that he is burdened only with venial sins, let him not be excessively confident of pardon, because sometimes a multitude of venial sins closely disposes one toward mortal sin. Therefore let him consult the priest concerning these matters. Nevertheless, they are frequently removed in general confession because they often slip from memory. Therefore let the sinner, gathering his sins by recalling them [Col. 0300B] and having the intention of repenting of each and not falling back, approach the priest and confess his offences with great sorrow, tears, and groaning. For if he remains in the will to sin, he speaks indeed, but does not confess. For three things concur in order that there may be confession: contrition of heart, confession of the mouth, and the intention not to relapse. If any one of these is lacking, when it could be present, there will not be a true confession. That one ought to grieve and be contrite for sin is proved by many authorities. For Augustine says in the book *On Penance*: “Penance is a kind of vengeance of one who grieves, punishing in oneself what one grieves to have committed.” The same Augustine says: “You do penance: you bend your knees

> [Note: Col. 0299D: “You fix them firmly” (*figis*).]

and laugh? You mock [Col. 0300C] God’s patience. If you do penance, you repent; if you do not repent, you are not penitent.”

### Interior Contrition Is Necessary

Behold, you have that contrition of mind is necessary for true penance. Exterior contrition, or frequent bathing in tears, does not suffice unless it proceeds from the fountain of the heart. Hence Isidore says: “We see some people receive tears for repentance, yet lack the disposition of repentance, because they shed tears through instability of mind, not through remembrance of sin.”

### Necessity of Confession. Confession prefigured (Gen. III)

One must also confess sin, because contrition of heart is not sufficient unless confession follows, if one has time to confess. For, to show that confession belongs to the fullness of repentance, the Lord, who commanded the healed leper to show himself to the priest (Matt. VIII), indicates [Col. 0300D] that the spiritual leper—that is, the sinner—ought to disclose to the priest through confession the sins [Note: [Col. 0299D] “the sores of sinners”]. That confession contributes to the removal of guilt [Note: [Col. 0299D] “sin”] may be inferred from the beginning of the human race. For the first parents, after their fault, were questioned by the Lord concerning that fault, so that they might erase by confession the sin they had committed through transgression (Gen. III). But the serpent was not questioned concerning its fault, because it is not restored to life through confession.

Cain, however, when he had added fratricide to the first transgression, was likewise questioned by the Lord concerning his guilt, [Col. 0301A] when it was said, “Where is your brother?” (Gen. IV). But because, in his pride, he would not confess his sin, and instead attempted to deceive the Lord by denial, saying, “Am I my brother’s keeper?” (ibid.), he was judged unworthy of pardon. Augustine likewise says concerning the passage, “Let not the deep swallow me up”:

> “The pit is the depth of human iniquity. If you fall into it, it will not close its mouth over you if you do not close your own mouth [Note: [Col. 0301] Another copy reads: “It will close its mouth over you if, by not confessing, you close your mouth.”]; therefore confess and say: ‘Out of the depths I have cried to you, O Lord’” (Ps. CXXIX).

Hence the Prophet says: “Enter his gates with confession” (Ps. XCIX).

### Satisfaction strengthens contrition

That outward satisfaction is also effective for contrition is indicated by many authorities. Even if a priest does not impose penance upon one who confesses—whether because he lacks discernment, is moved by natural compassion, or judges the penitent’s contrition to be superabundant—the penitent should nevertheless still redeem his sins by almsgiving, fasting, vigils, and 196 prayers. If a parishioner knows his priest to lack discernment, then, having obtained permission from him, he should consult a more learned person; or, having first confessed to his own priest, he should thereafter consult one more learned.

John shows that outward satisfaction has force when he says in the Gospel: “Bear fruits worthy of repentance” (Matt. III). The Ninevites also, whom the Lord commends in the Gospel, repented at Jonah’s preaching (Matt. XII; Luke XI), and through the Lord’s mercy deserved to obtain pardon and escape the ruin of being overthrown [Col. 0301C] [Note: [Col. 0301] “to evade it”]. Still clearer testimony is given us by that king, namely Ahab, who, shaken by the enormity of his crime, repented; clothed in sackcloth, he wept for his deed, and thus called forth God’s mercy toward himself, so that God absolved him of all his sins. For the Lord said to Elijah: “Have you seen how Ahab has been pierced with compunction before me? And because he has wept in my sight, I shall not bring evils in his days” (III Kings XXI). Therefore, lesser satisfaction is required for lesser sins, and greater satisfaction for greater sins.

### Venial sins are forgiven through prayer

That prayer makes satisfaction for venial sins is indicated by Augustine, who says in the *Enchiridion*:

> “For daily and slight sins, without which this life [Col. 0301D] is not lived, the daily prayer of the faithful makes satisfaction; for it belongs to them to say, ‘Our Father, who art in heaven.’ This prayer erases small and daily sins. It also erases those sins through which the lives of believers have been wickedly conducted, but which, through repentance changed for the better, have departed [Note: [Col. 0301] “depart”].”

### Almsgiving is forgiving those who have injured us

So that it may truly be said, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI), [Col. 0302A] let what is said be done. For this itself is almsgiving: namely, granting pardon to those who repent.

### Contrition is required even for venial sins

From these things it is now easy to understand what satisfaction ought to be offered for venial sins. The Lord’s Prayer with some fasting and almsgiving is sufficient, provided that a measure of contrition precedes it and confession is added if there is opportunity. For graver sins, however, these things also must be employed in satisfaction, but much more earnestly and strictly. For Augustine says:

> “For doing repentance, it is not enough to change one’s conduct for the better and withdraw from evil deeds, unless one also makes satisfaction to God for deeds already done through the sorrow of repentance, the groaning of humility, and contrition of heart [Note: [Col. 0301] Another copy read: “the sacrifice of a contrite heart, with almsgiving assisting.”].”

[Col. 0302B] From what has been said, it is clear how three things concur in true repentance: contrition, confession, and satisfaction, together with the resolve not to relapse. For repentance is to weep over sins and to will no longer to commit them. Hence Pope Pius says:

> “It profits a person nothing to fast and pray and perform other works of religion unless the mind is recalled from iniquity.”

Likewise Isidore says:

> “He who still does what he repents of is a mocker and not repentant; he does not seem humbly to seek God, but proudly to mock him.”

Therefore, since the penitent is bound to confess sin, he should take care to disclose his sin to the priest, and thus, through the priest, to God. For God granted priests the power of binding and loosing; and therefore those whom [Col. 0302C] they forgive, God also forgives [Note: [Col. 0301] “This was formerly practised, for greater humility, but was never a precept; the practice has long fallen out of use, though it was formerly observed. See St Thomas, *Supplement*, q. 8, art. 2.”].

If, however, a priest is lacking, confession should be made to a neighbour or companion; yet a priest should be diligently sought. Hence Augustine [Note: [Col. 0301] The *Book on True and False Repentance* (ch. 10), cited here, is not Augustine’s, because in ch. 17 Augustine himself is cited there. See Sylvius, on question 8, supplement A, 2, conclusion 3.] says:

> “Such is the power of confession that, if a priest is lacking, one should confess to a layman.”

Although the person to whom confession is made has no power to absolve, the penitent is nevertheless worthy of pardon because of his desire for a priest. For the lepers were cleansed as they went to show themselves to the priests (Luke XVII). But the person confessing should beware of confessing one matter in such a way as not to confess another; or of confessing one thing in such a way that another is concealed. For repentance of this kind is sophistical and not true.

For just as no half-complete 197 remission can be effected by God, so half-complete contrition has no force. Hence [Col. 0302D] Gregory says:

> “To repent is to weep over sins previously committed and not to commit the sins that must be wept over. For one who so laments some sins as to commit others again either does not know how to repent or pretends to repent.”

For what good is it if one weeps over sins of lust while still panting after the fires of avarice? Augustine says:

> “There are many who repent of having sinned, but who nevertheless entirely reserve for themselves certain things in which they delight. They do not notice that the Lord likewise delivered one who was mute and deaf [Col. 0303A] from a demon; by this he teaches us that we are never healed except from all things.”

Likewise:

> “It is a kind of impiety arising from unbelief to hope for half a pardon from him who is just and justice itself.”

Moreover, the sinner must beware of lying long in sin, but should repent quickly of sin, lest, lying as though four days in evil habit, he stink; lest, held fast by the birdlime of evil habit, he rise more difficultly. For authority says:

> “A sin not immediately washed away by repentance drags one by its own weight to graver sins; for crimes are punished by crimes. It is just that one who is filthy should become filthier still” (Rev. XXII).

David’s repentance should be our example that contrition ought to follow sin immediately. As soon as he recognized the sin [Col. 0303B] of adultery and homicide, he resorted to the remedy of repentance; descending from his throne, he sat in ashes and sackcloth (II Kings XII).

### Alms without repentance do not remit sins. Various kinds of almsgiving

Let sinners who remain in crime not flatter themselves by wishing to redeem their sins through almsgiving. Almsgiving cannot obtain pardon unless repentance intervenes. I do not deny, however, that alms may benefit sinners, as other good works do: God may more quickly turn their hearts toward good, or the punishment of the damned may be more tolerable. Yet remission of sin is not effected by them unless contrition of heart is present. Hence Augustine says:

> “There are some who live wickedly and take no care to correct such a life and conduct, yet amid their very crimes do not cease frequently to give alms. But they flatter themselves in vain on this account, because God says, ‘Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you’ (Luke XI). They do not understand this, though it is widely evident.”

For there are many kinds of almsgiving by which, when we perform them, we are helped. Not only does one who gives food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, and such things give alms; one who grants pardon to one who asks also gives alms. One who corrects by a beating a person over whom authority has been given, or restrains him by some discipline, or prays that some sin be forgiven him, gives alms, because he bestows mercy. Many benefits are bestowed even upon unwilling people when regard is had for their advantage rather than their will. But the greater almsgiving [Col. 0303D] is that by which we forgive from the heart when someone has sinned against us; and the greatest is to be benevolent even toward one who has done you much evil.

### Sins forgiven return through contempt. Doubts should be confessed as doubts

The sinner should also consider whether he has relapsed into any sin; for, as many authorities say, sins forgiven return through contempt. When a person frequently relapses [Col. 0304A] into the same sin, he seems, on account of his contempt, to remain liable for earlier sins. It is therefore safer to confess sins previously committed than not to confess them. Hence Ambrose says:

> “Forgive one another if one sins against another; otherwise God will demand back what he has forgiven.”

For if there has been contempt in these matters, without doubt he will revoke the sentence, as is read in the Gospel concerning the wicked servant (Matt. XVIII), who had not shown mercy to his fellow servant. On this Rabanus says:

> “The master handed the wicked servant over to the torturers until he should pay the entire debt, because he demands back not only the sins a person committed after baptism, but even original sins forgiven in baptism.”

If someone is uncertain whether he has at some earlier time committed this or that sin, he should carefully examine himself [Col. 0304B] as to whether he committed it or not. If he cannot become certain, remaining in doubt, he should not tell the priest that he committed it, but that he doubts whether or not he committed it. The priest will then regulate the penance accordingly, so as to impose some modest satisfaction.

The sinner should likewise be careful not to reveal his sins to a priest notoriously guilty of disclosing the sins confessed to him. But if this is his own priest, he should, with that priest’s permission, go to another. If the crime is secret, it is sufficient to disclose it to one person alone; but if it is notorious, so that public disgrace attaches to it, it may be disclosed to several, so that it may be punished by greater shame.

### How one who is guilty should aid an innocent person who is accused

If a sinner sees someone suffering the disgrace of a crime in which the sinner himself, rather than that other person, is implicated, he ought by every means to free that person from disgrace, though without accusing himself. But if someone is implicated in an offense for which he is accused before a judge and compelled to undergo trial by single combat, the counsel is that he confess his sin before entering the trial. For in every confession there is no danger to the soul, but salvation; whereas in the trial there is danger both of damnation of the soul and of temporal life.

If a priest accuses his parishioner of a crime in which that parishioner is implicated, the counsel is that he not confess to that priest but to another. If a parish priest has known a female parishioner, the counsel is that she consult another [Col. 0304D] priest. If someone is a thief, usurer, or similar robber, the counsel is that he restore what he has stolen if he can, because without this true repentance cannot exist. If he is guilty of simony, whether in giving or receiving, he should restore what was given and relinquish what was received. These remarks concerning the office of the spiritual physician and the manner of spiritually curing the sick are sufficient.

[AGAINST HERETICS.]

[Col. 0305]

## TO THE BENEVOLENT READER CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING BOOK

199 I had intended, in the first volume of the works of our Blessed Alan, to publish only moral and paraenetic writings. But when the following work, *On the Catholic Faith*, printed at Paris in 1612, recently came into my hands—wholly incorrect and mutilated, with points frequently substituted for words, or other words substituted in their place, and not infrequently whole sentences; such substitutions in many places wholly corrupt and twist the author’s genuine meaning into its opposite, not without grave injury to the author—to say nothing of the almost countless typographical errors which by themselves could nauseate any reader, I judged it worthwhile to examine and correct this work as well, restore it to its proper completeness, and publish it, together with the other works of the same author, for the public benefit of letters.

I therefore immediately sent letters to various monasteries known to possess libraries well supplied with more distinguished manuscript codices. In these I found a single copy, sufficiently commendable for its antiquity and correctness: namely, in the most celebrated Abbey of Park near Louvain. When the venerable abbot of that place very kindly sent it to me, I corrected the printed copy by careful collation with it and restored to the work that completeness which you, benevolent reader, will here be able to enjoy.

Moreover, although the author says in his Prologue that this work is divided into four books—the first written against heretics, the second against the Waldensians, the third against the Jews, and the fourth against pagans—nevertheless I have nowhere been able to find the fourth, however diligently sought. I found the third in the Park manuscript, but it is so brief that it scarcely deserves the name of a book; and one may reasonably doubt whether it is truly the complete book as written by the author, or merely a fragment. Meanwhile, because in the said Park copy it is honoured with the title of “Book,” I have included it here under that same title.

The first book, *Against Heretics*, was indeed written by the author against various heretics of his time, as may sufficiently be inferred from the Prologue mentioned above; but especially against the Albigensians, whose sect had then grown extraordinarily strong. In a short time, as Caesarius of Heisterbach—an exceptionally trustworthy writer of that time—testifies, it infected more than a thousand cities; and unless it had been suppressed by Catholic swords, there was reason to fear that it would overrun all Europe. Yet it taught the most absurd errors, stitched together from obsolete scraps of the heresies of Mani, Novatus, Tertullian, Origen, and other ancient heresiarchs. This is also taught by the cited Caesarius, *Dialogues*, book V, ch. 21, where he lists all the principal errors of the Albigensians [Note: [Col. 0305] Peter of les Vaux-de-Cernay also recounts the errors of the Albigensians throughout ch. 2 of his book *On the War against the Albigensians*.]; these are the same errors which our Alan refutes throughout his entire first book.

Alan wrote the second book against the Waldensians [Note: [Col. 0305] “Concerning the Waldensians, see also Caesarius above.”], because the Albigensians themselves had arisen from the Waldensians and still agreed with them in many respects. In any case, the work is filled with sound doctrine and worthy of its author. You too, reader, will acknowledge this with me when you have studied it attentively. Farewell.

F. Carolus de Visch,  
P. of the Dunes.

[Col. 0305]

# ALAN OF LILLE, ON THE CATHOLIC FAITH AGAINST THE HERETICS OF HIS TIME, ESPECIALLY THE ALBIGENSIANS, IN FOUR BOOKS

## PROLOGUE. TO THE PRINCE OF MONTPELLIER

[Col. 0305A] 201 To his most beloved lord William, by God’s grace prince of Montpellier, distinguished not only by the title of noble birth but still more pre-eminently by the nobility of a noble mind, Master Alan, wholly and in all things his own, offers his work.

[Note: [Col. 0305] The manuscripts of Bonne-Espérance and Park read “most reverend” instead of “most beloved.”]

Since, among all the princes of this world, I see you [Col. 0307A] especially clothed in the arms of Christian faith and not abandoning Peter’s little ship amid the many tumultuous storms of this age, I dedicate to your discernment this completed writing *On the Catholic Faith*.

Although the Catholic faith shines forth founded not only upon divine but also upon human arguments, and stands unconquered by the strongest theological authorities, as though by irrefutable supports [Note: [Col. 0307] The printed copy reads the preceding words thus: “May it excel, greatly fortified by most irrefutable theological authorities.”], nevertheless, because of new heretics raging with new—indeed, old and newest—heresies, devoted to philosophical speculations yet directed by the mirrors of their senses, I am compelled to give a reasoned account of reasonable faith in explicit arguments [Note: [Col. 0307] The printed edition omits the word “faith”]. They differ from ancient heretics in this: those attempted to assault our faith by human reason; but these, relying upon no human or divine reason, fabricate monstrosities according to their own will and pleasure.

In former times, different heretics are recorded to have dreamed up, at different times, diverse and contrary doctrines, which are known to have been condemned by the public decrees of the universal Church. But in our own times new heretics—or rather, old and inveterate heretics, making their doctrines old—combine the doctrines of different heresies into [Col. 0308A] one general heresy, as if making one idol from different idols, one monster from different monsters, and one common poison from various poisonous herbs.

But because their doctrines are old, we must not labour over novel inventions, but oppose them with authoritative arguments by which impious doctrines are said to have been destroyed by men of brilliant intellect, trained in every discipline: Augustine, Hilary, Jerome, and the other orthodox Fathers. Since the same seeds of heresy sprout again, the same defenses of the ancient Fathers must be set against them; and if some new heresy arises, it must be shattered by firm arguments [Note: [Col. 0307] The manuscript copy reads “shattered.”]. Because I see you, most valiant prince, as a special son and defender of the faith, I dedicate this work to you [Col. 0308B] and await from you an examination of it.

This work is divided into four distinct volumes [Note: [Col. 0307] The printed edition reads: “This work is divided into two distinct volumes.” This is because the codex of Papirius Masson, from which the printed copy was taken, contained only the first two books, although the author in fact wrote four, as other manuscripts repeatedly attest.]: the first is known to have been issued against heretics; the second against Waldensians; the third against Jews; and the fourth against pagans.

# BOOK I

[Col. 0307]

## 203 CHAPTER I. A comparison of pagans and Christians in material and spiritual valour

[Col. 0307C]

As is read in ancient treatises, the suitors and nobles of the Gentiles, pursuing human glory, nobly destroyed various kinds of monsters: Hercules, Antaeus; Theseus, the Minotaur; Jason, the fire-breathing bull; Meleager, the immeasurable boar; Chorebus, the Stygian monster; Perseus, the sea-monster [Note: [Col. 0307] The printed edition reads “mammum portentum,” but wrongly.]. So the noble leaders of holy Church are recorded to have vanquished with spiritual weapons the monsters of various heretics and heresies.

And just as Antaeus, recovering strength from the earth, became stronger, and the Hydra became more prolific through the loss of its heads [Note: [Col. 0307] In the manuscript: “more fertile through its own cutting-off.”], so, after ancient and antiquated heresies have been uprooted, they sprout again in [Col. 0307D] novelty. But there is this great difference: the strength of Antaeus was destroyed and the Hydra utterly extirpated, whereas among modern people there are none to oppose renewed heresies and uproot their new shoots. Yet I, the least among the sons of Jesse, taken from behind the nursing ewes, shall attempt to slay Goliath with his own sword and kill the Egyptian who insults the Hebrews.

## CHAPTER II. The authorities by which heretics maintain that there are two principles of things

[Col. 0308C]

The heretics of our time say that there are two principles of things: a principle of light and a principle of darkness.

They say that the principle of light is God, from whom spiritual things come—namely souls and angels—and that the principle of darkness is Lucifer, from whom temporal things come. They seek to prove this by authorities and arguments. By authorities, thus: “A good tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor a bad tree good fruit” (Matt. VII). Therefore, since God is supremely good, evils are not from him. But since evils exist and are not from God himself, they are from another than God himself. Therefore, since God is the principle of good things, another is the principle of evil things.

Again, at the beginning of Genesis it is read that darkness was upon the face of the deep (Gen. I), and thus the world had its beginning from darkness. Therefore the creator of the world was the principle of darkness, and thus the author of the world was evil, since [Note: [Col. 0307] In the printed codex, the preceding words are read in complete confusion: “the world had its beginning from the darkness of the world; therefore the Creator was the principle of the earth, and thus the author of the world was evil, because,” etc. But we have restored the text more correctly from the manuscript.] he began the beginning of his creation from darkness.

Again, Christ says in the [Col. 0309A] Gospel: “The prince of this world comes, and has nothing in me” (John XIV). There he calls Lucifer prince of the world rather than himself; therefore Lucifer was more the author of the world than Christ. Elsewhere it is said: “No one can serve two masters” (Matt. VI), namely God and Mammon. There Christ calls himself and Mammon—that is, the devil—masters. But Christ is called Lord only by reason of creation; therefore, by a like reason, the devil is called lord by reason of creation. Again, he says: “You are of your father the devil” (John VIII).

Again, the Apostle says: “It is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me,” that is, in my flesh (Rom. VII). If sin dwells in the flesh, and comes from the flesh, and flesh cannot exist without sin, flesh is evil and therefore is not from God. Again: “I perceive another law [Col. 0309B] in my members, resisting the law of my mind and making me captive under the law of sin which is in my members” (ibid.). If the law of the flesh is the law of sin and death, the flesh appears to be evil and therefore not from God. Again, the same Apostle says: “The flesh fights against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. V). If the flesh always contradicts reason, the flesh is evil, and thus comes from evil.

## CHAPTER III. The arguments by which heretics maintain that there are two principles of things

The heretics also prove their opinion by these arguments. If God made these visible things, he either could make them incorruptible or could not. If he could not, he was powerless; if he could and would not, he was envious. Again, if the cause is unchangeable, the effect is unchangeable; but it is evident that these bodily things are changeable; therefore their cause is changeable.

Again, since many things in the world occur by chance, they do not appear to occur by divine ordinance. Again, since human flesh is generated in sin and through sin, it does not appear to be from a good principle. Again, there are certain creatures which serve no useful purpose [Note: [Col. 0309] The printed edition has: “which tend to no usefulness.”], such as serpents, flies, and spiders, but serve manifold destruction. Therefore, since they are fitted for evil and not for good, they are from evil and not from good.

## CHAPTER IV. The Catholic reply to the foregoing heretical authorities concerning two principles

In reply to these authorities, we say that the saying, “A good tree,” etc. (Matt. VII), [Col. 0309D] must be understood of a good or evil intention. For only a good work proceeds from a good intention, and only an evil work from an evil intention.

We also say that the term “evil” sometimes stands for an evil action, and sometimes for the deformity of the action itself. Thus, when it is said, “There is no evil in the city which God does not do,” the meaning is: there is no evil action which he does not permit to be done. But he does not make evilness itself—that is, the deformity of the action—according to which it is called evil; for it is nothing. That very deformation of an action, by which an action is called evil, is nothing.

Therefore, insofar as the term stands for an evil action, evil is said to be something and to be from God—not in respect of its being evil, but in respect of its being. But insofar as it stands for evilness, it is said neither to be something nor to be from God; for it denotes a privation rather than the positing of a thing [Note: [Col. 0309] The preceding passages in the printed codex are all confused, in this fashion: “insofar as it stands for evilness, it is said not to be from God, nor to be from God; rather when it denotes,” etc. But here the text has rightly been restored from the manuscript.].

We also say that the term “darkness” denotes absence of light rather than the existence of a thing; and therefore the world did not have its beginning from darkness. Rather, the sense of “Darkness was upon the face of the deep” (Gen. I) is: there was no light. The devil is not called prince of the world because he [Col. 0310B] created the world, but prince of the world—that is, of worldly people—because he rules and reigns in their hearts through the desire for earthly things. For the same reason he is called lord of the world.

That “world” means lovers of the world is read in John: “And the world did not know him” (John I), that is, lovers of the world. Elsewhere in the Gospel: “My kingdom is not of this world” (John XVIII), that is, the lovers of this world are not my kingdom; that is, I do not reign in them. The devil is called father of human beings not by reason of creation, but by reason of imitation, because they imitate him through wicked deeds [Note: [Col. 0309] The printed edition reads “through perpetual deeds.”].

Sin is said to dwell in human flesh—that is, the tinder of sin, or concupiscence, which dwells in the flesh not by reason of substance but by reason of circumstance. For since Adam sinned, flesh has become prone to concupiscence—that is, the human being is so prone through the weakness of the flesh. Although concupiscence thus remains in the flesh incidentally, the flesh is not evil—that is, vicious—but vitiated, or weak; nor is it therefore any less from God. Just as a human being, though weak, nevertheless has existence from God.

The following authority is explained in the same way. Although the law of sin and death—that is, concupiscence—arises incidentally in and from the members, that is, from the weakness of the members, the members themselves, though vitiated, are from God in what they are; but their being vitiated—that is, weak—is not from God.

That the flesh is said to fight against the spirit must not be understood of flesh itself, but of the carnality [Col. 0310D] of flesh. For “flesh,” that is, carnality, always contradicts the spirit, that is, reason.

## CHAPTER V. The heretics’ arguments concerning two principles refuted

The arguments are answered thus. Although God could have made the world actually unchangeable and did not do so, he was not envious. For it belonged to supreme goodness that he made the world, but to wisdom that he permitted it to be changeable, so that through the changeable we might be changed into the unchangeable [Col. 0311A]. For everything changeable indicates that something is unchangeable; everything moving indicates that something is at rest [Note: [Col. 0311] “In the printed edition there is remarkable confusion here, which need not be reported.”].

I say “actually unchangeable,” because he could not make anything unchangeable by nature. Every created thing, precisely because it is created, has a beginning of its existence; for the same reason it has an end, either actually or by nature. Every thing is bounded by two limits.

Moreover, it does not follow that if the cause is unchangeable, the effect is unchangeable. An efficient cause is one thing, a formal cause another. An efficient cause moves and works in order that a thing may exist; an artisan, for example, is the efficient cause of his work, moves it, and works in order that it may exist. Yet it does not follow that what is predicated of the artisan is predicated of his work, or conversely. A work may endure a long time while its artisan does not.

Likewise, since God is the supreme artisan of all things and their efficient cause, he is unchangeable; yet things created by him are not unchangeable. Indeed, it is impossible for things created by him not to be changeable, because whatever has a beginning naturally has an end.

> Everything that has been begotten tends toward destruction.

But concerning formal cause it is true that, if it is unchangeable, its effect is also 206 unchangeable, and conversely: if whiteness is changeable, a white thing is also changeable. Thus, because humanity, which is the substantial nature of a human being and its formal cause, is changeable, its effect is also changeable: namely, making a human being [Col. 0311C]. Since, then, God is not a formal cause but an efficient cause, things are not unchangeable merely because he is unchangeable [Note: [Col. 0311] The printed codex is again wholly confused in the preceding text; its final words read: “yet things change.”].

And although many things in this age seem to happen by chance, they nevertheless do not happen contrary to God’s ordinance [Note: [Col. 0311] The printed text reads: “all things happen by God’s ordinance, that is, they happen because,” etc.], who knows how and in what manner each thing occurs. For, as the philosopher says, “There is no thing whose beginning is not preceded by a lawful cause and reason.” Hence Christ says in the Gospel that not even one sparrow falls to the ground without God (Matt. X).

The following argument receives this answer. Many things are done in sin and by means of sin, yet are not sins and are from God. For example, knowledge which one acquires with an evil intention—namely, for the sake of human favour or earthly advantage—is acquired by that person through sin, yet is from God. Likewise, authority acquired simoniacally is acquired in sin and through sin, yet is from God. Likewise, money acquired through usury is possessed in sin and through sin.

Similarly, although human flesh incidentally has its origin from sin, what it is comes from God. [Col. 0312A] Moreover, no creature exists which was not created for some usefulness. Some things were created by God for human food, others for other uses, such as beasts of burden. Some were created to humble us, such as venomous animals, so that a person, considering that these dumb animals can harm him even to death, may humble himself beneath the hand of God the Creator and recognize what he is and from whom he comes. Some were created for understanding the Creator, so that through the things made the invisible things of God may be intellectually discerned. Some were created for punishment, such as the punishments of Gehenna and other instrumental causes of punishment; some for exercise, such as certain harmful things through which a person is stirred to good by patience; and some for delight. Nothing in this world, therefore, was created which was not created for some [Col. 0312B] good use.

## CHAPTER VI. The authorities which prove that the good God created the world

After determining the authorities [Note: [Col. 0311] The printed edition wrongly reads: “the authorities of determinations.”] and refuting the arguments by which heretics seem to confirm their error, let us turn our pen to the authorities and arguments opposed to them [Note: [Col. 0311] The printed edition has “meet.”]. John says concerning Christ: “All things were made through him” (John I). Either this totality includes visible and invisible things together, or it does not [Note: [Col. 0311] The preceding text is again wholly confused in the printed edition.]. If not all things, it includes either visible things only, invisible things only, or some visible and some invisible things; but they do not grant this.

If it includes invisible things only, why invisible rather than [Col. 0312C] visible things, since visible things are more numerous than invisible things and therefore more properly belong to the totality? Hence it follows: “And without him nothing was made” (ibid.), that is, no thing was made without him.

Perhaps the heretics will say that by the term “nothing” is denoted a bodily thing which perishes and tends to nothing. But many bodily things neither perish nor tend to nothing, such as the sun and other stars; and it is said of the earth that it stands forever. If they say that the stars vary according to rising and setting, and according to the increase and decrease of light, then by the same reasoning souls vary and tend to nothing; for they change according to sorrow and joy, ignorance and knowledge, sin and [Col. 0312D] righteousness.

Accordingly, if every bodily thing, because it is changeable, is denoted by this name, “nothing,” by what reasoning would not every spirit, because it is changeable, likewise be denoted? [Note: [Col. 0311] The printed edition has this: “Therefore also all species, because every species of flesh is changeable.”] Again, in the same Gospel: “He came unto his own, and his own received him not” (ibid.). What is denoted by “his own,” except these visible and worldly things, into which Christ came by assuming humanity? They are called Christ’s own [Col. 0313A] not so much by right of possession as by right of creation and authority. If they say that they are Christ’s own by right of possession, then the possession of the devil is also the possession of God; for, if they were created by the devil, they are possessed more by him than by God, and yet there is no fellowship of Christ with Belial (II Cor. VI). Again, in the same Gospel: “He was in the world, and the world was made by him” (John I). Again, in the Apostles’ Creed one reads: “Creator of heaven and earth.” Again, Christ says in the Gospel: “Are not two sparrows sold for an assarion? And not one of them falls to the earth without your Father” (Matt. X). What is it for a sparrow not to fall upon the earth without your Father, except that the sparrow is under God’s power? Again, he says in the Gospel that God clothes the lilies of the field (Matt. VI). What is it for God to clothe [Col. 0313B] the lilies of the field except to give them an elegant nature, and thus for the nature of the lily to be from God? Again, the Apostle, speaking of Christ in the Epistle to the Colossians (ch. I), says: “In him all things were created, visible and invisible.” Again, in the Epistle to the Hebrews (ch. I): “In many and diverse ways, God, formerly speaking to the fathers through the prophets, has in these last days spoken to us through the Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom he also made the ages.” Again, in the same Epistle, by David’s authority, he proves that God created heaven and earth, in this manner: “In the beginning, O Lord, thou didst found the earth, and the heavens are the works of thy hands” (Ps. CI [102]).

Again, in the Acts of the Apostles (ch. XVII), Paul says to the Athenians: “I proclaim to you this unknown God, for whom you have made this altar: he is the God who made this [Col. 0313C] world and all things in it, in whom we live and move and are.” In Luke also (ch. III), where Christ’s genealogy is set forth, one reads: “Who was Seth’s, who was Adam’s, who was God’s.” Adam, moreover, is said to have been God’s son by reason of creation, and thus was from God, not from the devil. Again, Christ says to the Jews in the Gospel: “You have dishonoured me, but my Father glorifies me, [Note: [Col. 0313] The preceding period is omitted in the printed edition, so that the sense there is left incomplete.] of whom you say that he is your God” (John VIII). If, then, the Jews called God the Father their God, they did not believe the devil to be their God.

Of those heretics against whom we are speaking, the Apostle says to Timothy: “The Spirit said that in the last times certain persons will depart from the faith, giving heed to spirits of error and doctrines of demons, [Col. 0313D] speaking lies in hypocrisy; forbidding marriage and abstinence from foods which God created” (I Tim. IV). Do not the aforesaid heretics depart from the faith in the last times—from the faith, I say, which the universal Church holds? For they do not depart from the faith of the Jews, since they do not possess faith; nor from the faith of the Saracens, because they lack faith. Therefore, they depart from the faith of Christians. These are they who attend to doctrines of demons and, pretending to be righteous, speak lies in hypocrisy. They forbid marriage because they condemn marriage; they command abstinence from foods which God created. Again, in Matthew the Lord is introduced speaking thus: “He who made man from the beginning made them male and female” (Matt. XIX); and elsewhere: “So God loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son” (John III). Paul also says in the Epistle to the Corinthians: “God set the members, each one of them, in the body as he willed” (I Cor. XII). Again, Peter: “The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob raised up his Son Jesus” (Acts XXXVI).

208

## CHAPTER VII. By what authorities it is proved that God Almighty created the world.

The errors mentioned above are also refuted by the authorities of pagan philosophers. [Col. 0314B] For the Apostle said that God’s invisible things are perceived from the things that have been made (Rom. I), by philosophers; because through the magnitude of things the philosophers understood God’s power, through their beauty his wisdom, and through their order his divine goodness. Hence Plato, speaking of God, said: “To discover the Maker of the universe is as difficult as it is to declare him worthily once discovered.” [Note: [Col. 0313] The printed edition reads *proferre*, “to bring forth.”] Boethius also says in the book *The Consolation*:

> O thou who rulest the world by everlasting reason,  
> Begetter of earth and heaven.

## CHAPTER VIII. By what arguments it is proved that God Almighty was the Creator both of visible and invisible things.

[Col. 0314C]

The same is maintained by various arguments. If the devil is the author of visible things, one asks whether he had a beginning or not. Christ indicates that he had a beginning when he says: “He was a murderer from the beginning”; [Note: [Col. 0313] The printed edition reads *hominum*, “of men,” but the manuscript is better: “He was a murderer from the beginning; therefore he had a beginning.”] therefore he had a beginning (John VIII). If he existed from eternity, [Note: [Col. 0313] This is wrongly omitted in the printed edition.] there were two coeternal authors of things, and thus two coeternal creators of things, and consequently two gods—although all the Scripture of the Old and New Testament cries out that there is one God alone.

Again, since the devil is mutable and variable, there is in him some composition, at least of a property with a subject; since change is nothing other than the accession of one property to the subject of another and the departure of the other. But everything composite has a principle of its existence. [Note: [Col. 0313] The printed edition incorrectly reads: “at some time there is in him,” etc.]

[Col. 0314D] Again, if there are two principles of things, either one was imperfect or the other superfluous.

Again, the devil created the world either prompted by malice or by goodness. But not by goodness, because the author of evil and supremely evil cannot do anything except from malice. Yet if he created the world from malice, how did he arrange all things so that they should succeed one another so elegantly, [Note: [Col. 0313] The printed edition has: “so that the seasons should succeed one another so elegantly.”] with the moon and stars serving the night, and the sun the day, when supreme goodness rather than malice shines forth in these things? [Note: [Col. 0313] The printed edition reads “the righteous” in place of “in these things.”]

[Col. 0315A] Again, if the devil, namely Lucifer, existed from eternity, one asks whether the other demons were coeternal with him or not. If they say that there was only one demon, namely Lucifer, [Note: [Col. 0315] The printed edition wrongly reads “God.”] they are refuted by Gospel authority, which testifies that the devil, replying to Christ when asked his name, said: “My name is Legion” (Mark V), as if to say: “There is not only one demon here, but many.” Elsewhere it is written that the Jews said of Christ: “By Beelzebub, prince of demons, he casts out demons” (Luke XI). Therefore one asks whether the other demons were coeternal with Lucifer. If they were coeternal, then many things were coeternal with God.

Again, since good and evil spirits are of the same nature, just as good spirits had a beginning, so did evil ones. [Note: [Col. 0315] The printed edition has: “Just as good spirits have a good beginning,” etc.] Again, if [Col. 0315B] other demons were coeternal with Lucifer, one asks whether they could create the world as Lucifer could, since they were of the same nature as he. But if the other demons had a beginning, one asks: from whom? For it is plain that they neither composed themselves nor could come to be by chance. [Note: [Col. 0315] The printed edition reads “could be by cause.”] But if they had their beginning from Lucifer, Lucifer was the author not only of bodily things but also of spiritual things. But if from God, God was their author.

Again, since all creatures are mutable, there must be one immutable cause from which all mutable things proceed. Therefore, since Lucifer is mutable, he is from the immutable one, namely God. If he is from God, he was created by God either evil or good. But far be it that he was created evil, because an evil nature is not from God; for no creature, in so far as it exists, is evil. Thus Lucifer was created good by God; and if afterwards he was evil, he began to be evil through sin. But if he was created by God, and visible things were made by him after his creation, he created them either while evil or while good. [Col. 0315C] But if he created them while good, creature created creature. Yet how could the begotten be created by the begotten, or the created by the created? For it is necessary that that which creates be uncreated. For if it were created by another, that other would either be created or not. If it were created, an infinite regress of creatures would result. Therefore the Creator must be uncreated; nor is there any reason why one creature should create another rather than another another.

But if, while evil, he created the world from malice, as has been said, all things would have been made disorderly rather than orderly. It is therefore clear that all things were made by God and not by Lucifer. For if there were two principles of things, and one were the principle of good things and the other of evil things, then, as the principle of good things would be supremely and absolutely good, so the principle of evil things would be supremely and absolutely evil. Therefore, just as in the supreme good there is no malice, so in the supreme evil there is no goodness.

Again, if the devil created the human body and God the soul, one asks [Col. 0316A] by what authority the soul is joined to the body and the body to the soul. If they say that the devil and God agreed to this, there was some agreement of Christ with Belial. Far be it also that we should say God created the soul in order to unite it to an evil nature, for on this account the soul could throw back upon God the cause of its sin.

## CHAPTER IX. The opinion of certain heretics who say that there are no souls in human bodies except apostate angels who fell from heaven.

[Note: [Col. 0315] The heading in the printed codex reads: “And that all angels fell from heaven.”]

Certain of the aforesaid heretics, seeking aid for their ignorance, deny that souls are created each day and infused into bodies. They assert that only apostate angels, who fell from heaven, [Col. 0316B] [Note: [Col. 0315] The printed edition reads “descended,” but incorrectly.] are infused into human bodies by God’s permission, so that there they may be able to do penance. They also say of them that one spirit may successively be infused into eight bodies, so that, if it has not done penance in one, it may do so in another. Further, they say that no spirit of a human being exists other than an apostate angel, and that there are no spirits in heaven, because all the spirits that were in heaven fell with Lucifer.

They try to prove this by the authority: “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. XV). By the house of Israel they mean the assembly of angels who were created in heaven in order to see God, but fell through sin. By another authority they also say: “No one ascends into heaven [Col. 0316C] except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III).

210

## CHAPTER X. By what arguments and authorities it is proved that there is a soul in the human body, and not demons.

According to this opinion, when Christ cast an evil spirit out of a human body, since there was no other spirit in it, the body remained lifeless. Again, if the human body is from the devil and the human spirit is the devil, the whole human being is, as it were, essentially evil; and therefore cannot do good or merit eternal life.

Again, various authorities loudly declare that there is a soul in a human being, not an angel. For Christ says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can cast body and soul [Col. 0316D] into Gehenna” (Matt. X). Elsewhere he says: “What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers loss of his soul?” (Matt. XVI; Mark VIII). Again, he says: “He who hates his soul in this world keeps it for eternal life” (John XII).

Perhaps the heretic will object that in the Acts of the Apostles an angel is called a human spirit, where the faithful, assembled in one place, when Peter knocked, said: “It is his angel” (Acts VII), that is, the angel who is his spirit—as though they said: “It is Peter’s spirit and not Peter.”

To this we say that there Peter’s angel is called the angel assigned to Peter for his protection. For angels assigned to humans as guardians are often recorded as having appeared in their likeness. Or they called Peter’s soul Peter’s angel, supposing Peter to have been killed and his soul to be appearing and wishing to announce something about Peter. Therefore, because it performed the office of a messenger, they called it an angel; for *angel* means “messenger.”

## CHAPTER XI. On what ground heretics say that demons are punished in human bodies.

The aforesaid heretics also say that, because angels sinned [Col. 0317B] in a spiritual nature, God wished to punish them in bodily substance, and there to do penance. For, as they say, freedom of choice and the power of doing penance were not taken from them; otherwise they would be treated unjustly.

To this it must be said that they sinned through pride and, as authority says, are so hardened that they cannot repent. This results from their hardened malice, not from God’s injustice, just as good angels, confirmed by grace, cannot sin. Again, if demons enter different human bodies in order to do penance, why is their entrance allowed into as many as eight or sixteen bodies, and no more? Further, those who assert this fall into the Pythagorean error, which maintained that the soul of a human being, owing to sin, enters after death the body of another human being or of a brute animal.

Again, if demons wish to be saved, one wills another’s salvation; otherwise he would not have a good will and would not wish to be saved. [Note: [Col. 0317] The manuscript codex has: “can.”] But the devil does not will his neighbour’s salvation, since he suggests evil to the human spirit; and thus demons are divided among themselves, and so they shall be laid waste: “For every kingdom,” as Christ says, “divided against itself shall be laid waste” (Luke XI).

211

## CHAPTER XII. By what authorities and arguments it is proved that demons will not be saved.

[Note: [Col. 0317] The manuscript codex has “will be damned.”]

That demons [Note: [Col. 0317] The printed edition wrongly reads “human beings.”] will be damned seems to be indicated by the Lord in the Gospel, where he says: “Depart, ye cursed, [Col. 0317D] into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV). Again, by what argument or authority do the heretics say that demons are human spirits, or that they enter different bodies where penance is done by them? Where neither authority nor argument is present, an opinion is not probable. Again, in saying that other demons [Note: [Col. 0317] In the printed codex the word “human beings” is wrongly read in place of “demons.”] are infused into human bodies, they are compelled to assert that Lucifer himself must be united to some body in order to repent.

Perhaps they will say that he is to be infused into the body of Antichrist, [Col. 0318A] according to the authority which says that Lucifer will dwell bodily in Antichrist. But this must be referred not to essence but to fullness of power, so that the sense is: “He will dwell bodily in him,” [Note: [Col. 0317] The printed edition: “in that body.”] that is, he will possess him fully in order to carry out every will of his own. Again, if the reality of human nature consists in this, namely in a body and an evil spirit, [Note: [Col. 0317] The word *maligno*, “evil,” is omitted in the printed edition, but must be added, as is clear from the context.] Christ was not a true human being, because he neither had nor united to himself an evil spirit. But he was a true human being because he had a body and a soul; therefore either other human beings are not true human beings, or they have body and soul. [Note: [Col. 0317] The text here is wholly confused in the printed edition.]

## CHAPTER XIII. By what authorities it is proved that certain angelic spirits remained in heaven.

[Col. 0318B] That certain angelic spirits remained in heaven is indicated by John in the Apocalypse, who says that the dragon drew after himself a third part of the stars (Apoc. XII). He calls Lucifer the dragon, and the stars the angels created in the empyrean heaven. He did not draw all of them, but a third part. For among the angels there were some who were proud, such as Lucifer and certain other greater ones; others consenting to their perverse will; and others not resisting. Lucifer drew all these to himself through their perverse consent.

The Lord also, speaking in the Gospel about little children, says: “Their angels in heaven always see the face of your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVIII). This cannot be understood of [Col. 0318C] evil angels, for to see the Father’s face is to enjoy the divine vision, which cannot belong to evil angels. It must therefore be understood of good angels. But where are those who see the Father’s face, except [Note: [Col. 0317] The printed codex here omits the word “except.”] in heaven? Therefore some spirits are in heaven. Again: “The angel of the Lord descended from heaven and, approaching, rolled away the stone and sat upon it” (Matt. XXVIII). Again, the Apostle says: “If an angel from heaven should tell or preach to you otherwise, let him be anathema” (Gal. I).

212

## CHAPTER XIV. By what arguments it is proved that not all angels fell from heaven.

The same is proved thus. All angels were created by God in heaven. Therefore, if all had fallen from heaven through sin, [Col. 0318D] [Note: [Col. 0317] The printed edition reads “from God.”] the Lord could be charged with injustice or impiety if, knowing that all angels would fall, he had created them. It was fitting that, just as God’s justice appeared in those who turned away, [Note: [Col. 0317] The printed edition reads *adversis*, “adverse,” but incorrectly.] so his mercy should appear in those who turned toward him.

But perhaps opponents will object: if more angels remained in heaven, it does not appear that human beings were made to make up the number of angels.

To this we say: Even if no angel had fallen, human beings would nevertheless have been created, because more human beings will be saved [Col. 0319A] than there are angels who fell. Thus humanity was created not merely to replenish the fall, but rather to adorn the heavenly Jerusalem and to compose it, from citizens of different ranks, as it were from different walls. For it was fitting that both corporeal and incorporeal nature should share in divine goodness, enjoy it, and live happily. [Note: [Col. 0319] The printed edition reads: “should become happy.”] Perhaps they will say that certain angels are good but fell from heaven with the others; but how could those who did not fall into sin undergo a fall?

## CHAPTER XV. The opinion of heretics who say that the souls of the saints did not ascend into heaven with Christ, and that Christ did not descend into hell.

[Col. 0319B]

Likewise, they say that the souls of the saints did not ascend into heaven when Christ ascended, because they do not have this explicitly from the Gospel. They also say that Christ did not descend to the lower regions, nor free souls from hell, because they assert that the souls of all those who died before Christ’s coming are eternally damned. Yet in this they seem to contradict themselves, because they say John the Baptist was damned because he doubted Christ’s coming to hell. Thus, when he sent two disciples to Christ, he said: “Art thou he who is to come, or do we await another?” (Luke VII), as if he said: “Will you descend to the lower regions, so that I may be your herald in hell, as I was in the world?” Perhaps they will say [Col. 0319C] that John did not doubt [Note: [Col. 0319] The printed codex corruptly reads “always.”] concerning this, but whether Christ was the one to be sent into the world for the redemption of humankind.

## CHAPTER XVI. By what authorities and arguments it is proved that Christ descended to the lower regions and freed the souls of the saints from them.

Against this opinion John says: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John VII). And elsewhere: “He who comes after me has been made before me” (John I). But [Note: [Col. 0319] The printed edition wrongly reads “they are.”] those who say that John was damned oppose Christ’s words concerning John: “Among those born of women no one greater than John the Baptist has arisen” (Luke VII). And elsewhere: “What went you out into the wilderness to see? A reed [Col. 0319D] shaken by the wind? But what went you out to see? A prophet? Indeed, more than a prophet” (ibid.). Moreover, he himself underwent a capital sentence in defence of righteousness. While yet in his mother’s womb, he exulted at the Virgin’s coming. Sanctified in the womb, he was a prophet before his birth. On his account his mother prophesied and speech was restored to his father. He did not doubt whether Christ was God’s Son, or whether he would descend to the lower regions, since he had read this in the prophets. Rather, his disciples doubted; he sent them [Col. 0320A] to Christ so that they might be made certain concerning Christ’s coming.

Or John, under the form of a question, expressed an affection of piety and compassion when he said: “Art thou he who is to come?” (ibid.), as if to say: “You, who are such and so great, have already humbled yourself so far as to assume our weakness, [Note: [Col. 0319] The printed edition reads “humility.”] and you will descend to the lower regions.” It is therefore clear that Christ descended to the lower regions and freed the souls of the saints from them. Thus Christ says in the Gospel: “When a strong man armed guards his courtyard, the things he possesses are at peace; but when one stronger comes upon him and overcomes him, he takes away all his weapons [Note: [Col. 0319] The printed edition reads *conferet*, “will bring together.”] and distributes them” (Luke XI). Again, the Apostles’ Creed reads: “He descended to the lower regions.” Again, to show that Christ freed souls from the lower regions, the Apostle employs David’s authority, saying: “He led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men” (Eph. IV). Elsewhere he says that Christ descended into the lower parts of the earth (ibid.).

Again, elsewhere he says that whoever says, doubtingly, “He descended,” calls Christ back from the lower regions.

But if he descended to the lower regions, why did he descend except to free captives? For he did not descend by reason of any merit of his own, but in order to free those whom the devil unjustly held in hell. Again, authority says that many bodies of saints who had fallen asleep arose (Matt. XXVII). Did not they also ascend with Christ? For if they were afterwards reduced to ashes again, they do not appear to have been true witnesses of the resurrection. [Col. 0320C] [Note: [Col. 0319] All the preceding material is confused in the printed codex.] Again, if those souls which were freed from the lower regions ascended with Christ, where did they remain? In the earthly paradise? No, because that place belongs to bodily, not spiritual, beings.

## CHAPTER XVII. How this authority is to be understood: “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. XV).

What they say—that the phrase “I was not sent except,” etc., is to be understood of evil angels—cannot stand. For in Sacred Scripture, by “the house of Israel” is customarily understood only the Synagogue, descended by generation from Jacob, who was called Israel; or the Church, which now sees God through a mirror [Note: [Col. 0319] The printed edition reads “appearance.”] and will in the future see him face to face. Again, how [Col. 0320D] [Note: [Col. 0319] The printed edition has “that.”] can Christ call the assembly of evil spirits the house of Israel, when evil spirits have been banished far from the vision of God? Again, if evil angels are to be saved, how was humanity created to replenish the fall of angels, if the angels’ fall is to be repaired in themselves? Again, from the very sense of the words one may understand that Christ meant Jews, not angels, by the house of Israel. For the Canaanite woman, who was a Gentile, cried after him; but he answered: “I was not [Col. 0321A] sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. XV), as if to say: “I was sent principally first to preach to the Jews, convert them to faith, perform miracles among them, and heal their sick.”

214

## CHAPTER XVIII. How this authority is to be understood: “No one ascends into heaven except he who,” etc. (John III).

What Christ says of himself, “No one ascends into heaven,” etc., must be understood thus: an exclusive term joined to a name of the whole does not exclude a part. Thus, if I say, “Socrates alone is yours,” Socrates’ body is not excluded. Hence, if I say, “Socrates is rational,” his soul is not excluded. Similarly, when it is said, “No one ascends,” etc.—said concerning [Col. 0321B] Christ alone, who ascends into heaven—his spiritual body, [Note: [Col. 0321] The printed edition reads “spiritually.”] that is, his Church, is not excluded. For the meaning is: “I alone, who descended by assuming humanity, shall ascend into heaven through the glorification of human nature, I who am in heaven through divinity.” Here the supposition is for the person, not for the nature. In this supposition the Church, which is one with Christ, is not excluded. [Note: [Col. 0321] The entire preceding period is omitted in the printed edition.]

Again, if the body is the work of the devil, a human being cannot do good, because a good tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor a bad tree good fruit (Matt. VII). Again, if every body is the devil’s work, the Son of God did not assume a body, because he did not unite to himself the devil’s work; and so he had no true body and was not a true [Col. 0321C] human being. Certain heretics concede this.

## CHAPTER XIX. The opinion of heretics who say that Christ did not assume a true body, nor eat or drink.

Certain heretics also say that the Son of God presented to human beings a shadow of human nature, not its reality, just as it is read in the Gospel that he appeared to his disciples in another form, and was transfigured on Mount Tabor (Matt. XVII), representing a glorified nature which he did not possess. Again, if he had a body, how did he come out of the Virgin with her womb closed? How did he walk upon the sea with dry feet? (Matt. XIV.) Shall we also say that the Son of God truly died and suffered pain upon the cross, [Note: [Col. 0321] The printed edition reads “composition” in place of “cross.”] although Hilary says that there was no passion and no pain in Christ?

The Apostle also says of Christ: “Found in appearance as a human being” (Phil. II); he does not say: “He was found in appearance to be a human being.” The one whom he called God, he called the same one “as a human being,” not “a human being,” in order to suggest there the reality of divinity and here the shadow of humanity. [Note: [Col. 0321] The entire preceding period is confused and without sense in the printed copy.] Again, since Christ is read to have given his body to the disciples, if [Col. 0322A] it was a true body, how did he give it to them to eat? By the same reasoning, he neither truly ate nor truly drank, nor was truly crucified, nor truly rose from the dead. Certain heretics also say that he was neither truly born of the Virgin nor conceived.

215

## CHAPTER XX. Resolution of the foregoing objections, and that Christ was a true human being.

Replying to these objections, we say that Christ did not appear in another form, but the disciples thought that he appeared in another form. [Note: [Col. 0321] The preceding material is absent from the printed edition.] Perhaps they were struck by *aurisia*, [Note: [Col. 0321] The printed edition has *aurifia*.] that is, a certain kind of blindness by which what was presented to their eyes was not seen by them.

Christ truly showed the disciples [Col. 0322B] human nature glorified on Mount Tabor, not its likeness. For God could miraculously display the glorification of a body in his own body. Similarly, it was miraculously done that Christ’s true body came from the Virgin’s closed womb and that he walked upon the sea with dry feet.

He also truly bore our pains. Hence the Apostle says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you may follow his footsteps” (I Pet. II). And elsewhere: “If indeed we suffer with him, that we may also be glorified with him” (Rom. VIII). Therefore, unless Christ had truly suffered, we would not rightly be said to suffer with him. And elsewhere: “Christ became obedient to the Father for us unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. II). And [Col. 0322C] Christ himself, displaying his blood, says: “This is the blood which shall be poured out for many” (Matt. XXVI).

But how do they bring forward Hilary’s authority, when they have no faith in the authorities of the holy Fathers? Yet we may say that Hilary referred this not to punishment, but to the cause of punishment, that is, guilt. [Note: [Col. 0321] The printed edition has, by error, the opposite: “to punishment, not to the cause of punishment.”] For Christ had in himself no cause of suffering or death, that is, no guilt. Nevertheless, Claudianus, in his book *On the Soul*, says of Hilary: “Hilary of Poitiers is said to have erred in two of the most notable kinds of his disputations: first, in saying that the soul is from some [source]; [Note: [Col. 0321] The words “from some” are absent from the printed edition, though a blank space has been left.] and secondly, in maintaining that Christ felt no pain on the cross. Although during his life he endured the pen of censure, at his death, [Col. 0322D] led by repentance, he suffered no loss of his merits.”

The following objection receives this answer: the conjunction *ut* (“as”) is not always a marker of impropriety or resemblance, but sometimes expresses reality, as in “as was supposed, the son of Joseph” (Luke III). Likewise, the adverb *quasi* (“as if”) is sometimes a marker of propriety, sometimes of resemblance, and sometimes an expression of reality, as where it says: “And we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father” (John I). Similarly, here the conjunction *ut* expresses reality, so that the sense of “found in appearance as a human being” (Phil. II) is: “a true human being.”

Christ also gave his mortal body to his disciples. Yet it was miraculous that the body, extended in space, entered through the narrow opening of the mouth. On this ground they maintain that Christ [Note: [Col. 0323] The printed edition corruptly reads “Christians.”] neither drank nor ate, because it was unfitting for the Son of God to undergo the customary evacuations of nature, since he himself says: “Everything that enters the mouth is discharged into the privy” (Matt. XV). But we prefer to be uncouth Catholics with Jerome rather than polished heretics with Mani. Catholic faith, however, maintains that Christ assumed all the defects [Col. 0323B] of human nature except ignorance and sin; for it was fitting that he who was to free us from defects should assume our defects.

216

## CHAPTER XXI. By what authorities and arguments it is proved that Christ assumed true flesh.

That [Note: [Col. 0323] The printed edition corruptly reads “therefore.”] the Son of God assumed true flesh is shown by many authorities and arguments. For the Apostle says of Christ in the Epistle to the Romans: “Who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. I). Again, Matthew writes concerning the conception of the glorious Virgin: “Before they came together, she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit” (Matt. I). And the angel says to Joseph: “For what is born in her is of the Holy Spirit” (ibid.). And in Luke (ch. I) [Col. 0323C] the angel says to Mary: “Behold, you shall conceive in your womb.” And John (ch. I) says: “The Word was made flesh.” Therefore, if something was conceived in the Virgin, what was conceived except a human body?

The same is proved by arguments as follows. In appearing in human nature, Christ redeemed human nature; therefore, if he truly redeemed human nature, he truly assumed human nature. For it was necessary that, just as the ruin of the human race came about through a human being, so its redemption should come about through a human being. Therefore humanity’s liberation came about through a human being. But a mere human being could not redeem; for if he were a mere human being, he would be infected with the stain of human nature. Therefore it was necessary that he should be God and, by reason of divinity, be pure and unable to sin.

Thus it was necessary for God to become human, in this way to redeem humanity. But if Christ did not have a body, by the same reasoning he lacked a soul. Yet he says in the Gospel: “I have power to lay down my soul and to take it up again” (John X). Elsewhere the Gospel reads: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. XXVI). Again, if Christ was not a true human being, he did not truly rise; and if [Col. 0324A] he did not truly rise, neither shall we truly rise. But authority says that Christ was the first-fruits of those who have fallen asleep (I Cor. XV). And Paul says: “Christ, rising from the dead, now dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. VI).

## CHAPTER XXII. That Christ truly ate and drank.

That Christ ate and drank is demonstrated by many authorities. In Matthew we read: “John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, ‘He has a demon’; the Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, ‘Look, a glutton and a drinker of wine’” (Matt. XI). And elsewhere: “When evening had come, Jesus reclined at table with his disciples; and while they were eating he said: [Col. 0324B] ‘Truly I tell you that one of you will betray me.’ And, distressed, they began each one to say: ‘Is it I, Lord?’ But he answered and said: ‘He who dips his hand with me in the dish, he will betray me’” [Note: [Col. 0323] The printed edition varies this Scriptural text, substituting the text of St Mark.] (Matt. XXVI). And Luke (ch. XI): “A certain woman from the crowd raised her voice and said to him: ‘Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you sucked.’”

Likewise elsewhere: “When he entered, on the Sabbath, the house of a certain ruler of the Pharisees to eat bread, they were watching him” [Note: [Col. 0323] All the preceding material is omitted in the printed edition, and the text here is wholly confused.] (Luke XIV). And elsewhere: “When the hour had come, he reclined at table, and the twelve apostles with him” [Note: [Col. 0323] Here again certain things are omitted in the printed edition.], and he said to them: “I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer” (Luke XXII).

And after the resurrection: “‘Have you here anything to eat?’ [Col. 0324C] They offered him a piece of broiled fish and a honeycomb. And when he had eaten before them, he took the remainder and gave it to them” (Luke XXIV).

217 CHAPTER XXIII. By whom the bodies of the saints will be glorified on the day of judgment.

Furthermore, the foregoing heretics are asked: if every human body is from the devil, by whom will the bodies of the saints be glorified on the day of judgment? Not by the devil; nor, apparently, by God, for God will not glorify an evil nature. Thus it appears that the saints will not rise in glorified bodies [Note: [Col. 0323] The preceding material is all confused in the printed copy.]. If they say that they will rise in bodies of another kind, [Col. 0324D] newly created by the good God, while the other corruptible bodies have been reduced to ashes, Christ answers them in the Gospel, saying: “Not a hair of your head will perish” (Luke XXI), as though he said: Even the hair will rise again [Note: [Col. 0323] In the printed edition everything is again confused in this manner: “what he says, the hair will rise again.”]. And Paul says: “This corruptible thing will put on incorruption” (I Cor. XV).

CHAPTER XXIV. The arguments proving that our bodies will rise again.

The same is proved by arguments. The soul that has sinned mortally [Col. 0325A] will be punished eternally; by the same reasoning, so too will that flesh in which and through which it sinned. For it would be unjust that new flesh should be created to be punished, and in which the soul should be punished, while that flesh should not rise again [Note: [Col. 0325] The printed edition has “in that flesh,” but incorrectly.] in which and according to which the soul sinned, so that it might be punished in that flesh. By the same reasoning by which new flesh is created, a new spirit also will be created.

For the Apostle, proving the resurrection, employs this comparison: “Fool, what is sown will not be made alive unless it first dies” (I Cor. XIII). By analogy, unless the human body first dies, it will not be made alive through the resurrection. Likewise, since body and soul are the principal parts of a human being, if a human being does not rise in those principal parts of which he consists, it appears that no human being will rise. This [Col. 0325B] perhaps some will grant, agreeing with the heresy of the Sadducees. Many authorities cry out against this heresy. For Christ says in the Gospel: “Do not marvel at this, because the hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live” (John V). Likewise Paul, in the Epistle to the Corinthians: “If Christ is preached as having risen from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?
