But if there is no resurrection of the dead [Note: [Col. 0325] The printed edition has “of death.”], neither has Christ risen. But if Christ has not risen, our preaching is empty and our faith is also empty” (I Cor. XV). Likewise the Apostle: “We shall indeed all rise again” (ibid.). Likewise: “And the dead will rise incorruptible” (ibid.). And if all the dead will rise, then Peter and [Col. 0325C] the other apostles will rise in the flesh, since they did not die in spirit. Likewise Christ says in the Gospel: “But concerning the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was said to you by God: ‘I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? And he is not the God of the dead but of the living” (Matt. XXII). Likewise: “Unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved; but for the sake of the elect those days will be shortened” (Matt. XXIV). Likewise, in the Apostles’ Creed one reads: “The resurrection of the flesh.”

For this article of faith concerning the resurrection of the dead and the resurrection of one’s own flesh, we can offer further arguments. We read that Christ in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0325] The printed edition corruptly has “Christ in the Gospels.”] raised bodies that had formerly been animate and were afterward [Col. 0325D] deprived of soul [Note: [Col. 0325] The printed edition has “furthermore,” but incorrectly.]. Therefore, by the same reasoning by which those were raised, our bodies, from which souls will be separated, will be raised on the day of judgment. For particular raisings are witnesses to the general resurrection.

It is also written that many bodies of saints who had fallen asleep arose (Matt. XXVII). Christ also, whose resurrection is a witness to our resurrection, rose in his own body [Note: [Col. 0325] Here again the printed edition has the entirely absurd reading “will rise.”]. By analogy, the saints will rise in their own bodies.

CHAPTER XXV. The authorities and arguments by which heretics seek to prove that the flesh reduced to ashes will not rise again.

[Col. 0326A]

Heretics attempt to attack this article of faith by various authorities and arguments. Thus the Apostle says: “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. XV); therefore our flesh will not be glorified. Likewise John says: “Behold, I make all things new” (Apoc. XXI). If all things will become new on the day of judgment, then human flesh too will become new. Likewise it is written: “Heaven and earth will pass away” (Matt. XXIV). By the same reasoning, so will the human body. For if those things that are more enduring will cease to exist and will not begin to exist again, much more will human bodies, which are subject to every corruption. And [Col. 0326B] another authority says: “I saw a new heaven and a new earth” (Apoc. XXI). Likewise Christ in the Gospel: “In the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are as angels in heaven” (Matt. XXII). Thus they will not be bodily but spiritual.

Furthermore, since flesh always desires evil and not good, how then will it be glorified? And how will that which has been reduced to ashes again be formed in the likeness of a human body? Likewise, the human body, after dissolution, entirely ceases to be; and if anything remains, it remains as ashes. Therefore, when a human body is formed on the day of judgment, it will be very unlike this one; and whatever ceases to exist as an individual cannot begin to exist again [Note: [Col. 0325] Certain things are omitted here in the printed edition.]. It appears that the bodies which will exist on the day of judgment will not [Col. 0326C] be those which were reduced to ashes. We can prove this by an analogy: suppose whiteness ceases to exist in Socrates, and after ten years a certain whiteness begins to exist in Socrates. Shall we say that it is, or can be, that same whiteness which ceased to exist in Socrates ten years earlier? Certainly not!

Furthermore, from the analogy offered by the Apostle (I Cor. XV) to prove the resurrection, concerning a grain killed in the ground, we may say that the body reduced to ashes is one thing, and that which will be animated on the day of judgment another. For just as the grain that dies in the earth is not the same as that which comes forth or grows from it, so the body reduced to ashes will not be that which will be raised on the day of judgment.

CHAPTER XXVI. Reply to the foregoing authorities and arguments, and proof that that very flesh will truly rise again.

[Col. 0326D]

The following answer is given to the foregoing. We say that, when the Apostle says, “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. XV), he does not mean the substance of flesh and blood, but their condition—that is, corruption—so that the sense is: flesh and blood, that is, the corruption of flesh and blood, will not possess the kingdom of God. Hence he says later: “Neither will corruption possess incorruption” [Note: [Col. 0325] The printed edition has “incorruptible things.”] (ibid.).

[Col. 0327A] What is written, that God will make all things new on the day of judgment, must be understood thus: he will renew all things. For the seasons will be renewed, and the earth will be renewed in respect of its outward qualities, since the earth will be smoother than marble and brighter than crystal. 219 Thus the other elements will be new, that is, renewed; just as cloth is called new when it has been renewed by repair. And a man is called a new son when renewed by repentance [Note: [Col. 0327] This period is absent from the printed edition.]. By analogy, our flesh will be new, that is, renewed through glorification.

In the same way one must understand what John says in the Apocalypse: “I saw a new heaven and a new earth” (Apoc. XXI), that is, a renewed earth and renewed air. For here “heaven” means the air, [Col. 0327B] in accordance with the saying: “The birds of heaven will eat it” (Mark IV; Luke VIII). On the day of resurrection, moreover, the air will no longer be altered according to diverse qualities, as it is now altered. What is said, “Heaven and earth will pass away” (Matt. XXIV), must be understood as an accidental, not a substantial, passing away. For heaven and earth are not to be understood as passing away so that they cease to exist, or [Note: [Col. 0327] The printed edition erroneously reads “although.”] are changed into something else—which would be a substantial passing away. Rather, they will pass away in their outward qualities, as has already been said.

What Christ says, “In the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage” (Matt. XXII), must not be understood to mean that the saints to come will not be bodily but only spiritual. It must rather be understood with reference to incorruption, [Note: [Col. 0327] The printed edition lacks some material here, leaving the sense incomplete.] all corruption having been banished. [Col. 0327C] For in the bodies of the saints there can be no corruption, whether of sexual intercourse [Note: [Col. 0327] Omitted in the printed edition.], of a wound, or of any other suffering.

We answer the arguments in the same manner. We say that flesh is not by its own nature inclined to evil, but rather through the weakness which it contracted from Adam’s sin. Before Adam’s sin, flesh did not struggle against spirit, nor spirit against flesh. Therefore on the day of judgment flesh will rise in its substance, not in its condition; for the very corruption which impels it to sin will not rise.

To the following objection we say that he who created all things from nothing, and formed the human body from mud, can restore a body reduced to ashes to its former—indeed, to a better—state; just as a potter returns a badly formed and broken pot to earth and refashions that same material into a better state. A silversmith too, from unclean and foul earth, by repeated firing extracts silver, though the matter of the earth is not changed. Thus the universal fire will cleanse earth and air. But the supreme craftsman, by his authority, will restore [Col. 0328A] human bodies to a better state.

We also say that that individual body which was reduced to ashes will be raised, because both the matter of the body and its substance remain. For although the human body puts off its human shape, it does not cease to be a substantial body [Note: [Col. 0327] The printed edition has “body or substance.”] nor does it lose any of the other substantial elements pertaining to the body [Note: [Col. 0327] Printed edition: “admits.”]. Thus that individual body, which is now reduced to ashes, will be glorified on the day of judgment and will receive human form again, since neither its matter nor its substance perishes.

The analogy concerning whiteness does not hold. Whiteness wholly ceases to exist, because it has neither matter nor form; it remains neither in matter nor in form. But concerning a grain that dies in the earth, we say that diverse [Col. 0328B] grains are produced from it, not one which is that very grain; nor does the whole substance of the grain pass into the substance of another grain, but partly into the substance of the ear, partly into that of the stalk, and partly into that of the husks and roots. But the whole human body which was reduced to ashes will be that whole body which rises on the day of judgment. “Whole,” I say, according to the truth of human nature.

220 CHAPTER XXVII. The reply of heretics who say that the soul perishes with the body.

These people wish to say that there will be no resurrection because the soul perishes with the body, as many false Christians of our time—indeed, heretics—say. Many arguments and authorities contradict them, [Col. 0328C] although they try to establish their error by authorities and arguments. For, as they say, Solomon says: “There is one destruction of human beings and beasts, and the condition of both is equal” (Eccles. III). As a human being dies, so they too die.

Here Solomon appears to mean that a human being perishes completely just as a beast does; hence, just as the soul in a brute animal perishes with the body, so it perishes in a human being. Moses also says that the soul is in the blood; thus it seems that when the blood perishes the soul perishes, and that the existence of blood is the existence of soul. Another authority also says: “The spirit of a human being goes away and does not return” (Ps. LXXVII): it goes away in death and does not return to life [Note: [Col. 0327] Everything preceding, from the beginning of the chapter, was lacking in the manuscript copy.].

[Col. 0328D] This is also proved by arguments as follows. The spirit of a brute animal is either corporeal or incorporeal [Note: [Col. 0327] The printed edition reads “body, or incorporeal.”]. If it is incorporeal, like the human spirit, why does it perish with the body while the human spirit does not? For by what reason or force will the human soul be preserved in the body rather than the soul of a brute? [Note: [Col. 0327] Here too the printed edition has a confused sense.] That the spirit of a brute is incorporeal [Note: [Col. 0327] For *incorporeus* the printed edition again reads *incorpus*, as in many other places.] is proved in many ways. The genus substance is divided into these two [Col. 0329A] genera, body and spirit. This difference, “corporeal,” added to the genus substance, produces the genus body; likewise, this difference, “incorporeal,” added to the genus substance, produces the genus spirit [Note: [Col. 0329] The preceding material is also remarkably confused in the printed edition here, as is what follows immediately.]. Therefore, since the difference “incorporeal” constitutes the genus spirit, every spirit is incorporeal. Therefore the spirit of a brute either is not a spirit or is incorporeal. That it is a spirit is proved thus: it has all the powers of spirit, such as the power of perceiving sensible things and the power of imagining; and these powers both come from spirit and exist in spirit.

Boethius too posits this division of spirits: one is rational and another irrational; and thus the spirit of a brute is a species of the genus spirit [Note: [Col. 0329] Here too the printed edition omits certain things, and the rest is without sense.]. For what [Col. 0329B] spirit is irrational except the spirit of a brute? Therefore it is incorporeal. Likewise, every body has qualities perceptible by some sense, but the qualities of the soul are not such; therefore the soul is not a body. Likewise, a body is subject to a sense or the senses, but the soul is not so subject. Likewise, every body is either animate or inanimate. If it is animate, then it is animated by some other soul; thus it is a soul having a soul, and so on to infinity. But if it is an inanimate body, then it does not give life, for that which does not live cannot give life. Likewise, if a brute animal consists of a spirit which is a body within its own body, to what common third thing are those two bodies joined? [Note: [Col. 0329] Here again the printed edition omits certain things.] Likewise, the spirit of a brute is wholly in every part of the body, [Col. 0329C] as is the human spirit; therefore it is incorporeal, for this belongs to what is incorporeal and not to what is corporeal.

The soul of a human being is also proved to perish with the body in another way: just as after the death of a brute no trace of its soul appears, so after the death of a human being no trace of the soul remains.

221 CHAPTER XXVIII. Solution to the foregoing authorities and arguments: it is shown that the soul does not perish with the body.

Against the foregoing authorities, we give this solution. What Solomon says, that human being and beast have one destruction (Eccles. III), must be referred to the physical spirit, not to the rational spirit.

For there is a twofold spirit in a human being: the [Col. 0329D] rational and incorporeal spirit, which does not perish with the body; and another called the physical or natural spirit, through which the rational soul is united to the body. This spirit is subtler than air and even than fire [Note: [Col. 0329] All this is confused in the printed edition.]; through it sensation and imagination occur, and it perishes with the body. Such a natural spirit is in the body of a brute animal; it gives it life and perishes when the [Col. 0330A] body perishes. In this sense Solomon says that human beings and beasts have one destruction, with regard to body and physical spirit [Note: [Col. 0329] Here again everything is confused in the printed edition.].

That the soul is said to be in the blood is not to be referred to the soul proper, but to animal life [Note: [Col. 0329] The printed edition has “spiritual.”]. Here the term *soul* is used to signify temporal life, which resides in the blood. Hence we read also in the Gospel: “No one has greater love than that a person lay down his soul for his friends” (John XV) [Note: [Col. 0329] The preceding sentence is absent from the manuscript, but fits excellently here.]. What is said, “The spirit of a human being goes away and does not return” (Ps. LXXVII), must be understood thus: it goes by itself into sin and does not return by itself to good.

We answer the arguments as follows. We say that the spirit of a brute animal is corporeal, and that corruption belongs to corporeality; [Col. 0330B] but the rational spirit which is in a human being is incorporeal and therefore incorruptible, since incorruption belongs to incorporeality, as will be shown below. That the spirit of a brute animal is corporeal is proved in many ways. As natural reason testifies, the spirit of a brute animal originates in the second digestion which takes place in the liver, and is nothing other than a thin vapor arising from that digestion. It is called natural in the liver, vital in the heart, and animal in the head. Moreover, through it [Note: [Col. 0329] These two words are lacking in the printed edition.] the rational soul is united to the human body. Therefore that spirit must have some affinity with the rational soul in subtlety and agility, and with the body in [Col. 0330C] corporeality [Note: [Col. 0329] The printed edition here reads “the body is embodied,” with absolutely no sense.].

Moreover, five powers belong to an incorporeal spirit because of its subtlety and penetrative clarity: sensation, imagination, reason, intellect, and intelligence. But in the spirit of a brute [Note: [Col. 0329] The word *brute* is omitted in the printed edition.] there are only two powers, which operate upon bodily things [Note: [Col. 0329] The printed edition reads: “because they were turned against bodily things.”]. It thus appears that this spirit too is bodily, since no powers flourish in it except the powers of perceiving bodily things. Likewise, if two incorporeal spirits are in the human body [Note: [Col. 0329] The printed edition reads: “spirit in bodies, are in bodies of humans.”], it appears either that the body is animated by two souls or that one spirit is superfluous.

We also say that what gives life to the body of a brute is called *spirit* in a different sense: namely, from breathing, and it is situated in a corporeal subject. But in an incorporeal substance, *spirit* is so called from spirituality, because [Col. 0330D] it is of a spiritual nature. The spirit of a brute is called spirit because it is of a breathing nature, because it makes the brute animal breathe. The vegetative principle also, by which the body of a brute is nourished and enlivened, is included under this genus “spirit,” because it is not of a spiritual nature; and although certain powers of spirit belong to that vegetative principle, it does not follow that it is the same as spirit. Thus many [Col. 0331A] properties of a brute animal belong to a human being, such as capacity for grossness, mortality, and so on; yet a brute animal is not therefore a human being, nor is it of human nature.

When Boethius gives this division of spirits, namely that one is rational and another irrational, he does not take the term *spirit* to denote spiritual nature, but rather the vegetative principle which causes breathing. The sense is: of spirits—that is, vegetative principles which make things breathe—one is rational and another irrational. That vegetative principle which gives life to the body of a brute may also be called spirit comparatively, in relation to coarser [Note: [Col. 0331] The printed edition absurdly has “religious.”] bodies, because it is a subtler body than certain other animate bodies. Hence air is commonly called spirit, and certain consonants are called mute, not because they produce [Col. 0331B] no sound, but because they produce less sound than vowels and semivowels.

To the next objection we say that the spirit of a brute has qualities perceptible by sense in its nature, but is of such subtlety that it escapes sensory perception, like air.

Therefore, since it is subtler than air, it is not surprising if it does not appear [Note: [Col. 0331] The printed edition reads, “if sense does not encounter it.”]. Although it is not actually subject to the senses, it is nevertheless sensible by nature [Note: [Col. 0331] The printed edition again corruptly reads, “nevertheless it is not sensible.”]. And just as sense fails with things greatest and smallest, so it fails with things that are more subtle [Note: [Col. 0331] This final word is again omitted in the printed edition.].

The claim that every body is called either animate or inanimate is false, for a stone is neither animate nor inanimate. Those bodies are called inanimate which can naturally be animated and to which animation is due, [Col. 0331C] even if they are not animated. We say, therefore, that the spirit of a brute, even if it is a body, is neither animate nor inanimate. Or we may say that every body is animate or inanimate, and that the spirit of a brute is an inanimate body which nevertheless animates another body, namely the body of the brute. Although two bodies concur in constituting a brute, they need not be joined to a common terminus [Note: [Col. 0331] Here again the printed edition is confused and also omits some things.]; for this belongs to continuous parts. But the physical spirit of the brute enters into the constitution of the brute animal by infusion or union, not by continuity. Nor is the spirit of a brute whole in each individual part, but its different parts are in different places.

We also say that many traces of the [Col. 0331D] rational soul remain. For in the sacred Scriptures souls are recorded as having appeared to many after death (Matt. XXVII). And Christ says in the Gospel that Lazarus’s soul was carried by angels after death into Abraham’s bosom; but the rich man—that is, the soul of the rich man—was buried in hell (Luke XVI).

CHAPTER XXIX. The theological authorities proving that the human soul is immortal.

[Col. 0332A]

That the human soul is immortal is proved, as we said above, by authorities of theologians and philosophers as well as by arguments. Christ, proving against the Sadducees that the soul does not perish with the body, says in the Gospel: “Have you not read: ‘I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’—the God of the living and not of the dead?” (Mark XII). Likewise, as he himself declares, the wicked will be told on the day of judgment: “Go, cursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV). Those to whom this is said will be punished in soul and body, and eternally. Therefore the soul survives after death. Paul also says that the saints will be caught up [Col. 0332B] to meet Christ in the air, and thus will always be with the Lord (I Thess. IV). And John says in the Gospel: “Those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life; but those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment” (John V).

223 CHAPTER XXX. The authorities of pagan philosophers proving that the human soul is immortal.

And since nearly every little compendium [Note: [Col. 0331] The printed edition has “syllable.”] of the New Testament proclaims this, let us turn our pen to the authorities of pagan philosophers, so that Christians may be ashamed to deny [Note: [Col. 0331] The printed edition has “define.”] the truth which pagan philosophers confessed.

[Col. 0332C] Mercury says in the *Asclepius*: “For every soul is immortal” [Note: [Col. 0331] The manuscript added here: “But not all uniformly.”]. Likewise, in the *Aphorisms on the Essence of the Supreme Good* [Note: [Col. 0331] The manuscript attributed all that follows to Tully.] it is written that the soul is on the horizon of eternity, and before time by the name of eternity. Here perpetuity is indicated. Therefore the sense is: by the name of eternity, and before the time of eternity, the soul is on the horizon [Note: [Col. 0331] The printed edition gives the clearer wording: “The soul is on the horizon of eternity, that is, in the time of perpetuity.”], and also at the boundary of perpetuity—which is perpetuity in the soul, that is, what ends in the soul, that is, does not extend beyond the soul—and is above time, which here is called memory [Note: [Col. 0331] Printed edition: “death.”], having a beginning and an end. Therefore, although the soul has had a beginning, it will not have an end.

Virgil too, speaking only of the soul, says:

> “And life, indignant, fled with a groan beneath the shades.”

That is, the soul alone, departing from the body with indignation, [Col. 0332D] descends to the underworld. Here Virgil intimated that the soul survives after death. And Tully, in the *Rhetoric*, says that it seems probable to the wise that punishments are prepared for the souls of the wicked in the underworld. If punishments are prepared in the underworld for the souls of the wicked, then souls survive after death. Likewise Mercury says in the *Asclepius* that souls [Col. 0333A] after dissolution are compelled to believe in punishments [Note: [Col. 0333] The printed edition has “yield to punishments.”] which in life they refused to believe on the basis of words. Plato too, in the *Timaeus*, says that souls after dissolution are afflicted by diverse punishments. In the *Phaedo* he also proves the soul’s immortality in many ways. But because authority has a waxen nose—that is, it can be bent into divergent meanings—it must be strengthened by arguments.

CHAPTER XXXI. The arguments proving that the human soul is immortal.

Whatever is corrupted is corrupted either through discord among its parts, as a body is, or through the flux of matter, as a property is. For every property is immutable in itself; but that it ceases is due to the flux of the matter in which it exists. Hence Boethius, in the prologue to the *Arithmetic*, [Col. 0333B] [Note: [Col. 0333] The printed edition has “Aristotle.”] says: “Wisdom is the contemplation [Note: [Col. 0333] Printed edition: “mirror.”] of those things which possess an immutable substance of their own,” that is, a property. But the soul is not a corporeal substance. Therefore it cannot be corrupted through the substance of its parts, because it is simple. A property, however, is not without form, because it is a substance; and it cannot be corrupted through the flux of matter, because it is not in matter. Therefore it is incorruptible.

That it is incorporeal is proved by many arguments. For example, this genus, spirit, contains under itself these species: soul and angel. Therefore either an angel is not incorporeal, or the soul too is incorporeal. Likewise, the soul does not receive bodily dimensions; therefore it is not corporeal. Likewise, the soul has its power to [Col. 0333C] comprehend spiritual and incorporeal things either from itself or from another; but not from another; therefore from itself and by its own power. Therefore it is spiritual and incorporeal, for a human being does not perceive incorporeal things from himself but from the soul.

Furthermore, things which are moved by voluntary and sensitive motion do not have this from being bodies, for if they did, all bodies would agree in this. Likewise, if bodies themselves have sensation and motion from themselves, then they themselves are the cause of their motion and sensation. And if this were so, they would never rest from voluntary motion; for as long as a cause is a cause, why does its effect never cease? Therefore a body does not have voluntary and sensitive motion, but is moved by the soul; therefore the soul is incorporeal [Note: [Col. 0333] The printed edition corruptly has “in the body.”].

Likewise, no body does anything by virtue of being a body; [Col. 0333D] otherwise it would do that very thing. But there are many actions of the body; therefore the body performs none of them by virtue of being a body, but every action is caused by an agent, because it is not a thing existing through itself. Therefore, besides body, there is something else which is the cause of bodily actions.

Likewise, bodies are continuous and composed of parts; but continuity occurs only through the movement of the parts of the composite, through the withdrawal of some from others, and through each being retained in its own place. But it does not belong to parts to join themselves together [Note: [Col. 0333] The printed edition has “join themselves through themselves.”], since it is rather [Col. 0334A] their nature to go in different directions. It is therefore necessary that there be, besides the body, something in its essence which brings this about.

Likewise, we can conceive that which gives life to the body [Note: [Col. 0333] The printed edition omits “body,” incorrectly.] without conceiving corporeality. Therefore it is not a body; for if it were substantially a body, it could not be conceived without corporeality. From the foregoing it is evident that the soul is incorporeal and therefore incorruptible; for if the soul is incorporeal, it is like an angel. By the same reasoning by which an angel is immortal, the soul is immortal also.

Likewise, to prove the same point we may use the suggestion employed by a certain religious man against a philosopher [Note: [Col. 0333] The printed edition has “Philip.”] who denied that the soul is immortal. He said: “Either the soul is mortal or immortal. If the soul is mortal and you believe it immortal, no harm results to you from this; but if it is [Col. 0334B] immortal and you believe it mortal, some harm may result to you. Therefore it is better to believe it immortal than mortal.” For, as Aristotle says in the book *On Choosing between Two Alternatives*, if evil follows from one and good follows from the other, that from which good follows is more to be chosen than the other, from which evil follows.

Likewise, in the *Aphorisms on the Essence of the Supreme Good*, it is written that destructible things [Note: [Col. 0333] Printed edition: “deflectible things.”] are destructible through corporeality, not through incorporeality. Likewise, we would blow away all the merits of the saints of both Old and New Testament if we said that no rewards are to be given for their merits after death. For if this were so, as the Apostle testifies, [Col. 0334C] the saints would be more miserable than every creature (I Cor. XV).

CHAPTER XXXII. The authorities and arguments proving that Christ was truly the Son of God.

It is evident from what has been said that Christ assumed true flesh and was a true human being; that he truly suffered and rose from the dead; and that there will truly be a resurrection of the dead, in their own flesh. Because of the foregoing arguments, certain heretics say that Christ indeed had true flesh, but was not the Son of God. For they judge it absurd to assert that the Son of God assumed flesh. But both authority and reason proclaim that Christ truly was the Son of God.

For Christ says: “I and the Father are one” (John X). [Col. 0334D] But far be it from us that Christ should have lied! Therefore either the Father was not God, or Christ was God. But he calls God his Father; therefore he himself was the Son of God. Let heretics therefore be ashamed to deny [Note: [Col. 0333] The printed edition incorrectly has “define.”] what even demons were compelled to confess, saying: “Jesus, Son of the living God, why have you come before the time to torment us?” (Matt. VIII).

And John the Evangelist proclaims that he is God, saying: “And the Word was God” (John I). And Paul, in the Epistle to the Hebrews, says of Christ: “Who, being the brightness of glory and the figure of his substance” [Col. 0335A] (Heb. I). Likewise John, in the Catholic Epistle: “There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one. And there are three who bear witness on earth: the spirit, the water, and the blood” (John V). Here John intimates that Christ was true man, true God, and true Son of God.

Likewise, it may be proved through the miraculous works which he did, which no one else could do, that he necessarily was God. Hence he himself says to the Jews: “If you do not believe the words, believe the works” (John X). Likewise he says that he saw Satan falling from heaven like lightning (Luke X). But this occurred at the beginning of the world. Therefore Christ existed at the beginning of the world; but at that time he was not a human being or another creature; therefore he was the Creator. Likewise he says: “Before Abraham [Col. 0335B] came to be, I am” (John VIII). Likewise John says that every creature was made through him; therefore he is not a mere creature, through whom every creature was made.

CHAPTER XXXIII. The opinion of certain heretics who say that Christ assumed a heavenly body, and that blessed Mary was created in heaven and had neither father nor mother.

Other heretics, however, teach that Christ assumed a heavenly body, that the Blessed Virgin was created in heaven and was of a heavenly nature, and thus that Christ assumed heavenly flesh from the Blessed Virgin. They attempt to prove this in various ways. The Apostle says: “He who is of the earth is earthly; he who is of heaven is heavenly” (1 Cor. 15). [Col. 0335C] Here the Apostle seems to imply that, just as Adam’s body was fashioned from the earth, so Christ’s body was formed from heaven. Hence they say that on Mount Tabor he showed this heavenly substance to the disciples when he was transfigured (Matt. 17). They also maintain—though this is found in no canonical Scripture—that the Blessed Virgin had neither father nor mother.

And because Christ assumed such a subtle nature, he was able to come forth from a closed womb and likewise to walk dry-footed upon the sea. For this reason they say that Christ did not eat: for a heavenly nature had no need of nourishment; it was spiritual rather than animal.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Reply to the foregoing: that Christ truly assumed human flesh, and that the Blessed Mary had a father and mother.

[Col. 0335D]

In reply to what has been said, we state that Christ was truly heavenly: heavenly because he led a heavenly life; heavenly because he was born from heaven; heavenly because he is God. Nor is he therefore said to have been from heaven because he received a body from heavenly substance; but because he descended from heaven—that is, from the immensity of the Father—and, proceeding from his heavenly nature, came into the world.

[Note: [Col. 0335] The printed edition reads “altogether”; our reading is nevertheless more suitable.]

Adam, however, was truly formed from earth and truly earthly, because he was intent on earthly things.

[Note: [Col. 0335] The printed edition has “earthly destruction.”]

That the immensity of the Father, or his very nature, is frequently called heaven in sacred Scripture is evident. Thus: “He who is of the earth speaks of the earth; he who comes from heaven is above all” (John 3). And John says: “There are three who bear witness in heaven” (John 5), that is, in Christ’s heavenly nature, namely, the divine nature. Elsewhere: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven” (John 3). And, as was said above, he showed that glorification of human flesh which the saints are to have with Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0335] The printed edition wrongly reads, “to have that glorification of flesh.”]

If he assumed a heavenly nature, how did he suffer in it? How was he crucified? Further, if on Mount Tabor he displayed the heavenly nature which he possessed, how had he previously concealed it, or how was he going to conceal it? Did he veil it with our flesh, or not? If with our flesh, then he had a twofold nature, [Col. 0336B] heavenly and human. If not with our flesh, with what other substance? If with none other, why was the heavenly nature not visible?

That the Blessed Virgin had a father and mother, and was therefore of our nature, is manifest from sacred Scripture. For the angel says to Mary: “Behold, Elizabeth your kinswoman, she also has conceived a son in her old age” (Luke 1). Therefore, if Blessed Mary had a kinswoman, she was related to her either on her father’s side or on her mother’s side.

[Note: [Col. 0335] The printed edition reads *cognatio* (“kinship”).]

Again, in John we read: “Now there stood by the cross of Jesus his mother, and Mary, the sister of his mother, and Mary of Cleophas” (John 19). By the same reasoning by which she had a sister, it is true that she had a father and mother. Elsewhere in the Gospel mention is also made of the sisters of Mary, the mother of Jesus (Matt. 15). Furthermore, [Col. 0336C] James, the son of Alphaeus, is called the brother of the Lord—that is, his kinsman—because his mother and the Mother of Jesus were sisters. In Paul’s Epistle to the Romans it is also written: “Who was made to him from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. 1). If Christ descended from the seed according to the flesh, and descended only through the Blessed Virgin, then the glorious Virgin was of David’s seed and was of our nature, not a heavenly one.

If they say that David had two sons, one good and the other evil, and that Christ descended through Mary from the good one, it will no less be evident that Mary descended from David. Thus either the Blessed Mary was of our nature, or David, like her, possessed a heavenly nature, as likewise did those descended from David.

That Christ descended according to the flesh from David, who was a murderer and adulterer, Paul clearly shows in his Epistle to the Romans, saying: “God alone is true, and every human being a liar, as it is written: ‘Against you alone have I sinned, and have done evil before you,’” etc. (Rom. 3).

In these words the Apostle shows that God is true in his promises, because, although David had sinned by murder and adultery, God nevertheless wished to fulfil what he had promised him: that Christ would be born from his seed. And this came about, because he forgave [Col. 0337A] David’s sin and Christ descended from his seed.

That Christ came forth from the closed womb was not due to subtlety of nature, but rather happened miraculously, as was also said above. The same applies to his walking dry-footed upon the sea. For he who made all things from nothing was able to come forth from a closed womb and to walk dry-footed upon the sea.

That Christ ate has been proved above sufficiently and carefully.

Furthermore, since Christ is read to have raised many persons, it is probable that he had the power to create whose power it was to raise. All these incongruities follow for those who say that there are two principles of things. Further, if anyone confesses this, he is bound to concede that he is the devil’s servant and that he is obliged to obey [Col. 0337B] the devil and to do his will, rather than God’s will.

## CHAPTER XXXV. The authorities and arguments by which heretics attempt to prove that the Mosaic Law was given by the devil.

Let us now proceed to the second article of the heresy. The aforesaid enemies of the Christian religion assert that the Mosaic Law was given by the prince of darkness—that is, the evil god—but the evangelical law by the prince of light—that is, the good God—so that, just as there are two principles of things, two Testaments were delivered by them. They seek to establish in many ways that the giver of the Old Testament was evil, as follows. Evil was he who commanded that a man gathering wood on the Sabbath be stoned [Col. 0337C] without any mercy (Num. 15). Again, how could he be good who committed murder in many instances?

[Note: [Col. 0337] The printed edition reads: “perpetrated.”]

Again, what justice was there in sparing David—a murderer, perjurer, adulterer, and proud man (2 Kings 12)—while rejecting Saul because he had preserved alive the king of the Amalekites (1 Kings 15)? Again, the Mosaic Law is called the law of death and the law of sin; therefore it was evil.

[Note: [Col. 0337] The printed edition: “was from evil.”]

Again, the Apostle says: “The law entered in, that transgression might abound” (Rom. 5). Elsewhere he says that the law brings no one to perfection (Heb. 7).

[Note: [Col. 0337] The manuscript, correctly, reads “to the perfect [state].”]

Again, if the Mosaic Law was good, why was it abolished? Again, if anyone were to observe the Mosaic Law, he would sin mortally; therefore the Mosaic Law is now evil. Therefore it either was evil, or that which [Col. 0337D] was good began to be evil.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Refutation of the foregoing authorities and arguments; and that the Mosaic Law was given by the good God.

To these points we reply that, although almighty God was the author of the old Law, he was not thereby unjust in commanding that the man gathering wood on the Sabbath be stoned. Rather, he commanded this in order to curb the pride of the children of Israel, who said: “There is no lack of one to perform it, but there is a lack of one to command it”; and in order that, recognizing their own weakness through reverence for the Law, they might not presume upon themselves but rise up to the grace of God. We also say that God’s justice killed many people who were so stiff-necked that they could not be corrected in any way. They were therefore punished reasonably, so that the punishment of some might be a terror to others. This was also for our instruction: that we may know [Col. 0338A] that we, who have received Christ’s grace, shall be punished more severely if we go astray than they were.

[Note: [Col. 0337] The printed edition reads “feel.”]

For, as the Apostle testifies: “All things written in the Old Testament were written for our instruction” (Rom. 15). Many also of those who were punished temporally were punished by temporal punishment in order that they might not be punished eternally.

God also acted mercifully toward them in this: they were quickly taken away from the midst, because, if they had lived longer, they would have sinned more and thus been punished more severely. We also say that it is madness to dispute concerning God’s judgments.

Moreover, David repented of his sins, and therefore God spared him; in this, then, God was merciful. Saul, however, the more he sinned, the more he grew proud against God, and from day to day fell into greater sin.

The Mosaic Law is not called a law of sin or of death because it was an efficient cause of sin or an efficient cause of temporal or eternal death, but because it was an occasion of sin or death; because:

> We always strive toward what is forbidden, and desire what is denied.

[Note: [Col. 0337] The printed edition corruptly reads “and they deny those things.”]  
(Ovid, *Amores* III.4.17.)

[Col. 0338C] For concupiscence, somewhat dormant, was more aroused through the giving of the Law, and flamed up against the Law’s command;

[Note: [Col. 0337] In the printed edition the word “against” is wrongly omitted.]

and thus the Law was an occasion of sin. Yet it is not therefore to be blamed, but rather human concupiscence. The Law was given by the good, not by the evil. Just as medicine is given to a sick person for good and not for evil: if the sick person is disobedient, it will become his destruction rather than his health; yet the medicine is not therefore to be blamed, but the person’s disobedience.

Likewise, it was called a law of death because it commanded that a transgressor be punished temporally, and justly; or, if he was not punished for transgression of the Law, he was punished eternally. For the same reason the Apostle says: “The law entered in, that transgression might abound” (Rom. [Col. 0338D] 5). The Law itself made sin manifest, because before the Law was given certain sins were thought not to be sins, or were not thought to be as great as they were.

Therefore the Law is said to have brought no one to perfection, because the good work present in a person through observing the Law was not brought to completion at that person’s death, since he did not receive the reward. For the completion of merit is nothing other than receiving the reward.

[Note: [Col. 0337] In the printed edition everything here is confused and without sense.]

For, in the time of the old Law, one who died did not receive eternal recompense for the observance of the Law, because the gate of paradise was closed and a flaming sword stood before it. [Col. 0339A] We also say that the Law was not abolished because it was evil, but because it was less good; for things that are less good ought to yield to things that are better. Moreover, the old Law was one of promise; the evangelical Law, one of fulfilment. Once the thing promised has been fulfilled, the promise ought to cease; and when the truth comes, the shadow ought to cease. We also say that the Law was given for a time, not to remain permanently. Therefore, since the truth has come, the shadow ceases. Yet someone would not sin by observing the Law because the Law was evil, but because the old Law no longer has a place now.

That the Mosaic Law was good and given by God is loudly proclaimed by both authorities and arguments. For the Apostle says: “The Law indeed is good, just, and holy” (Rom. 7). The same Apostle, at the beginning of the Epistle to the Romans, says: “Paul, servant of Jesus Christ, called an apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made to him from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. 1). Behold: he calls the Scriptures of the Old Testament holy; and therefore the Scriptures of the Old Testament are good and were issued by the good God.

Again, the same author says in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “God, who at many times and in many ways formerly spoke to the fathers in the prophets, has in these last days spoken to us in the Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom he also made the worlds” (Heb. 1). Here the Apostle implies that God the Father spoke in the prophets, and similarly [Col. 0339C] in Moses; and thus he indicates that the Scriptures of the Old Testament were issued by God the Father.

Again, in Matthew we read: “I have not come to destroy the Law, but to fulfil it. Amen I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota or one stroke shall pass from the Law until all things are accomplished” (Matt. 5). And elsewhere: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do also to them; for this is the Law and the Prophets” (Mark 7). Elsewhere: “Behold, one came to him and said: ‘Good Master, what shall I do that I may have eternal life?’ And he said to him: ‘Why do you ask me concerning the good? One alone is good, God. But if you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments.’ He said to him: ‘Which?’ Jesus said: ‘You shall not murder; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; [Col. 0339D] you shall not bear false witness; honour your father and mother; love your neighbour as yourself’” (Matt. 19).

Again, in the Acts of the Apostles, Paul is presented as speaking in this way: “Men of Israel, and you who fear God, listen: the God of the people of Israel chose our fathers and exalted the people when they dwelt as strangers in Egypt, and with an uplifted arm brought them out of it” (Acts 13).

Again, Stephen in the Acts of the Apostles: “The voice of the Lord came to Moses, saying: ‘I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’” (Acts 7). Again Peter says: “First understand this: that no prophecy of Scripture comes by one’s own interpretation.”

[Note: [Col. 0339] The printed edition reads this differently, but our reading conforms to the text.]

“For prophecy was not ever brought by human will, but holy men of God spoke as inspired by the Holy Spirit” (2 Pet. 1). Again Peter: “We have the firmer prophetic word, to which you do well to attend, as to a lamp shining in a dark place” (ibid.). Again: “Every Scripture divinely inspired is useful for teaching, for correction, for instruction, that the person of God may be perfect, equipped for every good work” (2 Tim. 3).

And Peter introduces testimony from Joel, saying: “In the last days I shall pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh; your sons and your daughters shall prophesy” (Acts 2). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “A human being does not live by bread alone, but by [Col. 0340B] every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. 4). Again: “If you believed Moses, perhaps you would believe me also, for he wrote concerning me; but if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?” (John 5). Again: “They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them. If they do not hear Moses and the prophets, neither will they believe even if someone rises from the dead” (Luke 16). But Christ rose from the dead; therefore, whoever does not hear Moses and the prophets does not believe Christ, if that evangelical saying is true—which it cannot fail to be.

Again: “Beginning with Moses and all the prophets” (Luke 24). Again: “O foolish and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken” (ibid.). Again: “All things written concerning me in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms must be fulfilled” (ibid.). Again, in the Gospel: “We have found Jesus of Nazareth, of whom Moses and the prophets wrote” (John 1). Again Luke: “After the days of Mary’s purification according to the Law of Moses were fulfilled, they brought the child Jesus to Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord, as it is written in the Law of the Lord” (Luke 2).

Behold, you have the Law of Moses called the Law of the Lord. Therefore, whoever contradicts the Law of Moses contradicts the Lord. Again Paul: “Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all things written in the book of the Law, to do them” (Gal. 3). Again Paul: “Do not extinguish the Spirit; do not despise prophecy” (1 Thess. 5). And Peter in the Acts of the Apostles: “To him all the prophets bear witness that all who believe in him receive forgiveness of sins through his name” (Acts 10). Again Peter: “God thus fulfilled what he had foretold through the mouth of all the prophets, that his Christ should suffer” (Acts 3). Again James: “Whoever keeps the whole Law but offends in one point has become guilty of all” (Jas. 2).

Again Paul, in the Epistle to the Hebrews, cites the authority of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the other prophets (Heb. 11).

[Note: [Col. 0339] The printed edition has “Hedora” in place of Gideon, perhaps intending to say Deborah.]

Again Paul: “Thus I serve God, my Father, believing all that is written in the Law and the prophets” (Acts 24). And the four Evangelists quote the prophets Isaiah, Jeremiah, [Col. 0341A] and the other prophets. The Lord also brings David and other prophets forward as witnesses in the Gospel.

Furthermore, how can the Law be denied to be good, when the commandments it contains are good and holy, such as the commandments of the Decalogue: “Honour your father and mother”; “You shall not kill”; “You shall not commit adultery”; “You shall not steal”; and the like? Again, if the devil had given commandments, he would not have given commandments for avoiding evil, but rather for doing evil than good. Further, the Mosaic Law forbids evil and commands good; therefore it is good. Again, a person sinned mortally by transgressing the Law; therefore, by observing it, he merited [reward]. Christ also received the sacraments of the Law; therefore they were good, and so the Law was good.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. The authorities and arguments by which heretics prove that the Fathers of the Old Testament were evil and are damned.

[Col. 0341B]

They likewise say that the Fathers of the Old Testament were evil, and they attempt to prove this in many ways. They say that Moses was excluded from the land of promise because of sin: namely, because he doubted God’s power; because he was a murderer; because he married an Ethiopian woman (Exod. 2); and because he led an army to the destruction of the human race. They also adduce Aaron as damned because he made the molten calf (Exod. 32), because at the waters of contradiction he doubted together with Moses (Num. 20),

[Note: [Col. 0341] The printed edition confuses everything here as follows: “he contradicted at the waters, then he doubted.”]

and therefore did not enter the land of promise. They condemn Abraham [Col. 0341C] because he was willing to sacrifice his own son (Gen. 22), thereby opposing the law of nature; for, they say, the good God did not command this, but the evil one did. Likewise they condemn Isaac because he falsely said that his wife was his sister (Gen. 26), as Abraham his father had done (Gen. 21). They also condemn Jacob because he stole his brother’s birthright and deceived his father by a lie, saying: “I am Esau, your firstborn” (Gen. 27). Noah too is rejected because he became drunk and shamefully uncovered his thighs (Gen. 9). Likewise, they condemn Enos, son of Seth, because he first invented idols (Gen. 4). Nor do they except Enoch from this condemnation: for they say that he was taken away from the midst [Col. 0341D] and damned because of the enormity of his guilt (Gen. 5). They also condemn Joshua because, without judicial procedure, he sentenced countless people to death (Josh. 2, 7, etc.). Likewise Samson, because he married a foreign woman, was a fornicator, and killed himself (Judg. 14). They likewise condemn Jephthah because he sacrificed his own daughter (Judg. 11). Likewise Gideon, who, contrary to God’s command, made a tabernacle for himself and appointed himself priest (Judg. 6). For the same reason they reject Lot, because when drunk he knew his own daughters (Gen. 19). Likewise David, because he was [Col. 0342A] an adulterer and murderer (2 Kings 11). Job also, because he asserted that he had been punished unjustly (Job 3).

But why recount each instance? They subject all the Fathers of the Old Testament to eternal damnation,

[Note: [Col. 0341] The printed edition has “assign.”]

because they believe that, on account of the enormity of their sin, they descended into hell; and, besides their other sins, they observed a law handed down by the devil.

[Note: [Col. 0341] The printed edition reads: “who, deceived by other sins, observed the law handed down by God.”]

They also prove the same by their arguments, saying: Why did the Fathers of the Old Testament descend into hell unless because of enormous sin? But in hell there is no redemption (*Office of the Church*). Therefore they were not redeemed, and thus were damned. It is also written in the Law: “Cursed is he who does not fulfil all things written in this book” (Deut. 27). Peter also says: “This is a burden which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear” [Col. 0342B] (Acts 15).

[Note: [Col. 0341] The manuscript reads “we were able.”]

And Paul says that the Fathers of the Old Testament were subject to the curse of the Law (Gal. 3); and thus they were cursed, because they were transgressors, and thus damned.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Refutation of the objections; and that the Fathers of the Old Testament are not damned.

We refute the foregoing as follows. Just as the Mosaic Law was given by God and was good, so those who fulfilled it in charity merited eternal life; for every work done from charity merits eternal life. Hence Augustine says:

> “Have charity, and do whatever you wish.”

[Note: [Col. 0341] The printed edition has “the Apostle.”]

Of Moses we say that he was punished temporally in order that he might not be punished eternally. And if he doubted God’s power, yet, seeing that God himself had punished him for that sin, he repented of the same sin. That he killed a man was done by divine inspiration, because the man who was killed deserved death. That he married an Ethiopian woman was done by the divine will, or else he repented of it. That he led an army for the destruction of the human race was not done by his own authority but by God’s. It is evident, moreover, that Moses pleased God. For in the Gospel we read that, when Christ was transfigured, Moses and Elijah appeared speaking with him (Matt. 17; Mark 9; Luke 9). If Moses had been rejected, he would not have appeared after death speaking with Christ. Furthermore, if Moses had been rejected, Christ [Col. 0342D] would not have said in the Gospel: “If you believed Moses, perhaps you would believe me also” (John 5).

Paul also repeatedly commends him in the Epistle to the Hebrews, saying that he chose rather to be afflicted with the people of God than to enjoy pleasure in the king’s court (Heb. 11).

[Note: [Col. 0341] The printed edition reads: “than to flourish in royal dignity.”]

In the Epistle of Jude we also read that Michael disputed with the devil concerning Moses’ body, but repelled the devil by divine authority (Jude 9). If Moses had been rejected, Michael would never have disputed concerning his body. This dispute is to be understood thus: the devil [Col. 0343A] wished Moses’ body to be buried in the land of promise, so that the Israelites might worship it and thus become idolaters, as they worshipped the bronze serpent and therefore perished. But Michael, who presided over the Israelites, wished Moses’ body to be buried on a mountain outside the land of promise, so that Moses might thus be punished temporally in his body for sin, and so that the Jews might not be given an occasion for error.

Of Aaron we likewise say that he did not intend to make the molten calf. Rather, believing that the Israelites, on account of their avarice, would refuse him their earrings and other ornaments, he demanded them from them; and when they were handed over, he threw them angrily into the fire (Exod. 32).

[Note: [Col. 0343] Everything preceding is wholly confused and without sense in the printed edition.]

And just as he doubted with Moses, so he repented with him and was punished with him temporally for sin.

[Col. 0343B] Of Abraham we say that he wished to sacrifice his son at God’s command, but that same God called him back, and Abraham consented to the recall. God did not command this in order that Abraham might sacrifice his son, but in order to test his will. Nor was God evil in this, but good. Thus the text itself reads: “God tested Abraham,” etc. (Gen. 22). The Apostle too, commending him, says: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Rom. 4). Elsewhere he also says that God promised him that all nations would be blessed in his seed (Gen. 22). And Christ says of him: “Abraham saw my day and rejoiced” (John 8). If Abraham foresaw Christ’s advent by inspiration, he was more righteous than [Col. 0343C] evil. We also read in the Gospel that Lazarus’ soul was carried into Abraham’s bosom (Luke 16), but by Abraham’s bosom is understood rest.

Isaac, however, did not say that his wife was his sister with an intention to deceive, but out of fear of the malice of the inhabitants, lest he incur death because of her. And this may perhaps have been done by divine inspiration. Of Isaac Christ says: “Many shall come from East and West and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 8). Again, the Apostle says of Isaac that the Lord said to Abraham (Exod. 21): “In Isaac shall your seed be called” (Rom. 9).

If Jacob bought his brother’s birthright when his father was unwilling but his brother willing, in what did he sin? Nor did he deceive his father without cause; for since Jacob himself [Col. 0343D] was righteous and Esau rejected, the final blessing was more properly due to him than to Esau. If Noah, ignorant of the power of wine, became drunk, what fault was there in him? Of Enos—

[Note: [Col. 0343] The printed edition reads “Enoch.”]

—we say that he did not invent images, but certain spiritual prayers for invoking God. Enoch is not said to have been taken from the midst—that is, to have died—but rather to have been led by God into the earthly paradise or another place hidden from us. Of Joshua the same judgment must be given as was given concerning Moses: namely, that he acted by divine inspiration; that those whom he killed deserved death; and that it pertained to the just Judge to kill through ministers those whom he knew to deserve temporal death.

[Col. 0344A] Of Samson we say that he killed himself by divine inspiration and expiated by his death the sin that he may previously have committed. Since the Apostle commends Jephthah, likewise he freed himself from sin through repentance.

Gideon may be excused by a certain natural piety; and if he sinned, he was punished in his sons and acknowledged that he had sinned. We say that Lot sinned through drunkenness and incest, but his sin was forgiven through repentance. If he had been rejected, angels would not have appeared to him, nor would they have delivered him from Sodom, nor would it be read that he pleased God because of his hospitality.

The reply concerning David was given above. Job did not rebuke God, although the surface of his words seems to imply this. Rather, these things are to be referred to Christ, as Gregory testifies. All those mentioned here, [Col. 0344B] the Gospels and the other books of the New Testament declare to have been righteous, as has been proved above by various authorities.

Nor did the Fathers of the Old Testament descend into hell because they had been assigned to eternal damnation for sins. On the contrary, they merited eternal life; but because of the sin of the first parent—or rather, because of certain consequences of original sin and its effect—

[Note: [Col. 0343] The printed edition reads: “because of certain original [things], effect.”]

according to the saying of divine wisdom,

[Note: [Col. 0343] The printed edition has *sententiae* (“judgment”) instead of *sapientiae* (“wisdom”).]

the gate of paradise was closed to them. They descended only temporarily into hell,

[Note: [Col. 0343] The printed edition reads: “and they descended to the mouths of hell.”]

where they were not punished by material pain, [Col. 0344C] but by deprivation of the vision of God, while consoled by blessed hope. Nor did they descend to the depth of hell, of which it is said: “Who shall confess you in hell?” (Ps. 6), and elsewhere: “In hell there is no redemption” (*Office of the Church*).

Hence the Apostle says that Christ “died for our sins and rose again for our justification” (Rom. 4). For he died in order to free those who were held in darkness because of the effect of original sin, and he rose again in order to confer righteousness upon us. It was also proved above that Christ descended into hell in order to free the saints of the Old Testament from hell’s darkness.

The statement in the Law, “Cursed is he who does not fulfil all things in this book” (Deut. 27), is to be understood thus: “cursed,” that is, subject to a special reproach. Among the Jews, a person was reproached if he transgressed any commandment of the Law. Or it may be understood thus: “Cursed is he who does not fulfil all things which he is bound to fulfil.” What Peter said is true: no one fulfilled everything; yet no one was a transgressor if he fulfilled the things to which he was bound. In this respect all, according to the Apostle, were subject to the curse of the Law (Gal. 3), because no one fulfilled everything; and thus each person was subject to the Law’s spiritual reproach.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. The opinion of certain persons who say that baptism does not benefit children, and that children have no sin.

[Col. 0345A]

The aforesaid heretics oppose the Church’s sacraments. For they say that baptism is of no avail to a person before the years of discretion. But concerning this article of heresy different heretics hold different opinions. Some say that children have no sin and that baptism is therefore unnecessary for them. Others say that children have sin, but that remission of sin, or the efficacy of baptism, has no place without faith. The first group attempt to establish their position by these arguments.

First, let it be supposed that parents are without sin when they have carnal intercourse. Neither the one who begets sins, nor the one who creates sins, nor the one who is begotten sins. Through what chinks, then, does sin enter into children? Again, all merit depends upon willing and not willing; but children have neither willing nor not willing. Therefore in children there is no merit of good or evil. Again, where necessity exists, freedom is absent; but where freedom does not exist, neither does sin. But children are conceived by necessity in concupiscence; therefore they are not bound by sin because they are begotten concupiscently.

[Note: [Col. 0345] The printed edition has “in concupiscence” in place of “concupiscently.”]

Again, the soul is not unclean through creation or of itself; therefore it is not unclean,

[Note: [Col. 0345] The printed edition omits this final phrase.]

or else it is unclean from elsewhere: namely, because, when it is infused into the body, it contracts a stain, and thus seems to be punished unjustly for a stain which it contracts not from itself but from elsewhere. Again, the soul contracts [Col. 0345C] original sin either from itself or from the body; but sin is not in the body; therefore sin does not seem to be contracted from the body. But if it contracts sin from a soul, the soul seems to be from a soul, and thus by propagation.

## CHAPTER XL. Reply to the foregoing objections; and that children have original sin.

Against the first objection we say that, by God’s deep decree, it was established that, after the first transgression of the first human being, all who descended from Adam under the law of concupiscence would be held liable to original sin. From the first creation of the world God created nature,

[Note: [Col. 0345] The printed edition has “created marriage.”]

according to which it produced like things from like. Since, therefore, God was to beget things through the mediation of nature, he did not wish, because of Adam’s sin, to alter the law of nature. For this was the law of nature from the beginning: that like things should be generated from like, so that from a human being comes a human being, from a rational being a rational being. Therefore, after Adam’s sin, because Adam was subject to weakness, all who descended from him had to be weak; and, just as he was guilty, all who descended from him under the law of concupiscence were held guilty. Since every [Col. 0346A] human being is conceived in the stench of lust, which is sin, he or she is born guilty.

To the second objection we say that every actual sin depends upon willing and not willing, but not contracted sin—that is, original sin. Augustine nevertheless says that original sin is voluntary, not by a will of origin, or because it has the original will as its companion, but from the origin of the will: because this sin is originally contracted from the will of the first parent. For the perverse will of the first human being was the occasion of original sin.

[Note: [Col. 0345] In the manuscript, “origin” occurs in place of “occasion.”]

We also say that where freedom is absent, actual sin is absent; yet sin contracted by origin, that is, original sin, may be there. Indeed, because a child is conceived under a defective law of birth, it is necessary that the child be liable [Col. 0346B] to original sin. One could nevertheless also say that original sin depends upon freedom of choice, in respect of Adam’s freedom of choice, from which it proceeded incidentally.

The soul, moreover, is not unclean in itself; but because it is part of the person who is conceived in the stench of lust, just as that person is guilty, so also is the soul which is part of the person.

[Note: [Col. 0345] In the printed edition this entire discussion is presented without any sense.]

It is therefore not attributable to God that it is guilty or punished, but to the defective law of concupiscence. Thus a human being contracts original sin neither from body nor from soul, but, as has already been said, from the defective law of concupiscence. And even if the soul contracted a stain from the body, it would not yet follow that the stain was in the body; just as someone contracts a fever from an eel which [Col. 0346C] he has eaten, yet the fever is not in the eel, but it provides the occasion for becoming feverish. Similarly, the corrupted body is the occasion why there is a stain in the soul.

That sin is present in an infant is clear from David, who says: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Ps. 50). Paul also says that through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and thus death passed into all human beings (Rom. 5); and that through the transgression of one, all were made guilty (ibid.). And in the Gospel of John it is shown that an infant is born in sin, where it is said: “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he should be born blind?” (John 9). Here it is implied that being conceived in sin could result in his being born blind. [Col. 0346D]

### Chapter XLI. The opinion of heretics who say that baptism benefits no one before the years of discretion

Other heretics say that infants have sin, but that baptism does them no good before the years of discretion, because they do not have faith.

They seek to prove this by the authority which says: “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved; but he who does not believe shall be condemned” (Mark 16). As though the authority said: without baptism faith is of no avail, nor baptism without faith. Hence one to be baptized is customarily asked whether he believes in God the Father almighty. Therefore it would be pointless to baptize infants, since faith would be required of them in vain.

Likewise, if a pagan or an idiot were baptized, baptism would not benefit him; by the same reasoning, it cannot benefit an infant. Likewise, the other sacraments have no place with respect to infants—such as the sacrament of extreme unction, marriage, orders, the Eucharist, penance, and confirmation; by the same reasoning, baptism has no place with respect to those newly born. Likewise, it is not read that, at the institution of baptism, infants were baptized, but adults; nor was Christ baptized at a lesser age, but when grown. Thus he seems to have given this form of baptism: namely, that only adults should be baptized. Likewise, those who are baptized are first made catechumens and instructed; how, therefore, can those be baptized who cannot even be instructed? [Col. 0347A–B]

### Chapter XLII. Resolution of the foregoing, and that baptism benefits before the years of discretion

To this we say that the first authority, namely, “He who believes,” etc. (Mark 16), pertains not only to adults but also to infants. Infants are said to have faith not from the sacrament of faith, but from the faith of the sacrament. In the Gospel, however, mention is made only of adults to whom the Gospel is preached; therefore what is said, “He who believes and is baptized,” must be referred to them alone. For precepts in civil law are not given to infants and those without discretion, but to adults and those with discretion. Faith is required of infants in baptism not in order that they may possess it then, but that they may possess it at the fitting time. [Col. 0347C]

Hence the godfather answers for the infant, “I believe,” that is, “I pledge faith,” which he will possess at a determined time. We also say that if an adult pagan is so foolish that, through invincible ignorance, he adds no mortal sin to original sin, then, if he is baptized, original sin is remitted.

[Note: [Col. 0347] In the printed edition all the preceding material is imperfect.]

And although the other sacraments are not customarily administered to infants, nevertheless, because baptism was instituted against the wound of original sin, without whose remission neither infants nor adults have salvation, it is necessary both for infants and for adults. At the institution of baptism, moreover, because circumcision was still in force—and it removed original sin—it was unnecessary to baptize infants, since they had already been circumcised. Adults, however, were baptized so that they might thereby understand that regenerative power resides in the waters and might invite others to baptism.

[Note: [Col. 0347] In the printed edition certain things are omitted here, leaving the sense incomplete.]

Christ, moreover, just as he delivered the other sacraments in the years of discretion, so he wished to be baptized in the years of discretion, in order to provide them with an example of being baptized. Catechesis is proposed to infants, not so that they may then be instructed, but so that it may be shown how they ought to be instructed in the years of discretion. [Col. 0347D–0348A]

That baptism benefits infants is proved by that authority of John: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3). No one is excluded here, infant or adult; therefore baptism is necessary for all. Likewise, among the innocents slain by Herod, some were one or two days old (Matt. 2). Their original sin was remitted, because they were saved.

[Note: [Col. 0347] In the printed edition “by circumcision” is wrongly added here. But what follows immediately likewise admits no complete sense.]

But it was not remitted through circumcision, since this was not performed before the eighth day. By what power, then, was it remitted, unless by baptism of blood, because this is equivalent to baptism of water?

[Note: [Col. 0347] The printed edition reads *flaminis* (“of the Spirit”) in place of *fluminis* (“of water”).]

For baptism is threefold: of water (*fluminis*), of the Spirit (*flaminis*), and of blood. Of the first it is said: “Going into the world, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28). Of the second it is said: “He shall baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matt. 3; Mark 1). Of the third it is said: “I have a baptism with which to be baptized,” etc. (Luke 12).

Likewise, circumcision in the Old Testament was performed on the eighth day to remove original sin; baptism has the same power in the New Testament. Therefore baptism benefits infants for the same reason that circumcision benefited them. Perhaps the heretics will say that circumcision had no efficacy or sanctity. But what will they say of Christ, who was circumcised on the eighth day, and would not have received it unless to show in himself that the law must be fulfilled? Perhaps they will deny that Abraham circumcised his son Isaac. But the apostle Paul attests this and asserts that it was of old beneficial to those who received it.

Likewise, when the Lord commanded that all nations be baptized, he did not exclude infant or adult. Likewise Christ says: “Allow the little children to come to me; for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Mark 10). But they cannot come to Christ except through baptism, because without it they cannot be saved. Therefore they are to be baptized, so that they may come to God and be saved.

By many similar examples it can also be shown that a child can be saved through another’s faith, by baptism. For in the Gospel it is read that the centurion’s child was healed by the Lord on account of the centurion’s merit (Matt. 8). The dead daughter of the ruler of the synagogue was raised at his prayers (Mark 5). Likewise, the paralytic was healed by the merits of those who brought him (Matt. 9); and at the intercession of the Canaanite woman, her daughter was freed from a demon (Matt. 15). If, then, many were healed in soul and body through the merits of others, how much more can infants be saved through the faith of others by baptism? [Col. 0348B–D]

Likewise, if before baptism a child was to be condemned for another’s sin, namely Adam’s, why after baptism will he not be saved through another’s faith, namely the faith of the godfather or of the Church? Otherwise infants would be treated unjustly, since they have no free power to will or not will, if the sacrament of baptism in the faith of others could not benefit them.

The Apostle also, comparing Adam’s offense with Christ’s grace—

[Note: [Col. 0349] In the printed edition, *consensus* (“agreement”) is wrongly found instead of *conferens* (“comparing”).]

—shows that the offense is not like the gift (Rom. 5), because the gift is more powerful than the offense. For if one offense extended incidentally to all, Christ’s grace destroyed both original and actual sin. And just as original sin was transmitted to descendants, or infants, so the gift—that is, grace—is bestowed upon infants through baptism. Otherwise the gift would not be greater than the offense. Likewise, if sin cannot in any way be remitted to infants, why is it imputed to them? [Col. 0349A–B]

### Chapter XLIII. The opinion of heretics who say that baptism has no efficacy, either in infants or adults

There are those who say that the sacrament of baptism celebrated in the Church of God has no efficacy in infants or adults. For they assert that all merit depends on a person’s will, not on an external thing. They attempt to establish this in many ways.

First, thus: this man approaching baptism either repents or does not. If he does not repent, baptism does him no good; if he repents, he has already been justified and all sin has been remitted to him. Therefore baptism has no efficacy in him for remitting sin; thus baptism of water is not necessary for the remission of sin.

The Apostle also says: “Neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but God who gives the increase” (1 Cor. 3). As though he said: sin is remitted neither by preaching nor by baptism, but by divine grace alone. Likewise, if sacraments were instituted for the remission of sins, why were they not instituted from the beginning of the human race, so that the ancients, who had greater need of God’s grace, might obtain through them remission of sins? Likewise, what is this power of water, that it touches the body and washes the mind? [Col. 0349B–C]

### Chapter XLIV. Resolution of the foregoing, and that baptism has efficacy in infants and adults

[Col. 0349D]

We refute the first objection as follows. We say that all merit depends on the will. Yet we do not exclude a good work or a sacrament.

[Note: [Col. 0349] The printed edition reads, “the will does not exclude.”]

And if perhaps all sin is remitted to someone before baptism, he is nevertheless still bound to receive the sacrament of baptism, both in order to fulfill the divine command and also for a fuller remission of guilt and punishment, and for the bestowal of grace in the soul; for baptism does not require groaning or lamentation.

[Note: [Col. 0349] The printed edition wrongly has *sed* (“but”) instead of *vel* (“or”).]

The second objection is refuted by the foregoing answer, because in baptism not original sin alone but other sins too, even venial sins, are remitted, if they are present in the penitent when he is baptized; and, as has been said, grace is added.

To what the Apostle says, we reply that neither baptism nor preaching confers anything by its own power except through divine grace. To the other objection we say that, just as there was a development in faith, in God’s manifestation, and in the multiplication of saints, so there was in the administration of sacraments. Before the giving of the Law it was enough for a person to believe that God is one, the rewarder of the good and punisher of the wicked, while observing the natural precepts. Then faith itself developed during the Old Testament, because the more mature were bound to believe that God is three and one, and what was contained in the sacraments. But in the time of grace the faithful are bound to believe more things. Therefore, in accordance with the development of faith, there was development in the knowledge of God, in the multiplication of the faithful, and in the handing down of sacraments. It was therefore fitting that at the coming of the Lord, who was the redeemer of the human race, grace and sacraments that confer grace should be multiplied. [Col. 0350A–B]

The heavenly Word, that is, the Son of God, confers that power upon the water by which a human mind is cleansed, according to the saying: “The word comes to the element, and it becomes a sacrament—not what is spoken, but what is believed.” What, then, is that which is believed, if not the Son of God—

[Note: [Col. 0349] The printed edition has: “What then is that word which is believed?”]

—by whose power baptism is consecrated? [Col. 0350B–C]
