That all are bound to receive baptism is proved by many authorities. Christ says: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3). And elsewhere: “Go, preach the Gospel to every creature; baptizing them,” etc. (Mark 16). Likewise Peter says: “Repent, and let every one of you be baptized” (Acts 2). Likewise: “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark 16). Likewise, why was Christ baptized with such solemnity unless the greater power of baptism was thereby signified? For at Christ’s baptism the heavens were opened, the Father’s voice was heard, and the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove (Matt. 3).

But perhaps they will say that Christ was baptized, seeking to prove this: Christ did not need baptism, since he was free from sin.

[Note: [Col. 0349] These final words are omitted in the printed edition.]

Why, then, was he baptized? Further, how great would the presumption have been if John had baptized Christ?

To this we say that Christ was baptized not because he needed baptism, but in order to confer regenerative power upon the waters and to furnish others an example of baptism. [Col. 0350C–D]

And just as he was circumcised to fulfill the command of the law, so he received the sacrament of baptism in order to fulfill the highest degree of humility, by receiving baptism from one who was inferior. Nor was there presumption in John if he baptized Christ, because Christ so pleased.

[Note: [Col. 0351] The word “not” is omitted in the printed edition, producing an utterly contrary and absurd sense.]

Thus in Matthew it is read: “Jesus came from Galilee to John at the Jordan, to be baptized by him. But John was preventing him, saying: ‘I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?’ Jesus answered and said: ‘Allow it now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.’ Then he allowed him. And Jesus, having been baptized, immediately came up from the water” (Matt. 3). Here it is said that Jesus was baptized. And in Mark it is read: “Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee and was baptized by John in the Jordan” (Mark 1).

Therefore Jesus Christ wished to be baptized in order to confirm baptism and to provide others an example; and especially by John’s baptism—

[Note: [Col. 0351] The printed edition has “to John the Baptist” in place of “by John’s baptism,” again with a notable confusion of sense.]

—in which sins were not remitted, in order to show that he was without sin and did not need remission of either original or actual sin, since he had neither.

[Note: [Col. 0351] The printed edition reads *amisit* (“lost”), wrongly.]

For in John’s baptism bodies alone were washed outwardly, and sins were not remitted. This is clear from the fact that those whom John had baptized were afterwards baptized by Christ. Hence John himself says: “I baptized you with water, but he shall baptize you with the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 3; Mark 1). [Col. 0351A–B]

### Chapter XLV. The opinion of heretics who say that baptism does no good without the laying on of hands

[Col. 0351C]

There were some who said that baptism does no good without the laying on of hands, because it is read in the Acts of the Apostles that the apostles laid hands on those who had been baptized, and thus they received the Holy Spirit (Acts 8). But the Holy Spirit is first given when sin is remitted; therefore sin is not remitted before the laying on of hands, and thus baptism is of no avail without it.

The same heretics also say that every sin, however great it may be, is remitted through the laying on of hands, especially if one of those heretics whom they call “perfect” has laid hands upon a person. Thus, on this pretext, they invite many to sins, as those who abandon themselves to various sins place their hope in the laying on of hands.

They also distinguish between the “consoled” and the “perfect.” They call “consoled” those who have recently come to their heresy and are not yet confirmed in it; but such persons ought rather to be called “desolated” than “consoled.” They call “perfect” those who are confirmed in the heresy; but these stand rather in defect than in perfection. [Col. 0351C–D]

### Chapter XLVI. Resolution of the foregoing

We refute their foregoing objection as follows. When it is read in the Acts of the Apostles that certain people who had been baptized had not received the Holy Spirit, it must be understood thus: they had received him for remission of sin, but not in manifestation.

[Note: [Col. 0351] The printed edition adds, “in the manifestation of the Righteous One.”]

For in the primitive Church the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the baptized was signified by some special sign: either they immediately spoke in various tongues or some other special miracle occurred. Therefore, when it is said that some baptized persons had not yet received the Holy Spirit, it must be understood thus: the descent of the Holy Spirit upon them had not been signified by any visible sign. But after the apostles laid hands upon them, they received the Holy Spirit; that is, the descent of the Holy Spirit upon them was demonstrated by a visible sign. Nevertheless, it is not read that hands were laid upon all who were baptized. [Col. 0352A–B]

Nor is it found anywhere that hands were laid upon the eunuch whom Philip baptized (Acts 8), nor upon the centurion whom Peter baptized (Acts 10). Therefore, without the laying on of hands, sin is destroyed and grace is conferred.

The Holy Spirit is said to be received in many ways: with respect to remission of sin, the bestowal of righteousness, the distribution of gifts, or the strengthening of virtues.

### Chapter XLVII. The opinion of heretics who say that, after the remission of sins effected in baptism, penance has no place

Other heretics assert that after the remission effected in baptism, no other remission effected through penance has any place. They seek to prove this by various authorities. They also say that the sin against the Holy Spirit is the sin committed after the remission of sin effected in baptism, because it is a special injury to the grace of the Holy Spirit when, after receiving grace, a person returns to guilt. Hence they say that this sin will be forgiven neither here nor in the future.

Therefore, if one of them sins after receiving their baptism, he is expelled from their assembly without any injustice.

[Note: [Col. 0351] The printed edition reads *misericordia* (“mercy”), and rightly.]

This seems to be found in the Apostle’s Epistle to the Hebrews.

[Note: [Col. 0351] The printed edition reads: “which the Apostle seems to suggest.”]

For he says:

[Note: [Col. 0351] The printed edition reads “when he says.”]

“For it is impossible for those who were once enlightened, who have also tasted the heavenly gift, and have been made partakers of the Holy Spirit, who have nevertheless tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and have fallen away, to be renewed again to repentance” (Heb. 8).

Likewise in the same epistle: “If we sin willingly after receiving the knowledge of truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sin. But there is a certain fearful justice—

[Note: [Col. 0351] The printed edition reads “expectation of judgment” in place of “justice.”]

—and a zeal of fire, which has consumed [will consume] the adversaries” (Heb. 10). [Col. 0352C–D]

They also try to prove by reasoning that just as baptism, orders, or confirmation ought not to be repeated, so neither should penance. Likewise, one who repents once of his sins is bound to repent of the same sins all the days of his life, as an authority says; therefore, if he falls into sin, that penance is empty and futile.

Hence an authority also says: “To repent is to weep over sins and not commit again what must be wept over.” Augustine too is said to hold that penance cannot be repeated. Therefore, if the first penance must continue to the end, a second seems to have no place. [Col. 0353A]

### Chapter XLVIII. Resolution of the objections; why penance is repeated, but baptism and certain other sacraments are not

To the first authority we say that the Apostle there speaks against certain people who said that baptism could be repeated for the penance of sin.

[Note: [Col. 0353] The printed edition reads “for the remission of sins.”]

He therefore denies the repetition of baptism, saying—

[Note: [Col. 0353] The printed edition reads “suggesting.”]

—that it is impossible for those who have once received what is there written—

[Note: [Col. 0353] The printed edition reads “what is read in the foregoing authority.”]

—to be renewed again through baptism, after falling, unto repentance (Heb. 8). [Col. 0353B]

The second statement must be understood thus: “There no longer remains a sacrifice for sin” (Heb. 10)—understand, in the New Testament, as in the Old Testament a sacrifice for sin was appointed to be offered repeatedly. For Christ is not to be immolated again for sin, since this was done once and is not needed a second time. Rather, it is necessary to remain in faith and truth; if you do not do this—

[Note: [Col. 0353] In the printed edition the word *feceris* (“you do”) is omitted.]

—judgment awaits you unless you are renewed through penance. Therefore it adds: “But there is a fearful [thing],” etc. (ibid.). But in this it does not exclude penance, but a second baptism. For it did not say, “There is no longer penance or remission,” but “sacrifice,” that is, a second cross—

[Note: [Col. 0353] This final phrase is omitted in the printed edition, though it certainly must be included.]

—because the one cross is sufficient. It says this so that we may not expect anything further here, but may repent. [Col. 0353B–C]

We also say that baptism, confirmation, and orders cannot be repeated. For baptism represents Christ’s Passion: just as he was offered once and suffered once, so the representation of his Passion should not be repeated, because of its dignity. Likewise, orders, which are a sacrament of dignity, should not be repeated because of their dignity; similarly the sacrament of confirmation, on account of its own dignity. Penance, however, is like a second plank after shipwreck.

The first shipwreck is in original sin, against which baptism avails; the second shipwreck is in actual sin, against which there is the second plank, namely penance. And if sin occurs repeatedly, the remedy of penance ought to occur repeatedly. Hence it is said that a person is bound to repent throughout the whole time of life, because indeed throughout his whole life he sins. [Col. 0353C–D]

But if someone repents of sin and suffers a relapse into sin, the preceding penance is futile—

[Note: [Col. 0353] The printed edition reads “a futile remedy.”]

—because it does not result in eternal blessedness. Yet if he repents again of sin, the subsequent penance is efficacious and fruitful. The saying, “Penance is to weep over sins and not commit again what must be wept over,” must be understood so that it refers not to different times but to the same time: namely, that at the time when he weeps over deeds committed, he does not commit deeds to be wept over, with a settled will.

[Note: [Col. 0353] The printed edition reads “either by deed or by will” in place of “with a settled will.”]

Penance is more truly described thus: “Penance is to weep over sins previously committed and not to will to commit again sins which must be wept over.”

The words of Origen—

[Note: [Col. 0353] The printed edition reads “Jerome.”]

—by which he seems to hold that penance cannot be repeated, are these: “If some fault comes to delay us which does not consist in mortal crime or blasphemy against the faith, but lies in a fault of speech or conduct, this fault can always be repaired—

[Note: [Col. 0353] The printed edition reads *reprobari* (“be rejected”) instead of *reparari* (“be repaired”).]

—and one is not forbidden to do penance repeatedly; but for more grievous [crimes]—

[Note: [Col. 0353] The printed edition adds “crimes.”]

—room for penance is granted only once.”

Ambrose also says: “There are those who think penance ought to be undertaken often, who indulge themselves in Christ; for if they did true penance in Christ, they would not sin afterward so as to need it repeated, because as there is one baptism, so there is one penance.” But what Origen says—

[Note: [Col. 0353] The printed edition reads “Jerome.”]

—must be understood of solemn penance, which was public, outside the church, in ashes and haircloth, and which is imposed only for more grievous and dreadful sins. That penance is not to be repeated, out of reverence for the sacrament, lest it become cheap and contemptible to people. Likewise, Ambrose’s statement is to be understood in this way, as also what he says elsewhere: “Penance, once undertaken and not truly performed, both takes away the fruit of the former [penance] and loses the benefit of the subsequent one”; this too must be understood of solemn penance. [Col. 0354A–C]

### Chapter XLIX. Authorities and arguments proving that penance can be repeated

That penance is to be repeated not only once but often, and that forgiveness is frequently granted through it, is proved by examples, arguments, and authorities. We read that Peter sinned often. Did he not sin even before coming to Christ (Mark 3)? Hence the change of his name signified a change in the disposition of his mind, when it was said: “You are Peter” (Matt. 16). And when contention arose among the disciples as to which of them seemed to be greater (Luke 22), did Peter not then sin, if he disputed over precedence?

Likewise, when he wished to instruct Christ, saying: “Far be it from you, Lord!” (Matt. 16), and Christ said to him: “Get behind me, Satan” (ibid.). And perhaps when, from a certain presumption, he said: “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you” (Matt. 26). Likewise, when he cut off Malchus’s ear (John 18), and when he denied Christ (Matt. 26). But just as sins were repeated in Peter, so they were remitted to him through repeated penance. Hence it is read that, remembering his sin, he wept bitterly (Luke 22).

Likewise, when the other apostles sinned often before Christ’s resurrection, their sins were remitted through repeated penance. And if they give credence to the Old Testament, the same could be established from the example of David, who is read to have sinned frequently and repented frequently.

Augustine, too, writing against certain heretics who said that penance was useful only once for those sinning after baptism, says: “Still faithless, because they are wise beyond what is fitting—not sober, but exceeding measure—they say that even though penance is effective once after baptism, its repetition does not benefit those who sin often; otherwise remission would be an incitement to sin. For who would cease from sinning if he could always return?”

[Note: [Col. 0355] The printed edition reads, “they wickedly press this point.”]

They also say that God is an instigator to evil if he always forgives sins or helps those who repent, and that sins please him because he is always ready to remit them. But they err. It is plain that vices displease him who is always ready to destroy them; if he loved them, he would not always take care to destroy them.

[Note: [Col. 0355] The printed edition reads “would not always weep over them.”]

John Chrysostom also says, concerning the restoration of one who has fallen: “Such is God’s mercy toward human beings: he never rejects penance if it is sincerely offered to him.

[Note: [Col. 0355] The printed edition adds ‘sincerely and simply.’]

Even if someone has reached the summit of evils and then wishes to return from there to the way of truth, it suffices [manuscript: *suscipit*, “he receives”]; he gladly embraces [him] and does everything insofar as he may restore him to his former state. And what is still more excellent—

[Note: [Col. 0355] The printed edition adds ‘and more eminent.’]

—even if a person has been unable to complete the whole course of satisfaction, he nevertheless does not reject penance, however small and however briefly undertaken. For he receives it and does not allow the reward of even the slightest conversion—

[Note: [Col. 0355] In the printed edition, absurdly, *perditionis* (‘destruction’) appears in place of *conversionis* (‘conversion’).]

—to perish.” [Col. 0355A–C]

The same is also proved by arguments. This man sinned after baptism; neither penance nor any other sacrament can help him toward remission of sin. Therefore freedom of will has perished in him, so that he cannot act well or erase sin through penance. Therefore it ought not to be imputed to him if he does not act well, since he necessarily remains in sin.

Likewise, this man grieves for sin as much as he ought to grieve, is contrite, confesses his sin, and makes satisfaction for it; therefore he is treated unjustly if his sin is not remitted. [Col. 0355C–D]

### Chapter L. The opinion of heretics who say that penance does not avail for remission of sin

There are others who assert that no penance avails for remission of sin. They seek to prove it thus: God forgives sins freely; therefore not by good merits, and therefore not through penance. For if sin is remitted through penance, it is remitted by the merit of penance. Likewise, an authority says: “Not by works which we have done, but by grace alone he saved us” (Titus 3). Likewise: “It is not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9). Likewise, the first grace which God works in a person is remission of sin, which he works without the person. Therefore guilt is not remitted through penance.

[Note: [Col. 0355] In the printed edition, throughout this entire period there is no sense; everything is confused.]

### Chapter LI. Resolution of the foregoing, and that penance avails for remission of sin

We refute the foregoing by saying that sin is remitted by God’s grace alone, and penance is not the efficient cause of the remission of sin, but only God’s gratuitous will. Yet it is a necessary condition: unless a person repents, God does not forgive sin. Thus the sun illuminates a house because a window is opened; yet the opening of the window is not the efficient cause of illumination, but only an occasion, while the sun itself is the efficient cause of illumination. [Col. 0356A–B]

The statement, “Not by works which we have done,” etc. (Titus 3), must be understood thus: works do not exclude grace, nor grace works, because works come from grace and grace itself is the efficient cause of salvation.

Likewise, grace does not exclude penance, nor penance grace, because penance is a certain grace. Likewise, “It is not of him who wills,” etc. (Rom. 9), is to be understood in this manner: although running, that is, good action, or a good will, is an occasion of salvation, the efficient cause is God’s mercy. We also grant that God works the first grace in us without us, according to the understanding already set forth. [Col. 0356B–C]

### Chapter LII. The opinion of heretics who say that it is sufficient to confess to God alone

There are other heretics who say that it is enough to confess to God alone. They seek to prove this as follows. Ambrose says on Luke: “Peter therefore wept because guilt crept upon him.

[Note: [Col. 0355] The printed edition has *obrepsit* (‘crept upon’) instead of *subrepsit* (‘stole upon’).]

I do not find what he said; I find that he wept. I read his tears; I do not read satisfaction. What cannot be defended can be washed away: tears wash the offense which it is shameful to confess aloud; weeping provides both for pardon and for modesty.” Maximus the bishop says this as well.

Likewise John Chrysostom, on the Epistle to the Hebrews: “I do not tell you to expose yourself publicly, nor to accuse yourself before others; and I want you to obey the Prophet who says: ‘Reveal your way before the Lord’ (Ps. 36). Therefore confess your sins before the true judge with understanding—

[Note: [Col. 0355] The printed edition reads “with prayer.”]

—declare your offenses not with your tongue, but by the memory of your conscience; and only then hope that you can obtain mercy. If you keep your sins daily in mind, you will never harbor evil in your heart against your neighbor.” [Col. 0356C–0357A]

Likewise the same author: “Speak your sins so that you may erase them; but if you are ashamed to speak them to someone, speak them daily in your soul. I do not say that you should confess them to your servant—

[Note: [Col. 0357] The printed edition reads *conservo*, ‘fellow servant.’]

—so that he may reproach you; but speak them to God, who heals them. For even if you do not speak them, he does not fail to know them: when you were doing them, he was present; when you committed them, he knew.”

### Chapter LIII. Resolution, and that a person is bound to confess his sins

We resolve the foregoing as follows. Ambrose’s statement, “Tears wash the offense,” etc., must be referred to public penance. There, while showing the power of tears and confession, he intended to imply that hidden tears and secret confession made to a priest alone wash the offense which one is ashamed to confess publicly. That he says he read Peter’s tears but not his confession or satisfaction does not exclude either of these, for many things were done which were not written. Or perhaps the institution of confession now in force had not yet been established. Or it may be understood thus: “Tears wash the offense,” that is, one is cleansed by weeping where there is shame in confessing; because unless there is modest shame in confession, guilt is not removed.

[Note: [Col. 0357] The printed edition has *dicitur* (‘is said’) in place of *deletur* (‘is removed’).]

Chrysostom’s statement must not be understood as though, if a person has opportunity, he may fail to confess to a priest. Rather, where a crime is hidden, it is enough to speak to God alone through a priest, and to do so once; nor is one required to publish before many people what is hidden. Chrysostom himself noted this when he said: “I do not tell you to expose yourself publicly,” etc. For just as a public offense requires a public remedy, so a hidden offense is cleansed by secret confession and hidden satisfaction. [Col. 0357A–C]

Nor is it necessary that what we have once confessed to a priest should be confessed again. Nevertheless, if we wish our sins to be remitted, we must confess not only with the tongue of flesh but also with the tongue of the heart before the true judge. Hence the same John Chrysostom says—

[Note: [Col. 0357] The printed edition reads “John the Evangelist,” wrongly, because these are Chrysostom’s words, not those of John the Evangelist.]

—“If you remember your sins and frequently declare them in God’s sight and pray for them, they will more quickly be erased. But if you forget them, then unwillingly you will remember them when they are made public and brought forth before all enemies, friends, and holy angels.”

### Chapter LIV. Authorities proving that penance avails for the remission of sin

[Col. 0357D]

The efficacy of penitence for the remission of sins is demonstrated by many authorities. For John says: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” (Matt. 3). Christ says the same. And Peter, in the Acts of the Apostles, says to those who had been pierced to the heart by his preaching: “Repent, and let every one of you be baptized” [Col. 0358A] (Acts 2). Again Peter says: “Repent, that your sins may be blotted out” (Acts 3). The elements considered in penitence are required for the remission of sin: namely, contrition of heart, confession, and satisfaction. Yet heretics deny this.

## CHAPTER LV. The authorities proving that contrition avails for the remission of sin

That contrition avails for the remission of sin is evident from the Gospel, where we read that Peter remembered the word which Jesus had spoken to him: “Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.” And, going out, he wept bitterly (Matt. 26). See how, pierced in heart and remembering the evil he had done, he hastens to tears. Moreover, how can sin be remitted [Col. 0358B] to a person unless he is willing? But when a person wishes his sin to be forgiven, he wishes not to have sin; therefore he wishes not to be in sin; therefore he is contrite for sin. If the heretics just mentioned believed the prophets, it could be proved from them that contrition avails for the remission of sin. For Scripture says: “At whatever hour the sinner groans, I shall remember none of his iniquities” (Ezek. 18). And Joel: “Rend your hearts and not your garments” (Joel 2). David likewise says: “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Ps. 50). Contrition is the compunction of the heart arising from remembrance of past evils, together with the intention not to relapse, preferring to undergo every danger of death rather than to have incurred such guilt.

## CHAPTER LVI. The authorities proving that confession avails for the remission of sins

[Col. 0358C]

Likewise, oral confession is required for the blotting out of sin, although the heretics themselves also deny this. For James says in his Catholic Epistle: “Confess your sins to one another” (James 5). He did not say “to God alone,” as they say, but “to one another.” [Note: [Col. 0357] These final words are absent from the printed edition.]

Again Paul says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10). Christ also commanded those whom he had healed of leprosy to show themselves to the priests, thereby indicating that one who wishes to be cleansed from the leprosy of sin ought to show himself to a priest through confession. The same may also be established by many authorities of the saints; but perhaps the enemies of the Christian faith would not assent to them.

Perhaps some will also say that sin is remitted by contrition alone; why, then, is confession of sin required for its remission? To this we reply that one who is contrite [Note: [Col. 0357] The printed edition incorrectly reads “is converted” (*convertitur*).] is bound to have the intention of confessing; for unless he forms this intention, sin is not remitted. [Note: [Col. 0357] The printed edition reads: “unless he proposes to confess.”] He is therefore bound to confess for several reasons: on account of this intention, and on account of penitence, for the shame involved in confession is a great penitence [Col. 0359A]. Since confession of sin was instituted for other reasons, it was also instituted so that shame for sin might become a punishment. It is sometimes required also for satisfaction, because unless the sinner reveals his sins to the priest, the priest cannot heal them by assigning satisfaction.

## CHAPTER LVII. The opinion of heretics who deny that bread is transubstantiated into Christ’s body

The aforesaid heretics also say that bread is not transubstantiated into Christ’s body through the holy [Note: [Col. 0359] The printed edition incorrectly has *secunda* (“second”) instead of *sancta* (“holy”).] words spoken by the priest in the Mass. They attempt to prove this as follows: if bread were changed into Christ’s body every day, that body would be increased without limit.

They also ask whether that bread ceases to exist. If [Col. 0359B] it ceases to exist, it is annihilated, and is thus also corrupted. Again, they ask how a body of such size enters through a human mouth. Again, if Christ’s body is eaten, it is ground by the teeth and thereby divided into parts. Again, bread becomes Christ’s body; therefore it will be Christ’s body, and thus will be something other than it is. Again, bread will become body; therefore Christ’s body will come from bread, and bread will thus be the matter of Christ’s body. [Note: [Col. 0359] The printed edition has the confused reading: “bread was the matter [of] Christ’s body.”] Again, after transubstantiation the accidents remain; therefore they remain in another subject, or in the air. But if in the air, some part of the air is round, savory, and white; and as that form [Note: [Col. 0359] The printed edition reads *farina*, “flour.”] is carried through different places, the accidents change subjects. Again, the accidents remain in the same part of air, and thus solidity is in the air, since those things are solid; and so the air is solid. From these points it seems [Col. 0359C] that those accidents are not in the air; but neither are they in Christ’s body, nor can another body in which they are be assigned; therefore the accidents do not seem to remain. Again, when the form beneath which Christ’s body lies hidden is divided into parts, Christ’s body ceases to be under that form. How, therefore, is Christ’s body given under each portion of that host?

Again, if Christ’s body lies hidden under that tiny form, where are Christ’s head and feet? Thus its members are indistinct. Again, Christ gave his body to his disciples before the Passion; but he gave them either a mortal or an immortal body. If he gave a mortal body, yet at that time he was mortal; therefore, when he was mortal, he was immortal—a contradiction. [Note: [Col. 0359] In the preceding discussion the printed edition reads *immortale* (“immortal”) throughout in place of *immortalis* (“immortal [masculine]”).] Again, suppose that someone [Col. 0359D] had celebrated the divine office during Christ’s Passion: Christ’s body, being in Rome, would have suffered in Rome, because wherever it was, it suffered during the Passion; and thus it suffered not only in Jerusalem but in many other places. Again, suppose that a mouse approaches the pyx in which Christ’s body is present: the mouse eats something; therefore it eats air, or an accident, or Christ’s body. But that it eats air or an accident is absurd [Col. 0360A], and still more absurd that it eats Christ’s body. Again, since Christ’s glorified blood does not create local extension [Note: [Col. 0359] The printed edition adds: “extension from matter.”], it seems that another liquid could be poured into a chalice filled with blood. Again, Christ says in the Gospel: “Everything that enters the mouth is discharged into the privy” (Matt. 15). Therefore Christ’s body does not enter the mouth when given for eating, or else it is discharged into the privy.

## CHAPTER LVIII. Resolution of the foregoing objections, and that bread is transubstantiated into Christ’s body

To the first objection we reply that among changes, one is alteration, another is *alteritas* [substantial alteration], and another transubstantiation. [Note: [Col. 0359] The printed edition reads: “One change is alteration, etc.,” but our reading is to be retained.] Alteration is the change occurring through variation of accidents in the same subject, [Col. 0360B] as when a subject is first white and then begins to be black. With respect to this change, we grant these propositions: “What was white was black”; “what is white will begin to be black”; and “it will become black.” But we deny: “From white, black will come to be,” lest white be understood as the matter of black. [Note: [Col. 0359] The printed edition corruptly reads *nigra* (“black [feminine]”); furthermore, some things have been omitted in what follows, as a result of which the rest also lacks sense.] For *de* denotes matter. In this change the subject remains, and the substantial features remain; but certain accidental features do not remain.

*Alteritas*, however, is that species of change in which, while the same matter remains, the substantial features do not remain. This was the change made at Cana of Galilee, when water was changed into wine (John 2). For the matter remained there, because the matter of water and wine is the same; but certain substantial features were changed: that substantial reality which was water ceased to be water, and that which is [Col. 0360C] wine began to be wine. Certain accidents also changed. In accordance with this change, it is said that wine was made from water and that water was changed into wine. But water was not wine, did not begin to be wine, and was not going to be wine.

Transubstantiation is that species of change in which both matter and substantial form are changed, while the accidents remain. It is therefore called transubstantiation because nothing of the substance remains, whether with regard to matter or with regard to substantial nature. [Note: [Col. 0359] The printed edition reads *materiam* (“matter”) instead of *naturam* (“nature”).] Such a change occurs in the consecration of bread. Bread is so changed into Christ’s body that nothing of the matter of bread remains; nor do its substantial features remain, but certain accidental features do: [Col. 0360D] roundness, whiteness, and taste. Since the whole substance is changed into Christ’s body, that body is not increased, although bread is changed into Christ’s body many times: nothing remains in Christ’s body, nor does Christ’s body remain; and therefore Christ’s body is not increased.

There are two kinds of increase, or augmentation: one occurs by extension of parts, the other by addition. [Note: [Col. 0359] The printed edition reads *argumenti* (“of argument”) instead of *augmenti* (“of increase”).] In the first manner a twig grows in the garden; [Note: [Col. 0359] These words are omitted in the printed edition and replaced with several dots.] [Col. 0361A] in the second, a heap grows when something is added to it. [Note: [Col. 0361] Here again several words have been omitted and replaced with dots.] What increases in the first manner—for example, a twig—does not grow because something is added to it, but because its parts are extended by means of heat and moisture. By this kind of increase were multiplied the loaves with which the Lord fed five thousand persons (Matt. 16). Since, therefore, nothing is added to Christ’s body and its parts are not extended, we say that Christ’s body is not increased.

According to this change of transubstantiation, it must be said that bread is changed or converted into Christ’s body. We also grant other expressions signifying change, such as “bread will become Christ’s body,” but not “bread will begin to be Christ’s body.” We likewise say that bread ceases to exist, but is not corrupted; [Col. 0361B] for it ceases to exist not through the failure of natural things, but through a miracle.

Nor is it surprising that Christ’s body, though of some quantity, enters through a human mouth, since it is now glorified and does not occupy spatial extension in a place. Yet we deny that Christ’s body will be made from bread, because this denotes matter, and bread neither is nor will be the matter of Christ’s body. We also say that although Christ’s body is eaten, it nevertheless remains always incorruptible and indivisible. When Christ’s body is said to be divided or broken, this refers rather to the form of bread than to Christ’s body; for that breaking or division is not in Christ’s body, but in the form of bread.

Nor is it surprising [Col. 0361C] that he who made all things from nothing should make accidents exist without a material subject. [Note: [Col. 0361] The printed edition reads “without any subject” instead of “without a material subject.”] To their statement that bread is still upon the altar after consecration, because bread was previously there and the form of bread remains, we reply: bread truly was there, but it has been changed into Christ’s body, and the form remains, beneath which Christ’s body lies hidden. This occurs for several reasons. The first is that “faith has no merit where human reason supplies proof by experience.” Another is lest the Christian shrink from eating his Redeemer—lest, that is, the mind recoil from what the eye beholds; for eating raw flesh is not customary. The third is lest heretics mock us, saying: “You eat your Lord.”

We also see that certain things change into others while some [Col. 0361D] properties of the changed thing remain; for example, when wine is changed into vinegar, its fluidity remains. [Note: [Col. 0361] The printed edition incorrectly reads *siccitas*, “dryness,” for *liquiditas*, “fluidity.”] One thing often lies concealed beneath the form of another; thus angels are frequently said to have been concealed under human form, though human form was not in the angel. Similarly, Christ’s body is on the altar, but under another form—namely, the form of bread. The accidents that remain are without a subject, as has been said, because he who created them to be in a subject can make them exist without a subject; for their existence in this manner or another is from God [Col. 0362A]. We may nevertheless say that colour and taste are in the form of bread, and thus, miraculously, an accident is in an accident.

But it may similarly be asked here concerning the form itself: in what is it, since the form itself is also an accident?

Some say that after transubstantiation there are no accidents there, but that they appear to be there when they are not. Thus they do not say that whiteness or roundness is present there, but that such things appear in the sacrament; nor do they say that there is an illusion there, but a sacrament.

There are many kinds of visual deception. One occurs when we do not see what is presented to the eyes; this is called *aurisia* [Note: [Col. 0361] The printed edition reads *acrisia*.], that is, “non-seeing,” and it was by this that those seeking Elisha were struck (2 Kgs. 6). Another is called illusion (*praestigium*): when by magical art [Col. 0362B] the eyes are so deceived [Note: [Col. 0361] The printed edition reads *praestringuntur*, “are dazzled/deceived.”] that something appears to be which is not, and what is does not appear. This is done by magicians in order to deceive. A third kind occurs for instruction and as a sacrament; in this way prophets appeared to see what was not seen. Thus Jeremiah appeared to see a boiling pot from the north, and was told: “From the north every evil shall be opened out over the inhabitants of Jerusalem” (Jer. 1).

Likewise, taste and colour appear to be in the sacrament of the altar, yet there is no illusion there, because this does not occur for deception but rather for instruction and as a sacrament. But why should we wander through the winding paths of words? There is one answer to these matters: in a miracle, an explanation is not to be sought. We say [Col. 0362C] also that, when that form is divided into parts, just as Christ’s whole and entire body had previously lain hidden beneath the entire form, so afterward the same body, whole and entire, lies hidden beneath each portion of the broken host; just as an image appears whole and entire in an unbroken mirror, but when it is broken, the same image appears in each fragment.

We also say that Christ’s whole body lies hidden beneath that tiny form because, now glorified, it is of such subtlety that it makes no extension of air from air; and therefore [Note: [Col. 0361] The printed edition, by a gross error, has *non* (“not”) in place of *ideo* (“therefore”).] it can lie hidden in a small place, although its members are distinct. He also gave his disciples his body such as he had—namely, mortal. [Note: [Col. 0361] The printed edition reads *miraculosum* (“miraculous”) for *mortale* (“mortal”), and this is a gross error.] But it was miraculous that a body of such quantity entered through the narrow mouth of one eating it. By the same [Col. 0362D] miracle by which he was born while the Virgin’s womb remained closed, and by which he walked with dry feet upon the waters, he entered into the mouth of the eater.

We also say that if anyone had celebrated the sacrament of the Eucharist at Rome on the day of the Passion, Christ, being present in Rome, would suffer in Jerusalem, but would not suffer in Rome—just as, when something begins to exist, it begins to exist in that instant.

Concerning a mouse approaching the pyx, we say that it does not eat Christ’s body, but that form of bread [Col. 0363A], which miraculously becomes nourishment for it as though it were the substance of bread. Nor is this surprising, since in natural matters it happens that someone becomes intoxicated by the smell of wine alone. We also read that certain peoples are nourished by the smell of fruits alone. Yet some say that it eats nothing, but appears to eat, and is thus miraculously sated as though it ate.

When the chalice is full of Christ’s blood, another liquid cannot be poured into it while it remains full, although the blood does not occupy extension of air from air; for the species of wine beneath which the blood lies hidden occupies the place and fills the chalice, as miraculously as the glorified body does not fill a place. As for Christ’s saying, “Everything that enters the mouth,” etc. (Matt. 15; Mark 7), this must be understood of material rather than spiritual food. For as [Col. 0363B] material food goes into the privy, so spiritual food goes into the mind’s ecstasy. The former is food for the belly, the latter for the mind.

## CHAPTER LIX. Whether the transubstantiation of bread into Christ’s body is an article of faith

The heretics also ask whether the transubstantiation of bread into Christ’s body is an article of Christian faith, since no mention of it is made in any creed. For it is not found in the Apostles’ Creed—“I believe in God”—nor in the Nicene Creed—“I believe in one,” etc.—nor in the Athanasian Creed—“Whoever wishes,” etc. Since these creeds mention all the articles of Christian faith, why do they not mention that ineffable sacrament, against which human reason seems most strongly to object? [Note: [Col. 0363] The printed edition reads: “to which the rational soul seems most bound,” but our reading is to be retained.]

[Col. 0363C]

Some answer that in the early Church it was so evident to everyone that bread was transubstantiated into Christ’s body that no one doubted it, since Christ had testified to it in the Gospel. No heresy arose concerning this in the early Church which would have required that it be mentioned in an article of a creed in order to suppress it. Thus, because heresy concerning the Trinity arose in the early Church among Arius and Sabellius; concerning the Holy Spirit among Macedonius; concerning the Incarnation among Eutyches and Nestorius; and concerning the resurrection among others, as the Apostle testifies in his Epistle to the Corinthians (1 Cor. 15), these articles are mentioned in the creeds. Nevertheless, it may be said that the Apostles’ Creed mentions the Eucharist when it says, “the communion of saints.” For the saints communicate spiritually in this [Col. 0363D] when they receive Christ’s body not only sacramentally but also spiritually.

## CHAPTER LX. The authorities proving that Christ gave his body to his disciples

That Christ gave his body to his disciples Matthew plainly declares in the Gospel, saying: “While they were eating, Jesus took bread, blessed and broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: ‘Take [Col. 0364A] and eat: this is my body.’ And, taking the cup and giving thanks, he gave it to them, saying: ‘Drink from this, all of you. For this is the blood of the new covenant, which shall be shed for many for the remission of sins’” (Matt. 26).

Likewise Luke: “Having taken bread, he gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them, saying: ‘Do this in remembrance of me.’ Likewise also the cup, after he had supped, saying: ‘This is the cup of the new covenant in my blood, which shall be shed for you’” (Luke 22).

Again, the Lord says in the Gospel: “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John 6). Again: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him on the last day. For my flesh is truly food, [Col. 0364B] and my blood is truly drink. He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him. As the living Father sent me and I live because of the Father, so he who eats me shall live because of me. This is the bread that came down from heaven, not as your fathers ate manna and died; he who eats this bread shall live forever” (ibid.). Because of these words [Note: [Col. 0363] The printed edition wrongly reads *praeter* (“beyond”) instead of *propter* (“because of”).], some of his disciples said: “This saying is hard; who can hear it?” Therefore many turned back and no longer walked with him (ibid.). The aforesaid heretics are their imitators.

The Apostle also says in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you: that the Lord Jesus Christ, on the night in which he was betrayed, [Col. 0364C] took bread, and, giving thanks, broke it and said: ‘Take and eat; this is my body, which shall be given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.’ Likewise also the cup, after he had supped, saying: ‘This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me.’ For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you shall proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Cor. 11). Again: “Whoever eats the bread and drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER LXI. The opinion of heretics who say that Christ, in saying “This is my body,” pointed to himself and not to the body hidden beneath the form

[Col. 0364D]

Moreover, the heretics say that when Christ said, “Take: this is my body,” he did not point to the body hidden beneath the form at the completion of the utterance of the words, but to himself. It is as though he said: “I am the one who gives; that is, it is my body that I give you, not this bread; and what I give is therefore more worthy than bread.”

To this we say that this cannot stand if the sequence of the words is carefully considered. For the evangelist says: “Jesus [Col. 0365A] took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: ‘Take: this is my body’” (Matt. 26), as though saying: “That which I offer you is my body.” Moreover, why would he point to himself, when he and his body were visible to the disciples? Again, what will they say about the blood? [Note: [Col. 0365] The printed edition incorrectly reads: “Again, what also will they say about the blood?”] For we read in the Gospel: “Jesus, taking the cup, gave thanks and said to them: ‘Drink from this, all of you; [Note: [Col. 0365] Here again the printed edition has everything confused: in place of ‘Drink,’ etc., it has ‘This is my body.’] this is the blood of the new covenant, which shall be shed for many for the remission of sins’” (ibid.). Here they cannot say that he pointed to his blood except to that which he offered in the cup, which he gave to his disciples, saying: “This is my blood,” etc.

## CHAPTER LXII. Why Christ gave his body under an alien form

[Col. 0365B]

The heretics also ask: since so many authorities proclaim that bread is changed into Christ’s body, why do they deny so great a sacrament? If they say that it is contrary to nature, we may answer them that he who made all things from nothing can change one thing into another. And if the Son of God lies hidden under human form, what wonder is it if Christ’s body, hidden under the form of bread, does not appear? For just as there was reason for divinity to lie hidden under humanity, so there was reason for humanity to lie hidden under the form of bread. For, just as divinity could not appear to us without a veil, so glorified humanity did not wish to appear to us mortals and weak persons except by means of an alien form. [Note: [Col. 0365] The printed edition reads: “could not appear.”]

It was also fitting that he who had departed from men in the presence [Col. 0365C] of the flesh, sitting at the right hand of the Father, should sometimes visit us, although hidden under an alien form. They also strive to deprive us of the greatest grace who do not believe that Christ is on the altar by the power of the sacrament. What greater grace could he confer upon us than the sacrament of the Eucharist? Hence he himself says: “I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28). Although this is understood of his spiritual presence, it may nevertheless also be understood of his bodily presence.

To confound these heretics, in many churches a miracle is celebrated in which the appearance of flesh has been seen in the host. It would also be a long task to recount miracles [Note: [Col. 0365] The printed edition has the entire passage confused: “I could also recount long miracles, which through infirmity …”] which, on account of the weakness of certain persons, [Col. 0365D] occur concerning the Eucharist. It is also most foolish to deny what Christ confessed, what the apostles testify, what all the saints attest, and in the faith of which we see so many religious men end their lives.

## CHAPTER LXIII. The opinion of those heretics who say that marriage is blameworthy

The aforesaid heretics also condemn marriage. Some of them say that a person [Col. 0366A] ought by every means to cleanse himself from what he has from the prince of darkness—that is, from the body—and therefore ought to fornicate indiscriminately and in whatever manner, so that he may be more quickly freed from evil nature.

They therefore condemn marriage, which restrains the outflow of lust. Hence, as is reported, they commit most unclean acts in their conventicles. These are called Cathars, that is, those “flowing out” through vices, from *catha*, meaning “a flow”; or *Cathari*, as though “the pure,” because they make themselves out to be pure and righteous. Or they are called Cathars from *catus*, “cat,” because, as is said, they kiss the cat’s hindquarters, in whose form, they say, Lucifer appears to them.

They attempt to prove by authorities and arguments that marriage is blameworthy. First, thus: unless marriage were abominable, the Lord would not have recalled John the Evangelist from [Col. 0366B] the storm-tossed sea of marriage. And because marriage cannot be consummated except by carnal intercourse, and thus in sin, they say that marriage is abominable—as though they were lovers of chastity, whereas they are rather followers of incest [Note: [Col. 0365] The printed edition reads *incastitatis*, “unchastity.”] and lust.

They also say that marriage conflicts with natural law, because natural law dictates that all things are held in common; [Note: [Col. 0365] The printed edition most absurdly has *convivia*, “banquets,” for *communia*, “common things.”] whereas marriage appropriates what ought by natural right to be common. Again, if it is good to marry, why does the Apostle say: “I wish you all to be as I am” (1 Cor. 7), that is, continent? They also say that marriage is the cause of the greatest sin, namely adultery, because if marriage did not precede, adultery would not follow.

## CHAPTER LXIV. Resolution of the objections, and that marriage is not blameworthy

[Col. 0366C]

We reply to the foregoing that Christ did not recall John from marriage because marriage was abominable or evil, but in order to invite him to a greater good, namely virginity. For virginity is better—that is, freer and more ready for a greater good—than marital chastity. The married state is entangled in many occupations by which the necessities of life are acquired, and through these the state is less ready for good.

We also grant that marriage cannot be consummated without carnal intercourse, but carnal intercourse is not always sin. For through the sacrament of marriage it comes about that bodily [Col. 0366D] intercourse either is not a grave sin or is no sin at all. How many would not fall into the danger of fornication unless marriage existed? The sin of fornication is excluded within the honourable state of marriage. [Note: [Col. 0365] The printed edition gives the nonsensical reading: “It is excluded by marital honourableness, that it may be sin.”] Hence the Apostle, urging avoidance of fornication, says: “Because of fornication [Note: [Col. 0365] In the manuscript, after these words, *propter fornicationem* (“because of fornication”), there follows in parentheses: “understand, to be avoided.”], let every man have his own wife and every woman her own husband” (1 Cor. 7).

And since bodily [Col. 0367A] intercourse belongs to natural law, marriage does not in this respect conflict with natural law, but rather adorns it. For natural law and bodily intercourse are adorned in this: that a man does not indiscriminately know different women, but takes one woman to himself. This is also clear among brute animals, which, guided by natural law, do not delight in a plurality of mates but in unity.

To the last objection we reply that the Apostle did not wish those to whom he wrote to be free from marriage and continent because marriage is evil, but because the virginal or widowed state is freer. For marriage is holy; consequently, even the Gentiles held marriage in such great veneration that they judged children not born of marriage to be illegitimate.

## CHAPTER LXV. The authorities and arguments proving that marriage is good and holy

[Col. 0367B]

That marriage is good and holy, and that natural intercourse is excused through the goods of marriage, can be proved by various arguments and authorities. For the Apostle says: “Because of fornication, let every man have his own wife, and every woman her own husband. Let the husband render the debt to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband” (1 Cor. 7). Again: “The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; likewise, the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does” (ibid.). Again, the Apostle says in the First Epistle to Timothy: “I wish younger widows to marry, bear children, and be mothers of households” [Col. 0367C] (1 Tim. 5). Let the heretics also hear the Apostle testifying that neither husband nor wife can be continent unless both consent. Again Paul says: “Do not defraud one another, except perhaps by consent for a time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer; and return together again, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of continence” (1 Cor. 7). See how the consent of both must be present.

Again Paul says: “I say to the unmarried and widows: it is good for them to remain thus, as I also do; but if they cannot contain themselves, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn. But to those joined in marriage I give command—not I, but the Lord—that the wife should not depart from her husband, and that the husband should not dismiss his wife” (ibid.). Again: “If any man has an unbelieving wife, and she consents to live with him, let him not dismiss her; for the unbelieving husband is sanctified through the believing wife, and the unbelieving wife through the believing husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are clean” (ibid.). [Col. 0367D]

But perhaps the heretics will object to us the Apostle’s words: “Those who have wives should be as though they had none” (ibid.). These should be understood thus: they should serve God rather than bodily intercourse. Again: “He who gives his virgin in marriage does well, and he who does not give her does better” (ibid.). See how the Apostle commends both marriage and virginity, although he prefers virginity. Again Paul says: “A woman is bound to her husband for as long a time as he lives; but if he falls asleep, she is free to marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord” (ibid.).

They also object to the Apostle’s words: “Husbands, love your wives as Christ [loved] the Church” (Eph. 5). In this they think that continence among married persons is commended by the Apostle as though a commandment—far from it! The Apostle does not say this on account of continence, but in order to strengthen the bond of sincere love: so that, if necessary, a husband may not refuse to suffer something for his wife, just as Christ did not refuse to undergo death for the Church betrothed to him.

Again Paul says to the Romans: “For a woman who is under a husband is bound by the law of her husband while he lives; but if her husband dies, she is released from the law of her husband. Therefore, while her husband lives, she will be called an adulteress if she is [Col. 0368B] with another.” [Note: [Col. 0367] The scriptural text has: “with another husband.”] Again, when the Lord was asked in the Gospel whether a man might dismiss his wife for any reason whatever, he said: “Have you not read that he who made humankind from the beginning made them male and female, and blessed them, saying: ‘Increase and multiply’” (Matt. 19). And he said to Adam: “For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh. Thus they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let no human being separate” (ibid.).

Again, the heretics object: “Whoever has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or wife, etc., shall receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Luke 18). They say that, according to this authority, [Col. 0368C] God commanded wives to be abandoned. But the sense of the words is this: God commanded that, for the sake of divine love, we should set every creature below the Creator. [Note: [Col. 0367] The printed edition corruptly reads *proponamus* (“set before”) instead of *postponamus* (“set below”).] [Note: [Col. 0367] Printed edition: *respectu Creatoris*, “in regard to the Creator.”]

Again, how could the marital union of Zechariah and Elizabeth have been adultery, when their offspring, namely St John, was filled with the Holy Spirit while still in his mother’s womb? If he was filled with the Holy Spirit, then he was sanctified; if sanctified, then cleansed of every sin; therefore he was not conceived through adultery; therefore the union of Zechariah and Elizabeth was not adultery.

But perhaps they will say that John himself was not Zachariah’s son. But let them hear what the angel said to Zachariah: “A son shall be born to you” (Luke 1). Again: “On the eighth day they came to circumcise the child, and they called [Col. 0368D] him by the name of his father, Zachariah” (ibid.). Moreover: “The hand of the Lord was with him; and Zachariah his father was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied,” etc. (ibid.). And elsewhere: “The word of the Lord came upon John, the son of Zachariah, in the wilderness” (Luke 3).

Again, the sacrament of marriage was instituted by God in paradise, when He formed the woman from the man’s rib; and, establishing that one woman should belong to one man, He said: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. 1). Again, in order to commend the sacrament of marriage, Christ willed to be born of a married woman. And, to commend it likewise, He attended a wedding and performed a miracle there (John 2). We also read [Col. 0369A] of Peter that he had a wife, whom he would not have taken had he believed marriage to be sinful. Further, since through marriage the outflow of lust is restrained, it seems rather to be good than evil, since it is disgraceful before God and human beings to be born from persons not married.

Above all, those who condemn marriage contradict the effect of God’s mercy [Note: [Col. 0369] These two words, “God’s mercy,” are omitted in the printed edition.]; for it is chiefly in this that the effect of God’s mercy appears: that He instituted the sacrament of marriage [p. 251] for this purpose, that those who cannot be continent might be excused from the sin of incontinence.

## CHAPTER LXVI. The opinion of heretics who say that confirmation has no efficacy.

There are also heretics who disparage certain other [Col. 0369B] sacraments, such as confirmation, orders, and extreme unction. For they say that the sacrament of confirmation possesses no power, since it is not read in the Gospel or in the other books of the New Testament to have been instituted by Christ or by His disciples.

To this we say that, when Christ breathed upon the apostles, giving them the Holy Spirit for strengthening, He intimated to them the sacrament of confirmation. For the power which was conferred by the apostles through the laying on of hands is given to the faithful through confirmation. Nor do we read that this sacrament was conferred in the primitive Church except by the apostles. Hence later this sacrament was bestowed upon no one except the vicars of the apostles, who occupy the apostles’ place. [Col. 0369C] If others have presumed to confer it, it is considered void and without effect, nor is it reckoned among the ecclesiastical sacraments.

The power of this sacrament is the gift of the Holy Spirit for strengthening—the Spirit who was given [Note: [Col. 0369] In the printed edition: “by whom he was endowed.”] in baptism for the remission of sins. Therefore, since these heretics themselves judge the laying on of hands to be a great sacrament, and this sacrament of confirmation takes its place, they unjustly [Note: [Col. 0369] In the printed edition: “by an unjust judgment.”] disparage this sacrament. How, moreover, do they dare to disparage the authority of all the saints following the apostles, who testify that this sacrament is of the highest importance? It is of such dignity that it ought not to be repeated; no adult person of discretion departs without it without danger; and it must be administered by those who are fasting, unless necessity requires otherwise.

## CHAPTER LXVII. The opinion of those who say that orders are not a sacrament.

[Col. 0369D]

The enemies of the Catholic faith also say that orders [Note: [Col. 0369] The printed edition confusedly reads: “the orders of the Catholic faith.”]—such as the diaconate or priesthood—are not a sacrament. They attempt to prove this as follows: it is not read in any canonical Scripture that the apostles were ordained priests; why, therefore, must their vicars be so ordained [Note: [Col. 0369] This question is absent in the printed edition.]? Again, the apostles, who were called the greater priests, [Col. 0370A] are not read to have been anointed with chrism; why, therefore, are their vicars anointed? Past merits make and support [Note: [Col. 0369] The printed edition absurdly reads: “Many of their supporters do [these things].”] a person’s worthiness for an office; what, therefore, does ordination confer [Note: [Col. 0369] The printed edition reads *constat*, “is established,” for *confert*, “confers.”]?

To this we say that Christ made the apostles priests when, giving them His body, He said: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22; 1 Cor. 11). He also left many matters to be arranged by the apostles, which He Himself did not arrange, such as the conferral of orders and the consecration of priests. Furthermore, if orders conferred nothing for consecration, it would follow that laypersons also could consecrate as priests do, which is absurd.

We also read in the Acts of the Apostles that the apostles ordained seven deacons [Col. 0370B] (Acts 6); by analogy, it must be understood that others were ordained priests by the apostles. We likewise read that James, son of Alphaeus, was ordained bishop of Jerusalem by the apostles. Again, Paul ordained Timothy bishop. Again, in the Epistle to the Corinthians he says that God appointed in the Church some as apostles, some as prophets, others as teachers, and some as priests (1 Cor. 12). He says similar things in the Epistle to the Ephesians (Eph. 4).

What, then, is more absurd than to destroy the ecclesiastical order established by the holy Fathers and celebrated by mother Church with such reverence? Or should one rather believe simple and unlearned people—indeed, people estranged from the Catholic faith—than prudent and religious men? [p. 252] What is [Col. 0370C] more reasonable [Note: [Col. 0369] The printed edition reads: “as though it were more reasonable.”] than that those who effect the sacrament of the Eucharist should be endowed with a certain spiritual dignity? Did not Christ confer this dignity upon the apostles and their vicars—a dignity now conferred upon the vicars of the apostles at their consecration?

## CHAPTER LXVIII. The opinion of those who say that extreme unction is not a sacrament.

They also say that the final anointing with oil given to the sick is neither a sacrament nor has any effect, because this sacrament of the anointing of the sick is not read to have been instituted by the apostles.

But we say that the sacrament of anointing the sick is read to have been instituted by the apostles:

> “In this point Alanus subscribed to Hugh of Saint Victor, book II of *On the Sacraments*, part 15, chapter 2; to the Auxerre theologian, book IV of the *Summa*, treatise 7, chapter 1; to the Master, in book IV, distinction 23; to Saint Bonaventure, article 2, question 2; and to many other earlier theologians. They likewise taught that this sacrament was instituted by Blessed James—understanding, of course, not an original institution, by which some law is first established by a legislator’s authority, but a promulgation, by which Saint James [Col. 0371A] was the first of all to promulgate this sacrament, and not in just any way, but first transmitting it in writing and commending it to posterity. In this sense it is not absurdly said that he instituted it. For we likewise read that many things were instituted by different pontiffs, although it is evident that they are of divine or apostolic institution. But because they were promulgated by the pontiffs through written law, or restored by them to use after neglect, they are said to have been instituted by them. That these authors must be understood and explained in this way, see Saint Thomas, *Supplement*, question 29, article 3, reply to the second objection; and William Estius, on book IV, part 2, distinction 23, §3, letter C; and earlier, distinction 1, §16, where he expressly teaches that even after the Council of Trent Catholics still disputed whether all sacraments were instituted [Col. 0371B] immediately by Christ. Likewise, the opinion of those who say that certain sacraments were instituted by the apostles is to be tolerated.”

For James the apostle says in his Catholic Epistle: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him summon the priests of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the Lord will raise him up, and if he is in sins, they shall be forgiven him” (James 5). In this he shows that this sacrament was instituted for a twofold reason: for the remission of sins and for relief from bodily sickness. Hence it is evident that one who has received this anointing faithfully [Note: [Col. 0371] In the printed edition: “devoutly.”] is relieved both in soul and body [Note: [Col. 0371] There: “both in body and soul.”], provided, however, that relief in both is expedient. But if restoration of bodily health is perhaps not expedient for that person, he obtains in this sacrament [Col. 0371C] the health which belongs to the soul.

## CHAPTER LXIX. The opinion of some who say that a material place ought not to be called a church.

There are some who say that a material place is not a church, but only the assembly of the faithful, because, as they say, place has no bearing upon prayer. For just as God is everywhere, so He may everywhere be worshipped or prayed to. They attempt to prove this by Christ’s authority in saying to the Samaritan woman: “Woman, believe me, the hour is coming when you shall worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem. But the hour is coming, and now is, when true worshippers shall worship in spirit [Col. 0371D] and truth” (John 4).

Again, if place contributes to prayer, why did hermits in ancient times, dwelling in hidden places, have no churches? Why also do the sacraments have their effect even if they are not celebrated in a place called a church? Again, what do walls accomplish for one praying to Him who is everywhere, since He is no more in that place than in another? [p. 253] We also read that Christ prayed more fruitfully on mountains and in desert places, not in places dedicated to prayer [Note: [Col. 0371] The printed edition reads: “in a place dedicated to prayer, or in the temple.”]. Again, is prayer offered in a temple more fruitful than prayer offered in a field, if devotion is equal?

## CHAPTER LXX. Refutation of the foregoing, and the purpose for which the place called a church was instituted.

[Col. 0372A]

We say that place or time is not part of the substance of prayer, but a circumstance. Two things, however, belong to its substance: a good intention and a proper end. For prayer to be meritorious, it must be offered with good intention, devoutly and perseveringly, and for a proper end—that is, for eternal salvation. Hence Christ says: “True worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and truth” (John 4): in spirit, that is, with a good intention; in truth, that is, for truth [Note: [Col. 0371] The printed edition reads *prosperitate*, “prosperity,” for *pro veritate*, “for truth.”]—namely, for the eternal good, which is truly the true good because it is unchangeable.

Place, however, is not part of the substance of prayer; yet it was instituted for prayer, so that, by reason of a place [Col. 0372B] appointed for this purpose, human devotion may be stirred to pray. It was also instituted as a sign, because the material temple signifies the spiritual temple, which is the Church. Of this temple the Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, and that temple you are” (1 Cor. 3).

Likewise, time is not part of the substance of prayer, because God may be prayed to at any time [Note: [Col. 0371] In the printed edition: “at any hour.”]. Yet certain hours are specifically assigned to prayer, and not without reason: for example, the hour of midnight, because at that hour Christ was seized. Hence David says: “At midnight I arose to give thanks to you” (Psalm 118). The first hour of the day is likewise assigned to prayer, because then Christ was handed over by the Jews to Pilate; at that same hour He rose from the dead, and at that same hour He appeared to Mary [Col. 0372C] Magdalene.

The third hour is also assigned to prayer, because then Christ was crucified and scourged by the tongues of the Jews. At the same hour, on the day of Pentecost, the Holy Spirit was given to the apostles. Likewise, the sixth hour, at which Christ was crucified; and at which, on the day of the Ascension, He reclined with the disciples (Acts 1). Likewise, the ninth hour, because at that same hour, crying out, He yielded up His spirit, and blood flowed from His side (John 20). In the evening He was taken down from the cross, and earlier, at that same hour, He had reclined at supper with His disciples. At this hour also, on the day of the Resurrection, He was recognized in the breaking of bread by His two disciples going to Emmaus (Luke 24). At Compline He prayed to the Father for His disciples. At the same hour He was placed in the tomb. For these reasons, [Col. 0372D] the aforesaid hours have been especially assigned to prayer.

Their objection concerning hermits does not harm this argument, because place is not part of the substance of prayer, and the hermits themselves hid in solitudes and secluded places out of humility.

From these considerations the answer to the other objections is clear. Christ prayed in desert places in order to show that, when praying to God, a person should withdraw the mind from the tumult of worldly thoughts. Hence He Himself says: “When you pray, enter into your chamber, and, having shut [Col. 0373A] the door, pray to your Father in secret,” etc. (Matt. 6).

He also prayed in deserts in order thereby to show that God may be prayed to everywhere. We also say that devotion alone makes prayer meritorious; nevertheless, place stirs the fervour of devotion.

## CHAPTER LXXI. The authorities establishing that a material place is called the house of God and of prayer.

That a material place to which the faithful assemble to pray is called the house of God is proved by various authorities. For we read in Mark that the Lord entered the [p. 254] temple and began to drive out those buying and selling in it [Col. 0373B] (Mark 11), and that He said to them: “It is written: My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations” (ibid.). Likewise in Matthew: “Take these things away from here, and do not make my Father’s house a house of trade” (Matt. 21).

Paul writes to Timothy: “That you may know how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of the Lord, which is the Church of the living God” (1 Tim. 3). The same writer says to the Corinthians: “First, when you assemble in church, I hear that there are divisions among you” (1 Cor. 11). And below: “Do you not have houses in which to eat and drink, or do you despise the Church of God?” (ibid.).

It should therefore be understood that both the material place and the assembly of the faithful are called the Church of God. So Jerusalem was called a city, and so too was the assembly of people that was in it. Hence: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which kills the prophets and stones those sent to you” (Matt. 23). This cannot be understood [Col. 0373C] of timber or stone, but of the multitude. Likewise, a market is called both the place in which merchandise is sold and the people gathered in the market. Again, let them be asked whether they permit some churches to be built, or none. If they say none, they seem to oppose the apostles, who are read to have built churches.

## CHAPTER LXXII. The authorities and arguments by which heretics say that the prayers of saints do not benefit the living, nor the prayers of the living the dead, and that saints do not pray for the living.

Certain heretics also say that the prayers of saints do not benefit the living, nor the prayers of the living the dead. They further seem to prove that the saints do not pray for the living, because they know who will be saved [Col. 0373D] or damned. They do not pray for those whom they know will be saved, because prayer would be superfluous: whether they pray or not, those persons will be saved. But if they prayed for the damned, they would not obtain what they ask, and therefore would not be blessed; for blessed is the person for whom everything desired succeeds.

Again, each person will be judged according to his own works, not according to another’s merits; nor will recompense be made to him for another’s merits. Therefore the prayers of saints do not benefit persons either with respect to merit or with respect to reward, because they do not increase merits or rewards. [Col. 0374A] Again, the saints are not in a state of meriting but of receiving; therefore, by prayers or other good deeds, they merit neither for themselves nor for others. Again, in Luke’s Gospel we read that Abraham said to the soul of the rich man in hell: “A great chasm has been fixed between us and you” (Luke 16). By “chasm” he meant nothing other than so great a dissimilarity between the good and the evil that even the saints do not have compassion on the damned. But if they do not have compassion, neither do they pray for them.

## CHAPTER LXXIII. Resolution of the foregoing.

To the foregoing we say that the living pray for the dead, and it benefits the dead; and the souls of the departed—for example, Peter and Paul—pray for the living, and this benefits them [Note: [Col. 0373] The printed edition confusingly reads: “And the souls of the departed, so that they may openly pray for the living, and it benefits them.”]. For unless the saints who are in paradise [Col. 0374B] pray for us, the Church’s daily prayer, which is offered to the saints that they may pray for us, would be futile, and the litanies would have no place. But who would dare to say that God’s Church is deceived in these matters and frustrated in its prayers?

Since every person has an angel assigned to guard him, is it not true that angels desire their salvation and intercede for them? Paul also says [Note: [Col. 0373] The printed edition reads: “Does Paul therefore also preach?”] that Christ intercedes for us before the Father; and if the head intercedes, do not the members—that is, the saints—also intercede? Another authority likewise says that angels present our prayers to God. What is this except that angels pray for us and offer our prayers to God, that He may have mercy upon us?

Concerning the soul of the rich man, we also read that he prayed for his living brothers, lest they come [Col. 0374C] into the [p. 255] place of torments (Luke 16). Therefore, if one damned in hell and depraved by wickedness prayed for the salvation of his own, much more do the saints, who are endowed with mercy, pray for the salvation of the living. Do they not have compassion on the misery of the living? And if compassion and will are in them [Note: [Col. 0373] The printed edition corruptly reads: “therefore their will [is] salvation.”], and if they will their salvation, they appear to pray for them.

We also say that the saints do not know the future salvation or damnation of the living, but God alone does; likewise, they do not know the day of judgment. Because they do not know the salvation or damnation of the living, they are more ready toward good than toward evil, and are more inclined toward salvation than damnation. Thus they will the salvation of the living and appear to pray for them.

But Gregory’s authority, where he says, “What do those not see who see Him who sees all things?” seems to oppose this opinion. But the meaning of this authority is: “What do they not see”—understand, of those things which pertain to their salvation? As though he said: They have knowledge of all things which pertain to their salvation. It is not that they know everything, but those things whose knowledge concerns their salvation; thus this universality is fitting, not unrestricted [Note: [Col. 0373] The printed edition reads *universis*, “all things,” for *universitas*, “universality.”].

The heretics further object: if saints pray for the salvation of living persons who will be damned, they do not obtain [Col. 0375A] what they ask, and thus they are not blessed, since blessed is the person for whom everything desired succeeds. But to this we say that, although they do not obtain everything that they ask or will for others, they are no less blessed on that account. For the saying, “Blessed is the person for whom everything desired succeeds,” must be understood with the addition “for himself,” even if not for others. For if they knew someone’s damnation, they would not pray for him. Hence those who are in the heavenly homeland do not pray for those who are in Gehenna, whose damnation is eternal [Note: [Col. 0375] The manuscript better reads: “whose damnation is certain.”].

Again, although each person is judged according to his own merits [Note: [Col. 0375] The printed edition has “will be judged.”], nevertheless the prayers of saints benefit the living, so that the grace of remission of sins may be infused into them, that they may be justified, and that thus they may merit through their own righteousness. For if in this life one person can merit initial grace [Note: [Col. 0375] The printed edition adds: “for another to merit initial grace,” rightly.], or greater grace, much [Col. 0375B] more can saints through their prayers and petitions merit grace for the living, or make it greater [Note: [Col. 0375] Certain words are omitted here in the printed edition.].
