For the saints also merited this in life [Note: [Col. 0375] “On the way,” i.e. in earthly life.]: that the prayers of those existing in the heavenly homeland might benefit those still on the way. For God foresaw from eternity that, in answer to the prayers of saints, He would grant certain people remission of sins, multiplication of grace, or other benefits for body or soul. And although the saints now in the heavenly homeland do not merit for themselves, while they were on the way they merited that the prayers of those existing in the heavenly homeland should benefit wayfarers.

Abraham’s statement that a great chasm has been fixed (Luke 16) is to be understood thus: the saints do not have compassion on those in hell, because their damnation is certain; [Col. 0375C] but they have compassion only on those who stand open to either outcome.

The prayers of the living also benefit others. Thus in the Acts of the Apostles we read that Peter, by his prayer, healed a paralytic (Acts 9) and raised Tabitha from the dead (ibid.). And James the Apostle says: “The persistent prayer of a righteous person has great power” (James 5). Christ also said to Peter: “I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22). The Church also prays for schismatics and heretics, that God may convert them to repentance; it would not do so unless it believed that prayers could benefit them. Christ also prayed for His persecutors (Luke 23). Stephen interceded for those stoning him (Acts 7), many of whom afterwards were converted to the faith.

It is also manifest [Note: [Col. 0375] The printed edition: “clear.”] that the prayers of the living benefit [Col. 0375D] the dead, since the entire Church of God prays for the departed, that either their punishment may be more tolerable or their deliverance quicker. If saints such as Peter and Paul have the power to raise the dead by their prayers, they appear much more to have power to aid the dead in purgatory, so that they may be delivered more swiftly.

All the authorities of the saints proclaim this, and it is irreligious to oppose them by asserting that Augustine [Col. 0376A] and the others were liars. And if they accepted the books of Maccabees, they would find there an explicit authority on this matter, where it says: “The most valiant man Judas, after a collection had been made, sent twelve thousand drachmas to Jerusalem, that a sacrifice might be offered for the [p. 256] sins of the dead” (2 Macc. 12). Can the saints not also merit this before God by good works: that they may assist the souls of their friends by prayers and other good deeds?

## CHAPTER LXXIV. The opinion of heretics who say that we ought not to eat meat.

The aforesaid heretics assert that eating meat is a mortal sin. They attempt to prove it as follows. [Col. 0376B] We read that God cursed the earth (Gen. 3), and, in cursing the earth, cursed the animals which live from the earth; therefore, things cursed by God ought not to be used. Again, flesh comes from sentient flesh [Note: [Col. 0375] The manuscript reads *seminativa*, “generative,” for *sensitiva*, “sentient,” and rightly.], from uncleanness, through lust; but unclean things ought not to be used [Note: [Col. 0375] This entire passage is absent in the printed edition.]. Again, flesh supplies fuel for lust; therefore one must abstain from meat, because one must abstain from all things that provide incentives to sin. Further, we do not read that Christ ate meat; therefore He did not eat it, in order to give us an example of abstaining from meat, and thus He indicated that it should be avoided. We also read that saints abstained from meat, and not without reason [Note: [Col. 0375] The printed edition reads: “therefore there is reason why one ought to abstain.”]; therefore we too must abstain.

## CHAPTER LXXV. Resolution of the foregoing: it is not evil to eat meat.

[Col. 0376C]

To this we say that one ought not to abstain from meat because God cursed the earth, since by the same reasoning one would have to abstain from fruits. To curse the earth, however, meant nothing other than to subject it to barrenness. For whereas before Adam’s sin it was fruitful [Note: [Col. 0375] The printed edition: “exceedingly fruitful.”], spontaneously bearing every sort of fruit, after the sin, and because of the sin, it was condemned to barrenness, so that it yields scant fruit and not without human labour [Note: [Col. 0375] The final sentence is absent in the printed edition.], bringing forth thorns and thistles (Gen. 3).

Nevertheless, flesh was not thereby condemned such that it is unlawful to use it, even though it has been weakened because of Adam’s sin. And although flesh is propagated from flesh [Col. 0376D] by means of the prickling of lust [Note: [Col. 0375] The printed edition reads *principatu*, “rule,” for *pruritu*, “prickling,” incorrectly.], it is not unclean for eating. For what prevents from being eaten that which was conceived through lust [Note: [Col. 0375] Here again *per peccatum*, “through sin,” incorrectly stands for *per pruritum*, “through lust.”]? What uncleanness is there in flesh on this account that it should be forbidden for consumption? Nothing is considered unclean before God except on account of sin. Therefore, since the flesh of beasts is not subject to sin, why is it forbidden for human consumption?

We say that it is good to abstain from meat, [Col. 0377A] not because meats are evil, but because they furnish fuel to fleshly desire; nevertheless, it is not a sin to eat. For as the Apostle says: “All things are lawful to me, but not all things are expedient” (1 Cor. 6), which is to be understood concerning the eating of meat. Again, although we did not read that Christ ate meat, it would still not be true that He did not eat it, for Christ did many things which were not written. But Christ ate the paschal lamb with His disciples, as is beyond doubt since we read in the Gospel: “Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?” (Matt. 26). Here “Passover” means the paschal lamb.

The saints abstained from meat not because meats were evil or eating them was evil, but lest they should furnish fuel for concupiscence.

[p. 257]

## CHAPTER LXXVI. The authorities and arguments establishing that one is not bound to abstain from foods created by God.

[Col. 0377B]

This error can be opposed by many authorities and arguments. It has been proved above that all things were created by God; but nothing created by God is unclean. Therefore flesh too is not unclean. Therefore one ought not to abstain from meat because of its uncleanness.

Again, on what grounds do they say that one must abstain from meat but not from eggs, since eggs provide more fuel for lust than meat? Why, too, do they not abstain from fish, which likewise are born by a certain generative process, and some of which, being delicacies, [Col. 0378A] excite the prurience of lust? Further, why do they use legumes, such as beans and peas, which cause more flatulence and kindle lust?

We also read in the Acts of the Apostles that Peter was told: “What God has created, do not call unclean” (Acts 10). The Apostle likewise rebukes those heretics who forbid marriage and abstinence from foods which God created (1 Tim. 4). The Lord also, when sending His disciples to preach, said: “Into whatever house you enter, remain there, eating and drinking what they have” (Luke 10). The same Lord, as has been shown above, ate the Passover—that is, the paschal lamb.

Again, Christ says: “Whatever enters the mouth does not defile a person” (Matt. 15). Therefore neither does meat. Again, the Apostle says: “Eat whatever comes from the meat market, asking no question on account of conscience” (1 Cor. 10). Likewise: “Every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected which is received with thanksgiving, for it is sanctified through the word of God and prayer” (1 Tim. 4). Again, to Titus: “All things are clean to the clean; but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean” (Titus 1).

But the heretics object that the Apostle forbids eating meat and drinking wine when he says: “It is good for a person not to eat meat and not to drink wine” (Rom. 14). But we say that here the Apostle does not forbid the use of meat or wine, but gives counsel to abstain. Let these statements against the aforesaid heretics suffice. Now let us turn our pen to those called Waldensians.

# BOOK TWO. AGAINST THE WALDENSIANS.

[Col. 0377]

[p. 258]

## CHAPTER ONE. The authorities and arguments establishing that no one ought to preach unless sent by a superior prelate.

[Col. 0377C]

There are certain heretics who pretend to be righteous, though they are wolves clothed in sheep’s garments. Of them the Lord says in the Gospel: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves” (Matt. 7). They are called Waldensians, after their heresiarch, who was named Waldo. Led by his own spirit, not sent by God, he devised a new sect: namely, that he should presume to preach without a prelate’s authority, without divine inspiration, without knowledge, without learning. [Note: [Col. 0377] The printed edition reads: “without conscience, without letters.”] A philosopher without reason, a prophet without vision, an apostle without mission, [Col. 0377D] a teacher without an instructor [Note: [Col. 0377] The printed edition reads: “without instruction.”]; his disciples—or rather, his mousetraps—deceive the simple in various parts of the world, turn them away from the truth [Col. 0378C] [Note: [Col. 0377] The printed edition reads: “they lead them astray from the way.”], and do not convert them to the truth. They presume to preach in order to fill their bellies rather than their minds [Note: [Col. 0377] “They may be filled in belly rather than in mind.”]; and, unwilling to labour with their own hands to obtain food, they prefer to live idly and preach falsehoods [Note: [Col. 0377] The printed edition has *similia praecinere*, “to chant similar things beforehand.”] so as to hunt for food (1 Cor. 4), though Paul says: “He who does not work shall not eat” (2 Thess. 3).

First, in this they sail against divine authority and against the proclamations of Holy Scripture: they preach though they have not been sent by a higher prelate or by God. For their works do not prove that they were sent by God, nor do miracles confirm it. A mission given by God is proved by good works and confirmed by miracles. Nor do we read that any saint preached unless sent. Christ himself was sent by the Father, and he did not come to preach [Col. 0378D] except according to the Father’s good pleasure. The same is evident in the prophets, the apostles, and their vicars. We read that Jonah [Note: [Col. 0377] The printed edition incorrectly has “John” for “Jonah.”] was sent by God (Jonah 1). And the Lord says to Jeremiah: “Before I formed thee in the womb, I knew thee; and before thou camest forth from the belly, I sanctified thee; I gave thee as a prophet among the nations” (Jer. 1). Amos too says that he was sent by God while he was a shepherd of sheep (Amos 1). And the Holy Spirit is introduced in Malachi as speaking thus to the Father concerning John the Baptist: “Behold, I send my angel before thy face” (Mal. 3; Matt. 2). Isaiah too is read to have been sent by God (Isa. 1). And what need is there to enumerate each one? We read that all the prophets of the Old Testament were sent by God.

Likewise, Christ’s disciples were called apostles, as though sent above others [Note: [Col. 0379] The printed edition reads: “sent above others, and sent to others.”]. Likewise, their vicars were sent. Moreover, by Christ’s sending the apostles and others to preach, it is signified that lesser persons in the Church [Col. 0379B] of God ought not to preach unless they are sent by greater persons. And since ranks in the Church of God are distributed through superiors [Note: [Col. 0379] “By the authority of a superior.”], so too is the office of preaching, since it is the greatest office in God’s Church. And just as no one ought to be advanced 259 to the priesthood except in the manner of Aaron—that is, so that he does not usurp it for himself—so no one ought to undertake the office of preacher on his own authority. Hence Korah, as is read in Numbers, perished by fire with his companions because he usurped another’s office (Num. 16). We also read in the Fourth Book of Kings that King Uzziah, because he usurped the office of sacrificing, was struck with leprosy (4 Kings 15; 2 Chron. 26). Likewise, he who usurps the office of preacher is struck with spiritual leprosy, that is, mortal sin.

The Apostle also says to the Romans: “How shall they preach unless they are sent?” (Rom. 10), because they are not true apostles unless they are sent. [Note: [Col. 0379] This final clause is absent from the printed edition.] Likewise, in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians he rebukes pseudo-preachers [Note: [Col. 0379] “Reproves.”] because they had not been sent but preached on their own authority (2 Cor. 11). He himself, however, was sent by a superior, that is, by Christ. For he says also to the Romans, speaking of Christ: “Through whom we have received grace and apostleship” (Rom. 1). [Note: [Col. 0379] All this is absent from the printed edition.]

How, moreover, can the unlearned preach, when they do not understand the Scriptures? [Note: [Col. 0379] The printed edition reads: “who do not understand the mystery of Scripture.”] Is not their preaching more for the ruin of many than for their rising again? Again, how do those who have not learned know letters? We see also holier men, who possess an understanding of Holy Scripture, not preaching—for example, many Cistercians—because, of course, [Col. 0379D] they have not been sent. If preaching is dangerous for the wise and holy, [Note: [Col. 0379] The printed edition has “danger” rather than “dangerous.”] it is most dangerous for the uneducated, who do not know what ought to be preached, to whom, how, when, or where it ought to be preached.

They also oppose the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0379] The printed edition reads: “in this they presume against the Apostle.”] in that they bring little women with them and have them preach in the assembly of the faithful, although the Apostle says in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “Let women keep silence in church; for they are not permitted to speak, but are to be subject, as the law also says. But if they wish to learn anything, let them ask their husbands at home; for it is shameful for a woman to speak in church” (1 Cor. 14). Again, the Apostle says in the First Epistle to Timothy: “Let a woman learn in silence with all submission. But I do not permit a woman to teach, nor to exercise authority over a man” (1 Tim. 2).

The Apostle also says of these heretics in the Second Epistle to Timothy: “Know this: in the last days perilous times will come, and men will be lovers of themselves, covetous, haughty, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, wicked, without affection, without peace, slanderers, incontinent, savage, without kindness, traitors, rash, puffed up, lovers of pleasures rather than of God, having indeed an appearance [Col. 0380B] of godliness but denying its power. Avoid them; for among them are those who enter houses and lead captive little women laden with sins, who are led by various desires, always learning and never arriving at the knowledge of truth” (2 Tim. 3).

All these things especially suit the Waldensians: they are haughty, detracting from the prelates of the Church; proud, boasting of their own works; blasphemous against God through heresies; disobedient to carnal and spiritual parents [Note: [Col. 0379] “Carnal” is absent from the printed edition], because they deny obedience to their prelates; wicked, because they destroy their own souls and those of others by depraved teachings; without affection toward anyone [Note: [Col. 0379] The printed edition reads: “without affection of soul”]; without peace, troubling others; slanderers, because they charge others with crimes; incontinent [Col. 0380C] nevertheless, because in their conventicles they indulge their appetite and pursue lust, as those who withdraw from their associations testify; savage, in pursuing lawsuits; without goodness, because they are unwilling to assist others; traitors, because they reveal others’ secrets; swollen with hearts puffed up, insolent and brazen in a profane religion; having indeed an appearance of godliness but denying its power, because outwardly they profess religion while inwardly they are ravening wolves; blind, not understanding what they say or what matters they handle; lovers of pleasures, preferring carnal delights to spiritual ones. [Note: [Col. 0379] Much of the preceding material is absent from the printed edition.] These are they who enter widows’ houses and deceive them; they are they who labour continually in their schools in order to learn, yet never arrive at the knowledge of truth.

## CHAPTER II. The authorities and arguments by which the Waldensians, furnished with them, maintain that no one ought to obey anyone except God.

[Col. 0380D]

These Waldensians assert that no one ought to obey any human being, but God alone. They endeavour to prove this by the authority of Peter and John, who, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles, speaking to the Scribes and Pharisees, said: “Judge for yourselves whether it is better to obey God commanding [Col. 0381A] or you forbidding” (Acts 4 and 5). That is as if to say: You err in forbidding what God commands, and you are not to be heard; for where a superior commands and an inferior contradicts, the inferior is not to be heard.

They also say that, if one must obey a human being, one must obey for God’s sake and not for the human being’s sake; and thus God alone is to be obeyed. Again, if a human being obeyed another human being in matters in which obedience ought not to be rendered, he would sin, because in that he would not obey God. Again, Samuel says to Saul: “To be unwilling to obey is like the sin of divination” (1 Sam. 15). It is like divination, in a sense, to deny God through disobedience; but to be unwilling to obey a human being is not divination, but unwillingness to obey God. Therefore God must be obeyed and not man, because by not obeying man [Col. 0381B] we do not practise divination, whereas by denying obedience to God we do.

## CHAPTER III. Resolution of the foregoing, and that God and human beings are to be obeyed.

The answer to this is that God and man are to be obeyed, but God more than man; yet man also, because authority over human beings has been ordained by God. For, as the Apostle says: “There is no authority except from God” (Rom. 13). [Note: [Col. 0381] This final phrase is absent from the printed edition.] Hence Christ says to Pilate: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above” (John 19). If therefore Pilate, who had received earthly authority from the Roman emperor, possessed it over Christ, much more [Col. 0381C] [Note: [Col. 0381] The printed edition has “all the more.”] does one human being possess authority over other human beings.

Christ also was obedient to his putative father and his mother (Luke 2). Peter and John, however, by saying that God commanding must rather be obeyed than human beings (Acts 5), do not deny that human beings must be obeyed, but that God must be obeyed rather than man. Yet a human being must never be obeyed in evil matters, but only in good; and in obeying a human being in what is good, one obeys God.

Samuel’s statement, “To be unwilling to obey is like the sin of divination” (1 Sam. 15), is understood in the case where someone enjoins something on another by a divine command or divine inspiration; just as Samuel, by divine inspiration or divine command, had enjoined Saul to wait for him in order to offer sacrifice. Therefore, in failing to wait, [Col. 0381D] Saul was disobedient to God and not merely to a man; and this disobedience was in a sense like the sin of divination.

## CHAPTER IV. Authorities proving that human beings, especially prelates, must be obeyed.

The Apostle clearly shows in the Epistle to the Romans that human beings, and especially prelates, must be obeyed, saying: “Let every soul be subject to higher powers; for there is no authority except from God, and those that exist [Col. 0382A] are ordained by God. Therefore he who resists authority resists God’s ordinance” (Rom. 13). And below: “For this reason you also pay tribute; for they are God’s ministers, serving him in this very matter” (ibid.). Peter too says in the Catholic Epistle that one must obey one’s masters, not only the moderate but also the harsh (1 Pet. 3). Dionysius also says in the *Hierarchy* that angels obey one another, the lesser, namely, the greater. Even brute animals obey one another; this is evident even among the smallest animals, namely bees, for bees also have a king.

Therefore both ecclesiastical and secular powers are ordained by God, so that superiors may govern inferiors and subjects may receive praise [Note: [Col. 0381] The printed edition has “favour.”] from them if they act well, or, if they act badly, be punished. [Note: [Col. 0381] The printed edition reads: “if they act badly, let them bear punishment.”] Subjects ought [Col. 0382B] to obey their prelates, whether they are good or evil, in good matters, however, and not in evil ones. For obedience is the fulfilment, by a deliberating mind, of an honourable and just command; because we ought to obey prelates in those things which they deliberate justly and command justly.

There are certain things without which there is no salvation, such as fulfilling the moral commandments; in these we are altogether bound to obey prelates. There are other things in which there is no salvation, such as mortal sins; in doing these no one is to be obeyed. There are also intermediate things with which salvation is possible and without which salvation is possible, such as eating flesh or not eating it. But it is not lawful for a layman to preach, and it is dangerous for him [Note: [Col. 0381] In the printed edition everything here is confused, and for “it is dangerous” it has “it is not dangerous.”], because he does not understand what he says [Col. 0382C] and does not understand the Scriptures which he presumes to expound. [Note: [Col. 0381] The printed edition has “promised.”] Therefore, if a prelate orders him to be silent, he is bound to be silent; and if he is not silent, he sins mortally.

Hence, if under penalty of excommunication a prelate forbids him to preach, then, if he preaches, he incurs the sentence of excommunication. Accordingly, those Waldensians who preach against the command of the lord pope—indeed, against the whole Church—incur this sentence. At the Lateran Council too, a sentence of excommunication was passed against them. Therefore one must not communicate with them either, since by an apostolic sentence they have been cut off from the Church. They were excommunicated because they usurp an office not their own against the faith, and indeed preach the Church in words while impugning it in deeds; they set their mouth against heaven, detracting from the Roman curia, [Col. 0382D] whereas it is akin to sacrilege to dispute the act of the supreme pontiff. Whom, then, should one believe more: the unlearned or all the wise men of the Church? If therefore we obey the greater persons and prelates of the Church in things that are not dangerous but indifferent—such as abstaining from flesh or wine—then these aforesaid heretics are much more bound to obey the Church’s prelates in matters that it is dangerous to do, since a prelate’s sentence, as Gregory testifies, whether just or unjust, must not only be feared but also observed.

## CHAPTER V. The opinion of those who say that only good prelates ought to be obeyed, and its refutation.

[Col. 0383A]

Perhaps certain heretics will say that good prelates must be obeyed, those who are vicars of the apostles both in life and office; but not those who lack the apostles’ life and do not retain their office, because these are hirelings, not shepherds.

But Saint Clement opposes them, saying: “Priests and the other ministers of the Church, and all the people, ought to love their bishops and obey their commands, even if they themselves act otherwise—which God forbid—unless they have erred in the faith.” Likewise Pope Eusebius: “Sheep entrusted to their shepherd ought not to rebuke him unless he has departed from the faith,” [Col. 0383B] nor can they accuse him in any way, because the deeds of the shepherd are not to be struck with the sword of the flock. [Note: [Col. 0383] The printed edition has, quite contrarily: “The sheep are not to be struck by the shepherd’s sword.” Yet anyone can readily conclude that our reading must be retained.]

## CHAPTER VI. By authority the heretics seek to prove that only imitators of the apostles must be obeyed.

They endeavour to prove by various authorities that the power of binding and loosing was given only to those who preserve both the teaching and the life of the apostles. For Augustine says in the book *On Baptism*: “God himself effects the remission of sins, either by himself or through the members of the dove.” The same Augustine also says that sins, including those committed, are remitted by saints.

The same writer, commenting on Exodus where he speaks of the priest’s golden plate, which was always upon the priest’s forehead, says: [Col. 0383C] “This signifies confidence in a good life; and he who is truly and perfectly a priest, not merely in signification but in reality, possessing this confidence, alone can take away sins.” Likewise Gregory: “Only those who, while placed in the flesh, [Note: [Col. 0383] The printed edition reads: “placed in this cause.”] possess the power of binding and loosing like the holy apostles hold their examples together with their teaching.” Likewise, from Gregory’s sayings: “This power was granted to Peter alone and to Peter’s imitators; for whoever imitates Peter’s footsteps has this power of binding and loosing.”

It is also read in Malachi: “I will curse your blessings” (Mal. 2). And elsewhere: “Woe to those who make alive souls that do not live, and put to death souls that do not die” (Ezek. 13). For if the Lord curses their blessings, and if the souls whom they make alive do not live, how [Col. 0383D] is the grace of blessing given through them? [Note: [Col. 0383] The printed edition has “transferred” for “given.”]

## CHAPTER VII. Determination of the foregoing: all priests have the power of binding and loosing.

To this we say that all priests have the power of binding and loosing, but only those endowed with apostolic life and teaching use this power worthily and rightly. The foregoing [Col. 0384A] authorities, which say that unjust priests neither bind nor loose, must be referred to this point: that is, they do so neither worthily nor rightly. Absolutely speaking, however, remission or retention of sins takes place through those who are not holy. For God gives a blessing to one who worthily asks, even through an unworthy minister.

The saying read in Malachi, “I will curse your blessings” (Mal. 2), is understood thus: “I will curse your blessings,” that is, those things which you do not possess by our blessings, because, since you have abandoned me, they will turn to your harm. Or thus: even if they bless holy persons, they do not do this from a true heart, and so the blessing is turned into a curse for them. Or thus: what is blessed by you is cursed by me, because they bless evil-doers and flatter sinners, provided they are rich. [Note: [Col. 0383] All that follows is absent from the printed edition.] Or this may be understood as said against heretics cut off and excommunicated by the Church: their blessings [Col. 0384B] are curses for those who follow their errors. But the saying, “Woe to those who make alive souls”—that is, who say that they make themselves alive—is understood of those who presume to bind or loose without the key of knowledge and the pattern of a good life.

That all priests have the power of binding and loosing is attested by Jerome on that Gospel passage in which the Lord says to Peter: “I will give thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven,” etc. (Matt. 16). “The other apostles possess the same judicial power, and the whole Church possesses it in bishops and presbyters; but Peter received it specially for this reason: that all may understand that whoever separates himself from the unity of faith [Col. 0384C] and the fellowship of the Church can neither be loosed from sins nor enter heaven.”

Likewise, Augustine shows that even if a priest is evil, he nevertheless conveys grace by virtue of his office and rank, saying: “The Lord said in Numbers to Moses and Aaron the priests: ‘You shall place my name upon the children of Israel, and I the Lord will bless them’” (Num. 6). Thus grace is conveyed to people through the ministry of one who has been ordained; the priest’s will can neither harm nor benefit, but only the merit of the person requesting the blessing.

We perceive from this how great is the dignity of the priestly office and order. Augustine says in the book *Questions on the Old and New Testament*: “It was said concerning the utterly wicked Caiaphas, among other things: ‘He did not say this of himself; but being high priest that year, he prophesied’ (John 2),” whereby it is shown that the Spirit of graces follows not the person [Note: [Col. 0383] The printed edition has “part.”] of one unworthy or worthy, but the order of transmission. Thus, although someone may have good merit, he nevertheless cannot bless unless ordained, so that no ministerial office may be exercised [Note: [Col. 0383] The printed edition reads: “so that they may exercise the office of minister.”]. But it is God’s office [Note: [Col. 0383] The printed edition has “effect” for “office.”] to confer the blessing’s efficacy.

## CHAPTER VIII. The opinion of those who say that office or order contributes nothing to consecrating, blessing, binding, or loosing.

[Col. 0385A]

The aforesaid heretics also say that merit is more efficacious for consecrating or blessing, binding and loosing, than order or office. Hence, although they are not ordained, because they pretend to be righteous and to possess the merits of the apostles, they presume to bless in priestly fashion. They also say that they can consecrate, bind, and loose, because merit confers power, not office; and therefore those who call themselves vicars of the apostles ought to possess the apostles’ offices through merits. In this they sail especially against the Church and demonstrate themselves to be opposed to it.

They attempt to support this error by the authority of N. [Note: [Col. 0385] The author’s name was lacking in the printed edition; in the manuscript I could not read it. So far as I could conjecture, it was *Esitii*; the printed exemplar, however, substituted in its place: “the authority of one speaking by result.”], who says: “Priests do not bless by their own power, but because they bear Christ’s likeness, and through him who is within them bestow the fullness of blessing.” Therefore, not only one who has obtained the priesthood, but whoever possesses Christ within himself and bears his likeness through good conduct, like Moses, is fit to bestow blessing. They also say that it should be noted that the Apostle, in the Epistle to the Romans, when saying, “Through whom we received grace and apostleship” (Rom. 1), placed grace before apostleship. [Note: [Col. 0385] This entire period is absent from the printed edition.]

But we reply to the foregoing that one kind of blessing belongs only to priests, while another is rendered commonly by all. Indeed, priests [Col. 0385C] in whom Christ dwells are said to bestow the fullness of blessing, not because they alone convey grace, but because they alone do this lawfully and worthily. [Note: [Col. 0385] The printed edition reads, with the opposite meaning: “not because they alone do this lawfully and worthily.”] Nor does a priest’s evil life harm subjects, if they truly do what he says.

Hence Gregory says: “Many, while scrutinizing the priest’s life more than their own, slip down into the pit of error, considering too little that the lives of priests would not harm them if they humbly gave ear to the priests’ good admonitions.” [Note: [Col. 0385] The printed edition has “applied” rather than “gave ear.”]

## CHAPTER IX. Refutation of those who say that a person is not bound to confess to a priest if a layperson is available.

The aforesaid heretics also say that it is not necessary for a person to confess sins to a priest if a layperson is at hand to whom he can confess. But Augustine shows in the book *On Penance* that a priest, to whom God has granted the power of binding and loosing, must be diligently sought: “He who wishes to confess sins in order to find grace should seek a priest who knows how to bind and loose, lest, when he is negligent concerning himself, he be neglected by one who mercifully warns and seeks him.” The same writer says: “Let a person judge himself by his own will while he can, and turn his ways for the better, lest, when he cannot, he be judged by the Lord against his will. And when he has pronounced upon himself the judgment of the most severe—yet most salutary—medicine, [Col. 0386A] let him come to the bishops, through whom the keys may be ministered to him in the Church. [Note: [Col. 0385] Much is lacking here in the printed edition.] Let him receive from the governors of the sacraments [Note: [Col. 0385] The printed edition has “of priests.”] the measure of his satisfaction.”

Likewise Pope Leo: “The manifold mercy of God so assists human falls that hope of life is restored not only through baptism but also through penance. Thus the aids of the divine will have been ordained so that one cannot obtain God’s pardon except through the prayers of priests. For Christ delivered this power to the governors of the Church: that they should assign the satisfaction of penance to penitents confessing sins, and should admit those cleansed by wholesome satisfaction to communion in the sacraments through the gate of reconciliation.” Likewise Leo: “The confession which is first offered to God through a priest is sufficient; the sinner first approaches him on account of offences. For then more people may be moved to penance, if the conscience of the person confessing is not published in the ears of the people.” [Note: [Col. 0385] The rest is lacking in the printed edition.]

Likewise Augustine: “Let one who repents of sins show his sorrow by tears, and through the priest present his life to God. Let him anticipate God’s judgment by confession; for God commanded that sins be confessed orally to priests by those to be cleansed, not in writing or through a messenger, so that each may be ashamed for his own sins; for shame has a share in [Col. 0386C] remission.”

## CHAPTER X. In necessity a person may confess sins to a neighbour or companion if a priest is unavailable.

From what has been said it is clear that it is not sufficient to confess to God without a priest; nor is one truly humble and penitent unless one desires and diligently seeks a priest’s judgment. Yet if one cannot obtain access to a priest, it is sufficient to confess to a companion or neighbour. Hence Augustine says in the book *On Penance*: “Such is the power of confession that, if a priest is lacking, let him confess to his neighbour.” For it often happens that a penitent cannot bring himself to feel shame before a priest. And because neither time nor place is available to one who desires it, even though the person to whom he confesses does not have the power of binding and loosing, he nevertheless becomes worthy of pardon, by virtue of his desire for a priest, when he confesses his offence to a companion.

For the lepers were cleansed as they went to pray, or to show themselves to the priests, before they reached them. Hence it is clear that God looks to the hearts of those who cannot reach priests. [Note: [Col. 0385] The printed edition has the nonsensical reading: “while necessity prevents you from reaching priests.”] (Luke 17).

But they object to us as follows: If sin is wholly forgiven by God through contrition of heart, once the penitent has had the will to confess [Note: [Col. 0387] The printed edition reads: “the vow to confess.”], what is afterwards forgiven by the priest? I see by what bond he binds him, namely temporal punishment, but not from what he absolves him. For before repentance of heart, the soul has the stain and stench of guilt, and stands bound by the bond of eternal vengeance. But if before confession, through contrition of heart, God himself, without the ministry of a priest, both wholly remits the debt and inwardly cleanses the soul from the contagion and stench of sin, what then does the priest cleanse? What does he forgive?

To this we say that when a person sins, he offends against God and against his neighbour: against God, because he acts contrary to God’s command; against [Col. 0387B] his neighbour, through his bad example. Therefore, when sin is wholly remitted to him as regards guilt—that is, as regards the debt of eternal punishment—it is remitted as regards God. But because he has also sinned against his neighbour, a temporal punishment remains to be imposed on him. Moreover, because no one is certain whether he truly has that genuine contrition through which all sins are forgiven him, God gave priests the office of administering the sacrament of absolution to penitents and of imposing a greater or lesser satisfaction according as they see the penitents’ disposition. Thus the priest looses by remission of guilt and punishment, and when, through reconciliation, he admits someone into the Church; he binds when he strikes subjects with a sentence of excommunication. [Col. 0387C] [Note: [Col. 0387] All the foregoing was found, here and there, differently and very obscurely in the printed edition; yet scarcely any sense could be gathered from the manuscript either.]

## CHAPTER XI. The opinion of those who say that general absolutions made by bishops in various offices are not valid.

The aforesaid heretics also endeavour to prove that absolution made by bishops at the consecration of churches or in other offices should not be held valid. For they say: This man is bound to three years’ satisfaction; one bishop, at the consecration of one church, remits a third part to him; a second remits another third; and a third remits the remaining third, because the second and third have as much power to remit as the first. If this is done for three pennies and coins, a three-year penance will be remitted. Again, that remission seems undiscriminating, and an unequal recompense of satisfaction, if the satisfaction of one year is remitted for one penny or coin.

But we answer the foregoing as follows. The person to whom satisfaction is enjoined either possesses charity or does not. If he lacks charity, nothing is remitted to him by the bishop. But if he possesses, or is in, charity, charity itself dictates to him that he complete the penance imposed upon him and not deceive himself by avoiding bodily [Col. 0388A] punishment, without performing the penance imposed on him, if he can. For charity itself makes a person ready to complete not only that penance but an even greater one, if it were imposed on him.

If such a person performs that for which the bishop’s remission was made, not with the intention of having punishment remitted, but from the fervour of charity, and dies before completing the penance, then as much of purgatorial punishment will be remitted to him as the bishop remitted in this present world. We also say that spiritual punishment may lawfully be commuted into bodily or pecuniary punishment, which in very many cases is much more burdensome than bodily punishment. [Note: [Col. 0387] The manuscript has: “for in pecuniary [punishments], which nevertheless are for the most part more burdensome than bodily.”]

Nor, for the one who approaches out of charity, [Note: [Col. 0387] The printed edition has the nonsensical reading: “for this one who approaches out of charity.”] does a commutation of punishment take place as regards himself, because he does not do that for which remission is made with this intention—namely, that he may be released from the penance imposed upon him—[Col. 0388B] but solely from regard for charity. He does not wish it to be remitted, but intends to complete the penance if God grants him life. Because, therefore, he proposes to complete it, and it does not rest with him that he fails to complete it, if he dies before he has completed it, and if the bishop too remits with this intention, that something of the punishment may be remitted to him in purgatory: then, if he has been overtaken by death, as much of purgatorial punishment will be remitted to him as appears to have been remitted in this world from temporal punishment.

## CHAPTER XII. The opinion of those who say that the suffrages performed by those in mortal sin do not benefit the dead.

The aforesaid heretics also say that the prayers or [Col. 0388C] suffrages of those who are in mortal sins [Note: [Col. 0387] The printed edition reads: “who are in death.”] do not benefit the souls of the dead. For how can one who cannot benefit himself benefit others? Again, how can a prayer that is made to the ruin of the one praying contribute to another’s salvation? They endeavour to prove this by authorities and arguments.

For an authority says: “If the person sent to intercede is displeasing, the mind of the angry judge is provoked to worse things.” Again: “He who prays without devotion asks judgment for himself.” But how can one who asks judgment for himself in prayer ask a remedy for others? Again: “Let his prayer become sin” (Ps. 108). How then can it be for others’ salvation? Again, how can one who merits offence before God because he prays plead for another? For God said to the sinner: “Why do you recount my justices and take my covenant in your mouth?” (Ps. 40). Again, they endeavour to prove it by arguments: a priest existing in mortal sin, when he celebrates the divine offices or prays, performs an evil act and by it deserves eternal punishment for himself; therefore that same act does not merit remission of punishment for another, for by no action can a person merit both good and evil. Again, an authority says that one ought not to hear the Mass of a priest of whom it is certainly known that [Col. 0389A] he has a concubine. Another authority also cries out that one who is in mortal sin ought neither to pray in church nor teach the people. [Note: [Col. 0389] The printed edition reads: “nor ought he to say psalms.”]

## CHAPTER XIII. Resolution of the foregoing, and that prayer made by the Church, whoever utters it, benefits dead and living.

This can easily be answered. It is true that the person sent to intercede is displeasing to God through mortal sin when he presumes to pray for another. His condition is also made worse by celebrating the divine offices, especially if he is guilty of a notorious crime: for he sins both in presuming to do so and in being an occasion of scandal to others. Yet, because he prays in the person of the Church [Note: [Col. 0389] The printed edition corruptly has “his own church” for “person of the Church.”], saying, “Let us pray,” the thing signified [Col. 0389B] by the prayer, or the prayer’s own signification, [Note: [Col. 0389] In the printed edition everything here is confused and without sense.] benefits others, not by the efficacy of the prayer of the one praying, but by the efficacy of the Church, which instituted the prayer for the purpose that it might benefit living or dead persons. Therefore one who in mortal sin presumes to celebrate commits sin; nevertheless, the prayer benefits as regards the force of its signification, not as regards the act of the one praying.

It should also be known that there are two kinds of devotion: namely, that of nature and that of grace. Natural devotion exists when someone prays from natural piety and a certain humility, although he is in sin. If such a person prays, he does not sin by praying, because, as regards natural devotion, he does not pray without devotion. His prayer does not harm the one praying, and can benefit the person for whom he prays as regards the efficacy of prayer. The devotion of grace is [Col. 0389C] when someone prays from charity. Thus the meaning is: whoever prays without devotion—that is, without the devotion either of nature or of grace—calls down judgment upon himself; that is, he sins. But for one burdened by notorious sin and giving scandal to others, his prayer becomes sin to himself, not to those for whom he prays—I mean the act of the person praying, not the efficacy of the prayer. Therefore, although by his wrongful action he deserves offence before God, the efficacy of the prayer nevertheless pleads for another.

But when it is said, “And to the sinner God said,” etc. (Ps. XIX), “sinner” means one who glories when he has done evil, because he is guilty of a public crime, or one convicted or confessed in law. If such a person prays, preaches, or sings psalms publicly—that is, in church—he sins, as has been said. Likewise, if such a person celebrates the divine offices, he sins [Col. 0389D] so far as he himself is concerned; nevertheless, the efficacy of the prayer helps others. But if a heretic separated from the Church prays for others, he no longer prays in the person of the Church [Note: [Col. 0389] In the printed edition, *praesentia* (“presence”).], and his prayer benefits neither himself nor others.

From what has been said, it is clear that the act by which an obstinate sinner prays is evil and benefits neither him nor others; but the very signification of the prayer, because it has been instituted by God’s Church for the purpose of benefiting, does benefit others, and thus is not evil but good. But the assertion that one ought not hear the Mass of a priest who is certainly known to have a concubine [Col. 0390A] must be understood of a priest convicted or confessing in law, or in court. His Mass should not be heard, not because it is evil, but because this should be done to the priest’s shame and humiliation, so that he may thereby recognize his sin and repent.

## CHAPTER XIV. By what authorities and reasons it is proved that prayers instituted by the Church are beneficial, whether uttered by a good or a bad priest.

That prayers instituted by the Church are beneficial, if uttered in the person of the Church [Note: [Col. 0389] In the printed edition, *praesentia* (“presence”).], whether by a bad person or a good one, is proved by reason. If the merits [Col. 0390B] of ministers neither increase nor diminish the efficacy of the sacraments, it seems that neither do they affect the efficacy of prayer. But it is evident that the efficacy of baptism, the Eucharist, or any other sacrament is neither increased nor diminished by whoever administers it. By the same reasoning, neither is the efficacy of ecclesiastical prayers; for they possess in themselves a certain sacramental power.

Moreover, if the merits of ministers increased or diminished the efficacy of prayers, the unity of the Church could not stand; indeed, schism would arise. For some would follow the priest whom they believed better and avoid another whom they thought worse; again, some would follow one priest, others another.

Paul also, against those who gloried in their baptizers, says that there is one baptism and one who baptizes (1 Cor. 1). By the same reasoning, no one should glory [Col. 0390C] in the prayers of this person or that. For, as regards the signification of the prayer itself [Note: [Col. 0389] In the printed edition, “from the signification of prayer.”], a prayer uttered by one person has as much efficacy as one uttered by another, though not as regards the devotion of the one praying [Note: [Col. 0389] In the printed edition, *orationis* (“of prayer”) stands in place of *orantis* (“of the one praying”), but incorrectly.]. The devotion of the person praying can indeed be more efficacious in proportion as it is greater; but the prayer itself, so far as it is concerned, will not be more fruitful. For both divine and human Scriptures proclaim that words possess power. Is there not power in these words: “Baptize in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit”? “This is my body”? “This is the chalice of the New Testament”? Why, then, does power remain in ecclesiastical prayers when they are uttered in the person of the Church [Note: [Col. 0389] In the printed edition, with no small error, “the ecclesiastical parish” stands in place of “the person of the Church.”], not by virtue of the speaker but by virtue of the instituting authority?

## CHAPTER XV. The opinion of those who say that every lie is a mortal sin.

[Col. 0390D]

There is another error of the aforesaid persons: they maintain that every lie is a mortal sin. They attempt to prove it as follows. Scripture says: “You will destroy all who speak a lie” (Ps. V). And elsewhere: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1). Likewise: “Let your speech be, Yes, yes; No, no; and whatever is more than this is from evil” (Matt. 5; Jas. 5). It is as though Scripture said [Col. 0391A]: Simply affirm only what is true, and deny what is false. If this is a commandment, then whoever asserts a lie sins mortally. Again, whatever is done against conscience builds toward hell; therefore it is mortal sin. Again, when the Decalogue says, “You shall not bear false witness” (Exod. 20; Matt. 19), the whole is understood from the part. Therefore lying is forbidden to you; therefore, whoever lies acts against a prohibition. Therefore he sins mortally.

## CHAPTER XVI. Resolution of the foregoing, and that not every lie is a mortal sin.

To this it must be said that one kind of lie is a mortal sin, another venial, which [Col. 0391B] has in itself a ground of excuse [Note: [Col. 0391] In the printed edition, by an intolerable error, *excommunicationis* (“of excommunication”) stands in place of *excusationis* (“of excuse”).], as when it benefits someone and harms no one. Augustine clearly indicates this distinction among lies (on Ps. V), saying:

> There are three kinds of lies. For there are lies spoken for someone’s safety or advantage, not out of malice but out of kindness, as the midwives in Exodus are recorded to have done [Note: [Col. 0391] In the printed edition, again incorrectly, “are said.”], who told Pharaoh a falsehood in order to save the children of Israel (Exod. 1). There is also another kind of lie, made in jest, which does not deceive but is uttered solely from a desire to please or amuse; and the person to whom it is said knows that it is said in jest. These two kinds of lies are not without fault, but not with great fault. The third kind proceeds from malice and duplicity and must be very carefully avoided by all [Col. 0391C].

Therefore, the text “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1), and the text “You will destroy all who speak a lie” (Ps. V), refer to that species of lies which is mortal sin. But the statement, “Let your speech be, Yes, yes; No, no” (Matt. 5; Jas. 5), is not a commandment but counsel, and is especially directed against swearing. For sacred Scripture warns us not to swear without understanding the cause, since superfluous oaths are harmful. Hence it follows that “whatever is more”—namely, an oath—“is from evil”: not indeed from the evil of the swearer or of the oath, but from the evil of the one who compels another to swear [Note: [Col. 0391] In the printed edition, *jure* (“by law”) stands in place of *jurare* (“to swear”).].

But the statement that whatever is done against conscience is understood of mortal sin. For if conscience tells [Note: [Col. 0391] In the printed edition, “tells” is misprinted “may tell.”] someone that a certain [Col. 0391D] act is mortal sin and he nevertheless does it [Note: [Col. 0391] Everything here is confused in the printed edition, as follows: “nevertheless to do it builds him toward hell, and makes him worthy of eternal death.”], he builds himself toward hell and renders himself deserving of eternal death. But a lie that is venial, even if it is committed in this way against conscience—that is, though conscience declares such an act to be sin—does not, because it is venial by reason of its cause, build toward hell; nor does conscience thus tell the liar that such a lie is mortal. For if conscience told him that such a lie was mortal and he did it, he would sin mortally. But when it is said [Col. 0392A], “You shall not bear false witness,” etc. (Matt. 19), we say that only the kind of lie which is mortal is forbidden.

## CHAPTER XVII. Whether it is ever lawful to lie.

The heretics also ask whether it is lawful in any case to lie or not. If it is lawful, then in some case lying is not evil—which is false. To this we say that something is called lawful in two ways. In one way, what can be done without any sin is called lawful, according to which sense the Apostle says: “All things are lawful for me, but not all things are beneficial” (1 Cor. 6). In another way, something is called lawful which, although it cannot be done without venial sin, is sometimes done without mortal sin; and in this sense [Col. 0392B] it is lawful to lie in some case, and in no other sense.

That in some case someone may not only be able but even obliged to lie seems provable in this way. Suppose some people pursue a man in order to kill him. The fugitive hides with another person, and the pursuers ask the person with whom he is hidden where the hidden man is. That person strongly believes the hidden man to be in mortal sin and likely to die in that state if he were killed now. Therefore, since he is his neighbor, he is bound to preserve him for the life of body and soul, especially the soul. Therefore, it seems that he is bound to say that the hidden man is not there, and thus is bound to lie.

To this we say that [Col. 0392C] he is not bound to lie or say what is false, but may keep the truth silent. And if perhaps he lies in order to preserve his neighbor’s life, he sins venially, because he does not do this with the intention of deceiving anyone but with the intention of preserving someone’s life. Therefore, wherever the liar’s intention does not tend toward evil, the lie is venial; but where the intention tends toward evil rather than good—or indeed more toward evil than good—the lie is mortal. Thus lying is in no way good; but it is foolish to assert that every lie is a mortal sin.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The opinion of those who say that one must never swear.

The aforesaid heretics also maintain that one must never swear [Col. 0392D], a proposition which they seem to prove by many authorities and arguments. For Christ says: “Let your speech be, Yes, yes; No, no,” etc. (Matt. 5). Elsewhere in the Gospel he also says: “Do not swear at all, neither by heaven, for it is the throne of God; nor by earth, for it is his footstool; nor by a hair of your head, because you cannot make a single hair white or black” (Matt. 5).

To this we say that swearing is in itself neither good nor evil, but indifferent; yet sometimes [Col. 0393A] it is evil and sometimes it is not. To swear freely and without necessity, or to swear falsely, is a grave sin. But to swear from necessity—for example, to establish innocence, to confirm treaties of peace, or to persuade hearers of something useful to them [Note: [Col. 0393] The printed edition reads: “To persuade something which is useful to someone.”]—is not evil, for it is necessary. Hence Augustine, *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, says:

> An oath must be made in necessary matters, when people are slow to believe what is beneficial to them. For although swearing is not good, it is not evil when it is necessary.

Again, Augustine on the Epistle to the Galatians:

> Swearing is not contrary to God’s commandment; rather, the Lord is understood to have forbidden oaths in such a way that, so far as lies within him, no one swears. Many do otherwise, having an oath on their lips [Col. 0393B] as though it were something great and pleasant.

For the Apostle knew the Lord’s commandment and nevertheless swore (Rom. 1) [Note: [Col. 0393] The printed edition incorrectly has “forbidding one to swear” in place of “and nevertheless swore.”]. Therefore we are forbidden to swear out of a craving for, or delight in, swearing [Note: [Col. 0393] The printed edition has, “therefore he understood swearing.”]. Again Augustine, in the same sermon:

> Therefore, when Christ says in the Gospel, “But I say to you, do not swear at all,” he is understood to have commanded that no one should desire an oath as though it were good, and that, by habitual swearing, he should fall into perjury.

But what is added, “Let your speech be, Yes, yes; No, no,” is good and to be desired. And “whatever is more”—that is, if you are compelled to swear—know that it comes from the necessity arising from the weakness of those to whom you are seeking to persuade something. That weakness is certainly evil, from which we daily pray to be delivered, saying: [Col. 0393C] “Deliver us from evil” (Matt. 6). Thus he did not say, “Whatever is more is evil.” For you do not do evil, because you make good use of an oath; rather, it is from the evil of the person who does not otherwise believe—that is, from weakness, which is some punishment [Note: [Col. 0393] In the manuscript, “sometimes” stands in place of “some.”], sometimes both punishment and fault. Therefore there the Lord prohibited evil, advised good, and permitted what is necessary.

But the Lord’s command in the Gospel, “Do not swear at all, neither by heaven, nor by earth, nor by any creature,” was given so that the Jews, who were like little children in understanding, might not, by swearing through angels and elements, venerate creatures with divine honor; for such honor was better offered to God than to creatures. He therefore forbade this to the weak [Note: [Col. 0393] In the printed edition, everything following is confused, with some matters omitted here and there, spaces left blank, and dots scattered about.], but did not forbid it to the holy, who venerated the Creator in creatures. Hence [Col. 0393D] Joseph swore by Pharaoh’s safety, reverencing God’s judgment in him, since he had been placed as, in a sense, the savior of Egypt. But Christ forbade the weak to swear by creatures, lest they believe that something divine was present in them for which reverence was owed to them, or lest, by swearing falsely through creatures, people suppose themselves not bound by the oath [Note: [Col. 0393] Everything following is also absent from the printed edition.].

[Col. 0394A] Likewise, in the authority found in the Catholic Epistle, “Before all things,” etc., swearing is not forbidden, but readiness and rashness in swearing.

## CHAPTER XIX. That it is lawful to swear in certain cases.

From the aforesaid Gospel authorities [Note: [Col. 0393] In the printed edition, “Augustine” stands in place of “Gospel.”], it is clear that it is lawful to swear when one understands the cause; and this can also be proved [Note: [Col. 0393] In the printed edition, “in other ways.”] otherwise. For the Apostle says in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “An oath is the end of every controversy” (Heb. 4).

Therefore, how can someone suspected of a crime, when his simple word is not to be believed, be compelled to clear himself except by an oath, since other forms of purgation have been prohibited by the Church—such as the judgment of cold water, red-hot iron, [Col. 0394B] or fire? For to clear oneself in this manner is to tempt God. The Lord also swore by himself to Abraham [Note: [Col. 0393] In the printed edition, this sentence is preceded by the following words: “the author of all things is read to have sworn in many passages of sacred Scripture.”] that he would bless and multiply him. Hence the Apostle to the Hebrews says: “For when God promised Abraham, because he had no greater by whom to swear” (Heb. 6). And below: “God, wishing more abundantly to show to the heirs of the promise the immutability of his counsel, interposed an oath” (ibid.) [Note: [Col. 0393] Nothing of this or what follows is in the printed edition.]. On this passage the authority says: “He condescended to human custom in order to make them certain.” Again, in the Psalm: “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent” (Ps. 109). And elsewhere: “To whom I swore in my wrath” (Ps. 94). It is also read in the Apocalypse that an angel swore by him who lives forever and ever (Apoc. 10). The Apostle likewise, in the Epistle to the Romans, swears in this manner: [Col. 0394C] “God is my witness” (Rom. 1). What else is it to call God as witness than to swear by him? And how will anyone pledge fidelity to his lord except by an oath [Note: [Col. 0393] The printed edition adds, “or sacrament.”]?

## CHAPTER XX. The opinion of those who say that a human being must never be killed.

The aforesaid heretics and enemies of the Church also assert that in no case, on no occasion, and for no reason is a human being to be killed. For they say that God prohibited homicide, saying in the law: “You shall not kill” (Exod. 20; Matt. 5). Likewise in the Gospel: “All who take up the sword shall perish by the sword” (Matt. 26).

Again, Augustine, writing to Count Marcellinus [Col. 0394D] concerning certain criminals [Note: [Col. 0393] This word is omitted in the printed edition.], says:

> Fulfill, Christian judge, the office of a merciful father. Remember so to be inflamed against wrongdoing that you do not exercise a desire for revenge against the atrociousness of sinners’ crimes [Note: [Col. 0393] The printed edition reads, “in the sins of sinners.”], but apply a will to heal the wounds of sinners.

And below:

> I ask you that the punishment of those who have confessed such great crimes may be other than the penalty [Col. 0395A] of death, for the sake of our conscience and for commending Catholic gentleness. And if this seems unworthy, and resembling relaxation and negligence, to some among us stirred by the atrocity of the matter [Note: [Col. 0395] The printed edition reads, “to be silent.”], yet once the agitations of mind have passed—which usually arise more tumultuously over more recent deeds [Note: [Col. 0395] The printed edition reads, “those granting.”]—a notably clear goodness will appear.

The same Augustine says: “On the occasion of terrible judges and laws, we desire that they be corrected, lest they suffer the punishments of eternal judgment; we do not desire that they be killed.” Likewise Gregory: “Let the Church defend those guilty of blood, lest it become a participant in the shedding of blood.” Likewise the Lord says: “I do not will the death of the sinner,” etc. (Ezek. 18). The Gospel also prohibits the killing of Jews, because they are our book-carriers [*capsarii*; Note: [Col. 0395] The printed edition reads, “brothers.”] and serve as evidence [Col. 0395B] [Note: [Col. 0395] “Increase.”]] of our faith. Hence it is read in the Psalm: “Do not kill them, lest my people ever forget” (Ps. 58).

Augustine also, where it is read that Absalom went in to his father’s concubines (2 Kings 16), says that the concubines signify heretics, who are not to be killed but cast into prison and frequently admonished to return to the truth of the Christian faith. A wandering sheep, too, should not be killed but brought back to the folds. Likewise, heretics who bear the Christian character are to be compelled by words and blows to return to the unity of the Church.

## CHAPTER XXI. They try to prove the same by arguments.

They try to prove the same by many arguments. If [Col. 0395C] the severity of the Mosaic law was such that a thief was compelled to restore what he had stolen twofold or fourfold (Exod. 22), why is it that in the time of the Gospel, which preaches mercy, a thief is punished by death for theft? Should not the mercy of the Gospel take precedence over the austerity of the law? Under the law, it was judged a great severity in the law of retaliation when tooth was rendered for tooth and eye for eye (Exod. 21; Matt. 5); but in the time of the Gospel the severity seems much greater, when another man is condemned to death for the cutting off of a single foot (Matt. 18). What sort of mercy is this that approves homicide and makes laws more severe?

Moreover, one who kills a human being acts contrary to the natural law, which says: “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another” (Matt. 7; Luke 6). [Col. 0395D] Therefore no one ought to wish another killed or kill another, since he does not wish it done to himself. Again, someone sees another person to be in mortal sin [Note: [Col. 0395] Here again the printed edition is confused, reading: “He sees another to be younger in the death of the sinner.”] and not repent; consequently, his conscience tells him that, if that person were now to die, he would be damned. Therefore, if he kills him, he kills him in soul and body, and is thus guilty of that person’s damnation. Yet, since he is his neighbor, he is bound to love him as himself, and therefore to care for his eternal life and, consequently, to provide for his temporal welfare so that he may provide for his eternal welfare.

But if it is said that a judge does this, [Col. 0396A] since he is a minister [Note: [Col. 0395] The printed edition reads, “master.”] of the law, this contradicts the Lord, who says: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Deut. 32; Rom. 12; Heb. 13). Again, if someone objects and says, “Is it not lawful to repel the injuries of enemies?” they reply: “It is lawful to repel force by force, but with the moderation of blameless defense”—that is, by defending oneself, but not by killing another; or by capturing or putting our enemies to flight, but not killing them. For if we kill them, we act contrary to this commandment of the Lord: “Love your enemies, and do good to those who hate you” (Matt. 5).

## CHAPTER XXII. Reply to the foregoing, and that the punishment of murderers and sacrilegious persons is not shedding of blood but the administration of laws.

[Col. 0396B] We reply to these objections as follows. When a judge, justice so dictating [Note: [Col. 0395] In the printed edition, “sentence” stands in place of “justice so dictating.”], orders someone to be killed, he himself does not kill, but the law does. For the judge is a minister of the law—indeed, of God—in carrying out judgments.

The Gospel text, “Whoever takes up the sword,” etc. (Matt. 26), must be understood thus: whoever abuses judicial authority, or unjustly usurps it for himself on his own authority, or takes up the sword out of hatred or pride, shall perish by the sword—that is, he shall be condemned. Augustine’s intercession for criminals arose from mercy, not from the rigor of justice. For in justice the count could punish them by temporal death; but shedding blood does not belong to the ecclesiastical judge.

Gregory’s statement, “One guilty of blood,” etc., is to be understood [Col. 0396C] as meaning that shedding blood belongs not to the ecclesiastical judge but to the secular judge, who bears the sword by which he punishes the body; the ecclesiastical judge, however, punishes the soul rather than the body with his sword. And just as a temporal judge ought not usurp the office of an ecclesiastical judge, so neither should an ecclesiastical judge usurp that of a temporal judge. Therefore, for the Church to defend persons guilty of blood means nothing other than that it ought not punish them by bodily penalty, but rather intercede for them before the temporal judge.

When the Lord says, “I do not will the death of the sinner” (Ezek. 18), this is not understood of bodily death but of the death of the soul. For he does not will the death of the soul, but rather that it should be converted and live spiritually. Concerning Jews, we say that they are not to be killed. Yet if they are guilty of crimes [Col. 0396D] [Note: [Col. 0395] The printed edition incorrectly reads “but.”] for which the law dictates that a person is to be killed, the judge may kill them, thereby serving the law.

Likewise, heretics are not to be killed because of heresy; rather, because of the Christian character which they bear, they are to be brought back to the fold of the Church. Yet if they are guilty of sins to which temporal death is due, they can be punished by the secular judge, provided he punishes them with a view to justice and not from anger or rancor of spirit. We say of a thief that ordinarily he ought not be killed for theft, but compelled to restore the theft [Col. 0397A] and corrected by beatings. But a robber who lies in wait for travelers must be judged otherwise, because by law such a person may be put to death. Nor is the one who, as a minister of the law, kills him by command of the prince to be understood as a murderer [Note: [Col. 0397] Here again the printed edition has a confusion of meaning.]; indeed, he is not said to do this himself, but the law itself does it.

We also say that under the old law no dispensation could be made concerning offenders whom the law judged worthy of death. Even one who killed someone unintentionally was not safe unless he fled to a city of refuge. But under the New Testament [Note: [Col. 0397] In place of “New Testament,” the printed edition corruptly reads “will be noted below.”], no one who kills unintentionally is punished with death; rather, however he may kill, if he flees to a church he will be safe. For the Church grants greater immunity in the New Testament than a city of refuge did in the Old. An ecclesiastical judge [Col. 0397B] ought to punish no one by bodily penalty, but should intercede for those condemned before a secular judge.

Nevertheless, offenders are punished by the secular judge so that the punishment of one may be fear to many. Often, too, offenders are spared; whereas under the old law no dispensation could be made, but the offender was condemned without any mercy. We do not judge it just that if someone has cut off another’s limb, he should therefore be punished by bodily death. Yet by the rigor of justice he can receive retaliation, indeed be punished more severely, once the cause has been examined.

We also say that the judge does not [Note: [Col. 0397] “Not” is omitted in the printed edition, producing a contrary sense, most absurdly.] act contrary to natural law when he orders a murderer to be killed, because it is not he himself but the law itself that does this. The judge ought also diligently to admonish a condemned man whom he believes to be in mortal [Col. 0397C] sin, so that he may repent; he must omit nothing among the possibilities. Thus he frees his own soul and is not liable for the offender’s temporal or eternal death if he punishes according to the law.

But whoever does not have legal authority to kill and knowingly kills sins mortally [Note: [Col. 0397] In the printed edition, the following words are here attached without any sense or rationale: “Whence Jeremiah in the prophet Jonah.”]. When a soldier, obeying the authority under which he has been lawfully placed, kills someone, he is guilty of no homicide under the law of his state; indeed, unless he does so, he will be guilty of desertion and contempt of command. But if he had done it on his own initiative and authority, he would have incurred the crime of shedding blood. Thus, for the very act for which he is punished if he does it without command, he will be punished if he does not do it when commanded.

Many are of the opinion that a person must not kill another person lest he himself be killed. Hence Augustine, writing to Publicola [Col. 0397D]: “I do not approve the counsel to kill people lest one be killed by them.” For a person is bound to undergo temporal death rather than eternal death. He must prefer his own eternal good to his temporal good, and endure temporal death rather than incur mortal sin by killing his brother [Note: [Col. 0397] These preceding words of Augustine also are cited very imperfectly, with some omissions that confuse the sense.].

But when a judge exercises vengeance, God himself is said to exercise it. Hence the Apostle says: [Col. 0398A] “He does not bear the sword without cause”—that is, not without God’s authority—“for he is God’s minister, an avenger for wrath” (Rom. 13), that is, for vindicating or displaying God’s wrath. Therefore, when the Lord says, “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Deut. 32), he forbids a person to avenge himself on his own authority, but commands that vengeance be left to the judge or the law.

We also grant that “it is lawful to repel force by force with the moderation of blameless defense.” Yet it is not lawful, in repelling injuries, deliberately to kill a person. Nevertheless, if, for the purpose of defending himself, someone kills another without intending to kill him, he will not sin mortally. Likewise, if a judge kills a murderer or sacrilegious person for the correction of others [Note: [Col. 0397] The printed edition has *cor recidendum* (“the heart to be cut back”) in place of *correctionem* (“correction”).], so that he may be punished temporally and not punished eternally, he should not be said to hate the person [Col. 0398B] whom he kills, but rather to love him. For he punishes him so that, chastened by temporal punishment, he may repent in the punishment itself [Note: [Col. 0397] Again: “may be punished in death itself.”] and thus avoid eternal punishment.

But they object: “God does not judge twice concerning the same thing” (Nah. 1, according to the Septuagint). Therefore, if someone is punished by temporal death, he should not be punished eternally; or if punished eternally, he should not be punished temporally. Otherwise, if punished by a double death, he is treated unjustly, being judged twice concerning the same thing.

To this we say that a murderer or sacrilegious person sins against God and against his neighbor. Insofar as he sins against God, if he does not repent, he is punished eternally; insofar as he sins against his neighbor, he is punished temporally. Therefore he is not judged twice concerning the same thing, because he is not thus punished in respect of the same thing [Col. 0398C] but in respect of something else: insofar as he has sinned against God, he is punished eternally; insofar as he has sinned against his neighbor, temporally, for correction and for the warning of others. Thus, if sin is remitted in relation to God through repentance, it nevertheless remains to be punished by temporal penalty in relation to one’s neighbor.

## CHAPTER XXIII. That in many cases people ought to be put to death.

Jerome seems to maintain that people ought to be put to death in many cases, saying in his commentary on Isaiah: “He who kills a cruel man is not cruel; rather, he seems cruel to those who suffer.” For a robber hanging on the gallows thinks the judge cruel. Again, in his commentary on Ezekiel: “He who strikes evil people insofar as they are evil, and has cause for killing [Col. 0398D], namely, that he may kill the worst, is God’s minister.” And in his commentary on John [Note: [Col. 0397] The manuscript has “Jeremiah.”]: “To punish murderers, sacrilegious persons, and poisoners is not shedding of blood but the administration of laws.”

Likewise Augustine, *On Free Choice*: “If homicide is to strike down or kill a human being, someone can sometimes be killed without sin: for a soldier kills an enemy, and a judge or his minister a wrongdoer.” Likewise Cyprian, in the ninth kind of abuse: [Col. 0399A] “A king ought to restrain thefts, punish adulterers [Note: [Col. 0399] In the printed edition, *ad ultima* (“to the last things”) stands in place of *adulteros* (“adulterers”) or *adulteria* (“adulteries”).], remove the impious from the earth, not allow parricides and perjurers to live, and not allow children to act impiously.”

## CHAPTER XXIV. The opinion of those who say that preachers ought not to work with their hands.

The aforesaid heretics also say that preachers ought in no way to work with their own hands, but should receive necessities from those to whom they preach. They endeavor to support this by various authorities. For the Apostle says in the Epistle to the Corinthians:

> Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Who tends a flock and does not eat of its milk? Do I say this according to human judgment? For it is written in the law of Moses: “You shall not muzzle [Col. 0399B] an ox while it treads out the grain” (Deut. 23). Is God concerned about oxen, or does he say this for our sake? Indeed, these things were written for our sake. For one who plows ought to plow in hope, and one who threshes ought to thresh in hope of receiving fruit. If we have sown spiritual things for you, is it a great matter if we reap your material things? (1 Cor. 9)

And below: “Do you not know that those who work in the sanctuary eat what belongs to the sanctuary, and those who serve at the altar share in the altar?” (ibid.). So too the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live by the Gospel.

Again, the Apostle says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs” (2 Tim. 2).

## CHAPTER XXV. Resolution of the foregoing.

[Col. 0399C] To this we say that it is lawful for preachers in necessity to receive necessities from those subject to them. But these are false preachers, who, so that they may live in idleness, milk sustenance from simple people, though the authority says: “Always do some work, lest the devil find you idle.” Paul too worked with his own hands, lest his preaching be burdensome to those to whom he preached. Hence he says: “When I was with you and was in need, I was burdensome to no one” (2 Cor. 2). And [Col. 0400A] in the same place: “I preached the Gospel to you free of charge” (2 Cor. 7). Therefore, if a preacher has the means to support himself, he ought not demand expenses [Note: [Col. 0399] In the printed exemplar, much is omitted above and the remainder confused.].

But by what right will these people, who sow no spiritual things, reap temporal things? Therefore all the foregoing authorities bear on this point: that preachers may lawfully receive support in necessity, but ought not abstain from manual work. Hence the Apostle says to the Thessalonians: “Whoever does not wish to work shall not eat” (2 Thess. 3). Again, to the Ephesians: “Let the one who stole steal no longer, but rather work, doing with his own hands what is good, so that he may have something to give to one suffering need” (Eph. 4). Again, in the First Epistle to the Thessalonians: “Attend to your own affairs and work with your hands, as we commanded you” (1 Thess. [Col. 0400B] 4). Here the gloss says that manual work makes us tranquil and removes the evil of curiosity that arises from idleness.

Therefore, the aforesaid persons who refuse to work with their own hands seek here support for their idleness.
