But the authority, “No one serving as a soldier for God” (1 Tim. 2), etc., must be understood thus: no one who has left the world in order to serve as a soldier for God should entangle himself in secular business (ibid.); that is, he ought not devote himself to worldly cares. The aforesaid heretics, mere hirelings wandering about the world [Note: [Col. 0399] The printed edition reads *diffugientes*, “scattering/fleeing in different directions.”], pretend to be preachers so that they may milk victuals from simple people. Thus they prefer shamefully to be idle rather than work with their hands, though the Psalmist says: “You shall eat the labors of your hands,” etc. (Ps. XVII).

Again, let these false preachers themselves say why they refuse to work [Col. 0400C]. Is it a sin, or prohibited by law? Is it not better to acquire victuals by one’s own labor than shamelessly to demand them from others? Did not the Doctor of the Gentiles also set this example for preachers, acquiring his food by his own work? (Acts 20). They are like the false preachers whom the Apostle reproved, who, in order to avoid labor, took from those to whom they preached support beyond their need.

## BOOK THREE. AGAINST THE JEWS

[Note: [Col. 0399]

Dom Carolus Vischius published only the first two books of Alan’s *Treatise against Heretics*, together with the first three chapters of the third book [Col. 0401D], among Alan’s works issued at Antwerp in 1654. He later supplied this lacuna at the end of the second edition of the *Bibliotheca Scriptorum Cisterciensium*, published at Cologne-Agrippina by Johann Busaeus in 1656. Here are the author’s own words prefacing this supplement:

## TO THE READER.

“[These] little works constitute part of the fourfold work of Master Alan of Lille, *On the Catholic Faith*; namely, against heretics—that is, the Albigensians, Waldensians, Jews, and pagans or Mohammedans. Of these, the first two little works (that is, those against the Albigensians and Waldensians) I published two years ago, in 1653, together with several other works by Alan himself, as I had found them in an ancient manuscript codex of the abbey of Park, near Louvain. But these latter two, although I searched diligently for them far and wide in all the most celebrated libraries, I was then unable to find. Recently, however—after the other works had long since been published—they were discovered in the library of our chief monastery of Cîteaux and sent to me by the venerable prior of that place, Dom Francis Du Chemin, doctor of sacred theology. I judged it worthwhile now to publish them here, since perhaps I should not easily have another suitable occasion to publish them. Certainly, they are worthy of their author, and you, reader, will peruse them not without profit. Farewell.

“Brother Charles de Visch, prior of the Dunes.”

(“Library of Writers of the Sacred Cistercian Order,” etc., through the work and study of Dom Charles de Visch, prior of the monastery of St Mary of the Dunes, etc.; second edition, revised by the author, etc. Cologne, at the press of Johann Busaeus, 1656, quarto.)

[Col. 0399]

## Chapter I. The arguments by which the Jews attack the plurality of divine persons

[Col. 0399D]

The Jews say that God is one, but deny that there is a plurality of persons. Let us now turn our discourse toward the perverse beggary of the Jews, which still waits with the ass at the foot of the mountain and is not yet able to look upon the face of Moses; [Col. 0400D] and let us first see what they think concerning the author of all things. They say that he is the same God and creator of all things; but they do not believe that there are three persons in the Godhead, nor are they willing to consider what it is for there to be persons in the Trinity. They believe indeed in the unity of essence, but do not grant a plurality of persons.

They endeavor to prove this by arguments and authorities as follows. If there is one God, as Sacred Scripture proclaims, how does the Christian assert that three things distinct from one another—namely, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—are of one Godhead? For if they are several, they also appear to be several gods, and not one God. How, indeed, could the singular nature of one person, distinct from the others, be the nature of another person? Thus God seems to be threefold, [Col. 0401B] not one. Yet the Lord says to Israel through Moses: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one” (Deut. IX). Therefore God is not threefold, as Christians vainly say here: God is Father, God is Son, God is Holy Spirit. Again, the Father is one, the Son another, the Holy Spirit another; and yet they deny that there are three gods. What monstrosity is this: that there should be unity in Trinity and Trinity in unity? How is God one alone, if God is plural? Those who say this establish foreign gods, contrary to the Lord’s command, who says: “You shall not have strange gods” (Exod. XXX). For they say that God is one and alone, yet assert that there are several.

If God had wished the Jews to believe that three persons are one God and that Trinity is in unity, he would have explained it to them, as he explained other matters pertaining to faith. For, as the Christian says, just as unity pertains to faith, so too does Trinity; yet neither patriarchs nor prophets are read to have made mention of it. Again, if the Father begot the Son, then necessarily the begetter preceded the begotten in time, and some portion must have been cut off from the substance of the begetter. Again: no plurality can exist in God, where there is supreme and perfect simplicity. Again: what is simple in every respect cannot beget anything from itself.

## Chapter II. Resolution of the foregoing, and that unity is truly in the essence and plurality in the persons

We answer the first objection as follows. When God is called one, or of one nature, none of the three persons is excluded, because they themselves are one God [Col. 0402A] and of one nature. Thus one may say of the adjectival words *albus*, *alba*, *album* (“white,” masculine, feminine, and neuter): whoever utters one does not exclude either of the others, because they are one name. For although these words are several, they are not several names, but one name, established by one imposition. Similarly, the three persons are one God and of one essence.

Although in natural things it is true that there are as many substances or natures as there are subsisting persons, yet he who created nature is not subject to nature. Therefore, although there are three persons, they are nevertheless of one nature. For if there were a plurality of natures, there would be said to be several principles of things, which the Catholic faith abhors. And although God is triune, he is not threefold; for “threefold” denotes a plurality of parts or natures. [Col. 0402B] But in God the three persons are not like three parts which constitute God; for, if this were so, God would not be simple, and thus would not be the principle of his own essence, since every composite is generated. Nor are there several natures there, for then there would be several gods, or one God would be three-formed—both of which the Christian religion abhors.

Therefore we say that the Father is other, the Son other, and the Holy Spirit other; yet not that God the Father is another God, God the Son another God, and God the Holy Spirit another God—just as the word *albus* is other than the word *alba*, yet is not another name. We also say that, according to the Catholic faith, this is not some monstrosity, but a demonstrated truth, demonstrated by reason [Col. 0402C] and in a probable manner. We say likewise that unity is in Trinity and Trinity in unity, and that the three are one God; yet we do not establish a foreign god, since those three persons are one God and of one nature.

God veiled this mystery from the Jews in the Old Law by figures, just as he veiled other matters pertaining to faith, so that, as time advanced, the faith of the Christian religion might make progress. Before the Mosaic Law, it was enough for someone to believe that there was one God, who was also the rewarder of the good and the punisher of the wicked, provided that uprightness of life corresponded to uprightness of faith. In the Old Testament, however, or in the time of the Mosaic Law, the greater men, to whom it had been revealed, believed God to be triune and one; while ordinary people revered those greater men, believing what they believed, [Col. 0402D] and were saved in that faith. But after the apostles preached faith in the Trinity, all adults who possess discernment everywhere are bound to believe God to be triune and one.

Nor, if the Father begot the Son, need there have been a cutting-off. Since the Father is simple in every respect, he did not beget the Son from himself by a division of substance, but with the integrity of nature preserved, so that the whole substance of the Father is the substance of the Son. That the Father begot the Son will be proved below. In the Trinity, however, plurality is considered in one respect and identity in another: plurality in the persons, identity in the nature and essence.

We say also that among natural things, nothing simple can beget anything from itself; hence neither does soul beget soul, nor spirit spirit. But in divine matters [Col. 0403B] an entirely different order of reasoning applies, and divine generation does not correspond to human generation. For as God’s nature surpasses every nature, so God’s generation surpasses human generation. Hence Isaiah says: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. LIII).

## Chapter III. By what authorities of philosophers and theologians, and by what arguments and local resemblances, it is shown that there are three divine persons and one nature of them

That there are three divine persons and one nature of them can be shown by authorities, arguments, and various resemblances—not only by the authorities of theologians, but also of philosophers.

[Col. 0403C] At the beginning of Genesis, according to the Hebrew truth, one reads *Heloym* [Hebrew: *Elohim*], where we have “God”; while elsewhere *eloah* is the singular form of the name *Heloym*, just as “God” is the singular of the name “gods.” Therefore, where we have, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. I), the Hebrews have, “In the beginning gods, or lords, created heaven and earth.” But whom does Moses call gods or lords except the three divine persons? Not angels, since angels did not create heaven and earth; rather, they were created. Yet it is one God who created heaven and earth. Therefore, since Moses spoke in the plural, “gods” or “lords,” that plurality refers either to the divine nature or to the persons. But it does not refer to the divine nature; therefore it refers to the persons. Thus he intimated [Col. 0403D] three divine persons, who are one God.

There follows also God speaking in this manner: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (ibid.). Since God is here introduced as speaking, the question is to whom, or to whom plural, he speaks when he says, “Let us make.” He plainly does not seem to speak to angels, since the image or likeness of God and angels, according to which man was made, is not one. It remains, therefore, that God the Father speaks to the Son and the Holy Spirit; or that it is the common utterance of the three persons, in whose image man was made. Now the image of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one, because their nature is one.

Again, where the devil speaks to Eve, he says: “You shall be as gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. III). What does divine Scripture understand there by “gods,” except the three divine persons? Angels are not understood by that name. For, as Scripture says, Eve wished in this respect to be like God: she desired to be endowed with divine knowledge.

[Col. 0404A] Isaiah also records that angels cried: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth” (Isa. VI). But what does that threefold repetition of the name intimate, except the Trinity of persons—that is, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit? The sense is: holy Father, holy Son, holy Holy Spirit. And, so that the unity of nature may be intimated, there follows in the singular number: “Lord God of Sabaoth.”

Genesis relates that Abraham saw three and worshipped one (Gen. XVIII). By this it is intimated that in the three who appeared he understood the Trinity; and because he worshipped one, he understood unity in the Trinity. Thus he is understood to have worshipped God as triune and one.

David also says concerning the Son: “The Lord said unto my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Ps. CIX). If the Lord spoke to the Lord, one was he who spoke and another he to whom he spoke. But God the Father said these things; therefore another was he to whom he spoke. Yet David calls him his Lord; therefore he is either God or an angel. But he is not an angel, for God did not say to an angel, “Sit at my right hand.” Rather, this belongs to the Son, who, being God, sits at the right hand of the Lord—that is, is equal to the Father. For equals customarily sit at the right hands of rulers.

In another Psalm one reads: “The Lord said unto me: Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee” (Ps. II). [Col. 0404C] Most aptly he joined the present to the past. For the present contains newness, the past contains passing-away, and the future contains expectation. Hence we properly say that nothing “was,” except what has ceased to be; nor that anything “is” in the present except what has only recently begun; nor that anything “will be,” except what never was and is not. For example, a wall was white, is now black, and tomorrow will be yellow. Yet by comparison with what endures at the same time as something that has already passed, and still endures with what has now begun, and will endure with what is not but will be, we say that it was, is, and will be—for example, that a man was, is, and will be.

This author did not wish to say, “This day I beget thee,” lest, by joining two marks of the present, he might intimate the newness of the generation. [Col. 0404D] Nor did he say, “Long ago I begot thee,” lest, by joining two marks of pastness, he might intimate the passing-away of the generation. Therefore he said, “This day have I begotten thee,” in order to remove newness by adding the past, and to remove passing-away by adding the present.

Nebuchadnezzar also, though a gentile, said that he saw in the furnace a fourth like the Son of God (Dan. III). And Mercury the philosopher says in the *Asclepius*: “The eternal God makes eternal gods.” What did he understand by “God,” except the Father? What by “eternal gods,” except the Son and the Holy Spirit, who are called gods—that is, divine persons—and are truly eternal? But he used “made” in place of “begot,” slipping in his speech when he said that he made eternal gods.

The same Mercury, in the book entitled *Logostileos*, that is, “the perfect word,” says: “The supreme God made the second God, loved him as his only-begotten Son, and called him the Son of eternal blessing.” [Col. 0405A] How elegantly Hermes Mercury would have spoken had he put “begot” in place of “made.”

Jesus son of Sirach also, who was held in great esteem among the Jews, in his book called the Book of Wisdom, introduces the Son of God speaking thus: “I dwelt in the highest places, and my throne was in a pillar of cloud” (Ecclus. XXIV). And elsewhere: “Before he made anything from the beginning, I was with him, ordering all things” (Prov. VIII). Who speaks here except the Son, who from eternity ordered all things with the Father? And elsewhere he says: “And I was being brought forth” (ibid.). Who was being brought forth before the beginning of the world except the Son of God, whom he begot eternally and without beginning?

The Book of Genesis mentions the Holy Spirit where it says: “The Spirit of God was borne over the waters” (Gen. I). And in the Psalm: “The spirit blew, and the waters flowed” (Ps. CXLVII). And in another Psalm: “Take not thy Holy Spirit from me” (Ps. L). And in Isaiah: “The spirit of the fear of the Lord shall rest upon him” (Isa. XI).

## Chapter IV. The same is proved by arguments

The same may be proved by arguments. What is said concerning numbers must be referred to numbered things, because what is said concerning the properties of subjects must be referred to the subjects themselves. Thus, since arithmetic says that “unity alone, indivisible and simple, is the origin of all plurality,” this seems to be referred to subsisting things. But among creatures no subsisting being is found which is actually and naturally simple and indivisible, and not composed by some kind of composition. Therefore we must find that ineffable simplicity in another subsisting being. It remains, therefore, that it is in the Creator, since it cannot be found in the creature. For, just as every divisible plurality proceeds from indivisible unity, so everything changeable proceeds from the unchangeable Creator, because:

> He himself, remaining stable, gives all things to be moved.

And as the image of Creator and creature appears in unity and number, so too does a likeness of the Trinity. For in the property of unity there appears in some fashion a trace of the Trinity, because, as is read in the arithmetician, unity begets itself. [Col. 0405D] And between the begotten unity and the begetting unity a certain equality is found. In what subsisting being, then, can we find this except in God? For God begets God, not another God distinct from the begetting God; rather, he begot him who is the same God as the begetter. And there is perfect equality between begetter and begotten, or concord, or connection, which is called the Holy Spirit, in whom Father and Son are united. Hence the philosopher says: “The monad begets the monad and reflects its own ardor into itself” (Mercurius Trismegistus). Therefore either you will find in no subsisting being what is said concerning unity, or it is found in the divine unity and Trinity.

Moreover, just as God was wise from eternity, so his wisdom, which proceeds from him, was from eternity. Thus the Father’s Wisdom is born of the Father, and so is the Father’s offspring—therefore, the Father’s Son. [Col. 0406A] For that concept by which God knows both himself and all things created by himself is other than God himself, because it is from him and in him. Since it is not other in substance from him from whom it is, it is called Son by this resemblance: just as in natural generation a son is other than his father in person, though of the same substance, so God and the concept produced from him have one existence, yet another person, because, as we have said, the same thing cannot be from itself.

This, however, differs in the comparison given: in human generation, father and son are one in specific substance, not in individual substance; but God and his concept are one in essence individually.

Thus, therefore, what in theology is called Son because it is from God cannot be personally the same as God. Yet in God there is only one Godhead; therefore there is one essence in those who are personally distinct—or else that concept by which God knows all things is not God from God. But God loves his own concept. And what is the bond and concord of Father and Son except the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from both? Does not the Psalmist speak of this procession when he says: “Send forth thy Spirit, and they shall be created” (Ps. CIII)? For what is that sending forth of the Holy Spirit except the procession of the Holy Spirit from God?

## Chapter V. The same is proved by resemblances

The same is proved by resemblances, for a trace of the Trinity appears in the soul. The human mind remembers itself, loves itself, and understands itself in various ways. If we perceive this, [Col. 0406C] we do not yet perceive the Trinity of the Lord, but we perceive the image of God. For here a certain trinity appears: memory, understanding, and love. Let us therefore treat chiefly these three: memory, understanding, and will. These three are not three lives, but one life; nor three minds, but one mind, one essence.

Memory is spoken of in relation to something; understanding and will, or love, likewise are spoken of in relation to something. But life, mind, and essence are spoken of in themselves. Therefore these three are one insofar as there is one life, one mind, one essence, and whatever else each is called in itself; and they are spoken of together not in the plural, but in the singular. But they are three insofar as they are referred to one another. These three are in the human mind [Col. 0406D] and are one mind; yet understanding is not memory, memory is not will, and will is not understanding or memory.

The same is proved by another resemblance. There are two candles joined together, alike and equal to one another. If they are lit, they have one light; and the light is neither greater nor more the light of one than of the other. Yet the light of three is one and indivisible, just as there are three persons in one Trinity: no person is greater than another, nor is the nature of one greater or other than that of another.

The Father is spiritually called light, the Son radiance, and the Holy Spirit flame. The Father is called light because he shines from himself and not from another, and because from him shines the illuminating light, that is, the Son, and the inflaming light, that is, the Holy Spirit. The Son is called radiance [Col. 0407A] because, just as radiance proceeds from light and radiance, so the Holy Spirit proceeds from Father and Son. And just as flame does three things—it burns, shines, and kindles—so the Holy Spirit burns away vices, makes sins shine forth, and kindles grace.

Likewise, three things are considered in the sun: the substance of the sun, the ray proceeding from the sun, and the heat issuing from both. These three are considered in the sun and are in one substance of the sun: the sun is from none; the ray is born from the sun; heat proceeds from both. Both ray and heat are coeval with the sun. Therefore there are three—sun, ray, and heat—yet they are in one substance. Similarly, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are in one substance of Godhead: the Father from none, the Son from the Father, and the Holy Spirit from both; the Father eternal, the Son and Holy Spirit coeternal [Col. 0407B] with the Father.

## Chapter VI. The opinion of the Jews, who say that the Mosaic Law has not been abolished but must still be observed

They also endeavor to prove that the Mosaic Law has not been abolished but must still be observed, as follows. If the Law is good and given by God, it must be observed; for no decree would otherwise be binding if God’s command were not binding. If Christians exempt one part and say that another must be observed, let them advise us how we may escape that curse: “Cursed is the man who does not remain in all the things written in the Law” (Deut. XXVII). The Lawgiver exempts nothing, but universally commands that all commandments be observed; Christians, however, determine the observance of the Law and commandments according to their own judgment.

## Chapter VII. Determination of the foregoing

To this we first reply that the Law is good and was given by God. Therefore we hold that whatever is written in it, when understood in its divine sense, was observed and is to be observed in its proper times. But those things had to be understood by divine intelligence; if we take them literally, we see many things mutually contradictory.

For when Moses says, “God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good” (Gen. I), why are some things called clean and others unclean in the Law? Taken literally, nothing is unclean, because it is very good. Nor does the Law prohibit only things harmful by their nature for human consumption; it also prohibits things pleasant in taste and equally wholesome to eat. Therefore these things contain some sacramental meaning, and although they are spoken by God, taken literally they disagree utterly with one another.

At the beginning, among other commandments concerning the making of an altar, the Lord commands Moses thus: “You shall make me an altar of earth” (Exod. XX). But later it is read: “Moses therefore made an altar of incense from shittim wood” (Exod. XXXVII). And elsewhere: “He founded bronze bases at the entrance of the tabernacle” (Exod. XXVI and XXVII). It therefore seems greatly contrary that Moses himself should do something other than, and differently from, what the Lord commands through Moses. Thus these things must be understood otherwise than the letter sounds.

Again, how can it stand literally that God forbids: “A man shall not plough with an ox and an ass” (Deut. XXII)? The Law does not forbid you to place upon an ass whatever other burden you please. It does not forbid putting a yoke upon it with an ox, as though this were not permitted; while it permits one to lead ox and ass together to pasture, to be together in pasture, and to feed together, yet forbids and prohibits their ploughing together. If the author forbids this because the animal is said to be unclean, why does the Law not also forbid ploughing an ox with a horse or another unclean animal? We see this inconsistency not only in the commandments mentioned, but also in many other legal ceremonies, unless we understand them in a fitting sense. Therefore they must be understood and examined with discriminating and divine understanding.

But if we receive the Law in its due sense, we can observe all its commandments with due observance: understanding some as spoken literally and without any veil of figures, and others as belonging to figure and shadowed under a profound veil; understanding some as commanded to be observed for a time, and others without any determination of time. For those things which were foreannouncements of a sacrament and acknowledged the figure of truth had, in their own time, to lose their foreannouncement and figure when the reality and truth itself became present. For just as, in our own manner of speech, we use changes of verbal tense—saying “it will be” as long as the thing that will be remains future; then, when it is present, omitting that expression altogether and using “it is”; and, when we signify that it has now passed, using “it was”—so, in things foretelling some sacrament, when the sacrament itself is made present, its figure or sign would thereafter be preserved superfluously.

Those things which were not signs of some mystery, but either intimate the truth of faith or commend the edification of charity, are to be observed by Jews and Christians not temporarily but forever; and their transgression can in no way fail to be evil.

## Chapter VIII. The opinion of the Jews, who say that divine ordinances given then must not be changed

Again, the Jews object as follows. If God’s word is to be observed for a time, and, after that word has been annulled, another is to be observed at another time, then divine ordinances are changed through changes of time. How then will this statement stand firm: “For ever, O Lord, thy word remains” (Ps. CXVIII)? And this: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Mark XIII; Matt. XXIV)?

What difference is there, moreover, as to why God judges one animal unclean and another clean, permits the use of this one and forbids the use of that one? “For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor?” (Isa. XL), that he should permit one thing to be done and forbid another? Commands must be obeyed, and obedience to him is the highest virtue. He forbade it to be done; therefore it is not permitted; and if it is done later, it is a sin and deserving of the punishment due to it. Therefore, let us preserve the letter and disregard the figures; let us preserve the letter in order to preserve the other. What reason, then, is there for condemning the other? Let us therefore preserve the letter and preserve the figure of the letter as well. Let the letter remain for our limited understanding, and let there remain—and be added—the spiritual understanding of the hidden mystery, if God has granted it to us. Let us abstain from pork because the Law commands it (Lev. XI), and let us abstain also from whatever sin is signified by the pig. Let us not plough with ox and ass because the Lawgiver forbade it; and if we have understood something through the pairing of ass and ox, it is lawful to avoid it—indeed, it is sinful not to avoid it. So too with the rest. Thus the Law is considered to be fulfilled, and is fulfilled.

## Chapter IX. Resolution of the foregoing

[Col. 0409B] To this we say that the divine word is by no means annulled and that divine ordinances are not changed, because Christ did not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it (Matt. V). Hence he himself says: “Amen I say unto you, not one iota or one stroke shall pass from the Law until all things are accomplished” (ibid.). Therefore he does not wish to abolish it, but to fulfill it. The Law forbids homicide; Christ forbids anger and hatred. The Law forbids adultery of the flesh; Christ forbids even the desire of the heart.

The Law forbids us to use pork, and that abstinence was then necessary for us, since it was a figure of truth to come; and the figure had to be observed until the truth itself was present. But now it is not necessary for us, when the truth itself, of which it was a figure, is already present. Nevertheless, abstinence is permitted, and many of our people abstain [Col. 0409C] not only from it but from all flesh; and every one of us supports his own position before one and the same judge.

Moses called swine flesh unclean (Lev. XI), forbade its use, and therefore you say that it is not lawful to use it. But the same Moses, not another, calls swine flesh clean and very good; he writes that God made it good for eating just like all other things, and therefore we say that it is lawful to use it. For after he declared that God made all things—the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, and every animal of the earth in which there is a living soul—not far below he added: “God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good” (Gen. I). What is very good is evil in no respect; but what is evil in no respect, how is it evil and unclean? Therefore whatever is in swine flesh is not evil or unclean, but clean and very good, and may be used.

But because pleasure and impurity are figured by this animal, it is judged unclean on account of that which the animal signifies, and it is not lawful to participate in that impurity. Therefore, if the animal is understood to be both clean and unclean, both use and non-use of it are permitted to us.

For the same reason one may plough with an ass, and yet it is forbidden that we plough with ox and ass together. Therefore whoever tills the land may plough with ox and ass, if he cannot do better, because God permits this, he who created all these things for human use. But the ox, which divides the hoof and chews the cud, being altogether suitable for tilling the soil, signifies the discerning ruler of the Church, who has understanding in what he does and meditates upon God’s commandments, chewing them over within himself day and night, useful not only to himself but also to others. [Col. 0410A] No other person, undiscerning in morals, unlearned in understanding, and ignorant of letters, should be joined with him; for such a person is not only useless in speech but harmful to others by his corrupt example.

## Chapter X. By what authorities and arguments it is proved that the Law, as to the letter, is dead

That the Old Law has fallen into disuse may be proved by authorities and arguments. For the Lord says through the prophet: “I will complete a new covenant upon the house of Judah and upon the house of Israel” (Baruch II). What did he call the new covenant except the evangelical law? When it comes, the old is said to cease, because both cannot be observed together: when truth arrives, the shadow is said to cease.

Again David says in the Psalm: “For if thou hadst desired sacrifice, I would indeed have given it; thou wilt not delight in burnt offerings” (Ps. L). And Isaiah: “My soul has hated your sacrifices” (Isa. I). Again: “Sacrifice and oblation thou didst not desire, but thou hast perfected ears for me. Thou hast not required burnt offering and sacrifice for sin,” etc. (Ps. XXXIX). And elsewhere: “I will not rebuke thee because of thy sacrifices; thy burnt offerings,” etc. (Ps. XLIX). “I will not take calves from thy house, nor he-goats from thy flocks” (ibid.).

We also see that among the Jews a great part of what pertains to the Law has ceased. For among the Jews there is neither sacrifice nor victim, no prophet, no law, no priest, no temple, no place of sacrifice; and why need one go through each point? The Law has been abolished in very great part. Therefore it appears that the Law has no place.

In *Sehale* [reading uncertain], Elijah also says that the world will endure for six thousand years: two thousand years were of vanity, referring to the time before the Mosaic Law; two thousand of the Mosaic Law; and the following two thousand, of the Messiah. But it is manifest that more than four thousand years have passed. Therefore it is manifest that the Law has passed away and the Messiah has come.

## Chapter XI. By what arguments the Jews maintain that the Messiah has not come

The Jews also prove that the Messiah has not come as follows. Isaiah says: “In the last days, the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the summit of the mountains, and all nations shall flow to it. Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob” (Isa. II). But if Christ has already come, where throughout the whole world—except, it is said, among the poor Jewish people—does anyone say, “Let us go up to the mountain of the God of Jacob”? For some say, “Let us go to the house of Peter”; others, “to the house of Paul”; still others, “to the house of Martin”; but by no means, “to the house of the God of Jacob.”

Let Christians hear further matters concerning Christ’s coming: “They shall beat their swords into ploughshares, and their spears into sickles; nation shall not lift up sword against nation, nor shall they be exercised any more for war” (ibid.). Has the military order now beaten its swords into ploughshares [Col. 0411A] and its spears into sickles? Smiths scarcely suffice; iron scarcely suffices for making military weapons. Where on earth can one find the condition, “Nation shall not lift up sword against nation”? Nation fights against nation with forces poured out; kingdom rises against kingdom; from childhood itself everyone is trained for war. It is therefore clear that Christians believe about Christ and his coming something far different from what is true.

## Chapter XII. The Christians’ resolution

In reply, we say that those last days have now come, in which the mountain of the Lord was prepared on the summit of the mountains (Isa. II). That mountain is Christ, in whom all the ends of the earth now believe; all the families of the nations now worship in his presence and say with one harmonious voice: “Let us go to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob” (ibid.), that is, to the house of the God whom Jacob worshipped, whom Aaron worshipped. Thus it is shown that there is one God both of the faithful who were before the Law, of those who lived under the Law, and of those who now believe in God.

As for their objection against us because we say, “Let us go to the house of Peter,” “to the house of Paul,” or “to the house of Martin”: no one of sound mind understands these words in that sense. For we make no house for Peter or Paul; rather, in honor and memory of Peter or Paul, we dedicate it to God. Nor is it lawful for any bishop to say in the consecration of churches, “To thee, Peter,” or “to thee, Paul, we consecrate this house”; rather, it is said to be consecrated to God. And although all churches are consecrated to God, yet there is one house of God, one Church of God, which is the gathering of all the faithful.

[Col. 0411C] Whoever belongs to the unity of the Church approaches this house of God. In this house of God the mountain of mountains and Christ, the Holy of holies, is worshipped. Here sins are forgiven. Not only is homicide forbidden, but anger and hatred are removed; use of sword and spear is not permitted, because whoever renounces anger and hatred is rightly bound to renounce spear and sword. For it is far easier to beat one’s sword into a ploughshare and one’s spear into a sickle than, once the proud heart has been humbled by fear, to become humble from proud, a servant from free; to renounce wife, house, children, fields, arms, horses, and all one possesses, and moreover to deny oneself.

In this house of God is fulfilled what Isaiah says: “Calf, lion, and sheep shall dwell together, and a little child shall lead them” (ibid.). The little child leads lion and bear together with lamb when, in the house of God, the shepherd—that is, the prelate—commands noble and ignoble, powerful and powerless, strong and weak: a child little not in understanding, but in malice.

That Christ has already come is proved by various authorities. Jacob says: “The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a leader from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent; and he shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX).

The sense is that the kings or leaders of the Israelite people, descended from the tribe of Judah [Col. 0412A], would endure until the coming of Christ, who is the expectation of the nations. There were kings in Israel from the tribe of Judah, from David to Josiah, and afterwards leaders until the Nativity; but at the time of Christ’s birth the foreigner Herod reigned, and thereafter the Jews had neither leader nor king from the tribe of Judah. Therefore the Messiah has come.

The same is clearly shown from the words of Daniel. For in that chapter Gabriel is introduced speaking to Daniel in this manner: “Seventy weeks have been shortened concerning your people and your holy city, that transgression may be brought to completion, sin may receive its end, iniquity may be erased, everlasting righteousness may be brought in, vision and [Col. 0412B] prophecy may be fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies may be anointed. Know and observe: from the issuing of the word for Jerusalem to be rebuilt again, until Christ the leader, there shall be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks” (Dan. 9). By these words the angel signifies Christ’s incarnation: he fulfilled the Law and the Prophets, took away sins, brought in righteousness, and was anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions (Ps. 44). He sets forth weeks not of days but of years, so that one week is seven years. He calls them shortened, moreover, so that we may understand lunar years, which are shorter than solar years by eleven days. Thus seventy weeks of solar years make four hundred and seventy-five years. And indeed, from the issuing of the word that [Col. 0412C] Jerusalem should be rebuilt until Christ the leader, four hundred and ninety lunar years elapsed. They are counted from the twentieth year of Artaxerxes, in which Nehemiah, his cupbearer, obtained from him permission for Jerusalem’s walls to be restored, and restored them amid great distress. From that permission received from the king, I say, until Christ’s Passion, four hundred and ninety lunar years elapsed; and this total of years is calculated according to the years of the successive kings, down to the eighteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, and immediately thereafter came desolation (Dan. 9).

Daniel briefly interposes a reference to the rebuilding accomplished through Nehemiah, saying, “The street and the walls shall be rebuilt again in the distress of times” (ibid.). Of the seventy weeks Daniel reserved the last one, saying: “He shall confirm the covenant for one week” [Col. 0412D] (ibid.). This must be understood of the three and a half years during which Christ preached and confirmed what he had promised to the fathers. For the final three and a half years of that one week had already elapsed when the Lord was baptized; and in the remaining half of that same week, near its end, “sacrifice and offering shall fail” (ibid.). That is, when the truth comes, the shadows will cease, and in the Temple there shall be “the abomination of desolation” (ibid.); that is, sacrifices will be abominable and destined for desolation after Christ’s death, and this desolation shall endure until the end of the world (ibid.).

Above, Daniel set forth the time of Christ’s death, saying: “And after seventy-two weeks”—understand, together with the seventh and final week, which we have divided into two parts—“Christ shall be slain, and there shall not be [Col. 0413A] a people who will deny him” (Dan. 9). For they said: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 15 [sic]). And elsewhere: “We do not know where he is from.” But what follows—“And the people shall destroy the city and the sanctuary of God” (Dan. 9)—does not belong to the seventy weeks. Rather, the prophet foretold at the time of Christ’s coming and death what would happen to the people who refused to receive him, saying: “The Roman people, with its coming leader, shall destroy the city and the sanctuary; the end shall be devastation, and after the end of the war, desolation decreed by God for ever.” From these things it is evident that Christ has already come.

I also ask the Jews for what sin they have been placed in such misery and held in such prolonged captivity. For in former times their captivity is read to have been extended either for [Col. 0413B] seventy years or a little longer, as their sins required; but, led to repentance, they were freed from captivity. Yet after Christ’s Passion they have been continually held captive, now for a thousand years and more. For what sins are they held in such protracted captivity, when they now do not transgress the legal observances as they once transgressed them, and are never read to have kept the Law better than they observe it now? It remains, therefore, that they are now punished for the sin which they committed against Christ.

## Chapter XIII. By what authorities the Jews prove that Christ will not be God

[Col. 0413C] The Jews also attempt to prove by authorities that Christ will not be God, as follows: “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain” (Exod. 20). He takes God’s name in vain who attributes to a human being the name and worship of divinity. For if “every human being is vanity” (Ps. 38), whoever believes a human being to be God and calls him God attributes to a human being the name and worship of divinity. Likewise, it is written in the Law: “Whoever makes himself God shall be put to death” (Deut. 13). Therefore no human being is God.

Further, if with God there is no change, nor shadow of turning (Jas. 1), how can so great an alteration of things occur in him, that God should become human, the Creator a creature, and the incorruptible be believed to have become subject to corruption? How is this understood: “In the beginning, Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands; [Col. 0413D] they shall perish, but you remain, and all shall grow old like a garment; but you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Ps. 101). How is God himself the same if, having been changed, he can become human? If God is immeasurable, how could he be measured and circumscribed within the small division of human limbs? If God is immeasurable and uncircumscribed, by what reasoning is it said that, wholly enclosed by bodily dimension, he could be held within the narrow single womb of his Mother? Again, if God is that than which nothing greater or more sufficient can be conceived, by what necessity was he compelled to become a participant in human misery and a sharer in such great evils? Finally, if God became human, how can what he himself said to Moses stand: “No human being shall see me and live” (Exod. 33)? It seems greatly contradictory that God should have become human and yet could not be seen by a human being, even by his own mother. For far be it from us to believe that anything phantom-like existed with respect to God!

## Chapter XIV. The Christians’ answer

To these points we say that the greatest necessity caused God to become human and to redeem us through the mystery of his humanity. For it was reasonable that, just as the human race had perished through the sin of a human being, so it should be restored to life through a human being. But a mere human being could not redeem the human race, as was said above, because a good work does not belong to a human being but to God; for the good done in a human being is from [Col. 0414B] God, not from the human being. Therefore, in order to perform good from himself, he had to be of divine nature. Thus, because God was human, he could perform a good work, not only by action but also by authority, by which he could redeem the human race.

Therefore he became human, not ceasing to be what he was, but assuming what he was not. We say that he became human not by a conversion of divinity into flesh, but by an assumption of humanity into God. Just as a rational soul and flesh, because of the unity of person, are one human being, although the soul is of one nature and the flesh of another—nor is the soul changed into flesh, nor flesh into soul, but, both natures remaining, the unity of person is preserved—so God and human being, through the unity [Col. 0414C] of person, are one Christ. God was not converted into a human being, nor a human being into God; rather, the nature of God and human being is divided, while the person of God and human being is undivided, and its unity is preserved and adored.

For not everything that is in some manner made other than it was ceases to be what it was. In the alteration of certain accidents, when a black person becomes white or a white person black, one quality wholly perishes upon the arrival of the other. And when an unarmed person becomes armed, or a naked person clothed, or a clothed person naked, the person so altered receives or loses nothing whatever in himself. Therefore God assumed a human being into the unity of person, through his own uncreated goodness, not ours, out of great necessity—not his, but ours. Therefore God is immutable insofar as he is God, mutable insofar as he is human; uncircumscribed in divinity, circumscribed in humanity; invisible insofar as he is divine, visible insofar as he is human.

Thus God’s name is not taken in vain, because Christ is not merely human but God, to whom the name and worship of divinity are ascribed. Nor is he a recent or newly made God, since he is eternal God and God from eternity; nor did he make himself God, because he is God substantially. For the one who makes himself God is the one who pretends to be God when he is not. Nor is he an alien God who truly is God; but the gods of the nations, falsely called gods, are termed alien gods.

## Chapter XV. By what authorities Christ is proved to be God

Many authorities prove that Christ is God. [Col. 0415A] Jeremiah says: “This is our God, and no other shall be accounted before him. He discovered every way of instruction and gave it to Jacob his servant and Israel his beloved; he was seen upon earth and conversed with human beings” (Bar. 3). Likewise Micah says: “And you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, are by no means least among the thousands of Judah; for from you shall come forth the leader who shall rule my people Israel, and his going forth is from the beginning, from days of eternity” (Mic. 5). Amos says of the same: “Prepare, Israel, to meet the Lord your God” (Amos 4). Elsewhere Isaiah says of the same: “And his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isa. 9). And elsewhere: “Indeed, because of the crime of my people I struck him” (ibid.); not because of his own crime—as though the Father said: “I allowed [Col. 0415B] Christ to suffer, not for his own sin, but out of love for the people”—for, as Isaiah testifies, “He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth” (ibid.; 1 Pet. 2).

Therefore, if what blessed Job testifies is true [Note: [Col. 0415] Job 14, according to the version of the Septuagint. See Cyprian, Sermon 1 Against the Jews, and St Leo, Sermon On the Nativity.]: “There is no human being who does not sin, nor an infant whose life upon earth is one day old”; if what David testifies is true, “Every human being is a liar” (Ps. 115), and elsewhere, “No living human being shall be justified in his sight” (Ps. 142), then he who committed no sin is more than human. Christ was called Emmanuel, that is, “God with us”: God remaining in our nature.

## Chapter XVI. By what authorities they maintain that Christ was not conceived of a Virgin

[Col. 0415C] Those already mentioned also attempt to maintain that Christ was not conceived of a Virgin. For the authority says: “Drop down dew, heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down the Just One; let the earth be opened and bring forth the Saviour” (Isa. 45). What is signified by the earth except Mary, Christ’s mother? What is this opening of the earth except Mary’s defloration? In Ezekiel likewise it is read that the closed gate shall be opened for the prince (Ezek. 44). What is understood by the prince except Christ, Joseph’s son? And concerning Christ himself, his mother says: “Your father and I have been seeking you in sorrow” (Luke 2). Further, how can anyone conceive or give birth unless she has known a man? But where Christians say, “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isa. 7), the Hebrew text does not have “virgin” [Col. 0415D] but rather “hidden” or “concealed woman.”

## Chapter XVII. The Christians’ answer to the foregoing

In reply to these authorities, we say that “opening” does not mean defloration or the foulness of lust, but the fruitfulness of conception. She is said to have been opened with respect to Christ’s entrance—not opened by a man, but as a glass window is said to be opened to a ray of the sun, not through breaking or any division, but because the ray enters it in accordance with the subtlety of its nature. In this way—indeed, in a still more subtle way—the closed gate is said to have been opened for the prince, because Christ entered the Virgin’s womb, closed by virginity, [Col. 0416A] in an ineffable manner.

Christ is called Joseph’s son (Luke 3) with respect to human opinion and upbringing. In this sense, those who nourish others are called their fathers. It is true that, under the law of nature, no woman can conceive or give birth without knowing a man; but in miracles the law of nature is not to be sought. As for what the Jews deny to be written in Isaiah—“Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear,” and so forth—the Septuagint translators, men approved in faith and learning, translated it thus; and the prophet himself intended it to be translated thus when he said and wrote, “Behold, the hidden woman,” they say, “shall conceive and bear a son.” But if “hidden” is understood in the ordinary sense merely as shut up at home, what is wonderful or new in her conception? [Col. 0416B] Yet he intended it as the sign of that mystery when he said: “Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign: behold, the hidden woman shall conceive,” and so forth. Unless these words are understood more subtly, they must be regarded as uttered by the prophet in an altogether childish and empty sense. Since it is absurd to believe or say this, the meaning is: “hidden,” that is, kept from male love and every contagion of sin, shall conceive. Moreover, in the Syriac idiom, which is akin to Hebrew, *alma* means “virgin”; and where we have “virgin,” the Hebrew has *alma*.

## Chapter XVIII. By what authorities and reasons it is proved that the Blessed Virgin, remaining untouched, conceived Christ

That the glorious Virgin conceived while remaining a virgin, and without male seed, is indicated by manifold authority [Col. 0416C] and manifold reasoning. In Ezekiel it is read: “And the Lord said to me: This gate shall be closed and shall not be opened, and no man shall enter through it, because the Lord alone has entered through it; and it shall be closed for the prince. The prince himself shall sit in it, to eat bread before the Lord; he shall enter by way of the vestibule of the gate, and go out by its way” (Ezek. 44).

No one can fulfil this literally. For the Lord God, speaking through the prophet, says: “Heaven is my throne, but the earth the footstool of my feet” (Isa. 66). And elsewhere: “I shall fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23). If, I say, the Lord God of Israel is wholly everywhere, whence did he enter through that gate, and whither did he enter, if God is uncircumscribed? How ought one literally to understand that he sits in the gate? How shall it be closed to the prince, if the prince himself, the Lord God of Israel, entered through it and shall sit in it to eat bread before the Lord? What bread, or what kind of bread? From where was it made or brought? Shall the Lord God of Israel eat, and eat bread before the Lord? Who is this other Lord before whom the Lord God of Israel eats?

Since, therefore, these things cannot be understood literally, something else must be understood by the gate, so that all things may be considered and, once considered, may appear possible. The Lord God of Israel entered through that gate and came forth to us, because God became human in the Virgin’s womb from the Virgin’s flesh [Col. 0417A] (otherwise he would not be immune from original sin). As the Psalm says, “Like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber” (Ps. 18), he came forth to us as a human being; and, as Jeremiah testifies, “He was seen upon earth and conversed with human beings” (Bar. 3).

This gate shall be closed because it shall be closed to a man, and no man shall pass through it. It shall be reserved closed for the prince, so that he may enter through it, because the Lord God of Israel entered through it. For before conception and birth his mother had not known a man, since the gate was to be closed and no man was to pass through it; nor after Christ’s conception and birth did his mother know a man, because it was to be closed and preserved closed for the prince. For this whole mystery of the Lord’s incarnation was accomplished by divine power alone, without [Col. 0417B] human contamination.

What Isaiah says, “Drop down dew, heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down the Just One” (Isa. 45), means: by heavenly dew and cloud, that is, by God’s creation and operation alone, as he adds shortly afterwards: “I, the Lord, created him” (Isa. 46 [sic]). The earth was opened, that is, the Virgin’s womb, and brought forth the Saviour. “The prince himself shall sit in it,” because in that humanity too which Christ assumed for us, he received all things as subject to himself. Likewise Isaiah says: “Who shall recount his generation?” (Ps. 50 [sic]). If Christ was born by the same law of birth as another human being, why is his generation called unutterable? Therefore, because it is called unutterable, we understand that there was another mode of birth in Christ, according to which he was conceived without male seed, through the operation of the Holy Spirit. Thus his mother, remaining a virgin for Christ, conceived Christ.

Likewise, if Christ was conceived from male seed and conceived from the seeds of father and mother, then he was conceived in the itching of lust and thus born in sin, because everyone born in concupiscence is liable to sin. Hence David, speaking in the person of the human race, says: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother conceived me in sins” (Exod. 48 [sic]). And it was commanded in the Law that a boy should be circumcised on the eighth day, so that he might be freed from original sin. Hence it is written in the Law: “The man who has not been circumcised on the eighth day shall perish from his people” (Lev. 12), understand, eternally. And another authority says that an infant one day [Col. 0417D] old is not without sin (Job 14 according to the Septuagint).

But if Christ had been conceived in iniquities like any other person, and if his mother had borne him in sins, in what would he differ from another? How would he alone be free among the dead? How would his generation be called unutterable? But Isaiah marvelled at his generation and called it unutterable precisely because his mother neither conceived him in iniquity nor bore him in sins. Therefore he alone was free among the dead (Ps. 87); therefore, because he was conceived without sin, he was conceived without male seed; and thus his mother conceived him without sin. Therefore, since she did not know a man in conceiving, she remained a virgin in conceiving. And because Christ was without sin, he could free humanity from sin. And because every [Col. 0418A] human being was liable to original sin and, by God’s profound decree because of the transgression of the first parent, the soul descended after death to hell, it was fitting that the human race should be freed from hell through Christ and return to heaven through Christ.

## 278 bis. Chapter XIX. By what authorities it is proved that all descended to hell before Christ’s coming, and that, in order to restore the human race, it was necessary for God to assume humanity and subject himself to death

That all souls descended to hell before Christ’s coming is proved by manifold authority. Jacob says: “I shall descend to hell mourning for my son” (Gen. 37). And elsewhere he says to his sons: “You shall bring down my grey hairs with sorrow to hell” [Col. 0418B] (Gen. 42). Hence blessed Job, of whom, by the Lord’s testimony, there was no man like him on earth (Job 2), says: “Hell is my house, and in darkness I have spread my bed” (Job 17). Yet, raised up by the hope of deliverance, he adds shortly afterward: “I know that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth, and in my flesh I shall see God my Saviour” (Job 19).

He who testifies that he has a Redeemer does not deny that he has been sold or made captive and redeemed. Hear also blessed David: “God will redeem my soul from the hand of hell when he receives me” (Ps. 48); he says that the soul, once received from hell, is to be redeemed from hell. Hence elsewhere, rejoicing, he says: “Lord, you brought my soul out of hell; you saved me from those descending into the pit” (Ps. 9 [sic]). To whom does he say, “You brought me out, you healed me,” except to him of whom he says in another psalm: “Make a way for him who ascends above the setting; the Lord is his name” (Ps. 97 [sic])? And because he did not wish to ascend above the setting alone, hear what follows: “You ascended on high, you took captivity captive, you gave gifts to human beings” (ibid.).

Hezekiah also, when about to die, says: “I said: In the middle of my days I shall go to the gates of hell” (Isa. 38). And afterwards he adds: “But you have rescued my soul so that it should not perish” (ibid.). This, I say, was the hope of the righteous when they died then. Therefore no one ascended to heaven, but all who then died descended to hell. So that humanity might not perish eternally, it was necessary that humanity be restored. But it could not be restored [Col. 0418D] unless God assumed humanity, underwent our necessity, became our advocate against the adversary, and, conducting the business of our case by pleading and overthrowing the adversary by the judgment of just reason, brought our cause to its conclusion.

Humanity, then, had to be restored to God, and through a human being, since through a human being it had taken itself away from God. But who could restore it from the common mass? For scarcely does each person’s righteousness suffice for himself, much less for his neighbour; an infant whose life upon earth is one day old is not free from sin (Job 14, according to the Septuagint). If a new human being, or one born from elsewhere, or an angel made human, were to liberate humanity, humanity could not thereby be restored to its former state of inborn dignity; for humanity had been created equal with the angels, not in nature, but in reason and in the grace of freedom granted to it. Therefore, because humanity was bound to God the Creator alone, it could not be restored to that same state of freedom either through a human being or through an angel. For one who is redeemed from slavery by someone is judged to be bound to serve that person.

Since humanity’s full restoration could not occur through another, it was necessary that the Creator aid the creature, that the Creator undergo the creature, so that, restored through the Creator himself, humanity might be bound to serve the Creator alone and the enemy might lose jurisdiction over the human race. Therefore the enemy found nothing of his own in Christ, who was neither conceived in iniquities nor born in sins, nor had incurred any stain of sin whatever in his life. Since, then, death’s seizure of him in whom it found nothing and over whom it had no right at all was an unjust presumption, it rightly lost the jurisdiction which it had obtained over the first human being and his posterity through the first parent’s sin.

Christ’s death, therefore, was an offering and propitiation before the Father for original sin. First, it brought about the full and complete restoration of the human race: at his death the entrance to Paradise was opened, and that flaming, turning sword was removed, when, dying and fastened upon the gibbet of the cross, he said to the thief: “Today you shall be with me in Paradise” (Luke 23). Then too was fulfilled what was said in Hosea: “O death, I shall be your death; I shall be your bite, O hell” (Hos. 13).

Therefore we had the mystery of that restoration of ours promised in the prophets: sometimes through figures of things, sometimes through riddles of words, sometimes by clear and open promise. In those earliest times, God speaking to Abraham about this mystery said: “In your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 26). For surely the whole human race, oppressed under the curse of the first parent, is freed through him from that curse and restored to its former blessing and grace. For in Isaac no nation was blessed, nor is any nation read to have been subject to his rule. But in David and Solomon, who proved stronger and more powerful than the kings of that land, how should the nations be blessed, when all the neighbouring nations except the Jewish nation were hostile to them and continually fought against them? Any mention of their successors, expelled from their kingdom, taken captive, and disinherited, would be pointless. It remains that these things be understood in Christ and, once understood, be fulfilled in every way. Elsewhere also the authority says: “You who brought out the bound from the pit in which there was no water.”

## Chapter XX. By what authorities it is proved that Christ suffered in order to free us and blot out our sins

That Christ suffered in order to free us and blot out our sins is affirmed by many authorities. For it is read in the Psalm: “The Lord has reigned from the wood” (Ps. 95). This wood is called the Lord’s cross, through which Christ reigned in us [Col. 0420A] by grace.

Isaiah also says: “And he shall rise like a shoot before him, and like a root from thirsty earth; and he has no beauty, so that we did not esteem him. Truly he bore our infirmities, and he carried our pains; for he was wounded for our offences, bruised for our crimes; the chastisement of our peace was upon him; by his bruise we have all been healed. We wandered like sheep; each one of us turned aside into his own way; and the Lord placed upon him the iniquity of us all. He was offered because he himself willed it, and he did not open his mouth. He was taken away from distress and from judgment. Who shall recount his generation? Therefore he shall give the wicked for burial, and the rich for his death, because he committed no iniquity, nor was deceit found in his mouth; and his will shall be directed in the hand of the Lord” (Isa. 53).

All this is referred to Christ. Christ rose like a shoot when he advanced in age and wisdom before God and human beings (Luke 2). “Truly he bore our infirmities,” that is, he removed them; “and he carried our pains,” that is, he bore them away. For he was wounded for our offences and bruised for our crimes. And because he endured all these things voluntarily and not under compulsion, the text adds: “He was offered because he himself willed it, and he did not open his mouth.” This seems to concern his assumption of humanity; the remaining statements exceed humanity and belong to God alone: “He was taken away from distress and from judgment,” because, having died, he could not be held by death; and his generation is unutterable. For who can recount how God begets from himself before time, and eternally, a Son consubstantial with himself? Or who can recount how, at times predetermined, a human being was created from a mother without male seed, and God assumed him into the unity of person? “Indeed, because of the crime,” not his own but “of my people, I struck him.” For what crime did he commit who committed no sin, nor had deceit found in his mouth? And the Psalm reads: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones” (Ps. 21).

## Chapter XXI. By what authorities it is proved that Christ truly rose from the dead and ascended into heaven

We also have many testimonies in Holy Scripture concerning Christ’s resurrection. Hosea says: “In two days he shall revive us, and after two days he shall raise us” (Hos. 6). What clearer testimony is there concerning Christ’s Passion and death and resurrection? Likewise, in the Psalm the Son is introduced speaking to his flesh: “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp,” etc. (Ps. 56). Christ calls his human nature his glory, since in it he was glorified and performed glorious deeds. He calls it the psaltery with respect to the glorification and ascension of the flesh, because the psaltery gives sound from above. He calls it the harp because of the sufferings endured by Christ’s human nature, because the harp gives sound from within. And in the Psalm Christ says: “For you will not allow your Holy One to see corruption” (Ps. 15). Elsewhere: “And [Col. 0421A] my flesh blossomed again” (Ps. 27).

Of his ascension it is read: “He ascended on high; he led captivity captive” (Eph. 4). This indicates that Christ ascended into heaven and took with him the souls of the saints, who had previously been held captive in hell. Elsewhere concerning the same ascension of Christ it is read: “His going forth is from the highest heaven, and his course unto its highest point” (Ps. 18). And in Isaiah’s dialogue, where angels are introduced marveling at Christ’s ascension: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah?” (Isa. 63). And in the Psalm: “Who is this King of glory? The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Ps. 23). Let these statements suffice against Jewish errors.

## Book Four. Against Pagans or Mohammedans

[Col. 0421]

## 278 ter. Chapter I. By what authorities and reasons pagans, or Mohammedans, say that Christ was conceived from the common breath of God

[Col. 0421B]

Let us now turn the course of our pen against the disciples of Mohammed. Mohammed’s monstrous life, more monstrous sect, and most monstrous end are plainly found in accounts of his deeds. Inspired by an evil spirit, he devised an abominable sect, suited to carnal pleasures. Therefore many carnal people, enticed by his sect and cast down through the various beginnings of errors, have perished miserably and are perishing; people whom the common populace calls Saracens or pagans. They agree with Christians in affirming one God, Creator of all things; [Col. 0421C] yet they agree with the Jews in denying the Trinity within the divine unity. To refute them, what we have said against the Jews concerning unity and Trinity is sufficient.

They do not agree in everything with the Mosaic Law, but according to their own inclination select certain things from both sides and maintain that these must be observed, being led not by reason but by will. They maintain that Christ was born from a Virgin, that Mary remained a Virgin, and that Christ was conceived from the Spirit of God—that is, from God’s breath. But by the Spirit of God they do not understand the third person in the Trinity, but rather a natural breath, such as we find in a human being and every other living creature. They also say that God breathed into the Blessed Virgin, and that the Virgin thus conceived from that [Col. 0421D] breath. They seek to prove this by authority and reason.

For the authority says: “His Spirit shall blow, and the waters shall flow” (Ps. 147). They call this spirit God’s natural breath. And in Genesis it is read: “He breathed into his face the breath of life” (Gen. 2). They understand this as follows: God breathed or blew with his breath into Adam’s body, and thus a spirit was created in Adam by that divine breath. They understand the same breath in what is read in the Gospel: “Christ breathed upon his disciples and said: Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20). They also understand the same thing in what Gabriel says to Mary: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you” (Luke 1), and in the statement that Christ was conceived of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0422B] from the Virgin Mary.

They also seek to establish the same point by reason. The Virgin Mary did not bear Christ by herself—without anything else intervening—nor conceive him from male seed, nor from the divine substance; therefore, she conceived him from some intermediary between rational creature and God. But what is this intermediary above humanity and below God, if not the divine breath, by which the Virgin Mary, having been breathed upon, gave birth? If a material breath impregnates the earth and causes it to germinate, what wonder is it if the divine breath made Mary fruitful?

## Chapter II. The Christians’ answer to the foregoing.

We reply that those who attempt to maintain these assertions are in need of sense and punishment. For the divine breath is not material, because it exists in an incorporeal substance [Col. 0422C] and has none of the instruments of breathing, such as a throat, and so forth. For if it were bodily, it would be changeable and would not be uncircumscribed in every place. That it is incorporeal needs no proof, since every kind of reasoning, human as well as divine, affirms this beyond dispute. Therefore the breath of God, or Spirit of God, is called the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and the Son, of whom it is said in Genesis: “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters” (Gen. I); and: “The Spirit of Christ breathes where he wills” (Rom. VIII). If the Holy Spirit is the will of the mind, he is rational and is not a material breath. Likewise the Apostle says that the Spirit—that is, the Holy Spirit—intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings (ibid.). Christ also says: “Go, preach [Col. 0422D] the Gospel to every creature, baptizing in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII). This Spirit of God is compared with the Father and the Son, and thus is one person in the Trinity. Of this Spirit it is said: “His spirit will blow, and the waters will flow” (Ps. CXLVII). For when the Holy Spirit is breathed into sinners by grace—sinners who are called waters because of the flowing course of their sins—the waters flow; that is, sinners are converted, flowing in streams of tears through the lament of repentance.

That the Lord is said to have breathed the breath of life into Adam’s body is to be understood thus: in creating the human spirit, he infused it into the human body. By Christ’s bodily breathing upon the apostles, it was signified that he infused into them the grace of the Holy [Col. 0423A] Spirit. The Holy Spirit came upon the glorious Virgin because he infused his grace into her. For the same reason she is said to have conceived by the Holy Spirit—that is, through the work of the Holy Spirit, not from his substance. For the Virgin herself, by God’s authority alone, conceived Christ from her own flesh, without mixture of any other thing.

Nor, as has already been said, is any other material breath to be understood as proceeding from God and exceeding rational creation. For if another material breath proceeded from God, it would either be of the same nature as God or not. If it were of the same nature, then it would be God, and thus the Virgin conceived from the divine nature—an assertion horrible both to utter and to conceive. If that breath is not of the divine nature, the question is: of what nature is it? If it is of an incorporeal [Col. 0423B] and non-divine nature, it is an angel or a soul, since it is a spirit; and thus the Blessed Virgin conceived from an angel or from a soul. If it is bodily, it appears to be nothing other than air; and so the consequence is absurd, namely that we should say the Blessed Virgin conceived from air.

It is also asked whether that conception took place from breath alone. If Christ was made from breath alone, either that breath itself became a human being, or it was the soul of Christ, or it was the unity of Christ’s soul. If it was united to Christ’s soul, it appears to have been physical. Moreover, was the body Christ had from the Virgin’s flesh or not? If it was not from the Virgin’s flesh, he was not the Virgin’s Son. Whence, then, did it derive its origin? If it derived it from the Virgin, that breath was united to the flesh, so that conception might arise from those two things, and the flesh might be animated by that breath, [Col. 0423C] in order that Christ should become man.

The enemies of truth further object to us in this manner: How was Christ the Son of God, if he was not conceived from the divine substance or from God’s breath?

To this we say that Christ, according to his human nature, was the Son of the Virgin; according to his divine nature, the Son of God, begotten from eternity by the Father according to divinity, and in time from the Virgin according to humanity. That Christ was God and man has above been carefully proved against heretics and Jews, and therefore it need not be pursued here. Therefore, insofar as he is man, he is the Son of God only by grace; insofar as he is God, he is the Son [Col. 0423D] of God by nature. For if, insofar as he was man, he had been conceived from the divine nature, he would in no way have been changeable, nor would there have been any other defect in him.

## CHAPTER III. The opinion of pagans who say that Christ was impassible and immortal.

The aforesaid pagans maintain that Christ was immortal and impassible because he was conceived from God’s breath. Consequently, they say that he neither suffered nor died nor was raised from the dead; rather, they assert that when the Jews wished to fasten him to the cross, he put another man in his own place. They strive to establish this as follows: if Christ was conceived from the divine breath, then, just as the divine breath is incorruptible, so Christ [Col. 0424A] is impassible. Furthermore, it would be unfitting for Christ, conceived from the divine breath and thus in some manner the Son of God, to undergo the punishment of the cross.

## CHAPTER IV. Resolution of the foregoing.

To this it must be said that Christ, insofar as he is the Son of God, neither suffered, died, nor was raised; but he did so according to the weakness of the human nature which he assumed from the Virgin. For if he assumed flesh, did he have passible or impassible flesh? If impassible flesh, whence did he assume it, since all flesh was passible? If he assumed passible flesh, he could suffer and die, and by the power of his divinity rise from the dead. But the Virgin’s flesh was passible; and he assumed flesh from that passible flesh, and [Col. 0424B] thus he was passible.

That Christ was the Son of God and, accordingly, immortal; and the Son of the Virgin and, accordingly, mortal, has been carefully proved above. We have also proved above by diverse authorities that Christ suffered, died, and was raised. Thus, when Christ underwent death according to the weakness of the flesh, we do not reckon this Christ’s misery but his condescension. It was from God’s highest mercy and condescension that Christ assumed flesh and underwent death—not because he had deserved it, but so that through death he might redeem us from death. For if a king, taking pity on his servant lying in mud, entered the mud in order to free the servant, this would be ascribed not to the king’s misery but to his condescension.

## CHAPTER V. The opinion of pagans who say that, in eternal blessedness, human beings must be refreshed by material food and drink.

[Col. 0424C]

The aforesaid pagans also say that in eternal blessedness human beings will be refreshed by material food and drink. They try to prove this by authorities. For they say that God promised the Jews, if they acted well, a land flowing with milk and honey. But this cannot be understood of the material promised land, because it does not flow with milk and honey. Therefore it must be referred to paradise, where the blessed will be refreshed with milk and honey. And Christ, promising his own eternal refreshment, says: “That you may eat and drink at my table in the kingdom of my Father” (Luke XXII). Christ is also read to have eaten a honeycomb after the resurrection, so that [Col. 0424D] this may indicate that human beings after the resurrection will be refreshed with honey.

## CHAPTER VI. Resolution of the foregoing.

It must be said in reply that in eternal blessedness there will not be material refreshment but spiritual refreshment, because human beings will have spiritual bodies, needing neither drink nor food. For, as Christ testifies, in paradise people will neither marry nor be given in marriage, but will be like the angels of God (Rom. XIV); neither will they be refreshed with material foods, but will be like the angels of God, needing neither food nor drink. And the Apostle says that food and drink are not the kingdom of heaven; moreover, flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God (1 Cor. [Col. 0425A] XVI), that is, nourishment of flesh and blood will have no place in God’s kingdom.

What was said about the land flowing with milk and honey can also be understood literally of the promised land, for that land is most fertile. Or, by the land flowing with milk and honey is understood the heavenly paradise, which is said to flow with milk and honey because of the sweetness of eternal and inward refreshment. Christ likewise calls his table, which will be in the kingdom of his Father, the spiritual refreshment of the blessed. That spiritual refreshment will be nothing other than enjoyment of God. Hence in the Psalm: “You will give them drink from the torrent of your delights” (Ps. XXXV).

But what greater madness is there than to maintain that eating honey and drinking milk are the rewards of the blessed? Did the martyrs endure so many persecutions in order to attain these refreshments? Did Lawrence desire to be burned upon the gridiron in order to reach these joys?
