Was Vincent suspended upon the rack in order to enjoy this food? Certainly, if God were to give his own material dishes, I think he would give them more elegant fare. Christ, however, did not eat after the resurrection in order to indicate that the risen need food, but in order that his resurrection might thereby be proved true.

## CHAPTER VII. The pagan assertion that it is lawful for them to have several wives at once.

The aforesaid also say that it is lawful for them to have several [Col. 0425C] wives at once. They attempt to prove this by the authority of the Fathers of the Old Testament, who are read to have had two wives—Jacob, David, and many others. For by what reasoning was it lawful for them to have several wives simultaneously, but not lawful for modern people? Yet they assert this only in order to satisfy lust: their entire life is in the stench of lust. So be it.

## CHAPTER VIII. Resolution of the foregoing.

To this we say that one woman is said to belong to one man. Thus the Lord gave Adam one wife, not several; and this also serves a sacramental meaning, for it signifies that there is one Bride of Christ, namely the Church. Thus Lamech mortally sinned, he who first had several wives. But in the Old [Col. 0425D] Testament it was lawful for someone to have several wives for the multiplication of the human race and for divine worship. Then fertility filled the earth; now, however, in the New Testament chastity ought to fill heaven. For “from the time of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. XI).

Hence, as the Apostle says: “As long as a woman lives, she is bound to her husband, so that she cannot marry another”; likewise a husband is bound to his wife, so that he cannot take another (1 Cor. VII). Thus, if a man has several wives, he is an adulterer; and just as one woman cannot simultaneously have several husbands, so one man cannot simultaneously have several women. The Apostle likewise says that a man does not have power over his own body, but his wife does (ibid.); and thus, while his wife lives, a husband cannot approach another woman. Since, therefore, the aforesaid [Col. 0426A] pagans say that Christ was a great prophet, how do they dare contradict his words? He said that a wife was not to be put away except for the cause of fornication; but they put away their wives for many other causes.

There are also some among them who say that a woman left by her husband ought not to return to him until another has had intercourse with her; and thus they have become transgressors of the Law and the Gospel. For it is written in the Law that if someone dismisses his wife for any cause whatever and later wishes to return to her, it lies within his discretion, provided another man has not defiled her. If another has touched her, she is forbidden to him forever (Deut. XXIV). In the Gospel, however, it is not lawful for a man to dismiss his wife without the fault of fornication; and whoever takes another’s dismissed wife as his own is judged an adulterer and fornicator (Matt. V). Likewise, if they believe Christ to have been only a prophet, born of the Virgin and conceived by the divine breath, why do they not celebrate his conception or birth?

278, four times. ## CHAPTER IX. The opinion of those who say that washing the body with water alone suffices for the remission of sin.

The aforesaid also affirm that washing the body with water alone suffices for the remission of sin. They wish to prove this by many authorities. For Ezekiel says: “I will pour clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your defilements” (Ezek. XXXVI). And John was baptizing in [Col. 0426C] water only (Mark I). Naaman also, washed in the Jordan, was freed from the disease of leprosy (4 Kings V), by which it was signified that someone is freed from the filth of sin through washing with water alone. Led by these authorities, the aforesaid pagans assert that every mortal sin is forgiven to a person through washing with water alone, without contrition or confession.

## CHAPTER X. The Christian response.

To this we say that bodily washing, without contrition and confession, suffices for a person of discretion and maturity; but for a child it does not suffice without invocation of the Trinity, as has above been proved in many ways in the treatise against heretics. Ezekiel calls that water clean because it is sanctified by the word, according to the saying: “The word is added to the element, and it becomes a sacrament.” John, however, did not baptize for the remission of sins or for sanctification, but as a sign; nor were sins remitted by John’s baptism. The washing with water by which Naaman was cleansed of leprosy signifies Christ’s baptism, by which one is freed from guilt.

The washing with water by which remission of sin occurs in baptism must not be repeated, because it signifies Christ’s passion and death, which are not to be repeated; nor ought injury to be done to the sacrament of baptism. Therefore washing with water—that is, baptism—is effective once for child or adult; when repeated, it is of no benefit. Thus the pagans err who believe that mortal sin is forgiven them at each washing of their bodies [Col. 0427A]. For if this were so, it would appear to be an incentive to sin.

They also observe many things in the old Law and thus in some measure Judaize, because they do not eat pork and marry several wives at once. But above, against the Jews, we carefully proved that the Law has now been abolished. Paul also demonstrates this repeatedly, and that one who observes the Law of Moses according to the letter is, as it were, an idolater; for when the truth has come, the shadow ought to cease, and when the thing signified has come, the figure must cease. Christ also showed that it was completed and fulfilled in himself when he said: “It is finished” (John XIX).

## CHAPTER XI. The opinion of Jews and Saracens against Christians, because Christians have images in churches.

[Col. 0427B] Pagans together with Jews also reproach us because we have images and sculptures in our churches, in which we seem to oppose the divine commandment that says: “You shall not make for yourself graven images, nor any likeness that is in heaven or on earth or in the waters or beneath the earth” (Exod. XX; Deut. V). And the Prophet says: “Let all who worship graven images be confounded,” etc. (Ps. XCVI).

But Christians portray God seated upon an exalted throne and making a sign with outstretched hand; and around him, with great magnificence of dignity, they carve, fashion, and paint the eagle, the man, the calf, and the lion. Wherever they can, they adore and venerate these images.

## CHAPTER XII. Resolution of the foregoing.

[Col. 0427C] To this we say that, if the Mosaic Law prohibited the making of any carved image whatsoever, Moses sinned when he made images of cherubim and placed them in the Temple. Moreover, on the golden crown that was held in the land of the Philistines, as the Hebrews say, images of kings were carved. By the same reasoning it appears that images of saints and the image of Christ may be painted, so that by the things they see people may be invited to the invisible, and through the signs may venerate the things signified; for pictures are for laypeople what written letters are for clerics.

We also read in Isaiah that Isaiah saw the Lord seated upon a high throne, and seraphim stood above it (Isa. VI). If Isaiah wished to represent what he had seen in an imaginary, material, or bodily vision, it does not seem absurd that he should render in a picture what he had rendered in writing [Col. 0427D].

Likewise, Ezekiel is read to have seen (chapter I) likenesses of four animals, namely a man, lion, calf, and eagle. Therefore, may not a Christian paint in remembrance what Ezekiel is read to have seen and written? Thus the commandment of the Law must be understood suitably—or rather, it must be understood as the lawgiver himself explained it: “You shall not,” he says, “make a graven image,” and he gives the reason: “You shall not adore them or worship them.” Once the idolatry of faithless worship is excluded, graven images were made by them and may be made by us.

We make carvings and sculptures, but we neither adore nor worship them with divine worship. Nor do we say that the cross itself, once made, possesses power in itself or from itself. But after it has been sanctified by episcopal blessing in remembrance of the Lord’s passion, we exalt and venerate the cross, not with divine worship but with the worship of due veneration. For a human being adores God in one way and the cross in another: God is adored because of his divinity; the cross is venerated because of the passion of the Crucified One. Therefore, to state the matter briefly and in few words: a Christian does not at all adore any image of anything with divine worship; nevertheless, with the worship of due honor, he adores holy images and paintings of saints.

They also reproach us for this, saying that we make several gods because we adore several saints, such as Peter and Paul, and so forth. Yet no adoration is due except to God; anyone who attributes divine worship to a creature is an idolater. To this it must be said that the kind of adoration due to God, which in Greek is called *latria*, a Christian does not offer to a creature, but offers the kind called in Greek *dulia*, which is due to a human being and an angel [Col. 0428B]. The worship due to God consists in love, prayer, glorification, and offering: a person is to love God above all things and offer himself and what is his to him as Creator. No one offers this worship to a creature. But a person is obliged to love his neighbor as himself, to show him reverence—sometimes as a superior, sometimes as an equal—and kindness, sometimes as an inferior. Therefore we do not establish several gods, but adore one God with divine worship.

## CHAPTER XIII. The pagan opinion that they ought to greet no one unless he belongs to the same sect as themselves.

[Col. 0428C]

Those of whom the discussion has spoken also say that no one ought to be greeted unless he belongs to their own sect. For they say that they ought not to share the greeting of peace with those with whom they will not share the communion of salvation. For if greeting is not to be offered to excommunicated persons, much less should it be offered to those with whom there is no communion at all.

## CHAPTER XIV. The foregoing opinion refuted.

But they contradict themselves. For they say that it is lawful for them to take a wife belonging to another law, as the ancient Fathers are also read to have done: David, for instance, who took a Gentile wife, namely Absalom’s mother, and Solomon, the daughter of the king of Egypt. If it is lawful for them to take foreign women as wives, it is much more lawful to greet them or to pray for them. They worship a gnat and swallow a camel. In many other matters also they contradict themselves. For they accept some things from the old Law and reject others; likewise from the Gospel; and in many ways they are inconsistent with themselves. These are Samson’s little foxes, joined by their tails but separate and divided in their faces.

For they say that Christ was of such great dignity and holiness as Muhammad, or even greater; since they say that Christ did not die, while they maintain that Muhammad died—and it is also manifest that Muhammad died and was devoured by dogs.

[Col. 0429A] If Christ did not die, where do they say that he is: in heaven or on earth? It is evident that he is not on earth; therefore it remains that he is in heaven. But when did he ascend into heaven, since according to them he did not suffer, die, or rise again?

They are also asked whether Christ will judge the world. Is it not read in the book of Daniel (chapter VII) that the books of consciences will be opened on the day of judgment, and that the Ancient of Days will sit and judge each individual? These things he intimated on the way, so that he might attain this judgment in the homeland.

Let them also say by what miracles their opinion is marked. Miracles are performed among them by antiphrasis. It remains, therefore, that their opinion is false, since it is supported neither by reason nor by authority.

[Col. 0430A] ## Conclusion of this work

Let heretics, then, blush for their false error; Waldensians for their devised doctrine; Jews for their observance of the Mosaic Law; pagans for their abominable error. Let heretics be converted to Catholic unity, renouncing perverse doctrines; Waldensians, perverse persuasions; Jews, carnal observances; pagans, superstitious opinions, so that they may thus attain true unity, and from the true unity of faith may ascend to the true unity of eternal blessedness. May Jesus Christ our Lord deign to grant this to us: he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, one God, through all ages of ages. Amen.

Here ends the four-part work of Master Alan against heretics, Waldensians, Jews, and pagans.

Below was written:

Faithfully extracted from a manuscript preserved in the Cistercian Library. 18 March 1655.

Francis du Chemin, prior of Cîteaux.

[Col. 0429]

# ALAN OF LILLE: THE BOOK ON THE COMPLAINT OF NATURE

## TO THE READER

279 This book bears various titles both in manuscript copies and in citations by other authors. Sometimes, as in the copy from the Abbey of Cysoing, it is called the *Enchiridion on the Natures of Things*. At other times, as in the copy from the monastery of Saint-Bertin, it is called the *Book on Nature’s Complaint*. More frequently, however, it is entitled the *Book on the Complaint of Nature*, because at the beginning of the work the author introduces Nature lamenting the depravity of the human race and the foul dominion of vices—above all the unspeakable crime of sodomy, against which, more than against other vices, he inveighs, so strongly that various authors give the entire book the title: *Treatise against the Vice of Sodomy*. Yet he also most sharply censures many other vices and prescribes appropriate means by which each should be overcome.

Moreover, to use the words of the eminent doctor Robert Holkot, in the tenth chapter of the Book of Wisdom, lecture 118, letter A, this work is “composed with much learning and careful artistry,” and under that title it was familiar to all the most weighty authors, as is evident from their writings. So much so that the famous polymath Leo Allatius, professor of eloquence, judged it worthy of his most learned elucidations, as he himself attested in the book 280 *On the Urban Bees, or On Illustrious Men and Their Writings Who Were in Rome in the Year 1630 and the Two Following Years*; he published that book there in 1633 and dedicated it to Pope Urban VIII.

In that work, I say, after listing the various studies he had prepared, he added: “Allatius is now elucidating the book of Blessed Alan, *On the Lament of Nature*.” But, as Romanus Ferdinandus Ughellus, the most distinguished Cistercian abbot of our order, recently informed me by letter from Rome, death came upon the man untimely and suppressed the unfinished work, depriving this book, not without injury to literature and thus to the common good, of the benefit of the press. At length I myself have now provided that benefit, using two manuscript copies. The first was supplied to me by the exceedingly well-furnished library of the Abbey of Park near Louvain, but it was very mutilated, lacking both beginning and end. The second was most courteously sent by the Reverend and most eminent Lord Hugh Beekmans, most worthy archimandrite of the Abbey of Cysoing, of the Order of Canons Regular. Since it was wholly complete and perfect, and in addition highly commendable for its antiquity, I have followed it here almost throughout, noting here and there variant readings where the sense admitted both.

Charles de Visch, prior of Dunes.

# 281 THE BOOK ON THE COMPLAINT OF NATURE

[Col. 0431]

[Col. 0431A]

I turn laughter into tears, joys into weeping,  
Applause into lament, and jests into tears,  
When I see Nature’s own secrets fall silent,  
While a shipwrecked multitude perishes through Venus’s monstrosity.

When Venus, fighting against Venus, makes men into women,  
And by her magic art unmakes her own men.  
It is not deception that begets sadness, nor adulterous deceits that beget tears,  
Nor guile—rather grief brings them forth, indeed gives them birth.

The Muse asks, grief itself commands, Nature entreats,  
That in weeping I may give them a tearful song.  
Alas! Where has the grace of Nature withdrawn? Where the form  
Of good conduct, the rule of chastity, the love of modesty?

Nature weeps, morals are silent; every modesty,  
Orphaned from its ancient nobility, is proscribed.  
The active sex shamefully recoils  
[Col. 0431B] To degenerate into the passive kind.

Man made woman blackens the honor of his sex;  
The art of magic Venus makes him hermaphrodite.  
He predicates and subjects; the same thing becomes a double term;  
He extends the laws of grammar too far.

He denies that he is a man, made a barbarian in Nature’s art.  
Art does not please him—rather, a trope.  
Yet this cannot be called a tropological transfer;  
This figure falls more properly into vice.

Here now is a logician, by whom the simple conversion  
Of art makes Nature’s laws perish.  
He strikes upon an anvil that mints no seed,  
And the hammer itself shudders at its own anvil.

He stamps no material with the ideal matrix,  
But rather ploughs a barren shore with a ploughshare.  
[Col. 0431C] Thus Venus’s service is wrongly made iambic with a dactylic foot,  
In which the long syllable does not admit the short.

Although every form of man submits to the female species,  
Ever inferior to her in honor;  
Although, if the beauty of the Tyndarid were fashioned,  
The conquered beauty of Adonis and Narcissus would adore her;

Yet she herself is despised, though that beauty should plead for her  
And the deity of form argue that she is a goddess—  
She by whose love Jupiter’s thunderbolt would grow feeble in his right hand,  
And every active string of Phoebus would cease its leisure;

By whose love the free man would become a slave, and Hippolytus  
282 Would sell his own chastity;  
Whose kisses, once impressed, would sweeten with honeyed juice,  
And would give a honeycomb of honey in the mouth.

The spirit, given over to kisses of the mouth,  
Would depart, and wholly play with itself upon the lips.  
So that, while I thus die, dead in myself,  
I, another self, may enjoy happy life in her.

Not only does the Phrygian adulterer hunt the Tyndarid,  
But Paris produces unspeakable monsters in Paris.  
Not only does Pyramus seek Thisbe’s kisses through a chink;  
[Col. 0432A] No such little fissure of Venus pleases this man.

Not only does Achilles feign the acts of a maiden  
So that he may thus prove himself to be a virginal man;  
But he wrongly gives Nature’s gift in exchange for a gift,  
When for love of gain he sells his sex.

Such men deserve an anathema from the temple of Genius,  
Who deny to Genius tithes and his due rights.

As I repeatedly recited this elegy in a mournful melody, a woman—[Note: [Col. 0431D] She signifies Nature, whose beauty he has described.] [Note: [Col. 0431] Nature.]—seemed to hasten toward me, descending from the more inward palace of the impassible world. Her hair, shining not with borrowed light but with its own, not representing the image of rays by resemblance but surpassing their nature by native brilliance, gave the maiden’s head the appearance of a stellar body [Col. 0432B]. Parted by a double braid, it did not abandon the heights, yet did not disdain to smile upon the earth with a kiss. A small path like a lily-stalk, with a slanting crossing, divided the contention of the hair; nor was that slant ever a detriment to her face, but enhanced its beauty. A golden hairband, gathering the gold of her hair into the dance of lawful order, marveled to have found a face resembling itself. For the imaginative appearance of gold-like color produced a visual paralogism. Her forehead, spreading into a broad plain, lily-white with a milky hue, seemed to contend with the lily.

Her eyebrows, starred with golden brightness, neither straying into a thicket nor drooping into excessive scantness, held the mean between the two. The calm serenity of her eyes, caressing with friendly brightness, displayed the unfamiliar splendor of twin stars [Col. 0432C]. Each nostril, anointed with honeyed balm, neither unduly low nor improperly prominent, presented a certain distinction. The nard of her mouth offered the nostrils delicate feasts of fragrance. Her lips, rising in a slight swelling, invited Venus’s novices to kisses. By a certain harmony of their color, her teeth imitated the appearance of ivory. The purple fire of her cheeks, kindled with the crimson dye of roses, made her face friendly with a sweet flame; for the purple, wedded to the linen whiteness of her face, felt a pleasing tempering in its brightness. The polished flatness of her chin, more circumspect than crystal light, wore a silver gleam. The fair height of her neck, moderated by slenderness, [Col. 0432D] did not allow the neck to be joined to the shoulders.

The little apples of her breasts gracefully promised the maturity of youth. Her arms, fair to the viewer’s gaze, seemed to invite embraces. The even hollowing of her sides, stamped with the seal of proper proportion, carried the form of her entire body to the summit of perfection.

[Col. 0433A] As for the remaining parts, concealed by the more private chamber, faith declared them better still. For within the body lay a more pleasing countenance, of which the visible face displayed only a prelude. Yet though such was the joy of her beauty, a grief beyond estimation strove to extinguish the smile of that beauty. For a stream flowing from the fountain of her eyes proclaimed a sorrowing mind.

Her face itself, cast down to the earth in chaste modesty, seemed somehow to speak of an injury inflicted upon the maiden herself. But a gleaming crown of royal diadem, starred with dances of gems, flashed above upon her head. Its substance was not counterfeit gold, declining from its own dignity and misleading the eyes with sophistical light; rather, its own nobility supplied its essence [Col. 0433B]. By a wondrous circuit and eternal flight, the diadem itself, traveling from east to west, repeatedly returned in its course to the east. By perpetually performing this same action, its movement seemed frivolous because of its excessive seeking of the same beginning.

Some of the aforementioned gems for a time offered the sight new miracles of God through a new sun of their own light; but for a time, through an eclipse of their radiance, they seemed to be exiled from the palace of the diadem. Others, set in the throne, kept eternal watch in the uninterrupted vigilance of their sparkling. Among these, a shining circle, studded with precious stones in the likeness of the zodiacal obliquity, interrupted with kisses the necklaces of stellar adjacency. In [Col. 0433C] it a company of twelve gems, by a successive and privileged splendor, seemed to claim preeminence among the others.

On the front part of the diadem, moreover, three precious stones shone preeminently above the other nine in the proud audacity of their rays. The first stone commanded the cold of night to suffer exile in the fire of light. In it, as the witty falsehoods of painting declared, the represented image of a lion flashed.

The second stone, second to none in brightness, shone in the more prominent position of the aforesaid part and seemed, as if in indignation, to look down upon the other stones. In it, as painting—the ape of truth—showed, a crab seemed to advance backward in changing conflict, retreating as it moved forward [Col. 0433D].

The third stone repaid the impoverished brightness of the opposite stone with the abundant riches of its own radiance. In it, as the truth of the painting declared, the shadowy child of Leda went forward, rejoicing in mutual embrace. In like manner, three stones, possessing the same honor of rank, occupied the throne on the opposite side. The first of them saddened the gaze with a certain imaginary weeping, its drops of sweat imitating tears. In it, as the imagination of courtly writing taught by representation, the little pitcher of a certain youth received a flowing torrent. The second stone, driving winter from the lodging of its realm of heat with icy numbness, claimed winter as its guest. In it painting had woven Capricorn’s garment from the counterfeit fleece [Col. 0434A] of a goat’s wool. The third stone, wearing the face of crystalline light, foretold winter’s coming. In it old Chiron, by the continuous bending of his bow, threatened wounds, yet never repaid his threats with an effect.

On the other side, a kindly serenity of gems, playfully caressing, bestowed favor upon the eyes. The first, aflame with the crimson dye of rosy color, presented a rose to sight; in it a bull, displaying the emblems of his brow, seemed to thirst for battle. Another, privileged by the moderation of its light, attracted the fellowship of its sisters by the grace of its goodness; in it a ram, proud in the honor of its brow, sought dominion over the flock.

The third, displaying emerald greenness, bore within itself a remedy refreshing to the eyes [Col. 0434B]. In it, beneath an imaginary river, fishes exercised their natural practice of swimming along the shore.

On the opposing side of the throne, the beauty of stars sparkled in joyful applause. The first of these stones, shining tirelessly with the golden sun of its radiance, exalted the grace of beauty. In it, as the tropological figure of sculpture showed, Astraea contended with the stars by a certain prerogative of her brilliance. The second, neither luxuriating in excessive splendor nor begging sparks from impoverished brightness, rejoiced in a moderated flame. In it also, in equal balance and according to the rule of pictorial art, [Col. 0434C] a scale of weights promised judgments.

The third, alternating its expressions in turn, now promised the favor of serenity, now brought on clouds of darkness: in it appeared [284] the face of a scorpion, which threatened laughter with its face and tears with the sting of its tail. Beneath these twelve dwellings of stones, a sevenfold multitude of gems, perpetually moving in a circle, performed a delightful dance with marvellous playfulness; nor did the dance itself lack the sweetness of harmony: now sporting in semitones, now waxing youthful in the moderate sound of tones, now issuing in a more mature musical utterance of the trumpet, by its modulation it stirred the desire of our ears and offered the eyes preludes to sleep. Yet sparingness in hearing earns the ear’s displeasure; excess produces satiety: for an ear wearied by an overabundant supply of hearing grows dull.

These seven stones, although they were held subject to the diadem by no bonds of joints, nevertheless never, by their absence, made the companies of the higher stones orphaned. The upper stone was diamond, more niggardly than the rest in movement and more lavish in idleness; in traversing its wider circle it drew out an excessive delay of time. It grew sluggish with so icy a cold that its affinity of nature proved it to be born from the planet Saturn itself. The second was agate, which, when the nearness of its course made it more familiar to the others, transformed the enmities of certain ones. In it, since by the power of its imperial virtue it rendered even the favor and boyish goodwill of certain persons mature, and since through a close kinship of nature it was allied to Jovian fidelity, its effect was said to be gracious. The third was astrites, in which, with heat pitching camp in command, the effect of the planet Mars was read through a certain continuity of property; terrible in the threatening expression of its figure, it menaced destruction to the others. The fourth was carbuncle, bearing the image of the sun; beneath the waxen radiance of its rays it banished shadow, put to sleep the eclipsed lamps of its brothers, now commanding the rest to wander by the authority of its royal majesty, now granting stillness power over motion. Hyacinth, however, following in the sapphire’s tracks, serving it like an attendant, was never deprived of the sight of the aforesaid light; and, at the short intervening distance, their orbs run together or follow one another, or one following star grants to the other the service of going first. Of these two stones, one, by the correspondence of its nature, represented the planet Mercury; the other the effect of the star of Dione, Venus.

The last stone was a pearl. Set in the rim of the glittering crown and shining with another’s light, it begged the carbuncle for the assistance of light. Sometimes, when near the aforesaid light, it waxes; when its distance is prolonged, it wanes. In waxing, it reverences the carbuncle, as it were, by lowering the rays of its own light, so that, again adorned with fraternal fires and bearing about the renewed ornaments of its splendor, it now makes up, by its regular supplements, the losses of its diminished orb, now, orphaned of its proper lights, laments the loss of its own majesty. Silvered with a crystalline gleam, it shone with the character of the lunar planet. With all these splendors of stones, the serene nobility of the aforesaid diadem represented within itself the likeness of the firmament.

The garment, woven from silken wool and covered in manifold colors, served the girl’s body; a coloring diversity, varied by its colors, altered its appearance with multiple hues. At first, whitened with the whiteness of a lily, it offended the eye. Secondly, as though reduced by want and laboring toward improvement, it shone purple with the blood of blushes. Thirdly, at the summit of perfection, it delighted the eyes with green, like an emerald. But this fabric, made exceedingly fine and escaping the scrutiny of the eyes, had reached such thinness of material that one would have believed it and air to be of the same nature. Upon it, as painting imagined to the eyes, a gathering of animals was displayed.

There the eagle, after putting on old age for the second time after youth, returned again from Nestor to Adonis. There the hawk exacted tribute from its subjects by violence and tyranny. There the kite, assuming the role of a hunter, wore the hawk’s mask under a stealthy pretext of reverence. There the falcon stirred up civil war against the heron, though not divided by an equal balance; for it ought not to be counted as a fight when you strike while I merely hide. There the ostrich, setting aside secular life, inhabited the solitudes of deserts as though it had become a hermit. There the swan, herald of its own death, prophesied life’s end with the instrument of honey-sweet lyre-playing. There Nature poured such a treasury of beauty into the peacock that you would believe she later had to beg for it. There the phoenix, dead in itself and alive again in another, by a miracle of nature raised itself from the dead through its own death. There the stork, by tithing its offspring, paid Nature’s tribute. There, when the sparrow had been relegated to an atom of pygmy littleness, the crane, by contrast, rose to an excess of gigantic size. There the pheasant, having endured the confines of its native island and destined to be the delight of princes, flew forth into our regions. There the cock, like a common astrologer, spoke of the divisions of the hours by the clock of its voice. There the wild cock, scorning the idleness of the domestic cock, journeyed abroad and traversed woodland provinces. There the unholy owl sang psalmodies of misery in a funeral lament. There the little owl was filthy in a dung-heap with such deformity that you would believe Nature had been sleepy in forming it. There the crow, predicting things to come, was excited by its frivolous chatter. There the magpie, painted in ambiguous color, kept awake the sleepless care of logic. There the jackdaw, hoarding recovered goods by praiseworthy theft, displayed proofs of its inborn avarice. There the dove, intoxicated by the sweet apple, labored in the wrestling-school of Cyprian Dione, Venus. There the raven, abhorring the disgrace of jealousy, admitted that its offspring were not its own pledges, until, by the evidence of their black color, it proved this as though arguing with itself. There the partridge shrank from assaults of aerial power, hunters’ sophistries, and the prophetic barking of dogs. There the duck, with the goose, wintered in its riverine homeland under their rule of life. There the turtledove, bereft of its mate and disdaining to make an epilogue of its loves, rejected the consolations of bigamy. There the parrot, using the anvil of its throat, minted the coinage of human speech. There imaginary arguments of voice deceived the quail, ignorant of the dragon-form’s deceit.

There the woodpecker, architect of its own little dwelling, fashioned a closure in an oak with the adze of its beak. There the warbler, casting off its stepmother, adopted the cuckoo’s alien offspring as a son at the maternal breast of piety; yet rewarded with a capital penalty, recognizing the stepson, it did not recognize its son. There the swallow, returned from its journey abroad, plastered its nest’s lodging beneath a beam. There the nightingale, renewing the complaint of its deflowering and drumming with harmonious sweetness, excused the disgrace of its smallness. There the lark, like a noble lyre-player, trained in musical knowledge not by artful study but by Nature’s teaching, presented a lyre in its mouth; thinning tones into subtle particles, it divided semitones into divisible knots. There the bat, a hermaphroditic bird, held the place of zero among the little birds. Although these animals lived there allegorically, they nevertheless seemed to be there literally.

The linen mantle, green with an adulterated whiteness, which the girl herself had later woven in a distinctive, seamless manner, was not cheap through common material, but sported in subtle craftsmanship and performed the office of a cloak. Entangled in many folds, it represented the color of water; upon it painting’s fiction devised, beyond the nature of aquatic creatures, many different species divided into parts.

There the whale, contending with rocks, battered little towns of ships by the assault of its tower-like body, a reef by reason of its size. There the sea-dog, with the barking equivocation of its name, sparing no barks, hunted hares of its own kind in the groves of the sea. There the sturgeon offered to royal tables the nobility of its body by the individual blessedness of its body. There the herring, the most general kind of fish, comforted the fasts of the poor by the ample commonness of its body. There the plaice, by the sweet flavors of its body, redeemed the absence of flesh during Lenten austerity. There the mullet seduced the palates of eaters with the sweet enticements of its flesh. There the tritula, entering the marine bays and baptized in the sea, was called by the name salmon. There the dolphin, by the constancy of its appearance, foretold future voyages upon the sea. There, in the loins of the sirens there was a fish, while in the face a man was to be seen. To these inhabitants of the maritime region the middle portion of the cloak had been given; but the remaining portion of the mantle contained fish that were foreigners, wandering through different waves and making their homes in a country of sweeter water.

There the pike, by tyrannical exaction rather than the requirement of merit, imprisoned its subjects in the prison-house of its own body. There the barbel, famous for no lesser dignity of body, lived more familiarly with the common multitude of fishes. There the shad, accompanying the vernal season and offering the delights of its flavor among spring’s delights, greeted human tastes with the arrival of its body. There the moray eel, pierced with many window-like openings, read the onset of fevers to those at table. There the eel, representing the nature of a serpent by a certain similarity of property, was believed to be its niece. There the perch, armored with darts of sperm, did not greatly fear the attacks of the water-wolf. There the bullhead made up in its swollen head what it lost in the smallness of its lower body. These carvings, elegantly fashioned upon the cloak by the trope of painting, seemed miraculously to swim.

The tunic, figured in patterned embroidery with plumage-work, enclosed beneath itself the maiden’s body. Studded with many colors and gathered into a thicker material, it aspired to the likeness of the earthly element. In the foremost part of this garment, a man, putting off the sluggishness of sense and led by the charioteering of reason, penetrated the secrets of heaven. In this part the tunic, suffering the dissension of its own parts, displayed the insults of its injuries. Yet in the remaining places its parts, harmonious in elegant continuity, endured in themselves no discord of division. In them a certain enchantment of painting made terrestrial animals live.

There the elephant, advancing into the air with its monstrous bulk, doubled at manifold interest the mouth given it by Nature. There the camel, deformed by its humped body, served human needs like a purchased slave. There horns, taking the place of a helmet, seemed to arm the buffalo’s forehead. There the bull, tormenting the earth with its feet and thundering with its bellowing, sounded beforehand the thunderbolts of its duel. There oxen, refusing the warfare of bulls, aspired like rustics to servile occupations. There the horse, carried forward by fiery boldness and fighting beside its rider, broke the lance with the soldier. There the ass, loathing ears with horrible cries, as though making music by antiphrasis, committed barbarism in music. There the unicorn, lulled asleep in a virgin’s lap, incurred from enemies the sleep of death. There the lion, murmuring songs of roaring into the ears of its young, rekindled in them the little spark of life. There the she-bear, having produced deformed offspring through the gateways of her nostrils, shaped them more perfectly by frequently licking and correcting them with the stylus of her tongue. There the wolf, by hiding, usurped the office of a thief. There the leopard, playing Nero by more open robbery, plundered the herd not only of their garments but even of their very persons. There the tiger violated the commonwealth of its beastly citizens by frequent shedding of innocent blood. There the wild ass, casting off the servitude of the donkey and emancipated by Nature’s authority, inhabited the boldness of the mountains. There the boar, lightning-like in the armor of its tooth, sold its own death dearly to dogs with many a wound. There the dog, vexing imaginary wounds, bit the air with the importunity of its teeth. There the stag and doe, winged by swift feet, gaining life by running ahead, cheated the unjust bites of pursuing dogs. There the goat, clothed in sophistical wool, seemed to disdain a four-day smell with its nostrils. There the ram, draped in a more noble tunic and rejoicing in plurality of wives, defrauded marriage of its honor. There the little fox, putting off the simplicity of a brute animal, aspired to the superior cunning of man. There the hare, seized by a melancholy madness, terrified not by sleep but by the stupor of fear, dreamed of the coming of dogs. There the rabbit, tempering the anger of our cold by its skin and the attack of our hunger by its flesh, resisted both. There the beaver, lest it suffer dismemberment of its whole body by enemies, amputated its body’s extremities. There the lynx possessed such clearness of sight that the other animals seemed bleary-eyed by comparison. There the marten and sable, supplying the beauty of cloaks which demanded their help half-complete, brought it to completion by the nobility of their skins.

The representation of historical figure bestowed these figures of animals upon the eyes of beholders like feasts of delight. What the invention of painting imagined in the stockings and shirt, buried beneath the outer garments, I have not established by any authority of certainty; but only, as certain remedies of frail probability have taught, I suppose that there painting played with the natures of herbs and trees. There I would see trees now clothed in purple tunics, now crowned with green leaves, now giving birth to the fragrant infancy of flowers, now growing old in a more mature fruit. But because I have known this sequence of painting only through the slippery ground of probability, not the assurance of certainty, I pass it over, buried in the peace of silence.

The shoes, made from tawed leather, followed the forms of the feet so closely that they seemed born upon the feet themselves and marvellously inscribed upon them. On them, scarcely departing from true reality, shaded flowers were made lovely by the ingenuity of painting.

> There was the form of a rose, faithfully painted,  
> Slightly departing from its true appearance;  
> It matched purple with its own dye,  
> And stained the earth with its own blood.  
>
> Joining [variant: “Playing”] with companion flowers, there was present  
> The fragrant and pleasing flower of Adonis,  
> And the noble lily, in its silver,  
> Proclaimed the fields and the valley-depths.  
>
> There thyme, disputing to outshine all in scent,  
> Contended, envying the other flowers;  
> With the flower of narcissus as their companion,  
> The streams laughed in sportive murmuring.  
>
> The flower of columbine, with flower-bearing face,  
> Shone forth as the light-bringer of all flowers;  
> And the little violet flower, speaking of springtime leisure,  
> Starred the shrubs—  
> A painting’s countenance full of favor.  
>
> Here the gracious countenance of the painting  
> Had made the likeness of flowers live—  
> A little page royal in name,  
> Yet ignorant of the writer’s thumb.  
>
> These are spring’s riches and its own garments,  
> The earth’s appearance and its own stars,  
> Which painting brought forth by its arts,  
> Fashioning flowers with ingenious art.  
>
> By these green garments of flowers  
> The grace of a miraculous spring ennobles the meadows.  
> These furnish fine linen, and those purple,  
> Which the wise right hand of the west wind has woven.

## On the chariot, charioteer, and retinue of Nature

Although these ornaments of the garments blazed with the full fires of their own splendor, their brightness nevertheless suffered eclipse beneath the star of the girl’s splendor. On clay tablets, by the service of a reed stylus, the maiden joined together various painted images of things; but because the painting did not adhere closely to its underlying material, it swiftly died by vanishing, leaving behind no traces of its images. Though the girl often revived them and repeatedly made them live, the images could not persist in the intended writing.

Therefore, as we have said, the maiden emerged from the boundary of the celestial region into the cottage of the mutable world, borne in a glass chariot. It was drawn by Juno’s birds, trained by no service of a yoke but joined through their own spontaneous will. A man rose above the maiden’s head; his countenance breathed not of earthliness but rather of the secret of deity. Supplying the woman’s sex’s deficiency, he guided the chariot’s progress with a modest order of direction. When, to contemplate the beauty of his dignity, I gathered together the visible rays of my eyes as though they were sheaves, they did not dare confront the beauty of so great a majesty; dulled by the blows of splendor and excessively afraid, they fled to the companionship of the eyelids.

At the arrival of the aforesaid maiden, all the elements would seem to celebrate solemn rites, as though renewing their natures. The firmament, as though lighting the virgin’s path with its own candles, commanded its stars to shine more fully than usual. Thus even the divine light itself seemed to marvel at their audacity, because in its presence they dared to appear with excessive insolence. Phoebus too, showing a face more joyful than usual at the maiden’s approach, poured out all the riches of his light.

The sister whom he had impoverished of the ornaments of his splendor, clothing her again with a garment of delight, he ordered to meet the approaching queen. The air, putting off the tearful expression of clouds, burned with the favor of a clear countenance at the maiden’s progress. Once vexed by the madness of the north wind’s wrath, it now rested in the favorable bosom of Favonius, the west wind. Birds, as though by an inspiration of Nature, playfully sporting in the pleasing game of their wings, offered the maiden an expression of reverence. Juno, who long before had disdained Jupiter’s embraces, was intoxicated with such joy that by frequent preliminaries of the eye she incited her husband to Venus’s enticements. The sea, formerly raging in tumultuous waves, now, keeping holiday for the maiden’s arrival, promised a lasting peace of tranquillity. Aeolus had confined the winds of the storm in their prison-houses so that they might no longer wage civil wars before the maiden’s eyes. Fish swimming upon the brows of the waters, insofar as the dullness of sense allowed, adorned their mistress’s arrival with a certain festive cheerfulness. Thetis, even while celebrating her marriage with Nereus, intended to conceive another Achilles.

The beauty of the water-maidens, moreover, not only stole reason from human beings but compelled celestial beings to forget their divinity. Emerging from river places, they presented little gifts of perfumed nectar to their approaching queen as tributaries. The maiden graciously received these, and, joining them in a continual embrace and repeatedly kissing them, expressed her love for the maidens. The earth, long stripped of its ornaments by winter’s robbery, seized upon a fragrant tunic of flowers through spring’s prodigality, lest, inglorious in ragged clothing, it should appear unworthy beside the young maiden. Spring too, like an artist skilled in weaving, wove garments for the trees in order to applaud the maiden’s steps; by lowering their tresses, under a kind of appearance of worship and as though bending the knee, they made supplication to the little virgin. Maidens emerging from them enriched the material day with the riches of their beauty; they carried perfumes, made from choice kinds of herbs, in cedar vessels, and, paying these as their revenues to the little girl, purchased her favor with gifts. The nymphs, covering the royal chariot with flowers, at one time made it bloody with roses, at another made it white like lilies with flower petals. Flora generously presented to the maiden the fine-linen shirt which she had woven for her husband in order to earn his embrace. Proserpina, scorning her Tartarean husband’s bed and returning to the upper world, refused to be deprived of the presence of her empress. Even terrestrial animals, taught by I know not what Nature, learned the presence of the maiden by indulging more playfully in games. Thus the whole universe, flowing into obedience to the maiden, labored in marvellous rivalry to win the maiden’s favor.

> Flower-bearing Zephyrus had released the harsh year,  
> Extinguishing Boreas’s battles by his peace.  
> Showered with hailstones of flowers, he rained privet,  
> And commanded the meadows to possess snows of these flowers.  
>
> Spring, like a new fuller, renewing garments for the meadows,  
> Set their robes aflame with the fire of this purple dye.  
> It restored to the trees the hair that winter had shorn,  
> Renewing the dress which winter itself had formerly taken away.  
>
> It was the time when, with the applause of the Dryads,  
> The generous grace of spring spread its riches through the fields;  
> When the infancy of flowers has greater strength within it  
> And, rising higher, withdraws from mother earth;  
> When the violet, mirror of earth, licking its cradle,  
> Seeks the breath of air with a new mouth.  
>
> It was the time when earth, its head starred with roses,  
> Vied with heaven, full of its own stars.  
> The almond tree, bearing the banners of a rising age,  
> Proclaimed its birth and summoned spring’s joys with blossom.  
>
> Then the vine, its bosom gemmed, embracing its husbands,  
> The elms, began to think upon its own offspring.  
> The solar candle banished winter’s shadow,  
> Forcing every cold to endure exile,  
> When winter lay hidden in the deep forests,  
> Whose fresh leafy shade the woods had made.  
>
> Now Juno gave the little flower udders of dew,  
> So that the fosterling might first nourish its offspring.  
> It was the time when Phoebus’s power raises the dead grass  
> And commands all things to rise from their tombs;  
> When spring’s joyful countenance makes the world clear  
> And wipes winter’s tears from its face.  
>
> So that the flower may safely entrust itself to the air,  
> And winter’s cold may not burn its first blossom.  
> Then Phoebus visits the world groaning with winter’s torpor  
> And greets it with joyful light.  
>
> The season close at hand puts off its old age,  
> And the old world begins to be a boy.  
> Phoebus impoverishes night of its own hours,  
> And the pygmy day begins to be a giant.  
>
> Then the flock of sheep prepares lodging for Phoebus  
> And pays its tribute, the herd rejoicing in its sun-guest.  
> Then Philomela celebrates the rites of her own spring,  
> Singing the ode of her honey-sweet song:  
> At whose feast she strikes the instruments of her throat  
> So that with her own mouth she may proclaim her own god.  
>
> Then the lark counterfeits a lyre with sweet sound  
> When she flies upward and converses with Jupiter.  
> A silver splendor brought forth playful birds  
> And commanded the day to be its own in the rivers.  
>
> You might see the varied currents of the spring babbling;  
> Its murmur was a prologue leading into sleep.  
> And that spring, in the face of its splendor, invited  
> The weary man to take its cups.

## Nature speaks to Alan

In this youthful season of beauty, though cheered by no favorable things, the maiden could not moderate her former sorrow. Lowering her chariot to earth and making the ground beautiful with her own footprints, she came to me with a chaste step. When I beheld her from some nearness of place, I fell upon my face, lost my mind, wounded by amazement, and, wholly buried in the alienation of ecstasy, labored between the two, neither alive nor dead. The maiden kindly raised me, supported my drunken feet, strengthened me with the comfort of her hands, entwined me in her embraces, sweetened my mouth with chaste kisses, and cured my infirmity from the sickness of amazement with the honeyed medicine of speech. When she realized that I had been restored to myself, she painted for me in mental understanding an image of material speech, and, as though weaving together archetypal words ideally, brought them forth in act by voice.

“Alas! What blindness of ignorance, what alienation of mind, what weakness of the senses, what infirmity of reason has placed a cloud before [Note: [Col. 0441] Another copy reads: ‘opposed.’] your understanding, compelled your soul into exile, dulled the power of your senses, and made your mind sick, so that your intelligence is deprived not only of familiar knowledge of your nurse, but, struck as though by the novelty of a monstrous image, your discernment suffers eclipse at the rising of my appearance? Why do you make knowledge of me wander away from your memory—I, whose gifts speak me, I who have blessed you with such lavish gifts of benefits; I who, from your earliest age, as deputy of God the creator, by fixed dispensation ordered the lawful course of your life; I who once brought into true being the matter of your body, wavering with the adulterous essence of primordial matter? Taking pity on its deformed face, as though it repeatedly cried out to me [Note: [Col. 0441] ‘Turned aside.’], I sealed it with the signet [Note: [Col. 0441] ‘Seal.’] of the human form; and, when it was bereft of the honorable adornments of shapes [Note: [Col. 0441] ‘Deprived.’], I adorned it with garments of better forms [Note: [Col. 0441] ‘Of forms.’].

“In it, arranging [Note: [Col. 0441] ‘Arranged.’] the various workshops of limbs for the body’s service, I commanded the senses to keep watch in the same bodily city [Note: [Col. 0441] ‘Of the same [body].’], so that, as scouts against foreign enemies, they might defend the body from external attack; so that the whole material of the body, adorned with Nature’s nobler purple ornaments, might proceed to marriage and be joined more pleasingly to its husband, the Spirit—lest the husband, loathing his wife’s deformity, should reject her marriage. I also marked your spirit with vital [Note: [Col. 0443] ‘Potential.’] powers, lest, poorer than the body, it should envy the body’s successes. I assigned it the power of natural intelligence, which, hunting subtle things, might enclose them, once apprehended, in the investigation of knowledge. Why did I also imprint the seal of reason, which by the sieve of its discernment separates the empty things of falsehood from the serious things of truth? Through me too the power of memory serves you; in the storehouse of recollection it hoards the noble wealth of knowledge. Thus I blessed both [Note: [Col. 0443] That is, body and soul.] with gifts, so that neither might lament its own poverty nor complain of the other’s abundance. Therefore, just as the aforesaid marriage was celebrated by my consent, so at my will that same marital union shall cease [Note: [Col. 0443] ‘Shall be annulled.’].

“And the generosity of my power shines forth not only in you individually but in every member of the universe. I am she who fashioned human nature after the exemplary likeness of the worldly machine, so that in humanity, as in a mirror, the written nature of the world itself may appear. For just as the harmonious discord of the four elements, a unity in plurality, dissonant consonance, consenting disagreement, brings together the structures of the worldly palace, so the corresponding disparity of the four complexions, unequal equality, deformed conformity, divided identity, compacts the structure of the human body. And the qualities that mediate agreement among the elements establish the firmness of peace among the four humors as well. And just as, against the fixed revolution of the firmament, the army of planets marches with contrary motion, so continuous hostility of sensuality and reason is found in human beings. For the motion of reason, rising from the east of celestial things and passing through the west of earthly things, returns to heavenly things by contemplating them [Note: [Col. 0443] Another copy reads: ‘by contemplating earthly things, it returns to heaven.’]. On the contrary, the wandering planetary movement of sensuality sometimes slips, against the firmament of reason, into the west of earthly things.

“Sensuality [Note: [Col. 0443] That is, Sensuality.] leads the human mind into the setting of vices, so that it may set; Reason [Note: [Col. 0443] Reason.] invites it toward the east of virtues, so that it may rise. The former transforms man, by degeneration, into a beast; the latter potentially transfigures man into a god. The former extinguishes the mind’s light in the night of desire; the latter illuminates the mind’s night with the light of contemplation. The former makes man revel with brute beasts; the latter makes him converse with angels. The former compels man to live in exile from his homeland; the latter teaches man to find a homeland in exile. Nor can human nature accuse the ordering of my dispensation in this matter. For by the counsel of reason I ordained such a duel of opposition between these champions that, if in this contest reason can bend sensuality toward refutation, the preceding victory shall not lack its consequent reward. Rewards acquired by victories shine more beautifully than other gifts; gifts purchased by labors likewise shine more pleasantly than gratuitous ones.

“For he who receives a gift through labor deserves the praises of greater commendation than one who receives it in idleness. For preceding labor infuses a certain sweetness into the reward that follows and rewards the laborer with greater favor. In these, and in Nature’s more ample gifts, the world finds its qualities in man [Note: [Col. 0443] ‘It brings its qualities into man. God’s providence governs all things.’]. Consider how, in this world as though in a noble city, a certain majesty of the commonwealth is established by fixed governance. For in heaven, as in the citadel of the human city, the eternal emperor sits in imperial state; from him an edict has eternally gone forth that the knowledge of individual things should be inscribed in the book of his providence. In the air, as in the middle of the city, the celestial host of angels, serving [Note: [Col. 0443] ‘Fighting.’] in delegated administration, applies its diligent guardianship to humanity; humanity, dwelling like a foreigner in the suburb of the world, does not refuse to render obedience to the angelic soldiery. Thus in this commonwealth God commands, the angel acts, and man obeys.

> God creates man by acting [Note: [Col. 0443] ‘By commanding.’];  
> the angel procreates by acting;  
> man restores himself by obeying.  
>
> God orders a thing by authority;  
> the angel arranges it by action;  
> man submits himself to the will of the agent.  
>
> God commands by the mastery of authority;  
> the angel acts by the ministry of action;  
> man obeys through the mystery of regeneration.

“Now the course of our reasoning wanders too far abroad, daring to raise its discourse to the ineffable secret of deity—a matter whose understanding exhausts the sighs of our mind. Yet the image of this most orderly commonwealth is reflected in man. In the citadel of the head, sovereign Wisdom rests; the other powers obey her as demi-goddesses obey a goddess. For the power of natural intelligence, the rational power, and the power that remembers things past, inhabiting various chambers of the head, burn in her service. In the heart, as in the center of the human city, Magnanimity has established its dwelling. Having professed its military service under Prudence’s command, it acts as that command determines. The kidneys, like suburbs, grant the body’s furthest part to desirous pleasures; not daring to oppose Magnanimity’s command, they obey its will. Thus in this commonwealth Wisdom assumes the role of ruler; Magnanimity the care [Note: [Col. 0443] ‘Likeness.’] of the agent; Pleasure usurps the image of the obedient subject.

“In the other parts of the human body too the image of the world is figured. For just as in the world the benefit of solar heat heals languishing things, so in man heat proceeding from the foundation of the heart vivifies and invigorates the parts of the human body. Just as the moon in the worldly machine is mother of many humors, so the liver in man distributes corresponding moisture to the limbs. And just as the moon languishes when deprived of the sun’s light, so the liver’s power grows torpid when bereft of the heart’s life-giving aid. And just as the air is clothed in darkness by the sun’s absence, so without the heart’s benefit vital power breathes in vain. Besides, observe how the world is variously changed [Note: [Col. 0445] ‘Varied.’] by the succession of seasons. Now the infancy of spring sports; now it advances in the youth of summer; now it matures in autumn’s manhood; now it turns gray in winter’s old age. A like alternation of time and the same variety changes the age of man. When the dawn of human age rises, morning spring arises for man; when life’s course completes the further bounds of age, man experiences the midday of youth’s summer. But when a longer life has completed, as it were, the ninth hour of age, man enters the autumn of manhood; and, with age inclining toward its west, when old age announces life’s evening, winter’s icy chill of senescence compels man to whiten with its frosts.

“In all these things the effect of my power is reflected ineffably; yet I have decreed to veil the face of my power in many figures, protecting its secret from contempt, lest, if I imparted familiar knowledge of myself, things that first flourished as precious because unknown should afterwards become cheap through being known. For, as the common proverb testifies: ‘The sharing of a familiar thing is the mother of contempt.’ And the trumpet of Aristotelian authority proclaims: ‘He diminishes the majesty of secrets who divulges [Note: [Col. 0445] ‘Reveals.’] secrets to the unworthy.’”

But lest, in this prerogative of my power, I seem arrogantly to detract from God, I most certainly profess myself the humble disciple of the supreme Master. For I [Note: [Col. 0445] “I, Nature.”], though I work, cannot closely follow the footsteps of God at work; rather, from afar and, as it were, sighing, I gaze upon Him working. His operation is simple; mine manifold. His work is sufficient; mine deficient. His work is wonderful; mine mutable. He is unbegotten; I am born. He is maker; I made. He is the craftsman of my work; I the work of a craftsman. He works from nothing; I beg my work from something. He works in His own name; I work under His name. [Col. 0445D] He bids a thing exist by His nod alone; but my operation is a mark of the divine operation. And so that, in comparison with divine power, you may recognize my power as powerless, know my effect to be defect, and consider my vigor to be worthlessness, consult the authority of theological learning, to whose trustworthiness rather than to the firmness of my arguments you ought to give assent. For, according to its faithful testimony, man is born by my action and reborn by God’s authority. Through me he is called from non-being into being; through Him he is brought to a better being [Note: [Col. 0445] “Brought forth.”]. For through me man is begotten for death; through Him he is re-created [Col. 0446A] for life. Yet the ministry of my profession is excluded from this mystery of the second birth; nor does such a birth require such a midwife. Rather, I, Nature, do not know the nature of this birth; and, in attempting to understand these things, the sharpness of my intellect fails and the light of my reason is confounded: understanding is transformed by what is understood, and sense is confounded by insensible things.

And since natural reason languishes in all these matters, we reverence the secret of so great a thing by the firmness of faith alone. Nor is it surprising if theology does not show me familiarity in these things, since in most matters we think not contrary but differently. I compare faith by reason; she compares reason by faith. I know in order that I may believe; she believes in order that she may know. I assent knowingly; she perceives while assenting. I scarcely see visible things; she comprehends incomprehensible things [Col. 0446B] in a mirror. I scarcely measure the smallest things with understanding; she measures immeasurable things with reason. I walk, as it were, beast-like upon the earth; but she serves in the secret place of heaven.

And although it is not my office to treat of the aforesaid matters [Note: [Col. 0445] “The aforesaid matters are not the business of my treatment.”], nevertheless I have allowed my discourse to wander into them, so that, in comparison with God’s superlative power, you may not doubt that my own power is diminished. Yet although my effect fails when compared with divine power, when matched against human power it excels [Note: [Col. 0445] “Prospers.”]. Thus, in a certain dining-room of comparison, we may find three degrees of power: God’s power may be called superlative, Nature’s comparative, and man’s positive. All this, without any searching inquiry, affords you familiar knowledge of me [Col. 0446C]. And, to speak more familiarly, I am Nature, who by the gift of my condescension have made you a participant in my presence and have deigned to bless you with my companionship.

### How Alan speaks to Nature

When by these words Nature had unveiled her countenance to me, and by her admonition, as though by a preliminary key, had opened for me the door of knowing her, the little cloud of astonishment evaporated from the confines of my mind. Through this admonition, as by some medicinal draught, the stomach of my mind, nauseated, vomited forth all remnants of phantasy. Returning, therefore, from the wandering of my mind to myself, I again cast myself at the footsteps of Nature and, by way of greeting, marked her feet with many impressions of kisses. Then [Col. 0446D] raising myself up, I offered her, with reverent bowing of the head as though to divine majesty, a living libation of greeting.

Then, seeking the aid of an excuse, I implored her favor with prayers sweetened by the honey of humility—lest she impute it either to the error of my insignificance, or charge it to the disdain of indignation, or ascribe it to the poisons of ingratitude, that I had paid no festivity of gladness to celebrate her arrival, but had instead been struck by her appearance as by the strange apparition of a monstrous phantom and lulled into the false death of ecstasy—[Col. 0447A] saying that it was no wonder if, in the presence of so great a dignity, the shadow of my mortality grew pale; if, at the noon of so great a majesty, the little ray of my discernment vanished into the evening of error; if, at the appearance of such happiness, my littleness blushed. For the dark mist of ignorance belonging to human frailty, the dull incapacity for wonder, and the frequent shock of astonishment are joined by a kind of bond of kinship, so that, from their sociable cohabitation, human frailty is like a pupil dwelling with an instructing master who shapes the habits of his household: at the first encounter with novel things, in the service of great matters, it is accustomed to be darkened by ignorance, struck by stupor, and often wounded by wonder.

While this path of excuse was preparing for me a favorable entrance to the queen [Col. 0447B] and winning her favor more readily, it also gave me greater confidence in hearing things of greater moment. Setting before her judgment the uncertainty of a doubt of mine, which disturbed the lodging-place of my mind under the impulse of excessive agitation, I broke out in the following words of inquiry:

### Alan’s words to Nature

O offspring of God and mother of things,  
Bond of the world and abiding nexus,  
Jewel to earthly things, mirror to passing things,  
Light-bringer of the world.

Peace, love, strength, governance, power,  
Order, law, end, way, guide, origin,  
Life, light, splendor, appearance, form,  
[Col. 0447C] Rule of the world.

You who govern the world by your reins,  
Bind all things, established in a harmonious knot,  
And marry heaven to earth with the glue  
Of peace.

You who, recalling the many ideas of the *nous* [νοῦς],  
Fashion the individual species of things,  
Clothe things in forms, and with your thumb  
Shape the cloak of form.

Whom heaven favors, air serves,  
Earth cultivates, water venerates,  
To whom, as mistress of the world,  
All things pay tribute.

You who bind day to night in alternating turns,  
Give the waxen sun to day,  
[Col. 0447D] And lull night’s clouds with the bright  
Mirror of the moon.

You who gild the pole with diverse stars,  
Making serene the throne of our ether  
With gems of stars, and filling heaven  
With its varied soldiery.

You who, Protean, change heaven’s face  
With new shapes, giving the barren host  
Of our air a region,  
And binding it by law.

At whose nod the world grows young,  
The wood bristles with leafy hair,  
And Earth takes pride in the flowered garment  
[Col. 0448A] Which is your dress.

You who bury and swell the threats of the sea,  
Checking the sea’s course when it rages,  
Lest the flood of ocean  
May bury the land’s expanse.

### Alan’s first question

Reveal to one who asks the cause of your journey:  
Why do you seek the earth, a stranger to heaven?  
Why do you offer the gifts  
Of your divinity to our lands?

### Second question

Why are your cheeks moistened with the rain of weeping?  
What do the tears of your face foretell?  
Weeping is the faithful tongue  
Of inward sorrow.

[Col. 0448B]

### Nature’s reply

The aforesaid virgin, showing that the solution of this question stood watch in the vestibule, said: “Do you not know that the aberration of the earthly sphere, the disordering of worldly order, the negligence of the world’s court, and the injury done to law have compelled me to descend from the inner chambers of the heavenly mystery into the common brothels of earthly things? If you would gather in the affectionate disposition of your mind, and store in the treasury of your breast, what I am about to say, I would unravel the labyrinth of your doubt.”

To this I returned an answering requital, in a restrained modulation of voice: “Nothing, O heavenly queen, do I hunger for with more ardent desire than the untying of this question.”

[Col. 0448C]

### Solution of the first question

Then she said: “Since all things are held subject to the law of their origin by my laws and owe me the payment of their appointed tribute, almost all regularly obey my edicts by the lawful rendering of tributary service. But man alone is excluded from the rule of this universe by an anomalous exception: stripped of the robe of modesty and prostituted in the brothel of meretricious shamelessness, he dares to stir up the tumult of a lawsuit against the majesty of his mistress—indeed, to inflame his mother with the rage of civil war.

“All other things, to which I have granted humbler offices by my favor, are bound by voluntary submission, according to the condition [Note: [Col. 0447] “Condition.”] of their professions, to the sanctions of my decrees. But man, who has drained almost the entire treasury of my riches, [Col. 0448D] attempting to denaturalize Nature’s natural things, arms against me the injury of shameless [Note: [Col. 0447] “Meretricious.”] Venus.

“Observe how almost everything, according to the promulgation of my edict, renders the statutes of my law as the reason of its native condition demands. The firmament, encompassing [Note: [Col. 0447] “Circling.”] all things in its daily circuit, according to the teaching of my discipline, returns whence it proceeds and advances whither it goes, not by the idle sameness of its revolution. The stars, shining for the honor of that firmament, clothing it in their adornments, completing the short day-stages of their journey, and measuring its spaces by diverse revolutions, serve my majesty. The planets, as the edict of my disposition [Col. 0449A] has ordained, restrain the impetus of the firmament, travel eastward by a contrary striving [Note: [Col. 0449] “Course.”], and afterwards return homeward to the region of their setting.

“The air, disciplined by my teachings, now rejoices in a favorable breeze; now, as though in sympathy with the tears of clouds, weeps; now is angered by the clashes [Note: [Col. 0449] “Battles.”] of winds; now is lit by flashes of lightning; now is shaken by the threatening roar of thunder; now is baked in the furnace of heat [Note: [Col. 0449] “Burning heat.”]; now is made harsh by the severity of cold. Birds, stamped with various natures, under the government of my direction, crossing the waves of air by the rowing of their wings, earnestly attend to my disciplines. Through the intervention of my care, the sea, cemented to the earth by firm bonds of friendship, not daring to violate the sacrament of pledged faith with its sister, fears to wander beyond the appointed [Col. 0449B] boundary of its excursion into the dwellings of the land. At the sole discretion of my will [Note: [Col. 0449] “Nevertheless.”], it now swells into the anger of storm, now returns to the peace of calm, now, lifted by the pride of its swelling, assumes the image of a mountain, now is drawn out into a level plain. Fish, bound by the decree of my provision [Note: [Col. 0449] “Profession.”], fear to derogate from the canons of my rules. At the command of my decree, rains are married to the earth in a kind of nuptial embrace; and, laboring to fashion offspring, they do not cease, by untiring birth-giving, to bring forth diverse species of things.

“Earthly animals, under the examination of my strict authority [Note: [Col. 0449] “Disposition.”], profess the varied services of their obedience to my command. The earth now grows white with wintry [Col. 0449C] old age, now is crowned with a floral head of hair. The forest now is hair-covered with locks of leaves, now is shaved bare by winter’s sharp razor. Winter enfolds seeds buried in the womb of Mother Earth; spring releases what was confined; summer ripens the harvests; autumn displays its abundance.

“And why do I permit myself to wander through every stage of my account? Man alone spurns the lyre of my governance and raves under the lyre of deranged Orpheus. For the human race, degenerating from its own nobility, becoming barbarous in the coupling of genders, and changing Venus’s rules, employs an excessively irregular metaplasm. Thus man, made Tiresias by anomalous Venus, disorderly converts direct predication into contraposition [Col. 0449D]. Departing from Venus’s orthography, man is discovered to be a sophistical false-writer. Further, avoiding the analogy of the Dionaean art, he degenerates into a faulty anastrophe; and, while in such a matter he destroys me, in his frenzy [Note: [Col. 0449] “Siren-song.”] he contrives a *thesis* against me.

“I repent that I have generally endowed human natures with so many prerogatives of beauty, when they dishonor the glory of comeliness by abuse; deform the beauty of form with Venereal deformity; discolor the hue of beauty with the dark color of adulterous desire; and, by flowering into vices, deflower Flora’s flower. Why did I adorn the face of the Tyndarid woman—Helen—with godlike beauty, when she compelled the use of beauty to become the abuse of prostitution, abandoning the bond of the royal bed and shamefully binding herself to Paris?

“Pasiphaë too, driven by the furies of hyperbolical Venus, craftily celebrated bestial marriage with a brute under the guise of a bull; drawing for herself a still more shameful conclusion by a paralogism, she concluded with the bull’s astonishing sophism. Myrrha also, pricked by the goads of desire, in her father’s sweetness degenerating from a daughter’s love, performed a mother’s office with her father. Medea, becoming a stepmother to her own son, destroyed the glorious little work of Venus in order to seek Venus’s inglorious work. Narcissus too, deceived by his own shadow which feigned another Narcissus, [Col. 0450B] captivated by a shadow, believing himself to be another self, incurred from himself, for himself, the danger of love. Many other young men also, clothed by my grace in the honor of beauty, drunk with love of money, have transferred the hammers of their Venus to the offices of an anvil.

“So great a multitude of monstrous human beings roams through the entire breadth of the world; by their bewitching contagion chastity is poisoned. Of those persons who profess Venus’s grammar, some embrace only the masculine gender, others the feminine, others the common or promiscuous gender; certain others, as though of heteroclite gender, are irregularly declined in the feminine during winter and in the masculine during summer. There are those who, disputing in Venus’s logic, assign in their conclusions the law of subject and predicate by reciprocal relation. There are [Col. 0450C] those who, acting in the place of a subject, do not know how to be predicated. There are those who only predicate, and do not observe the lawful subjection of the subject. Others, disdaining to enter Dione’s royal palace, carry on a lamentable game beneath its vestibule. Against all these the laws complain; statutes are armed and seek to avenge their injuries with the sword of vengeance. Therefore do not wonder that I enter upon these profane novelties of speech, since profane people dare to revel still more profanely. I indignantly vomit forth such things so that modest people may reverence the character of modesty, while immodest people may be excluded from the brothels of shamelessness. Knowledge of evil is indeed a useful safeguard: it punishes those branded with culpable shamelessness, and rewards those free from it [Col. 0450D]. Now the file of my solution has removed the scruple of your question.”

### Solution of Alan’s second question

“For this reason, leaving the secretarial chambers of the heavenly palace above, I came down to the setting of this perishable earthliness: that I might lay before you, as before my familiar friend and secretary, a lamenting complaint concerning the execrable excesses of humankind; and that I might decide with you what response of punishment ought to be given to such an array of crimes, so that a penalty corresponding to the bites of the aforesaid deeds might bite back with the retaliation of punishment.”

[Col. 0451A]

Then I said: “O mediatrix of all things, unless I feared that the multitude of my questions might provoke weariness in your goodwill, I would set the darkness of another doubt of mine before the light of your discernment.”

Then she said: “Indeed, share with my hearing all your questions—not merely youthful ones, but even those ancient with the rust of old age—so that by the firmness of our solutions the agitation of your doubts may be calmed.”

### Alan’s third question

Then I said: “I wonder why, in treating poets’ fictions, you arm the stings of these invectives only against the plagues of humankind, when we read that the gods too limped with the same foot of aberration.”

[Col. 0451B]

“For Jupiter, carrying the young Ganymede up to the heights, transformed relative Venus into a transferred relation; and him whom he appointed to serve him drink at table by day he made subject to himself in bed by night. Bacchus and Apollo likewise, co-heirs of their father’s wantonness, not by the command of divine power but through the spell of superstitious Venus, turned into women by feigning boys.”

### Nature’s response

Then she, assuming with agitation the countenance of authentic serenity, said: “Do you clothe a question which is unworthy even of the appearance of doubt in the image of a question’s garment? Do you attempt to place faith in the shadowy inventions of poets, painted by the skill of poetic art? Are not the things discussed in the childish cradles of poetic instruction removed by the more elevated file of philosophical inquiry? Do you not know how poets, without any remedy of concealment, prostitute naked falsehood to their hearers, so that with a certain honeyed sweetness they may intoxicate the ears of listeners as though by enchantment?
