How they cloak falsehood itself with a kind of hypocrisy of plausibility, so that through images of examples they may stamp human minds upon the anvil of moral training?

“But while the lyre of poetry resounds falsely in the superficial bark of the letter, within it speaks secretly to hearers of a higher meaning, so that, when the outer shell of falsehood has been cast aside, the reader may secretly find within a sweeter kernel of truth. Poets also sometimes join historical [Col. 0451D] events to fabulous jesting by an elegant fiction, so that a more elegant picture of the narrative may result from the fitting union of diverse elements. Yet when poets dream of a plurality of gods, or say that the gods themselves have submitted to Venus’s rods, in these things the shadow of falsehood gleams, and the poet is not thereby found to have departed from the character proper to him.

“For now that Epicurus’s dreams are asleep, the Manichaeans’ madness healed, Aristotle’s subtleties refuted, and Arius’s deceptions exposed, reason proves, the world proclaims, faith believes, and Scripture testifies to the one unity of God. In Him no blemish is found; no plague of vice assaults Him; no movement of temptation contends with Him. He is splendor never failing, life untiring and [Col. 0452A] undying, a fountain ever springing, the wise seedbed of the seed of life, the principal principle, the originating beginning of goodness. Therefore, although, as poets have testified, many human beings have literally abused such ordinances of Venus, yet that narrative lies when it says that there are gods, or that the gods themselves have lurked in Venus’s gymnasia; it declines into the evening sunset of excessive falsehood. Therefore I have covered those things with the cloud of silence, while setting forth the others in the light of a true narrative.”

To this I said: “I now recognize that my question smells of the spark of excessive ignorance; yet, if some other little and poor question dared to gain the hearing of your dignity, I would seek something by asking.”

To this she said: “Did I not long ago set forth the free reins of inquiry, without any obstacle of restraint?”

[Col. 0452B]

### Fourth question

Then I said: “I wonder why certain portions of your tunic, which ought to be joined in the fabric of marriage, suffer divorces in that part of their conjunction in which the visions of a picture represent the image of a human being?”

### Solution of the question

Then she said: “From what has been explained you may now infer what mystery the figured parenthesis of the tear signifies. For, since, as we have said, many men arm themselves with the injuries of vices against their own mother, thereby establishing between themselves and her the greatest chaos of dissension, they violently lay violent hands on me, snatch away my garments piece by piece for themselves, and compel me—whom they ought to clothe in the honor of reverence—to be bereft of garments [Col. 0452C] and, so far as lies in them, to prostitute myself meretriciously. Therefore this tear in the covering depicts that, in the vicious insults of man alone, the ornaments of my modesty suffer the humiliations of rending.”

Then I said: “Now that the waves of my doubts have been stilled by the serenity of your solutions, they grant my mind a respite from questioning. If it pleased your inclination, I would ardently desire to know:

### Alan’s fifth question

“What rational reason, what undiscerning indiscretion, what misguided love so compelled the spark of reason to sleep in man that, intoxicated by the Lethean cup of sensuality, man became an apostate from your laws—indeed, even unlawfully warred against your laws?”

[Col. 0452D]

### Solution of the question

To this she said: “If you wish to know the origin of this most shameful plague, kindle the little fire of your mind more deeply, and you will find a keener desire for understanding. Subtlety dispels dullness of intellect; steadiness of attention restrains the waves of thought. Beginning from a higher point, I wish to weave the series of my account toward a more excellent object of inquiry.

“For I do not wish, as before, to explain the matters proposed in the flat plainness of words, or to profane profane things with profane novelties of speech. Rather, I wish to gild shameful matters with the golden trappings of modest words and clothe them in the varied colors of beautiful language. It is fitting to purple the dross of the aforesaid vices with gilded utterances [Col. 0453A] and embalm the foul stench of words with honeyed fragrance, lest, if the stink of so great a dungheap should reach ears through too public a proclamation, it should invite the people to the stomach of indignation and the vomiting of nausea.

“Yet sometimes, as we have noted above, because speech ought to be akin to the things of which we speak, the deformity of expression must be conformed to the deformity of the matter. In the following treatment, however, lest the explicitness of speech (*cathephaton*) offend the ears of readers or foulness find a place in a virgin mouth, I wish to grant the aforesaid monsters of vice the cloak of euphonious speech.”

Then I said: “The hunger of my understanding, the burning sharpness of my intellect, the fervor of my inflamed mind, and the steadiness and constancy of my attention demand what you promise.”

Then she said: “When God wished to bring forth the fabric of the worldly palace from the ideal chamber of preconception, and to portray, as it were, with the material word of its real existence the mental word which from eternity He had conceived concerning the constitution of the world, He—as the world’s elegant architect, as the goldsmith-maker of a golden fabric, as the skillful artificer of a wondrous craft, as the maker of an admirable work—created the marvelous form of the worldly palace, not by the laboring aid of an external instrument, not by the help of pre-existing matter, not through the compulsion of need, but by the command of His will alone. God, assigning various species of things to the worldly palace, tempered by the harmony of lawful order those things which were separated by the strife of differing kinds; He gave them laws and bound them by ordinances. Thus He transformed into the peaceful friendship of concord the conflict of opposition among things contrary by opposition of their kinds—between which opposition itself had placed distance—joining them by the reciprocal kisses of a mutual relation. [Col. 0453C]

“Therefore, all things being joined in harmony by subtle chains of invisible union, plurality returned to unity, diversity to identity, dissonance to consonance, discord to concord, in a peaceful union. But after the universal artificer had clothed all things in the faces of their natures and married them all to one another in lawful marriages of proportion, He wished to bestow upon perishable things, through the reciprocal circuit of birth and death, stability through instability, infinity through end, and eternity through temporality; and He wished the series of things to be woven continually by the ordered reciprocity of birth. He therefore decreed that, stamped with the seal of expressed conformity, things like should be brought forth from like along the lawful path of derived propagation. [Col. 0453D]

“He appointed me, then, as His vicar and minter for stamping the kinds of things, so that, coining the images of things upon their proper anvils, I should not permit what had been formed to deviate from the shape of the anvil; but that, by the skill with which I work, the copied face, deprived of no endowments of the exemplar, should in no way stray from the countenance of its model. Obeying, therefore, the command of Him who commands, I rendered the stamped faces of individual things: working as though stamping various related things, modeling the image of the copy after the image of the exemplar, and forming conformable things from conformable things. Yet I exercised the ministry of this operation under the command of divine power in such a way that the right hand of supreme majesty guided the hand of my attention, because the pen of my writing would wander through sudden deviation unless it were governed by the finger of the supreme disposer.

“But because I could not refine so many species of things without the supporting craftsmanship of a subordinate artificer, and because it pleased me to remain in the pleasant palace of the ethereal region—[Col. 0454A] where the quarrel of winds does not destroy the peace of serenity, where the accidental night of clouds does not bury the untiring ether, where no injury of tempest rages, where no madness of riotous thunder threatens—I placed Venus, skilled in ineffable knowledge and deputy of my operation, in the suburb of the world. There, under the direction of my command, aided by the diligence of her husband Hymenaeus and her son Cupid, she labors over the diverse shaping of earthly animals, regularly fitting her craft-hammers to their anvils, weaving the succession of the human race in tireless continuity, and repairing the injuries inflicted by the hands of the Fates.

“As, in this course of narrative, speech arose concerning Cupid, I inserted into the aforesaid narrative—interrupted by a parenthesis of my words—the tenor of this question.”

### Alan’s sixth question

[Col. 0454C]

“Ah, ah! Unless I feared that the interruption of your discourse and the pursuit of my questions might incur the offense of your kindness, I would wish to learn, from the picture of your description, the nature of Cupid, of whom your preceding discourse has made some small mention. For although many authors have portrayed his nature under the covering of enigmatic allegory, they have left us no traces of certainty. Yet in the human race his authority is read as so powerful in experience that no one—whether marked with the seal of nobility, clothed in the beauty conferred by the privilege of wisdom, armed with the armor of courage, arrayed in the mantle and robe of beauty, or endowed with the honors of other graces—can exempt himself from the universality of Cupid’s [Col. 0454D] dominion.”

### Solution of the question

Then she, with a measured movement of the head and words promising rebuke, said: “I believe that you serve as a soldier for pay in Cupid’s camp and are linked to him by some brotherhood of intimate kinship. For you eagerly strive to investigate his inextricable labyrinth, whereas you ought rather to apply your mind’s attention [Note: [Col. 0453D] “Intention.”] more earnestly to my account enriched with the riches of its meanings. Yet before the course of my speech proceeds to what follows, because I pity the weakness of your human condition, I wish, so far as my power permits, to uproot the darkness of your ignorance. Moreover, I am bound by the pledge of my promise to provide solutions to your questions. Therefore, whether by describing with a definite description or defining with a lawful definition, I shall show what cannot be shown and unravel what cannot be unraveled, although it, being bound under no natural combinations and awaiting no investigation of the intellect, could be designated by the seal of no description.

“Let this be the description of a circumscribed thing; let this be the explanation of an inexplicable nature; let this be knowledge of the unknown and science acquired concerning the knowable—though restrained by the loftiness of style:

> Love is peace joined to hatred, fidelity to deceit, hope to fear,  
> And madness mingled with reason.  
> A sweet shipwreck, a light burden, a pleasing Charybdis,  
> [Col. 0455B] A harmless sickness and a satisfied hunger.  
> Hunger that satisfies, drunken thirst, false pleasure,  
> Joyful sadness, joys full of evils.  
> A sweet evil, evil sweetness, sweetness bitter to itself,  
> Whose scent is savory and whose taste unsavory.  
> A welcome tempest, a bright night, a dark light,  
> Death alive, life dying, a pleasant evil.  
> A sin of pardon, a pardonable fault, a playful  
> Punishment, a pious crime—indeed, a pleasant wickedness.  
> An unstable game, a stable deception, strength  
> That is weak, mobility that is firm, firm movement.  
> Foolish reason, mad prudence, sad  
> Prosperity, tearful laughter, sick repose.  
> A caressing hell, a sorrowful paradise, a pleasant  
> Prison, a springlike winter, a wintry spring, an evil.
>
> A cruel moth of the mind, felt by a king’s purple,  
> Yet passing by not even a beggar’s cloak.  
> Does not Cupid, through antiphrasis, performing many wonders,  
> Make Proteus of every kind of human being?  
> While this madness rages, Scylla lays aside her fury,  
> And pious Aeneas begins to be Nero.  
> Paris thunders with the sword; Tydeus grows soft in love;  
> Nestor becomes young, and Melincta becomes old.  
> Thersites borrows Paris’s beauty; Davus, Adonis’s;  
> And all Adonis passes into Davus.  
> Wealthy Crassus is needy; Codrus, needy, abounds;  
> Bavius composes poetry; Maro’s muse is dull.  
> Ennius speaks eloquently, and Marcus falls silent; Ulysses  
> Becomes foolish, while Ajax becomes wise by folly.
>
> [Col. 0455D] He who formerly conquered the sophisms of authors by solving them  
> Is conquered by this monster, though he subdues other monsters.  
> Every woman runs into crime, and of her own accord,  
> If this madness infects her mind.  
> Daughter kills father, sister her brother, bride her husband  
> By deceit, forestalling the hand of fate.  
> Thus, by a wicked ascent, she brutally cuts short her husband’s  
> Body, when she reaps his head with a stealthy sword.  
> The mother herself is compelled not to know her parent’s name,  
> And, while herself giving birth, to face deceits in childbirth.  
> The son is amazed to have found a stepmother in his mother,  
> And fraud in faith, deceits in devotion.  
> Thus in Medea two names struggle together,  
> Since she desires to be at once mother and stepmother.  
> She did not know how to be a sister, or to preserve herself as a sister,  
> [Col. 0456A] When Byblis loved Caunus too much.  
> So too Myrrha, excessively subject to her own parent,  
> Was parent in her begetter, mother in her father.  
> But why teach more? Every lover is compelled to go beneath  
> Cupid’s spear and to pay him his dues.  
> He campaigns among all; his rule scarcely exempts anyone;  
> His thunderbolt and wrath strike everything.  
> Against him neither integrity, prudence, the grace of beauty,  
> Flowing wealth, nor the summit of nobility can prevail.  
> Theft, deceit, fear, anger, madness, fraud, impulse, error,  
> Sadness: these inhabit his realms as guests.  
> Here reason is to lack reason, and the proper measure  
> Is to lack measure; faith is not to have kept faith.  
> Proffering sweet things, he takes up bitter ones;  
> He brings poison, enclosing the best things in an evil end.
>
> [Col. 0456B] He attracts while ensnaring, smiles while mocking,  
> Anoints while pricking, affects while infecting, hates while loving.  
> Yet you may restrain that pain itself:  
> If you flee, no better remedy is given.  
> If you wish to avoid Venus, avoid places and times,  
> For place and time supply her fodder.  
> If you pursue, she follows; by fleeing she is put to flight;  
> If you yield, she yields; if you flee, she flees.”

“Now, from this workmanship of my teaching, the theory of Cupid’s art shines forth; but through the book of experience you will be able to acquire its practice. Nor is it surprising if I insert notes of censure into the foregoing depiction of Cupid, though he is linked to me by a clasp of close kinship. [Col. 0456C] It was not the dark rust of slanderous malice, the heat of burning hatred issuing outward, or the tyrant of envy raging abroad that drove me to these accusations of invective, but rather lest I seem to strangle by silence the evident truth that speaks for itself.

“For I do not condemn Cupid’s original nature as dishonorable if it is circumscribed by the reins of modesty and restrained by the reins of temperance; if the shoot of its excursion does not pass beyond its assigned bounds and its heat does not boil up into excessive swelling. But if its spark becomes a flame, or its little spring grows into a torrent, the luxuriance of its excess demands the pruning sickle, and the swelling of exuberance requires the remedy of medicine. For every excess disturbs the course of temperate moderation, [Col. 0456D] and the inflation of diseased abundance swells forth, as it were, into abscesses of vices.

First, therefore, the theatrical discourse, having wandered through the wantonness of buffoonery, is offered to your youth as a dish; now let the pen, somewhat more mature, return to the purpose of the proposed narrative. As I explained in preliminary fashion above, I assigned Venus to the propagation to be fashioned of terrestrial animals, so that, by stamping out various materials in the things to be fashioned, she might lay their foundations. But I, in the manifold purification of natures, in order that I might apply the hand of final polishing to the works, and in order that the fidelity of the instruments might exclude the leaven of faulty operation, fashioned for her two lawful hammers, by which she might both avoid the snares of the Fates and present things of manifold essence. I also assigned noble anvils, [Col. 0457A] workshops, to the same craft, commanding her faithfully to devote herself to the forming of things by fitting those same hammers to them, lest she permit the hammers to wander away from the anvils through any deviation.

For the office of writing I had likewise bestowed upon her a very powerful pen, so that, on suitable sheets requiring the writing of that pen—which she had obtained through the benefit of my gift—she might represent the kinds of things according to the rule of my orthography, and might not allow it to stray from the path of proper description into the byway of false writing. But since genial intercourse itself was obliged, by ordered combinations, to join together dissimilar things of different sexes, set in opposition for carrying out the propagation of things, I taught her, under masterly discipline and by courtly precepts, to cultivate that discipline which admits the canonical constructions of grammatical art in the artful unions of her own connections, so that the nobility of her craft might suffer no detriment to its glory through ignorance of any art; but excludes all other constructions, outside the ordinary ones and not redeemed by the excuse of any figure.

For although, as grammar attests, the order of nature recognizes especially two genders, masculine and feminine—although certain persons, impoverished in their sexual mark, might, in my opinion, be classed under the designation of the neuter gender—yet I impressed upon Cypris, under the most intimate warnings and the thunder of threats, that in her unions, according to the requirement of reason, she should celebrate only the natural construction of [Col. 0457C] masculine and feminine gender. For since the masculine gender, through the requirement of genial relation, takes to itself its feminine, if a construction of these genders is performed anomalously, so that things of the same sex are joined to one another, that construction can merit no pardon from me, either by the remedy of invocation or the support of conception. For if the masculine gender demands a like gender through the wrong of a certain irrational reason, no decorum of figure can excuse the fault of that conjunction; rather, it will be disgraced by the inexcusable monstrosity of solecism.

Furthermore, my command enjoined Cypris that she herself, in her constructions, should observe the ordinary rules of subject and predicate [Col. 0457D]: a thing marked by the character of the feminine sex she should assign to the office of subject; a thing specified as of masculine gender she should place in the position of predicate. Thus neither might the predicate decline into the place of the subject, nor the subject migrate into the region of the predicate; and although each is governed by the other, the predicate, under the property of the adjective, and the subject, under the property of the substantive, should retain its own proper character, as called for by the laws of requirement.

Furthermore, I added that the union of Venus should not receive the uniform character of a transitive construction, or the course of reciprocity, or the winding turn of retransition; content with the straight direction of transition alone, it should also not suffer any excessive interruption by some digressing nature. Thus the active gender might not, by usurping assumption, pass into the passive; nor might the same return into the active by the disposition of its own property; nor, retaining the nature of the active beneath the lettering of the passive, might it take upon itself the law of a deponent termination. Nor is it surprising if very many matters enrolled under the title of grammatical faculty suffer rejection from the dwelling of Venus’s art: she admits into the bosom of her familiarity those [Col. 0458A] that obey the rules of her prescription, but suspends in exclusion by an eternal anathema those that attempt, by the assaults of most eloquent contradiction, to overthrow her laws. For the authority of philosophical assertion acknowledges that many of the highest matters are common to diverse faculties, while some, beyond the dwellings of their own disciplines, have no license to range abroad.

But because I knew that Venus, as a new combatant, would enter the contest of disputation against the subtle objections of the Fates, I feared that Venus, through some evasive deceit, might shrink from the subtleties of Atropos’s constraining conclusion. Therefore I taught her that discipline by which she might exceed, according to the precepts of disputative art, the forms of their arguments; and how, in the fraudulent arguments of an adversary, she might discover the hiding-place of fallacy, so that she might conduct the contest of disputation more securely against the snares of the opposing party, and by an objection refute similar arguments of opposition.

I also ordered that her syllogistic combination, confined to the short compass of two terms and subject to no Aristotelian figures, should be woven in a suitable arrangement of three propositions—so much so that in each proposition the greater extreme should perform the office of predicate and the lesser be bound by the laws of being subject. In the first proposition, the predicate should adhere to the subject not by any mode of true inherence, but solely by reason of an intrinsic compact. In the assumption, however, by the eyes of relatives and reciprocal impressions, the greater extreme should be joined more expressly to the lesser. But in the conclusion, by a bond of most evident inherence, the carnal union of subject and predicate should be celebrated more truly.

This too was my intention: that, through no pernicious backward movement of conversion, the terms of Venus’s combination, preserving the laws of analogical predication, should exchange the positions of their seats. And lest the fallacy of the consequent, born from the arrangement of like terms, could hinder Venus’s skill, I marked the terms with special signs, so that by the familiar glance of free recognition she might boldly know which terms, by the right of their relation, required the lower rank of subjection and which the higher summit of predication; lest, if the combination of terms did not hold a consequent proportional relation in common, the deformity of uniform nonsense should arise.

And just as I wished, through an incursion of most hostile hospitality, to anathematize certain observances of grammar and dialectic from Venus’s schools, so I forbade the rhetorical propositions of metonymy to the craft of Cypris. Rhetoric, their mother, embracing these in the bosom of her amplitude, forms her arguments with many honors; but I forbade them lest, by the excursion of an excessively harsh transference, the prize should be alienated from its protesting subject into something else: wit into crime, urbanity into rusticity, trope into fault, excessive color into discoloration. [Col. 0459A]

Thus equipped with these distinctions and badges of nobility, Venus passed into the homeland of earthly habitation. There, laboring arduously with her auxiliary instruments to weave the sequence of human generation, and repairing more subtly with her subtle needle what had been destroyed by the hands of the Fates, she ties these things together more subtly. Thus she renders the duties of her hired administration with most diligent care.

But because a mind, wearied by the sameness of maternal abundance, grows indignant, and the onset of daily labor extinguishes the appetite for carrying out its purpose, the unity of work so often repeated harasses Cytherea with boredom, and the effect of continuous labor excludes the desire to labor. She therefore, more desirous of being enervated by barren leisure than exercised by fruitful labors, began, through the practice of holiday work preferred to business, to grow youthfully childish in desires for excessive idleness. And since from one in whom the torpor of idleness pitches camp every service of virtue is banished, the barrenness of leisure commonly produces a fecundity of evil offspring. Flooding drink likewise foams over into excessive lusts, and uncontrolled gorging on food belches forth similar nauseas of excess.

Venus, stung by these deadly furies, began to commit concubinous fornication with Antigamus against her spouse Hymenaeus, contaminating the chastity of the marriage-bed with the plague of adultery. Entangled by the deadly promptings of her adulterer, she shamefully changes liberal work into mechanical, regular into anomalous, civil into rustic; and, corrupting my command, she disinherits the hammers from fellowship with the anvils and condemns them to adulterous anvils. [Col. 0459C]

The native anvils themselves, lamenting the absence of their hammers, seem tearfully to demand them back. And she who used to oppose a shield of defense to Atropos as she mowed down everything with her sword is now bound to that same Atropos by a reciprocal pact of firm alliance. Allowing the sickle of fate to range too far through the harvest of humankind, she makes good no loss by the origin of any new seed. Rather, destroying herself by grammatical constructions, overturning herself by dialectical conversions, and stripping her rhetorical colors of color, she transforms her art into a figure and the figure into a fault. And while, in adulterous excesses, she perpetuates the allurements of concubinage with the adulterer, she receives from him, in place of a son, a bastard.

Since he enjoys the pleasantness of no delight and wishes to pass no midday in the pleasures of any playful enjoyment, usage has given him the name *Jocus* (“Jest”), as though by antiphrasis *jocus* were named from *jocositas* (“jocularity”). Thus two sons were given to Dione, different in disparate kind, unlike in the law of their birth, soon also differing in title and deformed in craft. For Hymenaeus, whom a lineage of higher dignity exalts at the boundary of affinity with uterine brotherhood, begets Cupid from Venus as his son. But Antigamus, descended from the stock of buffoonery or ignobility, begets for himself, in adultery, the adulterous son Jest in a jesting manner. The solemnity of marriage excuses the birth of the former; the common notoriety of public concubinage accuses the descent of the latter. In the one shines the urbanity of paternal civility; in the other darkens the rusticity of paternal uncouthness.

The former dwells among silver fountains bright with silvery sheen; the latter incessantly frequents places condemned to perpetual drought. The former pitches his tents upon a pleasant plain; wooded valleys delight the latter. The former spends every night in tents without fail; the latter continues day and night beneath the open sky. The former wounds with golden hunting-spears what he hunts; the latter pierces with iron javelins whatever he strikes. The former makes his guests drunk with bittersweet nectar; the latter kills his guests with the sour drink of wormwood.

My discourse has now inscribed upon the tablet of your mind [Col. 0460B] how the destructive ruin of idleness made Venus impassioned; how the flood of immoderate drinking brings about a poisonous conflagration; how, taking its origin from the gorging of food, the elephantine leprosy of luxury has struck very many. Behold: over people languishing with Venus’s acute fever I have sung a plaintive song of sorrow. Now let us likewise tune the lyre of a lamenting discourse in elegiac strain for others whom the diseased throng of other vices disturbs.

For many, while avoiding the gaping, voracious whirlpools of greedy Charybdis, suffer shipwreck through unforeseen danger in the abyss of malignant Scylla. Many also, while escaping the swollen encounters of an impetuous torrent, become stuck fast in the mud of a pond. Others, while prudence counsels them to avoid the precipices of an overhanging mountain, dash themselves down of their own accord upon level ground. Therefore fix in your mind, with the nail of tenacious memory, the things that I shall say; shake from your spirit’s vigilance the sleep of torpor, so that, aroused with me by motherly compassion, you may mourn in fellow-feeling for the shipwrecks of endangered people; and, armored with the shield of preliminary warning, meet the monstrous army of vices; and, if any evil seeds dare to sprout in the garden of your mind, uproot them with the sickle of timely cutting.

Then I said: “My mind, long gladdened by the brevity of your instruction, most willingly inclines its ear to your corrections.”

Then she said:

> Alas, with how headlong a pace  
> does Virtue, conquered by vice, struggle toward ruin?  
> Every semblance of virtue exults;  
> the reins of fury are loosened by vice.  
> The day-star of justice grows faint;  
> scarcely even the shadow of its shadow survives,  
> and, deprived of light and abounding in night,  
> it mourns its extinguished star of honor,  
> while the lightning-flash of crimes strikes the world  
> and the night of deceit clouds the south wind of faith.  
> Yet no stars of virtue redeem  
> the abyss of this night.  
> Evening falls upon faith in the world,  
> and the nocturnal chaos of deceit abounds.  
>
> Faith languishes through deceit; deceit too deceives  
> deceit by deceit, and thus fraud presses upon fraud.  
> Morals lack moral custom in a world deprived of morals;  
> laws lack law, and the laws of settled order  
> lose their own right. Now every right  
> is made without right; law flourishes without law.  
>
> The world degenerates; the world’s golden ages  
> are now, now degenerating. The poverty of iron  
> clothes the world which once  
> the nobility of gold clothed.  
> Now deceits seek the robes of hypocrisy,  
> and the fragrant stench of crimes seeks balms of virtue  
> in order that it may furnish a cloak  
> for its perverse odor.  
>
> Thus nettle conceals itself among roses, seaweed among hyacinths,  
> dross among silver, cosmetic dye among purple,  
> disguising poverty of appearance, so that  
> crimes may sometimes purchase a fair countenance.  
> But crime strips off every ornament  
> and does not color itself with the light of justice;  
> for vice openly glosses itself,  
> and fraud itself becomes the tongue of its own madness.  
> What safety remains when deceit arms  
> mothers themselves against their own entrails?  
> When brotherly love suffers through fraud  
> and the right hand lies to its sister?  
>
> The law of integrity is judged reprobate;  
> to honor worthy people, and the law of piety, are held wicked;  
> to be chaste is now shameful to all. A person made inhuman, without shame,  
> strips off the human practices of humanity.  
> Degenerate, therefore, he puts on the degenerate acts of a brute,  
> and thus making himself inhuman, deserves to be deprived of humanity.

### Alan’s Seventh Question

To this I replied: “Since the wanderer of this understanding ranges abroad in the air of generality, whereas particularity is friendly to understanding, I should like you to unfold in the varied intervals of most beautiful species the vices which you wrap up in a certain little ball of generality.”

### Nature’s Reply

“Since it would be improper for the deserving rationale of your request to be deprived of the merit of fulfillment, it is fitting that the individual vices be marked out for you one by one with particular notes. Since, therefore, it has already been said how almost the whole world is endangered by the general conflagration of impure Venus, it remains now to say how it is shipwrecked by the most general flood of gluttony.

“For gluttony is, as it were, a prelude to the execution of Venus, and, as it were, an antecedent to the Venereal consequent.

“Observe, then, certain daughters of ancient idolatry, uprooted from the very marrow, who at this present moment attempt to restore their mother’s dominion and by certain prophetic songs raise her again from the dead. Performing a harlot’s office, whitening their faces with the countenance of counterfeit love, they deceitfully entice lovers by alluring them. Under sad joy, friendly cruelty, and hostile friendship, like Sirens sweet unto destruction, outwardly displaying the melody of delight, they lead their lovers to the shipwreck of idolatry. One of these may, if I may speak in a coined term suitable to its property, be called *bacchilatria*, ‘Bacchus-worship.’

### On Excessive Drinking

“This *bacchilatria*, depriving her lover of the little spark of reason, exposes him to the darkness of brutish sensuality. In harlot-like fashion she makes her lover so drunk that he is compelled to desire Bacchus with excessive [Note: [Col. 0461] preposterous.] intensity, so that the drinker, bound to Bacchus by the tie of excessive delight, is believed to offer him the worship of divine majesty. Indeed, the Bacchus-worshipping man, often unable to endure the separation of Bacchus from himself even by a local interval, does not suffer his god to remain long lodged in the alien vessels of cups. Rather, that the divinity of this god may be more familiarly at hand, he encloses him in the cask of his belly. But since the container of the stomach often cannot sustain for long the divinity of so great a guest, this god shamefully evaporates either through the Arctic pole of the eastern gate or through the Antarctic region of the western one.

“Very often, too, a worshipper of Bacchus fashions for Bacchus a lodging in cups splendid in the dignity of their material, that the divinity may shine more divinely in a golden vessel. Hence, rivaling the heavens in brightness of sheen, competing with emeralds in greenness of color, and surpassing very many flavors by the majesty of its own flavor, it excites the children of drink by sophistical claims of its own excellences, so that they solemnly celebrate Bacchus as the mystery of an ineffable divinity with ineffable love. Stirred by these inducements, lest anything of that divinity remain undrained, they swallow Bacchus down to the dregs; and so they compel their god to descend shamefully into the Tartarean abyss of the belly. Passing thus from the special to the most general genus of drinking, they ascend to the superlative degree of drunkenness.

“This pest not only assails people of the common multitude; it also makes the haughty necks of prelates bend to itself. The favors that nature has poured out upon Bacchus do not suffice them; they even employ the attraction of reeds—now glorying in Bacchus joined with roses [Note: [Col. 0461] rejoicing.], now breathing the fragrance of another flower, now arrogating to themselves some privilege through association with hyssop, now enriched outwardly with the endowments of other things. These they swallow in the impetuous Charybdis of their gullet, so that they incur the shipwreck of drunkenness without a sea, weeping without sorrow, lethargy without sickness, and sleep without drowsiness.

“When, struck by the force [Note: [Col. 0463] frenzy.] of drunkenness, they devote themselves to psalmody, breaking up the verses by excessive interpolation [Note: [Col. 0463] interruption.], they importunately insert the north wind of drunkenness.

### On Excess of Food

“Not only does the aforesaid desire for drink ensnare many; the canine greed for food likewise entices them. Their disordered pleasures and discordant thoughts dream up new preparations of food. While they pay the daily debt of food to their collector far too abundantly, the collector, having an excess, is compelled to repay his debtor. Whatever they possess, they store up in the treasury of the stomach. And although rust’s corroding tooth does not gnaw away that deposit, nor does the cunning of a thieving robber steal it, yet it vanishes, more shamefully, through the more shameful theft of consuming heat.

“They invite their purse to vomit up coins and their money-chest to nausea, so that they may flatter the collector, the stomach, more carefully. Within, they enrich the belly with the wealth of foods; without, they are set in naked and utter poverty. Nor is this pest content with vulgar lowliness: it advances more deeply among prelates, who torture salmon, pike, and other fish distinguished by equal nobility through various martyrdoms of cooking, adulterating the office of baptism by baptizing them in the fountain of sacred pepper, so that, baptized by such a baptism, they may obtain the grace of manifold flavor.

“At the same table a land animal is submerged in a flood of pepper; a fish swims in pepper; a bird is bound in the same sticky substance. And while so many kinds of animal are imprisoned in the single jail of the belly, the aquatic creature marvels that it is buried with land and aerial kinds in the same tomb. Were they granted leave to emerge, scarcely would the width of the gate suffice for those coming out.

“These aforesaid pests make the bridge by which one reaches the brothels of luxury. These are the introductions through which one enters upon the art of theft. They breed diseases and sow poverty. They are nurses of discord, sisters of madness, mothers of intemperance, huntresses of uncleanness. Through them humankind exceeds the limits of modesty, sets aside the reins of temperance, breaks the seals of chastity, and does not attend to the grace of my bounty [Note: [Col. 0463] generosity.]. For although my bounty provides [Note: [Col. 0463] scatters.] dishes for so many people and showers down such abundant dishes, they, ungrateful for grace, unlawfully abusing lawful things too much and loosening the reins of gluttony, exceed the measures of eating and extend the lines of drinking to infinity. Seducing their palates by the sharpness of salty things, they are compelled to thirst more often so that they may drink frequently and much.

### On Avarice

“There is another daughter of idolatry which—if the propriety of its name retains in its sound the kinship of its meaning—it is fitting to call by the suitable term *nummulatria*, ‘money-worship.’ This is wickedness [Note: [Col. 0463] avarice.], through which money is deified in the minds of men and divine reverence is rendered to coin. Where coin speaks, the trumpet of Tullian eloquence grows hoarse; where coin marches in company, the flashes of Hector’s warfare fall silent; where money fights, Herculean virtue is conquered.

“For if anyone is armed with money, the rushing force of Tullius, the lightning assault of Hector, the strength of Hercules’ virtue, and the shape-shifting cunning of Ulysses are despised as though beside silver cuirasses. For the hunger to possess overwhelms men so much that dialectical subtlety is mute and the urbanity of rhetoric languishes. Where the abundance of coins pleads, Tully sells the currency of his own eloquence; Lucretia turns the jewels of her modesty into gold; Penelope sets the modesty of her twenty-year chastity at a price; even Hippolytus, if he hears the whispering prayers of money, does not refuse to play stepmother with his stepmother.

“For if money whispers in a judge’s ear, the lyre of Orpheus, the song of Amphion, and the Muse of Virgil are suffocated by the voice of money. The rich man, shipwrecked in the deep of riches, thirsts for wealth with the fiery thirst of dropsy, and, placed amid it, becomes a Tantalus. Even the poor man, although he cannot actually practice material avarice, nevertheless retains inwardly archetypal [Note: [Col. 0463] mental.] parsimony. Alas! Loads of metals bestow honors proportioned to the weights of metal. Caesar is no longer everything; money is everything, because it runs as mediator through every individual honor up to the most general.

“Money is our patriarch [Note: [Col. 0463] It performs the role of patriarchs.]; it enthrones bishops and archbishops. It fits some for archidiaconal offices, and makes others equal to the business of other dignities and offices. What more? Money conquers; money rules the world; money commands all things.

“What profit is it to pursue, with the course of subtlety, the evasions of elusive astronomy with Ptolemy; to investigate the prophecies of the stars and the voluntary wanderings of the planets; with Euclid to search out the secrets of geometrical riddles; to descend in understanding into the depths of the sea; to reach the height of heaven with intelligible measurements; with the Milesian to discover the harmonious friendships of musical proportions; with Pythagoras to examine the conflicts of numbers by the power of multiplication; with Tully to stud an oration with the starry constellations of rhetorical colors; with Aristotle to divide falsehood from truth by the two-edged sword of dialectic; with Zeno to clothe falsehood in sophistical plausibility; with Donatus to join words in the congruity of their accidents—when, in our times, wisdom is rewarded with the wages of no profit, no favorable breeze of renown raises it up, while money itself buys titles of honor and proclamations of praise?

“Yet wisdom alone truly surpasses every possession. It is a noble possession: gathered when dispersed, returned when bestowed, increased when made public. Through it the noble treasure of knowledge grows within the secret chambers of the mind, and the fruit of inward delight is acquired. It is the sun by which the mind becomes day in darkness; the eye of the heart; the delightful paradise of the soul. By the authority of divine transformation it changes the earthly into the heavenly, the mortal into the immortal, and the human being into God. It is the true [Note: [Col. 0465] sole.] remedy of pilgrimage, the sole comfort of human calamity, the unique day-star of human night, the special redemption of your misery. No mist of air confuses its brightness; no density of earth obstructs its operation; no height of water blunts its gaze.

“Therefore, although among many who grow brutish through sensual instability wisdom languishes in excessive cheapness, among those who have brought the spark of renown back to the original fire of reason [Note: [Col. 0465] the fame that sounds forth beforehand.] it is not deprived of the reward of fame. For although prudence disdains the pleasing applause of counterfeit flattery, the glorious property of true fame is this: it despises those who seek it and seeks those who despise it. By fleeing fame one attains it; by pursuing it one loses it. Therefore, even if you see money reigning among certain people, prudence lying low, riches serving in arms, and wisdom exiled, nevertheless trample underfoot, with a conquering spirit, the weight of riches subdued by contempt, and pursue prudence with the inward love of affection, that you may be able to behold with unoffended sight the chamber of mother Wisdom.”

Then I said: “I should like you, with the reins of reproach loosened, to attack more deeply the offspring of avarice.”

Then she, directing the course of her narrative toward the sharpest bites of invective, said:

> After the sacred hunger for gold pricks mortal hearts,  
> the human mind cannot remain fasting.  
> It loosens friendships, produces hatred, raises angers,  
> sows wars, nourishes disputes, and renews warfare.  
> It breaks bonds, tears treaties apart, stirs  
> children against fathers, mothers against their own entrails,  
> makes brothers fail to recognize the robes of brothers; and every  
> union of blood that joins them, one evil madness divides.  
>
> While the heat of possessing makes the stomach of the mind dropsical,  
> the mind thirsts while drinking; and another Tantalus  
> burns amid these waters, while abundance of wealth gives strength to thirst.  
> Thus, full, he hungers; drunk, he thirsts; abundant, he desires.  
> One person desires all things and by that very desire  
> becomes poor; rich outside, he remains needy within.  
> The wretch therefore possesses nothing, since he thinks he has nothing.  
> When his desires repay poverty with riches,  
> many enemies invade the lodging of his heart  
> and the walls of his avaricious mind,  
> troubling with great tumult the entire citadel of the human breast.  
>
> For fear attacks the mind, and desire likewise  
> shakes it and impoverishes the whole city of the mind.  
> The double whirlwind of cares thus disturbs the miser.  
> And while he fears things to be feared, his mind itself dreams fears,  
> often invents new anxieties, and through fear of loss  
> suffers losses, repaying the evil of loss with dread.  
> Thus dreams of terror display diverse misfortunes.  
> Fear tells him of his wife’s deceits, a thief’s tricks,  
> an enemy’s attacks, swords threatening his throat,  
> and the dreadful rivers of the powerful.  
> Now he recalls plagues and fires; now he conceives  
> the wrath of the ocean, and by fear alone is already shipwrecked.  
>
> The rich man’s mind philosophizes in the money-chest  
> while it buries a coin; and the buried coin dies  
> to the miser’s uses. It is not he who possesses it, but the chest  
> possesses the coin and claims its whole use for itself.  
> That he may furnish his coffers with varied dishes of coins,  
> the rich man imposes fasts upon his own belly.  
> The stomach abhors avarice and marvels that its own revenues  
> are denied it; it seeks aid from the coffers,  
> but the coffer lends a deaf ear to the stomach.  
> The eye has its food and feasts;  
> it is alone amid the silver; but the belly  
> is compelled to philosophize and suffers fasting by a long vow.  
>
> Neither tears, nor the honeyed persuasions of prayers, nor human  
> poverty itself prevails against the rich man’s devouring  
> the needy through usury and making the poor man’s purse still poorer.  
> He laughs at the poor man’s tears, feeds upon the wretch’s labor,  
> and makes rest a punishment for himself.  
> Pain holds this man, laughter that one; jest holds this man, sorrow that one;  
> this man groans, that one laughs; this one grieves, while that one is free of grief.  
> Every affection of the rich miser loosens into affection for money;  
> no pleasure is granted his mind  
> by which it can turn its face elsewhere.  
> The rich man does not possess riches; he is possessed by them.  
> He is not the possessor of coin; coin possesses him,  
> and the miser’s mind is buried in coins.  
>
> He worships these as gods; he honors these idols  
> with divine worship and gives divinity to coins.  
> Thus human reason [Note: [Col. 0465] minds.] is trampled down by desire  
> and serves the flesh, compelled to minister as its handmaid.  
> Thus the eye of the heart, blinded by the darkness of flesh,  
> languishes and, suffering eclipse, remains inactive by itself.  
> Thus the shadow of flesh miserably obscures the radiance of human sense,  
> and the glory of the mind becomes inglorious through money.  
>
> This discourse does not disparage riches or rich people,  
> but endeavors rather to bite at vice.  
> I do not condemn wealth, riches, or a rich person’s use of them,  
> if a conquering spirit, with reason as teacher,  
> tramples riches placed beneath it, and if noble reason,  
> as charioteer, directs the use of wealth.  
> For though a rich man scatter all his wealth, pour out gifts,  
> breathe after praise, and try to gain favor by a gift,  
> unless discretion is the author [Note: [Col. 0467] agent.],  
> guide, and charioteer of that gift,  
> there will be no fruit. Gifts do not deserve praise;  
> rather, they purchase it, unless deeds are fittingly  
> performed with discernment. For praise is often given to the hypocrite  
> in exchange for a gift: a false imitation of fame,  
> an ape of praise, the shadowy shadow of their favor.

“Behold how the birdlime of tenacious avarice takes away the wings of freedom from the human mind.

### On Arrogance

“We must now consider how the puffed-up swelling of insolent arrogance raises human minds into pride. A multitude of people corrupted by the deadly contagion of this infirmity, while insolently exalting themselves above themselves, descends ruinously beneath itself: diminishing itself by arrogating, depressing itself by raising itself, taking itself away from itself by lifting itself up.

“Among such people, either the solemn pomposity of speech, the silence that is mother of suspicion, a certain singularity of action, an insolent peculiarity of gesture, or an excessive corruption of the body betrays [Note: [Col. 0467] glosses.] inward pride. Some, though the humility of servile condition lowers them, boast of exalted freedom. Others, though they are made common by the baseness of buffoonish stock, verbally exalt themselves by nobility of blood [Note: [Col. 0467] mark themselves with distinguished eminence.]. Others, still babbling in the cradle of grammatical art and nourished at its breasts, profess the summit of Aristotelian subtlety. Others, though numbed by the icy chills of hare-like timidity, display leonine courage by the remedy of words alone.

“There are others who clearly speak by outward silence what the haughtiness of inward disdain conceals within. For, while others lie below them in moral rank, or are their equals in worth, or even possess a higher eminence of dignity, they disdain to share in mutual conversation. If someone asks them a word by the aid of a question, the answer will be separated [Note: [Col. 0467] divided.] from the question by such an interval of silence that it seems to have no kinship [Note: [Col. 0467] thought.] with it.

“Others, delighted to make their acts distinctive, labor to be singular among the multitude, special in the general, contrary in the universal, and diverse in unity in every way. While others apply themselves to conversation, these indulge in silence; while others are loosened by amusements, these seem to be entangled in serious affairs; while others are occupied with serious business, these idle away their time in amusements. While others are gladdened in countenance by a certain festivity of serenity [Note: [Col. 0467] are made serene by the festivity of cheerfulness.], these display upon their face a storm of malevolent severity.

“Others represent the gesture of inward pride by an outward peculiarity of gesture [Note: [Col. 0467] conception.]: as though they despised all earthly things, they look upward at heavenly ones with their bodies thrown back; they roll their eyes indignantly, raise their brows, tilt their chin haughtily upward, and bend their arms into arches. Even their feet touch the ground only by the contraction of their joints.

“Others make their bodies excessively effeminate by feminine adornments. With the aid of a comb they bring the assemblies of their hair into such peace that not even a gentle breeze can stir tumult in them. They cut down the fringes of luxuriant eyebrow with the help of scissors, or pluck them out by uprooting the excess from that same forest. They frequently set the razor’s snares for the sprouting beard, so that it may not dare to sprout even a little. Their arms complain of the narrowness of sleeves; their feet are imprisoned in the cramped jails of shoes.

“Alas! Whence come such arrogance and such pride to a human being whose birth is miserable, whose life laboriously destroys him by punishment, whose punishment is concluded by the still more punitive necessity of death; whose every being, every moment, and life itself are shipwreck, and for whom the world is exile; whose life is either absent or promises absence, whereas death is imminent or threatens imminence.

### On Envy
From Pride, indeed, is born a daughter who inherits her mother’s malignity. This is Envy, which, by the rusty gnawing of incessant detraction, destroys human minds. This is the worm whose diseased bite makes the granted health of the mind waste away into corruption; the mind’s integrity rot into decay; the mind’s repose melt away [Note: [Col. 0467] “Slip away.”] into [Col. 0468C] toil. This is the guest who, received as a guest in the house of its host, undermines that host’s dwelling. This is a possession that most ruinously possesses its possessor: while it harasses others with the barking of slander, it disquiets its own owner’s mind by piercing it with an inward bite.

This is Envy, which makes the stings of its indignant detraction lie idle [Note: [Col. 0467] “Does not send them forth.”] against those whom the hell that swallows vices absorbs; from whom nature’s law excludes the bodily gifts; whom mad Fortune spews out into poverty. But if someone swims in a torrent of wealth with Croesus, scatters riches with Cyrus, contends in beauty with Narcissus, thunders in courage with Turnus, rivals Hercules in strength, contemplates philosophy face to face with Plato [Note: [Col. 0467] “Contemplates.”], and is stamped with the mirror of chastity alongside Hippolytus—against him [Col. 0468D] Envy expends every sting of its slanders. For it ascribes courage to reckless madness; it twists prudence of mind into the craftiness of deceit or the bombast of verbosity. Through its slander, modesty too degenerates into hypocrisy.

This wasting disease of Envy consumes many people, who, while attempting to diminish the brilliance of another’s reputation, are the first to suffer losses to their own integrity. To them another’s prosperity appears adverse, another’s adversity prosperous. They grieve at another’s rejoicing and rejoice at another’s grief. They measure their own riches by another’s poverty, [Col. 0469A] and their own poverty by another’s riches. They try either to cloud the serenity of another’s fame with the cloud of detraction, or to steal that person’s glory by silence alone. They either sour the integrity of another’s virtue through perverse interpretations, or mingle the leaven of falsehood with truths.

Alas! What monster is more monstrous than Envy? What loss more damaging? What fault more blameworthy? What punishment more grievous? It is the abyss of erring blindness, the hell of the human mind, the goad of contention, the sting of anxiety [Note: [Col. 0469] “Wrangling.”]. What are the impulses of Envy but enemies of human tranquillity, attendants of mental plunder—hostile vigils for the toiling soul, sentries over another’s happiness? What benefits anyone if the serenity of prosperous Fortune smiles upon him, if his body [Col. 0469B] is made cheerful by the purple adornment of beauty, if his mind besides shines with the splendour of wisdom, when the brigandage of green-eyed Envy plunders the riches of the mind, turns the serenity of favourable Fortune into clouds of adversity, changes the gold of beauty into the dross of ugliness, and lets inglorious envy strip glory from prudence?

## Remedies against Envy

If anyone wishes to banish the rust of spite, the moth of Envy, from the treasury of the mind, let him find his own grief in another’s grief by sympathizing; let him make another’s joy his own by rejoicing with that person; let him reckon his own riches in the possessions of others, and mourn his own poverty in another’s poverty. If you see another’s virtue [Col. 0469C] celebrated with the solemnities of public renown, do not make the festal day of praise an unholy day by detraction; rather, at the midday of your own public declaration, let the lamp of another’s virtue, brought forth for the common good, shine more brightly. If you see any persons indulge in the barking of slanders against the titles of another’s fame, withdraw yourself from the pack of barking dogs; or, by the force of admonition [Note: [Col. 0469] “By the objection.”], blunt their slanderous tongues, break their teeth of biting criticism, and bite back the bites of detraction.

## On Flattery

To this aforementioned company of vices, Flattery attaches its share of malignity. By its pestilence are struck the attendants of princes, palace dogs, craftsmen of flattery, makers of praise, potters of falsehood. These are they who sound the great trumpet of commendation [Col. 0469D] in the ears of the rich; who belch forth the honeycombs of honeyed flattery; who anoint a rich man’s head with the oil of flattery in order to squeeze out gifts; who place cushions of praise beneath the ears of prelates, and from their cloaks either shake out imaginary dust or sophistically pluck a tunic already without feathers.

These men redeem by begged-for testimonials of praise the actions of the wealthy upon which indignant public opinion spits. They locate praise in gifts, favour in donations, and flattering public acclaim in payment. For if a torrent of lavishness shines forth in a rich man’s house, the flatterer pours himself wholly into praise of lavishness; [Col. 0470A] but if the rich man’s gift smells of the wintry numbness of avarice, the avaricious flatterer grows cold in the gift, though warm in laudatory praise. Yet if the gift seems, in the fullest sense, to demand the drums of praise, the poet of flattery swells with high-flown language in his panegyric. But if the poverty of the gift begs the aid of reputation, he impoverishes the dignity of reputation with a humbler style. For where the grandeur of the gift pleads its case, the flatterer belches hypocritical praises and shadowy reputations from the treasury of his heart.

For if the person on whose behalf the gift speaks has been cast down by so great a storm of ugliness that scarcely fragments of natural gifts remain in him, the poems of flattery will dream up for him the prerogative of beauty. The slightest confines of a cowardly spirit [Note: [Col. 0469] “Of a faint-hearted spirit.”] they will falsely call [Col. 0470B] palaces of magnanimity; the low lurking-places of sluggish avarice they will represent as an excess of generosity; and the lowliness of a plebeian lineage they will falsely dignify with the title of Caesarean nobility.

What more need be said? If, in some person not excused from vices by any virtue, a multitude of crimes has taken up camp [Note: [Col. 0469] “Fullness.”], then, when a gift-serving mediator appears, the mercenary flatterer lightly colours the appearance of vices with the superficial garment of commendation. Conversely, if the full noon of every excellence shines in someone’s face, if the tongue gleams with the silver pearls of eloquence, if the chamber of the mind shines with the ornaments of virtues—yet if the craftsman of flattery does not expect the favour of a gift, he labours to mingle clouds with the light of so great an integrity, [Col. 0470C] together with the heights of vices.

What, then, is the anointing of flattery but the squeezing-out of gifts? What is the sport of commendation but the mockery of prelates? What is the smiling of praise but their derision? For although speech is the faithful interpreter of understanding, and words are faithful pictures of the mind, while the face is the seal of the will, and the tongue is customarily the prophet of the mind, flatterers unfasten face from will, word from soul, tongue from mind, and speech from understanding, by a wide interval of separation [Note: [Col. 0469] “Separate.”]. They smile at many with the outward praise of whitewashing whom they mock with inward derision of mind; they publicly commend many with plausible applause whom inwardly they cheat with contrary mockery. Outwardly they applaud with a maidenly face; inwardly [Col. 0470D] they sting with a scorpion’s barb. Outwardly they pour down [Note: [Col. 0469] “Pour forth.”] the honeyed rains of flattery; inwardly they vomit forth storms of detraction.

## Alan’s Petition to Nature

Then I, checking the chariot-driving course of my uninterrupted narration, said: “Would that, by the rational fortifications of your instruction, you would strengthen the little city of my mind against the frenzied armies of these vices.”

Then she said:

## Remedies against the Vices

Let not the voracious Scylla of the abyss  
Plunge you into the deep night of lusts.

Offer your palate the reins of moderation;  
Pay a more modest tribute to your belly.

Let the path of your throat delight moderately  
In the Bacchic cups, the rain of Lyaeus.

Drink a little, so that your mouth may seem  
Almost to give kisses to Bacchus’s cups.

Let the water of Lyaeus break pride;  
Let Bacchus’s streams temper Bacchic frenzy.

Let Thetis offer herself as bride to Lyaeus,  
And as a bride restrain her husband’s tyranny.

Let plain, common, infrequent eating  
Crush the mutterings [Note: [Col. 0471] “Quarrels.”] of proud flesh.

So that the tyrant, ever proud in this flesh,  
May press you less severely,

[Col. 0471B] Sluggish Cupid will thus remain at rest,  
The reins of lust in you will be checked,

The languishing sting of flesh will grow numb,  
And flesh will thus become the spirit’s handmaid.

Set bolts upon the gateway of sight;  
Restrain your eyes, lest too shamelessly

They hunt abroad for assaults of light  
And the messenger offer its prey to the mind.

If the fever of possession intoxicates any,  
Let them compel wealth to depart from their mind;

Let ambition feel the mind’s triumph,  
Let the necks of conquered Cupid be pressed down.

Let money itself not linger enclosed  
In purses, sleeping idly [Col. 0471C]

And serving no one; rather, let it keep watch,  
The guardian of honour, for rich uses.

If time is present and place requires it,  
Let the buried mass of money rise;

Let purses vomit out their coins utterly.  
Let every gift serve honour.

If you wish to tread beneath your feet  
The neck of Pride, its swelling breath,

The thunderbolts of its spirit, weigh  
The burden of your perishable origin,

The labours of life, and death’s quittance [Note: [Col. 0471] “The paths of death.”].

## The Arrival of Hymenaeus

While Nature’s speech proceeded along this path of particular instruction, behold: a man, by the marvel of a sudden appearance and without any herald of our prior expectation, presented himself to our sight. [Col. 0471D] He seemed subject to no law of age: now he bloomed in the springtime of youth, now the serious face of riper age spoke forth, now his countenance seemed furrowed with the wrinkles of old age. As he fluctuated in the changing face of manifold ages, so his ambiguous stature was now humbled by a smaller measure, now enlarged beyond its deficiency by the balance of an even mean, now strove toward gigantic excesses with the bold height of its size.

No traces of feminine softness appeared in his face; the authority of masculine dignity alone reigned there. His face was neither drenched by the rains of weeping nor brightened by the wantonness of laughter; [Col. 0472A] free from both, it inclined with greater modesty toward tears. His hair, having made a truce with litigation, acknowledged the workmanship of the skilful comb; yet it lay arranged in the balance of moderate grooming, lest, if it wandered into extravagant arrangements, it should seem to pass over into feminine softness. And lest a little cloud of hair should bury the open space of his forehead, the ends of his hair felt the bite of scissors. His face, as masculine dignity required, departed in no respect from beauty’s grace.

His chin now put forth its first down, now a longer growth fringed it there, now it seemed to grow wild with the fleece of luxuriant beard. Now the severity of the razor chastised the beard’s excess. Rings studded with stars of gemstones, dazzling the hands with exceptional brilliance, made the sun seem newly born. [Col. 0472B]

## On Hymenaeus’s Garments

His garments now seemed to become common through the ordinary workmanship of coarser material, now to pride themselves on the most elaborate weaving of finer fabric. In them the fables of paintings dreamed of nuptial events. Yet the soot of age had almost compelled the painted images to grow dim. There, the language of painting confessed that there was woven a sacramental tableau of testimony: the purpose of marriage, the peaceable unity of wedlock, the inseparable yoke of marriage rites, and the indissoluble bond of those who marry.

For in the book of the painting one read, as though in shadow, what solemnity applauds the rejoicing of weddings; what sweetness of melody celebrates weddings; what special universality of guests smiles upon unions; and what general delight of the lyre concludes marriages. [Col. 0472C] A company, divided into groups of ten, of musicians also adorned the progress of the aforesaid man. But these musicians, representing in themselves their master’s sorrow, had imposed silence upon their instruments. Hence the workshops of instruments, rendered speechless by the torpor of silence, seemed to sigh in lamentation.

Therefore, when local nearness joined him to the neighbourhood of Nature, she, naming him, greeted him with a token of welcome and added a token of a kiss. From the indication of his name itself and from the eloquent signs of all the other circumstances, I recognized Hymenaeus as the one who had come; and Nature, placing him [Col. 0472D] at her right hand, endowed him with the dignity of her right hand.

## The Arrival of Chastity

While a certain festivity of conversation was being celebrated between Nature and Hymenaeus, behold: a virgin, whose dawn-like beauty delighted all, seemed, by the sudden presence of her arrival and the direction of her path, to draw near to us. In her beauty shone forth a solemnity of such craftsmanship that in no point did Nature’s polishing hand falter. Her face begged no hypocritical colouring from an alien hue; rather, the right hand of the Almighty had planted, by a wondrous mingling of Nature, a rose and lily contending upon her face. [Col. 0473A] Her eyes, disciplined by the modesty of simplicity, indulged in no wanton excursions. Her lips, retaining their native vigour, seemed neither worn out by caresses nor to have known Venus’s preliminaries through kisses. Yet you would have thought her face, sweating into tears, shipwrecked in a river of tears.

A wreath, materially composed of lilies fastened together in a crossed union, smiled as an ornament upon her head. Yet the whiteness of her swanlike hair, disdaining to yield to the whiteness of the lilies, displayed a rival brightness. Her garments would have surpassed snows in truer proofs of whiteness, had not painting, inventing diverse colours, deceived their whiteness.

In them, beneath the fiction of painting, was woven the manner in which the chastity of Hippolytus, fortified by the wall of constancy, resisted and refuted the attacks of his stepmother’s lust. [Col. 0473B] There Daphne, lest she suffer the loss of her virginal innocence, fled the enticements of Phoebus by flight. There Lucretia excluded the loss of violated modesty by the shortcut of death. There, in the mirror of painting, I could behold Penelope, the mirror of chastity. And, to encompass in the brief course of narration the copious details of the painting which must be passed over, the artistry of depiction deprived no daughter of birth of her due tribute of praise.

The nobility of a golden seal, which glittered like a starry multitude of jaspers, shone on the right hand of the aforementioned virgin. A turtle-dove, however, resting upon her left hand, in the form of an elegiac poem tuned the lyre of its voice to mournful lamentations. A company of young women [Col. 0473C] attended her footsteps, both as solace for the journey and as a serving retinue. When Nature saw her nearby in place, she came to meet her in solemn encounter and outwardly portrayed her inward affection by a prelude of greeting, a foretaste of a kiss, and the union of an embrace. As the virgin’s name shone out in the opening of the greeting, I recognized the present arrival of Chastity.

## The Arrival of Temperance

And while Nature welcomed her with festive conversation, behold: a matron, regulating her step by orderly modesty, seemed to trace the path of her journey toward us. Her stature was bounded by the limits of moderation. Her age tended toward the hour of noon, [Col. 0473D] yet the midday of her life encountered no winter in the love of beauty [Note: [Col. 0473D] “Winter.”]. The ruin of old age also tried to sprinkle her hair with its snows; but the virgin herself had not allowed it to flow disorderly across the expanse of her shoulders in youthful fashion, but constrained its excess beneath her discipline.

Her garments seemed neither to pride themselves on the glory of noble material nor to lament the lack of worth; obedient to the rules of moderation, they were neither curtailed by the truncation of excessive shortness so as to rise clear of the earth’s surface, nor did superfluous portions clothe the face of the earth. Rather, they touched it with the brief taste of a kiss; for a belt, moderating the fall of the tunic, recalled its excess [Col. 0474A] to rule. A necklace, guarding the entrances to her bosom, denied the hand entrance.

In her garments, painting, through the fidelity of its letters, taught what restraint ought to govern human words, what circumspection deeds, what moderation dress, what gravity bearing, what restraint of the mouth food, and what chastening of the throat drink. Therefore, Nature received this virgin, guarded by a small number of attendants, with the applause of a swift meeting; by the manyfold conclusion of kisses and the auspicious opening of a particular greeting, she displayed the fullness of her affection. The clear utterance of her own name announced the welcome arrival of Temperance.

## The Arrival of Generosity

While Nature honoured [Col. 0474B] Temperance’s presence with the gift of friendly greeting, behold: a woman whose beauty, aided by the brightness of material day, displayed the appearance of a more radiant face, hastening on her way, seemed to direct the course of her steps toward us. Her stature, scorning smallness, exceeded the ordinary measure of human height. Her head was not bent down to earth in abasement, making her face incline downward; but, with erect neck, lifting her gaze upward, she directed the course of her eyes toward higher things.

Nature sculpted her form, polished by refinement, so that in it she might admire the industry of her own artistry. A diadem, neither redeeming poverty by the distinction of its workmanship nor compensating for cheapness by the nobility of its material, but displaying singular sovereignty in both, burned upon her head without the bite of destructive possession. [Col. 0474C] Yet her golden hair, blazing with a more pleasing fire, seemed indignantly to take precedence over the golden diadem. It was neither cut short by the scissors’ workmanship nor gathered into braids, but luxuriated in freer course, passed beyond the limits of her shoulders, and seemed to descend in condescension to the poverty of the earth.

Her arms, not condemned to the poverty of shortness but flowing in an extension of tallness, seemed destined to move not backward in return but forward. Her hands, not folded back in any cramped clasping, but extended in the unfolding of lavish openness, aspired to the offices of giving. Her garments too, deriving their substance from gold and silken threads joined in an embracing union, rejoiced in such marks of exquisite workmanship, commended by the nobility of their material, [Col. 0474D] that you would have believed not merely a human but a heavenly hand had laboured upon the work.

In them, the plausible imagery of painting, through the prestidigitation of its sophistical contrivance, condemned with the reproach of anathema people suffering from the notorious crime of avarice; but it repaid the children of generosity, adorned with the public praises of fame, with the grace of blessing. Therefore, when this woman, attended by only three followers, pressed onward in the haste of her step, behold: Nature, accompanying her progress in notable encounter, divided a kiss with a greeting and interrupted the greeting with a kiss. While the particular distinction of her form, the courtliness of her specified dress, and the individuality of her bearing proclaimed [Col. 0475A] the arrival of Generosity, the name sounding forth in the greeting delivered me from the cloud of doubt and gave certainty concerning the matter.

## The Arrival of Humility

While Nature paid to Generosity the offices of an initial greeting and friendly welcome, behold: a maiden, slower in the sluggishness of her delayed step, more serene in the calmness of her dove-like face, humbler in the chastened smallness of her stature, seemed to turn aside toward us with the modesty of a tortoise’s gait. Yet beauty’s grace had come as patron to the humility of her stature. Not acquired through the deceitful artifices of human craftsmanship but springing from the living fountain of flowing Nature, it breathed ornament of beauty over her entire body.

Her hair [Col. 0475B] had been clipped by the bite of scissors so severely that the figure of truncation had nearly passed into a fault. Her locks, wandering in the divergent turn of a certain irregularity and intertwined in inextricable entanglement, seemed to be quarrelling among themselves. Her head, thrown down in deep lowering, inclined humbly toward the ground. Her garments, without degenerating from the native colour of their material through the adulteration of an added colour, defended the commonness of suburban cloth by the aid of artful workmanship.

There, in the fabulous inventions of painting, one read how Humility shone with the banner of distinction in the catalogue of virtues, whereas Pride, suspended by the mark of excommunication from the sacramental synod of virtues, was condemned to destruction by the extremity of exile. As she approached, Nature came to meet her [Col. 0475C] with more eager haste, sweetening the offering of her greeting with the honeyed seasoning of kisses, and displayed a face of deep affection. From the individual marks of her person, the arrival of Humility became apparent to me.

## Nature’s Complaint to Hymenaeus and the Aforementioned Virgins

While Hymenaeus and the aforementioned virgins displayed, in Nature’s presence, the countenance of inward complaint and endeavoured to express the forms of internal pain in outward images of tears, behold: Nature, anticipating words with words, said:

“O sole lights of human darkness, morning stars of the setting world, special planks for the shipwrecked, singular havens [Col. 0475D] amid the world’s waves! By the maturity of deep-rooted knowledge I know the purpose of your assembly, the occasion of your coming, the cause of your lamentation, and the beginnings of your grief. For men, fashioned solely in the outward form of humanity but inwardly debased by the deformity of brutish monstrosity—men whom I grieve to have clothed in humanity’s mantle—endeavour to disinherit you from the patrimony of earthly habitation. They wholly usurp earthly dominion for themselves and compel you to return to your heavenly dwelling.

“Since, therefore, my own cause is at issue when the wall of a household is set aflame, sympathizing with your compassion and grieving with your grief, I read my own groaning in your groaning and find my own loss in your adversity. Therefore, omitting nothing that pertains to the matter, having found its proper end in me, I shall, insofar as I can, extend the arm of my power and strike them with a vengeance answering their vice. But because I cannot exceed the boundary of my strength, nor is it in my power wholly to uproot the poison of this pestilence, I shall follow the measure of my ability and brand the men entangled in the windings of the aforesaid vices with the mark of anathema.

“Genius, who ministers to me in priestly office, ought to be summoned, so that, in the assisting presence of my judicial power and with the fitting assent of you all, he may expel them from the catalogue of natural things and from the boundary of my jurisdiction with the pastoral rod of excommunication. Hymenaeus shall be the most approved executor [Col. 0476B] of this embassy: in him shine the stars of radiant eloquence, and in him is lodged the treasury of discriminating counsel.”

## Hymenaeus’s Embassy to Genius with Nature’s Letter

Then those standing by, ceasing from the tears of their complaint, bowed their heads deeply and humbly rendered Nature abundant thanks. Hymenaeus, humbling himself on bent knees before Nature’s present gaze, acknowledged himself bound to undertake the assigned embassy. Then she marked a papyrus sheet with the following letter in verse-like form:

> Nature, by the grace of God first vicarious procreatrix of the worldly city, sends greeting to Genius, her other self and likeness, and wishes him friendship in every favouring caress of serene Fortune.

[Col. 0476C] “Because like things rejoice in the association of like things and in the admixture of unlike things, finding in you, as in a mirror radiant with Nature’s likeness, another self, I am bound to you by the knot of heartfelt love: either advancing in your advancement or declining in equal measure in your decline. Therefore love ought to be reciprocal, so that you may answer love with love in return.

“The evident fact of a perpetrated crime, bearing the image of a cry, speaks plainly to you of the shipwreck of humankind. For you see how men dishonour the integrity of original Nature by bestial enticements, stripping themselves of the privileged nature of humanity and passing over into beasts by degeneration of conduct: following the inclinations proper to Venus, [Col. 0476D] shipwrecked in the whirlpools of gluttony, boiling with the vapours of covetousness, soaring aloft on Pride’s fictitious wings, indulging the bites of Envy, and gilding others with the hypocrisy of Flattery.

“No one applies medicinal remedies to these diseases of vice; no one checks this torrent of crimes with a defensive barrier; no one restrains these waves of wicked deeds with the stability of a harbour. The virtues themselves, unable to bear the onslaught of so great a hostile conflict, flee to us alone as a refuge of defence and a remedy of life.
