Since, therefore, our cause is harassed by a common assault, both sweetening with entreaties and commanding you with the force of obedience, I admonish by commanding and command by admonishing that, setting aside every sophistry of excuse, you hasten to us. In the presence of myself [Col. 0477A] and my Virgins, separate the sons of abomination from the sacramental communion of our Church, and strike them, with the due solemnity of your office, with the severe rod of excommunication.”

After this, she gave the sealed letter to the envoy for delivery; on its seal artistic skill had engraved Nature’s name and image. Then Hymenaeus, concluding his thanks with a more solemn countenance of joy, beginning the assigned embassy, and rousing his companions from the sleep of sloth, ordered them to attend to their musical instruments, awaken them from the sleep of silence, and invite them to the measures of harmonious melody.

Then they, enticing their instruments with certain preludes, painted a grotesquely uniform voice, alike in its unlikeness, with varied rhythm:

Now the trumpet, greeting war with terrible blare,  
Has thundered forth the opening notes of kindred battle,  
Marking like tumult with a like bellowing.

The horn wounded the air with a false blow;  
Its wandering voice, its irregular voice, refuses  
To lie open to musical measures and to favour art,  
Scorns it, and admires unbridled song.

And the pleasing voice of the lyre, more sweetly calming,  
Bestowed upon these honeyed banquets of golden voice,  
Changing and colouring the face of varied song,

Now producing tears in its voice and feigning grief;  
Now painting the falsehoods of a sham laughter in sound.

[Col. 0477C] And the lyre, which always sings sweetly  
With the pleasant song of the nightingale, alluring more sweetly  
And reciting to the eyes the preludes of sleep;

And the pipe, which buries the murmurings of the offended mind  
And, vigilant and skilful, keeps watch by night—indeed,  
Repays with its voice the losses of sleep kept in vigil—

Smiled upon the ears, through which the stony hardness  
Of the heart is made to melt, and the harshness  
Of the hard mind is forced to soften and abandon its own rigidity.

The drums, with their dull voice and sluggish step,  
Delayed this course of sound and this birdlike keenness.

Yet song is not wholly deprived of its honour  
If someone strikes it with a delicate blow,  
Rouses it, and gently touches it with the drawing of his hand,  
Joined to the deep drawing of exhausted air.

[Col. 0477D] With sweet noise the organs belched their wind;  
Their unequal equality of song is divided while joined,  
And joined while divided: discordant harmony—  
Rather, a similarly dissimilar disagreement of voices.

The cymbals sounded with common noise and a beggarly voice;  
They never plead by their clamour in our ears,  
Scarcely worthy of winning the hearing of men.

There was none greater, better, or more pleasing than that  
With which one instrument concluded the songs aforesaid:  
The sweet song of five notes, in whose footsteps—  
Whose voice, whose song, the rival populace adored.

And the voice which disputes in discordant utterance with the lyre,  
Hid in the honeycomb of the psaltery, sweet in flavour,  
Sounded forth, bearing the little gifts of song.

The sistrums, demanding the touch of a maiden’s right hand,  
Prophets of feminine speech, of Mars and war,  
Sang, with their voice, the marvels of an unheard voice.

## Nature Resumes Her Complaint

Accordingly, while Hymenaeus was engaged in the mysteries of his mysterious embassy, Nature, weaving an elegiac speech of sorrowful complaint, rehearsed the injuries of those by whose advancing disgrace the majesty of her commonwealth had felt the abundant wound of profound loss. Among them she reproved one more sharply than the rest with the goads of rebuke: he struggled more disgracefully than others to dishonour Nature.

Though every grace of nobility smiled upon Nature, though prudence made alliance with her by its gifts, though magnanimity raised her and Generosity instructed her, nevertheless, because [Col. 0478B] the entire mass suffered from the bitterness of a small leaven, the setting of one virtue wholly clouded the rising of the others. The eclipse of one integrity compelled the stars of the other excellences to die in eclipsing retreat. When Generosity saw these reproaches directed at her foster-child, not daring to colour his vices with the cloak of defence, she fled, with a fallen lowering of her head, to the remedy of tears.

## Nature Consoles Generosity and Condemns Prodigality

Nature, perceiving what the lowering of her head and the shedding of tears signified, said:

“O Virgin, by whose prefiguring design the human mind is appointed as a palace of virtues; through whom men attain the rewards of favourable grace; through whom the antiquated ages of the Golden Age revive; through whom men bind themselves with the glue of heartfelt friendship; you have bestowed upon me a sister of the same womb, eternal *ousia* [being] producing eternal *nous* [intellect] by the everlasting kiss of its own *nous*. Not only does the bond of native consanguinity fasten you to me, but a direct chain of love also joins us together. Thus the scale of your judgment does not permit your will to deviate from the measure of my will. For such a union of conformity—indeed, a unity of unification—reconciles our minds in faithful peace that not only does that simulated union clothe itself in the image of unity, but, casting off the phantom of unification, it aspires to the reality of identity.

“Therefore no injury inflicted upon one of us rages without also assailing the other; no enticement acts as a stepmother to one without becoming hostile to the other. Therefore the man who, through the proclaiming blasphemy of an unchaste deed, labours to feminize the title of my dignity, endeavours by the force of injurious assault to diminish your honour as well. He also who, through the outpouring of excessive prodigality, abuses Nature’s gifts, is stripped of Fortune’s gifts by the loss of excessive dissipation. Thus the prostituted commonness of prodigality falsely professes the honour of generosity; the torrent of wealth is diverted into the dryness of poverty; the splendour of wisdom declines into the setting of folly; the strength of magnanimity slackens into the boldness of recklessness. Therefore I am wearied by a certain astonishment: why, at the condemnation of him who strives [Col. 0479A] to injure us more harmfully than all others, are you unable to restrain a flood of tears?”

Then Generosity, withdrawing the stream of tears from her face by a surer remedy and raising her bowed head toward heaven, said:

“O original source of all things born! O special aid of all things! O queen of the earthly realm! O faithful viceregent of the supreme heavenly ruler, who beneath the authority of the eternal Emperor corrupts your faithful administration by no taint! As the expressed equality of our deepest knowledge requires, the whole universe of worldly origin is bound to obey you in accordance with the demand of its proper kind; and a golden chain of love binds me to you.

“Therefore, the one who, selling his own nature to destruction, attacks you with the insult of excessive rebellion, opposes me with the violence of an equivalent assault. Although, deceived by the shadowy image of belief, he thinks himself an ally of my company, and although men deceived by the theatrical display of prodigality detect in him traces of Generosity, he is nevertheless held at a long distance from the benefit of our friendship. But because it is ours to sympathize compassionately with those caught in the windings of errant wandering, I cannot remain unmoved at the pestilential manifestation of his senseless will.

## The Arrival of Genius
While, amid these maidens, an interlude of discursive conversation was being celebrated, behold, Genius appeared, accompanied by the rejoicing applause of musical instruments, in a new resonance of manifestation. [Col. 0479C] His stature, suitably proportioned by the rule of moderation, neither complained of diminution through aphæresis nor grieved at excess through prosthesis. His head, clothed in the frosty hair of whitened age, bore the mark of wintry oldness; yet his face, polished with youthful smoothness, was furrowed by no traces of age. His garments, moreover, whose workmanship followed nature, knowing the poverty neither of this color nor of that, now seemed brightened by hyacinth-blue, now inflamed with scarlet; now made more distinctly white with fine linen. In them images of things, living only momentarily, so often expired that they slipped from the inquiry of our knowledge.

In his right hand he bore a reed pen of papyrus, never resting from the service of its writing; [Col. 0479D] in his left, a skin stripped bare of hair by the bite of a razor. With the assistance of an obedient stylus, images of things upon it migrated from the shadow of painting to the truth of being and were granted life proper to their kind; when these had been lulled by the death of erasure, others were recalled to life through the birth of a new creation. There was Helen, half-divine through her beauty, who, through the mediation of her own loveliness, might herself be called Beauty. There, in Turnus, flashed the thunderbolt of daring; strength reigned in Hercules. There giant stature rose in Capaneus; fox-like cunning flourished in Ulysses. There Cato was marvellously intoxicated with the nectar of chaste sobriety. Plato glowed with the starry splendor of genius. There gleamed the star-spangled tail of Tully’s peacock. There Aristotle wrapped his judgments in the hiding places of enigmatic expressions. [Col. 0480A]

After the solemn exercise of this writing, when the right hand had grown weary from the continuous labors of depiction, the left hand, like a sister assisting her weary sister, assumed the office of painting, while the right took possession of writing tablets. Departing from the path of orthography through the limp of false writing, it created figures of things—or rather, shadowy masks of figures—by a half-completed painting. There Thersites, clothed in the rags of ugliness, demanded the skill of a more accomplished craftsman. There Paris was portrayed in the softness of incestuous desire. There the verses of Ennius, barren of beauty of thought, transgressed the metrical art with unbridled license. There Pacuvius, not knowing how to regulate the course of narrative, placed the beginning of his treatise in a retrograde sequence.

[Col. 0480B]

### How Truth Accompanied Genius

While Genius was thus solemnly occupied in these ingenious exercises of painting, Truth stood beside him, obedient as a modest daughter serving her father. She had not been begotten by the indiscriminate itch of Aphrodite, but had sprung from this single genial kiss of Nature and her offspring: when eternal Idea greeted him as he contemplated the mirror of forms, kissing him through the vicarious mediation of the interpreter Iconia. In her face was read the divinity of divine beauty, scorning the nature of our mortality. Her garments, proclaiming the right hand of the heavenly Craftsman and kindled with splendors of untiring radiance, could not be moth-eaten by any age. They were united to her virginal body with so close a bond [Col. 0480C] that no division in undressing could ever make them strangers to that virginal body. Other garments, however, as though of an adventitious nature and added appendages to the preceding ones, now offered their tribute to the eyes of sight, now themselves took shape beneath the eyes’ scrutiny.

Opposite stood Falsehood, the watchful enemy of Truth. Its face, clouded by the soot of ugliness, acknowledged in itself none of nature’s gifts; but old age, lowering its face into valleys of wrinkles and enveloping it altogether, had gathered it up. Its head seemed covered neither by a garment of hair nor shielded from baldness by a veil of cloth; instead, an infinite multitude of little rags served as its garment—rags which the infinite multitude of its children had woven for it. This Falsehood, secretly lying in ambush against the painting of Truth, deformed in a shapeless way whatever Truth formed in conformity with its proper shape. [Col. 0480D]

### How Nature Met the Arriving Genius

Nature, then, giving freer reins to her pace, solemnly rendered a solemn reception. She offered kisses not fermented with the poison of illicit Venus, but signifying the embraces of a mystical desire and likewise representing the concord of mystical love, to the approaching Genius.

### Genius Addresses Nature

When their mutual rejoicing had reached its consummating end, Genius imposed silence, requesting it by a gesture of his hand; and then he cast the substance of his speech into this form of utterance:

“O Nature, not without the divine breath of inward inspiration did this imperial decree proceed from the balance of your judgment: [Col. 0481A] that all who, through abusive disuse, endeavor to render our laws obsolete, and who keep holiday on the feast-day of our solemnity, should be struck by the sword of anathema. And since the law of this lawful promulgation does not oppose the law of justice, and the balance of your judgment is subject to the scrutiny of my discernment, I hasten to strengthen the rule of your decree.

“For although my mind, distressed by the ugly vices of men and wandering in the hell of sorrow, knows not the paradise of joy, yet in this it perceives the beginnings of a pleasant delight: that it sees you sighing with me in longing for due vengeance. Nor is it strange that, through the concordant union of our wills, I find the melody of harmony; for the notion of one archetypal Idea has brought us into native being, and the condition of one official administration [Col. 0481B] conforms us. It is not a hypocritical love that joins our minds by a superficial bond of affection; rather, the modesty of chaste love dwells in the inward recesses of our souls.”

As Genius thus shaped the course of his speech into this brief utterance, and as the dawn, as it were, of his exclamation began to arise and somewhat dispel the darkness of sorrow, Nature, preserving the honor of her dignity, rendered Genius the dues of thanks.

### Here Genius Proclaims Excommunication against Those Previously Mentioned

Then Genius, having laid aside his ordinary clothing and adorned himself more splendidly with the vestments of a priest, summoned outward from the inner sanctuary [Col. 0481C] of his mind the aforesaid formula of excommunication in this form of words, prefacing it with the following declaration:

“By the authority of the superessential *Usia* [Being], and of His eternal Idea, with the assent of the heavenly host, and with the supporting ministry of Nature and of the other Virtues: [Col. 0482A] let every person be separated from the kiss of heavenly love, as the merit of ingratitude requires; let him be degraded from the grace of Nature; let him be severed from the harmonious council of natural things—every person who either turns aside the lawful course of Venus, or suffers shipwreck in gluttony, or experiences the sleeplessness of drunkenness, or, thirsting for avarice, endures its fire, or climbs the shadowy height of insolent arrogance, or suffers the inward destruction of envy, or shares in the counterfeit love of flattery.

“Whoever makes an abnormal exception to the rule of Venus, let him be deprived of Venus’s seal. Whoever is submerged in the abyss of gluttony, let him be chastised by the shame of beggary. Whoever is lulled to sleep by the Lethean river of drunkenness, let him be tormented by the flames of everlasting thirst. Let him in whom the thirst of possession burns incur perpetual want. Whoever, exalted on the precipice of arrogance, belches forth a spirit of self-exaltation, let him descend in ruin into the valley of abased humility. Whoever, by envying, gnaws with the moth of detraction at the riches of another’s prosperity, let him first find himself his own enemy there. Whoever, by the hypocrisy of flattery, hunts for little gifts from the wealthy, let him be cheated of the reward of sophistical merit.”

When Genius had brought his speech to an end with this devastating anathema, the company of attendant Virgins, applauding the imprecation, swiftly strengthened Genius’s decree with a word of confirmation. The candle-lamps in the Virgins’ hands, casting their noonday light upon the earth with a certain disdain and lowering, seemed to be cast down into the sleep of extinction.

[Col. 0482C]

### Conclusion of the Work

When the mirror of this imaginary vision was withdrawn, the former sight of the mystical apparition left me, awakened from ecstasy in sleep.

[Col. 0481]

# Alain de Lille’s *Anticlaudianus*, or *On the Office of the Good and Perfect Man*, in Nine Books, Revised and Variously Illustrated by the Reverend Dom Charles de Visch, Prior of Dunes, etc.

## To the Reader

Here for you, Reader, is the *Anticlaudianus*, most carefully corrected through an exact collation of various manuscripts and restored to its author. It had been taken from him by the man who brought it to light at Antwerp in the year of the Lord 1611, in a wholly uncultivated and confused state: without any division into chapters, without the author’s prefaces, in place of whose title and text he substituted some portion of the immediately following summary; indeed, without even the author’s own name. Yet this name is commonly given by all who catalogue Alain’s writings, and it is found in the older manuscript copies which are encountered everywhere. [Col. 0483]

Certainly, in the library of the College of the Society of Jesus at Louvain alone, I found two very ancient copies of this work, one of which expressly bore Alain’s name. A third, likewise marked with the author’s name, was in the library of Saint-Bertin at Saint-Omer. A fourth and fifth were in the possession of the most distinguished Balthasar Moretus at Antwerp. One of these was of such antiquity that the form of its characters suggested that it might even reach the author’s own time; the other, which also displayed Alain’s name, was written in a hand somewhat later, yet still of venerable antiquity. These last two copies were placed at my disposal; by their file I polished the printed copy and restored it to its native color.

First, I restored to the summary its true title and its last part, which had been unjustly cut off; in addition, I restored the author’s name and his two prefaces. I also removed the many errors by which the entire work was obscured. Although, where the sense permitted, I left here and there several words differing from the manuscripts, and sometimes even entire verses, I nevertheless carefully noted the variation of reading in the lower margin, in the following order: when both manuscript copies differed from the printed edition, I wrote “MS. V”; when only the most ancient manuscript differed, I marked “MS. A”; when the more recent manuscript differed, “MS. R.” Finally, for fuller elucidation, I added marginal annotations throughout.

The work is learned and endowed with rare acuteness; it is especially suited to instill true piety and other virtues in the minds of readers, and is nevertheless everywhere sprinkled with graceful charm. Therefore the venerable Adam of Basseya, a canon of Lille, a man most celebrated for learning in his time and believed to have lived about the year 1400, valued it so highly that he himself reduced it to a compendium in polished and elegant verse, illuminating it here and there with most learned moral digressions and various spiritual odes. He himself entitled this work: *The Play of Adam of Basseya on the Anticlaudianus of Master Alain of Lille*. It survives in manuscript at Tournai, in the monastery of Saint Martin, in two copies, one of which I had in my possession for some time. In its prologue the author speaks thus:

> “Needing the comfort of some recreation, I entered the meadow of that man once most renowned and excelling in grace, Master Alain of Lille, that I might gather there fragrant and most sweet flowers,” etc.

Moreover, Thomas Dempster, in his *Ecclesiastical History of the Scottish Nation*, printed at Bologna in 1627, gives this reason why Alain entitled his work *Anticlaudianus*: it was written in imitation of Claudian, not against Claudian. “Thus,” he says, “when Ennodius, bishop of Pavia, wishes to imitate Claudian’s epigram, he gives his own epigram the heading: ‘Against Claudian on Mules.’” So he says.

But the author of the following summary thinks it is called *Anticlaudianus* because of its subject matter: since Claudian, at the beginning of his book, introduces Vices to deform, or corrupt, Rufinus, the present book introduces Virtues at its beginning to fashion the blessed man.

For a clearer understanding of this explanation, one should know that Rufinus—against whom the poet Claudian wrote his invectives—had been appointed by the elder emperor Theodosius as prefect over several eastern provinces of the Empire, to serve as guardian for his sons Honorius and Arcadius. But, inflamed by the desire for kingship, he took up arms against his sovereigns; defeated by them, he perished miserably. Accordingly, Claudian, intending to describe this tragedy, introduces an infernal Fury in the council of the Vices, grievously complaining of the peace and reign of the Virtues under the emperor Theodosius; she incites each and every Vice to disturb this peace and expel the Virtues. She judges that this may be accomplished through Rufinus. The various Vices accordingly assailed him and easily overcame him; through him they stirred up a grave disturbance in the Empire.

Alain, on the contrary, presents Nature in the council of the Virtues, lamenting the corruption of the human race and the reign of the Vices throughout the world. By decree of the council, Prudence is sent to God to solicit the creation of a perfect man who, having overcome the Vices, may restore the Virtues to the world. Our Alain describes most beautifully how these events subsequently occurred. Hence it is clear that, in respect of its subject matter, this work is truly contrary to Claudian’s work and is therefore rightly called *Anticlaudianus*, even though in its manner of proceeding the two works have some resemblance to each other.

Meanwhile, candid Reader, if you do not think it burdensome to read these books attentively even once, you will soon perceive their elegance and wonderfully delight your mind. For, as the Basel editors who first published the work in 1536 rightly observed, they are endowed with singular festivity, charm, and elegance, embracing with incredible learning, order, and brevity all human and divine matters in which every person ought to be occupied and upon which he ought to meditate—matters which everyone should know, or at least admire and reverence in every way. Farewell.

Fr. Charles de Visch, Prior of Dunes.

# Summary of the *Anticlaudianus*, or Books on the Office of the Good and Perfect Man, Taken from an Ancient Manuscript Codex, in Which the Remarkable Design of the Entire Work Is Set Forth

Because this work treats of four makers—God, Nature, Fortune, and Vice—and because the first maker, that is, God, has four works: a work in the mind, a work in matter, a work in form, and a work in governance; while Nature has two works, one considered in pure nature, free from every corruption, such a work as did not exist before sin, and another deprived by various corruption; Fortune likewise has two works, one of prosperity and the other of adversity; while Vice has one, namely corruption—therefore this book, which treats of these matters, is not inconsequentially completed in nine divisions. [Col. 0485]

The works of Nature are treated first in this work, before the works of God, because through the things that have been made the invisible things of God are perceived. Secondly, then, it treats of the divine work; thirdly, of Fortune’s work; fourthly, of Vice’s work.

At the beginning of the first book, the author, in the manner of a proper writer, makes his proposition; yet in the proposition itself he does not give an advance taste of the matter he intends to treat, in order to suggest that the matter is, as it were, ineffable, and to avoid arrogance, lest by proposing to treat ineffable things he should create a suspicion of arrogance. Secondly, he invokes. Thirdly, he introduces Nature deliberating on the procreation of such a man as man would have been if he had erred in nothing.

But because the perfection of such a man consists not only in nature but also in virtues, a council of Virtues is introduced, with whom Nature deliberates; each Virtue is described according to its own rank. Next is described a most delightful place, starred with flowers, planted with trees, and made fertile by the waters of a fountain. On its brow is situated the royal palace of Nature, described as adorned with gold, silver, and diverse jewels, glittering with manifold paintings of men.

The army of Virtues is summoned to this court. Nature employs her deliberation; Prudence offers her opinion; Reason commends both, yet assents more strongly to Nature’s side. She advises that Prudence be sent to heaven, to present the prayers of Nature and the Virtues to God; in answer to their prayers, God is to send down a pure soul to earth, and by the union of that soul and body, through the mediation of Nature and the ministry of the Virtues, the blessed man is to be begotten on earth.

But since Prudence does not immediately assent to these words, Concord adds her counsel; complying with it, Prudence commands her seven handmaids to construct a chariot for her, in which she may swiftly be conveyed to heaven and fulfill her embassy. The handmaids strive without delay to fulfill the command. Thus the first fashions the pole; the second constructs the axle; the third adorns pole and axle with jewels and flowers. The remaining four attend to making the wheels.

When the chariot is complete, Prudence sits in it, and the four-wheeled vehicle, drawn by five horses and driven by Reason, is conveyed to heaven. As Prudence ascends, various natures of things meet her. She sees the causes of clouds, the origin of snows and hail, and the source of thunderbolts. She also sees demons wandering through the air, who, having fallen from heaven through the swelling of pride, lie in wait in the gloomy night of this air for human prosperity. She surveys also the diverse stages of her ascent and the varied courses of the planets. Finally, she is carried into heaven, where she beholds the various natures of the stars.

But because no further entrance lies open to her, Reason does not know the way, and the horses cannot climb higher, Prudence wavers in uncertainty concerning what she should do. While she is thus in doubt, she sees a maiden standing on the brow of heaven, under whose guidance she may be led as far as the empyrean heaven. Riding one horse, she leaves the others in heaven along with their driver Reason.

But in the course of her journey she marvels at the waters situated above the firmament. She perceives that they are neither fluid and prone to flow, nor suspended in the ether, but rather solidified by crystalline rigidity. Set in the empyrean heaven, she observes the orders and works of angels; she marvels at the glory of the saints, at the blessed Virgin placed above all others, and at the human nature of Christ reigning there. But struck by excessive splendor, she falls into lethargy. Her guide compassionately sympathizes with her and, summoning her own sister from a certain supercelestial region, frees Prudence from her languor through her sister’s intervention.

Then all three ascend together to the heaven of the Trinity, and Prudence sets forth before God the petition of Nature and the Virtues. God, assenting to their request, creates a soul according to the eternal exemplar in His mind; He entrusts the created soul to Prudence, warning her to lead it cautiously down to earth lest the malevolence of some raging planet corrupt it. Prudence therefore descends joyfully to the lower regions and places the soul in the hands of Nature and the Virtues. Nature fashions the body; Concord unites the spirit; the other Virtues, according to their respective right, adorn the man thus created.

Nobility, last of all, because she possesses nothing of her own, asks her mother Fortune for something to bestow. On this occasion the dwelling, house, dress, and wheel of Fortune are described. Nobility comes to her mother’s house and asks her mother not to withdraw herself by defrauding the new work of Nature of the gifts of the Virtues, but to contribute her gifts along with those of the others. At this request Fortune sets out and comes to Nature’s house, where she bestows her own gift. Reason stands by as she gives, lest Fortune, moved by some envy, introduce some ferment.

When the perfection of that man is completed, report of this work reaches Alecto’s ears. Alecto gathers an army, with which she prepares to attack that man and his companions. The man engages with the Vices; but when the Vices have at last been subdued, victory is given to him.

From these things it is clear what the subject matter of this author is in this work. Yet the matter is twofold: one historical, the other mystical. This is sufficiently clear to the attentive reader. And because the intention concerns the matter, knowledge of the intention is gained through the matter. The book, however, is bound to no single branch of philosophy: now it touches ethics, now tastes of philosophy, now ascends to mathematical subtlety, now approaches the depth of theology.

The cause for undertaking the work is twofold: one considered in itself, the other relative to others. The author undertakes the work for his own sake in order to exercise his genius; for the sake of others, in order to labor for their advancement. Its end is usefulness: the knowledge of human nature. Through this book a person learns what he possesses from God, what he receives from ministering Nature, what he receives from Fortune, and what he contracts from Vice.

The title of the book is: “Here begins Alain’s *Anticlaudianus, concerning the Anti-Rufinus*.” In this title both the author of the work is named, when it says “Alain’s,” and the author’s work, when *Anticlaudianus* is added. This book is called *Anticlaudianus* on account of its subject matter, because the matter of this book is contrary to the opening matter of Claudian. For whereas Claudian, at the beginning of his book, introduces Vices to corrupt Rufinus, at the beginning of this work Virtues are introduced to fashion the blessed man. Hence that man treated in this book is called Anti-Rufinus, as though contrary to Rufinus.

# The Author’s Own Preface

[Col. 0485A] 321

Since the onrush of lightning disdains to expend its force upon twigs, but assails the bold height of full-grown trees; since the imperious fury of wind does not spend its rage upon a reed, but its maddened blasts stir furious assaults against the summits of the loftiest things: let not the flame of envy strike down the lowly poverty of my work, [Col. 0486A] nor let the breath of detraction press down the humble indigence of my little book, where shipwrecked misery rather demands the harbor of mercy than prosperity calls forth the sting of envy.

In this work let the reader, not raging with the barking of mad quarrelsomeness but correcting with the file of amendment, cut away what is superfluous and complete what is deficient, so that what is unfiled may return to the file, what is unpolished may be brought back to the workshop, [Col. 0487A] what is unskilled may be referred to its craftsman, and what is wholly ill-made may be restored to its own anvil. And although the enormity of the workmanship accuses the craftsman’s lack of skill, and in a counterfeit work the hand of the maker leaves a trace of incompetence, nevertheless the work begs pardon for its own error, since the slight spark of reason is clouded by many errors of ignorance, and the spark of human intellect vanishes into many mists of error.

Therefore let the reader approach this work not led by the distaste of a nauseated mind, nor struck by swelling indignation, but attracted by the delight of novelty. For although the book does not bloom with the purple adornment of flourishing eloquence nor shine with the star of flashing thought, yet in the slenderness of a fragile pen the sweetness of honey may be found, and in the smallness of a drying stream the dryness of thirst may be tempered. [Col. 0487B]

Let no one therefore make this work base or subject it to the bites of reproach as though it smelled of modern crudeness; rather, let the flower of genius be preferred and the worth of diligence be held forth. For pygmy humility, placed above gigantic excess, surpasses the giant in height; and a stream gushing from its source increases and swells into a torrent.

Let not those who still cry in the cradles of lower learning and suck at their nurses’ breasts dare to disdain this work. Let not those who profess the service of higher knowledge attempt to disparage it. Let not those who strike the heaven of philosophy with their summit presume to deny it its due. For in this work the sweetness of the literal sense will soothe the childish ear; moral instruction will imbue the advancing understanding; and the sharper subtlety of allegory will sharpen the perfected intellect. [Col. 0487C]

Therefore let those be excluded from entering this work [Col. 0488A] who devote themselves only to the mirrors of the senses and are not guided by the progress of reason; who attain only the image of sensuality and do not seek the truth of reason, lest what is holy, prostituted to dogs, be defiled; lest the pearl, trampled beneath pigs’ feet, perish; or lest the sacred mysteries be diminished if their majesty is disclosed to the unworthy.

Since, therefore, in this work [Note: [Col. 0487] The edition printed at Basel in 1536 by Heinrich Petri reads as follows: “In this work resounds the rule of grammatical syntax, the maxim of dialectical expression, the common proposition of the orator’s thesis, the paradoxes of arithmetical mathematics, the axiom of musical melody, the theorem of geometrical writing, the excellence of astrological doctrine, and the heavenly emblem of theology.”] there graciously resound the rule of syntax, the charm of dialectic, the maxim of rhetorical thesis, the common pathway of arithmetic, the paradoxes of mathematics, the melody of music, the axiom of geometry, the theorem of grammar, the excellence of the astronomical week, and the heavenly emblem of theophany, untrained persons [Note: [Col. 0487] The same edition has: “unskilled persons.”] should not force their own notions upon this work—persons who do not extend the course of reason beyond the bounds of the senses, [Col. 0488B] who, according to the dreams of imagination, either recall things seen or, as artificers of fictions, invent things unknown.

Rather, let those enter the narrow passage of my work who do not allow the material of their reason to rest in shameful images, but dare to raise it to the contemplation of supercelestial forms; weighing with the sure balance of discernment what ought to be proclaimed to public ears and what should be entirely buried in silence. For just as I do not fear the commonplace assaults of certain detractors, so I do not expect the favorable breeze of commendation from others. It was not fear of pride rising within me and urging itself into public view that compelled me to fashion this work, nor did the favor of popular applause invite one swollen with presumption to the undertaking; rather, I did it lest my speech contract rust from the rarity of exercise, and that, through the labor of my study, I might toil for the advancement of others. [Col. 0488C]

# Another Preface by the Same Author

[Col. 0487]

[Note: [Col. 0487] Another copy reads “actor’s” instead of “author’s.”]

I beg the author for a style, the poet for his trappings,  
Lest my downcast Clio grow old in idleness;  
Lest my pen lie still, numb with rough rust.  
The old page rejoices to grow young through the novelty of writing  
And, desiring to emerge from its ancient hiding places,  
Laughs, while the Muse sports in the slender reed.  
Thus, Phoebus, from your fountain pour over your poet,  
So that a mind parched, drenched by your stream,  
May yield a shoot and bring the fruit of that shoot to fulfillment.

# First Book of the *Anticlaudianus*

## Chapter I. Nature, Reflecting upon Her Corruption in Human Beings, Desires That a Man Entirely Perfect Be Created. She Summons the Virtues. The Procession of the Virtues to the House of Nature.

[Col. 0487D]

[Col. 0488D]

That, more closely joined to herself, Nature’s gifts may resound more fully,  
And the mixture may give the gifts their own fear,  
The ingenious care of Nature, which had distributed separately  
Its individual gifts among others, gathers them into one;  
She fashions a work through which every work is brought to completion.  
Thus in one she repairs the former faults of her works,  
So that what she had failed in elsewhere she may make good in this one.  
Every work of beauty serves this work in supplication;  
And, desiring to be clothed in so great a dowry of favor,  
It seeks the aid of the anvil. But the anvil labors, weary—  
The anvil which has spent its powers on such great uses.  
Nature strives beyond her own capacity and measures her work  
Above herself; thus she is said to surpass other craftsmen  
Because she admits that she surpasses herself.  
Nor, enduring sudden impulses of mind, does she rush  
At once to these works; rather, she deliberates whether  
[Col. 0489B] she can accomplish them, and weighs each thing in Reason’s balance.

Therefore she immediately calls her sisters to join in her designs,  
From whom the rule of counsel may descend by a straight path  
And restrain the heat of her mind.  
Thus, relying upon Reason’s chisel, she may lead into the actual  
Effects of works the ideas of her mind,  
Or with a better file cut back what she has long conceived.

Therefore, not scorning the rigor of counsel,  
She summons the heavenly council. The glory of the heavenly host  
Journeys down from on high and makes the earth bright  
With its light, deigning to clothe the ground with blessed  
Footsteps and enduring the distastefulness of our world.  
The royal court of heaven descends from its splendor  
While for a time it grants its own light to earth.  
Now the earth marvels at these new footsteps; it rejoices  
To bear the burden, though the weight of the burden is balanced by honor.

## Chapter II. The Council of the Virtues

[Col. 0489C]

Concord, foster-child of Peace, takes the first steps;  
And Plenty, pouring all things from her full horn;  
And Favor; and Youth, steeped in abundant favor;  
And Laughter, banishing the clouds of our mind;  
And Shamefastness; and Moderation, content with a fixed limit;  
And Reason, the measure of good, whom ever-attendant  
Integrity happily accompanies with fortunate step;  
And Comeliness; and Prudence, weighing all things in her balance;  
And Piety; and true Faith, who in the shadow of deceit  
Knows not how to feign hypocritical love toward us;  
And Liberality, which scatters wealth and lavishes gifts,  
[Col. 0489D] in whose keeping treasure knows no idle rest,  
Nor can the mass of buried wealth sleep,  
But often changes its various temporary masters.

Last comes Nobility, second in the praise of beauty,  
Following from afar in the steps of these others. Although  
She bears some distinction beyond compare, nevertheless her face  
Could not equal, to the last degree, the beauty of the others.  
She is better by Fortune’s gift; but Nature’s grace  
Pours out her endowments more sparingly upon her.

This offspring of heaven hastens its steps to Nature’s citadel,  
And the chorus breathes its own honor upon the house.

## Chapter III. Where the House of Nature Was Situated. A Description of the Wood in Which Nature’s House Stood, and of the Fountain There

There is a place remote by a long distance from our region,  
[Col. 0490A] laughing at the corruptions of our places.

This place alone can do whatever all other places can do.  
Whatever is lacking in the rest is supplied more richly in this one.  
What Nature’s most generous hand can do, and in what place  
She pours forth her gifts more graciously, she displays in it.  
There the earth, budding with the tender down of flowers,  
Starred with its own constellations and kindled by the purple  
Of roses, strives to paint a new heaven.

There the grace of the flower does not perish as it comes to birth,  
Dying by being born; for the rose is no maiden in the morning  
And a languishing old woman in the evening. Ever with the same face,  
It rejoices to grow young through the gift of eternal spring.  
Winter does not burn this flower, summer does not scorch it;  
There the rage of raging Boreas is not wild, nor there  
Does the breeze of Notus thunder, nor do hailstones press their darts.

[Col. 0490B] Whatever feeds the eyes, intoxicates the ears,  
Entices the taste, suspends the nostrils with scent,  
And delights the touch, this place of places contains.  
Unafflicted by any plowshare, it produces whatever fights disease  
And restores to us health proscribed by the pestilence  
Of impending sickness.

Producing no common things but marvels of itself,  
The earth, needing no external cultivator and content  
With Nature’s hand and Zephyr’s favor,  
Brings forth and glories in so great a progeny of offspring.

Rejoicing in new blossom and crowned with green leaf,  
Neither gnawed away by decay nor suffering the anger of an axe,  
Neither cast down upon the ground nor wandering with scattered boughs,  
The wood surrounds the place, counterfeiting the form of a wall.

[Col. 0490C] Winter does not plunder the wealth of flowers  
Or shear the foliage’s hair, devouring the tender youth of flowers.  
Every tree that cannot pay Nature the tribute  
Of bud and fruit suffers exile.

Striving to purchase favor with better fruit  
And to surpass the others by its own gift,  
Every tree thinks always of giving birth.

The Sirens of the woods, the cithara-players of spring,  
The birds, have assembled in that place and improvise scattered  
Honeyed songs while they strike the instruments of their throats.  
They paint the lyre with their mouths; while hearing absorbs  
These songs, their sound offers sweet fare to the ears.

In the middle, the earth sheds tears; with blessed weeping  
It produces tears and, in perpetual sweat,  
Brings forth a fountain and sobs out sweet draughts of water.

[Col. 0490D] The silver stream casts off its native dregs;  
Returning to the condition of a pure element, it gleams  
In its own brightness, freed from foreign sediment.

This drink intoxicates the womb of the pregnant earth  
And invites the longings of the mother to give birth.  
The earth, not begrudging the trees a drink like its own,  
Gives it to them and inspires in them the desire of fruitfulness.

## Chapter IV. Nature’s House, Situated on a Mountain. The Paintings of the House. Painting Imitates Logic. Aristotle, Plato, Seneca, Ptolemy, Tully, Virgil

In the midst of the grove, a steep plateau of mountain  
Rises into the air and gives kisses to the clouds.  
Here Nature’s house is built—if it is right  
To call it by that name, since in majesty it can surpass  
[Col. 0491A] the starry houses and dwellings of heaven,  
And would not deign to compare itself with royal palaces:  
A court more blessed, excluded from our homes.

Suspended upon tall columns, it measures the air;  
It gleams with the constellations of jewels and burns with gold,  
Nor is it granted less than silver’s distinctive honor.  
No material lower than these has authority there  
Or can become common through its own condition.

Here the grace of painting records the customs of men,  
And writing adheres so faithfully to its own work  
That the thing painted scarcely deviates from the truth.

O new miracles of painting! What cannot exist passes into being!  
Painting, the ape of truth, playing with a new art,  
Turns the shadows of things into things  
And changes each separate falsehood into truth.

[Col. 0491B] Thus the powers of logic subtly repress  
The arguments of this art and overcome logic’s sophisms.  
Logic proves; painting makes. Logic disputes; painting obtains  
Everything that can be. Thus each wishes false things to appear true;  
but painting persists in this more faithfully.

There Aristotle prepares arms for the logician  
And paints the wrestling-school of logic; but Plato, more divinely,  
Dreams in his mind of the hidden things of reality  
And the depths of heaven, and endeavors to seek the meaning of God.

In his manner Seneca gives moral instruction by reason—  
The best cultivator of morals and tiller of the mind.

Ptolemy, with the overflowing vein of his rich genius,  
Carried in Reason’s chariot to the heavenly heights,  
Collects the numbers, places, times, and courses of the stars.

[Col. 0491C]  
He redeems poverty of expression through the splendor of colors.

Tully, too, adorns his sayings with flashes of brilliance.

Virgil’s Muse gives colour to many falsehoods  
and weaves false coverings with the appearance of truth.

Here vigour and intelligence weigh their gifts in an equal balance:  
vigour arms Alcides; intelligence, Ulysses.  
Lest a feast of riches ferment the mind, virtue  
pours forth abundant aid and compels gifts to depart.  
[Note: Ms. Titus: “riches” (*opes*).]  
The ardent boldness of threatening Turnus fights,  
thundering with the sword, knowing no fear, prodigal of life;  
and Hippolytus’ chastity, withdrawn from Venus’ reins,  
rejoices, while Cytherea mourns the chastity she has been denied.  
[Note: Ms.: “Cytherea mourns the chastity that has been taken away.”]

## CHAPTER V. Maevius, Nero’s cruelty, Ajax, Paris, Davus. The harmony of the elements.

[Col. 0491D]

The painted palace holds these forms, these tropes of things,  
these dreams of truth, in such festive splendour.

But painting, bearing a lesser emblem of modesty upon its face,  
[Note: Both manuscripts: “of beauty” (*decoris*).]  
has at the end somewhat sorrowful household gods.  
You might think that it had played too little,  
or at least suffered dreams,  
or felt the slight storms of anger;  
or rather, that Nature, forgetful of her present deed,  
had erred in it. The face of painting seems delirious,  
to demand a better form.

Yet neither the ray of gems, brightening with splendour,  
nor the sheen of silver, nor gold more pleasing in its glitter,  
[Col. 0492A]  
can excuse the grown-up fault of painting,  
unless painting itself, languishing, grows pale amid its gold.

There our Ennius is made common by ragged verse  
and thunders forth the fortunes of Priam. There Maevius,  
daring to raise his mute mouth to heaven,  
while he tries to paint the deeds of the Macedonian leader  
in the shadow of his obscure poem,  
sticks fast, exhausted, on the very threshold  
and complains that his sluggish Muse grows numb.

There Nero shakes the world with sudden lightning;  
indulging wickedness, he compels madness to desire more  
than madness itself would desire. Whatever wickedness  
distils from him, he distributes wholly throughout the world.

There the rich man is needy: Midas, all amid gold, thirsts for gold  
and grants his mind no limit to possession.  
Ajax, more a soldier than a soldier should be, exceeds  
the law of the soldier,  
[Col. 0492B]  
and the measure of soldiery runs into rage.

Paris, broken by love and melted in Venus’ fire,  
serves in Venus’ warfare while stripping off a soldier’s deeds;  
in this he ruinously compensates for what he loses in arms.

In Davus the owl marvels at its own form  
and consoles in him the faults of its own face.

Therefore whatever small gifts of Nature’s full heart  
[Note: Both manuscripts: “fully” (*plene*).]  
escape its modest art, the grace of painting displays, inscribed upon its chambers.  
[Note: The reading is unintelligible.]  
[Note: Ms.: “fable” (*fabula*).]

327 Nature, determining each thing by profound understanding,  
maintains its own rights in these abodes and providently fashions  
the laws which it proclaims everywhere throughout the world.  
It searches out the causes of things and the seeds of the world:

who redeemed ancient chaos with a better countenance,  
[Col. 0492C]  
when the forest sought the aid of a better form and beauty of face,  
and mourned its own disorder;

who, restraining civil wars and brothers’ quarrels  
with the bond of faith, bestowed upon the elements  
the kisses of peace and bound them with a better knot of number.

With faithful mind it beholds earthquakes, the thunder’s bellowing,  
the Ocean’s wrath, and battles of the winds;  
with sure and skilful inquiry it encloses  
the courses of time: why winter, saddened by white frosts,  
mourns; spring laughs; summer burns;  
[Note: Both manuscripts: “white” (*cana*).]  
autumn overflows in the deep torrent of things;  
or why earth rests, a river flows, air streams onward,  
fire flies, and, not grudging faith to the rest,  
does not dare violate its pledge; why the unstable wave  
keeps faith with the lands, content with its fixed course.

## CHAPTER VI. Nature speaks and laments humankind’s corrupted morals.

[Col. 0492D]

After the gilded seats of the heavenly assembly  
had been filled, and the very palace, shining  
with such great divinity, had gleamed, marvelling at the light  
of so great a day, Nature stood in the midst of the council,  
her head lowered for a little toward the earth.  
Displaying thoughts conceived with stern expressions  
and commanding silence beyond them,  
she held their minds in suspense and uttered these words:

Often, long, and much, with diligent mind I reconsider  
[Col. 0493A]  
every single thing which the skill of our right hand has fashioned.  
But I find nothing which lives blessedly in every respect,  
which could not bring us many complaints,  
if it chose to accuse our Minerva.

But because we regret that our hands have erred, the error  
does no great harm and stains our deeds less severely.  
Yet I cannot wipe away the clinging stains  
which long prescription of established habit preserves.

For medicine is silent; through the force of disease, the cause grows old.  
[Note: Ms.: “where the cause of disease grows old.”]  
Nor do old diseases require slow remedies.

There is one consolation for so great a plague;  
yet I do not wish to describe it in effect before  
the standard of your judgment approves our purpose.

This resolve has long remained inscribed in my mind:  
that all together, urgently, cautiously, skilfully, and with one purpose  
[Col. 0493B]  
we should labour upon a work into which each may pour so many gifts  
that, after these endowments, it may seem to lack something;  
that the fault of our works may be redeemed in one;  
that the uprightness of one may outweigh the crimes of many;  
and that one flood may wash away the stains of many.

328 Let there dwell upon earth—not a man smelling of earth’s dregs,  
nor a material man, but a divine man—fashioned by our labour,  
to grant remedies for our losses.  
Let him dwell in heaven in mind, but on earth in body.  
On earth he shall be human; among the stars, divine.  
Thus he shall become man and thus God; made both,  
he shall be neither, and shall travel most safely by the middle way.  
In him let our hand and our gifts speak.  
Let him be a mirror for us, that we may behold ourselves in him:  
what our faith is, what our power is, what our virtue is,  
[Col. 0493C]  
and how far it can advance toward what is better.

If labour indicts our defects in so great a task  
and our hand yields beneath our burden—  
[Note: Ms.: “and of men.”]  
this glory excuses it, dissolving the charges brought against our labour.

If Nature refuses, the strength of mind must come to the rescue  
and bring desire to completion by our effect.  
For what no one hand can accomplish by itself  
will be supplied by hands joined as one: what individual things do not help,  
many collected together will help. A very great river  
is produced as little streams grow; many sparks make a flame;  
many stones compose a heap.

Alas—  
[Note: Two manuscripts here insert the following verses: “Alas, let us be ashamed that our labour has erred so often, / and that its fruit has so often answered labour badly.”]  
let us be ashamed that our decrees are silent on earth;  
that our love languishes, that our renown grows cold  
and dull, and that we are contemptibly banished from the whole world;  
that Tisiphone grants the world loose reins for crime,  
[Col. 0493D]  
rejoices in triumphing over our race,  
and draws joys from our grief.

We are conquered; Erinys places us, conquered, beneath her feet  
and chastises our necks with heavy chains.

## CHAPTER VII. The beauty and clothing of Prudence.

Thus Nature fashioned the mind by her speech,  
and, having set an end to her words, ended her plea.  
Nature’s court rejoices and assents; it praises the wish,  
and the sisters’ wishes do not differ from that wish.

[Col. 0494A]

Then Prudence rises, with a gentle face and modest bearing,  
defined in due measure. A golden mass of hair ranges about her neck,  
but a parting made by the needle restrains the quarrel of the locks,  
and the rule of the comb is at work.

The line of her eyebrow is drawn in just balance,  
neither too thin nor luxuriant with a thick cloud of hairs;  
it shapes itself into twin arches.

The stars of her eyes, her brow’s lilies, her balsam-like nose,  
ivory tooth and rose-like mouth create, offer, render, and match beauty.  
Living colour breathes in her face; no counterfeit whiteness  
shamefully fashions a phantom of so great a loveliness.

Lilies wedded to roses correct the starry blush of her face;  
and lest clouds of pallor overshadow its whiteness,  
the flame of blush defends it,

329 brighter than silver, more conspicuous than yellow gold,  
[Col. 0494B]  
more luminous than ice, more pleasing than every crystal.

The calmness of her mind does not detract from her rosy face.  
Her neck sits well, not rising too high upon her shoulders,  
but standing distinct in moderate height.

The breasts’ rounded apples, suspended in modest swelling,  
do not hang slackly, broken by softness; rather, by their very firmness  
they mark out the signs of their own modesty.

The joint unfolds her arms in extended reach;  
you would think that her arms asked to give their embraces.  
The hollow of her sides counsels with the upper parts,  
the extremities with the first, in a valley lowered to fitting measure.

Who does not know that better things lie hidden beneath these,  
of which her gentle face alone displays the preliminaries?

No fixed canon of proportion delays her body’s extension  
or restrains it within a determined boundary.

[Col. 0494C]

Now, more fully emerging, it strikes heaven with its head;  
now, cheating the eyes, it dwells among heavenly things;  
now it returns to us and disciplines itself by our rein.

Her garment was woven of fine thread,  
not falsifying its own colour or deceiving the eye  
by any sophistry; indeed, its native redness intoxicates it.

There matter seeks no support from form,  
nor do the faults of form seek coverings for themselves.  
Neither yields to matter; neither yields to her sister;  
they contend equally to see which may conquer.

Here the responding painting dreams of forms of things  
which antiquity nevertheless commands to expire in part;  
and few traces of the old form remain.

Yet a tear in various places unravels this garment into pieces.  
[Col. 0494D]  
The garment seems to mourn and weep the insults brought upon itself.

Her right hand balances scales, by which she weighs each thing  
in number, form, measure, weight, and cause.

Adorned in these ways and festive in this attire,  
skilful Prudence prepares words. From her mouth the court hangs;  
sight and hearing run eagerly toward her,  
but they contend with unequal desire:  
sight, that it may seek feasts in so great a beauty;  
hearing, that it may catch the honeycombs of words from her mouth.

With these words, therefore, Prudence portrays her mind,  
[Col. 0495A]  
while so great attention holds the sisters intent.

## CHAPTER VIII. Prudence speaks and approves Nature’s speech.

This judgment savours of nothing but the divine:  
a provident counsel so great is refined in the fire of reason  
that no trace of dregs remains.  
It does not smell of an unstable mind,  
does not speak the sluggishness of a bloated intellect,  
does not press forward with sudden impulses  
spat out from the lips’ surface; rather, it rises  
from the depths of the mind and offers remedies for our diseases.

330 This mind has wisdom beyond humanity, seasoned  
with the flavour of the divine mind, from whose deep spring  
flows the rivulet of your mind’s discernment.

Therefore it does not lie lifeless, lacking right judgment,  
[Col. 0495B]  
bereft of reason; it is not an unbridled mind wandering astray,  
nor is it driven by chance, supported as it is by so great a patron.

What detraction could bite such a mind? What spur of envy  
could press it? What envy could mingle clouds,  
or hatred, when the royal boundary guides it  
and leads the traveller along a straight path?

Let not the conception of your mind miscarry;  
let so great a thing not fall; let not light die in shadow.  
Rather, let it shine forth when exposed: let this issue  
for the common good; it will appear better in the light.

For the good that often lies hidden degenerates in diminished brightness;  
it shines more brightly if it enjoys the light.  
Thus a flower will pass into fruit, an overflowing stream into a river,  
[Col. 0495C]  
and a rich ear of grain will grow into a month.

What better thing can an honourable conception of the mind hope for?  
What greater thing? What can it desire beyond this?  
If it is good, let it fix its steps in this purpose so far as is permitted,  
and not strive to go farther.

Yet what shakes the mind, opposes the purpose,  
troubles the soul, and delays its conception surpasses this:  
our hand, which thus brings man into being, does not understand  
the powers of so great a work and so many weights of things;  
it sighs for such labours. It does not bring him to completion,  
though it makes him; it does not perfect him himself.  
It always moves him toward being, but never advances him.  
It has power toward his being, but not over his origin.  
[Note: Ms.: “always.”]

[Col. 0495D]

A disparate nature, a disparate substance, a discordant form,  
a twofold being converge in man’s being.  
One part knows earth; the other knows heaven.  
This dwells in heaven; that upon earth.  
The latter is compelled to render tribute to death;  
the law of death exempts the former.  
This remains; that flows away.  
[Note: Ms.: “flees.”]  
This endures; that perishes.  
This bears the name of being; the other bears divinity.

The body has earth; the spirit has heavenly things: therefore earth holds earth,  
and heaven holds what is heavenly.  
The mortal body acknowledges our anvil,  
requires our craftsmen and seeks our art.  
The soul’s nativity requires other craftsmen.

[Col. 0496A]

A heavenly origin requires the aid of a better craftsman;  
its form escapes our coinage, and, speaking miracles  
of the divine work, scorns our work,  
laughing at the common things of our art.

## CHAPTER IX.

How something unbegotten, simple, animate, mobile, pure,  
may emerge outwardly from nothing—without form, seed, cause,  
matter, motion, sense, guide, or teacher—  
331 without any intervening patron:  
Prudence alone knows this, she from whose lofty breast  
proceeds whatever proceeds into being.

Here the elements are silent; the seeds of things languish;  
the star grows dull; Nature lies prostrate; the planet’s power  
fails, and it marvels that its own laws are silent.

[Col. 0496B]

Therefore, since our rule does not know such a generation  
and painting is astonished at so great a form—  
[Note: Ms.: “Nature.”]  
and since our hand suffers such a setting only at its rising—  
I neither see, desire, nor judge myself to know  
the methods, causes, reasons, seeds, forms,  
and instruments by which, with our Minerva intervening,  
the arising of the heavenly soul is brought forth.

Therefore I do not know how to cast the balance of counsel upon these matters;  
I cannot; I doubt; I cease; I am held back.  
My cause will lie orphaned of counsel, reason, and faith,  
nor will my will be enclosed within a certain end,  
unless Reason weighs each thing anew on a better balance.

She for whom the obscure, shifting, empty,  
unknown, and false are nothing—she to whom all things shine forth,  
[Col. 0496C]  
all stand open, and nothing is doubtful;  
to whom neither the high stars, nor dark air, nor the deep sea are obscure—

let her, the sun of the soul, eye of the mind, light of the traveller  
exiled from his homeland, comfort in death, source  
of justice, rule of virtues, line of right—  
separate doubtful things from certain, falsehoods from truths;  
fix the mind in certainty and cut off doubt;  
wipe away the darkness of error and make bright  
the mind’s day with truth’s light; drive away falsehood’s clouds.

May the more welcome breeze of Reason applaud the mind shaken  
by waves of doubts, soothing the mind’s surging  
with a gentle breath and holding back its waves.

Nor can so great a mass of labour accuse my sloth:  
I do not yield, defeated by so great a task,  
[Col. 0496D]  
nor beg for the refuge of idle rest.

I shall undertake whatever Reason dictates—indeed, commands—  
and shall not transgress in anything that belongs to contingencies,  
pursuing my proper end according to my power.

But since it is judged shameful, shifting, mutable, and foolish  
to enclose principles within no end,  
or to give principles ends proceeding from elsewhere—  
so that the middle does not accord with the first,  
nor the last with the middle—  
I prefer to yield to principles rather than yield to the end.

## CHAPTER X. Reason speaks. Her description.

So she spoke; and the whole court is shaken by so great a whirlwind  
of doubts, and the troubled crowd of sisters  
[Col. 0497A]  
surges amid uncertainties, while a loud voice holds their wandering minds  
in suspense and ranges only through murmurs:

as air roars, wind flows, and water surges,  
when first the west wind levels it with gentle breath,  
but the northern storm shakes sleep from the sea  
or forces the sea’s pressing storms to awaken—  
so souls surge and minds press upon minds.  
Nature had first breathed through them with a mild breeze;  
Prudence breathes through their minds with a stronger blast.

Reason rises and asks silence by nod,  
voice, hand, and face. The calmness of peace belongs to her face,  
and murmurs dying at her nod themselves nod in the maiden’s presence.  
Prudence greatly obeys her face  
and follows the traces of its expression.

Their faces are related: one bears the form  
[Col. 0497B]  
of the other and conforms itself to her in it.  
One face presents the countenance of both to itself.  
Their faces differ—the countenances of the two are different—  
yet they are not opposed, as sisters ought to be.

Their faces are alike, their garments alike, their bearing alike;  
their measure and beauty are alike, but their faces differ in years.  
For Reason, the greater,  
[Note: Ms.: “the elder.”]  
bore the banners of age, being fuller in age, riper in full years.

The radiant brightness of a triple mirror shines in her right hand;  
in the triple mirror a glassy softness is reflected threefold,  
which rejects every assault of touch  
and scarcely bears even the lightest blows of a finger.

She grants herself to the use of a single mirror.  
[Col. 0497C]  
In it attentive Reason examines herself in the mirror;  
she contemplates the sequence of causes and searches the abyss of things.  
She sees the marriages of subject and form;  
she beholds the kisses mingled by concretion or offered  
by native union, marrying the subject to forms.  
[Note: “Nature.”]  
She asks what form makes the subject, what perfects its being,  
what brings a thing toward being or brings it to being;  
what generates it, what changes it, what preserves it in being;  
what it is, how great, of what kind, or how it is disposed,  
and seeks its remaining states within it.

A countenance of silver, stripped of the dregs of metal,  
leaving daylight and stars below itself in brightness,  
rejoices, clothed in the form of the second mirror.

Here she sees the subject, bereft of forms, return  
[Col. 0498A]  
to ancient chaos and seek its own mother;  
and she sees form grow young in its proper state, pure,  
not mourning the weariness of its degenerate subject—  
how form, rejoicing in its own being, rests;  
how, shipwrecked, it feels none of the subject’s changing waves;  
how, a stranger, it returns to its proper origin,  
flees the subject’s decline, and escapes its deaths.

Youth, not despoiled by the subject’s old age,  
always makes the forms of forms into girls.

With unoffended face and in the depths of her mind,  
she sees how the composite becomes simple, the heavenly perishable,  
the different the same, the heavy light, the mobile fixed,  
the obscure bright, the precious cheap, the amusing  
[Col. 0498B]  
tearful, the perpetual mortal, the turning fixed.

The nobility of gold, refined beyond every gold  
and scarcely deigning to acknowledge its own race and kind,  
passes into the form of the mirror which, third among things,  
does not know how to falsify the shadows of things,  
but displays each thing more clearly  
[Note: Ms.: “more certainly.”]  
and fashions all things in a better form.

Here she beholds the spring of things, the race of the world,  
the idea of the universe, exemplar, species, cause,  
beginnings, and end; she measures each thing by sure causes:

by what reasoning, by what causes, why, how, when,  
this unstable, generated, flowing, mutable world  
received form, being, state, species, life, and origin  
from the unbegotten, stable, and certain.

How the heavenly idea generates an earthly form  
[Col. 0498C]  
and transcribes it into our abyss of offspring.

It sends to aid  
[Note: Ms.: “exile.”]  
the forms which it destines for the world.  
The offspring degenerates from the father and puts off its father’s face,  
forgetful of its ancient parent’s countenance.

How in the world a phantom of the idea is reflected,  
whose unharmed splendour is felt in shadow;  
how the rivulet wandering from the source of forms  
loses the unbegotten brightness through the subject’s blemish;  
what fate compels, what falls by chance, and what power  
of choice, weighed in the middle, can accomplish:  
Reason weighs herself wholly in these mirrors.

But her gaze gives freer rein to the present;  
she stirs her mind and expands her soul, that inwardly  
she may draw from the mirrors some word approved by Reason  
[Note: “Word.”]  
which deserves worthily to be borne to such great ears.

334 ## BOOK TWO.

[Col. 0497]

## CHAPTER I. Will, charioteer of sight. Reason’s discourse. Reason humbles herself and asks pardon. She approves Nature’s counsel. She desires on earth a man perfected in every virtue.

[Col. 0497D]

The whole palace is silent; the murmur expires,  
as the court raises peaceful faces upward with its gaze.

[Col. 0498D]

With sight the mind runs; and Will, charioteer of sight,  
desires to anticipate the flying gaze.

Therefore Reason’s overflowing eloquence calls the mind forth,  
and her speech proceeds in this manner:

You command me to be able beyond my capacity,  
when I am compelled, though untaught, to instruct your Minerva.

[Col. 0499A]

Thus myrtles are set over laurels, wild olives over olives;  
thus lavender is preferred to roses, cheap seaweed to hyacinths,  
mud to gems, and hemlock to violets.  
Thus a sheep begs a goat for the use of fleece;  
thus a swollen torrent asks a stream for water;  
thus a narcissus is accustomed to seek its form from a carrot;  
thus the flame of a candle adds light to daylight.

But since your will compels, commands, and urges  
that, upon the matters which your discernment has just raised,  
the begged-for support of my counsel should at last be given,  
I do not wish wholly to oppose your wishes.  
Thus my will begins to will together with yours,  
so that at last it desires whatever must be.

I prefer to set before you the less-refined secrets  
[Col. 0499B]  
of my counsel, asking for another form,  
rather than oppose your wishes with an openly displayed countenance  
or have my suspicious silences conjectured to be pride.

Therefore I ask pardon. May pardon’s grace not be slow  
to follow my fault; may compassion relieve the sickness,  
if the words offer reasons insufficiently refined,  
or if a speech destitute of reason labours in fasting.

Let no astonishment seize the safeguards of your mind  
[Note: Ms. A: “remedies.”]  
if my speech takes upon itself the stains of error.  
[Note: “may adapt.”]  
Error wanders tirelessly as companion among human affairs.  
Abundance of leaven is accustomed to blacken  
whatever human speech or human mind turns over.

Yet if the end answers the duty,  
there is no further error on the petitioner’s part, nor fault on the healer’s,  
if the first end is defrauded of a second end.

[Col. 0499C]

He who threatens does not always strike with his weapon.  
The physician does not always heal; the rhetorician does not always persuade;  
nor does the logician always reach the goal—indeed,  
often, exhausted, he lies gasping midway on the path.

I judge Nature’s counsel prudent, discerning, cautious, praiseworthy, and safe;  
I approve the wish, praise the proposal, and adore the undertaking:

335 that a new Lucifer may journey through the world, one whose rising  
no setting cloud of any stain may darken;  
that a new sun may rise on earth, at whose dawn  
the old sun may be thought to mourn its own setting.

Let him alone possess whatever all of us have possessed.  
Thus every human being shall be one; thus all that is one.  
One in his being, he shall nevertheless be all in virtues.

At the sun’s setting let another sun bring forth its rising.  
[Col. 0499D]  
Let him be  
[Note: “Thus.”]  
against the vices that try to extinguish us  
guardian, defender, judge, athlete, patron.  
When the world banishes us from our own homes,  
let this be our chamber; let our refuge be made firm.

## CHAPTER II.

Yet I do not deny the words of my sister born from the same womb,  
which savour of the file of so great an examination—indeed,  
these same things may more truly be called examinations—  
when she confesses our work and requires our anvil  
for the shifting machine of human bulk.

The rule of our art calls the body into being;  
but it excludes the human soul, which is always excluded  
[Col. 0500A]  
from these laws, led by a better thumb.

Yet the pressing purpose ought not withdraw from so great a wish  
or be conquered without battle,  
although Nature’s work sighs for such great tasks  
and so great labour, and falls short.

Yet the divine hand itself will supply what Nature’s rule leaves  
below the standard of perfection.  
What Nature makes, the divine author perfects.  
[Note: “actor.”]  
The divine creates from nothing; Nature produces the perishable  
from something. God commands; she serves.  
He rules; she acts. He instructs; she is instructed.

Therefore, if what is unworthy of favour inclines toward our wishes,  
relieving our sighs, it will more fully applaud those petitions  
which alone make their plea.

Wishes, though they do not pray more elegantly clothed  
[Col. 0500B]  
in the brightness of prayers, may nevertheless deserve to be sweetened  
more by our prayers, being better seasoned with such a flavour.

Therefore let us pour out wishes, prayers, and hearts toward him,  
that he may favour our wishes and prosper our prayers—  
he who alone can bring them to fulfilment.  
The divine mind will not be slow to follow if the mind sends prayers beyond itself:  
a mind which speech painted with rhetorical figures does not charm,  
nor an idle heap of riches, nor Virgil’s Muse,  
nor hypocritical love, nor honour hunting for love;  
but the sweetness of prayers alone makes its plea.

Yet, if prayer, drawn from the spring of the heart, is moistened thereby, it remains uncertain and does not appear in clear light  
which one of us, with what assistance and by what road,  
336 borne up to the heavenly house, may be granted the honour  
[Col. 0500C]  
of an envoy; which one may offer vows to God  
and, with a pressing rain of prayers, shower the divine ears with prayer.

But let the proper judgment of the mind speak.

## CHAPTER III. Prudence is declared most fitting to be sent to God. She searches out heaven’s secrets.

No one can better undertake the exercise of this office  
than our sister Prudence, whose strength  
no multitude of labours can overcome;

whose journey and steps no obstacles delay—  
not noise, not the sea’s anger, not a deep valley,  
not ridges, not the headlong boldness of a lofty mountain,  
not the stony roughness of the way,  
[Note: “Calloused” (*collosa*).]  
nor the windings of the path, nor deserts unfamiliar with footsteps;  
not the wind’s rage, not the cloud drunk with rain,  
[Col. 0500D]  
not horrifying thunder’s pestilence, not cloudy air—  
from reaching the gods above, visiting the stars,  
and drinking in God’s secret, moistened from the divine spring.

In the secrets of heaven she sees who is the world’s Creator;  
what God himself wills; what he prepares, foresees,  
provides for, or appoints for the world;  
what heaven’s secrets can do and what the stars declare;

why heaven’s course is trifled away in the same motion,  
always bending toward setting; while a planet  
[Note: “planets.”]  
moves in contrary motion  
[Note: “moves.”]  
and restrains the heaven;

what the sickly star of Saturn threatens the world;  
what aid of health Jupiter’s favour announces to the world;  
[Note: “wintry.”]  
or what wars Mars’ star prophesies.

[Col. 0501A]

By what leader, cause, stimulus, or patron;  
by what temperature, movement, life, brightness, and course,  
the Sun—eye of the world, source of life, waxen sphere of the world—  
foresees, applauds, flatters, and consults for the world;

what allurements Venus offers the earth; what sad joys, sorrowful  
delights, sweet evils, bitter cups;  
and how she showers the world with honeyed gall;

by what bond, law, and compact Lucifer and Mercury,  
attendant of our rising sun, travel:  
they bear the standards of the rising sun, serve it as it sets,  
and alternate the offices which each apportions to himself.  
One is transferred to the other’s use;  
one shines at the sun’s setting, the other at the sun’s rising;  
they give each other reciprocal names:

[Col. 0501B]

Hesperus accompanies the setting; Lucifer, the rising.

How the moon begs borrowed brightness;  
why Phoebe, diminished from her own light,  
briefly laments the losses of her light, but, more fully diminished below,  
mourns the great loss of all her brightness;  
yet, burning again in her brother’s fire, restores  
the losses of her worn beauty  
and finally, full, carries about perfect radiance.

337 Who binds rain in the cloud; why the air bellows;  
who produces the winds; who sows their angers  
[Note: Ms. V: “ends.”]  
why the cloud’s substance takes on so many forms—  
now full of the tears of rain, now white with frost,  
now clothed in snow’s appearance, now taking up  
the arms of hail—and why earth marvels at heaven’s arrows.

Therefore who can better undertake the office of envoy  
[Col. 0501C]  
than Phronesis—Prudence?  
[Note: That is, Prudence.]  
To her all God’s secrets speak.

Therefore, if she wishes to condescend to our wishes,  
all things will come about as law demands and order requires,  
and every thing will be bounded by certain limits.

Nor do I think that she wishes to disappoint such great enterprises,  
such efforts of mind, such weight of favour,  
or to reject such great gains.

No doubt remains when these things concur. Let us all undertake the work;  
a better fortune will follow. He who has begun has half of it;  
the grace of a happy end always answers honourable beginnings.

## CHAPTER IV. Concord described: the worth and power of her form, and so forth.

[Col. 0501D]

Thus Reason captures the souls and draws the sisters’ minds,  
compelling the willing throng to desire more.

Yet Prudence alone gives a lesser assent  
and denies that she is equal to so great a labour.  
She is compelled;  
[Note: “She is asked.”]  
she refuses; and her refusal deserved to be compelled.  
She wavers, denying that she does not wish it, yet does not admit wishing it.  
She flies between the two: she does not wish, and fears not to wish.

While her mind hangs, wavers, and sticks fast in doubt,  
Concord, mediating all things, comes forward into the midst.

[Col. 0502A]

In her face the image of divinity shines  
and disdains the weariness of a human countenance.

Her hair maintains peace of itself, more blazing than gold;  
it reconciles itself to itself and seeks no aid from a comb,  
but, self-sufficient, rests in so great a peace.  
Thus not even the sighs of the blowing north wind can disturb the hair  
or create the tumult of quarrel.

Form, figure, proportion, number, and joining  
[Note: “measure.”]  
are fittingly assigned to her limbs and render their due offices.  
Thus her limbs, bound in harmonious peace, answer one another,  
so that no discordant union appears in any part.

Her garment, of one face and content with one colour,  
passes into the adornment of her limbs, fitted so closely outwardly to them  
that it seems inscribed upon them.

[Col. 0502B]

There painting, by its art, grants a second life  
to those whom chaste love, simple concord,  
pure faith, and true devotion have joined  
and made two into one: the covenant of purified love.

For David and Jonathan are there, two yet one:  
though distinct, they are not two in mind but one.  
They divide their souls; each shares himself with the other.

That Pirithous may return himself to himself, Theseus, returned to the world,  
attempts the regions, monsters, and dangers of the underworld;  
he denies that he can live in himself unless he lives in the other.

Tydeus takes up arms that another Tydeus may reign:  
he fights in his Polynices, and, wishing his second self to reign,  
seems to seek kingdoms for himself.

One Nisus appears in his companion Euryalus, and another  
[Col. 0502C]  
Euryalus thrives in Nisus. Thus each renders both of them present,  
and each is measured from the one pair of companions.

The son of Atreus rages in madness; Pylades indicates  
that his frenzy is his own and suffers Megaera,  
lest his own other and same Pylades suffer it.

This painting speaks its mysteries in its signs.
