Neither the thing itself nor language has ever portrayed such things  
more faithfully; deceiving sight by such a sophistry,  
it encloses realities in shadow,  
of which the image is accustomed to be herald of goodness and peace.

In the maiden’s right hand, an olive branch,  
hairy with leaves, swollen with blossom, awaiting fruit,  
comes into youthful growth. It seeks no help from mother earth:  
through it Concord binds together the exchanges, connections, and bonds of things—  
[Col. 0502D]  
covenant, friendship, and peace.  
Assisting with marks of words  
[Note: Ms. V inserts here the following verse: “At the rod’s nod she asks peace for herself.”]  
[Note: “vows.”]  
she comes forward at those nods, and her thought dictates sound in words.

## CHAPTER V. Concord speaks. Many evils which have occurred in the world through lack of concord are enumerated.

If the world had once kept my rights, my laws,  
my compacts, or even now kept love’s bonds,  
the world would not groan under such great disasters.

[Col. 0503A]

Phoebus would not have mourned the brothers’ banquet  
or the banquet’s abuse; grieving the crimes of erring Nature,  
he would not have bequeathed to the world the darkness  
of an unnatural night.

The Theban king, Polynices’ brother and enemy,  
having cast off his brother, would not have turned himself into an enemy to his brother.

His homeland, devising deceits and casting off its parent,  
would not, breathing crime through ownership,  
have turned its degenerate right hand into its own entrails—  
a stepmother in place of a mother.

Troy’s nobility, Troy’s glory, Troy’s illustrious fame  
would still flourish  
[Note: “would be vigorous.”]  
and would not lack the flower of praise.

Crassus, thirsty for a draught of gold and drunk with gold,  
would not have drunk gold, disastrously drunk in gold.

Nor would civil crime, Caesar’s arms, the spirit of the boy king,  
the treaties of empire, the servile manner of death, and slaves  
have tested the great man; and, lifeless, mutilated, stripped  
[Col. 0503B]  
of the honour of burial, he would not have lain alone upon the bare sand.

After so many battle-cries of war, after Mars’ thunderbolts,  
after sword-furies and so many hazards, Caesar would not have felt  
deceits and the powerless battle of the stylus.

339 Antony could easily have avoided Caesar’s assaults,  
the crises of war, Fortune’s fury, and the changes of chance;  
nor would his wife, adopting  
[Note: Variant: “adapting.”]  
serpents to her breasts, have suckled snakes—  
[Note: Cleopatra is meant.]  
and, giving them drink from her teats, drunk death at her breast.

If I had not bound the elements with firm connection,  
harmonious compact, enduring peace, and my exchanges,  
internal tumult would still shake the discordant principles of things  
and stir up wars among kindred things.  
Released from their offices, ignorant of their courses,  
[Col. 0503C]  
rough with neglect, confused in locations, mixed in forms,  
driven by chance arrangements, the elements would lie in ruin.

And if the stars of heaven, the courses of heaven, and the seven planets  
had not of their own accord been subject to my laws,  
bound in order, peace, faithfulness, number, and connection,  
all things would flow uncertainly into chance ruin.

If my joining had not bound souls to bodies,  
the spirit, disdaining to inhabit the huts,  
the prisons of flesh, would depart  
and return to its proper origins.

Reason proves, says, argues, and teaches this;  
it shows that nothing is preserved in being  
which refuses to keep my laws and rights.

Therefore let one love bind us; let one will bind us;  
[Col. 0503D]  
let willing one thing bind us, sisters; let unwilling one thing bind us.

The rest are thus bound to preserve the rule of peace—  
we especially, at whose nod the world is ordered,  
to whom belong the decision, right, and rule of the world.

What bond, what true love, what covenant of love,  
what devotion, what pure faith, what line of rectitude  
will preserve in other things even traces of peace,  
if our own concord remains discordant?

The loss of an afflicted head will flow down into the limbs.  
The sickness of a bitter root will flow down into the branches.

[Col. 0504A]

The kindred wasting of the stream will flow down into the rivulets.  
What is the moon’s brightness if the sun’s light wanders astray?  
What are a stream’s waves if the river’s abundance dries up?  
What is grain’s fruit if the streaming ear,  
[Note: Ms. V: “numb.”]  
languishes?

If discord unweaves—indeed, breaks—our peace,  
our power perishes. For power that suffers decline  
is denied stability when divided against itself.

Since agreement gives us mature strength,  
[Note: “assent.”]  
our disagreement will exhaust those powers.

Divided medicine refuses its effects.  
A river is less in flood where streams distribute it among themselves.

Or the divided flame of the hearth glows less brightly.

A sharper assault of vices and a greater conflict will press upon us if error divides us. Once discord breaks the walls of cement,

[Col. 0504B] it exposes the unarmed walls to hostile battle. The sword attacks more fiercely and rages more deeply; parts joined together yield no barriers to force, nor does their joined sequence recoil before the sword. The bird of Jupiter hurls its thunderbolt more fiercely when the terror of its coming scatters the flock of birds. A torrent pours out more abundantly when no obstacle guards the way or denies passage to the stream.

Therefore, united in harmony, let us hasten toward one desire: that which nature seeks, reason commends, uprightness approves—indeed desires—and piety requires and wishes. Nor shall *phronesis* alone, distant, contrary, discordant [Note: [Col. 0503] “Distant, contrary, dissonant, discordant.”], divide all of us, bound under the harmonious law of peace, into factions, so as to loosen the bonds of love.

[Col. 0504C] Rather, steadfast, rejoicing together, harmonious, concordant, she shall enter our mind, lest, conquered by toil, she be thought to yield before the opening of the contest; or lest pride, with puffed-up breath, blow through the mind, or consuming envy gnaw at the inward recesses of the soul. Or shall she who alone is accustomed to seek good things alone reject this common good—our glory, our beneficial desire? She alone ought gladly and voluntarily to move all of us toward so great a work and so great a favor, if our inflamed will were less sluggish, and our spirit did not so greatly desire to ascend.

## Chapter VI. Prudence, inflamed by Concord’s words, undertakes the embassy. The construction of a chariot is ordered. The seven liberal arts are designated.

[Col. 0504D]

More inflamed by these words, Prudence steadies her mind and fixes the footsteps of her thought upon firm ground. The storm of the soul dies away, and its waves withdraw; she makes her own will common with the will of her sisters.

She thinks, searches, strives, finds, chooses: therefore, what road, what path, what track shall more rightly bear her herself to the heavenly beings and the secret realms of the Thunderer? And so that the roughness of the way may less trouble the traveller’s steps,

[Col. 0505A] so that her foot may know no stumbling-blocks—indeed, so that she may the more swiftly fulfil the duty at hand, in which she must traverse heaven, sea, stars—Wisdom commands that a chariot be forged. Nor does intention follow intention with slow foot; rather, they press on together. The effect is born when will itself is born. Thus birth is granted at once to mother and offspring.

Seven girls—cautious, prudent, beautiful, alike—who under seven faces render one countenance, whom one face, lineage, age, form, and power hold together, whom one faith holds and one will holds, stand beside Phronesis and follow Phronesis’ decrees, ever ready to burn with zeal in her service. The gifts of wisdom pour into them as many endowments as Prudence pours her whole self into them;

[Col. 0505B] she apportions herself among them and stores up treasure for herself in them. Thus divided, she nonetheless remains whole; scattered, she is at length gathered, and, diffused, returns with great increase.

Directing their faces into its recesses, this choir of sisters sees, attends, learns, notes, and is taught in the face, as though in a mirror, whatever parchment contains, whatever the mind conceives, whatever the tongue dares to utter; and it drinks without end the whole of wisdom. It drinks in without end the whole of wisdom: whatever the craftsman’s hand, the painter’s grace, the smith’s right hand, and the sculptor’s skilful industry require.

This choir paints as Zeuxis paints, shapes as Milo shapes, speaks as Fabius speaks, and pleads as Tully himself pleads;

[Col. 0505C] it perceives as the Samian perceives, is wise as Plato is wise, investigates as Hermes investigates, distinguishes as Socrates distinguishes, gathers as Zeno gathers, presses on as Briso presses on, studies as Crisius studies, observes as Argus observes; it constrains the course of time as Caesar does, examines the stars as Atlas does, weighs burdens as Zethus does; it counts like Chrysippus, measures like another Euclid, sings like Phoebus, plays the lyre like Orpheus, draws with compasses like Perdix, raises citadels like Daedalus, fashions like the Cyclops, forges arms like the Lemnian; instructs like Seneca, cajoles like Appius, presses like Cato, inflames like Curio, veils like another Persius, dissembles like Crassus, conceals like another Julius, entangles like Soldius [Note: [Col. 0505] MS R: “as the sun, when it doubles.”], and unravels like Naso; it blossoms like Statius and dictates like Maro.

[Col. 0505D] It conceives, expounds, imitates, bears, and fulfils Mercury’s intelligence, the passions of our Demosthenes, Ovid’s flowing stream, Lucan’s thunderbolt, Virgil’s abyss, the bites of Satire, and Solon’s refuge.

## Chapter VII. The liberal arts are designated. The liberal arts are charged with constructing Prudence’s chariot. Grammar makes the pole of Prudence’s chariot. The fruits, nature, and use of Grammar.

Therefore Minerva [Note: [Col. 0505] Minerva, goddess of disciplines, commonly Pallas. She is also taken to mean talent or nature, as when one does something *invita Minerva*, “against Minerva,” that is, with nature resisting.] sees the sisters shining with so great a splendour of Wisdom,

[Col. 0506A] with so many and such great gifts bestowed upon them. She directs, enjoins, commands, orders, and urges that each of these companions, with Wisdom accompanying her, strive, toil, pant, press on, and bring it about that the chariot may move into being—so that it may cross the expanse of earth, sea, clouds, stars, and heaven, and, passing beyond the third hinge of heaven, investigate the secrets of *nous* [Note: [Col. 0505D] Intellect or intelligence.], draw in profound meanings, and seek out the will of the supreme master.

She had scarcely expressed her desire when they strive eagerly to fulfil their commander’s wishes. The sisters gird themselves for the work: the mind does not differ from the deed, nor the hand from the mind; rather, the mind’s intention commits the mind to action. Thus the hand outwardly declares what the mind possesses within; so the hand becomes the faithful tongue of the mind,

[Col. 0506B] and portrays the mind in its own action.

The first of them strives that the pole may come forth as the forerunner of the axle, and as a kind of preface to the chariot yet to come, so that it may be the first part of so great a work. Watchful, studious, willing, attentive, labouring, devoted to her task, she leads thought into action. Neither cheap in dress, nor foul in face, degraded in bearing, disordered in speech, or barbarous in conduct, she nevertheless bears in her countenance the signs of labour: pallor—but moderate pallor, which does not banish from her face [Note: [Col. 0505] MS: “from the face.”] the purple fires and the honour of snowy colour [Note: [Col. 0505] “Colour.”], since the virgin flower is not stripped of bloom in her, nor does a breaking [Note: [Col. 0505] MS: “curbs.”] destroy Venus’ own modesty.

Yet breasts float in a great flood of milk, feigning the losses of withdrawn modesty.

[Col. 0506C] While she still sighs at the breasts of a nursing mother, this food nourishes the infant and cherishes him with liquid nourishment. Solid food does not yet feed him, while his milky age sips cups of milk; under this single drink, both food and drink issue forth in milk alone.

She roughens the hand with the whip by which she punishes the bad habits imbibed, in accordance with her own custom, by childish age. Thus she hardens breasts with blows and softens blows with breasts: in one act she becomes both father and mother. With the blow she compensates for the father; with the breast she performs the mother’s role.

Her other hand serves the office of the chisel: it frees teeth from foulness, applying boxwood to the tooth’s very ivory and restoring its beauty by its whiteness. Or if any one tooth alone strays from the troop of the others,

[Col. 0506D] she cuts back its excess by a just measure. She teaches infants to speak, loosens their bound tongues, and leads words into their proper coinage.

A white garment woven from Nile papyrus clothes her; it does not detract from her beauty, nor does her beauty harm it. The pleasing marriage of dress and beauty binds them, and they honour one another with their proper dignity. Inscribed and represented upon these garments remain

[Col. 0507A] the power, nature, capacity, order, matter, part, end, name, author, office, species, genus, instruments, and faculty of the art of Grammar.

There authority is granted to the art, rule reigns, and vice endures exile, unable to earn pardon. Defending itself by its own formal rationale, it keeps watch before the doors of the art, suffering Grammar’s endless rejection, and begs pardon. The art admits it, granting pardon to its suppliant, yet does not cherish it in her lap but merely tolerates it.

Here the art teaches, reason shows, doctrine declares: why a letter is called simple and undivided; why the letter claims the name of an element for itself, or why “element” is customarily used figuratively to mean a letter; what characters depict elements, what names they signify;

[Col. 0507B] what number encloses them, what order accords with them, what their power is; and under what fixed rule it confines these species. Why some, cast down with faint sound, demand voice, while others are silent, but the vowel openly cries out and gives the breath of voice to the rest; by what reasoning and for what causes the letter *h* is not one, though it lays claim to writing, name, and use; but instead occupies the places of a cipher and, defending for itself only a figure, bears the shadow of an element’s right.

How, when contending with itself in verse, a vowel melts away and loses its honour as voice; how in verse a letter loses its native strength and its prescribed force languishes for a time; how in verse one letter claims the powers and rights of two, making good the loss of its sisters.

[Col. 0507C] How one utterance assumes diverse forms; how the grave accent lowers it, the acute raises it, and the circumflex carries the same utterance in a curve. What a letter asserts as proper to itself, what a syllable does, what right a word preserves as its own; what a noun properly claims as its own, what a verb appropriates, what a pronoun adopts, and what the remaining parts reserve for themselves by their own right.

What a noun properly designates and what it suggests indirectly; what verbs denote and pronouns signify; since they designate things placed beneath them, why pronouns disdain the assistance of form,

[Col. 0507D] so that demonstration alone comes to their aid and makes up for the place of form in them. By what reasoning one part governs another and by what it is governed; why a noun, standing beneath others or depicting the rest, performs the office of matter or gives shape to form; why the action of a verb returns into itself or passes over to another.

Why nouns preserve a covenant of friendship with verbs, and a noun joined to a verb pays its due obligations; unless they agree, speech will be mute and silent [Note: [Col. 0507D] MS A: “will waste away.”], nor will a curtailed utterance speak full meanings. Why a word taking a part from each gives back to each

[Col. 0508A] what is owed it, and thus restores each what belongs to neither, and, holding the middle, mediates between both; why the remaining parts honour these and submit themselves to them, refusing not to serve them.

This ordered sequence of the art, portrayed one item after another, offers delights to the eyes and dishes to the mind. For a highly skilled painter had depicted it—or rather, a power greater than a painter and painting itself proclaims him.

## Chapter VIII. Grammar adapts raw material to the work. Authors of Grammar: Donatus, Aristarchus, Priscian. Grammarians delight only in the outer bark.

The aforesaid maiden, undertaking her proper labour,

[Col. 0508B] neither shaken by fear of the burden nor broken by toil, sweats over her assigned work; and much-rebellious matter, finally conquered, follows her will. For the instruments by which she cultivates childhood’s years lie aside for a time and remain at leisure. She feigns the smith and uses a smith’s tools; she overcomes matter’s flux and compels unwilling matter to serve her; she tames the stiffness of wood and clothes wood in the form of a pole.

Here, in a new birth of sculpture and fresh life, she places the craftsmen of Grammar and compels them to forge. There is Donatus, rhetor [Note: [Col. 0507D] “Teacher.”], patron, and heir, teaching the precepts of Grammar and cutting away vice.

[Col. 0508C] By learning, words, zeal, reason, and form, he enlarges, exalts, enriches, defends, and honours Grammar; and he earns for himself a special name, so that he is not called merely “a grammarian”: emphasis calls him “Grammar” itself, signifying divinity beneath the name.

Our Aristarchus pours gifts into the art of Grammar, enlarges its treasures, increases its riches, and measures his own powers within it. Dindymus gathers into one the scattered parts of Grammar and describes each in its proper forms. Our apostate treats the treatises of Grammar, being thought either to suffer the dreams of sluggish torpor in his sayings, or in his own writings to be mistaken, drunk, or rather mad, or asleep.

[Col. 0508D] He limps in fidelity, lest the reputation of his treatise should limp; he sells fidelity lest the rewards of the book perish, and fidelity goes wrong lest his reputation go astray.

This sculpture contains only those craftsmen whom mature fame has blessed with praise, and from whose achievement glory has not departed. It does not deign to acknowledge humble grammarians who delight in bark alone: the richness of the marrow does not admit them within; they seek scraps outside, content with the husk alone, and cannot taste [Note: [Col. 0507D] “Sip.”] the flavour of the kernel.

# Book Three

[Col. 0509]

## Chapter I. The second maiden is Logic. Logic makes the axle in Prudence’s chariot. Logic’s appearance, dress, and so forth. The character of Logic’s art. She exposes the sophists’ frauds. The use of Logic. How she makes an axle from iron. Authors of Logic: Porphyry, Aristotle, Zeno, Boethius.

[Col. 0509A]

Stretching farther, skilful, studious, and labouring, the second maiden strives; she enters the inner chambers of the mind and sets the hand in motion. The hand rouses the mind and presses talent and the proper senses to fashion the form of an axle and to advance it with great honour, so that, contending with its pole, the axle may be second neither in the praise of matter nor in that of form, but may surpass it in beauty and correspond to it [Note: [Col. 0509] MS: “investigating.”].

Beauty and comeliness would have breathed upon the maiden’s limbs,

[Col. 0509B] as the remarkable ordering of her members shows, had not her face lain sprinkled with a certain leanness. Leanness surrounds her; deeply surrounded by leanness she sinks in, and dry skin clings to bare bones. By her dress, bearing, thinness, pallor, and figure, she represents the sleepless movements of the soul, proclaims watchful Minerva, and declares that wakeful lamps have kept vigil with her [Note: [Col. 0509] MS R: “to keep vigil.”].

Her hair, contending in some dispute, strays down to her lower parts and foolishly quarrels with itself. No comb disciplines it, no bite of scissors presses it, no cutting’s apocope bites its end. While her eyes vie with the stars, they seem to burn; the sight of eagles yields, and lynxes revere such a gaze, confessing themselves and their eyes overcome

[Col. 0509C] and fearing to compare themselves with them.

Her right hand is adorned with the glory of a flower; a scorpion, threatening with the pointed sting of its tail, attacks her left. That hand tastes of honey; this bears the flavour of gall. The one promises laughter; the other ends in weeping. The one receives; the other drives away. The one affects; the other infects. The one strikes; the one soothes. The one anoints; the other is pricked.

Her garment lay neither in the squalor of dirt nor in proud brilliance, maintaining a middle state and drawn back on both sides [Note: [Col. 0509] “Drawn together.”]. There, by a new art, a new painter, an actor of truth, displays the combats of refutations and Logic’s duel: how the force of Logic, flashing with the double edge of a sword, clothed in the appearance of truth, cuts down falsehood, denying that the false can lurk under truth’s shadow. Why the pseudologician, thief and adulterer of the art,

[Col. 0509D] false man, hypocrite, secret robber, sophist, counterfeits the face of Logic and, relying on certain marvels, attempts to sell falsehood as truth.

What in Logic is called a “place,” what topical congruity is, what the cause of a place is, what a maxim is, and what is the force of an argument flowing from a topical source.

[Col. 0510A] Why a place establishes an argument and a maxim arms a refutation, granting its proper strengths to the refutation. How a refutation errs in matter or form and, by appearance alone, puts forward the mask of a refutation. Why a conclusion born from premises in speech is marked with the appearance of those premises; why the middle term, mediating between the extremes, binds them and fastens all things with a firm connection. Why the form of a shortened refutation arises when either aphairesis or syncope shortens the refutation. How induction, appropriating the forces and strength of a refutation, runs through particulars and gathers the whole, yet submits itself as inferior to refutation.

How an example gives rise from itself—or rather, a shortened parent, with a part of itself cut off, begets offspring for itself.

[Col. 0510B] How the topical art itself is fortified by places, yet is not confined to a place, since it does not seek places; indeed, ignorant of places, it takes a place and takes places. How it defines, divides, gathers, and unites individually the things it embraces in its capacious lap. How description, portraying things, encloses those same things and does not allow what has been described to run into diverse forms.

What separates a genus divided into species, or divides a whole into parts, and then binds together again what was previously scattered, compelling divided things into one. How the art of Logic, like a road, gate, and key, points out, unlocks, and opens the secrets of wisdom. How it bears arms and serves in every art, assigning to itself the causes and losses of its sisters.

[Col. 0510C] How it defends the rest, enriches the needy, strengthens the weak, instructs the speechless, adorns the unkempt, rouses the sluggish, and arms the unarmed. How it cleanses vice and drives away dross, lest any dross within should detract from the art. How it guards the anvil, lest the sophist, by secret fraud, coin false arguments upon it.

This writing [Note: [Col. 0509] MS A, MS R: “description.”] expressed on her garment makes you think that it demands the art’s own champions and contest. The maiden wears this dress, bearing, form, and appearance; but for the present she lays aside the flower in her right hand, devotes herself to other tasks, and the serpent leaves her left. Both hands press toward a greater desire.

Therefore, lest sloth intoxicate the maiden’s hands,

[Col. 0510D] the smith’s instruments stand ready for them—tools which the Lemnian himself [Note: [Col. 0509] The Lemnian is Vulcan.] supplies and in whose own arms he serves her. Giving herself wholly to labour, the maiden attempts to soften iron’s hardness, bend its stiffness, erase its sluggishness, and drive away its dullness,

[Col. 0511A] so that, taming iron’s defects, she may fashion it into an axle and give the iron material a better form. Now fire softens it; now the hammer bends it; and each yearns for the cultivation of iron. Thus iron contends with iron so as to refine it, reverencing its companion and being reverenced in it.

After much sweat of work, after struggles of conflict, unremitting labour conquers iron’s resistance, takes away its baseness, restrains its motion, and blunts its contention; it strikes matter into form and clothes it with shape. And matter, which had been discordant, crude, bristling, and sluggish, now recovers proportion, form, refinement, and motion, and, shaped, bears the figure of an axle.

There the sequence of the painting proclaims with renown the authors of Logic, whom life grants to everlasting fame and whom earth does not bury when it covers their buried bodies,

[Col. 0511B] but, remembering the dead, restores them to the world.

There Porphyry lays down a bridge by a straight path and shows the track by which the reader enters Aristotle’s abyss, penetrating the innermost chambers of the book. There Porphyry unfolds mysteries like another Oedipus of our age, solving the riddles of the Sphinx. Aristotle, our disturber of words, is present; he confounds many in a whirlwind and delights in concealment. Thus he treats Logic in such a way that he seems not to have treated it—not because he errs in this, but because he covers all things with a veil of words so that toil can scarcely uncover them. Yet he clothes his sayings in concealment for this reason: lest he cast down his secrets and, abandoning his mystery to the crowd, ultimately compel it to become cheap.

[Col. 0511C] For the majesty of a secret becomes cheap and is deprived of all its splendour if it becomes public; for things made common always breed disgust. From a thing made common arises the nausea of contempt.

Zeno, logical boxer, athlete of Logic, king and leader of wisdom, is present, seeking for himself the battles of Logic. He exposes its hidden places and deepest recesses, brings dark things into the light, puts new matters into use, excuses tropes, reduces figure to rule, and brings forth what is ambiguous. Under his leadership Severinus, leaving his native tongue, causes the power of Logic to travel into the use of our foreign speech and to speak Latin.

## Chapter II. The third maiden is Rhetoric. Rhetoric is described. She carries a trumpet in her right hand and a horn in her left. The office and use of Rhetoric. The parts of a rhetorical speech. Cicero’s distinguished service to Rhetoric.

[Col. 0511D]

Not inferior in dress or face, nor second in art, the third maiden does not cheat the chariot of her own contribution. She calls the mind outward, directs it when called by study, and, with mind leading, guides the hands. She puts on the finishing hands, completes her sisters’ work, and adorns what has once been made so as to make it more perfect.

She refines to the highest degree those things which had been made at the positive degree,

but had not attained the increase of the highest end, being content with secondary degrees. Nor is it surprising if she completes what was made before by adorning it more perfectly and gives beauty to the completed work through better refinement, since beauty and the grace of form smile more favourably upon her,

[Col. 0512A] who surpasses her companions by the painter’s abundant art, enclosing the entire art of the painter beneath her breast.

Her hair, polished by wondrous art, lies in imitation of gold’s appearance; it clothes her neck, and fiery colour floats in her face. Purple fire colours her countenance with rosy brilliance. Yet an alien whiteness clings to part of her face and strives to mingle its colour with the native colour. Now a changing flood of tears overwhelms her face; now the dawn of varied laughter makes it serene, wiping away the tears of weeping; now the maiden presents a stern countenance with the majesty of severity. Now her eye sends its light upward; now its point falls downward; now slanting the whole sharpness of its light to one side, it seeks winding paths and shadow.

[Col. 0512B] In her right hand she bears a trumpet, and she gives her left a horn; upon the horn she marks the opening signals of war. A garment encloses her, painted in many colours and smiling, clothed in varied hues. Here, through the painter’s skill, a picture of rhetorical colour shines; thus painting colours the painting.

Here, as in a book, one reads what Rhetoric’s end and author are; its form or office, its cause, its order, and its proper character and power; how it presses on—now thundering with threats, now flashing with the light of speech, now raining entreaties, now steeping the ear in praise. What type of cause it makes, toward what it tends, and at what end, when it arrives, it deliberates about the useful, judges the just,

[Col. 0512C] affirms the right, and demonstrates the honourable; what the parts of the art are and in what order they are woven.

How first the art invents, then orders, expresses, remembers, and delivers, so that order may answer itself in a lawful sequence. What parts, or how many parts, the rhetor’s speech contains within itself, and in what sequence they are woven into it. How the opening moves the mind, raises the ear, awakens the hearing, and prepares the judge’s heart, making the hearer more attentive, more teachable, and more favourable, and dedicating his mind to the ear.

How narration explains truth in brief words, or falsehood lurking under truth’s appearance. How, in sum, division gathers all that follows,

[Col. 0512D] collecting what is scattered and constraining what is diffuse. How assertion, acting on our side, marks, proves, expresses, establishes, and infers arguments. How refutation strikes the opposing side, destroys, weakens, dissolves, scatters, and presses it.

How a concluding conclusion gathers all points and, by its proper end, brings them to a close, checking the reins of speech. What question requires the deed, the kind of deed, and the name; what question rests on the diverse columns of arguments; what dispute contests a fact, what question concerns law; what kinds there are and how many—simple, relative, and the parts of the relative; why one establishes the charge of crime, another transfers it, another rejects it, while another compares and weighs disadvantages in an equal balance.

How contention takes strength on either side

[Col. 0513A] when one law disputes against another allied law, or a discordant interpretation fights against the written text, or a twofold interpretation produces ambiguity in a text; or when a name may be defined so that a certain description resolves the ambiguity of the name itself; or when the question transfers itself by the law of place, person, or time, stirring up other disputes; or if contention, ignorant of a fixed law, draws the strength of its reasoning from analogy.

How arguments give weapons of strength suited to persons, but those arguments totter with false force when they put forward uncertain name, nature, capacity [Note: [Col. 0513D] MS V: “mode of life.”], fortune, appearance, habit, disposition, deceptive purpose, pursuits, accidents, speech, and deed. What things contain the outcome; what the undertaking of the deed contains;

[Col. 0513B] what circumstances accompany the deed, or ordinarily follow it as the matter itself requires. What measure belongs to the deed, what its circumstances are, what place, time, occasion, cause, and capacity.

One part of her garment bears this representation of the art; the other speaks of its practitioners. There Marcus claims Rhetoric for himself alone—indeed, gives her birth. Therefore the art which Tully begets may deservedly be called Cicero’s daughter; since the art derives its origin from him, it could be reckoned Tullian.

## Chapter III. Other authors of Rhetoric: Quintilian, Symmachus, Sidonius. Rhetoric adorns the pole of Prudence’s chariot with gems and silver. She also engraves varied flowers upon the axle.

[Col. 0513C]

There he marks poems with many a distinguished flower and most clearly disentangles every feature of speech. Quintilian is present, veiling the semblances of cases under a kind of image of truth; he invents new disputes and compels them to enter litigation when no dispute exists.

Symmachus is sparing in words but profound in mind; lavish in thought, restricted in words; rich in mind but less ample in speech, blessed with fruit rather than foliage, he confines the riches of thought within the brevity of language. There the senatorial speech of Sidonius shines, radiant with many a star, glitters with jewels of colours, and in his sayings a painted peacock appears.

Now he cultivates a slender Muse with a fine reed,

[Col. 0513D] yet his speech does not mourn the fast of bloodlessness; now a middle style, neither rushing down to the depths nor swelling up to the heights; now he thunders, describing serious matters in lofty words, yet does not burst forth swollen with inflated roar.

The festively adorned maiden does not diminish her art by this adornment; rather, her workmanship overflows into its ornaments. She sets the pole’s jewelled appearance ablaze with stars, clothes the pole here and there in silver, and external honour comes to the aid of the material of the wood itself, which possesses lesser dignity, and redeems its inferiority. The adopted splendour buries the wood’s original birth and all its complaints;

[Col. 0514A] the plainness of the wood goes into exile and thus forgets its first origin. Therefore the constellation of gems gilds the pole; indeed, this light makes a true day, and day is indebted to matter, for the day’s native light marvels at and adores the wood’s adopted brightness.

Similarly, the maiden inscribes the axle with varied flowers, compelling iron to grow young with a new flower. Though iron is normally sluggish with the stiffness of cold and smells of winter frost, this iron knows no winter: abandoning its native cold, it claims for itself spring’s smiles and joys and assumes the aspect of a meadow in the image of flowers.

While the maiden thus cheers the pole with gems and the axle with flowers, bestowing a fullness of beauty,

[Col. 0514B] the trumpet yields to the painter’s stylus, and the horn yields as well; thus the two take upon themselves the functions of the other two.

## Chapter IV. The fourth sister is Arithmetic. Her appearance, work, and so forth. Her clothing. The use of Arithmetic. Arithmetic makes the first wheel in Prudence’s chariot. Authors of Arithmetic: Nicomachus, Gilbert, Pythagoras, Chrysippus.

The fourth sister follows; the first wheel is the fourth sister’s work, and she industriously devotes her efforts to it. Though she is fourth, she refuses to be second in the work, contending to be called first. Therefore she is beautiful, graceful, slender, subtle, and keen; abundance of mind is shown in her countenance.

[Col. 0514C] For our face is a book and a letter of the heart, a truthful messenger, interpreter, and image of the soul. She bears the appearance and form of an anxious countenance, prudent mind, honourable refinement, and attentive modesty; and in a manly mind she transcends her sex. No alien colour dwells in her rosy face [Note: [Col. 0513D] MS R: “colour dwells.”], but native colour reigns, and her face’s purple does not allow within it the ferment of a stolen colour.

She lowers her head to the ground and does not pursue the slippery pleasures of sight, granting the eyes repose in obedience to the mind. One hand holds Pythagoras’ table, which gives food to the mind, the wise delights of the soul rather than food for the body; the other hand displays battles. She arranges the troops of numbers, feigns combats,

[Col. 0514D] indicates their varied assaults and rebellious numbers, and finally brings the wars to a close with subtle triumph.

A garment woven of fine linen, clothed in its own beauty, covers the maiden’s starry limbs. The material was fine; the workmanship surpasses the material more subtly still. Thus use outstrips nature’s powers, and nature is conquered by art. Here a painting that speaks in writing and cries out through figures—though itself mute—proclaims the entire art of counting: what the power, law, connection, order, knot, love, reason, covenant, harmony, and limit of number are.

How number binds all things in a harmonious connection, composes individual things, governs the world, orders the universe,

[Col. 0515A] moves the stars, binds the elements, marries souls to bodies, earth to heaven, and what is heavenly to what is perishable. How it is the beginning, end, model, form, and seal for the world and things to be created [Note: [Col. 0515] MS A: “being born.”]. It was there, according to whose form the Idea of divinity impressed forms upon things and a shape upon the world.

How the monad is number’s beginning, fountain, mother, and origin, and, though one, gives birth from itself to the multitude of numbers. How the Virgin gives birth, remains whole in giving birth, multiplies herself though simple, begets from herself, and remains incorrupt within herself, her offspring imitating their parent.

What number is called “numbering” and what “numbered”; which repeats, distributes, gathers, subtracts,

[Col. 0515B] adds, and draws roots from the first origin. By what right or reasoning an even number is called female, an odd number male and virgin Minerva; why the doctrine of the wise represents soul, heaven, reason, joys, and life under odd number; why even number signifies body, earth, sense, what is tearful, and death, and speaks of worse destinies.

What number is called a point, what a line, what a plane figure or one with equal sides, what a sphere, what a square, what a solid, what a pyramid, or what a circle that bends around from itself into itself. What number is completed by its own divisors [Note: [Col. 0515] MS V: “parts.”], what exceeds its parts, and what, being exceeded by them, abounds.

[Col. 0515C] What harmony binds number to number, and whence it comes that the extremes are linked by intermediate terms. Why square numbers are joined in one middle term, or solid numbers by a connection of two intermediate terms.

Thus the highly refined maiden, not fleeing the burdens of labour lest, in avoiding the weight, she also avoid the weight of honour, surpasses feminine strength by the abundance of her excellence and skill: male in mind, female in sex. Thus she is male and thus female; in mind she is not she, but he.

She does not immediately express in action what she conceives by a sudden impulse, nor does she lead what the mind begets into sudden actions [Note: [Col. 0515] MS A: “immediately.”], lest the mind itself bring forth its conception before

[Col. 0515D] the conception of the mind receives form in the womb or takes the firm seal of the mind’s womb; lest, having long lived nourished by the fuel of reason, an abortive offspring rush forth suddenly into birth, die at its own birth unworthy of life, or at least, living, lament the defects of its form.

Therefore, lest the mind’s offspring deviate from lawful birth and utter no complaint against its mother, the mind begets and reason nourishes what action brings forth. In the bedchamber of the mind it fashions the mental work before

[Col. 0516A] it calls the material work forth outside. Therefore, by the labour of mind, the craftsmanlike soul, and the favour of study, the mental wheel is raised; afterwards she depicts it in material form. Thus she conceives the first in mind in order to bring it forth, while in action she gives birth to the second.

First setting aside the instruments assigned to her hands, she enters upon the work of a stonecutter. By art she tames the stiffness of marble and first levels its parts exactly. The roughness descends into a plane, the valley rises into an even surface, the angle is lowered into a curve, and the circle encloses flatness and turns the plane into a circle. Yet a swelling rises in the middle and stands above it; indeed, while stretching upward to the top, it does not leave the bottom.

Having rounded its parts by means of iron,

[Col. 0516B] the maiden hollows out the sections and, dividing the marble with openings, cuts the entire wheel through with spaces. She places the centre in the middle and crowns the middle with many a radius, around which the side of the circle is drawn. [Note: [Col. 0515] MS A inserts here nineteen verses found below at the end of Chapter V; we leave them there more appropriately, in agreement with MS R.]

Here the painting teaches the authors who discovered methods of calculation and taught the dormant art. There Nicomachus plays in the aforesaid art and, as it were, prophesies the secrets of things through numbers. There Gilbert holds the field, and as a soldier in the same art, by a deceptive leap, oversteps the art. Pythagoras, giving banquets to his own mind rather than to flesh, satisfying souls rather than feeding bodies, ascribes to fixed laws of number the origins, existence, changes, causes, motions, and bonds of things.

[Col. 0516C] Chrysippus gives himself to numbers with such love that number is always manifested in his speech and deeds, and you would think him counting even in dreams.

## Chapter V. Music is the fifth sister. Music’s dress. Authors of Music. Music’s efficacy. Music makes the second wheel in Prudence’s chariot. Michalus, teacher of music.

The fifth sister is like the fourth and bears her predecessor in her face. She portrays her in dress and returns to her in deed.

She is not free from similar study but follows her sister. In her studies she models herself upon her; looking to her sister’s work, she stamps her own works with that work. And she whom nature long ago made a sister

[Col. 0516D] becomes a sister in deed, increasing every right of sisterhood [Note: [Col. 0515] MS A: “of adornment.”]. For reason teaches, right demands, and order requires that work acknowledge what nature acknowledges.

This one bears her face as a noble mirror for the beholder. For whoever sees her face sees his own appearance in it, and the eye feasts upon the face in the mirror [Note: [Col. 0515] “The eye contemplates the face.”].

While one hand holds the lyre, the other plucks the strings, producing a sweet savor of sound, feasting the ear and giving the eyes the prelude to sleep.

[Col. 0517A] By this song the Thracian bard made stones soften, forests run, rivers stand still, wild beasts grow tame, and quarrels yield. He compelled the Eumenides to tears when their hardness was broken, forced Dis to be merciful, and made the Furies forget their fury.

By this song Amphion turned Tyrian mountains into city walls, thus mastering the stones; for no axe subdued the hard rocks which the lyre’s voice alone deserved to tame, while the iron was held silent.

Clothed in a distinguished robe, the maiden declares herself a foster-child of peace and does not seek the thunderbolts of war. There playful wantonness of painting smiles and plays, showing in diverse forms what music can accomplish: what bonds and knots join all things together; what is the nature of the art; how music gathers the hours,

[Col. 0517B] distinguishes the months, assigns the seasons of the year, restrains their courses, binds the elements, joins the planets, moves the stars, and varies their revolutions; how music joins the parts of the human body, orders the lesser world, and honors it with the likeness of the better world, so that the pygmy little brother may be painted as the image of the giant, lesser though worthy of the greater’s likeness.

It shows what parts music joins in the soul, what Euphrosyne binds together and confirms in faith. [Note: [Col. 0517] Manuscript V, instead of “Euphrosyne,” etc., has: “the flesh, and confirms faith,” etc.] It shows how music divides voices and how number varies the distinctions among sounds; why every melody and sweet song does not arise from one voice, but from the union of voices; sound unlike and like, different and the same, one and simple, double, dissimilar, and other.

It shows how music changes when the song changes,

[Col. 0517C] weaving laughter with tears and serious things with play. Now it resounds inharmoniously; now, shaping sadness, it mourns in a ditonic song; now it plays in chromatic mode. It shows what voice is double another, what song resounds in the octave (*diapason*), what sound stands in the ratio of a sesquialter to it, or harmonizes with it in the fifth (*diapente*); what combination of voices produces the fourth (*diatessaron*), in which one sounding together with three voices contends—or rather, plays.

[Note: [Col. 0517] The following nineteen verses occur in manuscript A above the preceding chapter. Yet they occur here in another manuscript, and more suitably.]

It shows why one part of a tone always exceeds the other; why a whole tone cannot be divided into equal parts, but one portion slightly exceeds the other and surpasses the smaller; why one part overcomes the other by its own chromatic refinement,

[Col. 0517D] yet the chromatic *diesis*, divided into two, does not refuse parts cut by an equal balance.

Thus the maiden, splendid in dress and radiant in elegant attire, lays aside the use of the lyre for a time. Taking up the work of a smith, at the command of heat she transforms stone into bronze; from bronze she makes the second wheel, which, commending the first through the excellence of its form, proclaims itself the first wheel’s sister. Although the matter which separates them was different, form nevertheless makes them twins.

There the written record perpetuates the fame of the craftsmen whom Music rejoices to have as partners, or deems worthy to embrace with the honor of her own name. The Milesian exercises the power of honeyed speech and, as it were, gives the ears a new dedication of song, softening minds by such an art.

[Col. 0518A] Another, at the opposite extreme, invented the tiresome drone of sluggish songs, the strife of dull-toned voices, and rebellious songs that attack the ears rather than greet them with their voice [Note: [Col. 0517] Manuscript R: “the mind.”], and offends our ears with song.

Our Gregory sails the middle course, leaves each extreme behind, and avoids the dangers of voices, fleeing the songs of the Sirens and avoiding Charybdis. Music rejoices in Michael as her teacher and corrects her errors under the direction of such a master.

## CHAPTER IV. Geometry is the sixth sister. Geometry’s appearance. Her work.

[Col. 0518B]

The sixth sister presses upon the work [Note: [Col. 0517] Manuscript A: “remains”; manuscript R: “pressing on.”], wholly applying herself to study and clinging to study more studiously than the others. Her bearing, dress, and beauty vie with one another in adding to her honor and in speaking alike in her praise.

She wears an inclined head, yet suffers no bodily loss, but directs her gaze downward [Note: [Col. 0517] Manuscript V: “one.”], so that the inclination itself may declare the things on which her mind is fixed. [Note: [Col. 0517] “Is placed.”] Her face reveals her mind and confesses her disposition. The maiden carries a rod with which she circles the whole world, measures the extent of the earth, confines the sea within fixed boundaries, and traces the heights of heaven with compasses.

Though her garment were sprinkled with a shower of fine

[Col. 0518C] dust, the dignity of its material and the beauty of its form are not darkened; rather, it shines adorned with many figures and prides itself on much distinction.

Here the language of painting recounts the whole art which sets forth and teaches the doctrine and practice of measuring: it confines the immeasurable, restrains the spacious, attains the small, measures the great, searches the depths,

355 dwells in valleys, and climbs to the heights. Here one reads what a point is [Note: [Col. 0517] Manuscript A: “what a point is.”]; what is called a curved, straight, equal, or bent line; what surface, bounded by a plane and knowing no depth, runs evenly without height.

What a tetragon is; what a triangular figure is; what is enclosed by triple measure; what a solid (*stereon*) is; and what a line drawn around its own center describes.

[Col. 0518D] Why the center lies in the middle; why every angle is either dull and obtuse or rises sharp and acute; and why the right angle is less than the obtuse but greater than the acute.

Why, according to the laws of the art and the rule of the given data, proceeding in a straight path above a given gamma, an equilateral triangle is described, in which the line, stretching itself out, supplies the given side.

How from a point a line equal to a proposed line is drawn, reproducing the given line; why a greater line produces from itself a smaller one by cutting off an end.

Why the “eleufuga” terrifies beginners in this art and compels them to go out first into the deep before they approach the shore, and to slip before they labor in the art. [Note: [Col. 0519] The manuscript reads both verses thus: “Before they approach the shore, and slip first before they labor in the art.”]

By what aid of reasoning a triangular figure finds another equal to itself; why a line is cut into equal parts, or an angle is divided by a similar art; and how one division divides one thing into two.

## CHAPTER VII. Geometry makes the third wheel.

Thus the maiden shines in this dress—or rather, this heroic woman concentrates her mind upon these things. Giving the rod rest, she puts on the smith’s clothing and gathers her scattered mind into one.

[Col. 0519B] With mind, hand, and study she attacks and corrects the material of lead itself, which the hammer repeatedly strikes.

[Col. 0520A] She impresses a form as she pleases; the old form departs, and the new form entering excuses the lead’s former defects. From lead the third wheel is born; born after the earlier ones, it takes their form in its own appearance.

There the written testimony calls out the names of craftsmen who, enclosing within fixed bounds the courses, measurements, weights, and limits of things—air, heaven, stars, sea, and lands—regard them by a like method.

Here the geometer traverses the wandering sphere of the airy expanse without motion; flies over the sea without wings; crosses the space of Ocean without an oarsman; walks into the stars without a step; and touches Olympus without reaching out.

Euclid, binding his precepts into a sequence and unfolding the art, places the parts of the art in proper order;

[Col. 0520B] he joins them as though bound by a certain cord of reason, so that you would think the rest sprang from one.

856 BOOK FOUR.

[Col. 0519]

## CHAPTER ONE. Astronomy, the last maiden. Astronomy’s face and dress. Her dignity and art. The spheres and motions of the planets. Astronomy makes the fourth wheel. Concord disposes and joins the parts of the chariot.

[Col. 0519C]

The last maiden follows, she who is first in beauty, first in attire, and bears the foremost mind beneath her breast. Her head does not decline toward earth through sickness, sadness, or at the mind’s command; rather, her face clings to the stars and hunts out heaven’s mystery and its fleeting causes. Her sight, the mind’s forerunner, announces them to the mind; and, as the mind’s frequent attendant, instructs the mind.

A brightness is present at her mouth which strikes our gaze with such splendor that sight, avoiding the mature brightness, fears to leave the coverings of the eyes. A sphere fills her hand; yet it might better be seen as the shadow of a sphere, for it receives shadow alone.

[Col. 0519D] [Note: [Col. 0519] Both manuscripts insert this verse: “And, not retaining the proper character of a sphere, it rises upward.”] Yet it lies on a plane, raised by no swelling.

Her dress blazes with gems and exults in gold; by its own splendor it seems to equal the stars. Here painting’s endowed power flourishes, speaks, instructs, teaches—indeed, gives precepts to her own: it teaches the laws, places, times, motions, signs, powers, courses, names, and causes of the stars.

Here one reads what the celestial sphere is; what axis divides the sphere into parts; what pole bounds the axis, whether rising upward or submerged below; why the world’s form is round; why the world is enclosed by five parallels, or cut by certain zones, freezing at the extremes, scorched by heat in the middle, and tempering the two lateral zones by their double removal, correcting flame with cold.

[Col. 0520B] Why the shortened circle encloses each colure, and neither can return to its former points,

[Col. 0520C] but the cutting-off gives each its name.

Why the obliquely running line, drawn on a sloping course, paints heaven with the twelve constellations of the zodiac and grants a welcome lodging to the wandering planet, sharing its own proper place with it.

By what principle the stars move; by what law a planet measures its direct course; by what law it retreats backward or remains fixed in a definite station.

By what principle the signs move in an oblique course; why a sign rises more directly in its own risings, taking its time of rising at the opposite point, and loses at setting the time which it spends more fully in rising.

What is the moon’s motion, what is the sun’s sphere, what is Mercury’s orbit,

357 what is Venus’s path, what is Mars’s route, what delay holds Saturn back, on what course the star of Jupiter runs,

[Col. 0520D] and what circle equalizes the wandering motions.

What, rising upward after leaving the earth’s point, goes forth and does not know how to fix its center in the earth.

Therefore the maiden, wearing the solemn attire of so great a dignity, does not bury her mind, nor distract herself in lazy leisure, nor weaken the powers of her mind; rather, with her body she exercises her whole mind in study. The sphere leaves her hand, because that hand is summoned to new tasks, claiming for itself the art of the hammering smith.

While her hand hammers gold and shapes the mass, the fourth wheel is born from gold. Excelling its companions in the honor of beauty, it makes the earlier wheels seem second.

The form of writing applauds those and gathers into its account those who, guided by the oar of mind,

[Col. 0521A] have gone to the heavenly dwellings and, searching heaven’s secrets, earned for themselves the honor of divinity.

There Albumasar consults the stars, the poles, heaven, and the seven planets, and brings their counsel back to earth, arming the earth and strengthening its frail things against celestial wrath and the anger of the gods above.

The strength of Atlas supports the stars while it is itself supported by the stars; without burden, it bears a burden—the sky. It bears heaven while it is borne; and while bearing it yields to the stars, the stars yield to it as it yields.

Accordingly, as rule requires, order demands, reason calls for, and prudence dictates, the purple-bordered company of sisters forges and refines, makes—indeed perfects—and adorns the parts of the chariot. With a finer file it adorns them together and leaves in them no deformation

[Col. 0521B] of excessive shape or complaint of blemish. Concord, setting the finishing hand to the work and bringing it to a blessed conclusion, unites the scattered parts by order, law, and place; binds them in alliance, makes them one, and brings them into proportion.

Thus the joined parts, bound by fastenings, nails, and connections, form the chariot. Shining beforehand with the light of beauty, it shows in its own appearance that within it the divine hand and Minerva of heaven have labored.

## CHAPTER II. Reason yokes five horses to Prudence’s chariot, namely the five senses. The first horse is sight. Hearing is the second horse.

Then Reason, taught by the counsel of instructing Nature, presents to herself five horses, which Nature has joined by a pleasing compact, harmonious peace, and faithful bond. She compels these untamed yoked horses, whom Nature’s favor nourished from their earliest years, to serve beneath the yoke. Nature has so formed the dispositions of these horses, giving them certain traces of mind, that, though brute beasts, they nevertheless revere their foster-mother.

Moreover, insofar as the nature of a harnessed horse permits, each boasts the gifts of its own nature.

358 No excellence of breeding or beauty is absent from them that could fully complete the appearance of a yoked horse.

The first horse surpasses his companions in breeding, beauty, and speed, and subjects the others to his own distinction. Breeding, form, color, appearance, boldness, and speed enrich him; nor does he suffer loss in this, that a ruddy color, sprinkled with whiteness, gilds him.

He does not run but flies. His hoof makes no mark upon the earth and bends no grass in passing; rather, as he goes he barely touches the earth with swift tread, leaving no tracks on the ground. The light breeze marvels that it has found his flights; Boreas wonders that his own course is slowed.

The breeze falls, the bird slows, and the flight of winged arrows grows dull. Everything is slowed in comparison with the horse’s course.

He anticipates the spur’s command and begins his course of his own accord, though he is easily restrained by the rein.

Moreover, the nobility of his stock itself heaps up his natural gifts: he is Pyrois,

[Col. 0522A] [Note: [Col. 0521] Pyrois is imagined by poets to be one of the horses of the Sun; it is also the star of Mars.] for he boasts of his father, and the father himself is reflected in the mirror of his offspring.

Jove’s favor gave him as a gift to mother Nature. The excellence of the gift increases Nature’s gratitude and favor toward the giver; nothing greater could so great a giver have bestowed upon so great a mother.

With such gifts, as the horse’s own nature requires, his appearance is ennobled. Beneath him the second horse has power, lesser in appearance and humbler in breeding; his adornment is inferior and his pace slower than the first’s. Although lesser than the first and second in beauty, he is nevertheless greater than all the others, first in the gift of beauty. Though he surpasses the rest, he is surpassed by one.

And though he cannot contend with the first horse on equal footing, the fleeting breeze nevertheless does not outstrip the second;

[Col. 0522B] rather, it competes with him in equal course.

No one color marks him, but he often disguises his face with the color of another. He thunders, snorting; he strikes the air with frequent flashes and wounds the thin air without causing a wound. [Note: [Col. 0521] Manuscript V: “the ear.”]

Rattles hung from his neck yield sweet sounds and flood the air with abundant song. In his face he bears his father, displaying Eous in his gestures and proving by form that he is his parent.

By gifts lavishly bestowed, Nature enriched her resources through this gift, earned divine favor, and portrayed her own love in the gift.

## CHAPTER III. Smell is the third horse. Taste is the fourth horse. Touch is the fifth horse.

[Col. 0522C]

The third horse turns somewhat aside from so great a radiance of beauty: he does not claim the gifts of the former horses but, possessing less, sighs after them.

359 Though his appearance is darkened in comparison with theirs, when compared with the rest it shines out; he is not defrauded of his own beauty. Though he is conquered by those already described in swift running, he rejoices triumphantly as victor among the rest, outflies them, and includes them within his own movement.

A subtle mixture of color is sprinkled over him, but that color eludes the eyes and refuses sight.

[Col. 0522D] A succession of intertwined flowers clothes him as with a fitting garment and breathes its own scents into him. The violet’s flower bathes him; the rose intoxicates the neighboring breezes [Note: [Col. 0521] “The rose intoxicates the ears.”]; and his nostril is satisfied with the scent of thyme.

A mare ignorant of natural mating bore him by wind alone, knowing no male and content with the breath of air as her husband, made pregnant by Zephyr as her spouse. By this gift Zephyr purchased the love of mother Nature and paid her his own tribute.

The fourth horse degenerates and has less power; he slows greatly, is low in form, and slackens in pace. He serves those previously described, almost reverently worshiping them;

[Col. 0523A] he attends on them and does not deny that he is their client, but serves them as masters like a household slave.

Yet he does not find Nature wholly ungenerous; indeed, he abounds in his own endowment by which he may sustain himself. He suffers no eclipse in this gift by which Nature customarily blesses a yoked horse.

Violets do not wither simply because the rose shines with the honor of its flower, or because the brightness of lilies arranges their adornment. Not everyone is mad whose understanding lacks Ulysses’ wit, nor mute because he does not know the Muse of Maro. Silver’s brightness does not grow pale if gold flashes; Hector does not take up arms less bravely if fuller Ajax thunders. In like manner, not all glory is absent from the fourth horse, although he is denied that degree

[Col. 0523B] of emphatic praise in which Nature places the earlier horses. Yet he does not complain that he has been cast down from every gift of Nature, but rejoices in the fortune by which rich Nature has blessed him.

A sea-green color smiles upon him; rain sprinkles him, and dew showers the yoked horse with watery rain. He retains and reserves as special and proper to himself this trait: swift to drink, he does not forget food. He indulges in drink; alone among all he runs to food, and in drink makes up the horses’ deficiencies.

The horse of Triton begot him; appointing him heir to his paternal right, Triton portrayed himself in him.

[Note: [Col. 0523] Triton is a sea-god and Neptune’s trumpeter.]

By this token of favor, Triton bestowed this gift upon Nature, giving mind along with the gift.

360 The fifth horse will scarcely defend the appearance and retain the form of a horse, if anyone tries to compare the earlier horses with him. For he will cease to be a horse; dressed in the mask of a yoked animal, he will taste of the ass, cast down into the same sluggishness and wholly stripped of equine habits.

[Col. 0523C] Yet if no comparison with the others diminishes this horse, but we examine him in himself, his adornment will not be excluded from his own gifts, nor will he suffer any degradation of beauty.

The fifth horse resembles and in part represents the fourth; yet in a small degree he is lower, for beauty smiled more sparingly upon this harnessed horse than upon the one mentioned before, who lowers himself less toward the earth as he goes.

[Col. 0523D] He does not raise his head fully enough; rather, with drooping countenance he bends his gaze downward. A dark color clothes him, possessed by blackness itself, which permits no other color beside it.

Yet the fortune of his lineage is not lowly. Aethon [Note: [Col. 0523] Aethon is said by poets to be a horse of the Sun; in Latin its name means “burning.”] begot him; Aethon rejoices in having the Sun’s horses as brothers and defends himself by the honor of his brothers.

Ops, mother of the gods above and wife of Saturn [Note: [Col. 0523] Ops is imagined to have been the mother of the gods and Saturn’s wife.], gave Nature to this horse as a sign of covenant; by it the bond of their love was made firmer and bound their desires.

## CHAPTER IV. Reason governs all the horses and yokes them to the chariot. Reason is the charioteer of Wisdom and Prudence. At Reason’s instructions Prudence mounts the chariot. She investigates the air and its nature.

[Col. 0524A]

Reason, under the guidance of Reason herself, forces the aforementioned horses beneath the yoke, joins them to the pole, urges the unbridled, binds the untamed, and reins in those that wander.

First she throws down the horse; mounted upon the fallen horse, she corrects his excesses with the reins, examines him with the rod, presses him with blows, voice, and threats. She scarcely makes him quiet, but at last, overcome, he is conquered; he obeys her and, exhausted, pants at Reason’s nod.

Thus Wisdom’s charioteer first sets the horses in order, lest, if Prudence mounts the four-horse chariot, the untamed horses range abroad, abandon the rule, follow devious courses, loosen the yokes, and dissolve the bonds. Then all would run loose, the chariot would sway, its structure would totter,

[Col. 0524B] each part would come apart, the connection would loosen, the reins would perish, and the whole substance of the chariot would collapse.

After the ordered arrangement, passing through the separate parts, has put each in order, Prudence, intending to mount the chariot, arranges herself for such a task.

The whole court sits beside her, applauds, rejoices with her, and takes pleasure in her. With abundant favor it cheers the maiden at her departure, prays for an auspicious return, and asks that the outcome of her return may be more serene.

361 Repeatedly it gives kisses, presses a seal upon her mouth, clasps her arms in embraces, entwines her neck, and greets her in heart and voice, doubling, repeating, and reiterating its farewell.

[Col. 0524C] Then, at Reason’s command, Prudence comes forward and mounts the chariot. The chariot’s beauty becomes more fully and abundantly complete, and her face is set aflame with rosy splendor.

Reason urges the horses with the guiding rod. The yoked horses begin their journey; the chariot rises, leaves the earth, and in its course enters the thin air.

Entering the regions of air, Prudence carefully examines in her mind all that air claims as its own; she investigates and penetrates the fleeting element. She asks what its material is and what gives rise to cloud; how the earth, wet with its own sweat, sweats itself out into clouds and fashions its garments in the sky.

Why Phoebus, thirsty and panting with the heat of his fire, drinks draughts from Ocean, turns his cups into clouds, and hangs in thick air the cloudy vessels, cups of rain, and bottles of showers.

[Col. 0524D] How fire, dying in a cloud, grows dull and produces thunderbolts as it dies; thus in death it presses more harmfully than in life, and when living cannot inflict what it inflicts when dead.

Whence winds arise; what seeds of things breathe movement into the winds and provide the causes of their motion.

Why the south wind, cupbearer of rains, serves rain to the earth and lavishly offers full cups to the world; how the thirst of Boreas drinks up southern showers and cleans the paths with rains as though it were a street-sweeper.

How Zephyr, a farmer without a plough, cultivates the earth and raises crops of flowers in gardens.

[Col. 0525A] Why the bird, safe with the oarage of its feathers, makes its plumes into oars and its wings into sails, crosses the airy sea like the likeness of a ship, and passes through such an abyss without shipwreck, safe and fearing no Charybdis in so great a sea.

## CHAPTER V. Prudence considers the spirits wandering in the air.

Prudence investigates more deeply the hidden entrances, secrets, and lurking places of the air. Searching with profound understanding, she sees with clearer sight the airy citizens who wander there: for them air is a prison, the abyss punishment, pain laughter, death life, and guilt triumph.

Their mind, wounded by the low poison of envy, pours its venom into the human race, so that it too may suffer from a like infection and the same disease.

[Col. 0525B] These are they who are always armed against us; they overthrow the unarmed, conquer the armed, seldom yield themselves, and, once conquered, cannot renew the duel.

As though clothed in an airy body and feigning our appearance, by many phantasms they deceive foolish human beings: sophists of falsehood and truth. In darkness they counterfeit light; in conflict, peace; they hide deceit beneath peace, fashion sweet things in gall, and offer corrupted things under the appearance of right.

God made these to be gods; true Day drenched them with true light; from their first origin the honor of divinity clothed them. Yet, leaving light behind, they went into their own darkness; leaving the fountain, they sought the pools of hell; stripped of the garment of beauty,

[Col. 0525C] they put upon themselves the garment of groaning and the sackcloth of sorrow. Cast down from heavenly majesty, they earned for themselves endless ruin.

O grievous outcome, wretched fall, singular plague! He who was free now serves; he who was wealthy begs; he who once reigned first in the court suffers exile; he who was second under the king suffers punishments from the king.

By this fall a jewel becomes mud, purple becomes sackcloth, light darkness, beauty confusion, glory downfall, laughter sadness, rest labor, seaweed hyacinth.

Thus the celestial star falls; thus Lucifer, ignorant of rising, is oppressed by setting; thus the citizen of Olympus, expelled, lives in exile and does not mitigate the fate of exile. Hope of return—every hope—is absent and yields to fear.

O pride: plague to be avoided, Charybdis to be fled,

[Col. 0525D] grievous fault, common disease, public pest, gate of sin, mother of vices, origin of wickedness, seed of hatred, pursuit of strife! It falls while rising, perishes when raised high, is lifted up only to perish, falls when promoted, and swells only in order to fall.

Unable to bear itself when carried above itself, it suffers ruin beneath itself; it cannot sustain itself, but is crushed by its own mass, falling beneath its own weight.

It compels a person to seek himself outside himself. When a person goes out from himself, made contrary to himself, he disagrees with himself; forgetting himself, he does not know himself. Going still farther beyond himself, he struggles to be more than he is; not content with his own origin,

[Col. 0526A] he wishes to be greater and labors to surpass himself. Losing what it seeks, it seeks while losing; desiring what lies to it, it pursues false honor.

This plague corrupts what is right, disfigures what is honorable, ferments morals, drives away justice, and destroys what is useful. It makes *saliunca* into roses and clouds the stars of virtues with clouds, through whose darkness they suffer eclipse.

By this light, the angel, banished from the court of the heavenly kingdom, pays for his sin with exile and atones for guilt by punishment—cast down from his own seat, broken by pride, overthrown by arrogance, ruined by envy.

## CHAPTER VI. Prudence visits the highest region of the air. The citadel of the sun is described. The sphere of Venus is described. Stilbon is the star of Mercury. The sphere of Mercury.

[Col. 0526B] Having traversed the space of air where clouds of heaven weave darkness with their own night; where a hanging cloud gathers waters into itself; where the shower of hail bursts forth; where winds contend; where the wrath of thunderbolt swells—Prudence passes beyond into the ether, where the grace of highest peace flourishes, pleasant rest abides, a still more pleasant air cherishes all things, all things are silent, purer ether smiles and drives away weeping, while cloudy air groans and blooms wholly with hidden light.

Having passed through the regions of ethereal light, she enters higher into that realm where splendor and fire hold sway. Pleasant light gleams there, but the force of heat, light’s companion, withdraws the caresses of light.

[Col. 0526C] Here the novelty of things, the glory of things, the unique form of things, the beauty of the world, delights the sight of the maiden as she travels; and a new kind of song intoxicates [Note: [Col. 0525] Manuscript V: “inebriates.”] her ear.

Yet she receives the sound with restrained hearing and a lesser tone, though she drinks it in with a discerning ear. Here the sound of the heavenly lyre expires in thick voices: where the moon’s sphere sighs with a subdued song, sounds hoarse—indeed, almost falls silent in sounding—languishes while sounding, and takes the place of the lowest, slackest string, scarcely deserving a place in the lyre.

Here Prudence sees openly the moon’s diminishings, changes, courses, phases, and labors: how Phoebus, joined to it, diminishes its light, or conversely how it steals from Phoebus the honor

[Col. 0526D] of light, compels the people to fear in deceitful night, and depicts the likeness of night where there is no night.

Why the moon produces moistures; why seas suffer the moon’s diminishings or rejoice in its fullness; what the moon’s mark signifies upon the moon, and what it signifies by marking. Nor can an accumulation of brightness erase the faint trace, while a small blemish confronts the fount of light and refuses to yield to that with which it contends; and in the ray of light the great shadow becomes daylit. [Note: [Col. 0525] “greater.”]

Ascending higher, the maiden climbs to the citadel where the sun holds sway, where the Sun’s waxen light burns, the living fountain of light gushes forth, the vein of heat flows, and the treasury of new splendor abounds.

[Col. 0527A] There the maiden sees what is the sun’s road, path, and course, and whence the begetter, fountain, shepherd, and source of ethereal light receives the fuel of his strength. [Note: [Col. 0527] Manuscript A: “heat.”]

How, reigning among the stars and compelling the planets by his authority to serve him, he now makes them halt in their motion, now by his majesty commands them to follow their swollen and devious solitary courses, and now, granting freedom of motion, restores to the planets the laws proper to their movements.

How, changing the face of his age at rising, he becomes a child; at mid-day grows into an adult youth; then rises to manhood; and at evening grows wholly old. Thus at each hour the sun displays the different forms of life’s ages, and a single day embraces an entire lifetime.

Already the maiden’s ear disdains the moon’s sound, because a sweeter and better sound entices and lures

[Col. 0527B] her ear and does not permit it to remember the former song.

This song is produced by the Siren that clings to the sun’s movements and reveals a lyre in the sweetness of its voice. Every voice marvels at her, reveres and adores her; the sound of the whole lyre sighs after her.

Leaving the sun’s realm, the maiden hastens her steps upward. But the winding uncertainty of the path and the many twists of the roads delay her pace. At last, after overcoming the hill [Note: [Col. 0527] “path.”] through the burden of effort and careful exertion, she reaches the region where Venus and Stilbon are joined in embracing bonds.

There Lucifer, the sun’s forerunner and herald of day, exults, signaling beforehand to earth the comfort of light; with his own rising he plays before the sun’s rising and predicts dawn through his own rising.

[Col. 0527C] Stilbon clings there as an inseparable companion to these steps, like a household servant following the footsteps of his sun. Veiling his tresses with solar rays, he tempers his fires and darkens his star with the sun’s cap.

The sphere of Lucifer, light in movement and swifter than the breeze, produces sound in its motion and sports with a high voice. In the lyre of Venus it is not thought a common Muse, but rightly gains the ear’s assent.

With equal voice, like manner, and neighboring song, Mercury’s Siren sings Venus’s melody and plays the lyre in friendly harmony with an equal sound.

## CHAPTER VII. The palace of Mars is described. The region of Jupiter is described. Jupiter’s star is good.

[Col. 0527D] Prudence proceeds, entering the fiery palaces of Mars. She marvels at the assaults and wrath of heat which that place produces, wholly steaming with fire and knowing nothing but boilings and storms of flame.

There winter does not mourn, spring’s grace does not smile, autumn does not swell; summer alone thunders.

Here Mars rules, hot with fire and fruitful in anger, sowing wars, thirsting for quarrels, and thirsty for our blood; he shakes peace loose and breaks treaties anew.

He delights in violating the pledged faith of kingdoms and changing rulers; he is clothed in the flaming hair of a comet. He prepares arms for men, compels madmen to hope,

[Col. 0528A] sows assaults, breeds anger, and loosens loves.

His face itself, by its redness, reveals what he bears within and proclaims the frenzy and plague of inner rage. By his infection he corrupts a companion planet; he teaches a cruel planet to rage more cruelly, or perhaps makes a kindly one savage by wickedness, harming it with poison.

His sphere rushes like a torrent and shouts in thunder, echoing lofty roars with its cry.

365 The Siren of thundering Mars cries out more loudly than the rest; but the sweetness of her song is itself weakened by the storm of sound. Harshness and rigor of voice diminish its favor and damage its charm.

Now the maiden’s journey passes beyond the Lemnian eruptions and vapors of fire; no flame touches the traveler or has dared touch her hair.

[Col. 0528B] Then she tests in her onward course Jupiter’s harmless fires, the joy of serene light, and the laughter of the sky.

This region is wholly bright with the lamp of Jupiter’s star and rejoices, blessed, in perpetual spring. Here Jupiter’s star gleams and announces salvation to the world; it restrains Mars’s anger and fury and meets the raging god with tranquil peace.

If a star foretelling evil and preceding misfortune is joined to Jupiter, he nevertheless makes the hostile star friendly. Alternating its conditions, he changes sad lamentation into laughter, applause, and grievous tears into joy.

Or if perhaps the health-bringing star Numia is joined to Jupiter, Jupiter’s star, with a more favorable aspect, increases health and doubles the omen of a better outcome. Loving covenant, sower of peace, nourisher of love,

[Col. 0528C] it uproots angers, banishes wars, restrains frenzies, erases quarrels, and checks Mars.

Generating sound by its movement, it does not strike the air with songs; Jupiter’s charming Muse makes it a sweet nightingale. Music rejoices in so great a fosterling of sound, one who heaps up the treasures of her own art.

## CHAPTER VIII. Saturn’s sphere is described. It moves slowly. Saturn’s star is harmful.
