Prudence, advancing farther, directs her steps to the heights. Passing beyond Jupiter’s courts in her course, she enters Saturn’s more distant dwelling-place and shudders at winter’s cold and brumal frosts, marveling at sluggish cold amid heat.

[Col. 0528D] There winter burns, summer grows cold, and heat is chilled; brilliance raves while flame becomes lukewarm. Here darkness shines, light grows dark, and there night flourishes with light while light grows daylike with night.

There Saturn traverses space with miserly motion, heavy progress, and a long day’s journey. [Note: [Col. 0527] Manuscript A: “serecta,” uncertain.]

Here by his cold he despoils spring of its joys, steals the beauty from the meadows and the stars of flowers. He grows cold while hot, burns while cold, overflows while dry, shines while dark, and grows old while young.

Yet his sound does not stray degenerate from song; his voice precedes those of his companions in mature

[Col. 0529A] harmony, a harmony which the dullness of song does not render tasteless, and to which the sweetness of voice gives flavor.

[Col. 0530A] Here reign pain and groaning, tears, discord, terror, sadness, pallor, lamentation, and injury.

366 BOOK FIVE.

[Col. 0529]

## CHAPTER ONE. Prudence ascends to the firmament. The zodiac and its signs are described.

[Col. 0529A]

The region of untroubled light and the fountain of brightness—

[Note: [Col. 0529] This entire verse is lacking in both manuscripts.]

—draws the ear by a muted yet sweet song: there stars shine, the constellations of the pole contend with much brilliance, and endlessly traverse their own day.

Where the stars paint heaven’s face, the joyful maiden ascends,

[Col. 0529B] having drunk in part of the burden of labor, and rejoices, refreshed by the serenity of the sky.

There shine forth among the stars and enjoy heaven those whom either fame made good by their deeds [Note: [Col. 0529] Manuscript A: “made gods”; manuscript R: “gods by deed.”] or fable fashioned in word, and who retain for themselves a name without divinity.

Here the new Alcides is admitted to heaven; there Perseus cuts down the face of burning Medusa with his sword. There Orion, lacking a sword but pretending to have one, threatens battles under the appearance of battle without war.

And the Haemonian old man, as the bow dictates, sets an arrow in motion, yet it does not flee in any flight or escape the command of the bow as it goes.

Here the Ledaean offspring gleams, nor the pledge of love
He lays aside among the stars that which he had previously borne upon earth.

He is changed into a constellation, starred by the star of renown—

[Col. 0529C] he by whose gift the star of medicine shone upon the mortal, giving weapons of health against diseases.

Parrhasis, translated to heaven, restores the faces that were taken away and the losses of modesty; to her Jupiter repaid the flower he had taken, granting that she should bloom eternally with the radiance of modesty in place of that flower.

Moreover, the court of heaven is inscribed with various stars, which the Muse of poets once entitled with diverse names, playfully beneath an image of truth.

The twelvefold company of signs shines conspicuously among the stars, bright with exceptional brilliance; it leaves the common multitude of stars below and surpasses the rest in starlight.

Here burns Cancer; Leo scorches; Virgo springs forth; Libra makes the day equal; Scorpius grows fierce; Chiron is cold;

[Col. 0529D] the Goat is stiff with frost; the Urn pours itself out; the Fishes are drenched. Aries exults; Taurus, bearing the banners of spring, foretells it; and the Laconian Twins do likewise.

The little eye of Prudence tastes this spectacle of heaven, which sight cannot penetrate; it seeks known matter and is amazed by the miracles of so great a light. [Note: [Col. 0529] Ms. A, *ocellis*, “with little eyes.”]

367 CHAPTER II. The horses, or external senses, cannot penetrate the secrets of heaven.

After she had traversed the heavenly approaches, the depth of heaven,

[Col. 0530A] and the wandering courses of the stars, and had halted upon the brow of the world, she wavers with anxious mind, is carried into varying impulses, and remains uncertain. Her mind falters, her spirit flows away; her will itself doubts along with her mind, and the anchor of her mind is fixed nowhere firm.

For she fears and, fearing, doubts that she may be led astray by the winding complexity of places to which the hazardous path stretches farther on: places that know no human steps or flights of birds,

[Col. 0530B] wholly untroubled by the onset of things or the noise of travelers, disturbed by no tumult.

Here a human step would fail as it went; the foot itself would wander drunkenly; dull sight, the foot’s lamp, would spend itself in idleness and deny guidance to the feet; light beneath light would be blind.

Not because the darkness of night reigns there, but because the splendor of purified, emphatic light kindles it. [Note: [Col. 0529] Ms. V, *euphaticae*.]

The ascent to it is difficult and retreat easy. Access is open to few, falling away to all. Hardly anyone can cross into it; everyone can turn aside from that path, which is passable to few and closed to many—far too narrow for virtue, broad for ruin.

Neither nobility of birth, nor the favor of beauty, nor a debased love of riches, nor worldly glory,

[Col. 0530C] nor worldly eminence, bodily strength, bold human wickedness, or rash daring makes for this place.

But only virtue of soul, steadfastness of mind, nobility achieved by deeds—not born, but implanted in the mind—inner beauty, abundance of virtues, rule of conduct, poverty toward the world, and contempt for honor.

Therefore, when Prudence sees the difficult approaches and the easy ruin, she is inflamed by the great heat of an anxious mind. She fears that the yoked horses, worn out by labor, may refuse to bear the yoke or obey their mistress’s reins; that, ignorant of the way, they may find the path unsuitable for their steps, denying the feet the conditions of walking; and that Reason may be unable to bend upward the reins which the horses stubbornly hold and resist their mistress,

[Col. 0530D] unbridled and refusing further service to her command.

While this double judgment draws Prudence’s mind in diverse directions, and she cannot test the hidden places by herself unless someone shows them to her beforehand or, regulating her progress, guides her along the way:

CHAPTER III. The adornment of Theology. She bears a book in her right hand and a scepter in her left.

Behold a maiden [Note: [Col. 0529D] This signifies Theology.] seated on heaven’s summit, looking down upon heaven, directing her eyes upward, striving with all the power of sight

[Col. 0531A] to seek something beyond the world—not pursuing anything bodily, but, transcending it, searching out the hidden cause of the incorporeal, and seeking the beginning and end of things. She is presented to Prudence; and, dazzling sight with the brilliance of her light, she relieves the mind by the novelty of the vision.

Nor is this surprising, since she surpasses all in such splendor of beauty that she adorns the stars with brightness, multiplying light by light and radiance by radiance, and does not cease to bestow borrowed light even upon Olympus itself.

Her face bears nothing earthly; her expression suggests nothing perishable, nothing mortal, nothing begotten. The maiden’s appearance displays only what is heavenly. The proofs of her beauty show that she is a goddess; no argument refutes what beauty itself establishes and a face most like heaven confirms.

[Col. 0531B] A diadem sets her head aflame; gold, radiant with the many lamps of gems, glows, and outside it glitters with the twelvefold starry splendor of precious stones.

In her right hand she bears a book; in her left she holds a royal scepter, and her eye most often returns to the book.

But it rarely returns to the rod; and when at last it does, it carefully circles the hand, lest the left hand falter beneath the rod’s burden and surrender the scepter.

A garment drenched in gold and gleaming with silver encloses her, more beautiful than clothing itself, more pleasing than a comely attire, and brighter than heaven’s pure star—than divine hand and Minerva’s skillful right hand ever wove, as the dignity of its form shows us.

[Col. 0531C] Here a subtle needle depicts the secrets of God and the abyss of the divine mind; it gives form to the formless, places the immeasurable, and displays the hidden.

It describes the uncircumscribed, offers to sight the unseen, and confesses in painting what speech cannot. [Note: [Col. 0531] Ms. A, *scriptura*, “writing.”]

How speech, subject to nature, is struck dumb when it attempts to speak divine things and loses the power of speech; how it longs to return to its former meaning; how sounds fall silent, scarcely able to stammer, and words, departing from their new meaning, lay down their complaint.

How God himself contains in himself all the names of things which the very nature of God does not reject; yet he bears them all through a mediating trope, as figure dictates, and adopts bare words without their things.

Being, just, without justice; living, without life;

[Col. 0531D] beginning without beginning; end without end; immeasurable without measure; strong without strength;

powerful without force; governing all things without movement; filling every place without being in a place; enduring without time;

remaining without position; possessing all things while ignorant of possession; speaking without voice; at rest without peace;

shining without new splendor; flashing without light.

369 Nor is he just merely in the true sense of the word, but is Justice itself; nor merely luminous, but Light itself, without night; nor is he called immeasurable merely by name, but is measure itself, describing each transient thing

[Col. 0532A] and fitting it within fixed bounds.

Nor is he strong merely in the sense of a saying, but Strength itself subsists, shining in eternal strength. [Note: [Col. 0531] Ms. A, *sistens*, “standing/subsisting.”]

He alone is rightly powerful, who is supreme power; he alone can do all things, and from him proceeds the power of the powerful.

Nor does he merely fill all places, but alone encloses each beneath himself, as the boundary and place of places.

Here one reads, though obscurely and in a slender figure, how one power, abiding, simple, eternal, is fountain, splendor, form, way, virtue, end, origin; the unbegotten begetter, the living God, the sole author; one in essence (*usia*), three in persons; he remains uniquely one, while this threefold relation makes him three, and in the three he remains one, three in one.

In what sense the Son is the mirror, light, splendor, and image of the Father:

[Col. 0532B] from God the Father, God one and the same; beginning from beginning; light from light; sun shining from sun; splendor produced from fire; like from like; true from true; one from one; eternal, born from the eternal; equal from the equal; good from the highest Good; sublime from the High One.

How ardor, love, concord, and the form of the two is the Spirit, in whom the Father properly gives kisses to the Son, and in whom the Father finds himself in the Son; in whom the Father sees himself, while another is born from himself, and the image of the begetter shines in the unbegotten one.

CHAPTER IV. Prudence greets Theology. She seeks her guidance and reveals the reason for her journey. Nature desires that a blessed human being be formed. Nature’s power is limited. A soul endowed with every virtue is sought.

[Col. 0532C]

Inspired by these observances, the queen leaves perishable things and consults the secret of God; she clings to divine things, raises her mind from earthly things, [Note: [Col. 0531] Ms. V, *exuit*, “strips off.”] and drinks in the *nous* with her mind, drunk with the draught of the divine stream—or rather, she should be called sober: for drunkenness born of such nectar flourishes in complete sobriety and does not compel the mind to depart from its proper function, but more nobly raises it, cleansing the contagions of our filth. [Note: [Col. 0531] *Elimans*, “polishing away.”]

With humble step, lowered face, and modest bearing, Prudence approaches her. First offering greeting, she fashions her conceived words in this speech:

“O queen of heaven, goddess of heaven, daughter of the highest

[Col. 0532D] Craftsman: for your divine face does not show you to be perishable or bear the stain of our race.

Your countenance proves you a goddess, and the scepter declares you queen; your glory shows that you are queen and born of God.

To you lie open the seat of the heavenly beings, heaven’s way, Olympus’s boundary,

370 the sphere beyond the world, the whole region of the Thunderer, the throne of God, and that which lies beyond fate.

Govern me as I wander; rule me in my dullness; steady me in my fear; teach me in my ignorance; correct me in my instability; gladden me in my sadness. Counsel me, a stranger, with joy; complete what I have begun; strengthen me when I waver; help me when I fall.

[Col. 0533A] For I wander, tremble, am astonished, untaught, laboring, failing, ignorant of the place, a stranger, exhausted. Though striving to surpass the heavens and invade the heavenly seats, to penetrate God’s inner chamber, the Thunderer’s bridal chamber, and Jupiter’s counsel, I approach them wavering, wandering, alone, and roaming; I attempt the hidden paths of heaven.

Yet I do not undertake these labors inconstantly, rashly, heedlessly, with chance hurling me into these paths. Rather, yielding to prayers and at last compelled to will it by Nature’s prompting, by the divinity of the virtues, and especially by Reason’s command, I am sent here in order that I myself may present Nature’s prayers to the supreme Thunderer.

Remembering that her hand has erred in many things, Nature wishes to recall the error and erase her former faults,

[Col. 0533B] or excuse the old blemishes by the newness of a blessed work. She attempts to form a human being, fashion one blessed, complete one perfect, and create one restrained, that she may cover her former offenses.

Out of so many thousands, she gives the erring world one person who may uphold rectitude for it, examine what is honorable, condemn avarice, distribute gifts, avoid excesses, hold to the mean, and ban abuses.

Nor does she decree this work of the virtues without their counsels, assent, governance, and desire; rather, the whole assembly of sisters nourishes these same conceptions by its assent. [Note: [Col. 0533] Ms. A, *eodem*, “by the same [assent].”]

But since mighty Nature’s office prevails only around earthly things, while her power languishes in the things above, having no jurisdiction there and unable to create the soul,

[Col. 0533C] which the hand of the heavenly Creator alone forms and which requires no prerogative of Nature in any respect: for this reason, striving long and struggling greatly, I am driven here and seek out the heavenly retreats alone, so that I may bring to God what Nature’s Reason conceives, what Virtue desires: [Note: [Col. 0533] *perferre Deo quod percipit ipsa*, “to bring to God what she herself perceives.”] that God’s own will may strengthen your will, [Note: [Col. 0533] Ms. V, *nostrum*, “our.”] hear our prayers, and let grace breathe upon our petitions.

May the divine hand send down from on high a soul keen in mind, filled with virtue, endowed with modesty, marked by faith, and shining with piety; a soul which, clothed in the robe of flesh, may so visit the world

that piety may redeem crime, virtue guilt, modesty incest, strength fraud, glory downfall.

May she overcome the earthly house, earthly force, the garment

[Col. 0533D] 371 of bodily mass, the mortal body; may the work of mighty Nature be enriched with such manifold endowment, deprived of no gift of beauty,

that the spirit may no longer disdain to have a bodily lodging, nor so great a guest lament the decay of its lodging, but may reign in the hall of flesh.

Therefore show me the way by which the path rises to the citadel of supreme Jupiter, lest wandering error carry me everywhere along byways, lest our mistaken wandering destroy the purpose and rob labor of its reward.”

CHAPTER V. Theology offers herself as Prudence’s companion, provided she leave behind the chariot and horses. As Prudence tends toward heaven, a second horse, Hearing, is granted her. The author’s most devout prayer to God.

[Col. 0534A]

Delighted by these words, the queen of heaven replied with gracious speech that she would offer herself to the traveler as companion, guide of the path, and mistress of her steps.

But she promises guidance to Prudence alone and urgently counsels her, mixing the force of command with counsel, to leave the chariot, set down the horses in heaven, and leave below the companion who is to be the firm guardian of so great a deposit, halting the chariot and restraining the yoked horses.

For if chariot, horses, and Reason strive to ascend, the heavenly path, acquainted with other ways, may not deign to admit such a traveler;

[Col. 0534B] the horse may stray, Reason may waver, and the chariot may totter.

The goddess’s commands are fulfilled and her wishes favored. Reason stands still, the horses are halted, and the four-horse chariot rests.

With all the others excluded, the queen grants her companion only a second horse, which marvels more sparingly at the journey and does not greatly deny the ascent, broken in by the rein of a better bridle. [Note: [Col. 0533] Ms. R, *fretus*, “relying upon.”]

Prudence is borne on the horse; the queen bears herself along; the horse is borne in flight; the goddess vies with the horse and, going on foot, overtakes the flying one and leads the way before her companion’s step.

Thus far my Muse has sounded in a faint murmur; thus far my page has played in fragile verse while the Phoebean lyre resounded. But, laying aside the small lyre, I now reach for a greater one; casting off the whole poet,

[Col. 0534C] I claim for myself the new words of a prophet.

Earthly Apollo shall yield to the heavenly Muse; the Muse to Jupiter; words obedient to heaven shall yield to the Word alone; earth shall give place to Olympus.

For this song I shall be the pen, or scribe [Note: [Col. 0533] “not scribe.”], the sounding bronze, the silent writer’s page, the singer’s pipe, the sculptor’s chisel, or the speaking Muse; the thorn bearing a rose, the reed offering new honey, night shining from another source, an earthen vessel flowing with nectar.

Highest Father, eternal God, living Power, sole form of the good, way of rectitude, boundary of what is honorable, fountain of life, sun of justice, refuge of piety,

372 beginning, end, measure, seal.

[Col. 0534D] Cause of things, abiding Reason, life-giving *nous*, true Wisdom, true day, light knowing no night, highest origin, perfect beauty of the world, everlasting life,

ruling things born, sowing things to come, preserving all things that arise; enclosing all beneath number, setting each beneath weight, restraining all beneath stable measure.

You draw the forms of things and the shadow of the sensible world from the exemplar of the intelligible world, painting it outwardly in the image of earthly form.

You clothe the old mass, complaining of the filth of its appearance, in a better garment; and, marking it with the seal of form,

[Col. 0535A] through the mediating bond you exclude tumult. [Note: [Col. 0535D] Ms. A, *excludens*, “excluding.”]

You are the efficient cause when you bring a thing into being; the formal cause when you shape it; the final cause when, preserving the thing in being, you confine it beneath a fixed end.

Shine before me with divine light; more fully bedew my mind with divine nectar; rain upon it, erase the stains of my soul, cut away its darkness, and make me serene in the splendor of your light.

Renew my pen; cleanse my tongue of rust. Grant, I pray, that I may speak your words; grant speech to one mute; give a fountain to the thirsty; direct the path for one wandering; guide the sailor’s ship; grant a harbor to one afraid, breathing a heavenly wind into my sails.

CHAPTER VI. Prudence marvels at the crystalline waters. She marvels at the concord of the elements. She examines the nature of the crystalline waters. Exact knowledge of things above the moon exceeds the powers of nature.

[Col. 0535B]

Now, with the goddess directing her, Prudence had surpassed the starry heights. Marveling at the new path and the knots of the ways, she wondered what could sustain the weight of so great a mass, unless the novelty of things refreshed her own sight and the queen bore part of her labor.

As she passes, she marvels at waters which an undivided order of place has joined with fire. Flame does not hinder the liquid, nor does that liquid struggle in opposition against the flame;

rather, they lay aside the weapons of their contention.

No longer do they care to recall their native tumults, which discordant assent binds: concordant discord, hostile peace, fantastic faith, the false bond of love,

[Col. 0535C] deceptive friendship, a shadowy covenant.

Wisdom fixes sight and mind upon them, searching keenly in spirit who made peace present where no peace abides; who commanded Mars to be absent where Mars holds sway; who bound a covenant there where there is no covenant; who mingled peace with anger, joined covenant to dispute, and love to strife.

Prudence inquires more deeply, pressing more eagerly: whether that liquid flows, wedded to it by the neighboring flame of heaven, and tempers the fierce angers of the flame; whether, wearing the appearance of mist and the form of vapor,

373 spread out in the likeness of a cloud in the highest ether, it hangs there and gives draughts to the thirsty flame; or whether it takes the form of ice and presents the shape

[Col. 0535D] of crystal, the liquid itself losing its liquidity.

Yet by living reason Prudence proves that no moisture can there make any turnings, nor can it range in its own flow, since no channel there offers it a bosom; no earthly womb spreads its recesses for it; nor, drawn by its native weight toward the center, can moisture rush downward to the depths, friend of its own gravity, since flame denies it descent and compels the waters to remain above, binding them there as though in a closed prison.

For whoever imagines that fire, by some stealthy fall, knows how to send dew down from above is a philosopher who lacks reason and prophesies falsehood.

[Col. 0536A] He pursues idleness and catches clouds and empty things, putting a knot in a rush, smoke in light, creating a stumbling-block on level ground, and darkness in light.

By this reasoning too she proves that no vapor there exhales into clouds, nor does suspended moisture veil the ether with waters, where earth emits no breezes and fire does not suspend clouds in the ether.

From these things Prudence concludes that heavenly moisture retains the appearance of crystal and takes the form of ice: ice ignorant of frost and unaware of winter, more familiar with summer and heaven’s heat, not deigning at the face of fire to melt into liquid.

Yet this is what most amazes and moves her: by what bond of trust, by what covenant of peace, cold things may agree with hot and flowing things with sluggish,

[Col. 0536B] where there is no mediator of peace and no binding covenant that, once peace is found, may destroy hostile quarrels and cut off conflict.

She fails in inquiry; inquiry overcomes her, conquered by her own search. But, defeated, she laments her own failures in complaints; thus that complaint becomes a question, leaving Prudence only sighs.

Nor is it surprising that Prudence yields before things which so exceed the laws of mother Nature, surpass her course, and cause the mind to fail, the intellect to halt, reason to grow dull, and wisdom to waver. Cicero himself is silent; the tongue of Maro grows hoarse; Aristotle languishes; Ptolemy’s understanding wanders.

CHAPTER VII. The delights of the empyrean heaven.

[Col. 0536C]

Prudence leads the journey farther, shaping her companion’s step by her own. At last, after great labor, manifold vision, and much effort, she ascends to places of joy, places full of favor, places pleasing to the heavenly God, pleasing to the Thunderer.

374 Here is laughter without sadness; serenity without cloud; delights without failure; pleasure without end; peace free of hatred; rest ignorant of labor; ever-ruddy light; the sun of true light; a rising that knows no setting; a welcome morning without evening.

Here splendor knows no night, satiety no weariness; full joys flourish, touched by no sorrow.

Here Fortune does not walk an uncertain path; she does not weaken laughter with tears, prosperity with adversity, joy with sadness;

[Col. 0536D] she does not spoil honey with vinegar, mingling harsh things with pleasant, dark things with clear, joining darkness to light and mournful things to merry.

Rather, tranquil rest remains; Fortune’s accidents do not know how to turn it, having no end, into clouds.

Here shines forth the heavenly royal court itself, which rejects human filth and the contagion of the world.

This sphere beyond the world, this blessed portion of the world, is cleaner than the world, purer than chastity itself, brighter than what is bright, more gleaming than gold. It shines with gentle splendor and flashes with harmless fire, lacking heat but abundant in radiance; it possesses the charm of splendor and rejects the harm

[Col. 0537A] of heat. It cherishes no wickedness with its brilliance and strikes no one with burning heat.

Here fire is less hot than fire, more bright than fire; and, remaining one, it is at once lesser and greater.

Since this place entirely sparkles with blessed fire and is graciously favored by the flame, it is judged to be the empyrean heaven, to which flame smiles with benign fires and adorns the court with brightness.

Here dwell the citizens above and the nobles of the Thunderer: angelic companies and divine powers, governors of the world, heavenly troops, hosts of heaven, our guards. Diverse rank, function, office, differing virtue, abundant power, and unequal degree and distinction of work divide them.

Here burn the seraphim, aflame with the heat of the higher

[Col. 0537B] light and irradiated by the splendor of the eternal sun.

The cherubim, filled with the liquid of the divine fountain, know more and cleave more perfectly to God’s mind.

And in the thrones resounds the balanced judgment of God, in which God himself sits and weighs judgments.

The ruling powers take their name from their office. As they yield to those above, so the rest yield to them; together they command and obey their commander.

The principality arranges its citizens in order and binds the wishes of its own subjects to its wishes.

The host of Powers overcomes with heavenly arms the rulers—or rather, tyrants—of this air.

Virtues oppose the laws of nature, loosen their bonds, and refashion old things in new forms.

The archangel uncovers mysteries, opens secrets, reveals

[Col. 0537C] hidden things, and announces to the world what lies still more concealed; he discloses heaven’s mysteries to earth.

Greater in service, but inferior to all these in power, the army of the angelic people renders the duty of obedience and proclaims lesser things to the world, ministering among us in diverse employments.

Here the citizens of the supreme King dwell in their city. The commonwealth of heaven is entrusted to these citizens for preservation. Among them this law is established: one commands, one acts, another obeys the rest.

Each learns in the book of the divine mind what must be done, and there reads what things are to come, consulting God and seeing all things in the mirror of divinity.

Nor does one angel alone claim so great a city for himself.

CHAPTER VIII. Saints assumed from earth inhabit heaven. The diverse merits of the saints.

[Col. 0537D]

Here dwells the one whom life and virtue made pious and blessed, and who on earth earned for himself the divinity of Olympus:

earthly in body, heavenly in mind; perishable in flesh, divine in life; living divinely, wise beyond earthly things, inwardly pondering divine things.

Whom neither pride nor the glory of worldly things raised up, nor love of the world cast down; whom slippery luxury did not break; whom excess of riches, the ardor of possession, devouring envy, the anxious plague of foul

[Col. 0538A] avarice, or blind desire for praise did not inflame.

Rather, patience lowered him, as did contempt of the world, poverty of possessions, strict regulation of sustenance, contempt for the flesh, [Note: [Col. 0537D] Ms. V, *dejectio*, “abasement.”] and direction of life.

He trampled riches with a conquering spirit, overcame evil, and forced the flesh to serve him.

The dignity of life, merit of virtue, and reward of labor enroll such persons among the angelic companies: those whom virginal brightness or the purple of martyrdom clothes, or whom the laurel of the teacher enriches.

Those whom the gift of a little crown does not receive, it crowns with the laurel of common reward, all relying on the same recompense.

Though their merit is diverse and unequal splendor, differing light, and unequal reward result, joy remains equal for all and laughter alike where recompense differs.

[Col. 0538B] Nor is it surprising that an equal grace of joy awaits all to whom one life is given as reward, in whom God himself is all things to all: both gift and giver, giving many things to one and one thing to many.

CHAPTER IX. The praises and prerogative of the Virgin Mary.

Here the Virgin surpasses the heavenly citizens by her distinctive honor: she who, not losing her own modesty under the law of giving birth, deserved the name of mother together with that of virgin.

In her two names agree, their conflict buried,

376 though they are accustomed to fight each other and stir up quarrels. Mother and virgin no longer disagree; with their disputes excluded,

[Col. 0538C] they turn to kisses of peace.

Here nature is silent, the force of logic is banished, every judgment of rhetoric perishes, and reason wavers.

She is the one who, by the wondrous operation of a divine gift, bore her Father and, herself a parent, conceived her Son, retaining virginal honor and not losing a parent’s rights.

In the bridal chamber of her womb, the highest divinity prepared a lodging for itself; the Son of the highest Craftsman wove a tunic for himself and put on the garment of our salvation, clothed in our covering. [Note: [Col. 0537D] Ms. A, *carnis*, “of flesh.”]

She is the star of the sea, way of life, gate of salvation; rule of justice, boundary of piety, source of virtue, mother of pardon, bridal chamber of modesty, enclosed garden, sealed fountain, fruitful olive, fragrant cedar, delightful paradise,

[Col. 0538D] rod of spices, wine-cellar endowed with heavenly liquor and offering heavenly nectar; rose blooming without knowledge of thornbush, grace ignorant of fault, fountain free of mud, light dispelling clouds; hope for the wretched, medicine for the guilty, protection for the blessed, return for the banished, path for the wanderer, light for the blind, rest for the cast down, respite for the weary.

She is the one who wiped away the first falls and the stains of the first parent, overcoming guilt by virtue; restoring what was destroyed, returning what was taken away, making amends for what was lost, renewing what had vanished, repaying what was driven out; giving new joys after evening laments, and shining with newness of life after death’s darkness.

[Col. 0539A] At her coming the golden age returns to the world; piety after crime, grace after fault, virtue after vice, peace after hatred, merriment after sadness.

As a rose compensates with its flower for the harshness of the thornbush, as an adopted branch redeems with its sweetness the fruit of a bitter root, so she atones for her mother’s crimes and causes her mother to be born again through her daughter.

Thus may she cleanse the guilty woman, she who is pure; the corrupt woman, she who is virgin; the shameless woman, she who is modest; the unhappy woman, she who is blessed; the proud woman, she who is humble; and may the daughter give birth to her mother for life.

The heavenly court depends upon her command; it stands ready in devoted mind for her command. With her, he governs the reins of the heavenly kingdom—he who is her Father and offspring, born from her and her author—ruling all things and ruling without end. Under this king the soldier triumphs

[Col. 0539B] in heaven and serves as an exile upon earth.

He is the one who, entering the prison-house of our flesh, bound himself in punishment in order to free all those bound; [Note: [Col. 0539] Ms. V, *se poenae vinxit, ut vinctos solveret*, “bound himself to punishment, that he might free those bound.”] who became sick in order to heal the sick; poor, in order that he might bring aid to the poor themselves;

[Col. 0540A] 377 dead, in order that Life itself might grant life to the dead; who suffered the lot of an exile, that as an exile he might draw the wretched from exile.

Thus envy perishes by envy, wound by wound; thus disease condemns disease, death is put to flight by death. Thus the living one dies that the dead may live; the heir goes into exile that he may make slaves heirs; the needy becomes rich, the poor powerful, that he may enrich the needy.

Thus the free one serves that he may free slaves; the heights seek the depths, so that the lowest may ascend to the highest.

That night may shine, splendor is darkened; the true sun grows faint in eclipse, that he may bring back the stars to their rising.

The physician is sick, that, diseased, he may heal the sick.

Heaven conforms itself to earth; cedar to hyssop; the giant himself to the dwarf; light to smoke; the rich to the needy;

[Col. 0540B] the healthy to the sick; the king to the slave; purple to sackcloth.

He is the one who, pitying our condition, departed from the court of the eternal Father and endured the indignities of our lot; though without crime, he fixed upon himself the punishments of crime and the losses due to our guilt.

378 BOOK SIX.

[Col. 0539]

CHAPTER I. Prudence cannot bear the splendor of the Empyrean heaven. Theology strengthens her. Theology implores Faith’s assistance. Theology teaches the articles of faith.

[Col. 0539C]

After the Virgin had entered the throne of God and the heavenly seats [the printed text reads *Post virgo*], she wished to sample new things beforehand by seeing them. [Note: [Col. 0539] V. Ms.: “After the Virgin of God, the ground, and the heavenly seats.”]

The splendor struck her eyes; the novelty of things struck her mind with astonishment; sight failed in them, and the inward mind grew dark before them.

Thus sleep invaded one awake; thus treacherous slumber oppressed Prudence’s spirit, and, lulled by sleep, ecstasy itself compelled her mind to serve its sleep. [Note: [Col. 0539] Ms. R, *dormire*, “to sleep.”]

And now, falling, she would have suffered headlong ruin, had not her companion run to her, embraced her as she fell, held her up in her hands, and, strengthening the maiden’s limbs with a gentle embrace,

[Col. 0539D] averted so great a fall. She approached her with mild words and soothed the mind’s stupefaction; yet her full mind was not restored to her.

But when she could by no means uproot the evil of stupefaction or bring back the entire mind, so as to bring help to Prudence, shake off all slumber, restore her mind, and compel it to return, the queen entreats with prayers her own sister, who sits upon the throne of heaven above, searches the heavenly depth, and clings only to God’s inner chambers.

Reason affirms nothing to her; belief itself suffices, and Faith alone, with reason removed.

[Col. 0540C] For Reason does not precede Faith; rather, Faith itself anticipates Reason, and Reason at last obeys Faith when Faith teaches, and follows its teacher.

She writes the articles of faith and the divine symbols on pages, writing in her mind what she depicts with her reed.

The garment in which this aforementioned woman shines glows purple in raised marks, with white color intermingled and its brightness subdued; her apparel declares the judgment of her mind, and the mind itself seems visible in it.

The garment yields to painting: it is wholly written with figures and, written, displays the form of a little book.

Here the living picture renews the teachers of old, through whom our Faith, spread throughout the whole world, shone forth and glittered illustriously with titles of praise.

Here [Note: [Col. 0539] Ms. R, *sic*, “thus.”] Abraham, father of our faith, casts off the role

[Col. 0540D] of father, as he strives with willing mind to obey the highest Father and refuses to be a father to his son.

In him Nature and Faith wage a conflict, being at odds and drawing one mind in contrary directions.

For Nature teaches a parent to spare his son. But Faith stands firm in opposition, commanding him to disregard his son, so that Nature may favor the highest Father.

Therefore the father desires what he does not wish; now attempting to spare, now willing to offer, at last he himself refuses what he desires.

Thus Nature yields to Faith and, grieving, gives way to the conqueror, forced to will what it does not wish.

[Col. 0541A] Peter shines in the strength of Faith with the light of virtues, and his power shines in its shadow.

Armed with the merits of life and the endowment of wisdom, Paul presses on with persuasion, reason, threats, and powers, and opens the entrance of Faith to the gentiles.

He conquers the rebellious not only by signs, but by reason. Nor is it enough to travel by a path granted him: he desires more and delights to make the way by reason.

There, protected by Faith’s shield and the armor of justice, Lawrence overcomes enticements, threats, prisons, beatings, and deaths; he surpasses his own fires.

Vincent, equal in the merits of conflict and a soldier in the same arms, conquering the world, tramples everything; fighting the living in death, he triumphs.

[Col. 0541B] Although the dignity of writing paints this clothing, no wantonness diminishes the garment. Rather, it was such as age requires in a matron who has reached the bounds of old age, full of days, her head sprinkled with grayness and the hoarfrost of age.

Yet mature old age does not plow her face with furrows; her face disagrees with her age. It shows youthful years, while her white hairs speak otherwise, since the grace of her face thus vies with her gray hairs.

CHAPTER II. At Theology’s urging, Faith comes to Prudence and frees her from ecstasy. Ecstasy is described. A heavenly drink is given to languishing Prudence. Faith offers Prudence a mirror in which she may see everything that is in heaven, though only obscurely.

[Col. 0541C]

This woman, moved of her own accord and touched by her sister’s prayers, directs her steps to where Prudence, struck by the taste of lethargy, languishes, portrays death’s image, dies while living, and lives while dead.

But when, on arriving, she recognized her from the signs that indicated her, saw her stupefied, and was astonished at her lying there, she grieves in pity at these misfortunes. She lays aside the hardness of mind; breaking into groans, the majesty of her spirit is compelled for a time to soften; hardness departs, and compassion alone possesses her mind.

Therefore she approaches more closely and visits the fallen woman at nearer range. She seeks the seeds of the languor and tests all things—place, time, causes, and symptoms—carefully investigating the disease. At last she finds its traces and knows that Prudence suffers the dreams of lethargy,

[Col. 0541D] as the outward signs of languor declare.

Having found the root of the evil and discovered the matter of the disease, she further investigates what remedy can remove the causes of languor, destroy the pest, overthrow the plague, and drive away the sickness.

Accordingly, by threats, prayers, shaking, and cries she prepares to overcome sleep; but such sleep resists.

Nor is it surprising that sleep strives to depart before these things. This was not the slumber of sleep, but the image of death: it darkens life’s light and puts life to sleep more than sleep does, but less than death; greater than sleep, less than death, yet nonetheless a sure preface to death.

[Col. 0542A] Since such medicine cannot repel the disease or overcome the strength of so great a malady, a drink is given to the languishing woman—prepared by a heavenly hand, compounded with honey-flowing flavor, honeyed in taste, sweet in scent, fragrant with secret spices, rejecting earthly seasonings, and offering a new incense of heaven.

It pervades the whole body, courses with life through it, enters the veins, searches the nerves, and penetrates the marrow.

At its coming Prudence returns to herself; when she returns, every error of mind is shut out.

Stupefaction itself, now driven away, is amazed that medicine can do this, and marvels that so great a disease yields to such medicine.

Yet although the eye of her mind shines again within, her outward eye still languishes and cannot endure the empyrean radiance or heaven’s excessive brilliance.

[Col. 0542B] Therefore the skillful matron returns to her art,
And especially splendid, graceful, glowing, admirable [Note: [Col. 0541] Utr. MS: “wonderful”], polished,

spread over a great expanse and written in figures, she presents to Phronesis a mirror in which are reflected all things contained within the empyrean realm, all that shines, all that the heavenly world possesses. Yet in these things there appears a discordant aspect: here is the thing, here its shadow; here hope [Note: [Col. 0541] A MS: “thing”], here the appearance; here light, there the image of light.

This mirror holds the mind and checks the gaze of Wisdom, lest a greater light confront her eyes, offend them, and weary sight together with the mind. This mirror is present as mediator, lest the radiant abundance of empyrean light impoverish the use of sight.

[Col. 0542C] In this mirror sight takes breath, finds a congenial light, and rejoices: light shining in light. In this mirror Wisdom beholds, with a gaze that mirrors, whatever the divine world embraces within itself. As she sees each new thing, she marvels at all things and delights in all; and the newness of things produces new joys. Her mind delights together with her vision, casts off every mist of error, and joys suffuse her mind; every symptom of its own pain perishes.

If she knows anything less fully, the attendant matron teaches her more fully, supplies her deficient insight, discloses what is hidden, and opens what has been shut up.

381 Here she sees the host of the angelic people and the heavenly senate; likewise the palm of victory and the sweet triumphs of the saints, their unequal merits and the fruits of their labours.

[Col. 0542D] She marvels at the merit of that Virgin; she adores the birth of her who gave birth while the flower of modesty did not wither or become worn away by the burning tide of lust. Wondering, she is astonished at the manner of conception and birth, and at the intact flower of modesty; she cannot discover how she can be a mother who has known no intercourse with a man.

She flees to the laws of logic. Accordingly, it denies the rights of a parent to her to whom virginity grants the honour of a virgin. By a similar case it wishes to overthrow the mother's virginal chastity: it argues that the mother is the parent of the birth, and that the birth belongs to its mother by natural right.

Yet this reasoning wavers when it finds a mother together with virginity,

[Col. 0543A] and sees the arguments of logic lying defeated. Wondering more deeply, it hesitates more; lingering longer, it asks by what law of heaven a blessed daughter brings forth her father, an earthly woman God, one who will fall the One who remains, a flower a cedar, a star the sun, a spark a furnace, and a rock sweats out liquid honey.

It marvels that God should clothe himself in our form and dwell in our houses: that the ruler of flaming Olympus should hide beneath seaweed, that a gem should clothe mud, a violet be covered by hemlock, life die, and the sun grow dark. What glue, what joint, what bond, and from where, can join human things to God, unite divine things to what is perishable, and by what order can God be joined in covenant with humankind?

While Phronesis marvels at each thing and attempts to trace all things

[Col. 0543B] by the laws of her own reason, the attendant matron—

## CHAPTER III

—warns her not to dream there of human laws, worldly covenants, the courses of nature, or our conditions, where these have no power. Rather, every decree is silent, laws stand in awe, rights are astonished, where the will alone of the supreme Maker reigns. It excepts whatever it wills from our rule; where rights favour, the rule yields to the Maker, and the canon falls silent when the Master gives command.

There reason is not sought, but faith alone. There the heavenly Cause transcends lesser causes; the highest Law surpasses laws, and the Rule of rules. Therefore let faith suffice there; let reason cease its inquiry

[Col. 0543C] there, and let faith restrain the reins of reason.

## CHAPTER IV. Prudence, abandoning Reason’s guidance, follows Faith. Faith also takes Theology as her companion. Prudence, accompanied by Faith and Theology, enters the heavenly places. She arms her eyes with a mirror. She investigates the causes of predestination. She considers the various dispensations of God and other wonders of the empyrean heaven.

At these admonitions Prudence assents, yields to instruction, follows Faith, and ascribes wholly to the heavenly Author what she sees surpasses our law and proceeds according to the rationale of an exceptional jurisdiction.

382 Thus instructed, she more quickly takes up the way. The queen directs her step and marks her gait with her own manner of walking; but lest the hidden place, the hazardous path, the twisting boundary, the strange road should hinder the Virgin’s steps,

[Col. 0543D] she appoints as companion for her the one who restored to Phronesis the mind that had been banished, restoring its function when the abuse of illness had yielded.

No road is unknown to her; no place is hidden from her.

[Note: [Col. 0543] A MS reads this verse thus: “No hard boundary, no wandering path deceives.”]

No confused boundary obstructs her; no path deceives her. Accompanied by these, Phronesis proceeds more safely on her way, crosses perilous routes, strange places, and unknown paths. Nor could she now overcome the winding turns of the places; but each sister supplies strength to her wavering, steadies her step, cuts short the burden upon her pace, and, lightening the punishment, removes weariness.

The mirror protects the vision offered to Phronesis from every encounter

[Col. 0544A] with light, lest the splendour of heaven intoxicate it and the fire strike back upon her eyes.

At last the weary, trembling, astonished Virgin completes her journey and enters the highest palaces of the eternal King. She rejoices that the weight of her completed labour has been overcome; yet she is amazed at everything that the messenger presents to her sight in the mirror, where nothing mortal, perishable, failing, or earthly shines, but only what is eternal, heavenly, abiding, immovable, and certain gleams.

Here she sees innate forms; she contemplates heavenly ideas, the forms of human beings, the first principles of things, causes of causes, seeds of reasons, the laws of the Fates, the sequence of destiny, and the mind of the Thunderer: why God rejects these, predestines those, prepares this person for life, and withdraws his gifts from that one.

[Col. 0544B] Why humble poverty oppresses some, crushes the needy, and want is satisfied with tears alone; why every channel, exceedingly rich in resources, rains wealth upon others, and the prosperous man swims in gold. Why wisdom enriches some, while impoverished understanding, a poor mind, and a beggarly will cloud others. Why the beauty of form makes Adonis radiant when purified; why Danus bears a misshapen appearance; why Hector flashes in arms; why Ulysses sparkles with the ray of intellect. Why Cicero is an orator, Tiphys a sailor, Milo a painter, Pollux a boxer, Cato stern, and Naso a poet.

These alone do not delight the sight of Phronesis. Advancing farther, vision charms the beholder with another novelty and brings back wonders on its return.

[Col. 0544C] Here she sees the brightness of a water-bearing fountain shine forth, which, rich beyond measure in waters and more conspicuous than any other stream, outshines the stars in light and surpasses honey in flavour.

383 Paradise yields to its delights; balsams are conquered by its fragrance, and nard submits to it. From it proceeds a stream which, not forgetful of the qualities possessed by that fountain, assumes for itself the fountain’s whole dignity and answers the fountain with equal honour; yet the grace breathing upon the irrigating fountain is not less.

Therefore the fountain produces the stream, and the stream together with the fountain produces the river, retaining the flavour of fountain and stream. Though fountain, stream, and river are distinct, they come together into one; the substance of the three is the same and simple, their flavour alike, their colour one, their splendour in them unique, and their appearance conformable and the same—

[Col. 0544D] like the appearance of a fountain, a sun surpassing a sun in light.

Here it pours forth a ray which the earthly sun adores, to which heaven and the stars are favourable, and before which the world makes supplication. This sun never suffers setting, nor any eclipse, nor does it feel the darkness of a cloud. The ray proceeding from it equals the Father in brightness and speaks of its parent by its own splendour.

The sun is the same, the form the same, the light one, the splendour coeternal, in no way declining from its own origin. It is another sun, but not something other; one sun and one thing, abiding with its begetter: light harmonious with light, radiance with radiance, splendour not forgetful of its own fire.

[Col. 0545A] From itself, together with the sun, the ray produces heat, which, soothing, burns; burning, soothes; blazing, moderates; inflaming, caresses; burning, tempers.

This heat dries up the streams of vices, cleanses filth, and refines virtue’s gold from vice. This heat destroys the chills of sin, the flames of anger, the winters of time, and the heat of Venus. Thus heat conquers fire, flame drives back flame, burning heat burning heat, and the splendour of a furnace the splendour of a furnace.

The mind touched by this heat blossoms into flowers, and this heat makes the soil of the mind purple with the blessed flower of virtues while it brings back the heavenly spring.

## CHAPTER V. Prudence, relying on her companions Faith and Theology, ascends the citadel of God. She prostrates herself before God. God raises and strengthens her.

[Col. 0545B]

Phronesis, having long marvelled at these things and repeatedly considered each thing that vision gives her a foretaste of, relies on the guidance of her sisters and ascends the citadel of the highest King. There dwells that King of heaven who restrains all things by the laws of his rule, who binds the heavenly divinities by his divinity, and at whose nod heavenly things themselves tremble.

Thus, being near to God, she can scarcely endure his immortal radiance, can scarcely await the overflowing light of majesty; but the flat surface of the mirror, which the attendant offers to her sight, protects her from that lightning-flash, moderating the light through the mirror’s mediation.

Then, with bent knees and a suppliant countenance, in a subdued voice and a fearful gesture,

[Col. 0545C] 384 the Virgin entreats the eternal King and begins a word of greeting; her words tremble, mingled with fear.

But the Father above, restoring to safety its due rights, raises her and commands her to stand and to restrain the motions of fear, lest terror delay her mind and voice. She rises and governs her mind, partly restraining fear. Mind stands with body; the upright mind matches the body’s posture. Thus her subdued voice regains its strength; her words follow her uplifted mind.

Her spirit breaks forth in these words and overflows in speech:

## CHAPTER VI. She addresses God with every humility. She sets forth the reason for her embassy. She laments that the whole world lies in evil. She asks that Nature be aided by the formation of a new human being. She continues to emphasize Nature’s need. She describes the qualities of the new human being whom she requests from God.

[Col. 0545D]

If we weigh our groans and the weariness of our condition, worldly misfortunes and worldly destinies, perishable births, imminent deaths, the near falls of life, and the omen of our origin, what pride can invade us so greatly that we should presume to hold conversation before the presence and face of God? Can the pestilence of night speak with the light? Can a servant approach a king, a poor person the mighty? Can a creature bring a complaint against its Maker?

But because we know you as the fountain of mercy, from whom innate goodness banishes the prick of envy;

[Col. 0546A] because the mercy joined to your justice tempers its severity and does not allow it to range too far: we, exiles whom the world drives away, flee to you. The world persecutes us; every human being rejects and condemns us who are living. Thus, if it is lawful to say it, the world is excepted from your laws while it assails our rights with wicked acts and so threatens war upon you. For your own cause is at stake when the neighbouring wall burns.

Nature sees these misfortunes and the falls of the falling world: virtue succumbing to vice, covenant to treachery, friendship to quarrelling, and peace to rage. She groans at these excesses, mourns these errors, laments these abuses, and grieves that the world lies beneath night.

In many matters she condemns her own works, wishing to excuse the blame

[Col. 0546B] by a better work and to wipe away the disease by new arts and a new remedy.

How she may overcome evil, cut back the disease, cut away putrid limbs lest the sound part be infected, and meet vice lest it overthrow the entire world—this she scarcely yet knows. But at last, trusting in the counsel of her sisters, she proceeds by a better way, arriving at this plan: to forge with all her strength one work by which she may aid her own honour.

That she may compensate for the old ruins of her works, she wishes to form a new human being, one who surpasses all others by the star-like excellence of form and character; who, cutting away every excess, proceeds in a royal course, holds the middle, and leaves extremes behind.

[Col. 0546C] 385 Thus at least one star may shine before the world, which lies buried in the dark night of errors; thus virtue may breathe again; Nature may excuse in this one her errors, confer upon one what she cannot confer upon many, and at least in one win the merit of favour and titles of praise.

For she lies condemned in many, and loses her own beauty, while now only her image of herself remains.

Yet what has been conceived remains established by no firm tenor unless your grace approves what has been conceived, strengthens the undertaking, and confirms Nature’s prayer by your divinity. Nature’s work would languish and lie wholly uncultivated [Note: [Col. 0545] A MS: “heaped together”], retaining the weariness of the old mass, unless your right hand strengthened Nature’s work, guided her weak hand, led the pen of this writer,

[Col. 0546D] and supplied the failing traveller.

She assigns to herself the fashioning of the body; she asks from you the good which surpasses Nature, the gift that you alone possess. She seeks a soul which alone demands the understanding and the finishing touch of the heavenly Maker.

For earthly workmanship demands only our hands; but the heavenly origin of the soul knows them not and assigns its own origin to you alone [Note: [Col. 0545] V MS: thus].

Therefore, at your nod, let the heavenly divinity visit what is perishable, and let a heavenly spirit enter the body, so that, placed on earth, it may live with a blessed mind in heaven and may be a pilgrim upon earth in body alone.

Rich in the resources of virtues, fruitful in heavenly love,

[Col. 0547A] may it restrain by reason the tyrant of the flesh. May it confess you to be your own work; may the creature proclaim what author made it and speak of its Maker.

Thus may the divine human being descend to us, so that by the very honours of his virtues he may improve the characters of others.

Let Nature’s losses at least move you: the exile of modesty, loss of goodness, the downfall of morals, the error of honourableness, the banishment of faith, contempt for laws, and our prayers. If we are of any weight or consequence, do not confound those long confounded. We too were once blessed.

If no crises among things move you, let your grace at least move you freely. Receive the prayers we offer and give weight to our devout petitions.

If you abandon us, exiled from the dwelling of our father, without fulfilment of any desire,

[Col. 0547B] we who are abandoned are overcome; we lose every function and abandon our arts.

The judge of the heavenly court grants assent to these prayers, and this voice calls forth an answer:

386 ## CHAPTER VII. God consoles Prudence and assents to her request. Mercy surpasses judgment. A new soul, adorned with every virtue, is promised.

Virgin, parent of things, sister of those above, and my daughter—heavenly in origin, yet an inhabitant of earth—you alone upon earth savour divine things, and possess an image of my divinity. You lift up those weary of the world and wipe away tears with your consolation. Your will does not degenerate from the supreme Mind; for the daughter sighs for the Father’s desire, and offspring not unlike the father follows the parent

[Col. 0547C] in its desire.

Reason long ago dictated this to me: that by one gift I should look upon the earth and bless the world through the divinity of a heavenly human being, who alone would possess so many riches of virtue, so many gifts worthy of favour, so many endowments of soul, that at least the wandering world might flourish through him, though withered by the vices of others—indeed, already stripped of blossom, it might rise again in one flower.

If, weighing the fault of earth, the wickedness of the world, and the crimes of humankind according to their desert, I wished to exact penalties, I would again veil the earth in floods, clothe the mountains again in waters, and the whole human race would perish in the deluge. No merit of life would escape the waves, nor would another Deucalion live, nor another Noah guide the ark.

[Col. 0547D] But rather, the world which lives in one sin would die by one punishment so as to deserve life. Or a new fire would consume the offences of earth, enveloping humankind beneath a single catastrophe, and no one would escape the rule of so great a universal disaster. Or the plagues of crimes would perish beneath another plague.

But because mercy surpasses the standard of justice, and the strictness of judgment [Note: [Col. 0547] V MS: “and of judgment.”] yields when softened by compassion, I shall not match penalties to evils, nor rewards to sins; I shall not cleanse pestilence by the sword, nor disease by a wound. But, overcome by the sweetness of your prayers and moved with pity for your

[Col. 0548A] exile, I shall give better remedies to the world.

Strengthened by a divine gift and heavenly endowments, a spirit sent from heaven will be a stranger in the earthly world; received into the lodging of flesh, this new guest will have a muddy covering.

What remains is that your hand should provide a worthy bridal chamber for this soul, a palace suited to its king, lest the new guest feel the contagions of its lodging; lest the rottenness of the shell injure the kernel, and the thing contained make the taste of a corrupted vessel its own.

## CHAPTER VIII. Prudence gives thanks to God. God fulfils his promise. Noys prepares the idea of the soul to be created. God entrusts the created soul to Prudence. The soul is anointed against sins. Prudence, having attained her desire, returns, and Reason meets her. Nature marvels at the perfections of the newly created soul offered to her by Prudence.

[Col. 0548B]

Made more joyful by these words and forgetting her own labour, the Virgin no longer complains of the burden of the road. She gives thanks and worships the divinity of heaven.

God himself carries the matter forward and brings into effect what he promised. Therefore he calls Noys [Note: [Col. 0547] Noys, that is, Intellect.] to prepare for him the model of the divinity, the idea of the human mind, after whose form there may be fashioned a spirit rich in every gift of virtues, which, overshadowed by the cloud of perishable flesh, may be veiled by the body’s shadow.

Then Noys, at the King’s command, searching out the patterns of each thing, seeks a new idea. Among so many forms she scarcely finds the form

[Col. 0548C] she seeks; at last what was sought is offered to the seeker.

In its mirror every grace takes its seat: the beauty of Joseph, the judgment of Judith, the patience of righteous Job, the zeal of Phinehas, the modesty of Moses, the simplicity of Jacob, the faith of Abraham, and the piety of Tobit.

Noys herself presents this form to God so that he may fashion a soul after its model. Then he takes the seal and, giving the soul a form according to the traces of that very form, imprints upon it the countenance required by the idea. The image takes on all the riches of the exemplary model, and the figure speaks through the seal.

The Fates stand beside the Maker and increase the beauty of the thing to be made, not grudging the soul’s gifts through the envy of spite, but greeting its birth with a rich endowment and closing its destiny with a fortunate omen.

[Col. 0548D] Enriching the creature with these gifts, the Maker entrusts it to Phronesis. He moves her and commands her, adding threats to commands and counsels, not to keep so great a charge carelessly, but to guide it more cautiously, regulating its course by a better way: lest, touched by Saturn’s icy cold, it feel excessive chill; or burn in Mars’s heat; or, wounded by the sweet itching of Dione, languish; or be made to fluctuate by the torrents of the moon.

Then Noys, in the form of an ointment which wholly arrests every assault of the air and storm of disease—the chill of avarice and the foul heat of lust—calms the prick of envy and moderates anger, anointing the soul by pouring over it heavenly dew.

[Col. 0549A] Thus the Virgin, powerful in her fulfilled wish, is sent down from high heaven. She hastens her step and returns whence she had come. Reaching the heaven ablaze with radiant stars, Reason meets her, praises her for having attained her desire, and marvels at the gifts of the heavenly Author.

Then Phronesis leaves the companions by whose guidance she had escaped upward, giving thanks and offering greeting; joyfully she returns to the chariot, resumes her accustomed driver and former road.

Then she passes through the regions near Saturn. Cautiously she deceives the old god, withdraws her step, flees far away from him, and enters a remote path so that she may overcome his frenzy.

[Col. 0550A] Yet she would have felt the wrath of Saturn’s spirit, had not the liquid of the ointment fought around [Note: [Col. 0549] V MS: “against”] her, and the heavenly shower, overcoming it, surpassed that heat.

Thus she escapes the plagues of Venus, the heat of Mars, and the lunar sphere; and, having finally conquered each of these, she completes [Note: [Col. 0549] A MS: “surpassed”] the immense journey. Prudence, long awaited by the wishes of her sisters, is restored to them. She offers Nature the heavenly gift. In it Nature marvels at the hand of the Maker, praises the blessed hand, and in the gift the grace of the giver is praised.

389 ## BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 0549]

## CHAPTER ONE. The virtues meet Prudence as she returns from God. Nature forms a noble body from the elements. The beauty of the formed body.

[Col. 0549B]

A throng of virtues meets Phronesis, clings in her embrace, throws its arms about her neck, and gives kisses. It praises her happy return, since a reward pleasing to labour is given back, bringing labour to a close with a happy end. Fear no longer harms hope’s laughter and joys, since the hoped-for thing swallows up fear and joys succeed a long desire.

Therefore, with diligent care, Nature seeks out the choicest material from which she may notably fashion the dwelling and house of flesh into which the heavenly spirit may enter, so that the house may shine as worthy of its guest.

[Col. 0549C] From earth she receives whatever earth contains most pure; from water, whatever pure moisture claims for itself; whatever purer air reserves as more pure for itself; and whatever purer fire retains, refined of dregs.

She separates these from the whole and, separating them, gathers them again into one mass and mixes them together. Thus, while she gives a foretaste of the work to come, she prepares the material of the human body, marking out the standards of the future work.

Therefore fiery power gives the material of yellow bile. Although it is accustomed to disturb the body’s entire peace and stir up a war more than civil, here it lies at peace, destined to cause no disturbance.

Pure air supplies blood as its material; it no longer luxuriates arrogantly in its own stream,

[Col. 0549D] but the sanguine humour keeps peace with the other humours and stirs no anger with its brothers.

Below these flows the watery humour, and it now refuses to decline into diseases. Although it is usually close kin to putrefaction and generates diverse plagues of sickness, here the dregs of humours cast off their dregs and, better disciplined, cut away all their inborn tendencies.

[Col. 0550B] From this derived material Nature coins a form, adapting the features of a human body to the material. Earth marvels at its beauty, and Beauty itself, its equal upon earth, marvels at the beautiful.

Nature’s most lavish hand pours out upon him every richness of form. After these gifts, mother Nature was almost poor; she deposits in one face the gifts of beauty and the treasures of form.

Narcissus breathes in this form, and another Adonis breathes in this appearance; if Venus herself [Note: [Col. 0549] V MS: “than if Venus”] should again behold it, she would lapse into her customary frenzy.

390 This likewise contributes to the token and gifts of beauty: no fat swells the body, but it tends rather toward leanness. Thus it possesses all things in due measure; its beauty fails in nothing; indeed,

[Col. 0550C] Nature can give nothing greater or beyond it.

This appearance displays such distinction that it can safely entrust itself to the praise of envy and deserves praise even from its enemy.

## CHAPTER II. Concord joins soul to body. Arithmetic and Music cooperate in the union of soul and body.

After Nature’s hand has endowed the material, Concord joins the soul to the flesh with human features and connects discordant things in a stable bond. By a fine joining she fits them with subtle fastenings, joins the simple to the compound, the subtle to the dull, and in a pleasing covenant marries the divine to the flesh.

[Col. 0550D] Thus she joins light to night and ether to earth. Thus disparate things keep peace; discordant things lay aside their own strife; the flesh no longer threatens war, yielding to the spirit, though not without much murmuring.

Nor does the spirit, recoiling, now disdain the bodily garment; it rejoices in such lodging and shadow. That Concord may more effectively complete her work, the Virgin who promises us the doctrine of numbers, and she

[Col. 0551A] who shows the bonds of sounds and their connections in the linking of notes, assist the work begun. They strengthen the marriage of the two, bind it with numbers, and join it by a fixed covenant, so that the substance of heaven may be wedded to flesh.

Thus the new human being is formed. Mighty Nature marvels that she has been able to accomplish so much in him; in amazement she can scarcely believe that the work she herself made is her own.

Abundance piles up the endowments already bestowed, pouring Nature’s gifts from a full horn and keeping no limit of measure in so great a gift. And the horn which no earlier little gifts and no gift had exhausted is poured out wholly in him, where it proves itself and measures how much it can do. Favour is added as a dowry, lest the great gifts already given should lose the praises due to their perfection.

[Col. 0551B] Therefore favour assists these things, enabling the gifts to please; and swift Fame breathes abroad so many gifts. Although she is accustomed to corrupt truth with falsehood, here she knows how to speak nothing but truth, casts off her old habits, and retains for herself the names proper to fame.

There praise is not without reality, nor reality without praise; and the reality worthy of favour guards its own praise from hypocrisy.

Pleasing youth bestows the gifts of joy. Though wantonness is usually its constant companion, it lays wantonness aside, puts on grave character, and imitates the age of an old man in its morals.

391 Youth passes into old age through gravity of character. Thus the young man flourishes in age because he grows old in mind. His understanding surpasses his years; the fruit comes before the first beginnings of blossom, and the river precedes its stream.

[Col. 0551C] The mind confines age while they struggle in a contrary manner: the one calls him young; the other approves old age.

Laughter is present—but not the laughter often produced as an abortive thing by malicious mockery, brought forth inwardly by envy, portrayed outwardly by the semblance of false affection, or painted by wantonness in an unstable brain. Rather, it possesses much gravity, inscribing itself modestly upon the face [Note: [Col. 0551] Ant. MS: “and smiling modestly in his face”], and disfiguring the features with no guffaw.

Such was laughter, corrupted by no abuse, such as cause, place, time, and person require.

Modesty joins these qualities, banishing far away the incitements of luxury and avoiding Venus’s sweet poison; the welcome satiety of chastity extinguishes the returning unchaste thirst.

[Col. 0551D] It [Note: [Col. 0551] A MS: “leanness”] drives from him the waves of lust, conquering Dione by flight rather than by Mars.

## CHAPTER III. The gifts of chastity and moderation.

Hippolytus returns to life; another Elijah returns to the world; another, new Joseph equals the ancient Joseph.

The form of chastity and moderation its guardian add their own endowments, and a gift surpassing all other gifts. Nor do they abandon measure in giving; rather, they prescribe each thing according to the moderation of a fixed limit.

They order the whole human being, moderate his actions,

[Col. 0552A] fashion [Note: [Col. 0551] V MS: “measure”] his words, weigh his silences, assess his gestures, balance his attire, and restrain his senses.

They urge him constantly to do nothing shameful, by which shame may mark his brow, guilt torment his mind, or disgrace injure the titles of his reputation.

They show what words must be silent, in what circumstances and at what time; and what should be said, lest silence choke what ought to be spoken, or too lavish speech vomit forth what should be silent and expose secrecy to an unrestrained mouth.

They prescribe the carriage of the head and graciously raise the face to the balance of what is right, lest, with his brow thrown back and raised toward heaven, he seem to despise mortals and scorn to look upon our earth; or, with his face cast too far down to earth, he should reveal

[Col. 0552B] a dull and desolate mind. Therefore he is raised more moderately: the steadiness of the face marks the mind, neither rising nor falling beyond measure.

They forbid buffoonish gestures and reject excessively severe walking, lest wantonness proclaim him a buffoon, or excessive stiffness display arrogant behaviour.

And lest he stretch out weak arms in a buffoonish way and shake his limbs with ugly gesture; or, displaying arrogance, shape his elbows into an arch, she warns the man. Or lest, as he walks, he merely skim the ground with the joints of his feet, scarcely touching earth, she fashions his footsteps according to its proper gait.

Lest his luxuriant hair, through excessive adornment, match feminine extravagance and diminish the dignity of his sex;

[Col. 0552C] or lest it lie too unkempt, degenerate in deep squalor, and the young man’s neglect of his own dignity prove him too much a philosopher, she holds to the mean between the two and arranges his hair in its appropriate fashion.

The eye does not hunt after things that should be avoided outside; the ear, seduced by the sweet melody of honeyed voice, does not lead the mind astray; nor does the deceived nostril, through scent, dissolve into luxury. She disciplines sight and hearing and restrains smell, lest taste, made foolish by the sweetness of flavour, deceive the mind by tasting too keenly. She moderates the perception of taste and orders the use of touch, lest it wander out of the way and inwardly

[Col. 0552D] trouble the mind, seeking the preliminaries of Venus outwardly and bearing the standards of our Dione.

## CHAPTER IV. The gifts of Reason.

Reason succeeds no less generously in gifts and pours forth every gift, now for the first time lavish with gifts [Note: [Col. 0551] A MS: “lavish with her own gifts”]. Long frugal, she now ceases to be sparing in giving; yet the gifts themselves return with interest.

She counsels the young man with the counsel of old age and grants an old man’s morals to the youth. She teaches him, therefore, to do nothing rashly or undertake nothing suddenly, but to anticipate every deed in mind, deliberate before

[Col. 0553A] acting, and first examine his own actions.

Let him divide truth from falsehood, distinguish honourable from shameful, flee vice, and pursue what is honourable. Let him promise seldom and give more frequently—indeed, anticipate the petitioner with a gift, so that the thing is not purchased by asking.

If he promises anything, let the gift bestowed equal or surpass the promise, lest hope prove greater than the reality and overcome joy.

Let performance accompany the promise, lest gifts come late, lest delay detract from the worth of the gift and the favour of the giver, and diminish the giver’s gift.

Let him not flow into varied impulses, but let his mind stand firmly in a single good, lest, attempting every individual thing, he hold nothing; lest his mind range everywhere and therefore nowhere. Let not a newly transplanted plant

[Col. 0553B] dry up through frequent transplanting, nor a disease become stronger through trying various remedies. Let the mind not be present to everything so as to be present to none; let it not approve all things in such a way as to lose each one.

393 Let him neither seek to be propelled by popular praise nor reject it when offered, unless it is veiled in the colour of hypocrisy, seeking to squeeze profit out by words.

For he who despises every reputation smells too strongly of severity; and he who seeks every flattery of fame, given over to the popular breeze, becomes too soft.

Let him not hear with a credulous mind or an ear drinking in favour the praises of hypocrites, the lies of fame, the trappings of a flatterer—words that sophistry paints

[Col. 0553C] and plays like a lyre in the rich man’s ear with the sweet sound of praise, selling praises in proportion to the weight of the gift.

## CHAPTER V. The gifts of Honourableness.

After Reason’s riches and so great an endowment, Honourableness opens her own treasury, appoints the young man guardian of her riches, deposits in him all that she possesses, and transfers to him every right over herself.

She warns him to avoid the disreputable, lest his reputation suffer and the contagions of neighbours harm good morals.

That he may flee vice, let him love Nature: condemning the deed that wrongdoing has produced and that perverse will has brought forth, but embracing whatever Nature has created.

Let him avoid not human beings, but monsters; let him shun crimes. Thus, opposing vice, let him spare the honour of things.

Let him be good in common, lest a hidden light shine parsimoniously and enclosed virtue yield lesser fruit. Let him live inwardly for himself as for a few, and outwardly for the many: inwardly for himself, outwardly for many.

Let him believe himself born for the world; let him serve all as all things, and let the wise person recognize himself in it.

Let not places blacken his reputation, nor times make

[Col. 0554A] him suspect, nor his manner of life or his means.

After these things comes Honour, colouring what was said before with her light and allowing no stain of disgrace to be felt. Rather, she illuminates all things with the honour of her gift and clothes every distinction in beauty with her own adornment.

She shines no less upon the deeds of the other sisters than the rose upon kindred flowers, Lucifer upon the starry fires, or the brilliance of the carbuncle increases that of gems. Phronesis, standing by, showers forth all the teachings [Note: [Col. 0553] V MS: “gifts”] of Wisdom.

She does not bestow those riches which often blind the minds of the powerful, lower the dignity of majesty, diminish laws, and impede rights. Rather, she gives the treasure of the mind and all riches of spirit; whoever receives them once has no further need—indeed, once enriched, is always abundant.

[Col. 0554B] Their love is upright, their possession noble, their use useful, their giving more useful, and their fruit abundant.

This is the treasure-house of heaven, heaven’s treasure, overflowing grace, which enriches the learned, desires its possessors to be lavish, and disdains the avaricious.

394 Shut up, it perishes; poured out, it returns. Unless it becomes public, it slips away; and it gains much strength as it goes forth.

Rust does not consume these riches, nor fire devour them; theft by a thief does not diminish them, shipwreck does not sink them, a robber does not take them away, and an enemy does not impoverish them.

Nor does Phronesis merely confer her gifts [Note: [Col. 0553] “gifts”]; she goes further and commands her handmaids [Note: [Col. 0553] “The handmaids are the more humane disciplines, or liberal arts.”] to display all that they can and to pour forth their gifts in a kind of contest.

[Col. 0554C] First, the teaching of Grammar completes Wisdom’s commands and descends wholly into the young man; it is not diminished in itself, but rather, growing, grows greater in him.
