Everything which its rule determines, the canon commands, and the authoritative judgment of the mistress-art dictates, it bestows as the young man’s dowry, lest he speak without grammar or err barbarously in speech. No barbarism marks him; thus he follows the art and way of speaking and writing correctly, gains mastery, condemns fault, and permits figure.

And, bathing the man in the nectar of the Pegasean spring, the throng of poets teaches him to bind words in metres and paint song in sweet rhythm.

## CHAPTER VI. The power of Logic; the gifts of Rhetoric, Arithmetic, Music, Geometry, Astrology, Theology, and Piety.

[Col. 0554D]

Keen Logic succeeds, and is not cold in a pygmy-sized gift. Rather, she strives to scatter riches in him and loosens the reins of giving.

She teaches him to enter the keen warfare of reason, to confute the opposing side, break its hostile strength, and defend his own position by reason; to trace the flight of truth and put falsehood to flight; to strike down schismatic brethren logically and false brethren, and to unmask pseudo-logicians and sophists.

The ornaments of rhetoric and the flowers of its colours are present:

[Col. 0555A] words by which speech shines like stars, language puts on beauty, and a period gleams with much brilliance. These riches of speech, these ornaments and stars of expression—
Rhetoric’s abundance displays itself, and paints the young man’s speech, marking his words in varied colours.

She teaches him to speak concisely, and to enclose profound meanings beneath brief speech, to contain much beneath few words, and not to wander in diffuse discourse: so that the word may be brief, the meaning rich, the speech eloquent, fertile in the weight of many meanings.

Or, if speech should perhaps flow beneath a flood of words, let the meaning flow yet more abundantly; let the abundance of fruit excuse the forest of foliage; let plenty redeem the wandering chaff by its grains, and meaning redeem speech.

That art bestows its riches—she which investigates by fixed laws the seeds of things,

[Col. 0555B] their compacts, combinations, causes, and bonds; traces numbers, and examines all

395 effects by which all things are held fixed, constrained under their several revolutions, and all bound together by numbers, maintaining peace when tumult has ceased.

Therefore Minerva unveils her secrets to the man, makes him her heir, and reveals to the youth whatever is knowable that she possesses, whatever her abundance pours forth: what principle, what virtue, or what power resides in numbers, and what such great potency rules in numbers, so that number binds all things in a stable knot of connection.

Music opens her riches, grants the man her gifts full of abundant favour, adopts that same man [Note: [Col. 0555] MS A: “adapts [it] to the same man”];

[Col. 0555C] she entrusts all that is hers to him as though to her heir.

She shows what sound displeases another sound and what accords with it; she teaches the friendships of sounds and the quarrels of tones, and what sound disturbs or what intoxicates the ear.

That art, which measures the expanse of earth, the tracts of sea, the lofty courses of air, and the bounds of heaven, and describes every body within a definite limit—neither hindered by height, delayed by immensity, nor drawn back by depth—loosens hands outstretched with gifts.

She teaches the man to enclose the earth in space, measure the air, confine the sea, enclose heaven within bounds, and describe the rounded form of the world.

The learning of the stars establishes its dwelling in him, no court being more pleasing to it than this.

[Col. 0555D] It teaches what motion drives the heavenly bodies and stirs the stars, or what spirit sets the sphere of heaven in motion.

By this title of gift, Wisdom of the world enriches and distinguishes the man; but, breathing upon him more divinely, the divine art of heaven—the school of truth, ignorant of falsehood—

the art which alone rejoices, supported by faith, and does not rely on art, shunning the refuge of human reason—

smiled upon him more graciously while heavenly fire still held his soul in the heights [Note: [Col. 0555] MS A: “on earth”], and serene radiance breathed upon it; while it had not yet endured the pressure of our lowly ether or the weariness of the world.

It teaches him to follow what is heavenly, to avoid what perishes, to live by the law of heaven, to suspend his mind on high,

[Col. 0556A] to disdain the ground, to ascend to heaven in mind, to bridle the assaults of the body, to refute the lusts of the flesh, and to subject unlawful impulses to reason.

Piety follows, giving and offering herself wholly as a gift, and entrusting so much to the man that he himself is thought to be Piety, the foster-child of such great piety.

She teaches him to smooth away the stains of the soul and cast off every cloud of hatred, so that the mind may become like wax.

If it has once been sprinkled with the olive of piety, yet let it be so that the steadfastness of a firm mind never departs from what is right; lest, if the youth grow slack through piety, softness effeminate his great deeds,

396 and his weakened mind lose a man’s vigour.

She teaches him to judge the tears, hardships, and misfortunes of the wretched as his own,

[Col. 0556B] and not to think himself happy while he sees in so many people grounds for sorrow still remaining.

Let him defend widows, comfort the wretched, support the needy, feed the poor, and cherish orphans.

## CHAPTER VII. The gifts of Faith

Faith adds her gifts; in this great gift she proves herself to be Faith, nor does she withhold herself from herself, but displays—and in her gift declares—herself faithful.

She teaches him to avoid deceits, despise frauds, preserve inviolate in faith the covenant of friendship, the force of trust, and love’s pledge, and not covertly feign a friend under the false name of pseudo-friend or hypocrite.

Moreover, she warns the man not to seek friends who are companions of Fortune,

[Col. 0556C] changing with her, present or fleeing as she does, and following the turns of chance and fate;

who truly withdraw when Fortune withdraws, avoiding the wintry storms and clouds of adverse fortune.

She teaches the youth never to purchase a friend by a gift, nor hunt for love by the merit of a present.

For love acquired at a price departs with the gift; and as long as generosity lasts, so long does the friend last.

Such love is for sale, filling the measure of the gift.

There is no true faithfulness where a gift bestows love.

Love does not bestow a gift while payment itself weighs the weight of the love given, and the abundance of the gift.

But, abandoning the mercenary law of entreaty and price,

[Col. 0556D] let him seek one whom he may thus embrace with true love and unviolated faith: so that love may gain the love of another, and one new friend may return new loves to another.

Let affection be reciprocal; let there be a mutual bond of friendship, which neither hostile Fortune may dissolve, nor misfortune shake, nor glory break.

Let him seek one to whom he can wholly entrust himself, declare his will, and expose his entire mind;

to whom he may entrust the secrets of his hidden soul, so that this person may preserve the treasure of his mind as though it were his own.

Let him have nothing secret that he does not disclose [Note: [Col. 0555] MS A: “reveal”; MS R: “make public”] to that same person,

so that in such a sign his friend may measure the weight of friendship, and repay it with the same balance.

[Col. 0557A] There follows the virtue which delights to pour forth gifts, scatter riches, and spread abroad a mass of wealth.

It forbids him to nourish estates or feed money, and does not allow an idle treasure to grow sluggish beside him [Note: [Col. 0557] MS V: “grow torpid”];

nor does it fill a purse with coins, but compels that same purse to vomit up whatever wealth it has ever swallowed.

Formerly sparing toward men, now lavish toward one man, it surpasses itself and exceeds its own powers in one person.

It teaches him to set his mind free from every gift,

397 to shake out his hand, and not succumb to the love of wealth, trampling riches beneath his spirit and triumphing in mind.

Thus let him trample wealth, lest he be trampled by it.

Let not his hand run toward a gift, nor let the sticky bond of avarice fasten upon a gift once received;

[Col. 0557B] nor let gifts seek a reciprocal recompense, nor profit thirst, nor a gift adore rewards.

Rather, let gifts be scattered without hope of return [Note: [Col. 0557] MS A: “everywhere”];

and let nobility alone and the simple generosity of the mind shape the gift and season its use.

## CHAPTER VIII. Nobility, daughter of Fortune

After the others, Nobility—the daughter of Fortune and close kinswoman of chance—would gladly and joyfully have given her gifts, if anything proper had fallen to her lot which she might preserve by the law of Nature.

But since she has nothing except what Fortune supplies, and accomplishes nothing without Fortune’s counsel, the daughter resolves to visit her mother’s house, sets out,

[Col. 0557C] and overcomes the hardships of the road by swift movement.

There is a rock in the midst of the sea, which the water continually beats and with which the wrangling wave contends;

tossed in diverse ways and struck by ceaseless motion, now wholly hidden and buried beneath the waves, now stripped of sea-water and breathing again the upper air.

It retains no form, since individual moments transform it into varied changes; it casts forth star-like flowers and the rock rejoices in abundant grass while the gentle Zephyr breathes upon everything with mild breath.

But fierce Boreas quickly strips the flowers and destroys the grasses: when the flower begins to exist, it ceases [Note: [Col. 0557] MS V: “is completed”], and the life of flowers is arrested in a moment [Note: [Col. 0557] MS R: “of forms”].

Thus raging Aquilo plunders everything, reaps flowers with the sword of cold,

[Col. 0557D] and destroys former joys.

Here an uncertain grove and diverse trees grow. One remains barren; another brings forth fruit. One rejoices in new foliage; another laments, bereft of leaves.

One grows green, many wither; one blooms, others lose their bloom; one rises high, the rest are cast down to earth; while one shoots forth, others fade away. Thus varying chance alters them and alternates all in diverse [Note: [Col. 0557] MS V: “various”] movements.

There chance’s dice bear many an antiphrasis: the pygmy sits in shortness, while the lowly cedar

[Col. 0558A] ceases to be a giant, and the dwarf tamarisk puts on the giant; thus one receives [Note: [Col. 0557] MS J: “puts on”] the form of another.

The laurel withers, the myrtle bears fruit, the olive dries up; the willow becomes fruitful, the pear barren, the apple tree bereft of fruit, and the elm vies with vines in bearing.

398 Here thorn-thickets, armed with their own darts, threaten a wound, and the rough yew, attacking hands, does harm.

Here the nightingale rarely sings, the lark plays the cithara;

more often here the owl foretells unhappy events, messenger of adverse chance and herald of grief.

Here run two rivers, divided by unlike sources, differing appearance, diverse form of colour, varying taste, and distinct substance of their springs.

One has exceedingly sweet waters and gives honeyed draughts; with its honey it seduces many, and waters once drunk are thirsted for the more.

[Col. 0558B] It intoxicates those drinking; indeed, while it satisfies, the wave produces thirst, and the river is thirsted for after it is drunk, hydropically afflicting countless drinkers.

It plays with a gentle murmur, murmurs with sweet whispering, and glides past the rock in placid water.

At the river’s entrance many stop, and access farther on is not open to them. They scarcely touch the sweet waters of the stream and sip only a little; touched by such a flavour, they desire more, long to be plunged more fully into the waters and have all their limbs drenched by the waves.

Others proceed, submerged in the deep gulf, and the fuller stream holds and carries them onward in a deeper wave.

Yet the light wave restores these men, steeped in so great a sweetness, to the bank and sends them back to land.

## CHAPTER IX. The river of Adversity

[Col. 0558C]

The other current rushes down with headlong fall, dark with sulphurous waters and producing wormwood; by its taste the wave resembles the heat of furnaces.

Thus its colour disturbs sight, its taste disturbs the palate, its violence disturbs hearing, and its tasteless stench offends the nostril.

Zephyr does not ripple these waters; rather, Boreas overturns them from their depths and raises them into mountains, declaring war upon the waves and mingling kindred battles.

Upon the riverbank, rivers of tears submerge many, who fear to be submerged in the torrent’s abyss by the raging stream and to endure the tumult of its waves.

A great people descends into this river and is buried together in its deep

[Col. 0558D] waters, driven onward by its swollen current.

Now the wave swallows men, now vomits them forth; it plunges these beneath the waves and permits those to breathe for a little while. But the abyss thus swallows far more, because they cannot retrace their step or escape to the upper air, and no traces of return remain [Note: [Col. 0557] MS A: “backward”].

Flowing in varied windings, this river enters the torrent of exceedingly sweet water, compels its current to degenerate, and communicates its own pollution to it.

Cloudy water darkens clear water; bitter ferments the exceedingly sweet; hot water the lukewarm; foul-smelling water that which has fragrance.

# BOOK EIGHT

[Col. 0559]

## CHAPTER I. 399 Fortune’s house is described. Fortune is nowhere stable

[Col. 0559A]

Suspended on a steep cliff and threatening ruin, Fortune’s house slopes headlong downward; it endures every fury of the winds and withstands storms of heaven. Rarely does the mild breeze of Zephyr make the house calm, and only sparingly does the gentle mercy of its breath wipe away the tears of Notus and the harshness of Boreas.

One part swells upon a mountain; another sinks in the depth of a valley and threatens, as though about to fall.

One part of the house flashes with silver, sparkles with gems, and shines with gold; another lies cast down in cheap material. This part is proud in lofty height; that gapes and falls apart.

[Col. 0559B] Here is Fortune’s dwelling—if indeed anything unstable remains anywhere, if anything wandering rests, if anything mobile stays fixed.

Her whole rest is falling, her constancy motion: rolling, standing, position, running downward, rising through falls.

For her, measure and reason are to lack reason; faithfulness is not to keep faith; piety is to lack piety.

She is inconstant, uncertain, changeable, double-minded, wandering, unstable, mobile; while she is thought to stand, she falls, and with a false smile lies about joys.

Harsh amid caresses, cloudy in brightness, poor and rich, gentle and fierce, exceedingly sweet and bitter; weeping while laughing, wandering while standing, blind while seeing, abiding in fickleness, firm in falling, faithful in falsehood, fickle in truth, and stable in motion.

[Col. 0559C] She preserves this as certain: that she is never certain; she retains this alone as faithful: that she does not know how to be faithful; she is truthful in this alone: that she is always proved false; stable in this alone: that she always wanders in motion.

With ambiguous countenance she deceives the beholder. For the forepart of her head luxuriates, clothed with hair, while the other part laments baldness.

One eye plays wantonly, while the other flows with tears; one is dull and languid, while the other flashes.

One part of the face lives, inflamed with living colour; another dies, possessed by pallor, where the grace of the countenance expires, the face grows faint, and beauty melts away.

One hand gives; the other withdraws the gift.

[Col. 0559D] This hand enlarges the gift, this one contracts gifts; that offers, this takes away; this presses tight, that relaxes.

Her step is unequal [Note: [Col. 0559] MS V: “backward-going, drunken, wandering”], varied, backward, wandering;

400 advancing, she retreats, and while moving forward she withdraws far away, equally swift and slow in going.

[Col. 0560A] Now Fortune shines in a better robe; now, vulgarized in poor attire, she lies low; now she stands exposed, bereft of clothing, and seems to mourn her ancient honours.

She turns a headlong wheel, and no rest ends the labour of its motion [Note: [Col. 0559] MS A: “day”], nor does leisure stop its movement.

For when that labour often wearies her right hand, her left hand succeeds it and aids her exhausted sister, driving the wheel’s motion more swiftly.

Its rapacious whirl, swift seizure, and uncertain impetus envelop men; it exempts no one from the whirlwind of falling, compels all to bear fate’s mockeries, and to descend into diverse fortunes.

It crushes some and raises others; casts some down and lifts others up.

[Col. 0560B] While Croesus occupies the top of the wheel, Codrus holds its lowest point; Julius rises, Magnus descends, and Sulla lies below while Marius rises. But when the pivot turns, Sulla returns and Marius is crushed: thus the whirl carries all away in turn, and Fortune’s will changes the vicissitudes.

## CHAPTER II. Nobility approaches the house of Fortune, her mother. Fortune and Nobility go to the house of Nature. Nobility’s gifts are of slight importance compared with virtues. Reason attends Fortune and does not allow her to give riches except in due measure

Nobility, joyful, seeks Fortune’s dwelling, marked with the equipment described above. Arriving, she greets her mother, briefly states to her the reason for her journey, and entreats her mother in prayer

[Col. 0560C] that, if she possesses anything distinguished and worthy of favour—something befitting the work of virtue and suited to Nature’s creation—she should not deny it to him

whom Nature creates, new grace renews, manners form, virtue shapes, prudence enriches, piety endows, dignity breathes upon, honour adorns, reason embellishes, beauty marks out, and for whose benefit the entire abundance of virtues comes together.

When these things had been said, Fortune, brightening her stern face with a slight smile, returned these words to her daughter:

“Nature’s act, virtue’s workmanship, does not seek our aid. So celebrated a work of God needs not our action; every gift of Nature enriches it, and divine gifts make it blessed, nor does it lack any honour of virtue.

[Col. 0560D] What can chance do where nothing is governed by chance? What can my changeableness do where constancy preserves the thing? What can fickleness do where the thing is stable? What can mobility do where everything remains fixed? Gold does not need iron, nor light darkness. Thus Nature’s act, virtue’s work, the creation of the heavenly Craftsman, does not require me and does not seek the service of our hand.

[Col. 0561A] But lest envy’s sting seem to rage against this good, or pride seem to restrain me,

401 I shall bring gifts. Yet I do not wish to deny whatever they may be, lest the giver rather than the gifts bear shame, and the faults of a gift be known as the crimes of its donor.

I shall add what is mine—if indeed anything may either be called mine or be fitting for me to confer upon another, which heaven forbid! I do not give so much as lend for a time, nor have I ever given anything that I could not reclaim at will.

Yet here I shall try to overcome my accustomed failings and exert force upon myself. I shall alter the familiar deceits and lay aside the weariness of my own caprice.

[Col. 0561B] I shall make myself stable, partly cutting off motion.

I shall begin to be industrious, wise, discerning, truthful, and stable. Foolish, reckless, deceitful, and headlong as I have been until now, I shall change my former excesses and marvel at my own conduct for a while.”

After this Fortune takes uncertain paths and hastens the journey she has begun; Nobility accompanies her going and follows in her mother’s footsteps.

Therefore Fortune, traversing the road by an uncertain route and ambiguous step, with chance as guide and error as teacher, seeks the house of Nature and at last, scarcely—wavering, wandering, headlong, mobile, erring—finds it. The court marvels and is astonished at her arrival. But although her altered dress, degenerate face, and inconstant bearing

[Col. 0561C] might terrify the beholder and divert a foolish mind from the right,

Nature nevertheless does not waver in fear. She marvels for a while at what she sees, but the constancy of her firm mind does not fail.

Nobility therefore presents dowries and gifts. Fortune, prescribing the measure, breathes her honour upon the young man, already blessed by Nature’s gift, virtue’s endowment, and heavenly dowry, and lying under no stain of sin. Yet these gifts shine with lesser light when joined to the former gifts; indeed, they have scarcely any splendour, being overwhelmed by the greater light. So a lesser flame languishes beside a furnace; so a star disappears near Phoebus.

[Col. 0561D] Yet august nobility, distinguished lineage, free-born parents, unfettered liberty, and noble birth are added for praise and the title of favour.

As Fortune prepares to add other dowries, Reason stands beside the giver, lest the gift of one thing ferment the prior gifts and the glory of many goods perish through one fault.

She does not allow favourable things to be mixed with adverse ones, nor joys with sorrows. She compels Fortune to deceive herself, takes Fortune from herself, makes the deceitful true, the false faithful, the changeable constant, and the blind seeing, and compels her wandering to cease for a time.

Fortune therefore bestows her riches, and Fortune’s Reason permits the gift to run neither beyond

[Col. 0562A] nor short of measure.

402 She measures riches and weighs all wealth, lest, if their channel should flow out too copiously, the torrent of riches carry the mind headlong and drown it, bend the soul toward unlawful uses, and effeminate the operations of the mind.

## CHAPTER III. Alecto grieves that man has attained such perfection. The council of Vices assembles to attack the man

That heavenly and divine man was now perfected in all things; slippery Rumour now proclaimed Nature’s work throughout the world, and report had reached the ears of many. Then sorrowful Alecto shuddered at these reports, yet did not

[Col. 0562B] readily assent to them, but was at last forced unwillingly to believe when fact and rumour spoke aloud.

Therefore she grieves that houses languish and laments that groans are silent; she mourns that her own sorrows grow numb.

When man rejoices, she weeps; when the world laughs, she mourns and languishes; when the world flourishes, she withers.

When virtue grows green, when human affairs grow vigorous, she fades; when man reigns, she is proscribed.

Therefore the aforesaid plague suddenly summons her own plagues. At her command the princes of Tartarus gather into one: rulers of night, offspring of wickedness, makers of crimes, masters of guilt—losses, deceits, frauds, perjuries, thefts, robberies, violence, anger, madness, hatred, discord, battles,

[Col. 0562C] sickness, sadness, wantonness, excess, poverty, luxury, pride, envy, fear, and old age.

That whirlwind of crimes, crowd of vices, assembly of evils, numerous pestilence and public plague rushes into the Tartarean realm, where the Fury reigns, Alecto commands, and Megaera dictates laws.

## CHAPTER IV. Alecto addresses Pride. She complains about humankind’s conversion. She resolves that the man must be attacked

After the raging crowd, discordant race, discordant assembly, diverse rabble, and misshapen people had seated themselves in those places, while their murmur still ran through the ears, Alecto, uttering swelling words and speech full of pride, broke out thus:

[Col. 0562D] “What laws, what order, what measure, whence such repose, such license of peace, that Nature should wish to proscribe our laws, make the world serve herself, condemn the guilty, and save the righteous? Shall Nature, inferior to our populace, whose strength our power outstrips, so often subdued beneath the laws of our empire, be able any longer to mutter and withdraw her neck from our chains?

Shame! Shall incest depart while modesty reigns? Shall crime languish while piety governs the world? Shall avarice yield [Note: [Col. 0561D] MS R: *avarities*], if the enemy of avarice scatters gifts everywhere?

[Col. 0563A] Shall the correction of fraud be silent while Faith holds the kingdom? Shall anger bear the silences of peace?

Shall peace steal away our right, which prescription, defending it for so long a time, claims for us, which use confers, and which settled possession preserves by a just title?

But let us be ashamed to follow laws by which it does not become us to live justly, or to employ prayers. Let force therefore be taken up in place of laws; let violence be brought forward in place of virtue.

It befits us to assume strength in place of right, dictate new conditions by arms, and write laws in blood.

Nature our mother has armed one boy—unskilled in war and inferior in virtue—against us, who are mature in years [Note: [Col. 0563] MS R adds: “and in war”], powerful in war, more numerous, and stronger. Thus a fawn rages against a bear; a twig arms itself against oaks; a valley against mountains; a hare against puppies; does against a tigress.

[Col. 0563B] If we wished to match strong against strong, nail to blunt nail, could not one of ours overcome one man, one whom Tisiphone fostered from his earliest age and whom the Fury nourished with her milk?

Could a new Sulla, another Nero, overturn the laws? Could Rufinus renew ancient frenzies again? Could a new Catiline overthrow the world?

But it is better that our whole people, gathered together, assail Nature’s fresh attacks and cast down her recent pride, restoring her to her ancient ruin.

Therefore, with equal clamour, concordant warfare, and equal fury, let us wage strife and war against him who alone, a boy and poorly acquainted with warfare, arms himself against us and desires to destroy cedars with a tamarisk.”

[Col. 0563C]

## CHAPTER V. The Vices conspire against the man. Discord first thirsts for war, with her servants—envy, rage, fury, strife, anger, and so forth. Other companions of Discord are enumerated

When this had been said, all the populace loudly declares its assent and promises to follow its mistress wherever she may go; their deeds immediately follow their resolve.

Discord is the first to thirst for war, the first to seek tumult, and the first to prepare to enter upon the preliminaries of battle. Her servants stand beside her and fulfil their mistress’s command, preparing the insignia of war.

Envy supplies the horses, rage the chariots, fury the weapons. Violence is charioteer, strife armour-bearer, anger a troop.

[Col. 0563D] Terror attends on the right side of its mistress as she goes, loss clings to the left, defeat follows, death overtakes her setting steps, and Pallor—the faithful Achates of death—together with slaughter accompanied by continual grief.

Discord draws these companions into battle, incites them all, and infuses into her allies the love of war.

But after them Poverty, drawn from the humble populace, rushes forward, with downcast face, poor clothing, and a sad gait; yet lavish of life, neither shaken by fear of death nor broken by terror.

In selling life at the cost of great slaughter, she ventures more, because, needy and poor, she does not know how to fear.

She goes on foot, surrounded by an innumerable throng of infantry,

[Col. 0564A] into whose arms rushes the plebeian cohort: punishment, toil, thirst, hunger, fasts, and cares.

Infamy follows, surrounded by her own monsters. The banners she bears are corruptions of life, deeds worthy of censure, and a life notorious in conduct.

Contempt accompanies her; shame clings to her as she goes.

There murmuring creeps, insults run about, Rumour pours forth praise by antiphrasis, and there is mocking laughter.

Sickly, sorrowful, trembling, frail, long-lived Old Age, leaning upon a staff and not firm in strength of mind, stirs war and grows young amid the heat of new battle.

Weakness, diseases, languors, weariness, and falls accompany her path; inflamed by love of war,

[Col. 0564B] they desire to encounter life in battle.

Mourning, raging for arms and clothed in a torn garment, burns and ploughs his face with nails, wetting it with tears.

Sadness, oppression, grief, laments, and disasters fervently serve him, acknowledge their master’s soldiery, and, servants with their king, burn hot for war.

Fiery Luxury kindles its inborn fires into the ardour of Mars, attended by a great following.

Perjuries swear aid to it; false love, fickleness of mind, deceitful wantonness, tasteless sweetness, savoury pain, sickly desire [Note: [Col. 0563] MS R: “pleasure”], adverse prosperity, a mournful place, bitter joys, rich poverty, and poor opulence pledge themselves.

After the others comes Excess, raging for war and inclined toward arms, raised high upon a horse, proud in bearing, excessive in dress and speech, and degenerate in deed.

[Col. 0564C] He anticipates the fury of battle and suggests to all the angers of war. Under his leadership drunkenness, pride, boasting, revelry, and extravagance bear standards and threaten battle with their voice.

## CHAPTER VI. The war of Folly. Its companions. The companions of Impiety; Avarice, infernal fury, and its retinue. Virtues vigorously oppose the Vices and defend the man

The continual tinder of crimes and tyrant of the flesh, the spur of sin, flame of transgression, beginning of guilt, plunderer and enemy of our reason, rushes into such a madness of fighting and fury of war. To aid it, guilt takes up arms: evil will, unlawful passion, and ruinous desire.

[Col. 0564D] No smaller or less numerous assembly of princes arms Folly [Note: [Col. 0563] MS A: “adorns”]: sloth, games, idleness, trifles, babbling, leisure, and sleep are its companions.

Impiety rages no less; proud with a great host, it thirsts for arms with a greater desire and rejoices in no path except the stream of shed blood.

Wickedness, slaughter, crime, violence, and destruction occupy its camp and acknowledge it in arms.

Bearing its weapons in quivers and its treacherous bow, armed Fraud rages; its companions are Deception, double Cunning, enticing Guile, and deceitful Craft.

A worse crowd of dependents attends Avarice: constant care, voracious usury, and shameful robbery.

[Col. 0565A] With vigilant care and an intent mind it takes stock of those who hunt the wealth of coins, of the coin that lies idle in the chest, and that serves its master for no purpose at all.

Low birth follows her, disgrace overtakes the one who follows, abasement clings to her, the lash sits beside her, constraint applauds, and misfortune adheres.

Although she was burdensome, abased, and malignant, she wins for herself more of the love of mother Fortune, pleases her mother more, and the love of Nobility grows colder by so much. Fortune the mother now desires to alter what she had earlier done, wholly favours the second daughter, and attempts to undo the deed first performed.

Reporting Fame flies, marrying falsehood to truth, and declares that the shades have conspired with the Furies above, the realms of silence with heaven, and the tyrant of Erebus

[Col. 0565B] has opened Tartarean Chaos, denied his brother his kingdom, and no longer granted peace to the world.

By speaking, she invents monsters greater than monsters, while she piles crime upon crime and adds fury to the Furies, declaring that the Eumenides have greater power than usual.

She heaps up the wrath of Tisiphone and magnifies Megaera. Pluto rises more savage, the Fury becomes greater, the three-headed porter of hell ceases to be three-headed and receives a thousand mouths, and Alecto doubles her own serpents.

Nature stands fixed in her purpose and is shaken by no fear, though assailed; in her mind she conquers fear. Her courage increases, her will for war rises, and the same disposition takes its seat among the virtues.

The heavenly man arms himself, and the blessed offspring of those above, who alone undertakes such grave perils of a new war.

[Col. 0565C] The Virtues give arms to the man and supply his strength, arming one man with their own insignia.

Peace gives greaves, uprightness spurs, piety a breastplate, prudence a helmet, true faith a weapon, reason a sword, and constancy a shield.

Hope grants horses; chaste fear adds reins. Concord performs the office of armour-bearer; Fame sings as herald and heaps praise upon the man’s renown.

Reason serves on the right, constancy holds the left side, modesty orders the whole host,

[Col. 0566A] and prudence checks the din of the infantry.

Each virtue bears arms corresponding to itself and swears to aid the man. Nature gives the youth the whole honour of Mars, for whom she stirs wars, and grants him the palm of war and the labour of battle.

## CHAPTER VII. The Vices burst out into the world with great force. Prelude to the conflict of virtues and vices

Now the plagues of Erebus, contagions of crimes, monsters of hell, citizens of Pluto, and children of night, having left Tartarean Chaos, pour out into the world.

Now they envelop our day in the dense darkness of night and strive to destroy the world’s radiance.

Light itself marvels at these new attacks, and that Night now has greater power than usual and lingers longer,

[Col. 0566B] neither observing her own alternations nor yielding to Phoebus.

Yet it compensates for its losses by this alone: there eternal light remains, cut off by no darkness, and unbroken day; there that heavenly senate and the troop of virtues serve in Nature’s army.

Now the battle-lines see one another; now foe beholds foe, and the sight kindles their spirits to anger.

Their souls catch fire, greater boldness raises their minds, angers rise. Now in their thoughts the cohorts outdo themselves; now their spirits imagine mutual wounds [Note: [Col. 0565] MS A: “inflict”].

The mind fights first in ardour, before the right hand with steel. Impatient of delay, the crowd of vices launches the first assaults of battle and first stirs up fury; the whole cohort thunders its anger with loud cries.

[Col. 0566C] It rises against the enemy first in word rather than steel; it anticipates war with words, assailing him with gesture, voice, and threats. Yet gesture, words, and threats do not break him. Rather, the youth, fixed steadfastly in the lofty resolve of his mind, rises against these things, and the constancy of his mind conquers fear.

But after their words, threats, and gestures had no force, words give place and have no further room; indeed, deed succeeds threats and contests of words yield to arms. Now mystical [Note: [Col. 0565] MS V: “words”] wars taste of reality [Note: [Col. 0565] MS R: “the thing”]; the thing itself acknowledges the battles of the mind.

# 407 BOOK NINE

[Col. 0565]

## CHAPTER I. Description of a notable battle. Discord begins the battle. The righteous man vigorously opposes the Vices. He attacks and slaughters Discord first. He also kills or puts to flight the remaining Vices

[Col. 0565D]

Now foot-soldiers rush into battle, now dare to shed the first offerings of blood, now desire to offer the first libations of gore and the earliest deaths of war.

Clouds of dust rise; a new rain floods the earth as weapons rain and a shower of dust

[Col. 0566D] is poured forth; clouds cover the heaven of heavens, and new lightning flashes with the new brilliance of steel.

Hot in mind, fervent in spirit, aflame with fury, Discord is first to assail the man [Note: [Col. 0565] MS V: “make assaults”], first to attack Mars, first to fall in the tumult.

Violence drives her horses; strife supplies arms; anger gives her an arrow; fury prepares a bow; envy a sword; and she burns more fiercely than the others for battle.

Therefore the arrow flies as herald of war [Note: [Col. 0565] MS R: “death”] and impetuously seeks the enemy. With all her force Discord directs it against the youth,

[Col. 0567A] yet the blow answers not the hand that launched it: his small shield rejects the arrow, and the opposing boss repels its whole force.

Then he gathers the strength of his soul and all his might into one, and wholly devotes himself to Mars.

The youth gives rein, presses the spur into his hoofed horse, and the charger does not become slow, dull, or languid from weariness, but serves in the same love of Mars, breaking the hostile ranks along with his rider.

He therefore invades the opposing side and, meeting the enemies themselves, frees his sword from its sheath.

He does not thunder with threats, but flashes with the sword alone.

He accomplishes all by steel and does not dispute in words; rather, by blows and in many ways he closes with the enemy [Note: [Col. 0567D] MS R: *hostis*, “the enemy” (nominative), for *hosti*].

He takes on, before the rest, her who was the first cause of fury,

[Col. 0567B] who first supplied the fuel of evils.

Attacking her with the sword-point, he tears life from her body and compels her to die, though to live in the world was death; and one death delays the death of the world.

Nor is it enough to have seen her die: the enemy demands more. Reaping her head from her trunk with his sword, he splits open her face.

And rightly, in her the head is at discord with the trunk, through whom strife, hatred, rage, dissension, and quarrel first arose; through whom came the first conflicts, angers, first fears, and the first desire for war.

Therefore she lies lifeless upon the ground, she who once made others lifeless. But as she dies, the strength of her own followers dies; one punishment spreads over many, and the disease of the head runs through them all.

[Col. 0567C] Now Fear itself is afraid; Strife falls silent; Anger grows cool; Rage is mute; Violence falls; Envy itself dies; Hatred languishes; Fury lays down its arms.

The Virtues stand beside the youth, kindled by the same spur of Mars, and arm themselves against the remaining enemies.

They kill some and put others to flight; they wage war against all. True Faith kills Hatred; Concord, Strife; Peace, Anger; Constancy, Rage; and Hope, Fear.

## CHAPTER II. Poverty’s weapons. She attacks the man. She urges her companions to battle. Poverty’s companions are enumerated. Poverty is overthrown, and her companions are put to flight

Poverty rises to anger no less for battle, indeed more fiercely: not swelling with sword, not threatening war with the flash of a weapon,

[Col. 0567D] not shining in any garment of armour, not defending her side with shield nor her face with helmet;

but hardened with various knots and unpolished by art.

Yet retaining her ancient features and original form, she employs a club in place of arms. But what arms give less, courage supplies; the mind gives what she loses in weapons.

Poverty rushes upon the youth and threatens with her club.

[The opening *Funera* is syntactically uncertain.] He poises her; once she is poised, he strikes; struck, he is stunned by the blow, while his helmet sinks beneath so great an impact; yet the steadiness of the assailing blows eludes part of it with his sword-point. Poverty therefore burns with still greater rage and riots with a great clamor, when she sees the club raging in vain and making no answer to her.

[Col. 0568A] Then she doubles—indeed, multiplies—her blows; but her club is powerless in its own stroke. For as often as Poverty opposes the stroke of her club, Virtue refutes her arguments with its own sword-point.

But after she sees that her own warfare can accomplish nothing, she spurs her attendants more fiercely to battle: Toil rushes on, Hunger presses hard, Thirst attacks, Fastings fight. Wakeful Cares rise up; they give weapons to Toil: clod, stone, cudgels, a missile from an oaken trunk. Armed Hunger seizes reeds; they furnish weapons to Thirst, while the rest rage with like arms.

But the young man meets them first, first confronts the enemy, first attacks Poverty; and, speeding on his hoofed horse and striving with his own effort, he adds force to the spear by which he casts her down.

[Col. 0568B] Cast down, she lies upon the ground. He therefore attacks her as she lies; yet he does not search her entrails with the steel, nor whirl her head away with the sword, nor make his weapons drunk with blood. Disdaining to end the enemy’s life by a celebrated death and to compensate her fall with an illustrious killing, he tramples her down, disfiguring the face of the fallen woman, and threshes her, cast upon the ground, beneath horses’ hooves. [Note: [Col. 0567D] Ms. A: “tramples.”]

Thus Poverty, long since dead to the world, is compelled now to die; yet death does not seize her spirit. Rather, the mind alone remains and languishes, restrained; death, weaker than the mind, resists it long and greatly, and at last the mind departs together with death.

While Poverty thus yields to fate and to the laws of fate, dying, she impoverishes her own company.

[Col. 0568C] The assembly that was rich while Poverty lived is needy; her riches perish, and every resource perishes with Poverty’s perishing. Her fellow-citizens, whom she had formerly enriched by impoverishing them, are compelled to be poor. Exhausted Toil languishes; Thirst flees; Hunger casts down its weapons; Fastings flee; Cares perish. Thus the lesser crowd is crushed by the greater ruin, and the people perish when their leader perishes.

Therefore rest drives away punishment, fullness fasting, and peace cares; abundance overcomes hunger, thirst languishes in plenty, and defeated want yields.

## CHAPTER III. Infamy attacks the man. She is repelled. The companions of Infamy. Infamy is overthrown. Her companions flee.

Then Infamy, wishing to make up the losses of her companions,

[Col. 0568D] rises more powerfully, attempts to avenge the death of her allies, and to sate her grief with an enemy’s death. She rushes against the young man, but forestalls the blow with a word, sharpening her insults with speech:

“Shame! Shall a race powerful in age, understanding, prudence, strength, and arms succumb to the unarmed warfare of one young man? Shall this boy bear a triumph from among our people?”

Without saying more, she sends a weapon against him, showing by deed what she threatens in speech. The flying missile lashes the air along with the word; and it does not announce peace in the manner of an envoy, but rather wages war. Rushing forward, Infamy follows her weapon and competes in speed with the missile; she attacks the enemy with her sword, wishing to aid the weapon with the blade:

[Col. 0569A] just as, if perchance a man’s weapons should evade the arrow, or the slight fury of the missile should miss its raging blow, the furious sword-point of the weapon might supply its cooling wrath.

Therefore the arrow, mindful of the right hand that sent it, strikes the young man’s forehead; but the helmet stops it as it comes, holds it fast, denies it passage, and obstructs its course. But Infamy, wishing to make up for the arrow’s failure, comes to the weapon’s aid with bare sword. Yet the helmet receives the blow in the middle; the sword falls away from the stroke and poorly repairs the loss suffered by its companion, the arrow.

But when the troop of followers sees that the assaults of its leader can do nothing, it is kindled into greater madness. It therefore seizes weapons more fiercely: Contagion fights, Murmuring rushes on, Insults rise, Disgrace presses forward.

[Col. 0569B] But the young man neither loses heart nor is broken by the enemy; neither does he grow afraid in terror nor wander wounded. Rather, with the horn he thunders forth the famous proclamations of his praise, makes Fame subject to his moment, and strikes the enemy with this sword-point. In the mighty wound he shows his strength, and at the blow the brain is revealed as it issues forth.

With the enemy’s fall, Shame dies; Murmuring lays down its weapons; Insults fall silent; Disgrace knows no wrath; Contempt dies; Contagions yield.

Thus favor extinguishes Disgrace; fame, Shame; glory supplants Murmuring; praises, Insults; honor destroys Contempt; virtue, Contagions.

## CHAPTER IV. The assault of Old Age. She attacks the man by wrestling. The weapons of Old Age. Old Age is conquered without a wound. Conquered, she flees, casting down her weapons and content with a staff.

[Col. 0569C]

Although sluggish, although idle, Old Age—although delirious, although wasting away in numbness—yet is eager for battle, grows young in arms. No longer, supported by rage, does she seek the help of a staff; nor does she ask for support, being sustained by anger. Powerful in weakness, robust in sickness, rich in pain, strong in lethargy, prompt in slowness:

Thus Old Age, near to death, neighboring death, blooming in grayness and furrowed with wrinkles, rushes upon the young man set against her. At first she does not press with sword, attack with missile, or strike with spear; but, in a kind of wrestling-match, she strives to throw him to the ground, draw his horse away, and, when he is stripped of arms,

[Col. 0569D] freely assail the enemy with her sword.

But the horse, fired by the spur’s prompting, rushes against her and lays the wretched woman upon the earth. Rising again, however, she recovers both her strength and spirit. She turns her hands to arms and places her hope in weapons; but her helmet lies useless through numbness, grows old in filth, and, through long neglect, dreads the biting of rough rust. Her small shield reckons its own age by its abundant rust and, stripped of its mesh, does not prevent the entrance of arrows. Rust, gnawing the fragile chains of the cuirass, tears them apart and adds separations to the young man’s scales. [Note: [Col. 0569] Ms. V: “to the conquered [scales].”] The sword-point sticks sluggishly in its sheath and does not easily emerge,

[Col. 0570A] resting in long torpor. Old Age prepares to draw it forth, but the degenerate sword rejects such an exit and denies obedience to the urging hand, preferring the numbness of rest to experience the varied tumults of war.

Yet at last the sword is drawn from its case—sluggish, blunt, lying in squalor, no longer mindful of the fury of battles. This blade seeks peace rather than weapons, if indeed this sword ought rightly to be called a sword-point rather than merely the image of one.

Old Age, armed with the sword, attacks the man. She seeks a wound from the blade, but the sword, forgetful of wounding, strikes in vain and does not know the way to wounds. In its varied blow it stares senselessly at the helmet. [Note: [Col. 0569] Ms. A: “senseless in varied blows.”]

[Col. 0570B] Therefore Old Age, seeing that her own fury can do nothing, marvels and grieves that she is conquered without a wound. Though she was near to death, wishing to hasten the death that was near, she provokes the enemy’s sword against herself.

But the young man pities her and, not repaying the enemy according to her deserts, grants life to one unwilling to live and denies death to one who desires her fate. He stops his horse, checks the reins, and, addressing Old Age in speech and restraining her fierce spirit and wishes, speaks thus:

“Why do you prepare fates for yourself, when nearest Death declares your end—when to live is to die, and to die is your destiny? Why do you seek what has been granted you? Why do you foolishly ask for what nature prepares, what neighboring death threatens? Use the life that remains, and do not seek to anticipate the approaching days.

[Col. 0570C] The shortening of life is compensated by death; life makes good the loss occasioned by death.”

Thus conquered Old Age flees and renounces war. She casts down her sword, throws away her shield and helmet, and, content with a staff alone, departs. Weakness loses its strength; sickness languishes as it retreats from war; languor becomes sickly; falls stick fast; failures slip away; weariness languishes.

## CHAPTER V. Weeping arms himself against the man to avenge his mother. He is conquered by Laughter. Venus attacks the man with a stronger assault. Her weapons. By fleeing, the man shoots an arrow and kills Venus. By fleeing, he puts Lust to flight. Lust boasts of her power and recounts her victories.

[Col. 0570D] Seeing now her companions stray and withdraw from battle, Weeping comes; he laments that his mother is succumbing in war and mourns in grief, with his veil torn away. Since he is impatient, he hastens his steps and fiercely approaches the enemy. He attempts to loosen the bindings of the helmet, so as to prepare an entrance for the sword toward a wound.

But Laughter comes to the rescue. With his sword-point he severs the arm from the trunk; the hand, clinging to the helmet, falters, dies while still clinging, and, bereft of its own power, is numb. Now Groaning groans over its own losses; streaming Grief takes itself upon itself; Weeping sheds tears, and the whole accompanying

[Col. 0571A] crowd mourns; lamentation mourns, and tears grow wet.

Now Pain itself suffers, losing the means that nourish pain; Oppression is crushed; Laments fall; Ruins perish; and every violence of grief perishes. Joy overcomes sadness; glory, oppression; prosperity, lamentation; jest, mourning; happy things, misfortune; and Laughter conquers the weariness of evil.

But Venus herself rages—hers is the stronger anger, the greater wickedness, the worse assault, and the more grievous power. She mourns that her companions’ hands are weakening, that the battle is thinning, and that the enemy’s ranks grow in spirit and in force; already she grieves that her own furies are dying. Yet she immediately snatches up a blazing torch, which matches the very appearance of lightning, and with which she is accustomed to dissolve stones, wear away crags,

[Col. 0571B] soften iron, and set rocks ablaze; she brandishes it against the enemy.

Trembling at these fights, avoiding these wars and battles, the young man fears to await them; flight counsels him, and by the counsel of flight he escapes the approaching blows. The burning torch falls, expires in the air, and loses its force when no fuel of heat remains.

Yet, in the Parthian manner, he directs an arrow from behind against Venus. Nor does it miss her: it first presents the blow, receives the wound, and then brings death to its conclusion. Nor can Lust bring forward arguments against this, when it is thus concluded against her.

Thus under a new Mars a new laurel is granted to the young man. [Note: [Col. 0571] Ms. V: “glory.”] While he flees, therefore, he puts to flight; while he yields, he is yielded to.

[Col. 0571C] While he falls, he rises; while he is conquered, he conquers; while he fears, he dares; while he abandons battle, he takes the enemy’s stronghold; absent, he presses on; and, forestalled in war, he forestalls the enemy.

As she dies, the Cytherean marvels at her own deeds and does not believe that death itself is present, though Death itself speaks. Since others are accustomed to succumb to death through her, she scarcely believes that she can die; but when she at last sees her fate close at hand, she pours forth these complaints as she is dying:

“Alas! Our hand, so often victorious, raves madly in one act! [Note: [Col. 0571] Ms. V: “blow.”] So often conquering, it now, conquered, wastes away—this hand that does not know how to be deceived, nor has Fortune ever deceived it! Now my heat—yes, my furnace—grows cold: it burns the flames of the sun, kindles Neptune in the waters, compels Bacchus to rage, and strikes Jupiter himself with fire; it steals the honor of divinity from the gods above

[Col. 0571D] and compels many powerful beings to serve.

“Now my weapons lie fallen, through which Achilles, once conquered, yielded, pretending to be a girl in a base garment. Turning his club into a distaff, his arrows into skeins, his quivers into a spindle, Alcides, degenerate from arms, wholly degraded himself into womanly acts.”

So she spoke, and left life together with her voice.

## CHAPTER VI. Excess attacks the man. He is conquered by Moderation. Sobriety conquers Luxury. Gluttony is subdued. Reason defeats the stimulus of the flesh. The war of Imprudence; she is conquered by Prudence.

Excess now fears and seeks to yield in war; her proud spirit falls, her ardor collapses in spirit, when she sees the fall of her companion, who was the greatest part of the battle and the first origin of the whole warfare.

Yet her hurled spear flies, but swerves from the enemy whom it seeks; and the hand that sends it counsels her badly: when badly directed, it wanders away from the enemy and does not even graze a part of the shield in its course.

Then Moderation gives aid to the young man; she draws her sword and routs and breaks the hostile troop. Moderation fights Excess; sober Reason attacks Pride; Endurance, Punishment; Sobriety, Luxury. But battle favors the virtues; victory defends their side. Therefore Pride is conquered, Luxury departs, Gluttony ceases, and Drunkenness yields.

[Col. 0572B] Then the stimulus of the flesh, resisting by stealthy warfare, attacks the young man from behind and attempts secretly to assail him. Yet provident Reason perceives these attacks; she is not sluggishly numb, but confronts it, restrains the untamed thing, and stops its rage.

But it long withstands the powers of Reason, struggles against her, and fiercely wrestles; at last, conquered, it submits to its enemy. Imprudence flies more fiercely into battle, observing no rule of fighting; turbulent in the whirlwind of war, she keeps nothing in her mind but love of Mars.

She seeks to tear from the topmost cliff a fixed millstone, beneath which Achilles would stagger, Alcides groan, and Atlas himself entirely collapse.

[Col. 0572C] But her strength yields to the burden; overcome by its weight, her force grows dull and suffers a grievous fall beneath the mass. Phronesis—Prudence—stands against her and conquers her, already overcome beneath the weight, compelling the conquered woman to be wounded by her own weapons.

Diligence overcomes Sloth; Seriousness, Play; Utility, Loss; Study drives away Leisure; Understanding condemns Folly; and Silence conquers Trifles.

## CHAPTER VII. The war of Impiety. Impiety is not moved by blandishments. She wears herself out by her own labor. The war of Fraud. She attempts to overcome the man by flattery. Faith conquers Fraud.

Impiety no longer restrains the angers and tumults of her mind. She declares herself by fighting, speaks herself by quarreling, quarrels in words, and completes her quarrels by a blow: with her sword she proves what she confesses with her mouth.

[Col. 0572D] She wanders in the error of war and rages more in war’s frenzy; on the path of Mars she becomes wayward, observing the law of combat without law, faithless without a compact. When her sword-point rages too feebly toward a wound, she seizes an axe, to repair with the axe the failings of the sword.

Therefore she strikes the man and exhausts her strength upon him. But the young man stands secure beneath the mass of the axe. Piety, standing by, does not fight with steel; rather, she seeks to soften the war by flattering words and prayers. Yet the ardor of battle is kindled more fiercely by the flood of prayers, and prayers furnish fuel to rage.

But after neither flatteries, nor words of favor, nor prayers avail, Piety sets aside her honeyed words,

[Col. 0573A] seizes the sword, and begins to repel war by war and steel by steel. With the interposition of her shield, she eludes the axe and beats back its varied blows.

At last Impiety, conquered by her own exertion, grows weary, yielding to Mars while subdued without Mars.

Fraud alone seeks what comfort remains to her in battle and returns to her old hiding-places and deceits. By a base fight, a servile warfare, and a treacherous assault, she brings war’s furies against the enemy.

[414] Yet Fraud, not herself kindly, entices him with blandishments. Accordingly she pours out these pleas and breathes sweet words, covering her art with the trappings of speech:

“O young man, whom earth favors, for whom heaven fights, upon whom God smiles, whom heaven serves, whom all

[Col. 0573B] the world applauds and the whole earth entreats: spare the remnants of the war, which scarcely and perhaps still survive, and let not the lion’s anger rage against the conquered. Why do you try to conquer the conquered? Why do you seek to wage war upon the defenseless? It is enough to have been able to conquer; nobility of spirit should seek nothing further than the power to conquer.”

While she falsely speaks the words of a petitioner in flattering prayers, she secretly calls forth her sword, bares the blade too hastily, and, redoubling her strokes, invites the steel toward wounds. But the helmet withstands this and despises the sword, refusing to yield to such steel.

Faith, on the contrary, bears arms, refutes Fraud’s snares, uncovers deceits, and reveals her tricks. But when Fraud sees that her deceits and the coverings of fraud can do nothing, she leaves the battle, commits herself to flight, strips off her arms, and by departing gains a share of life.

## CHAPTER VIII. The war of Avarice. She is overcome by Generosity. Prosperity. With the help of the Virtues, the man overthrows the Vices. The blessed man is described and exalted.

The tumult of Avarice remains; upon her alone rests all the madness of fury and the dangers of so great a warfare. Alone she bears them, alone she rages; though one, she offers herself against many, and in solitude despair gives birth to hope.

She hurls against the young man darts which the gleam of much silver has set aflame, and, like hail, weapons press on: spears rain down and arrows form a cloud.

[Col. 0573D] Thus the pest Avarice plants a forest of weapons and many arrows in the enemy’s shield, clothing it in arrows. But the weapon penetrates the shield only sparingly, and her darts do not stick firmly in the buckler.

But Virtue—who rains gifts and scatters presents, who neither buries coins nor imprisons wealth in a chest, but pours out riches nobly without hope of return—cuts down the grove of weapons with her sword and fells the forest. She presses Avarice, fights steadfastly, snatches away the sword she holds, conquers the enemy with hostile arms, and compels the arrows to rage against their mistress.

Therefore, conquered, she flees. Prosperity, Fortune’s daughter, alone survives the battle; but Fortune drives her from the war and warns her daughter not to wish to stir up civil wars, nor, as daughter, to mingle strife against her parent,

[Col. 0574A] or, as sister, to move battle against her sister.

Accordingly she agrees with her mother’s counsel and abandons the enemy, not knowing against whom she could more justly take arms. Thus, yielding to neither, she serves both. Now the conquered troop of crimes carries its weapons back into the realms of silence; it wonders that it has been conquered, scarcely thinks what it suffers to be real, does not believe what it sees, and indignantly flees beneath the Stygian shades.

Battle falls; victory yields to the young man; Virtue rises; Vice succumbs; Nature triumphs. Love reigns; Discord is nowhere; harmony is everywhere.

For that blessed man rules the kingdom of the world with the reins of laws: he whom wantonness does not break, pride does not overcome, crime does not defile, the spur of luxury does not urge, and the error of fraud does not infect.

[Col. 0574B] The Virtues now pitch their camps upon earth and earn kingdoms; they rule the world, and the stars and the dwellings of heaven please them no more than the earthly globe. Earth now contends with heaven; the land puts on ethereal brilliance; Olympus clothes the earth.

No longer is the field tilled by rake, injured by ploughshare, or made to lament the wound of the curved plough: though the earth, however unwilling, obeys the greedy farmer and returns seed with abundant increase.

No tree requires cultivation, no vine the pruning-hook; rather, it gives new fruits of itself and overwhelms the farmer’s wishes with fertility: hope is surpassed by abundant fruit. The tree bears apples freely and the vine clusters;

[Col. 0574C] the vine-leaf marvels at grapes born without it. The rose, emerging from its coverings, makes the gardens purple; it does not smell of its mother thorn, but springs up self-created and produces new growths without seed.

Thus the other flowers smile, and the primeval youth of flowers paints the earth in varied colors.

## CHAPTER IX. The author fortifies his work against the teeth of the Zoili.

O page much sweated over in unceasing labor, whose reputation detraction still diminishes: live, and do not try to equal the ancient poets. Rather, always revering the footsteps of the ancients, follow them and humble the lowly tamarisks beneath their laurels.

[Col. 0574D] Now the ship, escaping Scylla and the monster Charybdis, sails peacefully into harbor; now the sailor rejoices on shore; now the runner reaches the goal; the anchor holds the harbor. Yet after the storm of the sea the trembling sailor still fears assaults on land, lest, safe upon the waters, he perish shipwrecked on land; lest envy rage against him or detraction fix its bites in him—he who has exhausted the zeal of writing and the burden of labor, bringing his labor to its own conclusion.

Yet if envy now pours out its murmurs and wishes to destroy the poet’s reputation and undermine his new praises, at least after his death it will be silent.

[416] **ONE MUST ALWAYS BEGIN FROM GOD AND END IN HIM.**

[Col. 0575]

[Col. 0575A] Whoever addresses God in supplication should begin from him and, having turned the end back toward that same One, come to rest.

Many subjects indeed present themselves to this study for meditation, capable of raising the mind lying here below to heavenly things: namely, to contemplate how God once brought forth all things from nothing; what power, how great a wisdom, what ardor belongs to the Maker; how greatly his works excel and shine.

Yet do not so admire created things alone that you fail to follow the Creator with mind and heart. Therefore let all things that are read come before the gaze of light, lest anything lie inactive, without its proper service and office.

For many things meet the eyes, affording nourishment to every sense: the beauty of earth, the fire of heaven, the fluidity of the waters, and the courses through the vast void;

[Col. 0575B] then the beauty of heaven and the lights of the immense universe—the stars. Next, let the circuit of heaven make itself known to the sharpness of eye and mind, by whose revolution things having bodies are encompassed; and let that force of the axis be considered, which continually whirls the highest sphere.

Then let the outermost spheres, the whole work beneath the shining axis, the motions, risings, and settings of the stars, their varied changes, and the yearly revolutions be weighed. Consider how greatly heavenly things favor earthly things, and with what obedience the lowest mass obeys the heavenly.

Consider how all things subject to the globe of the moon are borne according to an order of birth and, consumed by old age, decay; and how nothing departs from nature’s prescribed boundary.

Hence also it becomes clear with what mad frenzy are stirred the minds of those who maintain that the stars serve humankind;

[Col. 0575C] that the world is not governed by reason but turned by the assault of Fortune, and that mortal things are distressed by varied chance.

Yet this is not now the place to investigate such abstruse principles of things, so often discussed beneath the Actaean shade. Rather, let the matters already traced by learned and keen intelligence, and already known, be sought with a sharp mind. Let each person’s own Minerva grant as much favor to the unlearned as they are permitted not to sweat over a work so great.

For divine power often teaches the untrained something wonderful, so that they may in turn teach those professing mysteries. Yet those who are knowledgeable and distinguished by so great a gift should go farther ahead, when the grace of the highest Father cultivates the intellect rather than destroys or perverts it.

[Col. 0575D] But the human race offers a twofold subject to those who contemplate it: on the one hand, the mind conscious of the divine breath; on the other, the sense devoid of all reason and sharing in beasts, which often cheats us of lofty Olympus.

It should also be frequently considered that, since that greatest Craftsman has placed us amid things as though we were the bonds of the world, how carefully we must guard against allowing our spirit to remain inactive; and with how much labor we must strive, since our final station lies above among the heavenly things. Consider also in what order the battle must be fought when opposites wage war against one another above and below.

[Col. 0576A] And how each person must take care to know himself inwardly to the very nail, and break the endeavors of the unknowing mind. For there is great danger in the matter concerning the extremes: while someone supposes himself to incline toward the love of one, he may turn toward the other; abandoning reason and enslaved to the senses, he may miserably grow dumb, ignorant of whence he came and whither he must hasten.

But things inferior to man offer subjects for the mind to ponder, just as those things which raise themselves gloriously by innumerable virtues preserve to so great a degree the powers bestowed by their Maker. Thus one is raised by a chaste mind, another by a stronger force, another by a wise spirit, or by fair moderation.

[Col. 0576B] God also, the great and loving Father, fashioned all these things with skill, so that he might implant in mortals their proper fire.

Having observed these things, the mind will gird itself for those things which do not come to be but simply are, as Plato’s own words proclaim. It will now seek nothing from sense, examining the natures and forms of things themselves; then, borne through angelic ranks, it will ascend Olympus. No longer looking on mortal things, but with the dark cloud now driven far away, it will see the things that shine divinely in the light and joyfully behold the effects of holy love.

[Col. 0576C] Then, looking about, it will see all things above and below praise God and refer every good thing to him—especially if it has surveyed with keen intellect and the sharp gaze of faith whatever lies open to our eyes.

For just as the sphere of heaven and of generative things, so that sacred choir and the spirits redeemed from death are, as it were, a world free from material, not visible. If you compare all these things together with the Thunderer, they will be utterly nothing. He is entire through himself; the same is part and whole; part always everywhere, always whole everywhere, lacking both beginning and end.

Nothing of these is lasting; nothing stands by its own strength. All would now collapse into nothing, if that greatest Ruler of hidden power refused the current of his force to flow.

Hence one may behold the Maker’s power, mind, and loving intention; although power is active in the lower world, wisdom shines in the higher, and light burns in the highest, while goodness is in each of these. Yet it is right to meditate upon all things, and upon all things in all things.

[Col. 0577]

# A MOST ELEGANT RHYTHM OF MASTER ALAN OF LILLE ON THE INCARNATION OF CHRIST

In it he sings with great ingenuity how that divine work set at naught all the rules of the liberal arts.

[Note: [Col. 0577] 418 NOTE.—John Buzelinus, of the Society of Jesus, published this rhythm together with the following one, “On the declining nature of man,” from a manuscript codex of the library of the Abbey of Marchiennes, Order of St Benedict, in his *Gallo-Flandria*, vol. I, ch. 7. There he rightly observes that these two rhythms admirably reveal their author’s genius and the devout dispositions of his soul.]

## Grammar

[Col. 0577A]

The Word of the Father receives  
an exceptional action,  
while it eludes reason,  
while it deceives nature.  
A substantive receives  
an inflected designation,  
and action receives passion  
in this Word.

In this union of the Word,  
every rule is astonished.

## Rhetoric

The condition of man,  
when it passes into God’s prerogatives,  
is a positioning of the noun  
foreign to nature.

[Col. 0577B]

A new trope in figure,  
a new transference is made;  
a new color in conjunction,  
a new construction is made.

In this union of the Word,  
every rule is astonished.

## Arithmetic

While unity does not depart from the One,  
it is altered;  
while it yields itself into one,  
otherness is united.

The same passes into diversity,  
diversity into the same;  
yet simplicity does not exceed  
its own limit.

[Col. 0577C]

In this union of the Word,  
every rule is astonished.

## Music

While the wondrous conjunction  
of Maker and made thing occurs,  
what is the mode of the bond,

[Col. 0578A]  
what its order, what its rationale,  
what are the ties, what the connections,  
what the knots, what the union?  
Music’s proportion, its own law broken,  
stands astonished.

In this union of the Word,  
every rule is astonished.

## Geometry

In judging its own art,  
the geometer is deceived,  
when the immeasurable is contained  
under the measure of earthly things.

Curvature is turned straight;  
curvature encloses the sphere,

[Col. 0578B]  
and is enclosed beneath it.

In this union of the Word,  
every rule is astonished.

## Dialectic

Among places, the place from contraries  
does not know a place;  
it is silent concerning its own place,  
being excluded from the others.

It becomes speechless, stands amazed,  
is deceived in its own principles,  
and Logic blushes  
at its own fallacies.

In this union of the Word,  
every rule is astonished.

## Astronomy

[Col. 0578C]

The Sun’s light, veiled by a cloud  
beneath the cloud’s covering,  
bears the obstacle of our flesh  
and does not grow dim in brightness.

The Sun born from the Virgin  
turns toward our eclipse.

[Col. 0579A]  
In eclipse it produces an effect—  
light within darkness.

[Col. 0580A]  
In this union of the Word,  
every rule is astonished.

# Another Rhythm of Master Alan, graphically depicting the unstable and perishable nature of man

[Col. 0579]

[Col. 0579A]

Every creature in the world  
is for us as a book,  
a picture, and a mirror:

a faithful sign  
of our life, our death,  
our condition, and our lot.

[Col. 0579B]

The rose depicts our condition,  
a fitting gloss upon our state,  
a lesson of our life.

When it flowers in the first morning,  
the flower, once flowered, fades  
in the old age of evening.

Therefore the breathing flower expires  
while it declines into pallor,  
dying as it rises.

At once old and new,  
at once old woman and girl,  
the rose withers as it rises.

[Col. 0579C]

Thus the spring of human age  
flowers again a little  
in the first morning of youth.

Yet life’s evening shuts out this morning  
when it encloses  
life’s twilight.

While its beauty makes its plea,  
Age, into which it flows away,  
soon makes its splendor fade.

[Col. 0580A]

The flower becomes hay, the jewel mud;  
man becomes ash, when man pays  
his tribute to death.

Whose life, whose being,  
is punishment, labor, and necessity  
to close life with death.

[Col. 0580B]

Thus death closes life, grief closes laughter,  
shadow closes day, and the wave closes the harbor,  
with evening closing morning.

Punishment, bearing the face of death,  
makes its first assault upon us;  
labor is death’s actor.

It sets us to labor,  
takes us into sorrow,  
and is death’s conclusion.

Therefore, O man, enclosed beneath this law,  
read your condition;  
consider your being.

[Col. 0580C]

Carefully consider  
what you were before birth,  
what you are now, and what you will be.

Mourn punishment, lament sin,  
rein in impulses, break pride,  
cast down arrogance.

Ruler and charioteer of the mind,  
govern your mind; irrigate its currents,  
lest they flow into stray paths.

[Note: [Col. 0579] NOTE.—The rhythm on the Blessed Virgin, said to be held in the library of the monastery of St Martin at Tournai, is found word for word at the end of Book V of the *Anticlaudianus*; it is therefore not repeated here.]

[Col. 0579]

# THE *DOCTRINALE MINUS*, OTHERWISE CALLED THE *BOOK OF PARABLES*, OF MASTER ALAN OF LILLE

## TO THE READER

[421] The elegance and usefulness of this book are sufficiently demonstrated for you, reader, by its many editions and annotations. For when it was first printed and brought to light at Deventer in 1492, it soon acquired such distinction that, furnished with learned Latin commentaries, it received the benefit of the press at Lyons in 1501, with a prefixed summary Life of the author, Master Alan of Lille, in small folio.

Again, in 1516 it appeared in quarto, printed at Leipzig, but without commentaries. Finally, translated also into French verse and honored with moral commentaries in the same language, it was printed at Paris in 1536, in sixteenmo, by Denis Janot; and this was done in honor of Charles VIII, king of the French, as the commentator himself testifies at the beginning of the work. Yet he does not state his name, nor does the Latin commentator.

For preparing this edition I had copies of all these editions except the Leipzig one. Although they were scattered with various errors through the negligence of printers, correctors, and scribes, and were even somewhat altered here and there by the rashness or ignorance of certain persons, nevertheless, when carefully compared with one another and with the very ancient manuscript of the Library of St Martin at Tournai—which the Reverend Lord Gilles du Quesne, librarian of that monastery, most kindly sent me—they supplied the true and genuine reading, which I here present. In the margin, however, I have noted variant readings of many words and several verses, especially where either reading admits some complete sense. [Note: [Col. 0581] We have also noted the variants which Leyser gives from the Helmstedt codex in his *Historia poetarum medii aevi* (Halle an der Saale, 1721, octavo), p. 1064. Editors of the *Patrologia*.]

**Fr. Charles de Visch, Prior of Dunes**

# BOOK OF PARABLES

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0581A]

Phoebe receives light from Phoebus; from the wise man  
the foolish receives understanding, by which he shines as though with light.  
[Note: [Col. 0581] The Lyons edition of 1501 reads: “the beginner.”]

Burning Aetna can do nothing but burn itself;  
thus the envious man consumes himself, not others, with fire.

A sow raises herself from filth, at least when gathering food;  
why does a man, wallowing in filth, never rise?

Do not put wine into old skins,  
nor understanding into old men, if you wish it retained.

The water strives to flow into forbidden fields;  
thus, as soon as a man begins what is unlawful, he sins.

More foolish than a fool is he who entrusts balsam to a sieve  
and words to a man full of words, words that ought to be silent.

A new path, not an old one, often misleads the traveler;

[Col. 0581B]  
so a companion misleads a companion—not an old companion, but a new one.

The thing viewed in it is not in the mirror;  
faith appears, yet is not in a woman.  
[Note: [Col. 0581] “Appears,” that is, “is visible.”]

In a barren field the plough makes barren furrows;  
and labor in wretched schools is without fruit.

From tiny grains comes a great sum for horses;  
[Note: [Col. 0581] “Greatest.”]  
from small faults comes an evil that is not pardonable.

The ram bears its fleece not for itself but for others;  
thus the miser always gathers wealth for others.

What he holds cannot easily be plucked away by the hook;  
nor can the bronze be taken from the chest which a tight hand holds.  
[Note: [Col. 0581] “Nor the thing from the chest which a tight hand binds.”]

One cupbearer can offer wine to a thousand men;  
one man can offer cups of learning to many.

The sea-monster Scylla receives what it has received and never gives it back;  
thus the bad debtor takes and retains money.

[Col. 0581C]

A dog cannot easily be drawn away from a greased hide;  
[Note: [Col. 0581] “Torn away from the greased [hide].”]  
nor a rogue from a dish while he is being filled by it.

Under a gentle shepherd the wolf fouls the wool; and the flock,  
if unguarded, is torn apart by him.  
[Note: [Col. 0581] That is, “defiles.” Two printed editions read: “seizes.”]

Phoebus is brighter than usual after many clouds;  
[Note: [Col. 0581] “Greatest.”]

[Col. 0582A]  
and love too is brighter after enmities.

Arrows can pierce a hard cuirass,  
and mockery and evil words my heart.  
[Note: [Col. 0581] Thus: *corderisum*.]

The anchor grips the ship firmly in harbor;  
thus certain hope holds hearts firm in their resolve.

Take wood from the fire if you wish to extinguish the flames;  
if the stirrings of the flesh, take away leisure, wine, and feasts.

The bank restrains the sea’s waters lest they migrate into fields;  
and a modest hand restrains the reins of anger.  
[Note: [Col. 0581] Two copies read: “thus.”]

Old scars often rise again into former wounds;  
a people ill healed returns to its evil deeds.

The neighboring nettle burns fragrant roses;  
thus the wicked man always troubles the just.

While grains lie in straw, they appear unclean;  
and he who remains among the wicked is like them.  
[Note: [Col. 0581] Other copies read: “is.”]

[Col. 0582B]

A motionless rock withstands the blows of waves,  
and a good man the continual billows of the world.  
[Note: [Col. 0581] “Of all [men].”]

A leaf, torn from a tree, flies with the moving wind;  
thus an unstable mind always flies like a breeze.

Foolish is he who takes a ship out into the deep without a helmsman,

[423]  
and he who takes up a heavy burden without assistance.

Through open cracks the shining sun enters a house;  
through the little ears, the teacher’s doctrine enters hearts.

Many a fish, once caught, is drawn from the sea by the hook;  
but no one draws good words from the mouth of an evil man.

The die, by the throws, impoverishes and enriches anyone [Note: [Col. 0581] “They enrich.” Other copies read “Ulphus,” who was once a famous dice-player; through gambling he was often rich, but more often poor.];  
but it punishes, so that he becomes still more destitute. [Note: [Col. 0581] “They forbid,” that is, “they ordain.” Another reading: “may they avoid.”]

If you touch extinguished ashes with sulphur, they will live again; [Note: [Col. 0581] “If you apply sulphur, they will live.”]  
so old love grows warm when the mind is again applied to it.

Dread Charybdis drinks and vomits waters at every hour;  
[Col. 0582C] so fortune gives, so she takes away her gifts from men.

A sharp spur beneath the rider drives the horse to run,  
and the rod drives the boy to apply himself to his task.
