He who sails by his own wind does not always perish, [Note: [Col. 0581] Two other copies read: “He who sails by his own proper wind does not perish.”]  
nor the man who must live by his own resources.

[Col. 0583A] The sea cannot be calm while it is stirred by a storm; [Note: [Col. 0583] *peste*, that is, *tempeste* for *tempestate*, “storm.”]  
nor can a gentle man be calm while anger stirs his heart.

Why does he open a gate who cannot shut it?  
Why does he promise me a thing which he cannot presently give me? [Note: [Col. 0583] Two other copies read: “which he cannot give.”]

A woman conceives so that she may give birth when her hour has come;  
you too, having received, may someday give to me.

No water can quench the thirst of those who burn;  
nor can abundance satisfy the heart of the covetous man.

The viper has venom, which, when it grows hot, it vomits out:  
close its breast; prevent it from becoming warm there.

A leaking vessel pours out; a sound one retains wine:  
so a good mind retains what it hears, while a dull one pours it out.

From a nut comes a hazel tree; from an acorn, a lofty oak;  
from a small boy, often an accomplished man.

[Col. 0583B] Deep snow melts away into nothing if rain  
falls upon it; and reputation destroyed by fault likewise perishes.

A vine lying on the ground needs the supporting elms;  
every poor man needs the help of a rich man.

I cannot prevent a dog from barking everywhere,  
nor can I close the lips [Note: [Col. 0583] “Words.”] of a lying man.

A chimney sends forth smoke, not fire, from a house [Note: [Col. 0583] “From its mouth.”];  
envy can harm by speech, [Note: [Col. 0583] “By eloquence.”] not by deed.

Let not the house, but its master, be praised, if he is good;  
but if not, we despise both master and house.

Neither the ibis nor the heron leaves the river, [Note: [Col. 0583] Two other copies read “the anus,” which the commentator says must be understood as “the tail.”]  
nor does a man lightly abandon the vice which he practises. [Note: [Col. 0583] “While.”]

A black cloud often takes the sun’s light from the earth,  
and a cruel stepmother takes from me my father’s help.

424 Birds for which the bow lies in ambush do not always die;  
[Col. 0583C] nor are arrows and spear threats to me.

The stars cannot add brightness to the sun,  
when the sun’s radiance surpasses every light.

Though you be Cato, and wish to turn black things white,  
let the court be your concern; [Note: [Col. 0583] “And let care be your concern.”] you may also become rich.

The fowler lures birds to birdlime with song;  
the flattering [Note: [Col. 0583] Leyser: “stammering.”] speech of a man lures peoples into deceit.

Lions have fierce impulses and immense wrath, [Note: [Col. 0583] “Forests.”]  
yet among themselves they maintain social law.

After night you may hope for day; after clouds, the sun;  
after tears, laughter and joy.

Caesar was everything, but ceased to be Caesar’s glory;  
and he scarcely had a tomb [Note: [Col. 0583] Leyser: “he scarcely has a tomb.”] eight feet long.

A ship does not rush upon rocks or lofty dangers  
[Col. 0583D] when its helmsman guides it amid the sea’s motions.

## CHAPTER II

Day wrestles with night, clear weather with cloud,  
light with darkness, vigorous life with death.

So there is struggle within us, for spirit and flesh always  
fight; and we die if the flesh conquers it.

The horse bears burdens; the ox ploughs the earth;  
the sheep supplies clothing; [Note: [Col. 0583] Other copies read: “The sheep bears fleeces.”] the dog guards the fold.

For all things pay the debts required by their own nature,  
[Col. 0584A] except the being which possesses more reason than they.

The heavenly motion moves all the stars except one;  
but that one always remains unchanged.

So the steadfast and faithful man will without end retain  
this measure in love [Note: [Col. 0583] Leyser: “custom.”] which he once adopts.

Phoebus is carried back from setting to rising,  
where before the revolving mechanism bore him here and there:

so in friendship the world stands, burns and grows cold, [Note: [Col. 0583] Two copies read “burns.”]  
falls and rises; what it hates most, it loves. [Note: [Col. 0583] “Loves, hates.”]

A place on the ground is safer than lofty towers:  
he who lies on the ground has nowhere from which to fall.

The force of winds, thunder, and lightning  
overturns towers with blasts, but leaves the low places standing.

Death and life, being opposites, cannot dwell together;  
[Col. 0584B] the one is far at variance with the other.

So there are two things which cannot inhabit one heart: [Note: [Col. 0583] “Enter.”]  
vain love of this world and love of God. [Note: [Col. 0583] “Vain love of the world, and true love of God.”]

What lies spread upon the ground does not rise; likewise, when with bent knee  
425 a horse bears a heavy burden under which it collapses:

so a man weighed down by a great mass of vices  
cannot rise unless the burden is laid aside.

A ship is carried not where the sailor wills, but where the wind carries it, [Note: [Col. 0583] “Wills.”]  
when the wave of the swelling sea has come.

A man must go not where he has purposed, but where fortune tends; [Note: [Col. 0583] One copy reads “leads”; another, “teaches.”]  
all men ought to go under this guide.

A phantom appears to men, but again from them  
turns into nothing, what before was nothing:

[Col. 0584C] so too the fleeting glory of the world is both present and absent; [Note: [Col. 0583] Another copy reads “wealth.”]  
it arrives no sooner than it departs like a dream.

While warmth and fair weather last, the ant labours,  
lest it perish of hunger when deep snow arrives:

so, while a young man has a season fit for exertion,  
let him seek that by which weary old age may live in enjoyment.

A light wing does not raise a bird so high  
that it does not return, seeking again the fields it left.

Nor does the rising wheel lift those borne upon it so high  
that, turning, it does not carry them down again.

The drunkard drinks before he is sick, gorges himself before  
he vomits, rises before he is steady on his feet:

the order is not so maintained among us;  
nowadays it pleases us to teach before we have learned.

[Col. 0584D] A thing purchased under the laws of the marketplace is not dearly bought;  
there seller and buyer are equal in the commodity. [Note: [Col. 0583] “In mind.”]

But there is nothing bought more dearly under heaven  
than what long prayers purchase, with brow bowed down. [Note: [Col. 0583] Leyser: “blushing.”]

The ox chews again the grass worn by its teeth,  
so that, though often chewed, it may be nourishment to it:

so, if you wish to retain your teacher’s lessons,  
often recall what you receive once through the ear.

The tireless smith stirs up air enclosed in bellows  
[Col. 0585A] while the fire itself softens hard iron:

so anger once arisen works within the fool’s heart,  
while the contest of strife renders his strength soft.

At the voice of Molossian hounds wild asses are kept from their hiding places; [Note: [Col. 0585] “Forests.”]  
the boar too comes forth, subdued by dogs’ teeth. [Note: [Col. 0585] The Lyons copy reads “to be held”; the Paris copy, “to be feared.”]

So priests also ought to seek out the vicious  
and, unless they repent, strike them with the sword of God.

King Midas too was both wretched and rich—rich  
426 in gold, but wretched in the condition of his life. [Note: [Col. 0585] Midas was king of the Phrygians. Poets tell that, when everything he touched, even food and drink, turned to gold, he would have perished from hunger, had not the gods, taking pity on him, set him free.]

So the guardian of wealth lives, and every miser:  
while he possesses much wealth, he himself possesses nothing good.

The western star first shows itself in the evening  
and produces the boundless radiance in which it gleams:

so he who possesses the bright light of twofold love  
shows himself swiftly, not slowly, to those in need.

[Col. 0585B] Aeolus restrains the great [Note: [Col. 0585] “Ungrateful.”] rage of the winds,  
and Neptune often tames the sea with his trident:

so the ruler who wishes to govern a great people  
should make himself feared for sternness.

A bull lacking horns begins war sooner  
than one able to strike with horned brow:

more often in a village we see boys fight  
than strong men in whom vigour is customary.

If an ox impatient in spirit [Note: [Col. 0585] Leyser: “of the plough.”] is yoked to the plough,  
in ploughing it makes a crooked, not a straight, furrow:

so there are men who often draw back those advancing,  
when they see them take the path of light. [Note: [Col. 0585] Leyser: “elsewhere.”]

We see goats turn about in snow, rain, and hail,  
and sheep strain with their foreheads against them:

[Col. 0585C] deceit, anger, wickedness, and injury drive the unjust;  
but the just man resists them with his whole heart.

A small boat cannot lightly cross the sea [Note: [Col. 0585] For “a small boat cross,” other copies read “a light vessel pass.”]  
unless someone compels it to move by oars.

A runner cannot bring his course to its goal  
unless hope and foot assist him. [Note: [Col. 0585] Leyser: “there.”]

He who looks with many eyes sees farther  
than the man to whom one eye alone gives sight:

therefore Juno, Jupiter’s bride, entrusted the cow to be guarded by Argus,  
not to you, Polyphemus.

A fire spread broadly exerts less force  
than torches gathered together confer:

he who collects his strength attacks an enemy more powerfully  
than he who presses him with scattered strength.

[Col. 0585D] The worst enemy is he who, when you have done him good,  
rises more fiercely against you by making war:

thus, if you wish war to be made against you, let the flesh have its will;  
if peace, subdue its neck by hunger. [Note: [Col. 0585] “To subdue.”]

## CHAPTER III

Do not take everything that glitters to be gold,  
[Col. 0586A] nor every beautiful apple to be good.

Virtue is not in many in whom it seems to be;  
they deceive our eyes by their deeds.

Such men, whom you might judge like saints because of their simplicity,  
have more aloes than honey in their hearts.

The goat attacks with bites the tree to which it is tethered, [Note: [Col. 0585] “To which it is tethered.”]  
when there is nothing else given it there. [Note: [Col. 0585] Two copies read: “When nothing is given it that it can tear apart.”]

Although everyone may desire pleasures, it is necessary  
that all receive what they are able to have.

It profits us nothing to wish or seek for more  
than what, or how much, God himself wills to give.

Springs and rivers run to Neptune’s shallows,  
and water runs wherever it can run.

The stream flows down through valleys, which it always loves,  
and flees the hills, which it hates.

[Col. 0586B] To those who have enough, more flows; from every side it is brought,  
given, and purchased for them; the poor man lies everywhere.

We often see Zephyr changed into Boreas,  
and then, with its name changed, the latter into the former.

Yet I do not wonder if it changes with the season,  
when the Creator of all things himself so wills;

but I greatly wonder at the wandering hearts of men—  
why they change themselves so often, although God forbids it.

A thief caught as a robber receives no law different  
from that received by the robber who goes by night, the thief by day.

He sins no less who hides wealth in the ground  
than he who keeps his teaching shut in his mouth.

Far be it from us to carry a talent entrusted without profit,  
lest God’s anger call us worthless servants.

He who enters among the Sirens has no need of sleep,  
[Col. 0586C] nor does he who wants by diligence to avoid false things.

He who must compose a verse often turns his stylus, [Note: [Col. 0585] Leyser: “compose.”]  
bites his nails with his teeth, and scratches his head with his nail;

he seeks what he can put first and what afterward;  
he cannot place just any words suitably.

Thersites increased the number, not the strength, of the Achaeans—  
poor in virtue, powerful in talk:

so among chessmen the bishop is useless,  
among birds the owl, and among bees the drone;

among storytellers he is a cipher; he delights to be a figure  
and often wishes to take first place.

A narrow isthmus separates the opposing waves;  
this single sea-water [Note: [Col. 0585] Leyser: “one.”] keeps peace between two seas.

Bulls cannot charge one another with threatening brow  
while the shepherd holds his staff between them.

[Col. 0586D] 428 The Apulian people and the Lucanian people threaten war, [Note: [Col. 0585] Some copies read this verse thus: “The Apulian and Lucanian peoples always threaten wars.”]  
but the people of Venusia in between restrains their fury.

In its own cage the fox becomes fierce and savage,  
though it would previously flee [Note: [Col. 0585] Likewise: “though it might rather flee,” etc.] if it were outside.

A wicked, biting dog is bold upon its familiar threshold  
[Col. 0587A] when it sees the aid which a pack of dogs gives to its strength:

among companions a worthless man is bolder  
than he is in foreign places where an enemy threatens.

We quickly lose a hare, found only with difficulty,  
among the thickets, for the hare is a fleeting thing.

We lose the eel while grasping it in our hands,  
whose slipperiness deceives hands in the river;

so a friend once found departs unless he is kept,  
and unless mutual freedom preserves him.

A knot which is loosened by one finger was not firmly tied,  
nor was faith strong if it was broken so quickly.

He who ceases to be faithful will never be faithful;  
he who is not faithful will never be a friend.

Since two hearts agree in one heart,  
it is right that the hearts remain the same heart.

[Col. 0587B] The man thought less sound in mind than sick in body  
is he who strikes his physicians with staff or sword.

Who is more insane than a blind man led upon steep ground,  
if, swollen with rage, he then despises his guide?

Black eye-salve heals a bleary-eyed man, not a one-eyed man;  
he who is once one-eyed will remain no more than one-eyed.

We do not wish to seek a knot in a reed where none exists,  
nor to put a great foot upon the weak.

Feed a dog: when fed, he will be gentle toward you, and,  
though beaten, will love you as master after he has been beaten.

Do good things for a wicked slave, and you will always lose  
whatever you give him, since he has love for no one.

Ridiculous is the mouse who rules mice,  
and thus governs them as though he were their king; [Note: [Col. 0587] “May be.”]

[Col. 0587C] no less laughter arises when a slave is raised  
to be master, when he rages with voice and hand. [Note: [Col. 0587] “Strikes.”]

Nothing is harsher than when a humble man rises to high station;  
the ape snarls [Note: [Col. 0587] “Is painted.”] while sitting on a lofty seat.

Different remedies avail for different diseases;  
as diseases vary, so they vary.

Teaching does not enter minds in one manner:  
fear is applied to some, admonition to others, love to others.

You cannot make four-footed animals drink by striking them,  
429 nor does the rod compel ignorant boys to study.

A little purse contains merchandise for sale  
and lies increased within a small place:

what then can satisfy the covetous mind—the world,  
landed estates, glory, riches, honour?

It is right that the little man be entirely deprived of the earth  
[Col. 0587D] who wishes alone to possess the whole earth.

With harmless jaws a young lion roams the wilderness  
when it finds nothing that it can tear apart;

the serpent does not always sting nor everywhere pour forth  
the venom it always carries in its mouth:

indeed it would not spare the sting or the poison  
if something were present which it could harm with it.

## CHAPTER IV

Thorns and briars are not well drawn from the feet  
while a short thorn remains within; [Note: [Col. 0587] Leyser: “remains.”]

the longer the delay, the more the wounds will fester,  
[Col. 0588A] and then they cannot be drawn out without pain.

He who draws faults from the heart should draw them while fresh,  
and all together, lest one bring death.

What profit is there in a physician’s having healed two hundred wounds  
if one remains through which a man may die?

A tree which branches broadly [Note: [Col. 0587] “Puts forth leaves.”], unless it is firm at its base, [Note: [Col. 0587] “One.”]  
falls with its branches when easily struck by the south wind.

But that which has roots deep in the earth  
resists, and cannot be torn up [Note: [Col. 0587] Leyser: “overturned.”] by raging pestilence.

He who spreads widely the branches of reputation, not the roots of merits,  
know that he himself will fall.

He who utters such vain things displeases not only heaven  
but also the soil through his fault.

Water drawn from a small spring is no less sweet  
than water borne from a great river.

[Col. 0588B] Both jar and cask sometimes contain Falernian wine,  
nor is the cask better than the little jar itself.

A drink does not become sweeter in splendid gold  
than in glass, which is worth less by an *as*.

Though each wretched man may bless good things, let no one  
consider cheap words worthless on account of a wretched body.

With intent gaze the kite searches the earth from the sky [Note: [Col. 0587] Leyser: “prey.”]  
and sees from afar scraps [Note: [Col. 0587] “Searchings.”] left behind.

Though hungry, it does not immediately descend from above,  
but continually circles the place in various turns.

For there are those skilled in setting snares beside placed food,  
430 so that unsuspecting birds may thus be deceived.

Finally, once it has perceived that none of the fowler’s craft is present,  
it approaches safely with its claws and takes the entrails.

[Col. 0588C] Worms generated from flesh show to the eyes something of the work of mortification: [Note: [Col. 0587] “Witnessing.”]

they attack with their teeth the flesh given to their bites,  
and seek no other while this lasts for them.

There is no counsel unless salt can come to aid:  
salt laid on plentifully bites and drives them away.

This is the worms’ practice; nor are they alone forsaken by it:  
there are men into whom that same madness now passes.

The diner does not praise a bird for its feathers,  
nor the eloquent slave-dealer [Note: [Col. 0587] A *mango* is one who knows how to polish merchandise so that it may be sold more dearly.] a horse for its hide;

indeed, the analogous use extends through every particular:  
every man honours garments, not men.

New actions establish a new custom for all ages, [Note: [Col. 0587] Leyser: “individual things.”]  
that nothing is cheap except the poor man.

[Col. 0588D] The poor man does nothing well; but whatever the rich man does,  
whether well or ill, is valued according to its supposed worth.

What good is food taken, which leaves as soon as it is taken?  
Nausea distresses the heart; loosened bowels ache.

When a disease in the belly does not tolerate remedies,  
I think it a sign not of life but of death.

As the belly needs food, so the spirit needs it;  
they are not well nourished when either lacks anything.

Not all who attend schools wherever they may be learn;  
for many come in order to be seen there.

[Col. 0589A] An ox was once a calf; a dog was once a puppy:  
why is a man twice a boy, though he may be one only once?

Nature makes an old man from a boy, as order demands;  
but vice in turn makes a boy from an old man.

It is not fitting to harness mice to an old man’s little cart, [Note: [Col. 0589] “Post-cart.”]  
nor thereby to multiply the changes of fortune.

A man is twice a boy and once a man, when white old age subdues him  
with strength and sense exhausted, [Note: [Col. 0589] Leyser: “relaxed, stammering.”] his powers spent.

The Molossian dog often takes a sheep from the wolf’s jaws  
in order to eat the sheep it has taken, not to let it go.

What difference is it whether it is eaten by the enemy wolf or by that dog,  
when the teeth of both are equally grievous?

Reason observes similar actions in many cases,  
concerning which experience can speak true words. [Note: [Col. 0589] “Can speak true words.”]

[Col. 0589B] Fierce Alcon defends men’s property from enemies  
so that he himself, not others, may safeguard that property.

A blind man is simply forbidden to lead a blind man,  
lest the blind lead the blind into his pit; [Note: [Col. 0589] Leyser: “with him.”]

yet we cannot prevent the mad Alan  
from wishing to lead the blind along an uncertain path.

He does not complain that his feet strike something shameful as he walks,  
but that so few follow him at night.

I wonder—and wonder greatly—that he takes the way of a guide of light [Note: [Col. 0589] “Light.”]  
whom it is certain has never known or travelled the road.

Achilles, who was hard for war, withdrew  
when Aegisthus entered the marriage-bed at home.

He who lies among feathers, having suffered nothing hard among them, [Note: [Col. 0589] Leyser: “arms.”]  
is unable, being unaccustomed, [Note: [Col. 0589] De Visch edition: “accustomed.”] to endure evil like a man.

Rain and wind change the colour of the weary cheek,  
[Col. 0589C] and tender skin is lightly burned by the sun.

A shoulder accustomed to soft things does not bear a shield well,  
nor does an anointed hand hold the sword firmly.

Not every companion is faithful, not every heart trustworthy;  
I do not wish to associate myself with everyone.

Whoever wishes to be my companion must become not another, but the same as I;  
for an alter ego is not enough.

Should I keep as companion one who knows what I do not know, or who,  
when I ask for what I do not have, has that very thing? [Note: [Col. 0589] Leyser: “I do not have—perhaps that thing,” etc.; Leyser: “to divide.”]

A wise companion deliberates everything with his companion  
when the consonant hearts of the two agree.

Tomorrow, in the fashion of the ungrateful, postpones everything;  
and from one tomorrow it makes a thousand tomorrows for me.

Why does he not multiply today who multiplies tomorrow?  
Does not each day mark its own sun?

[Col. 0589D] Tomorrow is customarily after today, returned with the sun,  
but it does not possess that tomorrow which it promises me.

That tomorrow will never come, nor will the sun rise in it,  
since its own coming tomorrow is without end.

## CHAPTER V

Not every acre cultivated in the world is worthy of cultivation,  
nor every vine of being dug by hand. [Note: [Col. 0589] “By whatever hand.”]

What profit is there in ploughing soil or digging a vine  
when this bears no fruit and that no yield?

[Col. 0590A] Let the barren untilled field rest; let the vine also rest,  
which I shall never harvest.

By analogy, I hold that the giver ought to refrain  
when he cultivates the unworthy and gives his goods to them.

He who gives his goods to the worthy sows, reaps, joins, and enlarges;  
but what is given to the unworthy wholly perishes.

The ass makes us laugh when it is painted in the manner of a lion,  
432 and the crafty fox brings about the same result.

Let this one strip off the skin in which it imagines itself a lion,  
so that, patient under burden, it may follow its master’s commands.

I exhort the fox also to rest in its own skin,  
lest, exulting in a lion’s skin, it provoke laughter.

The frog, puffing itself up, wished to be equal to the ox  
and to avenge in the waters its offspring, which the ox had crushed beneath its foot: [Note: [Col. 0589] Leyser: “ploughing.”]

but the ox swore that the little frog would burst first  
[Col. 0590B] through the middle before it became equal to him.

Drusus hastens to shave his growing beard  
lest the shadow of his cheek harm his eyes by night.

He sets up a mirror; with the mirror showing what remains,  
he removes hairs with scissors—using scissors for the hairs.

And lest itching seize his head, he has ready at all hours  
a washerwoman to wash it.

Besides, every day he supplies water for face and hands;  
he cleanses with brooms the place covered with dust. [Note: [Col. 0589] “Washes.”]

He does this outwardly, but gathers filth within  
and takes no care to shave away its growing growths.

It is fitting that the hand first be thoroughly washed  
which presumes to wash God’s vessels for him.

A clean hand makes clean the clean vessel which it washes;  
a filthy hand makes it filthier than it was before.

[Col. 0590C] A hem touched by mud draws filth to itself, [Note: [Col. 0589] “An implanted thing.”]  
and what was formerly white suddenly becomes black.

The man who spares the tumours he himself carries  
does not rightly rebuke me for having warts.

Let him first free himself, full of ulcers;  
then let him laugh at my warts.

No one can throw down a strong wrestler by a hold  
unless, enduring the struggle, he attacks him.

The fair walls of Troy would never have fallen  
unless the undertaking by which they fell had been begun.

Let whoever wishes to be good and devout begin:  
he who has begun well has half the deed.

How can a work be done unless it is first begun?  
All things are known to have their beginning.

[Col. 0590D] Fortune aids the bold; no great thing terrifies a bold heart;  
it has no disposition that shrinks from anything.

A great camel cannot, prevented by its hump,  
pass through the small, slight eye of a needle;

nor does the gate of heaven allow a rich man to pass,  
while the burden of riches compels the wretch to halt.

433 Why does a man seek his soul’s death with so perverse [Note: [Col. 0589] Leyser: “inclined.”] a heart?  
Why does he seek what takes away his life?

[Col. 0591A] Happy is the poor man whom will itself makes poor:  
there is nothing to weigh down his back when he seeks high things;

neither robber, brigand, nor crafty thief lies in ambush  
while he travels without fear on the roads he has undertaken. [Note: [Col. 0591] “He takes the undertaken roads.”]

A thousand ways lead men through the ages to Rome—  
those who wish to seek the Lord with all their heart.

There is a road which leads straight through high mountains,  
made arduous by thickets [Note: [Col. 0591] Leyser: “brambles.”] and thorns.

There is likewise a path which rough gravel  
makes rough and daily wears away the soles of the feet;

there is a road over sea, a road through deserts, through deep  
valleys, rocks, and places harsh to the foot;

through woodland and hiding places, through the fearsome haunts of wild beasts,  
through thorns, briars, and muddy shallows.

The raven is always gaping and always seeking corpses;  
[Col. 0591B] it always loves death, and death in turn feeds it. [Note: [Col. 0591] Leyser: “wild.”]

Those whom their own weakness and old age itself oppress  
make the raven rejoice when it thinks they are dying.

The raven alone does not lie in wait for the dying;  
the greater part of humankind now does the same.

A son desires his father’s death before its day, so that he may become  
his heir and seize miserable wealth by law.

Alas! grief and that crime pass into the clergy:  
one man buys a church while another holds it.

The ox is struck twice and feels the sharp goad twice  
if it kicks against its own goad:

the iron makes two wounds from one wounding;  
the second blow will be worse than the first.

Why, then, do servants created to obey their master  
[Col. 0591C] raise weapons against their master in the rage of their hearts?

This madness, this fury, this indignation  
offers laughter and seeks an evil that is hateful.

While Davus held his head obstinately opposed [Note: [Col. 0591] Two copies read “opposite.”] to his angry master,  
he barely escaped his master’s chains.

There is no measure in an unmeasured madman [Note: [Col. 0591] The same copies read “inconstant.”]  
while he gives whatever he can possess to the abyss.

The miser likewise exceeds the norm of reason,  
while spending nothing, he continually heaps up wealth.

Let no one follow them, for each is vicious;  
virtue teaches the path which lies between the two.

One is a dog, the other a wolf: one devours flesh,  
while the other, fox-like, conceals wealth. [Note: [Col. 0591] “While the fox conceals.”]

Let him who takes care to pursue life’s path  
avoid vices fighting one another with opposing fronts.

## CHAPTER VI

[Col. 0591D]

If anyone wishes to plough for himself a fruitful little field  
and afterward entrust his seed to it,

let him first uproot the thorns which hinder the crops,  
and cut down with the sickle whatever briars are there. [Note: [Col. 0591] “Reap.”]

Bracken too is harmful; [Note: [Col. 0591] Two copies read “brackens,” two others “flints.” Bracken is a harmful plant which grows in neglected fields.] he who wishes to cleanse the crops  
must strive to destroy harmful bracken.

Not every soil which receives seed produces a crop;  
weeds spring up from luxuriant manure.

[Col. 0592A] Watchful care tends fields well; negligence, indeed,  
makes them barren. Hence the poet says:

> “Bracken grows in neglected fields, awaiting the fire.”

By “bracken” he denotes a man’s vice.

A man who has never learned what hunger itself is  
does not know what sweetness sweet food possesses.

After the burning of thirst and after hunger,  
drink and food themselves are very sweet to us.

Honey clings more sweetly to the human palate  
if bitter taste has first bitten it.

He who endures cold values warm clothing;  
he who endures grave sickness rejoices in the lot of health.

Let him who considers the false goods of earth and the goods of heaven  
entirely abandon the false and seek the true goods.

Let him strip his heart of the unlawful things and misfortunes of the world  
[Col. 0592B] who wishes to take possession of a place in heaven beforehand.

The man whom concern for possessions  
torments, and fear exhausts [Note: [Col. 0591] Two copies read “examines.”] night and day, does not live well.

He who fears losing his life together with the things he possesses  
does not sleep securely.

Therefore, by way of example, we read that a tyrant showed  
that he was not happy, as his servant had said:

above the head of the man brought to the table  
a sword hung, scarcely held by a thin thread.

He ordered him to eat the banquet thus set before him; but the man  
did not dare, because he saw death on every side. [Note: [Col. 0591] “On both sides.”]

“Such,” he said, “is my condition: fearing a fall and calamity,  
I die, certainly, by my own death or by an enemy.”

An evil companion draws his companion to evil deeds, and thus  
[Col. 0592C] he who had previously been good becomes evil and worthless.

Nor is this surprising, since inclination toward evils is swifter  
than toward the work which God wishes to be done.

A weight seeks the depths more readily than it rises to the heights,  
which the necks of oxen scarcely draw from the ground.

Do not oxen that pull carts sometimes themselves get pulled  
when the wheel, set in motion down a sloping road, rushes downhill?

When one pulls upward with all its strength, the other pulls downward;  
this obstructs it, and it often falls back.

For the course is more downhill from a lofty summit  
than it is uphill from a western valley.

If some beast of the woods happens upon a pack of dogs,  
will it not perish there?

Do not those die by the bites of serpents  
[Col. 0592D] whom road or chance draws among them?

Who but a serpent joins itself with serpents,  
when they grievously sting whatever clings [Note: [Col. 0591] “Adheres.”] to them?

Flowers wither, and grasses are killed,  
when poured-out poisons scorch them by touch alone.

The Marsian people place doubtful children among them,  
wishing to know whether they have truly been born of them:

for, as is said, serpents spare only those children  
whom they make their friends by the charms of their mouths.

[Col. 0593A] While you can bend or straighten a bent twig,  
make the young plant conform to your will. [Note: [Col. 0593] Two copies read: “Thus make it stand as your planting wills.”]

Once it has been hardened with age into great strength,  
you will not easily bend its lordly head.

Again, if at first you allow it to grow crooked,  
it will always remain crooked as it was at first.

So, while a man is a boy, let him be taught to hold fast to what is right,  
lest he steep his heart in accustomed evils.

Although a potter may alter wet clay,  
he cannot impose a shape upon it once dry.

A puppy barks at a deer-skin through the house  
at first, so that it may learn to enter the woods.

You will see three slaves always serve in three ways—  
not three at once for one master, but for three masters.

For there is one who, trusting in the future reward of life,  
[Col. 0593B] submits to God’s commands and service.

This man is not a slave, since he who bears the reins  
of saving justice will be free and exalted.

There is also one who obeys, subjected to a wretched little man,  
as the ancient fathers once ordained;

yet the imperious man does not wholly subjugate him to himself:  
the inner man is not held in chains.

There is a third slave, who always obeys vice;  
he lives wholly as a slave in both ways.

436 A wall must be levelled by a plumb-line,  
lest the house collapse when this is lacking.

How can the structure of a wavering wall stand  
if a weak foundation fails beneath its weight?

Similarly, if anyone strives toward the higher arts,  
he must first learn their elements by heart.

[Col. 0593C] The poets of old learned the arts after the elements, [Note: [Col. 0593] “Through”; Leyser: “teachers.”]  
and thereby earned great honour.

[Col. 0594A] First they dictated, and afterward wrote verse;  
stretching out their hands, they placed them beneath the rod. [Note: [Col. 0593] Leyser: “those rejoicing.”]

Once steeped in the elements, wisdom led them to Athens,  
joining the Quadrivium [Note: [Col. 0593] Leyser: “Quadrivium.”] to the Trivium.

Restrain unlawful frenzies, pitiable boy;  
know that the enemy impels them toward death.

Turn your mind away from these, and behold their miserable pains:  
other things than these must be meditated upon by you.

Remember that you will be dust, food for worms,  
when you lie decaying in cold earth.

There will be no one in the world who wishes to see you any longer  
when your flesh, torn apart, becomes more rancid than a dog.

Why do you cut off your head with your own sword? Why do you voluntarily run  
into the devil’s chains? Why do you obey his commands?

Stand continually against rising impulses,  
[Col. 0594B] lest he whom you suppose you conquer overcome you.

Alas! why does man seek so much [Note: [Col. 0593] “Empty.”] while he passes like a shadow—  
he who now thinks himself standing, now falls seeking the depths?

What certainty remains for him except death and death’s image?  
It always follows him, holds him, and drags him away.

Alas! why does man rejoice, why is he proud—and to what end?  
Why does he assume a lofty bearing, [Note: [Col. 0593] “Station.”] who is and will be ashes?

Why does he desire and fear, and why does he attempt to subject  
all things to himself? Why does he always seek to live here? [Note: [Col. 0593] Other copies read: “thinks himself able to live.”]

Not so, no: for that belief is already perishing; [Note: [Col. 0593] Other copies read “vain.”]  
the dew falls, and life again rushes downward:

[Col. 0594C] so man stands; or say by what means the rest stand—  
what more are they? Each and every thing is vain, nothing.

## Supplement to the Edition of the Works of Alan of Lille Prepared by Charles Visch

[Col. 0593]

## On the Art, or Articles, of the Catholic Faith. (G)\*

## Notice

(Dom Bernard Pez, *Introductory Dissertation to* vol. I of the *Anecdota*, p. LXXIII.)

Charles Vischius wrote a historical account of the life and death of Alan the Great of Lille, doctor of sacred theology, surnamed “the Universal,” and illustrious master of the Parisian ecclesiastical school, a humble Cistercian convert; he prefixed it to the works of Alan, so far as these could be found, which he himself published in folio at Antwerp in 1654. In the preface to that edition is found a catalogue of Alan’s works, which the same learned Vischius reproduced, enlarged and more accurate, in the second publication of his Cistercian Library, issued at Cologne in 1656. From both sources we have certain knowledge that these distinguished and most learned Five Books on the Art, or Articles (for the manuscripts vary), of the Catholic Faith had never been printed.

Charles Vischius indeed, in his Library, lists only Book I *On the Articles of Faith*, preserved among the Regular Canons at Tongeren. But, apart from the testimony of our manuscripts—the Gemnicensian, namely, and the Emmerammian, a parchment octavo about four hundred years old—it is better to follow Alan himself, who testifies in the prologue that this work is divided into five books. The first treats of the one cause of all things, that is, the one and same triune God; the second, of the world, the creation of angel and man, and freedom of will; the third, of the Son of God incarnate for the redemption of man; the fourth, of the sacraments of the Church; the fifth, of the resurrection of the dead. Alan endeavors to demonstrate by natural reasoning alone these most weighty dogmas of the Catholic faith, together with the necessary truth and consequence of each, so that those who disdain to rest content with prophecy and the Gospel may at least be persuaded by human arguments.

Moreover, we have also seen this work of Alan in a Campililian manuscript, where there is likewise his unprinted writing *On Intelligences*, beginning: “The sum of our intention in this chapter is briefly to gather the more difficult matters of natural things.” Parchment manuscript, folio, in a fourteenth-century hand. Finally, the same manuscript contains another hitherto unpublished work of Alan, whose title and beginning are these: *Paradoxes on the Greatest General Principles*: “The opinion of Plato and Aristotle is,” etc. Vischius nowhere mentions this latter little work.

Furthermore, in the library of the monastery of Sainte-Croix there are outstanding sermons of Alan, not yet published in print, entitled *Mirror of the Church*.

> [Note: Col. 0595. They are not Alan’s, but Honorius of Autun’s. The *Mirror of the Church* was published in vol. CLXXII of the *Patrology*, from the manuscript of the monastery of the Blessed Virgin Mary of Rheinau among the Swiss. EDITOR.]

The manuscript is parchment, folio, compiled four hundred years ago. The preface begins: “When you first took up residence in our convent, and addressed the brethren according to the grace given you,” etc. Then follows the prologue, whose opening is: “The most skilled painters, Ambrose, Augustine,” etc.

In a parchment folio manuscript of the same library of Sainte-Croix, written four hundred years ago, is seen Alan’s *Eye of Sacred Scripture*, or *Compendium of Both Testaments*.

> [Note: Col. 0596. This is the same work as the *Distinctions of Theological Terms*, which we reprint below according to the Deventer edition of 1477. EDITOR.]

The preface begins: “To the most reverend father and lord Ermengaud, by God’s grace abbot of Saint-Gilles, Alan,” etc. The work begins: “Since, according to the proclamation of Aristotelian authority, those who are ignorant of the names of virtues,” etc.

Lastly, in the library of Kremsmünster there is Master Alan’s *Book on the Various Discourses of Theological Terms*. It begins: “Whoever seeks knowledge of sacred Scripture,” etc. Paper manuscript, folio, in a fourteenth-century hand. We have reported all these matters here in order that anyone who may someday undertake a fuller collection of Alan’s works may know whence the manuscripts are to be obtained.

# FIVE BOOKS ON THE ART, OR ARTICLES, OF THE CATHOLIC FAITH

(Extracted by the Reverend Father Dom Bernard Pez from the manuscript of the imperial monastery of St. Emmeram at Regensburg and from that of the illustrious Charterhouse of Gaming in Austria, and published in vol. I of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, p. 476.)

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0595A] Clement, Pope, whose subjects may experience the reality of your name and life, and may you receive from the Lord the zeal of one writing this work devoted to your name: attend graciously. Observing that the regions of the western empire were corrupted by the offence of so many heretical sects, I could scarcely endure this corruption in the confession of Christ’s name, so greatly prevailing through the deserts of sins; for, creeping like a cancer and no longer fearing openly to show itself—

> [Note: Col. 0595A. Gemnicensian manuscript: “to advance openly.”]

—it produces grave scandal in the Church and irreparable loss. Moreover, the inhabitants of the eastern lands, deceived by Mohammed’s ridiculous teaching, in these times persecute not merely in doctrine but even by arms those who profess the Christian faith. But since I cannot resist them with bodily strength, I have attempted to attack their wickedness by arguments.

The holy Fathers, indeed, turning Jews from obstinacy and Gentiles from errors by the power of miracles, and bringing forward the authorities of the Old and New Testaments, extended the faith thus proved. Yet neither has the grace of miracles been granted to me, nor is the adducing of authorities sufficient for overcoming heresies, since modern heretics either wholly reject them or distort them.

I have therefore more diligently arranged probable reasons for our faith, against which scarcely the keenest intellect can resist, so that those who disdain to rest content with prophecy and the Gospel [Col. 0597A] may at least be persuaded by human arguments. Yet, if these reasons lead people to believe, they are not in every respect fully sufficient for embracing faith. Nor does that faith possess merit to which human reason supplies complete proof. For this will be our glory: in our homeland to comprehend by perfect knowledge what we now behold as through a mirror, in an enigma.

Moreover, since you are Christ’s vicar and the successor of the apostle Peter, it belongs to you to spread the seed of the Catholic word throughout the earth. I have therefore devoted this work to be inscribed with the title of your name, so that, wherever it is read, the authority increased by the merits of your excellence may more effectively move its readers. Indeed, I rightly call this edition an *Art of the Catholic Faith*. For it is composed after the manner [indeed] [Col. 0597B] of an art: it contains definitions, distinctions, and propositions proving the intended matter by an orderly method.

This work, then, is divided into five books. The first treats of the one cause of all things, that is, the one and same triune God; the second, of the world, the creation of angel and man, and freedom of will; the third, of the Son of God incarnate for the redemption of man; the fourth, of the sacraments of the Church; the fifth, of the resurrection of the dead.

Definitions have been added in order that it may appear in what sense terms suitable to this art are to be used. Three postulates are appended. They are so called because, although, as first principles, they cannot be proved through other things and are not altogether self-evident, [Col. 0597C] nevertheless—

> [Note: Col. 0597C. Emmeram manuscript: “yet true.”]

—I ask that they be granted to me for proving the propositions that follow. Then follow the common conceptions of the mind, so called because they are so evident that, once heard, the mind immediately understands them to be true. These are introduced to prove what follows.

A cause is that through which something said to be created has being. A substance is that which consists of substance, matter, or form. Matter is a distinct thing capable of receiving form. Form is that which, arising from a concurrence of properties, makes its subject, as distinct from every other [Col. 0598A] substance, to be something else.

> [Note: Col. 0597C. Gemnicensian manuscript: “something.”]

A property is either substantial or accidental. A substantial property is that which is compounded—

> [Note: Col. 0597C. There: “is placed under.”]

—with underlying matter in order to complete a substance; an accidental property is of an adventitious nature. An accident is a property which exists through a subject, conferring not being upon it but difference. “To differ” is said of that which is informed by properties whose collection cannot be found in another thing. Properties and forms produce difference. “Distinct” is said of that which differs, or produces difference.

Motion is an accident considered according to some change in a subject.

There are six kinds of motion: generation, corruption, increase, diminution, change of place, [Col. 0598B] and alteration.

Likewise, things are said to exist actually when we apprehend them among existing things not merely by intellect but in actuality. Intellect is a power of the soul which apprehends a thing with the assistance of form. Nouns and verbs are utterances signifying, in part, those things which we apprehend by intellect. Number is the natural sum of distinct things.

These are the three things which I ask, or postulates. First: that every composition has a composing cause. Second: that the ascent through the causes of no thing proceeds to infinity. Third: that whatever we attribute to the causes of created things, and which is not present in them through an effect, must also be attributed to the cause of that thing.

The common conceptions are these. First: every thing has being through that which brings its cause—

> [Note: Col. 0598C. Gemnicensian manuscript: “produces”; and so always in what follows.]

—into being. Second: [Col. 0598C] every cause is prior and more worthy than its effect. Third: nothing is prior to, more worthy than, or higher than itself.

> [Note: Col. 0598C. Emmeram manuscript: “than it itself is.”]

Fourth: if a greater being possesses a lesser, the lesser is bound to direct itself and those things which belong to it to the honor and will of the greater. Fifth: an offender deserves a punishment so much the greater as the one against whom the injury is done is greater. Sixth: satisfaction ought to be rendered in proportion to the dignity of the one against whom the sin is committed. Seventh: things heard move minds effectively, and things seen more effectively.

# BOOK I

[Col. 0597]

## 437. I. Whatever is the cause of a cause is the cause of the caused thing.

[Col. 0597D]

A cause is that through which something has being, according to its definition; and every thing has being through that which brings its cause into being, according to the first common conception of the mind. Therefore, if something produces a cause, it is evident that it also produces the effect. Hence, if *a* is the cause of *b*, and *b* is the cause of *c*, it is clear that *a* is the cause of *c*. For if *a* is the cause of *b*, and *b* is the cause of *c*, then *c*—

> [Note: Col. 0597D. Both manuscripts: “a.”]

—has being through *b*, according to the definition of cause. By hypothesis, *b* [Col. 0598D] has being through *a*, for *a* is its cause; and *c* has being through *b*. But according to the first conception of the mind every thing has being through that which brings its cause into being. But *a* brings *b* into being, for it is its cause; and *b* is the cause of *c*. Therefore, according to that conception of the mind, *c* has being through *a*. Therefore, by the definition of cause, *a* is the cause of *c*; and thus the proposition is established.

## II. Every cause of a subject is a cause of its accident.

For an accident, according to its definition, has being [Col. 0599A] through its subject; therefore, according to the definition of cause, the subject is the cause of the accident. But—

> [Note: Col. 0599D. Gemnicensian manuscript: “and.”]

—the preceding theorem says: “Whatever is the cause of a cause is the cause of the caused thing.” Therefore every cause of a subject is a cause of its accident.

## III. Nothing composed itself or brought itself into being.

Indeed, the adversary says: something composed itself or brought itself into being. Therefore it has being through itself; therefore it is the cause of itself, according to the definition of cause; therefore it is prior to and more worthy than itself, according to the second conception of the mind. But this is contrary to the third common conception of the mind. For nothing is prior to or more worthy than itself. Therefore it is impossible that something should have composed itself or brought itself into being.

## IV. Neither underlying matter without form nor form without underlying matter can actually exist.

> [Note: Col. 0599D. Emmeram manuscript: “It must be held that neither underlying matter without form nor form without underlying matter can actually exist.”]

[Col. 0599B]

For if underlying matter exists, it is a distinct thing; therefore, according to the definition of the distinct, it differs or produces difference. But it does not produce difference, because—

> [Note: Col. 0599D. Emmeram manuscript adds: “the subject.”]

—it is neither a property nor a form; therefore it differs. Therefore, by the definition of that which differs, it is informed by properties; therefore it is subject to form; therefore it is not without form.

The same follows from the definition of form. For form makes its subject other than every other substance. Therefore form is in a subject, and thus in underlying matter. And so the proposition is established.

## V. The composition of form with matter is the cause of substance.

[Col. 0599C]

For substance consists of matter and form. Therefore matter and form are causes of the composition of substance, by the first postulate. Likewise, neither form can actually exist unless it is composed with matter, nor matter unless it is composed with form, as was proved above. Therefore form and matter actually have being through their composition; therefore composition is the cause of their existence. But their existence is the cause of substance. Therefore, by the first theorem, the composition of form with matter is the cause of substance. For whatever is the cause of a cause is the cause of the caused thing.

## VI. Every substance has a threefold cause: namely matter, form, and their union; and the cause of these three is the same.

[Col. 0599D]

The first part of this theorem derives its force from the preceding proposition. The second is proved by the first postulate. Since every composition has some composing cause, the composition of form with matter has some cause; therefore that cause is the cause of the composition and union, and of matter and form themselves, as is proved by means of the preceding theorem.

## VII. Whatever falls under number differs or produces difference.

> [Note: Col. 0599D. Emmeram manuscript: “and differs.”]

[Col. 0600A]

For number is the sum of distinct things. Therefore, if things fall under number, they are distinct; therefore, by the definition of the distinct, they differ or produce difference.

## VIII. Nothing is the cause of itself.

> [Note: Col. 0599D. Gemnicensian manuscript: “For nothing is,” etc.]

This derives its proof from the third theorem. For nothing composed itself or brought itself into being. Therefore nothing exists through itself; and therefore neither is it its own cause.

## IX. The being of every inferior thing has a supreme cause.

> [Note: Col. 0600D. Emmeram manuscript: “The cause is,” etc.]

For the ascent through the causes of no thing is infinite, as the second postulate proposes.

## X. The supreme cause neither is composed with anything, nor do any things compose it.

For whether this or that is the case, there is some composing cause of that composition, [Col. 0600B] by the first postulate. That composing cause is either the cause under discussion itself or another. But it cannot be the cause under discussion. For nothing is the cause of itself. Therefore it is another than that of which this is said. But every cause is superior to its effect, according to the second common conception of the mind; therefore it is superior to the supreme cause, which is impossible.

## XI. The supreme cause is neither property nor form.

For it is not composed with anything; therefore it is neither property nor form.

## XII. The supreme cause must be utterly simple. Hence it is evident that there is only one supreme cause of all things, which, for the purpose of reasoning, we call God.

[Col. 0600C]

The truth of this proposition is sufficiently apparent from the tenth theorem. The corollary introduced is proved as follows. If the adversary, together with the Manichaean heretic, says that there is not only one supreme cause, let several be posited; therefore at least two—

> [Note: Col. 0600D. Emmeram manuscript: “Let several, then, be posited.”]

—exist. Therefore they are subject to the number two and fall under number; therefore, by the seventh theorem, they differ or produce difference. But neither produces difference, because neither is a property or form, as the preceding argument taught. Therefore they differ. Therefore, according to the definition of that which differs, those causes are informed by properties or forms; therefore forms are joined to them.

> [Note: Col. 0600D. Gemnicensian manuscript: “unjoined.”]

But every composition has some supreme cause. Therefore they have some cause or causes; [Col. 0600D] therefore they are not supreme causes, contrary to the hypothesis.

## 438. XIII. No accident occurs in God.

For if an accident occurs in God, then God is the subject of the accident.

> [Note: Col. 0600D. Gemnicensian manuscript: “then God is an actual subject.”]

But an accident makes its subject differ, as was said in the definition of accident—

> [Note: Col. 0600D. Emmeram manuscript: “in the preceding [definition].”]

Therefore God differs from something; therefore he is informed by properties, which is contrary to the hypothesis.

## XIV. God can neither be altered, increased, diminished, nor moved locally.

[Col. 0601A]

For no accident occurs in God. Therefore no species of motion occurs in him.

## XV. God is eternal.

For if he begins to exist, then there is motion by generation. If he ceases—

> [Note: Col. 0601D. Emmeram manuscript: “has failed.”]

—to exist, then he will be moved by corruption; therefore an accident either will be or has been in him, which is impossible.

## XVI. God is immeasurable, incomprehensible, ineffable, and unnameable.

He is truly immeasurable because there is in him no fixed measure of quantity; for he is devoid of quantity, since no accident occurs in him. Who could doubt that he is likewise incomprehensible by place, time, and intellect? [Col. 0601B] For he is not confined by an interval of time, because he had no beginning and will not be enclosed even by an end.

> [Note: Col. 0601D. “Even” is absent in the Emmeram manuscript.]

Likewise, he cannot be contained by place. For if he were circumscribed by place, his solidity would be enclosed by fixed surfaces, and thus he would not be devoid of quantity and form, which was disproved above. Again, God, who eludes every kind of form, cannot be comprehended by intellect, since natural intellect does not apprehend a thing without the assistance of form, as appears from the definition of intellect.

> [Note: Col. 0601D. Gemnicensian manuscript: “being.”]

Therefore God cannot be grasped by human intellect.

In the same way he is rightly called ineffable, that is, one of whom we cannot speak properly. For human speech concerns two terms: the subject, [Col. 0601C] by which that concerning which discourse is made is expressed; and the predicate, which joins a property or form to the subject. This mode is foreign to the divine nature, since nature is subject to property, and property itself is not without a cause. Hence it is clear that God is unnameable. For names were instituted only to express things understood, and God cannot be grasped by human intellect; therefore neither can he properly be signified by a name.

> [Note: Col. 0601D. Emmeram manuscript: “therefore neither by name nor by reasoning can [he be] signified.”]

## XVII. We apprehend God not by knowledge but by faith alone.

For nothing can be known which cannot be understood. But we do not apprehend God by intellect, as is apparent from the preceding proposition.

> [Note: Col. 0601D. Emmeram manuscript: “the foregoing.”]

Therefore neither do we apprehend him by knowledge. Thus, led by reason, we presume that God exists, [Col. 0601D] and do not know it, but believe that he exists. For faith is an assumption arising from certain reasons—

> [Note: Col. 0601D. There: “notions.”]

—not sufficient for knowledge. Faith, therefore, is certainly above opinion but below knowledge.

## XVIII. God is in every time, in every place, and is capable of all things and of however much.

The immensity comprehended under this name embraces created or co-created things, and those things which, if they existed, would be created or co-created. Thus [Col. 0602A] let the false writer say: “God cannot do all things.” Let him posit something—

> [Note: Col. 0602D. Both manuscripts: “another thing.”]

—created or co-created, which God cannot do. It will be either a subject, a property, or a substance formed from both. But whatever it is, that union will have some cause, as is proved by the first postulate. Now every inferior cause has a supreme cause, as is proved from the ninth theorem.

> [Note: Col. 0602D. Emmeram manuscript: “The being of every inferior [thing] is [a cause],” etc.]

Therefore the supreme cause already established is the cause of the thing at issue.

> [Note: Col. 0602D. Gemnicensian manuscript: “the composite.”]

Therefore that thing has being through God; therefore God can make it to exist; therefore God can do it, which is contrary to the hypothesis.

Similarly, if it is denied that God can do all things at every time, let some time, or some thing [Col. 0602B] or things, be posited which God cannot do at that time; and we may argue in the aforesaid manner. The same argument must be made if it is denied that God is capable of all things—

> [Note: Col. 0602D. “All things” is absent in the Emmeram manuscript.]

—in every place and of however much.

## XIX. The admirable things which we observe in the creation and ordering of things are attributed to the Creator through effect and cause.

> [Note: Col. 0602D. There: “are observed.”]

Hence, because powers and good things have been created powerfully and well, we say that the Creator is powerful and good. And because in the ordering of things love, justice, mercy, humility, piety, and the like are perceived, we call him pious, humble, just, merciful, and wise. Moreover, by familiar likenesses he is called light—

> [Note: Col. 0602D. There omits “light.”]

—spring, rising, radiance, life, seeing, and by other terms borrowed from every kind of language to proclaim his greatness.

[Col. 0602C] The third postulate is required for proving this. Beyond doubt, God is called good, or goodness, through effect and cause, because every good proceeds from him and he brings about every good. He is likewise called just, or justice, because justice proceeds from him alone, who is the cause of all things, as the corollary to the twelfth proposition affirms. He is called “Spring” by a certain likeness, because, as streams proceed from a spring, so all things proceed from him. He is also affirmed to be Sun and Light, because “he enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1). And the same is clear with respect to each term.

## XX. God is the power by which he is called powerful; the wisdom by which he is wise; the love by which he loves. And the other names that belong to the divine nature predicate the divine essence of God, though improperly.

[Col. 0602D]

For these names—power, powerful, wisdom, wise—can attribute neither form nor property nor anything of that kind to God, since God, being utterly simple, is incapable in his nature of anything such, as was proved by the tenth theorem. Therefore, when, for the sake of reasoning about God, we join names to names, we predicate nothing that is not his essence; [Col. 0603A] and if by borrowed names we say something—

> [Note: Col. 0603D. Gemnicensian manuscript: “that which.”]

—about God which we believe, we stammer improperly, as is shown to have been proved by the sixteenth theorem.

## XXI. All things are in God, God is in all things, and God is said to be all things causally.

For all things are in God as in their cause. God is in all things as a cause in its effects. God is also said to be all things through causation.

## XXII. God is essentially everywhere and nowhere locally.

God is truly said by the eighteenth theorem to be capable of all things in every place. But this name “powerful” predicates the divine essence, as is clear from [Col. 0603B] the twentieth theorem. Therefore God exists everywhere. God is therefore essentially everywhere, but nowhere locally; for he is incomprehensible, as is set forth in the sixteenth theorem.

> [Note: Col. 0603D. Gemnicensian manuscript: “As theorem 16 sets forth.”]

## XXIII. The admirable union of every substance shows how great its Author is.

For since we know that no creature can create another, and reason teaches us that the cause of every product is superior to it, we believe every maker to be admirable.

## XXIV. Matter, form, and their union are three wholly distinct things principally required in the creation of every substance. Hence it is evident that, in the creation of one and the same substance, the effect proves that there is a Trinity in one and the same Creator. This Trinity is called three persons: the first Father, the second Son, the third Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0603C]

Their definitions and natures demonstrate that form and matter are wholly distinct. It is also evident that neither is its own union, since what composes is other than what is composed. That these three are principally required is also readily understood from the definition of substance. For substance consists of matter and form; and to consist is the same as to be composed. The corollary is proved by the preceding proposition: for the union of every substance is admirable.

## XXV. Although, in the creation of every substance, a fitting order may assign matter to the Father, form to the Son, and composition to the Holy Spirit, nevertheless the whole Trinity must work in each of the three.

[Col. 0603D]

Matter, the first foundation of substance, fittingly corresponds to the first person of the Trinity; form, which is born within it, we fittingly attribute to the Son; but their composition [Col. 0604A]—to whom else could we suitably assign it but to the third person of the Trinity, called the Holy Spirit? Hence that composition contains not only the joining of the extremes but also their adornment. But since each of these persons is God, who is the one maker of all things, it follows that the whole Trinity works the aforesaid three things indivisibly.

## 439. XXVI. Form born in matter, and the union proceeding from both, figuratively proclaim to us the Son as begotten of the Father, and the Holy Spirit as their bond and love proceeding from both.

> [Note: Col. 0603D. Emmeram manuscript: “proclaimed beforehand.”]

For, considering their nature, we set it before ourselves as an image of its author—

> [Note: Col. 0603D. Gemnicensian manuscript: “we set him before ourselves as an image of his maker,” etc.]

—and, contemplating the Creator’s nature through the creature as through [Col. 0604B] a mirror, judging substance in an enigma, we behold it figuratively by the aforesaid figure, as is clear from the twenty-third—

> [Note: Col. 0604D. In that place only theorem 24 is cited.]

—and twenty-fourth theorems.

## XXVII. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are equal in power and nature.

For nature proves that they are equal, since each is God and the three themselves are one God, as we have from the corollary to the twenty-fourth theorem. The twenty-fifth theorem proves them equal in power.

## XXVIII. The three persons have one essence, and none is another of the others.

The first part of this proposition is apparent from what has preceded. For since the three persons are one and the same God, it is evident that they are of the same essence. Next, we can establish that these persons are wholly distinct in the manner already stated. Just as the twenty-fourth theorem held that three things are distinct in the creation of substance, so we perceive the creating persons to be distinct. The same is indirectly proved.

> [Note: Col. 0604D. Both manuscripts: “Likewise.”]

For if anyone says that the Father is the Son and the Holy Spirit, then their person is the same; therefore there are not three persons, which is contrary to the twenty-fourth theorem.

## XXIX. Whatever predicates the divine essence belongs to the three persons.

For these three persons are nothing other than the one divine essence, as the preceding theorem confirms.

## XXX. The Trinity of persons is the unity of Deity.

> [Note: Col. 0604D. Emmeram manuscript: “divinity.”]

[Col. 0604D]

For the Trinity is three persons—

> [Note: Col. 0604D. There: “is the term ‘person.’”]

—which are one Deity. And that Deity is nothing other than the unity of Deity. Hence, from the first, that Trinity is the unity of Deity.

# BOOK II

[Col. 0603]

[Col. 0603D] Good is that which has being beneficially. Evil is the defect and privation of good. Useful is that which proceeds from a good cause. Love is that which wills for others the same good that it wills for itself, and brings it about insofar as it can and ought. [Col. 0605A] Justice is that which rewards those who deserve well and punishes the wicked, repaying reward or punishment according to the measure of merit. One properly said to deserve well is one who, compelled by no necessity, does what he is not bound to do for another’s honor or advantage. One deserves ill who does not render to the one to whom he owes it what is due, though able to do so. Humility is that which makes the greatest equal to the least. Mercy is that which remits something of a punishment due. Glory is joy arising from the felicity of good things. Grace is that which bestows something not by merit but gratuitously. Satisfaction for sin is something sufficiently done for the honor of the one against whom the sin was committed, though otherwise not due.

## I. God is the highest good; neither in him nor from him is there evil.

[Col. 0605B] God is good through effect and cause, as is proved from the nineteenth theorem—

> [Note: Col. 0605D. Gemnicensian manuscript: “is made clear.”]

—and nothing has being as beneficially as God. Therefore nothing is as good as God, according to the definition of good; therefore he is supremely good, and therefore the highest good.

Again, God is capable of all things and of however much, as is stated in the eighteenth theorem of Book I. Therefore there is no incapacity in him; therefore no defect; therefore there is no defect of good in him; therefore, by the definition of evil, there is no evil in him.

Again, whatever is from him is from a good cause, for God is a good cause. Therefore whatever is from him is useful, according to the definition of the useful; therefore whatever is from him has being beneficially; therefore whatever is from him [Col. 0605C] is good; therefore evil is not from him. Thus we have proved the three parts of the proposition.

## II. Everything, whether substance or accident, must be good in its nature as it exists.

For everything is from God. Therefore it has being beneficially; therefore it is good. Or otherwise: no evil is from God, and everything is from him; therefore everything is good. An argument from immediate premises.

## III. Supreme love, justice, humility, and mercy are perceived in God.

Understand love, humility, and the rest to be in God, as is explained in Book I, theorem XXI. But because he is the highest good, there is in him no lack of any good. Therefore love and every virtue are supreme in him.

## IV. Divine love proves that a thing sharing in divine wisdom and glory had to be created; and that thing is called a rational spirit.

[Col. 0605D]

Whoever considers the definition of love will recognize that God wills for another the same good which he wills for himself, and brings it about insofar as he can and ought, especially since love is supreme in him. But this could not be unless there were something other than him which could share God’s good. Therefore there had to be something from him for which he would will the same good that he wills for himself, and not merely will it but bring it about insofar as he could and ought. He could bring it about, since he is capable of all things, as is clear from the first [Col. 0606A] book. Therefore, in view of his love, he ought to do so. Thus there had to be something other than him which shared that good. But something other than him cannot exist except through his creation, as the twelfth theorem of Book I proves. Therefore such a thing had to be created, a participant in the divine good. But the divine good is wisdom, glory, and the other things mentioned above. Therefore a thing sharing in God’s wisdom, glory, love, and other admirable qualities had to be created; and thus the proposition is established.

## V. A rational spirit is bound to fear and serve God, and to minister in every obedience.

Anyone who considers the fourth common conception of the mind will find the necessity of this proposition. For since the lesser is bound to obey the greater in all things, [Col. 0606B] and the rational spirit has from God its life, wisdom, and power, it ought without interruption to direct itself and all that it has to God’s glory, honor, and praise.

> [Note: Col. 0605D. Emmeram manuscript: “without interruption.”]

## VI. The structure of the world, with its manifold ornaments, had to be fashioned as material for fear, praise, and service of God, and for the attainment of glory.

Since the rational spirit is bound to serve and minister to God, as the preceding proposition set forth, the wondrous power displayed in created things had to be set before it as material for service.

> [Note: Col. 0605D. Gemnicensian manuscript: “set before.”]

Therefore, by contemplating the craftsmanship of the world, it had manifest material by which it might fear and praise so powerful and learned a maker, minister to the Lord in the governance and ordering of things—

> [Note: Col. 0606D. Emmeram manuscript: “whose.”]

—and, from knowledge of all things, might more fully glory in its author.

> [Note: Col. 0605D. Gemnicensian manuscript: “Love as material for service.”]

## VII. On account of the manifold functions of service, many rational spirits had to be created in the structure of the world; we call them God’s messengers.

For one spirit could not suffice for such great administrations; it was fitting that so great an author should have an abundance of ministers; and the bounty of infinite love willed that God the author should bestow his glory upon many.

## VIII. Freedom of choice to act well or ill had to be granted to angels from the necessity of justice.

For since we say that justice is in God, it follows from the definition of justice that we believe him to reward those who deserve well and punish the wicked. Therefore, if an angel were bound by necessity [Col. 0606D] to do for God what it owes, it would not deserve well. Since one is said to deserve well before God who, compelled by no necessity, willingly does for God what one owes, even if it did deserve, it would not be rewarded.

Likewise, if an inborn necessity compelled him to evil, so that he could not render the honor due, this would not be imputed to him but to the one who had created him such; nor, therefore, would he merit ill or deserve punishment, since free choice had to be granted to the angel by the necessity of justice. [Note: [Col. 0606D] Codex Em.: “would not merit, nor [would he receive] reward, when free [choice], etc.”] For since justice rewards only those who merit well, and punishes only the wicked [Col. 0607A] [Note: [Col. 0607D] Both codices: “nevertheless.”], one does not merit well except because, through no necessity but by the free choice of one’s own mind, one inclines oneself from evil toward good; and the same would similarly apply in the case of evil. If angels were good or evil by necessity, they would receive no reward for a good work nor incur punishment for an evil one; and this would be contrary to divine charity and justice.

### IX. The nature of angels must be believed to have been strong and subtle, enriched with manifold grace.

Angels assigned to the ministries of such great matters as the sixth and seventh theorems have set forth could not suffice unless they possessed a very powerful nature. Moreover, since they attend upon the divine mysteries in order to minister in the highest offices, angels must be wise, prudent, and provident, enjoying free choice [Col. 0607B]. Thus it is clear that they were enriched with the gift of manifold grace.

### X. In order that angels may merit well, they are obliged to use free choice for good.

For since they possess free choice, as the eighth theorem has set forth, by the principle of subjection they are obliged to fear God and serve Him in all things, as was proved in the fifth. Therefore they are obliged to direct free choice toward this end; and if they voluntarily turn it toward another, it is clear from the definition of meriting well before God that the angel merits well before God who uses free choice for good. Thus the proposition is evident.

### XI. Angels using free choice wrongly were to be damned without remedy.

[Col. 0607C] When the tenor of the ninth theorem is considered together with the strength of angels—for they could and ought to resist sin—they were all the more bound, by their manifold gift of grace, to obey their Creator readily. Therefore, if in dishonoring God they had abused free choice, they were in no way worthy of a remedy.

### XII. God’s charity and humility extend to all things.

No charity can be greater than God’s charity, which is supreme in God, as the third theorem of this book states. Therefore charity in God is infinitely great; therefore it is infinitely extensive; therefore it extends everywhere; therefore to all things. Argue likewise concerning humility, and you will have the proposition.

### XIII. A thing having something in common in its nature with every thing, and sharing in God’s wisdom and glory, had to be created even from the basest material; and we call this thing man.

[Note: [Col. 0607D] Codex Gem.: “his own.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0607D] Omitted there: “even.”]

[Col. 0607D]

For since, from what has preceded, we hold that God’s charity extends to all things, it was fitting that He should communicate His glory either to every thing or to something having a nature in common with every thing. But He ought not to do this to every thing, for God’s glory would be useless in insensate and brute creatures. Therefore there had to be something having something in common with every thing [Col. 0608A], by a necessity arising from its capacity to attain that glory. But since humility in God is most extensive [Note: [Col. 0607D] Codex Em.: “most simple.”], as the preceding theorem proves, so that the least might be made equal to the greatest, it was fitting that this thing should be fashioned from the basest material. But nothing is humbler than earth. Therefore rational man was formed from earth, like an angel; living together with inanimate things, composed of the four elements, and destined to receive the highest glory.

### XIV. Free choice had to be granted to man.

I prove this in the same way in which I proved the eighth proposition.

### XV. All human thoughts, words, and acts ought by obligation to be directed to God as their lawful end.

For since man is capable by free choice, he is obliged, [Col. 0608B] as was proved in the fifth theorem.

### XVI. It is just that reward and punishment be apportioned to a person’s will together with its effect, insofar as this lies within that will.

[Note: [Col. 0608D] Codex Em.: “affection.”]

A good will is worthy of reward; an evil will, of punishment. This follows from the definitions of meriting well or ill before God. For one who willingly does what he is obliged to do for God merits well before God. Therefore, by the definition of justice, he is worthy of reward. But by “a good will” we mean one meriting well before God—that is, one which, so far as it lies within itself, directs itself toward God; this was proved by the preceding proof. Therefore a good will is worthy of reward.

The contrary is proved in the same way of an evil will. Reward and punishment, however, must be imposed in greater or lesser measure [Col. 0608C], according as the will has been more intense in good or evil, as is found in the definition of justice.

### XVII. A perpetual will to merit well is worthy of perpetual recompense.

For, as the preceding points teach, reward must be apportioned to the will [Note: [Col. 0608D] Both codices: “is to be.”]. If a person has the will perpetually to serve God effectively [Note: [Col. 0608D] Codex Em.: “to God affection.”], insofar as this lies within him, and it is not through his own fault that he does not live forever, perpetual reward must be given in recompense to his will. Thus the proposition is clear.

### XVIII. The recompense of those who merit well before God is not wages, but grace.

For properly speaking, someone is said to merit well who voluntarily does a benefit for another which he is not obliged to do. But we do nothing for God which we are not obliged to do, as was established in the fifth theorem of this book [Col. 0608D]. Therefore our merit before God is not properly merit, but payment of a debt. Yet wages exist only for preceding merit or debt. But we do not properly merit; therefore what will be given by God will not properly be wages, but grace.

### XIX. Every being that labors in meriting well or ill ought to enjoy reward or be condemned to punishment.

For otherwise there would not be justice in God, which rewards those who merit and punishes those deserving condemnation.

### XX. The good which is in God is bestowed upon those who merit well. Hence it is evident that God bestows Himself upon those who merit well.

[Col. 0609A]

The fourth and the tenth propositions proved this present point. For man and angel were made to receive divine wisdom, and thus they ought to receive the divine good that is in God. Thus the proposition is evident. But there is no good in God which is not God, as the twentieth theorem of the first book, if we remember correctly, demonstrates. Therefore God gives to those who merit well that which God is, and thus gives Himself. Hence the corollary is clear.

### XXI. Human frailty readily falls from a good state.
