For, as was proved in the thirteenth theorem, man was made from the basest material. Therefore he is made of something fragile, because he is made of earth; therefore he is easily corrupted and driven toward a fall [Col. 0609B] [Note: [Col. 0609C] Codex Em.: “we are driven.”].

### XXII. The defilement of the mind desires to be washed and wiped clean.

For when the mind is corrupted and soiled by vices, it desires to be washed and wiped clean.

### XXIII. Counsel must be sought in correcting evil thoughts, words, and deeds.

For when a disease in a person must be cured, as the preceding proposition has set forth, who doubts that a physician should be consulted about this?

### XXIV. Bodily frailty needs to be relieved by a remedy.

I prove this as I did the preceding point.

### XXV. A manifold cause of disease requires a manifold medical remedy.

[Col. 0609C]

Since man is of a fragile nature, as the twenty-first proposition states, and for this reason easily contracts the disease of meriting ill, he needs a remedy in order to be restored to the state which is due. But the causes of the disease are many. By this disease we mean evil, that is, the lack of a good state [Note: [Col. 0610C] Codex Em.: “we call evil the lack of goodness.”], as appears from the foregoing. [Col. 0610A] Therefore many remedies must be applied to many causes, which is the proposition.

### XXVI. Frequent falling requires frequent help in rising again.

You can prove this as you did the preceding point.

### XXVII. In order that a person may become healthier and stronger, he must persist in using manifold aids.

This proposition is evident from the twenty-fifth.

### XXVIII. The form of man, made deformed through abuse, needs to be re-formed.

If you attend to the definition of form in the first book, you will find that it consists of concurrent properties. Therefore, when man does not at all direct his motions and his other properties, both of mind and body, toward God’s will, he uses them wrongly. Therefore he abuses his form; therefore he deforms it; therefore he corrupts it [Col. 0610B]; therefore he needs to be restored to the state that is due; therefore to his former form; therefore he needs to be re-formed.

### XXIX. One who merits ill before God is injurious toward God.

As was established in the fifteenth proposition, man is obliged to devote himself and everything within him to God’s honor; and if he withdraws himself and everything within him from God, he dishonors God. Therefore one who merits ill is injurious toward God. But to withdraw oneself and one’s possessions from God is to merit ill; therefore he is injurious toward God.

### XXX. One who merits ill must be punished with an infinitely great punishment.

For one who merits ill is injurious toward God, as was asserted in the preceding proposition [Col. 0610C]; and according to the fifth common conception of the mind, one who inflicts injury deserves a greater punishment the greater the one upon whom the injury is inflicted. But God is infinitely greater than every thing. Therefore one injurious toward God deserves an infinitely great punishment.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0609]

### I. Fallen and repentant man ought to be visited by divine mercy.

[Col. 0609D]

For since man, through his own frailty, stands on slippery ground, as was proposed in the twenty-first proposition of the second book, if he falls and repents, it is merciful and just that he should obtain divine mercy—that is, release from the punishment due.

### II. Fallen man had to be restored in order to receive glory.

For since God’s charity and humility decreed that the fragile creature of human nature should rejoice together with angels in glory, man had to attain that glory, as is explained in the thirteenth proposition of the second book. But if through sin he fell and was rendered unworthy to attain that blessedness, then, in view of his frailty, he ought through mercy, as was stated above [Col. 0610D], to be raised up. Therefore, even though he had fallen, he was to be restored to the glory predestined for him. Thus the proposition is clear.

### III. Man had to erase man’s guilt by satisfaction.

For it was more just that a man should erase the guilt of man than that an angel or another creature should do so. But if you consider divine justice, which does not permit guilt ever to be remitted unpunished, satisfaction had to follow guilt. Therefore man had to make satisfaction for man’s guilt; and this was the proposition.

### IV. Neither an angel, nor a mere human being, nor any other creature could restore man by satisfaction.

The truth of the preceding statements will appear from the thirtieth proposition of the second book: one who merits ill must be punished with an infinitely great punishment. But man or any other creature could not suffice for so great a satisfaction [Col. 0611A]; thus the proposition is clear. Again, in another way:

Whatever man can ever rightly do, he is obliged to devote to God’s honor and praise, as is manifestly evident from the fifteenth proposition of the second book. But according to the definition of satisfaction for sin, satisfaction is an act owed solely on account of guilt; and satisfaction must be recompensed according to the dignity of the one against whom the sin is committed, as is stated in the penultimate common conception of the mind. But God is infinitely worthy. Therefore whatever man can do is not a sufficient satisfaction for sin; therefore man cannot make sufficient satisfaction for sin, and neither, therefore, can any other creature. Thus the proposition is clear. Moreover, even if he could make satisfaction for sin [Col. 0611B], he still could not restore man to predestined glory.

### V. It was fitting that God should make satisfaction for man. Hence it is a great thing that God, made man, would restore the human race.

[Note: [Col. 0611D] Codex Em.: “through man.”]

It was fitting indeed [Note: [Col. 0611D] The same manuscript: “best.”] that divine glory should be communicated to man, as was proved in the twenty-first proposition of the second book. But man had sinned; therefore the sin had to be erased by satisfaction, as was stated in the third proposition of this book. But no creature could make full satisfaction, as was proved in the fourth. Therefore it is evident that man had to be restored by God; thus the proposition is clear. But it was just that man’s guilt should be erased by God, as has been inferred from the third proposition. Therefore God, who would make satisfaction for the creature, had to be man [Col. 0611C]; hence the corollary is clear.

### VI. The second Person of the Trinity was more fittingly appointed to unite human nature to Himself.

The second Person in the Trinity is the Son, who is the author of form, as is clear from the twenty-fifth proposition of the first book. Consider its tenor. But God had to reform man, deformed through guilt, as was proposed in the twenty-eighth proposition of the first book. Therefore it was more fitting that the author of form, who would reform the form of fallen man, should be united to human nature.

### VII. The restorer of man had to offer Himself to God on behalf of fallen man.

For since man, who owes himself and all that he can do to God [Col. 0611D], withdrew himself from God through sin and his works, tending toward an end other than God, as was proposed in the twenty-fifth proposition of the second book, the restorer of man had to render [Note: [Col. 0611D] Codex Em.: “return.”] and offer Himself to God in place of the man withdrawn from God.

### VIII. The offering due for redeeming man must be sincere and free from every contagion of sin.

For God is offered on behalf of man, as the foregoing states, and He is the Son of God the Father; therefore He is God, in whom there is no evil, as was discussed [Col. 0612A] in the first proposition of the second book. Therefore there is in Him no contagion of sin.

### IX. The Son of God was to assume flesh from an uncorrupted woman; and He was called Christ.

For it was fitting that He who would make Himself a pure victim should come forth from a pure vessel, and from a woman, so that God the Redeemer might be born from the sinful race [Note: [Col. 0611D] “God” is absent in Codex Em.]; and from a Virgin, lest that most holy flesh should contract a stain through the sin of male intercourse [Note: [Col. 0612D] Codex Gem.: “lest it contract the stain of the sin of a man, or of male intercourse.”].

### X. For the sins of the fallen, it was fitting that the Redeemer should endure insults, terrors, and the punishment of death.

This is evident from the thirtieth proposition of the second book. Since an infinitely great punishment was due for the sin [Note: [Col. 0612D] Codex Em.: “for the sin of one.”] of one man, much more, for so many sins of so many human beings to be redeemed, the Redeemer had to endure the greatest punishment He could [Col. 0612B]. But there is nothing greater in man than death. Therefore, in order to make full satisfaction, He had to endure death, insults, and terrors.

### XI. That victim had to be offered to God the Father.

That it had to be offered to God is proved in the seventh proposition. That it had to be offered to the Father follows because He is the Son, and because a creature had to make satisfaction to its Creator.

### XII. This victim is sufficient to make satisfaction to the Creator for the greatest transgressions of any human beings whatsoever.

For He is God; therefore the victim is of however great worth. Therefore it is sufficient, however great the need, to blot out sin. Therefore it is sufficient for however many sins of any human beings; and thus for all those who have been, who are, and who will be. Hence the proposition is clear.

### XIII. This victim must be offered to God the Father by frequent ministries.

[Col. 0612C]

This theorem is suggested with the assistance of the twenty-fifth and twenty-sixth propositions of the second book. For frequent falling requires frequent help in rising again; and there is no help greater than the aforesaid victim. Therefore it must be set against our frequent falls.

### XIV. This remedy is useless to one who refuses it.

For one who refuses this remedy refuses God as helper. Therefore he sins; therefore he must be punished; therefore he renders himself unworthy of this remedy; therefore this remedy is useless to him. This is the proposition.

### XV. God could have redeemed the human race fittingly in another way.

For since, as is stated in the eighteenth proposition of the first book, God is omnipotent, He could have discovered another good and fitting mode of redemption [Col. 0612D] [Note: [Col. 0612D] Codex Em.: “fittingly.”], because whatever is from Him is good, and there is no evil either from Him or in Him, as the first proposition of the second book declares.

### XVI. One without this remedy can in no way attain glory, but rather punishment.

For since man is born in sin, he is not worthy to attain divine glory unless he has been restored by a divine remedy, as the second theorem of this book declares.

## BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0613]

[Col. 0613A] Preaching is speech persuading the soul toward salvation. [Note: [Col. 0613D] Codex Em.: “mind.”] A sacrament is a visible thing representing invisible grace by a certain likeness. Baptism is the washing with water sanctified through invocation of the Holy Trinity, signifying the washing away of sin. The Eucharist is the sacrament of Christ’s body existing under the appearances of bread and wine, when bread is changed into Christ’s flesh and wine into blood. This sacrament was instituted under this appearance so that, just as bread and wine are the principal nourishment of the body, so Christ’s body is the strongest sustenance of the soul above all others. Matrimony is the lawful union of man and woman, representing the union of Christ and the Church. Penance is contrition for sins, intending to cease from them, expressed through oral confession. The dedication of churches is manifold in the same order as the ministers of the Church. The anointing with chrism and oil, and certain other sacred rites [Note: [Col. 0613D] Codex Em.: “sacraments.”], through whose practice devotion is aroused and man made holier. The Church is the congregation of believers confessing Christ, and the support of the sacraments.

### I. Preaching and the sacraments of the Church are necessary.

For things heard effectively, and things seen more effectively, move minds; this is the final common conception of the mind. Therefore preaching moves the mind, and the sacraments more strongly, since they are outward signs. And because the Church, on account of the disease of manifold sin, needs the manifold remedy of medicine, as the twenty-fifth proposition of the second book states, sinners must be aroused both by words and signs [Col. 0613C]; for if individual means do not help, many help [Note: [Col. 0613D] Codex Gem.: “for the things which do not help individually may benefit through many [means], therefore, etc.”]. Therefore both preaching and sacraments are necessary, which was the proposition.

### II. To investigate the reason for baptism.

Since the soul united to flesh conceived in sin contracts a stain from the corrupt mass, it consequently requires a spiritual remedy of washing, as we established in the twentieth proposition of the second book, where it is said that the defilement of the mind desires to be washed and wiped clean. To remove this, the institution of an external washing was necessary; sanctified by invocation of the Holy Trinity, it has the effect of an interior cleansing.

### III. To examine the reason for the Eucharist.

Man, rising from sin through faith and penance [Col. 0613D], needed an effective remedy which would confer the grace of perseverance in good. But none was more effective than Christ’s flesh. Therefore it was necessary [Col. 0614A] for man to receive Christ’s flesh, which flesh of Christ, under the appearance of bread and wine, as Christ Himself instituted it, when received by worthy persons advances the salvation of body and soul and makes those who receive it members of Christ. And lest wickedness abound in us, this victim must be offered by frequent ministries, as is declared in the thirteenth proposition of the third book.

Moreover, all the prelates of the universal Church after the apostles departed in this faith, as did those through whose merits God performed great and wonderful miracles. Therefore let no believer recoil from the sacrament first instituted by the Lord [Note: [Col. 0613D] Codex Gem.: “utterly.”]. Rather, let him beseech Him with simple prayer that what we now perform under an appearance [Note: [Col. 0614D] Codex Em.: “what we now often perform.”] we may comprehend with certain knowledge in eternal glory.

### IV. To investigate the reason for matrimony.

[Col. 0614B] The human race had to be propagated for the worship of God rather than produced through the wantonness of the flesh. Hence, to those unwilling to remain continent, this remedy of marital intercourse was granted; and such sexual union or [Note: [Col. 0614D] Codex Gem.: “its own.”] conjunction is excused by the good of matrimony, so that recognized kinship among those joined may increase charity through the line of consanguinity, and thus bodily frailty may be relieved, as was proposed in the twenty-third proposition of the second book.

### V. To investigate the reason for penance.

Since the power of baptism imprints upon the baptized a Christian character which can in no way be erased when the guilt of a repeated crime is incurred, repeated baptism would be superfluous. For it would be doing what has already been done [Col. 0614C] if what a Christian already possesses were conferred on him again, and thus an injury would be done to the sacrament. Therefore one who has fallen after baptism, with a contrite heart consulting God and, by oral confession, man, had to apply the medicine of penance to the recurrent disease, as is proposed in the twenty-third proposition of the second book.

### VI. To explain the manifold reasons for the Church’s manifold sacraments.

Certain sacraments have been devised for erasing guilt, confirming man in good, remedying frailty, and conferring grace, as was decreed, as is proposed in the twenty-third proposition of the second book. Therefore [Note: [Col. 0614D] Codex Em.: “moreover.”] it was fitting to consecrate both the persons who confer them, the places in which they are conferred, and the instruments both which they use and from which [Note: [Col. 0614D] Codex Gem.: “from which.”] [Col. 0614D] they make them. Thus it was useful to establish manifold sacramental rites [Note: [Col. 0614D] Same manuscript: “restore.”].

### VII. Christ’s faithful are certainly possessed of faith in the sacraments.

[Col. 0615A]

For Christ’s faithful are Christ’s Church, and Christ’s Church is the congregation of believers confessing Christ and the support of the sacraments. Therefore they have faith in the sacraments, which was the proposition.

### VIII. Faith in the sacraments is required of those who merit well before God.

Let the heretic therefore say: “It is false.” [Note: [Col. 0615B] Codex Em.: “Therefore Tartarus.”] Suppose, then, that one who merits well before God does not have faith in the sacraments. Then he does not confess the support of the sacraments; therefore, by the definition of the Church, he is not of the Church; therefore he is not among Christ’s faithful; therefore he does not merit well—which is contrary to the hypothesis.

### IX. Baptism, conferred upon someone not yet baptized who neither refuses it nor has an evil conscience, confers something. Hence it is evident that baptism is efficacious for persons deprived of reason and for infants.

[Col. 0615B]

The proposition is proved thus: baptism is a sacrament of the faithful; therefore, by the definition of sacrament, it signifies invisible grace and inner washing; [Col. 0616A] therefore, when conferred upon a worthy recipient, inner washing is signified; therefore the worthy recipient is inwardly washed; therefore it confers something upon him. But if someone receives baptism and does not receive it worthily, then either he has previously been baptized, or he refuses baptism, or he approaches with an evil conscience; and, by denial of the consequent, it confers nothing on him. But if someone receives baptism and is neither such a person, he receives it worthily; therefore baptism confers something on him, because he receives it neither while sound [the text is uncertain] nor with an evil conscience, nor is he such a person.

But let the corollary be proved. [Note: [Col. 0615B] Codex Em.: “But if he receives baptism, [being] neither such nor such a person, he receives it. But he receives it; therefore baptism confers [Col. 0616B] something on him because he is neither such nor such a person; which was the proposition.”] Infants or persons deprived of reason are not such persons; therefore baptism is efficacious for them. But baptism confers nothing on one already baptized, lest, if it were repeated, injury be done to the sacrament. Nor does it confer anything on one who refuses it. For if he refuses, he does not believe; [Col. 0616B] if he does not believe, he is not among Christ’s faithful, as was proved in the seventh proposition of this book. Therefore it confers nothing upon him. Again, for one having an evil conscience it is not effective at present. For such a will is worthy of punishment, as is proposed in the sixteenth proposition of the second book. Therefore it is not worthy of reward; therefore it is not worthy of the washing away of sin, etc.

## BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0615]

### I. Resurrection is the renewed union of body and soul separated by death, conferring upon both soul and body reward or punishment according to the character of their deed.

[Col. 0615C]

For each labors in meriting well or ill. But every thing which labors in meriting well or ill ought to enjoy reward or be condemned to punishment, as the twenty-eighth proposition of the second book states. Therefore both body and soul, as was proposed, shall feel recompense made to them according to the character of their deed.

### II. The whole human being obtains perpetual recompense.

The whole person indeed obtains it because body and soul, as was stated above, obtain perpetual recompense; or because the human will will rejoice in perpetual recompense, as is maintained in the eighteenth proposition of the second book [Col. 0615D]. You can prove the same concerning recompense for sin.

### III. Man will rise in the flesh which he had, to be united anew with his own soul.

For unless he rose in the same flesh, recompense for merits would not be made to the whole person, though the whole person, as stated above, must obtain it. Flesh cannot experience condemnation or glory unless it is animated by spirit; therefore it will be united to the spirit. But at the resurrection a new flesh, which has not merited, must not be assumed; rather, the flesh in which the person merited, and likewise the same spirit. For if another flesh or another spirit were assumed, there would be another person [Col. 0616C], who had merited nothing before; and if the flesh which had merited did not rise, it would obtain no recompense at all. This is contrary to the nineteenth proposition of the second book.

### IV. Resurrection generally applies to all, both greater and lesser. Hence it is evident that Christ rose from the dead.

For if a human being has discernment, he merits well or ill; therefore he will rise for reward or punishment. But if he is a child or deprived of reason, he has either been aided by the sacraments or not. If he has been aided by the sacraments, and it is not through his own fault that he does not merit, he will nevertheless obtain glory, as is declared from the fourth and thirteenth propositions of the second book. But if [Col. 0616D] he has not been aided by the sacraments, he will nevertheless rise, to obtain that of which the final proposition of the third book has spoken. What flesh, moreover, is more glorious than Christ’s flesh? What flesh is more powerful in merits? Hence there is no doubt that it rose in glory.

### V. Resurrection will attain an incorruptible body, free from defect.

[Note: [Col. 0615D] Codex Gem.: “An incorruptible body is free from the defect which resurrection will attain.”]

For since it obtains perpetual resurrection, it will be such that it cannot decay or dissolve, since it must endure without end. And if it must be damned without end, because it is incorruptible it cannot [Col. 0617A] fail. Therefore it seems that no defect can be in it.

### VI. The saints in glory will enjoy the recompense of perfect knowledge and charity.

Glory is joy arising from the happiness of good things. But God, intending to communicate His glory to the saints, both angels and human beings, as the fourth and thirteenth propositions of the second book state, will make them abound in His goods. What goods, however, are greater than wisdom and charity? In that glory the saints, who according to the twentieth proposition of the second book will possess God as their reward, will contemplate Him eternally face to face; and the divine mysteries which they now imagine through a mirror in an enigma, they will then apprehend in the fullness of knowledge. [Col. 0617B] In that kingdom they will also be bound by such an affection of charity that the least will rejoice in the glory of the greatest [Col. 0618A] as greatly as though he himself had obtained the same glory. What wonder, when God, supreme charity and supreme wisdom, will be in them, and they in God? Let the Mohammedans therefore be ashamed, who promise to the risen body little women, foods of marvelous flavor, and delights that are bestial and earthly rather than heavenly—delights for the body, not the soul.

### VII. There is no punishment greater than the everlasting torment of the damned.

For what loss is greater than losing God, for the attainment of whose glory man was made, as the eleventh proposition of the second book states? And the lightest punishment, if perpetual, is more grievous than the most severe temporal punishment. Or consider those whom the worm of conscience will perpetually gnaw, who according to the final proposition of the second [Col. 0618B] book must be punished with an infinitely great punishment. Thus the proposition is clear.

[Col. 0617]

# THE THEOLOGICAL RULES OF ALAN OF LILLE, UNIVERSAL DOCTOR

(D. John Aloysius Mingarelli, *Fasciculus of Anecdota*, p. 171. Rome, 1756, quarto, published at the expense of Venantius Monaldini, bookseller on the Via del Corso.)

## PREFACE

As I am about to speak of the *Theological Rules*, I need not spend time investigating their author. For the most learned men agree that they were written by Alan the Great: above all Charles Visch [Note: [Col. 0617B] In the *Library of Writers of the Cistercian Order*.], who published most of his works at Antwerp in 1654; Casimir Oudin, in his *Commentaries on Ecclesiastical Writers* [Note: [Col. 0617B] At the year 1150, vol. II, p. 1407.]; and, to pass over others, John Albert Fabricius, in his *Library of Medieval and Late Latin* [Note: [Col. 0617B] Vol. I, p. 37, Padua edition, 1754.]. In my judgment, their agreement should carry great weight in this matter; moreover, it can be supported and confirmed by the authority of ancient manuscripts and copyists. For in several codices which Visch and Oudin attest still exist in the libraries at Bruges, Cambron, Saint Martin at Tournai, and Pembroke College, Cambridge—and also in the very ancient codex now before me—Alan’s name was inscribed by the copyist. This codex displays such antiquity that it may rightly seem to have been written in the very century in which Alan lived.

Oudin testifies that the *Theological Rules* which we publish were given many titles by ancient copyists. Sometimes, to distinguish them from another work of Alan’s called the *Lesser Doctrinal Work*, they are called the *Higher Doctrinal Work*; at other times they bear this title in old codices: *Book on the Maxims or Axioms of Theology*. Sometimes also, if Fabricius is to be believed, they bear this other title: *Book on Doctrine*. Finally, in our codex they are entitled: *Alan’s Rules on Sacred Theology*. We have retained the title of our codex, and did so all the more willingly because Alan himself seems to have indicated and, as it were, handed it down to us, when he repeatedly calls the propositions which he collects and interprets in this work “Rules.”

There are many matters in this little book worthy of notice; if I wished to enumerate them all, I should be far too lengthy. I shall offer only one example, namely what Alan writes in Rule 85 concerning attrition. Since John Morin had not seen this book of Alan’s, he had reasonably written in that distinguished *Commentary on Penance* [Note: [Col. 0617B] Book VIII, chapter 2, no. 14, p. 348.] that the term *attrition* was first employed by Alexander of Hales and introduced into the schools after 1220. “That name,” he says—namely, *attrition*—“began to become common after the year 1220, a little more than a hundred years after the birth of scholastic theology. They distinguished attrition from contrition as follows: they said that attrition arises from unformed faith, contrition from formed faith; that the principle of attrition is servile fear, and of contrition initial fear” [Note: [Col. 0618B] Please read what our Milliavacca wrote on this matter in the work published at Venice in 1753, entitled *On Proper Dispositions for the Sacraments of Baptism and Penance*, book I, chapter 15.]—and what follows.

But from Rule 85 we learn that the word *attrition* was current in theological discourse before 1220. For there Alan uses the word a second and a third time; and he seems to use it not as some new expression first devised by himself, but as one familiar to theologians. “Every meritorious evil in man,” he says [Col. 0619], “is either increased by continuance, lessened by attrition, or remitted by contrition.” And shortly afterward he adds:

> “The evil which is in a man, such as fornication or another criminal sin, is either increased by continuance … or lessened by attrition, as when someone grieves that he has committed this act and ceases from the deed, although he does not repent perfectly; or it is remitted by contrition, when he turns fully away from sin. For there are many who grieve that they have sinned and are bruised in heart, yet are not fully contrite: they neither have a firm purpose not to fall again, nor confess with the mouth.”

Yet two passages in these Rules will confront the reader which may perhaps provoke some criticism, or at least astonishment; and therefore something must now be said briefly about them. First, in Rule 106 Alan teaches that Christ never merited anything for himself. “Christ,” he says, “merited nothing for himself by his works; but whatever he merited, he merited for us by each of his works … Therefore, when he is said to have merited immortality and the name which is above every name, this must not be referred to himself, but to us; because he merited for us that we should have immortality and recognize him as equal to the Father.”

Now I freely admit that this opinion which pleased Alan has long since been rejected by the unanimous consensus of all theologians; nor does Chamier himself, a Calvinist, deny this in the work entitled *The Wars of the Lord*, or *Catholic Panstratia*. [Note: [Col. 0619] Vol. II, p. 266.] For although it is agreed that Christ our Savior merited neither grace, nor knowledge, nor the blessedness of his soul, nor divinity, yet it is the settled opinion of theologians that he merited for himself the glory of his body and certain other things of the same kind. Thus Peter Lombard certainly holds in the third book of the *Sentences*, distinction 18; St. Thomas Aquinas, *Summa*, Third Part, question 19, article 3; Cajetan, Vasquez, Hayus, and—to avoid naming each individually—Bellarmin, book V, *On Christ the Mediator*, chapter 9. Calvin therefore rightly deserves to be charged with impudence and falsehood for having written in book II of the *Institutes of the Christian Religion*, chapter 17, section 6:

> To inquire whether Christ merited anything for himself, as Lombard and the Schoolmen do, is a curiosity no less foolish than their definition is rash, when they assert this and the matters that follow.

To show that these things are false neither belongs to our present purpose nor accords with brevity in a preface. Yet, although these matters stand thus, Alan should not immediately be condemned as rash; for he wrote at a time when the opinion he preferred appeared tolerable. Peter Lombard, Alan’s contemporary, begins the very distinction in the third book in which he refutes the opinion followed by Alan with these words: “Nor must the merit of Christ be passed over; concerning which some are accustomed to say that he merited not for himself, but only for his members.” Yet Lombard brands none of those theologians, from whom he professes to dissent, with any mark of censorious severity.

Let us now proceed to the second of the two passages of Alan mentioned above. John Launoy, citing it in the book entitled *On the Sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick*, [Note: [Col. 0619] P. 353.] says that it was written by some Alan the Porretan, I know not whom. It occurs in Rule 113, where our Alan speaks thus concerning extreme unction: “There are those who say of this sacrament that it cannot be repeated, just as baptism cannot; but because it is a sacrament of repentance, and repentance can be repeated, it is probable that this sacrament can be repeated.”

Here also someone may find it surprising that Alan concedes that extreme unction may indeed be repeated, but embraces that view only as probable, not as certain. But whoever knows that in Alan’s age the matter was not wholly settled, but doubtful and disputed, will cease to wonder; Peter Lombard indicates this in the fourth book of the *Sentences*, distinction 23. Launoy judges that Geoffrey of Vendôme and Ivo of Chartres held the view that extreme unction could not be administered a second time to one and the same sick person, not even on account of different illnesses. I shall not now inquire whether their words ought to be taken more favorably than Launoy and Juenin have taken them.

Geoffrey, indeed, in his letter to Ivo of Chartres—letter 19 of book II of Ivo’s letters—says: “To pass over other matters, they err, as it seems to us, not a little in this: that they think the anointing of the sick ought to be repeated, although it is called a sacrament by the holy catholic and apostolic see, and although no sacrament ought to be repeated.” St. Ivo himself, replying to Geoffrey, [Note: [Col. 0619] Epistle 20, vol. XXI, *Bibliotheca Maxima Patrum*.] says: “I do not think the anointing of the sick should be repeated, because, as you yourself have maintained, according to the institution of the Apostolic See it is a kind of sacrament. But whoever repeats the sacraments of Christ and of the Church inflicts an injury upon the sacraments themselves. For the anointing of the sick is a sacrament of public penance, and Augustine testifies that it is not to be repeated, just as baptism is not; Ambrose testifies likewise.”

Others held the same view as St. Ivo, and are refuted by Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, in his letters, book V, letter 7. But on this subject one should certainly read the excellent work, filled with every kind of learning, which the most wise pontiff Benedict XIV published, *On the Diocesan Synod*. From it I shall transcribe here several matters relevant to my purpose:

> “As the eleventh century was declining and the twelfth beginning, some were imbued with the opinion that it was unlawful ever afterward to anoint with the same holy oil a believer who had once been anointed; and, if Ciacconius and Ughelli related the truth, the same opinion persisted, at least among some, even in the fifteenth century … Others thought that extreme unction could be administered again to the same person, provided only that three complete years had passed since the day on which he had first been anointed. The author of *The Ancient Monastic Discipline*, preface, chapter 128, reports that the monks of Hirsau adopted this false persuasion … Finally, others, according to Peter the Chanter, *Summa*, chapter 132, and Durandus, book I of the *Rationale of the Divine Offices*, chapter 8, no. 25, judged that extreme unction might not be repeated within the space of the same year, even if someone should again fall into a dangerous illness.”

[Note: [Col. 0619] Book VIII, chapter 8, no. 3, p. 355.]

But all doubt in this matter was long ago removed, first by the Council of Florence [Note: [Col. 0619] In the decree issued to the Armenians.] and then by Trent, whose decree occurs in session XIV, chapter III: “If the sick recover after receiving this anointing, they may again be aided by the help of this sacrament when they fall into another similar danger of life.”

It remains only to add a few words concerning the manuscript which I used in publishing this little work of Alan. It is a parchment manuscript, preserved at Bologna in our library of St. Savior; and it was through the supreme kindness of the most eminent pontiff Benedict XIV that it could be sent to me. It contains in all ten little works, [Note: [Col. 0619] They are titled in the manuscript as follows:

I. “Little book published by Brother Thomas of the Order of Preachers against the invectives of Master William of Saint-Amour directed against certain religious.” The name “Brother Thomas,” after what had previously been written was erased, was added by the scribe.

II. “Sermon of Blessed Augustine, bishop, on the praises of this psalm, *Out of the Depths*.”

III. “Sermon of Blessed Augustine on the Trinity and the Incarnation of the Lord.”

IV. “Work of Master Alexander, *On Fate*.”

V. “Treatise *On Miracles*, from the *Summa* of Master Alexander.”

[Col. 0621C]

VI. “Here begins the prologue upon a certain *Summa*, compiled by Brother Bonaventure of the Order of Friars Minor, on the truth of theology.” The *Summa* follows the prologue.

VII. “Treatise on being and essence.” The author’s name is lacking.

VIII. “Here begins the prologue to the book called *The Astonishment of Christ*, or *Lament concerning the Ministers of the Church*.” The *Lament* itself follows the prologue.

IX. “Rules of Alan on Sacred Theology.”

X. “Here begins a brief Compendium upon the Psalter.” The author’s name is lacking.], the ninth of which is Alan’s work; I believe it was copied in the twelfth century, certainly not long after that time.

# RULES OF ALAN ON SACRED THEOLOGY

[Note: [Col. 0621C] This little work bears this title in our manuscript, as I said above.]

[Col. 0621]

[Col. 0621A] 444 Every science rests upon its own rules as upon proper foundations. To say nothing of grammar, [Note: [Col. 0621C] The manuscript has *gramatica*. It would be superfluous to note other errors of this kind which occur throughout it.] which wholly depends upon human pleasure and will, and of its rules, which exist solely by human convention [Note: [Col. 0621D] Or opinion: for the manuscript has *pone* with a superscribed abbreviation mark.]; the other sciences have their proper rules upon which they rest and by which they are enclosed, as it were, within certain fixed boundaries. Thus dialectic has the rules it calls “maxims”; rhetoric, commonplaces; ethics, general propositions; physics, aphorisms; arithmetic, *porisms*, [Note: [Col. 0621D] Euclid calls *porismata* (πορίσματα) what Latin geometers usually call corollaries; for *porizesthai* (πορίζεσθαι) means to infer something from things that have been demonstrated.] that is, subtle rules which in some manner come to the inquirer as a reward for their subtle understanding; hence they are called *porisms*, as though prizes, for *porisma* in Greek means “prize” in Latin.

Musicians also have axioms, rules of the musical art. They are called axioms because they investigate commensurations, that is, consonances. For *axia* [Note: [Col. 0621D] The manuscript wrongly has *anxi* here, and *anxiomata* a little above. But one must read *axiomata* and *axia*, or ἀξία, although ἀξία has rather the meaning of value or worth than of weight.] in Greek means “weight” in Latin. Theorems, moreover, are the rules of geometers, called “theorems,” that is, contemplations; for *theoria* [Note: [Col. 0622C] The manuscript incorrectly has *Theorin*.] in Greek is “contemplation” in Latin, because through them geometry contemplates the truth of matters belonging to it. Astronomy likewise has its maxims, which it calls “excellences” [Note: [Col. 0622C] Du Cange does not mention this meaning of the word *excellentia* in his glossary.] because of their dignity and the subtlety of their understanding.

But the supercelestial science, that is, theology, is not deprived of its own rules. It has rules more worthy than the rest, surpassing the others by their obscurity and subtlety. And whereas the whole necessity of the rules of the other sciences is unstable, because it rests solely upon custom in accordance with the accustomed course of nature, the necessity of theological maxims is absolute and incontrovertible, [Col. 0621C] [Col. 0622A] because they establish matters which cannot be changed either in actuality or by nature.

Hence, because of their immutable necessity and their glorious subtlety, philosophers call them paradoxes—as though “glorious right propositions”; [Note: [Col. 0622C] *Paradoxon* (παράδοξον) means what is *para doxan* (παρὰ δόξαν), that is, beyond human opinion and wonderful. Thus *paradoxos* has no meaning connected with “right.”] because of their obscurity, enigmas; because of the inward splendor of their intelligibility, emblems, since they are understood by a purer sharpness of mind; enthymemes, as though hidden within the mind, from *en* (ἐν), meaning “within,” and *time*, or *timos*, meaning “mind”; [Note: [Col. 0622C] Thus it is written in the manuscript; but it should read: “from *en* (ἐν), meaning ‘within,’ and *thymos* (θυμός), meaning ‘mind.’”] and, because of their authority, hebdomads, that is, dignities. [Note: [Col. 0622C] The word *hebdomas*, or ἑβδομάς, certainly does not mean “dignity,” still less does *hebdam*, a word which Greek does not possess at all. But what Aristotle calls ἀξιώματα, or axioms, are called “dignities” by the ancient interpreters of Aristotle.] For *hebdam* in Greek means “dignity” in Latin. Hence Boethius entitled a book *On Hebdomads*, [Note: [Col. 0622D] Boethius’s book *On Hebdomads* also bears the title: “Whether Everything That Is Is Good.” At the beginning of this little book Boethius proposes certain axioms, which he calls *hebdomads*, because, as I suspect, they are precisely seven.] as though concerning the most subtle propositions of theologians.

The higher the understanding contained in these propositions, the more skilled a hearer they require. Therefore they should not be proposed to the unlearned and beginners, who are devoted solely to sense-perception, but to those who, guided by a purer mind, ascend to ineffable things and with a purer eye behold the secrets of philosophy. These propositions are hidden in the fuller bosom of theology and speak only with the wise. Therefore, since we are to treat of theological maxims, let us begin our discourse from the source and, as it were, the bosom of all maxims—that is, from the most general maxim.

A common conception of the mind is a proposition [Note: [Col. 0622D] Read *enuntiatio*, “proposition.”] which every intellect approves when it hears it. [Note: [Col. 0622D] This definition is drawn from Boethius’s little book *On Hebdomads*.] It embraces by its generality all maxims, whatever their discipline. It is elegantly called “common of mind,” that is, of many minds; for in order that it may be a maxim, it must come, through nature or art, to the knowledge of many, so that, if it is added to prove something else, it needs no proof from another proposition. Hence it is called indemonstrable, self-evident, and a maxim. Thus it is rightly added: “which every intelligent person approves when heard.”

Some theological maxims come to the knowledge of many, as this one: “There is one principle of things”; others to the knowledge of few, that is, of the wise, as this: “Everything simple has its being and that which it is as one.” We must therefore treat of those which come to the knowledge of few.

## RULE I. The Monad is that by which every thing is one.

445 God is called not only one, but also the Monad, that is, unity; and this for many reasons. He is called one, or unity, by reason of simplicity or singularity. For every plurality is excluded from God. Now every plurality is threefold: plurality of parts, found in bodily things, which are constituted out of parts; plurality of properties, found at least in corporeal things, for many properties are compounded in them by concretion, as in spirits; and plurality of effects, found in properties, for every property, although it has no structure of parts or concretion of natures, nevertheless has a plurality of effects. Thus whiteness makes something white, makes it colored, makes it qualified; and every such diversity is excluded from the heavenly Monad.

For God is not diverse by reason of parts, because he is incorporeal; nor by reason of properties, as Augustine says, [Note: [Col. 0623D] Read Augustine, Sermon 341, chapter 6, no. 8, vol. V, p. 1317.] because in him there is no number and no plurality; nor by various effects, because he is not a formal cause. Therefore he is truly one—indeed, unity. Hence Boethius, speaking of God in *On the Trinity*, says: “Truly, then, one is that in which there is no number or plurality.” [Note: [Col. 0624D] Chapter 3.]

He is also called one, or unity, by reason of immutability. For, as is found in the gloss on the book of Kings, where it says, “There was one man in Ramathaim-zophim,” and so forth, immutability is predicated of God under the term “one.” He is called one also by exclusion, so that the meaning is: God is one, that is, not many. He is called one also by similarity, because he has a manifold resemblance to unity. Unity descends from no one; every plurality flows from unity. Unity begets unity from itself and brings forth equality from itself. So God is from no one, while everything is from him; so from himself he begets another himself, that is, the Son; from himself he brings forth one equal to himself, that is, the Holy Spirit. From the foregoing you may therefore draw another rule.

## RULE II. In the supercelestial there is unity; in the celestial, otherness; in the subcelestial, plurality.

The supercelestial is God, in whom there is supreme unity. The celestial is the angel, in whom otherness first exists, because he was first created by God and first, after God, made mutable. Yet he is not said to have as much variety as the subcelestial has. Hence, because otherness is the first plurality, plurality is not said to exist in him, but otherness alone. In the subcelestial, however, as in these corporeal things, full plurality is said to exist, because it is subject to manifold variety.

Therefore God is truly one, or unity, by reason of simplicity, immutability, exclusion, and similarity. Thus the Monad alone exists, that is, God alone truly exists—namely, as being simply and immutably; but other things do not truly exist, because they never remain in the same state.

The conclusion of the first rule follows: every thing is one by the Monad. For nothing is one by any kind of unity unless it is one from the supreme Monad. There is the unity of singularity, according to which every thing is called numerically one. [Col. 0624B] Hence Boethius: “Whatever is, is because it is numerically one; and whatever is one in this unity has from him that it is one.” There is a unity of union, according to which several men are said to be one, not by unity but by union; and this too is from God. Hence the authority on John testifies: “All things were made through him,” etc. (John 1). Every concord is from God.

The unity of distinction or discernment likewise derives its origin from him. For whatever is discrete or distinct is from God. The unity of integrity also, which consists in the composition of parts, by which a human being is called one—that is, made whole from soul and body—is from God. Hence the authority: “Every joining together is from God.” The unity of unification also, by which several persons, coming together under the same rule of life and placed beneath the yoke of the same law, are called one people, is from God. The unity of agreement, by which it is said, “They had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4), is from God.

## RULE III. The Monad begets the monad, and reflects its own ardor upon itself.

This rule arises from the preceding one. For it was said that God is called the Monad because he begets God from himself and also produces the Holy Spirit from himself, just as unity begets unity from itself. Therefore the Monad begets the monad, that is, the Father begets the Son. For it was necessary that, if the Monad begot, it should beget a monad; since nothing can be begotten from what is simple by division, [Col. 0624D] as happens in natural generation. It was therefore necessary either that nothing should be begotten from the simple or that the simple should be begotten from the simple. Hence Augustine says that the Father poured his whole substance into the Son, because the Son is of the same substance as the Father not by division but by the fullness of nature.

And because the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, it follows: “and reflects its own ardor upon itself.” The Holy Spirit is called the ardor, love, kiss, and bond of the Father and Son, because the Father spiritually joins with the Son in breathing forth the Holy Spirit. And because their love for us is signified in the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which are given by the Father and Son—because the production of the Holy Spirit by Father and Son is the certain signification of the love of Father and Son, that is, of their unity; for unless they agreed in one nature, they would not breathe forth by one spiration—the Holy Spirit is called the ardor or love of Father and Son.

This ardor therefore proceeds from the Monad, that is, from the Father, in such a way that it does not leave him, because it is of the same essence as he; or the Monad reflects its own ardor, that is, the Holy Spirit, upon another within itself, namely the Son. But it proceeds from the Father in such a manner [Note: [Col. 0625D] The manuscript has *quia*, “because,” instead of *ita*, “thus.”] that it proceeds from the Son by the Father’s authority. [Note: [Col. 0625D] Because the Father is the source of the Son, Alan therefore says that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son by the Father’s authority. You will find the term “authority” taken in the same manner in Rules 53 and 54.]

## RULE IV. In the Father is unity; in the Son, equality; in the Holy Spirit, the bond of unity and equality.

[Note: [Col. 0625D] This rule is drawn from Augustine, book I, *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 5.]

446 This rule follows from the third and is, as it were, an explanation of it. The Father is called the Monad for the reasons stated: namely, he himself is from no one, while everything is from him; the Son also is from him by generation, and the Holy Spirit by procession. From himself, moreover, he begets the monad, that is, a thing of the same nature and simple.

Unity is said to be especially in the Father, equality in the Son. I do not say “otherness,” lest diversity of nature be understood there, but rather “equality.” For equality denotes both plurality of persons and unity of nature; nothing is equal to itself, nor is anything equal to another that is unlike it in nature. Equality is especially attributed to the Son for three reasons, although it also belongs to the Holy Spirit: first, equality appears in the Son; moreover, the Holy Spirit’s equality with the Father comes to him from the Son; and equality or likeness is especially found in a thing which proceeds from another through generation. Why the bond of unity and equality is said to be in the Holy Spirit is clear from what has gone before.

## RULE V. The Monad alone is alpha and omega, without alpha and omega.

This maxim arises from the first, where God was said to be the Monad by reason of simplicity, and every thing to be from that Monad insofar as it is numerically one. Thus the Monad alone is alpha and omega, the beginning and end of all things. “All things were made through him” (John 1), as Scripture declares; and so he is the beginning of all. All things likewise tend toward the one, that is, toward the highest end. For irrational creatures—even brute animals, and indeed insensate things, such as plants and trees, and even inanimate things, such as stones—naturally tend toward one and, as far as they can, resist cutting and division. Even a stone, from which one might least expect it, resists division by the natural joining of its parts.

It follows: “without alpha and omega,” since the same Monad lacks end and beginning; for, being simple in every way, it excludes every composition. A thing is called composite in four ways: by the joining of parts, as bodily things are; by reason of properties, as spiritual things are, because spiritual things have a manifold concretion of properties; by an aptitude for composing, as every property is, which, though not composed of parts, is nevertheless apt to be joined to a subject; or by an aptitude for being composed, as primordial matter was called composite by philosophers because it was apt to have something composed from it.

Every such composition is excluded from God. For he is not compacted of parts, like a body; nor composite by reason of properties, like a spirit; nor by an aptitude for composing, like some property; nor by an aptitude for being composed, like primordial matter. God is form without material substance and substance without a formal predicate. [Note: [Col. 0625D] Read Rule 13.] Therefore, because he is simple in every way, he lacks beginning and end. Where there is no composition, either actual or natural, and where no origin or beginning can exist, it is inappropriate to understand an end.

## RULE VI. Every thing bounded by alpha and omega is good either from alpha, or from alpha and omega.

[Col. 0626C] This follows from the saying, “The Monad alone is alpha and omega.” For if all things are from God as from a principle, then from alpha—that is, from that very good principle—they are good by possessing the good principle. But note that by “everything bounded by alpha and omega” is meant every created thing, which is enclosed by two limits, namely beginning and end, whether actually or naturally. For everything begotten naturally tends toward destruction. Thus even angelic nature is naturally dissoluble [Note: [Col. 0625D] That is, it can be reduced to nothing by God.]—of which Plato says: [Note: [Col. 0625D] In the *Timaeus*, p. 41, vol. III, Plato introduces the maker of the universe as saying: “Gods of gods, whose maker and father of works I am, things brought into being through me are indissoluble, so far as I will … and, since you have been begotten, you are neither immortal nor altogether indissoluble; nevertheless, you certainly shall not be dissolved.” Cicero translated these words thus: “Give heed, you who have sprung from the seed of the gods, whose parent and maker I am; the works which I have made are indissoluble, so far as I shall will … therefore, because you have arisen, you cannot indeed be immortal and indissoluble; nevertheless, you shall by no means be dissolved.”]

> Gods of gods, whose father and maker I am: by nature you are dissoluble; but, by my will, indissoluble.

Hence Augustine says in his work on Genesis: [Note: [Col. 0626D] Read *The Literal Interpretation of Genesis, Unfinished*, chapter 12, no. 36, vol. III, part I, p. 106.] “Every creature has morning and evening,” that is, a beginning and an end, at least by nature.

Thus every created thing is either good from alpha, that is, naturally a participant in goodness, and has this from its maker; or good from alpha and omega, as rational creatures are, which tend toward blessedness, the end of all things. Therefore only the rational creature is good from the end, since it not only naturally tends toward God, but also worships him as Father by the conduct of its life, recalls him by the understanding of its mind, and seeks him with the whole effort of charity, that he may be given to it as its reward.

## RULE VII. God is an intelligible sphere, whose center is everywhere and circumference nowhere.

[Note: [Col. 0627D] The scribe writes *spaera* everywhere.]

447 This rule is proved by the rule which said that the Monad alone is alpha and omega. For from the fact that God lacks beginning and end, he is called a sphere; for it is proper to spherical form to lack beginning and end. But he is not a bodily sphere; rather, an intelligible one. When we call God a sphere, we must not be led into imaginings, so as to imagine that he is a sphere resembling bodily objects; but, guided by understanding, we should understand God to be a sphere in this respect: that he is eternal.

Hence in Martianus [Note: [Col. 0627D] Martianus Capella, book I, *On the Marriage of Philology and Mercury*, p. 3, has this: “Jupiter had taken from Eternity, his more honorable daughter, the diadem,” etc.] eternity is said to have a diadem, because it is signified to lack beginning and end. Therefore this lack of beginning and end is called a diadem, as though *duo demens*, that is, “lacking two things,” namely beginning and end.

It follows: “whose center is everywhere and circumference nowhere.” O great difference between a bodily and an intelligible sphere! In a bodily sphere, the center, because of its smallness, is scarcely perceived to be anywhere, while the circumference is understood to occupy many places. In the intelligible sphere, however, the center is everywhere and the circumference nowhere. The creature is called the center, because just as time, compared with eternity, is considered a moment, so the creature, compared with the immensity of God, is a point or center. God’s immensity is called circumference, because, in disposing all things, it in some manner surrounds all things and contains all things beneath its immensity.

There is also this further difference between a bodily and an intelligible sphere: the center of a bodily sphere is immovable and its circumference movable; in the intelligible sphere it is the reverse, because God, remaining stable, gives all things motion.

## RULE VIII. God is whatever is; he is all being that is.

This rule is supported by the one which says, “The Monad is,” and so forth. Since God is simple, there is nothing in him besides that which he himself is, as Boethius says in *On the Trinity*. [Col. 0627D] For in him there is neither diversity of parts nor plurality of properties. Therefore, by whatever terms God is shown to be something, one and the same thing is predicated. For the same one thing is posited by these terms when it is said: God is God, mighty, patient, merciful. For it is the same thing for God to be God, mighty, and merciful. Hence Boethius says in *On the Trinity*: “For God, to be is the same as to be great.”

The meaning, therefore, is: God is whatever is; he is all being that is. That is, God is that of which, whatever term is predicated, the same thing is predicated by all the other terms concerning him. But this must especially be understood of the terms of three categories: substance, quality, and quantity. Therefore whatever terms of the first, second, or third category are spoken of God predicate the divine *ousia* (οὐσία, “essence”) of him: as when it is said, God is God, substance, spirit, devout, merciful, mighty, great, immense. Hence some have handed down the following rule:

## RULE IX. Whatever is in God is God.

That is, whatever term in natural things predicates inherence, predicates essence when said of God. But such universality, when it is said, “Whatever is in God is God,” or “Whatever is,” and so forth, does not refer to a plurality of things signified, but of signifying terms and effects. For the effects of one and the same cause are diverse when signified by diverse names, as when it is said: God is mighty, devout, wise. Thus there is universality in speaking and in effecting, but singularity in being.

## RULE X. Every predication made of the Creator is coupled and conjoined.

448 This rule follows from the preceding one. For if one and the same thing is predicated of God by the terms mentioned above, the predication is coupled and conjoined, because, when some term is predicated of him, nothing is left outside that predication. For when I say, “God is good,” I say as much as if I said: “God is God, good, mighty, devout.” But nothing is predicated of a creature in a coupled manner, but separately. When it is said, “Peter is just,” although something is predicated, many things which belong to Peter remain outside this predication and are predicated of him by other terms, as when I say, “Peter is devout, merciful.”

Hence Boethius says in *On the Trinity*: [Note: [Col. 0628D] Chapter 7.]

> In other things it is indeed separately; but in God it is distinctly and conjointly in this manner. For when we say “substance is man” or “God,” it is said as if that of which it is predicated were substance: “substance-man” or “substance-God.” Yet there is a difference, because man is not wholly that which man is, and therefore is not substance; for what he is, he owes to other things which are not man. But God is wholly that which he is, God; for he is nothing other than what he is.

## RULE XI. Everything simple has its being and that which it is as one.

This rule follows from the saying, “God is he for whom whatever is,” and so forth. Its meaning is therefore this: if anyone says simply, “is,” of that which truly is simple—as “God is”—and says that God is something, as “God is great” or “mighty,” no one should understand that the second proposition predicates something different from the first. Thus, if “is” is said of the Father, Son, or Holy Spirit, it does not predicate anything other than when it is said, “The Father is powerful,” “The Son is powerful,” “The Holy Spirit is powerful”; it predicates precisely the same thing. There must be no understanding in any respect that what is, and that by which it is powerful, are different, because for the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, to be and to be powerful are altogether the same.

## RULE XII. No simple thing can be a subject.

This follows from the preceding rule. For since in the simple there is no diversity and no plurality, in it there is nothing accidental or substantial; therefore it is subject to no property. For the same reason, nothing is predicated of the simple, since to be predicated is nothing other than to inhere. In a theological proposition [Note: [Col. 0629D] Here he calls “theological proposition” one which is stated concerning God.] the question is not what inheres in what, but what something is. For when it is said, “God is good,” it is not shown what belongs to what by inherence, [Note: [Col. 0629D] Namely, by inherence.] but rather what God is by essence. Hence no theological proposition of “being-in” is contingent, but is of pure being or necessity. Whether I say “God is” or “God is just,” the proposition is one of pure being. Hence Boethius, wishing to indicate that the simple cannot be a subject, says: “For it cannot be a subject.” [Note: [Col. 0629D] *On the Trinity*, chapter 3.]

## RULE XIII. The simple alone is form without a material subject and substance without a formal predicate.

Since form is truly said to be that which informs another and is informed by none, what is more truly form than God, who informs all things and is informed by none? For he participates in nothing in order to be. Yet he is not a form of the kind which inheres in a subject; rather, he is without every subject—that is, abstract. Hence it follows: “without a material subject,” and “substance,” not because he underlies a property, but because all things subsist through him. Hence it further follows: “without a formal predicate,” because no formal predicate is predicated of him.

## RULE XIV. All being is from form.

Since God is called form because he informs all things and grants being to all, it is rightly said that all being is from form.

## RULE XV. That which is being has no being.

That is, of God, who is the being of all things, since all things exist through him, there is no being, because he participates in nothing in order to be. From this follows:

## RULE XVI. Form alone is unformed, because form has no form.

[Col. 0629D]

For the divine form is informed by nothing in order that it may be, since it is form in the highest degree.

## RULE XVII. Every name given from form, when spoken of form, falls away from the form.

449. Since every name, according to its first institution, is given from a property or form—hence Boethius says, “Of things consisting of matter and form, the human mind alone arose which, as it pleased, imposed names on things”—when a name is transferred to signify the divine form, it falls away from the form from which it was given, and thus in some manner becomes formless. For a name is used pronominally when it signifies the divine *usia* [essence]; it signifies bare substance. And when it appears to signify its own form or quality, it does not in fact signify that, but the divine form—for example, when it is said, “God [is] just,” or “good.”

## RULE XVIII. All affirmations said of God are uncompounded; negations, however, are true.

An affirmation is called composite, or compounded, when it signifies the composition which it appears to signify. Thus, when I say, “Peter is just,” this affirmation appears to signify the composition of justice with Peter, and indeed does signify it. But an affirmation is called uncompounded, or uncomposite, when it does not signify the composition which it appears to signify. Thus, when it is said, “God [is] just,” no composition of justice with God is signified there: justice is not compounded with, or inherent in, him. Rather, being justice is signified rather than being just.

But negations said of God are both true and proper, by which is removed from God what does not belong to him by inherence. Hence Dionysius [Note: [Col. 0630D] Read the letter attributed to Dionysius the Areopagite, addressed to Titus the bishop.]—considering what is said of God by way of cause, attending rather to the sense from which the words arise than to the sense which the words produce, and considering rather what is said from what than what is said of what—says: “God is just, pious, strong.” Again, considering rather what does not belong to God by property than what is said of God by way of cause, he says: “God [Col. 0630C] is not pious, strong, merciful,” removing rather the warrant for speaking than the truth of being.

## RULE XIX. Everything simple is through one thing and is said to be through another.

This follows from the rule in which it was said: “Every name given from form,” etc. There it was said that no name properly belongs to God. Thus everything simple—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit alike—is through one thing, because it is its own proper essence; and is said to be through another, because it is called “being” from the effect which it has in creatures. For whatever exists has existence from God, as from supreme being; and thus, because God causes all things to be, he is called “being.” Yet he is his own essence.

Likewise, God is just through one thing and is said to be just through another: he is just through his own proper justice; but he is called just from the effect of justice which he has [Col. 0630D] in us. For he is called just because he makes just; but he himself is just because he is supreme justice.

## RULE XX. Everything simple properly is, and is improperly said to be.

It is clear that this follows from the preceding rule. For the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit alike properly are: they are unchangeably. Hence Hilary says [Note: [Col. 0630D] Book I, *On the Trinity*, no. 5, vol. II, p. 4.]: “Being is not an accident in God, but a property of the substantial genus.” Yet God himself is improperly said to be; for every name said of God is said improperly [Col. 0631A]. Thus there is propriety in being, but impropriety in speaking.

## RULE XXI. Every name fitting God fits him either causally, by likeness, adjectivally, or negatively.

Likewise, this follows from the preceding rule. Since no name properly belongs to God, any name said of him must be said in one of these ways. For even in natural things every name transferred from its proper signification is transferred in one of the aforesaid ways.

Accordingly, some names fit God by way of cause, such as “just,” “pious,” and “strong”; some by likeness, such as “Father,” “Son,” “splendour,” and “image”; some by reason of an accompanying circumstance, such as “to be angry” and “to repent.” Anger is attributed to God [Col. 0631B] by reason of the accompanying circumstance—namely punishment; for punishment is customarily associated with anger. Likewise repentance is attributed to God by reason of an accompanying circumstance, namely a change in work; for a change in work is customarily associated with repentance. Thus God is said to repent because he changes his work; to be angry because he punishes.

Hence Claudius Claudianus [Note: [Col. 0631D] Claudianus Mamertus, at the beginning of his book *On the State of the Soul*, writes similar things; for Alan frequently cites the Fathers’ opinions, not their words.] says in the book *On the Soul*: “God is said to repent, not through an affection of passion, but through the effect that follows.” Negatively, as when God is said to withdraw grace or to harden someone. To withdraw grace is nothing other than not to continue it; to harden is not to bestow grace. Hence an authority says [Note: [Col. 0631D] Read Augustine, Letter 194 to Sixtus, ch. 3, no. 4, vol. II, p. 719.] that God hardened Pharaoh’s heart not by imparting wickedness, but by not bestowing grace.

Those names [Col. 0631C] which are said of God by way of cause are said of God according to substance; the rest, for the most part [Note: [Col. 0631D] It seems one should read *ut plurimum*, “for the most part.”], are said of God relatively.

## RULE XXII. Every theological predication shows God to be either “what” or “relative to what.”

450. It is likewise clear that this follows from the foregoing. For all terms of the three natural categories—substance, quality, and quantity—when said of God predicate the divine *usia* of him, and show that God is “what.” A term from the remaining categories, however, shows him to be relative to something.

This rule agrees with that set forth by Augustine [Note: [Col. 0631D] Book V, *On the Trinity*, ch. 8, no. 9, vol. VIII, p. 837.] in this form: “Every term said of God is said either according to substance or relatively.” Thus the ten natural categories are reduced [Col. 0631D] to two theological categories: the category of “what” and the category of “relative to what.”

## RULE XXIII. Every term said of God according to substance is said separately of the three persons, in the singular number; and collectively of the three, in the singular number.

Two things must be understood in the phrase “according to [Col. 0632A] substance”: the property of signifying. For two things concur in order that a name be said according to substance: it must signify substance or a circumstance of substance, and it must have a substantial mode of signifying—that is, it must signify substantively.

By substance we mean the divine *usia*; by a circumstance of substance, a relation pertaining to the *usia*. There are relations pertaining to the hypostases [Note: [Col. 0631D] Namely, the relations called relations of origin.], such as paternity, filiation, and procession. There are relations pertaining to the *usia*, signified by the terms “principle,” “Lord,” “maker,” “creator,” and “author.” Therefore any term which signifies substance or a circumstance of substance, and does so substantively, is said separately of the three persons in the singular number, and so forth.

For example [Note: [Col. 0631D] The manuscript has: “for example, or for the sake of example, this name,” [Col. 0632D] etc.], the name “God” [Col. 0632B] signifies substance and does so substantively. Therefore it can be said separately of the three and in the singular number: “The Father is God; the Son is God; the Holy Spirit is God.” It may also be said collectively and in the singular number: “The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are God.” Likewise, the name “principle” signifies a relation pertaining to substance and is predicated of the three persons in the manner stated above.

We add “substantively” because names signifying substance or a circumstance of substance, if taken adjectivally—such as “powerful” and “just”—are said collectively of the three persons in the plural number [Note: [Col. 0632D] Hence, in the *Quicunque* Creed, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are called both one eternal [being] and three coeternal persons. That is, the word “eternal” has the force of a substantive name in the first instance and of an adjective in the second.]: “The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are just; they are powerful.”

## RULE XXIV. No substantive name which pertains to the essence either in sound and signification, or in sound alone, is said collectively of the three persons in the plural number, but only in the singular.

[Col. 0632C]

For example, the names “God,” “Creator,” and “principle” are said collectively of the three in the singular number. This rule is sufficiently demonstrated by the preceding one, which is broad enough to extend even to personal names.

Therefore one must not grant that the Father and the Son are “principles” of the Holy Spirit, but rather “principle”; nor “breathers” of the Holy Spirit, but rather “breathing” the Holy Spirit. For although Hilary says [Note: [Col. 0632D] Book II, *On the Trinity*, no. 29, vol. II, p. 43] that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son as authors, a substantive [Col. 0632D] is there used for an adjective [Note: [Col. 0632D] St Thomas explains Hilary’s passage in the same way: *Summa Theologiae*, I, q. 36, art. 4, ad 7.], so that the sense is: “as authors,” that is, “as breathing.” Yet an impropriety must not be drawn into a consequence.

## RULE XXV. Every adjective pertaining to the essence, when retained adjectivally, is said collectively of the three persons and in the plural number.

451. Thus: “The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are [Col. 0633A] just,” or “powerful.” Adjectival names derive from the subject, or from the substantives to which they are joined, whether they are singular or plural in number or have some other co-signification. For in themselves they have a variable signification or co-signification.

Hence when it is said, “Punishments are just,” or “The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are just,” the adjective, which is plural in number, has this from the subject or substantives on which it depends; it therefore derives the signification of plurality from it or them. Likewise, when it is said, “The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are,” the verb derives the signification of plural number from the supposita. For a verb is not judged singular or plural from its principal signification, but from its co-signification. [Col. 0633B] Number and person are co-accidents of the verb. Accordingly, from the singularity or plurality of the suppositum—which the verb co-signifies—the verb is judged to be singular or plural.

Yet adjectives are said collectively of the three persons in the singular number when they are substantivized, that is, taken substantively with the article understood: “The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are the Almighty.” This can be expressed better in French: *li tut pussant* [Note: [Col. 0633D] Thus it is written in the manuscript, for *li*, that is, *le tout-puissant* (“the Almighty”). It should be observed that the French formerly said *li* for the article *le* now in use. Thus in this very work, Rule L, Alan has *li Per* for *le Père*, “the Father”; and in Villehardouin, book 3, p. 53, we read: “Ainsi fut li chatiaus de Galathas pris li baron, et li dux de Venise” (“Thus the castle of Galata was taken by the barons and the doge of Venice”). From this the grammarian Dumarsais derives the origin of the barbarous little word *ly*, introduced into the schools by Peter Lombard; vol. I of the *Encyclopédie*, p. 731.].

## RULE XXVI. Every transfer in divine matters is of the name, not of the thing.

A threefold transfer can occur in natural things. Sometimes there is a transfer of both name and thing, when both the name and the thing are transferred from that whose property they are to that from which they are, or according to which they are. Thus [Col. 0633C] when it is said, “A line is long,” both the name “long” and the thing signified by this name, namely length, are transferred from that whose property it is—that is, from the thing having length—to that according to which it is, namely the line, according to which both length and the name “long” belong to the thing having length.

Sometimes there is a transfer of the thing but not of the name, as when I say, “The crop is joyful”: joy is attributed to the crop, but not every name signifying joy, such as “rejoicing” or “exulting.” Sometimes there is a transfer of the name but not of the thing, as when it is said, “The monk is white”: the name “white” is transferred so as to fit the monk, but not the thing of the name. For when the monk is called white, this does not mean that he is affected by whiteness, but that he wears a white habit.

[Col. 0633D] In divine matters, however, there is a transfer of the name but not of the thing. For when it is said, “God is just,” the name “just” is transferred from its proper signification so as to fit God, but the thing of the name is not attributed to God. Rather, divine justice itself is attributed to God—not another justice, from which the name “just” was given. For one thing is predicated when “God [is] just” is said, and another is co-predicated: divine justice is predicated, while the effect of justice in us is co-predicated.

[Col. 0634A] Hence, when it is said, “God is just and strong,” identity of predicate but diversity of co-predicate is understood. The copulative conjunction therefore has a place there because it joins the different effects co-predicated in these propositions: namely, the effect of justice and the effect of strength. For sometimes a copulative conjunction joins significata, and sometimes co-significata: significata, as when it is said, “Peter is pious and merciful”; co-significata, as when it is said, “God is pious and merciful.” Likewise, a disjunctive conjunction sometimes separates significata, as when it is said, “An animal is healthy or sick”; but sometimes co-significata, as when it is said, “That is white, or white [feminine].”

Yet one should not grant, “*Deus est justum et pium*” (“God is just and pious,” with *justum* and *pium* in the neuter); for there [Col. 0634B] predicates rather than co-predicates would seem to be joined, and since there is a single predicate, the copula is unsuitable. But it is asked what is joined to what when it is said, “God is compassionate and merciful,” since “merciful” pertains to nature and “compassionate” to effect. One may say that a repetition of the conjunction is understood, so that the sense is: “God is merciful, and he is compassionate.” But perhaps the capacity to effect, denoted by “merciful,” joins the effect of acting denoted by “compassionate.”

## RULE XXVII. Every distinctive noun or pronoun joined to a personal name, in the masculine or feminine, pertains to person; but in the neuter, to essence.

452. Thus: *Pater est alius a Filio* (“the Father is other [masculine] than the Son”); *persona Patris est alia a persona Filii* (“the person of the Father [Col. 0634C] is other [feminine] than the person of the Son”); but not *aliud* (“another thing” [neuter]). The Father is not he who is the Son, but he is that which the Son is.

Nor is it surprising that distinctive nouns or pronouns in the masculine or feminine pertain to person, and in the neuter to essence, since in natural things nouns in the masculine or feminine pertain to a thing of a gender, while neuter nouns pertain to the genus of the thing. Distinctive adjectives in the masculine and feminine are so by reason of gender; for masculine or feminine gender is distinctive. Therefore the adjective itself, because by its discriminating force it pertains to a thing of a gender, requires a subject which determines the thing of that gender: “a white horse,” “a white woman.”

But an adjective in the neuter gender is confused [Note: [Col. 0634D] Read “is confused,” or add some verb.].
