For the neuter [Col. 0634D] is not called a gender by positive designation but by negation. Thus an adjective in the neuter, because it is indeterminate, pertains to the genus of the thing, not to a thing of a gender. Hence it is customary to say that in an adjective of neuter [Note: [Col. 0634D] Read “neuter gender.”] gender the subject “thing” is understood; therefore it is also commonly taken substantively, as when it is said, “The white [thing] runs.”

Likewise, by *quis*, in masculine gender, one usually asks about a person, as when one says, “Who runs?” By *quae*, likewise, in feminine; by *quid*, in neuter, about [Col. 0635A] essence. Similarly, in divine matters, by reason of distinction distinctive words in the masculine and feminine pertain to person; but in the neuter, by reason of indeterminacy, to essence.

## RULE XXVIII. No partitive noun or pronoun is suitably joined to an essential name.

For it is less fitting to say “some God,” “a certain God,” or “this God,” because a partitive expression divides among things denoted which are actually or naturally many. Hence it is fitting to say, “some phoenix”: although there are not actually many, there can naturally be many. But we can understand gods to be many neither actually nor naturally. Although there are many persons, of which the name “God” is appellative, a partitive distinction has no place concerning this name [Col. 0635B], because, just as it divides among appellative names, so it divides among the natures denoted by appellatives.

For one could not truly say, “Peter is a different man from Paul,” unless he were a man through a different humanity from Paul. The name “one,” however, although it is sometimes taken partitively, is admitted because it is sometimes taken exclusively, so that one may say “one God,” that is, “not many.” And if anywhere a universal or particular sign is found joined to an essential name, that universality or division should be understood as referring to the plurality of persons, not of essence. Thus Boethius says in *On the Trinity* [Note: [Col. 0635D] Ch. 4.], “God differs from God in no respect”; the sense is: No thing which is God differs, in that in which it is God, from a thing which is God.

## RULE XXIX. Whenever an exclusive expression is joined to an essential name, the name makes rather for the genus of the thing than for a thing of the genus; there is no suppositum for which it stands, but an indeterminate statement [Note: [Col. 0635D] The manuscript has *sermone* instead of *sermo*.] is made concerning something.

[Col. 0635C]

Thus, when it is said, “one God,” “God alone,” or “only God.” For just as in natural things, when the exclusive “one” is joined to an appellative name, there is no suppositum for which it stands; rather, the name is directed to the genus of the thing, not to a thing of the genus. Thus, when one says, “Only a man,” or “a man alone, is in here,” the term does not stand for Peter or Paul, but for man indeterminately. So when it is said, “one God,” “God alone,” or “only God,” the term does not stand for the Father, Son, or Holy Spirit, but for a thing of this nature indeterminately.

[Col. 0635D] Therefore we do not grant: “One God begot one God,” or “God alone,” or “only God,” [begot one God]; nor “One God alone begets,” or “is begotten,” because the term stands for no one [Note: [Col. 0635D] Read “for no one [masculine],” or “for no person [feminine].”].

## RULE XXX. Every essential name is either quasi-mathematical or quasi-concrete.

Among natural philosophers, mathematical or principal names are those which signify a property [Note: [Col. 0635D] I think one should read “property,” not “impropriety.”] mathematically—that is, abstractly—without any regard to a subject, such as whiteness [Col. 0636A] and blackness. Concrete or derived names are those which signify properties concretely, that is, properties inhering in subjects, such as white and black.

In divine matters, quasi-mathematical names are those which signify deity without regard to person, such as deity, divinity, nature, *usia*, essence, and substance. Quasi-concrete names are those which signify nature as it exists concretely, such as Lord, just, and merciful.

## RULE XXXI. Every mathematical name is said of God less improperly than a concrete one.

453. For mathematical names tend more toward simplicity; and the simpler a thing is, the more fittingly it pertains to God. For God, as was said above, is simple in every way.

## RULE XXXII. Every name said of God is either essential, coessential, personal, copersonal, or partly personal and partly essential.

[Note: [Col. 0635D] The manuscript has: “either partly personal, or partly [Col. 0636D] essential.”]

[Col. 0636B]

Essential names are all those which stand for the essence and name [Note: [Col. 0636D] It seems one should read “name” (*appellant*).] it. They are either quasi-mathematical, or predicate the essence—that is, they are principal names—such as “Deity” and “Divinity”; or they name a person, such as the name “God.” For, as was said above, the name “God” predicates Deity and stands for a person. Yet sometimes it stands for deity, as in: “God is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.” Nor is this surprising, since Deity itself is person [Note: [Col. 0636D] Namely, the divine essence is identified with each person.].

For in natural things, where the thing of a nature differs from the nature of the thing, a name which properly stands for the thing of the nature sometimes improperly stands [Col. 0636C] for the nature of the thing. For example, the name “man” properly stands for a man, as in “Man runs”; but improperly for the species, as in “Man is a species.”

Coessential names are those which signify or predicate circumstances of substance, that is, relations pertaining to substance, and name persons: “principle,” “Lord,” “creator,” and “author.” Of these names some signify eternal relations, some temporal relations. “Principle” and “Lord” signify eternal relations, for God was Lord or principle from eternity. “Creator,” “author,” and “maker” signify temporal relations, for God began in time to be creator or author.

These names are sometimes used substantively, with the article understood: “The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are the principle,” or “the Lord.” In that case *usia* is understood to be predicated and relation co-predicated. Sometimes they are taken adjectivally, without an understood article, as when it is said, “The Father is lord and principle of all creatures”; then relation is understood to be predicated and *usia* co-predicated.

Personal names are those which stand for and predicate personal properties, such as paternity, filiation, and procession; or which predicate [Col. 0637A] personal properties and name persons, such as Father, Son, Holy Spirit, begotten, begetting, and proceeding.

Copersonal names are those which predicate distinctions pertaining to personal properties, such as distinct, differing, and other.

Names partly personal and partly essential are those which partly denote person and partly essence, such as “person” and “Trinity.” *Persona* is said, as it were, from “one through itself” (*per se una*). Therefore, in that unity understood there is an understanding of essence; while in the phrase “through itself” there is an understanding of personal distinction. Hence the Father is called a person, as it were “one through himself,” that is, distinct in such a way that he is one. The same is true of the Son, and likewise of the Holy Spirit. Hence they are called persons, as it were “one through themselves,” that is, distinct in such a way that each is one.

[Col. 0637B] Likewise, Trinity is, as it were, “three-one” [Note: [Col. 0637D] Isidore, Book VII, *Origins*, ch. 4: “It is called Trinity … as it were, Tri-unity.”], so that, in the fact that three are understood, knowledge of personal distinction is obtained; and in the fact that [they are] one, knowledge of essence.

## RULE XXXIII. No name denoting privation, liability, or violence applies to God.

Since, as has been said, names are said of God by way of cause or likeness, a name of privation cannot be said of God either by likeness or by cause. For privations have no causes, and God is not a destructive but a positive cause.

Names of liability do not apply to God because of the danger that he might be understood to be bound by some liability or necessity. Hence we do not say, “God [Note: [Col. 0637D] I have supplied the word “God”; it is absent from the manuscript.] must do this,” or “God is bound to do this.”

[Col. 0637C] Likewise, no name implying violence is said of God. For God is not said to be unwilling of anything, lest violence be understood there. God did not will many things, but he was unwilling of none. Nor should we grant that God *nolit* (“is unwilling of”) evils, but rather that he *non velit* (“does not will”) them.

## RULE XXXIV. Every theological expression must be catholic, general, customary, not discordant with understanding, and consonant with the thing of which we speak.

454. It must be catholic, because what is contrary to the catholic faith must not be admitted, such as saying that there are three essences or three gods. It must also be customary, because the Church avoids profane novelties of expression; general, so that it may be accepted by intelligent people—for example, that Christ is something insofar as he is human. It must also be intelligible; [Col. 0637D] for a catholic ought to avoid convoluted expressions. And it must be consonant with the thing of which we speak; for the theologian ought to have language suited to the things of which he speaks.

## RULE XXXV. Substantive names are said of God less improperly than adjectives.

For adjectives tend more toward concretion and composition than substantives. Likewise, positive names [Col. 0638A] are said of God less improperly than comparative or superlative names, because God’s substance does not admit more or less. Likewise, names of incorporeal things, or names pertaining to incorporeal things, are said less improperly. God is called Spirit, but not body; mercy, piety, merciful, pious; but not whiteness or blackness; not having lines or a line; not having a surface or a surface.

Although these might be said of God by way of cause, they are excluded in order to remove the suspicion arising from idolaters [Note: [Col. 0637D] Manuscript: “idolaters.”], who imagined the natures of things to be gods, and from anthropomorphite [Note: [Col. 0637D] It seems one should read “anthropomorphite.”] heretics, who believed God to be marked out by bodily features.

## RULE XXXVI. Whenever God is referred to by a demonstrative pronoun, it falls short of demonstration.

[Col. 0638B]

For every demonstration is either to sense or to understanding. But God cannot be comprehended either by sense, because he is incorporeal, or by understanding, because he lacks form. Indeed, we understand rather what he is not than what he is. Since understanding a true name arises from perception of form, by which a thing is understood to be what, what kind, or how great it is, and since in God there is no form [Note: [Col. 0637D] Manuscript: “there is not no form.”], he cannot properly be grasped by understanding. Rather, by the removal of another form alone, he is as it were understood to be separate from other things; and by separating, is understood.

Hence Boethius says in *On the Two Natures and One Person of Jesus Christ*: “God and nature cannot be grasped by a whole and perfect understanding, but are nevertheless grasped in some manner through the privation of other [Col. 0638C] things” [Note: [Col. 0637D] Boethius has “things” (*rerum*).].

Thus, when God is introduced as speaking of himself, proper demonstration has no place there, since it is made neither to the eye nor to the understanding of a true name. Rather, if one may speak thus, the demonstration is made to faith. In Donatus, demonstration is made to understanding; in the case of God, however, demonstration is made to faith. Therefore, when God is introduced as speaking of himself, a twofold prosopopoeia is understood: one called *anthropopathos* [Note: [Col. 0638D] The manuscript has *antopospatos*, but one should read *anthropopathos*: ἀνθρωποπαθεῖν means “to be affected in the manner of human beings.”], that is, human passibility; the other called *idiotheos* [Note: [Col. 0638D] The manuscript has *ydeotheos*, but one should read *idiotheos*: the word is formed from ἴδιος, “proper,” or ἰδιότης, “property,” and Θεός, “God.”], that is, divine property.

For when God is read to have said, “I am who I am” (Exod. 3), an angel [Col. 0638D] was speaking in God’s person, as though reciting what is read in the divine mind. The impropriety, then, lies in this: someone else, namely the angel, speaks as though the speech were about someone else, namely God. Thus this is *anthropopathos*, because the words of a creature—the angel—are attributed to the Creator. But *idiotheos* is discerned in this: what belongs to the Creator is attributed to the creature, because the words uttered by the angel are understood to be true of God alone.

Sometimes the Father is understood to be speaking in the property of the first person, as in: “My spirit shall not remain in man forever,” etc. Sometimes the Son, as in Genesis, where the Lord speaks to Abraham, saying: “At this time I shall return to you, and Sarah shall have a son” (Gen. 17). Sometimes the Holy Spirit, as in Malachi, where it is said: “Behold, I send my angel before your face” (Mal. 3); there the Holy Spirit speaks to the Father concerning the Son. Sometimes the whole Trinity, as in: “I am who I am” (Exod. 3); or perhaps *usia* itself is there introduced as speaking. The three persons [are speaking], however, where it is said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” etc. (Gen. 1).

Demonstrative names fit God more [Col. 0639B] improperly than relative pronouns. Possessive pronouns are sometimes said of God with the greatest impropriety, when they denote identity of essence; for possessives ought to denote a difference between possessor and possessed. The pronoun “my” is used most improperly where it is said: “Vengeance after I withdrew from my praetor” [materially uncertain wording]. Likewise, when it is said, “My soul has hated your sacrifices” (Isa. 1), “my” is used most improperly. For there is no difference between God’s soul and God: soul is the will itself, which is God himself.

Sometimes it denotes a lesser impropriety when it suggests the day of generation; but it denotes propriety when it is said: “This is my beloved Son,” etc. [Col. 0639C] (Matt. 3; 17). It is also taken less improperly when it denotes the author of creation, as in: “All things are mine,” by the authority of creation and governance. Sometimes possessives denote the grace of re-creation, as in the Gospel: “My children are with me in bed” [Note: [Col. 0639D] Luke 11:7: “My children are with me in bed.”]; there the saints are called God’s children because of the grace of adoption.

## RULE XXXVII. Verbs are said of God with greater impropriety than nouns or pronouns.

455. For they tend more toward composition. As Aristotle testifies [Note: [Col. 0639D] Book I, *On Interpretation*, ch. 3.], every verb signifies composition, which cannot be understood without composite things; for a verb is a sign of that which is said of another.

## RULE XXXVIII. No name in divine matters is a sign of that which is said of another, or of that which is another; rather, it is a sign of that which is selfsame.

[Col. 0639D]

Thus, when it is said, “God is,” the verb “is” is not there a sign of something which is said of another or which is other than the divine essence itself. Rather, it signifies that which is itself, namely that which is placed as subject. For essence is God and God is essence. Hence, whereas for Aristotle truth and falsehood consist in composition and division, for the theologian they consist in identity and diversity.

## RULE XXXIX. No verb is said of God less improperly than the verb “is.”

[Col. 0640A]

For this verb denotes substance and, among natural philosophers, is said to lack temporal motion. Unlike other verbs which signify successive actions, it does not have motion in its signification; rather, it signifies essence.

## RULE XL. Every verb in the present tense is said of God less improperly than one in the past or future.

For presentness belongs to God, not pastness or futurity. The same rule applies to participles in divine matters as to verbs, because participles are used in as many ways as verbs. Likewise, certain adverbs are said of God less improperly than nouns, because [Col. 0640B] they denote various circumstances or relations which are said of God according to *usia*.

## RULE XLI. Every local adverb said of God predicates divine immensity, or a certain relation of Creator to creatures, according to which the Creator is said to be in creatures as an efficient cause in its effects.

For when it is said, “God is everywhere,” or “somewhere,” this is not said as though God were understood to be circumscribed by place. Rather, God’s immensity is predicated, so that all things are understood to be contained beneath his immensity rather than he himself to be in a place.

## RULE XLII. By local circumlocutions, either divine immensity, relation, or union is predicated of God.

For example, when it is said, “God is in every place,” or “in some place,” divine immensity is predicated. But [Col. 0640C] when it is said, “God is in the saints,” the relation of divine grace is signified; for he is said to be in the saints by grace. When he is said to be in the assumed man, union is predicated: that is, human nature is united to Christ.

## RULE XLIII. Temporal adverbs said of God predicate eternity.

456. Whether I say of God, “He was yesterday,” “He is today,” or “He will be tomorrow,” eternity is predicated. Hence when we say, “God was before whatever was,” neither time nor temporal priority is denoted, but rather eternity. Hence Boethius says in *On the Trinity* [Note: [Col. 0639D] Ch. 9.]: “Our ‘now,’ as though running, produces time and sempiternity; but the divine [Col. 0640D] ‘now,’ remaining, neither moving itself nor changing, produces eternity.”

## RULE XLIV. Adverbs of likeness said of God signify either truth of essence, likeness, impropriety, or accompaniment.

For example, when it is said, “We saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father” (John 1), there *as* denotes the truth of the essence—that is, truly Only-Begotten; similarity, as in: “As the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son to have life in himself” (John 5); impropriety, as is read in Daniel [Note: [Col. 0639D] These words which Alan cites from Daniel are not found there. But in Daniel, chapter 7, [Col. 0640D] verse 9, it is written: “The Ancient of Days sat down.” In Psalm 77, verse 65: “The Lord awoke as one sleeping, like a mighty man overcome with wine.”], where it is said: [Col. 0641A] “The Most Ancient of Days will sit judging, as though overcome with wine”; addition, when it is said: “The Father is called the principle of the Son, just as he is called the principle of the Holy Spirit,” so that the sense is: the Father is called the principle of the Son, and is called the principle of the Holy Spirit. Likewise, prepositions have various meanings in divine matters.

## RULE XLV. The preposition *in*, in divine matters, sometimes denotes identity of essence and plurality of persons; sometimes quasi-diversity; sometimes eternal predication; sometimes identity; sometimes an efficient cause; sometimes a quasi-formal cause.

For example, when it is said, “The Son is in the Father,” plurality of persons is denoted together with identity of essence. For if, when it is said, “Atalanta resounds in [Col. 0641B] Parthenopaeus,” an explicit likeness of nature is denoted, it is not absurd that, when “the Son is in the Father” is said, identity of nature should be denoted along with plurality of persons. Quasi-diversity is denoted when it is said, “Deity is in the Father.” I do not say diversity, but quasi-diversity: there is no diversity between deity and the Father, because deity is the Father and the Father is deity; but a kind of transition is denoted when the preposition is there used through apposition.

Eternal predication is denoted when it is said: “What was made, in him was life” (John 1), as though everything that was to come into being lived in him by an eternal disposition. An efficient cause is denoted when it is said, “In the Son all things were made,” that is, through the Son. A quasi-formal cause is denoted when it is said, “Who, being in the form of God” (Phil. [Col. 0641C] 2). Identity is denoted in the statement that God, before the constitution of the world, was in himself or with himself.

## RULE XLVI. The preposition *according to* (*secundum*), in divine matters, sometimes denotes an order of cause and sometimes an order of understanding.

When it is said, “The Son, insofar as he is God, is a person,” if this denotes an order of cause, the proposition is true, so that the sense is: for the Son to be a person, it is required that he be God. But if it denotes an order of understanding, the expression is false: for person is not understood in the name “God.” But if it is said, “The Son, insofar as he is a person, is God,” so as to denote an order of understanding, the proposition is true, because God is understood in the name “person,” since to be a person is to be God.

## RULE XLVII. The preposition *according to* sometimes denotes a quasi-efficient cause, sometimes a quasi-formal cause, and sometimes a condition of nature.

[Col. 0641D]

457 For example, when it is said, “The Son is equal to the Father according to substance,” the preposition *according to* here denotes a quasi-efficient cause. For substance is, as it were, the efficient cause why the Son is equal to the Father. But when it is said, “The Son is equal to the Father according to equality,” *according to* denotes a quasi-formal cause. For equality is the formal cause why the Son is equal to the Father.

Likewise, in natural philosophy a thing is said to be [Col. 0642A] similar according to quality, so that *according to* denotes an efficient cause; and a thing is also said to be similar according to similarity, so that *according to* denotes a formal cause. It denotes a condition of nature when it is said, “The Son of God, insofar as he is man, forgives sins,” that is, being in human nature. Similarly, other prepositions used of God denote various circumstances; so too do conjunctions.

## RULE XLVIII. Of names said of God, some are said collectively of the three persons in such a way that they are said of none of them individually; others are so said collectively of the three that they are said of each individually; still others are said of one person in such a way that they are not said of the others.

For example, the name “Trinity” is said collectively of the three in such a way that it is said of none individually, because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are the Trinity, [Col. 0642B] but neither the Father, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit is the Trinity. But the name “God” is said collectively of the three in such a way that it is said of each individually, because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are God, and the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are each God. But the name “Father,” the name “Son,” and the name “Holy Spirit” are each said of one person and not of another.

## RULE XLIX. Of theological names [Note: [Col. 0641D] Read: “theological.”], some are appropriated to one person in name and reality; others in name but not in reality.

For example, the name “Father” is appropriated in name and reality, because neither the name “Father” nor its signification belongs to anyone other than the Father. Likewise, “Son” belongs to the Son. But the name “power” [Col. 0642C] is appropriated to the Father in name but not in reality; thus it is an appropriation in speech, not in being. The Father alone is called power, but he alone is not power; indeed, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one power. Likewise, the name “Wisdom” is appropriated to the Son in name but not in reality.

## RULE L. The name “Father,” when said of God, either predicates a person, a personal property, the Father’s relation to the Son, the Father’s relation to creatures according to creation, or the Father’s relation to humanity according to re-creation.

For example, when it is said, “Deity is Father,” a person is here predicated of *usia* [essence], so that the sense is: “Deity is Father,” that is, the one who begets. Accordingly, the name “Father” is used substantively, with the article understood, [Col. 0642D] and is thus explained in French: “Deity is Father,” that is, *li Pere* [“the Father”]. [Note: [Col. 0641D] The manuscript has *li per*. See what we noted a little earlier on Rule 25, p. 191.]

Nor is it surprising that, in divine matters, person is predicated, although in natural matters neither person nor a thing’s property is predicated. In natural matters, something is predicated by inherence when it is shown to inhere in, or belong to, something as a property of the thing. But in divine matters, where nothing inheres except what is added [Note: [Col. 0642D] Humanity was, as it were, added to the Word through the hypostatic union.], it is not shown what inheres in what, or what inheres in whom; rather, it is shown what something [Note: [Col. 0642D] For *quid*, the manuscript has *quidquid* (“whatever”).] is, or how it stands. Thus, when it is said, “Deity is Father,” the question is not what is said of deity or what inheres in it, since nothing is in it; rather, the question is what [Col. 0643A] deity is. Hence, to the question asked concerning deity—what is it?—the fitting reply is: “Father.”

For we cannot say that a relation is there predicated of deity, since deity is neither begetting, nor begotten, nor proceeding [Note: [Col. 0643D] After Alan’s death—namely, in 1215—the Fourth Lateran Council issued this decree against Abbot Joachim: “That reality, namely the divine essence, is neither begetting, nor begotten, nor proceeding; but [Col. 0644D] it is the Father who begets, the Son who is begotten, and the Holy Spirit who proceeds.”], nor are personal relations understood to exist in deity by which deity is distinguished from the Father, Son, or Holy Spirit.

But a personal property is predicated when the reply is made to the question, “Who is the begetting God?”—“The Father”—with the article again understood and the name used substantively. In natural matters, however, a personal property is called the proper state of a person, considered from the concurrence of all the substantial and accidental features of a thing, and is predicated by such terms as [Col. 0643B] “Socrates” and “Plato”; grammarians also commonly call this a proper quality. In divine matters, however, a personal state can be assigned not properly but by likeness: the personal property of the Father is called his singular state, considered from the concurrence of deity, unbegottenness, fatherhood, and spiration. It is not a personal property in the strict sense, but a quasi-personal property; it does not answer the question “what?” or “relative to what?” but “who?”

There are no proper terms in Sacred Scripture by which these personal states are designated, but rather certain circumlocutions: “God the Father,” “God the Son,” “God the Holy Spirit.” These answer a question asked with *who*: “Who is the Father?”—“God the Father.” “Who is the Son?”—“God the Son.” “Who is the Holy Spirit?”—[Col. 0643C] “God is the Holy Spirit.” Relations should not be given in answer to a question asked with *who*, but to a question asked with *how*: if it is asked, “How does the Father stand?”, the fitting reply is: “The Father is Father of the Son.” Likewise, “The Son is Son of the Father.” Therefore the name “Father,” when retained adjectivally, predicates a relation of the Father. At times “Father” predicates a relation to creatures according to creation, as when it is said, “I believe in God the Father almighty.” At times it predicates a relation to humanity according to re-creation, as when it is said, “Our Father, who art in heaven.”

## RULE LI. The name “principle” sometimes predicates fatherhood, sometimes spiration, and sometimes the Creator’s relation to creatures.

[Col. 0643D]

458 Thus, when it is said, “The Father is the principle of the Son,” it predicates fatherhood—that is, the Father’s relation to the Son. When it is said, “The Father is the principle of the Holy Spirit,” it predicates spiration, which is common to the Father and the Son, according to which the Father and Son breathe forth the Holy Spirit. Hence the name “principle” seems to be used equivocally when the Father is called the principle of the Son and the principle of the Holy Spirit: here fatherhood is predicated, there spiration [Note: [Col. 0644D] It seems that *spiratio* (“spiration”) should be read; p. 191.].

Hence it does not seem that one may truly say in a single utterance: “The Father [Col. 0644A] is the principle of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” Rather: “The Father is the principle of the Son. The Father is the principle of the Holy Spirit,” according to that signification in which spiration is predicated by the name “Father.” On this basis it can also be affirmed that the Father is the principle of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Yet one may say that only origin—which in some manner belongs to fatherhood and spiration—is predicated by the term “principle,” so that the sense is: “The Father is the principle of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” that is, their origin. On this basis there will be no equivocation in the name “principle” when the Father is called the principle of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

On this basis, the Father is the principle both of the Son and of the Holy Spirit; but he is not the principle of both the Son and the Holy Spirit. Just as, if Socrates is white [Col. 0644B] at two instants, one must grant that Socrates is white at each of the two instants by some whiteness, yet not that he is white by some one whiteness at both instants. Likewise, the Father and the Son are called one principle of the Holy Spirit because they breathe forth the Holy Spirit by one spiration.

But when it is said, “The Father and the Son are one principle of the Holy Spirit,” each of these terms, “one principle,” is taken adjectivally in signification, though the name “principle” is taken substantively in grammatical form. For “one” denotes the unity of spiration, while “principle” denotes spiration. Yet it cannot truly be said, “They are one breather-forth,” for *one* pertains to person, [Col. 0644C] while the Father and Son are not one person breathing forth. Nor can they be called “one breathing forth,” for *one* pertains to essence, and the Father and Son are not one essence that breathes forth; for essence does not breathe forth. But they may be called “two breathing forth,” with “two” used substantively and “breathing forth” adjectivally—that is, two who breathe forth—but not “two breathers-forth.” For “breathers-forth” would be used substantively and would thus denote a plurality of spirations.

Hilary nevertheless says [Note: [Col. 0644D] See what we noted on Rule 24.] that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son as authors; but “authors” is used in place of “those who breathe forth,” that is, a substantive for an adjective. Figurative expressions must be tolerated, not extended. But although one grants that the Father and Son are one principle, one must not grant that they are the same principle. For “the same” establishes an intrinsic relation; and thus, if the Father were one principle of the Holy Spirit, the Son would be the same principle, and identity would seem to exist in the Father and Son not only in spiration but also in person.

Furthermore, it must not be granted that the Father and Son are *some* principle of the Holy Spirit; for *some* is partitive, just as one does not admit: “The Father and Son are some God.” Nor is a relation admitted with an improperly used term, as when one says “is the same,” “is not,” “that is,” or “is some.” Hence some do not permit [Col. 0645A] the expression, on the side of the subject: “The principle of the Holy Spirit is the Father and the Son,” because a term taken so improperly cannot be used as subject, though it may be improperly used as predicate. Others say that it cannot be used as subject because it is retained adjectivally; an adjective, retained adjectivally, cannot supposit. But this seems to be no reason. For though it is adjectival in signification, it is substantive in grammatical form, like the names “Lord” and “author.”

Others admit: “The principle of the Holy Spirit is the Father and the Son,” saying that the statement there concerns spiration, which is the Father and the Son. But if so, spiration is the principle of the Holy Spirit, and thus breathes forth the Holy Spirit. Yet one must by no means admit: “The principle of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0645B] is the Father and the Son,” or “is both the Father and the Son,” because either there would be supposition for essence, and the expression would be false, or it would be for several persons, and then “principle” would be taken collectively. But there is no reason why this name should be taken for several persons.

Therefore we grant: “One principle of the Holy Spirit is the Father”; “one principle of the Holy Spirit is the Son”—but not “the same,” lest identity of person be understood; nor “another,” lest plurality of spiration be denoted. Hence one must grant: “The principle of the Holy Spirit is the Father, and the Son is not the same.” “The principle of the Holy Spirit is the Father, and is not the Son.” Yet not: “The principle of the Holy Spirit is not the Son.” For that would seem to remove from the Son not only person but also [Col. 0645C] spiration.

Therefore, because the Holy Spirit is breathed forth by the Father and the Son through one spiration, the statement in the hymn may be tolerated [Note: [Col. 0645D] In all the handwritten and very ancient breviaries in the possession of our abbot and visitor, Dom John Chrysostom Trombellius—indeed, they are quite numerous—it is written as the Church now reads it, namely: *Unus Patri cum Filio* (“One with the Father and the Son”); for he examined them all at my request.]: “One with the Father and the Son,” that is, proceeding from the Father and Son by one spiration, so that “one” denotes unity of spiration. If, however, *Patris* [“of the Father”] were found, the expression would be clear, with the sense: “one Spirit of the Father and the Son.” Yet some emend it by saying: “One with the Father,” that is, of one essence with the Father and the Son. But “principle” predicates the Creator’s relations to creatures when it is said, “God is Father of creatures.”

## RULE LII. Of names appropriated to persons in name and reality, some are said positively and others negatively.

459 For example, “Father” is said of God positively, but “unbegotten” negatively. For the Father is not called unbegotten through a positive assertion of a property, but through negation of origin, so that the sense is: “The Father is unbegotten,” that is, he is not from anyone. Likewise with “ungenerated.” These names belong especially to the Father, so that not nativity but [Col. 0646A] origin is removed. For negations are negative of more things than positive assertions are positive of. Hence the Holy Spirit is not called unbegotten or ungenerated, because he has being through origin; yet he may be called “not begotten,” or said not to be begotten.

Some, however, say that unbegottenness is a property. But if it is the property by which the Father is distinguished from the Son and Holy Spirit, the relation seems to have a correlative. Therefore it has either filiation or another correlative. If another besides filiation and procession, there will be more personal relations than five [Note: [Col. 0645D] The Prepositive and Gregory of Rimini excluded real relations and notions from God. Most theologians, however, say that there are four relations of origin in God and five notions: namely, unbegottenness, fatherhood, filiation, active spiration, and passive spiration. Scotus, however, posited six divine notions: these five which I have named, and the Son’s inspirability.]. But if it has filiation as its correlative, either one relation will have two correlatives, or unbegottenness will be fatherhood. This is impossible because, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0646D] Book V, *On the Trinity*, chapter 6, no. 7, vol. VIII, p. 835.], it is one thing to be Father and another to be unbegotten: a person is not unbegotten insofar as he is Father; for to be Father, and to have origin, is not to be from another [Col. 0646B] [Note: [Col. 0646D] The passage needs emendation.].

Moreover, birthable (*nascibilis*) and unbegotten (*innascibilis*) seem to be opposites more as privation and possession, or as affirmation and negation, than as relatives; and thus *innascibilis* is not said relatively to *nascibilis* or to the Son. But if some property is predicated of the Father by the name “unbegotten,” insofar as he is not from anyone, then by the same reasoning, if a term concerning the Holy Spirit were coined, a property would be predicated—for example, “unbegetter,” because no one proceeds from him or is begotten by him.

It should be known that birthable (*nascibilis*) and unbegotten (*innascibilis*) are not opposed as privation and possession, but as affirmation and negation; for privation has no place in divine matters, because it removes a possession [Col. 0646C] and implies something due. When it is said, “This man is blind,” the sense is: “He does not have sight though he ought to have it.” But *nascibilis* and *innascibilis* are opposed as affirmation and negation, like finite and infinite. For nothing is posited by the term “unbegotten”; rather, something is removed.

## RULE LIII. The circumlocution “Holy Spirit” predicates either a person, a personal property, or a relation in divine matters.

It predicates a person when it is said, “Deity is the Holy Spirit.” But it predicates a personal property when it is given in answer to a question asked with *who*, as when one asks, “Who is the third person in the Trinity?” and the answer is: “The Holy Spirit.” It predicates a relation when it is said, “The Holy Spirit is the Holy Spirit [Col. 0646D] of the Father,” as though one said, “The Father breathes forth the Holy Spirit.” For the circumlocution “Holy Spirit” is not properly said relatively, but was specially devised to express by circumlocution the personal property of the Holy Spirit; and it is taken with greater impropriety to predicate the procession by which the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

Having dealt with [Col. 0647A] names personal and appropriated in name and reality, we must treat those appropriated in name but not in reality. It should therefore be known that, although the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one power, the names “powerful,” “power,” “omnipotence,” and “omnipotent” are appropriated to the Father, not the reality signified by the names. The name “power,” and the other aforesaid names, are appropriated for this reason: lest the Father seem more powerless than the Son, since in natural generation fathers, on account of age, are usually weaker than sons; or because there is nothing of which the Father is not author—the Son by generation, the Holy Spirit by spiration, and every other thing by creation. But so that authority may be suggested to reside in the Father, the name “power” or “omnipotence” is appropriated to him.

## RULE LIV. He alone is truly omnipotent who can do everything that it is a power to be able to do.

[Col. 0647B]

This belongs to God alone. For he alone can do everything that it is a power to be able to do. Hence, although he cannot sin, his omnipotence is not thereby diminished, because the ability to sin is more an impotence than a power: it proceeds from weakness. But could not Adam, before sin, sin? Yet he had no weakness. To this it is said that weakness is understood in two ways: as privation and as negation. When understood as privation, it denotes a defect, and weakness removes a possession; in this way Adam was weak after sin. When understood as negation, [Col. 0647C] no defect is implied, but only the state of weakness is removed; in this way Adam was weak before sin, not because he had a defect or any weakness, but because he did not have firmness.

But God is not weak through any defect—whether because he has some inability or because he has weakness. But must it be granted that he can run or walk? No, because power and bodily exertion are jointly implied, and it is impious to understand this of God. Yet he is not less omnipotent for that reason, because, although he does not perform such actions, they are nevertheless subject to his power, and he brings them about by authority, not by action.

## RULE LV. The Omnipotent can do only what accords with his justice, his power, and his mercy.

[Col. 0647D]

For if something, should it occur, would be contrary to his power, justice, or mercy, the Omnipotent cannot do it, because this would derogate from his omnipotence.

## RULE LVI. God is called omnipotent because he can do not only things that exist or can come to be, but also things that cannot come to be.

For he can do many things that are impossible according to an inferior cause or according to nature, though they are possible according to a superior cause.

## RULE LVII. Whatever is possible according to an inferior cause is possible according to a superior cause; but the converse does not hold.

[Col. 0648A]

Possible according to an inferior cause means that which can happen according to the course of nature—for example, a human being being born from a human being, an ox from an ox. That is also called possible according to nature which, though it does not occur through inferior causes, is nevertheless customary—for example, the creation of a soul. Therefore, the creation of a soul is said to be according to nature because it customarily occurs; custom is called a second nature. Hence, if it were customary for a human being to be raised from the dead, raising a dead person would be called possible according to nature on account of custom, which we call a second nature.

But we call possible according to a superior cause that which the superior cause—that is, [Col. 0648B] God—can do, though it is not in nature that it can occur: for example, Balaam’s ass speaking, a virgin giving birth, and the like. What is possible according to nature is called simply possible; but what is impossible according to an inferior cause is not called simply possible, but possible to God.

## RULE LVIII. Every thing impossible according to an inferior cause, from which there follows an impossibility according to a superior cause, is impossible to God.

460 Impossible according to an inferior cause means that which cannot occur according to the customary course of nature, such as a virgin giving birth. But impossible according to a superior cause is that which the superior cause—that is, [Col. 0648C] God—cannot do: for example, making God not good. For God cannot make himself not good, since that would derogate from the divine majesty. Thus every impossibility according to a superior cause is an impossibility according to an inferior cause, but not conversely.

For a log being a calf is impossible according to the law of nature; yet God could remove the nature of the log from its subject and impress upon it the nature of a calf. If this were done, the log would cease to be a log and would begin to be a calf. Although this is contrary to nature, once it had happened, what previously was naturally a log would now, contrary to nature, be a calf.

But for white, while remaining white, to be black is impossible not only according to an inferior cause but also according to a superior one. For although God could alter matter with respect to substance, so that water became wine, he cannot make it the case that, while it is individually water, it is wine; while it is white, it is black; while it is, it is not. For if something were white while black, God would by his authority make not to be what by his authority he had made to be. Thus he would be at variance with himself, which is impossible. Therefore everything impossible according to an inferior cause from which impossibility according to a superior cause follows is impossible to God.

Likewise, this saying attributed to Jerome may be understood: “Although God can do all things, he cannot make a corrupted woman a virgin”; that is, God cannot [Note: [Col. 0647D] Add: “make.”] make someone at once [Col. 0649A] corrupted and a virgin. But it is asked: since Creator and creature differ more in their natures than white and black—for the former agree in no genus, whereas white and black agree in a subaltern genus—how could God make God, remaining God, to be man, while he could not make white, remaining white, to be black?

The answer is that a thing begins to be something, or to be of some mode, in two ways: either by mere connection, or by the union to it of another thing. For example, something begins to be white through the connection of a substance and a property, which becomes the cause in the subject of the predicate “white.” But God begins to be man because human nature is united to divine nature. Therefore God could make himself, while remaining God, [Col. 0649B] to be man, namely by union with human nature. But he could not do this through mere connection, so as to compose humanity with the divine person and not unite to that person a man—that is, a body and soul.

Likewise, he could make white, while remaining white, to be black: namely, by an ineffable union analogous to that by which he united human nature to divine nature, if he united black to white, so that, just as it is said, “God is man,” one might truly say, “White is black.” But this could not occur through mere connection, or through a union of white and black such that blackness were impressed on white while it remained white, rather than that black should be united to white.

## RULE LIX. Truth in essence does not entail possibility in nature.

The sense is: not everything that is true is possible [Col. 0649C] according to nature, such as those things that occur through a superior cause—for example, Balaam’s ass speaking. Considering this, some do not grant that everything true is possible, denying that, if one thing follows from another, the antecedent being possible implies that the consequent is possible. For example, “God makes Balaam’s ass speak” entails “Balaam’s ass speaks”; yet, even if this antecedent is possible, the consequent is not possible.

For it has been said that from what is possible according to nature another thing possible according to nature follows; but possibility according to an inferior cause does not follow from possibility according to a superior cause. For it has been said that it is possible for God to make Balaam’s ass speak, but not possible for Balaam’s ass to speak, because that would imply a possibility of nature.

Yet some things are so impossible that it is impossible for them to occur even before they occur; and after they have occurred, it remains impossible for them to occur according to nature. Thus, before Balaam’s ass spoke, it was impossible according to nature for it to speak. Of such cases the aforementioned thinkers say that they are impossible before they occur and while they occur.

There are other things which, before they occur, it is impossible for them to occur, but, after they occur, are possible: for example, “a blind man sees” is impossible; but after he sees, it is possible for him to see, for he sees through natural powers. [Col. 0650A] Of such cases they say that they are impossible before they occur, but possible after they have occurred.

But it is better, as others say, that everything true is possible: just as “true” extends to things occurring through a superior cause, so too does “possible.” For there is one species of the possible; nor should it be granted that something is possible unless it is true or can occur according to nature. Hence, “God’s making Balaam’s ass speak” is not granted to be impossible, because it is neither true nor can occur according to nature. But it is nevertheless granted that God can do this, so that the discourse is about the thing, not the proposition. It is also possible for God that Balaam’s ass should speak. Thus it was true and possible that Balaam’s ass spoke, but now it is neither true nor possible.

## RULE LX. The Omnipotent cannot fail now to be able to do what he once could do, nor could he not do what he now can do.

[Col. 0650B]

461 The sense is: whatever God could do, he can do, and conversely. But the objection is made: God could have made the world not to have existed; therefore he can do the same. The inference does not follow, for being able to make it the case that the world had not existed is not to be able to do something. But God could not make it the case that the world had not existed, for this would be contrary to his power. Since the world was made by his authority, if he made it the case that the world had not existed, he would be at variance with himself.

But whatever was subject to his power is subject to it, and conversely. Therefore, when it is said, “Whatever he could do, he can do,” although the expression is absolute, its meaning is not absolute. Rather, this verb requires an infinitive, [Col. 0650C] as do verbs of affection, so that the sense is: “Whatever he could make, he can make,” and “Whatever he could make actually, he can make.” But he cannot make it actually. For he can now make Peter’s soul, but he cannot now create it, since it is true that it exists. Yet he could now make it not to exist; at the same time he could make it exist again; but he could not now make it exist for the first time, since that would be self-contradictory.

## RULE LXI. The works of the Trinity are undivided.

The sense is: whatever the Father works, the Son works, and the Holy Spirit works. This universality is appropriate with respect to works that can be done by God, so that the sense is: every work subject to the Father’s power is subject to the whole Trinity. But if someone objects that the Father can beget whereas the Son cannot, and thus the Father can do something that the Son cannot, the objection has no force.

For the Father’s being able to beget is not the Father’s being able to do something, but rather an ability relative to something. The power of begetting in the Father is for his begetting; in the Son, it is for his being begotten; in the Holy Spirit, it is the same power for his proceeding. Nor should one grant that the power of begetting is in the Son, because power and begetting are jointly implied, and this would make the power in the Son a power to beget. Yet it may be granted that the power of begetting is in the Father and is the same in the Son, for the pronoun refers only to the power without any indication of relation.

## RULE LXII. Nothing can occur against the will of one who can will nothing but good.

[Col. 0651A]

This rule is sufficiently clear because, as the authority says: “Whatever he willed, he did” (Psalm 113). The will of God is described in several ways. Sometimes God’s will means his authority; and then for him to will something is nothing other than for it to exist by his authority. By a kind of metaphor, his operation is called will, because a work is usually a sign of the will of the one working. Therefore, when it is said, “God wills this,” divine *usia* [essence] is predicated and the effect of the essence is co-predicated. Nothing occurs against this authority.

Likewise, what is subject to God’s will is called will, and nothing occurs against this will; for it is impossible that something should be subject to God’s will and [Col. 0651B] not occur. Again, will is called counsel, as in: “He wills all people to be saved” (1 Tim. 2), that is, he counsels [Note: [Col. 0651D] The reader should consult what more recent theologians have written on this celebrated passage in the First Epistle to Timothy.]; and many things occur against this will. For God counsels many things that do not happen.

Will is also called permission, according to which God is said to will evils, that is, to permit them. Hence: “There is no evil in the city that he does not do” (Amos 3), that is, permit. By the same reasoning, nothing occurs against what he does not will in this sense, because it is impossible for something to be subject to God’s will and not occur. Therefore nothing occurs against the will of God which is God; but many things occur apart from his will.

Having dealt with what had to be said concerning God’s power and will, we must speak of Wisdom. Although the three persons have one wisdom, the name “Wisdom” is appropriated to the Son, either because he proceeds from the Father as wisdom from mind, or lest he seem less wise than the Father, since in natural generation a son is less wise than his father.

## RULE LXIII. First substance does not admit of more or less.

462. The first substance is called *usia* [Greek *ousia*, “being/substance”], which is the substance of substances, the form of forms, the cause of causes. Substance admits neither greater nor lesser degree: not in power, because whatever it was able to do, it is able to do; nor in will, because whatever it willed, it wills. For a volitional verb requires an infinitive verb; and therefore the meaning may vary when it is said, “Whatever it willed, it wills.” For if you understand it thus—“Whatever it willed to be, it wills to be”—it is false. But if [Col. 0651D] thus—“Whatever it willed to be, or to have been”—it is true. Yet one must simply grant that whatever it willed, it wills.

Likewise, God’s wisdom or knowledge does not admit more or less. But it should be noted that knowledge is sometimes called the divine *usia*, which can in no way change: it cannot be more knowing at one time than at another. “Knowledge” is also called the things known; and in this respect perhaps God’s knowledge can increase or decrease. But the question is asked whether he can know more things than he knows. That he can seems provable as follows: he can know more things to exist than he knows to exist; for only things which exist are known; therefore [Col. 0652A] he can know more things than he knows.

Conversely, it seems provable that he cannot, because his knowledge is infinite, and infinite things are subject to his knowledge. Again, all possible and all impossible things are in God’s knowledge; and thus all things are subject to his knowledge. Again, if knowledge is properly said to concern things that are, since it properly concerns propositions, if God begins to know one of two contradictorily opposed things, he ceases to know the other; and therefore he cannot know more things than he knows. But, as was said concerning other verbs, this verb “to know” requires an infinitive construction. Therefore, if you understand it thus—“He cannot know more things than he knows”—it is false; but if thus—“He cannot have knowledge of more things than he has knowledge of”—it is true. When, therefore, it is said, “What God knows once, he always knows,” this must be understood as “has been,” “is,” or “will be.” For he knows something to be or to have been, and he will know it to be going to be which he knows to be or to have been. And so it is of whatever he has knowledge, once and always.

## RULE LXIV. Divine providence cannot be deceived.

Just as knowledge cannot increase or decrease, so neither can it be deceived. For if, as Aristotle said [Note: [Col. 0652D] In Book I of the *Posterior Analytics*.], all knowledge is unmixed with falsehood, much more so is God’s wisdom. Thus it is impossible for what God foresaw not to occur—not because God’s providence imposes necessity upon the event and thereby removes the freedom of free choice, but because this cannot be: namely, that he should foresee and it should not occur. This is not because divine Providence is a cause attaining the event, [Col. 0652C] but a concomitant cause, a cause without which it would not occur. Hence follows this rule:

## RULE LXV. What God foresaw must occur by necessity of consequence [Note: [Col. 0652D] The manuscript has *consequendi*, “of following.”], not by necessity of the consequent.

For the thing foreseen need not occur; rather, it is necessary only that what has been foreseen should occur. Thus there is necessity of the consequence, not an incapacity in the thing itself. Just as this whole proposition is necessary: “Socrates is moving, if he is running”; yet it is not necessary that Socrates move or run. Likewise, it is not necessary that God have foreseen what is to be, or have predestined who is to be saved. For “God has predestined,” although stated in the past tense, nevertheless concerns the future, [Col. 0652D] just as it is not necessary that Antichrist will read. From this follows the rule:

## RULE LXVI. From the necessity of a superior cause follows the necessity of an inferior cause; but not conversely.

463. Something is called necessary in relation to a superior cause in two ways: either because the superior cause cannot prevent it, as that God is wise or good; or because it is so by the authority of the superior cause and not by the ministry of the inferior cause—something which the inferior cause cannot prevent—as a virgin’s giving birth. For that a virgin, remaining a virgin, should give birth, [Col. 0653A] occurred by God’s authority in such a way that an inferior cause could neither bring it about effectively nor prevent it. She herself indeed could, through the freedom of free choice, have prevented herself from giving birth; but she could not prevent herself, while remaining a virgin in mind and body, from giving birth. Hence authority says that the prophecy of predestination must be fulfilled in every way; that is, no inferior cause can prevent it.

Likewise, something is called necessary in relation to an inferior cause in two ways: either because inferior causes work toward it, as toward a human being’s being an animal; or because an inferior cause cannot prevent it from being, as the movement of the firmament. Necessity arising from superior causes is called absolute necessity; that arising from inferior [Col. 0653B] causes is called determinate necessity. Philosophers testify that determinate necessity follows from absolute necessity. Thus, if it is necessary for Socrates to move, it is necessary for him to move while he is running; but the converse does not hold.

In Aristotle, a necessity is called determinate when it is not stated simply, but with a qualification—for example, “Socrates moves while he is running.” In relation to a superior cause, the general resurrection of humankind is said to be necessary in the future, because it occurs by God’s authority alone and no inferior cause can prevent it. In accordance with this opinion, some say that Christ’s having spoken truly became necessary after he said to Peter, “Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times” (Luke 22), [Col. 0653C] because he had spoken in such a manner that it could not be avoided. But this seems false, because an inferior cause could have prevented it from being true: Peter could have refrained from denying him.

The following objection is also made: If Christ said it, it will occur; but it is necessary that Christ said it; therefore it is necessary that it occur. But according to the opinion set out above, this is resolved as follows. If one thing follows from another, and the first is necessary by a necessity of nature [Note: [Col. 0653D] Something appears to be missing here, which may be supplied thus: “If one thing follows from another, and the first is necessary by a necessity of nature, the last is necessary by a necessity of nature; but not if something, etc.”], the last is necessary by a necessity of nature. But if one thing follows from another and the first is necessary by a necessity of person, the last is not necessary by a necessity of nature. Christ’s having spoken truly is necessary, as it were, by grace of the term—namely, by reason of his person; and a necessity of nature does not follow from such a necessity of person.

Again, this objection is made: Something [Col. 0653D] is necessary and something else is possible; therefore the latter can be true together with the former. One may say that it was not necessary for Christ to have said or uttered anything. Although this statement appears to concern the past, it nevertheless concerns the future; just as the statement “Plato, who will be white, has read” is not necessary. Therefore neither is it necessary that Socrates spoke truly because he said this; for he could have made no assertion—that is, he could have spoken neither truth nor falsehood.

## RULE LXVII. The necessity of an inferior cause yields to the necessity of a superior cause.

[Col. 0654A]

For a superior cause can derogate from the rule of nature. Hence Hilary [Note: [Col. 0654D] Read *On the Trinity*, Book XII, §6.]: “That the Creator was made a creature is not an account of nature, but an exception of power.” Thus, before the Virgin gave birth, it was necessary that the Virgin should not give birth. The superior cause set aside this necessity when the virgin gave birth.

Likewise, some say that Lazarus’ salvation was necessary after he died, but that after he returned to life it was not necessary; for he could sin and thus die in mortal sin. Similarly, others say that Lazarus’ salvation was not necessary after he died, because that first death was not natural but miraculous, and he had not yet reached the prize, but had [Col. 0654B] been withdrawn, as it were, from the middle of the racecourse, and the worthiness of his merit depended on his future life. We say that Lazarus’ salvation was necessary after he died; nor could he sin after he returned to life, for the tinder of sin had been extinguished in him through death.

Just as the name “power” is appropriated [Note: [Col. 0654D] These matters seem to belong elsewhere.] to the Father, and the name “wisdom” to the Son, so the name “goodness” is appropriated to the Holy Spirit, although the Three have one goodness. Since this name, “Spirit,” seems to suggest swelling and pride, lest anyone here suspect such a thing of the Holy Spirit, the name “goodness” is appropriated to him; or because the Holy Spirit is the gift of the Father and the Son, in whom the manifold use of graces is given to us, through whom everything that is [Col. 0654C] good is good.

## RULE LXVIII. All things, insofar as they are, are good.

This rule is put forward by many and understood by few. Hence Boethius addressed a book to the deacon John concerning the interpretation of this rule [Note: [Col. 0654D] This little work of Boethius is the very work which many entitle *On the Hebdomads*.], carefully showing how all things, insofar as they are, are good: whether substantially or accidentally, and whether they are so in another way [Note: [Col. 0654D] Some word seems to be missing.].

Thus one commonly asks whether something natural is attributed to the subject when it is said, “All things, insofar as they are, are good.” If it is natural, is it substantial or accidental? If substantial, it will be superior to the genus substance, since every substance is good, but not every good is a substance. In like manner it will be superior to [Col. 0654D] every category, and thus all things are reduced to one. Again, if it is substantial, it is either a genus, a species, or a difference. If a genus, as has already been said, it will be superior to the most general genus. If a species, under which category will that be contained which is predicated of all things? But if a difference, of what genus will it be constitutive or divisive?

Again, if goodness belongs to God alone, and if the goodness of each thing, in that it is, is substance, then every thing, in that it is, [Col. 0655A] is God. But if an accident is predicated there, not every thing is good in that which it is, because, as that rule of Boethius [Note: [Col. 0655D] In *On the Hebdomads*.] testifies, to be something is one thing, and to be in that which it is is another. For here an accident, there a substance, is predicated.

The meaning is this: when something is predicated simply of something else, an accident may be predicated, as when I say, “Plato is white.” But when the phrase “in that which it is” is added, the thing predicated is shown to be the substance of the thing of which it is predicated, or of that from which the subject derives its being. Thus, when it is said, “This work is bronze,” what is predicated substantially of bronze is predicated in that which it is. But when it is said, “This work is human,” what is predicated in that which it is is that which is the being of the one from whom this work has its being—namely, human nature.

Therefore [Col. 0655B] we say that nothing accidental or substantial to a creature is predicated when it is said, “All things, insofar as they are, are good.” Rather, the divine *usia* is predicated, not essentially but denominatively, by a certain denominative transference. Thus all things are called good because they are from the highest good, just as, when pointing to a human being one says, “This nature is human,” and when pointing to a human work one says, “This is a human work,” the same thing is predicated in these two propositions, but in a different way in each.

For in the first, this species, human being, is predicated essentially; in the second, denominatively. Thus the sense is: “This work is human,” that is, it has being from a thing of human nature. Likewise, when it is said, “God is good,” [Col. 0655C] divine goodness is predicated of God essentially. But when it is said, “All things, insofar as they are, are good,” the same divine goodness is predicated denominatively. The sense is: “All things, insofar as they are, have being from that whose goodness is supreme.” To state it more expressly: in this proposition, possession of being from a good principle is predicated.

According to this rule, we say that every action, insofar as it is, is from God, but becomes evil through deprivation of its due end. That it is an action, it has from God; but that it is deprived of its due end, it has from the human being. For, as Augustine testifies [Note: [Col. 0655D] Alan perhaps has in view what Augustine writes [Col. 0656D] in *Eighty-Three Questions*, question 21, vol. VI, p. 5.], God causes human beings to do things that are unfitting; but human beings cause the things they do to be unfitting.

Likewise, we say that every power and all [Col. 0655D] knowledge are from God—but not the abuse of power or knowledge. For the magical art, insofar as it exists in itself, is from God, namely as a kind of knowledge; but that someone abuses it is not from God. For someone can learn magic not for enjoyment, but in order to avoid it, and can teach it for the same end. The same applies to the knowledge of heretics. But how can it be good when no one can use it well? For no one can use magical art well. Therefore it does not appear to be from God, or to be good. To this we say that someone can use it well by teaching it and presenting the things done in it, [Col. 0656A] directing everything to a good end. Thus it is universally true that all things are from God, both subjects of properties and properties of subjects.

## RULE LXIX. That whose end is good is itself also good.

464. This rule appears contrary to Boethius’ rule, who says: “That whose end is good is itself also evil.” But there is a twofold end: an end of consummation and an end of consumption. If the end of consummation is good, the thing of which it is the end is also good; for example, God is the consummating end of someone, and that person is also good. But if the consummating end of a thing is good, the thing itself is evil; for example, if the [Col. 0656B] consummating end of sin is good, sin is evil.

Therefore every thing whose final cause was God’s goodness is good. He made all things by that very will; and so God’s goodness is the final cause of every thing, and thus everything is good. For he elicits good even from evil action, because he who is supremely good would never permit evils to exist unless he drew goods from evils.

It is also generally true that the action whose end is good is itself good. For if anyone establishes a good and due end for his action, the action itself will be good. Likewise, if he establishes an evil end, the action too will be evil. Although certain Jews, having zeal for God but not according to knowledge, wish to establish a good end for the killing of Christ—namely, God—[Col. 0656C] they did not in fact establish it. They wished, therefore, to direct their action by zeal for God, but did not direct it, because they lacked knowledge, just as someone wishes to aim an arrow at a stag and strives to do so, but the arrow swerves.

The Jews who crucified Christ likewise seem to have set a good end to their action, namely Christ’s Passion. Yet, although Christ’s Passion was good in itself, most holy, and fruitful for the human race, they did not make it the end of their action for the good of the Passion itself, but in order to inflict evil upon Christ. Thus the same Passion which was a good end for the prophets, who desired Christ’s Passion for its resulting benefit, was an evil end for the Jews because of the depravity and manner of their action. [Col. 0656D]

Likewise, if someone steals in order to help his mother, the end of the theft is evil. For although helping one’s mother is good, helping her wickedly is evil; and it is the evil end of this action. Hence arises this rule:

## RULE LXX. One action cannot have different ends.

465. This appears false. For someone earns money in order to feed a poor person, and directs this act to that end; he also directs the same act to the highest end, namely God. But when one thing is for the sake of another, it counts only once in both respects. [Col. 0657A] For when one thing is called such for the sake of another, the one and the other are not both so called. Hence, when Plato is called rational [Note: [Col. 0657D] Thus it is written in the manuscript.] by reason of his soul, Plato and the soul are not called two rational things. And when a priest is called audible by reason of his voice, they are not called two audible things, but rather one audible thing.

So, although the ends of this action are distinct, they are not different, because one is referred to the other. Thus they are said to be one end rather than several ends. Or we may say: both this and that are ends of the action, but not one end or several ends.

But does one who begins to go to church in order to pray, and then moves his steps in order to see a woman so as to lust after her, establish two ends for his action, a good and an evil one? And what of one who [Col. 0657B] teaches sacred Scripture both for temporal gain and for God? To this we say that one action is the individual action by which he first moves in order to go to church; that action is good and has a good end. Another action is that which is directed [Note: [Col. 0657D] I should prefer to read *dirigitur*, “is directed.”] toward seeing the woman; that is evil and has an evil end. Likewise, the person teaching sacred Scripture makes either God his principal end or temporal profit. If he makes God his principal end, the action is good and the end good, and thus there is one end alone. But if temporal profit, there is one end alone, and it is evil.

## RULE LXXI. Every merit is voluntary either by a will of origin or by the origin of a will.

For every merit, whether good or evil, [Col. 0657C] has either a preceding or a concomitant will. Thus it is voluntary either by the will from which it proceeds or by the will with which it occurs. For example, someone wishes to kill a human being and kills him. The killing itself, which merits eternal punishment, proceeds from a concomitant will; and thus this merit is voluntary by a will of origin—that is, by the original will which [Note: [Col. 0657D] The word *quam*, “which,” is absent from the manuscript.] he had while killing.

But someone who undergoes nocturnal fantasies because, while awake during the day, he thought about some woman, undergoes at night the slippery impulse of the flesh. If, therefore, he sins in this, that sin is voluntary by the origin of a will, because it had its origin from a preceding will. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0657D] In *On True Religion*, ch. 14, §27, vol. I, p. 756. See also *Retractions*, Book I, ch. 13, §5, vol. I, p. 19.]: “Every sin [Col. 0657D] is so voluntary that, if it is not voluntary, it is not sin.” Accordingly, original sin too is voluntary, because it had its origin at least in Adam’s will.

Likewise, if someone directs an arrow at a wild animal intending to feed a sick poor person, and, omitting none of the relevant precautions, kills a man lying in the forest, that act merits [Col. 0658A] eternal life and is voluntary—not because he wished to kill the man, but because he willed the act by which he killed the man. Yet some say that such an act is indifferent, that is, neither good nor evil, because it proceeded not directly but indirectly from the will.

Again, if a saint, while sleeping, resists nocturnal fantasies after having restrained assaults of temptation while tempted during the day, he merits a reward; and this is voluntary because it had its origin in a preceding will.

## RULE LXXII. Every merit depends upon the will.

466. For one merits as much as one wills, the will is reckoned as the deed, and one’s disposition gives one’s work its name. The question, therefore, is whether someone merits as much through will alone as through will [Col. 0658B] and deed together. Some say this is generally true in the class of good things, except for privileged works such as martyrdom and preaching; for they say that martyrdom and preaching add something to merit. Others grant it true in the class of good things without any exception; nor do they say that martyrdom adds anything to merit except incidentally, because it is sometimes an occasion for charity to be kindled. They say the same of preaching.

But in the class of evils they say this is false: for one who wishes to kill someone and does kill him sins more than one who wishes to do so but does not kill him, because the act is evil in kind and thus adds something to merit. Yet by the same reasoning they could say that a good work adds to merit, because an act such as giving alms is good in kind [Col. 0658C] and, when added to will, likewise increases merit.

One may say that this is true in the class of evils because an act cannot accompany the will without there being greater contempt. Since a human being is bound neither to will nor to do evil, if he wills evil he ought at least to stop there. Therefore, when he goes farther, contempt is greater. But it is not so in good things, because a human being is bound both to will and to do good, and ought not to remain short of action if he can carry it into action. Therefore, God is not more pleased with one who wills and does than with one who only wills when he cannot accomplish it. Hence charity is not greater in accomplishing than in willing [Note: [Col. 0657D] The word *si*, “if,” is absent from the manuscript.].

[Note: [Col. 0657D] In the manuscript margin the copyist wrote: “Or because laws are more inclined to acquit than [Col. 0658D] to condemn; and therefore a person is not punished as much for will alone as for will and deed together.”]

## RULE LXXIII. Every sin occurs either by committing what ought not to be done, or by omitting what ought to be done.

[Col. 0658D]

A sin committed by doing is specially called *peccatum* (“sin”); but one committed by omission is called *delictum*, as though “abandonment” (*derelictum*) [Note: [Col. 0658D] Augustine, in *Questions on Leviticus*, question 20, vol. III, part I, p. 496, writes similar things: “The question is asked what difference there is between *peccatum* and *delictum* . . . Perhaps, then, *peccatum* is the commission of evil, whereas *delictum* is the abandonment of good . . . What else does *delictum* sound like but *derelictum*, ‘abandoned’; and what does one who commits a *delictum* abandon except good?”].

But the question is asked how an omission can be voluntary, since it occurs not in doing but in omitting. To this we say [Col. 0659A] that the omission is voluntary because either he wills to omit what he omits, though he ought not to omit it, or he wills not to omit it when he ought to will [Note: [Col. 0659D] That is, when he ought to will to omit it.] to omit it. Sin is called voluntary in two ways: either because it proceeds from the will, or because the will does not restrain it when it ought to restrain it.

## RULE LXXIV. Not doing avoids punishment; doing merits the crown.

For in not doing something, a person does not merit anything, but avoids the punishment which he would incur if he did it. But in doing good he merits a reward. To signify this, authority says: “Withdraw from evil, that you may avoid punishment; and do good, that you may merit the crown.” Therefore, not doing evil is expedient for caution; doing good is expedient for choice.

[Col. 0659B] Does the person who remains in charity and does not commit adultery fulfil this commandment, “You shall not commit adultery” (Matthew 19)? To this we say that, if he is not tempted by the desire for adultery and is not moved toward it, he does indeed act, but does not perform fully. But if he feels the desire and resists it, he not only avoids punishment but merits the crown. But if these circumlocutions—“not to commit adultery,” “not to steal,” “to withdraw from evil”—are taken merely negatively, I say that no one merits by them. But if an affirmation is implied with the negation, so that the sense is, “This person does not lust,” that is, “he resists lust,” then there is merit.

## RULE LXXV. No unformed or deformed action can be formed, nor conversely. Likewise, it cannot be more or less unformed or deformed, nor more or less formed.

[Col. 0659C]

Note that some actions are unformed, some deformed, and some formed. An unformed action is one lacking its proper office or its end. For two things concur in making an action formed: proper office and due end. Its due end is that the action be directed toward God. Proper office, as they say, is the fitting act of each person, and so forth. The proper office of a Christian must be the fitting act of each person according to the institutions of the Christian religion.

Therefore, one who, in a due office, directs an action toward its due end—that is, toward God—forms his action. An unformed action lacks its due office or due end; for example, a Jew who gives alms [Col. 0659D] finally for God’s sake does not give within a due office, because he does not give as the institutions of the Christian religion require.
