A deformed action is one lacking a due end, as when someone gives alms for vain glory or for earthly profit.

Accordingly, we say that a venial sin cannot become mortal, or conversely, although authority seems to assert this when it says: “No sin is so venial that it does not become mortal while it pleases.” [Col. 0660A] But this must be referred to the kind of thing, not to an individual thing of that kind. The sense is: no act belonging to the class of venial sins remains non-mortal if someone delights in it too greatly. Thus, if someone takes excessive delight in an idle word or a joking lie, that idle word or joking lie, which otherwise was venial, becomes mortal through delight and contempt. Yet one and the same act which was formerly venial does not later become mortal.

But suppose that someone does not lie in jest, then subsequently lies with intent to deceive, and persists in the lie: does not the lie which was previously venial become mortal? No: rather, the preceding act is one thing and the subsequent another. Again, someone commits fornication and does not turn from the sin: is he not held more guilty for fornication day by day, and does fornication not thereby become a greater sin? We reply that it does not. The sin of fornication is not increased, but contempt becomes greater. Yet the contempt by which he now despises more is distinct from that by which he formerly despised less.

But the question is asked concerning someone who kills two people with one shot of an arrow: first, one whom he kills unknowingly; second, one whom he kills knowingly. Does the action which was first a lesser sin later begin to be greater? We say no, because there are two actions there, and the first is a lesser sin than the second.

But if the question concerns ignorance in a subdeacon, who is obliged to know things which he does not know, and who later becomes a priest: does it begin in him to be a greater sin than it was? [Col. 0660C] We answer no. Since ignorance removes rather than posits, it is not sin. For he does not sin in what he does not know, but in despising to know. Thus the sin lies in contempt of knowing, not in the fixed state of ignorance. Yet because ignorance proceeds from contempt of knowledge, the name of the consequence is often taken in the sense of the antecedent. Hence contempt of knowledge is sometimes called ignorance, and in this sense ignorance is sin.

But the contempt of knowing in him after he has become a priest is distinct from that which was in him as a subdeacon. Accordingly, we may establish this rule: No privation can be a merit of reward or of punishment. For who of sound mind would say that deafness or blindness is a merit of reward or punishment, when they deprive one of a habit and entail what is due? By analogy, how can ignorance be [Note: [Col. 0659D] The manuscript mistakenly has *ignoraverit* (“he will have been ignorant”) for *ignorantia erit* (“ignorance will be”).] merit when it is a privation? Since we cannot merit through passions [Note: [Col. 0659D] Clearly, in what we suffer involuntarily there is no merit, good or evil.], how can we merit through privations, which lie outside all being? [Note: [Col. 0659D] The copyist placed a question mark twice here, evidently after the words *privatio* (“privation”) and [Col. 0660D] *sunt* (“are”). Yet it cannot be inferred from this that what I said in the preface about the age of our manuscript is false; for our Trombellius proves in his recently published book, entitled *The Art of Knowing the Age of Manuscripts*, etc., ch. 17, p. 100, that such punctuation marks were customarily written even in the eleventh century.]

## RULE LXXVI. Every sin is a punishment, either in the affection of suffering or in the effect that follows.

467. In the affection of suffering, as envy and hatred: these [Col. 0661A] sins affect their subjects with certain passions. In the effect that follows, as those sins which, although they contain no passions in themselves, nevertheless have passions following from them in some manner. Thus murder, although not a punishment in itself, gives rise to blindness of mind and corruption of natural goods, which can in some manner be called a passion. A sin which proceeds from another sin incidentally is also called a punishment, because it follows from that sin as punishment from merit, and is in some manner the effect of the preceding sin.

## RULE LXXVII. Every punishment either preserves a good in one who is good, tests a good, purges an evil, invites to a greater good, hardens in evil, torments by bitterness alone, or stains with sin.

[Col. 0661B]

It preserves a good in one who is good, as the punishment imposed upon Paul so that the greatness of his revelations might not exalt him; of this he himself says, “There was given to me a sting of Satan” [Note: [Col. 0661D] In 2 Corinthians 12:7: “There was given to me a sting of my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me,” etc.].

It tests a good, as Job’s punishment; for through it Job’s patience was tested. It purges evil, as penance, through which a human being is cleansed from sin; such also was Mary’s punishment, when she was struck with leprosy as a correction (Numbers 12). It invites to a greater good, as martyrdom, which is an act of greater charity and of greater reward. It hardens in evil, as the plague inflicted on Pharaoh, through which Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and so forth. It torments by bitterness alone, as the punishment of Gehenna. It stains with sin, as that which is sin by its very property [Note: [Col. 0661D] Perhaps *poenalitate*, “penality,” should be read.].

## RULE LXXVIII. Every movement of concupiscibility toward enticements is a vice arising from sin; every movement of concupiscence amid enticements is a sin arising from vice.

[Col. 0661C]

Concupiscibility is called the proneness by which someone is inclined to sin. Concupiscence is called the very act of desiring. Sometimes a movement proceeds from concupiscibility which is without pleasure and without freedom of choice: for example, when a person sees a woman and, willing or unwilling, is moved. Yet he does not take pleasure in this, and such a movement is not in concupiscence but toward concupiscence—not amid enticements but toward enticements. Such a movement is sin, that is, vice, but not sin in the sense that it makes one a sinner, because it does not merit punishment: for it is not in his power [Note: [Col. 0661D] It appears one should read *penes se* or *penes eum*, “in his power.”] to will or not to will. Thus this movement is a vice arising from sin, because every vicious movement [Col. 0661D] has its origin in the sin of the first parent, or original sin.

Sometimes pleasure follows the initial movement; this pleasure is amid enticements and in concupiscence. Then a person desires and is moved enticingly; and such a movement is a sin proceeding from such a vice.

## RULE LXXIX. Every will of affection contributes to merit; a will of effectuation completes merit.

A will of affection is called either that by which a human being naturally desires good, although he is in mortal [Col. 0662A] sin; or that by which someone, out of a certain weakness, desires evil although he is in charity. Of the first Paul says: “To will is present with me, but I do not find how to accomplish it” (Romans 7). Of the second he says: “I desire what I will” [Note: [Col. 0662D] I do not find these words in Paul. Alan seems, however, to have had in mind Romans 7:16: “But if I do what I do not will,” etc.; accordingly, one should read, “I desire what I do not will.”].

A will of effectuation is that by which someone effectively wills something: either good, of which Paul says, “But I do not find how to accomplish it” (ibid.), because no one has this without the consolation of grace; or evil, as when someone proceeds through pleasure to consent to evil or to the act of evil. Therefore, concerning one who is in mortal sin, although he has a will of affection toward good, it must not be granted that he wills good or wills to be good. Hence the Prophet, speaking in the person of a sinner: “I longed to desire your justifications” (Psalm 118). He does not say, “I desired,” [Col. 0662B] but “I longed to desire.” Likewise, one who is in mortal sin does not will to be good; rather, he wills to will to be good.

Therefore, a will of affection contributes in some manner to merit because from it a will of effectuation proceeds incidentally. But a will of effectuation either contributes to or completes merit.

## RULE LXXX. Equality of effect in pleasure does not produce equality in guilt; equality of disposition in will does.

Although two people take equal pleasure in something, they do not thereby merit equally, because their wills are unequal. For example, this layman and this bishop fall into simple fornication: perhaps their pleasure is equal, but their wills are not equal, because the bishop shows greater contempt than the layman. Therefore their merit is not equal. By analogy, a young man and an old man have unequal pleasure, which does not produce unequal merit; but because they have equal will, they merit equal punishment.

## RULE LXXXI. Every sin by which the punishment of penance is remitted is admitted to penitential punishment, not by the essence of the act but by equivalence of guilt.

468 The sense is: sins return, not in act but in guilt, in the case in which a person repents of having repented. For example: this man fell into fornication; afterwards he makes satisfaction, both as to punishment and as to guilt, for the fornication. Meanwhile he sees the woman with whom he committed fornication, desires her, and even regrets that he repented; and at this point the preceding fornication returns [Col. 0662D], not in act but in guilt, because he is now held troubled by the sin just as he was before. Likewise, a man is converted and has the will to confess and not to relapse, but afterwards does not wish to confess: in some sense he regrets having repented, and thus the sin in some sense returns. Likewise, if satisfaction is imposed upon someone and he scorns to perform it, in some sense he regrets having repented. To this point belong the authorities of the saints who say that sins return.

There are, however, some who say that all sins return generally: if [Col. 0663A] diverse sins have been forgiven to this man [Note: [Col. 0663D] The manuscript has *ista*.], and he afterwards falls into one sin, he will be guilty of all the preceding sins on account of ingratitude. Yet it seems dangerous to assert this, because on this account the desolation of human nature would be excessive. Others say that sins return in a like kind of sin: for example, if a man has suffered the slippery inclination of the flesh, his sin is afterwards forgiven, and then he falls into a similar sin, what had been forgiven returns, so that he is held liable to the same extent as before. Others say that sins return in hatred of a brother, and not in another act, because of the gravity of that sin: this is to sin against the Holy Spirit. Others say that sins return in the sense in which this was said: “Whoever offends in one point is guilty of all” [Note: In the Epistle of James, chapter II, verse 10: “For whoever keeps the whole law but offends in one point has become guilty of all.”]; that is, the other things are [Col. 0663B] insufficient for his salvation. Likewise, if grave sins have been forgiven to this man and he falls into some sin, the forgiveness of the preceding sins will be insufficient for his salvation, and thus he will be punished as though they had not been forgiven him.

REG. LXXXII. Every deserving of punishment belongs to man by action; every deserving of glory belongs above man by authorship.

The sense is: the evil which a man does belongs to man, and he is its author, because man is “a spirit that goes and does not return” [Note: Refers to Psalm LXXVII, verse 39.]. For he goes by himself, but does not return by himself. But man is not the author, by authorship, of a good work, but only its minister. Hence he is not properly said to merit eternal life. For four things concur in order that someone may properly be said to merit something: that the work which he does should properly be his own; that he should merit it before another [Col. 0663C]; that this other should have the power of rewarding; and that what was not owed should become owed.

Therefore Christ alone properly merited eternal life for us. For in that he had one greater than himself before whom he could merit, who was able to reward him because he was God, he was able by his own authorship to perform a good work worthy of the reward of eternal life; and, whereas previously nothing but punishment was owed to us, he made glory owed to us. But good works are properly ours only by ministry; they are God’s by authorship. And, as Augustine says [Note: *Expositions on the Psalms*, Psalm XCVIII, verse 5; and Letter 194 to Sixtus, chapter 15, no. 19, and elsewhere.], “God does not reward in us his merits [Note: I think that *our* should be read instead of *his*.], but his gifts”; because [Col. 0663D] “the sufferings of this present time are not proportionate to the future glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII). Evil works, however, are properly ours: for insofar as a work is evil, it is from man, not from God. Thus, when the rationale of meriting is considered, man is more properly said to merit punishment than reward.

REG. LXXXIII. By grace from the Spirit man has the ability by which he may will; by grace in the Spirit he has the willing by which he may be able.

Note that the term *grace* is sometimes taken so broadly [Col. 0664A] that natural endowments too are called graces, as though freely given; yet this term *grace* is restricted so that only superadded gifts are called graces. But among graces of this kind [Note: The word *kind* is lacking in the manuscript.] one is from the Spirit but not in the Spirit; for example, servile fear, which is both called gratuitous and a gift of the Holy Spirit, though not given in the Spirit, because it is not in charity. Yet it is from the Spirit, because “every best gift and every perfect gift,” etc. (James I).

Likewise, the grace bestowed on someone when he ceases from actual sin, although he does not repent perfectly, is grace from the Spirit but not in the Spirit. Therefore, whoever has a certain facility by which he can will the good has grace from the Spirit, but not always in the Spirit, since someone existing in sin can possess that facility also. But a man has the willing by which he can [Col. 0664B] will the good only from grace that is in the Spirit, namely, from liberating grace. Hence Augustine says concerning Genesis [Note: In the book *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 2, no. 32, vol. X, p. 768, Augustine writes concerning Adam: “He had received the ability, if he willed it, but did not have the willing by which he might be able.”] that Adam before sin had the ability by which he might will, but did not have the willing by which he might be able.

REG. LXXXIV. Every human choice is more free for evil by serving, less free for good by being liberated, so that the greater freedom is that of slavery and the lesser that of liberty.

469 Human choice is freer toward evil because there are more things impelling toward evil than there are aids working toward good: bodily and mental weaknesses, diabolical suggestions, and worldly pleasures invite a person to evil. By contrast, there is nothing that [Col. 0664C] works toward good except God’s grace alone. Therefore a man can do evil without another’s aid, but cannot perform good without its help, that is, without God’s benefit.

Yet the freedom toward evil is rather slavery than freedom, because “whoever commits sin is the servant of sin” (John VIII). The lesser freedom, which is toward good, tends more toward liberty. Hence, to serve God is to reign. But if free choice is freer toward evil than toward good, what does this mean: “If the Son shall set you free, you shall be truly free” (John VIII)? There “truly” is taken in the sense of “profitably.” Therefore free choice is more truly free toward evil by the truth of its essence, and more truly free toward good by reason [Col. 0664D] of usefulness.

REG. LXXXV. As every meritorious good in man either advances by progressing, languishes by growing lukewarm, or fails by ceasing, so every meritorious evil in man either increases by continuing, is remitted by attrition, or is forgiven by contrition.

It sometimes happens that through venial sin charity grows lukewarm in someone for a time and its fervour is diminished; sometimes, however, it is intensified more than before; and sometimes through mortal sin [Col. 0665A] it is extinguished. There are nevertheless some who say that charity does not depart through venial sin, denying, that is, that such venial sins can cause a descent from perfection to imperfection, although authority says that by the one-eyed eye is understood charity, which grows lukewarm from its fervour through venial sin.

Gregory also says on Job [Note: I do not find in Gregory the Great’s *Exposition on Job* what Alanus cites from it here. Read book VIII of his *Exposition*, chapter 6, where these words of Job are explained: “And again I shall await the evening.”] that by evening venial sin is understood, through which the light of charity is darkened. And since by omitting venial sins a person rises from imperfect to perfect charity, it appears that by committing them he might descend from perfect to imperfect. What is more absurd than to say that a man is bound to become better from moment to moment, when he may be in a most fervent motion of charity and, at the following [Col. 0665B] moment, in a less fervent one, although he has not fallen from charity?

But indeed [Note: It seems that *siquidem* should be read in place of *sed quidem*.] the statement that charity either advances in man or fails may be understood thus: it advances by continuing, or fails by ceasing. Another authority also says that venial sin does to charity what a drop of water does to a furnace. This should be referred to occasion: just as water poured into a furnace temporarily lessens its heat, yet subsequently occasions a greater blaze, so venial sin temporarily weakens charity but subsequently occasions greater fervour.

Likewise, evil in man, such as fornication or another mortal sin, either increases by continuation [Col. 0665C] if a man actually perseveres in sin; or is remitted by attrition, as when someone grieves that he committed it, ceasing from the deed although he does not repent perfectly; or is forgiven by contrition, when he turns fully away from sin. For many grieve that they have sinned and are inwardly bruised, but are not fully contrite: they neither have the firm purpose not to relapse nor confess with their mouth. Such persons become less evil, but do not cease to be evil [Note: I think the text should read: “but they do not cease to be evil.”] unless they are perfectly contrite.

REG. LXXXVI. Every righteous person can merit for another the merit of a reward, but not the reward of merit.

The sense is that one person can merit for another the first grace [Note: That is, congruously, not condignly, as St Thomas teaches, *Summa Theologiae* I–II, question 114, article 6.], namely justification, so that an unjust person may become righteous; by this justification [Col. 0665D] a man becomes worthy of the eternal reward. Yet no one can merit eternal life for another, although he can merit for him the first justification by which he is worthy of [Col. 0666A] eternal life. For it does not follow that, if someone can merit the antecedent, he merits [Note: In place of *quod mereatur*, read *mereatur*, both here and a little later.] the consequent; just as conversely it does not follow that, if someone merits the consequent, he merits the antecedent. Thus one who merits eternal life cannot merit the first grace for himself. The following Rule follows:

REG. LXXXVII. Grace unto merit comes about in us without us, with free choice accompanying but not cooperating; but grace in merit comes about in man through man, with free choice acting toward this but not being sufficient.

470 “Grace unto merit” means the first grace, that is, forgiveness of sin, which occurs in us without us. For freedom of choice does not work toward forgiveness of sin: guilt is forgiven by grace alone. Yet forgiveness of sin never occurs without free choice [Col. 0666B], not because free choice works toward it or cooperates in it, but because it accompanies forgiveness, so as to be a cause without which it does not occur. For “we were saved not from works of righteousness which we ourselves did, but by grace alone” (Titus III, 5); nor does forgiveness of sin rest with us. For if free choice worked or cooperated toward the forgiveness of sin, one could truly say that man merits first grace.

There are, however, some who say that God’s grace and the motion of free choice precede contrition causally, not temporally, whereas contrition precedes forgiveness of sin. These locate the first forgiveness in man’s power. For they say that, just as from the infusion of dew into the earth there proceeds a shoot in the earth, from the shoot a flower, and from the flower [Col. 0666C] fruit, so from the infusion of grace, as from dew, and from free choice, as from the earth, there arises contrition, as a flower, and from contrition there arises forgiveness of sin, as fruit. But “grace in merit” is this contrition, or the bestowal of virtues, with which free choice cooperates. For free choice contributes to the infusion of virtues, but is not sufficient for it.

REG. LXXXVIII. All virtues are given to man together and alike from creation, so that they may be by nature [Note: Namely, as St Thomas says, *Summa Theologiae* I–II, question 63, article 1: virtues are in us by nature according to aptitude and inception, but not according to perfection—except theological virtues, which are wholly from without.]; but from re-creation they are infused into man, so that they may be virtues by grace—together indeed in habit, but unequally in use.

Note that every virtue is, in genus, a quality; and naturally every virtue is a power of a rational creature, by which a rational creature is born fitted for doing this or that. Hence Tully also [Note: Read Cicero, *On Invention*, book II, shortly before the end. There he defines virtue as “a habit of mind consonant with nature and reason.” Augustine uses this definition in book IV *Against Julian*, vol. X, p. 594.] places virtues [Col. 0666D] among the species of natural law; and Aristotle says in the category of quality: “Further, sciences and virtues.” [Note: In the *Categories*, chapter 8, Aristotle writes: “Τοιαῦται δὲ αἵ τε ἐπίστημαι καὶ ἀρεταί,” that is, “Such are, namely, habits, sciences, and virtues.”] Augustine also says [Note: Book I, *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, chapter 6, no. 9.] [Col. 0667A] that virtue is, in genus, a quality. Moreover, since every virtue is a habit of a well-disposed mind, and every habit or disposition is a quality, every virtue is a quality.

Every virtue is understood to belong to man in three ways: by nature, by habit, or by use. Every power that is a virtue belongs to man by nature from creation, so that he is naturally fitted by this or that power for doing this or that; just as he is born fitted to reason or to understand, so he is born fitted to render to each person what is his, and to love God and neighbour. Aristotle sufficiently indicates this [Note: In *On Interpretation*, chapter 11 (p. 44, vol. I, Paris edition of 1639), Aristotle says that man is “καὶ ζῶον, καὶ δίπουν, καὶ ἤμερον,” that is, “both animal, biped, and gentle [or tame].”] when he says that man is gentle by nature. Under the name “gentle” he understood those natural virtues.

But then the powers are not virtues. Rather, after a man reaches the years of discretion, if he uses those powers in their due office and for their due end, directing their use toward God and as the Christian religion requires, those powers become virtues, as it were, standing in strength against vices. Virtues are therefore possessed in habit when, through those powers, a man has a certain aptitude and readiness to use them if occasion requires; and in this respect all virtues are possessed together and alike. For whoever has one virtue in habit has all virtues in habit [Note: In the margin of the manuscript the copyist wrote: “In Isaiah: Just as a lyre does not emit the sound of its harmonies if even one string is lacking, so spiritually the truth of the prophet, if one string of the virtues is lacking, will not sound forth sweet melody [the text reads *dulces*; read *dulce*]; nor will it cry out against a brick wall with all the inner powers of philosophers, whose opinion is that the virtues cling together.” And James: “If one is lacking, all are lacking.”].

But virtues are said to be possessed in use when someone employs them in acting well; and in this respect they are possessed neither together nor equally. For one virtue is sometimes possessed in use when another is not, and one is possessed more fully than another. Therefore those authorities [Col. 0667C] and arguments that seem to indicate that all virtues are possessed together and alike must be referred to habit; while those that seem to indicate that they are neither possessed together nor alike must be referred to use.

REG. LXXXIX. Virtue and vice are mediately opposed, not by the placement of a mean, but by the negation of each.

471 Note that the term *vice* is taken in many ways, negatively and positively, just like the term *sin*. Vice is sometimes said to consist in omitting what ought to be done; likewise, sometimes in committing what ought not to be done. Accordingly, insofar as vice is taken negatively, virtue and vice are immediately opposed, as affirmation [Col. 0667D] and negation—for example, rational and not-rational; I do not say irrational. Therefore, since virtue and vice in relation to a rational creature are opposed as affirmation and negation, insofar as vice is taken negatively, every rational creature that does not have virtue has vice, and conversely.

Thus, although a Jew or pagan possesses chastity, temperance, and the other powers that can be virtues, nevertheless, because he does not possess them as virtues, he has vices opposed to virtues by negation. In this he is vicious: that he does not possess virtues when he is bound to possess them. Just as failures are said to consist in not going to church or not giving alms, because we are bound to do these things and do not do them, so vices or failures are said to consist in not possessing temperance as a virtue or chastity as a virtue when we are bound to possess them.

Yet in this respect virtue and vice are not said to be immediately opposed except at a determined time. We do not say that a child has virtues or vices before the years of discretion; but when [Col. 0668B] he has reached the years of discretion, if he does not possess virtues, he will possess vices. Nor do we say that a puppy possesses sight or blindness before the determined time. Therefore a Jew or Gentile is not temperate, prudent, or chaste, although he possesses civic virtues; but he is not intemperate, imprudent, or unchaste, for these terms not only remove something but also imply vicious motions. The same judgment must be made concerning a Christian who is in some mortal sin, for example lying: although he is not moved toward lust, he is not to be judged chaste, lest chastity as a virtue be implied; nor is he lustful.

At other times vice is taken positively, insofar as lust, envy, and anger are called vice. [Col. 0668C] In this respect vice is divided into seven mortal vices: pride, anger, envy, avarice, acedia [Note: The manuscript has *accidiam*, but I think *acidiam*, or rather *acediam*, should be read; this word derives from the Greek ἀκηδία, “acedia” or “listlessness.”], gluttony [Note: Read *gastrimargiam*: a Greek word meaning gluttony, so named from γαστήρ, “belly,” and μάργος, “greedy.” Gregory the Great discusses these seven vices at length in book XXXI, chapter 17, on Job XXXIX.], and lust. In this respect intemperance, imprudence, and injustice are called vices. For since lust is called vice positively, and intemperance is a genus of lust, intemperance is called vice positively. In this respect virtue and vice are mediately opposed, as chastity and lust, for there is a mean between them by negation, namely non-chastity. Likewise, there is such a mean between faith and unbelief [Note: For instance, a Hebrew infant has neither faith nor positive unbelief, but is merely not faithful.], and between hope and despair.

Therefore, just as for the natural physician health and sickness are said to be mediately opposed, with neutrality by negation established between them as a kind of mean, so for the heavenly physician, between the health of virtue and the sickness of vice, there is established as a kind of mean a certain neutrality by negation: namely, not being virtuous. We do not call it a vicious motion, because vice is said to possess a substantial [Col. 0669A] quality from which it proceeds, just as a motion of virtue possesses a substantial virtue from which it proceeds. Thus no quality that is vice is opposed to a quality that is virtue; rather, motion is opposed to motion. For we call a disordered motion opposed to virtue, on account of the motion of virtue.

REG. XC. The merit of good consists in free choice occasionally, in virtue formally, in the motion of virtue essentially, in grace effectively, and in work instrumentally.

For freedom of choice is the occasion of merit: it belongs to free choice to will or not to will. It is not itself the efficient cause, but contributes toward this without being sufficient. Virtue is the formal cause of merit, from which, as from a form, proceeds the motion by which we merit. This motion itself is essentially merit, [Col. 0669B] because merit properly consists in the motion itself. Grace makes that motion merit; for without grace no motion or work is merit. Thus merit consists effectively in grace. An outward work is as it were the instrumental cause of merit; and thus merit consists instrumentally in the work itself.

REG. XCI. Among virtues charity is the prior cause, greater in duration, mother in informing, form in manifestation, end in recompense, more universal in operation.

472 Although faith is called first by reason of sign, because it principally signifies the inherence of virtues in man, and also by use, because one is moved to believe before hoping or loving, [Col. 0669C] charity is nevertheless called prior as cause, because it is especially the cause why a work is called good. A virtue chiefly becomes a virtue because it is exercised for God, namely for love of God. And every work is called good because it is finally done for the love of God. Hence charity itself is called the Mother of all virtues, because it informs all virtues, without which the others are not possessed.

It is also called form in manifestation. For just as a form impressed upon a thing makes the thing more manifest, so through works of charity the other virtues appear more clearly. It is greater in duration because the others will be done away with, such as hope and faith; but charity never fails, for death does not interrupt the order of charity. It is also the end in recompense: every true merit tends toward this, that in the future we may have charity as a reward. For the blessedness of eternal life consists in these two things: knowledge [Note: That is, vision or knowledge called intuitive.] of God and love. It is more universal in work because every good work signifies that charity is in the person who acts well. It is also so by reason of its end, because, as has been said, every good work is finally done for the love of God.

REG. XCII. Charity in one person is like a little stream and, as it were, like hay, which a stranger shares; but in another it is like a fountain and final, which none but one of the household shares.

For there is one who believes for a time and, in [Col. 0670A] the time of temptation, falls away (Luke VIII). In such a person charity is like a little stream and as it were like hay: as a stream now flows and now dries up, and hay now grows green and now withers, so charity in such a person now burns with the ardour of charity and now fails through temptation. But there is another who, once charity has been received, never falls from it. In such a person charity is like a fountain, because as a fountain always springs forth and never dries up, so charity overflows in such a person like a fountain. Such charity does not desert its possessor to the end; and a stranger does not share in charity that is like a fountain, namely one who is not predestined or written in the book of life.

REG. XCIII. A man is said to be justified from faith, not because justification comes from it, but because it proceeds from its article.

[Col. 0670B]

In sacred Scripture one frequently finds that man is justified from faith. Thus Habakkuk says: “The righteous lives by faith” (Hab. II). Elsewhere it is read: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Rom. IV). But this is not to be understood as meaning that first justification is from faith [Note: Certainly the ungodly person is not justified by faith alone, as the Fathers of Trent say, session VI, canon 9. But read St Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* I–II, question 114, article 5.], because in that case someone would merit first justification, and there would be no reason why a man should be said to be justified from faith rather than from charity. Rather, justification is said to be from faith because faith especially signifies that a man is justified, and because a man is justified through an article of faith, that is, through the grace which is an article of faith. For just as we are bound to believe other things, [Col. 0670C] so we are bound to believe this: that man is justified by God’s grace alone. The sense therefore is: man is justified from faith, that is, from the grace to which faith directs us.

REG. XCIV. No work done in charity is rendered deformed into the merit of eternal punishment; but a work done from charity is informed into the merit of glory.

A work done *in* charity is one thing; a work done *from* charity is another. Every work done from charity is done in charity, but not conversely. To be done from charity is to be informed by charity. But to be done in charity is for a work to be done by someone while he is in charity. For example, this religious man eats and drinks in charity, but not from charity, because this work is not informed by charity. Venial sins too are done in charity [Col. 0670D], but not from charity—unless this proposition is understood in an occasional sense. For charity is often the occasion of venial sin: in Peter, charity was the occasion why he struck the servant of the chief priest with a sword; and in the person who, out of charity, eats with guests and drinks beyond measure, charity is the occasion of drunkenness.

But every work informed by charity merits eternal life. Hence ceremonial observances done from charity, if they were informed by charity, merited eternal life. For if Abraham was willing to kill his son from [Col. 0671A] charity and thereby merited, although killing belongs to the class of evils, then much more was a ceremonial work done from charity meritorious of eternal life, since it did not belong to the class of evils. Since such a work lacks neither end nor due function, there is no reason why it should lack merit.

REG. XCV. As in man perfection is considered by the criterion of comparison, attainment, deed, vow, sufficiency, and conscience, so in charity perfection is considered by reason of sign, exclusion of impediment, continuance, rootedness, and intensification of fervour.

473 Comparative perfection is that attributed to someone in relation to another; according to this Noah is said to have been perfect in his generations (Gen. [Col. 0671B] VI), because he was better than the rest. Perfection of attainment is that which will be in the homeland, when neither body nor soul lacks anything for its own perfection. Perfection of deed is considered in the excellence of works, as in the works of religious persons. Perfection of vow is considered in solemn vows. Perfection of sufficiency is considered in someone’s having what suffices for salvation. Perfection of conscience is purity of conscience, of which Paul says: “I am conscious of nothing against myself” (I Cor. IV), etc.

Likewise, charity is called perfect by reason of sign when works proceed from it that signify perfect charity, such as laying down one’s life for Christ. Of this it was said: “No one has greater charity” (John XV), etc.; that is, no one has a greater sign of charity. The perfection of charity is also considered [Col. 0671C] in the exclusion of impediments. This perfection will be in the homeland, when all scandals are removed from the kingdom of God and then what is imperfect will be done away with. The perfection of charity is also considered in its continuance to the end: once a man receives it, he does not lose it. Perfection is also considered in rootedness, when charity is so rooted that it cannot easily be torn out; concerning this perfection Paul says: “I am certain that neither death nor life will separate me from the charity of God” (Rom. VIII). Perfection is also considered in the intensification of fervour, because the more fervour is intensified, the more charity is perfected.

REG. XCVI. Every good fear is either an initial terminus of faith, within its scope or outside its scope; or a final terminus of faith, within its scope or outside its scope.

[Col. 0671D]

Note the difference between human, worldly [Note: Peter Lombard does not distinguish human fear from worldly fear, *Sentences*, book III, distinction 34, letter D.], servile, initial, chaste, or filial fear. Likewise, it should be noted what is temporal good, eternal good, temporal evil, and eternal evil.

Human fear is a certain horror arising in the human mind from weakness, because [Col. 0672A] it fears incurring temporal evil, that is, temporal punishment. Such was the fear in Christ arising from the weakness of human nature [Note: Read Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, book III, distinction 34, letter L, where he distinguishes human fear from worldly fear.]. It is neither good nor evil in kind, but indifferent.

Worldly fear is that by which someone fears doing good in time—that is, a good meritorious of eternal life—lest he lose temporal good, that is, temporal life; yet he does not fear willing to do the good. Such was Peter’s fear when he denied Christ. This fear is evil and merits eternal punishment.

Servile fear is that by which someone fears doing evil in time, that is, sin, lest he incur temporal evil, that is, temporal punishment. Thus a thief who fears stealing lest he be hanged has servile fear. It is called servile because it is characteristic of servants [Col. 0672B] to fear in this way: they shrink from committing crimes lest they feel the lash. Hence an authority says [Note: Horace, *Epistles*, book I, epistle 16, verse 738:

“The good hate to sin for love of virtue.
You will admit nothing into yourself through fear of punishment.”]:

“The wicked hate to sin through fear of punishment.”

Those who fear in this way fear to do evil, but do not fear to will evil, because servile fear restrains the hand, not the mind. Hence Augustine says [Note: Read *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 8, no. 13; and the second *Exposition on Psalm XXXII*, vol. IV, p. 192.]: “The will to sin lives on, and the deed would follow if impunity were hoped for.” Such fear is good as regards flight from punishment, not as regards the merit of glory. It is called the beginning of wisdom not within its scope but outside its scope: a beginning that begins, not one that has been begun, because it leads toward wisdom while not being within wisdom.

Just as a bristle draws in a thread, so servile fear introduces [Col. 0672C] faith or charity. Initial fear is that by which someone fears doing evil lest he incur eternal evil, that is, eternal punishment, and lest he lose eternal good, that is, eternal life. Thus it consists partly in fear of punishment and partly in love of righteousness. Such fear is the beginning of wisdom within its scope, because it is in charity; and thus it is the initial terminus of faith within its scope.

Chaste fear is that by which someone fears losing eternal good more than incurring eternal punishment: that is, he fears being separated from the bridegroom more than being punished by eternal punishment. It is called chaste because it is characteristic of chaste women to fear offending their bridegroom lest they be separated from him. Such fear is the terminus of faith within its scope, because in it faith comes to an end and is brought to completion [Col. 0672D]. Reverence too is often called fear, because it accompanies fear; concerning it it is said: “The fear of the Lord is holy,” etc. (Psalm XVIII). Hence it is said of angels [Note: This seems to refer to Job XLI, verse 16: “When he is lifted up, the angels shall fear, and being terrified shall be purified.” Some refer this to the day of final judgment. Read St Gregory’s *Exposition on Job*, book XXXIV, chapter 7.] that they will fear on the day of judgment, that is, they will reverence. The saints too are said to fear in the homeland, that is, to reverence. Such fear is the terminus of faith outside its scope, because it will exist in the future after faith has been done away with.

REG. XCVII. Just as the flesh is said to obey reason when it does not act directly against [Note: The manuscript reads “against directly reason.”] reason, so reason is said to consent to the flesh when it does not restrain the flesh.

[Col. 0673A]

474 There is a continual duel between flesh and reason: for the flesh wills one thing and reason another. Although reason restrains carnality lest it proceed to unlawful acts, it is never so calmed that it does not murmur back [Note: The manuscript reads *remuneret*, “repays.”] at least in its first movements. Therefore it is said to obey, because it does not act directly against reason. Likewise reason is said to consent to the flesh, not because it gives consent, since it always condemns its works, but because, although it can restrain the flesh, it does not restrain it. Just as a king is said to consent to the city’s robbers, not because he consents, but because he does not drive them away although he can do so.

REG. XCVIII. Charity possessed by man causes something to be loved either because one possesses it, or in order that one may possess it, or in order that it may be possessed.

[Col. 0673B]

A father loves his son in order that he may possess something—namely, that the son may have honor or some temporal prosperity. But one loves riches or honors in order to possess them. One loves a just man, however, because he possesses virtues in himself. Thus one loves in one way when one loves in order to possess; in another when one loves because something is possessed; in another when one loves in order that something may be possessed. We may ascribe all these effects of love to charity. For by charity we love God for his own sake, because he is good—not merely in order that we may possess him, but because he is good in himself. Even if we expected nothing from him [Note: [Col. 0673D] The manuscript reads: “expected from him, namely.”], nevertheless, because he is good, we ought to love him [Note: [Col. 0673D] Read: “we would be bound.”]. Moreover, charity causes us to love ourselves in order that we may possess God; and our neighbor for the same end, namely eternal life, that we may enjoy it.

REG. XCIX. Just as a human being, through charity, ascending from the thesis of his nature to the apotheosis of grace, is deified; so God, through charity, descending from the apotheosis of his nature to the hypothesis of our misery, is made human.

Note that the thesis of human nature, apotheosis, and hypothesis are distinct things. Thesis is called the proper condition of a human being, which he is said to preserve when he uses reason to consider what is good, what evil, what ought to be done, and what ought to be avoided. But sometimes a human being exceeds this condition, either by descending [Col. 0673D] into vices or by ascending to contemplation of heavenly things; and such an exceeding is called ecstasy, or metamorphosis, because through such an exceeding one goes beyond the condition or form of one’s own mind.

The higher exceeding is called apotheosis, as it were deification. This occurs when a human being is rapt into contemplation of divine things; and it occurs through that power of the soul which is called intellectuality, by which [Col. 0674A] we apprehend divine things. According to this power, a human being becomes God [Note: [Col. 0673D] No one fails to see that Alan speaks metaphorically here.], just as, through that power of the soul called intellect, he apprehends invisible things; through this apprehension a human being becomes a spiritual human being, just as through rational speculation a human being becomes a human being.

The lower ecstasy, also called hypothesis, occurs when a human being is cast down from the state of human nature by degenerating into vices; and this occurs through sensuality, by which a human being becomes a bestial human being. God, however, has his own apotheosis, namely the excellence of his nature. Descending from it, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; he humbled himself even to the thesis of our nature—indeed, even to the hypothesis of our misery—not as regards guilt, but as regards punishment.

REG. C. Human nature is united to the divine, so that diversity of substance exists in one being, while the property of each nature remains in the united being.

[Col. 0674B]

475 One must consider how the Son of God united human nature to himself. Sometimes one thing is added to another in such a way that they do not become one, nor is either named from the other or does either acquire the other’s property—for example, if one stone is placed beside another. There is no composition of them, but a certain aggregation.

Sometimes a thing is so added to another that they do not become one, yet one acquires from the other a property—for example, when an apple is placed in a hand, the hand acquires the apple’s property, namely its scent.

Sometimes one thing is so added to another that [Col. 0674C] they do not become one, but one is named from the other—for example, when a cloak is put on a person, the person is called cloaked. Yet they do not become one. Nestorius the heretic assigned this kind of application to Christ’s incarnation, positing two persons in Christ, human and God: one, he said, was God and the other human; there was no union there [Note: [Col. 0673D] Namely, a substantial and hypostatic union.], nor anything made from them, but rather one person was added to the other by application.

Sometimes something is so added to another that one is absorbed by the other; as when a drop of wine is poured into the Seine [Note: [Col. 0673D] The manuscript has *secane*, and shortly afterwards *secana*.], it is absorbed by the Seine, and the two do not become one. Certain heretics [Note: [Col. 0674D] Namely, the Eutychians.] said that this kind of addition occurred in Christ’s incarnation: that human nature was absorbed by the divine, or [Col. 0674D] the divine by the human.

Sometimes one thing is so added to another that both are confused, and a third thing arises from them. Thus, when water is mixed with honey, both are confused, and hydromel arises from them [Note: [Col. 0674D] *Hydromellum* is an altogether barbarous word. This kind of honey-water of which Alan speaks is called *hydromeli*, or ὑδρόμελι, namely from ὕδωρ, “water,” and μέλι, “honey.” Pliny discusses *hydromelites* in *Natural History*, book XIV, chapter 17.], which is neither water nor honey. Eutyches the heretic wished to posit this confusion in Christ, saying that in Christ’s incarnation neither the divine nature remained divine nor the human [Col. 0675A] remained human; rather, when the natures had been confused, a third was made.

Sometimes one thing is so applied to another that something results from them while each remains in its own nature, as one human being consists of body and soul. But such a composition did not occur in Christ; for Christ, as Augustine testifies [Note: [Col. 0675D] *Against Maximinus*, book II, chapter 10, vol. VIII, p. 698.], does not consist of God and human being as of parts.

Sometimes, however, one thing is applied to another by union such that they do not become one thing, but that which is united to another becomes part of that to which it is united. For example, a shoot is united to a tree by grafting through the agency of heat and moisture; nevertheless, the shoot and tree do not become one thing, but the shoot becomes part of the tree. Similarly, body and soul are united to the Son of God, so that they are not the Son of God, but are of the Son of God. Thus the Son of God does not consist [Col. 0675B] of them and something else; rather, in one person there are two natures, the divine remaining divine and the human remaining human.

REG. CI. Just as a part cannot be the whole, nor a constituent that which is constituted, so that which assumes cannot be that which is assumed.

All philosophy proclaims that nothing can be from itself or belong to itself. Therefore a part cannot be the whole, because it is from the whole; similarly, that which composes cannot be the composite. By the same reasoning, since that which is assumed is from that which assumes, it cannot itself be that which assumes.

For something is assumed by another in three ways. At times something assumes another thing to itself but not in itself or from itself, as a soldier assumes weapons; through their application he is called armed, but the weapons themselves [Col. 0675C] are not the armed man. At times something assumes another to itself and in itself, as a cask assumes wine, but not from itself. At times it assumes something to itself so that it is from itself, as Christ so assumed human nature—that is, body and soul—that it is from Christ. Yet it is not Christ, nor is Christ it; for Christ is not the body and soul which he assumed, nor are the body and soul which he assumed Christ.

But through the assumption of body and soul he is human. Yet he did not assume some human being, although certain people fabulously assert that a certain human being was assumed by the Word and began to be the Word. Thus they say that a creature began to be Creator, and thus God, and thus deity; and so something made in time began to be eternal.

They endeavor to establish this as follows. The capacity for laughter belongs to Christ, but not according to his divine nature; therefore it belongs according to his human nature; therefore either according to body, soul, or the composite of both. To this we reply: according to none of these [Col. 0676A] taken singly, but according to body and soul united to himself. For he did not assume a composite of body and soul, but only body and soul united to himself; for in assuming he united, and in uniting he assumed. Therefore the body and soul united to himself composed Christ—that is, made him composite. For he began to be composite of body and soul; and they did not compose something other than Christ, nor something that would begin to be Christ or be united to Christ, but Christ himself. Thus something began to be composite of body and soul, insofar as he was human, who was simple and eternal insofar as he was God.

REG. CII. For Christ to be human, a threefold union concurs: compersonal union, so that he might be of human nature; subpersonal union, so that he might live; and propersonal union [Note: [Col. 0675D] The final words of this rule are absent from the manuscript. I judge that they may be supplied thus: “and propersonal union, so that he might be human.”].

[Col. 0676B]

476 Personal union is that which makes a thing a person. It is found in a pure creature, as in a mere human being: for from the fact that a human being becomes one through the union of body and soul, he begins to be a person, that is, a thing one in itself. Such a union was not in Christ as human; for Christ did not begin to be a person when he began to be human.

But a propersonal union was in Christ. The union of body and soul which was in him had a likeness to personal union; hence it could be called propersonal. It especially effected Christ’s being human. Subpersonal union is the union of the physical spirit with Christ’s body and soul. The physical spirit [Col. 0676C] is a certain body subtler than air but less subtle than fire, which vivifies the body. Such a spirit exists in brute animals and produces life; through it the soul is united to the body. For it has affinity with the soul in swiftness and subtlety, and with the body in corporeality. The soul is united to the Word without a medium; the spirit through the soul; the body through the spirit [Note: [Col. 0675D] Augustine writes similarly in *On the Christian Combat*, chapter 18, §20, vol. VI, p. 254: “If, therefore, clean visible things can be touched by unclean visible things and not be defiled, how much more did invisible and unchangeable Truth, receiving the soul through the spirit and the body through the soul, with the whole human being assumed, free him from all infirmities without any contamination of itself?” Please read Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, book III, distinction 2, letter B.].

Corporeal union [Note: [Col. 0676D] Alan perhaps refers to Paul’s words: “In whom dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily” [Colossians II].] was the union of body and soul with the Word. These unions concur in Christ’s incarnation; none was sufficient without the others. For if body and soul had not been united to him, nor soul to body, he would not have been human. Hence we do not say that during the three days he was [Note: [Col. 0676D] Understand: “human.” During those three days both body and soul were indeed united with the Word, but the soul was separated from the body; consequently Christ was not human during those three days.]. Likewise, if the soul had been united to the body but not to the Word, Christ would not have been [Col. 0676D] human.

REG. CIII. In Christ there occurs memorial number, by which the substantial hypostasis is numbered [Note: [Col. 0676D] Perhaps one should read: “by which the substantial hypostasis is numbered.”]; and material number, by which *ousia* is numbered with *ousiosis* [Note: [Col. 0676D] *Ousiosis*, or ἡ οὐσίωσις, is taken by Boethius in his treatise *Against Eutyches and Nestorius* to mean subsistence; by Dionysius, chapter 2 of *On the Divine Names*, to mean the communication of simple essence; and by Chrysostom, Homily 13 on the Epistle to the Ephesians, to mean the production of a thing when it begins to exist. Alan appears to take this word to mean existence or humanity.].

As Augustine testifies, memorial number is [Col. 0677A] the repetition of the same thing, which in some manner bears the image of number. For where there is repetition, there appears to be numbering; as if I said, “Sun, sun, sun”; “God, God, God.” Here there is repetition, not a numbering of different things; and such repetition is called memorial number.

Material number is numbering properly so called, when several things are counted; as if I say, “Socrates is one thing; Plato is another.” In Christ, then, there is memorial number as regards hypostasis: for Christ’s hypostasis, that is, his person, is one. But there is material number as regards nature, by which diverse natures are numbered, as when I say, “Christ is God and human.” For one nature is predicated when he is called God, another when he is called human. Hence Christ is called one thing according to [Col. 0677B] his divine nature and another according to his human nature.

REG. CIV. The necessity of dying was in Christ, not as an operation overcoming his mind, but as a will binding the event.

Among the other defects of human nature, the Son of God assumed the necessity of dying. Hence Augustine [Note: [Col. 0677D] The word “Augustine” is absent from the manuscript. I have added it on the authority of St Thomas, who writes in *Sentences*, book III, distinction 16, question 1, article 2: “Hence Augustine: If he had not been killed, he would have dissolved by a natural death, and the same work of redemption would have been accomplished as he accomplished through the Passion.”] says: “Although he had not suffered, he would have failed through old age.” Note that coercive necessity differs from voluntary necessity. We have coercive necessity whether we will or not; Christ had voluntary necessity, because he voluntarily assumed the necessity of dying: “He was offered because he himself willed it” (Isaiah LIII).

One necessity is imposed, another inborn, another assumed. Adam had the first, because he brought it upon himself [Col. 0677C]—the necessity of dying. Hence Augustine says: “They summoned death to themselves by their hands and feet.” We have an inborn necessity by original descent; Christ had an assumed one.

REG. CV. In Christ there was the fear of propassion, not opposing reason; but there was not the fear of passion that disturbs the mind.

477 The fear called propassion [Note: [Col. 0678D] Read Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, book III, distinction 15, letter F.] is a certain horror innate in a human being, by which one recoils from punishment. It is called propassion, as if *protopassion*, that is, first passion. Such fear was in Christ, because he naturally recoiled from death. But in him there was not the fear called passion, which disturbs reason, such as was in Peter when he denied Christ. Correspondingly, in Christ there was a will, proceeding from sensuality, by which he willed not to die.

REG. CVI. Christ merited nothing for himself by his works; but whatever he merited, he merited for us by each of his works.

[Col. 0677D]

Since to merit is to make what is not owed become owed, whereas from the time of the incarnation whatever he afterwards received was owed to Christ, he did not make owed from not owed [Col. 0678A], and thus did not merit for himself. For from the incarnation he was as worthy of all that he afterwards received as he subsequently merited it for us by each of his works: because, as Isaiah says, “He was given to us” (Isaiah IX). And the Psalm says: “His leaf shall not fall, and whatever he does shall prosper for us” (Psalm I). Therefore, when he is said to have merited immortality and the name above every name (Philippians II), this should not be referred to himself but to us [Note: [Col. 0678D] Read what I said in the preface, no. 6, p. 174.]; for he merited for us that we should have immortality and know him to be equal to the Father.

REG. CVII. Just as the Creator, made a creature by assuming a creature, so a creature becomes the Creator’s body by the transubstantiation of a creature.

Note that alteration, otherness, and transubstantiation are distinct. Alteration [Col. 0678B] of a subject occurs with respect to accidental properties: when white becomes black, or black white. Accordingly one may say, “The white thing will be black”; “the white thing will begin to be black”; but not, “Black will be made from white,” or conversely. For it is said in that manner because the term is materially posited, so as to suggest [Note: [Col. 0678D] The passage is corrupt and needs emendation.] that the white thing was the matter of the black thing.

Otherness is said to occur when the subject is changed with respect to substantial things, as happened at Cana of Galilee when water was made wine (John II). In accordance with this alteration one should not concede that water will be wine, but that wine will be made from water.

Transubstantiation occurs when neither matter nor substantial form remains, as in the change by which bread is transubstantiated into Christ’s body [Col. 0678C], where neither the matter nor the substantial constituents of bread remain, but only accidents. According to this change we may concede that bread becomes Christ’s body and will be changeably converted into Christ’s body. Here we ought not to concede statements that do not denote [Note: [Col. 0678D] The manuscript mistakenly reads: *non e notancia*.] change. Therefore one must not concede that bread will be Christ’s body or will begin to be Christ’s body, but that it will become Christ’s body; yet Christ’s body will not be made from bread.

Of the accidents which remain, it may be said that they exist without a subject; or it may be said that they are in the air. Yet there are those who say that the accidents are not there, but merely appear to be. Nevertheless there is no illusion or deception there, for this does not occur in order to deceive, but sacramentally. Others say that the whiteness and the accidents themselves which remain are in the form of bread. But on this account the question remains where that form itself is. Likewise, one must ask where the breaking occurs, or in what it occurs: whether in Christ’s body or in something else. Some say that Christ’s body is broken [Note: [Col. 0678D] Read Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, book IV, distinction 11, letter D.] and yet [Col. 0679A] remains whole; divided and yet remains undivided. Others say that the breaking is in the form itself. Others say that nothing is broken there, but that it appears to be broken, as stated above.

REG. CVIII. Christ’s body is in one species and under another species.

For in that form which he assumed from the Virgin, it is on the altar, but not under that form; rather, it is under the form of bread and wine. Hence Christ’s body is improperly said to be seen on the altar, since it is not seen through its own form; improperly said to be broken or ground by teeth, since this pertains not to Christ’s body but to the form.

REG. CIX. For bread to be transubstantiated into the Lord’s body, four concurrences occur: order in the person, intention in the agent, matter in the bread, and form in the words.

[Col. 0679B]

478 Note that some things belong to the substance of the sacrament and others to its circumstances. Those already set forth belong to its substance. The solemnity of priestly vestments, the prayers said beforehand, and certain other things belong to the circumstances. Order belongs to the substance of the sacrament, because unless someone is a priest, he cannot consecrate. Intention also belongs to it: not, indeed, an intention to consecrate, but an intention to observe the Church’s form. Thus a heretical priest, provided he has been ordained in the Church’s form, consecrates while celebrating Mass, even if he does not bring faith to the sacrament, so long as he intends to observe the Church’s form.

Matter also is said to belong to the substance of the sacrament. For transubstantiation to occur there, there must be bread made from wheat and wine. [Col. 0679C] So too is the form of the words: that form of words instituted by Christ when he said, “This is my body. This is the chalice,” and so forth.

REG. CX. Just as the Eucharist is a sacrament perfecting the righteousness of dignity, so baptism is a sacrament advancing toward righteousness by necessity.

Note that there are seven spiritual sacraments in the Church of God. Some are common: baptism, Eucharist, penance, confirmation, and extreme unction. Others are special: marriage and orders. Some are sacraments of necessity, such as baptism, without which there is no salvation for a child or an adult unless an emergency prevents it. Likewise, the Eucharist is a sacrament of necessity for adults; yet it is especially a sacrament of dignity.

[Col. 0679D]

For whereas circumcision only removed guilt, baptism extinguishes both guilt and punishment and also confers grace. The sacrament of the Eucharist adds an abundance of grace; hence Eucharist is said to mean, as it were, “good grace.” For this reason too it is called a sacrament of dignity.

REG. CXI. The sacrament of confirmation is not given in order that baptism may be had, but in order that it may be possessed more fully.

For baptism is given in order that the Holy Spirit may be had; confirmation, in order that he may be possessed more fully. This sacrament too is one of necessity for adults [Col. 0680A], because if an adult neglectfully omits it, it will be a mortal sin for him.

Just as certain things belong to the substance of baptism, so certain things belong to the substance of confirmation. Water belongs to the substance of baptism, because baptism is invalid unless it is in water. So too does intention: the minister must intend to observe the Church’s form. The form of words does likewise. Similarly, certain things belong to the substance of confirmation: the rank of the consecrator, namely that the confirmer be a bishop [Note: [Col. 0679D] The bishop, of course, is the ordinary minister of this sacrament.]; also the place of confirmation, namely the forehead; and the chrism with which confirmation is administered.

REG. CXII. Just as baptism is the first remedy against the fall of original sin, so penance is the second plank after the shipwreck of sin.

Sometimes those shipwrecked at sea, fleeing [Col. 0680B] to some [Note: [Col. 0679D] Read: “to some plank.”] plank of the ship, are brought by it to port. By this analogy penance is called the second plank after shipwreck. First, one shipwrecked in original sin flees to baptism and reaches the harbor of remission of that sin by the plank of baptism. If one is shipwrecked again by actual sin, one has recourse to the second plank of penance and is brought back to the harbor of salvation.

There is another reason why penance is called the second plank after shipwreck. Shipwrecked persons are accustomed to carry with them a board upon which the entire event of their shipwreck is described; when people see it, moved to mercy, they customarily give such shipwrecked persons aid. Likewise, God first gives aid to all through baptism and second through penance.

REG. CXIII. Just as baptism is the sacrament of faith, confirmation the sacrament of hope, and the Eucharist the sacrament of charity, so extreme unction is the sacrament of penance or contrition.

[Col. 0680C]

479 Baptism is called the sacrament of faith, for in it faith is sought [Note: [Col. 0680D] Perhaps one should read *requiritur*, “is required,” or *acquiritur*, “is acquired.”]. Before baptism, even if someone possesses some of the things pertaining to salvation, that person does not yet possess faith as a virtue, because in that person faith is not “the substance of things hoped for” (Hebrews XI). Hence a human being has nothing by which to hope for salvation until baptized.

Confirmation is called the sacrament of hope because one is confirmed through the laying on of the bishop’s hand so as no longer to be moved from the faith by heretical seductions. Thus it is called the sacrament [Col. 0680D] of hope, because there is hope concerning the confirmed person that he will no longer depart from the faith.

The Eucharist is called the sacrament of charity because through its reception there is signified the unity of the Church and of Christ the head, which in the present exists through charity: charity toward God and neighbor. Through charity toward neighbor, the faithful are united to one another such that, as members joined together, they are called one body; and through charity toward God that body is united to Christ its head. Although this union exists here in some measure, in the future it will be perfect.

Likewise, the sacrament of extreme unction is the sacrament of contrition. It is administered so that, through inward contrition, bodily health may be conferred upon the recipient together with health of mind; or, if not bodily health, at least health of mind. This sacrament is a sacrament of necessity. For if someone has time and is not prevented by necessity, and is not anointed, it will result in peril to that person’s soul. Some say that this sacrament cannot be repeated, any more than baptism can; but because it is a sacrament of punishment [Note: [Col. 0681D] I think one should read: “but because it is a sacrament of penance, and penance can be repeated,” etc. For above, in the rule, it says: “Extreme unction is the sacrament of penance.” Moreover, Launoy, citing this passage, read *poenitentiae*, as I said in the preface.], and punishment can be repeated, it is probable that this sacrament can be repeated.

REG. CXIV. Marriage is a sacrament of remedy for flight, not of necessity for choice.

For just as some sacraments are of necessity, such as baptism and the Eucharist, and of dignity, such as sacred orders [Col. 0681B], so marriage is a sacrament of counsel—indeed, a remedy against incontinence. It is called a sacrament for two reasons: because of the consent of minds signifying the spiritual union of Christ and the Church, and because of bodily intercourse signifying the fellowship of the two natures in Christ [Note: [Col. 0681D] Marriage is a sacrament not only for these reasons, but also because it confers grace, as the Fathers of Trent define, Session 24, canon 1, on the sacrament of marriage.].

Marriage before Adam’s sin was a precept of discipline, and after the sin [Note: [Col. 0682D] Perhaps something is missing.]; but after married chastity had filled the earth, so that virginal chastity might now fill the heavenly homeland, the precept of discipline was changed into a remedy of indulgence.

REG. CXV. Sacred order is the sacrament by which a human being is marked out, so as to preside over others through honor in such a way as to benefit them through the burden of prelacy.

[Col. 0681C]

In order three things must be considered: ordination itself, knowledge, and action. If you have order without knowledge, it will be folly; knowledge without action, sloth; action without knowledge, rashness.

Having discussed the rules specially suited to theological truth, we must treat those belonging to natural science and consider especially those that so suit natural science that they do not stray from theology. But of those common to both disciplines [Note: [Col. 0682D] Something is lacking in the manuscript.], the following is the chief rule of natural philosophy.

REG. CXVI. Every proposition depends so completely upon a cause that, if there is no cause, the proposition itself is empty.

[Col. 0681D]

This rule is common to both disciplines. For, as Hilary testifies [Note: [Col. 0682D] *On the Trinity*, book IV, §14, vol. II, p. 82.], “The understanding of statements must be drawn from the causes of speaking.” This is plainly true in natural science. Peter is called a human being because of humanity; [Col. 0682A] white because of whiteness; just because of justice. Even when a meadow is said to laugh, it is because of a cause: it is said to laugh because it possesses in itself the cause of laughter. Similarly, in theology every proposition is from a cause. God [Note: [Col. 0682D] I think “God” must be understood.] is called just because he makes just; and likewise in other cases.

REG. CXVII. A proposition is one thing; the cause of speaking is another.

480 This rule is suited to natural science. In natural science it is true that white is one thing and whiteness another; human being one thing and humanity another. In theology, however, God is not one thing and divinity another, although Hilary [Note: [Col. 0682D] Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book VIII, §22, vol. II, p. 229, writes: “For nature is not the same as the thing of nature, just as a human being is not the same as that which belongs to a human being,” etc.] seems to maintain that nature is one thing and the thing of nature another. But what Hilary says [Col. 0682B] must be referred to a difference in conception, not to a difference in being, just as one commonly says that human being is one thing and animal another, because we apprehend a human being by one concept and an animal by another.

REG. CXVIII. Every cause of a proposition is expressed in one way and explained in another.

A cause is expressed when it shows from what a thing itself is; for example, “A human being is good.” A cause is explained when it discloses what it is; for example, “That which is good is good by goodness and nature.” This rule is common to the two disciplines, natural and theological. For in divine matters, “God is good” is explained in one way; the cause by which he is good, in another. In the statement “God is good,” [Col. 0682C] the proposition is explained; in the statement “Goodness is the cause by which God is good,” the cause of speaking is explained.

REG. CXIX. The cause of speaking is distinct from the thing of which it is, as stated, the cause [Note: [Col. 0682D] Perhaps one should read: “distinct from the thing of which it is or is called the cause.”].

This rule is common to both disciplines. In any case, color, by which a body is called colored, is one thing; the colored body itself another. In divine matters, however, the cause by which God is called just is not distinct from God’s justice, by which God himself is just. Rather, he is called just from the effect of his justice—that is, from our justice, which he produces in us. For he is called just because he makes us just; and he is his own justice.

REG. CXX. One cause of a thing is intrinsic; another extrinsic.

[Col. 0682D]

An intrinsic cause is that by which a thing is what it is, or is something; for example, a body exists by corporeity. By color it is something, namely colored. An extrinsic cause of speaking is that by which a thing, of whatever nature it may be, [Col. 0683A] is something, but stands in some relation to something else outside itself. For example, paternity, by which the Father neither exists nor is something; but he has outside himself something which is neither Father nor paternity, namely the Son. This rule applies to natural as well as divine matters. In divine matters deity is, as it were, the intrinsic cause by which God is and is God. Yet there is this difference: God is not one thing and good by another; rather, for him, being and being good are identical. The extrinsic cause is paternity, filiation, procession.

REG. CXXI. Of causes, one is called through itself; another in relation to another.

A cause of speaking through itself is one spoken of in comparison with nothing else; for example, in natural matters, “a white human being”; [Col. 0683B] in divine matters, “a just God.” A cause is called in relation to another by comparison; for example, Father and Son.

REG. CXXII. Of causes, one is first; another second.

The first is that which has no cause in itself to which it belongs—for example, that by which a human being is human; in divine matters, that by which God is God. The second is that which in itself has another cause, because of which it belongs to a thing and to whose power it is added—for example, that according to which one who is human is capable of laughter. In divine matters, it is that according to which the Father is Father and the Son is Son.

REG. CXXIII. A first cause is either the nature of that which subsists or its property.

[Col. 0683C]

The nature of that which subsists is that by which the subsisting being subsists—for example, that by which a human being is human. The property of that which subsists is that by which the subsisting being is distinguished from all others—for example, that by which Plato is Plato. In divine matters the subsisting nature is deity, by which the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit exist; the property of that which subsists is the personal status of the Father, by which the Father is Father; the personal status of the Son, by which the Son is Son; and the personal status of the Holy Spirit.

REG. CXXIV. A second cause of speaking either belongs to nature or belongs to property.

481 Every cause belongs to nature [Col. 0684A] which is said of a subsisting being on account of the subsisting being’s essence—for example, that by which a human being is capable of laughter. For the capacity for laughter belongs to human nature, that is, humanity. So too does essence itself; for example, “human being is a species.” But whatever is said either of the subsisting being on account of its property—for example, “Plato is a person”—or of the property itself—for example, “Plato is an individual”—belongs to property.

Likewise, in divine matters, what is asserted when one says, “The Father is Lord of creatures,” or “The Father is principle,” belongs to the divine essence. What is asserted when one says, “The Father is a person,” belongs to personal property.

REG. CXXV. There is one cause of speaking which belongs to every cause of a proposition.

[Col. 0684B]

This cause is unity. For unity accompanies every property to its subject: Socrates’ humanity, for example. Thus, just as Socrates is called human by humanity, so he is called one by the unity which accompanies that humanity; and thus he is called one human being: human by humanity, one [Note: [Col. 0683C] The word *unus*, “one,” is absent from the manuscript.] by unity. Likewise, this animal is called one white thing: white by whiteness, one by unity added to whiteness; and so proceed through the other properties.

There are, however, those who except two causes: proper quality and duration. For they say that unity does not accompany proper quality to the subject, because unity itself belongs to that proper quality. For both the substantial and accidental features of a thing belong to proper quality. Hence one cannot say, “Socrates is one,” since unity does not accompany Socrates’ proper quality.

Likewise, unity does not accompany duration, because if unity accompanied duration, then, since unity endures in the subject, duration would accompany that unity; similarly, another unity would accompany that duration, and so we would fall into an infinite regress.

Likewise, in divine matters unity is considered in relation to deity, namely a certain singularity according to which God is called one. Likewise, three unities are considered in relation to the properties of the divine persons: according to one of them the Father is called one, according to another the Son one, and according to another the Holy Spirit one.

[Col. 0685]

THE BOOK OF THE VENERABLE ALAN, ON DISTINCTIONS OF THEOLOGICAL TERMS.

(From an undated and unlocalized folio edition, very kindly shared with us by Dr. JUNG, director of the Strasbourg Library. Concerning this precious specimen of early printing, Dr. Jung wrote to us: “This edition of Alan’s *Distinctions* was never reprinted afterwards. It appeared at Deventer about the year 1477, from the press of Richard PAFFROET of Cologne, and is to be counted among the earliest productions of this master of the printing art, who is known to have published nothing before that year. Its type is still not unlike that used by Gutenberg and Fust.” — The same volume contains the book called *Mammotrectus*, which a fifteenth-century binder bound together with Alan.)
