## ALAN’S PROLOGUE TO HERMENGALD, ABBOT OF SAINT GILLES

[Col. 0685A] To the most reverend Father and lord HERMENGALD, by the grace of God abbot of Saint Gilles, ALAN, called Master: may you be adorned in this present life with manifold grace, so as to be rewarded with glory in the life to come.

[Note: [Col. 0685A]

Hermengald governed the monastery of Saint Gilles from about 1179 until 1195. Accordingly de la Serna Santander must be corrected, who, in his work entitled *Dictionnaire bibliographique choisi du XVe siècle* (Brussels, 1806), part II, pp. 27–28, after listing the Strasbourg edition of Alan’s *Distinctions* (read: the Deventer edition; for they were never published at Strasbourg), adds:

“This work’s author must be distinguished from Alan the Great of Lille, who died in 1203. Thus this great Alan is to be regarded as nearly a century and a half older; for Hermengard, abbot of Saint Gilles, to whom the *Distinctions* are dedicated, died before 1060 according to Mabillon. At that time, in 1050, Hermengald was abbot of the monastery of Andaon (Saint-André de Villeneuve, near Avignon); afterwards he became abbot at Saint Gilles, where he died seven years later (*Annales SS. ord. S. Bened.*, vol. IV, p. 522). This is confirmed by the testimony of the authors of *Gallia Christiana*, vol. I, col. 873, who, while treating of the abbots of Andaon, write: ‘IV. [Col. 0686A] [Col. 0686B] Hermengald, during whose tenure Rostagnus I, bishop of Avignon, gave the church of Juncariae in the year 1050.’ Hence it is clear that Master Alan’s work, dedicated to Hermengald, was completed before 1038, the year in which Hermengald died.”

Santander writes learnedly, but heedlessly. A certain Hermengald did indeed govern the monastery of Saint Gilles about 1050: “X. Hermengald, abbot of Andaon,” say the authors of *Gallia Christiana* (vol. VI, col. 483), “about 1050; later abbot of Saint Gilles, where Mabillon says that he died seven years later, in vol. IV of the *Annals*, p. 722; nothing further about him could be discovered elsewhere.” But if Santander had continued through the succession of the abbots of Saint Gilles, he would soon have encountered (ibid., cols. 489–90) another Hermengald, the nineteenth abbot of Saint Gilles, who governed from before 1179, as we have said, until 1195. It is this Hermengald to whom Alan dedicated his *Distinctions*. — ED.]

When the world of old flourished with the varied excellences of wise men, and, like another firmament, shone with its own stars, now, as the diverse darknesses of vices press in and the stars of virtues have been driven away, it is wholly wrapped in the night of profound blindness and banished from the light of all truth. Yet, while all others have been banished, you alone, like a new Lucifer, illuminate the world with the rays of your discernment and, so far as lies within you, remove from it the shadows of indiscretion.

Therefore I dedicate the star of my work to such a star, equipped with the divine constellations of theological authorities. And just as it bears your name in its title, so may it be marked by your eminent protection, in order that the scales of your judgment may weigh the opinions of my book: so that, if anything has been insufficiently refined in the fire of reason, it may be buried in silence; but whatever appears polished in the workmanship of prudence may be celebrated publicly. For I do not wish my work to go forth disseminated into public ears before it has left the balance of your examination weighed in the scale: that it may either prevail, approved by the judgment of your wisdom, or be held cheap, rejected by the decision of your authority. For to you, first among the foremost, I first offer the first fruits of my work, so that, as you are first among prelates, you may be the first to taste this book’s novelty.

[Col. 0687A] Since I was wholly unwilling to present to your magnanimity the idle burdens of wealth, than which nothing is more serviceable for wrongdoing when the thirst for possessing burns hot, nor more contemptible when a victorious spirit has subjected it beneath itself in scorn.

[Note: [Col. 0687C] We have restored this passage with the aid of manuscript no. 73, preserved in the public library at Dijon. The Deventer edition reads corruptly: “Since … I was wholly unwilling to present the idle burdens of works, things akin to which nothing is more serviceable for wrongdoing when the desire of possessing burns hot,” etc.]

But this alone I ask of your fatherhood with all devotion of mind: that your kindness may preserve unimpaired and inviolate the glorious covenant of your friendship, which I have read not only in the book [Col. 0688A] of knowledge but also in the book of experience. For as long as my spirit animates my limbs, as long as I endure the various courses of temporal life, your glory, your name, and your praises shall ever remain with me. May you fare well forever, as I desire.

## ANOTHER PROLOGUE BY THE SAME AUTHOR

[Col. 0687]

[Col. 0687B] Since, according to the declaration of Aristotelian authority, those who are ignorant of the significations of terms quickly fall into paralogisms, it is dangerous in Holy Scripture to be ignorant of the significations of theological terms. There, the object of inquiry is more perilous, what is found is more difficult, we do not possess words adequate to the things of which we speak, language does not speak of the thing as it is, and terms wander away from their proper meanings and seem to take on strange new meanings. There divine excellence descends so that human understanding may ascend; nouns are used pronominally, adjectives substantivally; the verb is not the sign of what is said of another; predication occurs without inherence, subjecthood without matter, affirmation improperly, negation truly; construction is not subject to the rules of Donatus, metaphor is alien to the rules of Cicero, statement is strange to Aristotle’s teaching, and the matter of faith is remote from rational demonstration.

Therefore, lest the theologian affirm falsehood as truth; lest the heretic confirm error through a false interpretation; lest the Jew be excluded from the literal sense; lest the proud person impose his own understanding upon sacred [Col. 0688B] Scripture: we have judged it fitting to distinguish the meanings of theological words, to assign the reasons for metaphors, and to bring into light the hidden uses of tropes. Thus a freer entry may be opened into Holy Scripture, the theologian may not be deceived by an alien interpretation, and the path of understanding may become easier: it may invite the less understanding, rouse the sluggish, and delight the more learned. Thus the different senses of terms, lying unknown in different places of Holy Scripture, may be brought into the light of manifestation by the explanation of this little work: so that a shorter explanation may exclude prolixity, brevity remove weariness, exposition remove obscurity, and concise teaching [supplies a saving] of time. [Text uncertain; the printed reading is corrupt.]

The execution of our work will be arranged in this order: according to the order of the letters of the alphabet, the different meanings of theological expressions will be faithfully distinguished in accordance with the principles and causes of their usages; and, set down under the different chapter-headings of titles, the discussion will offer the reader, by the aid of distinctions, whatever he wishes. A follows.

## THE BOOK OF THE VENERABLE ALAN ON DISTINCTIONS OF THEOLOGICAL TERMS. HERE HAPPILY BEGINS.

# A

[Col. 0687D] **A** sometimes indicates place; hence in the Gospel: “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho.” It also indicates time; hence in the prophet Micah: “From ancient days.” It indicates eternity; hence the same Micah: “His going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity.” It indicates agency; hence in the Psalm: “This was done by the Lord.” It indicates birth or origin; hence in the Gospel: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world.” [Col. 0688D] It indicates breathing forth or procession; hence in the Gospel: “Simeon received an answer from the Holy Spirit.” It indicates separation or removal; hence in the Psalm: “And I shall be cleansed from the greatest sin.” It indicates the separation of a thing from a whole, with an exception, as when a righteous person is said to be separated from the mass of perdition.

All the meanings possessed by the preposition *a* are also possessed by the preposition *ab*. But it should be noted that *a* ought to be prefixed to words beginning with a consonant, and *ab* to words beginning with a vowel. Sometimes *ab* is used for “without”; hence in Cato: “Do not become angry *ab re*,” that is, “without a reason.”

**Fir tree** (*abies*), properly speaking, means a contemplative person; hence Isaiah: “I shall place a fir tree in the wilderness.” Because of its loftiness, the fir tree signifies contemplatives who, though still situated in earthly bodies, contemplate heavenly things. It also means contemplation; hence Isaiah: “In place of the bramble the fir tree shall rise,” when, in the hearts of saints, the height of heavenly contemplation arises in place of the rejection of earthly thought. It also means a heavenly power, as is said through the prophet concerning the apostate angel: “The cedars were not taller in God’s paradise; the fir trees did not equal his height,” because the other angels were not equal to Lucifer in dignity.

**To depart** (*abire*) properly indicates local movement from a place, or withdrawal; hence “he departed,” that is, “he withdrew from that place.” It indicates mental withdrawal; hence in John: Jesus said to his disciples: “Whoever eats my flesh,” etc. Therefore many of his disciples, hearing this, said: “This saying is hard; who can hear it?” And they departed—not locally, but mentally. It indicates a wandering course through vices; hence the Gospel’s account of the prodigal, who went away into a far country. It indicates consent to evil; hence at the beginning of the Psalms: “Blessed is the man who has not gone.”

[Col. 0689C] **Wormwood** (*absinthium*), properly, means the devil because of bitterness, since his teaching is bitter; hence in the Apocalypse: “And the name of the star is called Wormwood,” that is, the devil. It means bitter teaching; hence there: “And the third part of the waters became wormwood,” that is, bitter teaching. It also means punishment; hence Jeremiah: “Of wormwood and gall,” etc.

**Without** (*absque*) is used for “outside”; hence in the Gospel: “They will make you without the synagogues,” that is, outside the synagogue. Sometimes it is used for “without”; hence Job: “My days have passed more swiftly than by a weaver, without any hope.” It also indicates “apart from”; hence in the Song of Songs: “Apart from that which lies hidden within.”

**Abyss** (*abyssus*) properly means the depth of waters; hence in Exodus: “The abysses covered them.” The depth of waters is called *abyssus*, as it were *sine bysso*, “without fine linen,” that is, without whiteness. It means the fabric of the world as it was first created; hence in Genesis: “Darkness was upon the face of the abyss.” The world’s fabric is called an abyss because of its confusion and obscurity; hence the Greek called it *chaos*, that is, “confusion.” It means the deep and inscrutable human heart; hence in Daniel: “You who behold the abysses and sit upon the cherubim,” that is, “you search the abyss of the human heart and sit upon the fullness of knowledge.” It also means God’s hidden judgments; hence in the Psalm: “Your judgments are a great abyss.” It means hell; hence Job: “Have you entered into the depth of the sea and walked in the uttermost parts of the abyss?” As if to say: As I have entered not only the sea—that is, the world—by assuming humanity, but also, through that humanity, freely submitted to death and descended to the lowest parts of hell, as though to great depths, and walked in the uttermost parts of the abyss. Just as the abyss of waters is comprehended by none of our sight, so the hidden things of hell are penetrated by no faculty of our thought, etc.

[Col. 0690A] It means the judgment of human reason; hence in the Psalm: “Abyss calls to abyss.” For abyss to call to abyss is to pass from judgment to judgment. In the sin which a person commits, he finds against himself the judgment of his own reason; and afterwards he is brought before the strictness of the eternal Judge, unless he turns during his lifetime. It also means the devil’s deep cunning; hence in Job: “As the surface of the abyss is held fast,” because, while something like a good appearance of his persuasion is displayed above as though solid ice, his hidden malice in the depths is not seen. It means the heart of a wicked person; hence in Job: “The abyss said: ‘It is not in me.’” A wicked heart is elegantly called an abyss because it is dark through the fluidity of its fall and through the gloom of duplicity. It means the Testament; hence in the Psalm: “Abyss calls to abyss,” that is, one Testament accords with the other. It is fittingly called an abyss because in each Testament many things lie hidden that are in no way open to humankind. It also means persecution; hence in the Psalm: “The abyss is his garment.” As though he said: “He shall not be moved for ever and ever, although the abyss of persecutors is his covering like a garment.”

[Col. 0690C] It means a despairing mind; hence in Job: “Have you entered into the depth of the sea?” The sea, indeed, is the human mind, whose depths God enters when a person is troubled from the depths of his thoughts by his own reflection and the laments of repentance; when he recalls the wickednesses of his former life to memory and shakes his mind, tossed by the waves, in confession. God penetrates the depth of the sea because he transforms despairing hearts. He enters this sea when he humbles the worldly heart; he enters the depth of the sea when he does not disdain to visit minds oppressed even by crimes. Hence it follows: “And have you walked in the uttermost part of the abyss?” The abyss is a criminal mind which, since it cannot comprehend itself, lies hidden from itself in everything that exists, like an obscure abyss. Therefore, to walk in the uttermost parts of the abyss is to convert even the hearts of utterly wicked people and wonderfully reform despairing minds by touching them with the footprints of his visitation. For when, after immense crimes, each person is pierced with compunction, what else does he seem to have done than to have walked in the uttermost parts of the abyss?

[Col. 0690D] According to another exposition, abyss means a human being in the Psalm: “Abyss calls to abyss,” that is, one person calls another to God while preaching some truth. A person is called an abyss because the heart of neither—the caller nor the called—can be known. “The heart of man is deep and inscrutable,” as is found in Jeremiah. According to another exposition, it means punishment in the Psalm: “Abyss calls to abyss,” that is, the punishment inflicted on Adam, so grave for the eating of a single fruit, signifies the punishment to be inflicted on the wicked. It means a wind proceeding from hidden causes; hence in the Psalm: “Placing the abysses in storehouses,” that is, setting winds in the hidden recesses of nature. According to another exposition, it means a person deep in sins: “Placing the abysses in the treasury,” that is, he places among the saints by good works those who were in the depths of sins; and elsewhere in the Song of the Children of Israel: “They descended into the depth of vices.”

**To approach** (*accedere*) properly signifies local movement; hence in the Gospel: “The Pharisees approached Jesus.” It indicates an approach of knowledge or consideration; hence in the Psalm: “Man shall approach the lofty heart.” It indicates an approach of union, as there according to another exposition: “Man shall approach the lofty heart.” It indicates an approach of faith; hence in the Psalm: “Approach him and be enlightened.” For a person approaches God through faith; thus this is the Prophet’s utterance to beginners in faith.

[Col. 0691B] **To receive** (*accipere*), properly: hence in the Gospel: “Jesus took bread and broke it.” It signifies to give; hence the Apostle: “He received gifts among men.” It indicates the inherence of a property in a subject; hence the Apostle: “What have you that you did not receive from God?” It indicates the infusion of grace; hence in the Psalm: “The Lord looked down from heaven and received me.” According to another exposition, it indicates union: “The Lord looked down from heaven and received me,” that is, united me, etc.

**Hawk** (*accipiter*), properly, means a righteous person; hence Gregory: “The feather of the ostrich is like the feather of the heron or the hawk.” This authority will be expounded when the heron is discussed.

**Reclining at table** (*accubitus*), properly: hence the Lord says that the Pharisees desire the first places at table. It means Christ’s Incarnation; hence in the Song of Love: “While the king was at his table,” etc. It means Christ’s Passion, in the cited example according to another exposition. It means the Ascension or sitting at the right hand of the Father; for the cited authority can be expounded in all these ways.

[Col. 0691C] **Heap** (*acervus*), properly, means the Church, because, just as a heap is broad at the bottom and narrow at the top, so it has fewer people in the stricter commandments and more in the common precepts. It also means a mass of sins or idolatry; hence in Solomon’s Proverbs: “He who sacrifices to gods is like one who casts a stone into Mercury’s heap.” One casts a stone into Mercury’s heap who adds sins to sins, or who increases idolatry, signified by Mercury because Mercury, who was called the god of eloquence, was worshipped more especially than any other.

**Vinegar** (*acetum*), properly: as in the Gospel, “And they gave him vinegar mixed with gall.” It means the evil will which the Jews offered to Christ in his Passion; hence in the Psalm: “In my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.”

[Note: [Col. 0691] It seems one should read: “according to which they offered this,” etc.]

**Battle line** (*acies*), properly, means a wedge of warriors; hence the poet says: “Brotherly battle lines.” And in the Song of Songs: “Like an ordered battle line of camps.” It means visual sharpness; hence it is read that the eagle, with the unblunted sharpness of its eyes, penetrates the rays of the sun, etc. It also means the Church; [Col. 0692A] hence in the Song of the Most Beloved: “Terrible as an ordered battle line of camps,” etc.

**Sting** (*aculeus*), properly, means sin; hence in the Ambrosian hymn: “You, death’s … having been conquered”; and the Apostle says in the Epistle to the Corinthians: “Where, O death, is your sting?” It means the piercing deception of a heretic; hence in the Apocalypse: “And they had stings in their tails,” namely those of the locusts. There, heretics are understood by the locusts, and the wicked deceptions of heretics by the stings.

**Needle** (*acus*), properly, means compunction of heart; hence in Mark: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle,” that is, for a sinner, having laid aside the burden of sin, to pass through repentance into the kingdom of heaven, than for a rich person—that is, one who loves riches—to enter the kingdom of heaven. It also means Christ’s Passion, in the same passage according to another exposition: “It is easier for a camel,” etc. It means the malice of persecutors or heretics; hence in Isaiah: “On that day he shall remove the needle and darts.” On the day of judgment the Lord will remove the persecutions of the wicked and their pleasures, or their pride.

[Col. 0692B] **To** (*ad*) sometimes indicates local movement; hence in John: “Nicodemus came to Jesus by night.” Sometimes it indicates mental movement; hence in the Psalm: “For to you, O Lord, I shall pray.” Sometimes it indicates temporal movement; hence in Daniel: “There shall be seventy weeks unto Christ.” Sometimes it indicates vocal movement; hence in the Pentateuch: “The Lord spoke to Moses.” Sometimes it indicates sensory movement, according to our customary expression: “This man looks toward the poor.” Sometimes it indicates final movement; hence the Apostle: “Whatever things were written were written for our instruction,” etc. Sometimes it indicates the movement of comparing one thing with another; hence in the Apostles’ Creed: “He sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty,” etc. Sometimes it indicates likeness; hence it is said: “This is done after the model of that,” etc. Sometimes it is used for “according to”; hence in Genesis: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness.” Sometimes it is used for “before”; hence in Samuel: “The sons of Eli always slept at the door of the tabernacle,” that is, before it; and in the Pentateuch: “The Lord spoke to Moses while standing at the door of the tabernacle,” etc. Sometimes it indicates “against”; hence the Apostle: “In vain I fought against beasts at Ephesus,” that is, against bestial men at Ephesus. Sometimes it is used for “toward”; hence [Col. 0692D] the prophet Isaiah: “I shall set my throne toward the north.” It is also used for “for” [perhaps “through”]; hence the Psalmist: “They tested me at the waters of contradiction.”

**Diamond** (*adamas*), properly, means eternity, as is said through the prophet Jeremiah: “The sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus upon an adamantine nail.” Diamond is a stone so hard that it cannot be cut by iron. By the iron stylus is signified a strong judgment, and by the diamond nail an eternal end. The sin of the Jews is said to be written with an iron stylus upon a diamond nail because the Jews’ guilt is reserved to be punished at the end by God’s strong judgment.

**Fat** (*adeps*) means the fat of the entrails. It also means pride; hence it is said of the proud and rich person in Job: “His entrails are filled with fat,” that is, pride. It means the carnal understanding which the Jews had in the Law; hence in the Psalm: “They have enclosed their fat,” that is, they retained their carnal understanding in the letter of the Law, etc. It means the marrow of Holy Scripture; hence the Psalmist: “He satisfies you with the fat of wheat.” According to another exposition, it means charity in the same authority. It also means abundance; hence in the Psalm: “Their iniquity came forth as if from fat.” It means wisdom which is in hiddenness, the fatness of the soul, without which the soul withers; hence in the Psalm: “May my soul be filled as with fat and richness.” It means strength; hence: “The kingdom of David over Saul and Jonathan,” that is, “from the fat of the mighty [Col. 0693B] and the blood of the slain.”

**To be present** (*adesse*) indicates presence in a place. It indicates readiness to obey; hence in Genesis: “Abraham, Abraham,” and he answered: “Behold, I am present.” It indicates the giving of help; hence in a certain prayer to God: “Be present with us, O God.” It indicates likeness of nature; hence in Job: “One day, when the sons of God—that is, angels—had come, they were present before the Lord, and Satan among them”: not principally or locally, but by likeness of nature, because he is of spiritual nature, as an angel is. Here “day” indicates not time but the brightness of angelic nature.

**Young woman** (*adolescentula*), properly, means a believer newly converted to the faith; hence in the Song of Songs: “The young women loved you exceedingly.” Those are called young women who have already been reborn in Christ but are not yet strong enough to preach Christ’s name.

[Col. 0693C] **To adore** (*adorare*) properly means to render to God the worship due to him, whether *theosebia* (“worship of God”), *theosis* (“deification”), or *latriosis* (“service” or “worship”). This consists in contemplation, prayer, offering, and the like; hence in the Psalm: “Come, let us adore and fall down before God.” It also means to render worship to a human being or another rational creature, and is called *dulia*. This consists in obedience, kneeling, bowing the head, and the like; hence in Genesis: Abraham saw three angels and adored one, that is, rendered them the worship due to them. It means to venerate; hence in the antiphon: “We adore your cross, O Lord,” that is, we venerate it. It means to pray to God; hence: “I shall enter into your house; I shall adore.” To pray to God is to tend toward God in faith, hope, and charity.

**Against** (*adversus* or *adversum*) is used for “against,” as we commonly say: “This man fights against such a lord.” *Adversum* is not prefixed to a word beginning with a vowel.

**Egypt** (*Aegyptus*), properly, means the world; hence Isaiah: “I shall ascend upon a light cloud and enter Egypt,” that is, human nature, and shall come into the world through assumed humanity. It means gentile people; hence in the Psalm: “Envoys shall come from Egypt,” that is, holy preachers converted from the Gentiles to the faith will come by Christ’s mercy.

[Col. 0693D] **To emulate** (*aemulari*) indicates love; hence the Apostle: “I am jealous over you with God’s jealousy.” It also indicates indignation; hence the Psalmist: “Do not be indignant at evildoers.” [Col. 0694A] It indicates envy, as in the cited authority.

**Air** (*aer*), properly: hence Paul: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the principalities and powers of this air.” It means a prophet; hence in the Psalm: “Dark water in the clouds of the air,” that is, subtle understanding in the writings of the prophets. It means a changeable soul or the mobility of the worldly mind; hence: “Suddenly air is gathered into clouds.” Air is gathered when unstable minds are strengthened in the solidity of virtue by the grace of heavenly regard. It means the loftiness of contemplation by which we contemplate God; hence Paul: “We shall be caught up with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air.” It means emptiness or vanity; hence the same apostle: “You will be speaking into the air, however many kinds of languages there are.” It also means a demon; [Col. 0694B] hence Paul: “Thus I do not box as one beating the air,” that is, I do not merely resist the demon, but chastise my body and reduce it to servitude.

**Verdigris** (*aerugo*) is rust that consumes gold or silver. It means pride, which consumes every good habit in a person, in accordance with the saying:

> Pride, when joined to them, defiles noble virtues.

And in Matthew’s Gospel it is read: “Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither verdigris nor moth destroys.” It means lust, which consumes the treasures of human faculties; in the cited authority, lust may be understood by verdigris.

**Bronze** (*aes*), properly, means a prelate whose deed does not correspond to his word; hence the Apostle, speaking in the person of a false preacher, says: “I shall be like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal.” It means the hard and insensitive heart of the wicked; hence Job: “Neither is my strength the strength of stones, nor is my flesh bronze.” Here bronze signifies the hearts of the insensitive, who often receive heavenly blows yet are not softened by any blow of correction. Bronze means those persevering in goodness; hence it is said of Antichrist in Job: “He will regard iron as straw and bronze as rotten wood.” Iron is sharpened persistently in order that the adversary may be wounded, while bronze is scarcely consumed at all by rust. By iron is signified the dart of preaching; by bronze, perseverance in goodness. It means the resonant voice of preachers; hence Ezekiel: “And sparks, like the appearance of glowing bronze.” By bronze, a resonant metal, the voices of preachers are signified, because “their sound has gone out into all the earth.” Glowing bronze is aptly named because the life of a preacher resounds and burns: it burns with desire; it resounds in speech. Thus glowing bronze is preaching kindled by divine heat. But sparks issue from glowing bronze, because fiery words proceed from their exhortations to the ears of hearers. The words of preachers are rightly called sparks because they kindle into divine love those whose hearts they touch. It also means that bronze which does not abandon its malice; hence Isaiah: “The house of Israel has turned into dross.”

[Col. 0694D] **Summer** (*aestas*), properly, means the day of judgment; hence Solomon: “Because of the cold, the sluggard would not plough; therefore he shall beg in summer and nothing shall be given to him.” For one who now neglects to work well shall lack eternal life on the day of judgment.

**Heat** (*aestus*), properly, means labour or tribulation; hence in Matthew: “You have made them equal to us, who have borne the burden of the day and the heat,” that is, of daily toil. It means the ardour of vices; hence Isaiah: “A tabernacle shall be a shade by day from the heat.” The agitation of the sea is also called *aestus*.

**Eternal** (*aeternum*) is that which lacks beginning and end by nature, as God does. It means perpetual; hence Moses: “The Lord shall reign for ever and beyond,” that is, when the creature exists, he too shall exist; and beyond, that is, when other things cease to exist, he never shall. This is to say: although every creature can have an end, although by nature [lacuna].

[Note: [Col. 0695D] Something is missing.]

It means everlasting; hence: “For ever and unto the age of the age,” that is, everlastingly and unto the age succeeding this age. It means the continuation of temporal life; hence Horace:

> He shall be a slave all his life who does not know how to use a little.

That is, throughout the whole time of his life. Note that there is a difference among *aeternum* (“eternal”), *perenne* (“everlasting”), and *perpetuum* (“perpetual”), as is indicated in these verses:

> Give “eternal” neither beginning nor end, as with God;  
> Give “perpetual” a beginning, but let it lack an end, as angels and the soul;  
> Let “everlasting” have a beginning and an end, as certain bodies.

[Col. 0695B] **Field** (*ager*), properly, means the gentile world; hence in the Psalm: “The beauty of the field is with me,” because Christ benefited the Gentiles more than the Jews. It means the present world; hence Christ in the Gospel: “The field is the world.” It means our body; hence Solomon: “Cultivate your field diligently, that afterwards you may build your house,” that is, cleanse your body of the thorns of vices so that the structure of virtues may be built within. It also means Holy Scripture; hence Job says of heretics: “They do not reap their field,” that is, by perverting Holy Scripture they do not make it their own. It means Christ; hence in Genesis: “Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field.” Christ is rightly called a full field because he is refreshed with the flowers of virtues, and the Lord blessed him with diverse kinds of spiritual gifts. It also means the Church; hence in the Song of Songs: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys”; and elsewhere: “The beauty of the field is with me.”

[Col. 0695C] **To do / act** (*agere*), properly: hence in the Psalm: “He did not wish to understand so as to act well.” When said of God, *agere* does not indicate action, but authority; hence God is called *auctor* (“author”), not from *ago, agis* (“I act, you act”), but from *authentia* (“authority”). It means to render or pay; hence the Apostle Paul: “I give thanks to my God,” that is, “I render [thanks].” It means to undergo suffering; hence: “I do what I do not wish.” For “I desire” indicates not action but passion, just as neither “to fear,” “to will,” “to desire,” nor “to rejoice” indicates action. Some passions are soothing, such as joy; others are destructive, such as fear and the like. A person acts without acting, but by omission, as when someone neglects to go to church. It also means to lead; hence in Exodus: “Moses was driving the flocks into the interior of the wilderness,” that is, leading them. It means to govern; hence: “Those who are led by the Spirit of God are not subject to the law,” that is, are governed. It also means to say; hence one commonly says: “This book treats of this,” that is, speaks of it.

[Col. 0696A] **Lamb** (*agnus*), properly: hence the Law says that a year-old lamb was offered. It means Christ; hence in the Gospel: “Behold, the Lamb of God”; and in the Apocalypse: “I saw the Lamb standing,” and elsewhere: “They washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb.” It means the meek and innocent person; hence the Lord says to Peter in John: “If you love me, feed my lambs,” that is, the lesser members of God’s Church. By sheep we understand the greater; by lambs, the lesser. It means a predestined believer; hence in the Gospel: “The Lord shall set the lambs,” that is, the elect, at his right hand.

**Husbandman** (*agricola*), properly, means God the Father; hence in the Gospel: “I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman.” It means a preacher; hence the Apostle: “It is right that the husbandman should eat of his fruit.”

[Col. 0696B] **Husbandry** (*agricultura*), properly, means the faithful; hence the Apostle: “You are God’s husbandry.” It means the exposition of Holy Scripture, insofar as Holy Scripture is called a field.

**Wing** (*ala*), properly: as in “Jerusalem, how often I wished to gather your children.” It also means the protection of God’s charity and mercy; hence in the Psalm: “Protect me under the shadow of your wings,” that is, under the fortification of your protection. According to another exposition, it is God’s justice or mercy: “Under the shadow of your wings,” that is, under the protection of your justice or mercy; mercy is the right wing, justice the left. It means God’s commandment; hence [Col. 0696C] in the Psalm: “They shall triumph in the protection of your wings.” It also means human thoughts; hence in Job: “Does the hawk take feather by your wisdom, spreading its wings toward the south?” The hawk, each year at the season of the south wind, casts off its old feather when a new one grows. The sense is: Have you granted understanding to any chosen person, so that, as the Holy Spirit breathes, he may open the wings of his thoughts in confession, cast off the weights of his former way of life, and put on the feathers of virtues? It also means acts of pride and vainglory; hence Zechariah: “I lifted up my eyes and saw, and behold, two women going forth, and there was a spirit in their wings,” that is, pride and vainglory, in whose wings—that is, acts—is the spirit, that is, the devil, whom they always serve. It means the superstitions of hypocrites; hence in Job: “When they have opportunity, they will spread their wings on high,” because, when a hypocrite finds a favourable occasion, he displays a superstitious religion outwardly.

[Col. 0696D] **Elsewhere / at another time / otherwise** (*alias*) indicates place; hence one says: “It happened elsewhere,” that is, in another place. It indicates time, as when we say: “It was said at another time.” It indicates manner; hence in Genesis Abraham says: “Otherwise, she is my sister,” that is, “in another way I can say that she is my sister,” etc.

**Aloes** (*aloes*) is a kind of gum. It means good reputation; hence in the Song of Songs: “Myrrh and aloes with all the finest perfumes.”

[Col. 0697A] **Altar** properly denotes earth, as in Genesis: “You shall make me an altar of earth.” It denotes faith. As the Jews in the Old Testament offered material calves, so we offer the calves of our souls—that is, the good thoughts of the heart; and as victims are offered on a material altar, so good works are offered on the altar of faith. Hence in the Gospel: “If you offer your gift at the altar,” that is, your good work upon the altar of faith. It denotes Christ, as in the Apocalypse: “Beneath the altar of God I heard the voices of the slain.” It denotes Christ’s body, as in the Psalm: “Even to the horn of the altar,” that is, even to the eminence of the sacrifice. It denotes God in the Psalm: “I shall go in unto the altar of God,” which the exposition immediately explains: “Unto God who makes my youth glad.” It denotes eternal life, as in the Psalm: “Then they shall lay calves upon your altar.” [Col. 0697B] It denotes the Church; thus this authority may be explained: “Then they shall lay,” that is, the greater prelates, “calves,” that is, the lesser persons, “upon your altar,” that is, the Church—that is, through the preaching of the prelates the lesser persons shall belong to the Church, etc. It denotes the mind, as in the Psalm: “I shall go round about your altar, O Lord,” that is, I shall adorn my mind, in which, or upon which, I offer you a sacrifice of praise, with virtues. And as an altar is called a *high shrine* (*alta ara*), so too the mind is something higher and more worthy in a human being. In this sense that Gospel passage may be explained: “If you offer your gift at the altar,” that is, prayer in the mind. It also denotes an ecclesiastical sacrament, as in the Psalm: “Your altars, O Lord of hosts.” Above, the faithful person had said that the sparrow finds itself a house and the turtle-dove a nest; that is, the faithful person finds ecclesiastical sacraments in which he stores the increase of good works. And lest anyone should ask, “What is this nest?” there is added: “Your altars, O Lord of hosts,” etc.

**Fattened beast** (*altile*), properly, etc., denotes a martyr, as in the Gospel: “My bulls and fattened beasts have been killed.” The bulls are the greater persons, the fattened beasts the lesser, who were killed for Christ’s faith.

**Height** (*altitudo*) properly denotes depth, that is, the incomprehensibility of God’s secrets, as the Apostle says: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom of God!” It denotes the sublimity of power, as Paul says: “Neither height nor depth shall separate us from the charity of God.” It denotes the malice of the Jews, as in the Psalm: “I have come into the depths of the sea,” that is, into the malice of the Jews. It denotes [Col. 0697D] the greatness of tribulations, as in the preceding example according to another exposition; and the sense is: “I have come into the depths of the sea,” that is, I exposed myself to the manifold tribulation inflicted by the Jews.

**High / the deep** (*altum*) properly occurs in the Psalm: “Jesus ascending on high.” It denotes the high sea, as Virgil says:

> Scarce out of sight of the Sicilian land, into the deep.

It denotes noble birth, as the same author says: “From lofty blood,” that is, from a noble family. It denotes proudly, as the Apostle says: “Do not think high things,” that is, proudly, but fear.

**Bitterness**, properly, denotes the misery of this world, as in Job: “I have not sinned, and my eye remains amid bitterness,” etc. It denotes the evil desire for temporal things which one cannot possess; hence another says: “He dies in the bitterness of his soul, without any riches.” [Col. 0698A] It denotes the harshness of punishment, as in Job: “I shall converse with the bitterness of my soul.” It denotes the punishment of Gehenna, as Job says: “For you write bitterness against me.” It denotes harshness of speech; thus it is said of Antichrist in the Psalm: “Whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness.”

**Ambition**, properly, denotes an array or display. Thus it is read concerning Felix’s wife in the Acts of the Apostles that she came “with much *ambitio*,” that is, with much display; or “with much ambition,” that is, with many attendants.

**Circuit** (*ambitus*), properly. In Esther: “which are contained by the circuit,” that is, the revolution, “of heaven.” It also denotes desire for honour, insofar as desire is customarily divided into avarice and *ambitus*, that is, ambition.

**To walk** properly signifies progress in virtues, as in the Psalm: “I walked in the midst of my heart.” It signifies progress in good works, as in the Psalm: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord.” It signifies action, as the Lord says to Peter in John: “When you were younger, you girded yourself and walked where you wished”—you did whatever you wished.

**Amen** is said to derive from *a*, “without,” and *mene*, “defect”; hence: “Behold, I come quickly. Amen,” that is, without failure—that is, I do not cease to come to the faithful. Sometimes it is an indeclinable noun, as in: “I am Amen,” that is, Truth. Sometimes it is an adverb of affirmation when affirmatively used, as there: “Amen, I say to you.” Sometimes it is a concluding word when placed conclusively at the end of a prayer: *amen*, that is, “let it be so.”

**Amethyst**, wholly red and emitting from itself, as it were, little flames like a rose, signifies those who amid the torments of suffering which they endure for God emit, as it were, flames of charity from themselves, praying for those who strike them and grieving more over the persecutors’ sin than over the penalties they endure. It is placed last in the building of the heavenly Jerusalem because it signifies those who pray for enemies. For it is the virtue of virtues to pray for enemies and persecutors, and few are found to have done this. Yet in the Old Testament we find two, Moses and Samuel; and in the New, two, namely Christ and Stephen.

**Friend**, properly, is so called by reason of kinship; hence it is said to the Jewish people in Exodus: “You shall love your friend,” that is, your neighbour by race, namely a Jew, “and you shall hate your enemy,” that is, a Gentile. [Col. 0698D] A friend is so called by reason of nature, as in Luke: “Friend, lend me three loaves.” Here the soul is called friend by reason of nature, because when the soul returns to itself from the way—that is, from worldly wandering—it is said to return. By the three loaves is understood faith in the Trinity. A friend is so called by the performance of a work, as in the Gospel: “You are my friends if you do what I command you.” A friend is so called by pretence, as the Gospel says of the hypocrite: “Friend, for what purpose have you entered?” A friend is so called by reason of the sacrament—that is, by the sacrament of faith, not the faith of the sacrament. According to this exposition, the authority may be explained thus: “Friend, how did you enter here without a [Col. 0699A] wedding garment?” that is, charity. A friend is so called by reason of familiarity, as Christ says in the Gospel: “Friend, for what have you come?” For Judas had been familiar with Jesus. It is also so called by reason of a benefit conferred, as in John: “No one has greater charity than to lay down his life for his friends.”

**Love**, properly, denotes desire, in the sense in which we customarily say: “This man is held by love of earthly things.” It denotes charity, as in the Song: “Strengthen me with flowers, surround me with apples, for I languish with love.” It denotes the Holy Spirit, as a certain prose hymn calls the Holy Spirit “the love of the Father and the Son.” It denotes Christ, as in the Ambrosian hymn: “Jesus, our redemption, love.” It denotes natural affection, as in the book of Kings: “I grieve for you, my brother Jonathan, very lovely beyond the love of women.”

**Almond tree**, properly, denotes the primitive Church: “The almond tree shall flower, the locust shall grow fat, the caper plant shall be scattered.” In the *Moralia*: the almond tree flowers before other trees, and therefore signifies the primitive Church, in which the locust was soon made fat, because dry Gentiledom was filled with the richness of heavenly grace. But the caper plant shall be scattered, because Judaea, remaining in its barrenness, lost the order of life.

**Angel** is not the name of a nature but of an office. All ministering spirits can be called angels, as in the Psalm: “Who makes his angels spirits.” Yet the word is restricted to designate the lower order, because messengers are more frequently sent from that order. It denotes [Col. 0699C] Christ, as in: “Angel of great counsel,” and in Malachi: “The angel whom you desire.” It denotes John the Baptist, as in Malachi: “Behold, I send my angel, who shall prepare the way.” It also denotes a priest or bishop, as the Apostle says: “Women ought not to be in church except with veiled head, because of the angels standing around,” that is, the priests; and in the Apocalypse: “Write to the angel of Ephesus”; and in Malachi: “The lips of the priest guard knowledge, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.” It denotes concupiscence or the tinder of sin, as the Apostle says: “There was given to me a thorn, an angel of Satan, to buffet me.” It denotes the soul, as the maidservant said in the Acts of the Apostles when Peter, freed from chains, came to the door: “It is his angel,” that is, his soul. Angels are also called [Col. 0699D] demons, in many places.

**Corner** properly denotes faith, gathering the two peoples, namely Jew and Gentile, into one, as in the Psalm: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.” It also denotes concealment or obscurity, according to the customary saying: “Truth does not seek corners.” It denotes deviation from uprightness of conduct, as is read of one who abandons the narrow way that leads to life, because he passes through the streets beside the corner and near the way to that woman’s house.

**Soul** properly denotes the rational spirit which, together with the body, comes into the constitution of the human being, as in the Gospel: “I have power to lay down my soul.” [Col. 0700A] It denotes a human being, because it is a part of a human being; thus Genesis relates that eight souls were in the ark, that is, eight human beings. It denotes the animal spirit by which a brute animal is animated, as in Genesis: “Let the waters bring forth creeping things of living soul,” that is, possessing a living soul, that is, an animating spirit. And in the same place: “God created every living and moving soul.” It denotes a poor person, for Leviticus distinguishes between the offering of a ruler and that of a soul, that is, a poor person. A poor person is called a soul because, as the soul is something incomprehensible, so a poor person is said to be incomprehensible and is not counted among human beings. It also denotes life by cause, because the soul is the cause of life, as in the Gospel: “He who hates his soul in this world,” that is, whoever does not care for temporal life for God’s sake, [Col. 0700B] obtains eternal life. It denotes sensuality, which is the lower power of the soul, the name of the subject being used to designate a property of that subject. Hence in the canticle of the Blessed Virgin Mary: “My soul magnifies the Lord,” that is, I magnify the Lord according to the animal portion of my soul. It also denotes a demon, as in the *Asclepius* [Note: [Col. 0699D] The dialogue called *Asclepius*, concerning God, human beings, and the totality of things, survives only in a Latin [Col. 0700D] translation; though attributed by some to Apuleius, it is commonly believed to be by Mercury Trismegistus], where “Mercuries” are called enclosed souls. It denotes blood, as Virgil says: “He vomits forth his purple soul.” It denotes reason, as Job says: “My soul chooses hanging,” that is, reason, the higher part of my soul, is suspended from the desire for earthly things and raised toward heavenly things. It denotes the will proceeding from the soul, as in Genesis: “Simeon and Levi, vessels of iniquity in warfare—[Col. 0700C] may my soul not enter into your counsel,” that is, my will did not consent to your counsel when you killed the Shechemites. It also denotes an animal, as in Genesis: “God created great whales and every living soul,” that is, a living animal, because the soul is part of an animal. For the name of a part is used to designate the whole. It denotes animal nature, which man possessed from his origin. For from the first origin man possessed animality, namely an animal nature, requiring food and drink. Thus before sin man is said to have been animal, that is, alimentary, as though requiring the nourishment of food; hence: “Man was made into a living soul,” that is, possessing animality. It denotes gluttony, as in the Gospel: “Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years,” [Col. 0700D] as if to say: Through provisions which abound for me for many years I shall satisfy my soul, that is, my gluttony or appetite. It denotes the voracity that proceeds from gluttony; thus the name “soul” is used to designate voracity, as in the Psalm: “Hell has enlarged its soul,” that is, its voracity. It denotes bodily life, as in Leviticus: “Every soul is in the blood,” that is, every life. It denotes mind or thought, as in the Psalm: “How long shall I place counsels in my soul?” that is, in my mind or thought. Those are also called souls by whose example others live spiritually in the Church, just as teachers are called the eye of the Church because others see spiritually through their teaching, [Col. 0701A] and the weak in the Church are called its belly. Hence in the Psalm: “My eye is troubled in anger, my soul,” that is, in my mind, “and my belly.” It denotes intention, as in Job: “I carry my soul in my hands.” To carry one’s soul in one’s hands is nothing other than to display the intention of one’s heart in action.

**Animal** properly denotes an animate, sentient substance; thus a human being is called an animal. Sometimes it denotes only a brute animal, as when Moses, speaking of Noah and his sons, says in Genesis: “They and every animal entered the ark.” Sometimes it denotes only a rational animal, as in the Psalm: “You open your hand and fill every animal with blessing,” because he has opened the kindness of his power to all [Col. 0701B] human beings; for all things are in his power, and he fills with temporal and spiritual blessing every rational animal insofar as it can be blessed.

It denotes the likeness of an animal, as in the Apocalypse: “And the fourth animal was like a flying eagle,” that is, the fourth likeness of an animal. It also denotes one who is simple, meek, and humble, as in the Psalm: “Your animals shall dwell in the Church.” It denotes the Testament, as Habakkuk says to Christ: “You shall be known in the midst of two animals,” that is, between the Old and New Testaments. The faithful in the Church are also called animals, as in the Psalm: “Small animals with great,” that is, greater and lesser persons. It denotes thoughts somewhat raised from the earth but still seeking the rewards [Col. 0701C] of earthly recompense, as in Ezekiel: “And I entered and saw, and behold every likeness of creeping things and an abomination of animals.” For in creeping things thoughts that are wholly earthly are signified; but in animals, thoughts somewhat raised from earth but still seeking the rewards of earthly recompense. Creeping things cling to the earth with their whole bodies, whereas animals are suspended from the earth by their bellies, though by the appetite of the throat they are always inclined toward earth. It denotes the righteous, as in Ezekiel: “And I heard the sound of the other animals striking one against another.” By the wings of the animals we must understand the virtues of the saints, who, when they despise earthly things, are lifted in flight toward heavenly things. But the flying animals strike one another in turn with their wings, because the minds of the saints, in desiring things above, are stirred by considering one another’s virtues. For the wing of a saint strikes me by the example of holiness—that is, properly, inflames me toward better things—and I strike my neighbour with my wing if at some time I show someone a good work for imitation. [Col. 0701D]

**Animal-like** (*animale*) properly denotes a thing pertaining to the soul or to an animal. Thus in natural philosophy a distinction is made between the animal spirit which animates a brute animal and the rational spirit which animates a human being. It also denotes a person according to the sense of the soul, who judges concerning God by consideration of earthly things or by natural reasoning; hence the Apostle: “The animal man does not receive the things that are of the Spirit of God.” It denotes a person devoted to the senses of the flesh, who does not believe that anything can occur except according to natural causation. In this sense the aforementioned saying of the Apostle may be understood: “The animal man does not receive,” etc. It means, as it were, alimentary—that is, needing nourishment, food, or drink—such as our body is now; hence the Apostle: “An animal body is sown; in the future, a spiritual one.” It denotes carnal, as the Apostle says: “First indeed the animal, then the spiritual.” For in a human being there is first the animal or carnal, as vice before baptism is received; but after baptism, the spiritual, that is, virtue. [Col. 0702A]

**Ring** properly occurs where Genesis relates that Judah gave Tamar a ring, that is, a bracelet, as an earnest—that is, as a pledge. It denotes faith, as Luke relates that the head of the household, rejoicing with his returning son, said: “Bring forth the first robe and a ring”; there the ring signifies faith. [Col. 0702B]

**Year** properly occurs in Luke: “In the fifteenth year.” It denotes the preaching of heavenly grace, because as time is made up by days gathered into a year, so in heavenly grace a manifold life of virtues is brought to completion. Hence Isaiah: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me,” etc., “that I might preach an acceptable year to the Lord.” An acceptable year is preached to the Lord when it is preached that the faithful people are to be illumined by grace. Or a year denotes a multitude of faithful people, because as a year is named from a multitude of days, so the Church is completed from the gathering of the faithful. Thus Job, speaking of the devil, says: “May he not be counted among the days of the year, nor numbered among the months,” because the devil, oppressed by the darkness of his pride, sees indeed the advent of the Redeemer, but shall by no means attain pardon together with God’s elect. [Col. 0702C] It denotes the time of grace, as in the Psalm: “You shall bless the crown of your year of kindness,” that is, the multitude of faithful people converted to you in the time of grace. It denotes a revolution or turn, as Jacob says to his wives in Genesis: “Laban your father changed my wages ten years,” that is, ten times or revolutions, because each year he changed the wages twice. And by what was said, Jacob ought to have served him seven years, because he changed them in the sixth year; he departed, and so in the fifth year he changed them ten times. It also denotes a part of a year by synecdoche, so that what belongs to a part is attributed to the whole. Thus Christ is said to have lived thirty-three years, though he lived only thirty-two years and three months, which are taken [Col. 0702D] as a year. It denotes a month, as Daniel says Nebuchadnezzar was an ox for seven years, that is, seven months. It denotes God’s eternity, as in the Psalm: “You are the same, and your years shall not fail,” that is, eternity.

**Before** as a preposition denotes place, as in: “This man goes before that one.” It denotes time, as in John: “Before the feast day of Passover, he came there to Bethany.” It denotes eternity, as in the Psalm: “Before the morning star I begot you.” It denotes presence, as in the Psalm: “Come, let us adore and fall down before God.” It denotes unworthiness or inferiority, as in the Gospel: “He who comes after me is before me,” etc.

**Before** as an adverb sometimes denotes place, as when it is said: “This one goes before, that one behind,” that is, this one in this place, that one in another place. It also denotes order, as when it is said: “These go before, those behind,” etc. Sometimes it denotes time, as when it is said: “I came before he did,” that is, at an earlier time. Sometimes it denotes eternity, as in Wisdom: “Before he made anything.” Sometimes it is used negatively, as in the Gospel: “Before they came together,” that is, they never came together; she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0703A]

**Forewall** (*antemurale*) properly denotes a prophet, as Isaiah says: “A wall and a forewall shall be set in her.” Christ is called the wall because of the fortification of his protection: he prevents the incursions of evil spirits from reaching our hearts. Every prophet is called a forewall because, before the Lord appeared in flesh, he was sent by prophesying to preserve the faith. [Col. 0703B]

**Cave** properly denotes a wicked heart, as Job says of the devil: “The beast shall enter its hiding-place and dwell in its cave,” because the devil inhabits the hearts of all the reprobate. It denotes the thought or heart of the righteous, as the Lord says: “Will you take prey for the lioness and fill the souls of her cubs, who lie in caves?”

**To open** properly denotes the opening of sacred Scripture, as in: after the resurrection Christ opened—that is, expounded—to those going to Emmaus the Scriptures, that they might understand. It denotes preparation of the mind for faith and love of God, as in the Psalm: “Open your gates, O princes”; elsewhere: “Open the gates of justice.” It denotes dissolution, as in Genesis: “The floodgates [Col. 0703C] of heaven were opened,” that is, the clouds were dissolved into rains. See “floodgates” below. It denotes manifestation, as in: when Christ was baptized, the heavens were opened, and such great brightness appeared in the air as though, with the aerial and starry heaven unlocked, the empyrean heaven appeared.

**Bees** properly denote the Jews who plotted Christ’s crucifixion, not for their own advantage but for that of others, just as bees do not make honey for themselves but for others. This is what Christ means in the Psalm: “The Jews surrounded me in the Passion,” devising benefit not for themselves but for others, like bees, which, while they think they are storing honey for themselves, make it for others.

**With** (*apud*) sometimes denotes place, as in Acts: “He remained with him fifteen days,” etc. It also denotes a person, as Jacob says to Laban in Genesis: “With whomever your gods are found, let him die.” It denotes the inherence of a property in its subject, as we customarily say: “This man has great counsel within himself,” etc. It denotes identity, as in the Psalm: “With the Lord is mercy,” that is, because the Lord is mercy. It denotes authority, as in the Psalm: “With the Lord a man’s steps shall be directed.” It denotes distinction, as in John: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God.” Augustine explains it thus: as one person with another. [Col. 0703D]

**Water** properly denotes the material of the world’s fabric, as in Genesis: “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters,” that is, the Spirit, who is Lord, over the material of the world’s fabric, as an artisan’s mind is over an ark. Another book has: “He cherished the waters.” [Col. 0704A] It also denotes primordial matter, because as moisture supplies matter for every bodily thing, so that primordial matter does for every body. And as water receives the form of whatever thing it is poured into, so that matter was capable of receiving every form. It denotes wisdom, because “he gave him to drink of the water of saving wisdom.” And elsewhere: “All you who thirst, come to the waters.” It also denotes the infusion of the Holy Spirit, as in the Gospel: “He who believes in me, from his belly shall flow rivers of living water”; this is explained when it is added: “Now he said this concerning the Spirit, whom those believing in him were to receive,” etc. It denotes heresy, as the woman representing heresy flatters with crafty persuasions, saying in Solomon: “Stolen waters are sweeter,” that is, the opinions of heretics are sweeter to the simple and unlearned than Catholic doctrines, because heretics always wish to remain in the pleasure of the flesh, whereas the Church’s teaching commands abstinence from carnal desires. [Col. 0704B]

It denotes tribulation, as in the Psalm: “Save me, O God, for waters have entered even unto my soul.” It denotes a people, as in the Apocalypse: “Many waters,” that is, many peoples, because a numerous people both makes a sound in life through the tumult of the flesh and daily flows away through the deficiency of mortality. It also denotes the mind of the righteous, as Job says: “He weighs the waters by measure,” that is, the minds of the good, lest, when they are carried up to the heights, they become proud, are weighed down by temptations under a certain measure of virtues. For holy persons who, through the uplifting Spirit, are carried up to the heights are, so long as they are in this life, checked by certain temptations lest any become proud, so that they cannot progress as much as they wish. But lest they be puffed up with pride, a certain measure of virtues is brought about in them. The flesh draws downward lest the spirit exalt itself; and the spirit draws upward lest the flesh cast one down. The spirit raises us so that we do not lie in the lowest places; the flesh weighs us down so that we are not lifted up by the highest things. But if the spirit did not raise us, the flesh would tempt us and would without doubt cast us down to the depths by its temptation. [Col. 0704C] It denotes the soft hearts of the Jews, as Job says: “The waters are hardened in the likeness of stone,” because the hearts of the Jews, which had been softer and penetrable by faith, are changed into the hardness of the Gentiles, while the Gentiles by believing are changed into the softness of the Jews. It denotes sacred Scripture without understanding, as in the Psalm: “Dark water in the clouds of the air,” that is, obscure understanding in the prophets. It denotes falsehood, as Isaiah says: “Your tavern-keepers mix water with wine,” that is, your preachers mingle falsehood with truth. It denotes wicked speech, and also an outflow of speech, as Solomon says: “He who lets out water is the beginning of quarrels,” that is, whoever does not restrain speech destroys concord. It denotes the slippery desires of the wicked, as in the Psalm: “He placed waters as in a belly.” This occurs when God checks and confines the slippery desires of the wicked from carrying out evils by the straitness of impossibility. It denotes unbelief, as Job says: “They shall pass away from snowy waters,” as though to say: Whoever is not humbly restrained from unbelief [Col. 0705A] under the bonds of discipline slips into error through unrestrained wisdom.

It denotes weeping, as Job says: “My roaring is like overflowing waters.” It denotes the infernal torment of want, as Job says in the condemnation of the wicked rich man: “Want seized him as water,” who will be tormented by the want of hell. It denotes humility or compunction, as Job says: “If I have washed myself with waters of snow.” Note that spring water rises from the earth, while snow water falls from the air. Therefore, whoever weeps for earthly things washes himself, as it were, with spring water; whoever weeps for eternal things washes himself with snow water. It also denotes earthly delight, as Christ says in the Gospel: “Whoever drinks of this water shall thirst again,” because earthly delight does not remove the thirst of desire. It denotes a preacher, as in the Psalm: “The springs of waters appeared,” that is, the true teaching of preachers appeared. [Col. 0705B]

It denotes the Holy Spirit, as in the Psalm: “He shall be like a tree planted beside the courses of waters.” The Holy Spirit is called water on account of three properties common to him and water. Water cools; hence in the Gospel: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you.” Water satisfies; hence Ecclesiasticus: “He gave him to drink of the water of saving wisdom,” and the Gospel saying: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.” And it is so called on account of free movement, as in the Gospel: “The Spirit breathes where he wills.”

It denotes hell, as in Exodus: “They went down like lead in mighty waters.” It denotes refreshment, as in the Gospel: “Father Abraham, have mercy [Col. 0705C] on me, and send Lazarus.” It denotes the sacrament of baptism, as in the Psalm: “He took me out of many waters.” It denotes the frozen hearts of unbelievers, as in the Psalm: “His spirit shall blow, and the waters shall flow.” For when the Holy Spirit is breathed into sinners, who are called waters because of the flow of sins, the waters flow—that is, sinners turn back—and they flow through the outpouring of tears in penitential lamentation.

**Eagle** properly denotes the devil, as in Lamentations: “Our persecutors were swifter than eagles,” that is, evil spirits, surpassing others in devising malice against us. Or, according to another prophet, namely Ezekiel: “A great-winged eagle ate the marrow of the cedar,” that is, the devil desires to incorporate into himself the holiest and best persons in the Church. Hence in Job: “Behemoth is confident that the Jordan will flow into his mouth.” According to another exposition, it denotes Nebuchadnezzar. Thus the aforementioned authority can be explained: “A great-winged eagle ate the marrow of the cedar,” that is, Nebuchadnezzar destroyed the Temple, which was covered with cedar boards. For in Ezekiel Nebuchadnezzar is also called an eagle, where it is said: “A great eagle with great wings, with long extension of limbs, full of feathers and variegation, came to Lebanon and took the marrow of the cedar and tore away the top of its branches”; that is, Nebuchadnezzar, ruling many nations, surrounded by a great army, full of riches and innumerable adornments of earthly glory, came to the height of Judaea and the nobility of its kingdom, and by taking captive carried away from its kingdom’s summit the tender offspring [Col. 0706A] of the king, namely King Jeconiah with his mother, etc. It denotes Christ, who was human in being born, a calf in dying, a lion in rising, and an eagle in ascending. Christ is called an eagle because, with the gaze of the mind not dazzled, he penetrates the mysteries of the sun of justice. Hence in Job: “The eaglets lick blood,” that is, martyrs who imitate Christ through suffering; or the eaglets denote the faithful who are nourished by Christ’s body and blood. It denotes John the Evangelist, as Ezekiel, describing the four Evangelists under the image of four animals, says that the fourth animal has an eagle’s face. It denotes the dignity of the human condition, as in Job: “My days have passed like an eagle flying toward food.” For the eagle is suspended in high flight, but through the mind’s desire descends to earth and low places. So the human race fell in the first parent from higher things to low things, though the dignity of its condition had lifted it to the height of reason. Like an eagle flying toward food, our days pass swiftly, because as we seek low things, we are prevented from attaining lofty things. [Col. 0706B] It also denotes the subtle understanding of the saints, as in Job: “At your command the eagle shall be lifted up,” that is, the subtle understanding of the saints, obeying God’s commands, is raised to the heights. It also denotes the soul of an elect person, as in the Gospel: “Wherever the body shall be, there also the eagles shall be gathered,” because where I, incarnate, preside in the heavenly seat, when I have freed the souls of the elect from the flesh, I shall lift them up to heavenly things. [Col. 0706C] It denotes a saint who flies to heavenly things on the wings of charity, as in the Gospel: “Wherever the body,” that is, Christ, “shall be, there also the eagles,” that is, saints renewed by grace, shall be gathered, just as the eagle renews itself in old age.

**North wind** (*aquilo*) properly denotes the coldest wind, by which waters are frozen; hence *aquilo* is said as though “binding waters.” It denotes the region in which it blows, as Jeremiah says: “Behold, a whirlwind wind was coming from the north,” etc. It denotes a demon, as in the Song of the Beloved: “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind,” that is, depart, demon, and come, Holy Spirit; or otherwise: “Arise, evil spirit, from the hearts of Christians, which you bind with the frost of iniquity.” The devil is called north wind as though binding waters, that is, minds fluid with the chill of sin. [Col. 0706D] It denotes Gentiledom, as Job says: “From the north comes gold”: from Gentiledom true faith shines forth in the Lord. Elsewhere David says: “Say to the north, Come,” and “the sides of the north, the city of the king.” It also denotes the contrary, as in the Psalm: “I shall place my seat toward the north and shall be like the Most High.” It denotes the Synagogue frozen by the cold of unbelief, as the devil says in Isaiah: “I shall sit upon the mount of the Testament, in the sides of the north,” that is, in the hearts of the Jews to whom the law was given.

**Spider** properly denotes what is useless and unfruitful, as in the Psalm: “Our years shall meditate like a spider.” The spider weaves empty webs in order deceitfully to catch flies; and the sense is: “Our years shall meditate like a spider,” that is, in our years we devote ourselves [Col. 0707A] to deceitful and empty thoughts. Or *meditabuntur* may be taken passively: our years shall be reckoned like a spider, that is, as empty and useless. It also denotes a hypocrite, who deceives others by his pretence, as Job says of him: “His confidence is like a spider’s web.” It also denotes the spider’s web, as in the Psalm: “You made his soul waste away like a spider,” that is, like a spider’s web—that is, you caused the soul to waste away, that is, to become weak through humility after pride had been laid aside, like a spider, than which nothing is more frail: when lightly touched by a finger, it is both killed and reduced to nothing.

**To plough** properly occurs in Deuteronomy: “You shall not plough with an ox and an ass.” It denotes to preach, as the Apostle says: “It is right that he who ploughs should eat of his fruit.” Sometimes it denotes to know carnally, as Samson said to the Philistines in Judges: “Unless you had ploughed with my heifer, you would not have understood my riddle,” that is, unless you had known my bride, you would not have understood my proposition. [Col. 0707B]

**Plough** properly signifies remembrance of the Lord’s Passion. There are two things in the plough: iron and wood. The pricking iron signifies remembrance; the wood signifies the cross, in accordance with that Gospel saying: “No one who puts his hand to the plough.” According to another exposition, it denotes evangelical doctrine: “No one who puts his hand,” etc.

**Tree** properly denotes a human being; hence in Greek a human being is called *anthrōpos*, that is, a “turned tree.” For as a tree has its head attached to the earth and its members above, so conversely a human being has the head above and the limbs [Col. 0707C] below. Hence in the Gospel: “The axe is already laid to the root of the tree,” that is, judicial power is ready, or the judge’s sentence is imminent; and elsewhere: “Every tree which does not,” etc. It also denotes a good or evil intention, as in the Gospel: “A bad tree cannot bear good fruit.” It also denotes sacred Scripture or the Synagogue, as in the Song: “Under the apple tree,” that is, under sacred Scripture, where the Gentile people of the age rested, “there my mother,” that is, the Synagogue, “was wounded.” It also denotes one who seeks high things, as Job says: “They ate herbs and the bark of trees.” These wicked men are those who, when they see good things arise from evil actions, immediately pull them out by the hand of deadly reproach. It denotes Christ’s cross, as in the hymn: “Beautiful tree”; and also, according to another exposition, in “under the apple tree.” [Col. 0707D]

**Ark** denotes the Church, as in the Psalm: “You and the ark of your sanctification.” The Church is called an ark because, as Noah’s ark protected those who were in it from the flood, so the Church protects her own from the danger of eternal death.

Arcturus is the same as the north, that is, the seven stars which are toward the north. It signifies the Church, as in Job: “Can you join together the shining stars of the Pleiades, or scatter the circuit of Arcturus?” Arcturus is always turning and never setting; so the Church is wearied by various tribulations, but will not incline to ruin. It signifies the Mosaic Law, as in the aforesaid example according to another interpretation: Arcturus appears toward the north, and the Old Law came from the north [Col. 0708A], frightening those subject to it with much severity of constraint.

A bow, properly speaking, as when Isaac said to Esau: “Take your weapons, your quiver, and your bow.” It signifies the rainbow, as in Genesis: “I will set my bow in the clouds”; and it is a sign both of the judgment to come and of that which preceded it. It signifies Sacred Scripture: in a bow there are two things, namely, the string and the wood; the string signifies the New Testament, the wood the Old. As the string bends the wood, so the New Testament softens the Old; hence in the Psalm: “He bent his bow and made it ready,” that is, he gave us Sacred Scripture and expounded it to us. And elsewhere: “They bent their bow, a bitter thing,” namely, heretics by perversely expounding Sacred Scripture [Col. 0708B]. And elsewhere: “They bent their bow; they prepared their arrows in the quiver,” that is, heretics have diverted Sacred Scripture to themselves.

It signifies Christ, as in the Psalm: “Unless you turn back, he will brandish his sword; he has bent his bow.” It signifies persecution, in another interpretation of the same passage: “He bent his bow and made it ready.” It signifies a perverse intention, as in the Psalm: “They turned into a crooked bow,” that is, into a perverse intention. It signifies deception, as in another interpretation: “They bent their bow, a bitter thing.” It signifies hidden attack, as in the Psalm: “He will break the bow and shatter the weapons”: attack by the bow is understood as hidden, by weapons as open, and by the shield as wicked defence. It signifies power, as when Jacob said in Genesis to his son Joseph [Col. 0708C]: “I give you the field which I acquired from the Shechemites by sword and bow,” that is, by power. It signifies the strength or inflexibility of a good work, as in the Psalm: “You have made my arms like a bronze bow,” that is, you have made my good works inflexible. It signifies a threat or promise, as in the Psalm: “The sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow,” that is, issuing or making a threat or promise, saying: “Whatever you tell us, we shall do and obey.”

It signifies snares or deceit, again in the Psalm: “They bent their bow, a bitter thing,” that is, snares or deceits. It signifies the day of judgment, as in the Psalm: “That they may flee from the face of the bow,” that is, fear the day of judgment. It signifies the heavenly judgment; hence it is said of the wicked [Col. 0708D] in Job: “They fled iron weapons and rushed upon the bow.” Eternal damnation is prefigured: whoever evades present tribulation rushes into eternal damnation.

A threshing-floor, properly speaking, is a broad level place in a field where wheat is customarily winnowed; hence it is said in Judges of Gideon that, seeking a sign from God, he placed a fleece on the threshing-floor. It signifies the wheat winnowed on the threshing-floor: the name of the thing contained is taken to designate its container. Thus in Kings the king of the place answered a woman crying to him: “From where, from where can I save you? From the winepress?”—that is, from what is contained in the winepress; “or from the threshing-floor?”—that is, from the wheat contained on the threshing-floor, that is, the Church, in which grains are still mixed with chaff, that is, the good with the evil. Hence John, speaking of Christ in the Gospel, says: “His winnowing-fan is in his hand [Col. 0709A], and he will cleanse his threshing-floor and burn the chaff with unquenchable fire.” This will occur on the day of judgment, when the wicked will be separated from the Church not only in merit but also in place, etc. It signifies judgment, because, as grains are separated from chaff on the threshing-floor, so in judgment the good are separated from the wicked. Hence it is said: “The harvests are to be gathered to the threshing-floor,” that is, the peoples to judgment.

Sand, properly speaking: the wicked person is compared to sand because of its barrenness and innumerability. Hence in Genesis: “I will multiply your seed like the stars of heaven and like the sand of the sea.” The latter refers to the wicked, who are innumerable and barren. It signifies prudence, represented by sand both because of its multitude and because of its saltiness; hence in the Psalm: “He rained down like the sand of the sea.”

[Col. 0709B] A spice-bed, properly speaking, signifies the faithful person who is ashamed of his own sins and those of others, and through whom spiritual food is ground and served. Such a person is aptly compared to a spice-bed, because as a bed of spices, excellently arranged and ordered, delights the gaze of those looking upon it and offers them fragrance by reason of the multitude of aromatic herbs, so those who are beautiful cheeks are fragrant to God through their multitude of virtues and good works. Hence in the Song of Love: “His cheeks are like beds of spices.” It signifies Christ’s soul, cultivated by discipline or disciplines and carefully ordered; hence in Solomon’s Song: “My beloved went down into his garden, to the bed of spices.” The garden into which the Son of God descended [Col. 0709C] is human nature, into which he descended when, by making himself human, he emptied himself. It was like a garden full of fragrant kinds and laden with the shoots of virtues. Therefore, he came down into the garden to the bed of spices when, in assuming human nature, he united a soul to himself.

“To wither,” properly, denotes dryness. It denotes death, as in the Psalm: “For like grass they shall quickly wither,” that is, they shall die. It denotes failure of mind, as in the Gospel: “Men withering away from fear.” It denotes strengthening, as in the Psalm: “My strength dried up like a potsherd,” that is, through the fire of tribulation my strength was made firm, as a potsherd is hardened by material fire. It denotes reduction to ashes, as in the Psalm: “In the morning let it pass like grass [Col. 0709D], let it fall through death, grow hard through decay, wither through becoming ashes.”

Silver, properly speaking, as in the Acts of the Apostles: “Silver and gold I do not have.” It signifies eloquence, as in the most loving Song [sic]: “We shall make you golden chains, inlaid with silver,” that is, subtle statements in Sacred Scripture, as a fine chain is subtle; they are called golden because of wisdom and silver because of eloquence. And elsewhere: “Above thousands of gold and silver.” It signifies the writers of the divine utterance, as in Job: “Silver shall not be weighed in exchange for it,” by which silver divine sayings are frequently denoted.
