Under the name of silver its writers may be understood, whose life shone amid the crowds of men with the light of virtues. Note in the *Moralia* that [Col. 0710A] silver signifies the Sacred Scripture of the New Testament, bronze the Scripture of the Old Testament. Silver sounds and shines; bronze sounds but does not shine, because the preachers of the New Testament spoke openly what they were also able to show. But the preachers of the Old Testament, because through allegorical shadow they uttered obscure things concerning the heavenly mystery, gave a sound as it were without light. It signifies a good work, as the prophet says: “Your silver has turned into dross”; the prophet speaks to the Synagogue. Silver signifies temporal riches according to another interpretation: “Above thousands of gold and silver.” It signifies Christ’s humanity, as in: “In its midst, the appearance of electrum.” Electrum is a metal made from gold and silver. It signifies Sacred Scripture, as in the Psalm: “Silver [Col. 0710B] tried by fire.”

A ram, properly speaking, as in Genesis: “Abraham saw a ram caught by its horns among the brambles.” It also signifies an apostle or prelate who drives away enemies with the horns—that is, the authorities—of both Testaments; hence in the Psalm: “Bring to the Lord, sons of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams.” Elsewhere it signifies a prelate who ought to be offered for his subjects, as in Proverbs: “There are three things which go well: the strongest lion, the girded cock, and the ram; and none can resist him.” It also signifies a person, or devotion to a cause, insofar as one offers oneself to God; hence in Daniel: “Receive us as holocausts of rams.” It also signifies a ruler from among the Gentiles converted to the faith, as in Isaiah: “Let every flock yield to the rams [Col. 0710C] of Nebaioth.” It signifies Christ, as is said in a certain prose hymn: “Ram, lion, worm.” It signifies a siege-engine, as in Ezekiel: “Son of man, take a brick, and write on it the city, and set up rams.”

An ear of grain, properly speaking, signifies the reprobate rich man, as in Job: “And like the tops of ears of grain they shall be crushed.” When the ear is broken, the whiteness of the grains is displayed; so, when the wicked fall into eternal punishments, the extent to which the justice of the saints shines in truth is revealed. The meaning is: “The tops of ears of grain shall be crushed,” that is, the rigidity of the proud will be broken by fear of the final threshing, which now raises itself up in contempt of the life of the elect.

Weapons, properly speaking, as when Isaac said to Esau: “Take your weapons, your quiver.” They also signify doctrine, as in the Psalm: “Take up weapons,” that is, doctrine, “and [Col. 0710D] a shield,” that is, constancy. They signify open assault or attack by spiritual enemies, as in the Psalm: “He will break the bow,” that is, hidden attacks, “and shatter the weapons,” that is, open assaults, “and burn their shields,” that is, their defences, “with fire.” They signify the births of this present life, as in Job: “He will flee iron weapons and rush upon a bronze bow.” For the births of this present life press upon and pursue one in action. They also signify the members of the human body, as the prophet says: “They went down to the underworld with their weapons.” For the weapons of sinners are the members of the body, through which they carry out perverse desires. They signify virtues, which are fortifications against the devil’s snares, according to another interpretation of the Psalm: “Take up weapons and a shield,” that is, spiritual [Col. 0711A] virtues; the Apostle: “Take up the armour of God,” etc. They also signify the authority of divine Scripture, as in: “A thousand shields hang from it, all the armour of the mighty.” They signify the condition of penitents in contrition, confession, and satisfaction, as in: “Ashes and haircloth are the weapons of penitents,” as is clear in theology. They signify vices or suggestions by which the devil attacks us; hence Job said that Behemoth and Leviathan are weapons, that is, the devil’s suggestions.

A spice-mixture, properly speaking, is a preparation made from aromatic ingredients, and is called as it were *aeroma* or *agrimonia*; hence it is read in Genesis that Ishmaelites came from Gilead, carrying spices on camels. It signifies something delightful, as in the Song of Christ: “The fragrance of your ointments [Col. 0711B] is above all spices.” It signifies virtue, as in the Song: “Arise, north wind,” that is, “Depart, devil”; “come, south wind,” that is, “Come, Holy Spirit, and breathe upon my garden,” that is, the Church; “and its spices shall flow,” that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit in the Church. It also signifies saints encouraging others to good works, as in the Song of Love: “I shall go to the beds of spices of the saints.” It signifies the prayers of the saints, as in Revelation: “The smoke of the spices rose before the Lord,” that is, the prayers of the saints. It also signifies penitence, as in the Song: “Who is this who comes up through the wilderness like a little rod of smoke, from the spices of myrrh and incense?” By myrrh, which is a bitter spice, are understood the bitterness of contrition, confession, and satisfaction.

[Col. 0711C] An artisan, properly speaking, signifies God the Father, as in Solomon’s Epithalamium: “The things fashioned by the hand of the artisan,” that is, of almighty God, by whose generosity every virtue is bestowed upon a human being; or “by the hand of the artisan,” that is, the Son of God. For he is the hand of God the Father, who works through his hand as an artisan does—that is, God the Father works through the Son. It signifies a preacher, as in the Book of Wisdom: “Works shall be praised in the hands of artisans.”

A reed, properly speaking, signifies Sacred Scripture, as in the Psalm: “Rebuke the beasts of the reed,” that is, heretics, who are like beasts in the Scriptures. It signifies an unstable person, as in the Gospel: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind.” Such a person is aptly called a reed, because, as a reed is shaken by the blowing of the wind [Col. 0711D], so an unstable person runs after every breath of fortune. It signifies the Jew, as in Matthew: “He will not break a bruised reed,” and immediately, “the Jew will not be condemned.” It signifies the ordering of the Church, as in Ezekiel: “He who spoke with me had a golden measuring-reed to measure the city.” This golden reed is nothing other than the divine ordering by which he ordered the city, that is, the Church. It signifies sin; thus the passage may be expounded: “He will not break a bruised reed,” that is, he will not deny penitence to a sinner.

Fat, properly speaking, is the internal fat of an animal. It also signifies pride, as in: “Fatness has covered his face, and fat hangs from his side.”

“To ascend,” properly speaking, as in the Psalm: “You ascended on [Col. 0712A] high.” It signifies surpassing, as in the Psalm: “He ascended above the cherubim,” above the fullness of knowledge. It denotes the steps of virtues, as in: “Let us ascend from virtue to virtue, until we see the God of gods in Zion,” etc. It also denotes the excess of pride, as in Isaiah: “I shall ascend to the north, and shall be like the Most High.” It denotes the equality of the Father and the Son, as in the Gospel: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father,” that is, “Do not touch me with bodily touch, since you do not touch me with the touch of the mind”; as though he said: “You do not yet know me to be equal to the Father.” It denotes excellence of virtues, as in Isaiah: “Ascend the mountain, you who preach good news to Zion.” It denotes withdrawal of presence, as in the Psalm: “God ascended,” that is, he withdrew his presence or did not appear. It denotes [Col. 0712B] growth, as in the Gospel: “Why do thoughts arise in your hearts?” It denotes eminence of honour, as in: “Friend, go up higher.”

An ass, properly speaking, signifies an animal, as in Genesis: “Abraham saddled his ass.” It signifies a foolish person, as in: “You shall not plough with an ox and an ass,” that is, you shall not send a wise man to preach with a fool. It also signifies a lustful and wanton person, as in Ezekiel: “Whose flesh is like that of asses.” It also signifies the Gentile people, as in Isaiah: “The ox knows its owner, and the ass its lord’s manger.” The ox signifies the Jew placed under the yoke of the Law; the ass, the Gentile people, whom every deceiver saddled like a brute beast with whatever error he wished. The former rejected the God whom he worshipped; the latter received the God whom it did not possess [Col. 0712C]. The ass is the person who bears others’ necessities; hence it is said of heretics in Job: “They drove away the ass of the fatherless.” The ass which bears burdens is the person who provides the help of this life from possessions held here to one seeking heavenly things and despising earthly things; the heretic drives him away when he turns him from the bosom of holy Church. It signifies the Christian people generally, as the prophet says: “Rejoice, Jerusalem: behold, your king comes sitting upon an ass.”

An asp, properly speaking, signifies the devil, as in Isaiah: “The infant at the breast will delight over the asp’s hole and in the den of the basilisk.” What is meant by the infant except Christ? What by the asp’s hole except the devil’s cunning? What by the basilisk’s den except the hearts of the wicked? [Col. 0712D] It signifies the person who disdains to hear God’s word, as in the Psalm: “Their fury is like that of a serpent, like that of an asp.” It signifies a hidden and bland suggestion, or the violent and sudden temptations of unclean spirits; hence it is said of the hypocrite in Job: “He shall suck the head of asps, and the tongue of a viper shall kill him.” The asp is a small serpent and the viper is longer-bodied; therefore, hidden suggestion is denoted by the asp.

“To assume,” properly speaking, means to advance someone from a lower condition to a higher; hence in the Psalm: “He took me from behind those giving suck.” And elsewhere: “Mary was assumed into heaven.” It signifies conversion from unbelief to faith, as in the Psalm: “He took me up from many waters.” It also signifies taking human nature to oneself by uniting it to the divine nature [Col. 0713A], as in the Psalm: “Blessed is he whom you have chosen and assumed.” It signifies deliverance from tribulation, as in the Psalm: “He delivered me from tribulation and took me up.”

“To stand by,” properly speaking, as one person stands by another. It denotes rendering service, as in the Psalm: “The queen stood at your right hand,” etc., that is, the Church beside Christ. It denotes remaining or persisting in evil, as in the Psalm: “The kings of the earth stood,” that is, they persisted in evil. It denotes the raising of the mind to God, as in the Psalm: “In the morning I shall stand before you,” that is, I shall direct my mind to God. It denotes diligence or deliberation in evil, as in the Psalm: “He stood in every way that was not good.”

“But.” This conjunction is sometimes used copulatively, as in Luke: “But he said: Rather, blessed …” [Col. 0713B] Sometimes it marks opposition, as in the Gospel: “Friend, how did you enter here?” etc.; “but he was silent.” As if to say: He answered him no word, but was dumb and kept silence, etc.

An atrium, properly speaking, is a broad court around a palace. Hence it is said in the Gospel of John that John entered with Jesus into the court of the high priest. Thus also the broad space around the tabernacle or Temple was called an atrium; and Exodus says: “You shall make also the court of the tabernacle.” It signifies the beginning of good conduct, as in the Psalm: “Enter his gates in confession, his courts,” etc. It signifies the human heart enlarged by charity, as in the Psalm: “Worship the Lord in his holy court,” that is, in an enlarged and [Col. 0713C] sanctified heart. It signifies eternal life, as in the Psalm: “One day in your courts is better than thousands”; and likewise: “My soul longs for and faints for the courts of the Lord.” It signifies the present Church, as likewise in the Psalm: “Our feet stood in your courts, Jerusalem.” It signifies awareness of divinity, as in the Psalm: “Blessed is he whom you chose and assumed; he shall dwell in your courts.”

“To hear,” properly speaking, as in Kings: “I heard your voice.” It signifies understanding, as in John: “This saying is hard; who can hear it?” And elsewhere: “Lord, I have heard your report”; and in the Psalm: “Hear, daughter, and see”; likewise: “I shall hear what the Lord God speaks in me”; and in the Gospel: “All things which I heard from my Father.” It denotes hearkening, as in Kings: “Hear [Col. 0713D] the prayers of your servants,” that is, answer them. It signifies judging, as in the Psalm: “He who made the eye, does he not see? He who planted the ear, does he not hear?” that is, does he not judge? etc.

Hearing, properly speaking, means the ear, as the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be?” that is, where would the ear be? It signifies divine inspiration or divine command, as in Habakkuk: “Lord, I heard the report,” or: “Lord, I heard your divine command,” that is, I understood it. It also signifies understanding, as in the Psalm: “You shall give joy to my hearing,” that is, to my understanding. It signifies obedience, as in the Psalm: “A people whom I did not know served me at the hearing of the ear.”

A hall, properly speaking, signifies the virtue of the Blessed Virgin, as is read in a certain prayer: “God, who [made] the virginal hall.” It signifies the Church, as in the Psalm: “Worship [Col. 0714A] the Lord in the hall”; and a prayer reads: “He will defend all those dwelling in this hall of God.” It signifies eternal life, as in a certain prose hymn: “Let us joyfully sing jubilee in the hall of heaven. Alleluia.”

A breeze, properly speaking, signifies a mild judicial sentence, as in Genesis: “When the Lord walked in paradise in the breeze after midday,” namely, that he might judge Adam gently. It signifies the Scripture of the Holy Spirit, which soothes rather than terrifies, as in Job: “I heard a voice like a gentle breeze.” It signifies flattery, as in Isaiah: “The wind of the enemy takes away our days; the breeze will carry [them] away.” Flattery is aptly called a breeze because, as a breeze separates grains from chaff, so flattery separates the light-minded from the serious and the unstable from the steadfast.

Orichalcum, properly speaking, is what is brought to gold through many refinings [Col. 0714B], and it signifies saints purified in tribulation; in Revelation: “His feet were like orichalcum.” Orichalcum also signifies the final hypocrite, who will be at the time of Antichrist, who will pretend to be righteous and will not be so; and the aforesaid authority may be expounded accordingly.

An ear, properly speaking, as in Exodus: “If you wish the servant to remain in slavery, the priest shall bring him to the door of the Temple and pierce his ear with an awl.” And elsewhere, when the Lord sent Moses to Pharaoh: “He who made the ear, does he not hear?” It signifies spiritual understanding, as in the Gospel: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear,” that is, let him understand. It signifies obedience, as the Psalmist says: “A people whom [Col. 0714C] I did not know obeyed me at the hearing of the ear.” It signifies the mercy of hearing prayers, as in the Psalm: “Receive with your ears the voice of my prayer.” It signifies the appearance of ears, as in the Psalm: “They have ears and shall not hear.” It signifies a certain obstinacy or human negligence, as in the Psalm: “Their fury is like that of a serpent stopping up its ears,” etc. It signifies the presence of divine mercy, as in the Psalm: “Receive my words with your ears, Lord,” etc.

Dawn, properly speaking: in Genesis, “A man wrestled with Jacob,” that is, an angel in the form of a man; and here dawn is said to be before sunrise. Dawn of time is when the sun rises, as in Genesis: the angel said to Jacob, “Let me go, for dawn has now risen.” Dawn of the body is the faithful soul, as in Job: [Col. 0714D] “You have shown dawn its place,” that is, the heavenly homeland to the faithful soul. Dawn of the mind is the beginning of grace, as in the Psalm: “You fashioned dawn and sun,” that is, beginning and perfection. Dawn of heaven is the Church, as in the *Sir ha-shirim* [Song of Songs]: “Who is this that rises like the dawn arising?” It signifies Christ, as in the hymn: “Let dawn come forth wholly”; for as the material sun illuminates the world, so the spiritual sun, namely Christ, illuminates the holy Church.

Gold signifies contemplation, as in the Apostle: “Some build with gold, others with silver, others with precious stones,” that is, they contemplate. Gold also signifies faith, as in Job: “From the north gold shall come,” that is, faith from the Gentile world. It also signifies natural ability, as in Job: “If I have considered gold my strength [Col. 0715A],” that is, if I have made the ability of a distinguished intellect my strength. It also signifies the disposition of one acting well, as Solomon says: “As silver is tested in a refining vessel and gold in a furnace, so a person is tested by the mouth of one praising him.” For silver or gold is tested by fire; so too is the disposition of one acting well. For what sort of person he is in the matter for which he is praised is shown. It signifies the splendour of the heavenly city, as Revelation says that the city itself consists of pure gold like clear glass. It signifies the brightness of temporal glory, as is said of Babylon’s golden cup in Revelation. For temporal glory is called a golden cup because, while it makes temporal things appear beautiful, it intoxicates foolish minds with desire for itself. It signifies the brightness of innocence, as in Lamentations: “How darkened [Col. 0715B] is the gold,” that is, the brightness of innocence has turned into the blackness of fault. It signifies wisdom, as in Isaiah: “Kings shall come from Sheba, gold,” etc., that is, those spiritually governing themselves offer the finest gold in God’s Church. Gold signifies saints who surpass others, as in the Song of Songs: “Your head is finest gold.” Divinity is also called gold, according to another exposition of the same authority, namely, “Your head is finest gold.” God is meant, in the aforesaid example, according to another exposition. And in Ezekiel: “And in the midst of the fire, as it were, electrum.” There electrum signifies Christ, because, as gold is joined to silver in electrum, so in Christ the divine nature is united to the human: by gold [Col. 0715C] let divinity be understood, by silver humanity. It signifies angelic nature, as in Job: “Fine gold shall not be given for it”; by fine gold is understood angelic nature, which shines with the brightness of righteousness as fine gold does, because it has never had any contamination of fault. The saints who are in the heavenly homeland are called gold, as in Job: “Gold or glass shall not equal it”; by this we understand the saints in the homeland, whose hearts gleam with brightness and shine through with purity. It signifies charity, which excels other virtues, as the Psalmist says: “To him shall be given gold of Arabia.” Gold also signifies earthly riches, as in the Psalm: “More desirable than gold,” etc., that is, than all riches. It signifies the brightness of virtue, as in Job: “Its clods are gold,” because the gathering of the several orders [Col. 0715D] in Judaea shone with so much greater virtue as it bound itself more unanimously to God and neighbour. The person who suffers tribulation is also called gold, as in the Book of Wisdom: “He tested them like gold in the furnace.”

The south wind, properly speaking, is the hottest wind. It signifies the southern region, as in the Gospel: “The Queen of Sheba came from the south.” It signifies charity, as in Habakkuk: “The Lord shall come from the south,” that is, from the fervour of charity. It signifies the Son, as in the Psalm: “Turn, Lord, our captivity like a torrent in the south.” It signifies the Holy Spirit, as in the Song of Songs: “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind,” that is, “Come, Holy Spirit; fill the minds of human beings.” It signifies the Church, as in Job: “The inward parts of the south” are called the spiritual persons hidden in [Col. 0716A] the Church. It signifies Judaea. Isaiah says concerning the conversion of the Gentiles: “I shall say to the north: Give; and to the south: Do not forbid”—that is, I shall say to the Gentile world: “Offer a gift to God”; and to the south, that is, Judaea, which first received the warmth of faith from the true sun: “Do not forbid,” that is, do not reject and condemn the life of the Gentiles, as those who were idolaters did. It signifies a lax way of life, as in Job: “Consider the paths of Tema, the roads of Sheba, and wait a little.” *Thema* means “south”; *Saba* is interpreted “net.” By the south wind, which melts things upon which it blows with its warmth, is understood a lax and unrestrained manner of living; by the net, the entanglement of activity. Those walk with loosened steps into a net who, while not perfectly renouncing the world, bind themselves to worldly activities.

“Or.” This conjunction is sometimes used conjunctively [Col. 0716B], as in the Gospel: “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad”; sometimes explanatorily, as in the Psalm: “Will God forget to show mercy, or will he restrain [it]?” Sometimes as a comparison, as Moses said to the Lord: “Either forgive them this fault, or blot me out of the book of life”—that is, as it is true that I am not to be blotted out of the book of life, so it is true that you will forgive them this fault, since they sinned not through themselves but through another.

“Moreover” is used copulatively, as in the Gospel: “Moreover Mary said to the angel,” because there it joins Mary; sometimes adversatively, as in the Gospel: “But to whom shall I compare this generation?” [Col. 0716C] Sometimes affirmatively, as in the Apostle: “But I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers,” that is, I affirm that you are not ignorant.

A bird, properly speaking, signifies Christ, as it is said of the Jewish people in Job: “The bird did not know the path,” that is, the path of Christ, because it refused to consider the body which he assumed and raised into the air by ascending, and his humility, the paths by which he raises us to the heights; or Christ is called a bird because of the wings of virtues.

It also signifies the devil, as in Job: “Will you play with him as with a bird?” The devil is called a bird because, through the subtlety of his nature, he proudly exalts himself when by pride he pretends to be an angel of light. And God mocked him as one mocks a bird when, in the Passion, he showed him food to bite but hid the snare of divinity by which he would be caught [Col. 0716D]. And in the Gospel: “The birds of heaven,” that is, devils, “ate it.” It signifies the human mind, as in Job: “Man is born for labour and the bird for flying,” because when the flesh is afflicted by lashes, the mind is lifted up by desiring higher things. It also signifies pride, as in Jeremiah: “Woe to those who play among the birds of heaven,” because the proud person raises himself above himself.

An armpit, properly speaking, signifies a good work, as Leviticus says that the bone of the turtledove is to be twisted toward the armpits; that is, the preacher ought to possess in action the things which he sets forth in preaching. It also signifies deprivation of a good work, as in Proverbs: “The sluggard puts his hand under his armpit,” that is, he deprives himself of a good work, etc.

Unleavened bread is properly called *azyma*, from *a*, meaning “without,” and *zyma*, meaning “leaven.” Hence Mark says: “Now were the days of the unleavened bread,” that is, the days on which it was not permitted to use leaven. In this place it is neuter: *haec azyma*, “this unleavened bread”; *horum azymorum*, “of these unleavened breads”; *azyma* signifies unleavened bread, that is, bread without leaven. It also signifies the Paschal feast, as in the Gospel: “The Passover of Unleavened Bread was after two days”; and it is feminine, declined *haec azyma*, *hujus azymae*. [Col. 0718A] Sometimes it is an adjective: *azymus, -a, -um*, as in the Old Testament: “They ate unleavened loaves.” It also signifies a saint, as the Apostle says: “Purge out the old leaven,” etc., “as you are unleavened,” that is, holy and cleansed from vices; and then it is masculine: *hi azymi*, “these unleavened men”; *horum azymorum*, “of these unleavened men.” Sometimes it also signifies a good work, as the Apostle says: “Not in the old leaven,” etc., “but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth,” etc.

## B

[Col. 0717]

[Col. 0717A] Babylon, properly speaking; it also signifies the world, in which there is manifold confusion, as in the Psalm: “Upon the rivers of Babylon.” It also signifies a sinner, as in the Psalm: “I shall remember Rahab and Babylon.” It also signifies idolatry [Col. 0717B] or heresy, as in Revelation: “That great Babylon fell, which by wine,” etc. It signifies earthly delight, as in Revelation: “From Babylon’s golden cup.”

A staff, properly speaking, as Jacob says in Genesis: “With my staff I crossed this Jordan.” It also signifies pastoral rule, which consists in support and correction, as in the Psalm: “Your rod and your staff,” etc., that is, correction and support; or the staff signifies the greater correction and the rod the lesser. It signifies consolation or support, as Tobit’s mother says: “My son, that money, for which we sent you travelling, would never have existed—[you are] the staff of our old age,” that is, our consolation. Elsewhere the prophet says to the Egyptians: “I shall take away from you the staff [Col. 0717C] of bread,” that is, support. It signifies earthly power, as in Isaiah: “Woe to you who lean upon the reed-staff of Egypt,” that is, earthly power. It signifies the devil, as in the prophet: “The Lord will break the staff of the wicked,” that is, the devil.

Baptism, properly speaking, is merely the outward washing of the body without the inward washing of the mind. Hence, wishing to confound the Jews and Pharisees concerning John’s baptism, the Lord said: “Is John’s baptism from heaven or from men?” Sometimes it is the washing of the mind along with the outward washing of the body, as in the Gospel: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” etc.; and elsewhere: “John was in the wilderness, preaching a baptism of repentance.” It signifies the shedding of blood or martyrdom, as [Col. 0717D] Christ says in the Gospel: “I have a baptism with which to be baptized, and I am constrained until I accomplish it.” It signifies solely inward contrition of mind, which suffices when someone at the final point of death wishes to be baptized but is overtaken by death; hence the Apostle: “Our fathers were baptized in the cloud and in the sea in the wilderness.” Note that there is a threefold baptism: baptism of the river, which is performed in water; baptism of the breath, which is performed in penitence by the grace of the Holy Spirit; baptism of blood, which is performed in the struggle of martyrdom.

A beard, properly speaking, signifies strength, as in: “I shall take the beard from Ephraim,” that is, strength from the children of Israel, etc. It signifies a greater prelate, as in the Psalm: “Like ointment upon the head, which descended upon the beard [Col. 0718A] of Aaron,” that is, the ointment of divine grace, which descends from the Father into the head, that is, Christ; and from the head into the beard, that is, the peoples, who are called God’s beard, that is, strength, because strength and full age are denoted in a beard; from the beard into the garments, that is, the successors of the apostles and other prelates; and from the garments to the hem of the garment, that is, the final faithful—namely, Christians.

A barbarian is any person other than a Greek or a Latin. It signifies one alien to the faith, and is used for an unbelieving people, as the Psalmist says: “At Israel’s departure from Egypt,” etc.; “from a barbarous people,” that is, from an unbelieving people. It signifies a person not subject to the Roman Empire; hence it is said in the person of the Church: “Let us pray for our emperor, that our God and Lord may subject to him all barbarian nations.” It also signifies someone who does not understand, as Paul says: “He will be a barbarian to me.” It also signifies a bestial or uncultivated people [Col. 0718C], as Paul says: “Barbarian or Scythian.”

A basilisk, properly speaking, as Lucan says:

> [lacuna] The basilisk rules in the sand.

And *basilisk* derives from the Greek *basileos*, which is interpreted in Latin as “king”; that is, it is called, as it were, king of serpents because it surpasses all in venom. Its nature is to kill a human being by sight alone or by breath; hence the *Physiologus* says that it kills birds flying overhead by its breath. It also signifies the devil, as in the Psalm: “You shall tread upon the asp and basilisk.”

A foundation, properly speaking, signifies a doctor of the Church, as in Job: “Upon what were its foundations established?” The columns stand upon foundations, and the whole structure is raised upon the columns; so teachers, while they preach rightly, sustain the entire weight of the Church. It also signifies a prophet, because [Col. 0718D], when they properly first spoke of Christ’s incarnation, they placed themselves as certain foundations of our faith; hence the foregoing authority can be referred to this interpretation. It also signifies the intention of the soul, because virtue rests upon a good intention as a column upon a foundation; hence Job: “Upon what were its foundations established?” That is, “Unless upon me,” says the Lord, upon whom, when a righteous soul directs itself, it builds its good intention as a foundation.

**Blessed** denotes the blessedness of the heavenly homeland, whence in the Psalm: “Blessed are they who dwell in thy house.” It denotes the blessedness of the way, whence again in the Psalm: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way.” It denotes the blessedness of conscience, whence in the Psalm: “Blessed are they whose iniquities have been forgiven.” It denotes the blessedness of innocence, whence in Ecclesiasticus: “Blessed is the man who is found without blemish.” [Col. 0719A] It denotes the blessedness of experience, whence in the same place: “Blessed is the man who shall abide in his wisdom.”

**War**, properly speaking, whence in the Book of Kings David says of Saul and Jonathan: “How have the mighty fallen in battle!” It denotes the conflict of Christ and the devil, whence the Psalmist: “Blessed be the Lord my God,” etc., “and my fingers for battle”; he is called Lord with respect to creation, “my God” with respect to sanctification. It denotes the conflict of the good angels and the evil, whence in the Apocalypse: “There was silence in heaven,” while the dragon was waging war. It denotes the conflict of flesh and spirit, whence in the Psalm: “He removes wars unto the ends of the earth.” And it should be noted that, just as among secular authors there are many kinds of war, so too in theology, according to the different afflictions [Col. 0719B] of different persons. There is foreign war, which takes place between Jerusalem and Babylon; internal war, which takes place between neighbor and neighbor, and is called civil; and more than civil war, which takes place between body and soul.

**To bless** means to wish good things, whence Isaac in Genesis: “He blessed his sons Jacob and Esau,” that is, he wished them good things, speaking of the dew of heaven and the fatness of the earth, etc. It denotes speaking true things, whence the same Jacob blessed his sons, that is, he spoke truths to them. For he did not wish good things to all of them, as is evident from what he said in Genesis: “Simeon and Levi, let not my soul enter into your counsel.” It denotes giving good things, whence it is read in the Book of Kings that David sought a blessing from Nabal. It denotes multiplying, whence in Genesis: “God blessed Adam and Eve and said: Increase and multiply”; and the priest says: “Bless, O Lord, these gifts,” that is, multiply them. [Col. 0719C] It denotes praising, whence it is said in Daniel: “Let us bless the Father and the Son with the Holy Spirit.” It denotes giving thanks, when we say, “Let us bless the Lord,” that is, “Let us give thanks to the Lord.” It denotes supplying material for divine praise, whence in the hymn of the children: “Bless the Lord, all works of the Lord”; and in the same: “Bless the Lord, sun and moon,” that is, supply material for divine praise, etc. It denotes establishing a solemn and celebrated day, whence in Genesis: “God blessed the seventh day,” that is, he established it as solemn and celebrated. It denotes consecrating, whence the priest says: “Bless, O Lord, the bread on the altar,” that is, consecrate it. It denotes cursing, whence in Job Job’s wife says to him: “Bless God and die,” that is, curse him, [Col. 0719D] so that you may quickly be freed from your present distress. Likewise, III Kings 21: “Naboth blessed God and the king,” that is, cursed them.

**Beryl** shines like water struck by the sun; it warms the hand that holds it, and signifies those who are cold, yet, struck by the grace of the true sun, shine in good works and warm those among whom they live by the example of a good life. Of this there is mention in the Apocalypse.

**Beast**, properly speaking, whence in Genesis: “God created the beasts and creeping things of the earth.” And *bestia* is so called as though *vastia*, from *vastus*, “waste” or “vast.” It denotes the devil, whence in the Psalm: “Deliver not to beasts the souls confessing thee”; and elsewhere the Lord says to Job: “All the beasts of the field shall play there.” By beasts unclean spirits are signified, and by the field the present age. The beasts of the field therefore play among the grasses [Col. 0720A] when reprobate spirits draw human hearts toward unlawful thoughts, deceiving them now by terror, now by passing pleasures. A beast denotes the brutish, foolish man, whence the Apostle in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians: “If I fought with beasts at Ephesus,” that is, against beastly men at Ephesus, etc. It also denotes Antichrist, whence in the Apocalypse: “I saw a beast having ten horns.” According to another exposition it denotes the Roman Empire, which was divided into ten kingdoms; it also denotes heresy or an assembly of heretics, whence in the Apocalypse: “The beast came up out of the abyss which devoured all things.” It denotes a beastly impulse, whence in Job it is said that beasts shall not harm the righteous man, that is, beastly impulses.

**To drink**, properly speaking, denotes being united to the Church, because just as [Col. 0720B] wine consists of many drops, so the Church consists of many faithful persons; whence in the Gospel: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood,” etc., that is, unless you belong to the ecclesiastical union, you shall not have eternal life. It also denotes being spiritually incorporated, whence in the Gospel: “I will not henceforth drink of this fruit of the vine,” that is, I shall not incorporate the Jews, or any Jew, into myself, until I drink it, that is, incorporate myself with you; and this “new,” that is, I shall incorporate you when renewed, I say, in the kingdom of my Father, that is, in the state of immortality. It denotes spiritual refreshment, whence in John: “Whoever drinks of this water shall never thirst.” It denotes undergoing passion, whence in the Gospel: “Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink? You indeed shall drink [Col. 0720C] my cup,” that is, you shall undergo suffering. It denotes being instructed, whence in John: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink,” that is, if anyone desires teaching, let him come and be instructed.

**Byblus** is a rush which grows in the Nile, whence a certain writer says:

> “And I shall hand down many falsehoods on Nilotic bybli.”

It denotes a book, whose material is byblus; whence *bibliotheca* is a repository of *bibli*, in this book, etc.

**Biliber** is a weight of two pounds, of which one reads in the Apocalypse. Preachers of both Testaments are called *biliberes*: they are ground down by the tribulation of the present life and refined by the fire of suffering. Thus in the Apocalypse one biliber, made up of two sextarii, is understood as the Church composed of two peoples; it is therefore comprehended under the dual number [Col. 0720D] on account of the two Testaments or on account of the twofold commandment of love. A biliber of wheat is worth a denarius, because all the saints have been redeemed by precious blood. Hence “a biliber of wheat for one denarius” denotes merit consisting in good thought and good work. According to another exposition this text may be explained thus: “A biliber of wheat for one denarius,” that is, merit consisting in good work, in fulfilling the precepts of the New Testament, which is signified by grain, obtains for us the denarius of eternal blessedness.

**Bile** is the receptacle of gall. It also denotes anger, as when one says: “This man cannot contain his bile,” that is, his anger, etc.

**Bini**, properly speaking, whence in the Gospel: “He sent them two [Col. 0721A] by two before his face”; for here the expression is used distributively. It denotes “two,” whence in the Gospel: “There were six stone jars placed there, each holding two or three measures,” that is, two or three, etc.

**Biothanatus** or **biothematus** is a simple name expounded from *bis* and *ota, otae*, “ear,” because he has divided *otae*, that is, ears: in a simple person, what enters through one leaves through the other. Hence an *idiota* is also said to have divided ears, from *iduor, iduaris*, “I divide,” and *ota, otae*, “ear”; or *biota, biotae* is the same as “sheep.” Hence one is called *biothanatus*, that is, foolish; whence it is read in the Passion of Saints Gervasius and Protasius: “Do you wish to become a biothanatus,” that is, a fool, “like your brother?” It denotes one condemned in body and soul; according to [Col. 0721B] this derivation the word is composed of *bis* and *thanatos*, “death,” as it were “twice dead,” in body, namely, and soul. Hence it is read that Aegeas was buried among the *biothanati*, that is, among those condemned in body and soul; and concerning this, see the legend of Saint Andrew.

**Good** is sometimes used essentially and substantively when said of God, whence in the Gospel: “Why do you call me good? None is good but God alone,” because he himself is goodness. Sometimes it is used negatively, as: “It was good for him,” that is, it was less bad that he should not be punished except for original sin. Sometimes it is used denominatively, or denotes the source of a good principle, whence in Genesis: “God saw all things which he had made, and they were very good,” that is, made by the supremely good One. Sometimes it denotes an act of justice, [Col. 0721C] as: “This man is good,” that is, just. Sometimes it denotes the usefulness of a thing, as: “This is good,” that is, useful; or “works are good,” that is, useful. Sometimes it denotes what is pleasant, whence in the Psalm: “Behold how good and pleasant!” Sometimes it denotes an occasion, as when evil is said to be good, that is, an occasion of good; whence Augustine: “He who is supremely good would never permit evils to exist unless he drew good things out of evils.”

**Ox** denotes a preacher, because just as an ox, by means of the ploughshare, cuts open the earth and causes it to germinate, so a preacher by the ploughshare of his preaching cuts open the earth in order to make it fruitful in virtues. Whence the Apostle: “You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the grain,” that is, you shall not forbid the preacher to live from the Gospel, that is, from preaching, but shall provide for him; for the same [Col. 0721D] Apostle says: “If we sow spiritual things for you, is it a great matter if we reap your carnal things?” It denotes the devil, whence in Job: “He eats hay like an ox.” He seeks to eat hay like an ox because by the tooth of suggestion he seeks to grind down a pure life.

It denotes the Jewish people, whence in Isaiah: “The ox knew his owner,” that is, the Jew, “and the ass the manger of its lord.” It denotes Christ, because as an ox was sacrificed in the Old Testament, so Christ was sacrificed in the New Testament for our sins. It denotes the lustful person, whence [Solomon], speaking of a lustful and wanton woman, says: “He follows her as an ox led to sacrifice.” It denotes the virtuous or [Col. 0722A] just person, whence in the Psalm: “Thou hast subjected all things under his feet, sheep and oxen.” By sheep we ought to understand the innocent, by oxen the virtuous. It also denotes one made fruitful in good works, in the same passage.

**Cluster**, properly speaking, is that little bud which appears on the vine in spring, whence in the Song of Moses: “Their grape is a grape of gall, and their cluster is most bitter.” It denotes the gentile people, whence in the sequence of Master Adam [Note: [Col. 0721] Adam of Saint-Victor, Sequence V, *On the Resurrection of the Lord*, *Patrologia* CXCVI.]:

> The cluster of Cyprus is refreshed,  
> It spreads and grows;  
> The flower of the Synagogue withers,  
> And the Church blooms.

It denotes Christ in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is to me a cluster of Cyprus,” that is, comparable to a cluster for many reasons or causes. It denotes a grape, whence [Col. 0722B] in Numbers it is said of the scouts: “They carried a cluster on a pole.” It denotes a reprobate person, whence in the Apocalypse: “Put forth thy sickle and gather the clusters of the vines of the earth.” Here clusters denote the wicked, of whom it is read in Deuteronomy: “Their vine is of the vineyard of Sodom.” It denotes the beginning of grace, because just as the cluster precedes the grape, so the time of grace precedes the life of glory.

**Arm**, properly speaking, denotes the Son of God, whence in Isaiah: “And the arm of thy Lord has been revealed.” And he is called an arm because, just as the arm proceeds from the body and remains of the same nature as the body, so the Son proceeds from the Father without any diminution and remains of the same nature as the Father; and just as a man works through his arm, so the Father works through the Son. It denotes [Col. 0722C] Antichrist, whence the Lord says: “And the lofty arm shall be broken.” What else is understood by the lofty arm except the pride of Antichrist and that exaltation which is raised over the reprobate minds of men by the arrogance of worldly glory, so that a sinful man, scorning to be regarded merely as man, falsely claims to be God above men? It denotes severe vengeance, whence in the Psalm: “with a mighty hand and an exalted arm,” etc. It denotes authority or power, whence in the Psalm: “For the arms of sinners shall be broken,” etc. It denotes good action, whence in the Psalm: “Thou hast made my arms like a bronze bow.”

**Bruchus**, properly speaking, whence the Psalmist: “There was no number of the bruchi,” etc. It is the same as the locust called *atelebus*, though they have different meanings. *Bruchus* is called a brood and derives from *abromum*, “to consume.” A locust is so called as though “long spear”; its wings are innate. *Atelebus* means, as it were, “gliding high.” It denotes lust, because just as the bruchus is born from a locust dried upon a wall and, having no wings, clings to the earth and consumes and eats whatever it finds upon the earth, so lust devastates a man, takes away his reputation, empties his purse, weakens his body, defiles his soul, darkens his sight, loses God, and offends his neighbor. It is food for the devil and hateful to angels. Whence Joel: “What the bruchus has left,” that is, lust, “the locust has eaten,” that is, pride; for, when the penitence for lust has been accomplished, pride attacks and afflicts the man. It denotes fear or sorrow [Col. 0723A] over things lost, according to another exposition. And it should be noted that there are four states of man: hope concerning future goods, fear concerning future evils, joy concerning goods possessed, and sorrow concerning goods lost. Whence Boethius, *On the Consolation*:

> Drive away joys,  
> Drive away fear,  
> And banish hope.  
> Let no sorrow be present.

**Trumpet**, properly speaking, from *bucca*, “mouth”; it is otherwise called a *tuba*. It also denotes preaching, whence in the Psalm: “Sound the trumpet at the new moon,” that is, preach the New Testament. It denotes some eminent sign, whence: “The trumpet shall sound, and the saints who died in Christ shall rise first.” But this will not happen literally; rather, there will be some eminent sign by which all the saints shall be raised, which elsewhere in the Gospel is called a cry: “At midnight a cry was made.”

**Butter**, properly speaking, means any food, whence in Isaiah: “He shall eat butter and honey,” that is, he shall take any food, so that he may be shown to be true man; and he will be true man in such a way as also to be true God. It signifies the insults which he suffered, and according to another exposition the sense is: “He shall eat butter amid insults”; butter is sharp, while honey is [found] in miracles. It denotes the bitterness of the active life and honey the sweetness of the contemplative life. For then we eat butter and honey when we are afflicted with the bitterness of the active life and refreshed by the sweetness of the contemplative [Col. 0724A] life, so that we may know how to reject evil, that is, to despise the present life, and choose good, that is, the future life. It also denotes the teaching of elders, whence in Deuteronomy: “Butter from the herd and milk from the sheep,” that is, let the faithful receive greater teaching from greater persons, and lesser teaching from lesser persons. It denotes a good work, whence by butter good action and by honey Christ’s sweet speech are understood, so that he may know how to reject, that is, condemn, evil, and choose good unto life. It also denotes the fatness of milk; first impulses are called butter, whence someone is said to eat butter, that is, to destroy first impulses, and honey, that is, fleshly pleasures.

**Box tree**, properly speaking, denotes one who, blinded by infirmity, cannot perform good works, but nevertheless holds the faith of his parents; whence in Isaiah: “I will put in the desert the elm and the box tree together.” The box tree is a simple and lowly tree; it bears no fruit, yet remains green, and signifies those who hold the faith and flourish, yet, blinded by infirmity, are unable to perform good works, etc.

**Byssus** denotes a kind of flax growing in Egypt, which through much rubbing is turned white. It denotes a garment made of byssus, whence in Luke: “There was a certain rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen.” It denotes thread of byssus, whence in Exodus it is read that the curtain was of byssus, purple, hyacinth, and scarlet, that is, of purple, hyacinth-colored, and scarlet thread of byssus.

# C

[Col. 0723]

[Col. 0723B] **Corpse**, properly speaking, denotes one condemned, whence Isaiah the prophet: “And they shall go forth and see the corpses of the dead who have transgressed against me.”

[Col. 0723C] **To fall**, properly speaking, whence in the Book of Kings: “Eli fell backward from his chair and died.” Sometimes it signifies a fall from honor, whence Isaiah: “How hast thou fallen, Lucifer, who didst rise in the morning?” that is, from what honor? Sometimes a fall from virtue, whence Paul: “Let him who stands take heed lest he fall,” that is, let him who stands in virtue take heed lest he fall from virtue. Sometimes it signifies a fall from freedom from sin, though not into mortal but into venial sin. Sometimes a fall from the state of the present life, whence: “Where have the mighty fallen in battle?” Sometimes a fall from usefulness, whence Isaiah: “The Lord sent a word into Jacob,” that is, Christ preached the evangelical word to the Jews descended from Jacob, “and it fell in Israel,” and perished or bore no fruit. Or otherwise: “The Lord sent a word into Jacob,” that is, into the Synagogue, “and it fell in Israel,” that is, among the gentiles who were converted, and it bore fruit; [Col. 0723D] for Israel is interpreted “seeing God.”

**Blind**, properly speaking, denotes one blinded in mind, whence in the Gospel: “If the blind lead the blind, both fall into the ditch”; and elsewhere: “They are blind leaders of the blind.”

[Col. 0724B] **To strike**, properly speaking, means to beat, whence Christ in John: “Why do you strike me?” and elsewhere: “Without cause they struck me with scourges.” It denotes happening [Note: [Col. 0723] The old script does not distinguish *cadere* (“to fall”) from *caedere* (“to strike”), since both lack the diphthong.], whence it is said that matters [Col. 0724C] went badly for Herod Agrippa because of the death of the Lord. It denotes yielding place, whence in Cato: “Yield, yield to your superior.” It also denotes speaking, as in many passages in Terence, etc.

**Reed**, properly speaking, is a cane easily shaken and bent. It denotes a teacher’s skill, whence Isaiah says that in the haunts where dragons dwelt there shall spring up the verdure of reed and rush. It springs up because among those peoples whom the malice of the ancient enemy possessed, both the learning of teachers and the obedience of hearers are accumulated. It denotes the misery of temporal glory, whence Isaiah: “He shall not break the bruised reed.” He calls the shaken kingdom of Judaea a reed because they had no king of their own race, but a foreigner possessed the kingdom; but when Christ came, he did not break that kingdom by the power of judgment but endured it patiently. Temporal glory is rightly signified by a reed, [Col. 0724D] because inwardly it is empty in conscience through foolishness, but outwardly beautiful through appearance and display. It denotes the worldly man, who, like a reed, bends lightly toward good and evil, prosperity and adversity, [Col. 0725A] whence: “Behemoth lies hidden under the shadow of the reed,” because there he delights and rests, namely, in the worldly man. It denotes the prophet David, whence in the Psalm: “My tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe,” because he was the writer of the Holy Spirit. It denotes the Son of God, according to another exposition of the same example, because through him the will of his almighty Father is made known and shown to us.

**Heel**, properly speaking, is named from *calx*, that is, from the extremity of the foot. It denotes a final work, whence in Genesis: “I will put enmity between thee, O demon, and the woman,” that is, the Church; “and she shall crush thy head,” that is, thy first suggestions, “and thou shalt lie in wait for her heel,” that is, her final work.

It denotes the death or passion of Christ according to another [Col. 0725B] exposition: “I will put enmity between thee and the woman,” that is, the glorious Virgin; “and she shall crush thy head,” because through her, O demon, thy power has been weakened; “and thou shalt lie in wait for her heel,” that is, thou shalt plot to have Christ himself put to death. And elsewhere Christ says of the Jews: “They watched my heel,” that is, my death. It denotes hidden malice or deceitful thought, whence Christ says of Judas in the Psalm: “He who ate my bread with me raised against me,” that is, against me, “his heel,” that is, his hidden malice.

**Footwear**, properly speaking, denotes the incarnation of Christ, whence in the Gospel: “I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his footwear,” that is, the mystery or secret of Christ’s incarnation. And Gregory says: “Shod Divinity came to us,” that is, Christ in the flesh. And in the Psalm: “In Idumaea I will stretch out my footwear,” that is, in the world I will spread the faith of my incarnation and passion. It denotes the virtues of God, whence the Apostle: “Your feet shod for the Gospel of peace,” and in the Song of Songs: “How beautiful thou art in thy footwear, daughter of the prince!”

**Chalcedony** is a stone which does not shine while it is in a house; it grieves those wishing to carve it. When warmed by a ray of the sun or by rubbing with the fingers, it draws straws to itself. It signifies those who conceal their goodness and do their good works in secret, unwilling to be seen by men, according to that saying of Truth: “But thou, when thou fastest,” etc.; and again: “When thou givest alms,” etc.; [Col. 0725D] “But thou, when thou prayest.” And if anyone wishes to flatter or praise such persons, as though to carve and paint them, they do not receive their praise and vain glory. Touched, as it were, by the breath of the true sun or by fingers, that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit, they draw sinners to themselves by the word of their preaching and the example of their goodness. This stone is pale, and its pallor signifies patience.

**Pebble**, properly speaking, means a coal, whence Isaiah: “One of the seraphim flew to me and, taking a coal from the altar, touched my lips.” It denotes the reward of eternal blessedness, whence in the Apocalypse: “To him who conquers I will give hidden manna; I will give him a white pebble.” It denotes a judgment, according to our customary saying: “The decisive verdict has not yet been reached.”

[Col. 0726A] **Darkness**, properly speaking, denotes the devil, who is dark in himself, blinded through obstinacy, and blinds others by wicked suggestion; whence in the Psalm: “And darkness under his feet,” that is, the devil subjected to God. According to another exposition it denotes evil men blinded through unbelief, and the sense is: “Darkness under his feet,” that is, the damned shall be subject to God. It denotes stupefaction, whence the prophet Zephaniah says of the day of judgment: “That day, a day of error and darkness.” It denotes dimness of sight, whence in Genesis: “Isaac begot, and his eyes grew dim.” It denotes the confusion of error, whence Job, speaking of the devil under the figure of the day on which he was born, says: “Let darkness seize it,” because when the devil fell from the order of inward light, he inwardly confused himself with the darkness of error. It denotes [Col. 0726B] the confusion of mind arising from penitence; thus the aforesaid text may be expounded of the penitent: “Let darkness seize it,” that is, let the penitent be ashamed because of sin.

**Cup**, properly speaking, is a vessel by which drink is distributed in measured portions. It denotes the passion of the saints, whence Christ says in the Gospel: “You indeed shall drink my cup,” that is, you shall endure suffering for me. Passion is rightly called a cup because, as drink is measured by the cup for the drinker, so suffering is given in due measure to each patient person according to what he can bear. It denotes Christ’s blood, whence Paul: “Let every man prove himself and drink of the cup”; and elsewhere: “This is the cup of the New Testament”; and likewise: “My inebriating cup, how excellent it is!” It denotes the species of wine under which Christ’s blood is hidden, [Col. 0726C] whence it is said of Christ in the Gospel: “He took the cup and gave it to his disciples.” It denotes Sacred Scripture, whence in the Psalm: “A cup of pure wine in the hand of the Lord, full of mixed wine.” By pure wine spiritual understanding is meant; by mixed wine, literal observance; whence in the same place: “Yet its dregs have not been emptied,” that is, the literal understanding which the Jews still observe. It denotes eternal blessedness, whence David: “I will take the cup of salvation,” that is, I shall enjoy eternal blessedness. It denotes earthly pleasure, whence the Apocalypse speaks of Babylon’s golden cup by which God made all nations drunk, because all are intoxicated by earthly pleasure. It also denotes the vessel in which the sacrament of the Eucharist is celebrated on the altar.

[Col. 0726D] **Path** means a way. Paths denote the examples of the saints, whence in Proverbs: “May he guard the paths of the righteous.”

**Heat**, properly speaking, denotes the Holy Spirit, whence the Psalmist: “There is none who can hide himself from his heat,” that is, there are no thoughts in anyone’s heart which he does not see. It denotes concupiscence, whence in Paralipomenon: “These are they who came down from the heat of Rechab,” because concupiscence is exercised by means of heat. According to another exposition, and better in the foregoing example, it denotes charity, so that the sense is: He imitates Rechab, who had vowed not to drink anything by which he might be intoxicated and always lived in the open air, and all his descendants did likewise. The historical sense is: “Those who came down [Col. 0727A] from the heat of Rechab,” that is, those who observe Rechab’s religious rule or charity.

**Camel**, properly speaking, denotes a sinner burdened by the weight of sins, whence in Mark: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle.” It also denotes Christ, whence the Lord says that the Jews strain out a gnat and swallow a camel. The gnat wounds by buzzing; the camel willingly bends itself to burdens. The Jews therefore strained out the gnat when they demanded the seditious Barabbas; but they swallowed the camel because they tried, crying “Crucify, crucify,” to destroy him who willingly took upon himself the burdens of our immortality.

**Furnace**, properly speaking, whence Daniel says that Nebuchadnezzar cast the three youths into a furnace of fire. [Col. 0727B] It denotes tribulation, whence in the Book of Wisdom: “For gold and silver are tested in fire, but acceptable men in the furnace of humiliation.” It denotes tribulation of humiliation because in it man is humbled. It denotes charity, whence Isaiah says of it that “now there is fire in Zion, and there shall be a furnace in Jerusalem.” It denotes hell, whence the Gospel says that the wicked shall be cast into the furnace of fire.

**Field**, properly speaking, whence in Genesis: “Abel went out with Cain his brother into the field.” It denotes the world because of its pleasantness; hence it is called by the Greeks *cosmos*, that is, “adornment.” Whence in the Psalm: “Thou hast subjected all things under his feet: sheep,” that is, the innocent; “oxen,” that is, the virtuous; “and beasts of the field,” that is, worldly persons. It also denotes the Church of God, because just as there are varied flowers in [Col. 0727C] a field, so there are in the Church of God: there is the rose of martyrdom, the violet of humility, the lily of virginity, the grape of chastity; whence in the Song of Songs: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys,” etc. It denotes the breadth or extent of vices, whence in the Psalm: “We found her in the fields of the forest,” that is, wandering in vices. It denotes gentile lands, to which exposition the foregoing text may be referred: “We found her in the fields of the forest,” that is, the Church among the gentiles, that is, among wild men; and it is spoken in the person of the apostles. It denotes one descending in humility from the swelling of pride, whence in the Psalm: “Mountains rise and fields descend.” It denotes the saints, whence David: “And thy fields shall be filled with abundance,” that is, the saints shall be filled with the abundance of virtues and good works, etc.

[Col. 0727D] **Channel**, properly speaking, denotes the human heart, because as water runs through a channel, so contrition and remembrance of Christ’s passion run through the heart. Whence, in praises of the bride: “The hair of thy head [is] as the king’s purple joined to channels.” The king’s purple is joined to channels when Christ’s passion is impressed upon our hearts, so that we suffer with Christ in true charity. It also denotes the preacher through whom spiritual water descends into the beds of spices, that is, into the minds of the saints; whence it is said that water descends through channels into the beds. According to this signification the same text may be expounded: “The king’s purple is joined to channels,” when preachers set forth Christ’s passion.

[Col. 0728A] **Lattice** is a window broad within and narrow without. It denotes a gallery, whence in the Book of Kings it is said that the king of Israel fell through the lattice. It denotes obscure teaching, whence in the Song of Songs: “Behold, he stands behind our wall, looking through the windows and lattices.” Windows are broader, lattices narrower; by windows, therefore, is understood clear teaching proposed by Christ to lesser persons; by lattices, loftier and more obscure teaching offered to greater persons. It also denotes the human heart, whence in Proverbs: “From the window of my house I looked through the lattices”; these are the words of God looking down from the height of heaven into human hearts through the regard of their merits.

**Lampstand**, properly speaking. Sometimes it also signifies the cross, as in the Gospel: “No one lights a lamp [Col. 0728B] and puts it in a hidden place, but on a lampstand.” It also denotes Christ, to which signification the foregoing text may be referred, because one ought to light a lamp in faith in Christ. It denotes the flesh, because man ought to prefer the preaching of God’s word to love of the flesh. Sometimes it denotes the gift of the Holy Spirit, whence in the Apocalypse the seven lampstands signify the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

**To sing**, properly speaking, denotes making manifest, whence in the Gospel: “When thou givest alms, do not sound a trumpet before thee,” that is, do not make thy work known for the sake of human favor or earthly gain. Note that almsgiving is sometimes done in secret and sometimes openly: in secret, as in the foregoing example, namely, “when thou givest”; openly, as in the Gospel: “Let your works shine before [Col. 0728C] men, that your Father who is in heaven may be glorified.” It denotes prophesying, whence in a prose chant: “Isaiah sang,” that is, prophesied; “the Synagogue remembered, yet never ceases to be blind”; and elsewhere concerning the Sibyl: “Goddess, sing and prophesy,” etc. It denotes composing in metre, whence: “Moses sang a song to the Lord,” that is, he set forth a song to the Lord written in metre. And Virgil:

> “Arms and the man I sing.”

It denotes praising, whence Virgil:

> “... and they sang the king,”

that is, praised him.

**Dog**, properly speaking, denotes a preacher or good prelate. The dog has notable properties: some signify good shepherds; others, degraded hirelings [Col. 0728D] and thieves. These are the dog’s notable properties. A dog is an animal which shows familiarity toward man, guards its master’s house, drives away a thief, barks against an approaching wolf, puts a robber to flight, and has a healing tongue. By these properties it signifies the good shepherd, who is bound to show his subjects the familiarity of compassion, to discern their weaknesses, rejoice with the healthy, suffer with the sick, govern those on the way, and correct those who stray. He is also bound to guard the house of the Lord, that is, God’s Church, lest a thief, that is, a heretic, steal anyone from the Church by persuasion; lest a wolf, that is, the devil, devour anyone by temptation; and lest a robber, that is, a tyrant, rush into the Church by violent tyranny. Whence the Psalmist: “They shall suffer hunger like dogs”; and elsewhere: [Col. 0729A] “The tongue of thy dogs.” But in our times the dog has put on the wolf’s clothing, agrees with the robber, obeys the thief, and turns into a thief—if not in deed, at least in consent—because, led by negligence, he does not rebuke; darkened by ignorance, he does not know how to rebuke; or, touched by money, he allows him to remain in the Church. He does not bark against the approaching wolf because he does not expose the devil’s snares, either because he neglects to expose them or does not know how, or because, following the demon’s snares, he succumbs to its temptation. He flees from, rather than drives away, the robber, that is, the tyrant, because he is burdened by negligence, errs through ignorance, is softened by entreaty or payment, or enticed by greed. Of such persons Isaiah says: “Woe to you, dumb dogs unable to bark, because you despise.” A dog also denotes an evil prelate according to its [Col. 0729B] degraded properties. A dog is a mad, unclean animal, returning to its vomit. Thus prelates of our time rage indiscriminately against their subjects and, like mad dogs, disregard the lawful order and bark without discrimination: they soothe those whom they ought to rebuke, and bite with the bark of disordered severity those whom they ought to soothe. A dog is by nature an unclean animal; so prelates are unclean for many reasons: they overflow with lust, sink into gluttony, burn with anger, and blaze with avarice. Of these it is said: “Woe to you, dumb dogs unable to bark.” It also denotes a heretic on account of uncleanness, whence Christ said to the apostles in the Gospel: “Do not give what is holy to dogs.” It denotes the gentile people, [Col. 0729C] whence Christ said to the Canaanite woman in the Gospel: “It is not good to take the bread of the children,” that is, of the Jews, “and cast it to dogs,” that is, gentiles—the bread, that is, divine preaching, being for Jews and gentiles alike. It denotes an apostate, whence Peter says: “Like a dog he returns to his vomit.” It denotes someone lowly, whence in the Book of Kings Abner says to Ish-bosheth: “Have you regarded me as a dog’s head?” Whence David says in the same book concerning Saul: “A living dog is better than a dead lion,” that is, one living in the present life is better than one dead, with respect to the possibility of meriting, because the former can merit greater blessedness than anyone possesses in eternal blessedness. But one who is in the heavenly homeland is, conversely, called better by reason of certainty and blessedness. [Col. 0729D] This may explain what is said of John the Baptist: “Among those born of women none greater than John the Baptist has arisen,” and immediately there follows what seems contrary: “He who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.” It is explained thus: he who is in the heavenly homeland is called lesser in the possibility of meriting, and therefore is called dead, but greater by reason of this dignity; he is called a lion. He who is on the way is lesser in the possibility of sinning, greater in the power of meriting, and is called a dog on account of uncleanness, because so long as we are in this life, we are unclean.

A song (*canticum*) is properly the exultation of the mind concerning eternal things, breaking forth into voice. It signifies the preaching of the New Testament; hence the Psalmist: “He put into [Col. 0730A] my mouth a new song.” It signifies a prayer expressing God’s praise; hence in the song of Moses: “Let us sing gloriously to the Lord.” It signifies the exultation of eternal blessedness; hence in the Apocalypse: “The saints shall sing a new song before the Lamb.” Sometimes, by antonomasia, it means the *Song of Songs*, namely Solomon’s epithalamium, which sings of the ineffable union of Christ and the Church: “Let him kiss me,” and this by reason of its dignity. Note that “Song of Songs” is so called in two ways: either because of its antiquity in time, as Moses’ song, because no earlier work is recorded as having been composed; or because of the dignity of its mystery, as Solomon’s song, which is called *Sir Hasirim*, that is, “Song of Songs”: the Song of the Bridegroom or Bride, the poem of the beloved, the song of love, the song of the most beloved, or most loving, [Col. 0730B] or most desiring one, or the praises of the Bridegroom or Bride, etc.

To take (*capere*), properly; hence: “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy my vineyard,” that is, the heretics who destroy my Church. It signifies to happen, and is used impersonally; hence Christ, when his disciples told him not to return to Galilee because of Herod, who was plotting against him, said: “Tell that fox”—that is, Herod, who is called a fox because of his craftiness and deceit—“that it cannot happen,” that is, that it does not befall, “for a prophet”—that is, myself, who by antonomasia am called the Prophet—“to perish outside Jerusalem”; that is, I shall suffer in Jerusalem and nowhere else. It signifies to bear fruit; hence Christ says to unbelievers in John: “My word does not take hold in you,” that is, it does not profit [Col. 0730C] or bear fruit, etc. It signifies to take someone as an example; hence the Apostle in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians: “Take me”—it signifies an example, etc.

Hair (*capillus*), properly. It signifies saints or believers, who thin their bodies through abstinence for the adornment of their head, that is, Christ; hence in the Song of Songs: “Your hair is like a flock of goats.” For as hair adorns the head, so saints adorn Christ. It signifies venial sins; hence in the Psalms: “They are multiplied beyond the hairs of my head,” that is, sins and iniquities. Therefore clerics are commanded to remove their hair—for the length of hair signifies the multitude of sins—to signify that they are bound to put away mortal [Col. 0730D] sins and certain venial sins. Hair signifies the wicked; hence, according to another exposition, in the Psalm: “They are multiplied beyond the hairs of my head.” He compares enemies to the hairs of the head, which have been shaven off from Christ through their own unbelief. It signifies the loftiness of thoughts; hence in the Song of Songs: “Your hair is like a flock of goats which have come up from the washing-place.” The meaning is: Your hair, your thoughts, is like flocks of goats, that is, comparable to the movements of contemplation, since such thoughts pertain to contemplation, aptly signified by roe-deer. For just as roe-deer feed in the mountains and look about keenly, so such movements delight in heavenly things and contemplate the heavenly. “Which [Col. 0731A] have come up from the washing-place”: because, when the mind has been cleansed of love for earthly things, diverse movements of contemplation proceed from it.

The caper plant (*capparis*), properly, is a herb upon whose top a downy growth arises which is scattered by the blowing wind. It also signifies the Synagogue; hence in Ecclesiastes: “The almond tree shall blossom, the locust shall grow fat, and the caper plant shall be scattered,” that is, the Synagogue has lost its order of life by living in unbelief.

The roe-deer (*caprea*), properly; hence in the Book of Kings: “Azael was like one of the roe-deer,” etc. It signifies Christ, who is compared to a roe-deer according to his divinity. Those skilled in medicine maintain that this animal has within its entrails a certain moisture which drives away dimness of the eyes and sharpens dulled sight. Christ is therefore fittingly compared to a roe-deer, [Col. 0731B] because he not only sees the Father himself, but causes himself to be seen by those whose sight he has healed. Hence in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is like a roe-deer or a young stag.” Prophets are compared to roe-deer because of prophetic revelation: for as the roe-deer has keen sight, so the prophet has keen understanding in foreseeing future things.

Head (*caput*), properly, signifies God’s judgment. It signifies a beginning; hence David, speaking in the person of Christ: “At the head of the book it is written of me,” that is, at the beginning of the Psalter, where it says: “Blessed is the man,” etc. It signifies the human mind or reason: “His sorrow shall return upon his head,” that is, the punishment of a man’s sin shall return upon his head, that is, his reason shall be darkened. It signifies the first suggestion of the devil; hence in Genesis God said to the devil, [Col. 0731C] who was in the serpent: “I will put enmities between you and the woman,” that is, the Church; “and she shall crush your head,” that is, the first suggestion; “and you shall lie in wait for her heel,” that is, her final act. It signifies a woman’s husband; hence the Apostle: “The man is the head of the woman, Christ the head of the man, God the head of Christ.” It signifies the end of a thing; hence in Lamentations: “At the head of every street,” that is, at its end. It signifies the Synagogue, in relation to which the Gentiles are called the tail; hence: “The head is changed into the tail and the tail into the head,” that is, the Synagogue, which was the head before Christ’s coming, became the tail when the Gentiles were converted to the faith, in accordance with the Gospel saying: “The first shall be last.”

A coal (*carbo*), properly, is charity; hence James [Paul]: [Col. 0731D] “In doing this, you shall heap coals of fire upon his head,” that is, your patience shall kindle him in divine charity. It signifies a mind cold in sins; hence in Lamentations: “Their faces have become blacker than coals.” The minds of sinners become black after their whiteness because, having lost God’s righteousness, when sinners presume upon themselves they fall even into sins which they do not understand. It signifies the illumination of faith; hence in the Psalm: “Before the brightness in his sight the clouds passed, hail and coals of fire”: that is, most brilliant preachers, namely the apostles, passed through the whole world, threatening—which is signified when it says “hail”—and after the threatening hail followed coals of fire, that is, the illumination of faith, signified by coals. The apostles are called most brilliant also [Col. 0732A] in comparison with the prophets, because the prophets were obscure in their sayings; hence David: “Dark water in the clouds of the air,” that is, obscure understanding in the prophets. It signifies a preacher who by his preaching kindles others in the love of God; hence the Psalmist: “Sharp arrows of the mighty, with desolating coals,” that is, with God’s preachers, who desolate sinners from the love of earthly things and by their preaching console them to seek heavenly things. Coals signify preachers first alive through faith and grace, and afterwards dead through unbelief; hence David: “Coals were kindled by him,” that is, those long dead were illuminated by the grace of God through Christ our Savior.

A prison (*carcer*), properly, sometimes signifies the flesh; hence in the Psalm: “Bring my soul out of prison.” Sometimes [Col. 0732B] it signifies sin or hell: “Bring the bound out of the prison-house and the shadow of death,” that is, out of the prison of sin or hell. It signifies tribulation; hence the Apocalypse: “Behold, the devil is about to cast some of you into prison.”

A hinge (*cardo*), properly, is that around which a door turns; and it also means the subject matter around which a work turns. Hence: “The hinge of the external dispute was the commonwealth.” It signifies the east; hence in the hymn: “From the hinge of the rising sun,” that is, from the east where the sun rises.

Carmel signifies the mountain, Christ, who knows how to circumcise his faithful people from all vices by the true circumcision. For *Carmel* is interpreted “knowledge of circumcision”; hence in the Song of the Beloved: “Your head [Col. 0732C] is like Carmel.”

A poem (*carmen*) is a prayer written in metre; hence Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*:

> I who once, in flourishing study, composed songs,  
> Am now compelled, grieving—alas!—to enter wretched measures.

It signifies Sacred Scripture; hence in the Book of Wisdom: “Seeking out musical modes and recounting the songs of the Scriptures.” It signifies divine praise; hence in the Psalm: “He put into my mouth a new song, a poem for our God.” It signifies a word of incantation; hence it is said that enchanters deceive people by their charms.

Flesh (*caro*), properly, signifies a reprobate; hence of Behemoth Job says: “The limbs of his flesh cleave [Col. 0732D] together.” For the flesh of the devil consists of all reprobates who are joined to him in wicked action. It signifies the disciples of the Lord; hence Job, speaking in the person of Christ, says: “My bone clung to my skin, my flesh having been consumed,” as though to say: My disciples were consumed in my Passion through unbelief. It signifies punishment of the flesh; hence Job says to his friends: “Why do you persecute me as God does, and are you filled with my flesh?” that is, with the punishments of my flesh. It signifies carnal delight; hence in Job: “His flesh shall waste away, and the bones that had been covered shall be laid bare.” Flesh wastes away and bones are laid bare when, through scourges, carnal delight is diminished and the form of virtues which had lain hidden beneath the flesh becomes visible. It signifies carnal life; hence Job: “My flesh is clothed with rottenness and the filth of dust,” [Col. 0733A] as if he plainly said: The carnal life which I endure is polluted either by the wasting of slippery action or oppressed by the darkness of wretched thought arising from the memory of vices. It signifies substance; hence the Apostle: “One flesh of human beings, another of birds, another of fish, another of four-footed animals,” that is, substance. It signifies a human being; hence in John: “The Word was made flesh”; and the prophet: “All flesh is grass.” It signifies weakness; hence in Genesis: “My spirit shall not remain in man forever, because he is flesh,” that is, weak; “my spirit,” that is, my wrath, because he is of fragile nature and sinned through weakness; but the devil sinned through the fatness of iniquity. It signifies the carnal person; hence Paul: “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God,” that is, carnal people. It signifies carnality or sensuality; hence the Apostle: “The flesh [Col. 0733B] fights against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh”; and the Psalmist: “There is no health in my flesh.” It signifies the corruption of the flesh; hence, according to another exposition: “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God,” because there will be no corruption there. It signifies carnal knowledge; hence in Matthew: “Blessed are you, Simon Barjona, because flesh and blood has not revealed it to you,” that is, carnal knowledge. It signifies legal observance; hence the Apostle: “He renounced flesh and blood,” that is, legal observance. It signifies the form of bread, under which the body of Christ Jesus lies hidden. It signifies carnal intercourse; hence in Genesis: “The two shall be in one flesh,” that is, in one carnal act. It also signifies a righteous person; hence in the Psalm: “All flesh shall come to you,” that is, [Col. 0733C] the person who conquers the flesh.
