It signifies a relative; hence in Isaiah: “When you see the naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh.” It signifies a brother; hence in Genesis, Reuben, wishing to free Joseph, said: “For he is our flesh and our brother.” It signifies a woman; hence in John: “Who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh,” that is, of a woman, in whom pleasure is greater than in a man; hence in giving birth she is afflicted with a double pain.

Cartilage (*cartilago*), properly, signifies hypocrisy, because there are some who display in themselves an appearance of uprightness under which they conceal vices; hence in Job: “His cartilage is like plates of iron.” It signifies lesser Antichrists; hence Gregory: “Cartilage has the appearance of bone, but does not have the strength of bone.” There are certain lesser Antichrists in this time who are not distinguished by rank, but nevertheless strive to appear what they are not, and therefore become more wicked against the life of the good. [Col. 0733D]

Cassia is an aromatic species. It signifies baptismal faith, which is bestowed or nourished in waters, because cassia is nourished in waters; hence in the Psalm: “Myrrh and drop of myrrh, and cassia.”

Camps (*castra*), properly, signify the Church of God; hence in the Song of Songs: “Terrible as an army arrayed in battle.” It signifies a demon, since demons are said to be camps warring against God. It signifies the army of angels; hence Genesis records that an army of angels appeared to Jacob returning from Mesopotamia. Therefore the place where the angels appeared is called Mahanaim, that is, “camps,” etc.

[Col. 0734A] A fall (*casus*), properly, is the change of fortune from prosperity to adversity, concerning which Boethius says in *The Consolation of Philosophy*:

> He who has fallen did not stand on firm ground.

A natural fall is from life into death; concerning this it is read in the Book of Kings: “How have the mighty fallen in Israel!” A fall from grace is from virtues into vices; hence the Apostle: “Let him who stands take heed lest he fall.” A fall from glory; hence Isaiah: “How have you fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who rose in the morning?” A fall into the ruin of Gehenna; hence in the Psalm: “He shall fall when he has gained dominion over the poor.”

Cataclysm (*cataclysmus*) means a flood, from *cata*, “flow”; hence in the Book of Wisdom: “The cataclysm made the dry land drunk.” It signifies hell; hence in the book of Philo, who is also called Solomon: “All these things were created for the wicked, and because of them there is a cataclysm,” that is, hell, [Col. 0734B] because it was created to punish the wicked, etc.

Cataracts (*cataractae*) are said to be the branches of the Nile. For the seven streams into which the Nile was divided by Alexander are properly called cataracts and *cataduplae*, from *cata*, meaning “flow,” etc. They are also subterranean passages of the earth through which water runs; or dragons, or springs, are so called. Cataracts also signify clouds which were opened, that is, dissolved into rain, at the time of the Flood; hence in Genesis: “The cataracts of heaven were opened.” They signify preachers, because through preachers the rain of heavenly teaching descends upon those subject to them; hence in the Psalm: “Deep calls to deep at the voice of your cataracts.” They also signify the two Testaments which irrigate us with heavenly teaching, so that the meaning is: “Deep [Col. 0734C] calls to deep,” that is, the severe punishment inflicted on Adam for one sin indicates how great a punishment ought to be inflicted on sinners for many graver sins; and the two Testaments attest this, etc.

A chain (*catena*), properly, signifies the weakening of the devil’s power; hence: “I saw an angel descending from heaven, having the key of the abyss and a great chain in his hand,” etc.

A chair (*cathedra*), properly, signifies teaching or the love of ruling; hence in the Psalm: “He did not sit in the chair of pestilence,” that is, he did not give pestiferous teaching or entertain a love of dominion. This love is called by the name of pestilence because, just as the disease called pestilence spreads like pestilent milk and corrupts the whole flock, so the love of ruling infects [Col. 0734D] many. It also signifies a kingdom; hence in the Psalm: “Let them praise him in the chair of the elders,” that is, in pastoral government.

A cub (*catulus*), properly, is a lion’s cub. It also signifies Christ, because just as a lion raises its cubs on the third day after their birth, so God the Father raised his Son Jesus on the third day; hence in Jacob’s blessings: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you; Judah is a lion’s cub.” It signifies one inspired by a demon; hence in the Psalm: “I slept troubled in the midst of lion cubs,” and in many other places. It signifies lesser demons; hence David: “The lion cubs roar, seeking their food from God.” It signifies disciples of heretics; hence in Lamentations: “The lamiae uncovered their breasts and suckled their cubs.” A *lamia* is a certain [Col. 0735A] animal having a maiden’s face and horses’ feet. It represents those who at first put forward true things and at the end draw false conclusions, according to the saying: “Poisons often lie hidden, coated round about with the honey of words”; and the teacher pretends truth for as long as he speaks false words.

A tail (*cauda*), properly, signifies Antichrist; hence it is read in the Apocalypse that the dragon dragged a third part of the stars with its tail, because the devil will especially despise the righteous through Antichrist at the end of the world. It signifies earthly power; hence the Apocalypse says that there were stings in the tails of scorpions, because heretics, chiefly signified by scorpions, will harass the saints through earthly power. It also signifies the Gentile people; hence Isaiah: “The tail shall be turned into the head and the head into the tail,” because the Jews, who were [Col. 0735B] the first holy people, are last; and the Gentiles, who were last, have become first.

Heat (*cauma*) means burning heat; hence in the catalogue of creatures: “Bless the Lord, heat and cold.” It also signifies tribulation; hence Job: “My skin has grown black upon me, and my bones have dried up because of the heat,” etc.

An innkeeper (*caupo*), properly, signifies a false preacher who mixes falsehoods with truths; hence Isaiah: “Your innkeepers mix water with wine,” etc.

A cavern (*caverna*), properly, signifies Christ’s wound made by the lance; hence in the Song of Songs: “In the clefts of the rock, in the cavern of the wall.” By the clefts are understood Christ’s wounds made by the piercing of nails; by the cavern is understood the wound made by the lance. [Col. 0735C] The meaning, therefore, is: They dwell by faith in the wounds made either by nails or by the lance. It also signifies those less perfect persons who think lesser things concerning God; in the same authority, according to another exposition, the clefts signify those more perfect, while the cavern signifies those not so perfect in the faith of Christ.

It signifies the wicked human heart in which the devil dwells; hence in Isaiah: “The weaned child putting his hand into the cavern of the basilisk”; that is, Christ, after he has been weaned, will draw a human being out of the devil’s power, etc.; or Christ casts out the devil in the cavern of the basilisk, that is, from the wicked person inhabited by Lucifer, who is called a basilisk. Hence Master [Col. 0735D] Adam [Note: [Col. 0735] Adam of Saint-Victor, following *On the Resurrection of the Lord*, V, *Patrologia*, vol. CXCVI.]:

> Christ, hook and bracelet,  
> Pierces the serpent in its jaw.  
>   
> The weaned child puts  
> His hand into the basilisk’s cavern,  
> And thus, driven out, there flees  
> The ancient guest of the world.

“Hook,” he says, in accordance with: “Who shall catch Leviathan with a hook?” On the same subject the master says:

> “The weaned child puts his hand,” etc.

The cedar (*cedrus*), properly; hence it is read in the Book of Kings that Solomon made the Temple of cedars of Lebanon. It signifies [Col. 0736A] an angel; hence Isaiah: “What shall the shrub of the wilderness do when the cedar of paradise is moved?” that is: What shall the sinful human being do on the day of judgment when even angels tremble thus? Elsewhere Lucifer is called a cedar: “No cedars were taller than he in paradise,” that is, no angels. It also signifies one exalted in earthly honors; hence in the Psalm: “I saw the wicked exceedingly exalted and lifted up like a cedar.” A cedar rooted in place is of little use, but when uprooted it brings great usefulness. So a person powerful in earthly matters is useless, but when humbled through repentance confers great benefit; hence in the Psalm: “The voice of the Lord breaking cedars.” It signifies one possessing power over many; hence in the Book of Kings: “The thistle came to the cedar of Lebanon and said: ‘Give your daughter to my son as wife.’” This [Col. 0736B] was said by Joash king of Israel, who was very powerful, to Amaziah king of Judah, less powerful than he and wishing to fight with him. It signifies a saint, because as the cedar is a tall and fragrant tree and by its scent drives away serpents, so the saint excels in the height of virtues, emits the fragrance of good repute, and by word, deed, and example drives away serpents, that is, demons. Hence the Song of Songs: “The beams of our houses are cedar, our ceilings cypress”; and the Psalmist: “The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree; he shall multiply like the cedar of Lebanon.” It signifies the virtues of saints; hence Ezekiel: “A great-winged eagle ate the marrow of the cedar,” that is, the devil, who is called a great-winged eagle because of the subtlety of his suggestions, ate the marrow of the cedar, that is, [Col. 0736C] the abundance of virtues. It signifies a temple covered with cedar, where the material is put for the thing made of it. Thus, in the foregoing literal example, the great-winged eagle means Nebuchadnezzar, because of the multitude of his power; he ate the marrow of the cedar, that is, through his commander Nebuzaradan he destroyed the Temple built and covered with cedar, etc.

To assess or enumerate (*censere*) means to count; hence it is read that many thousands of the children of Israel were enrolled, that is, counted. Accordingly, *census* derives from *censio*, because in ancient times money was paid by number or weight, whence it is called “weighed out.” It signifies to recount; hence in the prayer for the Nativity of the Lord it is said: “the recounted birth.” Note that *recensita* is pronounced with a long *i*, and in that case derives from *recensio, -is*, which is of the fourth conjugation. Others say that it has a short vowel and is the supine of *recenseo, -es*, of the second conjugation, whose perfect is *recensui* and supine *recensitum*. Others say *recensetum*, deriving from *recenseo, -es, recensui*; and accordingly one may say *recensita nativitas* with *i* either long [Col. 0736D] or short.

Wax (*cera*), properly, signifies the human heart or mind softened or melted through repentance by the fire of charity; hence David: “My heart became like melting wax.” It signifies the wicked; hence in the Psalm: “As wax melts before the fire, so may sinners perish [Col. 0737A] before God’s face,” and they shall melt before the fire of Gehenna, etc.

The neck (*cervix*), properly, signifies pride; hence in Deuteronomy Moses said to the people of Israel: “For I know your contention and your most stiff neck”; and in the Psalm: “The Lord shall break the necks of sinners.” It signifies power; hence in Jacob’s blessings: “Your hand shall be upon the necks of your enemies.” It also signifies the uprightness of freedom; hence Job, speaking in the person of the Church, says: “He seized my neck and broke me,” that is, he bent down the neck which I held erect through the discernment of his Passion.

The stag (*cervus*), properly, signifies Christ, or Christ’s human nature, as appears in the title: “My God, my God, look upon me”; at the end of the psalm it is called: “For the morning hind.” Christ’s human nature is fittingly compared to a morning hind, because just as the morning hind, rising in the dawn, pierces and passes through thickets with its horns and sets itself upon the heights of mountains, so Christ, rising in the morning from the sleep of death, passed through the thickets of sufferings and mortality and set himself upon the height of the mountain: because after the Resurrection he passed into heaven. He also pierced the thickets, that is, he escaped human defects by the horns of his assumed divinity. Therefore Christ is compared to a hind and not to a stag, to mark that the human nature is inferior to the divine, etc. [Col. 0737B]

It also signifies prophets; hence in the Song of Songs: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the roe-deer and the young stags.” It also signifies saints; hence in the Psalm: “The high mountains are for the stags, and the rock is a refuge for hedgehogs.” The mountains are a refuge for stags: that is, saints who are troubled ought to have recourse to the high mountains, that is, to the apostles or their examples. The rock, that is, Christ, is a refuge for hedgehogs, that is, converted and penitent sinners, who are here signified by hedgehogs because of the hedgehog’s characteristic. It signifies either a neophyte or a perfect person, according to the twofold exposition of: “As the stag longs for springs of water.” This is expounded of neophytes with respect to baptism, or of the perfect with respect to eternal life.

A bit (*chamus*), properly, signifies a lesser tribulation, because a bit does not tighten a horse’s jaws as much as [Col. 0737C] a bridle. Thus a lesser tribulation is understood by the bit, and a greater one by the bridle; hence in the Psalm: “Constrain their jaws with bit and bridle,” that is, with lesser and greater tribulation. It signifies a diminution of power; hence in the Book of Kings the Lord says of Sennacherib: “I will put a bit in his head,” that is, I shall diminish his power. This occurred when the angel of the Lord in one night struck Sennacherib, while he was besieging Jerusalem, and killed eighty thousand of that king’s army.

A character (*character*) is a figure. It signifies imitation of Antichrist; hence in the Apocalypse: “A grievous and most severe wound came upon the people who have the character,” that is, who imitate the beast, that is, Antichrist. It signifies the reception [Col. 0738A] of sacraments; hence believers are said to possess the character of Christian religion or faith.

Charity (*charitas*) is a virtue; hence the Apostle: “Charity does not act perversely.” It also signifies God; hence in the Catholic Epistle: “God is charity, and whoever,” etc. It also signifies a sign of charity; hence in the Gospel: “No one has greater charity,” that is, no one has a greater sign of charity.

Cherubim (*cherubin*) is an order of angels. It also signifies fullness of knowledge; hence David: “He mounted upon the cherubim and flew upon the wings of the winds,” because however endowed with knowledge anyone may be, he cannot comprehend God. It signifies those filled with divine knowledge, because God is said to ascend over them, that is, to ascend over the cherubim. It signifies charity, because it is the fullness of knowledge without which knowledge is neither meritorious [Col. 0738B] nor perfect; hence in the Psalm: “You who sit upon the cherubim, show yourself before Ephraim,” etc. It signifies an image of an angel; hence in Exodus: “Moses made two cherubim from beaten gold.”

A string (*chorda*), properly, signifies a commandment of the Decalogue; hence in the Psalm: “Sing to him upon a psaltery of ten strings,” that is, fulfill the Decalogue, designated by the name of ten strings because it teaches the observance of the ten commandments. It signifies harmony between voice and deed; hence in the Psalm: “With strings and organ.” It signifies a virtue; hence on the passage in Isaiah, “My belly shall cry out for Moab like a harp”: As a harp does not emit a harmonious sound if one of its strings has been broken, so the spiritual belly of the prophet will not resound sweet melody if one string of the virtues is lacking. [Col. 0738C] The teachings of philosophers likewise maintain that the virtues cohere, so that if one is lacking, all are lacking.

A choir (*chorus*), properly, is an assembly of some persons; hence Augustine and Ambrose: “The glorious choir of apostles praises you.” It signifies a dance; hence it is read that girls led dances. It signifies an instrumental musical instrument; hence in the Psalm: “With timbrel and choir.” It signifies an order; hence it is said: “May the choir of angels receive her.” It is a measure; hence in Luke: “How much do you owe my master?” He said: “A hundred *choros* [measures] of wheat.” It signifies a wind; hence in Acts of the Apostles, where Paul’s shipwreck is described, it is read that those who were with Paul in the ship wished to [lacuna] spend the winter in a harbor of Crete facing Africus and Corus. It is also the name of a place; hence: “Custom gave him a stall in the choir and a voice [Col. 0738D] in the chapter.”

Christ (*Christus*) is a familiar name, arising from the Greek *Christos*, interpreted “anointed.” For *Christus* is Greek, *unctus* Latin, and *Messias* Hebrew. Accordingly, in a general sense anyone anointed with oil may be called a *christus*. But in a distinct and special sense, in the Old Testament kings and priests whose heads were anointed were so called. Hence David said to the man announcing Saul’s death in the Book of Kings: “Did you dare to stretch out your hand against the Lord’s anointed?” Likewise in the Psalm: “Showing mercy to his anointed, David.” These were called “anointed ones” as a sign of the honor and spiritual grace bestowed in anointing. Sometimes *Christus* is restricted so that only saints are called “christs,” anointed not with material [Col. 0739A] oil but spiritual oil; hence in the Psalm: “Do not touch my anointed ones.” Sometimes Christ is called, by antonomasia, the Son of God—Christ who is anointed with fullness of graces. Hence Peter in Matthew: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” In the name “Christ” he marked the Trinity: namely, the one anointing, the Son anointed according to his humanity, and the Holy Spirit with whom he is anointed. Note that Jesus was the proper name of the person, and he was Jesus from eternity because the person existed from eternity. The name Christ was an added name, because he acquired it from an event: in time he began to be anointed with fullness of graces. Of this anointing the Psalmist says: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness.” Thus he was not Christ from eternity. “Son of Man” or [Col. 0739B] “Son of the Virgin” was a surname.

Christ’s human nature is called Christ; hence Jerome: “Whoever denies that the Son of God assumed our Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema.” Certainly our Lord Jesus Christ was not assumed, but was the one assuming. The meaning is: Whoever denies that the Son of God assumed human nature, according to which our Lord Jesus is Savior and Christ—because the human nature is anointed and the divine nature anoints [Note: [Col. 0739D] The passage is corrupt.]—for it is not credible that he assumed a human person, namely a human being as one individual, namely human nature, that is, body and soul: let him be anathema.

Chrysolite (*chrysolithus*) shines like gold and sends out silvery sparks. It signifies wise and charitable persons [Col. 0739C] who show to others in deed and word what they know and understand; and this is to emit sparks. For *chrysos* means “gold,” and by gold are understood wisdom and charity, which is greater than all virtues. It is also read of in the Apocalypse, etc.

Chrysoprase (*chrysoprasus*) is purple in color and speckled with little golden spots, etc. It signifies those who always lead their life amid tribulation and the labor of sufferings while remaining always in charity. It signifies those who are pure, which is shown by the gold. *Chrysos*, “gold”; *prasus*, “horehound.” By gold are denoted purity; by the color of horehound, the greenness of faith and the whiteness of chastity. For horehound is white and green. It is read of in the Apocalypse.

To feed (*cibare*), properly, as in the Gospel: “If your [Col. 0739D] brother is hungry, feed him.” It denotes spiritual refreshment; hence in Ecclesiasticus: “The Lord fed him with the bread of life and understanding.”

Food (*cibus*), properly, signifies Christ’s spiritual refreshment; hence in the Gospel: “This is my food, to do the will of my Father”; and: “I have other food to eat which you do not know.” It signifies the flesh of Christ, both spiritual and material; hence in the Gospel: “My flesh is truly food.” It signifies the refreshment of spiritual wisdom; hence in Ecclesiasticus: “He fed him with the bread of life and understanding.” It signifies eternal life: the angel said to Tobit, “I use invisible food”; and in the Gospel: “That you may eat and drink.”

[Col. 0740A] Haircloth (*cilicium*), properly, signifies Christ’s human nature because of the harshness of its suffering; hence in the Psalm: “But when they troubled me, I clothed myself in haircloth”; and elsewhere: “I made sackcloth my garment.”

A lock or curl (*cincinnus* or *cirrus*) properly means a mass or entanglement of hair which girls commonly wear. It signifies saints joined together with one another; hence in the Song of Songs: “My locks are full of the drops of the nights,” because saints are sometimes drawn by the love of earthly things, which darken the eyes of reason, and are therefore called “drops of nights.” It also signifies the wicked, greatly entangled among themselves in vices, who are hairs in appearance but twisted toward unlawful things. Thus the foregoing authority may be expounded.

A belt (*cingulum*), properly, signifies chastity; because just as a belt [Col. 0740B] restrains the flowing folds of garments and does not allow them to wander here or there, so chastity constrains and restrains the flow and movement of lusts. Hence Solomon: “Who shall find a strong woman?” By the woman is signified the Church of God, which comes from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, that is, of Christ the Peaceful One. “And she gave a belt to the Canaanite,” that is, the Church offered chastity to Christ. Of this Luke says: “Let your loins be girded.” It also signifies justice; because as a belt holds clothes in order, so justice restrains excesses, giving to each what is his own. Hence the Psalmist: “Justice shall be a belt.”

Ashes (*cinis*), properly, signify a human being by reason of material; hence in Genesis: “Remember that you are ashes.” It signifies a human being by reason [Col. 0740C] of humility; hence in Genesis Abraham said to God: “Since I have begun, I shall speak to the Lord, though I am dust and ashes.” It signifies repentance; hence it is said: “Ashes and haircloth are the weapons of penitents”; and Job, speaking in the person of a penitent, says: “I have sewn sackcloth upon my skin and covered my flesh with ashes.” It signifies misery; hence in the Psalm: “For I ate ashes like bread.” Excessively subtle and useless inquiries concerning Christ’s human nature signify ashes; hence Amos: “Let not the bones of the king of Edom be reduced to ashes.” It is read in the Book of Kings that the king of Jerusalem and the king of the Edomites, who paid him tribute, wished to besiege the city of the Moabites because the Moabites wished to revolt from paying tribute. But the king of Moab, unable to withstand the attack of the besiegers, wished [Col. 0740D] to leave by the gate with his household. The king of Edom, who had been appointed to guard it, resisted him valiantly and did not allow him to leave, but forced him to return into the city. The king, however, inflamed with anger through fear, climbed to the top of the wall and there, in sight of the entire besieging army, sacrificed his own son, because he hoped that the Hebrews would be moved by pity. Seeing this, the children of Israel withdrew from the siege. Much later the king of Edom died. In revenge for that deed, the Moabites drew him from his grave, burned his bones, and scattered the ashes. By the king of Edom Christ is understood, because he himself said concerning Edom: “Over Edom I shall stretch out my sandal”; for Edom is interpreted “earth.” By the king of the Moabites are understood heretics and their supporters. The meaning is: “Let not the bones of the king of Edom be reduced to ashes,” that is, to excessively subtle and useless opinions devised concerning Christ’s human nature. For this would be to reduce the bones of the king of Edom to ashes and vanities. By bones are understood subtle, vain, useless, and hidden questions and opinions, which are scattered by the Moabites, that is, by heretics.

Cinnamon is an aromatic spice, signifying inward contemplation; because cinnamon has a most sweet bark, it signifies the sweetness of inward contemplation. Hence in the Song of Songs: “Nard, crocus, calamus, cinnamon.” [Col. 0741B] It also signifies good repute or esteem, hence: “Like cinnamon and balsam.”

To go round (*circuire*), properly, is to commit all divine good gifts or benefits to memory; hence in the Psalm: “I went round and sacrificed,” that is, by committing them to memory I considered all divine benefits. It signifies to search out in one’s mind, as: “that a man may fulfil all the wills of God”; according to this meaning the aforesaid authority may be expounded: “I went round,” that is, I searched my mind, in order that I might fulfil all His wills. It signifies looking round at the examples of earlier saints, so that each person may shape his life; and this is: “I went round and sacrificed.” Sometimes it signifies circumvention or a suggestion of the devil; hence the Apostle says of the devil: “He goes round seeking whom he may devour,” that is, whom he may deceive by suggestion and incorporate into himself. [Col. 0741C] And in Job the Lord says to Satan: “Whence do you come?” and he answered: “I have gone round the earth,” that is, “I have circumvented earthly people.” It signifies guarding; hence it is said of preachers in the Psalm: “And they shall suffer hunger like dogs,” that is, they shall hunger to sow the word of God and convert their subjects to the faith; “and they shall go round the city,” that is, they guard the Church. It signifies considering; hence in the Song of Songs: “I shall arise and go round the city.” It signifies clinging to changeable earthly things; hence in the Psalm: “The wicked walked round about.” It signifies wandering; hence the Apostle: “They went about in sheepskins, in goatskins,” that is, they wandered from place to place.

[Col. 0741D] A circuit, properly, signifies the changeableness of temporal things; hence in the Psalm: “The wicked walked round about.” It also signifies Christ’s human nature, which was changeable, in which the divinity lay hidden like an immovable point. Hence David: “I became like a ruined vessel, because I heard the reproach of many dwelling in the circuit,” that is, of the Jews, who considered in me only human nature, changeable through human defects, and did not reach the point of divinity. It also signifies deceit; hence in the Psalm: “The wicked walked round about.”

A circle (*circulus*), properly, exists when every part is equally distant from the centre. It signifies the polish of speech used by a heretic who, in order to veil his falsehood, employs brilliance of words to deceive simple hearts. Hence [Col. 0742A] Solomon: “A golden ring in its nostrils: a beautiful and foolish woman”; heretical perversity veils foolishness with the colour of words. It signifies restraint; hence the Lord, speaking to Job, says: “Will you put a ring in his nostrils?” that is, can you restrain the devil as I can? It signifies a cycle, hence it is customarily said: “This is sung through the cycle of the year.” It signifies a boundary or circularity; hence: “This Gospel is preached throughout the circuit of the world,” that is, through the circular regions or boundaries of the world.

A harp (*cithara*), properly, signifies the Son of God, who was a harp in dying, because the harp sounds from below; a psaltery in rising again, because the psaltery sounds from above; and glory in ascending. Hence in the Psalm: “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp.” [Col. 0742B] It signifies a time of tribulation; hence David: “I will confess to you upon the harp, O God, my God,” that is, in a time of tribulation. It also signifies service for earthly things, while the psaltery signifies service for eternal things; hence: “A pleasant psaltery with a harp.” It signifies the mortification of the flesh; hence in the Psalm: “Praise him with psaltery and harp,” that is, with devotion of mind and mortification of flesh. It signifies the exultation of the flesh; hence Job: “My harp has been turned into mourning.” It signifies suffering; hence Isaiah: “My belly and my harp cried out to Moab.”

“Quickly” (*cito*) denotes imminence of time. Sometimes it denotes the whole period up to the Day of Judgment; hence in the Apocalypse: “Things which must happen quickly,” that is, in the present [Col. 0742C] time. For all the time of this present life, compared with eternity, is like the tiniest moment of a single hour.

A city, properly, signifies the Church militant; hence in the Psalm: “Glorious things have been said of you, city of God”; and elsewhere: “The sides of the north, the city of the great King”; and again: “Great is our Lord and exceedingly praiseworthy in the city,” etc. It signifies this world; hence, in the same place: “In the fortified city.”

It signifies an assembly of evil persons; hence in the Apocalypse: “Babylon, that great city, has fallen.” It signifies eternal life; hence in the Psalm: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city,” etc. It signifies the soul of any believer, as in the Psalm: “That I might destroy from the city of the Lord,” that is, from the faithful soul, “all workers of iniquity,” that is, all evil thoughts, which are evil citizens. [Col. 0742D] It signifies hell; hence in the Psalm: “Who will lead me into the fortified city?” Hell is called a fortified city because before Christ’s Passion no one departed from it. It signifies the congregation of unbelievers; hence Isaiah: “I am the Lord and I do not enter the city,” that is, the congregation of unbelievers.

To cry out (*clamare*), properly, sometimes signifies devotion of mind; hence the Lord said to Moses in Exodus: “Why do you cry to me?” And in Daniel it is read that Susanna cried out to the Lord. Sometimes it signifies the evident character of a matter; hence the Lord said to Cain in Genesis: “The voice of your brother’s blood has cried to me from the earth,” that is, your criminal deed is evident and needs no accuser’s outcry. Hence Augustine: [Col. 0743A] “The evidence of a crime committed does not need the outcry of an accuser.” Sometimes it signifies prayer; hence in the Psalm: “I cried to you, O Lord, and hear me.” Sometimes, an invocation for help; hence in the Psalm: “From the ends of the earth I cried to you.” Sometimes, perfection of mind; hence in the Psalm: “I cried in my heart.” Sometimes, boldness or courage; hence the Lord to Isaiah: “Cry out, do not cease,” that is, preach boldly; and elsewhere: “The voice of one crying.” And I said: “What shall I cry? All flesh is grass.”

A cry (*clamor*), properly, is an evident and manifest sign at which all who have died before the Day of Judgment will rise; hence in the Gospel: “At midnight a cry was made.” It also signifies the voice uttered on the Day of Judgment; hence Zephaniah: “From the first gate there shall be a cry [Col. 0743B] and from the second a howling”: namely, from the first, from sight, when they see themselves being cast down into the abyss of hell; from the second, namely from hearing, there shall be a howling, when they hear that terrible word: “Depart, you cursed.” It also signifies religious devotion; hence David: “My cry is in His sight”; and elsewhere: “Understand my cry.” It signifies the manifestation or evidence of sin; hence the Lord said to Abraham in Genesis: “The cry of Sodom has come to me”; and elsewhere: “They have published their sins like Sodom,” etc.

Brightness (*claritas*), properly, signifies the divine nature; hence in John: “Father, glorify your Son with the glory which I had before the world was made.” It signifies nobility; hence in a certain prose: “Illustrious from the stock of David.”

[Col. 0743C] A nail (*clavus*), properly, signifies the word of God; hence: “The words of the wise are like goads fixed on high.” It signifies love of this world; hence Solomon: “A nail is blunted by a nail,” that is, love of this world is excluded by love of the Lord.

Clergy (*clerus*), properly, is the assembly of clerics, and it is a collective noun; it is called *clerus* from Greek *klēros*, “a lot” in Latin. Hence they are called clerics, that is, persons chosen by God’s lot. According to another translation, because *clerus* means “lot,” this noun *clerus* is used for the word “lots”; hence: “In your hands are my *cleri*,” where we say “my lots.” It signifies the New or Old Testament, as though given by lot, because through God’s grace, which is compared to a lot. Hence in the Psalm: “If you sleep among the midst of the *cleri*, the wings of the dove are silvered, [Col. 0743D] and the hinder parts of her back are in the paleness of gold, or the greenness of gold.” Construe it thus: O you preachers, if you sleep, that is, rest through contemplation, among the midst of the *cleri*, that is, in consideration and understanding of both Testaments, namely the New and the Old, you will be the wings of the spiritual dove, that is, of the Church, by which she is sustained. She is called a dove because of the many properties of the dove, by means of which wings she advances to higher things. The wings, I say, are silvered, that is, compared to silver on account of eloquence; for silver is a resonant metal. And the hinder parts of her back, that is, the perfect persons who are in the Church—namely active persons who bear the burden of day and heat for their subjects—are the hinder parts of her back, that is, of the Church; and these are [Col. 0744A] in the paleness of gold, or the greenness of gold, persevering in charity.

An oven (*clibanus*), properly, signifies a burning conscience; hence in the Psalm: “You will make them like an oven of fire in the time of your countenance,” that is, you will make them burn in their consciences, and this in the time of your countenance, that is, of your manifestation, when you appear in judgment or on the Day of Judgment. It signifies a heap of hay; hence in the Gospel: “If the hay which flourishes today is cast into the oven tomorrow, God so clothes . . . .” It also signifies any grave punishment, as: “This Day of Judgment will be an oven.” It signifies the devil; hence in Lamentations: “Our skin is like an oven because of the face of tempests,” that is, our carnality, that is, the devil.

A shield (*clypeus*), properly, signifies the devil’s opposition; hence it is said of [Col. 0744B] a holy preacher under the name of a horse: “Over him the quiver shall sound, the spear and shield shall flash.” The quiver is the hidden imagination of the wicked against God’s horse, that is, argument against the preacher. Therefore over the preacher quiver, spear, and shield flash, because the counsels of the wicked make open noise; from this arises an argument by which, as by a shield, the preacher is resisted.

Heaven (*coelum*) is called the air; hence in the Psalm: “The birds of heaven ate it.” It signifies the firmament; hence in Genesis: “God called the firmament heaven,” that is, the firmament which is heaven. It signifies heavenly judgment; hence, in Job, when the Lord questions him, it is written: “Do you know the order of heaven?” To know the order of heaven is to see the hidden predestinations of higher dispositions. [Col. 0744C] It signifies the divine immensity; hence it is said of the devil in Isaiah: “I will ascend into heaven,” that is, into divine immensity, “and I shall be like the Most High.” It signifies heavenly life; hence it is said in Job of the hypocrite: “If his pride ascends even to heaven, in the end he shall perish like dung.” The hypocrite’s pride is said to ascend to heaven because his exaltation seems to lead a heavenly life; but in the end he shall perish like dung, because from death he shall be led into torments. It signifies Sacred Scripture; hence in Isaiah it is said: “Heaven shall be folded up like a book,” and this at the time of Antichrist, because then there will be no interpreter of Sacred Scripture. And in the Psalm: “Stretching out heaven like a skin”: by heaven Sacred Scripture is signified to us; in it shine the sun of wisdom, [Col. 0744D] the moon of knowledge, and, to the ancient Fathers, the stars of examples and virtues. This heaven is stretched out like a skin because, formed through its writers by the tongue of the flesh, it is unfolded before our eyes by the words of teachers in exposition. By waters angels are signified; hence in the Psalm: “You cover its upper parts with waters.” The Lord covers the upper parts of this heaven with waters, because those things which it tells of the nature of divinity or of eternal joys, being still unknown to us, are known secretly to angels alone. Therefore heaven is both stretched out before us, and yet its upper parts are covered with waters, because some things of sacred utterance are already open to us through the revelation of the Spirit, while others, which can be manifest to angels alone, are still reserved for us. It also signifies God; hence in the Psalm: [Col. 0745A] “They have set their mouth in heaven.” It signifies a saint; hence in the Psalm: “He who dwells in the heavens shall laugh them to scorn”; and elsewhere: “The Lord’s seat is from heaven.” The heavens signify the apostles; hence in the Psalm: “The heavens declare the glory of God.” It signifies the Church; hence in the Apocalypse: “There was silence in heaven.” It signifies eternal life; hence in a certain antiphon: “The souls of the saints rejoice in the heavens.” It signifies the empyrean heaven; hence in Genesis: “God created heaven and earth,” that is, the worldly structure. It signifies reason; hence in the Gospel: “May your will be done, as in heaven so on earth,” that is, make our sensuality obedient to you as our reason is obedient to you—which will be so in the future. It signifies an incorporeal substance; hence in the Pentateuch: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth”: heaven, that is, spiritual things, namely [Col. 0745B] the angelic nature; and earth, bodily things, namely the matter of all bodies. It signifies the human mind; hence in the Psalm: “Truth sprang from the earth, and justice looked down from heaven,” that is, confession from the mind. Morally, it signifies Christ; hence David: “The Lord looked down from heaven upon the children of men,” etc. The heavens signify angels; hence in the Psalm: “Your magnificence is raised above the heavens,” that is, above the angels. It signifies the Holy Spirit or the operation of the Holy Spirit; hence the Apostle in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians: “The first man is earthly, from the earth; the second man is heavenly, from heaven, to reign,” that is, by heavenly operation or by the Holy Spirit; or “from heaven,” that is, of a heavenly nature, because both divine and human.

A supper (*coena*), properly, signifies evangelical doctrine; hence in the Gospel we read of the householder who made a great supper [Col. 0745C] and invited many. It signifies communion in the Lord’s body and blood, or the sacrament of the Eucharist itself; hence Paul: “When you come together into one, it is now no longer to eat the Lord’s supper,” etc.

God is said to know (*cognoscere*) by knowledge; hence David: “You have known all the last things and the ancient.” God is said to know by approval; hence in the Psalm: “Lord, you have tested me and known me,” that is, you have approved my sitting down, that is, humiliation in the Passion, and my rising up, that is, glorification in the resurrection. God is said to know causally; hence the Lord said to Abraham in Genesis: “Now I have known that you fear the Lord,” that is, I have caused it to be known; and elsewhere: “I have known you by name.” [Col. 0745D] God is said to know through eternal blessedness; hence the Apostle: “Then I shall know as I am known.” A human being is said to know by carnal intercourse; hence in Genesis: “Adam knew his wife.” An animal is said to know by an image; hence in Jeremiah: “The kite and the swallow knew the time of their coming; but Israel did not know me.”

To strain (*colare*), properly—hence a certain versifier says:

> He knows well how to strain out a gnat and swallow a camel,  
> Who bids the veil be taken away from acts of justice.

It denotes rejecting or cleansing; hence it is said in the Gospel of the Scribes and Pharisees: “They strain out a gnat and swallow a camel,” that is, they reject, confess, and cleanse lesser sins, but retain and commit greater ones.

[Col. 0746A] To cultivate or frequent (*colere*), properly, means to visit often; hence it is said: “I cultivate a house,” that is, I visit it frequently. It denotes to celebrate; hence: “Such a feast is cultivated,” that is, celebrated. It denotes rendering due worship to God; hence the Apostle: “They worshipped the creature rather than God.” Note that grammarians make the same distinction; hence the verse:

> He cultivates fields, the countryside, beauty, the gods above, and parents:  
> These he tills, this he inhabits, beauty he adorns, the gods he honours, parents he loves.

To gather (*colligere*), properly, signifies to remove; hence in the Gospel: “The Lord will send his angels as reapers, and they will gather out of his kingdom all scandals,” that is, they will remove from the Church all harmful things. It signifies bringing about ecclesiastical union; hence in the Gospel: “He who does not gather with me scatters.” It denotes acquiring; hence in the Gospel: [Col. 0746B] “From the fruit they shall gather eternal life,” that is, acquire it. It denotes proving; hence: “From this it is gathered in the decrees,” that is, proved; and Boethius: “All logic either defines, divides, or gathers,” that is, proves.

A hill (*collis*), properly, signifies a proud person; hence in Luke: “Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low”: by the valley we understand the humble, and by mountains and hills the proud, etc. Hills signify the less perfect in the Church; hence in the Gospel, concerning the Day of Judgment: “Then they shall say to the mountains, ‘Fall upon us’; and to the hills, ‘Cover us.’” Here mountains signify the more perfect and hills the less perfect. They signify the apostles and their vicars because of their eminence in virtues; hence in the Psalm: “The mountains leapt like rams, and the hills like lambs of sheep.” It signifies the excellence of Sacred Scripture, [Col. 0746C] hence in Joel: “On that day the mountains shall drip sweetness, and all the hills shall flow with milk,” that is, Sacred Scripture offers diverse draughts. It signifies eternal life because of the eminence of glory; hence among Jacob’s blessings, namely the one he bestowed upon Joseph, it is said: “The blessings of your father are strengthened by the blessings of his fathers, until the desire of the eternal hills should come,” that is, eternal life desired by the saints, which is signified by hills and is called plural because of the diversity of blessednesses, etc.

A neck (*collum*), properly, signifies a preacher, because just as food passes through the material neck, so preaching passes into the stomach of the hearers’ minds. Hence it is said of the Church in the Song of Songs: “Your neck is like an ivory tower,” [Col. 0746D] on account of the whiteness of chastity. In the neck is the throat, and in the throat is the voice; therefore by the neck of the holy Church sacred utterances are signified. It signifies pride; hence in Proverbs: “I have trampled down the necks of the lofty by my own power,” that is, humbled them. It signifies human discernment; hence in Daniel: “A chain shall be given upon his neck,” that is, a reward shall be given to human discernment.

A serpent (*coluber*), properly, signifies Antichrist; hence in Genesis: “Dan, a serpent in the way, a horned serpent in the path.” It signifies the devil; hence in Job: “By his labouring hand the twisting serpent was brought forth.” It is called a dragon when it devours the negligent, an asp when it strikes secretly, a bird when it deceives through pride, a basilisk when it poisons openly, and a lion when it persecutes violently. It also signifies Ahaz, the father of Hezekiah; hence it is read that from the root [Col. 0747A] of the serpent shall arise a basilisk, that is, from King Ahaz, Hezekiah, who will subdue his enemies.

A dove (*columba*), properly, signifies the Church; hence in the Song of Songs: “My dove, my beloved, in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the wall”; and elsewhere: “Your eyes are doves”; and in the Psalm: “If you sleep among the midst of the *cleri*, the wings of the dove,” because the Church is called a dove on account of the dove’s many properties. It signifies some saint because of simplicity; hence in the Psalm: “Who will give me wings like a dove?” and elsewhere: “And like doves to their windows.” It signifies God; hence in Jeremiah: “The land has been made desolate because of the presence of the wrath of the dove,” that is, because of the presence of the Lord’s wrath. For the dove is a very simple animal, and because no inequality creeps into any of the Lord’s [Col. 0747B] anger, he called the Lord’s fury “wrath,” in order to show the undisturbed force of the day of judgment, etc.

A column (*columna*), properly, signifies a gift of the Holy Spirit; because, just as a material building is supported by material columns, so a spiritual building is supported by the gifts of the Holy Spirit as spiritual columns. Hence: “Wisdom has built herself a house; she has hewn out seven columns,” that is, the Son of God made human nature a house for himself, and in it he hewed out the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Isaiah suggests this when he says: “A virgin shall come forth from the root of Jesse,” etc., “and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him.” It also signifies anyone strong against the devil’s temptations; hence the Lord says: “Whoever conquers, I will make him a column in the temple of God.” For whoever is made firm in God’s work by right intention is raised as a column in the structure of the spiritual building; or he is placed in this temple, which is the Church, for both usefulness and beauty, etc. [Col. 0747C] The four Evangelists are called columns; hence the Lord says to Moses in Exodus: “You shall make four columns and their bases, clothed in silver.” In the silver the brightness of the divine word is understood; by the bases we understand the teachers of the holy Church; and by the four columns we must understand the sayings of the four Evangelists. The chief preachers of the Church are called columns, upon whom in heaven the entire growing structure of the spiritual building rises; hence in Job: “The columns of heaven tremble.” But this trembling is not penal nor caused by fear, but by wonder. The apostles are called columns, because the primitive [Col. 0747D] Church rested upon the apostles as upon columns; hence in the Psalm: “He established its columns,” that is, the apostles. Peter and John are called so particularly; hence it is said in Acts that the Apostle, coming to Jerusalem, found no one except Peter and John, who were columns of the Church. Angels are called columns; hence Job: “The columns of heaven tremble before God,” that is, the angels. A saint is called a column; hence: “I shall dwell in the highest places,” says Wisdom, “and my throne is in a column of cloud,” that is, in a saint, who is a column of the Church, shaded by a cloud, that is, by the grace of the Holy Spirit. It signifies prophecy: for the Mosaic Law is like a base laid beneath; prophecy is set up as a column upon the base; and the Gospel is like an architrave. Thus after the Law prophecy was added [Col. 0748A] as a column, and after prophecy the Gospel as a capital.

Hair (*coma*), properly, signifies believers adhering to Christ and believing for his adornment; hence in the Song of Songs: “His locks are like the lifted branches of palms,” etc.

To eat (*comedere*), properly, signifies to wipe out or destroy; hence it is said in the Psalm concerning the Chaldeans: “They have eaten Jacob,” that is, destroyed the Jews descended from Jacob. It signifies to kill; hence David: “The zeal of your house has eaten me,” that is, the envy of the Jews for the Synagogue killed me. It signifies suffering or suffering with another; hence in the same example, according to another exposition, the meaning is: “Love of the Synagogue invited me to suffering, or set me aflame with the love of charity for the Synagogue’s suffering.” Sometimes it denotes spiritual incorporation; hence [Col. 0748B] in a gloss concerning Christ it is read that at the time of the Passion he ate only one thief, that is, incorporated him into the Church. Sometimes it denotes ecclesiastical union; hence in John: “Unless you eat flesh,” that is, unless you belong to ecclesiastical union, “you shall not have life in yourselves.” Sometimes it denotes spiritual food; hence Wisdom: “Those who eat me shall still hunger,” etc.

A fetter (*compes*), properly, signifies worldly misery or sin; hence in the Psalm: “That he might hear the groaning of those in fetters.” It also signifies a divine command; hence in the Psalm: “To bind their kings in fetters,” that is, in God’s commandments. And Solomon says: “Put your feet into fetters,” that is, into God’s commandments, etc.

*Con-* is an inseparable preposition. It always denotes completion, as is clear in these words: *contritio* (“contrition”), [Col. 0748C] *confessio* (“confession”), *contristatus* (“made sorrowful”). It can also denote accompaniment, so that *contristatus* means “made sorrowful with another.” It denotes plurality; hence *contristatus*, that is, “made sorrowful by many things,” and *conturbatus*, that is, “troubled by many things.”

A concubine (*concubina*), properly, signifies a soul that serves God not chastely, that is, not with true love, but for earthly advantage or human praise; hence: “There are sixty queens and eighty concubines,” in the Song of Songs.

To desire (*concupiscere*) sometimes denotes the most fervent movement of ardour; hence in the Psalm: “It desires and fails.” Sometimes it denotes the first movement of concupiscence; hence the Apostle: “What I do not will, this I desire,” that is, I am moved by first motions toward desire, not toward action or consent. Sometimes it denotes consent and action; [Col. 0748D] hence in the Law: “You shall not covet your neighbour’s property”; and the Apostle: “I did not know that concupiscence was sin, unless the Law said: ‘You shall not covet,’” that is, you shall not bring the first movements of desire into action or consent. Sometimes it denotes the first movement of reason; hence in the Psalm: “My soul desired to desire your justifications.” Note that the first movement of reason is not extinguished in a person living in mortal sin. For a person in mortal sin wills evil and does it; yet he would wish to do good, or to will good. He wills his willing to be good, but does not will to be good. This comes from the first movement of reason, which is not brought into effect because of mortal sin. Hence in the aforesaid example: “My soul desired,” etc.; it does not say “desires,” but “desired to desire,” [Col. 0749A] for it speaks in the person of a sinner. The same point is made by Paul’s saying: “To will the good lies near at hand to me,” through the first movement of reason, which could not be extinguished in me; “but to accomplish it I do not find,” through the will of nature, unless the will of grace be present.

To confer (*conferre*) means to give or bestow; hence in certain prayers it is said: “May God deign to confer his grace upon us.” It denotes to benefit; hence it is said: “This medicine conferred nothing upon me,” that is, it was of no use. It denotes to converse; hence in the Gospel it is said of those going to Emmaus: “What are these words that you are conferring with one another?” It denotes to place; hence in law: “They referred themselves to arbitrators,” that is, placed themselves before them. It denotes making a contribution, that is, putting in a share; hence those who put a share into a group of twelve are said to “confer.” And “I believe in God” is called the *Symbolum*, [Col. 0749B] that is, the collection of the Apostles, from *syn*, meaning “together,” and *bolus*, meaning “share,” because each added his own part to it. It also signifies gathering together; hence in the *Bucolics*:

> And Corydon brought together the flocks.

Confession is of compulsion, when it proceeds from coercion, as the confession by which demons confessed the Son of God, saying: “Jesus, Son of the living God, why have you come before the time to torment us?” There is confession of despair, proceeding from desperation, as that by which Judas confessed: “I have sinned in betraying innocent blood,” etc.; and Cain said: “My iniquity is too great for me to deserve pardon.” There is confession of repentance, proceeding from sorrow, that is, penitence, concerning which James says in his catholic Epistle: “Confess your sins to one another.” There is [Col. 0749C] confession of praise, by which we confess God’s goodness; hence in the Psalm: “Confess to the Lord, for he is good.”

To confess (*confiteri*) is to acknowledge or profess something and not deny it; hence it is said of John in the Gospel: “He confessed and did not deny,” that is, he professed. It denotes confessing all sins universally; for no one is said to confess unless he confesses all sins. Hence James: “Confess your sins to one another.” It denotes furnishing matter for divine praise; hence David: “Let all your works confess to you, O Lord.” It denotes praising; hence in the Psalm: “I will confess to you, O Lord, with all my heart”; and elsewhere: “Confess to the Lord, for he is good.” It also denotes thanksgiving, as John the bishop says in his exposition of Matthew’s homily: [Col. 0749D] “I will confess to you, Lord God.”

To confound (*confundere*) denotes confusion of nature, or the mixing of certain things in which both are corrupted, as happens in *hydromel* [a mixture of water and honey]. Sometimes it denotes the mixing of persons; hence Athanasius: “Neither confounding the persons, as Sabellius did, nor separating the substance, as Arius did.” Sometimes it denotes the confusion of blushing shame; hence Paul: “Hope does not confound,” that is, human hope in Christ causes no one to blush. Sometimes it denotes the confusion of penitence, when someone is ashamed of sin; hence David: “Let them be confounded and ashamed.” Sometimes it denotes the confusion of damnation; hence in the Psalm: “In you, O Lord, I have hoped; let me not be confounded.”

To consider (*considerare*) signifies to understand; hence Obadiah: [Col. 0750A] “Consider your works”; and in the Song of Love: “Do not consider me because I am dark,” etc. It signifies to see; hence: “He who formed the eye, does he not consider?” It signifies to lie in wait; hence David: “They considered me”; and elsewhere: “The sinner considers the just man.”

Counsel (*consilium*), properly, signifies suggestion; hence in the Psalm: “Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the wicked.” It signifies consent; hence in Jacob’s blessings concerning Simeon and Levi: “Let not my soul enter into your counsel.” It signifies judgment; hence in the Psalm: “Therefore the wicked shall not rise in judgment, nor sinners in the counsel of the righteous.” Because judgment ought not to be made without counsel, judgment is called counsel. It signifies Christ’s humble coming, made by the Son of God himself with supreme dispensation; hence in the Psalm: “You have confounded the counsel [Col. 0750B] of the poor.” It signifies a stricter precept; hence the Apostle: “Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give counsel.” It signifies deliberation; hence David: “How long shall I place counsels in my soul?” It signifies a gift of the Holy Spirit; hence Isaiah: “The Spirit of counsel and might.” It also signifies that which is subject to counsel; hence the Psalmist: “They are caught in the counsels which they devise.”

To consist (*constare*), properly, sometimes denotes composition; hence Augustine: “As a human being consists of soul and body, so Christ of God and man.” Sometimes it denotes steadfastness; hence in Chronicles: “Be steadfast, and you shall see.” Sometimes it denotes immovability; hence in the Book of Kings: “He stood in a field of lentils.” Sometimes it denotes price; hence it is commonly said: [Col. 0750C] “How much did this vessel cost?” Sometimes it denotes manifestation or certainty; hence it is said: “This is established,” that is, it is certain and manifest.

A consul (*consul*), properly, signifies an angel; hence Job: “Now, sleeping, I should be silent, and in my sleep I should rest with the kings and consuls of the earth,” because, had man not sinned, he would rest with angels. Angels are rightly called consuls, because they provide for the spiritual commonwealth while they join us to themselves as companions for the eternal kingdom. For, as they announce it, we know the will of the Creator; and in them, without doubt, we find counsel out of the distress of our tribulation.

To crush (*conterere*), properly, signifies to condemn; hence Jeremiah: “With a double crushing you will crush them, O Lord,” that is, you will condemn [Col. 0750D] them in body and soul. And elsewhere: “The stone, upon whomever it falls, will crush him.” It signifies repenting; hence David: “A contrite and humbled heart.”

To happen (*contingere*) means to occur: “It happened that the beggar died.” It denotes belonging to; hence in Luke the prodigal son says: “Give me the portion of the substance which falls to me,” that is, which belongs to me. It signifies touching; hence in Leviticus: “The walls of the temple touched one another.” Sometimes it denotes a relationship of kinship; hence it is said: “These persons are related in the first degree.”

*Contra* (“against”), properly, denotes opposition; hence in Job: “In all these things Job did not sin with his lips, nor did he say anything foolish against God.” It also denotes the presence of a thing; hence David: “My sin is always against [Col. 0751A] me,” that is, before my face, because I ought always to retain my sin in memory, etc. Sometimes it denotes material; hence Job: “Against a leaf which is carried by the wind,” that is, in respect to a leaf. Sometimes it denotes adherence to the property of a thing; hence Job: “For you write bitterness against me,” that is, you inflict bitter punishments. Sometimes it denotes “before”; hence in the Psalm: “All day long my shame is before me,” that is, my shame is before me.

Contrition. There is the contrition of penitents; hence in the Psalm: “A contrite and humbled heart, O God.” There is the contrition of the perfect; hence in the Song of Songs: “Who is this who ascends . . . and of every powder?” By powder contrition is figured. It signifies the contrition of the evil in the present; hence in the Psalm: “Contrition and unhappiness are in [Col. 0751B] their ways,” etc. It signifies the contrition of the evil in the future; hence Jeremiah: “With a double crushing crush them,” etc.

To come together (*convenire*), properly, signifies consenting; hence David: “The kings of the earth stood by, and the princes came together as one.” It signifies making an agreement; hence Matthew: “Wicked servant, did you not agree with me for a denarius?” It signifies summoning to court; hence Augustine: “I summon you, O Jews.” It signifies being suitable or fitting; hence common speech: “This garment suits this person,” etc.

A basket (*cophinus*), properly, is a vessel woven from palm leaves and rush; hence in the Gospel: “And they filled twelve baskets with fragments.” It signifies uncleanness of life; hence in the Psalm: “His hands served in the basket and in works of sin for Pharaoh,” that is, for the devil, etc.

[Col. 0751C] The heart (*cor*), properly, signifies the human soul; hence in the Psalm: “He who fashioned their hearts one by one,” that is, who creates souls individually. This is against those who say that souls are infused by propagation; rather, he creates souls daily, and in creating infuses them, and in infusing creates them. It signifies reason; hence David: “My heart is troubled within me.” It signifies will; hence in the Gospel: “From the heart proceed adulteries and thefts.” It signifies thought; hence the Psalmist: “God searches hearts and reins.” It signifies intellect; hence in Exodus: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart.” It also signifies the heart of Jerusalem; hence in the Gospel: “As Jonah was in the belly of the whale, so the Son of Man shall be in the heart of the earth,” that is, buried within Jerusalem, which is called the heart of the earth because it is in the middle of the earth, namely [Col. 0751D] between west and east, not between the northern and southern regions. It also signifies the higher power of the soul by which God and heavenly things are contemplated, and which is designated by various names. It is called intellect, intelligence, and intellectuality; hence: “Intellect belongs to God alone and to very few human beings.” — “Man shall approach the lofty heart,” and Paul was rapt to that. It signifies the Son of God, in the same example according to another exposition; and the reading will be different: “Man shall approach the lofty heart,” that is, divine and human nature come together in Christ. It signifies the depth of vices; hence in the Psalm: “The mountains shall be carried into the heart of the sea.” Or “the heart of the sea” signifies lesser persons among the Gentiles, for whose conversion the mountains, that is, the preachers, shall be transferred, etc.

[Col. 0752A] “Before” (*coram*) sometimes denotes the presence of a thing; hence in the Book of Wisdom: “And even if before men.” It denotes opposition to a thing; hence it is read of the prodigal son: “Father, I have sinned against heaven,” that is, against heaven, “and before you,” that is, against you. Sometimes it denotes approval; hence the Apostle: “For we provide good things not only before God,” that is, so that God may approve, “but also before all men,” that is, so that people may approve.

Cornu, properly “horn.” It signifies Christ’s human nature; for as a horn has its place in the more eminent part of the body, is harder than flesh and softer than bone, and by it an animal drives away creatures harmful to it, so Christ assumed flesh for himself from the more eminent stock of human nature; and according to his humanity he is worthier than every human [Col. 0752B] nature, yet inferior to the divine nature. And Christ, the horn—that is, human nature—drove away all his enemies, visible as well as invisible; whence in the Canticle of Zachariah: “He has raised up for us a horn of salvation in the house of David his servant,” that is, the family of David. It signifies the arm of the cross; whence Habakkuk: “Horns are in his hands”; and this is hypallage, that is, Christ’s hands are in the horns, namely, in the arms of the cross. Horns signify earthly power or pride; whence in the Psalm: “I shall break the horns of sinners.” They signify the good works of the righteous, namely virtues; whence David: “The horns of the righteous shall be exalted,” that is, the virtues of Christ, by which, as by horns, he drives away enemies. It signifies the resistance or assault of enemies; whence in the Psalm: “Deliver my soul [Col. 0752C] from the horns of enemies,” that is, of the Jews. It signifies eminence; whence in the Psalm: “Appoint the solemn day . . . as far as the horn of the altar.” It signifies abundance; whence Isaiah: “I planted my vineyard,” that is, the Church or the Synagogue, says the Father to my beloved, that is, Jesus Christ, “on a horn, the son of oil,” that is, in the abundance of the fullness of graces possessed by Christ, who is called the son of oil, that is, of charity, which is signified by oil. It signifies a kingdom; whence in the Apocalypse: “I saw a beast . . . from the sea, having seven heads and ten horns,” that is, Antichrist, who will subject to himself ten kingdoms of the world. It signifies the Holy Spirit or a gift of the Holy Spirit; whence it is read that John saw a lamb having seven horns, that is, the sevenfold Holy Spirit or the seven [Col. 0752D] gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Corona, properly “crown”; whence in the book of Maccabees: “They adorned the face of the temple with golden crowns.” It signifies eternal life; whence James: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation,” etc.; for just as a crown is given to a victor, so eternal life is given to those who triumph in Christ. It signifies the exaltation of pride; whence Isaiah: “Woe to the crown of pride of the drunken Ephraimites.” It signifies the sublimity of glory; whence Isaiah: “On that day the Lord of hosts shall be a crown of glory.” It signifies the order of saints; whence in the Psalm: “Lord, you placed upon his head a crown of precious stone,” because the saints are like stones in Christ’s crown. It signifies the time of grace; whence David: “You will bless the crown of the year of your goodness,” etc.

Corpus, properly “body.” It signifies the body of Christ; whence in the [Col. 0753A] Gospel: “Where the body shall be, there the eagles shall be gathered,” that is, in the empyrean the saints, renewed like eagles, will be with Christ. It signifies the Church; whence the Apostle: “We are one body.” It signifies a good work; whence in the Gospel: “If your eye,” that is, your intention, “is single, your whole body shall be full of light.” It signifies the totality of sin; whence Paul: “Let the body of sin be destroyed.” Because of solidity it signifies perfection and fullness; whence the Apostle: “In whom the fullness of divinity dwells bodily,” that is, solidly, fully, and perfectly. It signifies a spouse; whence in the Apostle: “He who commits fornication sins against his own body,” that is, against the honor of his spouse.

Corruptio, properly “rotting”; whence in the Psalm: “Nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption.” It signifies [Col. 0753B] wounding; whence David: “What profit is there in my blood, while I go down into corruption?” It signifies sin; whence in the Psalm: “They are corrupt and have become abominable.” It signifies defloration; whence in the Passion of Nereus and Achilleus: “Although God can do all things, he cannot make a virgin out of one who has been defiled.”

Cortex, properly “bark.” It signifies a saint who is not ashamed of Christ’s Passion; whence in the *Song of Songs*: “Your cheeks are like the bark of a pomegranate,” because the teachers of holy Church who expound sacred Scripture keep Christ’s Passion in memory, not only by believing but also by imitating it. It signifies the literal sense; whence in Job: “Those who ate herbs and the bark of trees”: they eat the bark of trees who in sacred volumes honor only the surface of the letter, and preserve nothing of spiritual understanding, since they suppose that there is nothing further in God’s words beyond what they have heard outwardly. [Col. 0753C] It signifies the work of one who makes a good beginning; whence, according to another exposition: “And they ate herbs and the bark of trees.” To eat herbs is not to keep the least commandments or works; to chew the bark of trees is to despise the greater commandments or good works.

Cortina, properly “curtain.” It signifies a faithful person; whence in the Apocalypse: “He who hears, let him say, ‘Come’; and let curtain draw curtain,” that is, one believer edifies another. This was signified by the curtains in the Old Testament joined together with hyacinth-colored loops, so that when one was drawn, the others followed.

Corvus, properly “raven.” It signifies the Gentiles; whence in Job, when the Lord questions [Col. 0753D] Job, it is said: “Who prepared its food for the raven, when its young cry to God?” By ravens and their young the Gentile people, in grace, are signified amid the soot of sins; food is given to the young ravens when their desires are refreshed by our manner of life. Food was prepared for this raven [reading uncertain], when the Church converted it to her faith. It signifies a holy preacher; whence Solomon: “Let the ravens of the torrents pluck out the eye that mocks its father and despises the bearing of its mother.” Those who despise God’s judgments mock the Father; those who deride the preaching of holy Church despise their mother’s bearing. But holy preachers, while they attack such persons with the streams of sacred Scripture, as ravens from the torrents extinguish their eyes, [Col. 0754A] that is, their arguments. They are called ravens because through the grace of humility they recognize themselves to be sinners. It signifies a hireling preacher. The raven has three qualities: it sends forth a hoarse cry, is black, and feeds upon corpses. Thus the hireling preacher becomes hoarse, either because he cannot or because he will not speak, since he preaches for the favor of earthly gain. He is black with the soot of sins; he feeds upon earthly honors, which are compared with corpses. Whence the Psalmist: “And the young of the ravens that call upon him.” The young ravens are the subjects of hireling prelates. A raven also signifies one who wears down his flesh by abstinence and reduces it to servitude; whence in the *Song of Songs*: “Your locks are like raised palm trees, black as a raven,” that is, like those who, mortifying [Col. 0754B] the flesh, have been blackened by the soot of tribulations. Of a similar blackness it is read in the *Song of Songs*: “I am black, but beautiful, daughters.”

Costa, properly “rib.” It signifies a faculty of the soul; whence: “Hunger shall weaken his strength, and want shall invade his ribs.” Want invades the ribs when, all spiritual refreshment having been withdrawn, the faculties of the mind fail and cannot govern or guard their thoughts. Each person’s ribs are the faculties of the soul which fortify hidden thoughts. Want invades the ribs of the wicked, because inward hunger weakens the faculties of the mind so that they cannot at all govern their thoughts. For when the faculties of the mind have become dull, thoughts emerge outwardly; and, as though the ribs were weakened, the inward parts that could have remained soundly hidden are poured forth outside.

[Col. 0754C] Cras, “tomorrow,” sometimes denotes the future; whence in Genesis: “Tomorrow he will answer for me,” that is, in the future. Sometimes it is used for what is uncertain; whence to be anxious about tomorrow, that is, about the uncertain. Sometimes it denotes the following year; whence Christ says in the Gospel: “Today and tomorrow I cast out demons and perform cures,” that is, in the first and second years of my preaching I shall work miracles; “on the third day I am brought to completion,” that is, in the third year I shall die and rise again.

Crassitudo, properly “fatness.” It also signifies charity; whence Isaiah: “Hearken diligently to me, and your soul shall delight in fatness.” It signifies the death of a martyr, and is called fatness because, just as fatness fertilizes the earth, so the death of one saint fertilizes the Church: through the death of one, many were converted [Col. 0754D] to life. Whence in the Psalm: “As the fatness of the earth has been broken up upon the earth.” It signifies pride; whence Job: “Fatness covered his face,” that is, pride blinds the human mind.

Crater, properly “bowl.” It signifies a preacher who gives others the cup of salvation to drink; whence in the *Song of Songs*: “Your navel is like a turned bowl,” etc.

Creare, properly, means to make something out of nothing, namely when matter and form are created together. Hence God may be called Creator, and his work creation. A created thing is called a creature, as though *concreature*, because matter and form are created together; whence in Genesis: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” It signifies to form or bring forth; whence in Genesis: “God created the great sea-creatures.” It signifies to recreate; whence [Col. 0755A] in the Psalm: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created,” that is, recreated. It signifies to renew; whence Isaiah: “I create a new heaven and a new earth,” that is, I renew them. It signifies to permit; whence Isaiah: “Making peace and creating evil,” that is, permitting it. It signifies to exalt; whence in the book of Kings, concerning David: “I created you from nothing,” that is, I exalted you, etc. It signifies to beget; whence Wisdom says: “From the beginning and before the ages I was created”; and elsewhere: “Wisdom was created before all things,” that is, begotten. Hilary explains it thus: “From this Arius drew support for his error, saying that the Son of God is not eternal, but was created before all temporal things.”

Creatura, properly, “creature,” signifies man, because he has a likeness with every creature: he exists with stones, lives with herbs and trees, senses with brute animals, and reasons [Col. 0755B] with angels. Whence in the Gospel: “Go, preach the Gospel to every creature.” It signifies a saint, for whose sake creation was made; whence in the Apocalypse: “Creation was subjected to vanity.”

Credere, “to believe,” sometimes denotes an unformed quality; whence James in the Catholic Epistle: “The demons believe and tremble.” In this sense faith is the apprehension of things with assent but without knowledge of their causes. Sometimes it denotes the virtue of faith, that is, faith working through love; whence in the Gospel: “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved.” Sometimes it denotes the pledge of a definite vow; whence a godfather answers for an infant: “I believe,” that is, “I promise that this child will believe.” Sometimes it denotes certainty about a matter; whence Paul: “I know whom I have believed, and I am certain”; [Col. 0755C] and in the Psalm: “I believed, therefore I spoke.” Here “I believed” does not denote faith but certainty.

Cribrare, properly “to sift.” Sometimes it signifies being cast down into love of earthly things; whence Christ said to Peter in the Gospel: “Simon, behold, Satan has demanded you, that he might sift you as wheat,” and might compel you to descend into love of earthly things or incline you toward the desire for earthly things. Just as wheat goes down in a sieve while it is being sifted, or settles [*residiat*, as printed], so it happened with Peter: he was cast down into love of earthly things when he denied Christ.

Crocus, properly “saffron.” It signifies divine Wisdom; whence in the wedding-song of Christ and the Church: “Nard and saffron, cane and cinnamon.” Saffron is golden in color; [Col. 0755D] therefore it signifies divine Wisdom.

Crus, properly “leg.” It signifies one who bears Christ’s name; whence in the *Song of Songs*: “His legs are columns of marble.”

Crux, “cross,” signifies a gallows; it signifies the mortification of the flesh, whence in the Gospel: “He who wishes to come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross.” It signifies faith or the preaching of the cross; whence the Apostle: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of the Lord.” It also signifies the sign of the cross.

Crystallus, properly “crystal.” It signifies an obstinate person whom God sometimes converts to faith; whence in the Psalm: “He sends his crystal like morsels,” because he frequently incorporates an obstinate person into himself through grace.

Cubile, “bed,” signifies conscience; whence in the Psalm: “The saints shall exult in glory; they shall rejoice in their beds.” It signifies lust or sloth; whence the Apostle: [Col. 0756A] “Not in beds and indecencies.” It signifies the hearts of the wicked, in which demons dwell; whence in the *Song of Songs*: “From the dens of lions and from the mountains of leopards,” etc.

Culmus, properly “stalk,” signifies a hypocrite; whence Hosea: “The stalk standing in them has no shoot, and it shall not make flour.” For a stalk has no shoot when the life of a hypocrite lacks virtues; the stalk makes no flour when it yields no fruit of good work to those who advance in the present age.

Cum, the preposition “with,” sometimes denotes a plurality or diversity of things and is taken copulatively, as in that catalogue of creatures: “Let us bless the Father and the Son with the Holy Spirit,” that is, the Holy Spirit. Sometimes it denotes the authority or dignity of the thing to which it is joined, as in: “Who lives and reigns with you”: authority is understood to belong to the Father, so that the Son may not be understood to be lesser. The reverse does not occur; whence in the Psalm: “With you is dominion,” so that the sense is: “O Son, with you and with me is dominion, with the Holy Spirit, who is the splendor of the saints.” Sometimes it denotes opposition; whence in the Apocalypse: “There was silence in heaven, while the dragon made war with Michael,” that is, against Michael. Sometimes it denotes identity of a thing; whence in the book of Wisdom: “You judge all things with tranquillity,” that is, you are tranquil in judgment. Sometimes it denotes abundance in a quality; whence in the Psalm: “They shall come with exultation.” It sometimes denotes bearing or attire; whence Josephus relates that Agrippa’s wife came “with great ambition,” that is, with great display. It sometimes denotes accompaniment in place; whence in the Gospel: [Col. 0756C] the maid said to Peter: “Were you not also with him?” Sometimes it denotes accompaniment in time; whence Luke relates that Anna lived with her husband for seven years from her virginity. Sometimes it denotes the instant of time. Sometimes in compounded expressions it denotes diversity of persons and identity of substance, as: “The Son is consubstantial with the Father,” that is, of the same nature with the Father. Likewise, when I say, “The Son is coeternal with the Father,” that is, eternal with him.
