Sometimes it denotes conformity of nature; whence it is said: “The Son is consubstantial with the Father.” Sometimes it denotes a thing’s benefit or advancement; whence in the Canticle of Zachariah: “To perform mercy with our fathers.” Sometimes it denotes authority, as in: “The Son is coeternal with the Father.” For [Col. 0756D] one rarely says, “The Father is coeternal with the Son.” Similarly: “This statue is like Hector,” yet one does not say, “Hector is like this statue.” And indeed this word *cum* has the same meanings in composition as it has in apposition.

Cum, the adverb “when/although,” sometimes denotes time; whence in John: “When the Paraclete comes,” etc. Sometimes it denotes cause and time together; whence in the Psalm: “They will praise you when you do him good.” Sometimes it is taken adversatively; whence the centurion says in the Gospel: “Although I am a man placed under authority.” Likewise: “Although he was God, he was made man.” Note that when the word *tamen* (“nevertheless”) follows, *cum* is always used adversatively. Sometimes it is conjunctive or consecutive; whence in John: “When he had tasted it, he would not drink.” Sometimes [Col. 0757A] it is taken copulatively, as: “When Socrates runs, Plato argues; therefore Socrates runs and Plato argues.”

Cuneus, properly “wedge.” It signifies prophets; whence in the book of Kings: “A wedge of prophets came to meet Elisha.” It signifies a battle-line; whence in the Life of Saint Martin: “He arranged the wedges in battle-array”; and elsewhere: “I shall safely penetrate the wedges of enemies.” It is called a wedge by reason of its resemblance: a wedge is broad at its upper part and sharp at its lower; so it is in wedge-shaped battle-lines, for the person [reading uncertain] is placed in the front.

Cur, “why,” sometimes denotes a final or rational cause; whence the glorious Virgin Mother says to her Son: “Son, why—or what—have you done thus to us?” And in Job: “Why do you hide your face?” Sometimes it denotes an impelling cause fitting to someone; whence the Lord: “Woman, why [Col. 0757B] do you weep?” An impelling cause is that by which something occurs suddenly, as shame is the cause of blushing and fear of pallor; whence one says: “Why is that man pale?” Sometimes it denotes authority; whence in the Gospel: “Why then do you baptize, if you are neither Christ nor prophet?” that is, by what authority or presumption?

Curare, “to care for,” denotes care and concern; whence in the Gospel: “Do not be anxious about tomorrow.” Sometimes it denotes treatment and healing; whence the Lord says through the prophet: “I treated Babylon, and she was not healed,” that is, I omitted nothing on my part among the means of healing, and yet she was not healed. Thus it denotes the care and diligence of the physician, so that the sense is: “I applied care, yet I did not heal.” It signifies to cleanse; whence one says: “Clean the wheat; clean the house.”

[Col. 0757C] Currere, properly “to run”; whence in the Gospel: “John ran more quickly than Peter.” It signifies passing through the course of this life; whence the Apostle: “So run through the course of this life that you may obtain the prize of eternal life.” Sometimes it denotes eagerness and diligence in doing evil; whence in the Psalm: “If you saw a thief, you ran with him.”

Currus, properly “chariot,” signifies worldly pleasure, vain glory, or worldly pomp; whence in the Psalm: “These in chariots, and these on horses.” It signifies an army of the good; whence in the Psalm: “The chariots of God are many thousands.” It signifies an assembly of the wicked; whence in the *Song of Songs*: “To my cavalry in Pharaoh’s chariots.” It signifies the likeness of a chariot; whence in the book of Kings: “Elisha saw a fiery chariot.” It signifies the host of angels; whence: “I saw [Col. 0757D] their chariots and horsemen.”

Cursus, properly “course.” It signifies the state of the present life; whence the Apostle: “I have finished the course; I have kept the faith.” It signifies the flow of our mortality; whence in the Psalm: “He shall be like a tree planted beside the courses of waters.” It signifies a distance greater than a day’s march; whence Vegetius, *On Military Affairs*: “The distance of an army’s day’s march is only twelve miles; but if an army advances farther in one day, it is not a day’s march but a course.” Lucan uses it in this sense; whence Lucan:

> . . . He had surpassed the icy Alps in his course—

that is, he had run through the Alps.

Custos, properly “guardian.” It signifies God; whence Isaiah: “What of the night?” is the voice of the Idumeans, who were in captivity and cried: “What will become of our night, O [Col. 0758A] guardian?” that is, of our misery, O God, since the Jews have been liberated from captivity by the Lord, who is the guardian of men. “What have you determined concerning the night?” that is, concerning the harsh captivity. The guardian answered them: “Morning comes,” that is, your liberation; “and the night of captivity recedes. If you seek by crying out, seek by devotion; turn through faith and come through good works.” Or it may be understood of the fathers of the Old Testament, who were in the mouth of hell and cried: “Guardian, what of the night?” that is, “What will become of our misery?” The guardian answered: “Morning comes, the time of liberation,” that is, the time of grace; “the night of guilt, punishment, and ignorance flees. If you seek with the mouth, seek with the heart; turn and come.” Elsewhere Christ too is called guardian; whence in the Gospel it was said to him: “Are you [Col. 0758B] a Samaritan and do you have a demon?” He accepted being called a Samaritan, which is interpreted “guardian.” It signifies a prelate of the Church; whence in the *Song of Love*: “The guardians of the city,” that is, of the Church, “found me, when I sought my beloved.” It signifies an angel; whence Isaiah: “Upon your walls I have set guardians.” A guardian angel presides over a province or a city of men, and likewise in similar cases.

Cutis, properly “skin.” It signifies the softness of weakness; whence in the *Lamentations*, Jeremiah says of the Nazarites: “Their skin clung to their bones; it dried up and became like wood.” By bones, the hardness of strength is expressed; by skin, the softness of flesh. Skin is therefore said to cling to bones because those who hold perverse opinions regard the weakness of vice as the hardness of virtue. For, deceived by confidence in their own pride, they join weak things to strong ones in their estimation. [Col. 0758C] And the more highly they think of themselves in these matters, the more they disdain to correct their wickedness. Hence it follows: “It dried up and became like wood”; for their fault is rendered all the more insensible insofar as it is held praiseworthy among them. It also signifies sin of the flesh; whence Job, in the person of a penitent: “I sewed sackcloth upon my skin, and covered my flesh with ashes.” By sackcloth and ashes, repentance is understood; by skin and flesh, sin of the flesh. Therefore, when some return to repentance after a fall of the flesh, as it were sackcloth is sewn upon the skin and flesh is covered with ashes, because the fault of the flesh is covered through repentance, so that it may not appear for punishment in the scrutiny of undiscerning judgment. It also signifies those who, in the body of holy [Col. 0758D] Church, serve outward concerns; whence Job: “My skin dried up and contracted.” Those who serve only outward concerns in the body of holy Church are rightly called skin. This skin, indeed, contracts as it dries up, because the minds of carnal persons, loving present things which they desire as though near at hand, refuse through faintheartedness to stretch toward future things. Since they neglect the richness of inward hope that would draw them onward, they dry up; for unless despair dried out their hearts, the heat of this faintheartedness would never contract them. Thus the drying skin contracts when the heart, devoted to outward things and dried by despair, does not stretch toward love of its Creator but folds back upon itself, so to speak, in wrinkled thought.

[Col. 0759A] Cymbala, properly “cymbals,” are small bells which give a sharp sound. They also signify those who preach with the mouth but by their works are discordant from their preaching; whence the Apostle says of such persons that they are “sounding brass and a tinkling cymbal.” They also signify the spiritual [Col. 0760A] harmonies of the faithful; whence David: “Praise him on well-sounding cymbals.” They signify ineffable praises that cannot be fully expressed by the mouth; whence: “Praise him on cymbals of jubilation.”

## D

[Col. 0759]

[Col. 0759A] Daemonium, properly, signifies one demon; whence the Jews say of Christ in John: “Do we not rightly say that you have a demon?” Note that *daemon* means “knowing one,” and *daemonium* comes from *daemon*; accordingly both good and evil angels can be called *daemones*, that is, knowing beings. God himself is called a *daemon*; whence in the *Asclepius*: “Those who are unwilling in the present to believe words shall in the future be compelled to believe by punishments; for they shall pass under the power of the highest judge,” that is, God. Hence good angels are called *calodaemones*, from *calo*, that is, “good,” meaning those who know good things; and rightly so, because they turn their knowledge to good uses. Evil demons, however, are called *cacodaemones*, from *caco*, which means “evil,” because they use their knowledge badly. The devil is also called a demon because, although every knowing being can be called a demon, the term is nevertheless restricted to signify malignant spirits only, so that demons are called such by antiphrasis because they turn their knowledge to wicked uses. Sometimes *daemonium* denotes a multitude of demons; whence in Luke: “Jesus was casting out a demon, and it was mute,” by its effect, because it made the possessed man mute. When [Col. 0759C] Christ asked it what it was called, the demon answered: “My name is Legion,” as if to say: “We are many.” It also signifies mortal sin; whence Mark relates that Christ cast seven demons out of Mary Magdalene, that is, seven mortal sins, which arise from the demon’s suggestion, and without which a woman of delicate body is rarely found. It signifies an open and grave temptation; whence in the Psalm: “From the arrow flying,” etc., “and from the noonday demon.” Here four kinds of temptation are denoted: open and light, in “from the arrow flying by day,” that is, from an open and light temptation; hidden and light, in “from the business that walks in darkness”; hidden and grave, in “from the assault”; and open and grave, in “from the noonday demon.” It also signifies lust; whence [Col. 0759D] in the Gospel: “This kind of demon is not cast out except by prayer and fasting.” It is called a demon because it withdraws with difficulty, because the devil frequently deceives through it, and because it supplies material for other vices.

Damnare, properly “to condemn,” means to inflict loss; whence: “This man is condemned to a monetary penalty.” It also denotes punishment by eternal penalty, as in this example: “You who came to save the lost, do not condemn those redeemed in body and soul.”

Dare, properly “to give,” means to bring forth with effect; whence David: “He gave forth his voice; the earth was moved.” It signifies to beget; whence John: “As the Father has life in himself, so he gave also to the Son,” that is, he begot the Son as having life in himself. It denotes to distinguish or divide; whence in Ecclesiastes: “Give portions to seven, and also [Col. 0760A] to eight,” that is, distinguish between the Old Testament and the New. For the fathers of the Old Testament served the number seven; the fathers of the New Testament served the number eight. It denotes to make what has been given manifest; whence the Apostle: “Therefore God gave him a name,” that is, he manifested to him in the resurrection what had been given, and what was given to no one else. Elsewhere in the Gospel: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given [Col. 0760B] to me,” that is, it has been manifested that I have power in heaven and on earth.

David signifies Christ; whence in the title of this Psalm, “My God, my God, unto the end, a Psalm of David for the reception and assumption of the morning,” the name David is taken as designating Christ. It signifies a penitent, as in the title of that Psalm in which it is said, “Unto the end, a Psalm of David: for the eighth”; here the name is taken as designating the penitent. It signifies the people established under the Mosaic law, as in the title of that Psalm: “How long, Lord, will you forget?” “Unto the end, a Psalm of David”; here the Jewish people, awaiting Christ’s coming, is understood through David.

De, “from/of,” sometimes denotes place, as in the Psalm: “He took me from behind those with young.” It denotes time; whence David: [Col. 0760C] “From day to day proclaim his salvation.” It denotes authority or agency; whence in the Creed: “Who was conceived of the Holy Spirit,” that is, by the authority of the Holy Spirit’s working. It denotes material; whence in the same place: “Born of the Virgin Mary”; and in the *Song of Songs*: “He made himself a litter of the woods of Lebanon.” It denotes origin; whence in the Creed: “God from God, light from light.” It denotes cutting off; whence in the Gospel: “They cut branches from the trees.” It denotes wholeness; whence the Apostle: “If the ear should say, ‘I am not of the body,’ is it therefore not of the body?” that is, not of the body’s integrity. It denotes that speech is made about someone; whence Christ says in the Gospel: “One of you is about to betray me.” He said this of Judas. It denotes final cause; whence John: “When the Paraclete comes, he will convict the world concerning sin,” that is, on account of sin. [Col. 0760D] It denotes a quasi-formal cause; whence: “From the fatness of iniquity.” It denotes emptying or humiliation; whence: “Christ descended from heaven.” It denotes transition from one state to another; whence in the Gospel: “No one ascends to heaven except he who descended from heaven.”

Decor, properly “splendor,” signifies immortal dignity; whence in the Psalm: “The Lord reigns; he has clothed himself with splendor,” that is, with the dignity of immortality. It signifies the beauty and loveliness of virtues; whence in the Psalm: “Lord, I have loved the splendor of your house,” that is, of the Church. It signifies the assembly of saints, who are Christ’s diadem and crown; whence Isaiah: “They shall see the king in his splendor.” It signifies divinity; whence in Isaiah: “We saw him as having neither form nor splendor,” that is, divinity.

[Col. 0761A] Dedicare, properly “to dedicate,” means to apply a thing to some use. Thus it is read in Deuteronomy that the fearful did not go to war, nor one who had newly planted a vineyard, nor one who had taken a wife and had not humbled her [as printed], nor one who had built a house and not dedicated it, that is, had not assigned it to common habitation. It signifies to consecrate; whence a church is said to be dedicated, that is, consecrated, as though assigned to the common use of the people. It signifies to glorify; whence the title of the Psalm *Exsultate* is: “A psalm of song at the dedication of David’s house.” This is understood of the glorification which the Church militant shall have in the future in body, that is, in soul.

Deducere signifies to lead upward; whence in the Psalm: “Lead me in the path of your commandments.” Elsewhere: “He led me upon the paths of righteousness,” that is, the narrower [Col. 0761B] commandments and more perfect counsels, in whose paths few walk. It denotes leading through various stages, that is, leading from good to better, namely from virtue to virtue; whence in the book of Wisdom: “The Lord led the righteous man through right ways.” It denotes providing guidance or safety; whence: “Pharaoh’s servants led Abraham out at his departure from Egypt,” etc.

Deficere, “to fail,” properly denotes bodily exhaustion; whence in the Gospel: “If I send them away fasting, they will fail on the way.” It signifies failing away from love of earthly things; whence in the Psalm: “My soul longs and fails,” namely, stretching toward the courts of the Lord: my soul, failing away from the threshing-floor of earthly things, stretches toward the courts of the Lord. And David elsewhere: “My soul fails for your salvation.” Only the Holy Spirit understands desire and failure of this kind, just as he understands: “My soul has melted because of the chariots of Aminadab,” that is, the soul of the righteous has melted from the love and fervor of charity, as wax from before fire. It denotes failure in evil, when someone intends to do evil but cannot; in the Psalm: “They failed while searching with searching,” that is, the Jews failed in their counsels and thoughts by which they wished to destroy Christ. It denotes failure away from good; whence in the Psalm: “My eyes have failed because of want.” These are Christ’s words, saying: “The eyes,” that is, the apostles, “have failed in faith because of poverty of spirit.”

Delere, properly “to erase,” in sacred Scripture denotes the deprivation of the effect of eternal predestination, when someone is erased from the book of life; whence Moses in Exodus: [Col. 0761D] “Either forgive them this offense, or erase me from the book of life,” etc. Note that the book of life is called eternal predestination, because, just as many things are contained in a book, so many are contained in eternal predestination; and as a book is written by someone’s hand, so eternal predestination is made by divine authority. A person is written in this book in two ways: with regard to eternal predestination, and in this sense it is impossible for anyone to be erased from the book of life; or with regard to present righteousness or human opinion, and in this sense it is possible for someone to be erased. Corresponding to the two modes of writing are two modes of erasing: one with regard to eternal reprobation, the other with regard to present righteousness. Of the first we have, as Moses says: “I beseech you, Lord, either forgive them this offense, or erase me from [Col. 0762A] your book which you have written”; as though he said: “Just as it is impossible for me to be erased from the book of life with regard to eternal predestination, so it is impossible that you should not forgive them this offense.” Yet someone may seem capable of being erased from the book of life even though he was written with regard to eternal predestination, according to what the Prophet says: “Let them be erased from the book of the living.” This must be understood thus: “They are erased and are not written with the righteous,” that is, they are not written. In the second mode many are erased, because, although they appear at present to be erased with regard to present righteousness and human opinion, they are nevertheless predestined—as Paul was, and all who are to be saved—because:

> The outcome crowns the deed, not the struggle.

This is clear from the fact that, although Judas was written [Col. 0762B] in the book of life with regard to present righteousness, he was not written with regard to eternal predestination.

Delictum, broadly understood, includes sins and offenses, that is, commissions of things that ought not to be committed, which are properly called sins; whence in the Psalm: “The offenses of my youth.” Strictly speaking, however, *delictum* is used when we omit what we ought not to omit; whence David: “Who understands offenses?” as though to say: “Either few or none.” Hence they are called *delicta*, as it were *derelicta*, “things left undone.” It signifies sin arising from ignorance; whence a distinction is made between the sacrifice for an offense, which is called a sin of ignorance, and the sacrifice for sin arising deliberately. It signifies a sin arising from inability [Col. 0762C] and weakness, and in this sense is restricted to sin arising from “the fatness of iniquity”; whence a distinction is made between the sacrifice for the sin of inability, which is there called *delictum*, and the sacrifice for the sin of iniquity. It also signifies pride; whence in the Psalm: “And I shall be cleansed from offense.”

Denarius is a kind of coin worth ten ordinary or current coins; whence in the Gospel: “Why this waste? For it could have been sold for three hundred denarii.” It signifies eternal life; whence in Matthew: “Did you not agree with me for a denarius?” Note that eternal life is called by the number ten because of the fulfillment of the Decalogue; or from the denarius coin, because it has two things, namely the king’s image and name. So the saints in eternal life will be Christ’s image [Col. 0762D] in respect of natural gifts, and his likeness in respect of gratuitous gifts; and the saints will have Christ’s name, being called by Christ’s name. It signifies Christ’s Passion or Christ; whence in the Apocalypse: “Two pounds of wheat for one denarius,” that is, the saints of the Old and New Testaments, signified by wheat, are bought with a denarius, that is, through Christ’s Passion or through Christ. Saints are rightly signified by grain, because just as grain is first ground, then made into dough, afterward baked in an oven, and finally brought to the table, so the saint is ground in tribulation, baked in suffering, and finally brought to the table of eternal blessedness. It signifies sin; whence in the Gospel one man is said to have owed five hundred denarii and another fifty. Since they had nothing with which to repay, he forgave both of them. [Col. 0763A] This is to be understood of sin; hence the devil is called an exactor, who lent the denarius to the first parents and demands it from us daily.

Teeth are called accursed words or detractions; hence the Psalmist: “You, O Christ, have broken the teeth of sinners,” that is, of the Jews: you broke the Jews’ accursed words through your Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension; for then, namely at the Resurrection, “the mouth of those speaking iniquity was stopped.” Evil preachers are called teeth, as also false preachers; hence it is said of Antichrist in Job: “Terror is round about his teeth,” that is, terror comes through Antichrist’s false preachers, who will go about the earth. For all will fear the preaching which Antichrist’s preachers will carry out in a circuit, that is, throughout the circuit [Col. 0763B] of the various regions of the world. A persecutor is called a tooth; hence the prophet: “He has gnashed against me with his teeth,” that is, with persecutions; and the Church speaks of the devil. Note that the devil is said to have teeth because he devours a human being through mortal sin, incorporates him through evil habit, or directs him to hell through an evil end. An evil suggestion is called a tooth; hence Job: “The roaring of the lion,” that is, of the devil, “and the voice of the lioness,” that is, of the Synagogue, which thundered against Christ, “and the teeth of the lion’s cubs,” that is, the evil suggestions of demons, “are broken.” An evil work is called a tooth; hence Job: “I broke the jaw,” that is, the sinner, “and from his teeth,” that is, from his evil works, “I snatched the prey,” that is, I prevented them [Col. 0763C] from sinning; or, “from his teeth I snatched the prey,” that is, I freed the human mind which a person plunders through evil works. A preacher of the Church is also called a tooth; hence in the Song: “Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep which have come up from the washing, all bearing twins.” By the teeth of the Church we understand holy preachers, who by their preaching convert the hardness of sinners. They are not undeservedly compared to shorn and washed sheep, because, taking up an innocent life in the washing of baptism, they lay aside the old fleeces of their former way of life. An apostle is called a tooth; hence Job, speaking in Christ’s person, says: “Only the lips about my teeth have been left.” For what is signified by lips but speech, and by teeth but apostles? Thus, in the Passion, lips were left about [Col. 0763D] the teeth, because they still indeed knew how to converse, but already feared to preach him or [Note: [Col. 0763] Something appears to be missing, as immediately after the words “Why, inwardly in my feelings,” etc.] the vices of unbelievers. Inward discernment is called a tooth, as Job says: “Why do I tear my flesh with my teeth?” As though he were plainly saying: Why do I examine inwardly, by my faculties, whatever carnal deeds have been done in me, if they cannot benefit those who behold me?

To put down (*deponere*) properly means to remove one thing from oneself; hence in Acts: “They laid down their garments beside [him].” It denotes removal from honour; hence the Blessed Virgin Mary: “He has put down the mighty.” It denotes removal from, or deprivation of, the burden of the flesh; hence the “deposition” of saints is so called, because then they are removed from, or deprived of, the burden of the flesh. It denotes [Col. 0764A] entrusting something to someone; hence the Apostle: “He is able to keep my deposit,” that is, my soul. It denotes giving security, that is, making a pledge; hence in the *Eclogues*:

> “I would not dare to stake anything from the flock with you.”

It denotes putting down below; hence in the Gospel: “Joseph took down the body from the cross.” It may be used thus in legal documents: “I will stake with you a hundred marks that this is so.”

God is said to descend through the humanity he assumed; hence in the Gospel: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven.” He is said to descend through the appearance of angels; hence in the Law God descended upon Moses’ tabernacle. It denotes punishing by the execution of vengeance; hence in Genesis: “I will go down and see whether they have completed their sins in deed,” that is, [Col. 0764B] I will punish, and by punishment prove—namely, I will make it known by vengeance—that they have committed such a sin. It denotes revealing; hence in Genesis: “Let us go down and confuse their tongues,” and let us reveal it to the angels, so that they may descend and confuse their tongues. It denotes descending by the bestowal of grace; hence in Acts the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles. Note that the Holy Spirit is said to descend because he signifies that he has descended; thus: “The Holy Spirit descended in bodily form like a dove upon him,” that is, the dove that appeared in bodily form signified that the Holy Spirit had descended into him from the moment of the Incarnation, but not for the first time then. Therefore he is said to have descended in bodily form because the dove was the sign of that [Col. 0764C] descent. A human being is said to descend through humility; hence Isaiah: “Come down, daughter Zion; sit in the dust,” that is, humble yourself. A human being is said to descend from good to evil; hence in the Gospel: “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho,” that is, from the vision of peace to the failure of sin. A human being is said to descend from a state of honour to a state of abasement; hence in Jonah: “The king of the Ninevites came down from his throne and sat in sackcloth and ashes.”

To describe (*describere*) means to make a thing manifest or to declare a thing’s property; and this is what is called, among logicians, a description. It denotes the profession of subjection to the Roman Empire, made by a poll-tax and entered in writing; hence in the Gospel: “A decree went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be enrolled.” [Col. 0764D] It denotes eternal predestination; hence Gregory: “It was fitting that the whole world should be enrolled by Caesar Augustus at the birth of him who had enrolled and predestined his own in eternity.”

Desert (*desertum*), properly, as in the Gospel: “Jesus was led by the Spirit into the desert”; and elsewhere: “John was in the desert preaching.” Judea, or the Jewish people, abandoned by God, is called a desert; hence in the Gospel: “The voice of one crying in the desert,” that is, in Judea abandoned by its king and by God. The world—that is, worldly people abandoned by God—is called a desert, as in the preceding example; according to another exposition in Isaiah: “The voice of one crying in the desert,” that is, in the world, that is, among worldly people. [Col. 0765A] The Gentile people, abandoned by God and estranged from the knowledge, love, and worship of God, is called a desert; hence Isaiah: “Send forth, O Lord, the Lamb, ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert.” “O Father,” say the saints, “send from your bosom into the bosom of the virginal womb the Lamb, that is, your innocent Son, ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert, that is, from abandoned Gentile stock, to the mountain of the daughter of Zion, that is, to the Jewish people.” They say this because Christ was to descend from both Gentile stock, on account of Rahab and Ruth, and Jewish stock; this is sufficiently clear in Job: “Who gave the flooding water its course, and who made a way for the sounding thunder, so that dew might rain upon land without moisture in the desert?” Flooding water is divine grace; sounding thunder, the divine threat. The sense, then, is: Who gave [Col. 0765B] divine grace its course, so that by its flooding it might reach the Gentile people? And who made a way so that the divine threat might reach that same people, so that the dew of divine grace might rain upon dry land without moisture—namely, without the moisture of divine grace—in the desert, that is, among the Gentiles? That is: who brought it about that the Gentiles were converted to faith? Paradise too is called a desert, because it was abandoned by angel and human being. “Which of you, having a hundred sheep,” etc., “in the desert?” Here “which” denotes dignity. He who has a hundred sheep is divine Wisdom, who had angelic and human nature, signified by the hundred sheep; for the number one hundred denotes perfection, and the sheep the original innocence of each Church. He therefore lost one sheep through the fall of the first human being; leaving the ninety-nine [Col. 0765C] sheep in the desert [Note: [Col. 0765D] Something is missing.], that is, the nine orders of angels in heaven, he came, by assuming human nature, to seek the lost sheep, that is, the human race; and, having found it, he placed it upon his shoulders and carried it back to the sheepfold, that is, the Church. Worldly happiness or earthly pleasure, which makes people abandoned by God, is also called a desert; hence Job: “In the deserts of torrents,” that is, in earthly pleasures. Yet misfortune is compared to a torrent because now it overflows and moves with force, now it fails like a torrent. The mind of a saint, deserted by worldly cares and by the tumult of evil thoughts, is called a desert; hence in Lamentations: “Like an ostrich in the desert.”

“God” (*Deus*) is used substantively; hence in Exodus: “Hear, [Col. 0765D] Israel: the Lord your God is one.” It stands for divinity, as: “God is Trinity.” It stands for the Trinity; hence in Genesis: “God said, namely: Let us make man in our image.” It stands for the Father; hence in Genesis: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” It stands for the Son, as there: “God from God.” It stands for the Holy Spirit; hence the Apostle: “The temple of God is holy, which you are.” It is also used adjectivally; hence: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” In Hebrew there is *heloim*, the plural of the name *hel*, which means “gods”; and this does not denote a plurality of divinity, but of persons, so that the sense is: [Col. 0766A] “The gods created,” that is, the three divine persons—just as “the deified Hadrian” (*divus Adrianus*) means “divine Hadrian.” It is also used by adoption for the perfected; hence the Psalmist: “I said: You are gods,” and elsewhere: “God stood in the synagogue of gods”; and the Apostle: “Whether there are many, whether gods, whether in heaven or on earth.” It is used nominally of demons, in name only and not in reality; hence: “The gods of the nations are demons.” It is taken for idols; hence in Genesis Laban says to Jacob: “Why have you stolen my gods?” that is, my idols. It is taken in the sense of power; hence in Exodus the Lord says to Moses: “I have made you a god to Pharaoh,” that is, powerful over Pharaoh. And Jacob says to Esau in Genesis: “I saw the face of God,” that is, of someone most powerful. It is taken for a priest; hence in Leviticus: “If a servant should wish to remain with his master, he shall live [Col. 0766B] for ever; his master shall pierce his ear with an awl and present him to the gods,” that is, to the priests.

The right hand (*dextera*), properly, is divine propitiation; hence in the Psalm: “Your hand protected me”; and elsewhere: “A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand.” It is called eternal life; hence in the Song: “His left hand is under my head,” namely in the present, while he grants me temporal things, says the Church, “and his right hand will embrace me,” in eternal blessedness. It is called power, or the Son of God; hence in the Psalm: “Your right hand will lead you forth wonderfully.” It is called the equality of the Son with the Father; hence in the Psalm: “Sit at my right hand”; for those whom we place at our right hand we make, or consider, our equals. It is called prosperity; hence: “Do not turn aside from the royal road,” namely neither to the right by pursuing prosperity, nor [Col. 0766C] to the left by fearing adversity. Spiritual things are called the right hand; hence in the Gospel: “If anyone strikes you on the right [cheek], offer him the other also,” that is, if some heretic wishes to wound you in spiritual things, set spiritual things before temporal things, so that you may be wounded first in temporal matters rather than in spiritual ones. According to another exposition, it is called the contemplative life, so that the sense is: If anyone wishes to scandalize you in the contemplative life, transfer yourself to the active life; that is, if you cannot maintain the contemplative life, transfer yourself to the active life, etc.

Devil (*diabolus*) means “falling downward.” He is called Leviathan, that is, “addition.” Some say that Leviathan is the fish called the whale, because just as a whale adds other fish to itself by swallowing them, [Col. 0766D] so the devil incorporates evil people into himself by suggestion. He is called Satan, that is, adversary, and *Satanas*, which is the same thing, because he opposes us. He is also called Sathael, that is, one contrary to God. A sinner who falls from the throne of righteousness into the mire of sin is called a devil; hence: “Did I not choose you twelve from the world, and one of you is a devil?”—namely Judas, who fell from the dignity of apostleship into apostasy.

A diadem (*diadema*) is properly a crown, and is called *diadema* as though “two lacking”: a beginning and an end. It is called duration or eternity because it lacks beginning and end; hence Martianus [Note: [Col. 0765D] *On the Marriage of Philology and Mercury*, ed. Ultr. [Col. 0766D] Frid. Kopp, Frankfurt, 1836, quarto, p. 27.]: “Jupiter took the diadem from the head [Col. 0767A] of the first-born daughter, Eternity, and placed it upon the head of Siches Endelechia, daughter of the Sun.” It is called eternal life; hence Isaiah: “And a diadem of the kingdom in the hand of your God.” It signifies eternal blessedness, because it is a kingdom; in its signification it has two circles, and in the future we shall be blessed in body and soul. Hence it was said of the saints in the Book of Wisdom: “They shall receive the diadem of beauty,” that is, beautiful blessedness, “from the hand of the Lord.” The human nature of Christ is called a diadem, as though “two lacking,” namely sin at its beginning and death in its continuance; hence: “Go forth, daughters of Zion, and see King Solomon.” And: “O faithful souls, go forth from the contemplation of earthly things to the love of heavenly things,” that is, see King Solomon—that is, Jesus Christ, the true peacemaker, who restored peace between [Col. 0767B] God and humankind, between angel and humankind, and between human being and human being—“in his diadem,” that is, in human nature, with which his mother, the glorious Virgin, crowned him “on the day of his espousals and on the day of his heart’s joy,” because he never had so much joy as on that day when the angel said: “Behold, you will conceive.” See the text. Or: “In his diadem,” that is, in the flesh which he assumed from his virgin mother; “on the day of his espousals,” that is, when he espoused the Church to himself. It is also called a crown, as in the aforesaid passage: “Go forth, daughters of Zion,” that is, O women who used to be in Jesus Christ’s company, go out of the city and see King Solomon, that is, Christ, “in his diadem,” that is, in the crown of thorns with which his mother crowned him—that is, [Col. 0767C] the Synagogue, from which he was born according to the flesh—“on the day of his espousals,” that is, of his conception, because after the years had revolved, on the same day on which he was conceived he also suffered.

To say (*dicere*) properly means to promise; hence in the Psalm: “The Lord said to me: I will give you the nations,” that is, he promised them to me. It is called preordaining; hence David: “He spoke, and they were made.” It signifies doing something else easily; hence in Genesis: “God said: Let there be light, and there was light,” that is, he made light as easily as someone utters a voice with ease. It denotes begetting a Son equal to himself; hence in the Psalm: “The Lord said to my Lord,” that is, God the Father begot God the Son, equal to himself in all things. It also signifies commanding; hence in the [Col. 0767D] Gospel: “Say the word, and my servant shall be healed.” It denotes inspiring; hence in the prophets: “And the Lord said to me,” that is, he inspired me. It denotes making manifest; hence it is said in Job that the Lord said to Satan: “Whence do you come, Satan?”—which is nothing other than revealing the devil’s perverse ways to all. It denotes being able to say; hence the Lord says to Pilate in the Gospel: “You say,” that is, with a brief change in the mode of expression: “You are able to say [so].”

A day (*dies*), properly, is the time of the present life; hence in the Psalm: “How long shall I take counsel,” etc. By “day” an undetermined time is meant; hence Isaiah: “On that day the mountains shall drip sweetness.” It is called the time of grace, as in the preceding example according to another exposition; and elsewhere: “This is the day which the Lord has made.” It is called the time [Col. 0768A] of judgment; hence Zephaniah: “That day, a day of wrath.” This does not mean that it is certain that it will take place by day, since it is written of it: “The day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night,” and it is said of it in the Gospel: “But at midnight a cry was made.” Yet it is called a day because then the books of consciences will be opened, clear, and manifest. It is called the light of grace; hence the Apostle: “The night has passed,” namely that of ignorance; “the day,” that is, the light, namely of grace, “has drawn near.” It is called eternal life; hence in the Psalm: “One day in your courts is better,” and elsewhere: “What is the number of [his] days?” There “days” is said in the plural on account of duration, etc. An evil conscience is called a day; hence Statius:

> . . . With unceasing wings  
> The savage day of the mind circles round.

It is called prosperity; hence in the Psalm: “In the day [Col. 0768B] the Lord commanded his mercy.” It is called human understanding; hence the Apostle: “But to me it is a very small matter that I should be judged by you or by a human day,” that is, by human understanding. Jews converted to the faith are called days; hence: “And night shall be illumined as day,” that is, like the apostles converted to the faith from the Jews. A spiritual teacher is called a day; hence in the Psalm: “Day utters speech to day,” that is, one spiritual person from fullness brings forth to another spiritual person the Word which was in the beginning with God. The souls of the elect are called days; hence Job, lamenting the night, says: “Let it not be counted in the days of the year, nor numbered among the months.” By the year we understand the preaching of heavenly grace, because, just as in a year a month is formed from accumulated days and time is completed, so in heavenly grace a manifold life of virtues is fulfilled. [Col. 0768C] Therefore, by days are signified the minds of the elect; by months, their multiplied Churches, which make one Catholic Church. Therefore let that night not be counted in the days of the year or numbered among the months, because the ancient enemy, signified by the night, oppressed by the darkness of his pride, sees the coming of the Saviour, yet in no way returns with the elect for pardon. The length of eternity is called a day; hence Job: “Times are not hidden from the Almighty; but those who know him do not know his days,” because, although he himself is eternity, we do not know what that eternity itself is like. For although we know God through faith, we do not see how eternity exists: without a past before the ages, without a future after the ages, without prolonged delay, without perpetual expectation. [Col. 0768D] The misery of time, or the delight of sin, is called a day; hence Job: “Let the day perish on which I was born, and the night in which it was said: A man is conceived.” By the day, the delight of sin is signified; by the night, the blindness of mind through which a person allows himself to be set in the commission of sin. The state of angelic nature is also called a day; hence Job: “When, on a certain day, the sons of God,” that is, the angels, “stood before the Lord, Satan also was among them,” not by essence, not by grace, but by possessing angelic nature like them, etc.

A finger (*digitus*) [is so called] properly. It is called the Holy Spirit because, just as there are different joints and inches in a finger, so there are different gifts of the Holy Spirit; and just as a finger proceeds from hand and body while remaining of the same nature as both, so the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son while remaining of the same nature as both; and just as we work with fingers, so the Father and Son work through the Holy Spirit. Hence in the Gospel: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God,” that is, by the power of the Holy Spirit, “by whom do your sons cast them out?” And Pharaoh’s magicians, failing at the third sign, said: “This is the finger of God,” that is, this occurs by the work of the Holy Spirit. It is called blessed eternity because, as different fingers are distinct within the same substance of a hand, so different persons are distinct in the same nature; and as we work with fingers, so all things are made by the work of the Trinity. Hence Isaiah: “Who has weighed the mass of the earth with three fingers?” that is, who created the earth and made it immovable? The Trinity. A good work is called a finger; hence the smallest finger signifies [Col. 0769B] the smallest good work. Thus the rich man in the Gospel said to Abraham: “Send Lazarus so that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame,” that is: If I had one smallest of his good works, I would have relief from the torment I suffer for the sin of the tongue. And elsewhere the Lord Jesus says to the Pharisees: “They lay unbearable burdens on people, but will not move them with their finger,” that is, they are unwilling to perform even the least good work. It is called discernment; hence in Job: “Attend to me and be astonished; put your finger upon your mouth,” that is, consider what I have done and marvel; considering the evils that I suffer, consider yourselves in relation to your own fault.

God is said to love (*diligere*), that is, to predestine; hence [Col. 0769C] in Malachi: “Jacob I loved,” that is, I predestined him from eternity; “but Esau I hated,” that is, I reprobated him from eternity. It denotes preserving in being, and in this sense God loves all things, and in this sense he also loves the devil; hence in the Book of Wisdom: “You hate none of the things which you have made,” that is, you preserve all things in their being. It denotes approving; hence in the Psalm: “You have loved righteousness,” that is, approved it, “and hated iniquity,” that is, rejected it. It denotes conferring spiritual goods, and in this sense God is said to have loved Judas, that is, he bestowed spiritual goods upon him; hence in Genesis (?) “The performance of a work is proof of love.” It denotes displaying signs of love; hence in John: “This is that disciple whom Jesus loved,” that is, to whom he displayed signs of love; [Col. 0769D] and elsewhere, of Mary Magdalene: “Many sins have been forgiven her, because she loved much.” Note that the following question may be raised here. There are two persons, of whom one is predestined to greater glory but is less good as regards present righteousness; the other is predestined to lesser glory but is nevertheless better as regards present righteousness. The question is whether God loves one of these more. Answer: We say that he always loves more the one whom he prepares for the greater good. — It also signifies directing a special movement of charity toward someone; hence in Exodus: “You shall love the Lord your God.” It is said of wishing good things to a person; hence in the Gospel: “You shall love your neighbour as yourself,” that is, to the same extent, not out of the same degree [of affection]: you ought to wish as great a good for your neighbour as for yourself, but not with so great a movement of charity. For if you wished a greater good for your neighbour than for yourself, that would be folly, if not actual envy. The sense is: “You shall love your neighbour as yourself,” namely unto eternal life. It signifies desiring; hence one says: “This man loves eternal life,” that is, desires it; and elsewhere: “Goods of those who love,” that is, of those who desire. It is said of praising, and in this sense we are bound to love every creature—that is, from every creature we are bound to take material for divine praise. Hence in the catalogue of creatures: “Bless the Lord, all works of the Lord.” The sense is: All you creatures, provide from all things material for divine praise. It denotes giving thanks to God; hence in the Gospel: “He to whom more is entrusted is bound to love God more,” [Col. 0770B] that is, he ought to be more grateful to God and is bound to give him greater thanks than one to whom less is entrusted; yet he is not bound to love him with a greater movement of charity. It denotes approving; hence it is said that anyone is bound to love a good stranger more than a bad father; hence it is said that dearer members are to be embraced with greater charity. But we say that Linus ought to love Peter more than himself, that is, to approve him more, because God approves Peter more than Linus, etc. It signifies conferring or showing benefits, and in this sense it may be said that we are more bound to love an unjust person whom we know than a just stranger, that is, to confer or show greater benefits upon him. Here it is asked in what sense the word ought to be taken when it is said: “A human being loves God.” [Col. 0770C] We say that they approve the following explanation: he desires, gives thanks, praises; therefore someone is said to love God, namely by directing a greater movement of my charity toward him, desiring him, approving him, praising him, and giving him thanks. Again, it is asked in what sense it should be taken when it is said: “I am bound to love God more than myself.” We say that it can be explained thus: I ought to love—that is, to direct a greater movement of charity toward God than toward myself.

Dawn (*diluculum*) properly means the same as aurora. It is called the light of divine knowledge; hence in Job: “You visit him at dawn,” that is, with the light of divine knowledge you visit a just person by enlightening him, namely by justifying that just person and immediately testing him. First a human being [Col. 0770D] is justified, afterward tested. It is called the beginning of divine grace; hence in the Psalm: “The Lord will help her in the morning at dawn.” It is called Christ’s Resurrection; hence Job: “He shall arise like the dawn”; for the Resurrection is called dawn because it occurred at dawn. It is called the Church of God in its primitive state, because as dawn is the beginning of day, so the primitive Church is the beginning of the triumphant Church; hence Job: “Have you, after its rising, provided for the dawn,” that is, for the primitive Church taken from the Jews, that is, the apostles, “its place,” that is, its state? And this “after its rising” means after the assumption of humanity, as though he said: indeed, after my rising, that is, after I assumed humanity.

A flood (*diluvium*) properly is a flow of carnal desires; [Col. 0771A] hence in the Psalm: “Nevertheless, in a flood of many waters,” that is, those who remain in carnal desires will not draw near to God. It is called the error of the various sects in which the Pharisees trusted; hence the aforementioned passage can be explained thus: “Nevertheless, in a flood of many waters,” that is, such people as trust in the errors of various sects will not draw near to God. A person flowing in carnal desires is called a flood; hence David: “The Lord makes the flood to inhabit,” that is, he makes the saints dwell unharmed among flooding submergers—that is, he preserved Noah’s ark amid the waves and inundations of waters. Baptism is called a flood; hence, according to another reading: “The Lord makes the flood to inhabit,” that is, the waters of baptism, through the grace [Col. 0771B] which cleanses the crimes of the world, just as the world was cleansed by the flood.

To dismiss (*dimittere*) properly means to satisfy a request; hence in the Gospel: “Dismiss her, for she cries after us.” It signifies withdrawing one’s presence; hence Exodus relates of the angel who dismissed Moses, that is, ceased to appear to him. It denotes forgiving; hence: “Forgive us our debts.” It denotes leaving someone to himself or withdrawing one’s counsel from him, as people commonly say: “He left him to himself,” etc.

*Diplois* is a double garment, as though “a double fold.” For *plois* is Greek and means “fold” in Latin; such is a mantle lined with silk or furs. It is called the double confusion of the damned, namely the confusion of body and soul; hence in the Psalm: “They shall be covered as with a *diplois* by their confusion.” [Col. 0771C] It is called the deceit of hypocrites, who have one thing in the heart and another in the mouth; hence they are said to be “clothed in a *diplois*,” that is, in duplicity; for they think one thing in the heart and speak another with the mouth.

A dish (*discus*) properly means a large platter. It is called a table; hence in the Gospel: “Give me on a dish the head of John the Baptist,” that is, on a table or platter. It is called a cloth or napkin; hence it is related that the Lord showed Peter every kind of animal in a dish hanging by four corners, that is, four angels or very fine cords. It is called a leaden body, namely a round object made of lead with which the ancients played; hence it is related that the Greeks played with a discus.

[Col. 0771D] To scatter (*dispergere*) properly means to spread in different directions, as one says: “He scattered seeds.” It signifies distributing among different persons; hence in the Psalm: “He scattered, he gave to the poor,” that is, he apportioned to various people; for all things should not be given to one person, according to that saying of Isaiah: “Break your bread for the hungry.” It denotes making schism; hence in the Gospel: “He who does not gather with me scatters,” that is, whoever does not remain with me in the unity of the Church makes a schism. Note that the Church has a threefold bond; hence Solomon: “A threefold cord is not quickly broken.” The first is that of faith, which heresy dissolves; the second, that of charity, which schism breaks; the third, that of obedience, which contumacy divides. It denotes destroying; hence in the Psalm: “In your power scatter them.” It denotes dividing; hence in Genesis: “I will divide them in Jacob and [Col. 0772A] scatter them in Israel,” that is, they will have no proper allotment in the land of promise. There Jacob speaks either in Christ’s person or in his own person, so that the sense is: “I will divide them,” that is, I will foretell that they are to be divided. This is understood of the tribe of Simeon and Levi, because, since they deceitfully killed the Shechemites, they had no proper portions but were scattered among other portions. Hence in Jacob’s blessings: “Simeon and Levi, let not my soul enter into your counsel.” Or this is understood of the Scribes and Pharisees descended from Simeon and Levi, who, because they plotted Christ’s death, were scattered.

To dissipate (*dissipare*) properly means to tear apart or divide in different directions, and it is composed of *dis* and *seps, sepis*, “a hedge,” because hedges are easily divided into different parts. It signifies destroying; [Col. 0772B] hence in the Psalm: “My bones have been scattered,” that is, strength has been destroyed. It signifies spending in different ways and uselessly; hence the Gospel speaks of the prodigal son who dissipated his substance, etc., that is, in various ways and to no purpose.

A rich man (*dives*) properly means one who loves riches; hence in the Gospel: “It is easier for a camel [to pass] through the eye,” etc. It means one who possesses and loves riches; hence in Luke: “There was a certain rich man,” so that both possession and love are denoted there. It means a proud person, because pride arises from riches; hence the Blessed Virgin Mary: “He has filled the hungry with good things and sent the rich away empty.” It means someone possessing spiritual riches; hence in the Psalm: “All the rich of the people shall entreat your face,” that is, those who love spiritual riches. It means God on account of the fullness and abundance [Col. 0772C] of every good, because of knowledge and power; hence the Apostle says: “But God, who is rich in mercy.” It also means the divine nature; hence in the Psalm: “Rich and poor alike,” that is, the divine nature, according to which Christ is called rich, and the human nature of Christ, according to which he was poor.

Riches (*divitiae*), properly; hence in the Psalm: “If riches abound, do not set your heart upon them.” Hence Job: “If I rejoiced over great riches,” as though he said: Even if I came to know many things that I ought to do, understanding did not lift up my heart. For saints do not chiefly rejoice when they know what to do, but when they perform the good things they have learned. Divine utterance is called riches; [Col. 0772D] hence Job: “Those who know shall drink his riches.” For Gentiles who come to know drink the riches of the Jews, because the converted minds of the Gentiles are watered by the flow of sacred speech which the Jews had first possessed. It means abundance; hence the Apostle: “O the depth of the riches of wisdom and knowledge!” And elsewhere: “Do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience, and long-suffering?”

To hew (*dolare*) properly means to strip rough timber not perfectly or completely but partly; hence *dolabrum*, “an adze.” Thus it is related in the Legend of Dionysius: “With blunted adzes.” It denotes preparing; hence Hosea: “Therefore I have hewed them by the prophets,” says the Lord—that is, the understanding of the divine Scriptures, which was rough in the prophets, was hewn: sacred Scripture in the prophets was prepared for understanding, though it had previously been rough. [Col. 0773A] Yet it remained hidden and, as it were, unstripped until the time of the apostles, through whom it was stripped, that is, made manifest and openly explained, and through other teachers of sacred Scripture.

*Doma, domatis*, properly means a flat roof; hence Joab took the city of Jerusalem by leaping over roofs. It is called tropology or moral interpretation; hence in the *Scholastic History* it is related that tropology is the roof laid upon the summit: history is the foundation; allegory raises the walls. Tropology is the roof that completes and finishes the building.

A house (*domus*) properly means the human body; hence Job: “Who dwell in houses of clay.” It means a sinful person; hence in Luke the devil says: “I will return to my house from which I came out.” It means the Church militant; hence the Psalmist: [Col. 0773B] “I rejoiced in those things,” etc. It means the material church, or temple of God; hence in the Gospel: “My house shall be a house of prayer.” It means the soul; hence in the Psalm: “From ivory houses.” The soul is also the temple of God; hence: “The Lord is in his holy temple.” It means conscience; hence Solomon says of the perfect soul: “She has considered the paths of her house,” etc. She considers the paths of her house because she minutely investigates all the thoughts of her conscience; “she does not eat the bread of idleness,” because what she understands from sacred discourse by precept, she displays outwardly in action. It means the dwelling-place of heaven; hence in the Psalm: “The sparrow has found itself a house, and the turtle-dove a nest.” By the sparrow our Redeemer is represented; by the turtle-dove, the holy Church. “The sparrow has found itself a house,” because our Redeemer entered the heavenly dwelling-place; [Col. 0773C] “and the turtle-dove a nest,” because the holy Church, moved by love of the Creator, makes use of frequent groans and builds, as it were, the most peaceful nest of the rest of faith. In this nest she cherishes in the bosom of charity her growing children, like fledglings warmed until they fly upward. It means a structure of virtues; hence Solomon: “Cultivate your field diligently, so that afterward you may build your house,” that is, chastise your flesh so that afterward you may build the structure of virtues. It means Christ’s body; hence in Proverbs: “Wisdom has built herself a house.” Wisdom built herself a house when the only-begotten Son of God, by means of a soul, created for himself a human body in the Virgin’s womb. It means the Church triumphant; hence in the Psalm: “I shall enter [Col. 0773D] into your house.” This is according to one exposition; according to another, it is understood of the Church militant. Elsewhere in John: “In my Father’s house,” and this concerns the triumphant Church. It means sacred Scripture; hence in the Psalm: “We walked with one accord in the house of God,” that is, explaining it in one manner. It means the tomb of the dead; hence David: “Their tombs are houses for ever.” It means hell; hence Job: “Hell is my house.” A house also signifies body and heaven; hence the Apostle: “We know that, if our earthly house is dissolved, we have a house not made with hands in heaven.”

[Col. 0774A] “Until” is sometimes used exclusively, as in the Gospel concerning John: “So I will that he remain until I come,” as though to say: Christ will not die except at my coming. It is also used inclusively, and then denotes absence of an end, or eternity, as in the Psalm: “Until I place your enemies,” that is, eternally. It is also used negatively, and then denotes impossibility, as where the Gospel says: “Until heaven and earth come together, I shall not do this,” that is, never. Likewise one finds there: “Before they came together,” that is, they never came together. It is sometimes used copulatively, as in Genesis: “May God give you both of the dew of heaven and of the richness of the earth abundance, until the desire of the eternal hills comes,” that is, the desire of eternal life signified by the hills.

[Col. 0774B] [Note: [Col. 0773] The second part of this chapter, which is the same as the first with a few changes, is printed separately in the old edition.]

“Gift” (*donum*) or “given thing” (*datum*) is broadly called whatever is given. There are natural gifts, namely memory, understanding, reason, and intelligence; hence James says in the Catholic Epistle: “Every good given thing, every perfect gift.” There he calls gratuitous gifts, namely virtues, “gifts.” At times it denotes the exercise of the grace of the Holy Spirit; thus the Holy Spirit was from eternity a gift, that is, capable of being given, in order to denote fitness for being given; but he was a given thing in order to denote the exercise of giving.

A gift (*donum*) properly so called is such that everything given may be called a gift. Spiritual gifts are, for example, the virtues of the Holy Spirit; hence James: “Every good given thing and every perfect gift is from above,” namely gratuitous gifts. The Holy Spirit is called the gift of the Father and the Son, and this denotes fitness rather than an act, because from eternity he was capable of being given; hence the Son gives a gift equal to himself. Yet the word is restricted, by antonomasia, to designate the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0774C] To sleep, properly, means to die; hence in the Psalm: “I slept and took my rest.” It denotes engaging in carnal intercourse; hence in Genesis Rachel says to Leah: “Let him sleep with you tonight in exchange for your son’s mandrakes.” It denotes lying in vices; hence the Apostle: “Rise, you who sleep.” It also denotes exposing saints to tribulations; hence in the Psalm: “Rise up; why do you sleep?” It denotes one who is soon to be raised from death; hence Christ says in the Gospel: “The girl is not dead, but sleeping.” It denotes freedom from worldly cares; hence in the Song: “I sleep, but my heart is awake,” as though to say:

[Col. 0774D] “I am free from worldly cares, and therefore attend to divine things.” It denotes resting; hence in the Psalm: “In peace I shall sleep in the selfsame place.” It denotes taking delight; hence Solomon: “Beware of her who sleeps in your bosom,” that is, carnality which delights in you and through which you take delight.

The back, properly, signifies the stronger persons in the Church; hence Christ or the Church says in the Psalm: “Sinners built upon my back,” that is, unbelievers persecuted the stronger persons in the Church. For just as the back is the stronger part among an animal’s limbs and is exposed to bearing burdens, so the prelates of the Church ought to be strong and bear the burdens of others’ tribulations

[Col. 0775A] and adversities. It signifies freedom of choice; hence in the Psalm: “And bend their back always,” that is, allow the freedom of choice of the Jews—upon which both good and evil works rest—to be continually bent, that is, bent down, like a back, toward desire. It signifies certain people set aside by God, whom he does not look upon with the eye of mercy; hence: “I place them below,” that is, I set them aside. It signifies active persons; hence in the Psalm: “The rear parts of his back.”

A dragon, properly so called; hence: “Praise the Lord from the earth, dragons”; and the passage does not have “dragons” [Note: [Col. 0775D] The passage is corrupt.]. For Augustine says: “He began with dragons, because there are no larger animals upon the earth.” It also signifies malice; hence: “It will be the lair of dragons and the pasture of ostriches.” By dragons he signifies malice; by ostriches, hypocrisy, which presents an image to all

[Col. 0775B] who behold it. For the ostrich has the appearance of flight but not its use, because hypocrisy suggests to all beholders an image of holiness in itself, yet does not know how to maintain a holy life. Therefore in a perverse mind the dragon lies down and the ostrich feeds: hidden malice is craftily covered over, while an appearance of goodness is set before the eyes of beholders.

It also signifies the devil; hence in the Psalm: “You shall walk upon the asp and basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and dragon”; and in Revelation: “There was silence in heaven,” etc.; and in Isaiah: “In the dens where dragons formerly dwelt there shall arise,” etc. By the reed is meant the preacher; by the rush, which always feeds or grows near moist water, are signified the little and tender hearers

[Col. 0775C] of sacred discourse; by dragons is expressed the malice of demons. Therefore in the dragons’ dens the greenness of reeds and rushes springs up, because among those peoples whom the malice of the ancient enemy possessed, both the learning of teachers and the obedience of hearers are gathered together.

It signifies the Gentile people; hence: “The beasts of the field, dragons and ostriches, will glorify you,” namely the Jewish and Gentile peoples converted to faith. By dragons openly malicious minds are expressed, which are reckoned as “earth” because of their lowly thoughts. By ostriches are signified those who pretend to be good, who retain the life of holiness, like the wing of flight, in outward appearance, but do not practice it in deeds. Thus the Lord declares that he is glorified by dragon or ostrich, that is, he often converts to his service, from their inmost thought, both those openly evil and those falsely good.

[Col. 0775D] It also signifies Antichrist; hence in Revelation: “The dragon moved his tail and drew with it a third part of the stars,” that is, the greatest part of the saints, because then scarcely will the just man be saved. And unless God had shortened the days, no flesh would be saved. For he is called a dragon because he will entice some secretly by miracles, and others openly by threats and gifts. By the dragon Antichrist is understood; by the tail, his final persuasion; by the stars, the pretense of hypocrites, who display to people the good deeds they do in order to receive praise. Therefore by the dragon’s tail a third part of the stars is drawn down to earth, because by the final

[Col. 0776A] persuasion of Antichrist some who seem to shine will be snatched down to earth. To draw stars to earth is to entangle in the earthly love of manifest error those who seem to cling, through devotion to the heavenly life. The most wicked leaders of the Jews are called dragons; hence in Jeremiah: “Wild asses stood upon the rocks; they drew in the winds like dragons.” By wild asses or dragons are understood proud Jews: they are called wild asses because of the exaltation of their minds, and dragons because of their muddy contamination. They stood upon rocks because they trusted not in God but in the highest powers of this world, saying: “We have no king but Caesar,” etc.

A *dragma*, -ae, properly is the name of a weight; hence in Maccabees: “Judas, a most courageous man, delivered an address,” etc.

[Col. 0776B] A *dragmatis* is half a *dragma*. A *didragmatis* is one *dragma*; a *didragma*, -ae, is a double *dragma*. According to some, it signifies a kind of chant, as in the antiphon: “Before the bedchamber of this Virgin, offer us sweet songs *dragmis*,” either in the ablative case, or *dragmatis* in the genitive. But it is truer that there *dragma* signifies the weighing of the chant or verses, and is metaphorically called a *dragma* as a mutual weighing; for just as a *dragma* is weighed, so the verses there are weighed when one person says one verse and another says another. The sense will be: “Offer sweet songs in *dragmis*,” that is, with mutual balancing of chant. Or it may there denote the mutual balancing of modulation. For in music there are mutual balances of harmonies and proportions

[Col. 0776C] made according to the rules of music, which are called axioms.

It signifies a question; hence an interrogative mode of speaking is called *dragmatic*. For there are three modes of speaking: the didactic (*didascalicon*), so called from *didaskalos*, which means “teacher,” such as is found in the Greater Donatus, the *Lucidary*, and dialogue, where the devil asks and the teacher answers; the hermeneutic, that is, interpretative, so called from Hermes—that is, Mercury—who was called Hermes, meaning “interpreter,” such as occurs in the Gospel, with Christ speaking in parables. There is also the *dragmatic* mode of speaking, that is, interrogative, such as in the *Eclogues*, as there: “Tell me, Damoetas.” But it is better to say that there *dragma* means mutual balancing, when one says one verse and another another, as is clear in the aforesaid example from Virgil and in Theodulus,

[Col. 0776D] where, in the person of Pseustis, he speaks four verses, and Aletheia four.

It also signifies a sum or weight; hence in Luke: “Or what woman having ten drachmas.” It metaphorically signifies angelic or human nature, as in the same example according to another interpretation. There the woman is called the Wisdom of God, who made nine weights, that is, the nine choirs of angels, and human nature, which she made by mutual balancing. But when one weight was lost, that is, human nature, she lit a lamp by assuming human nature. Before the assumption Christ was light; afterward he was a lamp, that is, light in an earthen vessel; and he overturned the house, that is, the power of the devil or the Synagogue, or, better, the Church.

[Col. 0777A] A dromedary, properly, is a running camel, named from Greek *dromos*, which in Latin means “swift.” There are two kinds of camel: one assigned to carrying burdens, the other to running. Hence very swift ships are called *dromones*, and a *hippodrome* is a circuit for horses. Thus it is read that blessed Sebastian was placed in a hippodrome, that is, in the broad street where horses ran around.

Sweet, properly. It signifies useful; hence David: “You who took sweet food with me.” It signifies pleasing; hence David: “How sweet are your utterances to my palate.” It signifies merciful; hence David: “The Lord is sweet and upright.” It signifies prosperity; hence Isaiah: “Those who call bitter sweet and sweet bitter.”

*Dulia*, taken broadly, is called the worship due to the Creator,

[Col. 0777B] which is called *latria* or *theosebia*, that is, the piety of Christ; hence in the Psalm: “Blessed be the Lord God.” The Gloss says: “Lord, to whom *dulia* is due; God, to whom *latria* is due.” It consists in prayer, prostration of the body, kneeling, offering—as in tithes and firstfruits—special love, and special fear. For *theos* is said to mean “fearing” or “seeing,” and accordingly this may be understood:

> Fear first made gods in the world.

Yet Augustine seems to intend that *latria* is due to Christ not only insofar as he is God but also insofar as he is man. It is nevertheless restricted to signifying worship due to God according to his humanity, which likewise consists in the things mentioned above.

Strictly speaking, it is service due only to a rational creature, such as

[Col. 0777C] bishops, prelates, and others; and in this sense it is called from *doulon*, “service.” This is, as it were, the positive form which we owe to superiors, consisting in love, service, obedience, and the like. The intermediate or comparative form is due to angelic nature. The greatest or superlative form is due to Christ’s human nature.

Hard, properly. It signifies terrible; hence Isaiah: “A hard vision has been announced to me from a terrible land.” It signifies striking grievously; hence Isaiah: “On that day the Lord will visit with his hard and great sword.” It signifies obscure or unintelligible; hence in the Gospel: “This saying is hard; who can hear it?” It signifies inflexible; hence in Exodus: “I have seen your contention and your most hard neck.” It signifies impossible; hence in the Acts of the Apostles: “It is hard for you to kick against the goad.”

[Col. 0778A] A leader, properly, is an apostle; hence in the Psalm: “The princes of Judah, their leaders.” By the princes of Judah, Zebulun, and Naphtali are understood the apostles, who perhaps came from these tribes; and these are their leaders who bless God in the churches. It signifies an author of error; hence Job says in the person of the Church: “The leaders restrained their voice,” because indeed the heretics who strove to draw erring peoples after themselves now dare not even speak perversities, and are restrained by the weight of authority and the power of reason.

It signifies a principal vice; hence Job says of the holy man under the designation of a horse: “From afar he smells battle, the exhortation of leaders and the shouting of the army.” For the saint considers with what a crowd of iniquities his heart may be assailed; hence follows: “The exhortation of leaders and the shouting of the army.” For the vices tempting us, which wage visible battle against us, partly go before in the manner of leaders, and partly follow in the manner of an army.

[Col. 0778B] It signifies Christ; hence in the Psalm: “The house of the herodion is their leader.” The herodion is a most rapacious bird, greater than all flying creatures, and victorious as well. By it are understood the rapacious; yet the Lord does not abandon even such persons. The sense is: “Like sparrows they will nest in cedars, and the house of the herodion is the leader of those sparrows,” that is,

[Col. 0778C] Christ, who is the house of those most rapacious persons converted to faith. Note that where we have “house of the herodion,” another text has “house of the coot.” The coot is a bird which lives in waters. These are those who trust in the grace of baptism, whose house is baptism. Thus this text may be read: Those who are cedars, those who are sparrows, are those who are baptized; and theirs is the coot’s house, that is, baptism, which is the house of the regenerate and is their leader, namely of the sparrows—that is, Christians—who ascend to heaven.

## E

[Col. 0777]

[Col. 0777D] Ivory, properly, signifies one who is chaste, or chastity; hence in the Psalm: “Myrrh and cassia from ivory houses.” It signifies one of the modern Fathers prepared to endure martyrdom or exposed to martyrdom; hence concerning the preachers of the New Testament it is read in Lamentations: “More ruddy than ancient ivory,” because they were more prepared for martyrdom, or more exposed to martyrdom, than the ancient Fathers.

“Behold” sometimes denotes evidence, as here: “For behold, from this.” Sometimes it denotes wonder, as in the Gospel: “Behold, a Canaanite woman from the borders of the kingdom.” John Chrysostom says that the evangelist spoke in amazement: “Behold, how wonderful!” Sometimes it denotes an awakening or summons; hence Isaiah: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive.” Scripture also, as Jeremiah says, arouses everyone as if from sleep to hear a marvel: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive.”

Church is the material place into which

[Col. 0778D] the faithful gather; hence: “Let women be silent in churches.” It also signifies the assembly of the faithful; hence in the Psalm: “In the midst of the Church I shall praise you”; elsewhere: “Bless the Lord in the churches.” It signifies an assembly of the wicked; hence David: “I hated the congregation of evildoers.” It signifies a prelate of the Church; hence in the Gospel: “And if he has not so complied, tell the Church,” that is, the prelate or superior, etc.

To pour out, properly. It denotes a son of luxury; hence in Jacob’s blessings: “Reuben, you were poured out like water.” For just as water is poured out cheaply, so you were wholly poured out in vile lust, because you mounted your father’s bed. It denotes giving birth; hence in the Preface of the Blessed Virgin: “She poured forth the eternal light upon this world,” that is, she gave birth to Jesus Christ. It denotes the flooding of divine vengeance; hence David: “Pour out your wrath upon the nations that have not known you,” etc. It denotes placing the ardor of charity

[Col. 0779A] in the soul; hence David: “And I poured out my soul into you.”

To go forth, properly. It also denotes the eternal going forth of the Son from the Father; hence in the Psalm: “His going forth is from the summit of heaven,” and elsewhere in the prophet Micah: “His goings forth are from the beginning, from the days of eternity.” It signifies being born, that is, the temporal going forth of the Son; hence Isaiah: “A rod shall go forth from the root of Jesse,” etc. It denotes the granting of help; hence David: “Will you not go forth, O God, in our forces?”—as though to say: You formerly granted help in tribulation through the prophets, but now you will not go forth in our forces, that is, you will not grant us help through our martyrs. It denotes passing from the contemplative life to the active; hence Christ says to the Church in the Song: “Go forth, go forth, that we may behold

[Col. 0779B] you,” that is: You, a contemplative man, who lie hidden in contemplation, come forth from the bosom of contemplation, so that it may appear how you will exercise yourself in the practice of the active life—and this is “that we may behold you.” She answers in the Song: “I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” that is, I have cleansed the affections of my mind; how shall I defile them by engaging with temporal things?

A he-goat is called an *emissarius*; hence in the Old Testament two goats were brought to the priest on the tenth day of September. One of these was offered for sin, while on the forehead of the other was placed a written sheet containing the sins of the people, which the people believed to have been forgiven. By the emissary goat is signified Christ’s divine nature, which was harmed in no respect; by the one

[Col. 0779C] that was sacrificed is understood the humanity which suffered. Hence in the prose of Master John [Adam]:

> Let the old leaven be purged,
>
> [lacuna]
>
> The emissary goat
>
> And the sparrow escape.

By the sparrow that was sent away is understood Christ’s divine nature; by the one sacrificed, human nature. It signifies a stallion put out with mares to recognize them; hence Jeremiah says of the Jews that they are like emissary horses neighing after women. It signifies attendants or officials, also called interrogators, because in every matter they extort the truth and torture persons by torments. They are also called *litores* from *lita, litae*, “punishment,” or *lictores* from *lito, litas*; and *apparitores*, that is, those who stand by punishments about to appear, from *paritura, -rae*, “punishment”; or because they make accused persons appear in court. Hence in Samuel: “Saul commanded the emissaries to kill the priests,” that is, the killers.

[Col. 0779D] To send forth, properly. It denotes the infusion or inspiration of the Holy Spirit; hence in the Psalm: “Send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created.” It denotes the incarnation of the Son of Man; hence Isaiah: “Send forth the lamb, O Lord.” It denotes doing good, or the fragrance of virtues and the diversity of good works; hence in the Song: “Behold, your outpourings are a paradise,” says Christ, that is, your virtues or works are delightful as paradise.
