*Energia* means fury; hence one possessed by a demon is called *energumenus*, as though inwardly troubled through a defect of mind.

[Col. 0780A] *Epiphania* is called that understanding possessed by the higher orders of angels. Thus John Scotus divides *theophania* into *epiphania*, *hyperphania*, and *hypophania*. Now *epiphania* is “the free resulting forth, distributed, of a warming affection and of a higher intellect and judgment.” By the first part of this description we understand the seraphim, whose name is interpreted “burning”; by the second, the cherubim; by the third, the thrones. It is called a resulting forth because, just as rays of the sun leap back from a shield, so the intellect of these orders seems to leap back when it cannot have full knowledge of God.

It signifies Antioch, which was first called Reblata, afterwards Emath—whence the Emathian plains, and Lucan’s “Wars through Emathia”;

[Col. 0780B] then Antioch, after Antiochus the Great, who restored it. And Antioch is interpreted as though *against ochis*; for *ochis* is interpreted “sea” or “swift,” and from it *oceanus*, “sea.” Afterwards it was called Epiphania after Antiochus Epiphanes, who was called Epiphanes as though “most illustrious.” It also signifies the feast of the star’s appearance above the house of lodging.

A horse, properly. It signifies the preparation of right intention; hence Job: “The horse is prepared for the day of battle, but the Lord grants salvation,” because the mind prepares itself against temptation, but unless it is helped from above, it does not fight successfully. It signifies a preacher; hence Habakkuk: “You sent your horses into the sea,” because holy preachers were sent into the sea of this world, and through their preaching the peoples were disturbed.

[Col. 0780C] It signifies earthly power; hence in the Psalm: “The horse is deceptive for salvation”; and elsewhere: “Those who mounted horses fell asleep,” that is, those who trusted in the honor of the present life closed their mind, unto the death of the soul, against the light of truth. It signifies the honor of earthly things; hence David: “These in chariots and these on horses.” It signifies the sinner; hence Moses: “He cast down horse and rider,” that is, sinner and devil. It signifies a saint; hence it is said that Judas was once Christ’s horse while he was good. It also signifies Christ’s humanity; hence in Genesis: “Dan, a serpent on the way, a horned serpent on the path, biting the horse’s hoofs,” that is, Christ’s human nature, “so that its rider falls backward,” that is, Christ’s soul is separated from his body. And according to

[Col. 0780D] [Note: [Col. 0779] “Or according to another interpretation,” as often elsewhere?] Dan is understood as Judas; yet Judas is read to have been of Issachar. It also signifies the body of a saint; hence in Revelation the saints are said to follow the Lamb upon white horses. And indeed the saints are reported to sit on white horses because their bodies shone with the brightness of justice and chastity. It signifies the proud person; hence in the Psalm: “Do not become like horse and mule,” that is, proud and foolish persons.

A hedgehog (*ericius* or *erinacius*) is, according to some, a rabbit, also called a *cyrogrillus*. It is also called a rabbit (*cuniculus*) because it goes through tunnels (*cuniculos*), that is, underground passages. But it is truer to call it a hedgehog. For the hedgehog is a spiny animal; hence it is read in the Passion of blessed Sebastian that blessed Sebastian was covered with arrows as a hedgehog with spines.

[Col. 0781A] It signifies a sinner covered with the thorns of sins; hence the Psalmist: “The rock is a refuge for hedgehogs,” that is, Christ for the wicked, etc.

A caterpillar, a worm, from *eruo, eruis*, because it tears out the blossoms of plants. It signifies the root of a certain edible herb. It signifies lust; hence in Joel: “What the caterpillar left, the locust ate.” And the caterpillar signifies lust because, just as the caterpillar clings to the ground, so lust clings to the flesh.

Food, properly. Saints are called food; hence it is read in Job concerning Behemoth, that is, the devil, that he seeks delicate things, that is, he wishes to incorporate saints into himself. And elsewhere David says: “Those who devour my people as the food of bread.” Necessaries are called food; hence in the Psalm: “Who gives food to all flesh.” The divine word is called food; hence in the Psalm: “Who gives their food to beasts of burden,” that is,

[Col. 0781B] the nourishment of the divine word to the simple. Divine kindness, which God shows to all, is called food; hence David: “The eyes of all hope in you, and you give them their food.”

“And” sometimes joins without distribution, as: “Father and Son and Holy Spirit.” Sometimes it joins with distribution, as: “Socrates and Plato run.” For there is a conjunction of terms and a distribution of the thing. Sometimes it is used causally; hence in the Psalm: “He was compared to senseless beasts,” because he was made like them. Sometimes it joins natures; hence: “Christ is God and man,” and “Socrates is just and good.” Sometimes it is understood explanatorily; hence “Marcus and Tullius”; and in the Psalm: “Judge me, O God, and,” that is, “distinguish.” Sometimes it joins what is uttered to a thought,

[Col. 0781C] as at the beginning of Ezekiel: “And it came to pass”; and in the Psalm: “And know that the Lord has made his holy one wondrous.” Since there is a *diapsalma* there, it is not connected with what preceded, but rather with what the Psalmist had been revealed in his mind concerning Christ.

Sometimes it denotes diversity of persons, as in the Gospel: “Who sees me sees also the Father.” This is used to signify unity of essence and to prove plurality of person; for if it were said, “Who sees me sees my Father,” the Father and Son would appear to be the same person, as concerning God: “Who sees me sees the Son.” Sometimes it denotes the effect of a thing, as: “God is just and good,” that is, the efficient cause of justice and goodness, etc. Sometimes it joins cause and effect, as: “Merciful by nature and compassionate in effect”; or it may be understood distributively and repeated thus:

[Col. 0781D] “Both merciful and compassionate.” Sometimes it denotes different applications; hence Paul: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!” He is called wisdom on account of heavenly things, which are subject to his knowledge; knowledge, on account of earthly things. Wisdom and knowledge are predicated identically of God. Sometimes it denotes the words rather than the meanings of the words; hence Boethius in *On the Trinity*: “Marcus and Tullius are the same in number.” On the same reasoning one could say, “Marcus is the same as Tullius,” or “is stronger than Tullius”; but it would be improper to say, “Marcus is the same as Marcus,” or “is stronger than Marcus.”

“Euge” sometimes denotes mockery; sometimes it testifies to flattery, as may be observed in this example: “Let all who say to me, ‘Euge, euge,’ be confounded.” The first *euge* is mocking, while the second is flattering.

[Col. 0782A] Sometimes it signifies congratulation, as in the Gospel: “Well done, good and faithful servant.” Sometimes it denotes exhortation, as: “Come now, do what you do.”

To pluck out, properly, means to extract. It signifies destroying sins; hence Isaiah: “That you may pluck up and destroy, and ruin and scatter, and build and plant.”

“From” (*ex*) sometimes denotes the material cause; hence: “What is born from flesh is flesh”; Paul: “Made from a woman”; and in the Creed: “Born from the Virgin Mary.” It denotes the efficient cause; hence: “From whom are all things, through whom are all things, in whom are all things”: he is the efficient cause. It denotes origin; hence: “O Wisdom, who came forth from the mouth of the Most High!” and in the Creed: “Who proceeds from the Father and the Son.” It denotes the formal cause; hence Paul: “The just lives by faith,” that is, one justified

[Col. 0782B] by faith lives, namely with eternal life; faith is the formal cause of his justification. It denotes the instrumental cause; hence it is said: “From the poison given to this man, death threatens him.” It denotes the occasional cause; hence the Apostle: “Dangers from my own people”; for the Jews, from whose race he was, were the occasion of dangers. It denotes removal or separation of one thing from another; hence David: “From usury and iniquity he will redeem their souls.” It denotes the passing of a thing; hence: “He inclined from this to that.” It denotes the state of a thing’s change; hence in the Acts of the Apostles: “From Saul he became Paul.” It denotes the constituent parts; hence in the Athanasian Creed: “Perfect God, perfect man from a rational soul,” etc., that is, divine and human nature constitute Christ. It denotes the concurrence or requirement

[Col. 0782C] of certain things into one; hence Christ consists of three substances, namely divine nature, body, and soul—that is, three substances concur for him to be Christ. The divine nature was not a part of Christ, but Christ. For no whole is its own part. The same is true of human nature. Otherwise, as Augustine says, Christ grew when human nature was added to him. We have a similar case in Porphyry, where he says that a statue consists of matter and form; for matter and form are not constituent parts of the statue, but are required for its being. Bronze is the matter of a statue, and the statue itself.

To exclude, properly, signifies to reveal; hence David: “Exclude those who have been tested by silver,” that is, reveal

[Col. 0782D] teachers who have been tested by the utterance of sacred Scripture. This occurs in the time of heretics, because then good clerics are revealed. By silver is understood discourse, according to that saying of the Psalmist: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire.” Note, therefore, that *excludere* is used for “to reveal,” because through the removal of certain things those things are revealed which previously lay hidden in the material. Hence goldsmiths are called *exclusores*, properly those who carve images in wood or stone by artful removal.

To shake off, properly. It signifies abstaining from or guarding against venial sin; hence in the Gospel: “Shake the dust from your feet,” that is, in your preaching you ought to beware of vainglory. There are some who do not seek vainglory, but none who reject it when offered, as Jerome says. And elsewhere: “Human glory reserves this one glorious thing for itself: it despises those who seek it and seeks those who despise it.” Hence the apostles are called shakers-off (*excussores*) or sons of those shaken out, that is, of the prophets, who were full of sacred grain, that is, spiritual understanding, and who were opened and shaken out by the apostles’ preaching. These apostles disclosed the spiritual understanding of the prophets which lay hidden in the prophets.

[Col. 0783A] To go out, properly. It denotes the eternal generation of the Son; hence in the Gospel: “The sower went out to sow his seed,” that is, the Son of God assumed human nature in order to sow divine teaching. Hence in Micah: “And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah; from you shall a leader go out.” It denotes dissemination of speech; hence in the Gospel: “A saying went out among the brethren,” that is, the saying was spread abroad; and elsewhere, “the issue of death”; and in Priscian: “He went out [toward] a man.” It denotes setting free; hence in the Gospel: “Cast him into the outer darkness, and let him not go out from there,” that is, let him not be freed. It signifies passing from rest to labor; hence the Psalmist: “Man shall go out to his work.”

[Col. 0783B] To drive out, properly. It denotes the leading force or overflow of charity; hence in Mark: “Then Jesus was driven into the desert by the Spirit,” that is, by an excessive affection of charity he allowed himself to be tempted. And there “driven out” denotes expulsion from the company of people and the ardor of his own charity.

To expound signifies to make manifest; hence in the Gospel: “Explain this parable to us.” It denotes making public; hence it is said: “A prostitute exposed herself to all.” It denotes presenting; hence it is said: “This man puts his horse on display for sale,” that is, presents it for sale.

[Col. 0784A] To rise up, properly. It signifies God being raised from the dead; hence in the Psalm: “I slept and took sleep, and I arose”; and elsewhere: “I arose, and the Lord received me.” God is said to rise when he stirs up faith growing lukewarm in a person. God is said to sleep when faith in him grows lukewarm in us; hence in the Psalm: “Rise up; why do you sleep, O Lord?” God is said to rise by granting protection to someone; hence David: “Rise up to help me.” God is said to bring help through vengeance; hence David: “Rise up, O God, and let his enemies be scattered.”

“Outside” sometimes denotes place, sometimes immensity, as when it is said of God: “Not enclosed among all things; not enclosed outside all things.” Sometimes it is used exclusively; hence in John: “They will make you outside the Synagogue.” Sometimes it denotes the separation of soul from body, as when it is said: “The soul is outside its body,” that is, separated from its body. Sometimes it denotes alienation of mind, as when it is said: “This man is beside himself,” that is, “He is not by himself” (*Der ist nit pei im selber*).

## F

[Col. 0783]

[Col. 0783C] A fable, properly; and it is said to derive from *olon*, “whole,” and *for, faris*, because a narration of false things is wholly in word and not in deed. Hence the Apostle says to Timothy: “Avoid old women’s fables.” It also signifies history; hence it is said in John the Apostle: “Hear a fable and not a fable.”

God is said to make by reason of predestination; hence David: “Who made the heavens in understanding.” He is said to make by reason of operation; hence in Genesis: “God saw all the things that he had made.” He is said to make by reason of speaking; hence: “And the word of the Lord came to me,” that is, he spoke to the prophet, etc. He is said to make by reason of permission; hence Amos: “There is no evil in a city which God does not do,” etc. A human being is said to make by reason of thought; hence the Lord says to Judas: “What

[Col. 0783D] you are doing, do more quickly,” that is, what you intend to do. A human being is also said to make by reason of speaking; hence: “Do not make a word about this,” that is, do not speak about this. By reason of operation, as the Psalmist says: “You did these things, and I kept silent,” etc.

A face, properly. It signifies the mind’s attention; hence it is read in Job: “Fatness covered his face,” because the face is the more honorable part of the body. By the face is signified the mind’s attention; by fatness, abundance. Thus fatness covers the face when the desired abundance of earthly things presses down the eyes of the mind. It also signifies a holy prelate; hence the Church says in her own person: “My face swelled from weeping.”

[Col. 0784C] The face of the Church consists of those set over others who lament the sins of the weak; and this is: “My face swelled from weeping.” It also signifies the devil’s thought; hence Job: “Want shall go before his face.” Want is called the lack of eternal blessedness or of virtues. Therefore want goes before the devil’s face, because no one joins the devil in thought by deliberate waking awareness unless he has first been stripped of the riches of virtues. It also signifies the Son of God, because the Father’s face, or will, is shown in the Son; hence in Malachi: “Behold, I send my angel before my face,” that is, John the Baptist before my Son. It signifies familiarity; hence in Exodus God spoke to Moses face to face, that is, he spoke familiarly with him. It signifies manifestation; hence the Apostle: “We shall see him face to face,” that is,

[Col. 0784D] manifestly. It signifies divine favor; hence David: “Why do you turn your face away from me?” It signifies one most like God; hence in Exodus Moses said to the Lord: “Show me your face”; and the Lord answered: “No man shall see me and live,” etc.; and Moses: “May your face go before us,” that is, someone most like you, namely an angel. It signifies presence; hence the devil says concerning Job: “Unless he blesses you to your face”; and elsewhere: “Then you shall see that he blesses you to your face,” that is, in your presence, etc. It signifies the human heart; hence in Genesis: “And he breathed into his face the breath of life.” There, by “face,” the whole body is understood, according to the figure called synecdoche

[Col. 0785A] (so written). It also signifies notice or regard; hence in the Psalm: “He turns away his face lest he see to the end”; and elsewhere: “Turn away your face from my sins,” etc.

A thing made, properly. It signifies that which is incarnate; hence in the Gospel: “Let us see this word which has come to pass”; and in John: “The Word was made flesh,” etc. It signifies that which is inspired; hence in Luke: “The word of the Lord came upon John.” It signifies that which was spoken beforehand; hence God is said to create things made, that is, things predestined or ordained by him, etc.

Facula, properly, a torch. It signifies the devil; hence in Revelation: “And a great star, burning like a torch, fell from heaven.” The devil is called a star because of his origin and the subtlety of his nature; he fell from heaven through pride, and burns through envy and malice [Col. 0785B] like a torch, because he sets others aflame for wickedness and works of iniquity.

Dregs, properly. The ceremonial observances of the Law are called dregs; hence in the Psalm: “And he inclined from this to that; nevertheless its dregs have not been emptied.” Mortal sin, or eternal punishment which has not been emptied out upon the Jews, is also called dregs; hence Origen, on that passage in the Gloss: “Nevertheless its dregs,” that is, “punishment for sin.” Carnal desire is called dregs; hence in the Psalm: “From the pit of misery and the mire of dregs.”

Sickle, properly. It signifies binding or loosing; hence: “No one ought to leave the sickle in another’s hand,” that is, no one may bind or loose another person’s parishioner. It signifies judicial authority; hence in Revelation [Col. 0785C]: “And in his hand”—that is, in the power of his disposal—“a sickle,” that is, judicial authority; “sharp,” that is, ready to cut off, namely to separate the good from the evil, etc. It signifies the day of death or the Day of Judgment; hence Isaiah: “They shall beat their swords into ploughshares and their spears into sickles,” because then rebellions shall cease, so that we may have fruit on the Day of Judgment, when it will be the time of harvest, since we reap with a sickle, etc.

Fame, properly, praise; hence it is read: “He is cruel who neglects his reputation.” It signifies every kind of report or public dissemination. The Philosopher, in the seventh book of the *Ethics*: “A reputation which all men report everywhere is not destroyed.”

Hunger, properly. It signifies the angel of hunger; hence in the prophet: “I shall send hunger into their land,” that is, the angel [Col. 0785D] assigned to this. It signifies the desire to convert some persons; hence in the Psalm: “They shall suffer hunger like dogs,” that is, they shall have a desire to convert others.

Household, properly. It also signifies the faithful people subject to their prelate; hence in the Gospel: “Who, do you think, is the faithful and prudent servant whom his lord has set over his household?” It signifies the Gentile people; hence in the Psalm: “And all the families of the nations shall worship in his presence.”

Flour, properly. It signifies faith, or the soul, or a people on account of multitude; hence in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour.” A *satum* is a measure containing one and a half modii. The meaning, then, is: the Church is like doctrine [Col. 0786A] which she herself hid in faith in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; or in three measures of flour, that is, in the three powers of the soul; or among the people descended from Noah’s three sons; or in the Church’s three orders—namely virgins, married persons, and the continent.

Bundle, properly, a heap of several things. It signifies Christ; hence: “My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh,” that is, “My beloved,” says the Church, “was a bundle of myrrh to me”: Christ endured the bitterness of the Passion for my benefit. It signifies the wicked gathered together in punishment, just as they were gathered together in guilt; hence the Gospel says that the angels will gather the tares into bundles to burn them, that is, the wicked to punish them, etc. It signifies the assembly of the good in their heavenly homeland; hence David, in the Book of Kings, when he wished [Col. 0786B] to kill Nabal, a foolish man, was met by his wife Abigail. Falling down, she worshipped him and said: “Lord, spare the man, so that your soul may be kept as though in the bundle of the living,” that is, may you be in the congregation of those who live, that is, who are ever green, just as bundles of vines are put into water that they may retain perpetual verdure.

To bewitch, properly, is to harm someone by word or sight; hence Virgil:

> I know not what eye bewitches my tender lambs.

It signifies to deceive; hence the Apostle: “O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you not to obey the truth?” that is, deceived you. It signifies to envy; hence, according to another interpretation: “Who has bewitched you?” that is, “Which false prophet [Col. 0786C] has envied you?”

Fate is called the sequence of temporal things proceeding according to divine Providence; hence Boethius, in the *Consolation of Philosophy*, distinguishes between providence and fate. It signifies divine providence; hence Statius:

> Foreknow the hands of the Fates and the destiny that lies beyond.

It is also commonly called generation, continuation in being, and corruption; hence three Fates are assigned by authors: Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos.

Jaws, properly. They also signify the human mind or thought; hence in the Psalm: “How sweet are your words to my jaws!” They signify the apostles, because through them, as through jaws, Christ sends forth his voice into the whole world; hence in the Psalm: [Col. 0786D] “My jaws became hoarse,” that is, the apostles failed in faith during the Passion. They signify death’s devouring; hence: “He delivered us from the jaws of death.” They also signify mountain precipices; hence: “Jonathan went down through the jaws of the mountains,” that is, through the mountain precipices, against the Philistines.

Spark, properly, something fragile; as: “Your strength shall be like a spark,” that is, fragile. It signifies what is vile; hence Job: “And I have been made like a spark and ash.” It signifies what has been annihilated, or annihilation; hence: “Their root becomes like a spark,” that is, their intention will be annihilated or will be useless.

Honeycomb, properly, honey in wax. It signifies the page of the Old Testament which contained evangelical teaching within itself, as honey; hence in the Song: “I have eaten [Col. 0787A] my honeycomb with my honey,” that is, I have inwardly incorporated the knowledge of the Old Testament, which is understood by the honeycomb, and the knowledge of the New Testament, which is understood by the honey. It signifies something more desirable in the world, as in the Psalm: “More desirable than gold,” etc., “and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.” It signifies the divine word; hence in the Song: “Your lips drip a honeycomb,” which is said of the Church. It signifies Christ’s resurrection because of the ineffable delight and joy which Christ had in the resurrection; hence, according to another interpretation: “I drank my wine with my milk,” that is, the resurrection. Thus Christ too is said to have eaten a honeycomb of honey after the resurrection.

Gall, properly. It signifies bitterness of mind, or the malice [Col. 0787B] which they offered Christ for food; hence David: “And they gave me gall for my food.” It signifies tribulation; hence Christ: “And he surrounded me with gall and travail.”

Thigh, properly. It signifies the weakness of the flesh; hence in the Song: “Sixty mighty men surround Solomon’s bed,” etc., “upon his thigh,” that is, upon the weakness of the flesh. It also signifies human nature; hence in the Psalm: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty,” that is, deity upon humanity. It signifies Christ; hence in Genesis Abraham said to his servant: “Put your hand under my thigh,” that is, swear by him who is to descend from my thigh. It signifies fleshly propagation; hence it is said of the Lord in Revelation: “He has written on his garment and on his thigh: King of kings and Lord of lords.” [Col. 0787C] Therefore, because the propagation of the human race came into the world from a virgin—that is, through the mystery of his incarnation—he made known to all nations that he would be King and Lord: on his garment, that is, in his flesh, and on his thigh, he had written: “King of kings and Lord of lords.”

Window, properly. It signifies the five bodily senses; hence Jeremiah: “Death entered through the windows.” For the five senses are an occasion for sinning mortally. It signifies the plain statements of Holy Scripture, just as lattices signify obscure ones; hence in the Song: “My beloved stands behind the wall, looking through the windows,” that is, through the manifest places of Holy Scripture, “peering through the lattices,” that is, through its obscure places; for God looks upon us through the plain [Col. 0787D] and obscure Scriptures. It signifies virtues; hence Isaiah: “Who are these that fly like clouds?” that is, the apostles, whose preaching was spread everywhere; “and like doves to their windows,” that is, persevering in virtues. It denotes the prelates of holy Church; hence Ezekiel, seeing the temple in his final vision, said: “Ground up to the windows, and closed windows in this temple,” namely, in the Church. The windows are priests who pour forth the light of preaching among the faithful people; but when there is ground up to the windows and the windows are closed, then earthly thought has grown within priests’ hearts, and the windows do not pour out light, because priests fall silent in the office of preaching. It signifies the contemplative mind; hence in Ezekiel: “Slanting windows [Col. 0788A] in the chambers,” by which are understood hearts aflame with God’s love. In slanting [windows], however, the part through which the light enters is narrow, while the inner part which receives the light is broad; for contemplatives’ minds, although they see in themselves but some slight portion of the true light, are nevertheless expanded into great breadth. It also signifies the Blessed Virgin; hence in the hymn: “You have become heaven’s window.”

Hay, properly. It also signifies human nature because of its corruption. For, just as hay now flourishes, now withers, and is presently cast into the oven, so human nature now flourishes in youth, now withers in old age; now it is raised up by prosperity, now pressed down by adversity. Hence Isaiah: “All flesh is hay.” It signifies venial sin, [Col. 0788B] hence: “Some build wood, hay, and stubble.” They build hay, that is, they commit a lesser venial sin; others wood, that is, a greater venial sin. It signifies earthly good; hence David: “Who brings forth hay upon the mountains,” that is, earthly good for rulers. It signifies earthly honor; hence in the Psalm: “Let them become like roof-hay.” It signifies the weak; hence in Revelation: “And he commanded them not to harm the hay of the earth.” Here, by hay, Holy Scripture signifies the weak, who cannot take solid food.

Wild beast, properly. It also signifies a heretic; hence in the Psalm: “Rebuke the beasts of the reed.” It also signifies an untamed people, that is, the Gentiles; hence in the Psalm: “For all the beasts of the woods are mine.”

Litter, properly. It may mean a tribunal carried [Col. 0788C] from place to place, or a bed; according to this sense, the words read in the Song are interpreted literally: “Solomon made himself a litter of the woods of Lebanon.”

Leaven, properly. It also signifies sin; hence Paul: “Not with the old leaven.” It also signifies a small and evil suggestion; hence in the Gospel: “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump”: a small and evil persuasion, or suggestion, corrupts the whole flock of the faithful. It signifies a public fornicator; hence the Apostle: “Purge out the old leaven.” It also signifies hypocrisy; hence in the Gospel: “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy.” It signifies charity; hence it is read that a woman mixed leaven into three measures of flour until the whole was leavened [Col. 0788D]. For just as leaven, by its dryness, converts into its own nature the whole lump to which it is added, so charity, by its fervor, strengthens good works, kindles the whole person, and invites him to the love of God.

Tools of iron, properly. They also signify the lesser scourges of the Lord; hence it is read of the building of Solomon’s temple: “Hammer, axe, and every iron tool were not heard in the house of the Lord while it was being built.” By that house is signified holy Church, in which the Lord dwells in heaven; for its building, the souls of the elect, like certain polished stones, are brought there. When they are built in heaven, no blows are heard, because in the eternal homeland all the clamors of persecutions are silenced. No hammer strikes there, because no punishment afflicts; [Col. 0789A] no axe cuts, because no sentence of outward severity casts out those received within; no tools clang, because thereafter even the slightest scourges are no longer felt.

To bear, properly, to take away; hence in the Gospel Mary Magdalene said: “They have taken my Lord,” that is, taken him away. It signifies to confer; hence the Apostle: “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord, having received [it], bears righteousness,” that is, confers it. It denotes to say; hence it is said: “This was borne among them,” that is, was spoken. It denotes to desire; hence Ovid, in the first book of the *Metamorphoses*:

> My mind is borne to speak of forms changed into new forms,

that is, it desired or desires. It denotes to endure; hence James: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation.”

Iron, properly. It signifies good consolation; hence [Col. 0789B] Solomon in Proverbs: “Iron is sharpened by iron,” because when the faithful instruct one another by mutual consolation, iron is sharpened by iron. It signifies one who does not abandon his malice; hence Isaiah: “The house of Israel has been turned into dross; all these are like bronze, iron, tin, and lead in the midst of a furnace.” Bronze, when struck, gives off more sound than the other metals; therefore one who, when subjected to a blow, bursts out into the sound of murmuring has been turned into bronze in the midst of the furnace. Tin, when artistically prepared, falsely imitates the appearance of silver; therefore one who is not free from the vice of pretense in tribulation has become tin in the furnace. Iron is used by one who lies in wait for his neighbor’s life; therefore he is in the furnace who does not abandon the malice of harming others [Col. 0789C] in tribulation. Lead also is heavier than other metals; thus, in the furnace, lead is found in one who is so weighed down by the burden of his sin that, even when placed in tribulation, he is not raised above earthly desires, etc. Iron also signifies preachers or the divine word; hence in Job: “He will reckon iron as straw, and bronze as rotten wood,” that is, the devil, deceiving men through Antichrist, will reckon iron—that is, preachers—as straw, and bronze as rotten wood—that is, those who persevere. It signifies the firmness of a person converted to faith; hence Job: “Iron is taken from the earth,” etc., namely because he had previously been weak and despised through earthly concerns, but afterwards became strong for heavenly teachings. It signifies mortal sin, [Col. 0789D] hence the Apostle: “Some build gold upon the foundation, others silver, others precious stones, others iron and lead,” that is, mortal sin. It signifies the inflexibility of the mind or of good intention; hence Ezekiel: “Set your face as iron and your forehead most hard,” that is, make your good intention inflexible.

*Fescenniae* are nurses’ songs by which they invite little children to sleep. They are called *fescenniae* from *fascia*, for a *fascia* is the binding by which a child is bound in the cradle. The songs which the angels sang at Christ’s birth are also called *fescenniae*, when they said, “Glory to God in the highest”; hence Jerome says that the angels sang in place of *fescenniae*.

A pregnant ewe is properly called *feta*. It also signifies a preacher [Col. 0790A] who brings others to birth in faith by his preaching; hence it is said: “He himself shall carry the pregnant ewes.”

To stink, properly; hence it was said to Christ concerning Lazarus: “Behold, he already stinks, for he has been dead four days.” It denotes becoming vile; hence in Exodus the children of Israel said to Moses: “May the Lord judge between us and you, because you have made us stink,” that is, become vile in Pharaoh’s sight. It signifies being manifest; hence a sin which is habitual and manifest is commonly said to stink, etc.

Fig tree, properly. It signifies a heretic or evil Christians; hence in Jeremiah: “What do you see, Jeremiah?” “I see very bad figs.” It signifies human nature; hence in the Gospel: “A certain man planted a fig tree in his vineyard.” This tree signifies human nature, [Col. 0790B] which was planted like a fig tree; but, having fallen voluntarily through its own guilt, it does not preserve the fruit of action. Since it was willing to fall into sin by its own will, it refused to bear the fruit of obedience; created in God’s likeness, when it did not remain in its own dignity, it despised preserving that for which it had been planted. It signifies the human mind; hence the prophet: “He made the vineyard a desert and stripped the fig tree.” When hostile spirits lie in wait, God’s vineyard is made a desert when the soul, full of fruits, is scattered by the desire for human praise; he stripped the upright fig tree, because, carrying off the deceived mind into the desire for favor, he removes the covering of humility. It signifies good action; hence in the Gospel: “Do you gather grapes from thorns or figs from thistles?” that is, do you believe that good works can be found among the wicked, and conversely? [Col. 0790C] It signifies the Synagogue; hence in the Gospel: “A certain man planted a fig tree in a vineyard, and it bore no fruit.” The Synagogue was barren of the fruit of good works; hence Christ cursed the fig tree that had no fruit. It signifies the primitive Church; hence in the Song: “The fig tree has put forth its early figs,” that is, the primitive Church, the apostles.

Faithful means truthful in promises; hence the Apostle: “God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted.” It also means truthful in things entrusted; hence in the Gospel: “Who, do you think, is the faithful servant?” It means one faithful by the faith of the sacrament, whence Christians are called faithful. Someone is called faithful from the sacrament of faith, as a baptized child is called faithful.

Faith, properly. It also signifies the virtue working through [Col. 0790D] love; hence Paul: “There are three: faith, hope, and charity.” It signifies grace; hence in Habakkuk: “The just man lives by faith”: he shall be justified by God’s grace and thus live eternally. It signifies the unformed quality possessed by false Christians; hence the Apostle: “Though I have all faith so that I could move mountains, but have not charity, I am nothing.” It signifies the act of faith; hence the Theologian: “Faith is believing what you do not see.” It signifies the subject of faith; hence the Apostle: “Christ is our faith.” It signifies the collection of articles of faith; hence Athanasius: “Whoever wishes,” etc., “must hold the Catholic faith.” It signifies knowledge; hence Corinthians: “Faith”—that is, knowledge—“has no merit when human reason supplies proof by experience.” It signifies fidelity; hence: “Zedekiah broke faith,” that is, fidelity, [Col. 0791A] with Nebuchadnezzar. It signifies the pledge of a certain vow; hence, in the sacraments, a little child is baptized in the faith of his parents, because they promise on his behalf that he himself will believe when he reaches the years of discretion, and the parents are bound to instruct him. It signifies certainty; hence: “Give me assurance,” that is, certainty.

To be made is said in one sense with respect to God, by reason of understanding; hence in Genesis: “Let there be a firmament,” that is, in the divine mind the creation of the firmament had been eternally preordained; and elsewhere: “Let there be light,” that is, God eternally preordained the future light. It is said by reason of matter, in Genesis: “Let there be a firmament, and the firmament was made.” It is said by reason of essence, hence in Genesis: “And light was made,” namely in its essence. God too is said to be made in two ways by reason of human nature, [Col. 0791B] hence Paul: “Who was made to him from the seed of David.” He is said to be made by reason of mercy, hence in the Psalm: “Lord, you have become a refuge”; and then it is more properly a change in the creature than in the Creator that is denoted.

A potter is properly so called, as in Jeremiah: “Go to the potter’s house.” It also signifies Christ, because, just as a potter by his labor makes a vessel from clay, so Christ by his Passion redeemed us from sin; hence in the Psalm: “You shall rule them with a rod of iron; you shall break them like a potter’s vessel”; and elsewhere: “Can a pot complain against the potter’s hand?” etc.

Figure, properly, is a quality discerned from the arrangement of features; hence Daniel records [Col. 0791C] that Nebuchadnezzar’s figure was restored—not because he had formerly had the form of an ox and subsequently that of a man, according to his own belief. This is said because, at the time of his transformation, he believed himself to be partly an ox and partly a lion. It also signifies a sign; hence it is said of the children of Israel that all things happened to them figuratively. Figure signifies the Son of God; hence the Apostle: “Who, being the brightness of his glory and the figure of his substance.”

Son, properly. It signifies a son by supposition or opinion; hence in Luke: “Jesus, beginning, was about thirty years of age, and was thought to be the son of Joseph.” It signifies a son by kinship; hence in the Gospel: “We have found Jesus, son of Joseph of Nazareth,” that is, of his kinship. It signifies a legal son; hence in the Gospel Jacob is [Col. 0791D] the son of Matthan. It also signifies a legitimate son, as Joseph in the Old Testament, and “legitimate” means as though born of lawful marriage. It signifies a son by adoption; hence in the Gospel Nathan is called David’s son. It signifies a natural son; hence in Genesis Perez and Zerah are called the sons of Judah. It signifies a son by upbringing, as Abraham, who was called the son of Aram, the father of his wife, because he brought him up; hence in Genesis Abraham said: “She is my sister and the daughter of my father.” It signifies a son by reason of evil action; hence in the Psalm: “They are filled with their sons,” that is, with evil works. It signifies a son by transformation; hence the Apostle: “Be sons of God,” that is, imitators. Someone is called a son of the earth, as Adam, who was formed from earth, etc. He is also called a son by nature, as Christ, who [Col. 0792A] remains in one and the same nature with the Father. He is called a son of grace; hence in the Psalm: “I said: You are gods and sons of the Most High.” He is called a son of wrath, as every human being conceived in sin; hence the Apostle: “We are all sons of wrath.” He is called the Son of Man, as Christ is called the Son of Man, that is, of a virgin. He is called a son of preaching, as Antichrist in particular, who will destroy himself and many others.

Thread, properly. It signifies a subtle proposition; hence Boethius, in the *Consolation of Philosophy*, says that Philosophy’s garment was woven of most delicate threads and indissoluble material. It signifies stability; hence Ovid:

> All human things hang by a slender thread.

Fringe, properly, the outermost part of a garment. It signifies a good work at the end; hence in the Psalm: “The glory [Col. 0792B] of the king’s daughter is from within, in golden fringes,” that is, in good works which persevere unto the end, etc.

To fashion, properly, to make; hence a potter is said to fashion, that is, make, a vessel; and the word derives from *fingo, -is, -ere*. It also signifies to feign; hence in Luke: “Christ pretended to go farther.” It signifies to create; hence in the Psalm: “Who fashioned their hearts one by one,” that is, created their souls. It signifies to mislead or deceive; hence: “The hypocrite fashions himself as righteous,” that is, deceptively presents himself as such.

End signifies a place; hence: “Reaching mightily from end to end,” that is, from heaven to earth, which is called an end because it is the last of the elements, and likewise heaven is; hence in the Psalm: “He turned his eyes away lest he see unto the end,” that is, earthly things. [Col. 0792C] It signifies the end of time; hence the Apostle: “We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come.” It signifies charity, called the end of consummation; hence in the Psalm: “I have seen an end of every consummation,” that is, charity. Eternal life also signifies the end of consummation; hence in psalm titles: “A psalm-title of David directing us unto the end,” that is, toward eternal blessedness. Christ too is called the end of consummation, because Christ fulfilled what the prophets foretold concerning him; thus, according to another interpretation: “A psalm-title directing us unto the end,” that is, to Christ. Death likewise is called the end of consummation, because at death all good or evil works [Col. 0792D] which a person has done in his life are completed. It also signifies the completion of a work; hence: “This is the end of this or that book.”

*Flamen*, properly, a light breath of wind. It signifies the Holy Spirit; hence it is sung:

> And to the holy Breath,  
> likewise poured forth from both, namely from the Father and the Son.

It signifies Christ; hence among the ancient Gentiles priests were called *flamines*, from *filum* (“thread”). Upon their heads were little caps, and at the top of each cap a small rod stood upright; at its summit a little wool was fastened by means of a thread, so as to drive birds away from sacrifices. They also had archflamines, that is, archbishops, and a protoflamen, that is, the pope.

[Col. 0793A] Flame, properly. It also signifies the gift of the Holy Spirit; hence in Revelation: “And his eyes were a flame of fire.” It signifies the heat of carnal desires; hence in Job: “Flame shall dry up his branches.” The branches are those who cling to the wicked. Thus iniquitous flame dries up branches, because those adhering to it are inflamed by earthly desires through its example. It signifies punishment; hence in the Gospel: “I am tormented in this flame.” It signifies an angel because of swiftness and the ardor of charity; hence in the Psalm: “Who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire.” An angel is called flame because it shines by the subtlety of knowledge and nature, burns with divine love, purifies human beings, and sets them aflame with charity—a charity which consumes human sins.

[Col. 0793B] Breath, properly, wind. It signifies the Holy Spirit; hence in the Psalm: “His spirit shall blow, and the waters shall flow.” It signifies the soul; hence Isaiah: “I made every breath,” that is, every soul. It signifies pride; hence one speaks of “the breath of pride,” and Isaiah says of the proud man: “Breath in his nostrils.”

To flourish, properly. It signifies possessing virtue or producing the fruit of righteousness; hence: “The almond tree shall flourish,” that is, the primitive Church from the Jews, which flourished in the winter of the Gentiles’ unbelief; “the locust shall grow fat,” that is, the Gentile world, converted to faith, by the richness of charity; “the caper plant shall be scattered,” that is, the Synagogue remaining in unbelief. The caper is a plant in whose power a downy growth arises, which is scattered by the wind. [Col. 0793C] It denotes the flower of youth; hence in the Psalm: “In the morning it flourishes and passes away.” It signifies rising again; hence it is said of Christ in the Psalm: “And my flesh flourished,” that is, rose again. It denotes the rose of martyrdom; hence in the Song: “I went down to the garden of nuts,” etc., “to see whether the vines had flowered,” that is, the martyrs. For just as the pomegranate seed has redness and whiteness in itself, so martyrs have the rose of martyrdom and the whiteness of innocence in themselves.

Flower, properly. It signifies Christ; hence in the Song: “I am the flower of the field”; and elsewhere in Isaiah: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower,” etc. By the rod the Virgin Mary is understood; by the flower, Christ. It also signifies human nature, which now flourishes in youth and now withers in old age; or now flourishes [Col. 0793D] in prosperity and now withers in adversity. Hence Job: “He comes forth like a flower and is crushed, and flees like a shadow.” It also signifies the glory of human life; hence: “The hay has dried up and the flower has fallen.” It signifies examples of the holy Fathers; hence in the beloved’s song: “Strengthen me with flowers,” that is, strengthen me with examples of the ancient Fathers; “surround me with apples,” that is, with examples of modern ones. It signifies souls beginning the good; hence in the Song, according to another interpretation: “Strengthen me with flowers”: the soul is strengthened by flowers when it rests in a good work, though it is not yet able to contemplate God’s face. It signifies the earliest faithful; hence in the Song: “The flowers have appeared.”

Waves signify the tumult of temptations; hence in Job the Lord [Col. 0794A] says to the sea: “Thus far shall you come, and here shall you break your swelling waves.” If we understand the sea as our heart, we may fittingly understand waves as temptations and the noise of vices. They signify the evil thoughts of the wicked; hence in Job: “They have overthrown my feet and obstructed his paths as though with waves.” They also signify the contradiction of unbelievers against the good; hence in the Psalm: “The rivers raised up their waves.” They signify an evil suggestion or worldly tribulations; hence in the Psalm: “All your heights and your waves passed over me.”

River, properly. It signifies the activity of this age, as the reprobate mind is reproached under the image of Babylon by the prophet Isaiah: “Strip off your shame, uncover your shoulder, reveal your legs, cross the rivers.” [Col. 0794B] For in the management of work, shame is exposed when a vile mind becomes known in the display of evil action, though it had formerly been thought great while quiet; it uncovers its shoulder when it displays its work which was unknown; it reveals its legs because it makes manifest the wicked worldly gains for which it longs with desire; and it crosses rivers, namely the activities of this age, which continually flow toward their end and which it incessantly seeks. Rivers signify holy preachers; hence in Ecclesiastes: “To the place from which rivers go forth, they return, that they may flow again,” that is, they direct all their actions to God, from whom every good action proceeds. It signifies the Holy Spirit; hence in the Psalm: “The rush of the river gladdens the city of God.” It signifies the gift of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0794C]; hence in the Gospel: “He who believes in me, rivers shall flow from his belly.” It signifies Holy Scripture; in the Psalm: “The river of God is filled with waters.” It signifies certain unbelievers who oppose the Catholic faith; hence in the Psalm: “The rivers raised up, O Lord, the rivers raised up their voice.” When the apostles preached, the rivers—that is, the Gentiles—raised their voice against them. It signifies the opposition of Gentiles or unbelievers; hence in the Psalm: “The rivers passed away on dry land,” through the apostles’ preaching. It signifies the flow of worldly tribulations; hence in the Psalm: “They rose up above the rivers of Babylon.” It signifies the present world; hence in the Psalm: “They shall pass through the river on foot,” that is, the saints shall pass into God without iniquity or defilement, etc.

[Col. 0794D] Stream, properly, the fire of the Last Judgment; hence in Daniel: “A fiery stream went out from before him.” It signifies the Holy Spirit; hence it is said of the hypocrite: “Let him not see the brooks of the stream,” that is, of the Holy Spirit. It signifies an unbelieving people; hence the Lord, speaking to Job, says: “He shall swallow up the stream and shall not wonder,” that is, the Lord, coming to judgment, will seize some who neglect to live rightly, namely unbelievers. It signifies those living negligently in this world; for those who have recognized the faith of truth but neglect to live faithfully may properly be called streams because they flow downward. It signifies the sayings of the ancient Fathers; hence Job: “He searches out the depths of streams,” that is, he brings the sayings and hidden things of the ancient Fathers into the light. It signifies the devil’s teaching; hence in the Psalm: [Col. 0795A] “You dried up the streams of Ethan,” that is, you destroyed the devil’s suggestions. It signifies the descent into mortality; hence Job: “The stream overturns the foundations of the wicked,” that is, of those who love earthly things. For the wicked neglect eternal things and do not see that present things are fleeting; rather, they fix their minds in love of this present life and build for themselves, as it were, a foundation for habitation in it when they are made firm in its things by desire. It signifies the course of the human race; hence in Job: “He shall swallow up the stream and shall not wonder, and he has confidence that the Jordan will flow into his mouth.” By the stream is signified the course of the human race, which, as it rises from the source of its birth, so, flowing down to the depths, passes away by dying. By the Jordan are signified those imbued with the sacrament of baptism, because our Redeemer [Col. 0795B] deigned to be baptized in this river. Here all the baptized are signified, because in the river Jordan the sacrament of baptism had its beginning. It signifies the present life; hence Job: “As waters withdraw from the sea and a stream, emptied, dries up, so a human being, once asleep, shall not rise.” The sea is the human mind; its waves are thoughts of the mind, some swelling with pride, others calm through grace. But when a person dies, the sea’s waters withdraw and the emptied stream dries up, because when the soul is removed, the body remains empty. And because while living we are sometimes afflicted by certain bitter things and sometimes found tranquil and gentle in sweetness, the course of the present life is expressed by comparison with sea and stream.

[Col. 0795C] To dig, properly, signifies to repent; hence in the Psalm concerning Christ: “They dug my hands,” etc. It signifies to humble or cleanse; hence in the Psalm: “I was digging and sweeping my spirit”: “digging,” that is, humbling; or “sweeping,” that is, cleansing—casting my spirit out from earthliness. It signifies consenting to sin; hence in the Psalm: “He opened a pit and dug it,” etc. He opens it by evil consent, digs it by evil action, and falls into the pit by perseverance. It denotes being crushed because of sin; hence in the Psalm: “Burned with fire and dug under.” It denotes indulging in earthly things or devoting care to them; hence in Luke: “I am unable to dig,” that is, I cannot indulge in earthly things.

Leaf, properly. It signifies Christ’s preaching or his word; hence: “And its leaf shall not fall.” It is called [Col. 0795D] a leaf for three reasons: just as a leaf covers fruit, so the word of God covers its meaning; and just as there is a greater abundance of leaves than fruits, so there is a greater abundance of words than meanings; and just as a leaf passes away, falls vainly, and decays, while fruit is stored in granaries, so the word of God passes away and falls vainly, but the meanings—that is, the senses of words—are placed in the storehouse of the mind. It also signifies human nature, which passes away after the likeness of a leaf; for as a leaf is easily moved and quickly passes away, so is human nature. Hence Job: “Against a leaf carried away by the wind.” It signifies a human being or lightness of mind; hence Job, according to another interpretation: “Against a leaf,” etc. A human being is called a leaf because he fell from the tree in Paradise, because he is carried away by the wind [Col. 0796A] of temptation and lifted by the gusts of desires. For the human mind is moved by as many gusts of wind as temptations it suffers. It signifies superficial understanding, or the letter of the Old Testament, which is signified by the fig tree, in which there was no fruit but only leaves. Thus superficial understanding has many leaves but lacks fruits; hence Christ found [nothing] on the fig tree except a leaf, that is, in the Synagogue, the letter.

Fountain, properly speaking. It signifies the gift of spiritual grace; hence in the Psalm: “You send forth springs in the valleys,” that is, you confer spiritual gifts upon the humble. It signifies a stream of truth; hence in the Psalm: “You broke open the springs,” etc. The Lord broke open springs and torrents when he opened streams of truth in the hearts of his apostles. It signifies a false preacher; hence Peter in the Catholic Epistle [Col. 0796B]: “These are springs without water.” It signifies Christ; hence Isaiah: “They have forsaken the fountain of living water.” It signifies the beginning of a good work; hence in the Psalm: “For with you is the fountain of life”; or, according to another exposition, Christ. It signifies the sacrament of baptism or a threefold blessedness; hence in the Psalm: “As the stag longs for fountains of water,” that is, someone first converted to the faith, as a catechumen longs for baptism; or someone perfect longs for eternal life. It signifies the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments; hence in the Psalm: “And the springs of waters appeared,” because the Scriptures of the Old Testament were unlocked at Christ’s coming. Springs also signify the apostles; hence in the Psalm: “You shall draw waters with joy from the fountains of the Savior.” It also signifies the Church of God [Col. 0796C]; hence in the praises of the Bride: “A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters.”

Form, properly speaking, is the same as figure, namely, that property considered according to the arrangement of the features. It signifies human nature; hence it was said of Christ that “he took the form of a servant,” that is, human nature. It signifies the divine nature, which gives form to all things and is itself informed by none; hence the Apostle: “Who, being in the form of God.” It also signifies fullness of graces; hence Christ is called in the Psalm “beautiful in form.” It signifies divine wisdom: namely, that preordination or prior conception which existed from eternity in the divine mind concerning things to be created; hence Boethius: “We ought not to be led away to imaginary [Col. 0796D] forms, but to the eternal forms from which the others proceed.” It signifies likeness; hence Dionysius in the *Hierarchy*: “We must be raised upward to anagogical and symbolic forms,” that is, figurative forms, which cannot exist without matter. It signifies a thing’s property; hence Boethius: “For it considers the forms of bodies,” that is, their properties. It signifies formation or instruction; hence: “A prelate is the form of the flock,” that is, he ought to instruct his subjects by good example.

To form, properly speaking, is to make something; hence in Genesis: “Therefore God formed man.” It denotes furnishing someone with virtues; hence Paul: “Until Christ be formed in you,” that is, until he has in you the form which he ought to have through the virtues. It denotes making like; hence the Apostle: “Do not be conformed to this age,” that is, do not become like worldly people. It denotes the union [Col. 0797A] of body and soul; hence Jeremiah: “Before I form you,” that is, before [the reference to the body is lost; lacuna].

Furnace also signifies the final tribulation to come in the time of Antichrist; hence in Revelation: “And the smoke of the pit ascended like the smoke of a great furnace.”

To commit fornication, properly speaking, is for the soul to sin mortally; hence in the Psalm: “You have destroyed all who commit fornication away from you,” that is, who sin against you. It denotes idolatry; hence in the Gospel of John: “We were not born of fornication.”

“Perhaps” sometimes denotes mockery; hence in the Gospel: “If you believed Moses, perhaps you would believe me.” At times it denotes the freedom of free will; hence in the Gospel: “Perhaps they will reverence my Son.” Elsewhere it denotes rebuke; hence the Apostle [Col. 0797B]: “I think that perhaps I have the Spirit of God,” etc.

Ditch, properly speaking. It signifies humility; hence Isaiah: “Enter into the rock,” that is, the hardness of your heart, “and hide yourself in the ditch of the earth from the face of the fear of the Lord,” that is, in humility. We enter the rock when we penetrate the hardness of our heart; we are hidden in the earth from the face of the Lord’s fear if we conceal earthly thoughts from the wrath of the strict Judge in the humility of our mind. We are commanded to enter the rock and to be hidden in the ditch of the earth, so that, breaking through the hardness of our heart, we may avoid invincible wrath. It also signifies patience; hence in the Law a ditch is said to exist in order that burnt offerings may be kept in it. If there were no ditch in the altar, every sacrificial offering found on it would be scattered over the altar by a passing [Col. 0797C] breeze. The ditch signifies the soul of the righteous person, that is, patience, which humbles the righteous person’s mind to endure persecutions. And as the ditch preserved the burnt offerings from being scattered by the breeze, so patience preserves the righteous person’s soul from being disturbed by the wind of impatience.

Pit, properly speaking. It signifies the delight of earthly things; hence in Job: “Hide them together in the dust, and plunge their faces into the pit.” According to another exposition, Job says concerning the proud: “And plunge their faces into the pit.” Their faces are rightly said to be plunged into the pit, because, following the weak things of the world, they head toward hell’s abyss. For by God’s just judgment, those whom voluntary turning-away blinds even here are there hidden from the sight of the true [Col. 0797D] light by the pit which is the fitting punishment. It signifies deception; hence Jeremiah: “They dug a pit for my soul,” that is, they prepared a deception. It signifies the manifestation of sin; hence in the Psalm: “And he falls into the pit which he made.” It signifies a hiding-place of defense; hence Job: “There the hedgehog had its pit,” that is, a defensive hiding-place. It signifies a harlot; hence Solomon: “The harlot is a deep pit, who lies in wait on the road like a thief.”

To cherish or foment, properly speaking, is to heal; hence Isaiah: “A wound, a bruise, and a swelling sore have not been bound up, nor treated with medicine, nor fomented with oil.” Hence people say: “This man’s wounds are fomented with medicine.” It denotes standing by or attending upon matter; hence, according to one translation: “And the Spirit of the Lord brooded over the waters,” so that he might make something else from them [Col. 0798A]. For as a hen attends upon eggs so that chicks may be produced from them, so the Holy Spirit attended upon the waters, that is, primordial matter, disposing future things; and elsewhere: “You will foster.”

A fragment properly signifies a portion of some thing; hence in the book of Judges: “A maidservant threw a fragment of a millstone upon Abimelech’s neck.” It signifies a saint or preacher; hence in the Song: “Your cheeks are like a fragment of a pomegranate,” because the saints themselves are the cheeks of the Church, chewing the food of doctrine; and they are a fragment of pomegranate, that is, red through suffering and white through chastity. This is to say: Your preachers, who ought to possess the whiteness of chastity and the redness of martyrdom, are like a fragment of pomegranate; and cheeks possess whiteness and redness.

[Col. 0798B] A sword (*framea*), properly speaking, is sharp on both sides. It signifies Christ’s soul, because, as someone vanquishes enemies with a sword, so God the Father vanquished the malignant enemy through Christ’s soul; hence in the Psalm: “Rescue the sword from my enemies.” It signifies divine vengeance; hence David: “Draw out the sword and bar the way against them.” It signifies death or the devil’s power; hence in the Psalm: “Rescue my soul from the sword, O God,” that is, from death, lest I be held in it.

To break, properly speaking, is to divide; hence in the Psalm: “Break your bread for the hungry.” It signifies to separate; hence the Apostle: “If the natural branches were broken from the olive tree,” that is, if the Jews were separated from the Church, what of you Gentiles, who are much more so? It denotes humbling; [Col. 0798C] hence Prudentius in the *Psychomachia*: “God breaks every proud person.” It denotes not keeping or breaking an agreement; hence: “Zedekiah, break Nebuchadnezzar’s covenant.” It denotes expounding; hence the Psalmist: “The little ones asked for bread, and there was none to break it for them.” It denotes openly; hence it is read of Mary Magdalene that, once the alabaster vessel had been broken, she openly poured ointment over Jesus’ head. It denotes making peace; hence: “He broke that man’s spirit,” that is, he pacified him. It denotes deflowering; hence it is said: “The woman is broken,” that is, deflowered.

Brother, properly speaking, means by nature, as Jacob and Esau. It signifies brother by nation, as all Jews are called brothers; hence: “If you buy your brother,” that is, a Jew. It signifies brother by kinship; hence in Genesis Abraham said to Lot, his brother’s son: “Let there be no strife between [Col. 0798D] you and me; for we are brothers.” It signifies brother by likeness; hence James of Alphaeus was called the Lord’s brother because he was like him. It signifies brother through conformity of conduct, agreement, or affection; hence in the Psalm: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity.”

To roar, properly speaking, is to be moved by the irrational motion of anger, as wild beasts are; hence in the Psalm: “Why did the nations rage?” that is, they were moved against the saints by the irrational motion of anger. It signifies shuddering; hence people say: “His whole soul roared,” that is, shuddered or feared.

To gnash, properly speaking, belongs to wild beasts. A person is also said to gnash when he is moved by such great anger that he cannot express in words what he has in his heart; hence in the Psalm: “They gnashed their teeth at me,” etc.

[Col. 0799A] Bridle, properly speaking. It also signifies greater tribulation; hence in the Psalm: “With bit and bridle,” etc., that is, with greater and lesser tribulation. It signifies any restraint by which someone is admonished; hence Isaiah: “I shall put a bridle in their jaws,” that is, I shall restrain them from their tyranny and wickedness.

Forehead, properly speaking, signifies conscience; hence in Revelation: “And his name [is] upon their foreheads,” that is, the remembrance of God’s name, written—that is, firmly fixed—upon their foreheads, that is, in their consciences. It also signifies the work or word of teachers; hence in Ezekiel: “At each treasury-chamber, a door in the fronts of the gates.” Treasury-chambers, as Gregory explains, are the hearts of teachers in which the riches of knowledge are stored. Understanding is signified by the door; by the fronts of the gates we understand the words and [Col. 0799B] works of teachers, by which we recognize outwardly what manner of life they live inwardly.

Fruit, properly speaking, is a work, whether good or evil; hence in the Gospel: “You will know them by their fruits”; and in the Psalm: “You shall destroy their fruit from the earth.” It also signifies a son; hence in the Psalm: “From the fruit of your womb.” It signifies usefulness; hence Paul: “What fruit did you then have in those things of which you are now ashamed?” It signifies virtue; hence the Apostle: “But the fruit of faith: hope, long-suffering.” It signifies eternal life; hence the Gospel says of the faithful who are in the Church that some bear fruit thirtyfold, some sixtyfold, and some a hundredfold. It signifies [Col. 0799C] temporal good; hence in the Psalm: “From the fruit of grain, wine, and oil,” etc.

To enjoy, properly speaking, as Augustine says, is to cleave to a thing and to use God solely for his own sake. It denotes using earthly goods; sometimes *uti* (“to use”) is put for *frui* (“to enjoy”), and conversely. Someone is also said to enjoy virtues because of their use; hence Ambrose, commenting on the Apostle, says that they are called fruits because we enjoy them. It denotes loving a person out of charity; hence Paul: “I enjoy you in the Lord.”

Grain, properly speaking, is Christ, who spiritually refreshes us; hence in John: “Unless a grain of wheat.” It signifies a temporal benefit in provisions; hence in the Psalm: “From the fruit of grain.” It signifies sacred Scripture, according to which exposition the foregoing [Col. 0799D] authority can be explained. It signifies the word of preaching; hence Solomon: “He who hides grain shall be cursed among the peoples.” For to hide grain is to keep to oneself the words of holy preaching; such a person will be cursed among the peoples when anyone is condemned to punishment for many whom he could have corrected, through the fault of silence alone. It signifies the flourishing of eternal blessedness or the spiritual work directed toward the mind; hence, after enumerating the good things he had done, Job says, striking himself with a sentence of curse if he had not done these things: “Let thistles grow for me instead of grain.” It is as if he plainly said: If I have done anything unjust toward my subjects; if I have exacted debts and have not myself paid what I owed; but have begrudged others the exercise of good work—then, instead of the goods that refresh eternally, let evils that prick be assigned to me at judgment. [Col. 0800A] It signifies the righteous person’s soul; hence Job: “The cloud desires grain,” that is, the righteous person’s soul desires the watering of heavenly doctrine. It signifies the perfection of righteousness; hence in the Gospel: “For the earth produces fruit of itself: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain.” The blade is devotion of mind, which, though green, is tender through weakness. Peter’s devotion was as it were in the blade when, at the servant-girl’s voice, he was bent away from good intention; but it was as it were found in the ear when Peter resisted the persecuting rulers, saying: “One must obey God rather than men.” But full grain was found when, in the threshing of persecution, he was by no means found like chaff.

To flee, properly speaking; hence in the Psalm: “That they may flee from the [Col. 0800B] face of the bow.” Or this authority may be understood concerning the day of judgment, namely, “that they may flee from the face of the bow.” It denotes the withdrawal of the mind from something; hence in the Psalm: “I withdrew”—namely, from temporal cares—“fleeing, and remained in solitude,” that is, in contemplation. It denotes avoiding; hence the Apostle: “Flee fornication.” It denotes the separation of the wicked from the good; hence in the Psalm: “Let those who hate him flee from his face.”

Lightnings, properly speaking, signify a miracle; hence Job: “Will you send forth lightnings, and will they go and, returning, say to you: ‘Here we are’?” Thus lightnings go when holy preachers display wonderful works; but in returning they say, “Here we are,” when in what they do they have recourse to the Savior’s power. They signify a threat; hence in the Psalm: “He made lightnings into rain,” [Col. 0800C] that is, he transformed terror and threat into the rain of heavenly grace.

Lightning, properly speaking, is the dreadful sentence of the heavenly judgment; hence the Lord, speaking to Job about the devil’s temptation, says: “He will send lightnings against him, and they shall not be carried to another place.” The sentences of his supreme judgment are aptly called lightnings, because those whom they strike they burn forever.

Smoke, properly speaking, signifies prayer or the power of prayer; for as smoke rises upward, so prayer inflamed by charity is directed to God. Hence in Revelation: “The smoke of the spices ascended,” that is, the prayers of the righteous, before the Lord. It signifies eternal punishment; hence in Revelation: “The smoke of his torments rises [Col. 0800D] for ages of ages.” It signifies the Church or compunction; hence in the Song: “Who is this that rises like a rod of smoke?” For as smoke becomes more subtle the higher it rises, so the more a contemplative person tends upward to God through contemplation, the more he chastises his body. It also signifies pride; hence Solomon: “There are three things which drive a man from his house: smoke, dripping water, and a bad wife.” For as smoke troubles the eyes of the body, so pride troubles the eyes of the mind. It also signifies repentance, because, as smoke moves the eyes to tears, so repentance moves human hearts through compunction [to] contemplate God. Hence in the Psalm: “Touch the mountains, and they will smoke,” that is, touch the proud through repentance, and they will smoke through [Col. 0801A] compunction. It also signifies the fall of human nature; hence in Job: “Man passes like smoke from the threshing-floor.” It signifies the obscurity of sacred Scripture; hence it is said: “The whole house,” that is, all Scripture, “is full of smoke,” that is, obscurity. It signifies murky uncertainty; hence it is said of Christ in Job: “Smoke proceeds from his nostrils.” Smoke is said to proceed from his nostrils because, from unbelievers in miracles, murky uncertainty is generated even for a moment in the hearts of the elect.

Rope, properly speaking; hence in the book of Judges the scouts were let down by a rope. It signifies lot or inheritance; hence in the Psalm: “The lines have fallen to me in pleasant places.” It signifies earthly pleasure; hence Isaiah: “Woe to you who draw iniquity with cords of vanity.” It signifies [Col. 0801B] sin; hence in the Psalm: “The cords of sinners have encompassed me.” It signifies virtue; hence Solomon [Col. 0802A]: “A threefold cord is not quickly broken,” namely faith, hope, and charity.

Thief, properly speaking. It also signifies the day of judgment; hence in the Apostle: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night.” It also signifies the mercenary prelate who entered office through simony; hence in John: “He who does not enter through the door into the sheepfold is a thief.” It signifies a heretic; hence in the Gospel: “The thief comes only in order to kill”; and elsewhere in the Psalm: “If you saw a thief, you ran with him,” etc. It signifies Christ or death; hence in the Gospel: “If the master of the house knew at what hour the thief would come.”

Fury, properly speaking, is divine vengeance; hence in the Psalm: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury.” It also signifies wickedness; hence in the same place: “Their fury is according to [Col. 0802B] the likeness of a serpent.”

## G

[Col. 0801]

[Col. 0801B] Cock, properly speaking, is a holy preacher; hence in Proverbs: “There are three things that walk well, and a fourth that advances happily: a lion, strongest of beasts, fearing no encounter; a cock girded about the loins.” The cock girded about the loins is a prelate of the Church, announcing the true morning amid the darkness of this night. He is said to be girded about the loins because he restrains the flow of lust in his members. For lust is said to be in the loins; hence in the Gospel: “Let your loins be girded.” And in Job: “Who gave intelligence to the cock, except I?” says the Lord, who instructed the minds of teachers to understand hidden things.

To rejoice, properly speaking, is to enjoy; hence in a certain antiphon: “They rejoice in heaven.” It signifies taking pleasure; hence in John: “I rejoice not because of myself, but because of you.” The devil is said to rejoice when he exults in our sins. It signifies spiritual exultation; hence in the Apostle: “Rejoice in the Lord always.”

Treasury, properly speaking, is a place in which *gazae*, that is, riches, are placed; hence it is said of the woman that she put two small coins into the treasury, as the Gospel relates. It signifies that portico in which [Col. 0801D] the ark stood; hence in the Gospel: “Jesus was in the treasury”—understand, of the second court—teaching in the Temple. It signifies the hearts of teachers; hence Ezekiel: “And he led me out into the outer court, and behold, treasury-chambers.” By treasury-chambers are denoted the hearts of teachers, full of the riches of wisdom and knowledge. It signifies sacred Scripture, in which heavenly treasures are stored; hence in hymns: “Desiring, from our poverty and scantiness, to put something with the poor little woman into the Lord’s treasury.”

Cheeks, properly speaking, are prelates of the Church; hence in the Song: “Your cheeks are like the bark of a pomegranate,” because prelates are red through affection or the shedding of blood.

Generation, properly speaking; hence Isaiah: “Who shall declare his generation?” It signifies the generation of the begotten one; hence in the Psalm: “From generation unto generation.” It signifies [Col. 0802B] people regenerated through grace; hence in the Psalm: “He shall be praised in the generation to come.” It signifies the glorification of body and soul; hence in the Gospel: “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man shall sit.”

Offshoots (*genimen*), properly speaking, are shoots of trees or vines. It signifies those born from others; hence: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” It signifies the Jews or the Synagogue; hence in the [Col. 0802C] passion of the Lord: “I shall not henceforth drink of this fruit of the vine until”—that is, I shall not incorporate into myself any of the Jews, until after the resurrection I incorporate some of them when renewed; and this in my Father’s kingdom, that is, in the state of immortality. Or literally: “I shall not drink until in my Father’s kingdom,” that is, in the state of immortality after the resurrection.

Knees, properly speaking, signify the strong in God’s Church, such as the apostles; hence in the Psalm: “My knees are weakened.” They signify works; hence Isaiah: “Israel, lift up your slack hands and feeble knees.” They signify the habit of sinning; hence Job: “Received upon the knees.” They signify the presence of a thing; hence in Genesis: Benjamin saw children to the third and fourth generation, that is, the children of Ahis being born upon his knees.

Kind, properly speaking, is lineage, according as it is said [Col. 0802D]: “This man is of Abraham’s kind.” It signifies a generation; hence Peter: “You are an elect race, a royal priesthood.” It signifies a sort; hence in Genesis: “Let the earth bring forth green grass bearing fruit according to its kind.” It signifies the principle of generation; hence Abraham may be called the stock of the Jews. It signifies a major substantial category; hence among logicians a question is said to concern genus, as the question whether Socrates is a human being is said to concern genus. It signifies a thing’s quality; hence: “The Son of God assumed flesh from the most excellent kind of human nature.” It also signifies that universal which is predicated of several things differing in species, in answer to the question “what is it?”; this is called genus. Augustine says (?) It signifies the divine nature; hence Hilary [Col. 0803A]: “Being is not an accident of Christ, but a property of his natural kind.”

To carry out, properly speaking, is to perform; hence: “He will render to each person according to what he has done in his body,” that is, according to what he has performed. It denotes possessing; hence: “He bore the cross in his breast,” that is, he held in his mind the remembrance of Christ’s cross.

Sprout, properly speaking, signifies the Son of God; hence in Isaiah: “And the sprout of the Lord shall be in magnificence.” It signifies virtue; hence Hosea: “Israel shall sprout like the lily.” It signifies a son; hence Isaiah: “Thus their root shall be like ashes and their sprout like dust.” It signifies wicked action: in the foregoing authority, intention can be understood through the root, and action through the sprout.

To sprout, properly speaking, is to bring forth a heavenly shoot; hence [Col. 0803B] Isaiah: “Let the root of Jesse sprout.” It also signifies doing a good work; hence Isaiah: “Israel shall sprout and flower like a lily.”

Giant, properly speaking, signifies Christ; hence in the Psalm: “He rejoiced like a giant to run his course.” For as a giant is of two substances because of his magnitude, so Christ was twofold in the substance of divine and human nature. And as a giant vanquishes enemies by his size and strength, so Christ vanquishes visible and invisible enemies. It signifies the obstinate; hence Job: “The giants groan beneath the waters,” that is, in the bosom. It signifies a powerful person; hence in the Psalm: “And the giant shall not be saved by the multitude of his strength.”

To beget, properly speaking. It denotes eternal generation; [Col. 0803C] hence in the Psalm: “Today I have begotten you.” It denotes regeneration; hence Peter in the Epistle: “Like newborn infants.” It signifies teaching or instructing; hence the Apostle: “I have begotten you all in Christ.”

Sword, properly speaking. It signifies judicial authority; hence in the Gospel: “He who strikes with the sword shall perish by the sword”: whoever abuses judicial authority will be struck, that is, condemned.
