Elsewhere: “Behold, two swords are here”; these two swords signify two judges, namely the judge of the forum and the judge of heaven, that is, king and priest. It denotes dissension; hence in Isaiah: “They shall forge their swords into plowshares and their spears into sickles,” that is, they will break dissensions with the plowshare of God’s word. It signifies martyrdom; hence Simeon: “And a sword shall pierce your own soul,” that is: O glorious Virgin [Col. 0803D] Mary, the soul of Christ himself, which you judge to be your own, shall be pierced by the sword, that is, martyrdom. Likewise in the Gospel: “He who has a tunic, let him sell it and buy a sword,” that is, the righteous person, if need be, exposes his flesh to martyrdom. It signifies discord or division; hence in the book of Kings Nathan says to David: “The sword shall not depart from your house.” It signifies plague; hence: “I shall send a sword into the land of Egypt,” that is, pestilence. It signifies a Christian; hence in the Psalm: “He brandished his sword.” It signifies a near temptation; hence in the Psalm: “You will break bow and sword and shield.” By the bow, with which one fights at a distance, is understood a remote temptation; by the sword, with which one fights close at hand, a nearby temptation; and by the shield, defense. It signifies eternal punishment; hence the prophet: “If his enemies are multiplied, [Col. 0804A] they shall be in the sword.” And in Job: “Rescuing his soul from corruption and his life so that it does not pass into the sword.” For every sinner is compelled to pass from this corruption of sins or vices to the sword of punishments, so that from that in which he took wicked delight here, he may be justly tortured there. It also signifies a razor; hence Ezekiel: “Take a sword and shave your hair and beard.” It signifies the fire placed before Paradise’s gate; hence in Genesis: “He placed cherubim and a flaming, turning sword”: the cherubim to bar angels, the sword to bar human beings. It signifies the divine word; hence the Apostle: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God”; likewise: “The word of God is living and effective and more piercing than any two-edged sword.” It signifies the sentence of the future judgment; hence in Deuteronomy: “My sword [Col. 0804B] shall devour flesh.” It will devour when, at the last judgment, its sentence kills those who think carnally. It signifies the devil’s anger or temptation; hence in the Psalm: “Deliver me from the evil sword”; and elsewhere: “You who delivered David your servant from the evil sword.” The sword of holy preaching is benevolent: by it we are struck in order to die to sin. The sword of diabolical persuasion is evil: by it a person is wickedly struck in order to be extinguished from the way of uprightness. And elsewhere: “Moreover, he will save the needy from the sword of their mouth, and the poor from the violent hand.” For the sword of the mouth is the wickedness of persuasion, whereas the violent hand is the adversity of one who sins; the poor person is one who is elevated within himself.

[Col. 0804C] Clod, properly speaking, signifies being united through charity; hence Job: “When dust was cast into the earth and clods were compacted.” Clods are compacted in the Church when the saints are united in the gathering of charity through the grace of the Holy Spirit poured forth, etc. It signifies the various orders of Old Testament saints; hence Job: “The clods of that land are gold,” that is, the various orders of saints, who are as gold by the excellence of the clods; for clods are bound together out of moisture and dust. Therefore all those upon whom the grace has been poured out truly confess themselves to be dust by the debt of death; while they shone with the power of life, they lay there like golden clods.

Glory, properly speaking, is praise; hence it is sung: “Glory to God in the highest.” It signifies vain glory; hence the Apostle: “Seeking glory from one another.” It signifies subjects [Col. 0804D]; hence the Apostle: “You are my glory.” It signifies nature; hence: “He sits at the right hand in the glory of God the Father,” that is, in the same nature. It signifies eternal life; hence in the Psalm: “The Lord will give grace and glory”; and elsewhere: “The saints shall rejoice in glory.” It signifies purity of conscience; hence the Apostle: “My glory is the testimony of my conscience.” It signifies the righteousness through which God is glorified in a human being; hence Paul: “All indeed have sinned and need the glory of God,” that is, righteousness, or forgiveness, or pardon of sins. It signifies the splendor of the glorified; hence the Apostle: “To those who by perseverance in good work [he gives] glory and honor.” It signifies Christ’s flesh; hence the Psalmist: “Arise, my glory.” It signifies the Son; the aforesaid authority can be expounded concerning the Son, etc.

[Col. 0805A] To glory, properly speaking, is to take delight; hence in the Psalm: “Why do you glory in wickedness?” It denotes being proud; hence Solomon in Proverbs: “They glory when they have done evil.” It denotes hoping; hence the Apostle: “But far be it from me to glory!” that is, except in the cross of the Lord. It denotes boasting; hence in the Apostle: “Let him who glories glory in the Lord.”

To walk, properly speaking, is to be seen walking; hence in Ezekiel: “They walked straight where the spirit led them.” It denotes ascending; hence Isaiah: “This one, beautiful in his robe, walking in the multitude of his strength.”

Step, properly speaking; hence in the Law the Lord commanded that the priest should not ascend the altar by steps, lest he stumble and his private parts be exposed. It signifies the state of innocence; hence, by the Lord’s commanding [Col. 0805B] Jeremiah to hide his loincloth in the river, and by the fact that the rotted loincloth could not return to its former brightness, it is signified that a person who has fallen into mortal sin cannot return to his former degree of innocence. It signifies a degree of blood relationship; hence it is said: “These persons are in the third or fourth degree.” It signifies a degree of dignity; hence Boethius in the *Consolation of Philosophy*:

> He who fell—the step was not stable.

Hail, properly speaking, is the hard and cold heart of a wicked person; hence in Job: “Have you entered into the treasuries of snow, or seen the treasuries of hail?” that is, have you understood the hard and cold hearts of wicked persons? It signifies participation in divine vengeance; hence [Col. 0805C] in the Psalm: “The clouds passed, hail …” It signifies the present punishment which God inflicts upon a person; hence in Job: “After hail follows snow.” It signifies the persecution carried out by a wicked person; for as falling hail is scattered and destroys something else, so the wicked, while persecuting the good, destroy themselves. Hence in Revelation: “And there were lightnings, voices, an earthquake, and great hail.”

Grain, properly speaking, signifies Christ; hence in the Gospel: “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth.” It signifies faith; hence in the Gospel: “If you have faith only as much as a grain of mustard seed.” Faith is signified by the mustard seed through an elegant metaphor; for as mustard seed, the more it is ground, produces the sharper [Col. 0805D] taste, so faith, the more it is ground by tribulation, becomes more refined and formed. It also signifies a saint; hence John: “And the grains shall be gathered into barns.”

Grace, properly speaking, is that which is given freely: from God, remission of sin; hence the Apostle: “Grace and peace from God the Father,” that is, remission of sin and tranquility of mind. It signifies honor rendered to God; hence Paul: “I give thanks to my God.” It signifies God’s gratuitous will; hence Paul: “By God’s grace I am what I am.” It signifies the apostleship bestowed upon the Apostle; hence Paul: “Through the grace of God that was given to me”; and elsewhere: “His grace in me was not empty.” It signifies eternal life or virtue; hence: “Grace for grace,” that is, the glory of glorification for the grace of justification. It signifies the Son [Col. 0806A] of God; hence Paul: “The grace of God has appeared to us.” It signifies a cause; hence people say: “I come for your sake,” that is, because of you. It signifies permission; hence people say: “I shall depart with your permission.” It signifies pardon; hence: “He does this when healed by grace,” that is, by pardon.

To weigh down, properly speaking, sometimes denotes oppression of the mind; hence: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down by anger and drunkenness.” At times it denotes hardening of the mind; hence: “Their heart has been weighed down.”

Heavy, properly speaking, as when it is said: “The righteous man is grievous to behold evil.” It signifies being heavy with the weight of sin; hence Isaiah: “Woe to the sinful nation, a people heavy with iniquity!” It signifies being weighty with the weight of virtue; hence in the Psalm: “I shall praise you among a weighty people.”

[Col. 0806B] Step, properly speaking, signifies a work; hence Job: “You indeed have numbered my steps.” It signifies an effect of the mind; hence in the Psalm: “My steps were almost poured out,” that is, hurled into evil. It signifies Christ’s incarnation; hence in the Psalm: “They saw your goings, O God.”

Flock, properly speaking, signifies a preacher; hence in the Song: “Your teeth are like a flock of sheep.” It signifies the Jewish people; hence in the Psalm: “He took him from the flocks of sheep; he took him from behind those giving birth.” For Christ was taken from the Jews, who were barren, to the Gentiles, a greater people. It signifies an assembly of believers; hence Isaiah: “As a shepherd feeds his flock.” It signifies an army of angels; hence the prophet Micah: “And you, the misty tower of the flock,” because there a flock [Col. 0806C] of angels appeared to the shepherds.

Throat, properly speaking, is gluttony, insofar as gluttony is counted among the seven vices, which are pride, envy, anger, gluttony, etc.

Whirlpool, properly speaking, signifies the onslaught and persecution of the wicked; hence Habakkuk: “The whirlpool of waters passed by.” It signifies the manifold preaching of expounders of sacred Scripture; hence Job: “He removes the stars of rain [one reading has ‘drops of rain’], and pours out showers like whirlpools.” The stars, that is, the prophets, who, set in heaven—that is, in the Church—shone for others by example and watered their subjects with streams of heavenly teachings. But those stars were removed when, their courses completed, the souls of the saints were laid up in the treasuries of the hidden dispensation. But because the earth would dry up if the streams of heavenly teaching ceased, it rightly follows [Col. 0806D]: “And he pours out showers like whirlpools.” For when the Lord removed the prophets, he sent the apostles in their place, that they might rain like whirlpools, because the preachings of the apostles were more abundant than those of the prophets.

Fish-trap, properly speaking, is a wicker instrument by which fish are caught. It signifies the Church; hence Job: “Will you catch fish in a fish-trap?” that is, will you incorporate the inquisitive and sinners into the Church?

To taste, properly speaking; hence in the Passion: “When he had tasted, he would not drink.” It denotes experiencing; hence in the Psalm: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet.”

Drop, properly speaking, signifies a sin arising from ignorance; hence in the Song: “My locks are full of dew,” that is [Col. 0807A], the Church says, the saints who are joined to me by the glue of charity are full of the dew of grace; “and my hairs are full of drops of the nights,” that is, some of them are held liable by sins of ignorance. It signifies humility; hence in the Psalm: “Myrrh, and drop, and cassia from your garments.” Myrrh, which is a bitter spice, drives away worms; thus through it the mortification of the flesh is signified. But the drop, called *ammoniac*, drives out every swelling and tumor: this is humility, which cures hardness of heart. Cassia is born and grows in watery places; Christ’s garment, from which these things flow, is the Church. It signifies Christ’s preaching, by which he softens hardness of heart through his preaching; and according to this, myrrh signifies Christ’s death, which benefited us, and cassia the redemption [Col. 0807B] accomplished through the water of baptism. And this is: “Myrrh, and drop, and cassia shall trickle from your garments,” that is, from Christ’s body.

Gullet/throat, properly speaking, means intention; hence in Proverbs: “Bind them,” namely peace, mercy, and truth, “about your throat, and write them upon the tablets of your heart.” Let mercy and truth never be absent from your mouth: truth in speaking, mercy in bestowing—both necessary for Christ’s throat, the organ of speech; the tablets of the heart suggest the breadth of thought. Thus the virtue of mercy and truth should be fixed in the root of the mind, [Col. 0808A] so that what is hidden may be uttered in the speaker’s voice, the secrets of intention may please the inspector, and the offices of speech may assist one’s neighbors. Virtues are fittingly said to be bound about the throat, since the voice of one speaking is ordinarily formed in the throat: for the voice of preaching flows rather from within, though it encircles outwardly. It signifies a prelate, whose spiritual understanding in preaching passes into the stomach of the mind; hence in the Song of love: “His throat is most sweet.” It signifies the mind; hence in the Psalm: “The exultations of God are in their throats.” It signifies accursed and venomous words; hence in the Psalm: “Their throat is an open sepulchre,” that is, comparable to an open tomb. For, just as a sepulchre is outwardly beautiful—whence it is called a sepulchre, because it is separately beautiful—and open to receive corpses, [Col. 0808B] yet foul-smelling because of what it contains, so the malicious outwardly offer fine words and draw others by malice, that is, they stink through a perverse intention. It signifies truthfulness; hence the foregoing authority concerning gluttons may be explained, whose throat is comparable to an open sepulchre, etc.

Circuit means the turning-round of things; hence in Proverbs: “I alone traversed the circuit of heaven,” that is, the revolution of the sun is open to me alone. “The spirit turns and turns”: that is, the solar spirit, namely the solar motion.

## H

[Col. 0807]

[Col. 0807C] To have signifies possession; hence in the Gospel: “My soul, you have many goods,” that is, you possess them, etc. It signifies the application of one thing to another; hence in the Book of Kings: “He had a spear in his hand.” It signifies a thing’s inherence; hence: “Have charity, and do whatever you wish”; and elsewhere: “To everyone who has, it shall be given, and he shall abound.” It signifies the union of one thing with another; hence we read that Christ’s body had a soul. Sometimes it signifies use or an external manner of having; hence one says: “This man has a wife,” that is, he makes use of her. Note that some have something in themselves, but not for themselves or from themselves: as a cask has wine and contains it in itself, but not for itself, because not through application; nor from itself, because it is not a part of it. Some have something in themselves and for themselves, but not from themselves, because it is not a part of them. Some have something in themselves, [Col. 0807D] for themselves, and from themselves: as Christ had body and soul in himself, because they belonged to him through application; and from himself, because they were his parts. Some have something in themselves and from themselves, but not for themselves, as a man has humanity: he has it in himself, because it is in him; from himself, because it is his property; but not for himself through application. Hence Augustine says that, with respect to the essence of a thing, nothing can be had which it itself is not, except what is said relatively.

To dwell, properly speaking, means to have; hence the Apostle says of God: “Who dwells in inaccessible light,” that is, has light to which human understanding cannot attain. It signifies being; hence in the Psalm: “He who dwells in the help of the Most High,” that is, etc. It signifies the union [Col. 0808C] of the divine nature with the human; hence Paul: “In whom dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily,” that is, the Godhead is truly and perfectly united not merely to the soul but also to the body. Hence in the Gospel: “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us.” It signifies the infusion of grace; hence Paul: “If the Holy Spirit, who raised Jesus from the dead, dwells in you.” It signifies the bestowal of glory; hence in the Apocalypse: “And he shall dwell with them” through glory.

A kid-goat, properly speaking, signifies Christ because of his simplicity, because of his innocence, and because he was born from sinners, such as Ruth, Tamar, David, and Solomon. And just as a kid was offered for sin in the Old Testament, so Christ was offered for our sins. Hence in Leviticus: “You shall not boil [Col. 0808D] a kid in its mother’s milk,” that is: O Jew, you shall not kill Christ on the day of his conception. The day of conception is called the mother’s milk because from that time the matter of milk is prepared in the mother; and this the Jews by no means observed, because on the very day on which he was conceived, after thirty-three years had elapsed, he suffered. Or it may be read concerning Herod: O Herod, do not kill Christ in his mother’s milk, that is, while he is still a child suckling his mother’s breasts, because at the fitting time he is to die for sins, according to the saying: “Scripture does not permit a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem.” It signifies a sinner; hence in the Gospel we read that Christ will place lambs on the right and kids on the left. It signifies a righteous person; hence in the Song: “If you do not know yourself, O fairest among [Col. 0809A] women,” that is, if you do not know who are yours, do not wander beside the flock of your companions, that is, of heretics, who pretend to be companions; but “feed my kids,” that is, your subjects, beside the tents of the shepherds, that is, according to the teaching of the apostles.

Inheritance, properly speaking; hence in the Psalm: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance,” that is, my hereditary portion. It signifies the Church, which is Christ’s inheritance; hence David: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance.” It signifies eternal life; hence in the Psalm the Church says to the Lord: “You are he who will restore my inheritance to me.” Eternal life is called the inheritance of the Church because it was given to the saints who are in God’s Church by reason of the first creation.

A hook, properly speaking. It also signifies a feigned pretence; [Col. 0809B] hence in the Psalm [Ecclesiasticus]: “Man does not know his end, but just as fishes are caught by a hook.” It signifies the Son of God clothed in humanity; hence Job: “He shall take him with a hook before his eyes.” There Leviathan signifies the devil, and the hook Christ. When a fish is caught by a hook, the hook is concealed by a little worm; and while the fish takes the worm, the hook takes the little fish. So the Son of God clothed himself with flesh so that his divinity might be hidden from the devil; but when the devil pursued the flesh, he experienced the power of the Godhead.

A spear, properly speaking. It signifies the Son of God; hence in Habakkuk: “They shall go in the brightness of your flashing spear.” The Son of God is elegantly called the Father’s spear: for as someone attacks enemies with a spear, so God the Father [Col. 0809C] repels unbelievers through the Son. But the apostles and apostolic men went through the world in the brightness of the flashing divine spear, that is, in the manifestation of divine wisdom. It signifies the open persecution of the wicked. As the Lord says under the name of a horse concerning the preacher: “Over him the quiver shall sound; the spear shall vibrate.” The quiver sounds against God’s horse when the counsels of the wicked resound; the spear vibrates when open punishment is exacted. It also signifies the dart of preaching; hence it is said of Leviathan in Job: “When the sword overtakes him, it cannot remain, nor spear, nor breastplate.” What, then, is signified by the spear except the dart of preaching, and by the breastplate except the strength of patience?

Grass, properly speaking, signifies the verdure of temporal glory; hence: “In [Col. 0809D] the early morning may he pass away like grass.” To flourish and pass away like grass in the morning is for the splendor of temporal glory, amid the prosperity of this world, quickly to wither. It signifies the support of preachers; hence David: “Who produces hay and grass upon the mountains,” by which is meant that the great ones of this world, called to faith, provide sustenance in this transitory life to holy preachers. It signifies knowledge or doctrine of eternal truth; hence Jeremiah: “Wild asses stood upon the rocks; their eyes failed because there was no grass.” These are the Jews who stood upon rocks because they trusted not in God but in their own powers; their eyes failed because their hope collapsed away from that to which they looked; and there was no grass because knowledge of eternity was lacking in their hearts. It signifies the [Col. 0810A] carnal man; hence the prophet: “They shall spring up among the grasses like willows beside flowing waters.” Carnal persons are signified by the grasses, among whom the saints spring up like willows, while amid the withering life of carnal people they endure in the perpetual verdure of the mind.

The herodion is a hawk. It is called *herodius* as though “hero of birds,” or as belonging to heroes; hence it is forbidden to be eaten or sacrificed. It signifies a saint; hence Job: “The wing of the ostrich is like the wing of the herodion or hawk.” By the herodion or hawk are understood the saints, because the herodion or hawk has a small body but appears large through the breadth of its wings. So the saints have little earthliness, but are great in the breadth of virtues; and it has many wings, that is, virtues, by which they are raised above the wind [Col. 0810B] of human favor. But hypocrites are signified by the ostrich: for just as the ostrich has a large body and seems to have wings by which it could fly, while it always clings to earthly things through its weight and cannot raise itself on high, so hypocrites, clinging to earthly things and possessing many vices, seem to have wings, that is, virtues through which they might be directed toward heavenly things; but they cannot be raised on high because of the weight of their vices. Thus hypocrites appear to resemble saints. It signifies the reprobate or wicked; hence in the Psalm: “The leader of their homes is the herodion,” that is, the Church to which the wicked flee. And just as the herodion is a bird intent on prey, so are the wicked. It also signifies Christ, as in the aforesaid example [Col. 0810C] according to another interpretation.

Winter, properly speaking. It signifies temptation or the frost of unbelief; hence in the Song: “Winter has passed.” It signifies adversity; hence in the Gospel: “Take heed lest your flight be in winter or on the Sabbath.” It signifies the day of judgment, which is called winter for the damned and most healthful for the saved; for then no escape will be open to anyone. It signifies the present life; hence in Job: “He commands the snow to descend upon the earth, and the rains of winter.” In this life, although hope raises us toward things above, yet the cold torpor of our mortality still binds us. Therefore he commands the rains of winter to descend upon the earth because, in the present life, the teaching of the saints is necessary. But when the heat of eternal judgment burns, no one will then have need of the words of preachers. [Col. 0810D] Yet now it is necessary for the rains of winter to descend upon the earth; this happens when the Lord, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, humbles saints to the ministry of preaching for the correction of sinners (*sic*).

To neigh, properly speaking, means to move lustfully; hence in Jeremiah it is read that the Jews of his time were like stallion horses, neighing after women. It signifies weeping; hence Isaiah: “Neigh with your voice, daughter of Gallim.”

A fawn is the offspring of a deer, etc. It signifies the Jewish or Gentile people who recognize themselves as sinners but, running in charity, pass beyond every obstacle of the world and ascend to higher things in the groves of contemplation; hence in the Song: “Your two breasts are like two fawns of a doe.” It signifies Christ, who in his assumption of flesh is compared [Col. 0811A] to a doe, and in the display of virtues and miracles to a fawn; hence in the Song: “My beloved is like a doe, and like a fawn of the deer.”

A he-goat, properly speaking, signifies Christ’s divinity; hence in the sequence:

> [Note: [Col. 0811] Adam of St Victor, Sequence V, “On the Resurrection of the Lord,” *Patrologia*, vol. CXCVI.]

> “The scapegoat  
> and the sparrow escape.”

It signifies wantonness; hence in the Psalm: “I will offer you bulls with he-goats,” that is, I shall put to death wantonness within myself. It signifies a sinner who repents of his sins; hence: “I will offer you bulls,” that is, teachers who labor in God’s vineyard, “with he-goats,” that is, with sinners who redeem their sins by alms.

Today, properly speaking. It sometimes also signifies the time of grace; hence in the Psalm: “Today, if you hear his voice.” [Col. 0811B] Sometimes it signifies the time of life; hence: “Give us this day our daily bread.” Sometimes it signifies eternity; hence David: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you.”

A holocaust is a victim wholly burned to the Lord; hence David: “Holocaust and sin-offering.” It signifies Christ, who offered himself wholly to God the Father upon the altar of the cross; hence the Psalmist: “May your holocaust be made fat.” According to another interpretation it signifies intention: “And your holocaust.” It signifies one who offers himself wholly to God, abandoning all worldly things and serving God alone; hence in the Psalm: “Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness, offerings, and holocausts.”

Man, properly speaking; and in this sense the word is used in the fullness of its meaning, according to Genesis: “Let us make [Col. 0811C] man in our image and likeness.” Sometimes it is used for a part of that fullness, and then sometimes to designate the higher part, when it is taken for the rational being, as we read: “According to your height you have multiplied the sons of men,” that is, rational beings. Sometimes it is used to designate the lower part, when it means the weak, mortal, or sinful person; according to David: “What is man, that you are mindful of him?” that is, weak, mortal, sinful; and elsewhere: “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?” Sometimes it is equivalent to the phrase “body and soul,” according as Christ is said to have assumed man, that is, body and soul. Hence Augustine, on [Col. 0811D] the Johannine text, “I have power to lay down my soul,” says: “Since the Son of God assumed man, that is, body and soul, he never laid aside body and soul.” Sometimes it is used to designate the substantial state by which man is man, that is, humanity; in the sense in which it is said: “Man is united to God,” that is, humanity to divinity in Christ. And elsewhere an authority says: “Whoever denies that Christ assumed man, let him be anathema,” that is, humanity; because, when he died, he ceased to have humanity, and in the resurrection assumed it. Sometimes it signifies the body, sometimes the soul; hence the Apostle distinguishes the inner man from the outer man, that is, [Col. 0812A] the body from the soul. Sometimes it signifies reason, sometimes sensuality; hence Paul, according to one interpretation, calls reason the inner man and sensuality the outer man. It signifies sin; hence the Apostle: “The old man was crucified with Christ.” It signifies grace repairing man; hence Paul: “Put off the old man with his deeds, and put on the new man,” that is, the newness of grace. It also signifies flesh; hence Job: “Man is born for labor, as a bird for flying.” Man is indeed born for labor because the one endowed with received reason considers how utterly impossible it is for him to escape without labor during the time of his pilgrimage here. A bird is born for flying because by that very means the mind flies up to the heights by which the flesh labors more harshly amid infirmities. [Col. 0812B] Man also signifies God the Father; hence we read, “A certain man planted a vineyard,” etc. By the man God the Father is understood; by the vineyard, the Synagogue; by the husbandmen, the prophets and other prelates of the Church; and by the heir, Christ. Sometimes it means the devil; hence: “An enemy man did this,” that is, the devil.

Honor, properly speaking; hence David: “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand.” It signifies the worship due to God, which is called *latria*; hence Job: “I will not give my honor to others.” It signifies divine glory or the divine nature; hence Paul: “To whom be honor and glory.” It signifies renown; hence David: “You have crowned him with glory and honor, O Lord.” It signifies eternal blessedness; hence the Apostle: “But glory, and honor, and peace.”

[Col. 0812C] An hour, properly speaking. It also signifies the time of grace; hence Paul: “Knowing that now is the hour for us to rise from sleep.” An hour signifies the time of the present life, which compared with eternity is like the tiniest moment of a single hour; hence John: “Little children, it is the last hour.” It signifies the final righteous persons, according to the exposition of the saying in the Psalm: “Like ointment on the head, which descended to the hem of his garment.” It signifies the office assigned to an hour, as we are accustomed to say: “This man prays his Hours.” It also signifies an apostle; hence the Lord: “Are there not twelve hours in the day and its parts?” So the apostles are from Christ and are members of Christ; and just as the hours are assigned to the day, not the day to the hours, so the apostles are assigned to Christ [Col. 0812D] and Christ is not assigned to them. The sense is: “Are there not twelve hours in the day?” That is, you ought to follow me, not I you. It signifies the extremity of a thing; hence David: “Like ointment,” etc., “to the hem of the garment.” It signifies a region; hence one customarily says: “I saw him in the eastern quarter.”

Barley, properly speaking, signifies the dispensing of earthly things; hence Job: “Let thistles spring up for me instead of wheat, and thorns instead of barley.” Job seems to say: I know that I have done great and small good deeds; but if this is not so, let small evils answer to me for great good deeds, and greater evils for small good deeds.

A garden, properly speaking. It also signifies the Church, because just as there are various kinds of flowers and herbs in a garden, so in God’s Church there is a diversity of saints [Col. 0813A] and variety of virtues; hence in the Song: “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind, and breathe upon my garden”; and elsewhere: “A garden enclosed, a fountain sealed.” It signifies Holy Scripture, because just as there are diverse flowers in a garden, so there are diversities of meanings in Holy Scripture; hence in the Song: “I went down into the garden of nuts.” It signifies eternal life; hence in the Song: “I have come into my garden,” etc. Christ invites the Church to eternal blessedness, saying that he has gathered myrrh, that is, by resurrection and immortality he has cut away from himself every bitterness of passibility and mortality.

A victim, properly speaking. It signifies a saint; hence Paul: “I beseech you, through the mercy of God, that from your heart you offer a victim.” It signifies Christ; hence in the hymn: “O truly worthy victim!”

[Col. 0813B] Humanity means human nature; hence Christ is said to have assumed humanity, that is, human nature. It also signifies God’s mercy; hence Paul: “The kindness and humanity of God our Savior appeared,” etc.

Human, properly speaking, means a human work; hence one customarily says: “This is a human work,” or “human reason.” It signifies something slight or tolerable; hence the Apostle: “I speak in human terms, because of your weakness,” or “of your flesh.” It signifies an excuse; hence the same Apostle: “Let no temptation seize you except a human one.”

A shoulder, properly speaking. It signifies divine power; hence we read in the Gospel concerning the heavenly Shepherd that, after leaving the ninety-nine sheep in the desert, he went to seek the one little sheep which had perished, and carried it back on his shoulders [Col. 0813C] to the folds—that is, he brought back by divine power the man who had perished. It also signifies Christ’s cross, which he bore on his shoulders; hence the Psalmist: “Sovereignty is upon his shoulders,” that is, he obtained sovereignty through the cross which he bore upon his shoulders. It signifies the conjunction of social life. Thus Job, recounting the excellence of his life, immediately calls down upon himself a sentence of curse if he did not fulfill in deed any of the things he had previously mentioned, saying: “Let my shoulder fall from its joint, and let my arm be broken with its bones.” It is surely clear that the arm is joined to the body through the shoulder. Therefore, if operation is signified by the arm, then the conjunction of social life is signified by the shoulder. Hence the prophet Zephaniah, seeing that the holy peoples of the universal Church would serve God in concord, says: [Col. 0813D] “And they shall serve him with one shoulder.” Therefore, when Job says, “If I have lifted my hand against the orphan, even when I saw myself superior in the gate,” he asserts that he preserved a remarkable virtue of patience, since he did not refuse to be burdened by persons of the least consequence, nor shrink from what might justly have belonged to him. But if he did not do this, he adds: “Let my shoulder fall from its joint,” because one who despises to preserve patience quickly abandons social life through impatience. It also signifies [Col. 0814A] action, as the reprobate mind, under the figure of Babylon, is reproached through the prophet: “Uncover your shame, bare your shoulder, uncover your legs, cross the rivers.” This was expounded above under “river.”

To humble, properly speaking, signifies to disparage; hence the Lord: “Whoever humbles himself shall be exalted.” It signifies to afflict; hence David: “I humbled my soul with fasting,” that is, I afflicted it. It signifies to grieve; hence David: “As mourning and sorrowful, so I was humbled,” that is, I grieved. It signifies to excel humbly in virtue; hence the Psalmist: “I believed; therefore I spoke exceedingly,” etc. It signifies to incline; hence one says: “In fasting humble your heads before God.” It also signifies to deflower; hence the law commands that if anyone has humbled [Col. 0814B] [perhaps: someone], he shall not take from him the price of defloration.

Humble means cast down; hence: “He has cast down the mighty from their seat and exalted the humble,” that is, the downcast. It signifies the virtuous; hence David: “And he will save the humble in spirit,” that is, all who are spiritually virtuous.

Humility, properly speaking, means lowliness; hence in the Psalm: “See my humility from my enemies,” that is, my devotion. It also signifies humiliation; hence: “Because he has looked upon the humility of his handmaid.” It signifies virtue; hence Gregory: “He who gathers virtues without humility carries dust into the wind.”

Moisture, properly speaking. It signifies divine grace; hence Job: “Can the rush grow green without moisture?” that is, without the grace of God.

Earth, properly speaking. It signifies the mind of the elect; hence [Col. 0814C] the prophet: “Upon the earth of my people.” Seek below under “Thorn.” It signifies Christ’s human nature; hence Isaiah: “Hide in the earth-pit,” that is, hide yourself by faith in Christ’s Passion. Or an earth-pit signifies the human mind cleansed of sins; hence: “Hide in the earth-pit.” Or, according to another interpretation, it signifies love of earthly things.

A water-jar, properly speaking. It signifies the heart; hence in the Gospel the six water-jars signify the hearts of human beings in the six ages, which shall be filled with water, that is, with the historical sense. The water-jar which the Samaritan woman left at the well signifies concupiscence. It signifies eloquence; hence in Genesis: “Rebekah set down the water-jar from her shoulder,” namely the arrogance of eloquence bestowed by the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0814D] A hymn is the praise of God with song. It signifies mental praise, because the saints will praise God in the future; hence in the Psalm: “A hymn for all his saints.”

Hyssop is a lowly herb: it clings to a rock and cleanses the chest. It signifies Christ’s humility; hence in the Psalm: “You shall sprinkle me, O Lord, with hyssop.” For just as hyssop cleanses swelling of the chest, so humility cleanses the mind’s pride; and just as hyssop clings to the rock, so humility was in the rock, namely Christ.

## I

[Col. 0813]

[Col. 0813D] An ibis is an Egyptian stork; hence: “Moses carried ibises in purple vessels.” It is also said to be a certain horned animal commonly called a *stempock*; [Col. 0814D] hence David: “He climbed to the most fortified places of Engaddi, accessible to ibises.”

An idiot, properly speaking, means a simpleton or fool, as though *iduatus*, that is, divided, from *iota*; or as though possessing *iduatae otae*, that is, divided ears. For *ota* is called an ear; hence *biotanatus*, that is, one having divided ears. It signifies a poor man; hence in Genesis Joseph says to his brothers in Egypt: “You are the sons of idiots,” as though to say: You are not the sons of Jacob, but of some poor man.

An idol, properly speaking, is so called from *idos*, that is, form. *Idos* is the model according to whose likeness something is made—“wood to be trampled” (?)—while an idol is that which has been formed as “a trampled thing” (?), [materially uncertain OCR]. It signifies the teaching of heretics; hence: “I shall ascend upon a light cloud,” that is, upon human nature, light through innocence; “and I shall enter Egypt,” that is, the world; “and the idols of Egypt shall fall,” that is, the perverse teachings of heretics. It signifies legal observances after evangelical teaching; hence the Apostle: [Col. 0815B] “What agreement has Christ with Belial, light with darkness, the law of God with idols?” It signifies a tabernacle made contrary to the Law; hence one reads: “Of Micah’s idol,” that is, of the tabernacle. It signifies the form of an idol; hence in the Gospel: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made,” that is, sin or an idol.

Fire, properly speaking, signifies charity; hence in the Gospel: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” That is: I came to send charity upon the earth, that is, into human beings; and what do I desire except that it burn, that is, consume sins? It signifies malice; hence in Job: “And now fire consumes the adversaries,” because a most evil heart wastes away through its own malice. As the fire of love raises the mind, so the fire of malice entangles it; because the Holy Spirit raises the heart he fills, while the heat of malice always bends it downward. [Col. 0815C] It signifies the flame of envy; hence Job: “The fire of God came down from heaven and consumed the sheep and servants that were struck,” that is, the flame of envy fell from the hearts of rulers and burned up whatever good was arising among the people. It signifies the Holy Spirit; hence the Apostle: “Our God is a consuming fire.” It signifies tribulation; hence in the Psalm: “You tested me by fire.” It signifies penitence; hence in the Gospel: “And he will baptize you in spirit and fire.” It signifies the punishment of Gehenna; hence in the Gospel: “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire.” It also signifies any grave punishment; hence the king of Babylon is said to have fried elders in fire, etc. It signifies angelic nature; hence in the Psalm: “Who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers burning fire.” [Col. 0815D] It signifies the heat of covetousness; hence in the Psalm: “Fire and sulphur and stormy wind.” It signifies the heat of anger or lust; hence in the Psalm: “As wax melts before fire.”

An image, properly speaking, signifies the divine nature; hence in Genesis: “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” that is, according to our divine nature. According to another interpretation it signifies man there: “Let us make man,” etc., that is, so that he may be our image. It signifies the Son of God; hence the Apostle: “Who is the image of God.” It signifies likeness or shadow; hence in the Psalm: “Yet man passes away in an image,” in the likeness of an image in a mirror or of a shadow, which quickly vanishes. It signifies natural endowments, according to another interpretation of the same text: for although he admits likeness, that is, gratuitous gifts, yet [Col. 0816A] he passes away in the image, that is, in natural endowments. It signifies reason; hence: “The image of God is re-formed in us.”

Rain, properly speaking, signifies tribulation; hence in the Song: “The rain has gone and passed away.” It signifies speech; hence Solomon: “He shall send forth his words like rain.” It signifies the dew of heavenly grace; hence Isaiah: “I will give you the early and latter rain.” It signifies the Son of God; Isaiah: “As rain and snow descend from heaven, water the earth, make it germinate, and give seed to the sower and bread to the eater, so shall my word be which goes forth from my mouth,” etc.

To send in, properly speaking, signifies an act of sending; hence David: “The angel of the Lord shall encamp around those who fear him,” that is, he shall make an encamping around those who purely fear him, and deliver them. It also signifies to inspire; hence [Col. 0816B] in the Psalm: “And he put a new song into my mouth.”

To immolate, properly speaking, signifies to offer; hence in the Psalm: “I went round and immolated in his tabernacle a sacrifice of joyful shouting”; and elsewhere: “Offer God a sacrifice of praise.”

To fill, properly speaking, means to complete; hence in the Gospel: “The time was fulfilled for her to give birth.” It signifies to satisfy; hence in the Gospel: “When they had been filled.” It also signifies to make up or restore; hence in the Psalm: “He shall judge among the nations; he shall fill up the ruins.”

To impose, properly speaking, signifies imposture, that is, to practise deception; hence in Genesis Abimelech, king of Gerar, says to Isaac, who called his wife his sister: “Why have you imposed upon us?” that is, deceived us. It signifies to suspect someone of evil; hence one commonly says: [Col. 0816C] “This man has imputed such-and-such a crime to me.”

When *in* is joined to the accusative, it sometimes signifies local motion; hence in Matthew: “Jesus came into the region of Caesarea”; sometimes temporal motion, hence in the Psalm: “From day to day declare his salvation”; sometimes sensual motion, hence in the Psalm: “They fixed their eyes to look down upon the earth”; sometimes mental motion, hence: “My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord.” It also signifies final motion; hence the Apostle: “All things work together for good.” It signifies a consequent accompaniment; hence in the Apostle: “To some we are the odor of life unto life, to others the odor of death unto death.” It signifies an accompanying adjunct; hence in the Creed: “He ascended into heaven, he sits at the right hand of the Father.” It signifies opposition; hence in the Psalm: “They rose up against [Col. 0816D] me,” that is, against me. It signifies likeness or is used for *iuxta*, “according to”; hence in the Apostle: “He was made in the likeness of men,” that is, according to likeness. It signifies the permanence of a thing, in the Song of Moses: “The Lord shall reign for ever and beyond.”

But when it is joined to the ablative, it signifies permanence in a place; hence: “There was a man in the land of Uz, named Job.” It signifies temporal motion; hence Isaiah: “On that day the mountains shall drip sweetness.” It signifies a place that is mental, not material; hence David: “I have hidden your words in my heart.” It signifies the likeness of a thing; hence the poet:

> “Atalanta leaps in Parthenopaeus.”

It signifies identity of nature; hence in the Gospel: “In the beginning was the Word.” It signifies inherence; hence in the Gospel: “I tell you in truth,” that is, in him who is [Col. 0817A] true. When joined to the ablative, it signifies immensity; hence: “God is in every place.” It signifies the infusion or indwelling of grace; hence in the Psalm: “The Lord is in his holy temple.” It signifies union; hence the Apostle: “In whom all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily.” It signifies identity; hence Augustine: “The Godhead is in God, and not there”; it signifies a distinction of being, but not of understanding.

Sometimes it is also used for *ante*, “before.” Then it is sometimes joined to the accusative (?): hence in Matthew: “Josiah begot Jeconiah and his brothers in the Babylonian deportation,” that is, before the deportation; or there it is used copulatively, so that the sense is: “And they were deported.” Sometimes it is joined to the ablative, as here in the Psalm: “I shall exult in your name, because it is good in the sight of your saints,” that is, before their sight; [Col. 0817B] and here: “Let my prayer enter into your sight,” that is, before your sight; and here: “This is marvelous in our eyes,” that is, before our eyes; and “he killed their sons in their eyes,” that is, before their eyes. Sometimes it is used for *iuxta*, “according to”: “They contended before the king in this manner,” that is, according to this manner. Sometimes it is used for *super*, “upon,” with the accusative: “Jerome on Matthew”; and likewise with the ablative: “You have set a crown upon his head,” that is, upon his head; and elsewhere: “Cast your thought upon the Lord,” that is, upon the Lord. Sometimes it is used for *inter*, “among,” whether it signifies a place or persons, and it is joined to the ablative, as here in the Psalm: “Moses and Aaron among his priests,” that is, among them; and in the Gospel: “And blessed are you among women,” [Col. 0817C] that is, among women. It is also used with the accusative; hence in Luke: “He took him in his arms,” that is, between them. Sometimes it is used for *intra*, “within,” and is joined to the ablative; thus in the Psalm: “And my prayer shall return into my bosom,” that is, within my bosom. It is also used for *per*, “through,” and then is joined to the accusative: “Justified in herself.” There is here the figure called *protheseos paraloge*, one preposition for another. Sometimes it is joined to the ablative; thus in the Apostle: “Speaking to the fathers in the prophets,” that is, through the prophets; and “he spoke in the Son,” that is, through the Son. It is also used for *ad*, “toward,” and is joined to the ablative, as in the Psalm: “As the eyes of servants are on the hands,” that is, toward the hands; and: “As the eyes of the maidservant are on the hands,” which in Hebrew is said: “At the hands, the Lord shall be at your side,” that is, at your side.

[Col. 0817D] Empty, properly speaking, means void. It signifies unfruitful; hence in Genesis: “The earth shall be empty.” It signifies vanquished; hence: “If I repaid those who repaid me,” etc., “empty.” It signifies vain things; hence the Apostle: “Do not be deceived by empty words.” It signifies air; hence the poet:

> “. . . they pursue empty things.”

It signifies that in which something is, according to Mercury in the *Asclepius*.

> [Note: [Col. 0817D] Something is lacking.]

Incense, properly speaking, signifies prayer; hence in the Psalm: “Let my prayer be directed, O Lord, like incense”; and in the Apocalypse: “Much incense was given to him.” It signifies sin set ablaze by the fire of covetousness; hence in the Psalm: “Burned by fire and dug up.”

To incline, properly speaking, signifies to humble; hence in the Psalm: “He inclined the heavens and came down,” that is, the Word [Col. 0818A] of God humbled himself when he assumed flesh. It signifies to present; hence David: “Incline your ear to me,” that is, offer me the presence of your clemency. It also signifies to transfer; hence David: “And he inclined from this to that.”

Hell, properly speaking, is the place around the center of the earth; hence Gregory, in the *Dialogues*, on the authority: “Neither in heaven nor on earth nor under the earth,” that is, in hell. It signifies the mouths of hell; hence in the Apostles’ Creed: “Christ descended into hell.” It signifies obstinacy; hence in the Psalm: “For who shall confess to you in hell?” It signifies the abyss of inward covetousness; hence in the Psalm: “They descend alive into hell,” that is, sinning knowingly. It signifies the lower places of the earth; hence in Numbers Dathan and Abiram descended alive into hell. It signifies [Col. 0818B] the devil; hence: “Deliver souls from the hand of hell,” that is, from the power of the devil. It also signifies one who is damned; hence in the Psalm: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present.”

To bring in, properly speaking, means to carry inward; hence in the Gospel: “Bring your finger here.” It signifies to gather; hence we read that this was a sign of God’s wrath: the Jews sowed much and brought in little, that is, gathered little.

**Infirm** properly means weak; hence Paul: “When I am weak, then I am stronger.” It denotes the frailty of a thing; hence Paul: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” And elsewhere: “Let him who is weak eat vegetables,” that is, let one prone to the fall of the flesh eat light and dry foods [Col. 0818C]. It denotes sin; hence in the Psalm: “Have mercy on me, O God, for I am weak.” It denotes lowliness; hence: “God chose the weak things of the world.” It is also understood negatively: thus one is called *infirmus*, that is, not firm. Hence Gregory says that Adam before sin was infirm, that is, not firm or not made firm.

**Below** sometimes denotes a temporal condition in the Gospel: “From two years old and under.” It denotes union, as when it is said: “The soul is enclosed within the body,” that is, it is united to the body. Sometimes it is used for “above”; hence John Chrysostom expounds the phrase “from two years old and under” thus: “from two years old and above.” It denotes a local position, as is evident.

**To enter**, properly. Sometimes it means to know carnally; hence it is commonly said [Col. 0818D]: “This man has entered unto that woman.” It means to appear; hence in the Gospel: “The angel, having entered unto Mary, said: ‘Hail, grace.’” It denotes exercising power; thus the devil is said to enter the human body, that is, to have the power of afflicting a person.

**Enemy** is one who injures another; hence in Matthew: “Love your enemies.” Among the Jews every idolater who is not a Jew is called an enemy; hence: “You shall love your friend,” that is, “you shall hate your enemy.” It denotes the devil; hence in Matthew: “An enemy has done this.” It denotes sin; hence in the Psalm: “I have grown old among all my enemies.” It denotes the flesh tyrannically raging in our members; hence Solomon: “Beware of her who sleeps in [Col. 0819A] your bosom”; and elsewhere: “Nothing is more effective for harm than a familiar enemy.” False friends also are called enemies; hence the prophet Micah: “A man’s enemies are those of his own household.”

**Iniquity**, generally, is any sin; hence the Apostle: “As you presented your members to serve uncleanness and iniquity.” It denotes a sin against equity and against one’s neighbour; hence in the Psalm: “Neither my iniquity nor my sin.” It denotes excess; hence in the Gospel: “Make for yourselves friends from the mammon of iniquity.” The iniquitous person himself is also called, emphatically, “iniquity”: “Iniquity opened its mouth against me.” It denotes unbelief; hence the Psalmist: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven.”

**Beginning** is the first principle of a thing. It is the cause of a thing; hence it is said of wisdom: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.” It denotes [Col. 0819B] God; hence: “God is the beginning of all things.” It denotes eternity; hence the prophet Micah: “His goings forth are from the beginning, from the days of eternity.” It denotes the cord by which a sheet is suspended; hence in Acts Peter saw a sheet descending from heaven by its four beginnings. It denotes consecration; hence in the Psalm: “They were initiated to Baal-peor.” *Initiae*, genitive plural of *initia*, are examples (sic); they are given at the beginning of the year; hence *initiari*, a deponent verb.

**Urgency** properly means nearness; hence it is said: “One’s birthday is at hand.” It denotes persistence; hence it is said: “He obtained this with great urgency of prayers.” It denotes distress; hence the Apostle: “Besides these things, my daily care, my urgency.” It denotes concern or glorification; hence it is said: “Give me urgency.”

[Col. 0819C] **Dealer**, properly, means a holy preacher; hence in Job: “The sons of dealers have not trodden it.” Dealers are holy preachers, who persist in good works; for not even their sons, that is, their imitators, have trodden the Synagogue, because they have ceased from its calling.

**Island**, properly, means the Church of God, as though set in the salt sea of the world and exposed to waves and storms; hence in the Psalm: “Let the many islands rejoice.” It also denotes the Gentile world; hence in the Psalm: “The kings of Tarshish and the many islands.”

**Understanding** is the power of the soul by which it grasps invisible things; hence Augustine, in the book entitled *Perisichen*, that is, *On the Soul*: “There are five movements of the soul [Col. 0819D]: sense, imagination, reason, intellect, and intelligence.” It also denotes intelligence; hence in the Psalm: “Good understanding to all who do it.” It denotes the gift of the Holy Spirit; hence Isaiah: “And there shall rest upon him the spirit of wisdom and understanding.” It denotes divine Wisdom; hence in the Psalm: “Who made the heavens in understanding.”

**Destruction** means death. It denotes the chastisement of the flesh; hence the Apostle: “I have delivered such a one to the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord.” It denotes eternal damnation, or death, or sin; hence the Psalmist: “They shall fall into the destruction which they made.”

**Within** denotes place; hence Christ in the Gospel: “The kingdom of God is within you,” that is, “I, the kingdom of God, am within you.” It also denotes the inwardness of the mind; hence [Col. 0820A] in the Gospel: “The husbandmen said within themselves: ‘Behold the heir.’” Likewise, *inter* has the same meanings as *intra*.

**To enter** properly means to deceive; hence in the Gospel: “Satan entered into the heart of Judas.” It denotes being pleasing; hence in the Psalm: “May my prayer enter into your sight.” It denotes beginning to belong to the Church by receiving the sacraments; hence in the Gospel: “Friend, how did you enter here without a wedding garment?”

**To go in**, properly, means to begin to belong to the unity of the Church through conferment; hence in the Psalm: “But I, in the multitude of your mercy, shall enter into your house.” It denotes rejoicing in the conscience; hence David: “His gates in confession or rejoicing.” It denotes beginning to enter into the mercy of God; hence David [Col. 0820B]: “Enter his gates in confession,” that is, begin from confession to enter into God’s mercy, etc.

**Entrance** properly means arrival; hence in the book of Kings: “Is your entrance peaceful?” etc. It also denotes a door; hence in Genesis: “God placed the cherubim and the flaming sword at the entrance of Paradise.” It denotes the beginning of life; hence the Psalmist: “May the Lord guard your entrance.”

**To find** properly means to approve; hence in the Psalm: “I have found David my servant.” It denotes imparting doctrine; hence David: “We found him in the fields of the wood.” It denotes knowing; hence: “I was found by those who sought me.” It denotes attaining; hence Paul: “The willing is present to me, but I do not find the accomplishing.” It denotes experiencing [Col. 0820C]; hence in Luke: “Seek, and you shall find.” It also denotes bestowing grace; hence in the Gospel: “He was lost and has been found.”

**Iota** is the same as *i*, etc. It also denotes the least commandment; hence in the Gospel: “Amen I say to you: until heaven and earth pass away, one iota or one stroke shall not pass from the law.”

**Wrath** properly means a sudden movement of the mind; hence the Apostle: “Let not the sun set upon your anger.” It denotes the zeal of God, that is, good anger; hence in the Psalm: “Be angry against vices, and do not sin.” It denotes purgatorial fire; hence in the Psalm: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury,” that is, do not condemn me; “nor correct me in your wrath,” that is, in purgatorial fire. [Col. 0820D] It denotes God’s vengeance; hence in the Psalm: “Then he shall speak to them in his wrath”; and elsewhere: “He shall store up wrath for himself on the day of judgment.” It denotes original sin; hence in the Apostle people are called vessels of wrath, and elsewhere children of wrath.

**Rainbow** is the heavenly bow. It denotes God’s communication, which God, seeing our iniquities, displays before us as a rainbow to frighten us, but without a string, which is propitiation. By showing the bow he demonstrates how powerful he is to destroy us; but by the absence of the string he reveals to us his ineffable mercy. Hence in the Apocalypse: “And there was a rainbow around the throne,” that is, divine propitiation was in the Church’s protection. It denotes Christ’s human nature; hence in the Apostle: “I saw an angel descending from heaven, clothed [Col. 0821A] with a cloud and with a rainbow upon his head.” By the angel Christ is understood; by his head, divinity; by the rainbow, humanity. For as a rainbow, when set against what is opposite to it, receives diverse colours, so human nature united to divinity receives diverse virtues, etc.

**Israel.** This name was first given to Jacob, as is read in Genesis. It denotes the Jewish people; hence in Exodus: “Hear, Israel: your God.” It denotes the Gentile people converted to faith; hence Isaiah: “The Lord sent a word into Jacob, and it fell in Israel,” that is, the Gospel was first set before the Jews, but when they rejected it, it fell in Israel—that is, it bore fruit among the Gentiles. It denotes, in a special sense, the Church triumphant [Col. 0822A], which sees God face to face. For Israel is interpreted “a man seeing God”; hence in the Psalm: “Jacob shall exult, and Israel shall rejoice.” At present the Church is called Jacob because it wrestles with vices; in the future, however, it shall be Israel, because it shall see God face to face.

**Way** properly means a good or evil work; hence in the Psalm: “The Lord knows the way of the righteous, and the way of the wicked shall perish.” It denotes the divine law; hence in the Psalm: “They placed a stumbling-block beside the way for me.” It denotes progress; hence in the book of Wisdom: “And the night should have a way in its course.” It denotes distance; hence in Jonah it is read that Nineveh was a city of a three-days’ journey.

## J

[Col. 0821]

[Col. 0821B] **To lie** properly means to be held cheap; hence the poet:

> “The poor man lies everywhere.”

And in the Gospel: “He who lay before the rich man’s door.” It denotes lingering or remaining; hence: “You are those who lie in graves,” that is, who remain in fleshly desires.

**Hyacinth** is a stone, or hyacinthine colour; hence in Exodus it is read that the veil of the tabernacle was made of twisted linen, hyacinth, purple, and twice-dyed scarlet—that is, of silk threads of hyacinthine, purple, and scarlet colour. In this passage, *hyacinth* may also mean a thread of hyacinthine colour. It also denotes the heavenly life, because hyacinth has warmth; hence Solomon: “Your hands are rounded gold, full of hyacinths.” By Christ’s hands are understood the saints, who [Col. 0821C] are prepared to endure all things for Christ. Thus they are called rounded hands and golden on account of divine wisdom, and full of hyacinths on account of life. It denotes a stone which changes its colour according to the appearance of the sun: if the sky is clear, it shines; if dark, it becomes dark. It signifies those who act wisely and fittingly with the wise, and accommodate themselves to those weak in understanding, adapting themselves to the capacity of their hearers. As Paul says: “We speak wisdom among the perfect”; but to those who understood little he said: “I could not speak to you as to spiritual persons, but as to carnal persons; I gave you milk to drink, not solid food.” On this, see the Apocalypse.

**Jacob** is the proper name of a man. It also signifies the Jewish people descended from Jacob; hence the Psalmist [Col. 0821D]: “They have devoured Jacob,” that is, they have destroyed the Jewish people. It denotes the Christian people who succeeded to the inheritance in the place of the Jewish people, just as Jacob the firstborn supplanted his brother; hence in the Psalm: “Jacob shall exult, and Israel shall rejoice.”

**To boast** is said of someone with respect to his good works. It also denotes to place; hence in the Psalm: “Cast your thought upon the Lord, and he shall sustain you.”

**Dart** properly means preaching; hence in the Psalm: “Their words are softened,” etc., “and they are darts.” The Lord’s darts are the words of the saints, which strike—that is, wound—the hearts of sinners until they yield.

[Col. 0822B] **Doorkeeper** properly means a prelate through whom access is open in the Church; hence: “And he commanded the doorkeeper to keep watch.”

**Door** properly means entrance; hence it is read that Christ opened the door of Paradise, and in the Gospel it is also said: “And the door was shut.” It denotes the Virgin Mary, who opened the gate of Paradise; hence in the hymn: “You are the lofty door of the King.”

**Jasper** is a somewhat dark stone, possessing greenness within. It signifies the Son of God, who, obscurely manifested by assuming humanity and suffering martyrdom for the redemption of humankind, nevertheless possesses within himself, by grace, the greenness and divinity of the most high Father. Its greenness signifies inward desire; hence the Lord says to the Church through the prophet: “I shall make your battlements jasper and your gates carved stones,” etc.

[Col. 0822C] **Liver** properly means *epar*; hence in Tobit it is read that Tobias took with him the fish’s liver and gall. It denotes the mind; hence Jeremiah: “My liver has been poured out upon the ground.”

**Fasting** is abstinence from food and drink; hence the Psalmist says of Christ: “I humbled my soul in fasting.” It denotes abstinence from temporal goods. It also denotes freedom from sin; hence a distinction is commonly made between the fast of mourning and the fast of rejoicing.

**Jericho** is the name of a place. It denotes the defect of mortality; hence in the Gospel: “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho,” as has been written above. It denotes the saints who presently endure human defects; hence Wisdom says: “For he himself is contemplation in Jericho, because he is present to the saints through [Col. 0822D] grace.”

**Jerusalem** is the proper name of a city. It denotes the Jewish people; hence in Matthew: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets.” It denotes the tribe of Benjamin; hence the Prophet: “Judah and Jerusalem, do not fear,” that is, the tribe of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin. It denotes the state of innocence in which Adam was created; hence in the Gospel concerning the man who went down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers—namely Adam, who descended from the state of immortality and innocence into the defect of mortality and guilt. It denotes the Church militant; hence in the Psalm: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city.” It denotes the Church triumphant; hence the prophet Isaiah says of charity [Col. 0823A] that it is “a fire in Zion,” that is, in the present Church, “and a furnace in Jerusalem,” that is, in the heavenly homeland. It denotes eternal blessedness; hence in the Psalm: “Our feet stood in your courts, Jerusalem.” It also denotes the first believers from among the Jews; hence: “From Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.”

**Jordan** properly denotes the elect; hence in Job: “Behemoth is confident that the Jordan will flow into his mouth.” It also denotes the wicked: for just as the Jordan flows down into the sea, so carnal people descend into the great sea, that is, the bitter malice of this age; hence in the Psalm: “The sea saw and fled; Jordan was turned backward.” For carnal people, at the coming of the Lord, were turned back to him. It denotes baptism; [Col. 0823B] for Jordan is interpreted “descent,” and one who is baptized must descend through humility; hence in the Psalm: “From the land of Jordan.” It denotes the stream which Jacob crossed when returning from Mesopotamia; it is called Jordan because it flows into the Jordan and is adjacent to the promised land; hence in Genesis: “With my staff I crossed the Jordan.”

**Joseph** is a proper name. It denotes the Gentile people increased by grace; hence in the Psalm: “You who rule Israel,” that is, Jews who see spiritually, “give heed,” that is, pour upon us the light of mercy; “you who lead Joseph,” that is, you advance the faithful people from among the Gentiles to greater things. It denotes the Jewish people; hence in the Psalm: “He established a testimony in Joseph.”

[Col. 0823C] **Jubilation** properly means an unformed and unintelligible voice, uttered to express the ineffable joy of eternal gratitude, as is a *neuma*. It denotes the joy of the apostles wondering at Christ’s ascension; hence in the Psalm: “God ascended with jubilation.”

**Judah** is a personal name. It is also the name of a tribe; hence in Genesis: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you.” And elsewhere in Judges, when the children of Israel asked who should go up before them into battle, the Lord answered: “Judah,” that is, the tribe of Judah. It denotes the kingdom of the two tribes; hence in the Gospel: “Mary arose,” etc., “into a city of Judah,” that is, a city then belonging to the kingdom of Judah.

**Judaea** means the whole promised land; hence in the Psalm: “Judaea became his sanctuary.” It denotes [Col. 0823D] the mountainous part of the promised land, divided between Judaea and Galilee; hence in Matthew: “Joseph, hearing that Archelaus reigned in Judaea in place of his father.” And it is written of Jesus that he went down from Judaea into Galilee. It denotes one tribe; hence it is commanded: “Judah and Jerusalem”—that is, the tribe of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin—“do not fear.” It denotes the Synagogue; hence in a certain hymn:

> Judaea then unbelieving,  
> Mad with a crooked spirit.

**Judgment** properly means reprobation; hence in John: “He who does not believe has already been judged.” It denotes judgments pronounced; hence in the Gospel: “The Father has given all judgment to the Son.” It denotes comparison; hence in the Gospel: “The Queen of the South shall rise in judgment against [Col. 0824A] this wicked generation,” that is, when she is compared with the Synagogue, the Synagogue is found more deserving of condemnation. Judgments also mean acts of vengeance, as Jerome observes to Fabiola concerning the forty-two stations, where, near the end of the first station, he says: “Moreover, what follows, ‘he executed judgments upon their gods’—or, as the Septuagint translated, ‘acts of vengeance’—the Hebrews maintain to mean that on the night when the people departed, all the temples in Egypt were destroyed without an earthquake, without the touch of lightning.” It denotes condemnation; hence in John: “And he does not come into judgment.” It denotes ascent for judgment; hence in the Psalm: “The wicked shall not rise in judgment,” that is, they shall not sit with, or assent to, Christ judging. It denotes equalization; hence in Genesis: “He judged me and made me equal to my sister [Col. 0824B].” It denotes purification; hence: “He shall be judged as through fire.” It denotes discernment; hence in the Psalm: “Judge me, Lord, and distinguish my cause.”

**Yoke** properly means Gospel teaching; hence in the Gospel: “For my yoke is sweet.” It denotes the devil’s power; hence in Isaiah: “The yoke of his burden,” that is, the devil’s power. It denotes earthly things subject to the five senses; hence in the Gospel: “I have bought five yokes of oxen.”

**Beast of burden** properly means a mind formerly brutish; hence in the Psalm: “He gives their food to the beasts of burden and to the young.” Beasts of burden receive food when minds formerly brutish are satisfied with the nourishment of Holy Scripture. It denotes one slower in understanding; hence in Job: “Ask the beasts, and they will teach you; the birds of the heaven, and they will tell [Col. 0824C] you.” By beasts of burden are understood those slower in understanding; by birds of heaven, those wise in high and sublime matters. It denotes a person decaying in sin; hence in the Psalm: “Man, though he was in honour, did not understand; he was compared to beasts of burden”; and in the prophet: “A beast of burden rotting in its own dung.” It denotes Christ’s human nature; hence in the Gospel concerning the Samaritan—that is, Christ—who places the wounded man upon his own beast of burden, because through assumed humanity he healed humanity. It also denotes Christ; hence in the Psalm: “I became as a beast of burden before you.” It denotes the simple person in the Church; hence in the Psalm: “He gives their food to the beasts of burden,” that is, the nourishment of the divine word is given to the simple in the Church.

[Col. 0824D] **Rush** properly means the attentiveness of hearers; hence in Job: “The greenness of reed and rush shall spring up,” that is, of the hearers of Scripture. It denotes an abundance of earthly goods, because the rush is usually abundant beside a river; hence Job: “Reed and rush shall wither,” that is, the abundance of earthly things shall be destroyed.

**To swear**, properly. At times it means to promise amicably; hence David: “The Lord has sworn, and he shall not repent of it.”

**Justice** properly means God; hence in the Psalm: “Deliver me in your justice.” It denotes the appearance of justice; hence the Apostle, speaking of the Jews, says that, “establishing their own justice, they are not subject to the justice of God.” It denotes the effect of justice; hence Paul: “For the justice of God is revealed therein from faith to faith,” etc.

[Col. 0825A] **Just** properly means one who exceeds justice; hence Solomon in Proverbs: “Do not be excessively just.” It denotes God; hence in the Psalm: “The Lord is just and loves just deeds”; for a just work is called “just,” etc.

**Young person** properly means one renewed through grace; hence in the Psalm: “Young men and virgins,” etc.

**Youth** properly means the renewal of virtues or eternal glorification; hence in the Psalm: “Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s.” It denotes the beginning of the Church; hence in the Psalm: “They have often assailed me from my youth.” These are the words of the Church speaking of her persecutions in this manner: “They have often assailed me”—this is said because of the frequency of her sufferings—“and this from my youth,” namely, from the first period of Abel’s age; for at one time the Church existed in Abel alone and was assailed [Col. 0825B] by his wicked and lost brother Cain. It denotes the state [Col. 0826A] of the Church; hence in the Psalm: “You, Lord, are my hope from my youth,” that is, the Church says, “since I was renewed through grace.” It denotes the confident and rash boldness of youth, which is usually found in young people; hence in the Psalm: “The sins of my youth,” that is, do not preserve for everlasting vengeance the sins by which I abandoned the way of equity—“of my youth,” that is, of my confident and rash boldness. It also denotes the state before conversion; thus the aforesaid text may be expounded: “The sins of my youth,” that is, those which I committed while still living in the house of my father, namely the devil. It denotes original sin found in little children; then the aforesaid text may be expounded thus: “The sins of my youth,” that is, original sin which is in little children, “do not remember,” that is, do not reserve for [Col. 0826B] eternal vengeance.

## L

[Col. 0825]

[Col. 0825B] **Lip** properly means a basin; hence in the Old Testament it is read of Solomon that he made a *labium*, that is, a basin. It was called a *labium* because at its opening it has, or seems to have, the form of a lip. It denotes a language, because it is the instrument of speech; hence in Genesis it is read that at the building of the tower of Babylon all were of one lip, that is, of one language. And in Theodulus: “There is a confusion of lips.” It denotes a word; hence in the Psalm: “May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips.” Likewise: “Our lips are our own”; those who speak deceitfully are called lips. And there “deceitful lips” means those who themselves are deceitful: “with heart and heart,” that is, with a double heart, they have spoken. It denotes prophets; hence in the Psalm: “And what proceeds from my lips I shall not make void.” It denotes the people; hence in the Psalm: “I shall not remember their names through my lips,” that is, through the apostles through whom God speaks. Or the lips denote the two Testaments, which harmonize in one, by which their wills are revealed; but neither the apostles nor the Testaments threaten judgment to the saints. It denotes preachers; hence in the Song: “Your lips are a dripping honeycomb,” etc.

**Labour** properly means tribulation; hence in the Psalm: “They are not in the labour of men.” It denotes the fruit of labour [Col. 0825D] or laborious activity; hence in the Psalm: “Because you shall eat the labours of your hands,” etc. It denotes iniquity; hence David: “Under his tongue are labour and sorrow,” that is, iniquity and destruction. It denotes thought concerning the toil of saints; hence, according to another exposition: “Under his tongue are labour and sorrow,” that is, his thoughts concern the toil of saints. It denotes contrition; hence David: “I have laboured in my groaning,” etc.

**To labour** properly means to repent; hence in the Gospel: “Come to me, all who labour and are burdened.” It denotes being patient; hence the Lord says: “I have laboured in enduring,” that is, I have been patient.

**Milk** properly means lesser teaching, set before those of lesser understanding; hence the Apostle: “As to little children in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not [Col. 0826B] solid food”; and elsewhere: “As newborn infants, desire milk.” It denotes the Old Testament, given to the Jews as to little children; hence in the Song: “Honey and milk are under your tongue,” that is, you possess knowledge of the Old Testament, represented by milk, and of the New, signified by honey because of the sweetness of grace. It denotes abundance of temporal things; in Exodus: “I shall give you a land flowing with milk and honey,” that is, abounding in provisions. It denotes the manifestness of apostolic preaching; hence in Lamentations: “Whiter than snow, more gleaming [Col. 0826C] than milk, more ruddy than ancient ivory.” The brightness of milk signifies the manifestness of preaching. It denotes infant age; hence it is said to Herod: “You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk,” that is, you shall not kill Christ, signified by the kid, in his mother’s milk, that is, in infancy. Or there milk signifies the sin drawn from the mother, concupiscence; hence it may be expounded thus: “Do not boil a kid,” that is, do not encourage a sinner in his sin through flattery. Or the Jews are commanded not to kill Christ on the day of his conception, and the day of Christ’s conception is called milk. From the time a child is conceived, milk is received in the breasts. The sense, then, is: “O Jew, do not boil the kid,” that is, do not kill Christ [Col. 0826D] on the day of his conception.

**Tear**, properly, means the bitterness of repentance; hence David: “I shall water my bed with my tears.” It denotes repentance or sorrow for sin; hence in the Psalm: “My tears were my bread,” that is, sorrow for sins was spiritual refreshment to me. It denotes tribulation, sorrow, or misery, because it brings tears from the eye; hence in the Apostle: “God shall wipe away every tear.” It denotes weeping; hence in the book of Kings: “I have heard your tear,” that is, your weeping, “and I have forgiven you your sin.” It denotes understanding, because as a tear proceeds from the material eye, so understanding proceeds from the mind; hence Wisdom: “Prick the eye, and it will produce a tear,” that is, exercise the mind, and it will produce understanding.

[Col. 0827A] **To nurse** properly means to nourish delicately; hence in Proverbs: “Nurse your son, and he will make you afraid.” It denotes flattering; hence: “If sinners nurse you, do not consent to them.” It signifies deceiving or teaching wrongly; hence in Lamentations: “The lamiae bared the breast and nursed their young.”

**To suckle** properly denotes being instructed by simple teaching; hence David: “Out of the mouth of infants and sucklings.”

**Lettuce** properly means the bitterness of repentance; hence in Exodus: “And they shall eat that night flesh roasted with fire, and unleavened bread with wild lettuces.” We eat the lamb at night because, in the sacrament, we receive the Lord’s body while we still do not see one another’s consciences. We eat the lamb’s flesh roasted with fire when we meditate in [Col. 0827B] our mind upon the burning of Christ’s Passion. We eat unleavened bread when we perform upright works without the corruption of vainglory. Wild lettuces are very bitter, and we ought to afflict ourselves for our sins, so that the bitterness of repentance itself may wipe from the stomach of the mind the moisture of a perverse life.

**Pool** properly means a pond or still water. It denotes a pit or den; hence Daniel is said to have been cast into the lions’ den.
