It denotes hell because of its depth and darkness; hence the prophet Zechariah says: “You brought forth the prisoners from the pit in which there was no water.” Hell is not improperly called a pool, because those whom it has once seized it swallows up, tossed and terrified by surrounding torments. It denotes the depth of fleshly [Col. 0827C] desires; hence in the Psalm: “You brought us out of the pit of misery and the mire of dregs.” It also denotes sin; hence in the Psalm: “He opened a pit,” that is, he began sin.

**To rejoice** properly means to exult in spiritual joy; hence in the Psalm: “Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous.”

**Left** properly means the left side. It denotes the reprobate; hence Isaiah: “You shall spread abroad to the right and to the left.” When the Church receives some converted from their wickedness, then she is said to spread abroad to the right. She also spreads abroad to the left when she admits to herself some who will remain even in iniquity. It denotes earthly good or temporal life, just as the right signifies eternal good; [Col. 0827D] hence in the Song: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me,” that is, in the present life I shall be sustained by temporal goods, and in the future I shall enjoy eternal goods. It also denotes adversity; hence: “Do not turn aside to the right or to the left,” that is, do not be [broken] by adversities nor exalted by prosperity. It denotes punishment or reprobation; hence it is said that the saints will be at Christ’s right hand and the reprobate at his left.

**Pitcher** properly is a vessel; hence Gideon in Judges, by breaking pitchers, terrified the enemies, namely the Midianites. It signifies the body, which must be broken by fasting so that the devil, who is signified by the Midianites, may be driven out. It also signifies reading the law; hence in the Passion: “A man carrying [Col. 0828A] a pitcher or an amphora of water will meet you.” There it also signifies frail human beings who are ministers of God’s grace.

**To lick** properly means to imitate; hence Job: “The young of the eagle lick blood.” The eagle is Christ; its young are the martyrs, who lick Christ’s blood, that is, imitate his Passion. It also denotes receiving; hence the aforesaid passage can be explained thus: “The young of the eagle,” that is, the faithful, “lick flesh and blood,” that is, receive flesh and blood in the Church of God, namely those of Christ Jesus. It denotes touching, according to our common expression: “A garment licks the ground,” that is, touches it.

**Lamia** properly is a monster having a maiden’s face, that is, serpent-like limbs [Note: [Col. 0827D] Thus in the text. Perhaps read: “and serpent-like limbs.”], which feeds upon human flesh. It denotes the devil, according to those who say [Col. 0828B] that demons appear in the form of little women in order to suffocate infants. According to what has been said, they are called *lamiae*, as though *laniae*, “butchers,” from *laniare*, “to tear in pieces.” Hence Bede, on the passage in Mark, “lest, coming, he bruise me,” says that *sugillo* is derived from *sugo, sugis*, “to suck,” or that *sugillare* means, as it were, “to place one’s hand beneath the throat”; and it is derived from lamiae, who kill infants by sucking them. It denotes false preachers or heretics; hence in Jeremiah’s Lamentations: “The lamiae bared the breast, nursed,” etc.

**Lamp** properly means the human heart, having the oil of charity with which it ought to be kindled; hence in the Gospel: “Give us some of your oil, because our lamps are going out.” It denotes saints who set before others the light of good example; hence in the Song: “Its lamps are lamps of fire and flame.” It denotes the gift [Col. 0828C] of the Holy Spirit, or the sevenfold Spirit; hence in the Apocalypse: “And seven burning lamps before the throne, which are the seven spirits of God.” By the seven lamps is understood the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, or the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. It also denotes Christ. In a lamp there are two things, namely glass and fire; so in Christ there are two: human nature, which was like fragile glass, and divine nature, which kindles and illuminates like fire. And as a lamp is fragile in courts, so human nature is subject to manifold frailty. And as a lamp has no brightness from itself, so human nature has no splendour of grace from itself. From the meeting of oil and flame a lamp pours forth light. Before Christ’s coming human nature was [Col. 0828D] a lamp without light, a lantern without illumination; but this lamp was kindled when human nature was assumed by Christ, and when the oil of divine grace was poured into the lamp of human nature. Hence it is said that his Saviour was kindled like a lamp when he flooded human nature within himself with the oil of divine grace and kindled the flame of deity; thus he supplied light to those journeying in the night of this world. It also denotes our works; hence in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like ten virgins who, taking lamps …” All have lamps, but not all lamps have oil, because the reprobate often show good things in themselves along with the elect. But when the Bridegroom comes, all the virgins rise, because the elect and the reprobate are awakened from the sleep [Col. 0829A] of their death. They trim their lamps because they reckon up with themselves the works for which they expect to receive eternal blessedness. But the lamps of the foolish go out, because their works, which appeared bright to people, are made dark within at the Judge’s coming. Therefore they find no reward, because for those works they have received from people the praises which they loved and cherished in this world.

**Wool** properly means virtue; for as bodily clothing or a garment is made from wool, so the garment of the soul is made from virtue. Hence in Isaiah: “And though your sins are red like scarlet, they shall be white as wool”; as if to say: “If you turn to me, in place of the grave sins which are in you there shall be the whitening of virtues.” It denotes divine nature or [Col. 0829B] Christ’s innocence; hence in the Apocalypse: “His head was white as wool.” It denotes the stronger persons in the Church, who provide the Church’s adornment and clothing; hence it is said of the Church in Solomon: “She sought wool and flax.” By wool, as has been said, are understood the stronger members of the Church; by flax, those who are repentant, who through great contrition of repentance assume the whiteness of justice.

**Spear** properly means the darts of temptations; hence Jeremiah: “He surrounded me with his spears.” The Church is surrounded by spears from her enemy when, in her members, she is impeded by the darts of temptations from the crafty assailant. It is fittingly said that she is surrounded by spears, because the ancient enemy hinders us by the wound of his temptation. For often gluttony is restrained so that lust may be subdued. [Col. 0829C] But if the body is not worn down by the affliction of abstinence, the flame of lust rises against the mind. Often, while we strive to preserve through simony, we slip into stinginess; and while we distribute our possessions lavishly, we are led into avarice, because we seek to gather again what we had given away. Therefore, while the darts of the ancient enemy hinder us everywhere, it is rightly said: “He surrounded me with his spears.”

### Lapidare — To Stone

Properly, to stone, that is, to overwhelm with stones; hence in the Acts of the Apostles it is read that unbelievers stoned Paul—not that they killed him with stones, but that they crushed him with stones. It also signifies to kill with stones; hence in the Acts of the Apostles: “The Jews stoned Stephen.” It signifies also [Col. 0829D] to condemn; hence in Ecclesiasticus: “The sluggard shall be stoned with the dung of oxen,” that is, one who is sluggish in fulfilling the divine commandments shall be condemned because he embraces dung—that is, earthly things. Hence, “instead of saffron they embraced dung,” which the ox rejects, that is, he who bears God’s yoke. Or, one sluggish in fulfilling the Jewish or Mosaic law shall be stoned with the dung of oxen: that is, he shall be condemned because he fulfils criminal acts and not the spiritual things given to the Jew for fulfilment. Of him the prophet aptly says: “The ox knew his owner.”

### Lapis — Stone

Properly. It signifies Christ; hence in the Psalm: “The stone which the builders rejected.” Likewise in Daniel: “A stone cut from the mountain without hands.” Christ is called a stone by several metaphors: for, as [Col. 0830A] a cornerstone joins into one two distinct walls approaching from opposite sides, so Christ gathered Jews and Gentiles—like distinct walls approaching from opposite sides, the one from idolatry and the other from the Mosaic law—into one faith. And as a stone provides a stumbling-block to the unwary traveller, so Christ incidentally gave an occasion of error to the unbelieving Jew.

It signifies an angel; hence Ezekiel: “Every precious stone was thy covering.” This is said of Lucifer: if the other angels are compared with him, the dignity and glorious nature of his own being shine out more brightly, because every angel contributed to Lucifer’s beauty and adornment. For when lesser things are joined to greater, both the greater will appear greater and the lesser lesser. An angel is called a precious stone both on account of [Col. 0830B] the stability of his nature and of his dignity.

It signifies a righteous person; hence in the Apocalypse: “I saw the holy city Jerusalem made of precious stones.” Here Jerusalem signifies the Church, to whose building precious stones—that is, saints—contribute. And elsewhere: “Thou hast set, O Lord, upon his head a crown of precious stone”: that is, the saints are Christ’s crown, set upon the head of the Church.

It signifies virtue; hence it is read of Jerusalem in the Apocalypse: “Adorned with every precious stone”; and Paul says: “Some build upon it gold, some silver, some precious stones.” Gold is contemplation of God; silver, love of one’s neighbour; a precious stone, virtue or a good work. A precious stone signifies virtue because, as a precious stone serves for the adornment of the body, so virtue serves for the [Col. 0830C] adornment of the mind.

It also signifies the unbelieving Gentile people; hence John the Baptist says: “God is able from these stones to raise up children to Abraham,” that is, to make Gentiles children of Abraham through imitation in faith. These Gentiles are called stones because of the hardness of their minds and a will hardened in evil.

It signifies the old law on account of its hardness; hence David: “Lest perhaps thou dash thy foot against a stone.” It signifies sin, because by its weight it draws one downward; hence: “Cast the stones out of the streets,” that is, sins out of your hearts. It signifies the assault of tribulation which oppresses a person like a stone; hence in the antiphon: “The stones of the torrent were sweet to him,” that is, tribulations endured for Christ.

It signifies hatred, contrary to [Col. 0830D] charity; hence in Luke: “Which of you asks his father for bread,” that is, love, “and he will offer him a stone,” that is, hatred? It signifies hardness of heart; hence in Job: “And the stone, melted by heat, is turned into bronze,” because a hard thought, melted by the fire of charity, is turned into praise of God, and so forth.

It signifies worldly pomp, which the stone represents because of its dignity; hence in the Psalm: “More desirable than gold and much precious stone.” It signifies the hardened habit of sinning; hence Jeremiah, speaking in the person of the Church, says: “And they placed a stone upon me,” that is, they were oppressed by a hard habit of sinning.

It signifies a hard thought; hence of Jerusalem in the Gospel: “They shall not leave in thee a stone which is not destroyed.” By Jerusalem the soul is understood; by stones, hard thoughts. [Col. 0831A] For when a perverse mind adds a still more perverse thought to a perverse one, it lays stone upon stone. But in the destroyed city no stone is left upon another, because, when the soul is led to its punishment, all that construction of its thoughts is scattered.

It signifies the words of sacred Scripture; hence Ezekiel: “Four tables for the burnt offering were constructed of squared stones.” By the tables we understand the hearts of holy teachers, by whose teaching the minds of hearers are refreshed. We offer a burnt offering when we renounce all that belongs to this world and turn to God in deed and thought. By the squared stones is understood the fourfold exposition of sacred Scripture. For the hearts of the holy are tables of God constructed for burnt offering [Col. 0831B] because, while they meditate upon God’s words, they sacrifice themselves to the Lord from the carnal life.

### Laquearia — Ceiling Panels

Properly, the ceiling panels attached to beams signify the bodily infirmities which adhered to the bodies of Christ and the Virgin. They are elegantly called cypress-wood, because cypress is customarily applied to bodies that are burned and gives forth from them a remarkable fragrance. Thus infirmities pertain to death; and, in both the Virgin and Christ, through the sufferings which they endured in infirmities, they wonderfully give forth fragrance. Hence in the Song: “Our ceiling panels are of cypress.”

They signify hearers who, through the teaching of their elders, adhere to God and the Church of God, as ceiling panels to beams, and complete the beauty of God’s house. The ceiling panels are called cypress because that wood [Col. 0831C] is incorruptible and of pleasant scent: these hearers of God’s word, and doers of it, are of good fragrance. This is the meaning: “The beams of our houses”—that is, the prophets, apostles, and other teachers of the Church—“are cedar,” that is, inflexible and firm; but the ceiling panels are cypress, that is, their imitators, namely apostolic men, are cypress: invincible and untiring in good work.

### Laqueus — Snare

Properly. It signifies the sweetness of the carnal life, a deception which ensnares a person; hence in the Psalm: “The snare is broken.” It signifies the ensnaring teaching of heretics, through which God permits sinners to be deceived, as their merits require; hence in the Psalm: “A snare rained upon them,” namely sinners. It signifies the habit or pleasure of sinning, as in the same [Col. 0831D] example according to another exposition.

It signifies fraud or deceit by which sinners strive to ensnare the righteous; hence the Psalmist: “They told how they might hide snares,” and elsewhere: “Their foot was caught in the snare which they hid.” It also signifies attachment to, or love of, earthly things; hence, according to another exposition: “In the snare which they hid.” It signifies liability to death; hence in the Psalm: “The snares of death came before me.” It signifies original sin, by which we are first ensnared and through which we subsequently come to death; hence the same saying can, according to another exposition, mean: “The snares of death came before me.” It signifies ensnaring captivity; hence the Psalmist: “Let a snare come upon him which he does not know,” and so forth.

### Later — Brick

Properly. It signifies human nature; hence Ezekiel: [Col. 0832A] “Son of man, take for thyself a brick,” that is, human nature—“for thyself,” that is, for thy honour—and write upon it the city Jerusalem, and so forth.

It signifies sin; hence Isaiah: “My belly cried out for Moab like a harp, and for the wall of baked brick.” The wall signifies the sinner who sets himself as a wall against God. He is said to be of baked brick, that is, baked in sin. For as a brick is made from mud and hardened by fire, so sin, born from the slippery weakness of human nature, is hardened through wicked habit.

It also signifies the sinner; hence it is commonly said: “In vain do I wash an earthen brick,” because the more a brick is washed, the more it is stained. So the more an obstinate person is corrected, the more he is scandalized and made worse. The bricks which the Jews were compelled to make in Egypt signify [Col. 0832B] works of cupidity, which are made in fire; and fire signifies cupidity. Hence in the Psalm: “Burned with fire and dug down.”

### Latibulum — Hiding Place

Properly, it signifies the immensity of the divine nature, which is a hiding-place because God hides in it so as not to be known; hence in the Psalm: “He made darkness his hiding-place.” It signifies the obscurity of the sacraments, in which divine grace is hidden: under the form of Eucharistic bread, and under the visible form of baptism, invisible grace. According to this interpretation, the foregoing authority is commonly expounded.

It signifies hidden hope in the hearts of believers, in which God lies hidden. This is what David means: “He made darkness his hiding-place,” that is, through hidden hope God lies hidden in the hearts of believers.

### Latitudo — Breadth

Properly. It signifies the extension of charity to [Col. 0832C] enemies; hence Paul: “That we may comprehend with all the faithful what is the length, breadth, height, and depth.” That is, that we may understand what is the breadth of charity, namely its extension even to an enemy; what is its length, namely perseverance to the end; what is its height, namely its raising up toward God; and what is its depth, namely the source from which charity proceeds.

It signifies the enlargement of the mind after the straits of tribulation; hence in the Psalm: “And he brought me forth safe into a broad place.” It signifies the abundance of eternal reward; hence David: “From tribulation I called upon the Lord, and the Lord heard me in a broad place.” It signifies abundance of knowledge; hence in the Psalm: “And I walked in a broad place, because I sought thy commandments.”

### Latro — Robber

Properly. It signifies the devil; hence in the Gospel: [Col. 0832D] “A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers,” that is, Adam, descending from the state of innocence, the vision of peace, and contemplation of God, through sin fell into the power of demons. The demon is aptly called a robber because he steals from us virtues and good works.

It signifies a heretic or a wicked prelate, because by a bad example or corrupt doctrine he kills; hence in the Gospel of John: “He who does not enter through the door,” and so forth, “is a thief and a robber.”

### Latum — Broad

Properly. It signifies the breadth of the commandment of the Decalogue; hence in the Psalm: “Thy commandment is exceedingly broad.” The commandment of the old law was narrow, because it was given to one people and one sex—namely, the precept of circumcision. But the evangelical commandment is [Col. 0833A] broad because it excludes neither people, sex, nor condition.

It signifies a plurality of things; hence in the Gospel: “Broad is the way which leads to death,” that is, there are many causes by which a person is led by crooked paths (*obliquis*, as printed) to eternal death.

### Latus — Side

Properly, it signifies the Gentile people: “The sides of the north, the city of the great King”; and the prophet says: “Thy sons shall come from afar, and thy daughters shall rise from the side.”

It signifies an intimate of a prince; hence it is commonly said: “This man has very bad sides.” According to this meaning, it is read in Daniel that the princes sought an occasion to accuse Daniel from the king’s side—that is, from his wife or concubines—so that by seeing, touching, or conversing with them they might accuse Daniel before the king [Col. 0833B] of wishing to have intimacy with his wife or concubines. Or “sides” denotes things belonging to the king; they wished to accuse him on the ground that he was taking away the king’s goods or possessions.

It signifies divine propitiation; hence in the Psalm: “They shall fall at thy side.” It also signifies a corner; hence it is read that the book of Deuteronomy was placed at the side of the ark, that is, in the corner.

### Laudare — To Praise

Properly; hence the Apostle: “I praise you; in this I do not praise.” It denotes glorifying God; hence David: “Praise the Lord, ye children.” It denotes furnishing material for divine praise; inanimate things are said to praise God because divine praise is elicited from them. Hence in the Psalm: “Praise him, sun and moon.” It denotes acting well in a manner that contributes to divine praise; hence [Col. 0833C] in the Psalm: “Praise the Lord, O my soul; I will praise God in my life.”

### Laus — Praise

Properly, the commendation of someone. It signifies the glorification of God; hence the Psalmist: “My praise, O God, for ever and ever.” It also signifies God; hence David: “For the Lord is my strength and my praise.” It signifies good action; hence in the Psalm: “Do not keep silence concerning my praise.” It signifies vain or empty praise.

### Lavacrum — Washing / Bath

Properly, baptism; hence Sedulius: “The washing of the pure stream.” It signifies martyrdom; hence in the Song: “Thy teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep which have come up from the washing.”

### Lavare — To Wash

Properly, to abstain from mortal sin; hence: “Blessed is the man who washes his hands.” It denotes being cleansed by baptism; hence: “Wash yourselves; be clean.” It denotes being free from venial sins; hence in the Song: “I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” It denotes repenting; hence David: “Every night I shall wash my bed.” It denotes undergoing martyrdom; hence in the Apocalypse: “They washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb.”

### Leaena — Lioness

Properly, the Church, because it is bold against adversities; hence Job says concerning Judaea’s rejection: “The sons of merchants have not trodden it, nor has a lioness passed through it.” The holy preachers are called merchants because they labour in good works; their sons, that is, their imitators, have not trodden the Synagogue because [Col. 0834A] they ceased from its calling. Nor has the lioness, that is, the holy Church, passed through it, because, after the gathering of the Gentiles, it did not preach to the Jews.

It signifies earthly glory; hence Job: “The roaring of the lion, the voice of the lioness, and the teeth of the lion’s cubs are broken.” As if he said: the Church, by overcoming through the merits of life, has trodden down the power of the ancient enemy, the desire for earthly glory represented by the lioness, and the persuasions of the reprobate.

It signifies the human mind because of pride; hence Job: “Wilt thou take me as a lioness?”

### Lectus — Bed

Properly, conscience: for as the sick suffer and the healthy rest in a bed, so the sinner suffers and the righteous rest in conscience. Hence David: “Every night I shall wash my bed,” and so forth.

It signifies a contemplative man in whom Christ rests through grace; [Col. 0834B] hence in the Song: “Our bed is flowering.” It signifies Christ’s human nature, according to which exposition the foregoing authority may be understood. It signifies eternal blessedness, as a certain rhythmic poet says:

> Now, in bed with the Beloved,  
> let us rest and sing psalms:  
>
> [lacuna]  
>
> For the wedding is at hand.

[Note: [Col. 0833] Adam of Saint-Victor, sequence XIII, “On the Dedication of a Church,” *Patrologia*, vol. CXCVI.]

It signifies sensuality; hence in the Psalm: “May the Lord bring him help upon his bed.” It signifies the flesh in the same authority.

### Lecythus — Oil Flask

Properly, it is a vessel in which oil is stored or carried; hence in the Book of Kings the woman of Zarephath said to Elisha: “I have only a little oil in the flask with which I may anoint myself,” that is, with which I may be refreshed.

It signifies the human heart filled with charity; hence in the prose sequence:

> Without the wood of faith,  
> neither the flask of oil  
> nor the little meal avails.

[Note: [Col. 0833D] The same author, sequence XX, “On the Finding of the Holy Cross,” ibid.]

By the wood is represented faith in Christ’s Passion; by oil, charity; by the little meal, hope.

### Legatus — Envoy

Properly, a preacher; hence in the Psalm: “Envoys shall come out of Egypt,” that is, saints converted from Gentile paganism to the faith shall be envoys, that is, messengers of Christ.

### Legere — To Gather; Read

Properly, to steal; hence the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0833D] “Apols.” always means “apostle.”] calls a sacrilegious person one who “gathers” (*legens*), that is, steals sacred things from a sacred place, and so forth. It signifies gathering; hence it is commonly said: “A maiden gathers flowers.” It denotes sailing; hence a certain versifier says:

> The thief gathers gold, the maiden flowers, the sailor the sea, books  
> [Col. 0834D] the cleric: each “gathers” in an equivocal sense.

### Legio — Legion

Properly, an assemblage of persons containing six thousand six hundred and sixty-six; hence in the Gospel the Lord says to Peter: “Can I not ask my Father, and he will provide me with more than twelve legions of angels?” It signifies an indeterminate multitude; hence in the Gospel the Lord asked the demon, “What is thy name?” He answered, “Legion,” as if to say: “You ask wrongly, for we are many, not one only.”

### Leo — Lion

Properly. It signifies Christ, because, as the lion is king of animals, Christ is king of all things; [Col. 0835A] and as the lion raises its young, so the Father raised the Son. Hence in the Apocalypse: “The lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered.”

It also signifies the tribe of Judah, which is called a lion because it received a certain privilege among the other tribes: because it first entered the Red Sea; because, before the other tribes, it fought the enemy in the promised land; because Christ descended from it; and because from it God chose kings. Hence in Jacob’s blessings: “Judah is a lion’s cub; from the prey, my son, thou hast gone up; resting, thou hast lain down like a lion.”

It signifies the powerful or wealthy; hence in Ecclesiasticus: “The prey of the lion is the wild ass in the wilderness, because the pasture of the rich is the poor.” It signifies the devil, because, just as the lion goes about seeking whom he may devour, so does the devil. Hence in the Psalm: “Thou shalt walk upon the asp and basilisk, and shalt trample the lion and dragon.”

[Col. 0835B] It signifies Antichrist because of his cruelty and power; hence David: “His eyes look upon the poor; he lies in wait secretly like a lion in his den.” Antichrist is rightly called a lion because he draws to himself those who are openly wicked by secular power, while he deceives holy persons through a pretence of holiness and the working of miracles: he will persuade the former to the pride of greatness, and deceive the latter by a display of holiness.

It signifies the righteous person living by faith on the way; hence Solomon says: “The righteous is confident like a lion; the righteous shall be without fear.” He is properly compared to a lion because, as the lion knows that he is stronger than all, so the righteous person, against any who rise against him, returns to confidence of mind and knows that by God’s power he overcomes all adversaries.

It signifies any plunderer; [Col. 0835C] hence Isaiah: “The calf, lion, and sheep shall dwell together.” The calf is one who sacrifices himself to God; the lion, one who plunders others; the sheep, the simple person. All of these, converted to the faith, dwell in the unity of the Church.

It signifies a Jew converted to the faith of Christ; hence: “A living dog is better than a dead lion.” The Gentile people is called a dog because of the filthiness of idolatry, and is therefore living when converted to the faith. But the Jew is called a lion because of the dignity conferred upon him above the former nations; he is dead when alienated from the faith, and so forth.

It signifies a righteous person in the heavenly homeland, and the foregoing authority may be expounded thus. A righteous person existing in the homeland is rightly called a lion because of the dignity of reward, but is called dead in regard to the capacity for merit, because in the homeland he cannot [Col. 0835D] merit. But the righteous person proceeding on the way is called a dog because of the misery of punishment and fault, for the righteous falls seven times in a day; he is called living because of the life of grace, and better than the dead lion—that is, the glorified righteous person—because he can advance in merit. Yet the righteous person who is not glorified is said to be better in this respect, because he is in a more certain and more worthy state. Hence in the Gospel: “Among those born of women none has arisen greater than John the Baptist; but he who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.”

### Lepra — Leprosy

Properly; hence the law contains a precept concerning leprosy. It signifies the Simoniacal heresy; hence in the Book of Kings Elisha said to Gehazi: “The leprosy of Naaman shall be upon thee and thy descendants.” Simony, represented by Naaman’s leprosy, shall remain upon thee and thine imitators. [Col. 0836A] It signifies a stain in a garment or wall; hence Leviticus contains a precept concerning the leprosy of a house and garment, and so forth.

### Levare — To Raise

Properly, to raise the mind; hence the Psalmist: “I lifted up my eyes unto the mountains.” It denotes making level or equal; hence Statius:

> Some make the round tables level with their hands and arrange them.

### Levis — Light

Properly, delightful; hence in the Gospel: “And my burden [is] light.” It signifies free from sin; hence Isaiah: “I will ascend above the light cloud,” that is, I shall assume flesh free from sin. In this sense the term *light* is opposed in meaning to *heavy*, insofar as something is called heavy because of the heaviness of sin, according to the Psalmist’s saying: “Sons of men, how long [will ye be] heavy of heart?”

It signifies free from the weight of virtues. For something is called heavy by the weight of virtues, according to the Psalmist: “I will praise thee among a weighty people.” In this sense one is called light who is moved from the state of a right mind by the light breath of corrupt teaching or pride; accordingly he is compared with dust. Thus someone is said to be light-minded, that is, changeable. [Col. 0836B] It signifies smooth; hence in Genesis the Lord says to Noah: “Make for thyself an ark of smoothed wood.”

### Lex — Law

Properly, written right, commanding what is honourable and forbidding the contrary, as Cicero says. It signifies the ceremonial observances of the law; hence the Apostle: “The law brought no one to perfection.” It signifies the moral precepts of the law; hence the Apostle: “The law indeed is holy, just, and good.” It signifies the Pentateuch; hence in the Gospel: “As it is written in the law and the prophets and the psalms concerning me.” It signifies the Psalter; hence in the Gospel: “Is it not written in the law?”—in the Psalm, “I said: Ye are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High.” It signifies sacred Scripture; hence law is divided into the old law and the new. It signifies the ten precepts of the Decalogue; hence: “The law was written upon two tables.” It signifies one single precept; hence: “Concerning the law of leprosy and jealousy.” It signifies the tinder of sin, the tyrant raging in our members. It signifies reason itself, written in our hearts; hence the Apostle: “I see another law in my members, resisting the law of my mind,” that is, reason. It signifies sanctification; hence in the Psalm: “But his will is in the law of the Lord.” It signifies the righteous person; hence the Apostle: [Col. 0836D] “The righteous are a law unto themselves”: for as the law governs someone, so the righteous governs himself.

### Libanus — Lebanon

Properly, a certain mountain. It signifies Solomon’s temple, made from the woods of Lebanon; hence Isaiah: “Open thy gates, O Lebanon.” It signifies the brightness of the age, that is, worldly dignity; hence in the Psalm: “The voice of the Lord breaking cedars, and the Lord shall break the cedars of Lebanon,” that is, through repentance he shall crush the cedars of Lebanon, namely those exalted by the splendour of earthly nobility. And elsewhere: “I saw the wicked man exalted and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon.”

It signifies the brightness of immortality; hence David: “The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree; he shall increase like a cedar of Lebanon.” The cedar is taller than other trees, especially in Lebanon, which is interpreted “whitening”; so the righteous person is lofty in virtues in the present [Col. 0837A] and in the future shall be white with the robe of immortality.

It also signifies the brightness of virtues; hence Isaiah: “The glory of Lebanon, the beauty of Carmel and Sharon, was given to him,” because the brightness of virtues was given to the Church. It signifies a saint made bright by virtues; hence in the Song: “Come from Lebanon, come.” Christ speaks to the Church, urging her to come with the saints to his contemplation and enjoyment.

It also signifies incense, for the name *Libanus* is used to denote incense; hence in the epithalamium of Christ and the Church it is said: “I will go to the mountain of myrrh and the hill of Lebanon.” Another translation has “of incense.”

### Liber — Free; Book

Properly, freed from sin; hence Paul: “He is no longer a servant but free”; and in this sense it is an adjective. At times it is a noun and signifies the likeness [Col. 0837B] of a book; hence it is read that the Lord showed Ezekiel a great book in which were written songs, lamentations, and woes, and the likeness of a book.

It signifies memory; hence in the Apocalypse: “Write this in a book,” that is, commit this to memory. It signifies divine predestination; hence Moses: “Either blot me out of the book of life, or forgive them this fault.” It signifies Christ; hence John in the Apocalypse saw a book sealed with seven seals, which no one could open except the Lion of the tribe of Judah. This book is Christ, in whom were seven benefits which could not be in another.

The first was Christ’s incarnation; the second, baptism; the third, Christ’s Passion; the fourth, the despoiling of hell; the fifth, resurrection; the sixth, the sending of the Holy Spirit; [Col. 0837C] the seventh, the coming to judgment. Elsewhere in the Psalm: “And in thy book they shall all be written.” It signifies conscience; hence Daniel: “The Ancient of Days sat, and the books were opened before him,” because at judgment each person’s conscience will be laid open.

### Licere — To Be Lawful

Properly; hence Paul: “All things are lawful to me, but not all things are expedient.” It denotes obligation; hence in the Gospel: “Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar or not?” that is, “Are we obliged to pay it?” and so forth.

### L igare — To Bind

Properly, it denotes subjecting someone to an ecclesiastical sentence. It denotes showing someone to be bound. It denotes imposing satisfaction; hence in the Gospel, with its threefold meaning: “Whatever thou shalt bind on earth,” and so forth. It denotes living; hence Boethius:

> Thou who bindest the elements by numbers, and so forth.

[Col. 0837D] It denotes depriving someone of every power; hence in the Gospel: “With hands and feet bound.”

### Ligatus — Bound

Properly, it also denotes someone bound to a wife; hence the Apostle: “Art thou bound to a wife? Seek not release.” It signifies someone subject to the Church’s sentence; hence in the Gospel: “Whatever thou shalt bind,” and so forth. It signifies someone deprived of the exercise of free choice; hence in the Gospel: “With hands and feet bound.” For those who will be in hell will have their hands and feet bound, because they will be able neither to do good nor evil, nor to bring wicked effects into actuality.

### Lignum — Wood; Tree

Properly. It signifies Christ; hence the Psalmist: “And he shall be like a tree.” Christ is elegantly called a tree because a tree is planted in the ground, watered by rain, grows green, puts forth leaves, blossoms, and bears fruit. [Col. 0838A] Thus Christ was planted in a foreign land when he was incarnate in the Virgin Mary; he was watered by the rain of heavenly grace; he grew green through virtue, put forth leaves through holy preaching, blossomed through fragrant conduct, and bore fruit through the redemption of humankind.

It signifies the Lord’s cross; hence it is said in the law: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree,” and “Let us put wood into his bread.” To put wood into bread is to apply the cross to the Lord’s body. It signifies Wisdom; hence in Solomon’s book: “Wisdom is a tree of life to those who embrace her.” It signifies the righteous person; hence in the Song: “Solomon made himself a litter from the woods of Lebanon,” that is, Christ constructed the Church from saints; and elsewhere, namely in the Gospel: “If they do these things in green wood, what shall be done in dry?” It signifies venial sin which is [Col. 0838B] more serious; hence the Apostle: “Others build upon it wood, hay, and stubble.” By wood is signified grave venial sin; by hay, a lesser one; by stubble, the least.

### Lilium — Lily

Properly, the image of a lily; hence in Exodus it is read that there were small spheres and lilies in the candlestick, that is, images of lilies. It signifies virtue; hence in the Song: “Thy breasts are like the fawns of a roe which feed among lilies,” that is, among virtues or good works. It signifies Christ; hence in the Song: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.” It signifies the Church; hence in the Song: “Like a lily among thorns.” It signifies the humble, because a lily grows in valleys; lilies signify the humble: “My beloved speaks to me, who feeds among lilies.” It signifies the Israelite people; hence Isaiah: “And Israel shall blossom like a lily.”

### Limus — Mud

[Col. 0838C] Properly; hence in Genesis: “And God formed man from the mud of the earth.” It also signifies Jewish iniquity; hence: “I am stuck fast in the mud of the deep, and there is no firm ground.”

### Lingua — Tongue

Properly, false doctrine; hence the Lord says to Job concerning the devil: “And thou shalt bind his tongue with a cord.” For when Christ came in the flesh, the falsity of the devil’s doctrine was restrained by the firmness of Christian faith.

It signifies the likeness of a tongue; hence in the Acts of the Apostles it is read that the Holy Spirit appeared in fiery tongues, because certain rays of brightness appeared above the apostles’ heads in the likeness of tongues. It signifies a word; hence the Psalmist: “May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips and the tongue that speaks great things.” It signifies [Col. 0838D] a language; hence in the Gospel and Acts: “They spoke in various tongues.” It signifies punishment inflicted for the sin of the tongue; hence it is read that the rich man’s soul spoke to Lazarus: “Dip the tip of thy finger in water, that it may cool my tongue,” that is, the punishment inflicted on me for the sin of my tongue.

### Linteum — Linen Cloth

Properly, it signifies an image of a linen cloth; hence in the Acts of the Apostles it is read that Peter saw a linen cloth containing within itself every kind of living creature.

### Linum — Flax

Properly. It signifies Gentiles possessing the natural law; hence Isaiah: “He shall not extinguish the smoking flax,” that is, he shall stir up the nations to the spark of faith. It signifies believers who acquire the brightness of virtues through much labour; hence it is said of the Church in Solomon’s book: “She sought wool and flax.” By flax [Col. 0839A] are understood penitents, who through much contrition of repentance assume the brightness of righteousness; by wool, the stronger members of the Church.

### Liquari — To Be Melted; Poured Out

It denotes being dissolved; hence the poet: “As wax melts.” It denotes being poured in, and in this sense is passive in force; hence the poet: “He liquefied the elements,” that is, he pours them in. Likewise, it denotes flowing forth or running down.

### Liquere — To Flow; Be Clear

It denotes to flow. It denotes to be dissolved; hence wax is said to melt. It signifies to become known, as when one says: “This is clear,” that is, it is manifest.

### Littera — Letter

Properly, a written sheet or epistle; hence in the Book of Kings it is read that Uriah carried with him letters of his own death. It signifies history, as we are accustomed to say: “This is expounded according to the letter,” that is, historically. It signifies the literal sense; hence the Apostle: “The letter [Col. 0839B] kills, but the spirit gives life.”

### Livere — To Envy; To Speak

Properly, to envy; hence also *livor* (“envy”). [Note: [Col. 0839] What follows belongs to the verb *Loqui* (“to speak”), which is in fact missing below in its proper place, and should be inserted after the entry *Loquela*.]

Properly, it also signifies to inspire; hence David: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me,” that is, what understanding inspires in me. It denotes to beget; hence David: “God spoke once,” that is, he eternally begot the Son. It denotes to exercise; hence Isaiah: “He who speaks righteousness and is a champion to save.” It denotes to reveal; hence David: “Then he will speak to them in his anger,” that is, he will then reveal his anger to them. It denotes to think; hence in the Psalm: “He who speaks truth in his heart.”

### Livor — Envy; Bruise

Properly, envy; hence Lucan:

> Devouring envy denies thee all things.

It signifies the livid colour which arises in the skin from a blow; [Col. 0839C] hence Lamech says in Genesis: “I killed a man to my wound, and a young man to my bruise.” The Jews relate that Lamech, when blind, was hunting while led by a youth. The youth, seeing Cain hidden beneath a shelter, believed him to be a wild animal; at his indication Lamech shot an arrow and killed Cain. Recognizing this, stirred by anger, he struck the youth violently and killed him. This is the meaning of his saying: “I killed a man.”

It signifies Christ’s Passion; hence Isaiah: “By whose bruise we are healed.”

### Locus — Place

Properly, the world, which is called the place of the wicked because the wicked delight in it; hence it is said of the impious person in the Psalm: “And his place was not found.” For, as the impious will be damned in the future, so [Col. 0839D] the world too will be dissolved.

It signifies a saint; hence David: “God in his holy place,” because the soul of a righteous person is called God’s place through grace. It signifies sacred Scripture; hence “in a place of pasture.” It is aptly called a place of pasture because it feeds us spiritually.

It signifies the Church; hence David: “In the place where his feet stood.” This place is called the Church, in which his feet—that is, Christ’s—stand. A foot is the lower part of an animal; Christ’s feet signify the saints who, persevering in goodness to the end, are in God’s Church.

It signifies Christ; in the foregoing authority “place” may be understood as Christ, in whom, through faith and charity, are his feet—that is, those of the Church. The feet of the Church [Col. 0840A] are called its preachers, through whom both the Church’s faith is extended and the Church itself spread abroad.

It signifies the triumphant Church or eternal life; hence David: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of thy house and the place of thy dwelling.” It signifies an opportunity; hence Paul: “Give no place to the devil,” that is, no occasion for possessing you. It signifies the sinner; thus the foregoing authority may be expounded: “Give no place to the devil,” that is, do not make yourselves a place for the devil. It signifies idolatry; hence in Deuteronomy: “He found him in a place of horror and vast solitude.” It also signifies a sheath; hence the Lord said to Peter: “Put thy sword back into its place.”

### Locusta — Locust

Properly. It signifies vain glory or pride; hence the prophet: “The locust ate what remained of the caterpillar.” By the caterpillar is signified lust, because, as the caterpillar, [Col. 0840B] which is the offspring of the locust, clings to the earth and gnaws away every plant, so lust corrupts the whole person. By the locust, whose flight falls downward, is represented pride or vain glory, which quickly falls.

It signifies a heretic; hence in the Apocalypse: “The sun and air were darkened by the smoke of the pit; and locusts came forth from the smoke of the pit and fell upon the earth.” The meaning is this: through the preaching of heretics the faith of Christ, signified by the sun, will be darkened. By the pit is understood the devil, from whose smoke—that is, from whose wicked suggestion—heretics arise; they fall into various heresies through desire for temporal things and empty glory.

### Loquela — Speech; Language

Properly, a language; hence David: “There are no speeches nor words.” It also signifies a manner of speaking; [Col. 0840C] hence in the Gospel: “For thy speech makes thee known,” that is, thy manner of speaking.

### Lorica — Breastplate

Properly, it signifies a fortification; hence in the Apocalypse: “And I saw horses in vision, and those who sat upon them had fiery breastplates.” For demons, through the tribulations which they inflicted upon saints by means of idolaters, fortified themselves against the faithful.

It signifies righteousness; hence Peter: “Stand therefore, having girded your loins and put on the breastplate of righteousness.”

Lotus, properly, one washed by the sacrament of baptism; hence in the Gospel: “He who has been washed does not need [to be washed again].” It signifies the humble person, or one pierced with compunction for heavenly things; hence: “Though I were washed with snow-water.” This was explained above under “Water.”

To shine (*lucere*), properly, is to offer or present; hence in the Gospel: “And the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” [Col. 0840D]. The sense is: Divine wisdom offers itself to all, both good and evil; but the darkness—that is, the wicked, deprived of inward light—does not comprehend the divine light, just as the sun offers its rays alike to one who sees and to a blind person: the one who sees apprehends the rays, but the blind person does not.

A lamp (*lucerna*), properly. It signifies the soul or life; hence in the Book of Wisdom: “The light of the saints brings joy, but the lamp of the wicked shall be extinguished.” It signifies John the Baptist; hence in the Psalm: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ.” It signifies the first believers from among the Jews; hence David: “For you light my lamp, O Lord my God; enlighten my darkness.” The Church prays [Col. 0841A] that, just as the first believers from among the Jews—such as the apostles and others—were converted to the faith and became the light of the Church, so her darkness, that is, the Jews now darkened through unbelief, may in the remnant be enlightened unto faith; and thus the remnant of Israel may be saved. It signifies carnal joy; hence Job: “And the lamp that is over him shall be extinguished.” The lamp in its earthen vessel is joy in the flesh; therefore the lamp over the wicked person shall be extinguished, because on the day of judgment carnal joy will be destroyed in the wicked when the recompense of evil pursues them. It signifies Christ incarnate, because, just as a lamp is light in an earthen vessel, so the light of the Divinity lay hidden in the vessel of humanity. Hence in Luke’s Gospel: “What woman, having drachmas, etc., lights a lamp?” This woman is the wisdom of God, who had ten drachmas [Col. 0841B], that is, the nine orders of angels and man, created by her. But she lost one drachma when man sinned. She then lit a lamp when she united the divine nature to the human, in order to recover the tenth drachma—that is, to redeem human nature. It signifies preaching; hence in the Gospel: “No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand.” The sense is: No one ought to refrain from preaching through fear of death, in order to spare his own flesh. It signifies intention; hence in the Gospel: “The lamp of your body is your eye,” that is, if the intention is good, the work is good, etc. It signifies charity in action; hence in the Gospel: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning.” The sense is: Bodily chastity is insufficient unless charity is [Col. 0841C] active in works. It signifies the word of God; hence David: “Your word is a lamp to my feet.” This is elegantly signified by the lamp, because, just as a lamp is light in an earthen vessel, so the word of God is contained in the slippery and fragile heart of man. Hence Paul: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels.”

The morning star (*Lucifer*), properly; hence: “May the morning Lucifer find its flame.” It signifies time; hence in the Psalm: “Before Lucifer I begot you,” that is, before time—as though he said, eternally. It signifies Christ; hence Peter: “Until Lucifer rises in your hearts.” It signifies the righteous person; hence Job: “When you find yourself consumed, you shall rise like Lucifer.” It also signifies the devil; hence the prophet: “How have you fallen, Lucifer?”

[Col. 0841D] Wrestling (*lucta*), properly, is the conflict between flesh and spirit; hence the Apostle: “Your struggle is not against flesh and blood”; and elsewhere: “Where the struggle is greater, the crown is greater.”

To play (*ludere*), properly, is to mock; hence it is read in Genesis that Sarah saw Ishmael playing with Isaac, that is, mocking him and compelling him to worship clay images. It denotes idolatry; hence in Exodus: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play,” that is, to worship the calf. It denotes divination; hence Isaiah: “Woe to those who play with the birds of heaven,” that is, who divine from the chirping or flight of birds. It denotes delight; hence in Proverbs: “Playing before him,” that is, rejoicing together.

Light (*lumen*), properly. It signifies Christ’s preaching and knowledge of the Father and the Holy Spirit; hence: “For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” [Col. 0842A]. The speech is addressed to Christ, and its sense is: With you is the fountain of life, that is, the beginning of every good; and in your light, that is, through your preaching, we shall see light, that is, we shall have knowledge of the Father and the Holy Spirit. It signifies confidence in the truth; hence in the Gospel: “What I tell you in darkness, say in the light,” that is: you who are in fear, preach in the light, that is, confidently; for confidence takes away fear. It signifies manifestation; thus the foregoing authority may be explained: “Preach openly those things that I said in secret.” It signifies Christ; hence John: “He was not the light, but [came] to bear witness concerning the light.” It signifies a saint illuminated by Christ; hence James: “Every good gift [comes] down from the Father of lights” [Col. 0842B]. It signifies understanding; hence in John: “Yet a little light is in you,” that is, a little understanding. It signifies eternal life; hence in John: “He who follows me, etc., shall have the light of life.” It signifies grace; hence David: “The light of your countenance is marked upon us,” that is, our reason, by which we are like you, is marked upon us as light—that is, impressed upon the higher part of the soul, namely reason. It signifies human reason; thus the preceding authority may be explained: “The light of your countenance,” that is, our reason enlightened by your grace, “is marked upon us,” that is, impressed upon the higher part of the soul. It signifies Christ’s cross; hence in the Psalm: “The light is marked upon us,” that is, the cross, through which you expressed your will to us [Col. 0842C], is marked upon us—on the forehead by its impress, in the mind by faith.

The moon (*luna*), properly; hence David: “He made the moon for seasons.” It signifies the mutability of temporal things; hence in the Apocalypse: “A woman clothed with the sun, and the moon beneath her feet.” In the sun is understood the illumination of truth; in the moon, which wanes monthly, temporal mutability. Holy Church, protected by the splendor of heavenly light, is as though clothed with the sun; and because she despises all temporal things, she treads the moon, as it were, beneath her feet. It also signifies a fool, as Solomon says: “The wise man remains as the sun; the fool changes as the moon.” It also signifies the Church. Thus, according to another exposition, the foregoing authority may be understood of the Church: [Col. 0842D] “He made the moon for seasons,” which was built in time through Christ’s Passion; and elsewhere: “For I shall behold your heavens, etc., the moon and stars.” The Church is elegantly figured by the moon, because, just as the moon begs light from the sun, so the Church receives the light of righteousness from the true sun, namely Christ. It signifies the Virgin Mary; hence in the Song: “Beautiful as the moon.” It signifies the reputation of a good work; hence Job: “If I saw the sun when it shone and the moon proceeding brightly.” By the shining sun is understood the splendor of a good work, but by the moon the good reputation of that work. It signifies those lesser in the Church; hence Habakkuk: “The sun and moon stood in their dwelling,” because both the sun—that is, the greater persons in the Church—and the moon—that is, the lesser—hold their own order. It signifies the frailty of mortals, because the moon suffers decrease and increase; thus through it is signified mortal frailty. Hence in the Psalm: “And he shall endure with the sun,” that is, as long as times revolve, which are understood through the sun because times change and are distinguished according to the sun’s course; “and before the moon,” that is, before all times, because in his immortality he precedes all temporal things [Col. 0843A]. It signifies the mortality of the flesh; hence David: “In his days righteousness shall arise and abundance of peace, until the moon is taken away,” that is, peace shall remain until death is destroyed and there is no longer the mortality of flesh signified by the moon. It signifies Christ’s human nature; hence in the Psalm: “By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night.” The sense is: If Christ protects you, the sun shall not burn you by day—that is, you shall not err concerning the Divinity or the wisdom of God—nor shall the moon burn you by night—that is, you shall not be scandalized concerning the flesh; that is, you shall not err in knowledge of the Divinity, nor in knowledge of the humanity [Col. 0843B]. It signifies the dejection sometimes caused by adversities; and the sense is: “The sun shall not burn you by day,” that is, you shall not be burned by the exaltation of prosperity; “nor the moon by night,” that is, neither shall you succumb to the depression of adversity.

A wolf (*lupus*), properly. It signifies the devil; hence in the Gospel: “The wolf snatches and scatters the sheep; the wolf comes and the hireling flees,” because when the devil arises, the false shepherd has no concernful care. And in the Life of Saint Martin it is read: “Why, Father, do you desert us, or why do you leave us desolate? For ravening wolves will invade your flock.” It signifies a robber; hence the prophet: “The wolf shall dwell with the lamb.” For what ought we to understand by the wolf [Col. 0843C] but one eager for plunder, and what by the lamb but the gentle person? Yet the wolf dwells with the lamb, because through faith in holy charity, in holy Church those who were robbers in the world rest together with the meek and gentle. It signifies a tyrant persecuting the Church of God; hence in the Gospel: “The hireling, and he who is not the shepherd, seeing the wolf coming, flees.” It signifies one persecuting a Christian; hence in the Gospel: “Behold, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves.” It signifies a hypocrite who deceives others by false religion; hence in the Gospel: “Beware of false prophets, etc., [who are] ravening wolves.” It signifies Paul the Apostle; hence in Jacob’s blessings: “Benjamin, a ravening wolf, devouring prey in the morning and dividing spoils in the evening” [Col. 0843D]. For Paul, who was of the tribe of Benjamin, in the morning—that is, in youth—persecuted the Church of God, plundering it and torturing the saints in prison; but in the evening—that is, in old age—having been converted to the faith, he divided the spoils: those whom the devil possessed, he took away from him by his preaching.

A *lustrum*, properly, is a period of five years; hence in the hymn: “Already six lustrums.” It signifies a woodland grove; thus authors frequently speak of the haunts of wild beasts, as: “He ranged through the haunts of wild beasts.” It signifies expiation; hence Ovid on peoples who performed expiatory rites . . . .

A *luter*, properly, is a washbasin; hence it is read in the Book of Kings that Solomon made ten basins. It signifies an animal that lives in water and feeds on fish; hence [Col. 0844A] Augustine says that the otter was not in Noah’s ark. In the sense of washbasin, it is *luter, luteris*; in the sense of animal, it is *luter, lutris*.

Mud (*lutum*), properly. It signifies man, because he was formed or fashioned from mud; hence Job: “Remember, I beseech you, O Lord, that you have made me like mud.” It signifies lust, because, like mud, it is clinging, foul-smelling, and corrupting. It clings, because one whom it has seized once it scarcely releases. It stinks because it stinks before God, before the angel, and before one’s neighbor through infamy. It corrupts because it corrupts body and soul; hence in the Psalm: “I shall destroy them as the mud of the streets.” It signifies the depth of sin; hence David: “You drew me out of the lake of misery and the mud of dregs.” It signifies desire for earthly things [Col. 0844B]; hence Peter: “Like a sow in the wallowing of mud.” It signifies Judaea; hence in Job: “Mud shall be restored as a seal, and shall stand as a garment.” The Lord found the Israelite people like mud when he found them devoted to idolatry; and when he led them to the promised land with so many miracles, he made them, as it were, a seal of mystery. It signifies the multiplicity of earthly things; hence the prophet: “Woe to him who multiplies what is not his, and heaps thick mud against himself!” For one burdens himself with thick mud who, through avarice, multiplies earthly things. It signifies a mind illumined by the Holy Spirit; hence: “Remember, O Lord, that you have made me like mud.” For our inner man is like mud, because the grace of the Holy Spirit is poured into the earthly mind so that it may be raised to understanding of its Creator. It signifies teaching [Col. 0844C] that savors of foulness; hence the Prophet: “You made a way in the sea for your horses, in the mud of many waters,” as though he said: You opened a path for preachers amid teaching that has a foul savor. It also signifies the enticement of carnal desire; hence David: “Rescue me from the mud.” To cling to mud is to be defiled by filthy desires.

Light (*lux*), properly, is Christ; hence: “I am the light of the world.” It signifies Gentiles converted to the faith; hence the Apostle: “Once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.” It signifies holy preachers, such as the apostles; hence in the Gospel: “You are the light of this world.” It signifies the luminous cloud; hence in Genesis: “Let there be light, and there was light,” that is, a luminous cloud which performed the office of the sun. It signifies the divine nature; hence in the Apocalypse [Col. 0844D] it is said of God: “Who dwells in inaccessible light.” It signifies eternal life; hence: “May eternal light shine upon them.” It signifies a good angel; hence in Genesis: “He divided light from darkness,” that is, good angels from evil ones. It signifies the time for acting; hence in the Gospel: “Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you.” It signifies faith and grace; hence Isaiah: “Upon those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death, light has arisen.” It signifies knowledge or happiness; hence Solomon: “The light of the righteous shall always be; the light of the wicked shall be extinguished,” that is, knowledge or happiness. It signifies manifestation; hence in John: “He who hates me hates the light of the Lamb.” It signifies brightness of the air; hence in the Canticle: “Bless the Lord, light and darkness.” It signifies the glory or prosperity of the present life; hence: “Shall not the light of the wicked be extinguished?” For the prosperity of fleeting life ends more swiftly with life itself [Col. 0845A]. It signifies knowledge of the law in the Gospel: “Their light shall be taken away from the wicked,” because the Jews refused to believe the truth and lost knowledge of the law. It signifies joy; hence Job: “Light shall be darkened in his tent,” because in the corrupt conscience which he inhabits badly, the joy he has in earthly things fails [Col. 0846A]. It signifies righteousness; hence: “Tell me, if you know all things, in what way light dwells,” that is, in whom it dwells.

M

[Col. 0845]

[Col. 0845A] A wall (*maceria*), properly. It signifies the spiritual body of Christ, that is, the Church, because, just as a wall consists of diverse stones, so the Church consists of saints. Hence it is said: “In the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the wall.” The rock is Christ [Col. 0845B]; the clefts are the wounds impressed upon Christ by the nails; the hollow is the greater wound by which his side was pierced. Therefore it is called the hollow of the wall, that is, of the Church, because it belonged to her through compassion and redounded to her benefit. It signifies the afterbirth, that is, the membrane in which a child is enclosed in its mother’s womb. It is called *secundina* because it is born second, after the child; it is called *maceria* because in some manner the child is protected by it, lest anything harm it. Hence the midwife said to Perez, because he was the first born of Tamar: “Was the wall divided on your account?” that is, was the afterbirth divided so that you might be born before Emron, who had first put forth his hand and whose arm the midwife had bound with a thread to preserve the indication of who was to be born first [Col. 0845C]? It signifies Christ, who consists of diverse members as a wall of diverse stones; hence in the Psalm: “How long do you rush upon a man? Do all of you kill,” supply, “pressing upon him, as upon a leaning wall and a tottering fence?”—wishing to destroy Christ as if he were a leaning wall and a fallen fence, as though you could erase his name from the earth, though he says: “God is my protector; I shall no longer be moved.” It signifies the difficulty of perfection; hence the Lord says through the prophet Hosea: “Behold, I shall hedge your way with thorns, and shall hedge it with a wall.” The ways of the elect are hedged with thorns when they encounter the pricks of idols; and their paths are obstructed as though by an interposed wall, whose difficulty of attaining perfection indeed opposes them. It signifies the protection of discipline; hence [Col. 0845D] in the Psalm: “Why have you destroyed its wall?” And Solomon: “I passed by the field of the slothful man and by the vineyard of the foolish man; and behold, nettles had covered it all, and the stone wall had been destroyed.” To pass by the field of the slothful man and the vineyard of the foolish man is to examine the life of anyone who is negligent. Nettles or thorns fill it because in the negligent person’s heart itchings after earthly desires and the pricking of vices spring up; and the stone wall had been destroyed, that is, the discipline of the Fathers had been dissolved from his heart. It signifies the obstacle between Jews and Gentiles before Christ’s coming, because Gentiles could not approach Jews because of idolatry, nor Jews Gentiles because of the Mosaic law. Hence it is read that the wall which stood between Jews and Gentiles was removed by Christ’s coming.

[Col. 0846A] To slaughter (*mactare*), properly. It denotes destroying sins in a person; hence Peter was told: “Slaughter and eat,” as though he said: Destroy vices in human beings, and thus incorporate them into the Church.

A blemish (*macula*), properly, is an injury to the body; hence it is read in [Col. 0846B] Leviticus that a lamb was offered without blemish—not, I say, in its fleece, but in its body—that is, one having no bodily injury: neither one-eyed, nor blind, nor lame, nor with a broken foot. It signifies a grave fault; hence in the Book of Wisdom: “Blessed is the man found without blemish.” It signifies sin; hence Christ is said to be without blemish, that is, free from sin.

To magnify (*magnificare*) means to proclaim great; hence David: “Magnify the Lord with me.” It denotes to make great; hence Wisdom: “He magnified him in his praise.”

Magnificence (*magnificentia*), properly, is power; hence David: “They shall declare your magnificence.” It signifies glory or renown; hence in the Psalm: “For your magnificence is exalted above the heavens” [Col. 0846C]. It signifies the Son of God, of whom the foregoing authority is also commonly expounded: for the magnificence of God the Father—that is, the Son magnifying the Father—has been exalted above the heavens.

Greatness (*magnitudo*), properly, is divine majesty; hence: “There is no end of his greatness.” It signifies the abundance of divine mercy; hence in the Psalm: “And they shall declare your greatness.” It signifies the dignity of one whom a multitude obeys; hence Statius:

> Great in majesty.

Great (*magnus*), properly, means immeasurable; hence David: “Great is the Lord and exceedingly praiseworthy.” It signifies insuperable; in the same place: “And great is his power.” It signifies firm or fervent; hence in the Gospel: “Woman, great is your faith.” It signifies wonderful; hence David: “Great are the works of the Lord” [Col. 0846D]. It signifies severe; hence in the Apocalypse: “These are they who came out of great tribulation.” It signifies abundant; hence in the Gospel: “A certain man made a great supper”; and elsewhere: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy.” It signifies numerous; hence in the Apocalypse: “I saw a great multitude,” that is, a numerous one. It signifies devotion of mind, either signifying a great matter or proceeding from one; hence it is read in Daniel that Susanna cried out with a great voice—not with respect to loudness of sound, but with respect to the devotion of her mind. It signifies intense; hence in the Gospel: “They rejoiced with exceedingly great joy,” that is, intense joy. It signifies deep; hence David: “This great sea.” It signifies hidden or useful; hence Isaiah: “Angel of great counsel.” It also signifies very solemn; hence in the Gospel: “For that Sabbath day was a great day.” It signifies [Col. 0847A] impassable or uncrossable; hence in the Gospel: “A great chasm has been fixed.” It signifies broad or spacious; thus a house is called great, that is, broad or spacious.

A magus, properly, is a person skilled in magic, such as Pharaoh’s magicians. A wise person is also called a magus; hence in the Gospel: “When Jesus was born, etc., behold, magi came.” They are called magi in this sense not because of magical art, but because of their greater knowledge.

Majesty, properly. It also signifies divine power; hence in the Psalm: “The voice of the Lord is upon many waters; the God of majesty has thundered”; and: “He who searches out majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory.”

Greater (*major*), properly. It signifies greater in merit; hence in the [Col. 0847B] Gospel: “Among those born of women none has arisen greater than John the Baptist,” that is, greater in the certainty or dignity of merit. Hence the Gospel continues: “But he who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he,” because the least of the angels who was then in the homeland was greater than John in certainty. It signifies greater in advantage; hence the virginal state is called greater than the married state, that is, more advantageous, because God is served more readily in virginity than in marriage. It signifies greater in duration; hence the Apostle: “Faith, hope, charity; but the greatest of these is charity,” that is, the more enduring. It signifies greater by sign; hence in the Gospel: “No one has greater charity.” It signifies greater in works; thus the office of a prelate is called greater than that of the contemplative, because it is more fruitful with respect to the multitude of works. It also signifies greater in origin [Col. 0847C]; hence the sin of pride is called greater than other sins because it is the origin of every sin. Hence David: “And I shall be cleansed from the greatest offense.” It signifies greater in harm; hence Adam’s sin is called greater, that is, more harmful. It signifies greater in commonness; hence the sin of lust is called greater because it is more common. It signifies greater in contempt; hence Judas’s sin is called greater than Adam’s sin because Judas showed more contempt than Adam. It signifies greater in habit; hence the sin of habit is called greater than the sin of a single act.

To curse (*maledicere*), properly. It denotes exercising vengeance; hence the Lord says to Abraham: “I shall curse those who curse you.” It denotes reproving something; hence the Lord says through the prophet: “I shall curse your blessings” [Col. 0847D]. It denotes wishing for the end of a thing; hence Job is said to have cursed the day of his birth, that is, to have wished for the end of the mutability into which he was born. It denotes foretelling evil; hence it is read that Noah cursed his son Ham, that is, foretold evils for his descendants. It denotes speaking evil of someone; hence: “Those who curse shall not possess the kingdom of God.”

A *malleolus* is a little hammer. It also signifies a bronze implement that supplies fuel to a fire; hence the prophet says that the king’s ministers kindled the furnace with *malleoli*. Others say that it is another kind of fire-kindling material.

A hammer (*malleus*), properly, signifies the devil; hence the Psalmist: “The hammer of the whole earth has been broken.” It signifies temptation; hence it is said that now the stones—that is, the saints—are between hammer and anvil [Col. 0848A], that is, between temptations and the tribulations of this world.

Evil (*malum*) signifies sin; in Amos: “There is no evil in the city which God does not do,” that is, does not permit to be done. It signifies one subject to wickedness; hence David: “From the evil man.” It signifies punishment; hence Isaiah: “Making darkness and creating evil.” It signifies weakness; hence: “Let your speech be: Yes, yes; no, no; what is beyond this is from evil,” that is, from the weakness compelling one to swear.

An apple tree (*malus*). It also signifies the mast set upright in a ship, to which the sail is attached. It signifies Christ; hence in the Song: “As the apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons.” It signifies Christ’s cross; hence: “Under the apple tree I raised you up.” Christ speaks [Col. 0848B] to the Church, as though saying: “Through my cross I raised you to faith.” It signifies a good work; hence in the Church’s Song: “Support me with flowers and surround me with apples,” that is, with good works.

A breast (*mamma*), properly, signifies spiritual teaching; hence in the Church’s Song: “How beautiful are your breasts,” that is, your spiritual teaching. It signifies a doctor of the Church, to which meaning the preceding authority may be referred. It signifies the doctrine of heretics; hence in Lamentations: “The lamiae bared their breasts and nursed their young,” that is, heretics made their doctrines manifest and deceived the simple.

The mandrake (*mandragora*), properly, is a medicinal and fragrant herb that bears fruits of its own kind. Their use, as many say, removes barrenness; but Augustine says that he investigated their effect carefully and did not find this property in them. It signifies a saint who, while bestowing examples of good works everywhere through holy renown, scatters, as it were, fragrance so that the sick may be healed; hence in the Song: “The mandrakes gave forth their fragrance” [Col. 0848C].

To eat (*manducare*), properly. It denotes being incorporated into ecclesiastical unity; hence John: “If anyone shall eat of this bread, etc.”; and elsewhere: “Unless anyone shall eat the flesh.” Augustine says that the eater does not eat: that is, someone who receives Christ’s body sacramentally does not receive it spiritually, because he is not of the unity of the Church. It denotes enjoyment; hence David: “Because you shall eat the labors of your hands, you are blessed,” that is, you shall enjoy eternal life [Col. 0848D] on account of your good works. It denotes being refreshed; hence David: “Rise up after you have sat down, you who eat the bread of sorrow,” that is, you for whom penitence is spiritual refreshment.

Morning (*mane*), properly, signifies prosperity; hence Isaiah: “Morning will come and night has departed,” that is, prosperity approaches and adversity will recede. It signifies the beginning of the time of grace; hence in the Psalm: “Weeping shall remain at evening, and joy in the morning.” It signifies the splendor of Lucifer’s wisdom, by which he surpassed the other angels; hence, according to another exposition, this may be understood: “How have you fallen, Lucifer, you who rose in the morning?” It signifies the beginning of the day; hence in the Gospel: “And very early in the morning, etc.” It signifies the beginning of life; hence in the Psalm: “In the morning, like grass.” It signifies the day; hence Job: [Col. 0849A] “Behold, now I shall sleep in the dust; and if you seek me in the morning, I shall not remain.” The day of judgment is called morning because human deeds will then be revealed. Its sense, therefore, is: Already in the present I suffer the death of the flesh, and yet I still dread the weightier sentence of your judgment at the coming judgment. It signifies the beginning of a thing; hence Isaiah: “How have you fallen, Lucifer, you who rose in the morning?” that is, in the beginning. It signifies grace; hence in the Psalm: “For to you, O Lord, I shall pray, and in the morning you will hear my voice.” It signifies the beginning of eternal blessedness; hence in the Psalm: “In the morning I shall stand.” It signifies the beginning of spiritual understanding; hence in the Song: “Let us rise early for the vineyards,” that is, rising from letter to spirit, from the threshold toward the mystical sense [Latin *ab ostio* is syntactically uncertain]. Let us approach the sacred Scriptures. In them the leaves of history are green, the flowers of allegory are fragrant, and the fruit of tropology satisfies; and this is morning, that is, the beginning of spiritual understanding [Col. 0849B]. It signifies the beginning of time; hence in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like . . . [a householder] who went out early in the morning.” The householder is Christ, the laborers are the faithful, and the vineyard is holy Church. He hired laborers for his vineyard at the third, sixth, ninth, and eleventh hour, because from the beginning of this world until its end he does not cease to gather preachers for instructing the faithful people. For the morning of the world was from Adam to Noah; the third hour, from Noah to Abraham; the sixth, from Abraham to Moses; the ninth, from Moses to the Lord’s coming; and the eleventh, from his coming to the end of the world. We may also distinguish these various hours in every individual by the stages of life [Col. 0849C]. Morning, indeed, is our childhood; the third hour may be understood as adolescence, because then the sun rises high as the heat of life increases. The sixth is youth, in which the sun is fixed, as it were, at its center, because the fullness of strength is established in it. The ninth signifies old age, in which the sun declines, as it were, from on high, because that age fails from the heat of youth. The eleventh hour is the age called decrepit or very old. Since one person is led to a good life in childhood, another in adolescence, another in youth, another in old age, and another in decrepit age, laborers are called into the vineyard, as it were, at different hours.

To remain (*manere*), properly. It denotes cleaving or bearing fruit; hence John: “If you remain in me,” that is, if you cleave to me; “and my words remain in you,” that is, bear fruit in you [Col. 0849D]. It denotes dwelling by grace; hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “He who remains in me and I in him.”

A sleeve (*manica*), properly, signifies divine judgment; hence in the Psalm: “And their nobles in iron sleeves,” because sleeves bind. They signify judgment, as in: “What God has joined, let no man separate.” It signifies eternal damnation, in the same authority.

Manna, properly, is the food given to the children of Israel in the wilderness. It is said that manna descended, and those who wondered at it said: “*Manhu?*”—that is, “What is this?” It signifies Sacred Scripture. It signifies Christ’s body; hence in the Apocalypse: “To the conqueror I shall give hidden manna.”

[Col. 0850A] A dwelling-place (*mansio*), properly, is one’s present state of being; hence the Apostle: “We do not have here a lasting dwelling-place.” It signifies a state of being in which God is present in someone by grace; hence in the Gospel: “We shall come to him and make our dwelling with him.” It signifies the state of reward; hence in John: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling-places.”

A hand (*manus*), properly. It signifies divine vengeance; hence the prophet: “And still your hand is stretched out”; and elsewhere: “For you consider labor and sorrow, that you may deliver them into your hands,” that is, into divine vengeance. It signifies divine power; hence the Psalmist: “Your hands, O Lord, have made me”; “Arise, O Lord God; let your hand be exalted”; and elsewhere: “Into your hands, O Lord, I commend my spirit.” It signifies the Son of God; hence [Col. 0850B] David: “Send forth your hand from on high.” He is called the Father’s hand because the Father acts through him. It signifies God’s generosity; hence David: “You open your hand.” It signifies an army; hence in the Acts of the Apostles: “King Herod sent hands.” It signifies the presence or readiness of a thing; hence it is read in the Book of Kings that David asked Abimelech for provisions, if he had them “at hand,” that is, present or readily available. It signifies a covering shadow; hence the Lord says: “I shall put my hand before my face,” that is, the shadowing of a cloud before the splendor in which I shall appear. It also signifies one who rules and sustains another; hence in the Gospel: “If your hand or foot causes you to stumble, etc.” That is: if someone closely attached to you wishes to cause you to stumble in faith, withdraw from him bodily rather than let him harm you spiritually [Col. 0850C].
