It signifies action; hence Job: “I put my hand over my mouth.” Action is signified by the hand, speech by the mouth; therefore to put one’s hand over one’s mouth is to cover the faults of evil speech through the virtue of good work. It signifies strength; hence Job: “Even now my speech is in bitterness, and the hand of my wound is heavier than my groaning,” as though he said: My friends, who ought to have reduced my grief, have instead increased it by their misguided intention of consolation. It signifies divine propitiation or mercy; hence David: “For there also your hand shall lead me.” It signifies the likeness of a hand; hence in Daniel it is read that King Belshazzar saw a hand writing on the wall, that is, the likeness of a hand. It also signifies the faithful who, although not capable in preaching, are nevertheless strong in works and in the generous giving of alms; hence in the Song: “His hands are rounded.”

The sea (*mare*), properly, is a collection of waters; for in Hebrew idiom every collection of waters is called a sea. Hence in Genesis: “The gatherings which are called seas.” It signifies the bronze basin in which the priests washed themselves; hence it is read that Solomon made a bronze sea, that is, a washbasin made of bronze. It signifies Sacred Scripture; hence in the Apocalypse: “And the second poured out his bowl upon the sea.” By this Sacred Scripture is figured, which was turned into blood for the Jews, that is, into a carnal understanding. It signifies the present age; hence David: “This sea, great and spacious.” The sea elegantly signifies the present age [Col. 0851A], for the sea is salty, restless, swollen, and foul-smelling; so the present age is salty through bitterness, restless through curiosity, swollen through pride, and foul-smelling through lust. The little ship is the Church. For as a ship reaches its desired land without sinking, so, if we remain in the faith of the Church, we safely attain original simplicity. But when the contrary wind blows, the sea is disturbed and the ship is covered by waves; so, at the prompting of the malignant spirit, the present age is shaken and agitated on every side, and a severe, persistent, and turbulent temptation or persecution is stirred up against holy Church. It signifies our heart; hence in Job: “Who shut up the sea with doors, when it burst forth as though proceeding from the womb?” By the sea we understand our heart, troubled by rage, bitter with quarrels, swollen with the exaltation of pride, and darkened by the deceit of malice [Col. 0851B]. It also signifies the active life, because, just as there is manifold tumult in the sea, so in the active life there is manifold noise of actions. Hence David: “Those who go down into the sea in ships,” that is, from the contemplative life to the active. It signifies the Gentile people; hence Isaiah: “Be ashamed, Sidon, says the sea.” That is, Gentile-ness, converted to the faith, taunting Judaea figured by Sidon, says: “You who have turned away from faith, be ashamed before me, who have been converted to faith; you should rather have been converted, because the oracles of God were entrusted to you.” Judaea is elegantly figured by Sidon, for Sidon is interpreted “hunting,” and Judaea hunts earthly things with all the intention of its mind. But the sea signifies Gentile-ness, which was bitter through the bitterness of idolatry; for the sea is so called from bitterness [Col. 0851C]. It signifies hell; hence Job: “Have you entered the depths of the sea?” It signifies baptism; hence in the Apocalypse: “And I saw something like a glassy sea.” It is called glassy because of the purity of faith which is manifested in baptism. Here the sea signifies baptism, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “Our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized in the cloud and in the sea.” Hence the Psalmist: “The wondrous swellings of the sea.”

Marble (*marmor*), properly, signifies firmness; hence in the Song: “His legs are marble columns, etc.” The bridegroom’s legs are preachers of Christ’s name, such as holy preachers who bear Christ through the world and proclaim him to kings and princes; they are strong and upright, and resist the vices and desires of this life [Col. 0851D].

Marsupium, properly, a possession; hence in the book of Wisdom: “Let there be one purse for all of us.”

Massa, properly, a lump or mass; hence the Apostle says that from the same mass the potter makes vessels for honor and vessels for dishonor. It signifies the Synagogue; hence the same Apostle says: “If the first offering is holy, so also is the mass,” that is, if the first Jewish believers are holy, it may come about that the rest are sanctified. It also signifies the totality of works; hence in the Gospel: “A little leaven corrupts the whole mass.”

Mater, properly, Eve, from whom we descend; hence David: “My father and my mother have forsaken me” [Col. 0852A], that is, Adam and Eve, by their sin, exposed me to punishment and guilt. It signifies concupiscence; thus the aforementioned authority may be expounded: “My father,” namely the devil, “and my mother,” namely concupiscence, “have forsaken me.” The sense is: I have forsaken the devil and evil concupiscence. It signifies corruption; hence Job: “I said to rottenness: You are my father and my mother.” It signifies grace through blessing; hence: “May mother grace bring forth into a new childhood.” It signifies the soul in which Christ is born through grace; hence in the Gospel: “Whoever does the will … is my mother.” It signifies the Church militant; hence in the Song of Love: “Go forth, daughters of Zion, and see King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him.” Here the diadem signifies the assembly of saints, with which the Church [Col. 0852B] crowns Christ as with a diadem; hence in the Psalm: “You have placed a crown upon his head.” It also signifies the triumphant Church; hence in the Song: “I held him and will not let him go until I bring him into my mother’s house,” that is, into the empyrean heaven, in which the triumphant Church reigns and is called the mother of the Church militant. It signifies the Synagogue, which instructed the Church from the Gentiles in faith by example and teaching; hence in the Song: “The sons of my mother fought against me,” that is, the Synagogue—namely Judaea, which is said to have been the mother of the Church from the Gentiles, because the first believers from Judaea, such as the Apostles, converted the Gentiles to faith. It signifies the earth; hence Adam is called son of the earth; by analogy, the earth is called Adam’s mother.

Maxilla, properly, the jaw. It also signifies a spiritual [Col. 0852C] or temporal good; hence in the Gospel: “If someone strikes you on the right cheek,” etc., that is, if someone wishes to injure you in spiritual things, you should rather allow yourself to be harmed in temporal things than in spiritual ones. It signifies the devil’s power; hence it is read in Job that the serpent’s jaw was pierced, that is, that the devil’s power was weakened by Christ’s coming. It is aptly called a jaw because, just as food passes through the jaw in order to be incorporated, so the devil incorporates the wicked into himself by his power. Hence a certain poet in rhythm says [Note: [Col. 0851] Adam of St Victor, following Book V, *On the Resurrection of the Lord*, *Patrologia*, vol. CXCVI]:

> He pierces the serpent in the jaw;  
> Christ is hook and bracelet.  
> Into the den of the basilisk  
> the weaned child puts his hand,  
> and thus, driven out, flees  
> the ancient lodger of the world.

Christ is called hook and bracelet: hook because of the humanity he assumed, bracelet because of the power of his divinity. The devil sought this hook when he swallowed the little worm of flesh upon the cross; but he was caught by the hook of divinity, which lay hidden beneath the flesh as beneath a little red worm. The bracelet—that is, the power of divinity—pierced Leviathan’s jaw when it diminished the devil’s power, shattered hell, drew the elect out through the opening, and restored Christ’s mortified flesh on the third day. Christ’s soul alone, without divinity, could by no means have done this, since [Col. 0853A] Christ’s soul was a creature and not a creator. It signifies a prelate, because through him the spiritual food of sacred Scripture is ground and conveyed into the stomach of the mind. For through prelates holy mother Church crushes the wicked away from their vices and, as though swallowing them, converts them into her own members; hence it is read in Jeremiah: “She wept bitterly in the night, and her tears are upon her cheeks.” For prelates sympathize with the weak with the Apostle, saying: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” It also signifies provisions, because food is ground by the jaws; hence David: “Constrain their jaws with hook and bridle,” that is, withdraw their provisions from them.

Maximum, properly, something called greatest because it concerns the greatest thing; thus the command concerning love of God is called greatest. For Christ, speaking in the Gospel about this [Col. 0853B] command, “You shall love the Lord,” etc., says: “This is the greatest and first commandment,” that is, it concerns the greatest thing—God or his love. It signifies greatest in origin; hence in the Psalm: “And I shall be cleansed from the greatest sin,” that is, pride, which is the origin of all evils. It signifies greatest in effect; hence in the blessing of water it is said: “The greatest sacraments also are performed by the substance of water.” Baptism is called the greatest sacrament in effect because it removes guilt and punishment and confers grace.

Medicus, properly, a physician. It signifies Christ; hence in the Gospel: “Those who are well have no need of a physician.” It signifies one who says one thing and does another; hence in the Gospel: “Physician, heal yourself.” It also signifies a teacher or preacher; hence in the Psalm: “Will physicians raise up and confess [Col. 0853C] you?”

Medius, properly, a mediator; hence, concerning Christ, in the Gospel: “In your midst stands one whom you do not know,” that is, Christ, the mediator between you and God. He is aptly called “in the midst,” because, as what is in the middle shares in the two extremes, so a mediator must have some relation to those whom he wishes to restore to concord. It also signifies present, because what is in the middle is more apparent than the extremes, since it presents itself to the extremes. Thus it may be explained: “In your midst,” that is, present among you. It signifies common; for what is in the middle stands in common relation to the extremes, and “middle” is taken for “common,” as the center in relation to the circumference. Thus the saying may be explained: “In your midst,” that is, common with you, having a common nature with you. It signifies lowly, because, just as “middle” means common, it also means cheap, since everything common is cheap; and the more common it is, the cheaper, just as everything rare is precious, and the rarer it is, the more precious. Thus the Jews called common things lowly and unclean. The sense, therefore, is: “In your midst stands,” that is, the one whom you regard as lowly. It signifies a middle thing opposed to another middle; hence in the Gospel: “Jesus was walking through the midst of the borders of Decapolis,” that is, by a road opposite the central districts of that region which contained ten cities; for *dekas* means ten, and *polis*, city. It signifies concord; hence Habakkuk: “You shall be known in the midst of two living creatures,” that is, in the concord of two testimonies; and in the Psalm: “If you sleep among the midst of the lots.” It also signifies what is straight; hence in the Law the Lord commanded that we walk in the middle way, turning neither to the right nor to the left.

Mel, properly, something pleasant; hence David: “More desirable than gold,” etc., “than honey and the honeycomb,” that is, than every delight. It signifies provisions; hence in Exodus the Lord says: “I shall give you a land flowing with milk and honey”; and in Isaiah: “He shall eat butter and honey,” as has been explained above. It signifies carnal pleasure, to which sense may be referred the statement in Isaiah: “He eats butter and honey,” that is, he will destroy in himself first movements and carnal pleasures. It signifies good action, according to which meaning [Col. 0854B] you should expound the aforementioned authority, so that the sense is: “He will reject evil and choose good.” It signifies spiritual teaching, which is sweeter; hence in the Song: “Honey and milk are under your tongue,” because the teachers of the Church give lesser teaching, signified by milk, to lesser persons, and spiritual teaching to greater persons. It signifies divinity; thus “honey and milk” may be expounded: honey, the divine nature; milk, the human. Honey comes from the dew of heaven, because the divine nature is above all things; milk is expressed below, because humanity was assumed below. Therefore, that honey and milk are beneath the Church’s tongue means nothing other than that the Church thinks rightly about Christ’s divinity and humanity. It signifies the New Testament. Just as by the honeycomb, which is nothing other than honey in wax, we understand the Old Testament, [Col. 0854C] in which truth was in shadow and the kernel in its shell, so by honey we understand the New Testament. Hence in the Song: “I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey,” that is, I have poured into the minds of my faithful the understanding of the Old and New Testaments. Or honey signifies Christ’s soul, which was separated from his flesh by death and incorporated into it again by resurrection. Therefore Christ ate the honeycomb with honey when, in the resurrection, he united both body to soul and soul to body; for the soul, previously like honey, became a honeycomb when it returned to the body. The body’s animation, the soul’s incorporation, and the glorification of both took place. It signifies the sweetness of sacred Scripture; hence in Revelation: “I received the book from the angel’s hand [Col. 0854D] and devoured it; and it was sweet as honey in my mouth.” It signifies wisdom; hence it is said: “My son, have you found honey? Take it soberly, lest perhaps, if you take too much, you vomit it out.” Hence Paul: “Do not be wise beyond what it is fitting to be wise.” The flatteries of heretics are called honey; hence Solomon: “The lips of a harlot drip honey.” It signifies the sweetness of Christ’s preaching; hence Deuteronomy: “They sucked honey from the rock, and oil from the hardest stone.” The rock signifies Christ, from whom, before his passion, his disciples sucked honey—that is, the sweetness of his preaching or the delight of his miracles. From him, after the resurrection, when he had become the hardest stone, that is, immortal, they sucked oil—that is, they received the grace of the Holy Spirit when the Holy Spirit was sent upon the disciples.

[Col. 0855A] Melior, properly, better. It signifies greater in body; hence it is read of Saul in Samuel that there was none better than he in the land, that is, none larger in body. This is not to be understood of merit, since many better men were in the land, that is, men of greater merit, such as Samuel and the sons of the prophets. It signifies more delightful; hence in the Song: “Your breasts are better than wine,” that is, evangelical teaching is more delightful than Mosaic teaching, whose austerity is signified by wine. It signifies more fruitful; hence Ecclesiastes: “A living dog is better than a dead lion,” because one who is on the way can produce a greater fruit of good work than one who is in the homeland. Hence the Apostle: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ; but to remain in the flesh is much better for the brethren.” It signifies safer or more glorious; hence the Psalmist: “One day in your courts is better.” It signifies more useful; hence David: “A little is better for the just man.” It signifies some good; hence the Apostle: “It is better to marry than to burn,” as though saying: It is good to marry, but not to burn. It signifies a lesser evil; hence the Lord in the Gospel: “It would have been better for him had he not been born,” that is, it would have been a lesser evil for him not to have been born.

Memor, properly, one who fulfills a promise; hence David: “Remember your word to your servant.” It signifies one judging or condemning; hence the Psalmist: “Nor will I remember their names,” that is, I will not judge them on the day of judgment, saying: “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire.” It signifies one conferring grace; hence David: “I shall remember Rahab and Babylon,” that is, I shall confer grace upon the sinners signified by Rahab and Babylon.

[Col. 0855C] Memoria, properly, memory. It signifies eternal life; hence in the Psalm: “The righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance.” It signifies fame or glory; hence David: “Their memory has perished with a sound.” It signifies a memorial punishment; hence David: “May the iniquity of his fathers return into remembrance,” that is, may he be punished by a memorial punishment.

Mendacium is a false signification of speech with the intention of deceiving; hence in the Psalm: “You will destroy all who speak falsehood.” It signifies an idol, which is called falsehood because it is not what it pretends to be; hence David: “Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” It signifies a temporal good that does not render what it promises, since it promises blessedness and does not deliver it; hence, according to another exposition: “Why do you love vanity?” It also signifies [Col. 0855D] sin; hence in Revelation: “Nothing defiled, and nothing doing abomination and falsehood, shall enter into it.”

Mendax signifies false; hence in the Gospel Christ says of the devil that he is a liar and the father of falsehood. It signifies deceitful; hence in the Psalm it is said that they are false in the balances, that is, deceitful in their denials. It signifies changeable; hence in the Gospel: “God alone is true; every man is a liar.”

Mens, the soul; hence the Apostle: “With my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin.” It also signifies reason; hence the Apostle: “I perceive another law in my members, resisting the law of my mind.” It signifies intention, [Col. 0856A] whence someone is said to lie, that is, to go against his mind. It signifies memory; hence in Revelation: “Therefore keep in mind how you received.” It signifies the wisdom of God, or the Son; hence Boethius:

> The Most Beautiful himself, bearing  
> the beautiful world in his mind.

Mensa, properly, a table. It signifies sacred Scripture, as understood perversely by the Jews; hence David: “Let their table become a snare before them,” etc. It signifies the Eucharist; hence David: “You have prepared a table before me.” It signifies eternal life; hence in the Gospel: “That you may eat and drink at my table.” It signifies the eating of idolaters, that is, things sacrificed to idols; hence the Apostle: “You cannot partake of the table of Christ and the table of demons.”

[Col. 0856B] Mensis, properly, a month. It signifies a plurality of graces, just as a month is a plurality of days. Thus Job, calling the devil night—because he both darkens others by sins and is himself darkened—says that he is not counted among the days of the year or numbered among the months, because the devil is separated and alien both from the plurality of graces and from the whole. Thus months signify the varieties of Churches; the preceding authority may therefore be expounded: the devil will not be counted among the days of the year or numbered among the months, because he will always remain estranged from the fellowship of the saints. It also signifies the Church; for as the completeness of a month consists of different days, so the Church consists of different faithful persons. The Church is therefore fittingly represented by a month; hence the prophet: “Month [Col. 0856C] from month, and Sabbath from Sabbath,” that is, from the present Church militant the triumphant Church is composed. It signifies an angelic order; for the months may be understood as the angelic orders, among which one who will not return to the dignity of the angelic order shall not be numbered. It also signifies human activity; hence Job: “As a stag desires shade, and as a hired laborer awaits the end of his good work, so I too have had empty months.” When saints serve God, they are often constrained by lack of resources; for those who do not seek present things through their actions pass months empty of the world’s gains.

Mensura, properly, a measure. It also signifies merit; hence Luke: “With what measure you have measured.” It signifies eternal life; hence in the Gospel: “A good and pressed-down measure.” It signifies the limit of a thing; hence it is read that the Lord created all things in number, weight, and measure—that is, distinctly, in their proper natures, according to which they are borne upward or downward, and within their proper limits; every thing is bounded by its own ends and limits. It signifies capacity; hence it is read that gifts and virtues are distributed according to each person’s measure. It signifies the distinction of teaching; hence in the Gospel: “Who, do you suppose, is the faithful and prudent servant,” etc., who gives the measure of wheat, so that greater things may be set before greater persons and lesser things before lesser persons.

Mercenarius signifies a merchant or trader; hence in Deuteronomy: “You shall not withhold the laborer’s wages until morning.” It signifies a false prelate; hence in John: “The hireling [Col. 0857A] who is not the shepherd.” It signifies a servant of God; hence in the Gospel: “Make me as one of your hired servants.”

Merces, properly, a reward; hence it is read of Judas in the Acts of the Apostles: “He acquired a field with the reward of iniquity.” It signifies Christ’s passion; hence the prophet: “Behold, the Savior and his reward are with him,” that is, he will endure the passion through which he will purchase eternal blessedness for us. It signifies eternal life; hence in the Gospel: “Rejoice and exult, for your reward …” It signifies vainglory; hence the Lord says in the Gospel of hypocrites: “They have received their reward.” It signifies punishment; hence Peter: “And they shall perish, receiving their reward.”

Mereri, properly, to merit. It denotes to claim as due; hence Augustine: “Charity once possessed merits to be increased, so that, increased, it may merit [Col. 0857B] to be perfected.” It denotes being fitting; hence of the blessed Virgin Mary it is said that she merited to bear the Savior—not because her merits demanded this as due, but because by reason of her innocence she was fitting for it. It denotes needing; hence: “O unhappy fault of Eve, which merited to have such and so great a Redeemer,” that is, needed such and so great a Redeemer. For merit and need agree in this: both merit and need demand that something be done. Therefore *mereri* is sometimes used for “to need”; nevertheless, “merit” is the more fitting term.

Meretrix, properly, a female innkeeper; hence the spies turned aside to the house of Rahab the harlot, who was not truly a harlot. But because she displayed wares for sale, [Col. 0857C] she was called *meretrix* from *mereri*, “to earn.” It signifies the teaching of heretics; hence: “The lips of the harlot drip honey.” It signifies idolatry; hence in Revelation: “Come, and I shall show you the condemnation of the great harlot.” Here idolatry, or the assembly of idolaters, is called the harlot. It signifies Judaea, which prostituted itself with idols and is therefore called a harlot by the prophets; hence in Isaiah: “How has the faithful city become a harlot?”

Meridies, properly, noon. It signifies an everlasting thing; for as the sun at noon does not appear to move upward or downward, so an everlasting thing is not subject to corruption. Hence in the Psalm: “At evening, and in the morning, and at noon,” etc., that is, I shall praise at evening for things past, in the morning for things future, and at noon for eternal things. It signifies the contemplative life; thus [Col. 0857D] this clause of the Song may be expounded: “Tell me where you rest, where you feed at noon,” that is, in whose mind you feed through good action, and in whose mind you rest through contemplation. It signifies the fervor of charity; hence it is read that, after Adam’s sin, the Lord walked through paradise in the breeze after noon, that is, when the fervor of charity had already failed in Adam. For what does it mean that after human sin the Lord does not stand in paradise but walks, except that, when sin burst in, he showed that he had moved away from the human heart? What does “in the breeze after noon” mean, except that the more fervent light of truth had departed and the coldness of guilt bound the sinful soul? Therefore he rebuked Adam while walking, so that he might reveal their wickedness to blinded minds not only by words [Col. 0858A] but also by things: so that sinful man might hear through words what he had done; see through the walking, having lost the state of eternity, the instability of his mutability; recognize through the breeze, after the expulsion of charity’s fervor, his own numbness; and know through the setting of the sun that he was approaching darkness. It also signifies ascension, because at noon Christ ascended to heaven; in the morning he rose from the dead; in the evening he died. The sense, therefore, is: At evening I shall praise you for your passion, in the morning for your resurrection, and at noon for your ascension. It signifies the day of judgment, because then God’s wrath shall burn fiercely, and human thoughts and works shall be manifest; hence in the book of Wisdom: “At midday he shall burn up the earth; and who shall be able to endure before the sight of his burning?” It signifies the time of Christ’s passion; hence in the book of Wisdom: “Tell me where you feed, where you rest at noon,” that is, in whose mind you feed through faith; where you rest, that is, in whose soul you repose through charity; and this at noon, that is, at the time of the passion. The state of the passion is aptly represented by noon, for just as the sun burns more fiercely at noon, so at the time of the passion charity burns more intensely in the faithful person.

Messis, properly, harvest. It also signifies the end of the age; hence the Lord in the Gospel: “The harvest is indeed the consummation of the age.” It also signifies conversion to faith; hence Job: “Lift up your heads,” etc., “for the harvest,” that is, human hearts are ready to receive faith. It signifies one who is converted; hence: “The harvest indeed is great, [Col. 0858C] but the laborers are few,” that is, many can be harvested through preaching, but few are laborers in respect to carrying out preaching. It signifies eternal life; hence Job: “The hungry man shall eat the harvest,” that is, through fulfillment of the divine word he attains the blessedness of eternal life. The hungry person is one who hungers for the bread of the divine word, acts according to what he hears, and thereby obtains the fruit of blessedness. It signifies sacred Scripture; hence, according to another exposition: “The hungry man shall eat the harvest”: certainly the Gentile people, by understanding, performs the words of the Law over which the Jewish people labored without understanding. It signifies the gift of right understanding; the same authority may be expounded thus: “The hungry man,” that is, the foolish man, has a harvest when [Col. 0858D] he receives the gift of right understanding and is taught by the sayings of sacred Scripture; he speaks good things, yet in no way performs what he says.

Metere, properly, to reap. It denotes attaining; hence in the Apostle: “He who sows in blessings shall also reap from blessings,” that is, shall attain eternal life. It signifies receiving a reward or prize; hence: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in exultation.” It denotes gathering; hence in the Song: “I have gathered my myrrh.” It denotes completing; hence the Apostle: “One is he who sows, another he who reaps.” The prophets sowed; the Apostles reaped, that is, completed. It denotes exacting or extorting; hence in the Gospel: “I knew that you are a harsh [hard] man, reaping where you have not sown.”

[Col. 0859A] Metiri, properly, to measure. It denotes rewarding; hence: “With what measure you have measured.” It denotes taking heed or looking about oneself; hence: “It is fitting that each person measure himself.” It denotes marking out the world within fixed limits; hence it is said of God in Isaiah that he measured the earth with his fist.

Miles, properly, a soldier. It signifies an attendant or lictor appointed to the office of punishing people; hence it is read that the soldiers crucified Jesus. We should not believe that persons honored with the military belt crucified him, but rather servants not endowed with such military honor. Yet an ordinary soldier is customarily called a *miles gregarius*; hence it is said of Nebuchadnezzar that he had been an ordinary soldier in the palace of the king of the Assyrians. Some, however, say that an ordinary soldier is one who belongs to the household of some prince along with other soldiers. The laws also speak of a *miles caligatus*, a common foot-soldier. A saint is also called a soldier, serving under God in good works; hence in the hymn: “God of your soldiers.”

Militare, properly, to serve as a soldier. It denotes opposing; hence the Apostle says that vices wage war against the soul. Demons are said to serve: “Hosts serving God,” that is, serving him.

Militia, properly, human life; hence Job: “The life of man upon earth is warfare.” It signifies the army of demons; hence Isaiah: “I shall visit the host of heaven.” It signifies the assembly of stars; hence it is read that the Jews in Egypt worshiped the host of heaven. It signifies the army of angels who serve under God, that is, perform different mysteries under him.

[Col. 0859C] Millia means the same as “a thousand”; hence: “And you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, are by no means the least among the thousands of Judah,” that is, among the thousand cities of Judah. Sometimes it means the same as “infinite”; hence in the prophet: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him,” that is, countless thousands. Sometimes it denotes perfection; hence in Revelation: “From the tribe of Judah, twelve thousand sealed.”

Minimus, smallest in body or age; hence in Genesis Jacob says of Benjamin: “The youngest is held,” that is, in chains. It signifies least in time; hence Paul calls himself the least of the Apostles because he was called by the Lord after the others. It signifies one least in temporal rank; hence in the Gospel: “What you did to one of the least, you did to me.” It signifies least in estimation; hence in the Gospel: “Whoever causes one of these least little ones to stumble.” It signifies least in severity; hence Augustine says that [Col. 0859D] the punishment of those who have added no actual sin to original sin is the least. It signifies what is easiest to fulfill; hence the Lord again says: “Whoever breaks one of my least commandments.” The greatest commandment is called such because it is harder to fulfill; by analogy, the least is what can easily be fulfilled.

Minister, properly, a servant; hence the Lord in the Gospel: “Where I am, there also my servant shall be.” It signifies an author; hence the Apostle: “We know that Jesus was a minister of the circumcision.” It signifies one who is lower; hence in the Gospel: “Whoever wishes to become greater, let him be a servant,” that is, lesser.

Minor, properly, less worthy; hence in Genesis: “When Noah awoke from wine and learned what his son had done to him, he said: ‘He shall be a servant, lesser than his brothers.’” For Ham was not lesser in age but in dignity. It signifies someone [Col. 0860A] lesser in merit; hence in the Gospel: “He who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.”

Minuere, properly, denotes making lower; hence in the Psalm: “You have made him a little less.” It denotes diminishing fame or glory; hence in the Gospel: “I must decrease.” It denotes depriving; thus the aforementioned authority may be expounded: “I must decrease,” that is, be deprived of my head; “but he must increase,” that is, be lifted up upon the cross.

Minus is used comparatively; hence David: “You have made him a little less than the angels.” It is used exceptively; hence Paul: “Five times I received forty lashes less one,” that is, lacking one lash. It is used negatively; hence John: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places; if otherwise,” that is, if anything were lacking, that is, if they were not prepared, “I would have told you.”

[Col. 0860B] Mirari, properly, to wonder. It denotes praising; hence it is said that people wondered at Christ’s works. It denotes imitating; hence Lucan:

> The fierce *haemorrhois* (“blood-flow serpent”), to Tullus,  
> the high-souled young man and admirer of Cato,

that is, imitator.

Misericordia, properly, the divine nature; hence David: “My mercy and my refuge.” It signifies the effect of mercy; hence: “I shall sing forever of the mercies of the Lord.” It signifies the manifestation of mercy; hence James: “Judgment without mercy shall be given to him who has shown no mercy,” that is, God will not show the damned the manifestation of his mercy. For although they will not be punished as much as they deserved, nevertheless the effect of justice rather than mercy will appear in them. [Col. 0860C] It signifies the first coming; hence in the Psalm: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth,” because in the beginning, or at the first coming, God displayed his mercy, while in the future he will display justice.

Mitis is the same as gentle; hence in the Gospel: “Blessed are the meek.” It signifies merciful; hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Learn from me, because I am meek.” It signifies lenient; hence one punishment is said to be milder than another, and God is said to deal more mildly with some than with others, that is, more leniently.

Mittere, properly, to send. It denotes making visible or incarnating; [Col. 0860D] hence in the Gospel: “God sent his Son into the world.” It denotes infusing into the human mind; thus the Son is said to be sent by the Father in a temporal mission, that is, infused into the human mind through grace. It denotes inspiring; thus the Holy Spirit is said to be sent by the Father, that is, breathed into or inspired. It signifies infusing the Holy Spirit into the human mind; hence in the Apostle: “He sent the Holy Spirit into our hearts.” It denotes making; hence in the Psalm: “He sends forth his crystal,” that is, “[he made it].” It denotes withdrawing or permitting; hence in Job: “Put forth your hand,” that is, withdraw your protection, or permit me to touch you; hence in the Gospel: “If you are the Son of God, cast yourself down.”

Modicum, little in quantity; hence in the Psalm: “A little is better for the just man.” It signifies little in time; hence in the Gospel: [Col. 0861A] “A little while, and you shall not see me.” It signifies little in faith; hence in the Gospel: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?”

Modius, properly, a bushel-measure. It also signifies the Mosaic Law; hence in the Gospel: “No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel,” because Christ is the true lamp and does not preach legal observances. It signifies the boundary of one nation, that is, Christ did not put his lamp under a bushel because he did not confine his faith within the bounds of one nation. It signifies temporal advantage, which contains grain. The lamp is not to be put under a bushel because one ought not to preach for temporal advantage; or no one ought to hide the lamp beneath a bushel, that is, cease preaching out of fear of bodily punishment, so that the bushel represents the body which contains the soul.

[Col. 0861B] Modus, a manner; hence the Apostle: “In many and various ways.” It signifies moderation or measure, as we commonly say: “This man does not know how to keep measure in his deeds or words.” Hence the author says: “The remedy exceeded its measure.” It signifies affection, as we commonly say: “In every way we beseech you to do this,” that is, with every affection of mind. It signifies musical modulation, as when one says: “He tunes his lyre to different modes of singing”; hence in the book of Wisdom: “Seeking musical modes and recounting songs of the writings.” It signifies intention; hence in the Psalm: “In what manner do you say to my soul: ‘Flee to the mountain’?”—where *quo modo* is two words: “with what intention?”

Moechari. It also denotes knowing someone illicitly, so that adultery may mean every unlawful sexual union; hence: “You shall not commit adultery.” It denotes lusting; hence: “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.” It denotes withholding the true understanding of Scripture and seeking a false one; hence the Apostle: “You who teach that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery?” It denotes practicing idolatry; hence Judah is frequently said by the prophets to commit adultery.

Mola, properly, a millstone. It signifies any temporal punishment, however great; hence in the Gospel: “Whoever causes … to stumble,” etc., “a millstone shall be hung.” It signifies a molar tooth; hence David: “The Lord shall break the molar teeth of the lions.” Mystically, however, this signifies the persecution of tyrants or the evil suggestion of demons. [Col. 0861D] It signifies the married state, because this entails manifold care and labor; hence in the Gospel: “Two at the mill: one shall be taken and the other left,” because among married persons some shall be saved and some condemned. It signifies hope or fear, because a Christian ought to grind between hope and fear; hence in Deuteronomy: “You shall not take the other millstone as a pledge,” because hope without fear is presumption, and fear without hope is despair. Among authors it also commonly signifies fleas, etc.

Molle signifies delicate; hence a word of sacred Scripture is called “soft” through exposition when it had previously been hard through obscurity. Hence in the Psalm: “His words are softer than oil, and they are darts.”

Mollire, properly, to soften. It denotes delighting; hence in the Psalm: [Col. 0862A] “His words have become soft.” It denotes soothing; hence Solomon: “That you may be delivered from the strange woman, who softens her words,” that is, soothes with words. It denotes troubling; hence it is read that the Lord softened his heart.

Monile, properly, a necklace. It also signifies a preacher or teacher who admonishes others by deed or example; hence: “Your neck is like necklaces.” The teachers are called the neck of the Church, because just as food passes through the neck into the stomach, so preachers, expounding sacred Scripture, convey the food of sacred Scripture into the soul. It signifies virtue; hence in Revelation: “I saw the holy city Jerusalem,” etc., “adorned with its necklaces.”

### Mountain

A mountain, properly speaking. It signifies a heretic because of pride; hence David: “How do you say to my soul, ‘Flee to the mountain like a sparrow’?” [Col. 0862B] According to another exposition or translation, this is not said with regard to the reality of the matter, but with regard to the opinion of heretics; for heretics pretend to be lofty in virtues. It signifies Christ because of the eminence of his virtue: “In the last days the mountain shall be prepared on the summit of the mountains”; this is from Isaiah. It also signifies the devil because of the eminence of his pride; hence in the Gospel: “If anyone has so much faith,” etc., “and says to this mountain.” It signifies a saint; hence David: “The high mountains for the stags”; and elsewhere: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains.” It signifies a proud person; hence David: “Touch the mountains and they shall smoke,” that is, touch the proud by compunction, and they shall smoke through the pouring forth of tears, because smoke produces tears and weeping; [Col. 0862C] and elsewhere: “The foundations of the mountains.” It signifies loftiness of virtue; hence in the prophet: “Go up upon the mountain, you who bring good news to Zion.” It signifies Holy Scripture because of the eminence of its teaching; hence Habakkuk: “God shall come from the south, and the Holy One from Mount Paran,” that is, “shady” or “thick.” Holy Scripture is a shady or thick mountain because of the difficulty of understanding it. It signifies the Church; hence the Psalmist: “And he shall lead me to your holy mountain.” It signifies eternal life because of its security, stability, and dignity; hence David: “Who shall rest on your holy mountain?” It signifies the primitive Church drawn from the Jews, because it first received the rays of faith; hence the Psalmist: “But I have been appointed king by him over Zion,” [Col. 0862D] “his holy mountain.” It signifies the Old or New Testament; hence David: “Waters shall pass through the midst of the mountains,” because theological teaching ought to agree with both Testaments. It signifies the Jewish people; hence Isaiah says of the devil: “I shall sit on the mountain of the Testament, on the sides of the north.” For the evil spirit held the mountain of the Testament when, through unbelief, he subjected to himself the Jewish people that had received the law. It signifies a holy mountain; hence Job: “A falling mountain melts away,” when, even in the mind of a righteous person, the representation of some event is acted out, so that he is suddenly tempted and shaken and overthrown by an unforeseen occurrence. It also signifies an apostle; hence: “The mountains shall be moved into the heart of the sea,” which happened when the apostolic preachers, driven from Judaea, came to the Gentiles. [Col. 0863A] It signifies lofty contemplation; hence Job says of the wild ass: “It surveys the mountains of its pasture.” For the saints, signified by the wild ass, the more they cast themselves down outwardly by self-contempt, the more abundantly they are fed inwardly by the contemplation of revelations. It signifies one of the ancient Fathers; hence in the Psalms: “You enlighten wonderfully from the everlasting mountains.” The Lord enlightens us from the everlasting mountains because, through the life of the preceding Fathers, he illumines us with the ray of his brightness. It also signifies the swelling pride of worldly powers; hence the Psalmist: “The mountains melted like wax before the face of the Lord.” Many who formerly swelled with broad rigidity were, when God appeared in the flesh, melted by great fear into repentance. And again: “Mountains rise and plains descend.” For [Col. 0863B] often the proud persecutors of the Lord come against him, but return from him humble; for mountains rise through the swelling of power, but plains descend, having been made level through knowledge of guilt or misery.

### Monster

A monster is a thing outside the course of nature, such as a man with two bodies, or a two-headed or three-headed animal. It signifies a monstrous—that is, cruel—man; hence it is written of Moses in the Book of Wisdom that “he calmed monsters by his words,” that is, he humbled Pharaoh and his companions, who were like monsters through their cruelty. Or the molten calf is called a monster, having arisen monstrously and been crushed at Moses’ command. Or the serpents made from rods by the [Col. 0863C] magicians are called monsters; Moses’ serpent devoured them—the serpent into which the rod was changed by Moses’ word. Or the fiery serpents are called monsters, whose malice Moses calmed by commanding the children of Israel to look upon the bronze serpent. It signifies demonstrations; hence Aristotle, in Porphyry’s *Analytics*, says: “Genera and species rejoice; they are monsters to him” [reading uncertain]. It signifies a miracle; hence in the Book of Wisdom: “He performed monsters for them and consumed them in the flame of fire.” The miraculous chasm of the earth by which Dathan and Abiram were swallowed up is called a monster. Thus what was said may be explained: “He calmed monsters by his words,” because by his words he calmed the plagues with which the Lord struck Egypt.

### Sickness

Sickness: infirmity. It also signifies guilt; hence [Col. 0863D] one reads in the Apostle that the Mosaic law showed sickness, that is, guilt.

### To Bite

To bite, properly speaking: to speak maliciously against; hence the Apostle: “Lest, by biting one another, you be consumed.” It signifies to draw out; hence Christ is said to have bitten hell, that is, to have drawn some persons out of hell. It signifies to torment; hence Leviathan is said to have bitten the little worm and to have been caught by the hook. The little worm is Christ’s humanity; the hook, his divinity. The devil pursued Christ’s humanity to the point of death and was caught by the sting of divinity.

### To Die

To die, properly speaking. It also signifies to sin; hence: “The soul that sins shall die.” It signifies to repent; hence someone is said to die to sin. It signifies to be condemned; hence in the prophet: “He shall live a living life and shall not die,” that is, he shall not be condemned. [Col. 0864A] And in however many senses death is used, in so many senses is “to die” used.

### Death

Death is the end of life, by which someone is called dying; hence the Apostle: “Christ became obedient for us unto death.” It signifies the separation of soul and body, by which someone is called dead; hence the same Apostle: “Death has been swallowed up in victory.” It signifies fear of death. It signifies the destruction of death; hence the prophet: “O death, I shall be your death,” as though Christ said: “O fear of death, I shall be your destruction.” For the ancient Fathers who lived before Christ’s coming feared death more than later people did; but after Christ’s coming the faithful, strengthened more by Christ’s example and grace, feared death less. Hence we read of many that they ran willingly to martyrdom. [Col. 0864B] It signifies sin, because there is a sin unto death; hence in the Psalms: “For in death there is none who remembers you,” that is, no one remaining in mortal sin remembers God so as to obtain pardon; and elsewhere in the Book of Proverbs: “Death and life are in the hands of the tongue.” It also signifies eternal punishment; hence David: “Death shall feed upon them.” It signifies the necessity of dying; hence it is written: “In whatever hour you eat, you shall die by death,” that is, you shall be subject to the necessity of dying. It signifies covetousness; hence in the Psalms: “You who raise me from the gates of death.” It signifies the devil, who was the cause of death; hence: “From Adam until Christ death reigned,” that is, the devil, who before Christ’s coming held greater dominion over human beings than he can exercise now; see under the word “Natural.” [Col. 0864C]

### Bite

A bite, properly speaking. It signifies diminution or despoiling; hence the prophet: “O death, I shall be your death; I shall be your bite, O hell,” that is, I shall diminish your power and draw out my own. Diminution of power or the taking away of saints is elegantly called a bite; for one who bites an apple cuts off a part and does not swallow it wholly. Thus Christ diminished the power of hell and freed his own from the lower regions. It also signifies the devil’s deception; hence man is said to have perished by the bite of the ancient serpent.

### Mortal

Mortal: able to die. Hence Adam is said to have been mortal before sin—not because he could not avoid dying, but because he was able to die. It signifies one who must die; hence the Apostle: “Man was made mortal through Adam’s sin”; for the Apostle says: [Col. 0864D] “This mortal shall put on immortality.” It signifies corruptible; hence the Apostle: “And likewise our mortal bodies.” It also signifies a cause of death; hence sin is called mortal sin.

### Dead

Dead, properly speaking. It also signifies a sinner; hence in the Gospel: “Let the dead bury their dead.” It signifies one justified and dead to sin; hence the Apostle: “You have died to sin once for all.” It signifies one condemned; hence David: “The dead shall not praise you, O Lord.” It signifies one who has ceased to be what he was; hence in the Gospel: “Unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies,” that is, unless through decay it ceases to be. It also signifies one unable to merit; hence in Ecclesiastes: “A living dog is better than a dead lion”; this was said above. It signifies something vile and cast down; hence David says of Saul: “Why [Col. 0865A] do you pursue me, a dead dog and a single flea?” It signifies that which contains nothing living in itself or allows nothing to live; hence the Dead Sea is so called because it sustains nothing living in itself. It signifies something dried up; hence a tree is called dead, that is, dried up.

### Moved

“Moved,” a participle: someone who slips through venial fault; hence in the Psalms: “When I said, ‘My foot has been moved.’” It signifies one falling through mortal fault; hence David: “They were troubled and were moved.” It signifies someone humbling himself through repentance; hence the Psalmist: “The foundations of the mountains were troubled and were moved.”

### To Be Moved

To be moved, properly speaking. It signifies to be changed; hence Boethius:

> Remaining stable, you cause all things to move.

It signifies to be deprived of good; hence the Psalmist: “He who does these things [Col. 0865B] shall not be moved for ever.” It signifies being stirred to anger; hence one commonly says: “This man is moved to anger.” It signifies doubting; hence someone is said to be moved concerning a question, that is, to doubt.

### Woman

Woman is the name of a sex; hence in the Gospel: “What is it to me and to you, woman?” It signifies one corrupted; hence: “Among those born of women.” It signifies a wife; hence the Apostle: “As long as the husband lives, the woman is bound to her husband; but if he has died, she is released from the law of her husband.” It signifies the Church; hence in Genesis: “I shall put enmities between you and the woman,” that is, between the devil and the Church; and elsewhere: “Who shall find a strong woman?” It signifies the wisdom of God, that is, the Son; hence in the Gospel one reads of the woman who, having lost a drachma, lit [Col. 0865C] a lamp; this was explained above. It signifies sensuality; hence the Apostle says that the man is the head of the woman, that is, reason is the head of sensuality. And just as a man ought to govern a woman, so reason ought to govern sensuality. It signifies heresy; hence Solomon: “That you may be delivered from the strange woman and the foreign woman who softens her words.” It signifies idolatry; hence in Revelation: “I saw a woman drunk with the blood of the holy martyrs.” It signifies carnal pleasure; hence Solomon: “Many, admiring the appearance of a strange woman, have been made reprobate.” It signifies a weak mind; hence the Wise Man says: “The wickedness of a man is better than a beneficent woman,” because sometimes the fault of the strong is an occasion of virtue, just as the virtue of the weak is an occasion of sin. By a man every strong and discerning person is signified; by a woman a weak [Col. 0865D] and undiscerning mind is understood. It also signifies vice; hence Zechariah: “I lifted up my eyes and saw; and behold, two women coming forth, and spirit was in their wings, and they had wings like the wings of a kite, and they lifted them between heaven and earth.” By the two women we understand the two principal vices, pride and vainglory, which are beyond any doubt joined to impiety. They are said to have spirit in their wings because in their actions they serve Satan as he flies. “And they had wings like the wings of a kite.” A kite always seeks to lie in wait for chicks; therefore these women have wings like the wings of a kite because their actions are undoubtedly like the kite’s, since they are always lying in wait for the lives of little ones.

### Many

“Many,” properly: great; hence Paul: “In much [Col. 0866A] patience, in many fasts.” It also signifies grave; hence in the Psalms: “Many are the tribulations of the righteous.” It also signifies all; hence: “Many are called, few are chosen,” that is, all. Likewise: “Her many sins have been forgiven,” that is, all. Similarly: “There many are gathered who sleep in the dust”; and in Luke: “He called many to supper,” that is, all.

### Mule

A mule, properly: foolish or mad; hence David: “Do not become like horse and mule.”

### World

*Mundus*: pure, and thus it is an adjective. *Mundus* as a substantive signifies the adornment of women with which they adorned themselves when about to go in to men; hence it is written that Esther’s guardian hastened the women’s adornment. It signifies a lover of worldly things; hence in John: “And the world did not know him,” that is, lovers of the world; [Col. 0866B] and elsewhere: “And the prince of this world shall be cast out.” The devil is not called prince of this world because he has power over worldly things, but because he reigns through sin in lovers of worldly things. It signifies the wisdom of God, according to which the world was made, and which the prophets call the archetypal world, as it were the principal image of the world; hence Boethius:

> Himself most beautiful,  
> Holding the beautiful world in his mind.

It signifies people of the world; hence it is said of Christ in the Gospel: “The whole world has gone after him,” that is, all people in the world. It signifies worldly manner of life; hence in John: “Jesus knowing,” etc., [Col. 0866C] “that he was to pass from this world to the Father.” It signifies the higher part of reason, which is so called from purity because it neither errs nor deceives; hence in John: “Who enlightens every person coming into this world,” that is, ascending to the higher part of reason. It signifies a human being, who is in many respects like the world. As in the greater world the firmament moves from east to west and returns to the east, so reason in a human being moves from contemplation of eastern things, that is, heavenly things—first considering God and divine matters—and then descends to western things, that is, the consideration of earthly matters, in order that through visible things it may contemplate invisible things; then it returns to the east, again considering heavenly things. And just as the planets move contrary to the firmament and retard its [Col. 0866D] movement, so the five senses move contrary to reason and impede its movement; nevertheless, reason carries them with it and compels them to serve. And just as in the greater world God rules in the heavens, while angels, as it were his soldiers, moving through the world, govern human beings subject to God and provide for them, and human beings dwell on earth as though in the suburb of the human city: so wisdom has its place on the throne of the head, will in the heart, and pleasure in the suburb of the loins. And just as the world consists of four elements, so a human being consists of four humors corresponding to the properties of the elements: melancholy, which performs the part of earth; phlegm, which performs the part of water; and blood, which bears the likeness of fire. A human being also has likeness with every creature: with stones in existing, [Col. 0867A] with trees in living, with brute animals in sensing, and with angels in discerning.

### Gift

A gift, properly: the Church; hence in the Psalms: “And the daughters of Tyre with gifts.” It signifies a good work; hence Matthew: “If you offer your gift at the altar and have something against your brother,” etc.—that is, if you wish to offer some good work to God in faith, first ask your neighbor to forgive you injuries. It signifies a person offering himself to God; hence David: “The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts,” that is, themselves to God. It signifies recompense; hence the Psalmist: “And he has not accepted gifts against the innocent,” that is, rewards. It also signifies an office; hence: “An order of angels is designated by the name of that thing which it possesses more fully in its office.”

### Little Lamprey

A little lamprey: a small eel, that is, a lamprey; hence someone says: “Lamprey is suspect food.” It signifies theological knowledge, which is elegantly called a little lamprey because, just as a little lamprey is slippery, so theological knowledge quickly slips away from the human mind. Hence in the Song: “We shall make for you golden little lampreys,” that is, in Holy Scripture we shall offer you various sayings, golden through wisdom, embroidered with silver, that is, shining with eloquence. [Col. 0867B]

### To Murmur

To murmur, properly: to be indignant. Hence in the Gospel it is written of the laborers who worked in the vineyard from the first hour that they murmured against the householder, who gave one denarius both to them and to those who had worked in the last hour. Those who came at the last hour signify the Gentiles. The same denarius shall be given to them according to the Jews’ opinion, not according to the reality of the matter. Therefore, seeing the Gentiles rewarded with the denarius of eternal blessedness, which they thought was owed to themselves, the Jews will be indignant. It also signifies doubting; hence: “But the Jews murmured among themselves, saying.” It signifies wondering; hence, according to another exposition, those who worked in the vineyard from the first hour until evening signify those who served God all the days of their life. But those at the last hour signify those who repent at the end of life. On the day of judgment those who always served God will murmur against God because he rewards others as much as themselves—that is, they will wonder at God’s grace and mercy shown to those who came last. [Col. 0867C]

### Wall

A wall, properly. It signifies Christ; hence Isaiah: “The city of our strength is Zion, the Savior; a wall and a fore-wall shall be set in it.” For he is the wall surrounding us by guarding us on every side. All the prophets were the fore-wall of the wall, having been sent to build faith before the Lord appeared in the flesh. It signifies the Church; hence in the Song: “I am a wall, and my words are a tower,” that is, my preachers, who offer others the drink of heavenly teaching, yet are comparable to a tower because they defend others as a tower defends a city. It signifies the defense of Christian faith; hence Job says of the persecutors of the faithful: “As through a broken wall [Col. 0868A] and an open gate, they rushed upon me.” The wall is, as it were, broken when faith in our Redeemer is destroyed in certain hearts through the wicked persuasions of evil people. As through a broken wall and an open gate, the wicked rush upon the good when, having received temporal power, they strive also to destroy in certain hearts the defenses of faith. It signifies a fortification; hence Jeremiah: “The Lord has destroyed the walls of the daughter of Zion,” that is, fortifications; and elsewhere in Job: “As through a broken wall the enemy enters when, by the crafty persuasion either of evil spirits or of wicked people, the defenses of discipline in the heart are destroyed.” It signifies the saints; hence Isaiah: “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have appointed watchmen,” that is, over your saints, O Church, I have appointed the guardianship of angels. It signifies Holy Scripture, by which God’s Church is fortified, and to whose guardianship saints have been assigned, that is, its writers [Col. 0868B] or interpreters. It signifies sin; hence in the Psalms: “And in my God I shall pass beyond the wall,” that is, through Christ’s grace I shall cast away from myself sin, which is an obstacle preventing my passing to God. For a wall is everything set in the way of our journey so that we may not pass to God, whom we love; but we pass beyond this wall when, for love of the heavenly homeland, we tread underfoot whatever belongs to this world. It signifies defense; hence: “You did not go up to oppose nor set yourself as a wall for the house of Israel.” It signifies the apostles; hence the prophet: “I have delivered your walls into the hands of the wicked,” that is, the apostles who are the walls of the faithful, whom Satan sought to sift like wheat. It signifies faith; hence Jeremiah: “The fore-wall mourned, and the wall was likewise destroyed,” that is, faith. It signifies divine power; hence Isaiah: [Col. 0868C] “Their heart cried to the Lord concerning the walls of the daughter of Zion,” that is, against divine power.

### Mouse

A mouse, properly: a mole; hence in the Book of Kings it is written that mice swarmed up from the earth and gnawed the buttocks of the Philistines. It also signifies the likeness of a mouse; hence it is written that the Philistines returned the ark with golden mice.

### To Bark; To Be Silent

*Mutire*, properly: to bark. Hence it is written that, when Egypt’s firstborn were struck by the destroying angel, not even a dog barked among the Hebrews. But *mutere* means to be silent; hence in the Gospel: “But he became mute.”

### Mute

Mute, properly. It signifies something making another mute; hence in Luke: “He was casting out a demon, and it was [Col. 0868D] mute,” that is, making a human being mute. It signifies one unwilling to speak; hence Isaiah says of wicked prelates: “Woe to you, mute dogs!” It signifies one unable, and one who ought not, to speak; hence idols are called deaf and mute. It signifies one rebuked so as not to speak; hence the Psalmist: “Let deceitful lips be made mute.”

### Myrrh

Myrrh, properly: bitterness; hence in the Song: “My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh,” because Christ’s passion was the Church’s greatest bitterness. It signifies mortification of the flesh; hence in the same book: “I shall go to the mountain of myrrh.” The Church is called a mountain of myrrh because many people in the Church mortify their flesh in many ways. It signifies the destruction of vices; hence in the Song: “My hands distilled myrrh,” that is, by good works I destroyed vices. It signifies passibility; hence in the same place: [Col. 0869A] “I harvested my myrrh.” These are Christ’s words speaking of himself according to his state of immortality, as though saying: “I cut passibility away from myself.” It signifies the Wisdom of God; hence in the Book of Wisdom: “Like choice myrrh.” It signifies the penitent person who chastises his flesh and reduces it to slavery; hence David: “Myrrh, and drop, and cassia.” It signifies the sweetness of virtues; hence according to another exposition: “Myrrh, and drop, and cassia.” Christ, coming, uses myrrh, drop, and cassia in his garment because he sprinkles the fragrance of myrrh from his chosen ones, with whom he mercifully clothes himself. For holy souls, brought forth by the ancient Fathers, delight their Redeemer in his honor, because from their good actions they claim nothing for their own praise.

### Myrtle

Myrtle, properly: a tranquil mind; hence Isaiah: [Col. 0869B] “In place of the saltwort the fir tree shall grow, and in place of the nettle [Col. 0870A] the myrtle shall grow.” For in place of saltwort the fir tree rises when, in holy hearts, the loftiness of heavenly contemplation arises in place of the casting away of earthly thought. In place of the nettle the myrtle grows when the minds of the righteous come from the itching of vices and burning to the moderation and tranquillity of chastity; for then they do not desire earthly things, when they extinguish the flames of the flesh with heavenly desires. Myrtles signify those who moderate their neighbors’ tribulations; hence Isaiah: “I shall give in the wilderness cedar, thorn, and olive wood.” By cedar, because it is very fragrant and of incorruptible nature, we understand the reward of eternal life. By the thorn, which pricks, we understand penance imposed for past sins. By the myrtle are signified those who know how to sympathize with the afflictions of their neighbors and moderate their tribulation through compassion.

## N

[Col. 0869]

### Nard

Nard, properly: an aromatic plant. It signifies something made from spikes of nard; hence in the Gospel, of Mary Magdalene, that she brought an alabaster vessel of spikenard. It also signifies the fragrance of good reputation, or good reputation itself; hence: “While the king was at his table, nard gave forth its fragrance,” that is, after Christ ascended into heaven and sat at the right hand of the Father, the fame of Christ or of the Church was spread throughout the whole world. It signifies charity; hence the aforesaid authority can be explained thus: [Col. 0869C] “While the king was at his table,” that is, after Christ was humbled through the Incarnation, “my nard gave forth its fragrance,” that is, my charity was inflamed and extended even to an enemy. It signifies good action providing others an example of acting well; hence in the Song: “Nard and crocus and reed.”

### Nostril

A nostril, properly. It signifies foolishness; hence Solomon: “A golden ring in her nostrils: a beautiful and foolish woman.” The golden ring is the brilliance of heretics’ speech, which is in their nostrils, that is, proceeds from the foolishness of heretics. It signifies the devil’s wicked suggestion; hence Job, speaking of Behemoth, that is, the devil, says: “Smoke proceeds from his nostrils,” because from the devil’s wicked suggestion proceeds the darkening of the [Col. 0869D] human mind. It signifies foreknowledge: “Therefore cease from man, whose breath is in his nostrils.”

### To Be Born

To be born, properly. It signifies proceeding from the Father by eternal generation; hence Origen says that the Son is always born, that is, proceeds from the Father by eternal generation. It signifies being born again through grace; hence Christ says to Nicodemus in John: “You must be born again.” It signifies arising or beginning to appear openly; hence the moon or sun is said to be born where it first appears. A river is likewise said to be born where it rises. It signifies beginning to exist; hence the Lord in the Gospel: “It would have been good for that man if he had not been born,” that is, no evil would have befallen Judas if he had not begun to exist.

### Nose

A nose, properly. It signifies a prelate excelling others [Col. 0870B] in virtues; hence in the Song: “Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon which looks toward Damascus.” It signifies discernment, as it is said in the Lord’s voice in praise of the Church: “Your nose is like the tower which is in Lebanon.” By the nose we distinguish odors and stinks, and therefore the prudent discernment of the saints is signified by the nose. A tower is set on high for watching, so that an enemy coming from afar may be seen; therefore the nose of the Church is said to be like a tower because the prudent discernment of the saints, set on high while carefully surveying all around, detects sin before it arrives. [Col. 0870C]

### Feast of Birth

A *natale* is a birth; hence Christ’s birth is customarily called his *natale*. It signifies the death of a saint, which is elegantly called a *natale*, because then the soul first truly begins to live when it leaves the state of our misery; hence the death of Saint Lawrence or Martin is called a *natale*. It is also called a *depositio*, because then it lays aside the prison of flesh. It is also called an *obitus*, because then angels come to meet the saint’s soul. It is also called a *transitus*, because the soul of a saint must pass through many places before arriving at the empyrean heaven. It is also called a falling asleep; because, just as someone rests in sleep, so after death the soul finds refreshment; and just as someone sleeping is awakened from sleep with complete soundness and integrity of limbs, so the saints shall be awakened from the sleep of death on the day of resurrection. But the death of the Blessed Virgin Mary alone is called an Assumption, according to the opinion of those who hold that she was assumed bodily into heaven. Or it is called an Assumption, that is, exaltation above the choirs of angels; hence in the antiphon: “The holy Mother of God has been exalted above the choirs of angels to the heavenly kingdoms.” [Col. 0870D]

### To Swim

To swim, properly. It signifies not reaching the depth of Holy Scripture; hence Holy Scripture is said to be a river in which both the lamb wades and the camel swims—that is, the simple person is sufficiently instructed, while the wise person [Col. 0871A] reaches the depth of Holy Scripture. It signifies abundance, according to our customary expression: “He swims in riches.” It is also taken for excelling; hence Statius: “Purple fire swims upon his face.” It is also taken for moving, because one who swims moves; hence Statius: “Eyes swimming toward death.”

### Nature

Sometimes *nature* is taken so broadly that everything which can in any way be understood is called nature; hence Boethius: “Nature is whatever can in some way be understood.” According to this explanation, both matter (*hyle*) and God can be called nature; for although matter cannot properly be grasped by the understanding, but only through the negation of form, nevertheless it is understood in some manner. Likewise, although the divine form is understood only through removal of matter, nevertheless it is grasped in some manner by the intellect. Sometimes it is taken as denoting substance alone; hence Boethius: “Nature is whatever can act or suffer.” According to this meaning, God can be called nature because he is the efficient cause of all things. Yet the name “nature” is restricted to bodily substance; hence Boethius: “Nature is a principle of motion through itself and not accidentally.” For it belongs only to bodily substance to be a principle of motion through itself, that is, to be moved principally and through itself: it alone is properly moved either from the center to the circumference, like light things, namely fire and air, or from the circumference to the center, like heavy things, namely earth and water. It is also restricted to the substantial and specific difference which, [Col. 0871C] coming to a genus, makes a species—for example, the universal “rational”; hence Boethius: “Nature is the specific difference giving form.” It signifies the substantial being of a thing by which the thing is born, that is, enters into its own being; hence Christ is said to be of two natures, because both humanity and divinity are Christ’s being. It signifies origin; hence an angel is said by nature to have had the capacity to sin, that is, from its origin to have had freedom of will for acting either well or badly. Hence Plato, in the *Timaeus*, introduces God speaking to the angels: “Gods of gods, by nature indeed indissoluble.” It also signifies constitution; hence: “Natural science asserts that the things of diverse natures are diverse,” that is, of diverse constitutions. It signifies a vice made habitual as nature; hence in law custom [Col. 0871D] is called a second nature, and a person is said to die “of nature,” that is, from a vice made habitual as nature. It signifies natural heat; hence the physician says that there is a struggle between sickness and nature, that is, natural heat. It signifies natural reason; hence the Apostle says that the Gentiles, who do not have the law, naturally do the things of the law, that is, by the natural prompting of reason. In this sense it is customary to say that nature dictates to a person that he should not do to others what he does not wish done to himself, that is, natural reason. It signifies a power implanted in natural things, producing like things from like; hence someone is said to come into being according to nature. Hence Hilary says that the Creator became a creature: this is not a principle of nature, but an exception of power.

### Ship

A ship, properly: a vessel. The rudder of a ship; [Col. 0872A] hence in John: “Cast the net on the right side of the ship.” It also signifies the act of sailing; hence elsewhere in the Gospel: “But the other disciples came by ship.”

### Ship

A ship, properly. It also signifies the Church, because just as someone crosses the sea by means of a ship in coming to harbor, so someone, by means of the Church as a spiritual ship, crosses this great and wide sea—that is, the world—and reaches the harbor of eternal blessedness. Hence it is written in the Psalms concerning the faithful established in churches: “Those who go down to the sea in ships,” that is, those who descend from the contemplative life into the active life, existing in churches. It signifies one who investigates earthly joy through carnal pleasures, honors, or riches; hence David says: “In a violent spirit you shall break the ships of Tarshish,” that is, [Col. 0872B] in the Holy Spirit, or in bitterness of heart, you shall convert to repentance those who investigate earthly joys. For Tarshish is interpreted “investigation of joy.” Or by ships the Gentiles are understood. For Tarshish is the metropolis of Cilicia, and by Tarshish is understood Cilicia, by Cilicia Gentile-ness, so that the whole is understood from a part. The sense, therefore, is: “In a violent spirit you shall break the ships of Tarshish,” that is, you shall convert the Gentiles to faith. It signifies one who fluctuates in the depth of carnal pleasures; hence the prophet: “Upon every fortified wall and upon all the ships of Tarshish.” It signifies commerce carried on in this world, yearning after earthly profit; hence John: “Woe, woe, great city Babylon, by which all who have [Col. 0872C] ships on the sea have become rich.”

### *Ne*

*Ne* is sometimes used interrogatively; hence Job: “Do you think that a dead man shall live again?” Consecutively; hence David: “O Lord my God,” etc., “lest at any time.” It is used negatively; hence: “See that you do not do it.” Assertively; hence Boethius in the prologue to the book *On the Trinity*: “But *ne*,” that is, “but.” Sometimes it is used for *ut* (“that”); hence in Theodolus, concerning Chatino, it is said: “*Ne patiatur*,” that is, he pretends to be a dragon.

### Mist

Mist, properly. Hence Solomon says: “The Lord said that he would dwell in mist.” The Lord is never read to have said this; but because he appeared on Mount Sinai in mist, went before Israel in a cloud, and before Moses passed by in the cavern of the rock also in mist, Solomon sets speech in place of action. The sense is therefore: “The Lord said,” that is, showed by his action. It signifies tribulation; hence: “A day of darkness and gloom, a day of mist and whirlwind.” This can be understood of the Babylonian captivity or the day of judgment. It signifies a preacher; hence Job: “Will he raise his voice like a mist?” It signifies ignorance; hence: “He scatters mist like ashes,” because Christ removes the darkness of ignorance arising from the gloom of sin through repentance and humility, signified by ashes. [Col. 0872D]

### Nor

*Nec* means both “not” and “and”; hence: “Woman, where are those who accused you?” etc., “Neither do I condemn you.” Sometimes it is used negatively; hence one commonly says: “Neither this nor that is true.”

### Necessary

[Col. 0873A] Necessary, properly: inevitable; and in this sense “necessary” is opposed to contingent. Hence God is said to be necessary. It also signifies that which someone needs; in this sense “necessary” is opposed to superfluous. Hence Solomon: “Give me neither riches nor poverty, but grant me only the necessities for my sustenance.” It sometimes signifies useful; hence the Lord in the Gospel: “But one thing is necessary.” And in however many senses “necessary” is used, in so many senses is *necesse* used.

### Necessity

Necessity signifies need; hence: “A friend is tested in necessity.” It signifies inevitability; hence in the Decrees: “Necessity breaks the law.” It signifies tribulation or adversity; hence David: “The tribulations of my heart have been multiplied: deliver me from my necessities.” Adversities [Col. 0873B] or tribulations are rightly called necessities because it is necessary that we suffer them until the end of life; or because they are situated near death (*necem*), they are called necessities, since they both precede death and signify it.

### To Deny

To deny also signifies not fulfilling divine commands; hence the Apostle says of sinners that they confess God with their mouth but deny him by their deeds. It also signifies not giving; hence one commonly says: “The earth denies fruit,” that is, does not give it.

Wickedness (*nequitia*) is called the malice by which someone wishes to undertake an evil which he cannot accomplish. Or it is called that malice by which a person continually strives to harm his neighbor; hence he is called *nequam*, that is, “not equitable,” because he acts against [Col. 0873C] equity. Thus the Apostle says: “Filled with all unrighteousness, etc., wickedness.”

Sinew, properly so called; hence Job: “You knit me together with bones and sinews.” It is also the instrument in which the condemned are placed; thus one reads in the book of Kings that Asa king of Judah put the prophet who rebuked him into the stocks. It means present misery; hence Job: “You have put my foot in the stocks.” It means the connection that exists among sins, when someone is so entangled that he seems unable to escape either of two sins; hence Job: “The sinews of Leviathan’s testicles are intertwined.” It means a strong judgment of discernment; hence, according to another exposition: “You have put my foot in the stocks.” God put a man’s foot in the stocks when He bound that man’s perversity by the strong judgment of His discernment. He “investigated his paths” because He judged each of his works minutely; He “considered the footprints of his feet” when He examined whether the intentions of his works were rightly directed.

Not to know, properly so called. It also denotes to reject; hence Matthew: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you,” that is, “I reject you.” It denotes not to cause to be done; hence in the Gospel: “But of that day no one knows, neither angel nor Son of Man.” He is said not to know because He does not make us know; He Himself nevertheless knows, but does not make us know. It signifies removing a perverse end from an act; hence in the Gospel: “Let not your left hand know what your right hand does.” The sense is: if you do good, do not do it with a leftward intention—that is, for human favor or earthly gain.

[Col. 0874A] Nest, properly so called: the heart of a saint, in which Christ dwells through grace; hence Job: “Will the eagle rise at your command and place its nest on high?” It means temporal things, because a nest is commonly made from hay and mud. By “nest” temporal things are signified, since they are of hay—that is, transient—and as it were muddy; hence David: “There the sparrows will make their nests,” that is, among the rich the poor will find temporal goods.
