It means faith in Christ, because through Christ’s incarnation, which is figured by hay, faith in Christ was enlarged; hence Job: “I shall die in my nest.” And David says: “Indeed the sparrow has found herself a house, and the turtledove a nest,” etc.—that is, sensuality finds faith in which it lays up good works, because works without faith are dead. It also means earthly honor or delight; hence the Lord says to the princes of the earth: [Col. 0874B] “I will draw you out of your nest.” It means a person in whom another deposits his teaching and delights; hence in the Gospel: “Foxes have dens and birds of heaven nests,” etc.—that is, heretics have the hearts of their followers, in which they lodge their teaching; likewise the proud, who are signified by birds. But Christ has nowhere to lay His head, since He scarcely finds any in whom He may deposit His teaching and who will preserve it.

Black, properly so called. It means darkened by tribulation; hence the Church says in the Song: “I am black, but beautiful”—black through the gloom of tribulations, but beautiful through the brightness of virtues. It means contemptible; hence in the Song: “Your locks are like the raised branches of palm trees, black as a raven.” For the saints were contemptible like an ugly and noisy bird.

[Col. 0874C] “Nothing” is used for “not”; hence in the book of Wisdom: “Riches profited you nothing.” It means sin; hence John: “And without Him was made nothing,” that is, sin. Sin is called nothing either because it separates from true being, or because it weakens human nature, or because, insofar as it is sin, it is nothing. It means an idol, because that which the Gentiles believed an idol to be—namely, something composed of an image and divinity—is nothing; or that idol which bears no resemblance to a natural thing is said to be nothing, that is, to bear the likeness of no natural thing. This is indicated by the Gloss on that passage of John: “And without Him was made nothing,” that is, sin or an idol.

[Col. 0874D] “Exceedingly” (*nimis*) sometimes denotes excess; hence David: “Tribulations found us exceedingly.” It denotes perfection or fullness; hence in the Psalm: “Your friends, O God, are exceedingly honored.”

*Nitrum* is named from the province of Nitra, where it is commonly produced, and differs little from a kind of sal ammoniac. For just as, on the seashore, the heat of the sun, hardening the waters of the sea upon rocks, produces this substance, so in Nitria, where longer rains soak the earth in summer, excessive heat boils the water into a stone very like salt or ice. The natives use it for washing; hence the Psalmist: “If you wash yourself with nitre.” It means a mind hardened through correction; hence Solomon: “Vinegar upon nitre is he who sings songs to a perverse man.”

[Col. 0875A] “To be unwilling” is taken as “not to will.” But when God is said to be unwilling—not to will—something, it sometimes indicates, if I may speak thus, a reality; and so it indicates that something happens against someone’s will. Thus the Lord says to Jerusalem: “How often I wished to gather [you], etc., and you were unwilling.”

Name, properly so called. Sometimes it is taken broadly, so that any word is called a name; hence the poet:

> “And with leaves you entrust marks and name.”

It means glory or renown; hence David: “O Lord our Lord, how admirable is your name!” And in the Song: “Your name is oil poured out.” It means the thing signified by the name; hence in the Gospel: “Whatever you ask the Father in my name,” etc., that is, in the reality of this name Jesus—for eternal salvation; Jesus is interpreted “Savior.” It means authority; hence the Apostle: “He gave Him a [Col. 0875B] name,” that is, authority over all things; and elsewhere: “All authority has been given to me.” It means power or divine efficacy; hence it is said: “I baptize you in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” that is, in their divine power or efficacy. It means invocation; hence John is said to have baptized in the name of the One who was to come, that is, in invocation. It means the Son; hence David: “And in your name we shall see light,” that is, in your Son. For a thing is known by its name, and the Father was made known through the Son; therefore the Son is called the Father’s name. It means knowledge of a thing; hence David: “He numbers the multitude of the stars and calls them all by names,” that is, He has knowledge of each one. It means merit; hence in the Gospel: “Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven.” It means the saint whose name is written in the book of life; [Col. 0875C] hence in the Apostle: “But you have a few names in Sardis.” By “names” we should understand the persons themselves. He uses “names” in order to show that He knows not only the number but also the names of His elect—He who knew Moses by name.

To know, properly so called. It denotes approval; hence the Psalmist: “For the Lord knows the way of the just.” It denotes discernment; hence it is said of God: “He knows both the deceiver and the one deceived,” that is, He discerns between the one and the other. It denotes predestination; hence the Apostle says of God: “He knows who are His.” It denotes causing a thing to exist; hence Origen: “For things do not exist because God knows them; rather, they exist because He knows them.”

Razor, properly so called. It also means Nebuchadnezzar, [Col. 0875D] who in Isaiah is called a hired razor. It means Antichrist; hence in the Psalm: “Like a sharp razor you have wrought deceit.” Antichrist is called a razor because it promises renewal and cuts: thus Antichrist will promise blessedness by his deceits and will kill. Or evil persons are called a razor, which shaves off superfluous and useless hairs: so the wicked shave the saints’ hairs, that is, they seize their useless and superfluous possessions.

New, properly so called. It also means wonderful; hence the prophet: “The Lord will make a new thing on earth: a woman shall encompass a man.” It means renewed; hence John: “I saw a new heaven and a new earth,” and in the Apostle: “Behold, I make all things new.” It means renewing; hence in the Gospel: “I give you a new commandment.” It means cleansed of the oldness of guilt; hence one reads: “Strip me, [Col. 0876A] Lord, of this garment,” that is, clothe me anew. It means firm; hence Adam is called the old man, Christ the new man, because Adam was weak and Christ was firm; for weakness comes from oldness, firmness from newness. It means unheard-of; hence in the Acts of the Apostles the Athenians are said to have told Paul and his companions, as they preached Christ: “Who are these preachers of new demons?” It means newly appearing; hence the moon is called new, and among the Jews it is called *neomenia*, that is, “new moon.”

Night, properly so called. It also means material blindness; hence the poet:

> “And a long night held the soul beneath it.”

It means ignorance; hence the Apostle: “The night has passed, the day,” etc. It means guilt; hence David: “Every [Col. 0876B] night I shall wash my bed,” that is, I shall cleanse my conscience from every sin. It means adversity; hence in the Psalm: “He shall meditate in His law by day and by night,” that is, in prosperity and adversity. It means the time before Christ’s coming; hence in the book of Wisdom: “While all things held the middle of silence and night in its course was completing its journey.” It means the Old Testament, according to which “The night has passed” may be expounded. It means temporal death; hence David: “And even unto night my reins rebuked me,” that is, Christ says: “The Jews, from whom I was born, persecuted me unto death.” It means the present life; hence in the Gospel: “In the evening, or at midnight, or at cockcrow, or in the morning.” It is fittingly called night because it is enveloped in many darknesses of ignorance and guilt. It means the hour [Col. 0876C] at which Christ will come for judgment, which is called night because the hour of His coming is unknown; hence in the Gospel: “But at midnight a cry was made.” It means a lesser temptation; hence David: “By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night”: this was explained above. It also means the misery of the time; hence Job: “May a dark whirlwind possess that night.” It means the devil; hence in Genesis: “And He called the light day, and the darkness night.” This is commonly expounded concerning the apostate angels. It means captivity; hence Isaiah: “One cried to me from Seir: Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?” For there the Idumeans are introduced as lamenting their captivity. It means a sinner; hence in the Psalm: “And night shall be illumined as day,” because sometimes a sinner is converted just like a just person. It means [Col. 0876D] a preacher who preaches to the less advanced; hence David: “Day pours forth speech to day, and night,” etc., because preachers proclaim greater things to the greater and lesser things to the lesser.

Cloud, properly so called. It means Christ’s human nature; hence Isaiah: “I shall ascend upon a light cloud,” that is, human nature free from the weight of sin, “and I shall enter Egypt,” that is, I shall come into the world through assumed humanity. It means a preacher; hence the prophet: “Who are these who fly like clouds?” And elsewhere: “I will command the clouds not to rain.” Preachers are aptly compared with clouds because they flash with miracles, rain down doctrine, and thunder threats. It means Holy Scripture; hence David: “Dark water in the clouds of the air,” that is, obscure meaning in the sacred Scriptures. [Col. 0877A] It means the grace of the Holy Spirit; hence the Apostle says of the ancient fathers: “They were baptized in the cloud and in the sea,” that is, in baptism through the grace of the Holy Spirit. It means an angel; hence the prophet: “Drop down, heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the Just One,” that is, let angels announce Christ’s coming. It means someone changeable; hence Solomon: “He who watches the wind does not sow, and he who considers the clouds does not reap.” Here the sinner is called a cloud, whom the devil drives hither and thither by various temptations. Therefore, one who watches the wind does not sow, and one who considers the clouds will never reap, because the person who, fearing the temptations of the evil spirit and perceiving the malice of the wicked, despairs of himself neither now labors in sowing good works nor afterwards is refreshed by the reward of just recompense. It means firmness [Col. 0877B] of mind; hence Job: “Suddenly the air is gathered into clouds.” Thin air is made solid; therefore by air the minds of worldly people are signified, and by cloud the firmness of the mind is figured. It means temporal good; hence Job: “My welfare passed away like a cloud.” A cloud rises high, but is driven by the course of the wind; so the temporal good of a wicked person seems to rise high through lofty honor. But because it is driven daily along life’s course, as it were by certain winds of mortality, it will not rise. A cloud is dissipated by the heat of the sun; so, under the stern gaze of the heavenly Judge, as by the sun’s heat, the pride of the damned in hell will melt away, and, once consigned to places of punishment, will not return again to the use of action.

Naked, properly so called: having nothing of one’s own. Thus [Col. 0877C] authority says that we must follow naked Christ naked; and Gregory says that we must wrestle naked with the devil. It also means uncovered; hence the Apostle: “All things are naked and open.”

To number, properly so called: to distinguish; hence David: “He numbers the multitude of the stars.” It denotes knowing; hence in the Gospel: “Even all the hairs of your head are numbered.”

Number is sometimes taken for counting or plurality; hence Boethius, in his *Arithmetic*, distinguishes between the numbering number and the numbered number. He calls the numbering number repetition, and the numbered number plurality in the proper sense. Number means a collection of things, as one commonly says: “He is of the number of men.” It means smallness in quantity; hence Jeremiah: “He broke my teeth to a number,” that is, by breaking them He reduced them to fewness. It means distinction; hence Wisdom says that God created all things in number, that is, distinctly. It means unity, and the aforementioned authority may thus be expounded: God created all things in number, that is, in unity, because each thing is one by unity; hence Boethius: “What is, is therefore because it is one in number.” It means dignity; [Col. 0878A] hence David: “They are multiplied beyond number,” that is, they are multiplied in sin, which lacks all dignity. It means eternal life; hence David: “And the number of my days,” etc. This is a number without number, a number truly so called because it does not pass away; but the number of present days is not truly a number for one passing away, though it seems to have being for one who abides.

“Now” signifies time; hence Peter said: “Now I know truly that He has sent,” etc. Sometimes it signifies eternity, as when it is said: “God is now.” Sometimes it denotes the time of grace; hence David: “Now I shall arise, says the Lord”; and elsewhere: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.”

Wedding, properly so called; hence in the Gospel: “A wedding was held at Cana of Galilee.” It means the union of two natures; [Col. 0878B] hence in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a wedding for his son.” It means the union of Christ and the Church in eternal blessedness, when the Church will be ineffably united to Him through glory and in some manner deified; hence the Gospel reads: “And those who were ready entered with him into the wedding.” It means a rational union of certain things; hence one reads of the wedding of Mercury and Philology, that is, of wisdom and eloquence. It means carnal intercourse; hence Eusebius’ *Chronicle* says that Nectanabus, ascending Olympias’ bed, consummated a wedding.

Nut, properly so called. It means a martyr; hence in the Song: “I went down … [among] nuts.” A nut has three things in itself: an outer husk, a shell, and a kernel. Similarly, a martyr has three things: the failings of the flesh, as the husk; the flesh, as the shell; and the soul, as the kernel. When a nut is broken, its husk is cast away, its shell is broken, and the sweetness of its kernel is tasted. Thus, through martyrdom, failings cease to exist in the martyr; the flesh, like the shell, is in some sense broken; and then the saint delights in his soul in the sweetness of eternal blessedness. The nut is also commonly said to mean Christ, because in Christ the body was like the outer husk, the soul like the shell, and the divinity like the kernel. So long as Christ remained in the world, the divinity did not appear in Him; but after death, when the body was separated from the soul, the shell as it were broken, humanity perceived the sweetness of the kernel because it was liberated through the power of divinity.

The night-raven (*nycticorax*), a bird that flies by night; hence it is called [Col. 0878D] *nycticorax*, as if “raven of the night,” from *nyctui*, meaning “night,” and *corax*, meaning “raven.” It means a faithful person living amid a perverse generation; hence David: “I have become like a night-raven in a dwelling.” It also means Christ, who came into the night of our misery and was crucified by the Jews, who ought to have been a dwelling but became ruins because they suffered destruction. Accordingly, what was said in the Psalm may be read: “I have become like a night-raven in a dwelling,” or “among ruins.”

## O

[Col. 0877]

[Col. 0877D] To obey means to do something for another’s sake, as when someone serves God for God’s sake. Hence [Col. 0878D] demons are said to serve God, but not to obey Him, because what they do, they do not do for God’s sake; indeed, so far as lies in them, they act against God. It denotes fulfilling divine commands; hence the Apostle: “But not all obey the Gospel,” that is, not all fulfill the Gospel. It denotes something being done at God’s nod and will; hence in the Gospel: “The winds and the sea obey Him.”

*Obesum* means fat, as one reads that Pharaoh saw in a dream seven cows fat with fat flesh, that is, full, as though enlarged by eating.

To stop up, properly so called: to impose silence; hence David: “The mouth of those who speak iniquity is stopped.” It denotes escaping; hence the Apostle: “They stopped the mouths of lions,” that is, they escaped, like Daniel.

To meet, properly so called; hence in the Gospel: “The children of the Hebrews met the Lord.” It denotes joining or agreeing; hence David: “Mercy and truth met [Col. 0879B] one another.” It denotes contradicting, as one commonly says: “This man opposes that one,” that is, he contradicts that person’s words or deeds.

Setting, properly so called; it also means death, hence David: “He who ascends above the setting,” that is, He who conquered death. It means the devil, concerning whom the same authority may be expounded: “He who ascends above the setting.”

To set, insofar as it means to fall, with the middle syllable shortened, is intransitive. Sometimes it means a fall; sometimes it means the withdrawal of grace, according to the twofold exposition commonly given to this saying of the Apostle: “Let not the sun set upon your anger.” The literal sense is: if you are moved by a sudden movement of anger, let that movement not last through the day or long endure, according to that Psalm: “Be angry and do not sin.” That is, let your anger [Col. 0879C] not cause the sun of justice to set within you, that is, to withdraw His grace from you. But when this verb *occidere* has its penultimate syllable lengthened, it is sometimes transitive and is used properly. Sometimes it means the delight of sin, according to the prophet’s saying: “I kill and I make alive.” Sometimes it denotes the death of the soul, according to the saying: “He who kills another in body first kills himself in mind.”

To come to meet, properly so called. It denotes repentance, for one who repents in some manner comes to meet God coming to him; hence authority says that God comes to meet those who come to meet Him. It denotes equality; hence David: “And His reaching is unto its height,” because Christ is equal to the Father.

[Col. 0879D] Eye, properly so called. It also means the contemplative life; hence in the Gospel: “If your right eye causes you to stumble,” etc., that is, if you are not sufficiently suited, by sound discernment, for the contemplative life, safely maintain the active life alone. It means a perverse counselor; hence Job says of the ancient enemy: “His eyes are like the eyelids of dawn.” By the eye, which is attached to the head and serves the usefulness of sight, is understood a counselor of Antichrist, who, while he foresees by perverse contrivances what is to be done, provides wicked people with a path as though displayed before their feet. It also means hope; hence Jeremiah: “The wild asses stood upon the rocks; they drew in the winds like dragons; their eyes failed.” By the wild asses the most wicked Jews are figured, who stood upon the mountains, trusting in earthly powers rather than [Col. 0880A] in God; their eyes failed because their hope in the things upon which they relied fell away from them. It means proud exaltation; hence the Wise Man: “He who humbles himself shall be in glory, and he who lowers his eyes shall be saved.” To lower one’s eyes is to despise no one by looking upon him with pride, but to judge oneself less and inferior to all whom one sees. It means reason, because, as visible things are weighed by the eye, so invisible things are weighed by reason; hence David: “My eye is troubled by fury.” It means intention; hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “The lamp of your body is your eye.” It means the stream of concupiscence; hence one reads that Adam’s and Eve’s eyes were opened after sin because they began to be aroused and to diffuse themselves toward the genital members. It means understanding; hence the Church is told [Col. 0880B] in the Song: “Your eyes are those of doves,” that is, your understandings concerning divine things are simple, not corrupted by the leaven of the Pharisees. It means the regard of divine mercy; hence David: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the just.” It means the gift of the Holy Spirit; hence the prophet: “His eyes are as a flame of fire.” The eyes of the Lord signify the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Of these it is read elsewhere that John saw a lamb as though slain, having seven horns and seven eyes; and in Zechariah that there were seven eyes upon one stone. It means a human being; hence John: “Every eye shall see Him.” Let us take “every eye,” by the customary manner of speech, as put here for every human being. Therefore every eye, that is, every person, when he rises again, shall see Christ bodily, whether unto life [Col. 0880C] or unto death. It means a wicked prelate; hence David: “Let their eyes be darkened so that they may not see, and bend their back forever.” Eyes are those set at the top in the very face of a person and entrusted with the function of foreseeing the way. The eyes are darkened and the back bent when they lose the light of wisdom and are bent down to bear the burdens of sins. It means one who provides for another; hence in the Gospel: “If your eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out,” etc., that is, if someone charged with oversight should wish to make you stumble in the Catholic faith or in spiritual matters, withdraw from his company rather than stumble in divine understanding. It also means a prelate of the Church, who enlightens others by word and example; in this sense may be understood [Col. 0880D] the saying of the Song: “Your eyes are those of doves.” It means Holy Scripture, which is called God’s eye, because by the eyelids of this eye—that is, by the plain and obscure passages of Holy Scripture—God tests the children of men, that is, distinguishes good from evil; hence David: “His eyes look upon the poor, and His eyelids among the children of men.” It means Christ, because as there are several coats in the eye, so in Christ there are several substances: body, soul, and divinity. In the middle of the eye is the pupil, called *pupilla*, as if *pusilla*, “very small,” through which the visible ray goes forth to distinguish light and darkness. So in Christ there is human nature, like the pupil, minimal in relation to divinity; through it God, coming to us, distinguishes between the light of the good and the darkness of the reprobate. [Col. 0881A] Hence David: “Keep me as the pupil of the eye,” that is, beneath the pupil of the eye.

To hate, properly so called. It denotes giving a sign of hatred or inflicting harm; hence David: “He who loves iniquity hates his own soul,” that is, he inflicts harm on his soul, which is a sign of hatred. It denotes rejecting; hence David: “I have hated the wicked,” and elsewhere: “You have hated all who work iniquity.” It denotes despising divine commands; hence the Psalmist: “The pride of those who hate you rises continually,” etc. It denotes not preserving a thing in being; hence one reads in the book of Wisdom: “You hate none of the things that you made,” that is, you preserve in their being those things that you made. It denotes not bestowing grace; hence: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” It denotes restraining carnal pleasures by the will of the soul; [Col. 0881B] hence in the Gospel: “He who hates his soul in this world,” that is, one who restrains the pleasures of the flesh by the will of the soul in this life.

Odor, properly so called. It also means renown; hence in the Song: “We shall run after the odor of your ointments,” that is, we shall do good works after the example and renown of virtues or good works. It means occasion; hence Paul: “To some we are an odor of life unto life, to others an odor of death unto death.” It means prayer, because one reads that the saints had bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints. It means burning; hence Daniel: “The odor of fire did not touch them,” that is, the burning of the fire did not touch the three youths. It also means devotion of mind; hence one reads that Noah offered a burnt offering to the Lord as an odor of sweetness.

[Col. 0881C] Wild olive, properly so called. It also means a Gentile. For when he was estranged from God, he was called a wild olive; hence the Apostle: “But you, when you were a wild olive.”

Oil, properly so called. It also means renown or glory; in the Song: “Your name is oil poured out.” It means spiritual grace; hence David: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness.” It means charity; hence in the Psalm: “You have made my head rich with oil,” that is, you have made my mind rich with charity. It means mercy; hence one reads of the Samaritan that he poured in oil and wine. It means flattery; hence David: “Let not the oil of the sinner make my head rich.” It means abundance of temporal goods; hence David: “From the fruit of grain, wine, and oil,” etc.

Olive tree, properly so called. It means divine wisdom; hence in the [Col. 0881D] book of Wisdom: “Like a beautiful olive tree.” It means a just person; hence David: “Like a fruitful olive tree.” It means the Church; hence the Apostle, speaking to the Gentile people, says: “But you, when you were a wild olive, were grafted among them and made a partner of the root,” that is, of the richness of the olive tree.

Pot, properly so called. It also means refreshment; hence David: “Moab is the pot of my hope.” For the Church is refreshed with spiritual refreshment when a sinner, who is figured by Moab, is converted to faith. It means every carnal heart; hence the prophet: “I see a seething pot from the north.” The seething pot is the human heart boiling with the burning of worldly cares and the anxieties of snares. The pot of the human heart is kindled from the quarter of the north when, through the instigation of the adversary spirit, it is inflamed with unlawful desires. It means the likeness [Col. 0882A] of a pot, according to the exposition: “What do you see, Jeremiah?” “I saw a seething pot from the north,” that is, the likeness of a pot. It means blackness or confusion, because various things are mingled in a pot; hence the prophet: “Their faces shall be turned into a pot.”

Vegetables, properly so called. They mean food without distinction; hence Paul: “He who is weak, let him eat vegetables.” They mean thin and dry food; thus the aforementioned authority may be expounded: “He who is weak,” that is, prone to the slipperiness of the flesh, “let him eat vegetables,” that is, let him use thin and dry food to chastise the flesh’s incitement. They mean the human race; hence David: “Like the green herbs they shall quickly fall.” They may also mean the married state, because it is common and light food; so one unable to remain continent may be told: “He who is weak, [Col. 0882B] let him eat vegetables,” that is, let him take a wife, etc.

Wild ass, properly so called. It also means a solitary person; hence Job: “Who has set the wild ass free, and who has loosed his bonds?” The wild ass, which dwells in solitude, rightly signifies the life of those who, removed from worldly crowds, live in the solitude of the mind. It means one who does whatever he desires; hence it is said of the vain person: “He thinks that he was born free like a colt of the wild ass.” The wild ass has freedom both to go where it desires and to rest when it is weary. Therefore, the person whom the reins of discipline do not restrain but who runs wandering through the forest of desires longs to be like a colt of the wild ass. It means one who, placed in the field of faith, is bound by the reins of no duty; hence: “Will the wild ass bray when it has grass?” When one burns with desire for the vision of contemplation after leaving worldly life, when he longs for the pasture of inward refreshment, he brays like a wild ass that cannot find grass. It means a Jew; hence the prophet: “Wild asses stood upon the rocks; their eyes failed because there was no grass.” This was said above about the Jews, whose eyes failed because they were frustrated in their hope; these things vanished from them because there was no grass, because knowledge of eternity was lacking to their hearts, and the food of inwardly verdant teaching refreshed them in no way. It means a heretic, as is written in Job: “Others go out like wild asses into the desert for their work.” There are some heretics who avoid mingling with peoples but seek the retirement of a more secluded life; and they generally infect those whom they find all the more with the pestilence of their persuasion [Col. 0882D] because they appear more worthy of reverence, as if on account of the merits of their life.

Onocentaur, properly so called. It means a lascivious and proud person; hence Isaiah: “It shall be a lair of dragons and a pasture of ostriches, and demons shall meet onocentaurs.” By dragons malice is signified, by ostriches hypocrisy. Therefore in a perverse mind the dragon lies down and the ostrich feeds, because hidden malice is craftily concealed and a simulation of goodness is displayed before the eyes of onlookers. By the onocentaur, slippery and haughty persons are signified; for Greek *onos* is called *asinus*, “ass,” in Latin. And lust is figured by the ass, while by the term “bull” the neck of pride is signified. Thus onocentaurs are those who, subject to the vices of lust, raise their necks precisely from that which ought to have humbled them. But demons [Col. 0883A] shall meet the onocentaurs, because evil spirits serve their desire greatly in those whom they see taking pride in what they ought to have mourned.

Burden, properly so called. It means the New Testament; hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “My yoke is sweet and my burden light.” It means the Old Testament; hence Peter in Acts: “This is a burden which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear.” It means something difficult to bear; hence: “Bear one another’s burdens.” It means sin; hence in the Gospel: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened.” It means adversity or tribulation; hence David: “He turned his back away from burdens.”

To work, properly so called. It denotes desiring; hence the Apostle: “It is no longer I who work it,” according as sin dwells [Col. 0883B] in me. It denotes furnishing a cause; hence Paul: “For when we were in the flesh, the passions of sins which were through the law worked in our members, that they might bear fruit unto death.” It denotes governing; hence the Lord: “My Father works until now, and I work.”

Opportunity is suitability or ease for doing something; hence one reads in the Gospel of Judas that he sought an opportunity to hand Jesus over. It means tribulation, which is called opportunity for three reasons: first, because of suitability, since it is fitting that saints suffer tribulation for their testing, according to what is said of the saints: “They were found worthy to suffer reproach for the name of Jesus.” Second, because of usefulness, since it is useful for saints to be assailed by tribulations. Third, because of necessity, because saints must suffer on account of eternal predestination. Hence one reads in the Psalm: “He looks in times of opportunity.” It means necessity; hence in the Gospel: “Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead.”

Work, properly, is that which results from working; hence Job: “You will stretch out your right hand to the work of your hands.” This accords with the customary distinction between the working work and the worked work. The working work of the Jews, by which they crucified Christ, was evil. The worked work, that is, Christ’s passion, was good. It means what is necessary; hence in the Gospel: “The Lord has need of them.” It means a kind of work; in Genesis: “God rested from every work which He had completed,” that is, from every kind of work, because after the sixth day He made no new kind [Col. 0883D] of work.

To pray, properly so called. It also denotes acting well, according to the Apostle’s statement: “Pray without ceasing,” that is, act well, in accordance with the saying: “Whoever works well prays well.” Or this should be understood literally: “Pray without ceasing,” that is, at stated hours assigned for prayer. It denotes presenting His humanity to God the Father; hence Christ is said to pray for us, that is, to present His humanity to the Father, in which He deserved to [save] the human race. It denotes directing the devotion of the mind to God; hence saints are said to pray for us.

World, properly so called. It means the week, revolving in a circle; hence in the hymn: “The world rolled seven times marks the blessed times.” It means the world; hence in the book [Col. 0884A] of Wisdom: “The Spirit of the Lord filled the world of the earth,” that is, preserves all worldly things in being. It means the earth; hence David: “And unto the ends of the world of the earth.” It means the Church; hence in the Psalm: “The foundations of the world were revealed,” etc., that is, the words of the prophets, by which the Church is united, were made manifest.

Order, properly so called: an ecclesiastical rank, in which sense the subdiaconate and diaconate are called orders. It means office; hence David: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” It means a uniform multitude of spirits, as sharing one mode of beholding God; in this sense the nine orders of angels are distinguished. It means suitability or harmony; hence Job: “Before I go to the dark land,” etc., where there is no [Col. 0884B] order.

*Organum* is the same as a psaltery; for *nablum* is Hebrew, *psalterium* Greek, and *organum* Latin. It means a musical instrument composed of diverse lead pipes which gives sound when bellows are blown; this instrument is commonly called an organ. It is also commonly used for any musical instrument. It means the harmony of virtues; hence David: “Praise Him with strings and organ.”

East, properly so called; hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Many shall come from the East.” It also means Christ; hence in the canticle of Zechariah: “The Dayspring from on high has visited us.”

Orphan, properly speaking. It also denotes the righteous person who leaves behind [Col. 0884C] the mother of concupiscence and the father who is the devil; hence David: “You will be a helper to the orphan.”

Mouth (*os, oris*), properly speaking. It denotes the heart or mind; hence David: “The mouth of the righteous will meditate wisdom.” For the mind is aptly called a mouth because the mouth itself is its instrument: what a person conceives in the heart, he expresses by the mouth. It denotes an entrance; hence we read in Joshua: “Roll huge stones to the mouth of the cave.” It also denotes a word, because a word is uttered by the mouth; hence the Lord in the Gospel: “By your mouth I judge you.” And in Job: “I shall put my hand over my mouth.” To put one’s hand over one’s mouth is to cover the faults of incautious speech by the power of good work. It denotes testimony; hence the Lord: “By the mouth of two or three witnesses every matter stands.” [Col. 0884D] It denotes the countenance; hence Statius:

> … Purple fire  
> swims upon his face.

It denotes devouring; hence David: “Deliver me, Lord, from the mouth of the lion.” It denotes urgency; hence in Exodus: “He slew them by the mouth of the sword,” that is, in its onslaught or devouring. It denotes presence or manifestation, as when we commonly say: “He spoke to him mouth to mouth,” that is, manifestly or in person. It also denotes God the Father, because from Him proceeds the Word, that is, the Son; hence in the antiphon: “O Wisdom, who came forth from the mouth of the Most High,” that is, from the mouth of the Most High Father. God the Father is aptly called a mouth because, just as the Word proceeds from a mouth without any alteration of the mouth, so the Son proceeds from the Father without any change in the Father. [Col. 0885A]

It also denotes the Son: for, just as someone speaks by the mouth, so the Father speaks through the Son. Hence in the Song of the Church: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” The sense is this: the Church prays the Father to kiss her—that is, to visit her—with the kiss of His mouth, that is, through the incarnation of His Son. The Son is called a mouth for three reasons: by the mouth we are refreshed, by the mouth we kiss, and by the mouth we speak. The Father, as it were, refreshes Himself by the Son as by His own mouth, because through Him He accomplished or fulfilled His own will. Likewise, through Him as through His own mouth, He gave a kiss to human nature when He united it to the Son; likewise, He spoke to it by this mouth, preaching to the world through Him.

It denotes the righteous person through whom the Lord speaks; hence: “The mouth of the Lord has spoken.” A righteous person is aptly called the Lord’s mouth, because in him the Father speaks forth, the Son speaks, and the Spirit [Col. 0885B] speaks. The Father speaks forth in a saint when the first and principal Word, that is, the Son, is sent into the saint. The Son speaks forth when He is infused into the saint in a spiritual and special manner, so that the saint then speaks outside the ordinary manner of speaking. The Holy Spirit speaks in the saint when He is wondrously infused into that person’s mind.

It also denotes a suggestion of the devil; hence we read: “Who shall enter into the midst of his mouth?” To enter into the midst of his mouth is to penetrate his crafty words, so that one considers neither what they sound like nor what they aim at. It denotes a preacher of Antichrist; hence we read in Job: “Lamps proceed from his mouth.” Just as those who see beforehand are called eyes, so those who preach are called a mouth. But lamps go forth from this mouth because they inflame the minds of hearers with love of the faith. It denotes the learning of teachers; hence John: “The power of the horses was in their mouths and in their tails.” In those most wicked preachers, running everywhere under carnal impulse, there is power in mouth and tail: they indeed preach their perverse doctrines about God, but, supported by temporal powers, they exalt themselves by things behind them. [Col. 0885C]

Bone (*os, ossis*), properly speaking. It denotes one who is stronger in the Church of God; hence David: “My bones have dried up like firewood.” It denotes strength or power; hence David: “Heal me, Lord, for all my bones are troubled.” It denotes an apostle; hence David: “They pierced, etc.; they numbered all my bones.” It denotes reason, because, just as bone is harder than flesh, so reason is harder than sensuality; [Col. 0885D] in this sense, “All my bones are troubled” may be interpreted. It denotes Christ, as is said through Job in the Lord’s person: “When the flesh of my skin was consumed, my bone clung to me.” For strength is signified in bone, but bodily weakness in flesh. Since Christ and the Church are one person, what is figured by the bone except the Lord Himself? What by the flesh except the disciples, who in the time of His passion had a weak understanding of Him? And what is figured by the skin, which remains outwardly upon the body beyond the flesh, except those holy women who served the Lord outwardly, in ministries concerned with preparing bodily necessities?

It denotes one more wicked and more crafty in the body of Antichrist; hence Job: “His bones are like pipes of bronze.” Antichrist has flesh—those who are held in error by others—and bones—those who hold others in error. [Col. 0886A] It denotes the strength of the flesh; hence Job: “My soul has chosen hanging, and my bones death.” What is signified by the soul except the mind’s intention, and by the bones except the strength of the flesh? Everything that is hung is undoubtedly raised from below. The soul, therefore, chose hanging so that the bones might die: when the mind’s intention is raised to things above, all strength of the outward life dies within it. It also denotes the strength of secular rank; hence Job says of the proud man: “His bones are full of marrow,” because pride arises from secular dignity. The woman taken from the man’s side is also called a bone in Genesis. Adam said: “This now is bone of my bones.” It also denotes that residue which remains from olives after the oil has been pressed out, according to which we call the remains of olives “bones.” [Col. 0886B]

Kiss, properly speaking. It denotes the incarnation; hence in the Song: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” Why the incarnation is figured by a kiss has been explained above. It denotes evangelical teaching; thus the aforesaid authority may be interpreted: “Let him kiss me with a kiss,” that is, with the presence of evangelical teaching. It denotes flattering speech; hence in the Book of Wisdom: “Better are the words of a correcting friend than the kisses of one who flatters.” It denotes the union of peace; hence the Apostle: “Greet one another with a kiss of peace,” that is, with the union of peace.

Door, properly speaking; hence in the Gospel: “He who does not enter through the door.” It denotes Christ, as He Himself says: “I am the door.” It denotes a branch of the Nile; hence the Nile is said to have seven mouths, called *cataduplae* or cataracts. [Col. 0886C] It denotes the human heart; hence John in the Apocalypse: “Behold, I knock at the door.” Christ knocks at the door when He invites freedom of choice to work well. And in the Apostle: “A door has been opened to me in the Lord,” that is, hearts opened to receive the Gospel. It denotes the desire of carnal concupiscence; hence in the Gospel: “When you pray, go into your chamber, and, having shut the door, etc.” We shut doors when we restrain unlawful desires. It denotes a holy preacher; hence Job: “Who shut up the sea with doors?” The sea—that is, the swelling of persecutors—is shut up when holy men are set against the swelling of persecutors as certain doors. It denotes understanding; hence in the Prophet: “And for each treasury-chamber a door in the fronts of the gates.” [Col. 0886D] The treasury-chambers are the hearts of teachers, which preserve the riches of knowledge; the fronts of the gates are the words and works of teachers, by which outwardly we recognize what manner of life they live inwardly. There is a door for each treasury-chamber in the fronts of the gates, because every teacher opens understanding in the hearer’s heart through the sayings and deeds of the ancient Fathers.

Sheepfold, properly speaking. It also denotes the Church; hence the Lord in the Gospel: “He who does not enter through the door into the sheepfold of the sheep.” It also denotes eternal life; hence the Lord in the Gospel: “I have other sheep that are not from this sheepfold.”

Sheep, properly speaking. It denotes the innocent person; hence David: “You have subjected all things beneath his feet, sheep and oxen.” It denotes [Col. 0887A] Christ; hence Isaiah: “Like a sheep He shall be led to slaughter.” He is called a sheep because of His singular, simple innocence; because His flesh is food; because of the sacrifice of His passion; and because He supplies His own with wool, that is, the clothing of virtues. It denotes an angel by reason of its innocence; hence we read in the Gospel concerning the shepherd that, having left the ninety-nine sheep—that is, the multitude of angels in paradise—he went, through assumed human nature, to seek the sheep that had perished, that is, humankind. It denotes the Christian people; hence David: “But we are His people and the sheep of His pasture.” It denotes the Gentile people; hence the Lord in the Gospel: “I have other sheep.” It denotes the Jewish people; hence David: “You who lead Joseph like a sheep.” It denotes a martyr; hence David: “We have been counted as sheep for slaughter.” [Col. 0887B] It denotes the damned; hence David: “Like sheep they have been placed in hell.”

Egg, properly speaking. It also denotes hope, because, just as an egg contains the hope of a living creature, so hope contains expectation of eternal blessedness; hence in the Gospel: “If anyone asks for an egg.” It denotes the counsel of evil persons; hence it is said of the wicked [Col. 0888A] through the prophet: “They have hatched the eggs of asps and woven spiders’ webs. Whoever eats of their eggs shall die, and what has been warmed will hatch into a basilisk.” For evil persons to hatch eggs of asps is to disclose by perverse works the counsels of malignant spirits that lie hidden in their hearts. To weave spiders’ webs is to undertake any actions for the concupiscence of this world; because they have no stability, the wind of mortal life undoubtedly carries them away. It is well added: “Whoever eats of their eggs shall die,” because one who receives the counsels of unclean spirits kills the life of the soul within oneself. “And what has been warmed will hatch into a basilisk,” because the counsel of a malignant spirit that is covered in the heart is nourished into complete wickedness; for the basilisk is called king of serpents. [Col. 0888B] Now Antichrist is the head of the reprobate. Therefore, “what has been warmed will hatch into a basilisk,” because one who receives within himself the counsels of the asp to be nurtured, becoming a member of iniquity, grows into the work of Antichrist.

## P

[Col. 0887]

[Col. 0887B] Covenant, properly speaking: a vow or commandment; hence: “They have made void my covenant.” It denotes a sacrifice; hence: “By the law, a covenant of salt.” It is called a sacrifice because salt was placed in every sacrifice. It also denotes a promise; hence the Father says in Genesis: “I shall remember my covenant [Col. 0887C] which I made with you.”

Chaff, properly speaking. It also denotes an evil person; hence the Lord: “But He will burn the chaff with fire.” Chaff also signifies empty glory, namely pride, which, like chaff, is scattered by the wind and is windy. It denotes sacred Scripture; hence Isaiah: “The lion, like an ox, will eat chaff,” that is, proud persons from among the Gentiles who have been converted to the faith will be refreshed by the understanding of Scripture, like a Jew converted to the faith. The literal sense is denoted; thus the aforesaid authority may be interpreted: the lion—that is, the heretic proud of his own ingenuity—will cling to the literal sense just as the ox, that is, the Jew, does. It denotes what is worthless; hence Job, speaking of Antichrist: “He will regard iron as chaff,” that is, he will despise the preachers of his time.

[Col. 0887D] *Paliurus*, properly speaking, a thorny plant. It denotes anyone powerful in malice and defending others in evil, as the prophet, under the figure of Babylon, rebukes the crowd of wicked persons and every perverse mind, saying: “Thorns, nettles, and *paliurus* shall spring up in its houses and fortifications.”

Cloak, properly speaking. It denotes charity, which adorns the human mind; hence Isaiah: “A short cloak cannot cover both,” because Judaea cannot love God and the devil at the same time. It denotes the sin of the flesh; hence the Lord: “If anyone wishes to take your tunic, let him also have your cloak,” that is, if you have confessed the sins of your mind to your superior, confess also the sins of the flesh, so that all may be forgiven you. Because [Col. 0888B] the cloak is exposed, the sin of the flesh, which is more manifest, is figured by the cloak. The tunic, which is more concealed, figures the inner sin that is not apparent. It denotes the robe of eternal blessedness; hence: “A rotten tooth and a weary foot is one who trusts in the faithless person in the day [Col. 0888C] of distress, and loses his cloak in the day of cold.” Gloss: “Because accursed is the person who puts his hope in man and does not know how to put hope in God, such a person can neither receive the word of life nor attain the dwelling of desired salvation; and he loses his cloak in the day of cold, because, even if in the calm of this present life he appears clothed in the habit of religion, on the day of judgment he will appear or be revealed naked.” It also denotes the adornment of virtues; hence Isaiah: “And a cloak of praise instead of a spirit of sorrow.”

Palm tree, properly speaking. It also denotes an outstretched hand. It denotes a blow of the hand; hence it is said of Christ: “Others struck His face with the palms of their hands.” It denotes the cross of Christ, which was made of palm wood; hence in the Song: “I shall climb the palm,” that is, the cross. The palm is called the cross [Col. 0888D] for three reasons: because of its substance, its circumstances, and its efficacy. Because of its substance, because the transverse wood of the cross was palm wood. Because of its circumstances, because we read in the Gloss on the Song of Love: “The characteristics found in the palm correspond mystically to the Lord’s cross.” The palm is dreadful in its root, rough in its bark, [firm in its strength], upright in charity, beautiful at its summit, sweet in the pleasantness of its fruit. So the Lord’s cross was dreadful in its root, because at first it was detestable by reason of the shame of the punishment; rough in its bark because of the penalty; firm in its strength because of Christ’s patience; upright in charity by reason of its end; beautiful at its summit in view of the resurrection; sweet in its fruit in view of our redemption. [Col. 0889A] Because of its efficacy, because, just as the palm is the reward of victors, so Christ through the cross attained triumph. It denotes victory, or eternal rewards; hence John: “And palms in their hands.” It denotes the righteous person; hence David: “The righteous shall flourish like a palm.”

By an elegant metaphor the righteous person is compared to the palm. For the palm is a tree dreadful in its root, rough in its bark, firm in strength, lofty in summit, delightful in flower, sweet in the sweetness of its fruit, upright in charity, and a sign of victory. So the life of saints or religious persons is dreadful in its root—that is, at the beginning to those entering religious life—because it inspires horror in foolish persons; hence in the Book of Wisdom: “We fools considered their life madness.” It is rough in its bark, namely in food, manner of life, and clothing; firm in strength, namely in constancy and patience; lofty in the eminence of virtues and works; delightful in flower, because virtues and good works flourish in it; sweet in the sweetness of fruit, because in return for labor it receives the sweet fruit of eternal life; upright in charity, because it raises the mind to contemplate heavenly things; and a sign of victory, because by the struggle through which it conquers the world, the flesh, and the devil, it will deserve a crown. [Col. 0889B] It also denotes the Church for the reasons stated above; hence Job, in the person of the Church, says: “And like the palm I shall multiply my days.” The palm grows slowly but remains green for a long time; so the Church reaches the state of faith through many difficulties, and, for the gathering of very many people, desires the glory of that same faith to endure longer.

[Col. 0889C] Branch, properly speaking. It denotes a saint adhering to Christ through grace; hence the Lord: “I am the vine; you are the branches.” It denotes someone converted through the preaching of the apostles; hence an authority of Jerome says: “Apostolic fellowship, unwashed, extended its branches as far as the sea,” that is, the apostles, regarded as vile, rejected, or cast down, converted many Gentiles to the faith of Christ.

Eyelids, properly speaking. They denote the open and hidden places of the Scriptures, through which sacred Scripture is opened and closed. These are, as it were, the eyes of God, by which He questions and tests the children of men—namely, those made new from their former state by faith—because good people are not wearied by obscure Scriptures but exercised by them, and are not puffed up by knowledge but strengthened by it. [Col. 0889D] Hence David: “His eyelids question the children of men.” His death and resurrection are called His eyelids. By these two things He tested the children of men, that is, His disciples; and this is what He says: “His eyelids question the children of men.”

They denote the intentions of the heart, through which the heart is opened and closed; hence David: “If I give sleep to my eyes and slumber to my eyelids,” that is, if I give carnal delight, signified by sleep, to my eyes—that is, to my wills or intentions, signified by eyes—and, to say more, if I give slumber to my eyelids, which is less than sleep, as though he said: “I shall not give it.” The person who sleeps clings firmly to sleep; but one who does not sleep but slumbers is sometimes repelled from sleep and sometimes returns to it. Similarly, one is said to sleep who attends wholly to earthly things; one is said to slumber who is sometimes drawn away from them and sometimes returns to them. [Col. 0890A]

They denote prelates of the Church; hence Job, in the person of the Church, says: “My eyelids have grown dim.” Those who watch carefully over the journeying of feet are rightly called eyelids; but when they do not understand many of God’s judgments, the eyelids of holy Church grow dim. They denote the prudent persons of the world, adhering to the perverse counsels of Antichrist; hence Job: “His eyes are like the eyelids of dawn.” By the eyelids of dawn we understand the last paths of night, in which night, as it were, opens its eyes while showing the way of the coming light. Therefore the prudent persons of the world, adhering to the wicked counsels of Antichrist’s malice, are like the eyelids of dawn, [Col. 0890B] because they assert that the faith which they find in Christ is, as it were, the night of error, and promise that veneration of Antichrist is the true morning.

Bread, properly speaking, daily food; hence David: “Those who devour my people like the eating of bread.” It denotes the necessities of life; hence the Lord: “Our daily bread.” It denotes the manna given to the children of Israel, and signifies the bread of angels, that is, Christ. It denotes charity, which refreshes us spiritually; hence Luke: “Which of you asks his father for bread?” It denotes one of the persons of the Trinity; hence in the Gospel: “Lend me three loaves,” that is, faith in the Trinity. It denotes refreshment; hence David: “My tears became my bread,” etc. It denotes sacred Scripture; [Col. 0890C] hence in Lamentations: “Little children asked for bread, and there was no one, etc.” It denotes the delight of eternal life; hence it is said in the Gospel: “Blessed is the one who eats bread in the kingdom of heaven.” It denotes the form of bread under which Christ’s body lies hidden; hence the Lord distinguishes visible bread from invisible; and the Apostle says: “And the bread which we break.” Thus Christ too is said to be eaten in parts, not with respect to His body but with respect to the form of bread. It also denotes Christ’s body; hence Paul: “Let a person examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread.” It denotes ecclesiastical unity; hence Paul: “We who are many are one bread in Christ our Lord,” etc.

Cloth, properly speaking. It also denotes higher and more stringent [Col. 0890D] teaching, which ought not to be offered to carnal persons; hence the Lord: “No one puts a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment,” that is, no one ought to offer higher teaching to carnal persons. It denotes impurity, because impurity is usually wiped away with cloth and clings to it; hence Isaiah: “All the righteous acts of man,” etc.

Paradise, properly speaking; hence in Genesis: “The Lord planted a paradise of delight in the beginning.” It denotes the present Church; hence in the Apocalypse: “To the conqueror I shall give to eat of the tree which is in paradise.” It denotes eternal life, according to the usual interpretation of the aforesaid authority. It denotes rest; hence in the Gospel: “Today you shall be with me in paradise.” This is not to be understood of the earthly paradise from which Adam was expelled, nor of the angelic paradise, [Col. 0891A] because before Christ no one ascended to that; but [of paradise], that is, of being in rest, which is to be with Jesus.

To prepare, properly speaking. It signifies to make ready; hence David: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ,” and elsewhere in the Gospel: “Prepare the way of the Lord.” It signifies to give or appoint; hence John: “In my Father’s house, etc., because I go to prepare a place for you.” It signifies to adorn, as when it is said: “He prepares the church,” that is, adorns it.

To spare, properly speaking. It also signifies to forgive sin; hence Job: “You have indeed numbered my steps, but spare my sins.” It signifies to restrain the evil persuasions of wicked people or demons, not so that they may not exist, but so that they may not condemn; hence David: “Cleanse me from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those of others.” It signifies not to spend, as when it is said: “He spares his money.”

[Col. 0891B] Leopard, properly speaking. It also denotes a heretic who deceives by various frauds, just as a leopard is marked by different colors; hence in the Song: “From the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards.” Thus by mountains of leopards are understood teachers of heretics who, when at times converted to the faith, become a crown to the Church. It denotes the devil; the aforesaid authority may be interpreted in the same way: the mountains of leopards are those in whom the devil dwells, and the Church is crowned from them when their hearts are converted to the faith. It denotes a sinner; hence Isaiah says concerning sinners to be converted: “The leopard shall lie down with the kid.” By the leopard is understood the sinner stained [Col. 0891C] with various sins; by the kid, the person who humbly recognizes himself as a sinner. The leopard lies down with the kid when one who was mottled with the stains of sins consents to humble himself with the one who despises himself and confesses that he is a sinner.

To give birth, properly speaking. It is used for making manifest or bringing into effect; hence David: “Behold, he conceived injustice and gave birth to iniquity,” that is, he brought it into effect or made it manifest. It signifies to create or reform through grace; hence in Jeremiah: “The partridge cries out: it has gathered eggs which it did not lay.” The partridge signifies the devil, because, just as a partridge broods over another’s eggs, so the devil often nourishes and cherishes in evil by seducing those whom God created or regenerated through grace, and gathers them for evil. This is the meaning of “The partridge cries out: it has gathered [Col. 0891D] eggs which it did not lay.” The devil cries out through heretics; he cries out through earthly tyrants; he cries out through tribulations; he cries out through varied temptations or suggestions. It signifies to renew; hence in the blessings of the candle: “May grace the mother bring forth new infancy.” It signifies to preordain vengeance or eternally beget the Son; hence the Lord says through the prophet: “Shall I not give birth?”—as though He said: “Indeed, because I have eternally begotten the Son, or have preordained within myself the punishment to be inflicted upon the wicked.”

Wall, properly speaking. It denotes Christ’s human nature; hence in the Song: “Behold, He stands behind our wall.” Christ stood behind our wall when He assumed human nature. It denotes the Gentile and Jewish peoples; hence we read that Christ is the cornerstone [Col. 0892A] joining two walls into one, that is, two peoples into the unity of faith. Sometimes it denotes human or angelic nature; hence we read that heavenly Jerusalem will consist of two walls, that is, angels and human beings. It denotes Christ; hence David: “Like a leaning wall and a tottering fence”; this was explained above. It signifies the hardness of sin, as it is written: “He built a wall.” To build a wall is to construct obstacles against oneself. It also denotes mortality, which prevents us from seeing—that is, comprehending intellectually—the divine nature of Christ. Hence, according to another interpretation: “Behold, He stands behind our wall,” because mortality is placed between us and God as a wall, preventing us from comprehending Him. Christ stood behind the wall when He took mortal flesh from the Virgin. [Col. 0892B] We lie crushed beneath the wall because we are naturally mortal; but He did not stand behind the wall substantially, because He was mortal by will, not by nature. He stood behind the wall in order to push it over. Gregory: “By dying, He destroyed our death.”

Part, properly speaking, God; hence David: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance,” that is, my inherited portion. It denotes division; hence Solomon: “Give portions to seven and also to eight,” that is, divide the sevenfold and eightfold order, giving the sevenfold to the Old Testament and the eightfold to the New. For the fathers of the Old Testament observed the seventh day, the seventh week, [Col. 0892C] and the seventh month; but the fathers of the New Testament observe the eighth day, namely the Lord’s Day, and the octaves of saints. It denotes a place adjacent to some region or city; hence we read in the Gospel that Jesus withdrew to the region of Caesarea Philippi, that is, to places adjacent to that city. It denotes a reason: “What part have we in David, or what inheritance in the son of Jesse?”—as though to say: “What reason is there for one to be chosen from a single tribe to rule the others?” It denotes a state, as is commonly said: Christ is immortal on His Father’s side and was mortal on His mother’s side, that is, according to His paternal or maternal condition.

To travail, properly speaking. It denotes thinking evil; hence David: “Behold, he conceived injustice.” It signifies laboring to instruct or form subjects; hence the Apostle: [Col. 0892D] “My little children, for whom I again travail weeping until Christ is formed in you.” It signifies God the Father’s generating the Son; hence Wisdom says that she is brought forth, that is, generated by the Father.

Little one, properly speaking. It also denotes first impulses; hence David: “Blessed is the one who will seize and dash the little ones against the rock.” It denotes Christ, who is called little both on account of human deficiencies and on account of innocence; hence Isaiah: “For a little child is born to us.” It denotes the humble; hence David: “Giving wisdom to little ones.” It denotes the simple and less intelligent; hence Jeremiah: “Little children asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them.”

To feed, properly speaking. It also signifies to instruct or form; hence the Lord to Peter: “Feed my sheep.” [Col. 0893A] It signifies to draw in wind; hence in the prophet Hosea: “Ephraim feeds on wind and follows the scorching wind,” that is, the ten tribes, signified by Ephraim, will be drawn into captivity to different parts of the world, from which diverse winds blow; and, as they feed on winds, so they will draw in various winds to breathe. It signifies to persevere, because from feeding comes persistence in life; hence one says:

> Envy feeds on the living; after death it rests.

Passover, properly speaking, means “passage” or “passing over.” It also denotes the evening hour at which the lamb was sacrificed on the fourteenth moon at evening; hence John reads: “Before the feast day of the Passover,” that is, before the ensuing evening hour in which the lamb was sacrificed. It denotes the paschal lamb; hence in the Passion: “Lord, where do you wish us to prepare the Passover for you?” It denotes Christ; hence the Apostle: [Col. 0893B] “For Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed.” It denotes unleavened bread; hence John: “They did not enter the praetorium, lest they should be defiled, but that they might eat the Passover,” that is, the unleavened breads. It denotes the Paschal solemnity; hence we read that Herod put Peter in prison, intending to bring him before the people after Passover. It also denotes the Sunday feast of the resurrection, which is evident.

Pasture, properly speaking. It also denotes sacred Scripture; hence David: “In a place of pasture He will set me.” It denotes the Church; hence the Psalmist: “But we are His people and the sheep of His pasture.” It also denotes eternal life; hence the Lord: “Whoever enters through me will be saved and will find pasture.”

Sparrow, properly speaking. It also denotes the light or unstable person; [Col. 0893C] hence David: “I trust in the Lord, etc., like a sparrow.” O heretics, how can you say to my soul: “Migrate to the mountain,” that is, to the Christ who is among us? For if I do this, I shall be like a sparrow, that is, light and unstable. It denotes a saint winged with virtues; thus the aforesaid authority may be interpreted: “Migrate to us, who are mountains, and so you will be like a sparrow, fortified with the wings of virtues.” It denotes Christ; hence David: “Like a solitary sparrow on the roof.” Christ was alone upon the roof when, rising from the dead, He alone in human nature ascended into heaven. And elsewhere: “The sparrow found herself a house, and the turtledove a nest,” etc. Our Redeemer is expressed by the sparrow, and the Church by the turtledove. For the sparrow has now found itself a house, because our Redeemer has entered His eternal dwelling; [Col. 0893D] and the turtledove has found a nest, because holy Church, moved by love for her Creator, employs frequent groanings and builds for herself, as it were, a nest—that is, the most peaceful rest of faith. In that nest, she cherishes in the bosom of charity her growing children, like fledglings growing feathers and warmed until they fly upward. It denotes reason, according to another interpretation: “For the sparrow found herself a house.” It also denotes the poor; hence the Psalmist: “There sparrows will make their nests,” because the poor receive the necessities of life from the rich.

Passion, properly speaking, shameful desire; hence Paul: “Therefore God gave them up to passions of dishonor.” A passion is called shameful because it both leads to the punishment of Gehenna, kills the powers of the soul, weakens [Col. 0894A] the body, and separates from God. It denotes concupiscence; hence the Apostle: “When we were in the flesh, the passions of sins, which were through the law, etc.”

Shepherd, properly speaking. It also denotes Christ; hence He Himself says: “I am the good shepherd.” It denotes a prelate; hence in the Gospel: “The hireling, who is not a shepherd”; and in the Song: “Feed your kids beside the tents of the shepherds.” *Pastor* is the name of a certain book among the Hebrews which we do not possess.

Father, properly speaking: someone who is a father by reason of upbringing or reputation, as Joseph; hence it is said in the Gospel: “I and your father,” etc. Father by reason of creation or re-creation; hence in the Gospel: “Our Father, who are in heaven,” etc. Father by reason of eternal generation; hence Christ says: “Father, if it is possible.” He is called father [Col. 0894B] by reason of spiritual conception, insofar as the human mind conceives Christ through grace; hence Christ says: “Whoever does the will of my Father.” Father by reason of lineage; hence John: “Your fathers ate,” etc., that is, your predecessors. He is called father by reason of antiquity; hence Abraham calls his brother his father, according to the saying: “Otherwise, she is my sister, the daughter of my father,” that is, of Aram, my older brother. He is called father by the law’s institution, according to which legal fathers were so called. For the law commanded that, if a brother died without offspring, the surviving brother should raise up offspring for his brother; and the child born was called the son of the dead man and not of the living one. Hence Heli was called Joseph’s father because, when Heli died childless, Jacob, his brother, raised up offspring for him and begot [Col. 0894C] Joseph; hence: “Jesus, as was supposed, son of Joseph, who was of Heli.” He is called father by adoption; hence David was called Nathan’s father because he adopted him as a son, as Luke says: “Who was of Nathan, who was of David.” He is called father by imitation; hence in the Gospel: “You are of your father the devil.” He is called father by invention; hence Christ says of Lucifer: “He is a liar and its father,” that is, the inventor of lying. He is also called father by reason of instruction and governance; hence Elisha says to Elijah: “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel.”

To be open, properly speaking. It also signifies to be widened; hence the Apostle: “My mouth is open to you, O Corinthians.” [Col. 0894D] It also signifies to be made manifest, as when it is said: “Scripture is thus open,” that is, clear.

To suffer is sometimes taken from “passion”: “The more patient a person is, the more merit he gains.” Sometimes it denotes patience: “The more someone suffers, the more patient he is.”

Poor, properly speaking. It also denotes the humble; hence the Lord: “Blessed are the poor.” It also denotes Christ, who was called poor with respect to worldly possessions and human deficiencies; hence David: “I am an only one and a poor man.” It also denotes the sinner who lacks spiritual riches; correspondingly, and by contrast, the person possessing spiritual riches is called rich. Hence John: “I know your tribulation and poverty, but you are rich,” etc.

[Col. 0895A] Pavement, properly speaking. It denotes the humility of hearers; hence Ezekiel: “And a pavement laid with stone around the court.” The pavement is rightly said to be laid, because souls, joined to one another in the height of reciprocal charity, are both called stones because of the strength of faith and laid in a pavement in the bond of humility. It denotes an earthly good, because, just as pavement is outwardly adorned with cement, so temporal good outwardly displays a certain sweetness of delight. Hence David: “My soul has clung to the pavement; give me life,” etc.

Peace sometimes denotes peace in time; hence in the Gospel: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.” Sometimes it denotes eternal peace; hence the Apostle: “And the peace of God which surpasses [Col. 0895B] etc.” And elsewhere: “I give you my peace.” It denotes the peace of the undivided Trinity; hence Paul: “And the peace of God which surpasses.” It denotes the peace of reason and sensuality; hence the Apostle: “Grace to you and peace in Jesus Christ.” It denotes feigned peace; hence the Lord in the Gospel: “I came not to bring peace upon earth, but a sword.” It denotes the peace of charity; hence David: “Let peace be in your strength.”

Sinner: one who is in sins. In an emphatic sense, “sinner” also denotes an obstinate person who is burdened by notorious crime and scandalizes others through wicked deeds; hence David: “But to the sinner God said.” Likewise, in an emphatic sense, Antichrist is called sinner; hence the Psalmist: “For the sinner is praised.” Likewise, “sinner” is also said in a depreciative sense, according to which [Col. 0895C] the statement “Break the arm of the sinner” may be read even of Antichrist.

Sin, properly speaking. It is called the punishment inflicted for sin; hence the Apostle: “Christ bore our sins upon the wood,” that is, the punishment for our sins on the wood of the cross. It is called the tinder of sin, or concupiscence, because every sin arises from it; hence Paul: “But sin, that it might appear as sin, by means of the good worked death in me.” For the tinder, or concupiscence, taking occasion from the law—because it was the more inflamed and burned, since a person always strives after what is forbidden and desires what is denied—worked death, that is, mortal sin, through the good, that is, through the commandment of the law, which was given by the Good and is directed toward the good. The devil is called sin, because the beginning of sin is from the devil [Col. 0895D], and he invites us to sin; hence the Apostle: “Concerning sin he destroyed sin in the flesh,” that is, he weakened the devil’s power concerning sin, that is, for sin. According to this exposition, the aforesaid authority is customarily explained thus: Christ destroyed sin, that is, he wiped away every sin through the things which he endured in his flesh; and this “concerning sin,” that is, on account of the fact that he himself was made sin, that is, a sacrifice for sin. It is called the guilt of a crime, that is, liability to the punishment by which someone is bound on account of sin; accordingly, after a homicide has been committed, the “sin of homicide” is said to be in someone, that is, guilt. It is called unbelief; hence Christ says: “When the Paraclete comes, he will convict the world concerning sin.” Concerning sin—understand, its own sin—that is, unbelief, because “they did not believe in me.” Concerning righteousness [Col. 0896A]—understand, yours, for he speaks to the apostles—because they did not imitate it; because righteousness and hope will be in you when you no longer see me, since then, inflamed with greater charity, you will be endowed with greater righteousness. And concerning my judgment, which they did not fear, because they did not believe that I would come to judgment; nevertheless, concerning that judgment it is already evident that the prince of this world has already been judged.

Breast, properly speaking. It also signifies a thought of lust; hence in Genesis it was said to the serpent: “You shall crawl upon your breast and belly.” The serpent—that is, the devil—crawls on its belly when, through human members subjected to itself, it exercises lust to the completion of the act. It crawls on its breast when it defiles in thought those whom it cannot defile in the work of lust.

[Col. 0896B] Money, properly speaking. It also signifies the mystery of holy teaching; hence in Job: “If I have eaten the fruits of my land without money.” The land is the holy Church; therefore, to eat the fruits of the land without money is to receive support from the Church but not to offer that same Church the price of preaching.

Cattle. It signifies someone devoted to carnal pleasures; hence David: “You have subjected all things beneath his feet,” etc., “and moreover the cattle of the field.” It also signifies the Gentile people, compared to cattle because of the foulness of idolatry; hence in Isaiah the cattle of Kedar and the rams of Nebaioth are mentioned.

Skin, properly speaking. It also signifies a temporal good; hence Satan says in Job: “Skin for skin will a man give” [Col. 0896C]; that is, a man would rather suffer loss in his outer skin, that is, in temporal good, than in his inner skin, that is, in the flesh; that is, he would rather lose a temporal good than suffer punishment in his body. It signifies the righteous person; hence martyrdom is signified by the dyed-red skins which covered the tabernacle. Thus in the Epithalamium of the Bride, that is, the Church: “I am black, but beautiful,” etc., “like the skin of Solomon.” There “skin” signifies the saints, who contribute to the adornment of Solomon’s temple, that is, to the adornment of God’s Church. It signifies a corrupt habit in which the sinner is entangled; hence the prophet Jeremiah: “Can the Ethiopian change his skin?”—that is, the sinner oppressed by a corrupt habit. [Col. 0896D] It signifies a human being subject to punishment; hence: “Why do you stretch yourself out, dead skin?” It signifies holy Scripture; hence David: “Stretching out the heaven like a skin.” It signifies a fool; hence Job, speaking of the conversion of unbelievers, says: “Will he fill a net with his skin, or a fish-trap with his head?” By the net or fish-trap are signified the faithful of the Church, who make one catholic Church; hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like a net.” It signifies holy women who, cleaving to the Lord, served bodily needs through outward ministries; hence Job, in the person of the Lord, says: “When my flesh was consumed, my bone clung to my skin”—which was explained above. It signifies a carnal impulse; hence Job: “You clothed me with skin and flesh.” The inner [Col. 0897A] person is clothed with skin and flesh, because when raised toward higher things, he is besieged by the assault of carnal impulses.

Feather or wing, properly speaking. It signifies the contemplative person; hence David: “The wings of the dove silvered,” because the contemplative man who belongs to God’s Church, signified by the dove, flies upward through contemplation and shines in eloquence. It signifies virtue or contemplation; hence the Psalmist: “Who will give me wings like a dove’s?” It signifies protection; hence David: “He will overshadow you with his shoulders, and under his wings,” etc.

*Per* (“through,” “by,” “during”) sometimes signifies time; hence David: “I will bless you through every day.” Sometimes place; hence in the Gospel: “They returned by another way.” It signifies instrumentality; hence in the Gospel: “The law was given through Moses.” It signifies occasion: “Through one man death [Col. 0897B] entered into the world.” It signifies formal cause, as one commonly says: “This was done through his malice,” or: “He did this through his wisdom or power.” It signifies entreaty; hence the Apostle: “I beseech you through the mercy of God.” It signifies personal distinction; hence Paul: “The Son is through himself, not from himself,” because he is from the Father, but is distinct from the Father. It signifies accompaniment; hence the Apostle, speaking of God the Father, says: “Through whom he also made the ages.” God the Father is said to have made all things through the Son because he worked all things with him. Yet in a higher consideration, the Father is said to work through the Son because the name of wisdom is appropriated to the Son. The Son is also called the Father’s hand, and the Father works all things through his wisdom; and just as someone works through his hand [Col. 0897C], so the Father is said to work through the Son. And lest he appear inferior to the Father, the Father is said to work through the Son rather than the Son through the Father; hence the Father says to the Son: “With you is the beginning,” not “with me is the beginning,” so that inferiority may be excluded from the Son.

*Per-* in composition sometimes signifies completion; hence in Genesis: “Therefore the heavens and the earth were completed.” Sometimes it signifies opposition, as when one says: “This man is perjured” or “faithless,” that is, acting against his oath or faith. Sometimes it is used for “very,” as when one says: “This man is exceedingly beautiful,” that is, very beautiful; as Priscian shows by adducing this example: “Very beautiful goods, not at all like yours.”

To strike, properly speaking.
