It signifies to kill; hence Saul: [Col. 0897D] “He struck a thousand, and David ten thousand.” It signifies permitting to be killed; hence God the Father says, “to the right” (*dextro*, sic): “I will strike the shepherd, and they shall be scattered,” etc., that is, I will permit Christ to be killed. Another text has “strike,” so that the prophet is understood to be speaking to God the Father. It signifies removing guilt in a person; hence in Deuteronomy: “I will strike, and I will also heal.”

To destroy, properly speaking. It signifies to condemn; hence David: “You will destroy all who speak falsehood.” It signifies to reject; hence: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise.” It also signifies to render shapeless; hence David: “I became like a destroyed vessel.”

Partridge, properly speaking. It signifies the devil, as we said above; hence Jeremiah: “The partridge cries,” which is called *perdix* because it often destroys those whom it had possessed in sins. [Col. 0898A]

Perfect is sometimes said of someone by reason of his action; hence in Genesis: “Noah was perfect in his generation,” that is, in comparison with those who belonged to his generation. Sometimes it is said by reason of a sign; hence in the Gospel: “If you wish to be perfect,” that is, if you wish to possess the signs of perfection, “go, sell everything.” It is said by reason of a vow; hence Augustine: “The perfect ought not to lie in order to preserve someone’s life.” It is said by reason of fullness; hence the Apostle: “We shall attain to a perfect man, to the measure.” Someone is called perfect by reason of the way; hence in the Gospel: “Be perfect,” that is, possess that perfection which you ought to possess on the way. He is called perfect in whom there is nothing superfluous [Col. 0898B] and nothing diminished, whether in act or nature, as God is; hence in the aforesaid authority one reads: “As your heavenly Father is perfect.” It is said by reason of consummation, in which sense those who are in the homeland are called perfect; hence the Apostle: “Then that which is imperfect shall be done away.” He is called perfect who has perfect charity; hence John: “Perfect charity casts out fear,” because imperfect charity casts out servile fear, while perfect charity casts out initial fear.

To perish, properly speaking. It also signifies to sin; hence in the Gospel: “He was dead and came to life; he was lost and was found.” This is understood of the Gentile people signified by the prodigal son, who had perished through guilt and came to life through [Col. 0898C] grace. It signifies not to rise again; hence the Apostle, disputing against those who denied the resurrection of the dead, says: “Therefore those who have fallen asleep have perished.” It signifies that a person ceases to be ungodly; hence in the Psalm: “You rebuked the nations, and the ungodly man perished,” that is, ungodliness ceased to be in him. It signifies to be rejected; hence David: “For the Lord knows,” that is, approves, “the way of the righteous; and the way of the ungodly shall perish,” that is, shall be rejected. It signifies to be condemned; hence the Psalmist: “They shall be weakened and perish from before your face.”

To permit signifies to allow; hence one commonly says that an abbot permits monks to eat meat, that is, allows it. It signifies not to forbid; hence in the Gloss on the Psalmist’s “Be angry, and do not sin”: “The law permits what is necessary,” that is, does not forbid it. [Col. 0898D] It signifies not to punish; hence it is read that Moses permitted the Jews to dismiss their wives, that is, did not punish the sin of dismissal. It signifies not to hinder; hence it is said that he permits evils to be done, that is, does not prevent their being done.

Person, properly speaking. It is called an individual substance of rational nature, that is, a substance which is so of rational nature that it is distinct from every other thing, such as a human being, an angel, or God; each of these is of rational nature and is a substance distinct from every other thing. Therefore the soul is not a person, because although it is of rational nature, it is nevertheless not an individual substance, since it is not separated from every other thing; for it is part of a human being and is not divided from him. For an individual is said to be what is fully divided from every other thing. [Col. 0899A] Hence Boethius, in the book *On the Two Natures and One Person of Jesus Christ*: “A person is an individual substance of rational nature.” Sometimes “substance” means the same as “subsistent”; hence: “The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons,” that is, three subsistents. It signifies someone endowed with a certain rank; hence in the Gospel: “Rabbi, we know that you are truthful, and you do not regard the person of a man.” It also signifies a property; hence: “The Father differs from the Son in person.” It signifies essence; hence Augustine: “To be a person is not one thing and to be an essence another; it is altogether the same.” It signifies one who holds some office in the Church; hence the Apostle calls them persons of different faces. Among rhetoricians, too, a person is one who, on account of an act, statement, or possessions, is brought into a case; [Col. 0899B] hence: “The subject matter of rhetoric is person and case.” Likewise, among those who treat comedies or tragedies, a person is an actor who, by playing roles in various ways, represents the different conditions of human beings; and it is called *persona* from *personando* (“playing a role”), as Boethius plainly shows in the book *On the Two Natures and One Person of Jesus Christ*. Among grammarians, a person is also the thing presupposed to speech; in this sense three persons are distinguished: first, second, and third.

Foot, properly speaking. It signifies Christ’s divine nature, insofar as footwear, that is, human nature, is said to be united to it; hence in the Gospel: “I am not worthy to loosen the strap of the shoe of his feet”; and elsewhere: “Do not swear by heaven, because it is God’s throne, nor by earth, because it is the footstool of his feet.” [Col. 0899C] It signifies Christ’s human nature, because as the foot is the lower part of a human being, so humanity is Christ’s lower nature; hence David: “Until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet,” that is, I shall subject them to you according to your humanity. It signifies preachers who run throughout the world; hence Isaiah: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim the Gospel,” etc. It signifies the latter-day righteous who will suffer persecution in the time of Antichrist; hence John: “His feet were like bronze.” It signifies the human affections that were in Christ; hence it is said: “When I saw him, I fell at his feet.” It signifies the human affections of others; hence in the Gospel: “He who has washed does not need except to wash his feet,” that is, to cleanse the affections of the mind from venial sins; and elsewhere David: “In [Col. 0899D] the snare which they hid, their foot was caught.” It signifies the weak in God’s Church; hence Job, in the person of the Church, laments over the conversion of the weak, saying: “They overturned my feet and oppressed my paths as with waves.” While these persons serve earthly works, they can be deceived by adversaries all the more quickly because they do not understand sublime things. Therefore adversaries overturn these feet because they draw the weak in God’s Church into the error of their doctrine. Feet that have been overthrown cannot keep the way, because all weak persons, persuaded by their persecutors’ promises, terrified by threats, or broken by tortures, turn aside from the straight path; and when any weak person sees the perverse prospering, the wave of imitation miserably plunges him into the sea of perversity.

[Col. 0900A] Rock, properly speaking. It signifies Christ; hence the Apostle: “And the rock was Christ”; and elsewhere: “They sucked honey from the rock”; this was explained above. It signifies faith in Christ; hence in the Psalm: “Blessed is he who shall seize and dash your little ones against the rock,” that is, who will restrain the first impulses from rising into consent and action, and dash them against the rock, that is, curb them through faith in Christ. It signifies the exalted power of heaven; hence the Lord, speaking to Job of a holy man under the name of an eagle, says: “He dwells among rocks.” By rocks are understood the lofty powers of the heavenly virtues; for among them the eagle—that is, the righteous person—dwells while awaiting their everlasting glory. It signifies the Gentile people, comparable to a rock because of the hardness of unbelief; hence in Isaiah: “Send forth the lamb, [Col. 0900B] O Lord, ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert,” that is, send Christ descending in the flesh from both Gentiles and Jews. It signifies the hardened heart of the Gentiles; hence Job says of the Lord: “He cuts out streams in the rocks.” By rocks we understand the hard hearts of the Gentiles; by streams, the rivers of preaching. Therefore the Lord cuts out streams in the rocks because he opened rivers of preaching in the hard hearts of the Gentiles.

Quiver, properly speaking. It signifies Christ’s flesh; hence Isaiah: “He hid me in his quiver,” in human flesh. It signifies God’s hidden judgment, as though the Son were saying: “The Father hid me in human flesh.” It signifies God’s hidden judgment or holy Scripture; hence in Lamentations: “He sent into my kidneys the daughters of his quiver,” that is, arrows, namely, words communicating judgment or holy Scripture. It signifies the scheming of the wicked; hence David: “They prepared their arrows in the quiver,” that is, heretics cloak their words with hidden contrivances. [Col. 0900C] It signifies God’s hidden counsel; hence Job, in the person of the Church, says: “He opened his quiver and fastened me.” Gregory: “As arrows are in a quiver, so judgments lie hidden in God’s secret counsel. An arrow is drawn from the quiver when an open judgment is shot forth from God’s hidden counsel.” And this is the meaning: “He opened his quiver and fastened me,” that is, he revealed his hidden counsel and wounded me by a public blow.

Phial, a glass vessel, is called from the Greek *phialim*, which in Latin is interpreted “glass,” or from *hio, hias*, because that vessel was very wide in the upper part [Col. 0900D] but narrow below; hence in the law God commanded the Jews to make phials. It signifies the persecution which the devil brings upon the saints; hence in the Apocalypse: “The fourth angel poured out his phial upon the sun,” that is, the devil poured persecution upon the saints, who shine in knowledge as the sun with its rays. It signifies preaching; hence in the Apocalypse one reads of the angel “who had seven phials”; by the angel is understood the order of preachers, by the seven phials useful preaching. It signifies the hearts of the holy faithful, in which devout prayers proceed; hence in the Apocalypse: “Each having harps and phials,” that is, having pure hearts like gold, full of adornments, that is, prayers.

Piety is the virtue by which someone is moved with compassion toward another. It signifies the worship owed to God [Col. 0901A], which is called *latria*; hence idolatry is customarily called impiety because it is opposed to piety. Thus the Apostle says that the wrath of God will come upon all impiety.

Sluggish, properly speaking. It also signifies one afflicted by acedia, who is lukewarm in his work; hence in Ecclesiasticus: “The sluggish man shall be stoned with the dung of oxen,” which was explained above.

Hair, properly speaking. It signifies a superfluous thought belonging to the old life; hence in Job: “When a spirit passed before me, the hairs of my flesh stood on end.” The sense is: when the human mind is raised to the height of contemplation, thoughts of its former life as it were arise, so that it does not contemplate God fully.

Fatness, properly speaking. It signifies an abundance of earthly things; hence of the ungodly man Job says: “He is armed with a fat neck” [Col. 0901B]; the fat neck is wealthy pride, supported, as it were, by many fleshly things through abundant possessions.

Fat, properly speaking. It signifies the proud; hence David: “Fat bulls surrounded me,” that is, Jews proud through abundance of earthly things. It signifies joyful: “May your burnt offering be fat,” that is, may it be pleasing to God; that is, may he turn the cross on which he was wholly offered into the joy of resurrection. Or, according to another exposition, “fat” means kindled with the ardor of charity, as: “May your burnt offering be fat,” that is, may your intention be enriched with the oil of charity.

A *piscina* is a pool in which there is no fish. It is called *piscina* by antiphrasis. It signifies a washing-place in which, formerly, the limbs of sacrificial victims were washed; hence John: “Now there was at Jerusalem the sheep-pool [Col. 0901C], having five porticoes.” It is called *probatica* from *probaton*, which means sheep or cattle, because the limbs of animals were washed in it. It signifies saints who do not cease to provide streams of teaching to their hearers; hence in the Song: “Your eyes are like the pools of Heshbon,” which is interpreted “girdle of sorrow” and signifies saints who, neglecting the transitory joys of the world, bind themselves with a girdle and live chastely and soberly.

Fish, properly speaking. It also signifies one occupied with worldly cares; hence David: “The birds of heaven and the fish of the sea.” It signifies Christ suffering; hence: “The roasted fish, Christ suffering,” in a certain prose hymn.

*Pisticum* means genuine; hence it is said that Mary Magdalene brought an alabaster jar of *nardus pisticus* [Col. 0901D], that is, uncorrupted by any foreign admixture; or the ointment was called *pisticum* from a place. Or *pisticum* means mixed, that is, blended with various aromatic spices; hence *pisticum* is said as though *pixicum*, because it was enclosed or stored in a box (*pyxis*).

Pitch, properly speaking. It signifies the seepage of sin; hence Solomon: “Whoever touches pitch shall be defiled by it,” that is, whoever imitates others’ sins is infected by them, because evil conversations corrupt good morals, and habits are formed through association.

Plant, properly speaking. It also signifies one lower in God’s Church; hence Isaiah: “From the sole of the foot to the crown there is no soundness,” because both lesser and greater persons in God’s Church suffer from the diseases of vices. It signifies intention; hence the prophet: “The sole of their foot is like [Col. 0902A] the sole of a calf’s foot.” A calf has a cloven hoof, and the intention which the Evangelists had in the Scriptures was twofold, because it invited to the two arms of charity, namely, love of God and neighbor. It signifies the end of life; hence of the wicked it is read: “His sole shall be caught in a snare”; for one whose life is bound by sin even to its end has his sole held in a snare.

To plant, properly speaking. It signifies to be incarnated; hence David: “And he shall be like a tree that has been planted,” that is, incarnated. Where something is planted, one thing is that which is planted, another that in which it is planted; thus in the incarnation the human nature united to the divine is one thing, and the divine nature to which the human is united is another. The sole of the foot is taken for a preacher; hence in the Apocalypse, of the four living creatures: “The sole of their feet was the sole of a calf,” [Col. 0902B] because holy preachers are signified by the name of oxen. It signifies converting to faith; hence Paul: “I planted, Apollos watered.” It also signifies planting by grace; hence David: “Planted in the house of the Lord, they shall flourish in the courts of our God.”

Plain, properly speaking: easy to understand, according to the way we are accustomed to say, “The letter is plain,” because it lacks the difficulty of obscurity. It signifies a heart polished free from the roughness of vices; hence Isaiah: “The impassable places shall become straight, and the rough places smooth ways.”

Plane tree, properly speaking. It also signifies God’s wisdom, which reaches from end to end; hence in the Book of Wisdom: “And I was exalted like a plane tree.” It signifies an angel; hence the prophet Ezekiel: “The plane trees were not equal to its branches.” Lucifer is said to have been made with many thick branches, because the greater his beauty, in that he was set over the other legions, the more beautiful he was rendered by the multitude of angels placed beneath him. Thus the tree in God’s paradise had so many closely packed branches because it held beneath itself the legions of heavenly spirits. [Col. 0902C]

Street, properly speaking: the broad way which leads to death; hence Wisdom says: “I see little children and observe a foolish youth who passes through the streets.” It signifies a heart enlarged by charity; hence it is said: “I was exalted like a plane tree beside waters in the streets”; or there “streets” signify saints enlarged by wisdom and charity. It signifies a multitude of people; hence it is said: “Wisdom cries out in the streets”; or there “streets” signify doctors through whom wisdom cries out. [Col. 0902D] It signifies the freedom of one’s own will, as Jeremiah says of certain persons of remarkable abstinence and continence who had returned to depravity: “They are not recognized in the streets.” Those who, in confidence of holiness, set aside the judgment of better persons and follow themselves, proceed as if through streets. But they are not recognized in the streets as though they showed something of their life when, by breaking their own wills, they kept themselves in the narrow path. It also signifies a more general command, just as by a lane is understood a stricter command; hence in the Song of the Bride: “Through lanes and streets I shall seek him whom my soul loves.” Or by lanes are understood the prophets, by streets the apostles; or by lanes those living the narrow spiritual life, by streets secular people who walk on the broader [Col. 0903A] way. Therefore everyone makes the circuit who mentally beholds all the saints who are or have been, and imitates them among secular people. Sometimes he finds what he can accomplish toward seeking the Bridegroom.

Cart, properly speaking. The Lord also called himself a cart laden with hay. It also signifies the bond of sin; hence: “Woe to you who draw iniquity with cords of vanity, and your sin as with the binding of a cart,” etc.

The Pleiades are certain stars called Pleiades, either because they are many, or because they bring rain. They signify saints; hence the Lord, speaking to Job, says: “Can you bind together the shining stars of the Pleiades?” The Pleiades were created so near one another and yet separate that they are together, yet cannot in any way be joined. They signify the saints, who amid the darkness of the present life illuminate us with the light of the sevenfold grace of the Spirit; sent to preach at different times from the very origin of the world to its end, they are in one respect not joined, because appearing at different times they were in some manner divided by reason of time, but they are joined through the intention of their minds. [Col. 0903B] It signifies the grace of the New Testament; hence this authority can be explained in another way: those Pleiades are seven stars, and therefore they indicate the grace of the New Testament all the more clearly because we plainly see that through it the sevenfold Spirit enlightens his faithful. Therefore our Redeemer, coming in the flesh, joined together the Pleiades, because he possessed the operations of the sevenfold Spirit both united and shining; hence Isaiah: “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom [Col. 0903C] and understanding.” Yet no human being possessed all the operations of the Holy Spirit at the same time: some had prophecy, others knowledge, and so with the rest. Therefore the sense is: “Can you bind together the shining Pleiades?” That is, some persons can possess the lights of certain virtues, but can they exercise all of them at once? As though he said: no.

Fullness, properly speaking. It also signifies totality; hence Paul says that blindness came upon Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter. It signifies charity; hence in the Apostle: “Charity is the fullness of the law.” It signifies abundance; hence: “From his fullness we have all received.” It signifies the time of grace; hence the Apostle: “But when the fullness of time came.”

[Col. 0903D] Full, properly speaking. It also signifies abundant; hence: “Full of grace and truth,” that is, abundant in grace and truth. It signifies one who is disgusted or rejects; hence in Isaiah, the Lord, speaking of Jewish sacrifices and rejecting them, says: “I am full”; as though he said: “I am disgusted by, or reject, your sacrifices, because they are not performed in the manner in which they ought to be performed.” It signifies someone consummated in good; hence in the Old Testament it is read of Abraham and Isaac that they died “full of days,” that is, consummated in good. It signifies laden; hence in Samuel it is read that Jesse sent Saul a donkey full of loaves, that is, laden, etc.

To rain, properly speaking. It sometimes signifies to water; hence Isaiah: “I will command the clouds not to rain,” that is, I will command the preachers [Col. 0904A] not to water you with spiritual teaching. It signifies that fullness of graces abounds; hence Isaiah: “Drop down, heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the righteous one,” that is, the Holy Spirit bestows upon Christ fullness of graces. It signifies that someone abounds in covetousness; hence David: “He rained snares upon sinners.”

Embroidery is work made with a needle, for *plumos* is interpreted “needles”; hence in the Old Testament it is read that the garments of the high priest were made with embroidered work, that is, woven with a needle. It may also be called embroidered work from a feather (*pluma*), because birds’ feathers are commonly painted in diverse colors.

Lead, properly speaking. It also signifies a sinner; hence of the wicked it is said in the Psalm: “They sank like lead in mighty waters.” It signifies sin, [Col. 0904B] hence one reads of iniquity sitting upon a talent of lead; for just as lead draws downward by its weight, so does iniquity. It signifies Judaea; hence Job: “Who will grant this to me,” etc., “or a plate of lead,” etc. What is written on lead is more quickly erased because of the metal’s softness. On flint, letters can indeed be impressed more slowly, but they are erased with greater difficulty. Therefore Judaea is not unfittingly represented by a plate of lead: it received God’s commandments without effort and did not wish to keep what it had received. Gentile society, on the other hand, is rightly figured by flint, because it could scarcely receive the words of sacred discourse to be kept, but kept firmly what it had received; while the iron stylus signifies God’s strong knowledge.

“More” properly means “greater”; hence the Lord: “You are worth more than many [Col. 0904C] sparrows”—understand, in value; and the sense is “of greater value,” that is, of greater worth. Sometimes it is used positively; hence the Apostle: “Much more the grace of God and the gift in the grace of one man, Jesus Christ, abounds unto more,” that is, unto many, in place of the word “many.”

Rain, properly speaking. It signifies divine grace; hence: “The Lord came down like rain upon the fleece,” that is, Christ’s grace first descended upon the Jews, while the ground of all Gentile peoples was dry; but afterwards it descended upon the ground of the Gentiles, while the Jewish fleece was dry. This alludes to Gideon’s deed, of which it is read that, as a sign of victory, rain first descended upon the fleece while the threshing-floor remained dry, and afterwards descended upon the threshing-floor while the fleece remained dry. Or this can be understood of Christ’s [Col. 0904D] incarnation; for as rain descends without noise upon the fleece, the fleece remaining whole and in no way corrupted, so Christ descended into the Virgin’s womb without the disturbance of flesh, the integrity of virginity remaining. It signifies the promise of eternal blessedness; hence David: “He made lightnings into rain.” Preachers sometimes flash with threats and sometimes rain with consolation and the promise of eternal things. It signifies prosperity, because rain produces joy; hence: “For protection and concealment from whirlwind and rain,” because Christ guards the Church, which is neither broken by adversities nor lifted up by prosperities.

Cup, properly speaking. It signifies the divine word; hence in the Song: “Your navel is a turned bowl, never lacking cups.” The preacher is the navel of the Church [Col. 0905A]: considering the weakness of human nature, he preaches it to others. If he is perfect, he expects only a heavenly reward and, as though revolving, works well with a ready mind. This bowl never lacks cups, because the word never fails preachers. It signifies the desire for the heavenly homeland through love; hence David: “And my cup with weeping . . .”

Punishment, properly speaking. It is also testing, as in Job; humbling, as in Paul; tormenting, as in hell; and so forth. It is purging, as in Mary the sister of Moses, whom the Lord struck with leprosy for correction because she had spoken against Moses, and who was put outside the camp for seven days. It is signifying, as in the man born blind, who neither sinned nor did his parents, but that the power of God might be manifested in him. It is initiating, as in Herod of Ascalon [Col. 0905B], in whom temporal punishment was a sign of eternal punishment. It increases merit, as in the saints whom God permits to suffer tribulations, so that they may thereby be humbled and so merit more, because power is perfected in weakness. It defiles in sin: this kind is not from God; all the others are from God. Hence a theological authority says: “Every punishment is from God.” It signifies sin, because sin, like punishment, defiles and afflicts, and often follows from a preceding sin; hence the Apostle: “Every sin from the apostasy of the first man to the final sin is both sin and punishment for sin.” Accordingly it is said: “It is just that he who is in filth should become filthier still,” that is, the things which delight a person while sinning are instruments of sin.

[Col. 0905C] Penance signifies outward satisfaction; hence in the Gospel: “Do penance, for [the kingdom] is near,” etc. It also signifies inward contrition of heart; hence in the Acts of the Apostles: “Do penance, and let each one of you be baptized,” which must be understood of inward penance. It signifies sorrow; hence in the Gospel it is read of Judas that, led by repentance, he hanged himself with a noose. It signifies change; hence the Apostle: “For the gifts and calling of God are without repentance,” that is, God calls his own and grants them spiritual gifts without repentance, that is, without changing his counsel and preordination; for as he preordained, so he does. It signifies baptism, because penance ought to accompany baptism in those who have discretion and are adults; and as sins are remitted in baptism, so also in penance. [Col. 0905D] Hence the Apostle, speaking against those who said that baptism could be repeated, says: “It is impossible for those who were once enlightened, who have also tasted the heavenly gift and become partakers of the Holy Spirit, who have nevertheless tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and have fallen away, to be renewed again unto repentance”—that is, unto baptism, that is, through baptism. Solemn penance is also so called by appropriation; Origen says of it that penance ought not to be repeated, out of reverence for the sacrament and lest it become cheap and contemptible.

To repent properly means to bewail sins. It signifies changing one’s work; hence the Lord says: “It repents me that I made man,” that is, I shall act in the likeness of one repenting, by changing [Col. 0906A] my work; for I shall destroy the man whom I created. Or: “It repents me,” that is, punishment holds me because I made man; as though he said: “I shall suffer for the human being whom I made.”

To defile. It signifies to destroy; hence the Lord threatened that he himself would defile his sanctuary, that is, destroy the temple. It signifies someone’s defiling himself with sin; hence David: “But God said to the sinner: Why, etc., through your defiled mouth.” It also signifies touching what is defiled; hence in the Old Testament someone was said to defile himself when he touched something defiled; and that defilement was not of the mind but of the flesh.

Pomum, properly. It signifies Sacred Scripture; hence it is said: “I have kept for thee all fruits, new and old,” that is, all the Scripture of the New and Old Testament. [Col. 0906B] It signifies the fragrant coming of the Lord, or the inward allegorical sense; hence Job, speaking in the person of the ancient fathers longing for Christ, or of the whole human race, says: “My days were swifter than a runner; they passed like ships bearing fruits.” It signifies a saint; hence in the Song: “Thy shoots are a paradise,” etc., “with fruits of apples”; for the growths of faith are a paradise of pomegranates, that is, of holy martyrs, who are aptly called pomegranates because they are red through outward suffering and the shedding of blood. By fruits are understood confessors, whose works are pleasing to the holy martyrs.

Ponere, properly. It also denotes to place beneath; hence David: “Until I place thine enemies,” that is, “I place them beneath.” [Col. 0906C] It denotes to impose; hence David: “Set, O Lord, a watch over my mouth.” It denotes to appoint; hence in the Gospel: “I have appointed you that you may eat.” It denotes to lay or produce; hence it is customary to say: “A hen lays eggs.” It denotes to permit to be placed; hence the Psalmist: “Make them like a wheel,” that is, permit them to be made so.

Populus, properly, a multitude of vices; hence David: “Hear, daughter, and see, and forget thy people.” It signifies the company of angels; hence it is read of Abraham that, when dying, he “was gathered to his people,” that is, joined to the fellowship of angels, then in hope of the future kingdom. It signifies the assembly of the Jews, who, in comparison with the Gentiles, are rational because of their worship of the one God; for *populus* is said to derive from *polis*, “city,” where men are governed under the same rule of life. [Col. 0906D] Hence David: “Why have the nations raged, and the peoples?” It signifies the assembly of the faithful, which is more rational than the Synagogue; thus it is customarily called the Church in comparison with the Jewish assembly called Synagogue, which means “congregation” and may also be a congregation of inanimate things. But the assembly of the faithful is called *Ecclesia*, as though “convocation,” which is not ordinarily said except of rational beings; hence David: “I will praise thee among a weighty people,” and elsewhere: “Save thy people.”

Porta, properly. It also signifies Christ; hence David: “Then he shall speak with his enemies in the gate.” The statement concerns the just man who, trusting in the gate—that is, in Christ—speaks securely against his enemies. Christ is aptly called the gate, because through him entrance [Col. 0907A] into the Church and into eternal life lies open. It signifies what is common; hence, in the same example, another exposition may be made thus: “Then he shall speak with his enemies in the gate,” that is, commonly and publicly; because a gate is something common and open to all, and by the gate what is common is understood. It signifies judgment, because judges used to sit in the gates; hence Solomon: “Her husband is noble in the gates,” that is, Christ in judgment. It signifies love of earthly things or fear of losing earthly things; hence speech is directed to the demons as follows: “Lift up your gates, O princes,” that is, remove the fear and love of earthly things through which entrance to man lies open to you. It signifies mortal sin; hence, according to another exposition: “Lift up the gates,” that is, O leaders of heresy, remove [Col. 0907B] from yourselves the mortal sins through which death enters. It signifies the day of judgment; hence: “They are shut up in the gate, and there shall be none to deliver”; for lovers of this world are proud in the present life, but at the very entrance to the kingdom they shall be struck by eternal punishment. It signifies a good action; hence Job, speaking in the person of the Church: “When I went forth to the gate of the city, I prepared my seat in the street.” For Holy Church goes forth to the gate of the city, that is, she exercises herself in holy actions so as to obtain entrance into the heavenly kingdom. It signifies a preacher; hence it is read that Jerusalem had twelve gates. It signifies a bodily sense; hence David: “Thou who liftest me up from the gates of death,” that is, who deliverest me from the appetite for earthly things around which bodily senses revolve. It signifies virtue; hence the Psalmist: “That I may declare [Col. 0907C] all thy praises in the gates,” etc., that is, among those established in virtues, which are the gates of the daughter of Sion, that is, of the Church. It signifies an ecclesiastical sacrament; hence the aforesaid authority can be expounded thus: “That I may declare all thy praises in the gates,” that is, among the faithful established in ecclesiastical sacraments. It signifies the devil’s power by which he held captives in hell; hence the angels who go before Christ’s soul as it enters hell say: “O princes of darkness, lift up your gates, O princes,” that is, remove from yourselves the power of holding captives in hell. It signifies the entrance to paradise; hence the angels going before Christ descending from heaven said: “And be ye lifted up, eternal gates, [Col. 0907D] and the King of glory shall enter,” that is, let the entrances of paradise be opened to Christ descending. It also signifies a heretic; hence: “The gates of hell shall not prevail against her,” that is, against the Church. It signifies the glorious Virgin; hence in Exodus: “This gate is closed.”

Portare, properly. It denotes to conceive; hence in the Gospel: “Blessed is the womb that bore thee.” It denotes to suffer with another; hence the Apostle: “Bear one another’s burdens,” that is, sympathize with one another’s infirmities. It denotes to imitate; hence the Apostle commands those to whom he writes to bear Christ in their body, that is, to imitate him in bodily afflictions.

*Posse* sometimes denotes the power by which someone is able, [Col. 0908A] as is said of Christ’s body, that is, the Church: “He was able to transgress and did not transgress.” This is said of Christ on account of his members. Sometimes it denotes ease or capacity, as when one deprived of his feet, although he has the natural power of walking, is said: “This man cannot walk.” Here natural power is not removed, but capacity. Sometimes it denotes possibility, as when it is said: “This man can be condemned.” This *can* should rather be referred to the outcome of the matter than to the thing itself, so that the sense is: “It is possible that he may be condemned for such a sin,” etc.; “that he cannot celebrate the divine offices,” that is, “that he ought not.” Sometimes it denotes obligation, as when it is said: “Offer sacrifice, thou who art lesser.” [Note: [Col. 0907] What these words mean, and how they relate to the word *posse*, we do not see.] Sometimes it denotes impotence rather than power, as when it is said: “This man [Col. 0908B] can die.”

Postulare, properly. It denotes to merit; hence David: “Ask of me”—that is, these are the words of the Most High Father—“O Son, by assuming flesh, suffering, and dying, ask this of me, and I will give thee the nations.” It denotes to cause to ask; hence the Apostle says of the Holy Spirit that he asks for us with unutterable groanings, that is, makes us ask. It denotes to present Christ’s human nature to God the Father; hence Christ is said to ask for us with the Father, that is, to present to God the Father his human nature and the things he did in human nature, so that he may have mercy on us. It denotes to demand, according to the customary expression: “This man’s merits demand that he be punished,” that is, require it.

[Col. 0908C] Potare, properly. It denotes to refresh with doctrine; hence in the Book of Wisdom: “He fed him,” etc., “and shall give him to drink of the water of saving wisdom.” It denotes to offer someone the bitterness of a corrupt mind; hence the prophet, speaking in Christ’s person: “They gave me gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.”

Potestas signifies a powerful person; hence the Apostle: “He who resists authority resists the ordinance of God.” It signifies the power by which someone is able; hence in the Gospel: “Knowest thou not that I have power to release thee?” It signifies grace which shapes a human being’s power to act well; hence John: “But as many as received him, he gave them power.” It signifies divine power; hence in the Gospel: “All power has been given to me.” It signifies an angelic order; hence “principalities and powers.” [Col. 0908D] It signifies the devil; hence the Apostle: “Your struggle is not only against flesh,” that is, against the powers of this air.

Potus. It signifies temporal delight; hence in David: “I mingled my drink with weeping.” It signifies Sacred Scripture; hence, according to another exposition, this authority may be understood thus: “My drink,” that is, Sacred Scripture, which recalls ancient things, “I mingled with weeping,” etc. It signifies the material and spiritual blood of Christ; hence in the Gospel: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood [is] drink.” It signifies lesser doctrine; hence the Apostle: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food.”

[Col. 0909A] *Prae* is sometimes used comparatively; hence Paul, speaking of Christ, says: “He has inherited a more excellent name than they.” It is used exclusively; hence in the Psalm: “How great is the Lord above all gods.” It denotes adherence, as when it is said: “This man died from grief,” that is, grief afflicting him or adhering to him; hence in the Gospel: “But the guards were terrified from fear.” It denotes presence; hence it is customary to say here: “We have this before all things,” or “before our eyes.” — In compounds *prae-* denotes precedence in place; hence in the Gospel: “The two ran together,” etc., “he ran ahead of Peter more swiftly.” It is also used for “very,” as when it is said: “God is all-powerful,” that is, very powerful. It denotes precedence in time; hence David: “Let us go before his face.”

[Col. 0909B] Praeco, properly: it is read that when Ahab, king of Israel, had been wounded, a herald sounded throughout the whole army, saying: “Let every man return to his city and to his own land.” It also signifies a preacher; hence John too was called Christ’s herald, that is, the voice of the Word.

Predestination is the preparation of grace, that is, that eternal preordination by which God from eternity ordained that the grace of justification should be bestowed upon his elect in the present, and in the future the grace of glorification. Hence predestination is the preparation of grace. It signifies foreknowledge of a future good according to higher causes, not according to lower ones—that is, miraculously, not naturally. Hence a prophecy concerning a future thing by miracle is called a prophecy of predestination; whence [Col. 0909C] in the commentary on Matthew: “A distinction is made between prophecy of predestination and prophecy of threat,” etc. It signifies merely the preparation of the grace of justification alone, which is given to someone in the present; hence it is customary to say that Judas was predestined with respect to present grace. It signifies foreknowledge, insofar as those foreknown are called predestined, if this term “predestination” is taken broadly.

Praelium, properly. It signifies a conflict between good and evil angels; hence John: “While Michael was fighting,” etc. It signifies a conflict between Christ and the devil; hence David: “The Lord strong and mighty,” etc., that is, mighty in conflict against the devil.

Praeputium, properly, that which was cut away by circumcision from the organ of generation; hence it is read in [Col. 0909D] Samuel that Saul promised David his daughter if he gave him a hundred foreskins of the Philistines, etc. Or perhaps there those called foreskins are the uncircumcised men. For Saul asked David to bring him the heads of two hundred uncircumcised Philistines, etc. It signifies a Gentile; hence the Apostle: “If therefore the uncircumcision keep the righteousness of the law, shall not his uncircumcision be counted for circumcision?”—that is, if the Gentile people keeps the law. It signifies the rite of the Gentiles; hence the Apostle: “Was anyone called in uncircumcision?” that is, in the state of the Gentiles: “Let him not be circumcised,” that is, let him not be compelled into Jewish rites. It signifies what is unclean; hence according to the law, the fruits of trees or vineyards in the first or second year were called “uncircumcisions,” that is, unclean.

Praesepe, properly. It also signifies the Church; hence [Col. 0910A] Isaiah: “The ox knew his owner, and the ass his master’s manger.” By the ass is understood the Gentile people, not subjected to the yoke of the law, which, having been converted to Christ’s faith, knows the Church through faith and charity. In it Christ, who was the grain of angels, became the fodder of men. Or “he knew the manger,” that is, he understood Sacred Scripture.

Praeter is sometimes used for “beside,” etc. Sometimes it is used exclusively; hence David: “For there is none other besides thee.” It is also used inclusively; hence it is read in the Gospel that God fed five thousand men, besides women and little children.

Pretiosum, that which is acquired at great price; hence David: “More desirable than gold and precious stone.” It signifies rare; hence it is said: “The word of the Lord was [Col. 0910B] precious,” that is, rare. It signifies meritorious; hence the Psalmist: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints”; and in the Book of Wisdom: “Not every sinner’s death is precious.” It signifies dear; hence it is read in the Gospel that the centurion’s sick servant was precious to him, that is, dear.

Primitiae signifies a certain portion between Pentecost and Lent. It signifies Christ, of whom the Apostle says that he is the firstfruits of those who sleep. It signifies the innocents; hence in the Apocalypse they are called firstfruits offered to God and the Lamb.

Primogenitus, properly. It signifies one before whom there was no one and after whom there was no one else; hence David: “Who struck the firstborn of Egypt.” One is also called firstborn before whom there was no one, even if after him [Col. 0910C] there is no other; hence Christ is called firstborn also according to his human nature, because before him and after him no one was born of the Virgin Mother, though he was born of her in a certain spiritual and principal manner. He is also called firstborn because he was the first to rise from the dead never to die again, and because he received the fullness of grace above all measure; hence the Apostle calls him the firstborn among many brethren.

Primus signifies someone by reason of eternity; hence Christ says: “I am the first and the last.” It signifies first in time; hence the Lord: “Thus the last shall be first.” It signifies first in place; hence in the Gospel Christ says of the Pharisees that they desired [Col. 0910D] the first places at table. It signifies first in dignity; hence: “Wisdom is first of every creature,” which must be referred to dignity, not to temporal order; for angelic nature was not created before the fabric of the world.

Princeps, properly. It signifies one who rules his thoughts by the judgment of great counsel; hence Job says of the Lord: “He pours contempt upon princes.” Those who rule their thoughts by the judgment of great counsel are often lifted up into the height of pride, and fall beneath the vices over which they rejoiced to have been victorious. Rightly, therefore, is it said: “He pours contempt upon princes.” But because those who seem at times to lie in vices run to the lament of repentance and raise themselves against the faults beneath which [Col. 0911A] they lay, it aptly follows: “And he lifts up those who had been oppressed.” It signifies an author of heretical depravity; hence Job, in the person of the Church: “The princes ceased to speak and laid a finger upon their mouth,” as though to say: When I was allowed to preach publicly, everyone not subject to my truth was terrified. It signifies Christ; hence it is read that the prince sat in the closed gate, eating his bread. The closed gate is the Blessed Virgin Mary. The prince sitting in the gate is Christ incarnate from her, eating his bread—that is, through the humanity he assumed, redeeming the human race and fulfilling the counsel of God the Father. Hence he himself says: “This is my food: to do the will of my Father.” It signifies the devil; hence in the Gospel: “For the prince of this world comes.” It signifies the angel [Col. 0911B] of providence appointed to guard; hence Gabriel says to Daniel: “I would have come to thee, but the prince of the Persians resisted me.” Gabriel was appointed to deliver the Jews in captivity; but the angel appointed over the Persians wished them still to be punished under the king of Persia, so that they might be more fully purified. It signifies an apostle or apostolic man; hence David: “Thou shalt appoint princes,” etc.

Principatus signifies honour or dignity; hence David: “Their dominion has been exceedingly strengthened.” It signifies an angelic order; hence the Apostle: “Neither angels nor principalities,” etc. It signifies Christ’s cross, through which Christ obtained dominion; hence Isaiah: “His dominion is upon his shoulder,” because he bore his own cross on his own shoulders.

[Col. 0911C] Principium is the same as beginning. It signifies a cause; hence at the beginning of the glosses on the Epistle to the Romans one reads: “The principles of things must be investigated,” that is, their cause. It signifies God the Father, from whom are all things; hence in the Gospel: “In the beginning was the Word,” that is, the Son was in the Father. It signifies Christ; hence John: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you.” It also signifies the whole Trinity, which is the beginning of things. It signifies one who breathes forth; hence the Father and Son are called one principle of the Holy Spirit.

Pro denotes place; hence David: “Sons have been born to thee in place of thy fathers,” that is, in the place of fathers. It denotes final cause; hence Stephen said: “My flesh was stoned for thee, my God.” It is also used for the expression [Col. 0911D] “according to”; hence in the prayer: “According to thy mercy, have pity on the soul of thy servant.” It is also used for “concerning”; hence in the title of this Psalm, “My God,” it is read: “At the end, a Psalm of David: concerning the reception or morning assumption,” that is, concerning the reception or morning assumption.

Probare is the same as to test or try; hence David: “They tested and saw my works.” It denotes to cleanse; hence Wisdom: “As gold in the furnace the Lord tested them.” It denotes to approve; hence David: “Lord, thou hast approved me,” etc. It denotes to demonstrate, as when one says: “Prove this to be true.”

Procedere sometimes denotes movement in place; hence it is read of Peter and the angel that they passed through one street. Sometimes it denotes movement in time; hence [Col. 0912A] Luke says of Zacharias and his wife Elizabeth that they had advanced in their days. It denotes to enter; hence in the Psalm: “Like a bridegroom coming forth,” etc. It denotes to be begotten; hence Christ: “I proceeded from the Father.” Or there it is used for “to assume,” so that the sense is: “I proceeded from the Father,” that is, I assumed human nature by his authority. It denotes to be breathed forth; hence in the Gospel: “The Spirit who proceeds from the Father.” It denotes to be manifested; hence in the Psalm: “Attend; proceed prosperously.”

Profundum, properly. It also signifies what is hidden and incomprehensible; hence it is read: “The heart of man is deep and unsearchable.” It signifies divine immensity; hence: “That we may comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth, length, height, and depth.” It signifies obstinacy; hence David: “The Lord said: From [Col. 0912B] Bashan I will bring back; I will bring back from the depth of the sea,” that is, from the depth of contempt for vices. It signifies Jewish iniquity; hence Christ says of himself in the Psalm: “I am fixed in the mire of the deep,” that is, in the mire of Jewish iniquity. It signifies the immensity of divine Wisdom; hence the Apostle: “The Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God.” It signifies hell; hence the prophet Isaiah: “Thou hast made the depth of the sea a way for the redeemed to pass over.”

Prope. Sometimes it denotes nearness in time; hence the prophet: “The day of the Lord is near.” It denotes nearness in place, as when it is said: “This man is near Seneca.” It denotes usefulness; hence: “The word of the Lord is near,” that is, the preaching of the Gospel is useful. It denotes harmony; hence the aforesaid authority can be expounded thus: “The word of God is near,” that is, consonant with reason. [Col. 0912C] It denotes propitiation; hence David: “The Lord is near to all who call upon him.”

Propheta, properly, one who by divine inspiration announces hidden events with unchanging truth. It signifies an expositor of Sacred Scripture; hence the Apostle says that the Lord established some in the Church as apostles and others as prophets, that is, expositors of Sacred Scripture. It signifies a wise man instructed by God; hence the Lord says to Abimelech concerning Abraham: “Now therefore restore the man’s wife, for he is a prophet.” It signifies one who pretends to be a prophet; hence false prophets are sometimes called prophets.

Prophetare is nothing other than to announce hidden events by divine inspiration with unchanging truth. [Col. 0912D] It also denotes to utter prophetic speech; hence: “But Caiaphas, being high priest in that year, prophesied, saying: ‘It is expedient,’” etc. For he was not a prophet in respect to himself, but in respect to us; Caiaphas did not utter this with the intention of prophesying. Yet the faithful person understands in this speech a prophecy concerning Christ’s death, made for the redemption of the human race. It denotes to expound Sacred Scripture; hence the Apostle says: “It is better to prophesy than to speak with tongues.” It denotes to speak strange things; hence Saul is said to have prophesied, that is, to have spoken things foreign to him.

Prophetissa: a woman who prophesies; hence in the Law Mary, the sister of Moses, or Deborah, is called a prophetess. Perhaps Mary was not called a prophetess [Col. 0913A] because she prophesied, but because she uttered Moses’ song, in which many things were prophetically said which perhaps she did not understand. It signifies the Holy Spirit; hence: “I approached the prophetess,” that is, the Holy Spirit, who is called prophetess because mysteries are revealed through him. He is designated in the feminine gender because the name *Ruha*, corresponding to the name “spirit,” is feminine among the Hebrews; or because he is second in spiritual gifts, he is called prophetess rather than prophet. For a prophet to proceed or approach the Holy Spirit is nothing other than for heavenly secrets to be revealed to him.

Proprium, one’s own; hence John: “He came unto his own.” It signifies what is appropriated; hence the aforesaid authority can be expounded thus: “He came unto his own,” that is, into the human [Col. 0913B] nature appropriated to himself and pure, such as it befitted him to assume; and here *propria* is in the ablative case. It signifies consubstantial; hence the Apostle: “God did not spare his own Son.” It also signifies that which belongs to one person alone; hence in the prayer: “O God, whose property it is to have mercy,” etc.

Propter sometimes denotes an end; hence David: “For thy sake we are put to death all the day.” It denotes benefit; hence: “Who for us men and for our salvation.” It denotes final cause; hence the Apostle: “Wherefore a name was given to him.” It denotes formal or moving cause; hence in the Song it is said: “Each man’s sword upon his thigh because of the terrors of the night.” It is also used for “according to”; hence [Col. 0913C] David: “Save me according to thy mercy.” It is also used for “lest”; hence the Apostle commands women to veil themselves “because of the angels,” that is, lest the angels—that is, the priests—see them, etc.

Proximus. It signifies one who is near by reason of place; hence it is said: “You shall call your neighbour who is close to your house.” By reason of time; hence in the Gospel: “The Passover was near,” and elsewhere: “For tribulation is near,” that is, the passion is near in time. By reason of conformity or imitation in action; hence good men are said to be like God, because they are conformed to him in goodness, as in Cato:

> Nearest to God is he who knows how to be silent by reason.

By reason of original origin, in which sense every person is a neighbour; hence it is said in the Law: [Col. 0913D] “Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.” It also signifies one by reason of a benefit bestowed; hence in the Gospel: “Which was neighbour to him who fell among robbers?” By reason of kinship; hence it was said to the Jews: “Thou shalt not lend at interest to thy neighbour”; and elsewhere: “Thou hast removed friend and neighbour far from me,” that is, kinsman.

Pruina, properly. It signifies the benefit of continence by which the concupiscence of the flesh cools or contracts; hence David: “For I have become like a skin bottle in the frost.” The skin bottle is our flesh; the frost is the heavenly benefit by which, as by ice, the concupiscence of the flesh is restrained. It signifies an evil man; hence the aforesaid authority may be expounded thus: “I have become like a skin bottle in the frost,” that is, retaining things entrusted to me among evil men. It signifies carnal desire; hence another exposition may be given: [Col. 0914A] “I have become like a skin bottle in the frost,” that is, just as a skin bottle does not feel frost, so I have extinguished carnal desire in myself. It signifies temporal tribulation; hence Solomon: “He who escapes frost shall fall upon snow,” that is, he who refuses to suffer tribulation in the present shall incur eternal condemnation.

Pruna, properly. It signifies the earthly mind, burning concupiscence, as the Lord says to Job concerning the devil: “His breath makes coals burn.” By burning coals we understand the minds of reprobate men aflame in earthly desires. Therefore the malignant spirit blows with his breath among coals insofar as, by hidden suggestion, he inflames human minds toward unlawful things. It signifies charity; hence Solomon: “Thou shalt heap coals upon his head,” that is, thou shalt change him to charity. [Col. 0914B]

Psalterium, a stringed instrument which, struck by the hand from its upper side, gives forth sound. It also signifies the book of David, which is sung to the sound of that instrument. It signifies devotion of mind; hence David: “A pleasant psaltery with a harp.” It signifies observance of the Decalogue; hence David in the Psalm: “Upon a ten-stringed instrument with a harp.” It also signifies Christ’s divine nature; hence in the Psalm: “Praise him on the psaltery and harp,” that is, according to his divine and human nature. It signifies Christ’s flesh, according to which he rose and ascended into heaven; hence David: “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp.” A psalm is the modulation of the aforesaid instrument produced by the touch of the hand. [Col. 0914C] It also signifies a section of the Psalter sung according to that modulation; hence: “At the end, a Psalm of David.” It signifies divine praise; hence David: “Praise the Lord, for the psalm is good,” that is, because divine praise is good. It also signifies good action; hence in the Psalm: “Thus I will sing a psalm to thy name,” that is, I shall act well to thy praise. It also signifies Sacred Scripture; hence David: “I will confess to thee in vessels of psalm,” that is, in the various parts of Sacred Scripture, in which spiritual meanings are contained as drinks in vessels.

Puer, properly; and *puer* is said to come from *pure*, that is, “under custody,” because he is under custody. It signifies a fool, and then is derived from childishness; hence Isaiah: “The child of a hundred years shall be cursed.” And after his resurrection the Lord calls his unbelieving disciples children, saying: “Children, have you any food?” Christ is called a child because of his innocence and humility; hence Isaiah: “A child is born to us.” It signifies a servant, and is said to come from *pure*, that is, custody, because just as a child is under custody, so too is a servant; hence it is read that, hearing the report of Jesus Christ, Herod said to his servants, that is, to his slaves. [Col. 0914D] It signifies one pure or just, and then is derived from purity; hence the Lord says in Luke: “My children are with me in bed,” that is, the saints are in eternal blessedness.

Pugillus, properly, is a diminutive of the noun *pugnus*, “fist.” It signifies what is contained in the fist; hence it is read in Exodus that on the table were twelve loaves of presentation, and upon each [Col. 0915A] golden dishes with a handful of incense. It signifies divine power; hence Isaiah: “Thou dost hold the earth in thy fist.”

Pugna, properly, also signifies a dispute of words when contradiction is not according to law, which among rhetoricians is called *antinomia*; hence the Apostle says: “Knowing nothing, but sick concerning questions and disputes of words,” etc.

Pulchritudo, properly. It signifies the adornment of the Church’s virtues; hence: “The beauty of the field is with me.” It signifies divine immutability; hence in the passion of Blessed Agnes: “Whose beauty sun and moon admire.” It signifies the fullness of Christ’s graces; hence David: “With thy comeliness and thy beauty.” It signifies cleanness from sins; hence the same writer: “Confession and beauty.”

Pulex, properly. It sometimes denotes worthlessness and lowliness; [Col. 0915B] hence David says to Saul in the Book of Kings: “Why dost thou pursue a dead dog and a living flea?”

Pullus. It signifies one subject to a wicked prelate; hence David: “And the young of ravens that call upon him.” It signifies one who imitates Christ through suffering; hence Job: “The young of the eagle lap blood.” It signifies a believer nourished by Christ’s body and blood; hence the aforesaid authority may be expounded concerning a believer. It signifies a penitent; hence Hezekiah: “Like the young of a swallow, so shall I cry.” The swallow departs in winter and comes in warm weather; therefore God is aptly figured by the swallow, who withdraws from man in the frost of unbelief and comes to man in the heat of charity. Hence the young of the swallow figures the penitent, who through renewal by grace becomes God’s child and is, as it were, the child of the swallow; and he cries to no other for remission of sins except God.

Pulsare, properly. It denotes perseverance in prayer; hence the Lord: “Knock, and it shall be opened to you.” It denotes frequent admonition; hence John says of Christ: “Behold, I knock at the door,” that is, I frequently admonish you to be converted.

Pulvis, properly. It signifies a sinner because, just as dust is barren, is not held together by moisture, and is scattered by a light breath of wind, so the sinner is barren of every work, is not watered by the rain of heavenly grace, and is scattered by the light breath of pride. Hence David: “Not so the wicked, not so, but like dust.” [Col. 0915D] It signifies venial sin; hence the Lord in the Gospel: “Shake the dust from your feet,” that is, venial sins from the affections of the mind. It signifies Christ’s disciples, alienated from faith during the Passion; hence Job: “Behold, now I shall sleep in the dust.” It signifies an assembly of virtues; hence in the Song: “Who is this that ascends,” etc., “and of every dust?” Sometimes it denotes lowliness or vileness; hence Abraham says to the Lord: “Let the Lord God hear me, though I am dust and ashes.” Sometimes it denotes repentance; hence Isaiah: “Sit in the dust, daughter of Sion,” that is, humble thyself through repentance. It signifies an earthly occupation or desire; and thus the Lord says to Job concerning the proud: “Hide them in the dust together, and plunge their faces into the pit.” For by a just judgment the Lord hides the proud [Col. 0916A] and wicked in dust, because he permits their hearts, which despise love for the Creator, to be oppressed by the earthly affairs that they choose. It signifies the obscurity of earthly thought; hence Job: “My flesh is clothed with rottenness and filth of dust,” as though to say: The carnal life which I endure is either defiled by the corruption of slippery action, or oppressed, from the memory of vices, by the darkness of miserable thought.

Pungere, properly. It denotes to pierce; hence the prophet says of evildoers: “They saw him whom they pierced.” It denotes to exercise; hence Solomon: “Prick the eye, and it will produce tears,” that is, exercise the mind, and it will produce a stream with labour. It denotes to crush in contrition; hence it is customary to say: “This man has been pricked unto repentance.”

[Col. 0916B] Pupilla, properly. It also signifies Christ’s human nature, as it were the pupil of the Father’s eye. And just as an inner ray is directed outward through the pupil, so God’s Wisdom comes to us through human nature; hence David: “Keep us as the pupil of the eye.”

Pupillus, properly. It signifies a saint whose father, the world, and whose mother, concupiscence, have died; hence David: “Judge the orphan and the humble, that he may add no more to magnify himself,” etc.

Purgare, properly. It denotes to winnow; hence the Evangelist says of Christ that he “will cleanse his threshing-floor.” It denotes to remit sin; hence it is read in Malachi that he “will cleanse the sons of Levi,” that is, will remit sins to the faithful.

Pusillus, properly. It also signifies humble; hence in the Gospel: “Fear not, little flock.” It signifies fearful; thus one is called faint-hearted, as though having a little heart.

Putatio signifies opinion, derived from *puto, -as*, “to think.” It signifies the cutting away of superfluities from vines or trees, and in this sense is derived from *puto, -as*, “to cleanse.” It signifies the cleansing of sins; hence in the Song: “The time of pruning has come.” The time of pruning is called the time of grace, in which human beings are cleansed of vices through the grace of Jesus Christ.

Puteus, properly. It also signifies the Church; for as a well gives material drink, so the Church gives spiritual drink. Hence in the Song: “Fountain of gardens, well [Col. 0916D] of living waters,” etc. It signifies a heretic; hence John: “The smoke of the well rose up,” that is, the corrupt doctrine of heretics. It signifies the depth of sin; hence David: “Let not the well shut its mouth over me.” It signifies hell, according to another exposition in the same example.

Putredo, properly. It also signifies concupiscence; hence Job: “I said to rottenness: Thou art my father.” It signifies sin; hence Habakkuk: “Let rottenness enter into my bones.”

Putrere, properly. It denotes to be corrupted by sin; hence David: “They have grown rotten and corrupt.” It denotes to persevere in sin; hence the prophet: “The beasts have utterly rotted in their dung.”

Putridum, properly. It also signifies a heretic, who [Col. 0917A] is called a rotten member of the Church because he corrupts both himself and others; Sacred Scripture frequently speaks of such rotten members.

Pyrgus signifies a square on a chessboard. It also signifies the critical point [Col. 0918A] of life; hence a certain versifier says in a poem:

> At the final square of life,  
> Protect us, gracious Virgin.

Q

[Col. 0917]

[Col. 0917A] Quadrans signifies the smallest weight, containing two *minutae*; hence it is read that a poor little woman offered two *minutae*, which is a *quadrans*. It also signifies the smallest sin; hence in the Gospel: “Amen I say to thee: Thou shalt not go out from there until thou hast paid the last [Col. 0917B] quadrans,” that is, until thou hast atoned even for the smallest sin—which will never happen, etc. Or the last *quadrans* signifies earth, because there are four elements, and earth is the lowest and basest quarter: fire signifies charity, air eternal life, water baptism, and earth every corruption. And this is “until he pays the last quadrans,” that is, all sins signified by earth.

Quadriga, properly, a four-horse chariot. It signifies evangelical doctrine, which rests upon four wheels, that is, the four Evangelists. This chariot is said to be Aminadab’s, that is, Christ’s; for Aminadab is interpreted “willing,” while Christ willingly offered himself to God the Father upon the altar of the cross. Hence in the Song: “My soul was greatly troubled because of the chariots of Aminadab.” This chariot, moreover, is called Christ’s [Col. 0917C] because evangelical doctrine was set forth concerning Christ and tends toward God, and through it faith in Christ has been spread throughout the whole world. It signifies the assembly of the saints; hence Habakkuk: “And thy chariots are salvation.”

Quadruplex (“fourfold”) is singular in expression but plural in meaning; for it is equivalent to the noun “four,” so that the sense is: “The understanding of Holy Scripture is fourfold,” that is, there are four understandings of Holy Scripture. Sometimes it does not refer to a plurality of things but of modes, as when one says: “Holy Scripture is fourfold,” that is, it is understood in four ways. Sometimes “fourfold” also means repeated four times. Thus Jerome says in the Prologue that Jeremiah lamented [Col. 0917D] the destruction of Jerusalem with a fourfold alphabet, that is, with the alphabet repeated four times, because he repeats the letters of the alphabet four times according to their order, placing them at the beginnings of the verses.

Quadrus or quadratus: a square or squared stone has four equal sides. It also signifies one made square by holy virtues; hence we read in the Apocalypse that the heavenly Jerusalem was built from squared stones, that is, saints.

To seek, properly. It also signifies to imitate, because whoever seeks another follows that person’s footsteps; hence Isaiah: “Seek the Lord while he may be found; seek, and you shall find.” It denotes to ask or inquire; hence the Lord says through the prophet: “I was found by those who did not seek me,” that is, by the Gentiles who did not inquire about me. It denotes to investigate; hence: “I sought and did not find,” that is, I investigated Jesus in the Holy Scriptures, but did not [Col. 0918A] find him through repentance, that is, through understanding.

Question. It signifies a proposition brought forward in doubt, as when it is asked whether some righteous person is saved by merits. “Question” also means the doubtful matter about which a question is made; accordingly, a question is divided [Col. 0918B] into the question that seeks and the question sought. It also means an answer extorted from an accused person by tortures; hence we read that one must trust interrogations under torture. Accordingly, interrogators are called executioners, because they extort truth from accused persons by tortures.

Qualis (“of what sort”) is sometimes used indefinitely; hence: “God is not qualis,” that is, he is without quality. It is used interrogatively and signifies quality; hence it is said in the Song: “What sort is thy beloved?” It is used relatively and predicates the divine nature, as when it is said: “Such as the Father is, such is the Son.” The sense is: by whatever qualitative name the divine nature is predicated of the Father, by that name it is predicated of the Son: if the Father is just, the Son is just; if the Father is good, the Son is good. The uses of the word quantus (“how great”) [Col. 0918C] in Holy Scripture are likewise the same as those of qualis.

Quam (“than,” “how”) is used comparatively; hence Cain: “My iniquity is greater than that I may deserve pardon,” that is, my iniquity does not deserve pardon, or pardon is not due to my iniquity. It is also used in a preferential or negative sense; hence David: “It is good to hope in the Lord rather than to hope in princes.” It is used admiringly or commendatorily; hence David: “Behold how good and how pleasant.” It is used copulatively; hence: “God will repay both the good and the evil according to their merits,” that is, the good and the evil. It is used equivalently; hence Statius: “God is good as well as just,” that is, equally good and just. And Seneca says: “Let it be as much to you to be praised by base persons as to be praised for base things.”

[Col. 0918D] Quando (“when”) denotes eternity; hence Boethius: “There was a when when there was time.” It denotes time, and then is sometimes used interrogatively; hence David: “When shall I come and appear?” It is used indefinitely; hence David: “Lest at any time he seize my soul like a lion.” It is used relatively; hence the Lord says to the Samaritan woman: “There will be a time when God will be worshipped neither here nor there,” that is, in which time.

Fourth. Sometimes it denotes rank in dignity, as when I say: “This man holds the fourth place in the Church.” Sometimes it denotes order in the world; hence in Daniel: “Behold, I see four men walking in the midst of the fire, and the appearance of the fourth is like the Son of God.” Sometimes it denotes chronological order; hence we read: “Job was fourth in Esau.” Sometimes it denotes order in place, according to the common saying: “This man or that sits fourth at table.”

[Col. 0919A] Quasi (“as if”), properly. It denotes the truth of a thing; hence John: “We saw his glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father,” that is, truly that of the Only-begotten. It is used doubtfully in the sense of “about”; hence Luke: “He was there beginning at about thirty years of age.” It denotes likeness; hence Job: “He comes forth like a flower and is crushed.” Likewise: “Who is this that comes up like the dawn?” It denotes impropriety; hence of the Lord: “He will judge as a mighty man made drunken by wine.”

Shaking. Properly, it signifies the crushing of a thing. It also signifies God’s vengeance; hence David: “And the shaking ceased,” that is, the execution of vengeance which God exercised upon the children of Israel, etc.

-que is sometimes used merely as an expletive, as here: “And God said.” It is used copulatively. It is also used comparatively, [Col. 0919B] as appears from various examples.

The oak, properly, is a tree. It signifies someone exalted in secular dignity; hence the prophet: “The Lord shall be exalted above the oaks of Bashan.” It signifies a believer: “And it shall be for a display like the terebinth, and like the oak that has cast off its fruits: the holy seed shall be that which remains in it.”

Gain, properly, means profit. It also signifies piety; hence Paul: “Piety with sufficiency is great gain.”

Quia (“because,” “that”) is used expletively and causally, as is clear. It is used in place of quod (“that”), as in the Gospel: “I told you quia I am,” that is, “that I am.” It denotes ease; hence the Apostle: “I obtained mercy [Col. 0919C] because I persecuted the Church of God through ignorance,” that is, I obtained mercy more readily because of ignorance.

Quidam (“a certain one”) sometimes denotes division, as when I say: “A certain man runs”; and elsewhere in the Gospel: “There are certain persons among those standing.” Sometimes it denotes impropriety; hence Boethius: “Blindness is a certain form,” as though to say: it is not properly a form. Sometimes it denotes ignorance of the matter; hence Christ says of himself: “A certain man made a great supper.” It denotes low rank or abasement; hence in Christ’s Passion we read: “They compelled a certain Simon of Cyrene,” that is, one lowly and abased; and in the Acts of the Apostles: “A certain Simon,” that is, a lowly man.

Quin is an adversative conjunction. Sometimes it is used [Col. 0919D] adversatively; hence we say: “I shall not desist until I do that.” It is used preferentially; hence Luke: “Quinimo quin,” that is, “why not?” Then imo is not used [Col. 0920A] adversatively but preferentially; or quinimo is one word and is used for imo, “rather.”

Quis (“who?”) sometimes denotes impossibility; hence Isaiah: “Who shall declare his generation?” It denotes charity; hence the Psalmist: “What is man, that thou art mindful of him?” that is, how lowly and how frail he is. It denotes quantity; hence David: “What man shall live and not see death?” that is, how great a man? It denotes wonder; hence Isaiah: “Who is this that comes from Edom?” The angels marvel at Christ’s ascension into heaven and therefore ask, saying: “Who is this?” It denotes removal or incomparability; hence David: “Who is like thee among the gods, O Lord?” It denotes likeness; hence Job: “Who can make the clean from the unclean?” It denotes doubt; hence in the Gospel: “Who art thou, that we may give an answer [Col. 0920B] to these?” It denotes origin or country; hence Adrastus, asking the origin or native country of Polynices, says:

> “From what Argos do you come?”

That is, from what people or country? And if quis in Holy Scripture commonly asks either the property of a thing, its name, or its origin—as concerning the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin: “Who is this who comes up like the rising dawn, beautiful, etc.?”—or, in the second way, quis asks concerning quality, that is, the substance of a thing and what that substance is like. Thus, if someone in the night asked concerning a person arriving, not knowing whether it was a human being or a beast, a man or a woman, that person would be asking about the substance of the thing in itself.

[Col. 0920C] Quod (“that”) is used determinatively; hence the Lord says to Satan: “Hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on earth?” It is used causally; hence the Lord: “Because thou didst not know the time.” It is used adjunctively for ut (“that,” “in order that”); hence in Judges Achsah says to her father: “I desire that thou give me the lower watered land.” It is used concomitantly; hence: “God, in that he is just, has mercy.”

Quoniam is a rational conjunction. Sometimes it is used as a sign; hence in the Gospel: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much,” that is, the forgiveness of many sins was a sign of great love in Mary Magdalene. Sometimes it denotes a cause from what precedes, as David: “He saved me, because he willed me.” Sometimes it denotes a cause from what follows, as in the Psalm: “Because thou hast struck all who opposed me without cause, thou hast broken the teeth of sinners.”

## R

[Col. 0919]

[Col. 0919D] Root, properly. It signifies origin; hence in the Epistle to Timothy: “Covetousness is the root of all evils.” It signifies the Lord’s incarnation; hence Job, speaking in the person of the Church: “My root is laid open beside the waters.” By the root of the Church we understand the incarnation itself of the Redeemer, which was laid open beside the water when the invisible Lord, through the assumption of his humanity, became visible to our sight. Hence David: “And he shall be [Col. 0920D] like a tree planted beside the streams of waters,” which are the daily passing-away of dying peoples. It signifies holy preaching; hence Job says of the righteous under the designation of a tree: “Though his root grow old in the earth, and his trunk die in the dust, at the scent of water it shall bud and put forth foliage as when first planted.” The root of the righteous is holy preaching, because he arises from it and is sustained by it. [Col. 0921A] Earth or dust is the sinner, to whom by the Creator’s voice it is said: “Thou art earth and shalt go into earth; thou art dust and shalt return to dust.” Therefore the root of the righteous grows old in the earth, because his preaching is despised in the hearts of the wicked; and the trunk dies in the dust, because his body is worn away among the hands of persecutors. It signifies a foundation or support; hence it is said of Antichrist: “Thou shalt pluck up thy root from the land of the living,” that is, those upon whom you rest or who support you. It signifies Christ; hence Isaiah: “In that day there shall be a root of Jesse, who stands.” It signifies charity; hence in the Gospel: “And these have no root.” It signifies intention; hence in the Gospel: “And the axe is laid to the root of the tree,” that is, God judges only according to intention. It signifies an end; thus the foregoing authority may be explained: “Now the axe is laid to the root of the tree,” that is, God judges the end of a human being or of a work. It signifies a predecessor; hence: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse”; and the Apostle: “If the root is holy, so also are the branches.” It signifies hidden thought; hence it is said through Job concerning the unrighteous rich man: “His substance shall not be inhabited or endure, nor shall he send forth his root into the earth.” He is rooted in virtues whose mind God inhabits; but because the thought of the proud man is not inhabited under the grace of its Maker, he is surely not rooted in virtues, because inwardly he is empty. For this reason it is said: “It shall not be inhabited”; but because he is transitory, it rightly follows: “Nor shall his substance endure.” Therefore it is openly added: “Nor shall he send forth his root into the earth”; by earth eternal blessedness is signified. [Col. 0921C] Thus the unrighteous man does not send his root into the earth, because he never plants the thought of his heart in the desire for eternal life.

Branch, properly. It signifies one descended from another, who is metaphorically called a branch; because, just as branches proceed from trees, so descendants proceed from predecessors. Hence the Apostle: “If the root is holy, so also are the branches,” that is, the descendants.
