It signifies a work; hence Truth says through the prophet, signifying the malice of ancient enemies: “He made the vine desolate, or into a desert; he stripped and laid bare the fig tree”; elsewhere: “Its branches were broken.” For when malignant spirits lie in wait, God’s vine is made a desert when the soul, full of virtues, is scattered by the desire for human praise. [Col. 0921D] This people strips God’s fig tree, because, seizing the deceived mind into the appetite for favor, in order to draw it into display, it removes from it the covering of humility. And it strips it bare, because, once the bark is taken away, the branches of this fig tree wither. Here one must carefully observe the deeds of the arrogant displayed before human eyes; hence: “They desire to please; therefore they wither.”

Frog, properly. It signifies a philosopher, comparable to a frog because of the overflowing abundance of speech; hence David: “And he gave their land,” because philosophers and heretics concern themselves with earthly things. It signifies worldly fear or earthly love; hence it is said that a frog thrown into a dog’s mouth renders the dog mute, because often a prelate ceases from correction or from pronouncing an ecclesiastical sentence, touched by worldly fear or earthly love.

> [Note: [Col. 0921D] Perhaps it should more correctly be read: “ceases from correction or from the pronouncement of an ecclesiastical sentence.” The edition has, corruptly: “ceases from correction [Col. 0922D] or from the Church’s pronouncement of an ecclesiastical sentence.”]

To seize, properly, means to merit; hence Christ: “I paid what I had not seized.” It denotes to seduce; hence David: “Lest at any time he seize my soul like a lion.”

Robbery, properly, means the usurpation of another’s property; hence Paul says of Christ that he did not consider equality with God a robbery, because he is equal to the Father according to divinity and less than the Father according to humanity.

Reason is the power of the soul by which the soul comprehends the inherence of a property in a subject, according to which it considers what a thing is, how great it is, and what sort of thing it is. Hence Augustine: “There are five excursions [Col. 0922B] of the soul: sense, imagination, reason, intellect, and intelligence.” Boethius likewise says in the book *On the Trinity*: “In natural matters one ought to proceed rationally, in mathematical matters according to discipline, in divine matters intellectually.” It signifies the power of the soul by which the soul is moved toward contemplation of heavenly things; in this sense a distinction is commonly made between sensuality and reason. Ratio signifies arrangement; hence Jerome says that Christ confounded the Jews by a two-pronged argument. It signifies instruction; hence the Apostle says that the believer is bound to render an account to almighty God concerning faith. It signifies cause; hence Gregory: “Faith has no merit where human reason supplies proof,” that is, knowledge gained of things through inferior causes, [Col. 0922C] namely through the substantial natures of things, is not faith but knowledge. In this sense we commonly say: “What is the reason for this saying?” It signifies reckoning; hence in the Gospel: “Render an account of thy stewardship.” It also signifies dialectic; hence Boethius: “Every method of reasoning is an argument, producing belief concerning a doubtful matter.” It signifies the firm connection of existence with its subject; hence Hilary: “Truth is the ratio of a thing’s substance,” that is, the settled connection of a substantial property with its subject. It signifies punishment; hence in the Gospel: “For every idle word thou shalt render an account,” that is, thou shalt pay a fitting penalty. It signifies the Son of God, who is for the same reason called the Word—not in the sense of an uttered word, but of an inward word, that is, intellect or reason—because, just as reason or intellect [Col. 0922D] proceeds from the soul and is distinct from it, so the Son proceeds from his Father and is distinct from him. Hence among the Greeks he is called *logos*, that is, “reason.”

To depart, properly. It signifies to delay help; hence David: “Why hast thou departed far away?” It denotes not applying correction; hence the Lord says to the Synagogue through the prophet: “My zeal has departed from thee.” It denotes withholding grace; hence we read in Samuel that the Spirit of the Lord departed from King Saul.

To recount. It denotes to repeat; hence we read in a certain prayer: “The necessity having been recounted and the feast of the Nativity repeated.” It denotes to count; hence in Numbers [Col. 0923A] many thousands of Israelite men are said to have been counted.

Right, properly. It signifies just; hence the Psalmist: “The Lord is sweet and right.” It signifies something formed with a distinct end; hence David: “Rejoice in the Lord, etc., all ye upright in heart.” It signifies something erect; hence the Psalmist: “Praise befits the upright,” that is, those who do not bend down toward love of earthly things, but rise up toward divine love.

To render is the same as to pay; hence in the Gospel: “Pay what thou owest.” It denotes to recompense; hence we read that God will render to each according to his works. It also denotes to emit, according to our customary saying that fire gives off harmful heat.

To redeem, properly, means to free; hence David: “Redeem [Col. 0923B] me from the calumnies of men.” It denotes setting down an equivalent price for a thing bought. Hence we read that Christ redeemed the human race with his own blood, because, when man had been bought by the devil through pride, Christ gave an equivalent price for man’s liberation—indeed a greater one—because humility in Christ was greater than pride in Adam.

Referre. It signifies to stand; hence it is customary to say: “It concerns the emperor,” that is, it pertains to the emperor. In this sense the verb is impersonal and is compounded from *res* and the verb *fert*, and the first syllable is lengthened. Sometimes it is formed from the inseparable preposition *re-* and *fero, fers*; in this sense it is used for *reporto*, “to bring back,” as when it is said that the children of Israel brought all questions to Samuel. [Col. 0923C] It denotes to relate, as when one says: “He referred this to me,” that is, he narrated it.

To reign, properly, means to rule; hence the Apostle: “Death reigned from Adam,” and elsewhere: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body,” that is, let it not rule. It denotes to govern; hence God is said to reign in the saints. It denotes to glory; hence it is said of the righteous: “They shall judge nations,” that is, they shall reign eternally.

Kingdom, properly. It also signifies evangelical doctrine; hence the Lord: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.” It also signifies the Church militant; hence the Lord: “The kingdom of heaven is like a net.” It also signifies the Church triumphant; hence in the Gospel: “Thy kingdom come,” that is, [Col. 0923D] let the kingdom militant come to the kingdom triumphant. It also signifies the eternal homeland; hence David: “Thy kingdom is a kingdom of all ages.” It also signifies the assembly of the wicked; hence in the Gospel: “Every kingdom divided against itself.”

Rule, properly, is a regular order of life; hence we read that blessed Benedict wrote the Rule of monks. It also signifies a geometrical instrument, that is, a measuring rod. It signifies evangelical doctrine; hence the Apostle says that those to whom he writes had quickly fallen away from the rule, that is, from evangelical doctrine.

Regulus, properly, a little king. Hence the Lord: “There was a certain royal official.” It signifies the devil; hence Isaiah: “The weaned child shall delight over the hole of the asp, and in the den [Col. 0924A] of the regulus.” The hearts of the wicked are those which the devil has inhabited through malice. The Lord put his hand into the hole of the regulus or asp when he seized wicked hearts by divine power, that is, he drew forth from there the regulus—the captive devil. It signifies Antichrist, as is written in Isaiah concerning certain wicked persons: “They have broken the eggs of asps and woven spiders’ webs; whoever eats of their eggs shall die, and what has been warmed shall hatch into a regulus.” For wicked people break the eggs of asps when they disclose in wicked works the counsels of malignant spirits hidden in their hearts. To weave spiders’ webs is to perform whatever one does for the desire of this world; since these works are established upon no stability, the wind of mortal life undoubtedly carries them away. But when it is said, [Col. 0924B] “Whoever eats of their eggs shall die,” the meaning is that whoever receives the counsels of unclean spirits kills within himself the life of the soul. And “what has been warmed shall hatch into a regulus,” because the counsel of a malignant spirit which is concealed in the heart is nourished toward complete wickedness and is finally fulfilled in Antichrist, who is signified by the regulus; for, as the regulus is king of serpents, so Antichrist will be prince of the wicked.

To leave, properly. It signifies to withdraw grace; hence in the Gospel: “I will not leave you orphans.” It denotes exposing to tribulations; hence David: “My God, my God, etc., why hast thou forsaken me?” It denotes subordinating love for one thing to another; hence in the Gospel: “Unless someone leaves father, etc., for my sake,” that is, unless one sets divine love above the love of earthly things, one is not [Col. 0924C] worthy of me. It denotes to reserve; hence the Lord says to Elijah in the Book of Kings: “I have reserved for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal,” that is, I have kept them for myself.

Remains, properly. They also signify things left behind as if worthless and few; in this sense what remains from food on the table is called leftovers. They signify the bodies of the saints, which are called remains in comparison with souls, which are more worthy, and because they are left in the earth to be dissolved into it. It signifies earthly covetousness; hence David: “In thy remains thou shalt prepare their face,” that is, in the desires of an earthly kingdom which thou dost not love, thou shalt prepare their face—that is, their intention—[Col. 0924D] namely that of the Jews, because through the desire to retain their kingdom they killed Christ. It signifies the Gentiles whom Christ left for himself to convert; thus the foregoing authority may be explained: “In thy remains thou shalt prepare their face,” that is, among those whom thou leavest to thyself from the Gentiles to be taken up, thou shalt prepare the face—that is, knowledge—of thee; I mean their face, that is, the Jews’, because that knowledge ought to have been theirs, to whom the sayings of the Law and Prophets had been entrusted. It signifies eternal goods; hence in the Psalm: “Keep innocence and behold equity, because there are remains for the peaceful man.” It signifies Christ’s passion and death; thus the foregoing words may be explained: “Thou hast prepared their face,” that is, their evil intention, “in thy remains,” that is, thou hast prepared it [Col. 0925A] for thy passion and death, so that, when they thought they were killing thee, the salvation of the world might come about. Thus Christ prepared their intention by disposing good from it. It signifies sins; hence the Psalmist: “They left their remains to their little ones,” that is, they left sins to their descendants, crying: “His blood be upon us.” It signifies a curse; the foregoing authority may thus be explained: “And they left their remains,” namely of the curse, “to their little ones,” that is, their descendants. It signifies the Jews at the end who will be converted to the faith; hence we read that the remnant of Israel shall be saved.

To remember, properly, means a deed; hence David: “Remember thy mercies, O Lord,” that is, show us mercy as thou didst show it to the ancients. It denotes to judge; hence in Tobit: “Remember not, O Lord, our iniquities.”

To remit, properly, means to pardon; hence the Lord: “Thy sins are forgiven thee.” It also denotes to lessen or diminish; thus heat is said to be remitted; and David: “Remit to me, that I may be refreshed.”

Reins, properly. They signify delight; hence David: “Searching the reins and hearts,” because God considers what a man thinks and what delights him. They signify the Jews from whom Christ descended according to the flesh; hence the Psalmist: “Until night my reins rebuked me”: those from whom I descended according to the flesh persecuted me even to death. They signify Christ’s human nature; the foregoing authority may thus be explained: “They rebuked me, etc.,” that is, according to my human [Col. 0925C] nature I was led even to death.

To fill, properly, means to be essentially in all things; hence: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world,” that is, the Holy Spirit is essentially in all things; or “the Spirit of the Lord,” who is Lord, if the phrase is read transitively. It denotes bestowing fullness of grace; hence it may be explained thus: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world,” that is, the Holy Spirit bestowed upon the Church the fullness of graces; and the Church is called “the world” because it has been gathered from different parts of the world.

Creeping thing. It signifies a fish; hence in Genesis: “Let the waters bring forth the creeping thing with living soul.” Moses calls fish creeping things because they dart themselves forward by a certain impulse. It signifies [Col. 0925D] an animal that moves about the earth: either drawing itself by its mouth, like a worm or serpent; dragging itself by the force of its flanks (*vi castrorum*, as printed), like a snake; or creeping on feet, like a lizard or a *botrata* [uncertain animal-name]. Hence: “Let the earth bring forth the living creature in its kind, cattle and creeping things.” It signifies a person intent upon earthly cares, as though creeping around earthly matters; hence David: “This great sea, etc.; there are creeping things.”

Thing (*res*) is sometimes taken so broadly that the three persons in the Trinity are called things; hence Augustine: “Of things, some are to be enjoyed and others used.” Sometimes it is restricted to the Church in body; hence Donatus says that nouns are significative either of things or of bodies. Sometimes only incorporeal things are called *res*, because true knowledge can be had of these; hence bodies are called things of things, and [Col. 0926A] the reason that comprehends bodily things is called reason. Thus, among things consisting of matter and form, the human mind alone existed which, as it wished, imposed names upon things. It signifies truth, because one says: “It is not in fact,” or, “Thus stands the matter.” It signifies sexual intercourse, as when one says: “This man had relations with that woman.” It signifies usefulness; hence the Apostle forbids those to whom he writes to have buffoonery among them “which does not pertain to the matter,” that is, which is useless. It signifies purpose; hence one says: “Nothing to the point.” It signifies possession, as when one says: “This man took away my things.” It signifies a person; hence Gregory: “A thing that is free from fault ought not to be called into damage,” etc.

To look upon, properly, means to show mercy; hence [Col. 0926B] David: “Look upon me and have mercy on me.” It denotes to approve; hence we read in Genesis that the Lord looked upon Abel and his offerings, that is, approved Abel. It denotes to attend to; hence the Lord: “No one putting his hand to the plough and looking back,” that is, attending to earthly things, “is fit for the kingdom of God.” It denotes to turn; hence David: “Look upon my enemies,” that is, turn them. It denotes to pertain, according to the customary expression: “This regards that,” that is, pertains to that.

Answer, properly, means something equal or equivalent to another thing; hence the Apostle says that he had received the answer of death, that is, had endured a suffering equivalent to death. It signifies divine inspiration; hence we read concerning Simeon that he received an answer from the Lord, not from a man. It signifies instruction; hence we read [Col. 0926C] in the Gospel concerning the Magi that, having received an answer in a dream. It signifies the counsel of a prudent person given for someone’s consolation; hence the laws speak of the responses of jurists.

Net, properly. It also signifies preaching; hence Peter’s nets are said now to be cast out for a catch, now drawn together, because not every time is suitable for teaching. For just as fish are held in a net, so people are held by preaching; hence the Lord: “Cast out your nets for a catch.” It signifies the devil’s deception; hence David: “Sinners shall fall into his net.” It signifies heretical persuasion; hence Solomon: “In vain is a net cast before the eyes of winged creatures,” because the saints, who are winged with virtues, are not deceived by the persuasions of heretics. [Col. 0926D]

Retro (“back”) denotes posterity in time or place, as is clear. It denotes subjection; hence Christ says to Peter: “Go behind me, Satan,” as though saying: Do not oppose me, but be subject to me. It denotes abasement; hence the Lord: “No one putting his hand to the plough and looking back,” that is, to earthly things, which are base and low. It denotes the past; hence we read that Ezekiel saw the living creatures full of eyes before and behind: these living creatures are the Evangelists, who have eyes before and behind, that is, understanding of past and future things. It denotes partial knowledge; hence John says that he heard a voice behind him, to signify that full knowledge of divine things cannot be had in the present.

[Col. 0927A] To return, properly. It signifies approaching God through grace. Hence in the Song: “Return, return, O Shulamite.” It denotes remembering; hence in the Acts of the Apostles: “But Peter, having returned to himself, said,” that is, having recalled the things he had seen. It denotes conferring a benefit; hence in Genesis the angel says to Abraham: “At the appointed time I will return to thee at this same time, life accompanying,” that is, on the same day when a year has elapsed, I shall cause thee to have a son. And this is what is said: “And Sarah shall have a son.”

King, properly. It signifies the saint who rules himself and others; hence David: “And now, O kings, understand.” It signifies an angel; hence Job: “Now, sleeping, I should be silent and rest in my sleep before the kings and counsellors of the earth.” It signifies Christ, who rules us; hence the Psalmist: “But I have been established king.” It signifies the devil, [Col. 0927B] of whom it is said in the Apocalypse concerning the wicked that they have over them as king the angel of the abyss. It signifies the God of eternity, who is King of kings and Lord of lords.

Buckthorn (*rhamnus*), properly. It signifies sin; hence David: “Before the buckthorn should produce your thorns.” The buckthorn produces thorns, that is, torments. The buckthorn is a shrub initially soft, but when mature it puts forth thorns; so sin first delights and afterward pricks. It signifies Gehenna, and accordingly another reading is found in the Psalm: namely, “Before the thorns should produce the buckthorn,” that is, sins produce Gehenna.

Rhinoceros is the same as unicorn. It is called *rhinoceros* from *rinos*, “nostril,” and *ceros*, [Col. 0927C] “horn,” because it has one horn upon its nostril. It signifies one powerful in this world; hence the Lord says to Job: “Would the rhinoceros be willing to serve thee?” as though saying: Will those who are proud in foolish exaltation submit to thy preaching without my help? It signifies the devil; hence in Job: “Wilt thou bind the rhinoceros to plough in thy place?” For Christ alone bound the devil and weakened his power.

Stream, properly. It signifies a principality; hence Isaiah says that the Lord will strike the river of Egypt into seven streams, that is, he divides the rule of Egypt into seven principalities. This was done in the time of Caesar Augustus, who, after subjugating Egypt to himself, established seven principalities in Egypt in order to diminish the power of its kingdom. [Col. 0927D] It signifies mortal sin; hence the Lord is said to have struck the river of Egypt into seven little streams, because when Christ came in the flesh he destroyed concupiscence in the seven capital vices. It signifies a movement of concupiscence; hence we read in the Pentateuch that the eyes of the first parents were opened through sin, that is, the streams of concupiscences. It signifies sayings of Holy Scripture; hence we read in the Song: “I saw one beautiful as a dove descending above streams of waters.” It signifies a preacher; hence David: “Making his streams drunk,” because the first teachers were first made drunk with the gifts of the Holy Spirit. But when they are made drunk, the generations of the Church are multiplied, because when preachers receive a more abundant grace of the Spirit, the number of believers increases. Then holy [Col. 0928A] Church rejoices in its drippings. By the dripping that falls from the roof to the earth is signified the grace of the Holy Spirit, which comes from heaven into believers’ hearts. It signifies the books of the Evangelists; hence Job speaks under the type of the Church, saying: “And the rock poured out to me streams of oil.” The rock is Christ, who, like a rock, poured forth streams of oil because diverse books of Holy Scripture came forth from him: the book of Matthew, Luke, Mark, and John. It signifies the explanations of interpreters of Holy Scripture; hence Isaiah: “A place of rivers, broad and mighty streams.” It signifies the flowing of preaching; hence Job says of the Lord: “He cuts out streams in the rocks.” By rocks we understand the hard hearts of believers; by streams, the rivers of preaching. Thus the Lord cuts out streams in rocks because in the hard hearts of Gentiles [Col. 0928B] he opened rivers of preaching.

Red, properly. It signifies bloodstained; hence in Isaiah angels are introduced speaking to Christ and wondering at his coming, in this manner: “Why is thy garment red?” that is, the garment of humanity bloodstained by the blood of the Passion. It signifies deformed by malice; hence Isaiah: “If your sins are red as scarlet, they shall be white as wool.”

Ruddy, properly. It signifies reddish; hence in Kings David is said to have been ruddy, that is, reddish. It signifies stained red with the blood of sin; hence we read of the great red dragon, that is, of the devil, who in Isaiah is called a garment woven with blood; and [Col. 0928C] elsewhere we read of a red horse, by which the assembly of the wicked is understood.

Ruin, properly. It signifies the fall of the angels; hence David: “He shall judge among the nations; he shall fill up the ruins.” For Christ, by raising the human race to heaven, filled up the ruins of the angels. It signifies a cause of ruin; hence it is said in the Gospel: “This shall be for the ruin and resurrection of many in Israel.” It signifies destruction; hence David: “There is no ruin of the wall.” The wall signifies the teaching of the Pharisees, which could not be destroyed except through Christ, the Son of almighty God.

### Rock

A rock, properly speaking. It also signifies Christ, as David says: “He turned the stone into pools of water, and the rock into springs of waters.” Before the resurrection and passion, Christ was like a stone and a rock, because there was no understanding in the Scriptures until, when they had been opened, he flowed forth and flooded all believers like a spring, saying: “Let him who thirsts come to me and drink.” It signifies worldly power, as in Lamentations: “The wild asses stood upon the rocks,” because they trusted in the powers of this world. It signifies the Gentile people, who were first hardened in wickedness and afterward converted to faith and sent forth streams of doctrine; and this is: “He turned the stone into a pool of waters,” that is, the hard hearts of the Jews into water, that is, baptism; and the rock, that is, the Gentiles, into springs of water, so that they too might pour forth the watering springs of preaching.

## S

[Col. 0929]

### Sabbath

[Col. 0929A] Sabbath is called the seventh day of the week, as in the Gospel: “That Sabbath day was a great day.” A week is called a Sabbath from the dignity of the Sabbath, as in the Gospel: “I fast twice in the Sabbath,” that is, twice a week. It signifies a solemnity, as in Lamentations: “Her enemies saw her and mocked her Sabbaths.” It signifies rest, as it is said: “Whoever escaped the sword, having been led into Babylon, served the king and his sons until the king of the Persians should enter, so that the word of Jeremiah might be fulfilled and the land might keep its Sabbaths.” It signifies the whole time of the present life, as in the Gospel: “Remember to keep the Sabbath day,” that is, to keep holy the sevenfold course of the present life by resting from every servile work and from sin. It signifies purity of mind and the state of eternal blessedness, as in Isaiah: “There shall be Sabbath after Sabbath,” that is, the Sabbath of eternity [Col. 0929B] follows after the Sabbath of the sinner.

### Sack

A sack, properly speaking. It signifies Christ’s human nature, which is compared to a sack because of the harshness of the punishment he assumed; and, as a sack contains grain, so the nature of his humanity veiled the nature of his divinity. Thus David says: “You have cut my sack asunder.” This occurred in Christ’s death, when the soul was separated from the body; and it follows: “And you have girded me with gladness.” This occurred in the resurrection. It signifies mortality, which, because of its harshness, is compared to sackcloth; and the preceding authority may thus be expounded: “You have cut my sack asunder,” that is, you freed me from mortality and thus girded me with gladness. It signifies haircloth, as it is read that Ahab, king of Israel, was clothed in sackcloth, that is, haircloth. It signifies a prophet, because, [Col. 0929C] as grain is contained in a sack, so the marrow of spiritual understanding is contained in the prophets. Hence the apostles are called sons of “those who have been shaken out,” that is, of the prophets, whom they shook out like sacks when they opened their prophecies.

### Priest

A priest, properly speaking. It signifies Christ, as David says: “You are a priest forever.” It signifies a saint, as David says: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness.” A priest means a chief man, as Exodus says that Jethro was priest of Midian, that is, prince of the Midianites. It signifies one who offers sacrifice for the people and prays for others; thus Melchizedek was called priest of God Most High.

### Priesthood

Priesthood properly signifies the assembly of saints offering itself to God as a sacrifice. Thus Peter says in the Catholic [Col. 0929D] Epistle: “You are an elect race, a royal priesthood,” that is, kings and priests: kings, because you govern yourselves; priests, because you are anointed with spiritual oil and offer sacrifice to the true God. It signifies holiness, as in Ecclesiasticus: “And he gave him a great priesthood.”

### Sacrament

A sacrament signifies the sign of a sacred thing. Thus Augustine says: “A sacrament is the visible form of invisible grace.” It signifies a sacred thing signified, or a sacred mystery, as Paul, speaking of the Incarnation, says that it had been hidden from the ages. [Col. 0930A] It signifies an oath confirmed by sacred things; hence one commonly says: “He confirms this by a sacrament.”

### Sanctuary

A sanctuary, properly speaking, is the place where the priest washes his hands after communion. It also signifies the place into which only priests enter. Thus the Council of Laodicea says: “Deacons ought not to have the right of entering the sanctuary.” It signifies the place in which sacred vessels are kept; hence the same council says: “Priests should not ask except by themselves or through the one who keeps the sanctuary.” It signifies the Church, as Prosper, from the sayings of Augustine, says: “Let those who labor in the sanctuary eat of the things that belong to the sanctuary.”

### To sacrifice

To sacrifice, properly speaking, is to offer; thus David says: “I will sacrifice to you a sacrifice of praise.” It also denotes doing good works; thus David says: “Sacrifice a sacrifice of righteousness.”

### Sacrifice

[Col. 0930B] A sacrifice, properly speaking. It signifies a contrite spirit, as David says: “A sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit.” It signifies good action, as the Psalmist says: “Sacrifice a sacrifice of righteousness.” It signifies divine praise which shall be in the future, as David says: “A sacrifice of praise honors me.” It signifies the injuries and insults which Christ bore for us, as the Psalmist says: “May he remember all your sacrifice,” that is, may he make us mindful of all the injuries and insults which you bore for us. It signifies the sacrament of the Eucharist; and the preceding authority may thus be expounded: “O Church, may God remember all your sacrifice in order to reward you.” The prophet foresaw by the Spirit the sacrifice of the Church, which offers not the sacrifice of beasts but that of the Lord’s body and blood.

### Sacred

[Col. 0930C] Sacred means the same as holy; hence an order is called sacred, that is, holy. It signifies consecrated; thus chrism is called sacred, or an altar is called sacred. It signifies sanctifying; thus the words said in the Mass are called sacred, that is, sanctifying. It denotes a sacrifice offered to God; hence sacrificial victims in the Old Testament were called sacred. It signifies execrable, as in the Life of Saint Nicholas:

> To what does the accursed hunger for gold not drive mortal hearts?

### Net

A dragnet is the same thing as a net. It signifies the Church of God, as Matthew says: “The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea,” because good and bad fish are contained in the net—that is, good and bad persons are gathered in the Church. [Col. 0930D] It signifies Holy Scripture, according to which meaning the preceding authority may be expounded: for Holy Scripture has been set forth and explained by the holy Fathers to people of different regions, and through it different persons are gathered into the unity of the Church, some good and some bad.

### Arrow

An arrow, properly speaking. It signifies a reed sent by a boy in the likeness of an arrow; hence: “Their wounds became the arrows of little children,” that is, the persecutions of the Jews by which they persecuted Christ were comparable to the arrows of little children: so ineffectual that they harmed neither Christ nor his members. [Col. 0931A] It signifies the words of preaching, according to another exposition: “Their wounds became the arrows of little children,” because the words of the humble pierced the hearts of the exalted. The words of preaching are rightly compared to arrows because they pierce the sinful hearts of the wicked. It signifies the doctrines of heretics, as the Psalmist says: “They prepared their arrows in the quiver,” that is, heretics devised perverse doctrines to deceive the simple; hence it follows: “That they may shoot in darkness at the upright in heart.” These are elegantly called arrows because, just as a material arrow wounds even unto bodily death, so those doctrines wound as well. It signifies a saying of Holy Scripture, as David says: “He made his arrows burning,” that is, God made the sayings of Holy Scripture effective for unbelievers [Col. 0931B] burning with charity. They are aptly called arrows because they wound a person unto compunction of heart. It signifies a preacher, as David says: “Sharp arrows of the mighty”; and elsewhere: “Like arrows in the hand of the mighty.” It signifies vengeance, as it is written: “I will make my arrows drunk with blood,” that is, I shall inflict a most grievous vengeance upon the wicked because of their sins. It signifies the devil, because, just as a person is punished by an arrow, so God punishes through evil demons. Hence he himself says in the prophet: “Assyria is the rod of my fury.” In accordance with this statement, the preceding authority is commonly expounded: “I will make my arrows drunk with blood,” that is, I shall punish demons with a most grievous punishment; by blood punishment is signified, and by drunkenness the severity of punishment. It signifies a light and manifest temptation, [Col. 0931C] as in the Psalm: “From the arrow flying by day,” because an arrow sent in daylight is visible and can easily be avoided; by it a light and manifest temptation is signified. It also signifies the treacheries of the wicked, according to another exposition: “They prepared their arrows in the quiver.” For when the wicked devise deceits and conceal them from the good by secret machinations, they prepare arrows as though in a quiver; and in the darkness of this present life, as though in darkness, they strike the upright in heart, because their malicious missiles may be perceived, yet cannot be seized as they approach.

### Salt

Salt, properly speaking. It signifies wisdom, as in the Gospel: “Let the salt of wisdom therefore be in you,” that is, wisdom; and: “If the salt has lost its savor, with what shall it be salted?” [Col. 0931D] that is, if a prelate goes astray, by whom shall the prelate be corrected? Or wisdom is aptly called salt because, just as salt makes the earth barren, seasons food, keeps worms away, and frees flesh from decay, so a prelate ought by his wisdom to make his flesh barren of evil works, season spiritual food with wisdom, drive away the worms of evil thoughts, and preserve his flesh from the decay of sin. It signifies seasoned food, as Ezra says that they were to remember the salt which they ate in the palace. It signifies rebuke or detraction, as the venerable Seneca [ed. *Sene*] says: “May your teeth be without salt,” that is, may you not have words [materially uncertain; the quotation appears incomplete].

### Saliunca

[Col. 0932A] *Saliunca*, properly: an unfruitful person, one barren in good works. Thus Josias says [Note: [Col. 0931D], ed.]: “And sometimes the delicate rose turns into *saliunca*”; and in Isaiah: “In place of *saliunca* a fir tree shall rise,” that is, in place of vices, exalted virtues shall arise.

### Saliva

Saliva, properly: discernment or wisdom. Thus Job says: “That I might swallow my saliva,” that is, that I might fully employ discernment or wisdom. Saliva descends from the head into the mouth, then flows from the mouth, and is swallowed by the stomach. The head is divinity; the stomach, the mind; saliva, knowledge full of heavenly brightness; the mouth, human thought. Saliva therefore descends from the head into the mouth because knowledge of divinity touches our understanding through God’s authority, but does not fully nourish the mind. We therefore cannot swallow saliva, because in the present life we are not permitted to be satisfied with the good of brightness.

### Willow

[Col. 0932B] A willow, properly speaking. It signifies the Gentile people, because the willow easily believes and comes to faith. [Note: [Col. 0931D] Something appears to need supplying, so that the passage should read thus: [Col. 0932D] “because, as the willow easily grows, so the Gentile people easily believed,” etc.] It signifies the righteous person by reason of its greenness, because the willow is so green that it can scarcely wither unless it is cut off at the root and cast away. Thus the Prophet says: “They shall spring up among the grass like willows beside running waters.” It signifies a wicked person barren in good, as David says: “Upon the willows in its midst we hung our instruments.” Upon those wicked persons, that is, who are in the midst of Babylon, situated in the depth of concupiscence, we hung our instruments—that is, we laid aside and withheld the Holy Scriptures and the promises of God. For we turn the Scriptures away from them as from pigs and dogs: we do not fasten them to them, but suspend them by deferring them, and [Col. 0932C] estrange them from them.

### Salvation

Salvation, properly speaking. It signifies bodily health, as David says: “A horse is deceitful for salvation,” that is, temporal power cannot confer health upon a person or preserve it. It signifies purity of mind, as David says: “O Lord, God of my salvation.” It signifies eternal life, as the Psalmist says: “But the salvation of the righteous is from the Lord.” God himself is also called salvation, because he is the cause of salvation; hence David says: “The Lord is my illumination and my salvation; whom shall I fear?”

### Savior / Salvation

“Salvation” [*salutare*], properly speaking, is Christ through whom there is salvation; hence Jacob says: “I shall await your salvation,” and Simeon: “My eyes have seen your salvation.” It signifies God the Trinity, as David says: “The salvation of my countenance, my God.” [Col. 0932D] And elsewhere: “Be my helper; do not abandon me nor despise me, O God of my salvation.” It signifies salvation, as Wisdom says: “Who shall give from Zion the salvation of Israel?” that is, who from the Jews shall confer salvation on the faithful people, if not Christ? It signifies eternal life, as David says: “My soul has failed for your salvation.”

### To save

To save denotes deliverance from danger, as in the Gospel: “Save us, Lord; we are perishing.” It denotes justifying, as likewise in Jeremiah: “Save me, and I shall be saved.” It denotes glorifying: “Save us, Christ the Savior, by your power.”

### To heal

To heal, properly speaking. It denotes remitting sin or [Col. 0933A] justifying, as the Psalmist says: “Heal my soul, for I have sinned against you.” It also denotes glorifying, as the Prophet says: “Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed.”

### To sanctify

To sanctify denotes making holy, as it is said of Christ in John that the Father sanctified him and sent him into the world. It denotes confirming, as in Matthew: “Hallowed be your name,” that is, may the name of sonship be confirmed in us. It denotes showing to be holy, as the Apostle says: “Sanctifying the Gospel,” that is, showing it to be holy. It denotes holding solemn and celebrated, as in Exodus: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day.”

### Holy

Holy. It signifies sanctifying; hence God is called holy, that is, sanctifying. It signifies sanctified, as: “The saints rejoice in glory.” It signifies profitable, as David says: “The fear of the Lord is holy.” By this servile or worldly fear is excluded. It signifies steadfast, and the preceding authority may thus be expounded: “The fear of the Lord is holy,” that is, unchangeable. For servile, worldly fear is changeable, because it makes a person change according to temporal things possessed or lost. But the fear of the Lord is without all disturbance. It signifies heavenly, as the Psalmist says: “I shall worship toward your holy temple.” It signifies given by a holy one; hence a commandment is called holy because it is given by a holy one. Thus David says: “The chariots of God are many tens of thousands, etc., in holiness.” Chariots signify the saints, through whom God—that is, faith in him—is proclaimed throughout the whole world. That chariot is manifold in ten thousands, that is, composed of innumerable peoples, who are holy thousands rejoicing because [Col. 0933C] they rejoice in hope until they are brought to the end. And why do they rejoice? Because the Lord is in them; and this is in holy Sinai; or “holy” means by fulfilling the commandment which was given. What profit is the commandment unless the Lord who gives both willing and working is there? It denotes a holy thing that sanctifies; hence the Blessed Virgin Mary says: “For he has done great things to me,” etc., “and holy is his name.” It also signifies the front part of the Temple, which in the Old Testament was called the Holy Place; the rear part of the Temple was the Holy of Holies, that is, the place following after the Holy Place. It signifies the occasion or cause of our holiness, or that which touches a holy thing; hence the cross is called holy.

### Blood

Blood, properly speaking. It signifies the wickedness of a bloodthirsty mind, as the Prophet says: “Her blood is in her midst; she poured it out upon [Col. 0933D] the clearest rock. She did not pour it upon the earth, that it might be covered with dust.” By earth and dust he signifies sinners, and by the clearest rock the righteous person, who is not embittered by the grave contagions of sins. Blood is poured out upon the clearest rock when the wickedness of a bloodthirsty mind rages in the affliction of the righteous person’s soul. It signifies sin, because an abundance of blood is often the cause of the sins of lust, anger, and pride. Sin is represented by the name of blood; hence Isaiah says: “Blood has touched blood,” that is, sin has been added to sin; and elsewhere: “Blessed is he who washes his hands in the blood of the sinner.” It signifies punishment inflicted for the shedding of blood, as: “His blood be upon us and upon our children,” that is, may the punishment to be inflicted for the shedding of [Col. 0934A] Christ’s blood remain upon us and upon our posterity. It signifies vengeance, which is customarily carried out by shedding blood, as Deuteronomy says: “I will make my arrows drunk with blood,” that is, I shall punish demons with a most grievous punishment. It signifies the shedding of blood, as David says: “What profit is there in my blood?” that is, in the shedding of blood. It signifies suffering or death, which ordinarily comes about through shedding blood, as Job says: “The young of the eagle lick blood.” It signifies kindred, as Virgil says:

> … sprung from the lofty blood of Teucer.

It signifies wine, because it has the color of blood, or because it works toward the multiplication of blood; hence Deuteronomy says of the Jews that they drank most bitter blood, that is, wine of the grape. It signifies the union of the Church from diverse saints, as the Lord says: “Unless you eat [Col. 0934B] the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood.” It signifies a thing acquired at the risk of blood, as it is written that David said he would not drink the blood of those who had brought him water from the cistern of Bethlehem at the peril of their blood—that is, water brought to him at the risk of death. It signifies carnal knowledge, which has its seat in heat; intelligence flourishes in the blood, whence knowledge arises. Thus the Lord says: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you,” that is, carnal knowledge. It signifies corruption, because blood easily corrupts; hence the Apostle says: “Flesh and blood [lacuna],” that is, the corruption of flesh and blood. It signifies the carnal observance of legal ordinances, because the material sacrifices of the Law were frequently performed through the shedding of blood; hence the Apostle says that, after his conversion [Col. 0934C] to the faith, he did not confer with flesh and blood, that is, with carnal observances.

### Health

Health, properly speaking. It signifies the state of righteousness, as Isaiah says: “From the sole of the foot even to the crown there is no health,” that is, from the greater to the lesser no holy person is found. It denotes the power of resisting sin, as David says: “There is no health in my flesh.”

### To understand

To understand, properly speaking. It denotes understanding or comprehending, as Paul says: “When I was a child, I understood as a child.” It denotes investigating, as he likewise says: “Do not understand more than it is fitting to understand.”

### Wisdom

Wisdom is sometimes taken broadly, so that any knowledge whatsoever is called wisdom. Hence it is said in the Book of Wisdom, or in Jesus son of Sirach, or in Ecclesiasticus: [Col. 0934D] “All wisdom is from the Lord God.” Sometimes it is restricted to knowledge of the quadrivium, which is called mathematical or disciplinary knowledge. Thus Boethius, in his prologue to Arithmetic, says: “Wisdom is the contemplation of those things which have a mutable substance by their nature.” Sometimes wisdom means shrewdness or cunning which someone has concerning earthly matters, as the Apostle says: “The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God.” It denotes knowledge of divine things, as Paul says: “We speak wisdom among the perfect.” It denotes the divine nature, as Paul says: “O the depth of the riches of wisdom!” It also signifies the Son of God, as Solomon says: “Wisdom has built herself a house.” It signifies the gift of the Holy Spirit, as Isaiah says: “And the Spirit of wisdom shall rest upon him,” that is, the gift of wisdom [Col. 0935A] bestowed by the Spirit. It signifies angelic nature, as the Book of Wisdom says: “Wisdom was created before all things.”

### Sapphire

A sapphire is properly a stone. It signifies a saint who longs for heavenly things, because sapphire retains the color of the sky; hence the heavenly Jerusalem is said in Revelation to be built from sapphires. It denotes contemplation of heavenly things, as in the Song of Songs: “His belly is ivory, adorned with sapphires.” It denotes angelic nature, as Job says concerning the price of wisdom: “It is not compared with the most precious sardonyx stone or sapphire.” By sardonyx, which resembles red earth, human beings are signified; by sapphire, which resembles the air, angels. Neither the first human beings on earth nor angels in heaven are comparable to God’s wisdom, that is, to Christ.

### Sardius

A sardius is a stone having the appearance of red earth. It signifies [Col. 0935B] a martyr made red by the blood of suffering; it is likewise mentioned in Revelation.

### Sardonyx

A sardonyx, properly speaking, is a stone black beneath, red in the middle, and white above. It likewise signifies a saint black in contempt, red in suffering, and white in mind; likewise mentioned in Revelation.

### Branch

A branch, properly speaking. It signifies an unbeliever cut off from the unity of the Church and reserved for eternal fire. The prophets, especially Ezekiel, frequently speak of this branch.

### To satisfy

To satisfy, properly speaking, denotes refreshing spiritually, as David says: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears.”

### *Satum*

*Satum* is the same as *natum* (“born”); hence among authors the noun *satus* is used for *natus* (“born”). It signifies what has been sown; consequently a crop is customarily called *sata*, from *sero, seris, sevi* (“to sow”). Hence it is said that the apostles went through the sown fields [Col. 0935C] and rubbed ears of grain. It signifies a measure that receives what is put into it, as it is written that a woman mixed leaven into three *sata* of flour, that is, three measures.

### To fill

To fill, properly speaking, denotes filling up, as the Psalmist says: “The children are filled,” that is, filled with evil deeds.

### Rock

A rock, properly speaking. It signifies Christ made immortal after his resurrection, as Deuteronomy says: “They sucked honey from the rock and oil from the hardest stone.” This has been explained above.

### Footstool

A footstool, properly speaking. It signifies the body of Christ, as the Psalm says: “Worship his footstool,” that is, the body of Christ, which is the footstool of divinity; for by the feet the unfailing stability of the Godhead is understood. [Col. 0935D] It signifies earthly dignity, as Isaiah says: “Heaven is my throne, but earth is the footstool of my feet.” Heavenly things, because they are worthier, are called God’s throne; earthly things, because they are less worthy, his footstool. It signifies a person subject to Christ in his humanity, as the Psalm says: “Until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet,” that is, subject to you as man.

### Ladder

A ladder, properly speaking. It signifies the likeness of a ladder, as Genesis says: “Jacob saw a ladder,” that is, the likeness of a ladder. It signifies the cross of Christ, as the prose hymn says: “This is the ladder of sinners.”

### Scale

A scale, properly, or *squama*. It signifies a ring of a coat of mail, because the rings of a coat of mail are woven together in the likeness of scales; in this meaning it is frequently found [Col. 0936A] among authors. It signifies a sinner by whom the devil protects himself, as Job says: “His body is compacted with scales pressing one another, because one is joined to another.” It signifies a covering, as Jerome [printed *Iere*] says that he does not care for the Atlantic scale as a covering. This refers to the fable that Atlas supported the stars on his own shoulders, by which it is signified that he was an astronomer and that astronomy flourished through him.

### Scandal

Scandal is derived from Greek *skandalon*, which in Latin is interpreted “stone,” because, lying hidden in the road, it provides an obstacle for the traveler. Scandal signifies someone’s error occasioned by the deed or word of another; hence the Lord says: “It is necessary that scandals come,” that is, that some may be scandalized. It signifies someone’s grief, as Paul says: “Judge this rather: that we [Col. 0936B] do not place a stumbling-block or scandal before a brother,” that is, that we do not grieve a brother. Hence the Apostle subsequently says: “If your brother is grieved through food, you no longer walk according to charity, causing scandal.” One who causes scandal is one who offends another; hence it is written that Christ shall remove all scandals from his kingdom, that is, all those causing scandal. It also signifies the occasion for scandal, as David says: “They set a scandal for me beside the path.”

### Shoulder

A shoulder, properly speaking. It signifies the working of miracles, as David says: “He shall overshadow you with his shoulders.” God’s grace is promised to the faithful person who hopes. For shoulders are miraculous works, by which the power of God is displayed as by shoulders. Feathers are the admonitions of the prophets, which carry people to heaven. And the sense is: “He shall overshadow you with his shoulders,” [Col. 0936C] that is, he shall instruct you by miraculous works; “and beneath his feathers,” that is, in the admonitions of the prophets—which are protection—you shall hope.

### Schema

*Schema* means material; hence in the legend of Blessed Michael it is said that his oratory was made from cheap material. It signifies a figure, according to the grammatical distinction between *schema lexeos* and *schema dianoias*, a figure of expression and a figure of thought.

### Knowledge

Knowledge, properly speaking. It signifies teaching concerning movements, as David says: “Day pours forth speech to day, and night declares knowledge to night.” It signifies thought of earthly things, as Paul says: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!” It signifies the gift of the Holy Spirit, as Isaiah says: “The spirit of knowledge shall rest upon him.”

### Spark

[Col. 0936D] A spark, properly speaking. It signifies an insect which shines at night and is therefore called a glow-worm. Thus Solomon says: “The righteous shall shine,” etc., “and like sparks,” etc. Four properties of the glorified body are implied: splendor and incorruptibility when it says “like the sun”; agility and subtlety when it says, “And like sparks in a reed-bed they shall run about.” Yet some read this of a material spark. It also signifies a mother’s only son, as it is written in the Book of Kings that the widow, speaking to David under a certain *paradigma*, that is, likeness, and wishing to reconcile Solomon to David, said: “They seek to extinguish the spark that is left to me.” It also signifies a transitory, even useless, work; hence the prophet says: “Our work is like a spark.”

### To know

To know, properly speaking. It denotes having regard for, as the Apostle says: [Col. 0937A] “I know in whom I have believed, and I am certain.” It denotes making known, as the Apostle says: “But of that day no one knows, neither the angel of God nor the Son of Man.” He is said not to know because he does not make us know. It denotes experiencing, as Paul says: “I know that neither death,” etc.

### Rush

A rush, properly speaking. It signifies a hypocrite, as Job says: “Can a rush grow green without moisture?” Therefore a hypocrite is signified by the name of rush: he has the appearance of greenness, but has no useful fruit for human uses.

### Broom

A broom is an instrument by which a threshing-floor is cleaned, made from tamarisks. It signifies ceremonial observance, as the Lord says: “When an unclean spirit has gone out of a man, it goes through dry places; and, finding no rest, it says: ‘I will return to my house from which I came,’” etc., “and it finds it swept with brooms and adorned.” [Col. 0937B] The synagogue was the devil’s house, devoted to idolatry before the giving of the Law; he was cast out from it through the worship of the one God. Then he went through dry places, because he then found a place among the Gentiles, dry from the moisture of heavenly grace. But afterward, when the Gentile world was converted and Judaea had turned away from faith through Christ’s death, the devil returned to the synagogue. Taking with himself seven spirits more wicked than himself, because stubborn Judaea was more grievously bound by the seven deadly sins than it had been before the giving of the Law, he then found it swept with brooms: that is, observing ceremonies which cleanse outward things but not inward things—that is, the body but not the soul—just as a broom cleanses the outside, not the inside. It signifies penitence, which cleanses the soul; hence [Col. 0937C] David says: “And I swept my spirit,” that is, I cleansed my soul through penitence.

### Dross

Dross is the sediment of metal. It signifies sin, as: “I shall smelt away your dross unto purity.”

### Scorpion

A scorpion, properly speaking. It signifies a kind of scourge, as the Book of Kings says that Rehoboam told the children of Israel: “My father chastised you with rods; I shall chastise you with scorpions.” It signifies a type of military engine, treated in the Book of Maccabees, where ballistae and scorpions are mentioned. It signifies the name of a sign, as one says in the zodiac: “The sun is in Scorpio.” It signifies a heretic, as Revelation says: “Power was given to it as the scorpions of the earth have power.” It signifies despair, as Luke says: “Or if he asks for an egg, will he offer him a scorpion?” The egg, which is the hope of an animal but is not an animal, signifies hope; against the egg, that is, hope, he sets the scorpion, that is, despair, which stings backward like a scorpion. For hope extends itself toward what lies ahead, whereas despair affects one backwardly.

### Scribe

A scribe means the same as counsellor, as in the Gospel: “Sent by the chief priests and scribes and elders,” etc. It signifies someone who gives moral teaching, as the Apostle says: “Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe?” It also signifies a Jew; according to this meaning the preceding authority may be expounded: “Where is the wise man?” that is, the Gentile; “where is the scribe?” that is, the Jew.

### To write

To write, properly speaking. It denotes committing to memory, as John says: “Write: Blessed are the dead who,” etc. It denotes predestining, as Moses says to the Lord in Exodus: “Either forgive them this sin, or blot me out of [Col. 0938A] the book in which you have written me.” It denotes inflicting, as Job says: “For you write bitter things against me,” etc.

### Scruple

A scruple is a weight. It signifies something projecting above a plane. It signifies an instrument by which smoothed ivory is made bright; hence the Gloss, on the Psalmist’s words “From ivory palaces,” says that ivory is first dull, and is made bright by irons, that is, scruples; others say, “by scruples.” It signifies obscurity; hence one commonly says: “How is this without a scruple?” It is also said that to find obscurity in what is plain is to find a knot in a rush, a scruple on a plane, or an angle in a circle.

### To search

To search, properly speaking. It denotes comprehending, as in the Book of Philo: “The Spirit searches all things,” that is, comprehends them. It denotes acting deceitfully, as David says: [Col. 0938B] “They failed while searching with searching.”

### Search / Examination

A search, properly speaking, is an examination; hence an examination is called a *scrutinium* when someone is tested in knowledge or life to see whether he is worthy of receiving orders. It signifies fraud; hence concerning the Jews, who deceitfully plotted Christ’s death, the Psalmist says: “They failed while searching out a search.”

### Shield

A shield, properly speaking. It signifies God’s gratuitous will or divine protection, as David says: “Lord, you have crowned us with the shield of your good will.” He speaks according to the custom of the land of Palestine, where round shields were formerly used, by which they sometimes protected the breast and sometimes the head. The sense therefore is: “Lord, as with a shield,” etc., that is, by your gratuitous will you protect us in the present against [Col. 0938C] vices; in the future you shall crown us in glory. It signifies defense of sin or human resistance, as the prophet says: “He has broken bow, sword, and shield.” In the bow is signified the envy of those striking from afar; in the shield, the obstinate hardness of defenses; in the sword, a victim struck down; in battle, the movement of the mind against the Lord. All these are broken in the holy Church when the minds of those resisting God are tamed beneath the imposed yoke of humility. It signifies faith, as Paul says: “Taking up the shield of faith.” It signifies the body of the wicked, as is said of Behemoth, that is, of the devil: “His body is like cast shields,” because the devil defends himself against the good through the wicked as through a shield. It signifies Christ’s soul, as the Psalmist says: “Take hold of weapons and shield,” that is, govern and defend Christ’s soul in this way, and through it defeat your adversaries. [Col. 0938D] It signifies constancy; thus the preceding authority may be expounded and read in the person of Christ speaking to the Father: “O Father, take hold of weapons,” that is, cause me to possess teaching and miracles, “and shield,” that is, constancy.

### Cup

A cup, properly speaking, means the joining of two parts which were joined in a candlestick; hence Exodus says: “In the candlestick there were cups, lilies, and little spheres.”

### According to

“According to” sometimes denotes the efficient cause, as one says: “The beginning of the holy Gospel according to John.” It denotes the formal cause, as David says: “He shall render to each according to his works.” It denotes a quasi-formal cause, as David says: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy.” It denotes the material cause, as it is written that Christ suffered according to [Col. 0939A] his human nature. Sometimes it denotes attestation, as: “And he rose on the third day according to the Scriptures.” It denotes time, as: “Today, if you hear his voice,” etc., “according to the day of temptation.” It denotes likeness, as David says: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” It is used for “as,” as the Lord says: “Do not judge according to appearance,” that is, as outward things show.

### Axe

An axe, properly speaking. It signifies judicial power or the execution of judgment; according to this meaning the authority “Now the axe is laid to the root of the tree” may be expounded. It signifies Christ, according to another exposition: “Now the axe is laid to the root of the tree,” that is, Christ is set to uproot human intentions. The tree of this world is the human race; the axe is Christ, who is held, as it were, by a handle and iron through his humanity, but cuts through his divinity. The axe is laid to the root of the tree because, although he waits through patience, he nevertheless sees what he is going to do: for every perverse person who here disdains to bear the fruit of good action will quickly find the prepared burning of Gehenna. [Col. 0939B] It signifies the gift of understanding, as the Book of Kings says that, when the sons of the prophets were cutting wood at the Jordan, one man’s axe fell from its handle into the depths and disappeared. The iron in the handle is the gift of understanding in the heart; cutting wood by it means rebuking wrongdoers. This gift is sometimes lost, when in acting carelessly one incurs the fall of vain glory in the knowledge received. The iron, I say, is lost because understanding is made foolish through disordered action. It signifies a power established under another power, as Isaiah says: “Shall the axe glory against him who wields it?”

### To sit

To sit, properly speaking. It denotes judging, as in the Gospel: “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man shall sit.” It denotes enjoying greater goods; thus Christ according to his human nature is said to sit at the right hand of God the Father Almighty. It denotes being equal, as David says: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand,” that is, God the Father begot a Son equal to himself. It denotes being humbled or cast down, as in Lamentations: “How does the city sit alone?” and elsewhere: “Sit in the dust, daughter Zion.” It also denotes consenting, as David says: “I hated the assembly of evildoers, and with the unjust I shall not sit.”

[Col. 0939D] A seat or throne, properly so called. It signifies the Church of God, whence John says: “And behold, a throne was set in heaven,” because the Church is God’s throne. Although by grace she still lives here in the flesh, nevertheless in mind she inhabits heaven; whence the Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven.” It signifies judicial power, whence David: “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever”; and elsewhere: “Your throne has been prepared from that time.” It signifies the divine majesty, whence in the Book of Wisdom: “While all things were in quiet silence,” etc., “from the royal thrones came,” that is, heavenly things are said to come from the divine majesty; whence Isaiah: “Heaven is my throne.”

“Once,” properly, means unchangeably; whence David: “Once have I sworn by my holiness.” Man swears often, but God once, because he does not change. It signifies eternally, whence David: “God has spoken once,” that is, [Col. 0940A] eternally—that is, he has disposed all things, among all which things I have heard this: that power belongs to God.

Seed, properly so called. It signifies someone’s descendants, whence in John: “We are Abraham’s seed, and have never been enslaved to anyone.” It signifies Christ, whence in Genesis: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed.” It signifies a good work, from which follows the fruit of eternal blessedness, whence David: “Going forth they went and wept, casting their seeds.” It signifies an imitator of someone, whence the Psalmist: “To David, his Christ, and to his seed for ever.” It also signifies the word of God, whence in the Gospel: “The seed is the word of God.” Note that *semen* properly belongs to animals, *sementis* to trees and crops, and *seminium* is the beginning of each thing.

To sow, properly so called. It signifies doing good works, whence David: “Those who sow in tears.” It signifies preaching, whence the Lord: “Behold, the sower went out.” It signifies giving alms, whence Paul: “He who sows in blessings will also reap blessings.”

*Semis* or *semissis* is the same as a half; thus in Exodus it is read that the ark was two cubits and a half in length. It signifies a kind of measure; thus one reads in the rhetoric of inventions that someone proposed a law of forced public service in halves and thirds. *Semis*, too, is indeclinable, means “half,” and is of every gender; thus it is said that a vowel has one time-unit and a half. Hence a certain versifier erred in the declension of the noun when he said:

> You three and a half  
> Solidi, I lavishly bought.

[Col. 0940C] A path, properly so called. It signifies counsel or a higher commandment, whence Isaiah: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.” It signifies the Incarnation, whence it is said of the devil in Job: “The bird has not known the path,” that is, Christ’s path. It signifies a work, whence Job: “Consider the paths of Tema.” It signifies the subtle preaching of a holy teacher, whence the Lord says to Job: “Do you know the paths of the clouds?” The clouds are preachers; the paths are the most subtle ways of holy preaching. It signifies thought, whence Job says to the Lord: “You have placed my foot in the stocks and considered all my paths.”

Old age, or agedness, properly so called. It signifies the final age of the Church, whence the Psalmist: “They shall still multiply in a fruitful old age.” The Church begins especially to be most fruitful [Col. 0940D] when she has been brought to the end of the world. For then the number of the elect will swiftly be completed in her through their sufferings. It signifies the end of the Church, when souls will be rewarded with eternal blessedness, whence David: “And my old age in abundant mercy”; for the final things of the Church, which will be in joy, are called her old age. It signifies weakness, whence David: “Do not cast me away in the time of my old age; when my strength fails”—that is, when patience, assailed, grows weak—“O God, do not forsake me,” because then it will have greater need of help. It signifies the last time, when the love of many will grow cold; whence David: “O God, you have taught me from my youth, and until now, and unto old age and decrepitude.”

Note that four ages of the Church are distinguished here. The youth of the Church was the time of the martyrs, when they were strong; “until now” signifies the advancing time now present, when faith makes progress through the churches; “old age,” the period in which love will begin to grow cold as the times of the world decline; and “decrepitude,” the end of the world, when iniquity has abounded and the love of many will grow cold. The meaning, therefore, is: “O God, you have taught me from my youth,” that is, from the time of the martyrs, “and until now,” that is, up to the advancing time; “and unto old age,” that is, when love begins to grow cold; “and unto decrepitude,” that is, to the end of the world: “O God, do not forsake me.” It also signifies the end of human life, so that the meaning of the statement is: “O God, you have taught me from my youth,” that is, from the beginning of the faith by which you made me new, “and until now,” that is, also after faith; and therefore, not ungratefully, I shall proclaim your wonders. And, Lord, as you then began, [Col. 0941B] so bring it to completion; and this is “unto old age and decrepitude,” that is, to the end of life. “Do not forsake me,” because unless grace remains with me until my very last end, I shall be nothing.

An old man, properly so called. It also signifies a fool, whence it is said: “Cursed is the almsgiving old man.” It signifies a wise man, whence David: “Old men with the younger”; thus among the Greeks elders are called *presbyters*.

Sense, properly, signifies understanding, whence Luke: “He opened their minds that they might understand the Scriptures.” It also signifies wisdom, whence in the Book of Wisdom: “The gray hairs of a man are understanding.” It signifies the meaning of a statement; accordingly, a statement is said to have multiple senses, that is, multiple meanings. [Col. 0941C] We commonly say: “This is the meaning of these words.”

To bury, properly so called. It signifies cherishing someone in sin, whence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Let the dead bury their dead,” that is, let sinners encourage others in sins.

A hedge, properly so called. It signifies angelic protection or a good ruler of the Church, whence David: “You have destroyed all its hedges”; and in the Gospel: “He set a hedge around it.” It signifies the faith, woven together from many articles, whence Ecclesiastes: “Whoever breaks through a hedge will be bitten by a serpent.” It signifies earthly love, by which someone is enclosed, whence the Lord: “Go out into the roads and hedges, and compel whomever you find to come in.” For through preachers those who run along the broad way that leads to death, and who are enclosed by the hedge of love for earthly things, are converted to the faith and become members of the unity of the Church.

[Col. 0941D] “Sevenfold” signifies perfectly, whence David: “The words of the Lord are pure words,” etc., “purified sevenfold,” that is, perfectly; for the number seven signifies perfection and universality. It signifies seven times, so that the meaning is: “purified sevenfold,” that is, by the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. For holy people who preach divine words, ready to undergo death in testimony to the divine word, are proved to possess the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. It signifies the sevenfold Spirit, so that the meaning is: “purified sevenfold,” that is, by the sevenfold Spirit; whence: “Whoever kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold.” For Lamech, who killed Cain, was punished more severely than Cain, who killed his brother Abel, etc.

A tomb, properly so called. It signifies the palaces of princes, whence David: “Their tombs are their houses for ever,” [Col. 0942A] because they built palaces for the eternity of this world, yet remain as though in tombs, not in the palaces which they constructed. It signifies the words of hypocrites or heretics. For just as a tomb is outwardly beautiful and open to receive corpses, but inwardly stinks, so the words of heretics are outwardly pleasing and open to corrupt others, but inwardly stink because of their perverse meaning; whence David: “Their throat is an open tomb.” It signifies gluttony, because it is open to devour many things; in this sense the foregoing authority can be interpreted. It signifies carnal desire, in which a human being decays as though buried; whence it is said: “You who lie in tombs, come out to meet the Savior”; and elsewhere David says: “Those who dwell in tombs.” It signifies hell, whence in the [Col. 0942B] Gospel the rich man in purple is said to have been buried in hell.

To follow, properly: to imitate; whence the Lord: “He who follows me does not walk in darkness.” It signifies rewarding, whence in Revelation: “Their works follow them.”

A bar, properly: the impossibility of entering paradise after the day of judgment, when the prudent virgins have been admitted and the foolish excluded; whence David: “For he has strengthened the bars of your gates.”

A word, properly so called. It signifies teaching, whence the Lord: “My word finds no place in you.” It signifies the Son of God, whence in the Book of Wisdom: “While all things kept a deep silence and night was in the midst of its course,” etc., “your word, O Lord”; because in that silence in which the prophets were silent—which was as it were midway between the New and Old Testaments—[Col. 0942C] the Son of God descended from the Father’s bosom into the womb of the inviolate Virgin Mary.

Late, properly so called; whence in the Gospel: “When it was late that day.” It also signifies the evening of the world, whence the Gospel says: “At evening, or at midnight, or at cockcrow, or in the morning,” etc.

A serpent, properly so called. It signifies the devil, whence Isaiah: “Upon Leviathan, the bar-serpent,” and “upon Leviathan, the twisting serpent.” It signifies the image of a serpent, whence one reads that Moses raised up a serpent in the wilderness, etc. It signifies Christ, whence John: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up,” for the salvation of humankind.

A saw is an iron instrument by which wood is cut. It also signifies power subject to God, whence the prophet says: [Col. 0942D] “Shall the axe boast against him who wields it, and the saw against him who cuts wood with it?”

A servant, properly a slave or attendant; whence in Exodus: “If anyone buys a Hebrew servant,” that is, an attendant. It signifies one who keeps the divine commandments, whence David: “And your servant keeps them.” It signifies one entangled in sin, whence John: “Whoever commits sin is the servant of sin.” It signifies one who fears slavishly, whence the Lord: “I will no longer call you servants,” etc. It signifies a child while under guardianship, whence Paul: “As long as the child is under guardianship, he differs in no respect from a servant.”

“If,” a conjunction, is sometimes used conditionally, whence the Lord: “If I had not come and spoken.” Sometimes it is used causally with a negation, whence in the Psalm: “If I lie concerning David,” that is, because I do not lie concerning David.

[Col. 0943A] To hiss, properly so called. It signifies inspiring, whence the prophet: “The Lord will raise a standard among the nations, and will hiss to him from the ends of the earth.”

“Thus” is used demonstratively, whence in the Gospel: “Son, why have you done thus to us?” And elsewhere: “Thus I wish him to remain until I come.” It is used locally, whence it is said: “Thus I preached the Gospel,” that is, in the place where Christ had not been named. It is used comparatively, whence the Psalmist: “Not so, not so, the wicked.”

“Just as” is sometimes understood copulatively, whence the Lord: “Be perfect as the Father,” that is: “Be perfect, just as your Father also is perfect.” Sometimes it expresses reality, whence in Luke: “And the Holy Spirit descended upon him as a dove,” that is, in a true dove. Sometimes it signifies similarity, whence [Col. 0943B] the Lord: “As the Father sent me, so I send you.” Sometimes it signifies identity, whence in the Gospel: “As the Father has life in himself, so,” etc. Sometimes it signifies an inexpressible likeness to something else, whence: “We shall see him face to face as he is.” “As he is,” he says, not “most exactly as he is,” because not thus expressly as he is.

A seal, properly, is an instrument by which something is closed or marked. It signifies a secret, whence one reads that John saw a book sealed with seven seals. Here the seals signify certain mysteries fulfilled in Christ and by Christ: the first, Christ’s conception; the second, Christ’s baptism, sanctifying the waters; the third, Christ’s death, conquering death; the fourth, the despoiling of hell; the fifth, [Col. 0943C] Christ’s resurrection; the sixth, his ascension into heaven; the seventh, his second coming, in which he will reward his own. It also signifies a signet, whence in the Song of Songs: “Set me as a seal upon your heart,” that is, seal your heart with love for me, lest the devil gain access to you. It signifies likeness, whence the Apostle says to the Romans: “Abraham received the sign of circumcision as a seal of faith,” that is, as a likeness of the righteousness of faith. And the prophet, speaking to Lucifer, says: “You are the seal of the likeness of God.”

“Sealed” signifies impressed, whence David: “The light of your countenance has been sealed upon us,” that is, the grace illuminating your countenance—that is, our reason, by which you are apprehended—has been sealed, that is, impressed, [Col. 0943D] upon us, that is, upon our higher part, namely the soul. It signifies closed, whence the book John saw is said to have been sealed with seven seals, that is, closed. It signifies marked, whence in Revelation: “From the tribe of Judah, twelve thousand sealed,” that is, marked. It signifies distinguished, according to which interpretation one may explain: “Twelve thousand sealed,” that is, distinguished.

A sign, properly so called. It signifies a miracle, whence one reads concerning Saint Stephen: “Stephen, full of grace, performed great signs among the people.” It signifies a likeness, whence it is sung: “This sign of the cross shall be in heaven.” It signifies a signification, whence in the Gospel: “There will be signs in the sun,” etc., that is, indications. It signifies the cross or faith of Christ, whence in the Gospel: “He will be for downfall and a sign that will be opposed.”

[Col. 0944A] Silence, properly so called. It signifies the cessation of the prophets, whence Wisdom: “While all things kept a deep silence,” etc. It signifies tranquillity of mind, whence John: “There was silence in heaven.”

To be silent, properly so called. It signifies the Word of God the Father being separated from human nature; for that separation is metaphorically called silence. One who speaks to someone in a manner sends his word to him. Therefore the Father in a manner spoke to the Son when he sent his Word to him, that is, united it to him. By a similar comparison, silence would be spoken of if a word were separated from a human being; whence David: “To you, O Lord, I cry; my God, do not be silent from me.” It signifies resting, whence one reads: “All the earth was silent,” that is, rested. It signifies ceasing from battles, whence in the Scholastic History: “And the land of Judah was quiet [Col. 0944B] for two years.” It signifies being deprived of life, whence Job: “For now, sleeping, I should be silent.” It signifies concealing, whence the same author: “Have I not been silent?” that is, have I not concealed it?

*Silica* or *siliqua*, according to some, is a root hidden in the earth, which pigs dig up and eat. Others say that *silica* is a pod proceeding from a certain tree, empty of fruit. It also signifies the husk of a legume, such as a bean or pea, as is read in Virgil’s *Georgics*. Metaphorically, *silica* signifies carnal desire, by which the devil incorporates a human being into himself. Thus one reads of the prodigal son that he desired to satisfy himself with the pods which the swine ate—that is, with the carnal desires in which the Gentile people delighted before conversion, and which were pleasing to demons.

[Col. 0944C] A wood or forest, properly so called. It signifies a multitude, whence Jerome, in his Prologue on Joshua, calls the multitude of Hebrew names a forest. It signifies what is uncultivated and wild, whence on the Psalmist’s passage, “Blessed be the Lord, who has made his mercy wonderful,” etc., the Gloss says that Christ set the whole forest on fire by the fire of the Holy Spirit, that is, the wild and uncultivated people. It signifies primordial matter, which among the Greeks is called *hylē* (ὕλη), and in Latin *silva*, and which Plato also calls *silva*. For just as a forest supplies material for buildings, so primordial matter supplies material for all bodies. It signifies the Gentile world, whence David: “We found it in the fields of the forest.” It signifies the saints, whence in the Song of Songs: “As an apple tree among the trees of the forest.” It signifies the material [Col. 0944D] of works, whence James in the Catholic Epistle: “Behold how great a fire kindles how great a forest; so also the tongue is a fire of all iniquity,” because through it all crimes are committed.
