“Likewise.” Sometimes it signifies similarity, whence it is read in the Gospel: “Likewise of the fishes, as much as they wished.” It is used copulatively, whence Abraham is introduced speaking to the rich man’s soul: “Son, you received good things in your life; Lazarus likewise evil things.”

Likeness, properly so called. It signifies the divine nature, whence it is said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” It signifies man, according to which meaning the foregoing authority is customarily explained, so that the meaning is: “Let us make man,” etc., that man may be image and likeness. It signifies the Son, whence [Col. 0945A] Augustine says that the Son is the first likeness of the Father. It signifies the cause of likeness, whence Boethius says that spirit is the likeness of many different species, that is, the cause of likeness.

“Simple” signifies that which lacks parts; thus the soul is called simple because it has no parts. It signifies someone without a fold, that is, without doubled deceit; whence Christ says: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves.” It signifies someone lacking plurality, whence Boethius: “God alone is called simple, because in him there is no plurality.” Thus Boethius, in the book *On the Supreme Good*: “Every simple thing possesses its being and that which it is as one.” In God, who is truly simple, to be is not different from what he is; for one thing is not predicated when I say, “God is,” and another when I say, “God is just” or “God is good.”

[Col. 0945B] “Simply” signifies immutability, whence Boethius says: “God has simply preordained all things,” that is, immutably. And among logicians a proposition is said to be changed simply, that is, immutably, when neither the quality nor the quantity of the proposition changes, as when it is said: “Some human being is an animal; some animal is a human being.” Sometimes it signifies innocence or right intention, whence Wisdom: “He who walks simply walks confidently.”

“Together” sometimes signifies concomitance of place or concomitance of time, as when it is said: “These were born together.” It also signifies the union of the two natures in Christ, whence David: “Together in one, rich and poor.” The poor is the human nature; the rich, the divine nature; these were united together in Christ. It signifies unity of faith, [Col. 0945C] whence, according to another explanation: “Together in one, rich and poor,” that is, in one faith. It signifies unity in wickedness, whence David: “When they gathered together against me.” It signifies identity of divine nature, as when it is said: “The Father and Son and Holy Spirit work together”; or it signifies coeternity, as in the foregoing authority.

Mustard, properly so called. It signifies Christ, whence in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard, which a man took and put in his garden; and it grew and became a great tree, and the birds of heaven rested in its branches.” This grain is Christ, who, planted in the garden of burial, rose as a great tree. For he was a grain when he was dead, [Col. 0945D] and a tree when he rose. A grain through the humility of the flesh; a tree through the power of majesty. The branches of this tree are holy preachers. In these branches the birds of heaven rest, because holy souls, which raise themselves aloft in heavenly contemplation as though on wings of virtues, recover breath from the weariness of this life through their consolations. It signifies the strength of a faithful man, whence in the Gospel: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard and say,” etc. Unless it is crushed, a grain of mustard’s force is not at all recognized: uncrushed, it is mild; but if it is crushed, it burns, and reveals the intense sharpness hidden within it. So every holy person, if not assailed, appears contemptible and slight; but if some crushing persecution oppresses him, [Col. 0946A] he immediately displays all that tastes of heat, and whatever seemed contemptible and weak in him is turned into ardor of virtue. What he had gladly covered within himself in times of tranquillity is compelled to become known when he is shaken by tribulations.

*Sincerus* means what is pure, whence Virgil:

> Pure and unadulterated flour follows,

It descends lower. [Note: [Col. 0945D] Thus the old edition, corruptly.]

It signifies innocence, whence Paul: “Be sincere.”

Sincerity is the same as purity. It signifies innocence, whence Paul: “But with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth,” that is, innocence and righteousness.

A *sindon* is a linen cloth made of fine linen, whence in the Gospel one reads of Joseph that he wrapped the body of Jesus in a clean linen cloth. It signifies faith, which [Col. 0946B] consists of diverse articles just as a linen cloth consists of diverse threads; whence Solomon says of the Church: “She made linen cloth.”

“Without,” a preposition, sometimes signifies removal, but sometimes removes the causal power of a thing; whence in the Gospel: “Without me you can do nothing.” Sometimes it removes union, as when it is said: “This person’s body is without a soul,” or “Christ’s body was without a soul during the three days,” that is, it was not united to the soul. Sometimes it removes inherence, whence in the Book of Wisdom: “Blessed is the man found without blemish.” Sometimes it removes essence, as when it is said: “Carnal intercourse between husband and wife may be performed without sin,” that is, the action itself will not be sin. Sometimes it removes concomitance, whence David: “You sold your people without a price.” Sometimes it removes presence, whence David: “Without [Col. 0946C] help, among,” etc.

The left hand, properly so called: the glory of the present life, whence the Lord: “When you give alms, do not let your left hand know what your right hand does,” that is, let the glory of the present life by no means mingle with pious dispensation, but let the desire for approval be ignorant of the work of righteousness. It signifies the misery of the present life. It signifies the misery of hell.

A bosom, properly so called, whence in Exodus: “Put your hand into your bosom.” It signifies a harbor, whence a ship is said to be in the bosom of the sea, that is, in harbor. It signifies the region of hell in which the saints before Christ’s advent were consoled by blessed hope; whence in the prayer: “May you deign to place the soul of your servant in Abraham’s bosom.” That region of hell was called a bosom because, [Col. 0946D] just as in a gulf of the sea there is greater tranquillity than in the open sea, so in that region of hell there was repose, as in the depth of the abyss. It signifies a bend or inlet, whence the sea is said to make many bosoms, that is, many windings. It signifies thought, whence David: “Of him who reaps did not fill his hand, nor his bosom who gathers sheaves,” because the angels, who are reapers, will not fill hand or bosom from evil people, that is, they will not gather from them good work or good thought. It signifies secrecy, whence Job: “My hope is stored in my bosom,” that is, away from the desire that has its place in the flesh. It signifies conscience, whence David: “And my prayer shall return into my bosom,” that is, it shall purify the conscience.

[Col. 0947A] Zion is the name of a place. It signifies the primitive Church from the Jews, whence the prophet: “From Zion the law shall go forth.” It signifies the universal Church, whence David: “But I have been established by him as king over Zion, his holy mountain.” It signifies the Synagogue, whence David: “Will Zion say: ‘Man and man was born in her’?” As if to say: God was born in her as man; but will man say it—that is, will any man be able to persuade Zion, that is, the Synagogue, of what I am about to say, namely that man was born? It signifies the triumphant Church, whence David says that “the God of gods shall be seen in Zion.”

To thirst, properly so called. It signifies to desire, whence the prophet: “You who thirst, come to the waters.” It signifies to crave, whence the Lord: “Whoever drinks of this water shall thirst again,” that is, for carnal delight. It signifies to burn with love, whence [Col. 0947B] the Psalmist: “My soul thirsted for you.” It signifies to dry up, whence the hymn says: “Thirsting earth,” that is, drying up.

Thirst, properly so called. It signifies desire, whence the prophet speaks in Christ’s person: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst,” etc. For Christ desired the conversion of the Jews, and they gave him the vinegar of wickedness to drink. It signifies lack of spiritual understanding, whence David: “All the beasts of the field shall drink; the wild asses shall await in their thirst.” The wild asses are proud Jews, and the meaning is: “The wild asses,” that is, the Jews, “will await in their thirst to drink these waters,” that is, they will defer understanding of Holy Scripture until the final time.

A bucket is a vessel for water and is called *situla* because it removes thirst; whence Isaiah: “All nations are like a drop [Col. 0947C] from a bucket.” It signifies a serpent whose poison removes thirst, concerning which Lucan writes.

An emerald is a stone of such greenness that it surpasses all herbs, all leaves of trees, and all gems in its greenness. By its greenness it refreshes the sight of the eyes, and it is produced in Scythia, a land uninhabitable because of excessive cold. It signifies the saints, who are greener in faith than others, surpass in the verdure of faith those believers who are cold in chastity, and enlighten those blinded by the stain of ignorance. It is also mentioned in Revelation.

The sun, properly so called. It signifies Christ, whence John: “I saw a woman clothed with the sun,” that is, the Church illumined by grace, that is, the glorious Virgin Mary. It signifies a saint, whence in the Book of Wisdom: “The righteous shall shine like the sun.” It signifies the Church, whence in the Song of Songs: “Chosen [Col. 0947D] as the sun.” It signifies the brilliance of a good work, whence Job: “If I saw the sun when it shone”; for the sun in brightness is a good work made manifest. It signifies the light of truth, whence one reads that the wicked, on the day of judgment, knowing their condemnation, will say: “We have strayed from the way of truth, and the light of righteousness has not shone upon us, and the sun has not risen for us,” etc. It signifies the brilliance of preachers, whence Job: “He commands the sun, and it does not rise, and seals up the stars as under a seal.” For what is understood by the name of the sun except the brilliance of preachers? And through John it is said: “The sun became like a sackcloth of hair.” It signifies tribulation; for just as the sun burns by reason of its heat, tribulation is figured by the sun. Thus in the Song of Songs: “Do not marvel that I am dark and blackened, because [Col. 0948A] the sun has discolored me,” that is, tribulation, not sin. It signifies time, because times are distinguished according to the sun’s motion; therefore time is figured by the sun. Thus David: “His name remains before the sun,” that is, before time, because from eternity. It signifies manifestation, whence: “He set his tabernacle in the sun,” because Christ made himself manifest to humanity according to his human nature, which is called a tabernacle. Since the sun manifests by illuminating, the name “sun” rightly signifies manifestation. It signifies the gift of wisdom, which excels the other gifts, whence David: “The sun to rule the day, the moon and stars to rule the night,” that is, he gives the gift of the Holy Spirit to the higher spirits, signified by the day, and lesser gifts to the lower, signified by the night. [Col. 0948B] It signifies Christ’s divine nature, which illumines Christ’s human nature just as the sun illumines the moon; whence David: “The sun shall not burn you by day, nor the moon by night,” that is, you shall not be tempted concerning Christ’s divine or human nature. It signifies temptation; in this sense the foregoing authority may be explained thus: “The sun shall not burn you by day, nor the moon by night,” that is, temptation shall not overtake you in prosperity, signified by day, nor in adversity, signified by night. It signifies Antichrist, who will pretend to be Christ; whence Revelation says that an angel poured out a bowl upon the sun. By the angel is meant a preacher, such as Elijah and Enoch, who will preach against Antichrist and his accomplices.

[Col. 0948C] Solitude, properly so called, whence the Apostle: “Wandering in deserts.” It signifies separation from the Church, whence Job says concerning heretics: “They gnawed in the wilderness, bleak with calamity and misery.” Heretics separated from the Church do not eat Scripture, because they do not understand it; yet they somehow gnaw it, because they presume to comprehend it by their own power. It signifies the absence of earthly thoughts, whence David: “Behold, I fled far away and remained in solitude”—not the solitude of the desert, but of the mind, etc. It signifies the Gentile world, once abandoned by God, whence Isaiah: “The wilderness shall rejoice, glad and praising.”

A throne, properly so called. It signifies power or dignity, whence Isaiah, speaking in the person of Lucifer, says: “I shall ascend into heaven; above the stars of God I shall exalt my throne.” It signifies a seat, whence Isaiah: “All the princes of the earth [Col. 0948D] rose from their thrones.” It signifies the angelic nature in which God dwells through grace, whence Isaiah: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne.” The high throne is the angelic nature; the exalted throne is said to be human nature, which through Christ has been raised from a lower to a higher state. It signifies divinity or eternity, inasmuch as God surpasses and subjects all things to himself. In this sense the statement “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne” may be explained, so that the high throne is understood as Christ’s divine nature or eternity, and the exalted throne as God’s human nature.

To loose, properly so called. It signifies remitting sin, whence God is said to loose sins, that is, forgive them. It signifies declaring loosed or remitting punishment, [Col. 0949A] whence the Lord: “Whatever you loose on earth shall be,” etc. It signifies destroying, whence in a certain hymn:

> Now that groans have been loosed  
> And the pains of hell.

Sleep, properly so called. It also signifies Christ’s death, whence David: “I slept and took sleep.” It signifies love of earthly things, whence the Psalmist: “If I give sleep to my eyes.” It signifies the torpor of sloth in doing good, whence Paul: “Knowing that it is now the hour for us to rise from sleep.” It signifies an ecstasy of mind in which something is revealed to a person by an angel from God; thus in Genesis, when Jacob heard that his son Joseph was alive, he awoke as though from a heavy sleep and did not believe them, that is, his sons.

To sound, properly so called. It signifies inspiring, whence in the Song of Songs: [Col. 0949B] “Let your voice sound in my ears,” that is, let your inspiration be poured into my mind, etc. It signifies contradicting the faith of Christ, whence David: “They sounded, and were troubled,” etc.

Sound, properly so called. It signifies the praise by which the saints praise God in eternal blessedness, whence the Psalmist: “In the voice of exultation and confession, the sound of one feasting,” that is, the praise of saints spiritually feasting in eternal blessedness. It also signifies divine inspiration which, through a human intermediary, fights against the devil, sin, and the world; whence David: “Praise him with the sound of the trumpet,” that is, because, through divine inspiration, the saints conquer the devil, that is, vices; for by a trumpet we are summoned to battle, etc. It signifies preaching, whence the Psalmist: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth.”

[Col. 0949C] Deep sleep signifies ecstasy, because the soul is received into contemplation of heavenly things; whence in Genesis: “The Lord sent a deep sleep upon Adam,” that is, ecstasy, because he was caught up to the heavenly court and many things concerning the future were revealed to him. It signifies death, whence the Psalmist: “I slept and was in deep sleep and rose again,” because just as one easily rises from deep sleep with bodily members intact, so Christ easily rose from death with the perfection of human nature. It signifies ignorance, whence Isaiah: “For the Lord has mingled for you a spirit of deep sleep; he will close your eyes.”

A sister, properly so called. It signifies a kinswoman, whence Abraham says to Abimelech: “She is also my sister, the daughter of my father.” The meaning is: Sarah is my kinswoman, the daughter of her father—understand, his brother. For Haran was Sarah’s father and Abraham’s brother. [Col. 0949D] The Church is also called Christ’s sister by reason of nature and grace, because she is conformed in nature and grace; whence in the Song of Songs: “My sister is still little, and has no breasts.” These are Christ’s words concerning the Church. It signifies a companion, whence Job: “I said to corruption: ‘You are my father,’” etc., “and to the worms: ‘My sister.’” A believer, or the soul, is called Christ’s sister, whence in the Gospel: “Whoever does the will of the Father.”

A lot, properly, is not something evil, but in human uncertainty expresses divine judgment; for the apostles used lots. Divine election or predestination is called a lot because it expresses the divine will and does not regard merits; no one knows why it falls upon one person rather than another. Thus predestination proceeds from the divine will and does not regard merits; [Col. 0950A] no human being knows why God chooses this person rather than that one. Whence David: “My lots are in your hands,” that is, my gratuitous election is in your power. It signifies possession, because Joshua distributed possessions to Israel in the promised land; therefore a possession is called a lot. For one reads in Joshua that Israel was in Benjamin’s lot. It signifies principal capital, whence it is said: “Whatever is received above the principal is usury.”

Form or appearance, properly so called. It signifies beauty of mind, whence David: “In your form and your beauty.” In logic, *species* is also called a universal. Augustine says that God is not predicated under this term as genus or species. It signifies a saint, whence David: “The king of powers, of the beloved, of the beloved, and of the beauty of the house, divides spoils.” God the Father is king of the powers of the beloved, that is, of the angelic powers, which are also Christ’s, because he rules them. He then repeats “of the beloved” in commendation of the beloved Son. I say, not only over the others, but also for dividing the spoils, and those snatched from the devil, whom he divides—some as apostles, others as prophets—thus making spoils. I say, “of the beauty of the house,” that is, of the saints who make the house—that is, the Church—beautiful. [Col. 0950B] It signifies eternal inheritance, whence David: “He chose for us his inheritance, the beauty of Jacob,” as if to say, eternal life, which he calls the inheritance and beauty of Jacob, that is, of the later people; this beauty Jacob loved. The heavenly inheritance is the beauty of the Christian people, in which it shall be beautiful, shining like the sun. It signifies a likeness of a thing, according to which [Col. 0950C] interpretation the foregoing authority may be explained in the person of the apostles: thus he chose to give us the inheritance of many peoples, so that we might worship him, striking their hearts with the sword of preaching and destroying wickedness. He calls this “the beauty of Jacob,” that is, those like Jacob, or signified by Jacob, who give earthly things for heavenly, as Jacob did when he gave a dish of lentils for Esau’s birthright.

A watchtower (*specula*) is properly a high place in which someone is stationed to watch for enemies; hence in Isaiah: “Set the table; keep watch from the watchtower.” It signifies the Church; hence Isaiah: “Upon the watchtower of the Lord I stand, holy.” It signifies contemplation; hence: “Set up for yourself a watchtower,” that is, direct your heart upon the straight way.

A mirror (*speculum*) signifies pride or worldly pleasure, [Col. 0950D] whence Isaiah: “On that day the Lord will take away the pins and the mirror.” It also signifies Holy Scripture; hence the Apostle: “If anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, such a person shall be compared,” etc., that is, to one looking in a mirror. For someone considers in the Scriptures, as in a mirror, the face of his birth—how man is born, how frail he is, what he will become, and amid how many miseries he is placed. From this he acquires great compunction; yet immediately, when some temptation arises, he forgets and departs from repentance. It signifies the Son of God, because in the Son the image of the Father is reflected, as in the book of Wisdom called *Ecclesiasticus*. It signifies enigmatic knowledge; hence the Apostle: “Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma.” To see through a mirror and in an enigma is to apprehend God through visible things as through certain images.

[Col. 0951A] A cave (*spelunca*), properly speaking. It signifies the Church; hence in the Gospel: “My house shall be called a house of prayer,” etc., “a den of thieves.” It signifies faith in Christ’s Passion; hence Isaiah: “And the Lord shall be exalted on that day, and the idols shall be utterly crushed, and they shall enter into the caves of the rocks.” It signifies hope in earthly things; thus the foregoing authority may be explained: “They shall enter into the caves of the rocks and into the chasms of the earth,” that is, they shall hide themselves from the knowledge of God in the love of earthly things, or shall place their hope in the merits of the saints.

Hope (*spes*), properly, is that which is hoped for; hence Paul: “Hope does not put to shame.” It signifies God; hence David: “My hope from my mother’s breasts.” It signifies certainty; hence the Psalmist: “My flesh shall rest in hope,” etc.

A sphere (*sphaera*), properly speaking. It signifies Jerusalem insofar as [Col. 0951B] it was surrounded on every side by enemies; hence Isaiah: “I shall surround you round about like a sphere.”

An ear of grain (*spica*), properly speaking. It signifies a small amount; hence Isaiah: “His arm shall gather ears.” It signifies the progress of a good work; hence in the Gospel: “So is the kingdom of God, as if a man should cast seed upon the earth, and sleep and rise night and day, and the seed should germinate and grow while he himself does not know how. For the earth bears fruit of itself: first the blade, then the ear, then full grain in the ear.” For a man casts seed into the earth when he implants a good intention in his heart; and after casting the seed, he sleeps, because he rests in hope of a good work. He rises by night and day, because he advances amid adversities and prosperities. The seed [Col. 0951C] germinates and grows while he does not know, because he is not yet able to measure its growth. Yet what has been conceived is brought forth toward progress, and the earth bears fruit of itself, because, grace preceding, the human mind spontaneously rises toward the progress of a good work. Accordingly, this same earth first bears the blade, then the ear, then produces full grain in the ear. To produce the blade is still to have the assurance of a good beginning; the blade comes to the ear when the virtue conceived in the mind draws itself onward to the progress of a good work; and it bears full grain in the ear when virtue has advanced so far that it can become the work of one strong and perfect. Sometimes an ear signifies an utterance of the Holy Spirit, as Job says of heretics: “They took ears of grain from the naked, [Col. 0951D] walking without clothing, and from the hungry.” They take them away because, whether some people are idle and exercise themselves in no good works, or proceed along the path of imprudence without the covering of a good work, even when at last they wish to return to repentance and desire the nourishment of the word, these heretics take ears away from them while they are hungry, because by destructive persuasions they destroy in their minds the sayings of the Fathers.

A thorn (*spina*), properly speaking. It also signifies the sting of retribution; hence Job: “Let thistles spring up for me instead of wheat, and thorns instead of barley”; see above under “wheat.” It signifies riches that prick through anxiety; hence the Lord: “Another fell among thorns and was choked.” It signifies a sinner; hence in the Song: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among daughters,” etc., because just as

> [Note: [Col. 0951] Something is missing here, for what follows cannot be referred to the sinner.]

[Col. 0952A] the more a thorn pierces the lily, the greater the fragrance it emits, so likewise the more one is afflicted by evils, the greater the fragrance of virtues one emits. It also signifies sin; hence David: “I was turned in my misery, while the thorn is fastened,” that is, because sin is fastened, that is, sins carry one as far as consent, action, and habit. It signifies reason; hence, according to another reading: “The Lord is fastened by a thorn,” that is, reason, broken, is bent down toward earthly things, though it ought to be raised upward, just as the spine of the back raises a man up. It signifies pride; thus the foregoing authority may be explained: “While the thorn is fastened,” that is, pride, once broken, does not raise one up unto destruction but unto salvation. It signifies conscience; thus it may be explained: “While the thorn is fastened,” that is, conscience has been pierced. [Col. 0952B] For then I felt pain and found my weakness. It signifies eternal punishment; hence: “Before the branch should produce thorns,” that is, pleasure produces torments. It signifies the sting of temptation; hence the prophet: “Thorns and briers shall rise over the ground of my people.” The ground of God’s people is called the minds of the saints, over which thorns and briers sometimes rise because vices sometimes oppress even it.

A breathing organ (*spiraculum*) is properly an instrument for breathing in. It also signifies the soul; hence in Genesis: “And he breathed into his face the breath of life.” It signifies the Holy Spirit; hence, according to some, in the foregoing authority *spiraculum* is understood as designating the Holy Spirit. It signifies the cessation of the Devil’s persecution, who persecutes either in person [Col. 0952C] or through his human agents; hence Job: “His body is like molten shields, compacted with pressing scales; one is joined to another, and not even a breath passes through them.” The Devil’s body consists of the wicked, who are called molten shields because he instructs them toward evil and defends himself through them against good deeds. They are called compacted scales because all agree in evil and are joined to one another in the Devil’s persecution, so that his persecution or perverse suggestion never ceases. This is what Job says: “Nor does a breath pass through them.”

To breathe (*spirare*), properly speaking. It also means to inspire; hence Job: “The Spirit breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice.”

Spirit (*spiritus*) signifies that vital spirit which animates the body both of a brute animal and of a human being. Thus Saint [Col. 0952D] Gregory distinguishes two spirits in man: the vital spirit, which ceases to exist with the body, and the rational spirit, which survives the body’s dissolution and is immortal. Hence it is said in the Gospel of Christ that, bowing his head, he gave up the spirit. It also signifies an angel in the same sense. Spirit also signifies life, because spirit is the cause of life; hence Job: “My spirit shall be weakened; my days shall be shortened.” And in Isaiah: “Keep yourselves from man, whose spirit is in his nostrils.” It signifies reason; hence the Apostle: “The flesh fights against the spirit.” It signifies spiritual understanding; hence in the Gospel: “It is the spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing,” that is, spiritual understanding; and in the Apostle: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life.” It signifies [Col. 0953A] a spiritual person; hence the evangelical law is called by the Apostle “spirit,” that is, spiritual; and in the Psalm: “Who makes his angels spirits,” because Christ makes his preachers spirits, that is, spiritual persons. It signifies divine inspiration; hence it is said of Simeon in Luke that he went in the Spirit into the Temple, that is, led by divine inspiration. It signifies spiritual intention; hence John: “The hour comes, and now is, when true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and truth,” that is, with spiritual intention and for things true and eternal. It signifies a human being; hence the prophet David says that man is “a spirit that goes and does not return.” It signifies God; hence John: “God is Spirit.” It signifies wrath; hence David: “In a violent spirit you shall shatter the ships of Tarshish.” This is explained of Herod, who, returning from Rome and finding [Col. 0953B] at Tarshish the ships by which the Magi had crossed, burned them in violent anger. It signifies pride; hence in the Gospel: “Blessed are the poor in spirit,” and blessed are those free from pride, that is, the humble. It signifies wind; hence in Genesis: “God remembered Noah,” etc.; “he brought a wind upon the earth, and the waters diminished.” It signifies a rational question arising from human reason; hence we read that the queen of Sheba, for whom Solomon resolved every question, had no spirit left, that is, no question which she could put to him. It signifies the Holy Spirit; hence in the Gospel: “Jesus was led into the wilderness by the Spirit.” It signifies a gift bestowed by the Holy Spirit; hence Isaiah: “And the spirit of wisdom shall rest upon him,” that is, the gift [Col. 0953C] of wisdom bestowed by the Spirit. It signifies a mortal sin suggested by an evil spirit; hence we read in the Gospel of the Devil that he takes seven others, that is, seven mortal sins.

To despoil (*spoliare*), properly speaking. It denotes delivering; hence in the Song: “They stripped me of my tunic.” The tunic signifies temporal things, or love of temporal things, from which holy preachers deliver the faithful people. It denotes preventing someone from possessing what he is prepared to receive; hence we read in the Gospel that robbers, that is, demons, stripped the man descending from Jerusalem to Jericho—like Adam from the state of innocence to the state of guilt—of gratuitous gifts: that is, through sin they prevented him from possessing the gratuitous gifts which he had been prepared to receive.

[Col. 0953D] Spoil (*spolium*), properly speaking. It signifies the assembly of the faithful, freed by Christ from the Devil’s power; hence David: “To divide the spoils of the beauty of the house.” Thus, in Jacob’s blessings, by the grace of Paul, he who descended from Benjamin is a ravening wolf, “in the morning devouring prey and in the evening dividing spoils,” because through Paul’s preaching the Devil was despoiled of many. Those whom the Devil despoiled from the Church are called spoils; hence it is said: “Woe to Assyria, the rod of my fury … I shall send him against a deceitful nation, and against the people of my wrath I shall command him, that he may take spoils and seize prey.” It signifies Holy Scripture, which was taken from the Jews by Christians; hence David: “I shall rejoice over your words as one who finds abundant spoil.”

A bride (*sponsa*) is the same as a wife. It signifies the Church; hence [Col. 0954A] in the Song: “My sister, my bride.” And elsewhere: “He adorned [her] as a bride.” The faithful soul too is frequently called Christ’s bride in Holy Scripture.

A basket (*sporta*) is a vessel woven of palm and reed; hence in the Gospel the disciples took up seven baskets. It signifies a purse; hence Saul says in the book of Kings: “Bread has failed in our provisions, and we have no little basket,” that is, nothing in a basket or purse.

A bastard (*spurius*) is called the son of a prostitute because of the uncleanness of his generation; hence a distinction is customarily made among the *spurius*, the *hybrida*, the *manser*, and the *nothus*. A *hybrida* is one born of an ignoble mother. A *nothus* is one born of adultery, whose father is unknown; as one says “the smith’s bastard,” or “a bastard name.” A shoot from a lower root after cutting is called a *spurius*, [Col. 0954B] because in some manner it is the adulterous offspring of no one and is born outside the ordinary course of shoots. Hence we read in the book of Wisdom: “Bastard shoots shall not put down deep roots.” The aforesaid branch is called a shoot because of its new growth, and bastard because it has arisen outside the natural or artificial union of trunk and shoot. A perverse and adulterous thought is also called a bastard shoot; thus the foregoing authority may be explained: “Bastard shoots,” that is, perverse thoughts, “shall not produce useful fruits.”

A stable or inn (*stabulum*), properly speaking. It signifies the Church, where Christ’s animals—that is, the faithful—are refreshed; hence in the Gospel: “Setting the wounded man upon his beast, he led him to an inn,” because Christ led man into the Church [Col. 0954C] and entrusted him to the innkeeper, that is, the prelate. It signifies the world, in which pleasures are like dung; hence the teacher Cassiodorus: “God mixes bitter things in, lest on the road we love the inn in place of home.”

A stadium (*stadium*), properly, is the space in which people run in order to gain the prize, that is, the reward of the race. It signifies the condition of the present life, in which we ought to run by good works so as to attain the prize of eternal blessedness; hence Paul: “In a stadium indeed they run, but one receives the prize,” etc.

Tin (*stagnum*), properly speaking, is a metal. It signifies a pool of water, namely, motionless water. It signifies baptismal water; hence David: “Who turned the rock into pools of waters,” that is, the hard hearts of the Jews toward baptismal water. [Col. 0954D] It signifies the stream of teaching; thus the foregoing authority may be explained: Christ was like a rock and crag before he opened Holy Scripture to the faithful; but after he opened their understanding to his disciples so that they might understand the Scriptures, he was turned into pools of waters. It signifies a pretender to holiness, according to the meaning of *stagnum* as tin; hence in Ezekiel the Lord reproaches the Israelite people, saying: “Israel has become to me dross: bronze and tin, iron and lead, in the midst of a furnace.” As if to say: I wished, or sought, to purify them through the fire of tribulation and make them silver or gold; but in the furnace they became to me bronze, tin, iron, and lead, because in tribulation they break out not into virtue but into vices. When struck, bronze [Col. 0955A] produces a sound more than other metals. Therefore one who, set amid persecution, breaks forth into the sound of murmuring has become bronze in the midst of the furnace. Tin, however, when artfully compounded, falsely imitates the appearance of silver. Therefore one who is not free from the vice of pretense in tribulation has become tin in the furnace.

To stand (*stare*), properly speaking. It denotes being raised toward heavenly things; hence Paul: “Let him who stands take heed lest he fall.” It denotes rendering help; hence Stephen: “I see the heavens opened and Jesus standing.” It denotes no longer increasing or being abundant; hence we read in the book of Kings: “And the oil stopped.” It denotes being steadfast; hence in the book of Wisdom: “The righteous shall stand in great steadfastness.”

A balance (*statera*) is an instrument in which weights are weighed. It signifies the Devil’s perverse persuasion; hence John: “And [Col. 0955B] he who sat upon it had a balance in his hand.” The Devil’s balance, therefore, is his perverse persuasion, which promises earthly things in order to take away heavenly things. It signifies Christ’s cross, on which the price of our redemption—that is, Christ’s body—was weighed; hence in the hymn, “the balance was made of his body.” It signifies the judgment by which merits are weighed, just as weights are weighed in a balance; hence Job: “Would that my sins and the calamity that I suffer were weighed in a balance.” It also signifies justice; hence David: “The sons of men are liars in the balances,” that is, in the scales of justice.

Stature (*statura*), properly speaking; hence the Lord: “Which of you, by thinking, can add one cubit to his stature?” It signifies the condition of the Church; hence: “Your stature is likened to a palm tree,” because the Church is raised toward higher things [Col. 0955C] by hope, is exalted by virtues, brings forth the sweetness of good works, and obtains triumph over her many enemies.

A star (*stella*), properly speaking. It signifies Christ; hence John: “And I shall give them the morning star.” And elsewhere, the prophet Balaam: “A star shall arise from Jacob.” Properly speaking, Lucifer is called the morning star, which is the herald of light and drives away darkness. Figuratively Christ is called the morning star because he drives away the clouds of unbelief. It signifies the glorious Virgin Mary; hence Mary is said in Hebrew to mean, as it were, “star of the sea”; hence in the hymn:

> Hail, star of the sea.

It signifies a gift of the Holy Spirit; hence in Revelation: “He who has the seven spirits of God and the seven stars”—that is, Christ [Col. 0955D] who has the Holy Spirit and the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. It signifies a saint, because just as star differs from star in brightness, so saint differs from saint in the worthiness of reward; hence David: “I shall see your heavens, the works of your fingers, the moon and the stars.” By the moon the Church is signified, by the stars the saints. And elsewhere David: “Who numbers the multitude of the stars.” And elsewhere Job: “May its stars be darkened by its gloom.” It signifies a hypocrite who feigns righteousness; hence John: “The stars of heaven fell to earth,” that is, hypocrites, who are thought to be righteous and feign themselves righteous, fell into love of earthly things. And elsewhere John: “The dragon,” that is, the Devil, “with his tail,” that is, through Antichrist, “shall draw with him a third part of the stars,” because through Antichrist many who appear holy shall fall [Col. 0956A] into sin. It signifies an apostle: “I saw [a woman] clothed with the sun, with the moon beneath her feet, and twelve stars in her hand.” It signifies the Devil, who was first called Lucifer because he was created in a good state; then he could likewise be called a star, but through pride he fell and became the Devil. Hence in Revelation: “And the third angel fell, and a great star, burning like a torch, fell from heaven.”

Dung (*stercus*), properly speaking. It signifies the ceremonial observances of the Law, which are to be cast aside as dung; hence Solomon: “The sluggard shall be stoned with the dung of oxen”; this has been expounded above. It signifies carnal pleasure; hence David: “Raising the needy from the earth and lifting the poor from dung.” It signifies temporal good; hence Jeremiah: “Those who embrace dung instead of saffron.” It signifies teaching [Col. 0956B] that makes the hearer’s mind fruitful; hence in the Gospel it is said of the householder who commanded that the fig tree be cut down, and it was said to him: “Leave it also this year, until I dig around it and put on dung.” Here the fig tree signifies the Synagogue, which is dug about by preachers, separated from carnal observances, and instructed in spiritual teachings. It signifies the stench of lust; hence the prophet: “The beasts have rotted in their dung.” For beasts to rot in their dung is for carnal people to end their lives in the stench of lust. It signifies a little dwelling in which the keeper of a vineyard or garden, and the like, lives.

Sterile (*sterilis*) means unfruitful. It signifies one estranged from good work; hence Isaiah: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear,” that is, the Gentile world, which is now sterile [Col. 0956C] in good works because it does not bear spiritual children: rejoice, because at that time the spiritual children of the deserted woman—that is, the Gentile world formerly abandoned by God—shall be more numerous than those of her who has a husband, that is, the Synagogue, which observed the worship of one God. It signifies one estranged from evil work; hence David: “Who makes the barren woman dwell in a house.”

To saddle (*stertire*), properly speaking, means to put straw upon a horse or donkey; hence: “Abraham saddled his ass.”

A dripping (*stillicidium*), properly speaking. It signifies lust; hence Solomon: “Three things drive a man from the house: smoke, dripping, lust, a bad wife”—our evil flesh. It signifies preaching; hence: “He descends as rain upon fleece, and as drippings falling upon [Col. 0956D] the earth.” Then drippings fall upon the earth when divine preaching makes the hearts of earthly-minded people fruitful unto grace.

Straw (*stipula*), properly speaking. It signifies one dry for lack of the moisture of grace, who is carried about by every wind of doctrine; hence Job says: “Against a leaf driven by the wind,” etc., “do you thus pursue straw?” It signifies the least venial sin; hence the Apostle says that some build upon the foundation wood, hay, straw. Wood signifies a greater venial sin, hay a lesser one, straw the least. It signifies an ear of grain remaining after the harvest, in which sense this word occurs in the laws. It also signifies a saint despised by the Devil; hence it is said of Behemoth that he will count a hammer as straw.

[Col. 0957A] A stock or root (*stirps*), properly speaking. It also signifies Nebuchadnezzar; hence Isaiah: “You are cast out from your tomb like a useless stock.” The Hebrews relate that, after Nebuchadnezzar’s death, his son Evil-merodach, fearing that he might rise again—for he had previously returned to his former state—on the advice of Joachi [as printed] drew his father’s body from the earth, divided it into three hundred parts, and gave it to vultures. It signifies one who is the origin of a family; hence we read that the Blessed Virgin Mary descended from David’s stock, according to that saying, “the stock of Jesse,” etc.

A robe (*stola*) is an ankle-length garment, named from *telon*, meaning “long”; hence in Genesis we read that Joseph gave to Benjamin, his brother by the same mother, five robes. It signifies the state of innocence which the baptized person receives through baptismal grace; hence a baptized child is clothed in a chrismal [Col. 0957B] robe made of white linen cloth and sewn with red thread. The white garment signifies the brightness of innocence; the red thread indicates that baptism has its efficacy through the Passion. Or this implies that the baptized person ought to be prepared to shed blood for Christ. Hence in the Gospel, the householder, rejoicing at the return of the prodigal son to himself, says: “Bring forth the first robe.” By the householder God the Father is understood; by the prodigal son, the Gentile people, who departed into the region of dissimilarity through sin, then returned to God through faith, and received through baptism the first robe, that is, the state of innocence. It signifies the body, which is as it were the garment of the soul; hence [Col. 0957C] we read of the martyrs that “they washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb,” that is, they cleansed their bodies through martyrdom by imitating Christ. It signifies the glorification of the soul after death; hence we read in the book of Wisdom concerning the second judgment that the Lord clothed him in a robe of glory. It signifies the glorification of the body; hence we read that at the resurrection the saints will be clothed in a double robe, that is, the glorification of body and soul. To signify that robe of the body, the angel appeared in a white robe at Christ’s resurrection.

A coverlet (*stragulum*) is a garment distinguished by varied color, or a double garment; hence we read in the book of Kings that Asahel took a coverlet, poured water on it, and spread it over the face of the sick Benadad, etc. It signifies a good [Col. 0957D] work of the Church made firm by charity; hence we read in Proverbs: “She made herself a coverlet,” that is, she adorned herself with good works.

A bed or bedding (*stratum*), properly speaking. It signifies a bed upon which a heap of garments is placed. It signifies sensuality; hence David: “I shall water my bed with my tears,” that is, by the bitterness of repentance I shall water sensuality, that is, make fertile that which was formerly barren of good works. It signifies a heap of sins, because a pile of garments is usually laid out upon bedding. By the bed is signified the multitude of sins; thus the foregoing authority may be explained: “I shall water my bed with my tears,” that is, by tears I shall dissolve the heap [Col. 0958A] of sins. It signifies one’s own flesh; hence David: “If I ascend onto the bed of my couch,” that is, if I yield to the flesh—as if to say: I shall not yield. He says “ascend” because private possession makes people proud. It signifies the right hand of God the Father; thus the foregoing authority may be explained as the words of Christ, who says: “David entered,” that is, Christ saying: “If I enter into the tabernacle of my house,” namely, the heavenly dwelling; for the tabernacle is the heavenly dwelling; “and if I ascend onto the bed of my couch,” that is, to the Father’s right hand, where there is rest—that is, the end of labors—until the holy Church is supported by preaching: this is an aposiopesis, as if to say, “Let me no longer be believed.” It signifies human nature; hence David: “You have wholly turned his bed in his infirmity,” [Col. 0958B] that is, you have exposed all human nature to misery. It signifies worldly prosperity; thus the foregoing authority may be explained: “You have wholly turned his bed in his infirmity,” that is, you have providently turned man’s worldly prosperity into his distresses. It also signifies some earthly good which a sick person holds and chooses as good for himself, in which he may rest; hence a good wife, when she could not lift the labor of her mind toward God,

> [Note: [Col. 0957D] The passage is corrupt.]

but God, wishing us to have love only for eternal life, mixes bitter things with pleasures and turns them into our infirmity.

A *strophaea* signifies a turning; hence islands which float and turn are so called. It signifies a new purpose; hence in the hymn of Saint Nicholas: “O new turning of Jacob,” [Col. 0958C] against the Devil, against lust: he gave three golden apples to maidens whose father, because of poverty, wished to expose them to prostitution.

An ostrich (*struthio*), properly speaking. It signifies a hypocrite; hence Job: “The ostrich’s feather is like the feather of the heron and hawk”; this has been expounded above. It signifies the Church deserted by the faithful; hence it is said that the Church is like an ostrich in the wilderness. It signifies the Synagogue, which has the wings of the Law but, crawling in its heart among lowly things, never raises itself to higher things. By the heron and hawk, however, the ancient Fathers are denoted, because they were able to discern those things which had to be understood. The ostrich’s feather is like the feather of the heron and hawk because the Synagogue, in speaking, held the teaching of its predecessors, but did not know it in living. Hence the foregoing authority can be referred to this [Col. 0958D] exposition. It signifies the Gentile world; hence the Lord says through the prophet: “The beast of the field, dragons, and ostriches have glorified me.” For beasts of the field, dragons, and ostriches glorify God when the Gentiles exalt God through faith; and he reproves them as dragons because of their malice and marks them as ostriches because of their hypocrisy. It signifies hypocrisy itself; hence Isaiah: “It shall be the lair of dragons and the pasture of ostriches.” By dragons malice, and by ostriches hypocrisy, are signified. The ostrich has the appearance of flight but not its use, because hypocrisy presents to all who look upon it an image of holiness, but does not know how to maintain a holy life. [Col. 0959A] In a perverse mind the dragon lies down and the ostrich feeds, because hidden malice is craftily covered, while a pretense of holiness is put forward before the eyes of beholders.

A stylus (*stylus*), properly speaking. It signifies a mode of speaking; hence, according to authors, three styles are distinguished: the low, the middle, and the elevated. It signifies ordering or arrangement; hence Job: “Who will grant me that these things be inscribed in a book with an iron stylus,” that is, with an unchangeable arrangement. Elsewhere we read that Judah’s sin was written with an iron stylus. And in Martianus we read that the patriarchs wrote with an adamantine stylus.

*Sub* (“under”) is a preposition sometimes joined with the accusative, sometimes with the ablative when action is involved. It denotes place. It also denotes protection; hence the Lord: [Col. 0959B] “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often I wished to gather,” etc., “under [my] wings, and you would not.” Sometimes it is joined with the ablative and likewise denotes place; hence it is said that all things which were under him filled the Temple. Similarly it denotes protection; hence David: “Under the shadow of your wings.” Sometimes it denotes subjection; hence the Psalmist: “You have subjected all things.” *Subtus* and *subter* are used in the same ways.

To draw under (*subducere*) denotes placing beneath; hence: “And we too have sometimes put our hand under the rod.” It denotes drawing or leading; hence in the Gospel: “When the ships had been drawn up onto land.”

To undergo or go beneath (*subire*), properly speaking. It denotes placing oneself beneath; hence we read in Maccabees: “Eleazar went beneath the elephant,” that is, placed himself under the elephant. It denotes coming into the mind; hence people commonly say: “This came into my mind.” It denotes undertaking or enduring; hence people commonly say: “This man undertook this great work.”

To subject (*subjicere*) denotes placing beneath; hence David: “You have subjected all things under his feet.” It denotes replying; hence: “Phoebia replies to Mancho.” A pronoun, among dialecticians, is also the thing about which speech is made in a statement. It is said to be subjected to a statement or predicate, and is therefore called the subject.

Sublime (*sublime*) signifies proud; hence in Proverbs: “I have trodden down the necks of the lofty by my own strength,” and in the book of Kings: “Do not multiply lofty words in boasting.” It signifies the height of eternal blessedness; hence in the Canon of the Mass: “Command these things to be carried by the hands of your holy angel to your sublime altar.”

To mock (*subsannare*) denotes deriding. It denotes scattering the Jews throughout [Col. 0959D] the world; hence in the Psalm: “He who dwells in heaven shall laugh at them; the Lord shall mock them.” Christ laughed at the Jews when, guards having been posted, he rose again. He mocked them when they were scattered throughout the world. Laughter is customarily made with the mouth, as by a grimace (*sinna*). We mock with the nose, wrinkling it, because a wrinkle is called *sanna*; and this is less laughter than mockery.

Benches or seats (*subsellia*) are seats. Hence Juvenal, speaking of Statius, at whose book-recitation many Romans had gathered so that the seats seemed to be breaking, says:

> … “He broke the benches with his verse,”

as if to say: So many gathered to hear Statius’s verses that the seats in which the Romans sat were broken, or appeared to be breaking. It signifies the angelic order called Thrones; hence in the sequence: “To the renowned [Col. 0960A] celestial ruling powers and divine seats.”

Substance (*substantia*), properly speaking, signifies a thing existing and distinguished from other things by its own quality. Hence in the book of *Categories*: “Primary substance is that which is called substance properly and principally.” In this sense it is equivalent to the term *hypostasis*; accordingly, in divine matters the term is transferred so that an individual person in the Godhead is called a substance or hypostasis, as Jerome calls the three persons three hypostases or three substances. It is transferred to mean a substantial property or substantial nature; hence Boethius says that for man to enter into substance is for him to enter into the most specific species itself. He also says that a species is the substance of its individuals; and in this sense [Col. 0960B] it is equivalent to the term *usiosis*, whence substantial differences are said to be placed among *usiones*, that is, among substantial properties. The term *substance* is also transferred to signify this most general genus of the category; hence Porphyry: “Substance is a certain thing, and is itself a genus.” In this sense it is equivalent to the term *ousia*; therefore it is transferred to signify the common nature of the three persons, so that divinity is called *ousia* or substance. Hence Christ is called a giant of double substance, and the three persons are said to be of one substance, *homoousion* and not *homohypostasion*, that is, of one substance, not of one person. It signifies possession; hence in the Gospel the [Col. 0960C] prodigal son is introduced speaking to his father in this way: “Give me the portion of substance which falls to me,” that is, possession or inheritance. It signifies faith; hence the Apostle: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen,” that is, that through which hoped-for things subsist in us. It signifies the power to escape suffering; hence Christ: “I am fixed in the mire of the deep,” that is, in the deep weakness of human nature, “and there is no substance,” that is, in me there is no power of the flesh to escape the Passion. It signifies stability; thus the foregoing authority may be explained: “There is no substance in me,” that is, no stability of life.

A sweat-cloth (*sudarium*), properly speaking. It signifies understanding or love of earthly things; hence in the Gospel we read of the wicked [Col. 0960D] servant who hid his lord’s money in a sweat-cloth. He hides his lord’s money in a sweat-cloth who negligently preaches the word of God or keeps silent through love of earthly things. It also signifies the cloth by which the sweat of the face is wiped away.

Sweat (*sudor*), properly speaking. It signifies labor because sweat arises from labor; hence in Genesis: “In the sweat of your face,” that is, “you shall eat bread”: this God the Father said to Adam.

To bear or endure (*sufferre*) denotes suffering; hence James: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation.” It denotes taking away; hence Mary Magdalene, thinking Christ the gardener, says: “Lord, if you have taken him away, tell me.” It denotes filling; hence we read that Christ’s disciples took up twelve baskets from the fragments which remained; nevertheless, *sufferre* may there be used for *deferre*, “to carry away.”

[Col. 0961A] To choke (*suggilare*) denotes strangling and is said to come from *sub* (“under”) and *gula* (“throat”), as if to put one’s hand beneath the throat. Bede, however, says that the verb *suggilare* derives from the verb *sugo, sugis* (“I suck”), and is drawn from the *lamiae*, who kill little children by sucking. It signifies making manifest; hence the unjust judge says of the widow: “Lest, by coming, she *suggilet* me,” that is, harass me.

A furrow (*sulcus*), properly speaking. It signifies someone well cultivated by the ploughshare of the tongue; hence Job: “If the earth cries out against me and its furrows weep with it.” Land uncultivated by any works often produces some food for human use; but when ploughed, it bears crops for satiety. So there are some who, not cut by any ploughshare of exhortation, bring forth from themselves certain gifts, however small, like earth not yet ploughed. But there are others who are always intent upon hearing [Col. 0961B] holy preaching. Cut through their former hardness of mind as by a certain ploughshare of the tongue, they receive the seeds of exhortation and render the fruits of good work through the furrows of voluntary affliction. Yet it sometimes happens that those in authority harm subjects whom they ought to benefit. When the untrained see this, they are stirred to murmur against their ruler, but do not sorrow for their neighbors in diverse compassion. But when those already worn by the plough of speech and cultivated for the fruits of good work see innocent people burdened even in small matters, they are immediately turned to lamentations through compassion. Therefore every ruler who acts perversely toward his subjects finds both the earth crying out against him and the furrows weeping, because against [Col. 0961C] his injustice the untrained break out in the voice of murmuring, while the perfect afflict themselves in tears over his evil deed.

Sulphur (*sulphur*), properly speaking. It signifies the stench of evil works; hence David: “He shall rain snares, fire, and sulphur upon sinners.” It signifies the stench of hell; hence in Daniel we read that fire and sulphur came forth from the furnace.

*Sum* properly signifies a thing’s essence; hence it is called the substantive verb, because it was instituted to preserve the substantial nature of a thing. Hence it is called *inpracticon*, that is, “without motion,” because it signifies the substantial nature, which is not in motion. Sometimes it signifies the divine nature, as in Exodus: “He who is has sent me to you.” Sometimes the immutability of a thing, as Boethius says [Col. 0961D] in the second prologue to his *Arithmetic*: “Wisdom is the comprehension of the truth of those things which are and which possess an immutable substance of their own”; that is, the properties which they possess in themselves are immutable, for mutable things derive [their properties] from subjects. Sometimes it denotes God’s eternal foreknowledge, as in the Gospel: “What was made in him was.” Sometimes it denotes the material cause, in the sense in which it is said that we all are in Adam. Sometimes it denotes adherence to God through grace, as the Apostle says: “Who calls those things which are not”—that is, sinners who do not adhere to God through grace—“as though they were”—that is, as though they were those who do adhere. It denotes seeming to be, so that the aforesaid apostolic authority may be explained thus: “Who calls those things which are not,” that is, the Gentiles, who were reckoned as nothing, “as though they were” [Col. 0962A]—that is, as the Jews, who seemed to be something. Sometimes it denotes an event, as Boethius says: “There was [a time] when time was not.” Sometimes *to be* is taken to mean *to belong*, as when it is said: “It is yours to do this,” that is, it belongs to you.

*Super* or *supra* is used in many ways. Sometimes it denotes place, as in the Gospel: “He set him upon the pinnacle of the temple.” Sometimes it denotes pre-eminence, as David says: “More desirable than gold and precious stone.” Sometimes it stands for “beside,” as the Psalmist says: “Upon the rivers of Babylon.” Sometimes it stands for “except,” as if we were to say: “Besides those mentioned, another did this,” that is, except for those mentioned. Sometimes it stands for “for,” as in the Gospel: “Daughters of Israel, do not weep over me, but over your sons,” that is, for yourselves. Sometimes it means “with” or “among,” as the Psalmist says: “I became a reproach among my enemies, and exceedingly so among my neighbours.” Sometimes it denotes oppression, as David says: “He rained snares upon sinners,” and so forth—that is, as a burden or oppression upon them; and elsewhere: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.” Sometimes it denotes subject matter, in the customary expressions “Augustine on John,” “Jerome on Matthew”: that is, Matthew is the subject of Jerome, and John the subject of Augustine’s treatise. Sometimes it is joined with the ablative, and then stands for “concerning” or “for,” as David says: “Concerning your mercy and your truth,” that is, concerning your mercy by which you turn the ungodly—that is, spare sinners—and concerning your truth by which you judge those who do not come [to you] [Col. 0962C] and restore the promised rewards to the good.

Sometimes this word *super* or *supra* is used adverbially and means “very,” as the poet says:

> O you, the sole image to me of my Astyanax!

that is, “very much an image.” Priscian, however, says that there is here an apocope and removal of part of a compound word, so that *super* stands for *superest* (“survives”). Sometimes it means “otherwise,” as it is read in the Apostle: “Let no one be puffed up for one against another beyond what is written,” that is, otherwise than is written; thus *supra* there means “otherwise.” Sometimes it denotes place, as in the Gospel: “There was above the pool five porticoes,” that is, in a higher place. Or *super* there may mean “besides,” so that the sense is: “There was, besides the sheep-pool, [another pool],” that is, besides the other baths. [Col. 0962D] There was there a pool in which the limbs of sacrificial victims were washed; hence it was called *probatica*, from *probaton*, which means “sheep” or “cattle.”

*Superare* properly means “to remain over”; hence the Lord says: “Gather up the fragments that remained, lest they perish.”

*Superbia*, properly: hence David says, “The pride of those who hate you.” It denotes riches, as in the Catholic Epistle: “But now you glory in your prides,” that is, in your riches.

*Supercilium*, properly. It also means pride, because a raising of the eyebrow commonly signifies pride; hence Sedulius says:

> Put on haughtiness, if you know yourself to be a friend.

Elsewhere it is read that the Jews have much concerning the brows of the Pharisees. It denotes the summit of a thing; hence [Col. 0963A] the summit of mountains is customarily called a *supercilium*, because, as an eyebrow is in the upper part of the body, so a mountain’s height is in its upper part—according to the customary phrase, “This city is situated …” [sentence incomplete].

*Superliminare*, properly, means a lintel. It denotes the intention of the mind. Thus Moses says concerning the eating of the lamb: “They shall take of the blood of the lamb and put it upon both doorposts and upon the lintels of the houses in which they will eat it.” The blood is set upon both doorposts because the blood of Christ is received not only with the mouth of the body but also with the mouth of the heart. It is set upon both posts when the sacrament of his Passion is received with the mouth for redemption and also contemplated with an attentive mind for imitation. By houses we understand our minds, in which we dwell through thought; [Col. 0963B] the lintel of any house is the very intention which precedes an action. Therefore, one who directs the intention of his thought to imitation of the Passion sets the Passion of the Lamb upon the lintel of his house. Or our houses are our bodies themselves, in which we dwell while we live; and we set the blood of the Lamb on the lintel of the house because we bear the cross of his Passion on our forehead.

*Supplantare* is to throw another to the ground by placing one’s foot upon the sole of his foot. It denotes hindering, as David says: “Those who plot to trip up my steps,” and so forth. It denotes deceiving, as Esau says of Jacob in Genesis: “For he has supplanted me a second time,” that is, deceived me.

[Col. 0963C] *Supponere* properly denotes putting one thing in place of another; hence Genesis relates that Laban substituted Leah for Jacob—that is, put her in Rachel’s place. Among grammarians, it is to place beneath another thing the thing about which the discourse is concerned.

*Surdus*, properly, means deaf. It means one who does not understand, as Isaiah says: “On that day the deaf shall hear the words of the book,” that is, those who previously did not understand will understand Holy Scripture. It means one who prevents himself from hearing, as David says: “Like a deaf asp that stops up its ears.” It means one who pretends not to hear, as David says: “But I, like a deaf man, did not hear.”

*Surgere* denotes being awakened from the sleep of sin, as Paul says: “Knowing that it is now the hour for us to rise from sleep.” It denotes being raised from the dead, as Augustine says [in the Gospel] of Christ: “He has risen; he is not here.” It denotes rising up against someone, [Col. 0963D] as in the Gospel: “Then two false witnesses arose,” that is, rose up against him.

*Sus*, properly, means a pig. It denotes the heretic; hence Wisdom says: “A golden ring in its snout, a beautiful and foolish woman.” It denotes the sinner; thus the Catholic Epistle of Peter says that the sinner is like a pig in the mire of mud. For just as the pig abandons the clean flatness of the threshing-floor, the flowering field, and the green meadows, delights in mud, frequents the dungheap, takes pleasure in slime, and keeps company with marshes, [Col. 0964A] so the sinful person, abandoning the paradise of eternal blessedness, casts himself into the mud of lust and gives himself up to the mire of gluttony. And, just as the pig keeps company with marshes, so the sinful person passes by the utterly clear fountain of charity, gives himself up to earthly affection, and embraces the dung of worldly riches.

*Suscipere* denotes uniting something to oneself, as the Psalmist says: “But you are my upholder”; these are the words of Christ’s human nature, which the Son of God united to himself. It denotes raising from the dead, as Christ says to the Father: “Because you have received me,” that is, raised me from the dead. It denotes taking to oneself, as Stephen said: “Lord, receive my spirit.” It denotes glorifying, as David says: “I arose, because the Lord received me,” and so forth.

[Col. 0964B] *Suscitare*, properly, means to rouse. It denotes exalting, as the Psalmist says: “Raising the needy from the earth.” It denotes inspiring, as the Lord [did] in Daniel: “He stirred the spirit of the younger boy whose name was Daniel.” It also denotes raising from the dead; hence God the Father is said to have raised the Son from the dead.

*Sustinere*, properly, means to wait, as the Psalmist says: “I waited for you all day,” and elsewhere: “Wait a little.” It denotes providing for necessities, according to the customary expression: “This man supports that man.”

*Susurrium* means a murmur. It denotes detraction, whence in Paul whisperers are called detractors. It denotes God’s secret inspiration, as the prophet says: “My ear received the veins of his whisper.”

*Sycomorus* is a tree like the fig; hence *sycomorus*, as it were “a foolish fig,” because it resembles the fig not in its fruit but in its leaves. Thus it is read of Zacchaeus that he climbed a sycamore tree. [Col. 0964C] It also denotes what is fragile, as Isaiah says: “The sycamores have been cut down, but we shall replace them with cedars.”

*Symbolum* means a sign; hence Dionysius, in the *Hierarchy*, calls symbolic those likenesses that are transferred from earthly things to heavenly ones. It denotes a sacrament; hence Augustine, on the passage “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit,” calls it a *symbolum*. It denotes a contribution in which several portions are placed together for a banquet; and it is called *symbolum* from *syn*, “together,” and *bolus, boli*, “a portion,” since each person puts his own portion into it. It denotes a formula in which various articles [Col. 0964D] of faith are contained; hence one says “the Nicene Creed” or “the Apostles’ Creed.”

*Synodus* means an assembly of the faithful for establishing, renewing, derogating from, or abrogating some new matter; hence it is called the Nicene Synod. It denotes the conjunction of other things, as: “The moon directly placed beneath the sun: sun and moon joined in the same conjunction.”

## T

[Col. 0963]

[Col. 0963D] *Tabernaculum*, properly, means a tent. It denotes the present Church, as the Psalmist says: “Who shall dwell in your tabernacle?” A tent is made for a time, not for permanent dwelling. The tent [Col. 0964D] of soldiers or travellers is exposed to various storms and tempests; thus, with elegance, the Church militant is represented by a tent, [Col. 0965A] since it has here no abiding city, wages war against visible and invisible enemies, and is exposed to the varied tempests of temptations and tribulations. It denotes the Church triumphant or eternal blessedness, as the Lord says: “Make friends for yourselves from mammon,” and so forth, “that they may receive you into eternal tabernacles.” It denotes Christ’s human nature, which for the same reasons is called a tabernacle as is the present Church; hence David says: “He has set his tabernacle in the sun.” It denotes an assembly of evil persons, as in the Song of Songs: “I am black, like the tents of Kedar.” It denotes the human body, as in: “I am certain that the putting off of my tabernacle is swift.” It denotes the Synagogue, as David says: “God loves the gates of Zion above all the tabernacles of Jacob,” that is, the Church above the Synagogue. It denotes the dwelling-place [Col. 0965B] of the mind, as Job says in the person of the Church: “Who will grant me that I may be as I was in the days of my youth, when God was secretly in my tabernacle?” The Church was small in Abel’s time, but grown in the time of grace, when she bore many children in faith. Therefore, in order to show how greatly she advanced inwardly in the time of grace, the Church says: “When God was secretly in my tabernacle,” that is, in the dwelling-place of my mind. It denotes thought, as in: “Fire consumes the tabernacles of those who gladly accept gifts.” For as the body dwells in a tent, so the mind dwells in thought; but fire devours tents when the heat of avarice lays waste thoughts. It denotes the construction of earthly happiness, as Job says: “The tent of the wicked shall not stand.” A tent is constructed to protect the body from [Col. 0965C] heat and cold. The tent therefore signifies the construction of earthly happiness, which the reprobate labour to multiply in order to protect themselves from the necessities of this present life as from heat and rain; but such a construction will perish.

*Tabes*, properly, means wasting disease. It denotes sin; hence it is read that Adam infected the whole human race by the wasting disease of sin, and so forth.

*Tabescere* denotes rotting away. It denotes grieving, as in the Psalm: “My zeal caused me to waste away.” It also denotes drying up from the moisture of virtues and divine knowledge, as the Psalmist says: “You made me waste away like a spider.”

*Tabula*, properly, means a tablet. It also denotes the human heart: the Old Testament is said to have been written on stone tablets, the New on the tablets of the heart. It denotes penance, [Col. 0965D] which is said to be the second plank after shipwreck. By shipwreck is understood first sin; therefore, shipwreck is original sin, in which an infant suffers shipwreck, after which baptism appears as the first plank. This is said by a certain analogy. Often a shipwrecked person, when the ship has broken apart, clings to a plank of the ship and so escapes; so a person, escaping the shipwreck of original sin through baptism, encounters another shipwreck through actual sin, in which the penitential “second plank” has its place. Others say that shipwrecked people used to tie around their neck a tablet on which the circumstances of their shipwreck were described, so that those seeing it might be moved to mercy. Thus baptism is the first plank after shipwreck: for every person of discretion and adulthood, before receiving baptism, [Col. 0966A] is bound to confess his sin and thus describe his shipwreck. Likewise, after he has suffered a relapse, penance comes to meet him, through which he must confess his sins.

*Taedere*, properly, means to be weary or disgusted. Thus Paul says: “We were so burdened that we were weary of living.” It also denotes grieving, as Mark says: “Jesus began to be afraid and distressed.”

*Talentum* is a kind of weight. It denotes eternal punishment, as John says: “And a great hailstone, like a talent in weight, descended from heaven to earth.” Eternal punishment is aptly called a talent because each of the reprobate will receive according to his merit, and so forth. It denotes human sense or understanding, as is read of the householder who gave five talents to one of his servants, two to another, and one to another. By the five talents are understood the five [Col. 0966B] bodily senses, given to a person so that he may use them well. Similarly, by two talents are understood reason and intellect, given to a person that he may be guided well by them; by one talent intellect alone is designated.

*Talis* is sometimes used demonstratively and sometimes relatively, and signifies the quality of a thing. Sometimes it signifies the divine nature; hence Athanasius says: “As the Father is, so is the Son.”

*Tantus* is sometimes used relatively and sometimes demonstratively, and signifies continuous quantity. It also signifies discrete quantity; hence the Gospel says: “But what are these among so many?” that is, among so many persons. Sometimes it signifies the divine nature, as when I say: “As great as the Father is, so great is the Son.”

*Taurus*, properly, means a bull. It denotes the company of the Shechemites, which, [Col. 0966C] because of pride, dominion, or lust, is called a bull. Hence in Genesis: “Simeon and Levi, let not my soul enter into your counsel.” It follows: “They dug through a wall.” Another text has: “They hamstrung a bull,” which is to be understood of the king of Shechem, whom Simeon and Levi killed. It denotes Christ, who was sacrificed for us; the foregoing authority may thus be explained: “Simeon and Levi hamstrung the bull,” because this is said of Simeon and Levi, who plotted Christ’s death. It denotes the Jew, because of the fatness of carnal understanding or of pride, which is compared to a bull; hence David says: “Fat bulls surrounded me.” It denotes the heretic, who resembles a bull in pride; hence the Psalmist says: “A herd [Col. 0966D] of bulls among the cows of the peoples,” because heretics gather for the purpose of deceiving the simple, who are signified by cows. It denotes the saint, who is spiritually sacrificed to Christ as the bull was formerly sacrificed to God; hence the Gospel says: “My bulls and fattened cattle have been slaughtered,” as though to say: “Look upon the deaths of the preceding fathers and consider the remedies of your life.” By bulls are understood the saints who suffered for Christ the Lord.

*Taxus* denotes a tree mentioned by both Ovid and Virgil, which has sharp, prickly leaves and remains green in winter. It also denotes an animal otherwise called a *melos* or *melota*.

*Tectum*, properly, means a roof. It denotes the empyrean heaven; hence David says of Christ: “Like a solitary sparrow [Col. 0967A] on the roof,” because Christ alone with his own ascended into the empyrean heaven. It denotes the world, as the Psalmist says: “May they become like grass on roofs”; for roof-grass signifies the glory of the world. It denotes the mind, which is in a person as an upper roof in a house; hence the Lord says: “Those who are on the roof must not come down to take anything from the house,” that is, those who transcend bodily acts should not return to them. It denotes mortality, as it is said that in the spiritual building history lays the foundation, allegory builds the walls, and tropology completes the roof.

*Tegmen*, properly, means a covering. It denotes protection, as David says: “But the children of men shall hope under the covering of your wings.”

*Tela*, properly, means a web. It denotes the present life, as Job says: “My days passed more swiftly than a web is cut from the loom by a weaver, [Col. 0967B] and they were consumed without any hope.” It denotes a sequence of sins, as the prophet says: “Weave a web, but not by my Spirit, that you may add sin upon sin.” It denotes eternal damnation, as Isaiah says: “And the web which I have woven over all nations.”

*Telonium* is the place where a tax or toll is collected. It is also the office of receiving taxes; hence it is read that Christ saw Matthew sitting at the tax-office, either in such a place or appointed to such an office.

*Temperantia* is the harmony of things. It denotes the virtue by which a person resists enticements; in this sense the four cardinal virtues are identified: prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice.

[Col. 0967C] *Tempestas*, properly, means a storm. It denotes sedition, as the Psalmist says: “I expected him who would save [me],” and so forth, “from the storm,” that is, from sedition. It denotes judgment or a sentence of equity; or it is called a storm by comparison, because it will come unexpectedly on the day of judgment and suddenly snatch [people away]. Hence David says: “And a mighty storm around him,” that is, in his saints and angels; for the circle is the angels and saints who, seated with Christ himself, will judge.

*Templum*, properly, means a temple. It denotes the Church militant, as the Apostle says: “The holy temple of God is what you are.” It denotes the soul of the just, as David says: “The Lord is in his holy temple.” It denotes Christ, as David says: “He heard my voice from his holy temple.” [Col. 0967D] It denotes the world, as Isaiah says: “And those things which were beneath him filled the temple,” that is, his works filled the world. It denotes Christ’s human nature, as the Lord says: “Destroy this temple.” It denotes eternal life, as David says: “I shall worship toward your holy temple in your fear.”

*Tempus*, properly, means time. It denotes a division of time; hence it is said of the stars that they shall be signs of fair weather, storm, and seasons—that is, divisions of time. It denotes variety of conditions, as is said of the damned in the Psalm: “Their time shall be for ages”; hence in Job: “They will pass from the heat of fires to the cold of snows.” And in Revelation the angel is said to have sworn that henceforth there will be no time among the saved—that is, no variety of conditions; henceforth there is perfect uniformity. It denotes [Col. 0968A] a fitting opportunity, as Cicero says that an argument may be drawn from time, that is, from the opportunity of time. It denotes the air, because the seasons of the year are distinguished by the qualities of the air; hence weather is called fair or cloudy.
