Sometimes it is restricted so as to mean only a year, as it is read that Antichrist will reign for “a time, times, and half a time”—that is, for one year, two years, and half a year, namely three and a half years.

*Tendere*, properly, means to stretch. It denotes bending, as David says: “He stretched his bow and made it ready.”

*Tenebrae* is sometimes taken negatively, as in Genesis: “Darkness was upon the face of the deep,” that is, light did not yet exist. It denotes the lament of penitence, as [Col. 0968B] Job says: “Let that day be turned into darkness.” We turn the day into darkness when, strictly punishing ourselves, we torment the very alluring pleasures of wicked delight by the lamentations of rigorous penance. It denotes adversity, as is said of heretics: “They dig through houses in darkness.” The house is conscience, in which the soul in some manner dwells in darkness; therefore heretics dig through houses because they strive to corrupt the minds of good persons by their own adversity. It denotes the present life, as Job says: “Thus they walk in darkness as in light.” The present life is rightly called darkness, for in it the consciences of others are not seen. The eternal homeland, however, is light, in which the hidden things of hearts will be made manifest. Thus the impious walk in darkness as in light because they are as happy in their present blindness as though they already [Col. 0968C] enjoyed the light of the eternal homeland. It denotes the quality of the air, as in the catalogue of creatures: “Bless the Lord, light and darkness.” It denotes the gloom of ignorance, as Isaiah says: “The people who sat in darkness.” It denotes the darkening of sinners, as Isaiah says: “And darkness shall cover the earth.” It denotes deprivation of the highest good, as in the Gospel: “Cast him into the outer darkness.” It denotes demons darkened through sin, as in Genesis: “And he called the light day and the darkness night.” It denotes incomprehensibility, as David says: “He made darkness his hiding-place.” It denotes sinners, as in the Psalm: “You are he who lights my lamp; my God, enlighten my darkness.” It denotes the horror of hell, as Job says: “I shall go to a land of darkness and covered with the gloom of death”; and elsewhere: “In darkness I have spread my bed.”

[Col. 0968D] *Tenere*, properly, means to hold. It denotes observing or keeping, as John says: “Hold fast what you have.” It denotes embracing through grace, as in the Song of Songs: “I held him and shall not let him go.” It denotes being valid, as one customarily says: “This judgment does not hold,” that is, it is not valid or has no force or strength.

*Tenerum*, properly, means tender. It also denotes young, as Virgil says:

> I know not what eye bewitches my tender lambs.

It denotes humble, as is read of David that he was “the tenderest worm of wood.”

*Tentare* is the same as to test or prove, as in Genesis: “God tested Abraham.” It denotes suggesting evil, [Col. 0969A] whence the devil is said to tempt a person. It denotes enticing, whence our flesh is said by the Apostle to tempt us; and elsewhere: “Let no temptation seize you except what is human.” It also denotes lying in wait, as David says: “Where your fathers tested me.” Hence it is customarily said that God tempts in order to test, the devil in order to deceive, the flesh in order to entice, and a human being in order to know.

*Tentorium*, properly, means a tent. It denotes an assembly of evil persons, as the prophet says: “For iniquity I saw the tents of Ethiopia,” that is, the secret places of evil persons.

*Tenuis* also means cheap or poor, as the poet says:

> Eloquence is rare in a cheap garment.

It also means subtle, as is customarily said: “A fat belly does not produce a subtle mind.”

*Tepidus*, properly, means lukewarm. It denotes one who departs from the faith, [Col. 0969B] as John says: “Would that you were hot or cold; but because you are lukewarm, I shall vomit you out of my mouth.” Cold is one who has never been in the faith; hot, one who remains in faith and good work; lukewarm, one who departs from the faith.

*Terminus*, properly, means the end of a thing; and there is a boundary beyond the field and a boundary within the field. A boundary beyond the field is that which separates or marks off one field from another, such as a stone or stake. But a boundary within the field is the outermost part of the field. Hence the prophet rebukes those who join field to field as far as the boundary of a place or of a plot. It denotes the end of life, as David says: “You have set a boundary which they shall not pass.” It denotes distinction, as it is read that he established the boundaries of peoples according to the number of the children of Israel.

[Col. 0969C] *Terra*, properly, means the earthly fabric of the world; hence Moses says: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth,” that is, the empyrean heaven and the earthly world-order. It denotes bodily substance, as Isaiah says: “Heaven is my throne, but earth the footstool of my feet”; for incorporeal things are more worthy than bodily ones. Heaven, which signifies incorporeal things, is said to be God’s throne, while earth—that is, bodily things, which are less worthy—is called his footstool. It denotes a subject people or household, as in: “If my earth cried out against me.” Everyone who governs the Lord’s household and presides over faithful peoples for the common benefit possesses the rights of governance among the faithful entrusted to him, holding nothing other than land to cultivate. It denotes [Col. 0969D] earthly action, as the prophet says to an iniquitous mind under the name of the daughter of Babylon: “Come down, sit in the dust, daughter of Babylon; sit on the earth.” By dust we understand thoughts; by earth, earthly action. For the mind of the reprobate is first led to think wicked things and afterwards to do them. It denotes a person formed from earth, as is said: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go.” It denotes someone intent on earthly things, as in Genesis the devil is told: “You shall eat earth all the days of your life,” that is, you shall incorporate earthly persons into yourself. It denotes human flesh, as Job says: “The earth is given into the hand of the wicked.” It denotes sensuality, as in Genesis: “The earth shall bear thorns and thistles for you,” that is, sensuality [shall bear] the pricks of sins and the distress of offences. It denotes Holy [Col. 0970A] Scripture; and according to that interpretation the preceding authority may be expounded thus: “The earth shall bear for you,” because a person gains an understanding of Holy Scripture through many hardships and sorrows. It denotes the Synagogue, as David says: “Therefore we shall not fear when the earth is troubled.” It denotes the Gentile people, as Isaiah says: “As rain and snow descend from heaven and soak the earth and make it germinate,” and so forth, “so shall the word be.” It denotes the Virgin Mary, as David says: “Truth sprang up from the earth,” that is, Christ from the Virgin; and elsewhere: “Let the earth be opened and bring forth the Saviour.” It denotes the present Church, as the Psalmist says: “You have blessed, O Lord, your land”; this is the good earth which produces a hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold fruit. And elsewhere: “The earth is full of the Lord’s mercy.” It denotes the present [Col. 0970B] age, as David says: “In a desert and trackless land.” It denotes eternal life, which is called land because of its stability, as the Psalmist says: “Not so the wicked,” and so forth, “from the face of the earth.” It denotes hell, as Job says: “I shall go to a land of darkness and covered with the gloom of death,” and so forth.

*Terribilis* is the same as dreadful, as Jacob says: “How dreadful is this place!” It denotes someone displaying terror, as David says: “You are terrible, and who shall resist?” and so forth. It denotes wonderful, as the Psalmist says: “How terrible are your works, O Lord.”

*Tersum* means cleansed. It denotes pure; hence Plato calls a purer mirror *tersius* (“more polished”).

*Testa*, properly, means a potsherd. It denotes Christ’s human nature, as David says: “My strength dried up like a potsherd,” that is, [Col. 0970C] the strength of my human nature was strengthened by the fire of the Passion, just as a potsherd is hardened by the heat of fire. It denotes uselessness; the preceding authority may thus be explained: “My strength dried up,” that is, it became contemptible in human opinion, “like a potsherd”; for a potsherd is a fragment of a pot that is useful for no purposes. It denotes the Old Testament, in which the New Testament is said to have lain hidden as in a potsherd.

*Testamentum* denotes a promise, as in Luke: “To perform mercy,” and so forth, “of his holy covenant.” It denotes Christ’s Passion, as David says: “Those who seek his covenant,” that is, those who seek his Passion through faith and imitation of him. It is aptly called a covenant because through it the eternal inheritance was confirmed [Col. 0970D] to us. It denotes the evangelical law, as in: “This is the blood of the New Testament,” that is, the confirmer of the new law. It denotes the Mosaic law; hence the customary distinction between the New and Old Testament.

*Testimonium*: in the law lepers were commanded, once healed, to present themselves to the priests “for a testimony to them,” that is, for attestation. It denotes the Holy Spirit, as David says: “The testimony of the Lord is faithful.” The Holy Spirit is called the Lord’s testimony because through the Holy Spirit God the Father testifies that the saints are his own, since through him they have now received the Holy Spirit. It denotes a divine promise, according to another interpretation: “The testimony of the Lord is faithful,” that is, because he fulfils whatever he promises. And elsewhere: “Your testimonies have become exceedingly credible.” [Col. 0971A] It also denotes God’s creation, which bears witness to God’s goodness and greatness, as David says: “Wondrous testimonies.”

*Testitudo* [sic] is a kind of creature in a shell; hence Avianus says: “Once a tortoise spoke to winged birds.” It also denotes a vaulted roof, as is evident in Lucan.

*Tetragrammaton* may mean any word made up of four letters; hence Theodulus says: “To utter *tetragrammaton* in the mind.” But by antonomasia it is restricted to the ineffable Name composed of the letters *joth*, *vau*, *he*, and *thet*.

*Thalamus*, properly, means a bridal chamber. It also denotes the virginal womb: in a bridal chamber intercourse is celebrated, it is adorned with flowers, and secret matters are discussed. Similarly, in the womb [Col. 0971B] of the glorious Virgin Mary the union of the two natures was celebrated; for she was adorned with virtues, and in her the mysteries were completed. Hence David says: “Like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber.” It denotes the Church; according to this meaning, the foregoing authority may be explained. For Christ then came forth as a bridegroom from his bridal chamber when he sent preachers into the world. It denotes the union of Christ and the Church; hence the book of Canticles is called an *epithalamium*, that is, a song composed concerning the bridal chamber of Christ and the Church—that is, concerning their union. It denotes the human mind, as it is said: “Adorn your bridal chamber, O Zion,” that is, O human being, adorn your mind with virtues. In the bridal chamber bridegroom and bride are united by covenant and joined to one another in love; [Col. 0971C] thus the Church, or the perfect soul, is rightly called a bridal chamber, because it is so joined in love to the invisible bridegroom that it burns with desire for him and desires nothing that is now in the world. Therefore the mind which has become such receives no consolation from the present age, but sighs from its depths, burns, hastens, and is made anxious for her whom it loves.

*Theophania* means the Lord’s manifestation—that is, the manifestation of God which angels and saints possess in the homeland. Hence John Scotus says that in the future God will be seen through certain theophanies; because, just as the sun is seen in the air by means of a ray mingled with the air, so the divine nature [is seen] through a certain illumination by which the human mind will be illuminated. It also denotes that manifestation of the Holy Spirit and the Father, made over Christ when he was to be baptized through a voice and the appearance [Col. 0971D] of a dove.

*Thesaurizare*, properly, means to store up. It denotes accumulating, as the Apostle says: “He who stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath.” It also denotes meriting, as the Gospel says: “Store up for yourselves treasure in heaven.”

*Thesaurus*, properly, means a treasure. It denotes Christ, as the Gospel says: “The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field.” The field is Holy Scripture; the treasure is Christ hidden within it. It denotes Wisdom, as the Apostle says: “In whom are hidden the treasures of wisdom and knowledge”; and elsewhere Paul says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels.” It denotes eternal life, as the Lord says: “Store up treasures in heaven.” It denotes a hidden cause, as the Psalmist says: “He brings forth winds from his treasuries,” that is, from hidden causes. [Col. 0972A] It denotes Holy Scripture, as David says: “Placing the deeps in treasuries,” that is, by converting the depths—that is, the obstinate—to faith, you make them your treasuries. It denotes divine preordination, as David says: “He brings forth winds from his treasuries,” that is, from the Church he sends preachers according to divine preordination. It denotes the Church, according to another interpretation: “He brings forth winds from his treasuries,” that is, preachers from the Church. It denotes the human heart, as the Lord says: “A good person brings forth good things from the good treasure of his heart.” It denotes heavenly desire, according to another interpretation: “The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field.” The field in which the treasure is hidden is the discipline of heavenly study. He indeed buys that field after selling [Col. 0972B] everything who, renouncing the pleasures of the flesh, tramples every earthly desire through observance of heavenly discipline. But the treasure, once found, must be kept hidden, because one does not sufficiently protect the pursuit of heavenly desire from evil spirits if one does not hide it from human praise. In the present life, we are as it were upon a road by which we travel to our homeland. Evil spirits lie in wait for our journey like certain robbers. Therefore the one who carries treasure publicly on the road desires to be plundered. Thus let the work be public while the intention remains hidden: by good work let us provide an example to our neighbours, yet by the intention through which we seek to please God alone, let us always desire secrecy.

[Col. 0972C] *Thorax* is the same as *lorica*, a breastplate. It denotes faith or justice, as the book of Wisdom says: “They shall put on justice as a breastplate.” It also denotes spiritual fortitude, as is read in Job concerning the power of the devil: “When his sword has seized him, he will not be able to stand, neither spear nor breastplate.” By the sword is signified the devil’s malice or deceit; by the spear, missiles of precipitous assault; by the breastplate, the strength of patience. We strike an adversary with a spear; with a breastplate we are protected against an adversary so as not to be wounded. And this is the meaning: “When his sword has seized him”—that is, the devil’s deceit or malice—preaching and defence, and so forth, will not be able to stand.

Throne, properly speaking, a seat. It denotes the angelic order, whence it is sung: “Thrones and dominations.” It denotes the soul of Christ [Col. 0972D], whence David says: “You have sat upon the throne, you who judge.” It denotes equality; thus the statement “You have sat upon the throne” may be explained as meaning, “at the right hand of the Father,” that is, equal to the Father. It denotes heavenly things, whence: “Do not swear by heaven, because it is the throne of God.” It denotes judicial power, because a throne is judgment; whence Christ says to the apostles: “You shall sit upon twelve seats”; and David: “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever.” It denotes the Church, whence John says: “Beneath the throne of God I heard the voices of the slain.” And elsewhere in the same book: “Salvation belongs to our God who sits upon the throne, and to the Lamb.” It also denotes the faithful soul, whence it is read that the soul of the righteous person is the throne of God.

A censer (*thuribulum*) is a vessel in which incense is burned. It denotes Christ’s human nature, whence in the Apocalypse: “An angel stood [Col. 0973A] beside the altar of incense, holding a golden censer.” Here the angel is said to be Christ; the altar, the Church; the censer, Christ’s human nature. Or the censer is Christ’s flesh, and the fire is his soul, the Holy Spirit. It denotes the devout mind, whence a certain versifier says:

> The vessel, incense, and fire are mystical things: by the vessel  
> A devout mind is signified; by incense, prayers; by fire, heavenly love.

Incense (*thus*), properly speaking. It denotes devotion of heart, whence in the Song: “Who is this that rises like a little column of smoke, from the spices of myrrh and incense?” and so forth. By myrrh is signified mortification of the flesh; by incense, devotion of heart. It denotes a saint who refreshes others by the fragrance of a good reputation, whence: “I shall go to the mountain of myrrh and incense.”

*Thymiama* is a compound made from various kinds of spices; hence the altar of incense was so called, upon which [Col. 0973B] aromatic substances were burned. It denotes devotion of mind, whence it is sung after the feast of Michael also: “Glorious,” etc., “incense upon the altar,” that is, upon the altar of the cross let us offer God devotion of heart.

A pipe (*tibia*), properly speaking. It also denotes an uncomposed gait, whence David says: “Not in the strength of a horse, nor in the legs of a man”—that is, in the unrestrained gait of one presumptuous and bold. It denotes a musical instrument, whence the prophet says: “Harp and lyre, tambourine and pipe, are at your banquets.” It denotes the poetic Muse, whence Virgil:

> Begin with me, my pipe, the Maenalian verses.

A beam (*tignum*) is the same as a timber. It also denotes one greater in the Church of God, whence in the Song: “The beams of our houses are cedar; our ceilings, cypress.” The beams signify those greater persons in the Church of God who excel in knowledge [Col. 0973C] and virtues; the ceilings, lesser persons who adhere to the greater.

The Tigris, properly speaking. It denotes a river, whence Genesis says: “The name of the third river is the Tigris.” It denotes the devil or a heretic, who, when he finds no one to deceive, in a manner fails within himself; whence Job says: “The tiger perishes because it has not,” etc.

The linden (*tilia*), a tree. It denotes the world, comparable to the linden on account of its barrenness; for just as the linden produces the pleasantness of foliage yet yields no sweetness of fruit, so the world produces false pleasure but provides no benefit. Hence it is read in Theodulus, in *Pseustis*, that he had placed little she-goats beneath a pleasant linden. By Pseustis is understood paganism and [Col. 0973D] pagan philosophers, who delight in worldly things.

Fear (*timor*) is the dread by which someone naturally fears punishment; whence David says: “Fear and trembling came upon me.” This is called natural fear. It denotes the impulse by which someone fears to do evil, even though he does not fear to will it; whence Paul says: “You have not received again the spirit of slavery in fear.” This is called servile fear. It denotes the impulse by which someone fears to do spiritual good lest he lose a temporal good, as Peter feared to confess Christ lest he lose his temporal life; and this fear is called worldly fear. It denotes the impulse by which someone fears to do evil, or to will to do it, partly from fear of punishment and partly from fear of justice; whence the Psalm says: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.” This is called initial fear. It also denotes the impulse [Col. 0974A] by which someone fears to sin lest he be separated from God; whence David says: “Come, children, hear me: I shall teach you the fear of the Lord.” It denotes reverence, whence David says: “The holy fear of the Lord endures for ever and ever.” God himself is also called “fear”; for, according to some, *Theos* in Greek means “fear” in Latin, because he is especially to be feared. Jerome says: “Emphatically, *Theos*, or ‘fear,’ is so called”; whence Ecclesiastes says: “Fear God and keep his commandments.” In as many ways as *fear* is used, so also is *to fear*, and so forth.

A moth (*tinea*) is a worm. It denotes infernal punishment, whence Isaiah says of Nebuchadnezzar that a moth shall be spread beneath him. It denotes corruption, whence Job says: “And like a garment consumed by moths.” The garment is the human body; the moth, corruption that consumes it. [Col. 0974B] It denotes spiritual sin, whence the Lord says: “Where neither rust nor moth destroys.” Rust darkens and consumes, and is seen; but the moth consumes and is not seen. Rust therefore signifies carnal sins, which are visible; the moth, spiritual sins, which are not visible, such as anger and envy. It denotes temptation of the flesh, whence Job, speaking in the person of a tempted man, says: “I am to be consumed like rottenness and like a garment eaten by moths”; for an impure thought, arising not from elsewhere but from the person himself, consumes the flesh, like the garment from which the moth comes forth, in the mouth of the moth. It denotes heretical perversity, whence Job says of the heretic: “He built his house like a moth.” A moth builds itself a house by corrupting it; so the heretic makes a place for his unbelief only in minds that he corrupts.

[Col. 0974C] *Tinum* [*thyinum*] denotes an incorruptible tree. It also denotes obstinacy of mind shaded by enduring constancy, whence John says: “Every thyine wood and all vessels of ivory.” This is said of the wicked who remain in obstinacy of mind.

A firebrand (*titio*) is the same as a burnt stick (*tirsus*), that is, a piece of wood partly burned. It also denotes a declining power, whence the Lord says to Ahab: “Do not fear the tails of two smoking firebrands.”

A title (*titulus*) is a brief inscription indicating the work that follows. A *titulus* is also customarily called a memorial epigram or epitaph inscribed upon the tombs of the dead. It denotes a laudatory inscription, which in antiquity was written upon a triumphal arch in remembrance of a victory. Another kind [Col. 0974D] was written upon the thresholds of cities or houses as a sign of their founder. It also denotes the rule of the Fathers; whence, according to the rulings of the ancient Fathers, written under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, clerics caught in adultery cannot return to honour. It also denotes a *guiffa* or public seizure by auction, whence the administrators of the Church’s patrimony are to imprint *tituli* with a small pipe upon urban or rural estates wherever they suspect that its right applies. Likewise, a *guiffa* is a sign placed upon another’s property for the purpose of acquiring possession. It denotes a benefice, whence Pope Urban says: “By the harmonious enactment of the holy Fathers we have decreed that an ordination performed without a title is to be held void.” It denotes a reason, whence Saint Augustine says in *The City of God*: “By these two titles the wicked or unclean Satan revealed the subtlety of his deceit.” [Col. 0975A] It denotes a beginning or cause, as people commonly say, “By what title do you possess this?” It denotes praise, whence in the passion of Saint Vincent: “It is sufficiently credible, to the glory of the martyr Vincent, that the enemy begrudged him the title drawn from accounts of his deeds.” It also denotes a sign, whence it is read: “Jacob therefore took a stone and set it up as a title.” It denotes an example, whence Augustine says that lesser persons are formed by titles, that is, examples. It denotes faith, whence it is frequently read that pagans reproached Christians with the title of Christianity.

A toga is a kind of garment worn by Romans in time of peace. It also denotes peace, whence Lucan says:

> Will you endure a degenerate toga?

Or there *toga* is spoken of as a prohibition, or the toga-wearer himself, [Col. 0975B] that is, Pompey.

To take (*tollere*), properly speaking. It denotes receiving, whence the Gospel says: “Take what is yours and go.” It denotes removing, whence the Gospel says: “Take him away, take him away, crucify him”—that is, remove him from the midst. It also denotes cutting off, whence: “The Hebrew children taking branches.”

To thunder (*tonare*), properly speaking. It denotes threatening, whence David says: “The Lord thundered from heaven.” And elsewhere: “The Lord thundered over many waters.” And Isaiah: “God will thunder with his voice,” that is, he will threaten human beings.

Thunder (*tonitrus*). It also denotes a divine threat, whence it is said: “Who can hear the voice of his thunder?” Or it denotes enduring strength, and this will be in the time of Antichrist.

[Col. 0975C] Thunder (*tonitruum*), properly speaking. It denotes a divine threat, whence David says: “The voice of your thunder, O God, is in the wheel”—that is, the voice of your threatening, made through preachers, was in the wheel of the whole world. For the wheel is the circle of the earth; hence a small wheel is also called a circle, as he later explains when he says, “the world.” It denotes vengeance, whence Isaiah says: “He shall be visited by the Lord of hosts with thunder.” It denotes open preaching, whence it is read in the Apocalypse that John heard the voice of thunder.

A tone (*tonus*) is a musical proportion of one sound to another; hence a tone is said to be divided into a greater and a lesser semitone. It denotes variety of chant, whence: “Eight tones are distinguished in music,” etc.

[Col. 0975D] Topaz (*topazion*) is a precious stone found on an Egyptian island called Topanozi. It has two colours: one most pure, like gold; the other like the sky. It is bright and surpasses all gems in brilliance, and nothing is more beautiful to behold. If it is polished, it becomes dark; and if anyone wishes to see his image there, as is usually done in a mirror, the image of the beholder always appears reversed, if he looks upon heavenly things, and so forth. It also signifies a saint adorned with diverse virtues, who, having purged away the filth of this age, is pure gold and ever attends to heavenly things. Whoever possesses this virtue is brighter and more wondrous than all saints; whence John, speaking of the foundations of the heavenly Jerusalem, says: “The ninth, topaz.” It also denotes [Col. 0976A] earthly riches or earthly honour, whence the Psalmist says: “Above gold and topaz,” etc.

A winepress (*torcular*), properly speaking. It denotes Christ’s Passion, whence the prophet says: “I have trodden the winepress alone.” It denotes martyrdom, whence certain psalms are inscribed “For the winepresses,” because they treat of martyrs. Martyrdom is elegantly compared to a winepress, because just as wine is separated from grape-skins in the press—the skins being thrown upon the ground and the wine taken into the cellar—so through martyrdom the body is separated from the soul: the body is reduced to earth, and the soul is received into the storehouse of eternal blessedness. It denotes the Church, because in the Church the good are separated from the evil; hence it too is compared both to a threshing-floor and to a winepress. It denotes the separation of spiritual understanding from the letter, as in Solomon: [Col. 0976B] “The winepresses shall overflow with wine”—that is, expositions in which the meaning is separated from the letter shall overflow with mystical understanding. It denotes the Mosaic law, which pressed the people, whence the Gospel says: “The householder planted a vineyard and dug a winepress in it,” because he gave the Jews the law of the Lord.

Torment (*tormentum*), properly speaking. It also denotes an instrument of torture, whence in the prayer concerning Christ it is said that he did not disdain to be delivered into the hands of evildoers and to undergo the torment of the cross. And elsewhere: “Those whom you wish to serve by torture”—that is, by the cross—“make them not feel the torments.”

Rounded (*tornatile*), properly speaking: that which retains nothing of harmful excess; whence in the Song: “Your navel is a rounded bowl.” This means some saint offering teaching to others [Col. 0976C] and retaining no malice in himself. It also denotes blamelessness, whence it is read: “His hands are rounded”: these are saints whose duty it is to act so well that they are blameworthy in nothing.

A necklace (*torques*) is an ornament for the neck, whence Isaiah says: “On that day the Lord will take away the ornament of the shoes, the little moons, and the necklaces.” It denotes victory or the adornment of wisdom, whence Solomon says: “A necklace for your neck,” that is, the adornment of discourse seasoned with the salt of wisdom.

A torrent (*torrens*), properly speaking. It also denotes divine vengeance, whence the prophet says: “The breath of the Lord is like a torrent of sulphur.” It denotes the Passion, whence David says: “He shall drink from the torrent on the way.” And elsewhere: “Our soul passed through a torrent.” It denotes the human race held captive under the devil, which was converted to God through the grace of the Holy Spirit: [Col. 0976D] “As a torrent is turned in the south,” that is, when the south wind blows. It is a warm wind by which torrents are loosened so that they run; by these is figured the Holy Spirit, through whom people frozen by the icy cold of unbelief are released from sins and run to God. Hence David says: “Restore, O Lord, our captivity like a torrent.” It denotes the abundance of eternal blessedness, whence David says: “You will make them drink from the torrent of your delight.” It denotes overflowing iniquity, whence the Psalmist says: “Torrents of iniquity troubled me,” that is, iniquities abundant and swift like torrents. It denotes an unrighteous multitude stirred up for a time but soon to cease, like rain-fed streams. In this sense the preceding authority concerning Christ may be explained thus: “Torrents of iniquity troubled me,” that is, the wicked [Col. 0977A] crowds of the Jews acted so that I might be troubled. It denotes a judgment swift and suddenly tending to evil, or one who believes only for a time—that is, who falls away in the time of temptation—as a torrent quickly dries up; whence David says: “You have broken up fountains and torrents.” It denotes the world, which is in varying flux, whence Job says: “The willows of the torrent surrounded me,” because people unfruitful in good works, clinging to worldly things, surrounded the devil, obeying his suggestions. It denotes the fire of Gehenna, whence Job says: “The torrent separates the stone of darkness and the shadow of death from the pilgrim people; and those whom the foot of the needy man has forgotten.” The needy man is called Christ, who became needy for our sake; the foot is the holy preachers, through whom the fame of Christ traversed the whole world. The stone of darkness and [Col. 0977B] the shadow of death are the Jews, who remain in hardness of mind and in the darkness of ignorance. They were separated from the people of the saints when, having rejected the word of God, the apostles were sent to the Gentiles. The torrent—that is, the punishment of Gehenna—separates these Jews from the blessed. It denotes the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, whence Job says of the hypocrite: “Let him not see streams of the torrent of honey and butter,” that is, he shall not experience the grace of the Holy Spirit. It denotes someone who loves transitory things, whence Job says: “My brothers have passed away like a torrent.” It denotes the flowing stream of Sacred Scripture, whence Solomon says: “Let ravens from the torrents dig out the eye of him who mocks his father and despises his mother’s bringing forth.” For the perverse, when they criticize divine judgments, mock their father; and when they corrupt through derision the fruitfulness of [Col. 0977C] Holy Church, they despise, as it were, their mother’s bringing forth. But ravens come from the torrents when the preachers of Holy Church draw forth streams of holy teaching from Sacred Scripture. They are rightly called ravens because, through the grace of humility, they confess in themselves the blackness of sins. These dig out the eye of the mocker because they overcome the intention of wicked people. It denotes a heretic, whence Job, speaking of the followers of heretics, says: “They dwell in the wildernesses of torrents.” We call torrents the streams gathered from winter waters, which also dry up at fixed times. Therefore the inventors of wicked doctrines are rightly called torrents, because, cold from the warmth of charity, they grow up as though in the numbness of winter weather. Those, therefore, who follow their error dwell in the wildernesses of torrents—that is, they trust in the preaching of men whose utterances have been dried up by Catholic reasoning. It denotes a preacher, who, while in the present life he pours divine utterances upon us, floods like a multitude of waters in winter; but when the summer sun comes he withdraws himself, because, when the eternal light of the homeland has shone forth, he has ceased to preach. The wildernesses of this torrent are the comforts of temporal life. The righteous abandon these and turn to gain heavenly profits. But the wicked desire to acquire in this life what the righteous leave behind in contempt; therefore they are said to dwell in the wildernesses of torrents. In this sense too the authority may be explained: “They dwell in the wildernesses of torrents.”

[Col. 0978A] To scorch (*torrere*) denotes to burn. It denotes setting human hearts ablaze with the flame of sins, whence Theodulus says:

> The burning summer has now scorched the lands of the Ethiopians,

that is, the heat of sins has set human hearts ablaze.

A torturer (*tortor*) is the same as an officer or executioner who punishes the accused for crimes. It denotes the devil, whence the Gospel says: “The angry master handed him over to the torturers, until,” etc.

A marriage-bed (*torus*), properly speaking. It also denotes the union of Christ and the Church, whence the Church is called an immaculate marriage-bed. It also denotes an ornament hanging from the neck of an ox.

“Whole” (*totus*) sometimes gathers together integral parts, whence it is read that Christ made the whole person well on the Sabbath. Sometimes it does not denote the parts but the integrity of the whole, whence it is said that the whole Christ [Col. 0978B] is received at the altar—that is, entire. In this sense one customarily says: “The whole cloak is worth twenty shillings.” It denotes a person, not a nature, whence an authority says that during the three days Christ was whole in hell, not wholly there: whole, that is, in person, but not wholly in both substances. It is used negatively, whence an authority says that the Father transmitted the whole substance to the Son; and this is said against corporeal generation. For in corporeal generation the father’s substance is transmitted to the son by division: the son does not possess the whole substance, but only a portion. But in eternal generation the Father begot the Son in such a way that the whole substance of the Father is the substance of the Son, not by division but by fullness. It denotes [Col. 0978C] the two persons, the Son and the Holy Spirit; whence an authority says that the Father is the principle of the whole divinity—that is, of the Son and the Holy Spirit, in whom the whole divinity consists.

A *trabea* is a garment worn by Roman nobles. It denotes the flesh of Christ, clean from sin. Pope Leo says that the Son was clothed in the *trabea* of flesh.

A beam (*trabes*), properly speaking, denotes a grave sin, whence the Lord says: “First cast the beam out of your own eye, and then cast the speck out of your brother’s eye”—that is, first cleanse yourself of the greater sin before correcting another person.

To hand over (*tradere*), properly speaking. It denotes betraying, whence it is read in the Gospel concerning Judas that he sought an opportunity to hand Jesus over without the crowds. It denotes permitting someone to be handed over, [Col. 0978D] whence: “For this reason God handed them over to a reprobate mind.” It denotes exposing, whence it is sung of the martyrs: “They gave over their bodies.”

A shoot (*tradux*), properly speaking, is a branch produced from a tree. It denotes [flesh] from which other flesh is produced; hence in the *Scholastic History* it is read that the human body is “from a shoot,” that is, derived from another.

To draw (*trahere*), properly speaking. It also denotes infusing grace, whence the Lord says: “No one comes to me unless my Father draws him.” It denotes prolonging, whence Isaiah says: “Woe to you who draw iniquity with cords of iniquity.” It denotes joining, whence the Lord says: “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, shall draw all things to myself”—that is, I shall unite to myself by grace some people from every class of humankind.

To transfigure (*transfigurare*): to assume another’s form or likeness, whence it is read in the Apostle that the angel of Satan transfigures himself as an angel of light [Col. 0979A].

To pass over (*transire*), properly speaking. It denotes departing, whence Christ says in the Gospel: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” It denotes undergoing, whence David says: “We have passed through fire and water,” that is, we have experienced them.

A passage (*transitus*), properly speaking. It denotes the death of a saint, who passes through many places before coming to the place of the empyrean heaven; hence the death of blessed Martin is called his “passage.” It denotes that hour when the children of Israel were ready to depart from Egypt, when the destroying angel passed over the houses of the Israelites. “On my first passage I shall come to you,” that is, while passing through.

To tremble (*tremere*) is the same as to move; hence the earth is said to tremble, that is, to move, when an earthquake occurs. It denotes [Col. 0979B] fearing, whence the Psalmist says: “The earth trembled and was still when he arose.”

To grant (*tribuere*) is to confer something by divine authority, whence the Psalmist says: “He asked life of you, and you granted it to him.”

Tribulation (*tribulatio*) denotes adversity, whence David says: “In tribulation you made room for me.” It denotes death, whence Christ says: “For tribulation is near.”

A thistle (*tribulus*), properly speaking, is a kind of thorn, whence the poet says:

> With thistles and timber.

It is also an instrument by which grain is separated from chaff, otherwise called a flail. It denotes heretics, whence the Gospel says: “Do they gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles?” It denotes the piercing of pain, whence Job, binding himself under a curse among the goods he had enumerated if he had not acted thus, says: “Let tribulation arise for me instead of wheat, and a thorn instead of barley”—that is, may I receive the piercing of eternal damnation. It denotes labour, whence: “The earth shall bear you thorns and thistles,” that is, Sacred Scripture entails manifold labour of understanding.

A tribunal is the seat of judges. It denotes the judgment of God, whence the Apocalypse says: “We shall all stand before the tribunal of God,” that is, we shall all be presented to God’s judgment. It denotes excellence or height, whence it is sung in a certain hymn:

> Ascending the tribunal of the right hand  
> Of the Father, the power of all things.

A tribe (*tribus*), properly speaking, signifies an assembly of those of the same lineage, whence the Apocalypse says: “From the tribe of Judah, twelve thousand sealed.” It also denotes a nation, [Col. 0979D] whence the Gospel says: “You shall sit,” etc., over the tribes of Israel—that is, over all nations.

Tribute (*tributum*), properly speaking, whence the Apostle says: “To whom tribute, tribute.” It also denotes a debt, in accordance with our customary saying: “That man has paid tribute,” that is, the debt of nature.

A triclinium is a house in which there is a threefold arrangement of couches; hence in the Gospel, concerning the wedding at which Christ was present, mention is made of the master of the feast (*architriclinius*), that is, the chief of the triclinium. It denotes an assembly of women, whence it is read in Esther that they passed from the women’s triclinium to the king’s chamber, to be joined in the king’s embrace. But *triclinium* may mean either a threefold arrangement of diners reclining at table or a threefold arrangement of tables, as [Col. 0980A] is customary in monastic refectories. It denotes the blessed Virgin Mary, with whom divine Wisdom lodged through the humanity assumed, and the whole Trinity through grace. For the Father reclined in the virginal chamber by his operation, the Holy Spirit by overshadowing, the Son by incarnation. Hence a certain rhythmic poet says:

> Hail, Mother of mercy  
> And noble triclinium  
> Of the whole Trinity.

A trireme (*trieris*) is a ship having three banks of oars, whence the prophet says: “They shall come in triremes from Italy.” It also denotes deception occurring in three ways: by consent, by deed, and by habit; whence the Lord says in Isaiah concerning the triumphant Church: “Through it there shall not pass [Col. 0980B] a great trireme.”

Trinity (*Trinitas*). In natural philosophy this name could have the same force as the term “the number three” (*ternarius*). Yet it is transferred, with equivalent force, to theological discourse and becomes the name of three persons. According to some, it is equivalent to the expression “unity of three”; according to others, “threefold unity”; according to still others, “three are one.”

Sadness (*tristitia*), properly speaking. It denotes acedia; acedia is the torpor of mind by which one either neglects to begin good things or is weary of completing them.

Wheat (*triticum*), properly speaking. It denotes a saint, whence John says in the Apocalypse: “Two pounds of wheat for one denarius”; this was explained above. Elsewhere, concerning saints, it is read in the Gospel that Christ will winnow his threshing-floor, burn the chaff [Col. 0980C] with unquenchable fire, and store the wheat in his barn. It denotes the divine word, whence the Lord says: “Who do you think is the faithful steward, to give them their measure of wheat at the proper time?”

Threshing (*tritura*), properly speaking. It denotes the divine judgment that will separate the grains from the chaff. It denotes Jerusalem, to which the Lord says in threat: “Threshing of the threshing-floor.”

To thresh (*triturare*), properly speaking. It denotes destroying, whence the Lord says to Israel: “I shall make you like a threshing-sledge; you shall thresh mountains and crush them,” etc. It also denotes preaching, whence it is written in the law: “You shall not muzzle the ox that threshes,” that is, you shall not deny it necessities.

To triumph (*triumphare*), properly speaking. It denotes overcoming temptations, whence Christ is said to have triumphed over the enemy [Col. 0980D] and overcome death. It denotes attaining eternal life, whence the distinction is made between the Church triumphant and the Church militant.

A crossroads (*trivium*) is a place where three roads meet. It denotes the combination of the three liberal arts, which proceed as though hand in hand; hence the usual distinction between the trivium and the quadrivium.

Troy (*Troja*), properly speaking. It denotes a military conflict instituted by the Trojans, whence:

> And now the boys play at Troy;

a Trojan troop, as Virgil says.

A trophy (*tropaeum*) is something acquired in victory, whence Lucan says:

> And when proud Babylon was to be despoiled of Italian trophies.

[Col. 0981A] It denotes victory, whence it is sung in the hymn:

> Faithful Cross, etc.

And:

> Upon the trophy of the cross,  
> Proclaim the noble triumph.

Tropology (*tropologia*) is a particular allegory: when, through the deeds of one or more persons, the general Church militant or malignant is not understood, but rather, within the Church militant, either the perfect or the imperfect; or, within the malignant Church, heretics. It also occurs when a deed is understood as something to be done by us; hence tropology is called, as it were, discourse turned toward us. Thus, from Christ’s hands being nailed to the cross it is signified that we ought to restrain our hands from the guilt of sin.

[Col. 0981B] A trope (*tropus*) is a turning. It is also a figure in which a word is turned from its proper meaning; hence an expression is called tropical, that is, figurative.

A trowel (*trulla*) is a mason’s instrument with which he plasters a wall with mortar, whence the prophet Amos says: “He who sees a man standing upon a wall holding a mason’s trowel in his hand.”

A trunk (*truncus*), properly speaking, whence the poet says:

> With a trunk, not leaves, it makes shade.

It denotes a human body deprived of its head, whence Virgil says:

> A huge trunk lies upon the shore;

and this is also read in Judith. It also denotes a useless person, whence people commonly say: “That man is like a trunk.” It denotes a stock or origin of kinship, whence it is said: “He descends [Col. 0981C] from this stock.”

To weigh (*trutinare*), properly speaking. It also denotes examining, whence someone says:

> Supreme Aristotle, weighing the heights of things,  
> Divided into two whatever exists in the world.

A trumpet (*tuba*), properly speaking. It also denotes the manifest sign at which the dead will rise, whence the Apostle says: “In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet,” etc. It denotes open preaching, whence John says: “And another angel sounded the trumpet,” etc. It denotes a preacher who, having been brought through varied tribulation into the breadth of charity, whence David says: “With beaten trumpets and voice,” etc. By antonomasia David is also called the trumpet of the Holy Spirit, and he is compared to a trumpet for many reasons. [Col. 0981D] For we use trumpets at banquets, festivals, and wars. He, like a trumpet sounding the signal in war, says: “Blessed be the Lord my God, who teaches my hands for battle.” He also sounds joy for a banquet, saying: “With the voice of exultation and confession: the sound of one feasting.” As a sign of our solemnity he says: “Sound the trumpet at the new moon, on the day of your solemn feast.” Therefore the Gloss on the Psalter calls him the trumpet of the Holy Spirit. It denotes a threat, whence the prophet says: “Sound the trumpet in Zion.” It denotes proclamation, whence the Gospel says: “When you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before yourself.”

A hut (*tugurium*) is a small house customarily made in gardens or vineyards. It denotes desolate Jerusalem, whence Isaiah says: “And it shall be like a hut in a cucumber-field.”

[Col. 0982A] To swell (*tumere*), properly speaking. It signifies being proud. It denotes cleansing, whence it is said: “A man or the sea swells.”

A swelling (*tumor*) is an inflation. It denotes pride, as we customarily say: “He does this through the swelling of pride,” and “the swelling repels what has been poured in.” The inundation of the sea is also called a swelling.

A mound (*tumulus*) is an elevation of earth. It also denotes a tomb, whence Augustine says that rich people die in ivory beds and are carried with great pomp to the tomb; and in the hymn:

> When Christ rises from the tomb.

It denotes a heap of stones, whence Genesis records that Jacob and Laban gathered stones and made a mound.

[Col. 0982B] “Then” (*tunc*) sometimes denotes time, whence David says: “Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness.” Sometimes it denotes eternity, whence the Psalmist says: “Your throne, O God, is prepared from then”—that is, from eternity.

A tunic (*tunica*), properly speaking, is a garment worn beneath a cloak and signifies inward sins, whence the Lord says: “To one who wishes to take your tunic, let go your cloak also”—that is, if a teacher seeks to remove your inward sins, such as envy, confess to him also outward sins, such as fornication. The tunic also, because it clings to the body, signifies worldly care, whence the Lord says: “Let him who is in the field not return to take his tunic”; and again: “I have taken off my tunic.” It is also taken for clothing, whence the Lord says: “He who has two tunics, let him give to one who has none.” It also signifies the human body, whence the Lord says: “He who [Col. 0982C] has a tunic, let him sell it and buy a sword”—that is, if necessity arises, let a faithful person expose his body to martyrdom; for here the sword signifies martyrdom.

A crowd (*turba*), properly speaking. It denotes a disturbed multitude, whence Augustine says: “What is a crowd except a disturbed multitude?” And in the Gospel it is read that many crowds followed Jesus. They were called crowds because of their diverse intentions in following Christ: some followed him to be healed of their diseases; others to be refreshed bodily; others to see him working miracles; others to catch him in speech; others followed him from zeal for righteousness.

To be troubled (*turbari*), properly speaking. It denotes being distracted by various thoughts, [Col. 0982D] whence the Lord says: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things.” It denotes being driven by waves, whence the sea is said to be troubled, that is, agitated or driven. It denotes becoming weak, whence David says: “For all my bones have been troubled,” that is, weakened. It denotes being angry, whence David says: “They have been troubled and moved.” It denotes repenting, whence Habakkuk says: “The tents of the land of Midian shall be troubled,” etc.

A whirlwind (*turbo*) is a storm. It denotes tribulation, whence the prophet says: “A hiding-place from the whirlwind and the rain.” It also denotes the malice, persecution, or damnation of the devil, whence Job says: “May a dark whirlwind possess that day.”

Shameful (*turpe*), properly speaking. It also denotes dishonourable conduct, whence: “In a shameful vow, change your decree.” It denotes blameworthy conduct, [Col. 0983A] whence the *Ethics of Cato* says: “It is shameful for a teacher.” It denotes something horrible, whence Dionysius says: “… compelling the material part of their soul to rest in shameful images.”

A tower (*turris*), properly speaking. It denotes a proud person, whence Isaiah says: “On the day of the slaughter of many, when towers fall.” It denotes a preacher, who is compared to a tower because of strength and because of the lofty contemplation of heavenly joys, whence the Song says: “Your neck is like the tower of David.” It denotes those more eminent in the Church of God, whence David says: “May there be peace in your strength, abundance in your towers.” It denotes Christ, whence Isaiah says: “He built a tower in its midst.” The tower built in the vineyard, which signifies the Jewish people, is Christ made man, taking flesh [Col. 0983B] from the Jewish race, or the temple built by Solomon. It denotes circumspection, whence the Song says: “Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon.” Through the nose we distinguish fragrances and stenches, and therefore by it is signified the provident discernment of the saints. A tower is set on high so that an approaching enemy may be seen from afar. Thus the nose of the Church is rightly compared to a tower, because the provident discernment of the saints, placed on high while it looks carefully in every direction, apprehends fault before it arrives. It denotes height, whence Jeremiah says: “The city shall be built for the Lord, from the tower of Hananel to the gate of the corner.” The holy city is the Church; Hananel is interpreted “grace of God.” At a corner, moreover, [Col. 0984A] a double wall is joined. Therefore the city of the Lord is said to be built from the tower of Hananel to the gate of the corner, because Holy Church, beginning from the height of heavenly grace, is constituted unto the entrance [Note: [Col. 0983D] Something is missing.] and reception of the two peoples, namely the Jewish and the Gentile.

A turtledove (*turtur*), properly speaking. It denotes sensuality, whence the Psalm says: “The sparrow has found herself a house, and the turtledove a nest.” It denotes the preaching of the apostles, whence the Song says: “The voice of the turtledove has been heard in the land.”

A guardian (*tutor*) is one who defends another. It also denotes one appointed to the custody of a child, whence the Apostle says: “So long as the heir is a little child,” etc., “but under guardians,” etc.

A tambourine (*tympanum*) is a musical instrument [Col. 0984B] made from hide stretched upon wood. It also denotes mortification of the flesh, whence David says: “Praise him with tambourine and dance.”

A female tambourine-player (*tympanistria*) is a woman who plays the tambourine. It also denotes a faithful person chastising and reducing his own flesh to servitude, whence David says: “In the midst of young maidens playing tambourines.”

A type (*typus*), properly speaking, is a figure. It denotes a mystery, whence the Apostle says that the commandments of the Old Testament were given in type—that is, in mystery. Yet *typus* there may be called a figure; hence it is read in the *Histories* that David sent the Ammonites away in the brick-kiln (*typolaterum*).

U

[Col. 0983]

[Col. 0983C] **Breasts**, properly speaking. They signify Christ’s teaching and the refreshment of his presence; hence in the Song of Songs: “Your breasts are better than wine,” that is, your teaching and the refreshment of your presence surpass the fervour of the Law or any ordinances whatsoever. They signify the greater persons in God’s Church, who nourish the unlearned; hence in the Song: “Your two breasts are like two young roes.” They signify spiritual gifts; hence in the same place: “We shall rejoice and be glad in you, remembering your breasts more than wine,” that is, your spiritual gifts. They signify Jew and Gentile; thus the preceding authority may be explained: “Your two breasts,” that is, the two peoples coming from Judaism and Gentilehood into the body of holy Church, are attached to the hidden heart by the intention of wisdom. They signify the words of sacred utterance; hence Solomon: “He who presses the breasts hard to draw out [Col. 0983D] milk expresses butter; and he who wrings very violently draws out blood.” We press the breasts hard when we weigh the words of sacred utterance by subtle understanding; while, through that pressure, we seek milk, we find butter. For while we seek to be nourished even by a slight understanding, we are anointed with the abundance of inward richness. Yet this must neither be done excessively nor continually, lest, while milk is sought from the breasts, blood result. For often those who examine the words of sacred utterance more than they should fall into a carnal interpretation. They signify the increases of vain hope or confidence, or the encouragements of wretched despair. Hence Job, speaking in the person of the human race or of any penitent, says: “Why did I not die in the womb? Why did I not perish immediately when I came forth from the belly? Why was I received upon knees? Why was I suckled at breasts?” The womb of the sinful person is hidden fault. A person comes forth from the womb when a sinner is not ashamed openly to commit what he committed secretly. He is received upon knees when he is no longer ashamed of his iniquity. He is suckled at breasts when he is nourished either by a false hope in the Lord’s mercy or by the manifest misery of despair.

**Elm**, properly speaking. It signifies the worldly mind; hence the prophet: “I shall set in the desert the fir-tree and the elm.” The elm is the worldly mind which, while serving earthly things, bears no [Col. 0984D] spiritual fruit.

**Ulnae** are arms. They also signify measures; thus a cloth is said to be six *ulnae* or more in length. They also signify deeds or preachings; hence Isaiah: “They shall carry their children in their arms,” that is, O Church, preachers from the Gentiles shall bring you their children through preaching unto faith.

**Beyond** (*ultra*) is sometimes used with the force of a preposition, and sometimes denotes excess in time; at other times excess in place and in many other respects, as is evident from the various [Col. 0985A] words joined with it. It is sometimes also used adverbially. Sometimes it denotes excess in expression, as if I should say: “This man is wise beyond what can be said.” Sometimes excess in faith; hence: “Isaac was seized with a very great astonishment beyond what can be believed.” Sometimes in understanding; hence in the Psalm: “The Lord shall reign for ever and beyond,” that is, beyond what can be understood. Sometimes it denotes excess of time, that is, eternity; thus the foregoing authority may be explained: “The Lord shall reign for ever and beyond.” “For ever,” that is, as long as creatures shall exist; and creatures can cease to exist by nature, because whatever has a beginning also has a limit to its existence. “And beyond,” because he cannot cease to exist either in actuality or in nature.

**To howl**, properly speaking. It also signifies to weep; hence Isaiah: [Col. 0985B] “Howl, ships of Tarshish.” It also signifies to sympathize or grieve with another; hence the prophet: “Therefore Moab shall howl for Moab.”

**Howling**, properly speaking, is that of wolves or dogs. It signifies a horrible cry; hence: “A voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and great howling.” It signifies the cry of combatants; hence in Isaiah the howling of an army is mentioned.

**Navel**, properly speaking. It signifies lust; hence in Job: “His strength is in his loins, and his power in the navel of his belly.” The sources of intercourse are said to reside in men in the loins, but in women in the navel; for both sexes are very much subjected to the devil’s power through the weakness of lust. Thus his strength against males is said to be in the loins, and his power against females [in the navel]. It signifies the imperfect in God’s Church, because, although they lawfully cleave to the world, they nevertheless rightly proclaim Christ; hence in the Song: “Your navel is like a rounded bowl, never lacking cups.” Jerusalem is also called a navel.

**Shadow**, properly speaking. It signifies protection; hence David: “Protect me under the shadow of your wings.” It signifies sin which leads to eternal death and bears a certain likeness to death; for as death separates the soul from the body, so sin separates the soul from God. Hence Isaiah: “Those sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death.” It signifies a human being, who is compared to a shadow because of his transience, since he never remains in the same state; hence Job: “Man born of woman, living for a short time,” etc., “flees as a shadow.” [Col. 0985D] It signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit; hence in Luke: “The power of the Most High shall overshadow you.” It signifies forgetfulness; hence: “To enlighten those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death.” To sit in the shadow of death is to lie hidden in forgetfulness, away from the knowledge of divine love. It signifies the ignorance or error of this present life; hence: “Until the day breathes and the shadows decline.” It signifies the end of the age; hence: “Until the day breathes and the shadows decline,” that is, until the end of the age. It signifies death; hence Virgil:

> And life, groaning indignantly, fled beneath the shadows.

It signifies the soul; hence Lucan:

> And while proud Babylon was to be despoiled of  
> Ausonian trophies, the unavenged shade of Crassus wandered.

It signifies the figures of the Old Testament; hence it is customary to say [Col. 0986A] that, when Truth arrives, the shadow ought to cease. It signifies the obscurity of the Law; hence Habakkuk: “His shadow covered the mountains,” that is, the obscurity of the prophets enveloped the teachers. It signifies care or anxiety; hence, according to another exposition, the shadow—that is, his anxiety—covered the mountains. It signifies virtue; hence in the Song: “I sat under the shadow of him whom I desired,” that is, under the virtues which are the shadow of divine majesty. It signifies rest or refreshment; hence Job: “Servants desire the shadow.” It signifies torpor of mind, as is written of a sinful person: “He has attained the shadow”; for, fleeing the warmth of charity, a person forsakes the sun of truth and hides himself in the shadow of the earth’s coldness. It signifies the repose of eternal refreshment; hence in Job: “As a servant desires the shadow, and as a hired labourer awaits the end [Col. 0986B] of his work, so I have had empty months and have counted laborious nights for myself.” For a servant to desire the shadow is, after the heat of temptation and the sweat of labour, to seek the restful peace of eternal refreshment. Aptly, moreover, one who desires the shadow is called a servant, because every elect person, so long as he is bound by the condition of weakness, is held beneath the yoke of a master as under the anxiety of heat; but when he has been stripped of corruption, then he is revealed to himself as free and tranquil. It signifies one ignorant of the Lord; hence David: “Though I should walk in the midst of the shadow of death,” because the gloom of death is dark and leads to death. It signifies the present life; hence: “Though I should walk in the midst of the shadow of death,” that is, of the present life. It signifies a heretic or schismatic, who is the shadow of death; thus the foregoing authority may be explained: [Col. 0986C] “Though I should walk in the midst of the shadow of death,” that is, among heretics and schismatics.

**To anoint**, properly speaking. It signifies to restore by divine grace; hence: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness,” that is, with divine grace, etc.

**Ointment**, properly speaking. It signifies the gift of the Holy Spirit; hence in the Song: “Because your breasts are sweeter than wine, fragrant with the best ointments.” It signifies God’s grace; hence David: “Like ointment on the head which descends,” etc.; for here ointment signifies the fullness of grace that was in Christ. It signifies virtue; hence in the Song: “We shall run after the fragrance of your ointments,” that is, after the reputation of your virtues. It also signifies a miracle, as in the aforesaid example: [Col. 0986D] “We shall run after the fragrance of your ointments,” that is, after the fame of your name. It signifies faith in eternal goods, which are comparable to ointments; hence again: “We shall run after the fragrance of your ointments.”

**Nail**, properly speaking. It signifies what is plain; thus it is customary to say: “This was done *ad unguem*,” that is, fully and plainly. It signifies the end of a matter; hence it is said through the prophet: “The sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus, with a diamond nail.” This was stated above. The Jews’ guilt is reserved to be punished at the end by God’s strong judgment.

**Hoof**, properly speaking. It signifies persecution or the devil’s suggestion; hence in Job: “He digs the earth with his hoof,” that is, the devil’s suggestion reaches the hearts of earthly people. It signifies the perfection of virtues; hence Job says of the preacher: “He digs the earth with his hoof,” because the preacher, by the perfection [Col. 0987A] of virtues in his hearers, drives out and removes earthly thoughts.

**Unicorn** is an animal having one horn upon its nose, whence in Greek it is also called *rhinoceros*. It signifies Christ; hence David: “He built his sanctuary like a unicorn.” It signifies the Jew trusting in one horn, that is, in the Mosaic Law; hence David: “Deliver me from the mouth of the lion and from the horns of unicorns.” It also signifies singular power; hence the Psalmist: “My horn shall be exalted like that of a unicorn,” that is, my strength, consisting in the unity of the faithful—which is like the singular power of the unicorn—shall be exalted when heresies are destroyed. It signifies the devil; hence Job: “Will you bind the rhinoceros to plough with your strap?” For *rhinoceros* is interpreted “unicorn.”

[Col. 0987B] **Only one** (*unicum*) signifies what is singular. It signifies one; hence David: “I am only one and poor.” It signifies Christ’s human nature, which is singularly called “only one,” because it was singularly conceived and singularly born; hence David: “Rescue my soul, O God, from the sword, and my only one from the hand of the dog.”

**One** sometimes denotes unity; hence Boethius, in *On the Holy Trinity*: “Whatever is, is because it is one in number.” It denotes the simplicity of the divine nature; hence Christ in the Gospel: “I and the Father are one.” It denotes the unchangeableness of eternal blessedness; hence David: “One thing have I asked of the Lord; this will I seek.” It denotes integrity; hence it is said in the Creed: “As a rational soul and flesh are one human being, so God and man are one Christ.” It signifies agreement; [Col. 0987C] hence in the Acts of the Apostles: “They had one heart and one soul.” It signifies union, whence all are called one Church; and David: “Behold how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in one”; and the Philosopher says: “By participation in the species, several human beings are one.” It signifies mutual assistance; hence: “Several stones are one heap.” It signifies likeness; hence the Apostle: “He who clings to God is one spirit with him.” It signifies distinction; hence it is said: “An emerald is one stone,” that is, distinct from another. It signifies the exclusion of plurality; hence the Lord in Exodus: “Hear, son of Israel: the Lord your God is one.”

**City**, properly speaking. It signifies the mind; hence Solomon: “Like a city lying open and without a circuit of walls is a man [Col. 0987D] who cannot restrain his spirit in speaking.” For if a person lacks the wall of silence, the city of his mind lies open to the enemy’s darts. It signifies the Church; hence the prophet: “Zion, the city of our strength,” that is, the Church.

**To burn**, properly speaking. It also signifies to cleanse; hence David: “Burn my reins.” It signifies to inflame a person with lust; hence the Apostle: “It is better to marry than to burn.” It signifies to dry up; thus winter is said to burn herbs. For the poet says:

> For the crop of flax burns the field; oats burn it too.

**To urge** signifies to compel. It signifies to press upon; hence it is said in the histories: “Necessity was urging,” that is, pressing upon; and in the hymn:

> The solemn day was pressing on.

[Col. 0988A] It also signifies to close in; hence David: “Nor let [lacuna] press its mouth over me.”

**Bear**, properly speaking. It signifies a tyrant or an unbeliever; hence: “The calf and the bear feed together.”

**Nettle**, properly speaking. It signifies an unjust person who pricks others by corrupt speech and example; hence Isaiah: “In place of the nettle the fir-tree shall grow,” that is, the good shall occupy the place of the evil. It signifies the itching of evil thought; hence the Lord, rebuking the confused mind under the figure of Babylon, says through the prophet: “Nettles and thorns shall arise in her houses.” By nettles are figured the itchings of thoughts; by thorns, the pricks of vices. Nettles and thorns therefore spring up in the houses of Babylon because, in the confusion of a reprobate mind, both desires of thoughts arise that irritate, and [Col. 0988B] sins of deeds that prick.

**Usia**, properly speaking, is something composed of matter and form. It also signifies the divine nature; hence: “Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one *usia*.”

**Usiosis** is a thing subsisting in its own substantial property; hence a human being and a donkey are called *usioses*. It also signifies substantial property; hence, as stated above, Augustine says that substantial differences are to be admitted among *usioses*.

**Until** (*usque*), a preposition. It sometimes denotes place, sometimes time, and many other things, as is found in different passages of Scripture. Sometimes it marks the beginning inclusively, as there: “From the sole of the foot unto the crown,” that is, not even at the crown. Sometimes exclusively, as there: “All have turned aside,” etc., “there is not [Col. 0988C] one,” that is, except for Christ alone, namely, etc. *Usque*, as an adverb, denotes a turning about. Sometimes it denotes time, sometimes place: time, as there: “But you, Lord, how long?” Place, as when it is said: “How far shall we go?”

**Usury**, properly speaking. It signifies sin, because more is repaid in punishments than was committed in faults. It signifies robbery; hence an authority says that it is permissible to exact usury from those against whom it is permissible to wage war. It signifies the multiplication of the Lord’s talent, that is, the teaching which a teacher ought to multiply in the minds of hearers; hence it is read in the Gospel that the master of the household exacts usury from his servants. This master of the household is Christ, who demands multiplication from his servants, that is, from teachers, [Col. 0988D] of teaching.

**Ut** is sometimes used for “after”; hence in Luke: “When he learned that Jesus had reclined,” that is, after. Sometimes it means “although,” and this is evident. Sometimes it means “lest”; hence in the Psalm: “For he dealt deceitfully in his sight, that his iniquity might be found unto hatred,” that is, lest he acknowledge and hate his iniquity. In this sense we customarily say: “Take care that you do it,” that is, do not do it. Sometimes it denotes consequence; hence the Apostle: “The Law entered in, that offence might abound,” that is, this followed. Sometimes it denotes occasion, as may be understood in the same example, so that the sense is: “The Law entered in,” that is, the Law was the occasion of an abundance of offence. Sometimes it denotes truth; hence Paul: “Found in appearance as a man.” Sometimes [Col. 0989A] likeness; hence the same writer: “Like a wise architect, I lay the foundation.” Sometimes it denotes an efficient cause; hence Christ says: “For this I came into the world, that those who do not see may see.”

**Wineskin**, properly speaking. It signifies a person retaining God’s commandments, as a wineskin retains liquid; hence David: “I have become like a wineskin in frost,” that is, retaining God’s commandments among sinners. It signifies one in whom desire has been extinguished, because a wineskin is made from the hides of a dead animal; hence, according to another exposition: “I have become like a wineskin in frost,” that is, dead to desire. It signifies a carnal person; hence the Lord: “Neither do they put new wine into old wineskins, but new wine into new wineskins,” because spiritual precepts are not to be put into carnal persons, but into spiritual persons. [Col. 0989B] It signifies fear of death; hence David: “Gathering the waters of the sea as into a wineskin,” because unbelievers, signified by the waters of the sea, do not dare to murmur, fearing for their skins; and thus they keep within the evils which they do not dare to send out. It also signifies the Church; hence David: “God gathers the waters of the sea as into a wineskin,” that is, he consolidates wavering peoples into the unity of the Church, which Church mortifies its flesh. It signifies the confession of mortified sin; hence: “Gathering the waters of the sea as into a wineskin,” that is, gathering the peoples of the world into confession of mortified sin, lest they flow freely away.

**Womb**, properly speaking. It signifies God’s hidden substance; hence David: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.” It signifies the first movement of conscience; hence Job: “I would have been as though I had not been, carried from the womb to the tomb,” that is, from the first movement of conscience. It also signifies the Jews’ carnal observance; hence Christ says to the Father: “Upon you I was cast from the womb,” that is, from the Law’s carnal observances. It signifies the mind; hence it is said of the hypocrite in Job: “He conceived sorrow and gave birth to iniquity, and his womb prepares deceits.” The hypocrite’s mind conceives deceits when it thinks perversely; it gives birth to iniquity when it begins to carry out what it thought. It signifies thought; hence the Psalmist: “They went astray from the womb and spoke falsehood.” It signifies divine preordination; [Col. 0990A] hence in Job: “From whose womb came the ice? And who begot the frost from heaven?” that is, from whose providence proceeded the grace which cools the incitements of vices. It signifies legal observance; hence the Apostle: “But when it pleased him, he set me apart from my mother’s womb,” that is, from legal observance, etc.

**To use**, properly speaking. It signifies to have temporal things in use for God’s sake; hence Augustine: “To use is to refer a thing which one has in use to the obtaining of that in which one delights, namely God.” Sometimes it is also taken for “to enjoy”; sometimes it is taken for possession, but improperly.

**Grape**, properly speaking. It signifies the worldly mind; hence the prophet: “I expected it to produce grapes, but it produced wild grapes,” etc. It signifies Christ’s flesh; hence in Genesis: [Col. 0990B] “He shall wash his robe in the blood of the grape,” that is, Christ shall wash his flesh in his own blood. It signifies an evil deed; hence: “Their grape is a grape of gall,” that is, their deed is corrupt. It signifies the fervour of love; hence it is said of hypocrites: “Do they gather grapes from thorns?” Thorns—that is, briars—are heretics who tear and prick human minds; the grape is fervour of love; the fig is sweetness of conduct. Therefore, just as grapes do not grow from thorns, nor figs from briars, so heretics neither burn with love nor devote themselves to good works. It signifies sin; hence Ezekiel: “Your fathers ate a sour grape, but their children’s teeth are numbed,” as though to say: Posterity is punished for the sins of predecessors.

[Col. 0990C] **Wife**, properly speaking. It signifies the Church: “Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife,” that is, to the Church, “and the two shall be one flesh,” that is, of like nature. It signifies desire; hence in the Gospel: “I have taken a wife.” He takes a wife who cleaves to desire and thereby begets evil deeds as though they were children. It signifies sensuality; hence Gregory: “There are three things that force a person to leave his house: smoke, dripping water, and a bad wife”; and in the Psalm: “Your wife [shall be] like an abundant vine.”

# V

[Col. 0989]

[Col. 0989D] **To be free** (*vacare*), properly speaking. It signifies to give attention; hence the Apostle: “Do not defraud one another, unless perhaps by mutual consent, that you may be free for prayer.” It signifies to be absent or to cease; thus it is customary to say: “This is not devoid of mystery,” and the Jews were free from servile work on the Sabbath. It signifies to have no office; hence it is read that Sunday is free, that is, it has no office. It signifies to be left; hence the poet:

> Although renowned very greatly  
> In song . . . yet much remains undone.

It signifies to be permitted or to take pleasure; hence Ovid:

> It is not permitted to put spur to a horse given to wrongdoing.

**Cow**, properly speaking. It also signifies a foolish or undiscerning person; hence the Psalmist: “The assembly of bulls among the cows of the peoples,” or, according to another reading: “Among [Col. 0990D] the cows of buffaloes.” Bulls signify heretics because of their pride or wantonness; cows, simple people who are deceived by heretics because of their simplicity.

**To waver**, properly speaking. It signifies to grow weak; hence: “Your words strengthened those who were wavering.” It also signifies to doubt; hence someone is said to waver in faith.

**To go**, properly speaking. It signifies to be withdrawn from human sight; hence the Lord: “I go and I come to you.” It signifies to obey or to be moved by an impulse of mind; hence in the Gospel: “Go, and do likewise.” Again: “Go, and sin no more.”

**Woe** sometimes indicates temporal misery, sometimes eternal damnation; hence in the Gospel: “Woe to you, Chorazin; woe to you, Bethsaida!” and elsewhere: “Woe to you, hypocrites!”

[Col. 0991A] **Sheath**, properly speaking. It signifies Christ’s humanity, by which he was covered in his first coming; hence: “The sword of God is Christ, who in his first coming was covered by the sheath of humanity.” It signifies hidden and evil thought; hence Job: “Coming forth from his sheath and flashing in his bitterness,” that is, he shall reveal his malice—that is, evil thought. It signifies weakness, in which sense it is frequently found in medicine (?).

**Health** (*valitudo*). It signifies strength; hence a person is called *validus*, that is, strong. It also signifies weakness, and *validus* [may mean] weak, etc.

**Valley**, properly speaking. It signifies Jerusalem, which is called a valley because of the abasement caused by sins; hence Isaiah: “The burden of the valley of vision.” It signifies the world; hence David: “In the valley of tears, in the place which he has appointed.” It signifies [Col. 0991B] the penitent; hence: “Every valley shall be filled.” It signifies humility; hence in the Song: “I went down into the garden of nuts, to see the fruits of the valleys,” that is, the fruits of humility. It signifies a humble person; hence David: “The valleys shall abound in grain.”

**Vanity**, properly speaking. It signifies something earthly; hence: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.” It signifies mutability; hence the Apostle: “Every creature has been subjected to vanity,” that is, to mutability. It signifies an idol, which is not what it appears to be; hence David: “Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?”

**Vain** signifies false or lying; hence the Psalmist: “Each one has spoken vain things.” It signifies transient; hence all transient things are called [Col. 0991C] vain; and David: “Who has not taken his soul in vain,” that is, whose soul has not clung to earthly things. It also signifies useless or superfluous; thus someone’s words are called vain, that is, idle or superfluous.

**Vapour** signifies smoke.
