It signifies a person who never remains in the same state; hence a human being is called “a vapour appearing for a little while.” It signifies the Son of God; hence it is said of the Son of God in Wisdom, which is Philo’s book: “He is a vapour of the power of God.” For just as vapour proceeds from a thing and is of the same nature as the thing from which it proceeds—indeed, through vapour some knowledge is had, in a manner, of the thing itself, though nevertheless the vapour is one thing and the thing from which it proceeds another—so the Son proceeds from the Father while remaining of the same nature as the Father. The Son is [Col. 0991D] one person, the Father another; but through the Son knowledge of the Father is obtained.

**Vessel**, properly speaking. It also signifies a priestly garment signifying virtue; hence it is said of Aaron in the Book of Wisdom: “And he shall crown him with vessels of virtue.” It signifies weapons; hence in Isaiah implements of war are called weapons. It signifies a musical instrument; hence Jeremiah: “From vessels of lyres unto every musical instrument.” It signifies the heart or conscience; hence it is read in the Gospel that they took oil in their vessels, that is, in their hearts or consciences. It signifies Scripture, in which the food of the soul is contained; hence David: “I shall praise you upon instruments of psalmody.” It signifies a heretic who gives others the cup of death; hence David: “And in it he prepared vessels of death,” that is, heretics. Or obscure [Col. 0992A] passages of Holy Scripture are called vessels of death, because they are an occasion of death to some. Holy preachers are also called vessels of death accidentally; hence the Apostle: “To some we are the aroma of life unto life; to others, of death unto death.” It signifies a hearer who receives teaching; hence Isaiah: “The vessels of the deceitful are evil”—that is, the deceitful hearers of a teacher. It signifies a wife; hence the Apostle: “Let each one of you know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification,” for a wife is like a vessel used by a man and must herself be governed chastely. It signifies the Church or Christ; hence David: “I have become like a ruined vessel.” It signifies eternal blessedness; hence the Lord: “They gathered the good into their vessels,” that is, into eternal blessedness. Paul is also, by antonomasia, called the vessel of election. The good are also called vessels made [Col. 0992B] for honour, but the evil vessels of dishonour. In Isaiah vessel also means ship: a papyrus vessel is mentioned, whence Isaiah calls ships papyrus vessels.

**Vastness** is the same as greatness. It signifies destruction or desolation; hence Isaiah: “As in an enemy’s devastation.”

**Bar** (*vectis*) signifies wood or iron placed crosswise in a wall so that the wall may be stronger; hence bars adhering to the wall are mentioned. It signifies the wooden pole by means of which something is carried; hence it is read that bars were put through rings when the Ark was carried. It signifies the devil; hence Isaiah: “Against Leviathan, the bar-serpent.” By this he indicates the devil as both hard and soft. He calls him a serpent because he is soft in his flatteries; he calls him a bar [Col. 0992C] because he is hard in malice. It signifies strength; hence Isaiah: “My heart shall cry out to Moab; its bars as far as Zoar, the heifer that brings devastation,” that is, its strength. Zoar was called a heifer because of the luxury of its inhabitants, and it was called destructive because it was utterly overthrown by an earthquake for the third time. It signifies a fortification; hence, concerning the Chaldeans, the Lord says through Isaiah: “And he brought down all their bars.” It signifies a nail; hence it is read that Amos, pierced through the head with a bar, was carried into his own land and died. It signifies the state in which souls were so held in hell before Christ’s coming that they could not leave; hence it is read of Christ that he broke “the bronze gates and iron bars,” that is, he freed some from hell. The state of the blessed is also called a bar, because they could not be deprived [Col. 0992D] of paradise, nor can any of the wicked enter it after the day of judgment; hence David: “For he has strengthened the bolts of your gates,” or “bars,” according to another reading. It signifies the shore of the sea; hence the Lord says to Job: “I surrounded it with my bounds and set bar and doors.”

**Vehement** means the same as frenzied, because it is borne outside the mind. It signifies the Holy Spirit, either because he is “woe, eternally mindless,” that is, eternal damnation, or because he carries our mind upward.

**Or** (*vel*) is sometimes used disjunctively, as if I said: “This animal is healthy or sick.” Sometimes it is conjunctive or elective, as when it is said: “Take this or [Col. 0993A] that.” Sometimes it means “at least,” as when it is said: “You do not wish to do that; at least do this,” that is, at least. Sometimes it denotes a division between parts of time, as when it is said: “This man prays or reads all day,” that is, in one part he prays and in another he reads. Sometimes, however, it distinguishes between names, as if I said: “Matthew or Levi.”

**Veil**, properly speaking. It also signifies shame; hence Abimelech said to Sarah: “Behold, I have given a thousand pieces of silver to your brother; this shall be to you as a veil for the eyes,” that is, for shame, because you have been found unclean. It signifies the obscurity of the Law; hence the Apostle says that a veil is still placed over Moses’ face. Moses signifies the Law, the face understanding, and the veil obscurity.

[Col. 0993B] **Covering**, properly speaking. It signifies protection; hence David: “In the covering of your wings.” It also signifies a figure; hence it is said that the Gospels lay hidden beneath the covering of the Law.

**To will**, properly speaking, signifies to be moved by reason; hence the Apostle: “The will is present with me, but I do not find how to accomplish [it]”; and elsewhere in the same writer: “For I do not do the good that I will.” It signifies to bring into effect; hence it is said of God: “He did all things whatsoever he willed.” It signifies to counsel; hence it is said of God that he wills all people to be saved. It signifies to display signs of will; hence in the Gospel: “Jerusalem, how often I wished to gather [you].” It signifies to approve; hence it is said that God wills the wicked to be damned.

**Fleece**, properly speaking. It signifies the Jewish people, first watered with the rain of divine grace, yet to be stripped of their fleece, like a sheep, by the Church. It signifies the blinded Synagogue; [Col. 0993C] hence in the Psalm: “He shall descend like rain upon the fleece,” because God’s grace first descended upon the Jews, from whom he chose the apostles. It signifies the glorious Virgin Mary; thus the foregoing authority may be explained: “He shall descend like rain upon the fleece,” because Christ shall descend into the Virgin’s womb without any disturbance of flesh. The comparison is fitting: for fleece remains whole both in receiving and giving back water, just as the Virgin’s integrity remained before childbirth, after childbirth, and in childbirth.

**Vein**, properly speaking. It signifies the beginning of divine inspiration; hence Job: “My ear received the veins of a whisper.” [Col. 0993D] It signifies the source of a spring. It also signifies the tongue; hence Solomon: “A corrupted vein and a just man falling before the wicked.” For it often happens that those who shone endowed with greater knowledge, at last wishing to know more than human frailty permits, fall into the pit of folly. It signifies intellectual capacity; hence it is customary to say: “This came from the vein of my talent.” It signifies a mineral vein of earth; hence Job: “Silver has the beginnings of its veins.”

**To sell**, properly speaking. It also signifies to preach; for holy preachers distribute preaching and bring faith back to the apostles. Hence John in the Apocalypse: “That no one may be able to sell or buy unless he has the mark or the name of the beast”; because they will not be able to preach Antichrist as holy; they will preach only those [Col. 0994A] who imitate Antichrist. It also signifies to be subjected to another’s dominion; hence it is read that Adam sold himself to the devil by eating the apple. It also signifies to set forth; hence David: “You sold your people without sin.”

**Poison**, properly speaking. It signifies deception; hence David: “The poison of asps is beneath their lips.” It signifies magical art; hence he calls those who practice magical arts poisoners or sorcerers. Saint John likewise calls them sorcerers in the Apocalypse.

**To come** is the same as to go. It also signifies grace being infused; hence Christ says to Nicodemus concerning the Holy Spirit: “You do not know whence he comes or where he goes,” that is, into whom he infuses himself by grace.

**Belly**, properly speaking. It also signifies memory, because as [Col. 0994B] the belly contains foods, so memory contains thoughts; hence: “Their belly is filled from your hidden things.” It signifies legal teaching; hence Christ says to the Father: “From my mother’s belly you are my God,” that is, from the time you received legal teaching, which belonged to the mother, that is, the Synagogue. It signifies the heart; hence in the Song: “My beloved put his hand through the opening, and at his touch my belly trembled,” that is, at divine inspiration my heart trembled. It signifies the weaker persons in God’s Church; hence David: “My heart became like wax melting in the midst of my belly”; and elsewhere: “Your belly is like a rounded bowl.” The belly, which is the softer part of the body, signifies the weak in God’s Church, to whom Christ’s wisdom and will are also manifest; the manifestation of these [Col. 0994C] is figured by the melting of Christ’s heart. It signifies sensuality; hence in the Psalm: “Our belly is glued to the earth.” It signifies compassion; hence Isaiah: “My belly shall cry out to Moab like a lyre,” that is, the affection of my compassion shall accord with Moab’s misery as strings accord in a lyre. It signifies conscience; hence Jeremiah: “I am pained in my belly.” It signifies paradise; hence Job: “Why did he not close the doors of the belly that bore me, nor take evils from my eyes?” For the human race came forth from paradise as from a belly: there our conception began, there the first human being, the origin of humankind, dwelt. But the serpent opened the doors of this belly when, by wicked persuasion, it expelled humanity from paradise. It signifies [Col. 0994D] flesh; hence in the Psalm: “My eye, my soul, and my belly are troubled in anger.” It signifies avarice; hence it is said of the wicked person in Job: “Breaking in, he stripped the poor man’s house; he seized it and did not build it, and his belly is not satisfied.” In the *Morals*: “He breaks in and strips the poor man’s house who, having stripped and crushed one by power, is not ashamed also to despoil him through avarice. He seizes and does not build it, because he not only gives nothing of his own, but also takes what belonged to another. Therefore it is aptly added: ‘And his belly is not satisfied.’ For the belly of the wicked is avarice, because in it is gathered whatever is swallowed by perverse desire. It is clear indeed that avarice is not diminished by desired possessions but increased.” It signifies lust, as the Lord says to the serpent: “Upon breast and [Col. 0995A] belly you shall crawl,” that is, through pride and lust you shall deceive earthly people.

**Winnowing fan**, properly speaking, is an instrument that separates grain from chaff. It also signifies judgment; hence in the Gospel: “His winnowing fan is in his hand.”

**To winnow**, properly speaking. It signifies to cleanse; hence the Gospel says that the Lord will winnow his threshing-floor. It signifies to agitate; hence Theodulus:

> He agitates with frenzy . . . Io adorned with horns.

It signifies to repel; hence the authority that preachers are compared to rams because with horns—that is, with the authorities of the two Testaments—they drive back enemies. It signifies to be moved; hence in Job, the just person is not winnowed by every wind, that is, is not moved by every temptation.

Vent, properly so called. It signifies the course of human life, as in Job: “My life is like a scorching wind,” that is, the course of human life. It signifies divine vengeance, as in Job: “A scorching wind shall carry him away,” that is, divine vengeance. It also signifies an evil spirit, whence, according to another exposition: “For what is called in this place a scorching wind but the evil spirit, who kindles the flames of desires in the heart in order to draw it to eternal punishment?” It signifies transient prosperity, as is read in Job: “You lifted me up, setting me as it were upon the wind; you dashed me down violently.” By the wind the prosperity of transient life is denoted; and because the glory of the present life is seen as though on high and is founded in no stability, he who [Col. 0995C] rejoices in transient prosperity is set up as it were upon the wind. But he is violently dashed down when he is cast from that glory into the depth of adversity. It also signifies a transient thing, whence Job says in the person of the weak: “Like a wind you have taken away my desire.” By the name of wind a transient thing is understood; therefore wind takes away desire when a transient thing takes away the longing for eternity. It signifies the upheaval of the last judgment, whence the prophet says: “I saw, and behold, a storm-wind came from the north.” By the wind is denoted the disturbance of the final judgment, and by the north the coldness of sinners. Therefore the storm-wind comes from the north, because surely the causes of sins demand that the upheaval of strict judgment should throw all the elements into confusion at once. It signifies pride, whence David says: “[Col. 0995D] Not so the ungodly, not so; but like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth.” It signifies a severe temptation, whence the Psalmist says: “Let them be like dust before the face of the wind,” that is, let them yield to a lesser temptation before the onset of a greater one. It signifies the fruitfulness of doctrine, whence the light and unstable are said to yield to every wind of doctrine. It signifies a region of the world, whence it is read that the elect are gathered from the four winds, that is, regions. It signifies a preacher, whence David says: “He brings forth the winds from his treasuries,” that is, he sends preachers according to what he has foreordained. It signifies the soul, whence David says: “And he flew upon the wings of the winds”; for when his comprehensibility surpasses the powers of souls, which, by means of these wings, free themselves from earthly fears, they are lifted up into the breezes. It signifies uselessness or falsehood, [Col. 0996A] whence: “You utter words into the wind,” that is, idle or false words.

To sell is the same as to vend, whence: “Joseph was sold.” It denotes being subjected to sin, whence Job, in the person of the human race, says: “I was sold under sin.”

Briers properly signify sins, whence Isaiah says of the Synagogue that briers shall grow up over her. It signifies God, who punishes the wicked with eternal punishment, whence Isaiah says: “Who will make me a thorn and a brier?” It signifies a wicked person, whence Isaiah says: “Wickedness has been kindled like fire; it shall devour brier and thorn.”

A person is called truthful (*verax*) by reason of immutability. A person is called truthful by reason of a promise, by which he performs what he promises, whence: “God alone is truthful,” because he performs what he promises and is able to perform it. A person is called truthful by reason of utterance, because he declares what is true, whence: “God alone is called truthful, because he cannot speak falsehood.”

A blow, properly so called. It signifies correction, whence: “The blows of a correcting friend are better than the kisses of a flattering enemy,” because the former punishes through zeal for justice, etc.

Word, properly so called. It signifies understanding, and *verbum* (“word”) is said to derive from *verber* (“a blow”), that is, an affection of the soul. For the understanding of the soul is called an affection; whence Aristotle says: “Things in the voice are signs of those affections which are in the soul,” that is, of acts of understanding. It signifies an outward voice signifying understanding, whence: “Receive my words with your ears, O Lord.” The Son of God is also called the Word, because, just as understanding proceeds from the mind and is coeval with the mind, yet distinct from the mind, so the Son proceeds [Col. 0996C] from the Father, coeternal with the Father, yet distinct from the Father. Thus a material voice is called a word either because it signifies the word of the mind, that is, understanding, or from the striking of the air, because it is formed by the plectrum of the tongue; hence Plato too calls the voice a striking of the air. That the Son of God is called the Word is indicated by John the Evangelist, saying: “In the beginning was the Word.” Augustine affirms this on the same passage. It also signifies a thing worthy of mention. It is read in the Book of Kings: “There was nothing in the house of the Lord which Hezekiah did not show them,” that is, a thing worthy of mention. A word can also be a useless thing, whence David says to his brother Eliab: “Is there not a word?” that is, is it not a useless matter? Or: do I not have in my mind what I say with my mouth? It signifies what is false and idle, whence one commonly says: “These are words,” that is, [Col. 0996D] false or idle things.

Shamefacedness signifies shame, whence the Apostle says: “I speak this to your shame.” It signifies fear, whence the Psalmist says: “Let them be clothed with confusion and shamefacedness.”

Truth, properly so called. It signifies God, whence the Gospel says: “For this I came into the world, that I might bear witness to the truth,” etc. Christ himself also says of himself: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” It signifies eternal good, whence the Gospel says: “God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth,” that is, with good intention and for eternal things. It signifies the virtue by which a person performs what he promises, whence Tully places truth among the kinds of virtue. It signifies good action, whence the Apostle says: “But in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth,” that is, in the purity of innocence, that is, good action. It signifies [Col. 0997A] confession of truth, whence David says: “Truth has sprung up from the earth,” that is, confession has arisen from sinful man, so that he may accuse himself. It signifies fulfilment of a promise, whence David says: “In truth destroy them,” that is, as you promised; and elsewhere, according to another exposition: “Mercy and truth have met together.” It signifies justice, whence: “Mercy and truth have met together,” that is, mercy and justice have come together in Christ. It signifies the effect of justice, whence David says: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth,” that is, in every work of God there is an effect of mercy and justice. It signifies the manifestation of the effect of divine justice, whence, according to another exposition: “All the ways of the Lord,” that is, the two comings of the Lord are called the ways of the Lord. The first was when he came in the flesh to be judged; [Col. 0997B] the second will be when he comes for judgment, so that the world may be judged by him. In the first the effect of mercy was manifested; in the second the effect of justice will be manifested, when all generations are judged by him.

Little worm, properly so called. David too is called a little worm because of his humility and strength, whence it is read of him in the Book of Kings: “He is the tenderest little worm of the wood.” It signifies a red colour, whence: “Though your sins be red like the little worm [scarlet], they shall be white like wool.” It signifies distinction or variety, whence it is said in the Song of Songs: “We shall make for you golden ornaments variegated with little worms,” that is, distinguished or varied.

Worm, properly so called. It signifies Christ, whence David says: [Col. 0997C] “I am a worm and not a man.” A worm is born from the earth without seed, without noise; it crawls, is trodden underfoot, and is despised. So Christ was born of the Virgin without male seed, lived humbly among men, and—as the prophet says of him—“did not open his mouth,” that is, like a lamb he was silent before the one shearing him; despised and trampled upon by the Jews, he was killed. It signifies sin, whence Job says: “I said to corruption: You are my father; and to worms: my mother and my sister.” By saying, “You are my father,” he indicated that every human being descends from a corrupted origin. Hence he adds, “My mother and my sister are worms,” because both from corruption itself and together with it we come into this world. With respect to the matter of corruptible flesh, worms are my mother and sister, because we proceeded from corruption and came with the corruption that we bear. It signifies bitterness of conscience, whence: “Their worms shall not die.” It signifies man, whence it is read: “And the son of man is a worm.” It signifies carnal delight, whence Job says of the lustful person: “The worm is his sweetness,” because one who burns with desire for carnal corruption pants after the stench of decay. It also signifies carnal care, whence Job says of the wicked rich man: “This man dies strong and healthy, rich and happy; his inward parts are full of fat, and his bones are moistened with marrow. But another dies in bitterness of soul, without any possessions; and yet together they come to dust, and worms cover them,” because carnal thoughts oppress either the former so that he may possess what he desires, or the latter lest he lose what he possesses.

[Col. 0998A] A home-born slave (*vernaculus* or *verna*) is a slave born in his master’s household. It also signifies a servant, whence it is read in Genesis that Abraham took with him three hundred home-born servants.

A verse is metrical speech; a verse is also a proposition, as when it is said: “He answers against that party.” It also signifies a clause, whence the clauses of a psalm are called verses. Likewise in readings, a person may be said to be suited (*versus*) to this undertaking or that business.

To turn, properly so called. It also denotes to overthrow, whence David says: “Overthrow the wicked, and they shall be no more.”

The crown of the head (*vertex*) signifies the summit of a thing, whence the summit of a mountain is called its *vertex*; every head is also called a *vertex*. The Arctic pole, which is always visible to us and seems to rise above [Col. 0998B] us, is also called the *vertex*, whence the poet says:

> This summit is ever lofty for us.

It also signifies faith, whence Jeremiah says of Judah: “The children also of Memphis and Tahpanhes have violated you even to the crown of the head.” By the crown of the head is understood the loftiness of faith; to be violated even to the crown is, after the practice of evil deeds, to be corrupted even in the very loftiness of faith. It signifies a superior in the Church, whence Isaiah says: “From the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no soundness in him,” that is, from the greater to the greatest; hence Peter was called the crown of the apostles. It signifies reason, whence David says: “His sorrow shall return upon his own head and shall descend upon his crown.”

[Col. 0998C] Dizziness (*vertigo*) signifies a turning or rolling. It also signifies illness, as is read in medical writings. It also signifies stupefaction or fear, whence Isaiah says: “The Lord has mingled in their midst a spirit of dizziness.”

True (*verus*) is the quality by which someone is called true because he declares what is true, whence David says: “There is no truth in their mouth.” It is also the disposition by which someone intends to speak truth, whence Paul says: “I tell you the truth and do not lie.” Someone is called true by reason of essence; thus God is called true because he is unchangeable, or because he exists unchangeably, whence the Creed says: “True God from true God.” God is also called true in contrast to false gods, which are not true gods. A man too is called true because he utters a true word; a word is called true because what is said is true; a proposition [Col. 0998D] is called true because it signifies truth. Understanding is called true because it beholds truth. An oath is also called true when it has three companions: judgment, justice, and truth. Judgment too is called true, that is, right. Doctrine is called true because it teaches truth, whence the maxim: “Everything true is from God,” that is, every true doctrine.

A wasp is properly a kind of fly. It signifies terror, whence the Lord promises in the Law to the children of Israel that he will send wasps before them, that is, at their coming he will send terrors of spirit upon the inhabitants of the land of promise.

Evening. The noun *vesper* and the noun *vespere* have the same meaning. They sometimes denote the evening of a day or time, whence Genesis says: [Col. 0999A] “And there was evening and morning, one day.” Sometimes they denote the evening of grace, that is, the failure of grace, whence the Psalm says: “Weeping shall tarry at evening,” that is, misery, beginning from evening—that is, from the failure of grace in Adam and in many—will endure through many calamities. Sometimes they denote the evening of life, whence the Psalm says: “Man goes forth to his work until evening.” Sometimes they denote the end of the world, whence Christ is said to have been born in the evening of the world. Sometimes they denote adversity, whence Isaiah says: “From morning until evening you will make an end of me.” Sometimes they denote night, whence Matthew says: “But in the evening of the Sabbath,” that is, at night, so that this may be understood plainly. And lest you understand the night preceding the Sabbath rather than the following one, it is added: “Which dawns on the first [day] of the Sabbath,” that is, at the end of which the first day of the Sabbath dawns, namely the Lord’s Day. Sometimes they denote the torpor of idleness, whence Job says: “If I sleep, I say: When shall I arise? And again I await evening.” Sleep signifies torpor; rising, the stirring of action; evening, the torpor of idleness. But holy mother Church, so long as she is led through the life of corruption, does not cease to lament the losses caused by her mutability. As though she said: While at rest I seek the exercise of action, and while exercised I seek the leisure of rest.

A footprint, properly so called. It signifies a foot, whence in the hymn:

> His inmost parts pierced with nails,  
> stretching forth hands and feet,

that is, stretching forth hands and feet on the cross. It signifies [Col. 0999C] a work, whence the saints are said to imitate Christ’s footprints, that is, his works. It signifies a saint imitating Christ’s works, whence David says: “That my footprints may not be moved,” that is, the apostles and other saints will not be moved away from good works. It signifies Christ’s teaching, whence, according to another exposition: “That my footprints may not be moved,” that is, my teachings. It also signifies the rationale of God’s works, whence it is said: “Perhaps comprehending the footprints of God,” that is, the reasons for his works. It signifies the mark Christ left for his own to imitate, whence David says: “You enlarged my steps, and my footprints have not been weakened,” because the virtues which he left to his own for imitation have not been weakened either in himself or in his own. It signifies a perverse work, whence the Song of Songs says: “Go out and go after the footprints of the flocks,” that is, follow the various [Col. 0999D] acts of those who go astray. He does not command, but permits, and foretells what will happen. It signifies an inward disposition, whence Job says: “You have considered the footprints of their feet,” that is, their dispositions.

A garment, properly so called. It signifies Christ’s human nature, whence the prophet says: “Why then is your garment red, and your clothing?” It signifies the saints, who clothe Christ or are clothed by Christ, whence David says: “Myrrh and drop and cassia [come] from your garments”; and elsewhere: “Like oil upon the head, which runs down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, which runs down to the edge of his garment.” It signifies the state of innocence and immortality, whence Revelation says: “Blessed is he who watches and keeps his garments.” He keeps his garments who does not stain himself with more grievous sins. Holy Scriptures or the sacraments of the Church are also called Christ’s garments, whence David says: “They divided my garments among themselves.” By those who divided the garments are understood corrupters of the Scriptures. For just as they actually divided the garments, so those who do not aim at unity corrupt spiritual sacraments and holy Scriptures through heresies and perverse interpretation. It signifies a work, whence Solomon says: “Let your garments always be white.” It signifies divinity, which surrounds man like a garment, whence David says: “Clothed with light as with a garment,” because Christ is invisible in his divinity. It signifies man, whence man is called like a garment consumed by a moth. It signifies an assembly of the wicked surrounding the devil, whence [Col. 1000B] in Jeremiah a garment clotted with blood is mentioned. It signifies the heavens, which will be changed on the day of judgment, whence David says: “They shall perish, but you remain; and all shall grow old like a garment.” It also signifies the human body, and the aforesaid authority may be explained concerning the saints: “Like garments they shall grow old,” that is, the body is consumed.

To clothe. It denotes to surround or adorn, whence it is said to the Church: “The Lord lives, for with all these you shall clothe yourself as with an ornament.” It denotes to veil, whence divinity is said to be clothed with humanity, that is, veiled.

Clothing, properly so called. It also signifies charity, which cannot be divided because it is bestowed from divine grace alone. Thus the Psalmist says: “They cast lots for my clothing,” because divine charity, figured by the seamless tunic, is bestowed by divine grace alone, which is signified by the lot. It signifies Christ’s body, whence Isaiah says: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah?” It also signifies God’s Church, whence John says: [Col. 1000C] “He was clothed in a garment sprinkled with blood,” because the Church in the martyrs has been drenched with its own blood.

Old, properly so called. It signifies weak, whence Adam is called old because he was weakened through guilt and punishment. It signifies a carnal person, whence the Gospel says: “Neither do they put new wine into old wineskins,” because the austerity of the Law was not to be imposed upon the apostles [sic], because they were old, that is, carnal. It also signifies what weakens, whence guilt is called old because it brings us to the weakness of guilt and punishment. Thus the Apostle says that, [Col. 1000D] with Christ, the old man was crucified. It signifies what has been abolished, whence Leviticus says: “You shall eat the very oldest of old things, and when the new things come, you shall cast away the old,” that is, the ceremonial observances which have been abolished. The very oldest things are the precepts of nature; the old things are the precepts of the Mosaic Law; the new things are the precepts of the Church’s teaching.

Oldness is the same as antiquity. It signifies the weakness of punishment or guilt. [Note: [Col. 0999D] Something is lacking.] Hence it is read that Christ, by his simple oldness, namely by the weakness of punishment and guilt. It signifies the abolition of the Mosaic Law, whence the Apostle’s authority says that we ought to walk in newness of life, not in oldness, etc.

Way, properly so called. It signifies the repentance by which one must travel, whence the prophet says: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight [Col. 1001A] in the wilderness the paths of our God.” It signifies a prelate who ought to provide us with an example of life, whence Lamentations says: “The ways of Zion mourn, because there are none who come to the solemn feast.” It signifies the divine law by which we ought to walk, whence David says: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way.” It signifies a divine command or good action, whence the Book of Wisdom says: “The Lord led the righteous man by straight ways.” It signifies the world, whence David says: “Blessed is the man who has not gone,” etc., “in the way of sinners.” It signifies faith or the Virgin Mary, whence the Psalmist says: “My God, his way is undefiled,” that is, holy faith and the immaculate Virgin Mary. It signifies Christ, whence the Gospel says: “I am the way.” Likewise: “They have not known the way of peace.” It signifies Christ’s spiritual coming, whence Job says concerning wisdom: “God sees its way, and he himself knows its place.” Whoever, by preaching, cleanses the hearts of hearers from the filth of vices prepares the way for wisdom that is coming. Wisdom therefore has a way, and it also has a place: the way by which it comes, and the place in which it remains. “If anyone,” he says, “loves me, he will keep my word.” The way is that in which Christ comes; the place, that in which he remains. And because it is uncertain to everyone in whose heart he comes, or in which heart, after coming, he rests by remaining, it is rightly said here: “God understands its way, and he himself knows its place,” because it belongs to divine sight alone to see both by what means the understanding of wisdom comes to the heart and by what means the mind does not lose the understanding of life which it has received. It signifies the path of uprightness, whence: “If my step has turned aside [Col. 1001C] from the way.” What is the way but the path of uprightness? Our step turns aside from the way as often as our thought leaves the path of uprightness after an erroneous perception. It signifies the breadth of one’s own freedom, whence the Gospel says: “Enter by the narrow gate, for broad is the gate and spacious the way that leads to destruction.”

Viaticum is the same as provisions for a journey. It signifies Christ’s body, whence it is read that viaticum, that is, the sacrament of the Eucharist, must be denied to no penitent who is at the point of death.

Neighbour, properly so called. It signifies a person willing to approach the Christian faith, whence David says: “I have become a reproach to my neighbours.” It signifies an angel who cleaves to Christ through charity, whence the Gospel says of the woman who, having found the drachma, summoned her women-neighbours; for Christ rejoices with the angels over the redemption of the human race, and there is greater joy among God’s angels over one sinner doing penance.

A victim, properly so called, whence Isaac says: “Behold fire and wood; where is the victim for the burnt offering?” It also signifies divine vengeance, whence Isaiah says: “For the Lord has a victim in Bozrah.” It signifies Christ’s sacrifice, or Christ himself, whence we frequently read in Holy Scripture that Christ is called a victim.

Victory, properly so called. It signifies constancy in martyrdom, whence in a certain prayer: “O God, who among the other miracles of your power bestowed even upon the weaker sex the victory of martyrdom.” It signifies the destruction of death, whence the Apostle says: “Death has been swallowed up in victory.”

A lane (*vicus*) is called a narrower way, just as a street (*platea*) is called a broader way. [Col. 1002A] It signifies a village, whence Jerome says that Jeremiah was native to the village of Anathoth. It signifies the spiritual person who, while advancing toward heavenly things, follows the narrow way; just as a street signifies one who lawfully uses this world, whence the Song of Songs says: “Through lanes and streets.” Yet sometimes the lane signifies the carnal person who runs about through the various windings of lanes, whence the Gospel says: “Go quickly into the streets and lanes of the city.”

To see. It denotes to imagine, whence: “What do you see, Jeremiah?” Elsewhere it is read that Pharaoh saw a dream. It denotes to hear, whence it is read that the people saw voices and heard, because sight is the more excellent of the senses; under the name of sight another sense is sometimes designated. Thus, when a demonstration is made to any sense, grammarians say that it is “made to the eye.” It denotes [Col. 1002B] to understand, whence the Lord says: “He who sees me sees my Father also.” It denotes to beware, whence Revelation says: “See that you do not do it.” It denotes to experience, whence the Gospel says that Simeon received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death. It denotes to act for sight, whence the eye is said to see because it is the instrument of seeing. God is said to see, that is, to know, whence the maxim: “What does he not see who sees the One seeing all things?” God is said to see, that is, to judge, whence David says: “See my humiliation from my enemies.” It denotes to have mercy, whence the Lord says: “I have seen the affliction of my people,” that is, I have had mercy on their affliction. It denotes to approve, whence: “God saw all things which he had made,” that is, he approved them. God too is said to see when he causes something to be seen; thus the aforesaid authority may be explained: [Col. 1002C] “God saw,” that is, he caused it to be seen.

A widow, properly so called. It signifies a people infected with heretical perversity, whence Job says of a heretic: “And his widows shall not weep.” Whom do we understand by his widows but subject peoples left bereft by his death? They do not weep for the death of the heretic because, remaining in their error and thinking that their preacher was holy, they comfort themselves with a false hope so as not to grieve. It signifies the soul which recognizes itself as bereft of every aid except that of God alone, whence: “Blessing I will bless his widow.” It signifies the Church, whence it is read that a widow by her persistence moved the judge. It signifies one deprived of worldly hope, for whom even error as husband has died, whence the Psalm says: “They shall be troubled at his presence, the father [Col. 1002D] of orphans and judge of widows.”

To watch, properly so called. It denotes to take care, whence the Lord says: “I watch over my people.” It denotes to beware, whence: “Watch therefore, because you know neither the day nor the hour.” It also denotes to labour, whence it is said of the sinner: “He shall be led to the graves, and shall keep watch among the heap of the dead.”

A watch, properly so called. It also signifies a part of the night; for the night is divided into four parts called watches, whence Genesis says: “It came to pass in the morning watch.” It signifies thought, whence Solomon says: “The watchfulness of honour wastes away the flesh.”

A country estate, properly so called. It signifies worldly ambition, whence the Gospel says: “I have bought an estate and must go to see it.” For those who seek worldly dignities cannot [Col. 1003A] come to God’s supper. It signifies one who receives faith, because faith dwells in him, whence the Song of Songs says: “Let us remain in the estates.” Or the estates there are understood as pagans, from whom Christ wishes to make a city for his preaching, etc.

A steward (*villicus*) is the keeper of an estate. It signifies Christ’s vicar who makes bad use of his spiritual office, as in the parable of the steward of iniquity. Jerome, however, says on that parable that Paul is signified by the steward of iniquity.

To conquer, properly so called. It denotes triumphing over the devil, whence John says: “The lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered.” It also denotes to overcome or confound, whence Paul says: “Overcome evil with good.”

Bound, properly so called. It signifies one entangled in sins, whence a certain antiphon is sung: “Lead forth the bound from [Col. 1003B] the prison-house.” It signifies one detained in hell, whence Isaiah says: “You brought forth the bound from the pit in which there was no water.” It signifies one oppressed in tribulation, whence the Psalm says: “Those bound in poverty and iron.”

A bond, properly so called; it signifies sin, whence David says: “You have broken my bonds,” that is, my sins. It signifies charity because it binds together all the other virtues, and is thus called by the Apostle “the bond of perfection.” It signifies a binding ordinance, whence someone is bound by the bond of anathema. It signifies eternal punishment, whence the Psalmist says: “He shall cast down upon this mountain the torch of the binding bond.” It signifies flatteries and threats, whence the Psalm says: “Let us break their bonds.” It is as though Christ said: Thus do the faithless act wickedly against; but, O faithful, let us break their bonds, [Col. 1003C] that is, their flatteries and threats. It signifies argument, whence the aforesaid authority can be explained thus: “Let us break their bonds,” that is, the arguments of Christ and the disciples by which they wish to bind us. Thus these are the words of Christ’s persecutors.

Vintage, properly so called, whence Isaiah says: “The vintage has mourned and the vine has grown weak.” It signifies divine vengeance, whence the same prophet says: “And the Lord of hosts shall make,” etc., “a banquet of vintage,” etc.

To gather grapes, properly so called. It denotes to destroy, whence it is read of Judah: “All who pass along the way gather her grapes.” Those who pass along the way are said to be those who exercise temporal dominion, such as those who have often destroyed Judah.

A vineyard, properly so called. It signifies an activity which we ought to cultivate through the practice of daily [Col. 1003D] labour. Yet, though appointed as keepers in vineyards, we do not keep our own vineyard because, while we are entangled in activities foreign to us, we neglect the ministry of our own work. This is the meaning of: “They made me a keeper in the vineyards.” It signifies a collection of trees bearing balsam, whence the Song of Songs says: “My beloved is to me a cluster of cypress in the vineyards of Engaddi.” It signifies the breadth of Holy Scripture, whence Job says of heretics: “They reap a field not their own, and they gather the vintage of the vineyard of one whom they have violently oppressed.” Therefore the breadth of Scripture may be signified by the name of field, which heretics reap though it is not their own, because from it they take up statements far different from their own views. It is also expressed by the name of vineyard because it brings forth clusters of virtues, namely pure teachings. Heretics gather this vineyard’s grapes because from [Col. 1004A] it they heap up clusters of statements according to the tendency of their own interpretation. It signifies a soul fruitful in good works. Indicating the malice of evil spirits under the figure of a certain nation, the Lord says through the prophet: “I have set my vineyard in the wilderness for those lying in wait.” God’s vineyard is placed in the wilderness for evil spirits when a human soul full of fruits is dissipated through the desire for human praise. It signifies the life of any negligent person, as Solomon says: “I passed through the field of a slothful man and through the vineyard of a foolish man; and behold, nettles had filled it all, thorns had covered its face.” To pass through the field of a slothful man and the vineyard of a foolish man is to observe the life of any negligent person and consider his works, which nettles and thorns fill; because in the hard ground of negligent hearts earthly desires and the pricking shoots of hostile vices spring up. It signifies the Synagogue, whence: “A certain man planted a vineyard.” It signifies the Church turned away from the Gentiles, whence the Song of Songs says: “My mother’s sons fought against me; they made me a keeper in the vineyards.” It also signifies the first believers, whence the Epithalamium says: “The flowering vineyards gave forth fragrance,” that is, the fragrance of good conduct.

Wine, properly so called. It signifies contemplation of heavenly things, whence David says: “And wine gladdens the heart of man.” This wine is the rapture of the mind from earthly to heavenly things, which so inebriates people that it makes them sober. It signifies concupiscence, whence the Apostle says: “Do not be drunk with wine, wherein is debauchery.” It signifies temporal abundance, [Col. 1004C] especially because it consists in wine, whence the Psalm says: “From the fruit of grain and wine,” etc. It signifies higher teaching, whence Solomon says: “Wine kills little ones.” It signifies perverse action, whence Deuteronomy says: “Their wine is the gall of dragons.” It signifies a prelate of the Church who so inebriates others that he makes them sober, whence Christ is said in Jacob’s blessings: “His eyes are more beautiful than wine.” It signifies divine preaching, whence Isaiah says: “Your tavern-keepers mix wine with water.” That teacher or preacher mixes wine with water who teaches or preaches with a view to human favour or earthly gain. It signifies a soul received into the storehouse of eternal blessedness, whence John says: “And he himself treads the winepress of the wine of the wrathful fury of God.” For as grapes are crushed in the winepress in order that storehouses may be filled with wine, so indeed the elect are crushed by the afflictions of pressures in order that they may remember the heavenly dwelling-place; and because they patiently endure the pressure due to sinners, they are rightly now called the wine of the wrathful fury of God. It signifies the austerity of the Law, whence the Song of Songs says: “Your breasts are better than wine,” that is, the Gospel teaching is better than the austerity of the Law. It signifies the spiritual seasoning of virtues and good works, whence the Epithalamium says: “And I will give you a cup of spiced wine.” It signifies the office of divine preaching, whence the Song of Songs says: “Your throat is like wine.” It signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit, whence: “He brought me into the wine-cellar”; this is the Church of God, in which the gifts of the Holy Spirit resound. It signifies a greater person in the Church of God who presides over others through spiritual grace, whence the Epithalamium says: “I drank my wine with my milk,” because into the Church [Col. 1005A] of God are incorporated both the greater, signified by wine, and the lesser, signified by milk.

A viper, properly so called. It signifies the ancient Jews, intoxicated with the venom of malice, whence the Lord says: “Brood of vipers, who,” etc. It signifies the devil deceiving man through perverse persuasion, whence: “He shall suck the head of asps, and the viper’s tongue shall kill him.” Or here a viper means a heretic who kills the simple by his perverse doctrine. It signifies a king of Jerusalem who is compared to a viper on account of malice, such as Zedekiah or Jehoiakim, whence Isaiah says: “In the land of tribulation and anguish are lion and lioness, and from them viper and flying basilisk.”

Man, properly so called. It signifies a virtuous man, whence David says: “Blessed is the man who has not gone.” It signifies a husband, whence the Gospel says: “Jacob begot Joseph, the husband of Mary.” It signifies a male, whence it is read in Holy Scripture that men and women were taken captive, that is, males and females. It also signifies a person mature in age, whence the Apostle says: “Let us all attain to a perfect man, to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ”; thus a distinction is commonly made between an adolescent, a man, and an old man. It signifies an angel, whence Daniel says: “Behold, the man Gabriel.” It signifies the devil, whence Jeremiah says: “Cursed be the man who announced to my father, saying: ‘A male child has been born to you.’” Why did that man who announced his birth to his father receive a sentence of cursing from the prophet? By the prophet is signified the mutability of the human race, which came through deserved punishment; by his father is expressed that world from which we are born. And who is he who announces our birth to our father, except the devil? When he desires us to fluctuate in thought, he incites the minds of evil persons who excel through the authority of this world, so as to persuade us to deception. When he sees us doing weak things, he exalts them with favours as though they were great deeds; and he speaks as though males had been born when, through falsehood, he rejoices that we have become men who corrupt. Thus he announces to the father that a male has been born when he shows to this world the one whom he has persuaded to sin as a corrupter of innocence.

To grow green, properly so called. It denotes to flourish in charity, whence Job says: “Can a rush grow green without moisture?” As though he said: The Gentile people cannot flourish in charity without the moisture of grace.

[Col. 1005D] **Rod**, properly speaking. It signifies correction, whence David: “Thy rod and thy staff”; and the Apostle: “Shall I come to you with a rod?”—that is, with inflexible justice. It signifies divine justice, whence David: “Thou shalt rule them with a rod of iron.” It signifies Christ’s dominion among the faithful, whence David: “The Lord shall send forth the rod of thy strength.” The Prophet is not speaking of that kingdom in which Christ reigns with the Father, but of the temporal, dispensational kingdom by which, through the Incarnation, he called us to eternity and reigns in us. And this began with the Jews, because the Jews were first made subject through faith. It signifies the authority necessary for receiving provisions from subjects, whence it is read in Mark that the Lord commanded his disciples, when sent forth to preach, to carry nothing with them save a rod only—that is, that they should have authority to receive necessities from their subjects.

[Col. 1006A] It signifies the persecution of the devil, by which he formerly persecuted the human race, whence Isaiah: “For thou hast broken the yoke of his burden, the rod and sceptre of his oppressor, as in the day of Midian.” It signifies the governance by which Christ rules his own, whence David: “Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the rod of uprightness is the rod of thy kingdom.” It signifies the Church, whence in the Song: “Who is this that comes up through the wilderness like a little rod of smoke?” It signifies the glorious Virgin Mary: “There shall come forth a rod from the root of Jesse.” It signifies Sennacherib, through whom God punishes the Jews, whence in Jeremiah: “Assyria, the rod of my wrath.” It signifies Christ, whence: “What seest thou, Jeremiah?” “I see a waking rod”; and the Lord says: “And I will watch over my people.” From these words it is suggested that Christ called himself the rod of watchings; for properly speaking,

[Col. 1006B] a “rod of watchings” is called the rod which a thief secretly inserts into a house, testing whether the people in the house are awake or not.

**Virginity** is manifold; for there is virginity of the flesh . . . There is also a superficial virginity, which belongs to hypocrites, of whom Sacred Scripture speaks in various places.

**Virgin**, properly speaking, whence the Apostle: “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.” A virgin is also said to be one who, though corrupted in mind, is nevertheless whole in body, seeking not God’s regard but human favor; whence we read of the five foolish virgins who took no oil. In an appropriate sense the mother of Christ is also called the Virgin, as Rome is called the City. The earth too was called

[Col. 1006C] virgin before Adam’s sin, because it was in no way corrupted; whence it is read that Adam was formed from virgin earth.

**Shrub**, properly speaking. It signifies the Church, whence: “He shall grow up like a shrub before him”; this is said of Christ.

**Greenness**, properly speaking. It signifies earthly delight, whence: “All greenness has perished.” It signifies a teacher of charity, whence David: “Its hind parts are in the pallor of gold, or in the greenness of gold,” according to another translation.

**Virtue**, properly speaking. It signifies Christ’s human nature, whence David: “O Lord, in thy strength the righteous man shall be delivered”—that is, Christ’s human nature shall rejoice in being united to thy Word. It signifies bodily strength, whence David: “The giant shall not be saved by the multitude

[Col. 1006D] of his strength.” It signifies divine power, whence in Luke: “The power of the Most High shall overshadow thee”—that is, divine power. It signifies secular power, whence the Psalmist: “A king is not saved by his great power.” It signifies an angelic order, whence in the Gospel: “And the powers of heaven shall be moved.” It signifies the Gospel, whence the Apostle: “For it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth.” It signifies a miracle, whence Christ, concerning the woman with the issue of blood healed by touching the hem of his garment, says: “I perceive that power has gone out from me”—that is, a miracle; and in many other places Christ and the saints are said to have worked powers, that is, miracles. It signifies an apostle or preacher, whence David: “The king of the powers of the Beloved”—that is, of Christ—“of his powers,” that is, of his apostles; and this is said in the manner of the Old Scripture. Thus it is read in the Old

[Col. 1007A] Testament: “Moses did as the Lord commanded him.” It also signifies the effect of a thing; hence herbs and stones are said to possess great virtues, that is, effects. It signifies perfection of strength, whence David: “Cast me not off in the time of my old age; when my strength fails.” Or “powers” there means virtuous persons. Virtue is also sometimes called fortitude, according to the distinction between prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice.

**Force**, properly speaking. It signifies violence, whence one commonly says: “This man used force against me.” It signifies divine correction, whence in Isaiah’s Canticle: “O Lord, I suffer force.” It signifies the assault of sin, whence the penitent says: “O Lord, I suffer force”—that is, the assault of sin.

**Entrails**, properly speaking. They signify those who minister to the spiritual

[Col. 1007B] sacraments in the Church, whence Job, speaking in the person of the Church, says: “And he poured out my entrails.” For what else should we understand by the entrails of holy Church except the minds of those who contain within themselves certain of her mysteries? But when the ancient enemy draws away into secular occupations some who seemed to minister to the inner sacraments, he undoubtedly pours her entrails upon the ground, because he tramples down in lowly things those who formerly lay hidden in secret and spiritual matters. It signifies the human heart, whence David: “Renew my spirit within my entrails.” It signifies compassion, whence it is read: “His entrails were moved.” It signifies inward parts, whence Habakkuk says of an idol: “There is no spirit in its inward parts.”

[Col. 1007C] **Viscus** is the same as glue. It also signifies the bond of an evil habit, whence it is commonly said that someone is held fast by the glue of an evil habit.

**Vision** is the perception of some thing by means of sight, and this vision is called bodily. It signifies imagination, whence Daniel says to Nebuchadnezzar: “Thy dream and the visions of thy head”; and this vision is called imaginary or spiritual. It signifies ecstasy, by which a man is carried away to the contemplation of heavenly things, whence: “The vision of Isaiah the prophet”; and this is called intellectual or mental. The first is called the first heaven, the second the third; whence Paul: “I know a man caught up even to the third heaven.”

**To visit**, properly speaking. It denotes healing, whence in the Canticle: “The Dayspring from on high has visited us.” It signifies correcting, whence

[Col. 1007D] David: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod.” It also denotes condemning, whence the Lord says of those to be condemned: “And after many days they shall be visited.”

**Life**, properly speaking, whence Job: “The life of man upon earth is warfare.” It signifies grace, whence Ezekiel: “He shall live, life, and shall not die.” It signifies eternal blessedness, whence in the Gospel: “Those who have done good shall come forth unto the resurrection of life.” It signifies resurrection, whence David: “He asked life of thee, and thou gavest it him”—that is, resurrection; whence Christ also says of himself: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” It also signifies the divine nature, whence in the Gospel: “As the Father hath life in himself,” etc.

**Vine**, properly speaking. It signifies Christ, whence in the Gospel: “I am the true vine.” It signifies the Church

[Col. 1008A] or wisdom, whence: “I have borne fruit like a vine,” etc.

**Glass**, properly speaking. It signifies penetration of intellect, whence it is said in Job: “Gold or glass shall not be equal to it”—that is, human wisdom or penetration of intellect cannot be compared with God’s wisdom. It signifies purity of heart. For if some vessel is made from other metals, whatever is placed within is by no means seen outside; but in glass whatever is placed within is wholly seen through, and therefore glass signifies purity of heart. Whence John says: “And the city itself was pure gold, like clear glass.” It signifies purity of faith, which the saints who hold it also make manifest by speech; and thus the passage “And the city itself,” etc., may be expounded.

**Ribbon**, properly speaking. It signifies a preacher, whence in the Song: “Thy lips are like a scarlet ribbon.” A preacher is called a ribbon

[Col. 1008B] because by his preaching he constrains the wandering thoughts in human hearts, lest they flow away and weigh down the eyes of the heart.

**Heifer**, properly speaking. It also signifies the ten tribes, whence Hosea calls Ephraim a heifer trained to love threshing, because the people of Israel had become accustomed to endure tribulations and pressures. The city of Zoar is called in Isaiah a collapsing heifer, because it fell in the third earthquake. It signifies the carnal mind, whence the prophet says under the figure of Ephraim: “A heifer trained to love threshing,” etc. For a heifer accustomed to the labors of threshing often returns to the same work even when not compelled. Thus the mind of the wicked, devoted to this world’s service and accustomed to the fatigues of temporal affairs, even when it may freely rest,

[Col. 1008C] nevertheless hastens to submit to earthly sweats and, through the habit of its miserable manner of life, seeks the threshing of labor; so that it does not wish to cease from the yoke of worldly servitude even when it is permitted to do so.

**Calf**, properly speaking. It also signifies Christ, whence it is read of the householder that he offered the fatted calf to the prodigal son upon his return. It signifies prayer, whence: “Let us render to God the calves of our lips.” It signifies a saint, fattened with the richness of virtues, whence David: “And he shall break them in pieces like a calf of Lebanon.” It signifies the new people, free from the yoke of the Law and from sin, whence the Psalmist: “Then shall they lay calves upon thine altar”—that is, the reaping angels shall lay new peoples upon the altar, that is, upon the heavenly Jerusalem. It signifies a preacher who fills the Church with lowings, that is, preachings;

[Col. 1008D] whence, according to another exposition: “Then the greater ones,” namely the apostles, “shall lay calves,” that is, preachers, “upon thine altar,” that is, the Church.

**To live** sometimes denotes temporal or bodily life, whence it is read in a certain prayer: “In whom we live, and move, and are.” Sometimes it denotes spiritual life, whence Paul: “I live, yet no longer I.” It denotes the bestowal of the cause of life, whence follows: “But Christ lives in me.” It signifies enjoying eternal blessedness, whence the Lord: “He that believes in me, though he were dead, shall live.” It denotes existing eternally, whence: “The Lord lives”; and elsewhere: “I live because of the Father.” All things are said to live for God through knowledge. A tree too is said to live, that is, to be green; whence in a homily: “They live not by a soul but by greenness.” It denotes being

[Col. 1009A] in memory, whence Priscian says of Virgil: “Virgil, who wrote the *Bucolics*, lives”—that is, in memory.

**Vocal**, that is, sonorous, whence the poet says: “Vocal Orion.” It signifies a letter which produces a sound by itself, whence the grammarian distinguishes vowels and consonants.

**To call**, properly speaking. It denotes bringing from non-being into being, whence the Apostle: “Who calls those things which are not as though they were.” It denotes predestining, whence: “Who calls those things which are not”—that is, who predestines the Gentiles, who appear not to exist because of idolatry, as those who exist—that is, the Jews, who appear to exist because of their observance of the Law. It denotes infusing grace, whence: “Who calls those things which are not”—that is, he thus infuses his grace into the Gentiles as into the Jews. It denotes inspiring, whence the Apostle: “Whom he called, them he also predestined.”

[Col. 1009B] **To fly**, properly speaking. It denotes ascending ineffably to heavenly things, whence David: “He flew upon the wings of the winds.” It denotes the most rapid spreading of Christ’s fame among all people; whence, according to another exposition, Christ is said to have flown—that is, his fame was most swiftly proclaimed throughout the whole world. Hence fame too is said to fly, and Virgil says: “Fame flies.”

**Bird** or **winged creature**, properly speaking. It signifies the devil, whence the Lord: “The birds of heaven ate it.” It signifies the proud man, whence: “The birds of heaven and the fishes of the sea.” It signifies the contemplative man, whence: “And the birds of heaven lie hidden”—with the wisdom of God understood. It signifies the spiritual mind, whence in the Gospel: “To what is

[Col. 1009C] the kingdom of God like?” etc.: “to a grain of mustard seed, which a man took and put into his garden; and it grew and became a great tree, and the birds of heaven rested in its branches.” He is the grain of mustard seed who, planted in the burial-place of the garden, rose as a great tree. He was a grain when he died, a tree when he rose again. The branches of this tree are preachers, in whose branches the birds of heaven rest, because holy souls, which lift themselves up by the thought of eternal things as though on certain wings of virtues, take breath from the weariness of this life through their sayings and consolations.

**Will**, that is, what is subject to will. It signifies the divine nature, whence it is read: “Who can resist his will?” It signifies the effect of the divine will, whence

[Col. 1009D] Christ: “I came not to do my own will.” It signifies that which is subject to the divine will, whence in the Gospel: “Thy will be done.” A threefold will of Christ is also commonly distinguished: the will of his divinity, by which he immutably willed to die; the will of reason, by which he steadfastly willed to die; and the will of sensuality, by which he willed not to die, whence he himself says: “Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me.” Will is also used properly. It signifies a movement of the will, as one commonly says: “This is my will,” as though saying, “I am moved toward this.”

**Pleasure**, that is, delight. It also signifies eternal blessedness, whence David: “They shall be made drunk with the abundance of thy house, and with the torrent of thy delight.”

**Wallowing-place**, that is, a rolling in mud. It also signifies

[Col. 1010A] the uncleanness of sin, whence it is said that a sinner is like a sow in a wallowing-place of mud, etc.

**Ploughshare**, properly speaking. It also signifies a preacher, whence it is read that the preacher cleaves the hearts of hearers with the ploughshare of his preaching.

**Vomit**, properly speaking. It signifies apostasy, or turning away from God or from the faith, whence it is said that a Christian who falls into mortal sin is like a dog returning to its vomit.

**Vow**, properly speaking. It signifies the offering by which a saint offers himself to God, whence David: “I will pay my vows unto the Lord,” and this before all his people, that they may take an example. It signifies the will by which a saint wishes to offer himself to God through suffering; thus the foregoing authority may be expounded as though it said: “I will take the cup which is

[Col. 1010B] in my vow,” that is, in my desire, “and afterwards in the act itself I will pay my vows.” A vow also signifies the saint himself, who offers himself to God, whence in the Psalm: “My vows,” etc., as though saying: “I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise, namely in such a way that I will pay my vows to the Lord,” that is, myself, because I am his image; for the image must be rendered to God, according to the Lord’s saying in the Gospel: “Render therefore unto Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and unto God the things that are God’s.” It signifies devotion of mind, whence David: “Offer unto God the sacrifice of praise, and pay thy vows unto the Most High”—that is, devotion of mind.

**Voice**, properly speaking. It signifies evidence, whence the Lord the Father says to Cain in Genesis: “The voice of thy brother’s blood,” etc.—that is, the evidence of blood shed. It signifies a sound formed in the air, which is called the voice of the Father that sounded:

[Col. 1010C] “This is my beloved Son.” It signifies a command, whence Christ says of his own in the Gospel: “They shall hear my voice.” It signifies the desire of the elect, who desire the salvation of human beings, whence John says in the Apocalypse: “And I heard a great voice from heaven.” It signifies John the Baptist, whence in the Gospel: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness,” because, as a voice precedes a word, so John preceded Christ. It signifies attestation, whence David: “Deep calls unto deep at the voice of thy cataracts”—that is, the Old Testament accords with the New, as the prophets and apostles, signified by the cataracts, bear witness. It signifies contraction, whence David: “The floods have lifted up, O Lord,” etc., “because of the voices of many waters.” It signifies preaching, whence in the

[Col. 1010D] Song: “The voice of the turtle-dove is heard in our land; arise, my beloved.”

**To wound**, properly speaking. It denotes being the cause of Christ’s Incarnation, whence in the Song: “Thou hast wounded my heart, my sister”; these are Christ’s words, as though he said to the Church: “For love of thee I assumed flesh.” It denotes extinguishing earthly love in the unbelieving, whence: “They struck me and wounded me”; the Church says this of preachers who extinguish earthly love in the hearts of the faithful.

**Wound**, properly speaking. It signifies the guilt or stain of the soul, whence Augustine says that, if we could behold the wounds of the soul, we would find them graver than bodily wounds; and elsewhere in Isaiah: “A wound and bruise and swelling sore is not bound up.” It signifies eternal damnation,

[Col. 1011A] whence in the Apocalypse: “And there came a grievous and very evil wound upon men.” It also signifies compunction, whence it is said: “The arrows of Christ,” that is, the sayings of Sacred Scripture, “pierce the soul unto wounds.”

**Fox**, properly speaking. It signifies a heretic, whence: “Catch for us the foxes.” It signifies Herod the tetrarch because of his deceitfulness, whence the Lord: “Tell that fox: It is not fitting for a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem.” It also signifies deceitful people, who delight in the deceits they have contrived in their hearts, whence in the Gospel: “Foxes have dens.”

**Vulture**, properly speaking. It also signifies Christ because of the keenness of his sight: “The bird has not known the path, neither has the vulture’s eye beheld it.” This is said of the devil, who did not know Christ’s paths—that is, how through the ways of his humility he raised up man, and for what reason he assumed the garment of humanity.

[Col. 1011B] **Countenance**, properly speaking. It signifies presence, whence the Psalmist: “Thou shalt fill me with gladness with thy countenance”—that is, with thy presence, when I desire nothing else than thy presence, that is, to see thee face to face as thou art. It signifies reason, whence David: “The light of thy countenance, O Lord, is marked upon us.” Here “countenance” means reason, because, as one obtains knowledge of a human being through the countenance, so of God through reason. It signifies the Son of God, through whom the Father is known, whence in the Psalm: “The light of thy countenance, O Lord, is marked upon us”—that is, the wisdom of thy Son is marked upon us, that is, impressed upon our higher part, the soul. It signifies the conformity of believers or the unity of the Church,

[Col. 1012A] whence David: “All shall entreat thy countenance”—that is, thy conformity, O Church, lest they act while outside; but in the countenance of the bride, that is, in the unity of the Church. For the countenance of the Church benefits those who give alms, lest they act outside the nest of the Church. It signifies God’s wrath, whence David: “But the countenance of the Lord is upon those who do evil”—that is, upon the voluptuous; namely, vengeance. It signifies God’s power, by which he makes himself known to the worthy, whence David: “His countenance saw equity.” It signifies human disposition or mind, whence in Samuel: “His countenance is no longer changed in different directions.” It signifies divine knowledge, whence David: “Let my judgment come forth from thy countenance”; these are the words of Christ speaking to the Father—that is, according to what thou knowest in me, since I have no sin, let judgment be seen to proceed in my case, not according to the intention of the Jews. This was manifest in the Resurrection, when, contrary to their expectation, he rose again.

[Col. 1012B] **Womb**, properly speaking. It also signifies hidden guilt, whence Job: “Why did I not die in the womb?” For hidden guilt secretly conceives the sinner and still conceals its guilt in darkness. The sense, then, is: “Why did I not die in the womb?”—that is, why, in the secret commission of sin, was I unwilling to be mortified to the life of the flesh? It signifies the abyss of the earth, whence Job: “Who shut up the sea with doors when it burst forth as though proceeding from the womb?” etc. It signifies the charity of the Church, in which converts are conceived and born while they receive the rudiments of faith, whence the Psalmist: “Sinners have been estranged from the womb,” etc.

## Z

[Col. 1011]

[Col. 1011C] **To be jealous** signifies loving one’s wife with excessive love, whence it is read in the Passion of Saint Clement: “I was jealous of my wife.” It denotes envying, whence David: “Do not emulate evildoers, nor be jealous of those who work iniquity”—that is, do not envy those who commit iniquity. It also denotes imitating, whence, according to another exposition: “Nor be jealous of those who work iniquity”—that is, do not imitate them. But thanks be to God, who has given us victory through Jesus Christ our Lord.

**Jealous one.** It signifies one who loves his wife with excessive love. God too is called jealous, because he shows the greatest signs of charity to human beings, whence in the Law: “I am a jealous God.”

**Jealousy**, properly speaking, is envy, whence David: “The zeal

[Col. 1011D] of thy house hath consumed me”—that is, Judaea, which ought to be thy house, killed me out of envy. It signifies love; thus the foregoing authority may be expounded: “The zeal of thy house hath consumed me”—that is, through the love which I had toward the Synagogue, I submitted myself to suffering and death. It signifies the natural affection by which the simple among the Jews thought that, in exposing Christ to death, they were rendering service to God; whence Paul, speaking of them, says: “They have zeal for the Law, but not according to

[Col. 1012C] knowledge.” It signifies correction, which is a sign of love, whence it is said: “My zeal has departed from thee.”

**Zephyr** is the name of a wind and the name of a god; both are found in Ovid, especially in the *Metamorphoses*.

**Zeta** is the name of a letter. It signifies the vestibule of a house, whence it is read in the Passion of Blessed Thomas: “I will make for thee winter zetas and summer zetas.” According to some, they are promenades; according to others, chambers.

**Tares**, properly speaking. They also signify the wicked, whence in the Gospel: “Gather the tares to burn them.”

**Belt**, properly speaking. It also signifies secrecy, whence in the Gospel: “Do not have money in your belts”—that is, do not conceal wisdom. It is also called a belt because it binds tightly, and it signifies continence, as is found

[Col. 1012D] in the Apocalypse; for John says that he who appeared to him had a golden belt upon his breast.

**Leaven** properly means ferment. It also signifies malice, whence in a certain prose hymn:

> Let the old leaven be purged,
>
> That the new Resurrection
>
> May be celebrated sincerely.

Whence also the Apostle: “Purge out the old leaven.”

[Col. 1011] Here end the *Distinctions of Theological Terms*, published by Master Alan.
