## BOOK ONE

Chapter I.—Nature, observing her corruption in human beings, desires that a wholly perfect human being be created. She summons the virtues. The virtues’ procession to Nature’s house, 487.  
Chapter II.—Council of the Virtues, 489.  
Chapter III.—Where Nature’s house was situated. Description of the wood in which Nature’s house stood, and of the spring that was there, 489.  
Chapter IV.—Nature’s house situated on a mountain. Paintings of the house. The painting imitates logic. Aristotle, Plato, Seneca, Ptolemy, Tully, Virgil, 490.  
Chapter V.—Maevius, Nero’s cruelty, Ajax, Paris, Davus. Concord of the elements, 491.  
Chapter VI.—Nature speaks and laments the corrupted morals of humankind, 492.  
Chapter VII.—Prudence’s beauty and garments, 493.  
Chapter VIII.—Prudence approves Nature’s speech, 495.  
Chapter IX, 496.  
Chapter X.—Reason speaks. Her description, 496.

## BOOK TWO

Chapter I.—Will, the charioteer of sight. Reason’s course. Reason humbles herself and asks pardon. She approves Nature’s counsel. She desires on earth a human being perfected in every virtue, 497.  
Chapter II, 499.  
Chapter III.—Prudence is judged best fitted to be sent to God. She searches out the secrets of heaven, 500.  
Chapter IV.—Concord described: the worth, power, and so forth of her form, 501.  
Chapter V.—Concord speaks. Very many evils that have occurred in the world through lack of concord are enumerated. [Col. 1047]  
Chapter VI.—Prudence, stirred by Concord’s words, undertakes the embassy. The construction of a chariot is ordered. The seven liberal arts are designated, 504.  
Chapter VII.—The liberal arts are designated. The liberal arts are charged with building Prudence’s chariot. Grammar makes the pole of Prudence’s chariot. The fruits of grammar. Grammar’s nature and use, 505.  
Chapter VIII.—Grammar adapts raw material to the work. Authors of grammar: Donatus, Aristarchus, Priscian. Grammarians delight in the bark alone, 508.

## BOOK THREE
### Book Three

Chapter I.—The second maiden is Logic. Logic makes the axle in Prudence’s chariot. Logic’s face, bearing, and so forth. The character of the art of logic. It exposes the deceits of the sophist. The use of logic. How it makes an axle from iron. Authors of logic: Porphyry, Aristotle, Zeno, Boethius. 509  
Chapter II.—The third maiden is Rhetoric. Rhetoric is described. In her right hand she bears a trumpet, in her left a horn. The office and use of rhetoric. The parts of rhetorical discourse. Cicero, who has rendered outstanding service to rhetoric. 511  
Chapter III.—Other authors of rhetoric: Quintilian, Symmachus, Sidonius. Rhetoric adorns the chariot-pole in Prudence’s chariot with gems and silver. She also engraves various flowers upon the axle. 513  
Chapter IV.—The fourth sister is Arithmetic. Her appearance, work, and so forth. Her clothing. The use of arithmetic. Arithmetic makes the first wheel in Prudence’s chariot. Authors of arithmetic: Nicomachus, Gilbert, Pythagoras, Chrysippus. 514  
Chapter V.—Music is the fifth sister. Music’s bearing. Authors of music. The power of music. Music makes the second wheel in Prudence’s chariot. Michalus, teacher of music. 516  
Chapter VI.—Geometry is the sixth sister. Geometry’s bearing. Her work. 518  
Chapter VII.—Geometry constructs the third wheel. 519  

### Book Four

Chapter I.—Astronomy, the last maiden. Astronomy’s countenance and bearing. Her dignity and art. The spheres and motions of the planets. Astronomy makes the fourth wheel. Concord arranges and joins together the parts of the chariot. 519  
Chapter II.—Reason, the fifth, harnesses to Prudence’s chariot the horses, namely the five senses. The first horse is Sight. Hearing is the second horse. 521  
Chapter III.—Smell is the third horse. Taste is the fourth horse. Touch is the fifth horse. 522  
Chapter IV.—Reason governs all the horses and harnesses them to the chariot. Reason, charioteer of Wisdom and Prudence. Prudence, instructed by Reason, mounts the chariot, examines the air and its nature. 524  
Chapter V.—Prudence considers the spirits wandering through the air. 525  
Chapter VI.—Prudence visits the highest region of the air. The citadel of the sun is described. The sphere of Venus is described. Stilbon is the star of Mercury. The sphere of Mercury. 526  
Chapter VII.—The palace of Mars is described. Jupiter’s region is described. Jupiter’s star is good. 527  
Chapter VIII.—Saturn’s sphere is described. It moves slowly. Saturn’s star is bad. 528  

### Book Five

Chapter I.—Prudence ascends to the firmament. The Zodiac and its signs are described. 529  
Chapter II.—The horses, or outward senses, cannot penetrate heaven’s mysteries. 529  
Chapter III.—The adornment of Theology. In her right hand she bears a book, in her left a sceptre. 530  
Chapter IV.—Prudence greets Theology. She seeks her guidance. She reveals the purpose of her journey. Nature desires that a blessed human being be formed. Nature’s power is limited. A soul endowed with every virtue is sought. 532  
Chapter V.—Theology offers herself as Prudence’s companion, provided that she leaves behind the chariot and horses. To Prudence, as she advances toward heaven, the second horse, Hearing, is granted. The author’s most devout prayer to God. 533  
Chapter VI.—Prudence marvels at the crystalline waters. She marvels at the harmony of the elements. She investigates the nature of the crystalline waters. Exact knowledge of things above the moon exceeds the powers of nature. 535  
Chapter VII.—The delights of the empyrean heaven. 536  
Chapter VIII.—Saints taken up from earth inhabit heaven. The differing merits of the saints. 537  
Chapter IX.—Praises and prerogative of the Virgin Mary. 538  

### Book Six

Chapter I.—Prudence cannot endure the splendour of the empyrean heaven. Theology strengthens her. Theology implores Faith’s assistance. Theology teaches the articles of faith. 539  
Chapter II.—Faith, at Theology’s urging, approaches Prudence, [Col. 1048] and frees her from ecstasy. Ecstasy is described. A heavenly draught is given to the languishing Prudence. Faith offers Prudence a mirror in which she may behold all things that are in heaven, though only obscurely. 541  
Chapter III. 543  
Chapter IV.—Prudence, abandoning Reason’s guidance, follows Faith. Faith also takes Theology as a companion. Accompanied by Faith and Theology, Prudence enters the heavenly places. She arms her eyes with a mirror. She investigates the grounds of predestination. She considers God’s various delays. She contemplates other marvels of the empyrean heaven. 543  
Chapter V.—Relying on her companions, Faith and Theology, Prudence ascends to God’s citadel. She prostrates herself before God. God raises and strengthens her. 545  
Chapter VI.—She addresses God with all humility. She explains the reason for her embassy. She laments that the whole world lies in evil. She asks that Nature be aided through the formation of a new human being. She continues to stress Nature’s need. She sets forth the qualities of the new human being whom she seeks from God. 545  
Chapter VII.—God consoles Prudence. He gives assent to her petition. Mercy surpasses judgment. A new soul, adorned with every virtue, is promised. 547  
Chapter VIII.—Prudence gives thanks to God. God fulfils his promise. Noys prepares the idea of the soul to be created. God entrusts the created soul to Prudence. The soul is anointed against sins. Prudence returns with her wish fulfilled, and Reason meets her. Nature marvels at the perfections of the newly created soul offered to her by Prudence. 548  

### Book Seven

Chapter I.—The virtues meet Prudence as she returns from God. Nature forms from the elements a noble body. The beauty of the formed body. 549  
Chapter II.—Concord joins the soul to the body. Arithmetic and Music cooperate in joining soul and body. 550  
Chapter III.—The gifts of Chastity and Modesty. 551  
Chapter IV.—The gifts of Reason. 552  
Chapter V.—The gifts of Honourableness. 553  
Chapter VI.—The power of Logic. The gifts of Rhetoric, Arithmetic, Music, Geometry, Astrology, Theology, and Piety. 554  
Chapter VII.—The gifts of Faith. 556  
Chapter VIII.—Nobility, daughter of Fortune. 557  
Chapter IX.—The river of Adversity. 558  

### Book Eight

Chapter I.—Fortune’s house is described. Fortune is nowhere stable. 559  
Chapter II.—Nobility comes to the house of Fortune, her mother. Fortune and Nobility go to Nature’s house. The gifts of Nobility are of little consequence in comparison with the virtues. Reason stands beside Fortune. She does not allow her to give riches except in due measure. 560  
Chapter III.—Alecto grieves that humankind has reached so great a perfection. A council of vices assembles to attack humankind. 562  
Chapter IV.—Alecto addresses Pride. She complains about the conversion of humankind. She resolves that humankind must be attacked. 562  
Chapter V.—The vices conspire against humankind. Discord is the first to thirst for war, together with her servants, Envy, Rage, and so forth. Other companions of Discord are listed. 563  
Chapter VI.—The war of Folly. Her companions. The companions of Impiety: Avarice, infernal fury, and its following. The Virtues vigorously oppose the Vices and defend humankind. 564  
Chapter VII.—The Vices burst violently into the world. Prelude to the conflict of virtues and vices. 566  

### Book Nine

Chapter I.—A remarkable description of the battle. Discord begins the fight. The righteous human being vigorously opposes the vices. He first attacks and slays Discord. He likewise kills or puts to flight the remaining vices. 565  
Chapter II.—The weapons of Poverty. She attacks humankind. Poverty’s companions are listed. Poverty is cast down. Her companions are driven away. 567  
Chapter III.—Infamy assails humankind. She is repelled. The companions of Infamy. Infamy is cast down. Her companions flee. 568  
Chapter IV.—The assault of Old Age. She attacks in wrestling. The weapons of Old Age. Old Age is conquered without a wound. Defeated, she flees, casting down her weapons and content with a staff. 569  
Chapter V.—Weeping, avenging its mother, arms itself against humankind. It is defeated by laughter. Venus attacks humankind with greater violence. [Col. 1049] Her weapons. By fleeing, the human being discharges an arrow and kills Venus. Lust is routed by flight. Lust boasts of her power and recounts her victories. 570  
Chapter VI.—Excess attacks humankind. It is defeated by Moderation. Sobriety conquers Luxury. Gluttony is overcome. Reason defeats the goad of the flesh. The war of Imprudence: it is conquered by Prudence. 571  
Chapter VII.—The war of Impiety. Impiety is not moved by blandishments. It is exhausted by its own labour. The war of Fraud. Fraud attempts to overcome humankind by flattery. Faith overcomes Fraud. 572  
Chapter VIII.—The war of Avarice. It is overcome by Generosity. Prosperity. With the Virtues’ assistance, humankind defeats the Vices. The blessed human being is described and exalted. 573  
Chapter IX.—The author fortifies his work against the teeth of the Zoili. 574  
Epilogue.—One must always begin with God and end in him. 575  
Rhythm on the Incarnation of Christ. 577  
A second rhythm, graphically depicting the fleeting and perishable nature of humankind. 579  
The Lesser *Doctrinale*, otherwise the Book of Parables. Admonition to the reader. 579  
Book of Parables. 581  

## Supplement to the Edition of Charles de Wisch: On the Art or Articles of the Catholic Faith

Admonition. 593  
Prologue. 595  

### Book One

I.—Whatever is a cause of a cause is a cause of the caused thing. 597  
II.—Every cause of a subject is a cause of its accident. 598  
III.—Nothing composed itself or brought itself into being. 599  
IV.—Neither matter without form nor form without underlying matter can actually exist. 599  
V.—The composition of form with matter is the cause of substance. 599  
VI.—Every substance has a threefold cause: matter, form, and their union; and the cause of all three is the same. 599  
VII.—Whatever falls under number either differs or causes difference. 600  
VIII.—Nothing is the cause of itself. 600  
IX.—The being of every lower thing has a supreme cause. 600  
X.—The supreme cause is neither compounded with anything nor compounded by anything. 600  
XI.—The supreme cause is neither a property nor a form. 600  
XII.—The supreme cause must be utterly simple. Hence it is evident that there is only one supreme cause of all things, which, for purposes of reasoning, we call God. 600  
XIII.—No accident belongs to God. 600  
XIV.—God can neither be altered, increased, diminished, nor moved locally. 601  
XV.—God is eternal. 601  
XVI.—God is boundless, incomprehensible, ineffable, and unnameable. 601  
XVII.—We apprehend God by no knowledge, but by faith alone. 601  
XVIII.—God is in every time and every place, and is able to do all things, however great. 601  
XIX.—The admirable qualities which we contemplate in the creation and ordering of things are attributed, through effect and cause, to the Creator. Thus, because power and good things have been created powerfully and well, we say that the Creator is powerful and good; and because charity, justice, mercy, humility, piety, and the like are discerned in the ordering of things, we call him pious, humble, just, merciful, and wise. Moreover, by familiar analogies he is called light, fountain, dawn, radiance, life, seeing, and by other terms borrowed from every class of language to proclaim his greatness. 602  
XX.—God is the power by which he is called powerful, the wisdom by which he is wise, the charity by which he loves. The remaining names that belong to the divine nature predicate the divine essence of God, but improperly. 602  
XXI.—All things are in God, God is in all things, and all things are said to be causally. 603  
XXII.—God is everywhere essentially, and nowhere locally. 603  
XXIII.—The wondrous union of every substance shows how great its maker is. 603  
XXIV.—Matter, form, and their union are three wholly distinct things principally required in the creation of every substance. Hence it is evident that [Col. 1050] the effect in the creation of one and the same substance proves a Trinity in one and the same Creator. This Trinity is called three persons: the first Father, the second Son, the third Holy Spirit. 603  
XXV.—Although, in the creation of every substance, a fitting order may assign matter to the Father, form to the Son, and composition to the Holy Spirit, yet the whole Trinity must operate in each of the three. 603  
XXVI.—Form innate in matter, and the union proceeding from them, figuratively declare to us the Son begotten of the Father and the Holy Spirit proceeding from both as their bond and love. 603  
XXVII.—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are equal in power and nature. 604  
XXVIII.—The three persons have one essence, and none of them is another than the rest. 604  
XXIX.—Whatever predicates the divine essence belongs to the three persons. 604  
XXX.—The Trinity of persons is the unity of the Godhead. 604  

### Book Two

I.—God is the highest good; neither in him nor from him is there evil. 605  
II.—Whatever exists, whether substance or accident, must be good in the nature of its own being. 605  
III.—Supreme charity, justice, humility, and mercy are discerned in God. 605  
IV.—Divine charity proves that a thing sharing in divine wisdom and glory had to be created; and that thing is called a rational spirit. 605  
V.—A rational spirit is bound to fear and serve God and to minister in every obedience. 606  
VI.—The fabric of the world, with its many ornaments, had to be made as material for the fear, praise, and service of God, and for the accompaniment of his glory. 606  
VII.—Because of the many purposes of their ministries, many rational spirits had to be created in the fabric of the world; these we call God’s messengers. 606  
VIII.—By the necessity of justice, angels had to be granted free choice to act well or ill. 606  
IX.—It must be believed that the nature of angels was strong, subtle, and enriched with manifold grace. 607  
X.—In order to merit well, angels are bound to use free choice for good. 607  
XI.—Angels who used free choice wrongly had to be condemned beyond remedy. 607  
XII.—God’s charity and humility extend to all things. 607  
XIII.—Since something having something in common with every thing in its own nature, and sharing in God’s wisdom and glory, also had to be produced from the lowliest matter, we call that thing the human being. 607  
XIV.—Free choice had to be granted to the human being. 608  
XV.—All human thoughts, words, and deeds ought by duty to be directed to God as their lawful end. 608  
XVI.—It is just that the human will, together with its effect insofar as that lies within it, be repaid with reward or punishment. 608  
XVII.—A will to merit well that endures forever is worthy of everlasting recompense. 608  
XVIII.—The recompense of those who merit well before God is known to be not wages but grace. 608  
XIX.—Everything that labours by meriting well or ill ought to rejoice in reward or be condemned to punishment. 608  
XX.—The good that is in God is bestowed upon those who merit well. Hence it is evident that God bestows himself upon those who merit well. 609  
XXI.—Human frailty easily falls away from a good state. 609  
XXII.—The defilement of the mind desires to be washed and wiped away. 609  
XXIII.—Counsel must be sought for correcting evil thoughts, words, and deeds. 609  
XXIV.—The frailty of the body needs the relief of a remedy. 609  
XXV.—A manifold cause of disease needs a manifold remedy of medicine. 609  
XXVI.—Frequent falling requires frequent help in rising again. 610  
XXVII.—That a human being may become healthier and stronger, one must persist in employing many aids. 610  
XXVIII.—The form of the human being, made deformed through misuse, needs to be reformed. 610  
XXIX.—One who merits ill is held guilty of injury against God before God. 610  
XXX.—One who merits ill must be punished with an infinitely great punishment. 610  

[Col. 1051]

### Book Three

I.—The fallen and penitent human being ought to be visited by divine mercy. 609  
II.—The fallen human being had to be restored in order to receive glory. 609  
III.—A human being had to wipe away human guilt by satisfaction. 610  
IV.—Neither an angel, nor a mere human being, nor any other creature could restore humankind by satisfaction. 610  
V.—It was fitting that God should make satisfaction for humankind. Thus it is a great thing that God, made human, was to restore the human race. 611  
VI.—The second person of the Trinity was most fittingly appointed to unite human nature to himself. 611  
VII.—The human restorer had to offer himself to God for fallen humankind. 611  
VIII.—The offering owed for redeeming humankind must be sincere and free from every contagion of sin. 611  
IX.—From an incorrupt woman the Son of God was to assume flesh; and he was called Christ. 612  
X.—For the sins of the fallen, it befitted the Redeemer to endure insults, terrors, and the penalty of death. 612  
XI.—That victim had to be offered to God the Father. 612  
XII.—That victim is sufficient to satisfy the Creator for the transgressions of any human beings, however great. 612  
XIII.—This victim must be offered to God the Father in frequent ministries. 612  
XIV.—This remedy is useless to one who refuses it. 612  
XV.—God could fittingly have redeemed the human race in another way. 612  
XVI.—One deprived of this remedy belongs in no way to glory, but rather to punishment. 612  

### Book Four

I.—The preaching and sacraments of the Church are necessary. 613  
II.—To investigate the reason for baptism. 613  
III.—To examine the reason for the Eucharist. 613  
IV.—To investigate the reason for matrimony. 614  
V.—To explore the reason for penance. 614  
VI.—To explain the many reasons for the many sacraments in the Church. 614  
VII.—It is established that Christ’s faithful possess faith in the sacraments. 615  
VIII.—Faith in the sacraments is required of those who merit well before God. 615  
IX.—Baptism, conferred upon one not yet baptized who neither refuses it nor has an evil conscience, confers something. Hence it is evident that baptism is effective for persons deprived of reason and for little children. 615  

### Book Five

I.—Resurrection is the renewed union of body and soul separated by death, conferring upon both soul and body reward or punishment according to the quality of what has been done. 615  
II.—The whole human being receives everlasting recompense. 615  
III.—The human being will rise in the flesh which he or she had, to be reunited with his or her soul. 615  
IV.—Resurrection belongs universally to all, both greater and lesser. Hence it is evident that Christ rose from the dead. 616  
V.—At the resurrection the body will obtain incorruptibility and freedom from defect. 616  
VI.—The saints will rejoice in glory through the recompense of perfect knowledge and charity. 617  
VII.—There is no punishment greater than the everlasting torment of the damned. 618  

## Theological Rules

Preface. 617  
Prologue. 621  

Rule I.—The monad is that by which every thing is one. 623  
Rule II.—In the supercelestial is unity; in the celestial, otherness; in the subcelestial, plurality. 623  
Rule III.—The monad begets a monad and reflects its own ardour into itself. 624  
Rule IV.—In the Father is unity, in the Son equality, in the Holy Spirit the connection of unity and equality. 625  
Rule V.—The monad alone is alpha and omega without alpha and omega. 625  
Rule VI.—Everything limited and possessing alpha and omega is either good from alpha, or good from alpha and omega. 626  
Rule VII.—God is an intelligible sphere (*spaera*, sic), whose centre is everywhere and circumference nowhere. 627  
Rule VIII.—God is he for whom whatever is, is all the being that is. 627  
Rule IX.—Whatever is in God is God. 628  
Rule X.—Every predication made of the Creator is joined and united. 628  
[Col. 1052]  
Rule XI.—Every simple being has its own being and that which it is as one. 628  
Rule XII.—Nothing simple can be a subject. 629  
Rule XIII.—Only the simple is form without a material subject, and substance without a formal predicate. 629  
Rule XIV.—Every being derives from form. 629  
Rule XV.—Of that which is being, there is no being. 629  
Rule XVI.—Form alone is formless, because form has no form. 629  
Rule XVII.—Every name given from form and spoken of form falls short of form. 629  
Rule XVIII.—All affirmations spoken of God are inadequate, but negations are true. 630  
Rule XIX.—Everything simple properly is, and improperly is said to be. 630  
Rule XX.—Everything simple is by one thing and is said to be by another. 630  
Rule XXI.—Every name fitting God fits him either causally, analogically, adjectivally, or negatively. 631  
Rule XXII.—Every theological predication shows either what God is or in relation to what he is. 631  
Rule XXIII.—Every term said of God according to substance is said of the three persons severally and in the singular number, and of all three together in the singular number. 631  
Rule XXIV.—No substantive name which pertains to the essence in sound and meaning, or in sound alone, is said of the three persons collectively in the plural number, but only in the singular. 632  
Rule XXV.—Every adjectival name, retained adjectivally and pertaining to the essence, is said collectively of the three persons in the plural number. 632  
Rule XXVI.—Every metaphor in divine matters is a metaphor of a name, not of a thing. 633  
Rule XXVII.—Every distinctive noun or pronoun joined to a personal name in the masculine or feminine pertains to person; in the neuter, to essence. 634  
Rule XXVIII.—No partitive noun or pronoun is fittingly joined to an essential name. 635  
Rule XXIX.—Whenever an exclusive expression is joined to an essential name, the name signifies rather a kind of thing than a thing of that kind; no supposition is made for a definite subject, but speech is made indeterminately of something. 635  
Rule XXX.—Every essential name is either, as it were, mathematical or, as it were, concrete. 635  
Rule XXXI.—Every mathematical name is said of God less improperly than a concrete name. 636  
Rule XXXII.—Every name said of God is either essential, co-essential, personal, co-personal, or partly personal and partly essential. 636  
Rule XXXIII.—No name signifying privation, liability, or violence applies to God. 637  
Rule XXXIV.—Every theological expression must be catholic, general, customary, not discordant with understanding, and consonant with the thing of which we speak. 637  
Rule XXXV.—Substantive names are said of God less improperly than adjectival names. 637  
Rule XXXVI.—Whenever speech is made of God through a demonstrative pronoun, it falls short of demonstration. 638  
Rule XXXVII.—Verbs are said of God with greater impropriety than nouns or pronouns. 639  
Rule XXXVIII.—No name in divine matters is a mark of that which is said of another, or of what is another, but rather of that which is the very same. 639  
Rule XXXIX.—No verb is said of God less improperly than this verb, “is.” 640  
Rule XL.—Every present-tense verb is said of God less improperly than a past- or future-tense verb. 640  
Rule XLI.—Every local adverb said of God predicates divine immensity, or a certain relation of the Creator to creatures, according to which the Creator is said to be in creatures as an efficient cause in its effects. 640  
Rule XLII.—By local circumlocutions one predicates of God either divine immensity, relation, or union. 640  
Rule XLIII.—Temporal adverbs said of God predicate eternity. 640  
Rule XLIV.—Adverbs of likeness said of God signify either the truth of essence, impropriety, or conjunction. 640  
Rule XLV.—The preposition *in*, in divine matters, sometimes denotes identity of essence and plurality of persons; sometimes a sort of difference; sometimes eternal predication; sometimes identity; sometimes an efficient cause; sometimes a quasi-formal cause. 641  
[Col. 1053]  
Rule XLVI.—The preposition *secundum* (“according to”), in divine matters, sometimes denotes an order of cause and sometimes an order of understanding. 641  
Rule XLVII.—The preposition *secundum* sometimes denotes a quasi-efficient cause, sometimes a quasi-formal cause, and sometimes a condition of nature. 641  
Rule XLVIII.—Of names said of God, one kind is said of the three persons in such a way as of none of them; another of the three collectively in such a way as of each severally; another of one person in such a way as not of the others. 642  
Rule XLIX.—Of theological names, some are appropriated to one person in name and in reality; others in name but not in reality. 642  
Rule L.—The name “Father,” when said of God, predicates either a person, a personal property, the Father’s relation to the Son, the Father’s relation to creatures in creation, or the Father’s relation to humankind in re-creation. 642  
Rule LI.—The name “Principle” sometimes predicates fatherhood, sometimes spiration, and sometimes the Creator’s relation to creatures. 643  
Rule LII.—Among names appropriated to persons in name and reality, some are said by affirmation, others by negation. 645  
Rule LIII.—The circumlocution “Holy Spirit” predicates in divine matters either a person, a personal property, or a relation. 646  
Rule LIV.—He alone is truly omnipotent who can do everything such that to be able to do it is to be able to do something. 647  
Rule LV.—The Omnipotent can do only what accords with his justice, power, and mercy. 647  
Rule LVI.—God is called omnipotent because he can do not only those things which are or can come to be, but even those which cannot come to be. 647  
Rule LVII.—Whatever is possible according to a lower cause is possible according to a higher cause; but the converse does not hold. 648  
Rule LVIII.—Everything impossible according to a lower cause, from which impossibility according to a higher cause follows, is impossible for God. 648  
Rule LIX.—If truth is in essence, possibility is not therefore in nature. 649  
Rule LX.—The Omnipotent cannot fail to be able to do what he could do, and could not fail to be able to do what he can do. 650  
Rule LXI.—The works of the Trinity are undivided. 650  
Rule LXII.—Nothing can be done against the will of him who can will nothing but good. 651  
Rule LXIII.—Primary substance does not admit greater or lesser. 651  
Rule LXIV.—Divine providence cannot be deceived. 652  
Rule LXV.—What God foresaw must come to pass by necessity of consequence, not necessity of the consequent. 652  
Rule LXVI.—The necessity of a lower cause follows upon the necessity of a higher cause; but the converse does not hold. 652  
Rule LXVII.—The necessity of a lower cause yields to the necessity of a higher cause. 654  
Rule LXVIII.—All things, insofar as they are, are good. 654  
Rule LXIX.—That whose end is good is itself also good. 656  
Rule LXX.—One action cannot have different ends. 656  
Rule LXXI.—Every merit is voluntary, either by a will of origin or by an origin of will. 657  
Rule LXXII.—Every merit depends on the will. 658  
Rule LXXIII.—Every sin is committed either by doing what ought not to be done or by omitting what ought to be done. 658  
Rule LXXIV.—Not doing avoids punishment; doing earns the crown. 659  
Rule LXXV.—No unformed or deformed action can be formed, nor conversely. Thus it cannot be more or less unformed or deformed, nor more or less formed. 659  
Rule LXXVI.—Every sin is a punishment either in the character of suffering or in its consequent effect. 660  
Rule LXXVII.—Every punishment either preserves good, tests good, purges evil, invites toward a greater good, hardens in evil, torments by sheer bitterness, or defiles with sin. 661  
Rule LXXVIII.—Every movement of concupiscibility toward enticements is a vice arising from sin; every movement of concupiscence in enticements is a sin arising from vice. 661  
Rule LXXIX.—Every will of affection produces merit; a will of effecting completes merit. 661  
[Col. 1054]  
Rule LXXX.—Not equality of effect in the will, but equality of affection in the will, produces equality in guilt. 662  
Rule LXXXI.—Every sin whose punishment is remitted by penance admits the punishment of penance, not by the essence of the act but by the equivalence of guilt. 662  
Rule LXXXII.—All merit of punishment belongs to humanity by action; all merit of glory exceeds humanity in authority. 663  
Rule LXXXIII.—By grace from the Spirit, a human being has the ability whereby he or she wills; by grace in the Spirit, the human being has the will whereby he or she is able. 663  
Rule LXXXIV.—Every human choice is more free in serving evil, less free in being liberated for good, so that there is greater freedom of servitude and lesser freedom of liberty. 664  
Rule LXXXV.—As every meritorious good in a human being either increases by progressing, languishes by growing lukewarm, or fails by ceasing, so every meritorious evil in a human being either increases through continuance, is remitted through attrition, or is forgiven through contrition. 664  
Rule LXXXVI.—Every righteous person can merit for another the merit of a reward, but not the reward of merit. 665  
Rule LXXXVII.—Grace toward merit comes to be in us without us, free choice accompanying but not cooperating; grace in merit, however, comes to be in a human being through the human being, free choice acting toward this end but not sufficient for it. 666  
Rule LXXXVIII.—All virtues are given to the human being simultaneously and alike in creation, so that they are by nature; but in re-creation they are infused into the human being so that they are virtues by grace—alike indeed in habit, but unlike in use. 666  
Rule LXXXIX.—Virtue and vice are opposed mediately, not by the presence of a mean, but by the negation of each. 667  
Rule XC.—Merit of good consists, with regard to free choice, occasionally; with regard to virtue, formally; with regard to the movement of virtue, essentially; with regard to grace, effectively; and with regard to work, instrumentally. 669  
Rule XCI.—Among virtues, charity is prior in causation, greater in duration, a mother in informing, a form in manifestation, an end in recompense, and more universal in operation. 669  
Rule XCII.—In one person charity is like a stream and, as it were, final, to which an outsider imparts; in another it is like a fountain and final, in which only one of the household shares. 669  
Rule XCIII.—A human being is said to be justified by faith, not because justification comes from faith, but because it proceeds from faith’s article. 670  
Rule XCIV.—No work performed in charity is deformed into merit of eternal punishment; rather, a work performed from charity is formed into merit of glory. 670  
Rule XCV.—As perfection in a human being is considered in relation to comparison, comprehension, accomplishment, vow, sufficiency, and conscience, so perfection in charity is considered in relation to sign, exclusion of impediment, continuance, rootedness, and intensity of fervour. 671  
Rule XCVI.—Every good fear is either an initial limit of faith, within expenditure or beyond expenditure, or a final limit of faith, within expenditure or beyond expenditure. 671  
Rule XCVII.—Just as flesh is said to obey reason when it does not act directly against reason, so reason is said to consent to flesh when it does not restrain the flesh. 673  
Rule XCVIII.—The charity possessed by a human being causes something to be loved either because it has, that it may have, or that it may be possessed. 673  
Rule XCIX.—As the human being, ascending through charity from the *thesis* of his or her nature into the *apotheosis* of grace, is deified, so God, descending through charity from the *apotheosis* of his nature into the *hypothesis* of our misery, is made human. 673  
Rule C.—Human nature is united to divine nature, so that diversity of substance is in one, while the property of each nature remains in the united being. 674  
Rule CI.—As a part cannot be the whole, nor the constituent the constituted, so the one assuming cannot be the one assumed. 675  
Rule CII.—For Christ to be human, a threefold union concurs: a co-personal union, that he might possess human nature; a sub-personal union, that he might live; and a pro-personal union. 676  
Rule CIII.—A memorial number applies to Christ, by which the substantial hypostasis is numbered; and a material number, by which *usia* (“essence”) is numbered together with *usiosi* [reading uncertain]. 676  
Rule CIV.—In Christ the necessity of dying arose not from an action overpowering the mind, but from a will binding the event. 677  
[Col. 1055]  
Rule CV.—In Christ there was fear of pre-passion, not opposing reason; but there was not fear of passion disturbing the mind. 677  
Rule CVI.—Christ merited nothing for himself by his works; but whatever he merited, he merited for us by each of his works. 677  
Rule CVII.—As the Creator became a creature by assuming a creature, so a creature becomes the body of the Creator through the transubstantiation of a creature. 678  
Rule CVIII.—Christ’s body is in one species and exists under another species. 679  
Rule CIX.—For bread to be transubstantiated into the Lord’s body, four things concur: order in the person, intention in the agent, matter in the bread, and form in the words. 679  
Rule CX.—As the Eucharist is the sacrament perfecting the justice of dignity, so baptism is the sacrament advancing the necessity of justice. 679  
Rule CXI.—The sacrament of confirmation is not given in order that baptism may be possessed, but in order that it may be possessed more fully. 679  
Rule CXII.—As baptism is the first remedy against the fall of original sin, so penance is the second plank after the shipwreck of sin. 680  
Rule CXIII.—As baptism is the sacrament of faith, confirmation the sacrament of hope, and the Eucharist the sacrament of charity, so extreme unction is the sacrament of penance or contrition. 680  
Rule CXIV.—Marriage is a sacrament of remedy for avoiding, not of necessity for choosing. 681  
[Col. 1056]  
Rule CXV.—Holy orders are the sacrament by which a human being is marked out, so as to preside over others by honour and benefit them through the burden of prelacy. 681  
Rule CXVI.—Every utterance depends so completely upon a cause that, if the cause is absent, the utterance itself is empty. 681  
Rule CXVII.—An utterance is one thing; the reason for uttering it is another. 682  
Rule CXVIII.—Every reason for an utterance is expressed in one way and explained in another. 682  
Rule CXIX.—The reason for speaking differs from the thing of which, as stated, it is the reason. 682  
Rule CXX.—One cause of a thing is intrinsic, another extrinsic. 682  
Rule CXXI.—Of causes, one is called per se, another relative to something else. 683  
Rule CXXII.—Of causes, one is first and another second. 683  
Rule CXXIII.—A first cause is either the nature of a subsisting thing or its property. 683  
Rule CXXIV.—A secondary cause of speech either concerns nature or concerns a property. 683  
Rule CXXV.—There is one reason for speaking that pertains to every reason for an utterance. 684  

## Book on the Distinctions of Theological Terms

Alan’s prologue to Hermengald, Abbot of Saint-Gilles. 685  
A second prologue by the same author. 687  
Here begins the Book on the Distinctions of Theological Terms. 687  
Analytical index. 1013  

[Col. 1055] End of the Two Hundred and Tenth Volume
